consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A testator can dispose of leasehold goods as long as the lease lasts; it is otherwise once the time has ended, because he cannot dispose of them to the prejudice of the lord.
body: By themselves

† proper goods are to be considered, and leasehold goods (bona libellaria) are to be considered by themselves. For in the proper goods of the testator, his testament must be observed, as in ff. de ver. si. l. verbis legis. However, in leasehold goods, so long as the third generation lives, the testament is still to be observed, de leg. 1. l. si domus. §. fi. But once the third generation is ended, that is, the property having freely reverted to the church, the testament is not to be observed, because the emphyteutic right has ended. C. de leg. l. vxor patrui. de vsuf. leg. l. Sticho. ff. de pig. l. lex vectig. From this it is concluded that the legatee has no right in the aforesaid emphyteutic goods, neither by reason of dower, nor by reason of a legacy of maintenance, nor of the legitime; because the testator could not make the condition of the church worse. In other proper goods of the testator, however, the testament is to be observed, saving the legitime, and the other fourth, c. Rayn. and c. Ray. de test., which by reason of the person of the pupillus belong to the mother, who ought also to have maintenance; I do not say usufruct by virtue of the legacy, because in the legacy no mention is made of usufruct. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that all cases shall be at rest during the time of holidays, an examination of witnesses for the perpetual memory of the matter may be conducted during that time up to the publication thereof; but the publication of the said witnesses may not.
2. During the time of holidays, a sentence may not be rendered under the pretext of witnesses received for the perpetual memory of the matter, but the order of judicial proceedings must be observed.
body: The matters set forth in my aforementioned opinion being confirmed as true: both regarding the possible reception of witnesses for the perpetual memory of the case, and that when the said legacy is sought as the cause of action arising from the will, the procedure is ordinary, not summary or executory. Nevertheless, at present, it is not necessary to give a response to the new doubts.

† It is asked. Whether the oaths and depositions of the said witnesses were valid, since they swore and gave testimony during a holiday period, on account of the harvest, pursuant to a statute which provides that during the said time cases shall cease, with no tacit or express renunciation of the said holidays having been made. And it must be said that the oath was not valid, and consequently neither was the deposition, the said holidays being an obstacle: as in D. de feriis, l. 1; and as noted in c. 1, de officio delegati, in the Clementines, because the clause is one of jurisdiction, since the statute uses the word "cease" [conquiescant], C. de dilationibus, l. sive pars. Moreover, since the statute does not provide for more than one exception, therefore in all other cases the prohibition remains firm: because an exception confirms the rule, as is fully noted in l. 1, D. de re iudicata. Moreover, if the statute does not distinguish, therefore we cannot distinguish either, as in l. de pretio, D. de publicaniis; because this determination is general, D. de militibus testamento, l. in fraudem, §. si; D. de aleatorio, l. 1, §. quod autem; D. de legibus praestandis, l. 1, §. et generaliter. Moreover, this statute not only expresses the common law, but must be interpreted strictly, as if it were precise and not admitting of gloss, since it must have some effect, as in D. ad municipalia, l. 1; D. de legibus, l. 1, l. si quia omnia; and as noted in l. si quando, in principio, C. de inofficioso testamento.

To the contrary it seems, because when a thing or proof is about to perish in time, there are no holidays, since they were introduced for the sake of men, and by statute, D. de feriis, l. 2; and there Cynus expressly holds that statutory holidays do not then apply. And it was the opinion of Azo: "Necessity has no law," D. de officio consulis, l. 1; "Necessity makes probable that which otherwise is not probable," D. de manumissione testamento, l. qui potuerunt. Indeed, even if they were holidays in honor of God, according to the note in C. de feriis, l. si.

Solution: I think that up to publication, exclusively, everything could have been done notwithstanding the said holidays; but I believe that the publication itself could not have been done during the said holiday time. And the reason is, because publication could have been deferred without danger to a judicial time. And since publication is a judicial act in itself, and there is no danger of delay in time regarding it, the judicial day ought to have been awaited. Since therefore they could not publish then on account of the holidays, they do not make faith, C. de re iudicata, l. gesta. I readily admit that they can be lawfully published anew, if and when they would make faith from that time. Secondly

It is asked, assuming that the publication is valid, whether the statement of Francis is applicable in the case of condemnation. And it seems that it is, in *l. emptorem*, *de acquisitione per hereditatem* [or *de acquirenda possessione*?], and in *l. at qui natura*, § *cum me absente*, *de negotiis gestis*, C. *qui et adversus quos*. On the contrary, it seems that it is not, because the libel must be offered, and the cause must be contested, an oath against calumny must be taken, and terms for proving must be given on both sides, as in *l. prolationi*, C. *de sententiis et interlocutoribus*, *de iudicibus*, c. *exhibita*, *de electione*, c. *dudum Ecclesia Rotomagensis*, *de probat.*, c. *quoniam contra falsam*, as if the cause were not contested, throughout. And this is the truth, because the order of judicial proceedings should not be omitted when an action is brought: as is the case here, because a useful action on a will is brought, and therefore unless the cause is contested and the ordinary procedure is followed, the judge cannot condemn or absolve. Hence, let advocates observe how much time they have lost, and are at the beginning of the litigation: as in ff. *de usuris*, *l. vulgo*, and *l. in fideicommissa*, with similar cases. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Against an instrument having ready execution by virtue of a statute, the exception of usury may be opposed, which may be proved before an ecclesiastical or secular judge.
2. Where the term given for proving the exception is too short, another term ought to be granted.
3. Jews are almost all moneylenders, which is relevant to the statute.
4. Given a statute that instruments of usurers are not to be put into execution, whether instruments of Jews ought to be put into execution, since all of them are commonly moneylenders.
5. One who amends the libel is not heard unless the expenses are restored.
body: Dor. The statute of the land of Gualdo has been given in general form concerning the execution of judgments and public instruments; yet it sets forth certain exceptions in the following terms: namely, excepting, however, usurious instruments, and the instruments of the usurious massarii of the said commune, and other public instruments made ten years ago, in which the order of law is observed. Now a judgment has been rendered for a certain Jew, whose execution is sought. It is objected that it does not deserve execution, but that the ordinary course of action should be pursued, since the said Jew is a usurer.

† It is asked whether the aforementioned execution proceeds according to law. And it must be said that it does, because those words, “reckoning back ten years,” serve to limit the species, which have their own proper and separate rationale, especially against usurers, who are odious to God and to the world. D. ad Maced. l. 1. And to prove this, the following authorities are helpful: D. de leg. 1. l. talis scriptura; D. de verb. oblig. l. stipulatio; D. de alim. leg. l. alimenta § basilicæ; and D. de mil. test. l. Stichus.

But it is asked whether, after the lapse of the first term of three days, another term ought to be granted; and certainly a term of three days is too short, as C. de iu. l. pe. and the strictness of the first term must be remedied by a subsequent term, or by the extension of the first. ff. de fer. l. oratione. and l. si. especially since one asks for a delay to prove that which is probable, as is the case that the Jew is a usurer. For

† By the place commonly occurring, we see that almost all are usurers. This usurious exception, raised against a Jew or a Saracen, can be proved in the secular court, even though it could be proved in the ecclesiastical court. And thus this exception, which is not raised on account of sin, but on account of another cause, and against one who is not of our law, yet is subject to Caesar, is of both forums. C. de iudic. l. quotiens. It supports what is noted in l. Titia, § 30, de mat., according to Bartolus.

But whether, without proof of usury, because he is a Hebrew, he is excluded by that verse of the statute: “Receiving all instruments of the Hebrews, or Jews, which instruments prescribe within a period of six years, and after the said time totally vanish, and merit no execution whatsoever: and this shall have effect in past and future instruments of the Hebrews.” I answer that these words can be explained in two ways. In one way, that there are two statutes against the Hebrews: one concerning the prescription of time, and another that their instruments never merit execution, but that they must proceed by the ordinary course of action. In another way, that there is only one statute against the Hebrews, namely, that after the prescription of six years, their instruments do not merit execution; therefore, *a contrario sensu*, if prescription has not occurred, they merit execution, unless they were usurers, as stated in another chapter of this statute. And this interpretation is supported by the nature of the conjunction, which repeats the immediately preceding words; and the inference from the preceding to the following is valid, regarding the interpretation of words (*de verbis obligantibus*), as in *l. Titia*, § *idem respondet*, in the Institutes on the Lex Aquilia; § *hoc tamen capite*, on legacies, book 3; *l. in repetendis*, in the Institutes on the division of things; § *item lapilli*, in the Decretals on appeals, c. 2, *requiris*. But the proper understanding is supported by the hatred of the person and the care for life, because they usually lend at interest. And because there should be no superfluous word in laws or statutes, as in § *quibus*, in the first constitution, and *l. si stipulatus*, on usury, and as noted in *l. certi condictionis*, in the beginning, if certain performance is demanded, and as I said above: if we understood that after the said time they totally vanish, and also that after the said time they merit no execution, this provision regarding execution would be very superfluous, since it was already stated that they totally vanish. Therefore, so that those words, “and merit no execution,” may have some effect, I understand them to mean that they merit no execution for any cause whatsoever, which can be said with sufficient probability.

† Another question is put to me, whether he who appeals ought to be heard without the costs having been refunded. I say that he ought not, as is stated in the law *Edita*, in the title *De edendo*. And this is due to his own temerity, as in the Digest, in the title *De iudiciis*, in the law *Eum, quem temere*. Hence, the judge ought not to hear him unless the liquidated costs have been refunded, or unless security has been given for the unliquidated costs, by argument from the Code, in the title *De iudiciis*, in the law *Sancimus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the mother is to be admitted to the share owed to her according to the form of the statute.
2. An inventory that is less complete, yet approved by the judge, suffices.
body: The case is as follows: Petrucius, son of Jacob of Todi, being on his deathbed, made a will, in which he appointed his son Jacob as universal heir, and left as co-guardians to him his brothers Fredutius and Bartholomew, and Lucia, his wife. The said Petrucius died, with the said brothers and the said wife surviving, and with the said Jacob, his son, surviving as a minor, whose guardianship the said Lucia assumed, without requesting the said co-guardians appointed in the said will. She made an inventory of one house and one plot of land, however, with the usual protestation, and she had nothing else written in the said inventory regarding the other hereditary goods of the said minor. Finally, the said Jacob died in minority, with the said mother surviving, and with Thomas, son of the said Bartholomew, cousin of the said Jacob, and with the said Fredutius, his uncle, surviving. The question now arises, having seen the testimony and the statute of the community of Todi placed under the heading “on intestate succession,” and presupposing that the common usage of speech in the city of Todi is such that anyone, whatever his age, who dies without having made a will is said to be intestate: what is the law concerning the inheritance of the said Petrucius, and whether the said Lucia can claim that part of it touching her, except for the goods described in the inventory made by her at the time of assuming the said guardianship.

† According to what is proposed, and it is that if the mother had never assumed guardianship, she is admitted to the share due to her according to the form of the statute: and the reason is that the ward had other guardians, as noted in C. ad Tertullianum, l. matres, and l. si, §. personis, C. de administratione tutorum. But concerning male guardians, it should be known that if the mother had not assumed guardianship, they would have been excluded; but because she assumed it and administered it, it benefited everyone; it suffices in legitimate matters that one administers, as noted in l. 2, qui petant tutores.
† Moreover, although the inventory is not complete, yet since it has been approved by the decree of the judge, it is understood to be formal, as in l. fina. C. arbitrium tutelae. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a cleric, acting against a layman in the secular forum, can be compelled to submit the case to arbitration by law and in fact, is distinguished according to the form of the statute.
2. Where there is doubt whether a statute of laymen is contrary to liberty, clerics are not included in such a case.
3. Add the opinion beginning "dictat statutum civitatis castelli" in the third part.
body: Whether

Whether a cleric suing a layman in a secular court can be compelled to submit the case to arbitration both as to law and as to fact, according to the form of the statute. I say he can be compelled, causatively by way of denial of jurisdiction, if he does not wish to submit to arbitration. And it seems that he can be compelled, because he ought to observe the statutes of that forum where he sues, as in Extra, De foro competenti, c. Quod clericis. And there is the gloss, Ordo. It is supported by C., De senatus consultis et interlocutionibus, l. Cum Pomponio, in the reason of the letter. To this effect it is also true that residents are compelled to this, if they sue. D., De iudiciis, l. 2. But if they sue, for the custom of the forum binds all litigants. C., Quemadmodum et quando res apostolicae, l. 2.

On the contrary, it seems that laymen can enact nothing regarding clerics, as in Extra, De consuetudinibus, c. Ecclesia sanctae Mariae. The contrary arguments do not prevail, because they speak concerning the mere order of judicial proceedings. But this matter is not of the mere order; rather, it touches the substance of the case and tends toward its decision. And this is held by Iacutus de Caltabiano and Ioannes de Lignano.

But if a cleric litigates concerning the goods of the church, then he is neither compelled against his will nor, if willing, can he submit to arbitration as to law and as to fact regarding the rights of the church. Or if he litigates concerning his own private patrimony, then he can submit to arbitration if he wishes. But whether he is compelled is our question. And I say that either the statute provides that arbitration be held as to law, so that it is an arbitration of justice, and he is compelled causatively, and there is a transfer of the instance as if to a certain delegated judge, just as if the ordinary judge were to delegate to himself, which he could do even against the cleric’s will. And just as a cleric suing before an arbitrator is compelled to choose arbitrators in a case of suspicion, D., De iudicibus, l. Penultima. Or the statute commands arbitration as to fact, and it tends toward settlement, and he cannot be compelled, nor is the statute valid in this regard, because it is contrary to the liberty of clerics. And much more so, in a general statute, nothing is included, either directly or indirectly, against the rights of churches or clerics, as noted by Bartolus in l. Si quis sub conditione, D., De conditionibus et demonstrationibus.

† Moreover, if there is doubt as to whether it is contrary to liberty, in such a doubtful statute clerics are not included on account of the ambiguous peril, to which the enactors do not appear to have bound themselves. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a woman may not make a will without the consent of two relatives, if two male relatives were present and a female relative, who was more closely related, was omitted, the will shall be valid.
2. Whether one who gives consent as the next of kin to a woman making a will may give such consent so that a substitution may be made.
body: This is the text of a certain statute found in the volume of the statutes of the commune of Bitonto, in book 2, speaking of civil causes under the rubric that a woman cannot make a will without the presence of blood relatives. Furthermore, we establish and ordain that no woman may make a will without the presence and consent of her husband, if she is married, and of two nearest and most suitable blood relatives; and if she has no husband, and has children, without the consent and presence of the children, if they are of age; but if she has no children, without the consent and presence of two nearest and most suitable blood relatives. And if it were done otherwise, what was done shall not be valid, nor shall it have effect by the law itself. And the aforementioned provisions shall apply to present, past, and future cases. We do, however, will and enact by this present law that if the husband, children, or blood relatives of the woman wishing to make a will should refuse to give their presence and consent to the will made by the said woman, such woman may, in that case, make and validate her will at her pleasure, provided that those refusing and unwilling to give their presence and consent to the woman’s will are first cited and warned by the Bailiff of the commune of Bitonto, by commission of the lord podestà or his vicar, that they go to give their presence and consent to such will made by the woman. And the will subsequently made by such woman, after the aforementioned citation and warning have been made, shall be valid and obtain full force by the authority of this present ordinance and decree. It is proposed that Margaret made a will with the consent of Frances, the wife of Lola, and of Laurentius Polte, in which she instituted her daughter Sanctucia, to whom she substituted the said Laurentius after her death, and the case of substitution has arisen. Now the question is asked, considering the said statute, whether the will is valid while the said Lola lives, and thus, since she is nearer than Frances.

It appears that the will is invalid, because the statute requires that the person be the next of kin and more suitable. To the contrary, it appears that the law speaks of a male, not of a female; because the uncertain counsel of a woman ought not to be supplied by a woman; and because a male is naturally more suitable than a female, as l. ult. ff. de fideiussoribus sufficiently shows. It could be said that if the woman, who is the next of kin, is wise and discreet, her consent is required; nevertheless, the contrary appears to be truer, by l. ult. C. de legitima tutela, in the reason of itself. But whether the said Laurentius could consent that he himself be substituted, it appears that he could not, as l. 1, in fine, ff. de auctoritate tutorum, and there by Bartolus.

But I say that he could, because this is not authority, but consent, and it suffices that consent be given for him to act, even if not that he act in this specific manner. And therefore it is different from what is said in the case of a tutor in the aforementioned law 1. It remains, therefore, that the said testament is valid; however, because the mother could not burden the son in his legitime, and the Trebellonian half is owed to the said fideicommissary substitute, the other half pertains to the intestate successors of the said ward. And thus there are three, and this half is divided into three parts. Many, who say that the masculine gender includes the feminine in statutes, will say that the said testament, by virtue of that statute, is invalid by operation of law. I, however, more rightly believe that a woman cannot suffice for another, who does not suffice for herself. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a son who has been exiled during his father’s lifetime, with all his property confiscated, is to be considered dead while his father is still alive, so that the fisc does not succeed.
body: Secondly

As for the things that are placed, the fisc has no right, because the son is understood to have died while the father was alive, since he was stripped naked of all his goods, having been deprived of them on account of a capital crime. The text is in l. Gallus, §. et quid si tamen, de lib. et posthum.; and l. 1, in fine, ff. de contrah. emptione. It is supported by ff. pro socio, l. actor, §. si publicatione; and C. de bonis damnatorum, l. si filius. But caduca do not pertain to the fisc. C. de caducis tollendis, §. cum triplici. It is supported by what is noted by Cynus in ff. qui sui iuris sunt, l. si qua poena, and there is the case of our question. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a substitution is made to several persons, some of whom are minors under guardianship and others not, whether such a substitution is called a fideicommissary or a pupillary substitution.
body: All

† These substitutions were fideicommissary, as noted in l. precibus, C. de impuberibus, and in c. pater and c. Raymundus, de testamentis. Although the gloss in cap. qua ratione, eodem titulo, and Cynus in l. precibus seem to say that a substitution within the pupillary age is pupillary, nevertheless the first opinion is more approved. Moreover, Bartolus seems to say that when a brother is substituted for a brother, it is understood to be direct. But the ordinary gloss expressly says that these words are fideicommissary even between brothers, C. de fideicommissis, l. si frater. And custom interprets it thus, and it is not to be changed, etc. And note those words in the plural number, “he substituted to them,” on account of the note in l. cohæredi, § cum filiae, ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione. The gloss in the last paragraph of l. precibus, in the words “or therefore,” does not obstruct, if it is said in breviloquy. For it is not that which is said in breviloquy, but here he speaks of a fideicommissum expressed in breviloquy. For it is more fitting in favor of the substitute than a fideicommissum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Instituted by the father, and substituted to a minor if he assisted from the institutions, does not transmit the pupillary substitution even while the condition is pending.
2. In the legitimate portion, one cannot be substituted.
3. Instituted in a certain thing, one does not deduct the Trebellian portion.
body: The deceased is Fortiguerra Nelli of Monte Fascon. He died having made a will, in which he instituted as heirs his posthumous son or sons, to be born from the womb of his wife, Lady Paula. And if a daughter were born, he endowed her with the dowry, in accordance with the law of institution, with boundaries, etc. And in this case, wherein a daughter would be born, he instituted for himself as heir Lady Fiordelisia, the mother of the said testator. And if the said daughter, to be born, should die in pupillary age, or at any time thereafter without children, he substituted for himself the said Lady Fiordelisia, as you will be able to see in the will. The said Fortiguerra died, survived by the said Lady Fiordelisia, his mother, and Lady Paula, his wife, from whom Lady Paula was born a single daughter named Alamana. Then the said Lady Fiordelisia died, survived by the said Alamana and her mother, the said Lady Paula. This Lady Fiordelisia died having made a will, in which she left several legacies to the same Alamana and to the said Lady Paula, and instituted as her universal heirs Lady Joanna, Lady Francesca, and Vincella Barutii, as appears in the said will, which you will be able to see. Then the said Alamana died in pupillary age, survived by her mother, Lady Paula, and the aforementioned substitutes. Now it is asked, what and how much the said Lady Paula ought to have, both by right of the legacies left to her in the said wills, and also by right of the dowries or alimonies owed to her, or by right of succession to Alamana, her daughter, or by any other right, since she has always observed and still observes a widowed life, and is in the house of the said testators, and possesses all the goods.

† In the estate of Fortisguerra, Lady Fiordelisia was instituted as universal heir by his will. If she had accepted the inheritance from the will, or acted as heir, Lady Alamana, being posthumous, succeeded to the quantity left to her. And if that said quantity did not cover the legitime, which is one-third of the goods of the said Fortisguerra, she would have succeeded also in that up to the due supplement of the goods, as in C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. omnimodo; and l. si quis filium; and l. scimus. And upon the death of Alamana, Lady Paula, her mother, succeeded in all the rights of the said Alamana, as in Auth. de haereditatibus ab intestato, §. sequens; and in Auth. defuncto, C. ad Tertullianam. For since Lady Fiordelisia died before Lady Alamana, she did not transmit the right of conditional institution. D. de suis et legitimis heredibus, l. si ex pluribus. Note, this opinion seems true, and is founded on the rule of law that a conditional substitution does not admit of transmission. C. de caducis tollendis, l. 1, §. si autem aliquid. But looking more subtly, one will consider that when a minor instituted by his father accepts, he transmits the pupillary substitution from the father, or the right of accrual, and this has the same effect even while the condition is pending, as is a very special case. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. qui pater, quae non est alibi. This passage is among the subtleties of the law, yet this last opinion is the very truth. And therefore Lady Paula, her mother, does not succeed to Alamana, but the heirs of the said Lady Fiordelisia, which is remarkable: and this would not be believed, unless jurists were well grounded in the law. And this concludes the matter of the succession of Fortisguerra. It remains to consider the succession of Fiordelisia.

And it should be known that, with respect to what came to Alamana from the testament of Fiordelisia, Paula, her mother, succeeds to Alamana, notwithstanding C. de fideic. l. si in personam, saving the substitution made to the same Alamana by the lady Fiordelisia; which substitution could be made, except in the legitime due to the said Alamana from the goods of the said lady Fiordelisia, which legitime is one-third of all the goods of the said testatrix, as in Auth. de trien. et semisse § 1, and in Auth. nouissima C. de inoff. testam.

† However, it does not seem that the Trebellianic action should be discussed here, because Alaman was instituted heir to specific things, and therefore she does not deduct the Trebellianic share. ff. ad Trebel. l. mulier. §. ii. And thus the chapter Ray. and the chapter Raynal. do not stand in the way, because there the text speaks of a universal heir. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A ward who has reached majority cannot bring an action based on the act of B, his tutor, if he alleges that B was never his tutor. See also in consilium 15.
body: I will say that if someone has made a contract with another in the name of another, or has received a promise, or an obligation, or has stipulated for something to be given or done for someone: the person for whom the contract was made, or the stipulation, or the receipt of the promise, or the obligation, may sue the obligor by a direct action, as if a testament, and a cession of right and action, had been made to him without any other cession. And such person, for whom the stipulation was made, or the contract, or the receipt of the promise, is bound to restore to such agent, or procurator, without the offering of a libel, and without the noise and form of judicial proceedings, all that he had expended out of his own funds on the occasion of such management, or mandate, just as if he were bound by a confession made in legitimate court, with the debt purified and liquidated. This statute being presupposed, and notwithstanding the said statute, it is asked: a certain person, as tutor, and in the name of tutor, had sold the usufruct of a certain piece of land for nine years for a certain sum of money. Now, the said nine years having ended, the pupils, now of age, sue the said buyer, that the said buyer restore and surrender the possession of the thing, which he holds by virtue of the stipulation. The said pupils, now of age, allege in the libel, or in the narration, that they sue on the contract made by the said tutor, although in truth he was not a tutor.

† Now it is asked, since the said agents deny that he was a guardian, and in their petition assert that he was not a guardian, whether on this pretext the said agents can be repelled. The mode of acting must be derived from the mode of contracting. D. de manumissionibus, l. Gayus. And from whose person I act, I must approve that person, not disapprove it; for when I ground myself on his person, I cannot impugn it, as in l. cum minor, §. si rem ratam haberi. No one can rely on the person of an author when the author is disapproved, as in Extra, de hereditatibus, c. fraternitatis. And because he says his author is lying, he cannot avail himself of his act, for it is more unworthy to obtain a benefit from that person whom he endeavors to impugn. l. 1, C. si servus extero. Likewise, no one can impugn that from which he derives fruit, as noted in c. ex eo, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Likewise, a contract having two parties, one contracts through the other, and it has two correlative extremes, and if one is destroyed, the other does not subsist, as in l. si, D. de acceptis. But he who denies him to be a guardian says that he is not bound by his act; therefore, he cannot act on the same act. This is proved by what is noted by Cynus, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam, in the first and second question. And this is the truth, for if someone contracted as a guardian in a contract obligatory on both sides, the ward who acts on it must affirm him to be a guardian, for he cannot waver regarding the same contract. D. de administratione tutorum, l. cum quaeritur. And the above are proved by the conjunction of two paragraphs, in one it is said that from the contract of the selling procurator a useful action arises without cession; in the other it is said that the master must simply approve or simply disapprove. D. de actionibus emptoris, l. Iulius, §. si procurator, and §. si quis colludente. For this, D. iudicatum solvi, l. 3, §. si quidem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Inferiors may not collect tolls from the prince unless by privilege of the prince, or by custom, of which contrary memory does not exist.
2. By whom the privilege of the prince may be proved.
3. When witnesses are taken for the perpetual memory of the matter by the mere office of the superior, a libel is not required; but when at the request of a party, then a petition is required.
4. Whether instruments suffice for the perpetual memory of the matter.
body: In the case of Passigi of Montefano

It must be premised for the sake of clarity that subordinates may not collect tolls from the prince, because these are royal prerogatives, as in c. 1, quae sint regalia, col. 10. And because passage through public roads is free and lawful. ff. de via publica, l. viam publicam; ff. ne quid in loco publico, l. 2, § viarum. And this is true, unless one has a privilege from the prince, or by custom, of which contrary memory does not exist, they may legally claim this: for such custom has the force of a royal privilege. And because this is generally observed in Italy, it is presumed from the conscience of the prince that the prescribed use of imposing and collecting tolls exists. extra de versigiis, c. super quibusdam; and in c. quiquis, de censibus, lib. 6; and noted by Roffredus in that rubric, ut liceat ire agere per viam publicam, in his libelli. And fully noted by Hostiensis in the Summa, de censibus, § ex quibus. Secondly

It must be premised that a prince’s privilege is proved by those who have read and seen it, provided they are prudent persons, as in the chapter *Olim essemus apud Perusium constituti*, Extra, *De censibus*, and as noted by Jacobus de Belvis and Cynus, Codex, *De fidei instrumentis*, law *Sicut iniquum*. Thirdly, it must be known that

† Who, in order that witnesses may be examined for the perpetual memory of the matter, sometimes proceeds from the mere office of the superior commanding this to be done, and then no other petition is required, except the production of his letters: because the rescript is held in place of the petition, that is, the production of the rescript. Sometimes it is the party, and then a petition is required. It is established by what is noted in c. Accepimus, De aetate et qualitate, in the Novella, and in D. De interdictis et actionibus, in the rubric. From these, however, it is thus concluded: since the matters contained in the supplication of the aforementioned common body of Montis Fani have been proven, there is no longer any doubt to be had about their right.

† since public documents suffice for perpetual memory of the matter. C. de re iud. l. gesta. since the rights to retain possession can be proved in this way, de testi. c. significauit. nor is it said to act wrongfully, that he collects the fruits of the toll even from unwilling parties: because the fruits are to be retained as part of possession. The conclusion is clear, because the common law of Montefano has a most certain right to collect the said toll in the usual manner. I say, however, in the usual manner, because it ought not to be increased, but that which was customarily collected in the past may be collected in the future. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a substitution is made by the word "succeed," it ought to be interpreted as a direct fideicommissum, in order to exclude or not exclude the mother.
2. If one party wishes that witnesses be examined regarding the testator's intent, they ought to be examined.
3. Witnesses who are not written in the will may be examined regarding the testator's intent.
body: A certain person named Angelutius Lelli of Triuo made his last will and testament of his goods, in which, among other things, he left to Nicolutia, his daughter, for her dowry 200 pounds, and in the same will he instituted as his universal heirs Antonio and Lellus, his beloved sons: and he willed that if the said Nicolutia should die without sons and daughters legitimately born to her, that the aforementioned Lellus and Antonio, his heirs, should succeed to her. And he willed that if any of his said heirs should happen to die without legitimate sons or daughters, that one should succeed to the other; but if all his said heirs and the said Nicolutia should die without legitimate sons and daughters, he willed that Datutius Petri Martini, Paulus Petri Martini, and Petrus Tollettae Petri Martini should succeed to them in equal parts. This Angelutius, having thus made his will, died, the said Nicolutia, Antonio, and Lellus being surviving and living, and Andreutia, his wife and mother of the said Nicolutia, Antonio, and Lellus, also surviving. Afterwards, Nicolutia died, the said Antonio, Lellus, and the said Andreutia surviving. After this, the said Lellus died, the said Antonio and the said Andreutia, his mother, surviving and living. Afterwards, the said Antonio died, the said Andreutia, his mother, and the said Datutius, Paulus, and Petrus surviving and living. And all the said sons of the said Angelutius died as minors after the death of their father, perhaps within 25 days. It is now asked, what is the law, and what and how much of the goods of the said late Angelutius, and subsequently of his sons, pertains and belongs to the said Andreutia: and what and how much to the said Datutius, Paulus, and Petrus. Points,

† The matters transmitted to me do not agree on this point. The substitution was made by the word “let them succeed to them.” And thus the words are directed toward the succession of the children, whereby in the case of pupillary age there is a pupillary substitution on account of the word “to them.” For from a pupillary substitution one succeeds to an impubes. L. 1, de vulgari substitutione; and L. moribus; and in § sed nec impuberis. And on this point the mother is entirely excluded, since the pupilli have died, as in L. precibus, C. de impuberibus; and in c. si pater, extra de testamento. On another point there is a distinction of times, and the same result follows, because the mother is entirely excluded, as fully noted in the aforementioned L. precibus. On another point there is no distinction of times, nor is there the word “to them,” but rather the word “let them succeed,” simply uttered, which can be understood to mean that they succeed by fideicommissum to the testator himself, de vulgari substitutione, L. cohæredi, § cum filiae. And because the word “let them succeed” is common, if the mother is in the middle, it ought to be interpreted as fideicommissary and not direct, lest a doubtful substitution be admitted against the mother. And the same we say in a doubtful substitution as we say in a tacit one, C. de institutione et substitutione, L. si. And thus the mother would deduct the legitima and the Trebellian portion, as stated in the aforementioned laws and in c. Raynaldus, de testamento. And therefore, according to the diversity of the points, I give diverse advice: according to the first two points, against the mother; according to the other, for the mother. And whatever the case may be, the said substitutes did not fall from their right of apprehending vacant possession, and without force, as in L. 1, § redigant, quorum legibus; and noted in C. de edicto divi Adriani tollendo, L. edicto, in the gloss on the word. Also, whether a universal fideicommissary.

† Regarding the matter in question, namely whether, if one party wishes that witnesses be examined concerning the testator’s intent, such witnesses ought to be examined, I say that yes; the text is noted in C. de testamento militis, l. testamento, at the end.

† Furthermore, regarding the question whether other witnesses, who are not described [in the instrument], may be examined concerning the testator’s will, I say that yes, if they were called [to testify]; otherwise, the substance is not proved by them. Hence, they could nevertheless contradict the written document; because where no falsity is found, no examination of witnesses is required. Thus, it must be proved by whatever witnesses that it is outside the instrument. See infra, c. Cum Ioannes, de hereditate instituta; de inutilibus stipulationibus, § Item puberum; Codex, de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. Optimam; and what is noted in l. 1, at the end, Quem ad modum testamentum apertum, where it is stated that what the testator says outside the testament may be proved by witnesses not described in the testament. l. Cum proponebatur, ff. de legatis 2. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether he who petitions for a will to be insinuated tacitly petitions that it be declared effective; and whether the judge pronouncing that it ought to be insinuated appears tacitly to pronounce that it is effective; and whether such tacit intention is definitive.
body: A nille.

† He who seeks the insinuation of a testament tacitly seeks that it be declared effective; for an ineffective one cannot be insinuated. If, therefore, it is declared that it must be insinuated, it is declared that the legacy is due, or that the inheritance pertains to the claimant, if he was instituted as heir. Hence, it includes within itself a definition; just as, conversely, if it is declared that it need not be insinuated, it is declared that it is invalid, and the matter is defined not only as to the instance, but also as to the obligation and the principal fact. Therefore, I hold this sentence to be definitive, as in l. 1, ff. de re iudicata. And although the procedure is extra ordinem according to the form of the statute, nevertheless the outcome of the controversy is definitive, if it is declared that it must be insinuated, and the actio in factum, or the officium iudicis, arises as from a definitive judgment. And this is true if it was declared in a contradictory judgment with the adversary appearing and opposing; for a judgment consists of three persons, as noted in C. de bonis quae liberis, l. 1, ff. § 1, noted in the gloss, major, ver. item quid in præcepto. And that passage serves well for the purpose, because here he scarcely commanded it to be insinuated, by which he receives the testament ready for execution. Hence, since the judge could not do more by a definitive condemnatory sentence, by this insinuation it should be called definitive, and it can be appealed without stating the cause, as noted by Io. And. extra de appellationibus, c. peruenit. In the Novella. And it is proved by l. 1, C. de bonis possessoribus secundum tabulas. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if the testator in his first will instituted Titia, his wife, to receive 300, which he confessed he owed her by way of her dowry, and afterwards he revokes that will and makes another, the first confession nevertheless remains valid. And where he distinguishes.
body:
Antonius made a will. In the said will, he left, made, or bequeathed a legacy to the aforementioned A., in the following terms, namely: “Furthermore, he left to the said A., by way of institution, the dowry of his wife, Lady B., daughter of Q., which amounted to, and amounts to, 355 Aquilian pounds, as should appear from the dowry instrument written by B. And if the said instrument is not found, nevertheless the testator willed that the said Lady B. should receive the said 355 Aquilian pounds for the aforementioned reason; since, however, she had received the aforementioned dowry, as he himself confessed, etc.”

After the aforementioned will, the said Antonius, the testator, lived for some time, and the said Lady B., the aforementioned wife, died, the said A., the aforementioned testator, surviving her, with three daughters born to the said A., the testator, and the said Lady B., the aforementioned wife.

After this, the said A., the testator, made another will, in which, by way of institution, he left to the said daughters certain sums for dowries and suitable support, and beyond what constitutes the legitime of the said daughters. In this last will, he made no mention of the first legacy left to the said first wife, because at the time of this last will he had taken a second wife. In this last will, he revoked the first, of which mention has been made.

Now it is asked whether the said daughters have any right against the universal heir of the said A., named in the said last will, by virtue and on account of the said legacy, or of the words contained in the said first will and the aforementioned legacy, or not; and if so, what right, and to what extent.

† In this question there are various opinions: some say that by such a confession an effective proof of the debt is produced, so much so that from such proof the confessor himself, upon recovering his health, can be effectively convicted; and this is proved first by the general rule in all contracts, as in D. de deposito, l. Publius, §. si; D. de probat., l. Cum de indebito, §. si. Secondly, by those things which are specially laid down in the law concerning dowry, C. de dote causa, l. 1, in the gloss. Thirdly, by natural equity, because it is equitable to abide by the statement of the testator, since he has acknowledged good faith, which men often acknowledge under the contemplation of death, Extr. de successione ab intestato, c. Cum dilectus. Fourthly, because the absence of the party is supplied by the repentance of the deceased, arg. C. de iudiciis, l. Properandum, §. Cum autem heremodicium. Fifthly, because in a last will it can be celebrated as an obligatory act rather than a probative one, l. Haeredes palam, §. si, de testamentis; and l. Assignare, de assignandis liberis. Sixthly, because if the testator left the confession in his memoranda, it would prove, C. de probat., l. Rationes, with its subject matter; therefore, why should it not be the same if he leaves it in his written will, or reduced to writing? The reason does not seem to be able to be given. Seventhly, because he cannot say that he is dead if he survives. Moreover, the heir cannot allege the falsehood of the deceased, D. de non numero pecuniae, l. Generaliter; D. de donationibus, l. Si patronus; D. de probat., l. Per tuas; D. de pignoribus, actio rem alienam. Eighthly, because although the party is absent, ratification fakes her presence, D. de iureiurando, l. Labeo. Ninthly, because the husband is bound to make an instrument of the dowry for his wife, and he is obliged to do this, l. 2, D. de solutione matrimonii; hence this act of confession tends to the liberation from this obligation of making the instrument; and therefore it seems valid, even in absence, according to us in l. Non solum, §. Si liberis, de liberatione legis. Tenthly, it is evident if the heir of the husband wished to claim the dowry from the pact of gaining; for if in the will he had confessed that he had received it, the exception of fraud would stand in the way, D. de solutionibus, l. Si ex pluribus. Eleventhly, and lastly, this is proved by the authority of Peter and Cynus, C. de non numero pecuniae. On the contrary, it is argued that the law provides that either such a confession is made simply or with an oath. In the first case, such a confession does not prove that a contract preceded, as in D. de lege legatorum, l. Aurelius, §. si. In the second case, it is either made between persons between whom a donation has not been granted, and it does not prove, as in D. de probat., l. Qui testamentum; or from the premises, every contract, and then it is proved, D. de lege 3, l. Cum qui decedens, §. Titia, and §. Codicilli; and in Auth. de iureiurando a moriente praestando, and there by Jacobus de Belvis. But here we are between husband and wife, therefore the confession does not bind between those present, and even with an oath. And thus says Bartolus in the said §. Titia. But this statement is very harsh in the case of dowry, because all the laws speaking of the confession of dowry, and setting times, and for opposing the exception of non-numbered dowry, C. de dote causa, l. si; and we in the same title, l. 1, and this unless it appears that the confession was made for the purpose of giving; because then it is not valid, the marriage being established, C. de dote ante nuptias, l. 1, where note that these laws speak of a confession made between the living, but we speak when it is in a last will, and since the confession tends to bequeathing.

† There are three cases to be noted: sometimes the testator confesses and bequeaths; sometimes he confesses and does not bequeath; sometimes he bequeaths and does not confess. In the first case, the confession does not prove the debt, because the legacy would not be valid in the entire amount, but only by way of representation in the case of a dowry; in other cases, it is not valid in any way, as stated in l. 1, l. si creditor. This is the case in l. aurel. §. fi. de li. le. l. lucius. §. quisquis. In the second case, it occurs between prohibited persons, and so forth, as I have said above. The third case is clear: therefore, if the testator, by confessing, made a bequest, and the legatee died during the lifetime of the testator, it must be said that, according to written law, the said legacy has lapsed, and the confession [is ineffective], as noted in d. l. 1. C. de dona. ante nupt. per gl. et Cy. Nevertheless, I advise the said heir, if he had any knowledge of the said dowry, to acknowledge good faith and to pay out of conscience. But according to written law, he is not bound. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. He who denies that someone was a guardian may not bring an action based on a contract entered into by him as guardian; and see above, opinion 0.
2. A party bringing an action based on a produced instrument must necessarily admit that all matters contained therein are true.
body: What? One ought to beware of those who truncate true legal issues: because they perhaps do not know the facts, or pretend not to have seen what they ought to have seen. Namely, the instruments which their clients use, or declare in their bill that they will use. Hence, omitting the fictitious issue, the true issue is this: Lady Gnesola, in her capacity as guardian of four sons and in her own right, sold certain revenues from half of a certain field for nine years. And the words of the instrument state, and in the guardian capacity of Angelo, Antonio, Agatella, and Claveia, her sons, and of Martin, formerly her husband: binding herself and them jointly and severally. And at the end is placed such a stipulation, that the buyer of these fruits promised and agreed with the said Lady Gnesola, stipulating and receiving for herself and the said her sons and their heirs, to hold the property of the due thing for them, and upon expiration of the term to restore possession vacant and unencumbered. It is also a true issue that two of the said sons, namely Agatella and Claveia, through a procurator, sought to enforce the said instrument and to have the said half restored to them by way of execution: yet denying that the said guardian, or lady, was a guardian. It is also true that there are two statutes in the city of Perugia: one provides that confessed instruments, in which a promise is made to make confession before a judge, shall be put into execution. The other provides that if anyone stipulates in the name of another, the action shall be sought without assignment. These things therefore being presupposed as true, it is asked whether the said petition for execution proceeds. It is also to be added to the issue that the procurator of the said Agatella and Claveia says that Angelo and Antonio renounced the paternal inheritance. Now it is asked whether the said execution sought proceeds, considering the form of the bill, or not? I advised,

† That this bill does not proceed, and thus I advise, and thus I hold, and this is evident, because when execution of an instrument is sought, the instrument is the formal part of the petition itself. And he who denies that which is formal to the instrument is contrary to his own petition, as in l. 1, C. si seruo extero; Extra, de app., c. solitudinem; l. 1, C. de furt.; l. si, C. de codic.; l. ubi repugnantia, de re iud.; c. nullus plurib., per Dy., q. 6, tit. 1, lib. 6. But here that which is formal to the instrument is denied in the petition; therefore the petition does not proceed. For observe, that it is established there that this is formal. Thus, it must be known that form is that which gives being to a thing, ad exhib.; l. Iul. But the guardian gives being to the thing, i.e., to the contract; therefore this quality is formal. It is evident that it must pertain to the thing, because if he is a guardian, the contract is valid on both sides; but if he is a false guardian, it is not valid in any respect, l. antepen., §. si, quod fals. tut. aut. extr., n. contracts, which are two, s. obligations on both sides with a false or null guardian are undertaken by a woman, because the person is lacking. So it is in lawsuits, in which there is a quasi-contract. C. de proc., l. licet; Iu. sol., l. 3, §. si quis. Nevertheless, it is verified that the name under which one contracts, as though under a final name, must be true; otherwise the contract would not be true in name, nor in those things dependent on the name, such as acquisition. Here, the law in the case of a slave who stipulates for someone as though he were the master, when he is not the master: because there is no stipulation. ff. de stip. serv., l. servus hereditarius. Secondly

† It is clear, because the party who produces the instrument, being the plaintiff, is bound to confess that all and each of the assertions contained therein are true, as noted in Inn. de cens., c. Cum olim. And if he denies this, the production of the instrument does not benefit him. Thirdly, it is clear, because when qualities differ in substance and in form, it matters greatly what results from the differing qualities. C. de iud. delict., l. Cum aliquis; ff. qui sat. cog., l. Filius, according to Jacobus Butrigarius. Now let us demonstrate the difference, and it is most certain: for if this mother was a guardian, the action was acquired by the four sons, against their will and without their knowledge, by virtue of the guardianship, which is a force and power, and so forth, regarding the acquisition of goods, l. Est inuitis. But if she was not a guardian, then if any action were acquired, it would not be acquired unless they ratified it; hence the difference is as great as that between two and four. This is clear even to barbers. Another difference is that he who contracted with four, and divided the obligation, insofar as it can be divided, just as a field can be restored in part undivided, as it touches upon virile shares. If two of them sue in a conforming and proper manner, they cannot sue except for their virile share. l. Reos, §. Cum tabulis, de duob. reis. Now he sues in a conforming manner by demanding the whole. C. si serv. pecc., l. Si singuli. Another difference is as if between something done legitimately and something null by law itself: for if the buyer had known, there would have been no contract. l. Antepen., in fine, quod falso tutor. Therefore, consent is lacking. Fourthly, this is clear, because the buyer, therefore, promised to hold the thing for all four; therefore, he cannot restore it to two of them. l. 1, §. Apud Iul., depositi. And thus two cannot sue. ff. depositi, l. Si plures: because the pact so states. The mother in this contract contracted in her own name, and by virtue of the stipulation, in her name only, and for her heirs; certainly, the said daughters of this mother cannot sue while this mother is alive, as noted in ff. de pact., l. Si tibi, §. Si pactum. For whenever a mother stipulates for herself and her heir, the daughter does not sue unless she is the heir, which cannot be the case unless the mother is dead. And therefore, the said petition is impossible, contrary to the instrument, inequitable, and evidently caviling, and this would seem to be one beast. Fifthly, and by another demonstrative reason, this is clear: for unless the instrument is confessional, i.e., a true promise is made, or presumed, of a confession made or to be made, this instrument does not merit execution, but the ordinary course of action must be taken. But this instrument is not confessional, except insofar as it states, i.e., that such a guardian, with a tutelary person, etc. Nor was it promised to confess otherwise; therefore, removing the tutelary name, the instrument remains non-confessional, i.e., without a promise to make a confession. And if anyone knows something, he should at least recall what is said in the law and noted in ff. de iureiur., l. Iusiurandum, quod ex coniunctione, §. 1, where the glossa says: note, a good argument in all contracts which those who enter into do not choose by law. Hence all things are annulled. And l. Quae neque, ff. de reb. eor. qui sub tutela. Let the procurator therefore look, and recite that glossa. Sixthly, and by another reason, for the statute says, if anyone stipulates in the name of another, he acquires for him. And this proceeds from the force of the name: and a name is not a name unless it is a true name impressed upon the subject, as in l. 2, ff. quena. test. apud, ff. de ver. sig., l. Paulus. But here it was a tutelary name; therefore, with the word "tutor" circumscribed, the statute ceases, for if he is not a tutor, it was not done in that name, of which name the instrument and statute speak; this word "in that name" signifies identity and truth. ff. de publ., l. Eum qui, §. Fin. And it should be known that ratification is equivalent to the mandate of a procurator, not to the mandate of a tutor: for the mandate of a tutor, if the tutor is false, as Agesias says, cannot arise from the agent. And the same quality of tutor is not verified by any ratification, nor does it have the privilege of truth: for the benefits of law and of the prince are accommodated to true qualities, not to those feigned by ratification, extra de rescript., c. Nonnulli. Seventhly, observe, because the statute says, the direct action is sought by law itself: and it must be understood through a true and capable person contracting, and consummating the extremes of the contract, as in l. Ut gradatim, §. Si lege, ff. de mun. et hon. But he who alleges a false tutor alleges the incapacity of the person. Eighthly, observe, because the statute says the action is sought: it therefore gives an action, for an action is not built when one sues for execution, but it intends the office of the judge against the common law, as in C. de exec. rei iud., Nimis propere. And because this statute does not say this, nor can we say it. It is certain that one thing is an action, another is the office of the judge, as fully noted in Inst. de act., in princ. And the statute does not dispose anything regarding the office of the judge. Ninthly, because this execution, or office, should not go beyond the power of the convention contained: which here is none, except in the formative quality of the contract. Hence fraud and falsehood are found. ff. de dolo, l. 1, and elegantly in princ. Tenthly, because he from whom rights arise is called the author of him to whom rights are derived. Hence a derivative successor is excluded by the fraud of his primitive ancestor, nor can he allege his turpitude. C. de revoc. his, quae in fraud. cred., l. Filios, and there noted. To allege to the contrary, that from contrary qualities the effect is not changed, does not help: on the contrary, certainly not only in effect, but in origin, they are contrary. Nor does it help to allege that the act can be approved, and not the quality, as in l. Cum interdictae, cum si. This has place if it is sued from fault to impugn the contract: otherwise, if from the form of the contract, and for its execution, the action must be born. But to allege that she did not stipulate as a guardian is contrary to the principle of the instrument: for from the principle of the title, etc. And it is a trick, and I marvel at your collateral and prudence, for you understand the truth, yet you fear the barking. I conclude therefore that the petition does not proceed, and that the narration of the petition is exclusive of the conclusion from all the reasons aforesaid, or at least from the majority of them demonstrating the truth to be so. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one must adhere to the father's confession made in the official records, that his legitimate son is present.
body: A father,

† by confessing in the judicial acts that he is his legitimate son, established proof of legitimacy on behalf of the son, as noted in C. de lib. causa. l. iubemus; C. de fideic. l. pe.; C. de proba. l. non epistolis; and l. neque natales; ff. de iureiu. l. 3. §. quaecunque; and with respect to the article of proof it is of no consequence whether he has other legitimate children or not, but with respect to the introduction of a new legitimation the opinions of the Doctors are conflicting, as was fully written above by the distinguished Doctor Dominicus Petri; and therefore it is safer to adhere to the confession made in the judicial acts. Nor does what is noted in ff. de prob. l. fi. in prin. stand in the way, because there it was outside of court; but in court one must stand by that which someone confesses in his libel on behalf of another, C. de li. ca. l. cum praecu., and l. rura, de omni agro deserto, lib. 11, especially in our case, where many presumptions assist, extra de prob. c. per tuas, and C. de nat. lib. auth. Item si quis, in the words sub gestis monumentorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the omission of the mother renders the son’s will void, if the testating son has children.
2. A substitution made simply is understood to refer to the first one made, if any formal requirement has been observed.
body: Omission

† The mother does not invalidate the will of a son dying with sons, because in succession the primary right belongs to the sons, as in the Authentica de haeredibus ab intestato, after the principal paragraph. And because the mother at the time of the son’s death does not hold the first place, she cannot break the son’s will, as in the Authentica de haeredibus quae ab intestato deferuntur, and in the law Si quis filio, et haeres, in the principal paragraph, de inofficioso testamento. Nor is the legitime due to this mother, because she would not have succeeded intestate. Codex, de inofficioso testamento, law Cum quaeritur. And by this response, two points concerning the testator’s mother are answered. To the third point, I say,

† That the substitution made to the sons was made among them in a threefold form, namely, vulgar, pupillary, and by fideicommissum; and, with the discourse continued, the following substitution was made to all of them, which, on account of the conjunction of the speech and the continuity, must be understood as repeated under the same threefold form; and thus the mother is excluded, if she wishes to be admitted by virtue of the pupillary substitution, as in c. Si pater, De testibus, lib. 6. By this reasoning, the sister of these pupils is excluded, nor is she admitted to anything else, except to what was left to her in the will, as in l. Pomp., § Sed nec impuberis, De inofficioso testamento. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a direct pupillary substitution, which excludes the mother on account of those words “without children,” becomes an oblique substitution, and thus does not exclude her.
body: The testator substituted heirs for his instituted daughter, in the event that he should die without issue, in the following form: in the other residual goods, after the death of the aforementioned Fran., his daughter, he ordered and expressly willed that Io., his brother, and Grassutia, his sister, should succeed; and he substituted them for the said Fran., and made them universal heirs after the death of the said Fran. The said Fran., after the death of her father, died in pupillary age. It is asked whether her mother is excluded from the legitime and the trebellianic portion by the aforementioned substitutes.

And it must be said briefly that this is so, because the substitution was direct and occurred within the time limits, that is, before the time of puberty. This is the opinion of the gloss in *l. precibus*, under the word "but in the pagan," in the Code, *de impuberibus*. This is not obstructed by what is noted in the same gloss, under the heading "if, however, he died without children, let him be the heir, etc.," because in this passage, when it says "let him be the heir," it speaks incorrectly according to all the Doctors, insofar as the term "heir" is applied to the impubes, that is, let him be the heir of the impubes, as is the case here, because one does not succeed an impubes except through a pupillary substitution. Since this is expressly made, it excludes the mother, as stated in *l. Pomp.*, § *sed nec impuberis*, in the Digest, *de inofficioso testamento*, and in *c. si pater*, *de testamentis*, Book 6. I therefore conclude that the mother is entirely and completely excluded. For a direct substitution, by reason of the added words "if he died without children," does not become an oblique substitution, as stated in *l. Centurio*, in the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*. All the Doctors say this, and another gloss states this in the Institutes, *de pupillari substitutione*, § *qua ratione*. Also, Johannes Andreas in the aforementioned *c. si pater*, in the Novels, and Cynus in the aforementioned *l. precibus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a usufruct is bequeathed to one person and fruits to another, the legatees concur simply in the usufruct; the same applies if a usufruct is bequeathed to one person in respect of all goods in general.
2. When the heir and the legatee concur and make a part in the legacy. And no. 3.
body: Ciioa

†Regarding the aforementioned doubt, it must be known that when the use of a fund is bequeathed to one person and the fruits simply to another, the legatees concur in the usufruct. ff. de usufructu legato, l. si alii. And similarly, when the usufruct in general of all goods is bequeathed to one person and a certain estate simply to another, they concur as legatees in the usufruct of that estate. eo. tit. l. Sempronio, in principio, and there noted. Nor is that species, specially bequeathed, excluded from a general legacy of usufruct as a species from a genus, as otherwise occurs in a special and general legacy, de legatis 3, l. uxorem, § codicillis, and § felicissimo, and eo. tit. l. servis legatis, § si. For since ownership and usufruct do not stand in the relation of genus and species, as noted by Dy. in c. generi, de regulis iuris, but rather stand in such a relation that one cannot be fully performed without diminution of the other: therefore, concerning the usufruct, the legatees concur, as stated in l. si alii and l. Sempronio, and there by Bartolus. Item

It must be known that when a legacy is left to an heir and to another person, either the legacy was left in full to the legatee, and subsequently the same thing is also left to the heir, and thus the legatee is joined with the heir both by the thing and by the words: in this case, the heir does not make a share for the co-legatee, because the legacy does not consist in his person; and the legatee comes to the heir’s share by the right of non-decrement; therefore, the heir has no right to use retention against the legatee, D. de leg. 1, l. plane, § si duobus. Or they are joined by words, because the legacy is left to them together in one sentence: and then the heir makes a share for the legatee, because then the legatee would wish to be admitted to the heir’s share by the right of accretion, and thus to acquire, not to retain; therefore, the heir could at least by hereditary right retain his share: this is proven by D. de usufr. accresc., l. si quis Titio, and l. si mulieri, § 1, and noted by Bartolus in the said l. plane, § si duobus, although there he does not cite those laws for this purpose; but this branch is better proven by the said laws than by the laws cited there by Bartolus.

† Now, as to the point: since the said testator bequeathed to the said ladies the usufruct of all his goods, and then bequeathed a certain estate to his said heirs, it appears that the said heirs and the said ladies concur in the usufruct of the said estate, as stated in the law *Sempronio* and the glosses thereon. However, because the legacy in the person of the said heirs is entirely useless, according to the law *De legatis* 1, *Legatum* § 1, and as is proven in *De legatis* 2, *Cum pater* § *Pater*, the said ladies would be admitted, and after their death, the said monastery would not acquire the entire usufruct of the said estate by right of accretion, because a solid legacy was made to them, nor would the said heirs make them a share, as stated in the law *Plane* § *Si duobus*. It would be otherwise if the usufruct of the said estate had been bequeathed simultaneously and in one sentence to the said ladies and the said heirs; for then, although the legacy in the person of the heirs would be useless, they could nevertheless not retain their share by hereditary right, so that the will of the deceased might be observed, who in that case seems to have intended to bequeath all the less to the co-legatees, whose legacy he modified by the addition of the heirs, as stated in the law *Si quis Titio* and the law *Si mulieri* § 1, and the glosses and notes thereon. And thus should be understood what Bartolus writes in the law *Huiusmodi* § *Si Titio* *De legatis* 1, where he cites the aforementioned laws; otherwise, his statement would be unreasonable, not conformable to the letter of the said laws, and would deviate from what he wrote in the said § *Si duobus*. And the aforementioned determination applies, especially if the said ladies were admitted to the petition of the said usufruct; for in those cases in which the heir, by virtue of a legacy made to him, can use the right of retention against the legatee, he is not admitted in any way if he has proceeded to delivery, or if he does not possess. And thus Bartolus understood it in the said § *Si Titio* and the law *Proinde* § 1 *De stipulationibus servorum*, and it is proven by the law *Per servum qui* in the Codex *De acquisitione rei dotis*. And this is true, unless some of the said heirs repudiated the inheritance; for insofar as there had been a repudiation of the legacy, it would be valid for the part of the repudiating heir, and concurrence would occur with the said ladies in the usufruct of the said estate, *Digestum* *De legatis* 2, *Milites* § *Pro parte*. And this I state and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It must be understood regarding this necessity, when it is said that, notwithstanding the fideicommissum, alienation may be made for one’s own necessities, since there are three kinds of necessity.
2. Likewise, what if he alienated something improperly, and not for necessities, whether he appears to be prohibited from alienating for other necessities.
body: What these words mean,

† That notwithstanding the substitution, he may alienate for his necessities and for the redemption of his person. Response: Necessity is threefold, namely, fatal, as if someone should fall into the hands of robbers by chance; natural, as necessity arising from illness and the support of one’s family; and necessity incurred by one’s own act, as if someone voluntarily contracted debts or committed some wrongful act. Therefore, either we are speaking of fatal or natural necessity, or some other just necessity, such as for paying taxes, for the repair of a house, or for the preservation of lands, and for these necessities he may alienate, D. de legatis 2, l. pater filium, in principio; D. de legatis 1, l. filius familias, §. diui; and §. pater, D. de legatis 2, l. peto, §. praedium, eodem titulo. Or we are speaking of necessity incurred by one’s own act, and then, if the act was done with the intent to defeat the fideicommissum, it cannot be alienated, D. ad Trebellianum, l. Titius rogatus. But if he contracted a debt in some youthful heat, or committed some wrongful act out of enmity or for some cause, then he may alienate for the redemption of his own person, because the testator expressly granted this; otherwise he could not freely alienate except up to the amount of the legitime. C. communia de legatis, auth. res, quae.

But the question remains whether, on account of the first alienations made prodigally, this power of alienating is lost for the future: it seems that it is. D. 36.1.12 (matrem et auunculum), at the end, where the text seems to indicate this. It does not seem right to say that, although he alienated badly in the past, he is prevented from alienating in the future in a case permitted by the testator; because the will of the testator must be observed. And because these matters are divisible: past wrongful acts [are distinguished from] present necessity. D. 46.3.1 (de illo). Therefore, on account of family necessities and fortuitous events, the faculty of alienating still endures. But the alienations first made wrongfully can be revoked upon the advent of the condition. D. 36.1.12 (res quæ). Thus, if this person contracted debts for just reasons, so that he might not be thrown into prison, he may alienate, as in D. 39.6.1 (si quis pro redemptione), C. 8.53.1 (usque admodum congruum et necessarium), and not beyond. D. 26.10.1 (fi). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the usufructuary makes the fruits his own before providing security.
2. Whether "to remain" is the same as "to be together," or "to dwell together," or "to live together," or whether these are different.
3. Whether heirs alone are bound to pay debts, or whether heirs and legatees are bound.
body: The first point of the question is stated in this,

Whether a usufructuary makes the fruits his own before security has been provided: some say that he does not, by the law *Uxori*, On the use and usufruct bequeathed. Others say that he does. And this was the opinion of Azo. The Codex touches upon this in the title On usufruct. For the first opinion is the gloss in the law *Si fur*, On the action for theft; in the Digest, On usucaption, the law *Si homo*; in the Code, On second marriages, the law *Hac edictali*; in the section *Is illud* of the Digest, On use and usufruct; the law *Si cuius* in the first gloss; and the law *Utifru* in the Digest, On usufruct; the law *Pe* in the Digest, On the action for recovery of property; the law *Ex diverso* in the principal gloss, which is great. The doctors say that sometimes the usufructuary himself does not collect the fruits, but the owner or another person does; and then the fruits ought not to be restored to the usufructuary before security has been provided, as stated in the aforementioned law *Uxori*. Sometimes the fruits are collected by the usufructuary himself, and then either with the knowledge and consent of the heir or the owner; and then he makes the fruits his own, as stated in the aforementioned law *Hac edictali*, in the section *Si autem*. But if the owner is ignorant, or knows and objects, then he does not make the fruits his own. Thus says Bartolus in the aforementioned law *Uxori*. And from these it is clear that if the heirs knew and allowed the usufructuary to collect the fruits, such fruits accrue to the women themselves to whom the usufruct was bequeathed.

† On another point, it must be said that those who stand in the same house are said to stand together, but they do not live together, since they do not dine together, but separately, 32. distinction. Moreover, on counsel, distinction 5. c. in omnibus. 12. q. 2. c. necessaria de vita, et hone. cle. c. quoniam vt ait. Although they do not live together, i.e., they do not dine together, they do not thereby lose the legacy of usufruct, for it was not bequeathed conditionally, namely, "if they live together." For if it had been a conditional legacy, no obligation arises, nor does an action before the fulfillment of the condition. ff. de verb. sig. l. cedere diem. Nor is it likely that the testator intended to deprive them of the legacy, although they do not dine together, since they have observed a widowed and honest life, and have not reclaimed their dowries, and have remained together in the same house. They have therefore sufficiently complied with the mode inserted in the testament by observing a widowed and honest life. For they lived together, although they did not dine together. For "living together" can be said of those who commonly cohabit. It is made clear in de sta. mon. c. cum ad monasterium. de sta. regularium. c. 1. li. 6. Therefore, they do not lose the legacy, since they have complied and observed the mode. C. de his, quę sub mio. l. 1. ff. de admi. le. l. liberto. de condi. et demon. l. 1. et l. qui haeredi. §. fi. et l. quibus diebus. §. fin. et l. eas. et de fideicom. li. l. cum in testamento.

† On another point, I say that the usufruct left to the lady of the legacy and to the lady of Iaco. ought to devolve to the hospitals of Saint Mary. For the legacy of usufruct was transferred to the hospital after the death of those ladies. Therefore, that right which was with the legatees was transferred to the hospital. D. de adimendis legatis, l. translatio.

† On the last point, I say that satisfaction must be given to the hereditary creditors by the heirs, not by the legatees: the heirs are also bound for the hereditary burdens in proportion to their hereditary shares. C. de rei vend. l. cum a matre; de privileg. cred. l. si creditores; ff. ex quibus caus. in possess. eatur. l. apud Iulianum, in fine; cum. l. sequ.; instit. de oblig. quae ex quasi contractu, §. heres; see below. And thus I say, and I, Baldus, advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Another opinion on the same subject matter.
body: On

† On the first point concerning usufruct, I say the same as was advised: the heir, by tolerating the situation, appears to give consent, especially because in corporeal things one is a debtor by toleration, nor is it necessary to offer security, but the right of demanding should not be denied.

† On the second point, I say the same, as it has been advised, because living together is understood according to the quality and convenience of the persons; hence a husband and wife are said to live together if they dwell under the same roof and in harmony, even if the wife maintains her own household, as nobles do.
