For that which prevents living together is discord, not separation. C. de fruc. l. manifestissimi. §. fi.

† On the third point, Bartolus states that the usufructuary of a universitas is bound to pay the debts, whereas another is not. D. de usufr. l. 1, according to Bartolus. Whether he is a legatee of the usufruct appears from the aforementioned D. de usufr. l. Si quis ita. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a testator bequeaths to an heir and to a legatee, whether they concur.
body: In another opinion, I say,

† That the subtlety of the law *alii* and *legis Sempronio* on usufruct, and the law *et l. plane*, § *si duobus*, on legacies 1, has application where the mind of the testator is not established, but where the will of the testator is established, one must adhere to the right of will, as noted in *l. si alij*, praetor’s edict, and Codex on fideicommissa, *l. cum virum* by the doctors. But when there is doubt about the will, we recur to the reason of the laws, and we dispute. In our case, it must be considered that either the testator bequeaths to the heir and the legatee uniformly, or differently. In the first case, either he bequeaths uniformly the ownership, and then the legatee has the whole, whether in fact and in words, or if he merely joins them, *de leg. 1*, *l. plane*, § *si duobus*. And the reason is, because since the testator considers the heir in that thing as a legatee, and in this way in the person of the heir the joint bequest does not hold, the whole must be had. Or he bequeaths the usufruct: and then they concur. And the reason is, because the ownership retained by the heir influences the casual usufruct by the nature of dominion, *de usufruct. actio*, *l. et mulieri*, and *l. si qui Titio*. In the second case, when he bequeaths differently, and this can happen in two ways. In one way, because to one he bequeaths the fund, to another the usufruct of the same fund specifically. And then in the usufruct, the legatee of the fund and the legatee of the usufruct concur, if the bequest holds in the person of both. *d. l. si alij*. But in the heir and the legatee, if indeed there are several heirs, if it is the bequest of one, the same, as noted in *d. l. Sempronio*. But if there is one heir alone, I say the same, because it accrues to him not by the right of legacy, but by the right of ownership. *l. si mulieri*. In another way, it can happen that there are two differences, for to one he bequeaths the usufruct of all goods, to another as heir he bequeaths, although uselessly, a certain estate. And this is our question, in which Bartolus says that they concur in the usufruct of that estate. By *d. l. Sempronio* in the principle, with the gloss. Thus he holds there, and *l. fi*, on usufruct, legacies, and *l. si quis seruum*, § *fi*, on legacies 2. For the difference is according to him between a predicable genus and a species. And this bequest, which cannot be performed by the nature of the thing without diminution of the subject, and has no other law for itself except the said *l. Sempronio*. But the gloss says otherwise in *l. quaesitum*, § *pe*, on funeral instruments, where it says that the legatee of Ricardina, who is in the village, has nothing to do with the paganella, which is bequeathed to another by name, which is a particular estate of the village; because special designation in that which is designated shows a singular and proper affection of the mind, *de conces. pręben.*, c. *quia cunctis*, lib. 6. And thus the part is separated from the whole. *l. si quis duas comunia prędio*. Nor does it object that one is heir; for what does not hold in him by the right of legacy, holds by the right of inheritance, and by the right of deduction from another universal. Because, as I said, Bartolus was prompt in deciding, and he bases himself on *l. Sempronio*, which does not say what he says: for there by the virtue of the relative, the species is shown; for he said, which I used to perform while alive, thus *ff. de leg. 1*, *l. si domino Stichus*. For the genus does not preserve its confused and general nature when a declarative is joined. And therefore of the said holding, the legatee will have either nothing, or certainly not more than half the usufruct. For of the half it seems sufficiently able to be defended on account of those universal words "of all goods"; but of the whole I do not believe it can be sustained, because the intention of the testator is shown not only once, but twice, declaratively and palpably, to which one must adhere, as *d. l. si alij* in the gloss, and *d. l. cum virum* by Cynus. A subtle inquirer will also weigh another thing in *l. Sempronio*, and that which Bartolus teaches, my master in the course of his lectures, could not weigh: for hasty and long-considered things do not have the same grace even among sublime minds. And by the foregoing, the sense of the gloss in *l. huiusmodi*, § *si Titio*, appears, as far as the passage of the said § *si duobus* is concerned. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if the Pope commands that a quest pertaining to the abbey be let or sold, the new abbot ought to observe the contract made by the authority of the Pope.
body: The dignity of the Abbot and his members is thus recognized to be vested in the new Abbot, so that, nevertheless, no prejudice shall arise to the purchasers of the said fruits, but the agreements made with them shall be observed to the letter. And this is proved first by the reason of the supreme pontifical power of the Lord Pope: for he can administer and dispose of the things and goods of all the churches of the world according to his will, especially when the causes subsist. And what is done by him is deemed to proceed from the mouth of God, 19th distinction, *Sic omnes*. And therefore he ought to strive to be like God. And although it is tolerated that he does whatever he does, even if it detracts from the rights of others, as noted by Innocentius, *De officio ordinarii*, chapter *Duo*; nevertheless, he sins more against himself, and indeed Hostiensis says more strongly that the Pope is not properly the owner, nor can he alienate prodigally, as noted by Johannes Andreae, *Extra*, *De iudiciis*, chapter *Cum venisset*, in the Novels. And his goodness is the salvation of all, and to the contrary, 40th distinction, chapter *Papae*. From the said power, therefore, by which he presides over all churches, he could enter into the said contract: for even the Abbot

† Saint Anthony. He may sell his acquired property before the Papal interdict; therefore, there is no doubt regarding the Pope, C. de praescri. l. omnes. and l. bene a Zenone. C. de quadri. praescri. Secondly, it is proven by the reason of faith owed, for the faith of the contract must be observed both by the Pope and by Caesar, as fully noted by Cynus, C. de legibus. l. digna vox. Indeed, even God binds Himself by the law of His promise. Thirdly, it is proven because not observing the faith of a contract is to lie. l. dolus. ff. mandati. But lying and fraud are abominable and horrible in the mouth of the Vicar of Jesus Christ; and therefore he is bound to keep his promises. Fourthly, because his acts must be free from all malice and diminution, as in Auth. constitutio, quae de digni. §. illud. Fifthly, because although the Pope does not impose law upon his successor, he does impose law upon the successor of the Abbot: for whatever pleases the prince has the force of law. ff. de consti. prin. l. 1. And the contract of the prince is law, and therefore it does not admit an exception of nullity. C. de don. inter vi. et vxo. l. pen. Sixthly, it is expressly stated that Caesar must observe his convention in good faith. ff. de pub. l. Caesar. And it would be fitting to his majesty to say that all his contracts are of good faith by special right, and especially of his dignity, since he is God on earth, as in Auth. de consulibus. Seventhly, this is proven because not nothing of speciality is preserved in him who has leased a public place for enjoyment. For he has a useful thing for a short time. ff. de loco pub. fruendo. l. 1. according to one opinion. Moreover, he has a possessory action from that interdict according to all. Therefore, this case is similar to that one. l. fi. de sa. san. ec. Eighthly, because it is certain that the Pope could bind the successor in the abbatial prelature, therefore the successor is bound to stand by this tenant or buyer of acquired property, extra ne praelati vices suas. c. fi. per Innocentius and others. Moreover, this privilege has been granted to the fisc, that one having a cause from it cannot expel the lessee. ff. de iure fisci. l. Valerius. Moreover, the Pope does not have less administration than a husband, etc., as noted ff. sol. matri. l. diuortio. and locati. l. emptore. per Cynus. Ninthly, because it is not likely that the Pope intended to take away the right acquired by the buyer from his contract, nor could he do so unless he made special mention of this with a derogatory clause. ff. ne quid in lo. pu. l. 2. §. si quis a prin. ff. de vul. sub. l. ex facto. C. de emam. li. l. nec auus. de autor. et vsu pallii l. ex tuarum. C. de praeci. impe. offe. l. quoties. and l. nec damnosa. and C. si contra ius, vel vti. pub. l. fi. and in c. quanuis. de rescri. li. 6. And finally, because the Church, which is the cultivator and promoter of justice, does not permit anything to be done against justice in itself or in another; a private person does not often obstruct justice, as c. 1. de alie. feud. coll. 10. And therefore it does not befit the Church to labor against good faith, which wishes pacts to be observed. ff. de pac. l. 1. extra eo. c. antigonus. ff. depo. l. bona fides. And if it were lawful for the Church to rescind its contracts, no one would contract with the Church. ff. de min. l. et si sine. §. enim. Moreover, the prelature passes to the new Abbot with its cause, its honors, and its burdens. ff. de contrah. emp. l. si aquaeductus. Moreover, the inferior, i.e., this Abbot, cannot rescind the act of the Pope. ff. de mino. l. minor autem magistratus. And for the buyer against the Abbot, every civil and canonical reason concludes: and I similarly say in this that the Abbot ought to stand by the contract of the Pope, even if he is unwilling, although by this no one finds the acquired property exhausted: because the Pope, and the lord of the end, and of all things, did this, i.e., ordered it to be done by another. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a codicillary clause has any effect in the case of the omission of grandchildren.
body:
The case concerns Joan of Casto, son of Castellione, who had three sons, namely Nardolus, Angelus, and Petrus, and from the said Angelus three grandchildren born of a lawful marriage, namely Iacobus, Mattheus, and Antonia. In the year of our Lord 1372, indiction 11, on the 1st day of the month of May, he made a testament, in which he instituted the aforementioned sons of Angelus, Petrus, and Nardus, his legitimate and natural sons, as his universal heirs. He ordered, willed, and commanded that if the said heirs should die without legitimate children descending from their bodies, his goods should remain in the male line or house. He also willed that half of his goods be given for the love of God, for the remission of his sins, to needy persons. For all the aforementioned legacies and fideicommissa to be paid and distributed, he appointed the aforementioned sons and heirs of the testator, Angelus, Nardus, and Petrus, and the good John, also called Tretia, and Cecchus, son of the good John. And the said testator willed this to be his last testament, revoking any other testament and last will that he might have made at any time. And if the said testament should not be valid as a testament, he willed that it should be valid as a codicil, and these are the words of the testament present here.

After the aforementioned events, from the said Angelus, legitimate and natural son of the said testator, and from the lady Florutia, legitimate wife of the said Angelus, was born a certain girl who was called Vuia. This girl died during the lifetime of the aforementioned testator and the said Angelus, her father, with the aforementioned testator surviving, and with the aforementioned Iacobus, Mattheus, and Antonia, grandchildren of the said testator and children of the said Angelus and the said lady Florentia, wife of the aforementioned Angelus, alive and surviving. Then the said Mattheus, grandson of the said testator, died, with the aforementioned testator surviving, and with the aforementioned Iacobus and Antonia, and the aforementioned Florutia, their mother, surviving. Then the said testator died, having made no other testament, with the aforementioned Nardus and Petrus, his sons and heirs instituted in the said testament, surviving, and with the aforementioned Iacobus and Antonia, his grandchildren omitted in the said testament, surviving, and with the said Florutia, mother of the aforementioned Iacobus and Antonius, grandchildren of the said testator, surviving.

After the aforementioned events, the aforementioned Iacobus and Antonia died in the year of our Lord 1384, namely Iacobus in the month of September and the aforementioned Antonia in the month of October of the immediately preceding year. Now it is asked whether, by the omission of the grandchildren who survived Angelus, that codicillary clause is broken.

† It might be doubted, because some say that such a clause has no effect in the case of posthumous omission: but these nephews are regarded in the place of posthumous children, as is noted in C. de posthumis haeredibus institutis in the response, and in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. filius a patre, and l. Gallus, §. nunc de lege, and de inofficioso testamento, l. in posthumorum. Others say that, since these nephews were born at the time of the will, they were omitted knowingly; and thus their birth does not break the codicillary clause, according to what is noted in l. sicut certi, and l. si cum vel in utero, de testamento militis. And if it be said that certainly one girl was conceived after the will, I answer that she does not break the will, because she died before her father; and thus, with the father existing in the middle, she does not break the grandfather’s will. D. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quis filio exheredato, in principio. Consider that here this dispute is not necessary, because when Angelus died with his sons, although he died while his father was alive, the condition of the substitution vanished, because he left living children after him. D. ad Senatum consultum Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. penultimo. And the codicillary clause, because the condition of the substitution fails, can have no effect, as C. de caducis tollendis, §. si autem aliquid. Since therefore the condition of the substitution fails, the share falls to the said nephews free and clear, and upon their dying, their mother succeeded in the said third portion of theirs by full and free right. See C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter; D. de fideicommissis, l. acutissimi; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum auus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How an uncle by the father’s side succeeds to a collateral nephew together with uncles by the mother’s side.
body: A paternal uncle

† succeeds per capita to a transversal nephew along with maternal uncles, as in the Authentica post fratres, C. ad Tertullia.; and the paternal uncle, who is the father's brother, must first have by his own person half of the common patrimony, which he would also have had during the lifetime of his brother Baldutius, in which half the dowries given to the said Baldutius do not enter, because if Baldutius were alive, he would deduct them in their entirety for himself alone; ff. fami. her. l. si maritus. However, these dowries, into the remaining dowry estate of the marriage of Baldutius and of his son John, are thereafter divided into three parts, and each uncle comes to his third, since they are three. It must also be known that if the inheritance of John's mother was not accepted, the dowry would revert to the said brothers of the mother, and the paternal uncle would have nothing from that dowry. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a procurator may declare the principal’s will, and whether a special mandate is required.
body: These reasons

† they act against the said lady. First, because her procurator did not produce the instrument of mandate, nor did he give proof of the mandate. And therefore the said priors and syndics were not placed in default. D. de deposito (16,3), l. si quis inficiatus. And although the procurator alleged it, he nevertheless did not exhibit it. Hence, his words ought not to have been believed. Furthermore, because the said power of attorney was not sufficient for this purpose by reason of its form: because it did not contain a mandate to relinquish and freely and expeditiously release the said properties and rights in the said properties. And the words state, insofar as the said Piera wished: which wish the procurator could not declare without a special mandate. D. de acquisitione hereditatis (29,2), l. Paulus. Furthermore, the said power of attorney does not extend to these matters: because the procurator had been appointed long before the said transaction was made. Hence, it does not extend to them, l. quod dicitur de tutela per Cynus, and l. omne, de procuratoribus. Furthermore, because no proceeding was had for the real division and distribution of the said properties, as ought to have been done within the year, for the word "wished" is understood with effect and with a subsequent act. D. de statu liberorum (40,12), l. 3, § si quis sic. From which reasons I say that the said lady does not uphold justice. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A legatee, to whom something is bequeathed after the death of the testator’s children, if he dies before the children, the legacy expires.
2. Pupillary substitutes exclude the mother.
3. The mother is not owed a legitime when the testator has children.
4. A wife who repudiates her children loses the legacy, but not the dowry, nor the paraphernal property.
body: On

† On the first point, it must be said that, since Peter Carrigiae died before the testator’s children, he did not transmit to them the legacy left to him after the death of the children. C. de caducis tollendis, §. autem si sub conditione; and fully known, C. de his qui ante apertas tabulas, l. 1; de regulis iuris, l. quae legata; and Institutiones, de verbis obligatorum, §. ex conditionalibus. And therefore, the said legacy remains with the heirs of the deceased, i.e., the testator, as caducary, as in §. pro secundo. On the second point

Having seen the will, in which a pupillary substitution is expressly stated, it must be said that those substituted pupillarily succeed, excluding the mother of the minors, according to the law on undutiful wills, Papinian, § but not of a minor; and the law Precibus; and in the chapter If a father, with similar authorities. On the third point, it must be said,

† that no legitime is due to the testator’s mother in the testator’s goods: because the testator died while his children were living, who had the primary right in the succession: and therefore, by his will, his children could be entirely passed over, in Auth. de haer. ab intest. § 1. On the fourth point, it must be said,

† That the fruits which were found in the inheritance pertain to the testator’s estate, not to the wife, who, having survived her children, fell from the legacy for the future time. ff. de leg. 3. l. qui concubinam. §. vxori. and in Authen. de nup. §. fiunt tutelam. And by this response is answered the other points, because the wife lost all usufruct, but she must recover her dowry and all her paraphernalia from the husband’s heirs. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a gift made to a church, with the usufruct reserved for oneself during one’s lifetime, is said to be a donation, or whether it is said to be inter vivos, or causa mortis.
body: The point is as follows. Cecchus made a certain donation by means of a notarial instrument, namely: In the name of the Lord, Amen. In the year of our Lord 1383, indiction 7, during the pontificate of Pope Urban VI, on the 6th day of the month of February, the chapter and convent of the church of Saint John of Fratta having been summoned and assembled, in the said church, in the choir, in which chapter were present Lord Peter, Prior of the said church, and Lord Peter Andreoli of Gubbio, a monk of the said church, while Lord Antonio Cecchi, a monk of the said church, was absent. Cecchus Vannis Cecchi of the castle of Fratta, of the community of Perugia, and Lord Bartolutia, his wife, appeared before the said Lord Peter Prior, and the said Lord Peter, and me, the notary, and the above-mentioned witnesses. First, one house situated in the castle of Fratta, with its roof, building, and boundaries, bounded on one side by a road and on the other by a neighboring house. Also, one garden plot situated in the said castle, bounded on two sides by roads and on the other by the commune of the said castle. Also, one piece of land planted with vines, situated in the district of the said castle, bounded on one side by Meus Tutii, and on the other by the heirs of Simonelli, or others, with appurtenances, to have and to hold, etc. This donation and conveyance they made to the said Prior for the salvation of the souls of their deceased relatives, always reserving the fruits of the said properties and the inheritance of the said house during their lifetime; and after the death of the said Cecchus and Bartolutia, the said properties shall remain to the said church. Done in the church of Saint John, in the district of the said castle, in the presence of Antonio Vannis, and Fran. Conueneuoli, and Paulutio Berrardelli, all of the said castle.

† Now it is asked whether from the aforementioned words it appears that there was any donation to the said church of the said goods; and if a donation is alleged, or can be alleged, whether it is a donation causa mortis or inter vivos? This donation was valid, but it is doubtful whether it was inter vivos or causa mortis. It seems that it was inter vivos, because in case of doubt a donation is presumed to be inter vivos, as in l. Seya, de don. causa mortis. To the contrary, because mention was made of death, whence it is deemed to be causa mortis: de dote praelegata, l. Seya; l. miles, in princ., de legatis; 2. glossa, in fin., C. de pactis; l. non firmatur. In this doubt, therefore, recourse must be had to the intention, which can be gathered from the words, as in l. non omnis, si certum petatur. For a donation causa mortis is one whereby a person wishes to retain possession for himself more than for the donee, and wishes to retain possession for the donee more than for his heir: ff. de donationibus causa mortis, l. 1. But thus it seems to have been here, because he wished to retain possession for himself during his life more than for the donee; therefore it is a donation causa mortis, and thus it could be revoked. But to this it is answered that it is true that he wished to retain the fruits for himself, but he wished the ownership to pertain more to the church, as in C. de donationibus, l. quisquis. Moreover, here mention of death was not made by way of a final cause, but by way of a certain postponement inserted on account of the fruits of the intervening time; for the final cause was for the soul, as shown by the doctrine of l. quae dotis, soluto matrimonio. But this part was not true on account of those words, “after death they shall remain.” For these words suspend the entire donation until death, and the word “remain” indicates this, notwithstanding that dominion was transferred during life; for this occurs whenever a donation causa mortis, on account of the mention of death, remains in the word “remain.” This passage is not clear, but it is commonly held that it would be a donation causa mortis; however, as I said, the reasons to the contrary are very strong. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When one is said to have, or not to have, the means to support oneself.
body: As he said, so do I say,

† That within the year she must be provided with alimony from the dowry, if she has no other source of sustenance. But what if she has means by selling and converting the proceeds into alimony? It seems that in such a case this rule is understood to apply, because she can support herself from the revenues; for she is not obliged to sell her own property in order to support herself from the price, as stated in the Digest, De cessione bonorum, l. Qui bonis. Otherwise, she would always have a source of sustenance, because she could sell the claim against the debtor who is bound to provide the dowry, and thereby support herself. But this is not true. It may be said that if she has means of support from things whose nature is to be converted into alimony—for example, she harvests much wine and no bread—yet by selling the wine she can obtain enough bread and wine, then she is obliged to sell. But if the things are not customarily sold for alimony, but are kept in the wife’s possession at her risk, such as linens and sheets, then she is not obliged to sell, but must be maintained from the dowry, just as during the marriage. For where we speak of alimony, we have regard to revenues, as stated in the Digest, Ubi pupillus educari debeat, l. Ius alimentorum, § 1. Skins, however, are not to be sold by one who has them, because they are included under the name of alimony, and therefore she asks in vain for what she already possesses within herself. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the paternal and maternal grandfathers succeed to the grandson.
2. One must prove the acceptance of the inheritance, and in what manner it is proved.
3. Knowledge of the death must be alleged even in the person who is presumed to know.
body: Angelus

† the claim is well-founded, because the maternal grandfather, to whom the dowry ought to revert, has no descendants from his daughter; or, if there were such descendants, they died without having accepted their mother’s inheritance. And Bartolus says that even if there had been heirs, nevertheless the property originating from the maternal grandfather would belong to that maternal grandfather, and not to the paternal one; but it is commonly held that both the paternal and the maternal grandfather succeed equally to the grandchildren, as there in the Authentico *Defuncto*, Codex, *Ad Tertullianam*; and in the inheritance, that the said grandchildren can transmit [their rights] to them, following the gloss in the law *Apud hostes*, *De suis et legitimis haeredibus*. But if the granddaughters did not transmit, only the maternal grandfather would come to recover the dowry which he had given to his daughter, as in the law *Dos a patre*, Codex, *De solutionibus*. However, the father of the children would exclude both grandfathers, if he alone had accepted their inheritance, as in the law *Infanti*, *De iure deliberandi*, fully noted.

† Whether the father of the boys accepted their inheritance or not. Since this is a matter of fact, it must be clear from the acts and the evidence. And because this is a matter of fact, he who alleges that the inheritance was accepted by another must prove it. Which in the present case has not at all been proven by the paternal grandfather in order to exclude the maternal grandfather. For the party pleading is deficient, because he entirely fails to plead the knowledge of the boys' death. E.g., that the mother, knowing of the boys' death, gave clothes for the love of God, etc.

† For it must be alleged, as is fully read and noted in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, in the law *Is potest repudiare*, that there was knowledge of the death, even in the person who is presumed to know. And even assuming that this reasoning does not apply, because the sentence would be included under the article concerning the intention to accept the inheritance, nevertheless the witnesses do not prove this knowledge. Nor is it proved that, after the woman’s death, the husband gave these garments out of love for God; nor that these garments belonged to the woman; nor that they were possessed by her, as clearly appears from the testimonies themselves. And therefore, the management of affairs as an heir (*gestio pro haerede*) is not proved. Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, in the law *Pro haerede*, in the beginning, and in § *Papinianus*. Furthermore, it is not proved that these boys died as infants, from which fact, upon their death, the doctors commonly state that the father cannot accept the maternal inheritance, in the aforementioned law *Si infanti*, and as noted, and in the law *Cum non solum*, in the beginning, *De bonis quae liberis*, by Cynus. Since, therefore, the defendant has not proved those matters which induce acceptance on behalf of the claimant, namely the maternal grandfather, judgment must be given in his favor. And if the maternal grandfather had claimed the whole, things being thus situated, he would have prevailed in the entirety, because the action is not concerning an inheritance, that is, of the grandchildren, but concerning the dowry of the daughter. Law *Finis*, *Communia utriusque iudicii*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a seller, who sold a thing as if it belonged to one person, when it in fact belonged to two, and stipulated for its return after a certain period, may bring an action against the other co-obligor who ratified the contract, so that he may sue on the stipulation and obtain restitution for his share.
2. Whether ratification is divisible.
3. And add [this] in consilium 34.
body: Let it be presupposed

†infaco. He asserts that the guardian did not sell, claiming that he was guardian only for a time of the property which he asserts belonged to two wards; and he stipulated that it be restored after the time. One of the wards has ratified pro rata. The question is whether he can sue pro rata, the other not ratifying, and the time indicating that it was not his intention to buy for a part, nor to bind himself by stipulation in a case in which the contract would not be valid, and he could not be asked for a right in solidum. And it is presupposed that it was for one price. And it seems that yes: because the obligation to restore the thing is divisible by nature and by performance, or by nature and effect, as is common knowledge among all students, in l. stipulationes non diuiduntur, D. de verb. oblig. To the contrary it seems, because this transaction cannot be carried out in part: for this contract made for one price must be ratified in its entirety or rejected in its entirety, otherwise from this contract one cannot sue here or there, de in diem adiecto, quod si uno. Nor can the stipulation to restore be separated into two parts, because from this contract a stipulation was interposed, and it does not stand by itself. And a contract which, by reason of this stipulation, is not valid in part, therefore neither is the stipulation. For this part I advised that the contract, or the stipulation arising therefrom, could not be valid in part and not valid in part: because he would not have contracted, nor promised, for a part, nor could the buyer have received the benefits of the contract: because a part does not bring as much utility with respect to a part as it does with respect to the whole. And a particular ratification could then properly be sued for pro rata, or per capita.

† Someone might say, in the case of a promise, ratification can be divided, as stated in the law *eadem*, on obligations arising from words, in the section *Cato*. Nevertheless, it is true regarding divisible matters, but otherwise regarding indivisible ones. Hence, if I purchase one thing from two managers for one price, it cannot be divided, since it was concluded by one and indivisible consent, which the other party did not contract. Bartolus says in consultation 32, which begins *Angelettus*, that if the contrary were said, one would be compelled against his will to a joint possession, which breeds discord and sometimes arms. See the law *in re communi*, on servitudes. And more is bought in the whole with respect to the whole than a part with respect to a part. See the law *Meuius*, on legacies, book 2. Hence, it must be noted that a lie in the office of guardianship sometimes does not harm the other party after ratification has followed, and then no one is so captious as not to say that ratification suffices, as noted in the law 1, in the beginning, *quod falsum*, on tutors. Nor is there anyone there so captious as not to say that ratification is necessary, and that one fiction applies to the tutor, another to the manager. And whoever does not grasp this, let him look at Bartolus, who explains this in the law *si tutor*, in the title *in quibus causis in integrum restitutio non est necessaria*. But when the lie in the office of guardianship also harms the other contracting party even after ratification, where the administrator’s fraud gives cause to the contract, and the contract is null if it is one of good faith, and ineffective if it is one of strict law. And if fraud is argued from the form of the libel, as is the case here, he is contrary to the libel and hostile to the libel who drafts the libel: spare me, colleague, because if the libel contains a defect in the cause, an exception is not necessary, says Bartolus there. Moreover, such a libel is invalid, since it does not contain in itself the ratification of the contract: for it does not ratify the contract, but tears it up and absorbs it, and he who does not wish to rejoice in the contract seems to repudiate the benefits of the contract. See the law *cum quare*, on the administration of tutors. Nor can one rejoice in part and not in part, because the whole is one structure with its honors. See the law *neminem*, on legacies, book 2. It is also established that the tutor could not sell, as stated in the law *qui neque*, on the things of those under guardianship, nor deliver possession of the wards. And delivery is not presupposed here by the libel, nor in the point on which I was consulted, and therefore the plaintiff suing for restitution is suing for the impossible and for the unjust: because restitution is a restoration to the former state, which is not proposed here, but rather the open contrary: because in the instrument delivery was promised, and the obligation to deliver is presumed to endure unless delivery is proven. See the law *quinquaginta*, on proof. Just as I promise to lend and then demand repayment, I must prove that I gave the money. See the law *qui pecuniam*, on certain actions; and the law 1, on dower secured. Moreover, this mother, acting as guardian, by observing the entire contract, promised ratification under penalty. But here the whole is not ratified, and the penalty is incurred, and for it all the legacies. And know that the little client causes the mother to incur the penalty, and if she ratifies, it is penal for her, because the goods are bound by the name of the penalty, and if this thing were in any way among her own goods, it can be retained for this penalty. Moreover, you demand a thing which, if it was ever yours, you lost by your own act, and therefore I bought it from you, and you do not believe it, therefore wrongly, as the law *Tuae* states. Your reasons are very beautiful and elegant, but they do not apply to the facts. Let the same Lord Collateral either expedite the matter or commit it openly, because we will certainly win, with the Lord Jesus Christ granting it. I, Baldus.

My first conclusion was this: The plaintiff acting on an instrument must act according to the quality of the instrument: so that the effect of the instrument with its modes and times is preserved on both sides. Second conclusion: the formal power of acting on an instrument is according to its form, therefore the instrument is the formal part of the petition. Third conclusion: no one can act on an instrument by rejecting the cause from which the instrument derives its action for him. Fourth conclusion: when by the libel itself it is revealed that the plaintiff is attempting without an action, the libel is inept and contradictory. Fifth conclusion: that if the obligation to deliver the thing sold, even among several joined persons, is divisible. Sixth conclusion: that if the obligation to restore the thing arises, and it is answered that the thing ought first to be delivered: for where there was no delivery, there is no restitution. Seventh conclusion: that the obligation to restore the thing, even if not dependent on the thing being delivered, can be indivisible by the form of the pact and the quality of the thing. Eighth conclusion: that assuming the truth and apparent truth of the guardianship, the plaintiff acting on the ground of being a tutor acts ineptly. Ninth conclusion: that ratification is not valid unless by the ultimate cause of the contract, which can be observed if reconciled on both sides. Tenth and last conclusion: that where mandate is lacking, ratification is necessary, and in such a way that it represents the same mandate. These were the conclusions included in my consultation. You, who marvel, bear a little of my foolishness, and answer briefly in order. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether those who receive from a person paying of their own accord, even without a cause of fear, are said to commit a wrongful act or robbery.
2. Cities which have the right to reclaim from the unworthy.
body: In the first place

† It must be considered that receiving payment from one who pays voluntarily, even on account of fear, is not a wrongful act, because voluntary payment purges every defect, nor is this an acquisition tainted by turpitude, but rather a release. D. de condictione ob turpem causam, l. si ob turpem. And therefore, in this case, the fiscus must remain silent. Secondly

† It must be considered that no land of the Roman Church, unless all fiscal rights were granted to it, has the right to claim back from unworthy persons, but it only has those [rights] which are granted by statutes confirmed by a superior. L. 1, C. de bonis vacantibus; L. 10 and the note in L. Item veniunt, § cum ante, and § ait senatus, D. de petitione hereditatis. And therefore it does not have the gualdum [forest jurisdiction] except by statutory ban. Thirdly, it must be considered that this is not a robbery, because the free will of the giver intervened, and it is made gratuitously, as is expressly noted by the Glossa and Cynus in L. 2, C. quod mea causa, and C. si rector provinciae, L. 1, § impleri autem. Fourthly, it must be considered that the statute regarding "like to like" does not apply here, because where there is not the same reason, there is no similarity. D. de legibus, L. non possunt. Baldus, Tractatus de materia consilii 32, placed above, immediately preceding.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether it appears that one who acts on the basis of a stipulation or a transaction thereby ratifies it.
2. When a contract is conditional, the writ must mention the existence of the condition.
3. A contract cannot be ratified except together with its clauses.
body: In that case, several points are alleged against the plaintiff. First, because the libel does not hold from the fact that restitution is sought, yet it is not stated that the delivery, which was promised to be made, was effected. And thus he improperly seeks restitution without claiming delivery. Second, it is alleged: because the principal contract was a sale, which was not ratified as is required, in the absence of a mandate; for whoever denies a mandate declares that the contract was not valid from the beginning, as in l. qui neque, de procu. and l. iusiurandum, quod ex conuentione, de iureiu.; and therefore the action is brought ineptly, unless a ratification should rehabilitate the contract, whence, absent ratification, the libel does not hold. And although it is sought without a cession, nevertheless the act of the gestor must be ratified, de neg. gest. l. si ego. But if a mandate had preceded, there would be no need for ratification, l. possessio quoque, §. et si possessio, and de procur. l. si curator absente; and I do not know why such an outcry has been made, because, setting aside ratification, the petition is impossible and inept. And thus I have advised, and thus it is true; and Bar. holds this expressly in l. si tutor, C. in quibus causis in inte. resti. non est ne., where it is to be seen. But

† it is to be seen whether one is said to hold as ratified by the very fact that he acts upon the stipulation. On this I have not given counsel, and that ratification ought to be made expressly, or it is tacitly inherent in such acts, if it were possible to be done; but I am moved to say that a contract of sale for a single price cannot be held as ratified unless it is ratified in its entirety, by l. quod si vno, de in diem adiec.; and Bar. gives the reason in consi. 32, which begins Angeletus, and is noted in l. stipulationes non diuidunt; and because one would not have purchased in part, whence a ratification of a part does not suffice in this case. And this is true with respect to the contract of purchase. But there is doubt regarding the contract of stipulation, because the obligation that a thing be restored is divisible. But since that stipulation contained in itself a tacit condition, "if the thing is delivered," and delivery could not be performed in part, therefore the stipulation lapses.

† And because, when a stipulation is conditional, the libel must make mention of the fulfillment of the condition, and here no mention was made of the fulfillment of that tacit condition, the libel appears inept, and the libel cannot be helped by proofs. And if it is said that it is not true that this is a tacit condition, properly speaking, as in l. quaero, §. inter locatorem, ff. loca., I respond that it is equivalent, because an action for restitution does not arise by operation of law without a preceding delivery. But let us grant that the libel would hold notwithstanding this; nevertheless another obstacle stands in the way, because the conclusion of the libel is uncertain: for either he intends to conclude for the restitution of the entire thing, and that is impossible, C. locati, l. si diuisae, si cert. pet. l. si non singuli, de duobus reis, l. reos, §. cum tabulis; or for a virile share according to the number of persons, and then the conclusion does not harmonize, nor does the cause of the conclusion, since he says that it belongs to him through the repudiation by the males. And these words also do not relieve the defect, de verb. ob. l. si mihi, et Titio; and that libel is inept from which, based on the allegations in the libel, it appears that one proceeds unjustly or without an action, as noted by Inn. in c. 1, de offic. vica. But let us grant that the libel would hold; nevertheless the plaintiff ought entirely to succumb for several reasons. And first, because delivery of possession has not been proven, nor indeed that these ladies ever possessed, and thus neither could they deliver; and let the acts speak on this point. Nor does it follow: if the father was able, therefore the son is, l. cum miles, quibus ex cau. ma. And if it is said to have been proven that the buyer held possession, and therefore he seems to have held from the title of purchase, as in l. minus instructus and l. quaedam mulier, it is answered by l. duo fratres, de ac. hęre., and l. non hoc, vnde legitimi; and because this is true when the contract is not void, as it was here, especially then because she was not a guardian. Likewise, that is true when delivery could take place according to the form and nature of the contract, and in the persons of the contracting parties, which is not the case here, for a particular delivery does not apply here; let the acts speak also on this point. The second reason is because there was a promise of ratification by those males, who did not ratify, but rather tacitly acted so that it could not be ratified. The libel is true, and thus the penalty has been incurred, and these things are bound for the penalty. And I argue thus: either the women ratify, and then the things are bound; or they do not ratify, and then, as has often been said, the libel does not hold.

† And a contract cannot be ratified except with its clauses, ff. de l. Gayus man. non ob. l. Pomp. and l. cum interdictae, where the act is approved and not the qualification, because it is one thing to say the qualification, another the cause and clauses; for if I reject something in which the strength of the contract resides, I cannot approve the remainder, and thus the allegation is not to the point. Likewise, it is no objection that even under the common law an action is acquired from the stipulation of a thing that remains one's own, because this is true if he to whom the stipulation is made ratifies it, C. si cert. pet. l. si absente, de admi. tuto. l. cum quaeritur, and it is also clear that the thing is his own. If therefore he ratifies, the thing is perpetually bound and can be retained as a pledge. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution made by the word "succeed" is direct, so that by means of it the mother is excluded.
2. Whether a substitution made to an underage son, in case of doubt, is to be interpreted as direct or as a fideicommissary substitution.
body: The father made his underage son his heir and instituted a substitution in the following form. Furthermore, the said testator ordered and willed that if Frances, his daughter, should die without legitimate sons and daughters descending from her own body, then from the goods of the inheritance of the said Frances, his daughter, ten pounds of denarii should be given and distributed by his said commissioners for the building and church of Saint John of the Cross. As for the remaining goods, after the death of the said Frances, his daughter, he ordered and expressly willed that John, his brother, and Gasutia, his sister, should succeed, and he substituted them and made them universal heirs after the death of the said Frances, his daughter. After the death of the father, the said Frances died within the age of pupillarity. Now there is a dispute between the substitutes and the mother of the said Frances, for they claim that they ought to succeed in the entirety, excluding the mother; but the latter says that she ought to succeed to the legitime and the trebellianic portion. The question now arises, what is the law, having regard to the will and the foregoing narrative? On the point and question aforesaid, it seems to be said briefly and without doubt that

† that the said substitutes ought to succeed in their entirety, the mother being entirely excluded: for the said substitution is a direct pupillary substitution, as is noted in l. Centurio, ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, and in l. precibus, C. de impuberibus, and in ca. si pater, extra de testibus, lib. 6, where the case is expressly stated today, and where the case falls under the law, and there is no question, as in l. ancillae, C. de furtis; therefore the mother is excluded, as is proven by the aforementioned authorities.

And not only where the direct substitution is expressed and clear, as in the aforementioned case; but even where it is doubtful, it is judged and assumed to be direct. For in doubt, by reason of natural affection, the father is presumed to wish to provide for his son, not to burden him, as in D. de usur. l. in fideicomm. §. cum Pollidius; and D. de inoff. test. l. filius matre; and l. si quis in suo; and D. de cur. fur. l. si furioso puberi. For an outsider does not wish [to burden] another outsider; therefore, much more so does a father [wish to provide for] his son, as in l. quidam cum filium, D. de haer. inst. Since, therefore, the pupillary substitution is favorable, and the fideicommissary substitution is a burden, as noted in l. ex tribus, C. de inof. testa., it is presumed that the father provided for his underage daughter by substituting pupillarily, and did not burden her by substituting fideicommissarily. This is confirmed by the said c. si pater, where it is openly stated that a doubtful substitution is interpreted as direct, if it agrees with the words and the persons; but here there is no doubt regarding the persons, and the words allow it; therefore, and c. ar., D. de leg. 1, l. ab omnibus, in princ., accedes to this. C. de haer. inst. l. si; and the glossa ordinaria in l. verbis civilibus, D. de vul. et pupi., which states that a doubtful substitution received the interpretation of direct. To the same effect is the fact that in wills a fuller interpretation is made, as in D. de re iur. l. in testamentis; but the pupillary substitution is fuller than the fideicommissary, as in D. de vul. subs. l. cohaeredi, §. cum filiae, ver. nec fideicom. And this opinion is precisely held by the glossa in Inst. de pupil. sub. §. qua ratione; and Cynus. Thus he advised, as reported in l. precibus; and Ioannes Andreas holds this, as in c. si pater, in nouella. And if this is so in a doubtful case, how much more in our case should it be judged direct, where the words are merely direct. It is pertinent that the disposition and the testator’s will are equivalent, as in Auth. de nup. §. disponant, coll. 4. But the law in doubt must be drawn to the more necessary case, as in l. 1, §. quid ergo, D. de vend. inst.; l. quod Labeo, ad car. Therefore, the same applies to the testator’s disposition. But it is certain that direct substitution is more necessary than fideicommissary, since by the direct [substitution] provision is made so that the son does not die intestate; for he is drawn to the goods of the father and the son; whereas by the fideicommissum provision is made only for the testator, since only his goods come into play, as in the said §. cum filio. Therefore, this substitution should be understood to have been made by the father as direct, not fideicommissary, in case of doubt.

Moreover, I weigh the words of the said substitution, when the testator said, “and he made the said Franceschina and others heirs,” etc., and did not say, “he made heirs for himself.” And this cannot be, except from a direct pupillary [substitution]; and this is sufficiently clear in the present case. And it is proved by those things which are noted in the said laws.

It does not avail that some wished to say the said substitution was fideicommissary, on account of the addition of those words, “without children,” which seem to draw the said substitution to puberty and make it fideicommissary, by l. credendum, §. hoc autem, D. qui pot. in tut.; and by the glossa in l. precib. For, as said above, the case is to the contrary, in the said c. si pater; and in the said l. Centurio, upon correct examination; and the glossa in Inst. de pu. sub. §. extraneo. And the condition “without children,” etc., operates nothing, nor alters the effect and nature of the said substitution, since it is always inherent, tacitly even if not expressed, as in l. cum acutissimi, C. de fideicom.; and l. cum auus, D. de condi. et dem. Nor does the said l. credendum avail, because there the words were merely oblique, whence it is always fideicommissary. But in our question the words are merely direct, and to say otherwise would be contrary to the testator’s intent and words.

From which I conclude, as said above, that the substitutes are to be admitted in whole, the mother being excluded. And this opinion is held by Dynus, Bartolus, Raynerius de Forli, and Franciscus de Pignis, and commonly by all doctors. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Substitution is conditional when the institution of an heir or the restitution of an inheritance is conditional.
body: All

† Substitution is either a conditional institution or a conditional restitution. If it is an institution, it is direct, according to the Falcidian law, *l. in ratione*, § *filio*. If, however, it is a restitution, it is oblique, that is, a fideicommissum, C. *de institutionibus et substitutionibus*, *l. generaliter*. When there is doubt whether it is a conditional institution or rather a conditional restitution, the following method is given for determining this. For when the wording is such that it has no other nature than a direct one, as the word “let him be heir,” then it is direct. If, however, it has no other nature than that of a fideicommissum, as the word “restore,” it is oblique. If it has an indifferent nature, it is said to be common, adapted to both. Nevertheless, I admit that if the condition under which it was made does not fall except in the form of a direct substitution, it is direct; but if the conditions are such that they cannot be attributed to a direct substitution, as the condition “if he should die without children,” the substitution is presumed to be fideicommissary, as noted in *l. precibus*. From this theoretical principle appears the solution to the question: for since the principal word is direct, because the testator said “he makes universal heirs,” and the word “makes” is the same as saying “institutes,” the said substitution is most direct, and in the case of a girl dying in pupillary age, the substitute excludes the mother, as in c. *si pater*, *de testamento*, lib. 6, in the word “restoring the heirs”; hence the mother succeeds in no way, which is a case according to the letter. D. *de secundis tabulis*, *l. si ita*, § *qui filio*. It is a case in c. *centenario*, and this is noted by all learned doctors in *l. precibus*, on the understanding of the great gloss in the verse *si non ita*, and it is the gloss in *l. 1*, D. *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a woman, who has ceded her rights for the price of her mother’s dowry, or who has renounced her father’s succession, may succeed to her father in all his goods by will; and whether the price of said cession is subject to collation. Nos. 3 and 4.
2. What effect is produced by this clause inserted in the cession, namely, “and by any other right whatsoever.”
3. Whether daughters wishing to succeed their father by will are bound to preserve their dowries.
4. Whether a daughter to whom a legacy has been made, if she is married, is considered to be endowed.
5. Whether the mother succeeds to her deceased daughter in pupillary age, or whether the sisters succeed, given the existence of a fideicommissary substitution.
6. Whether a father may burden his daughter with her mother’s dowry.
body: Since a matter more thoroughly understood is better resolved, the following grounds, fortified by legal reasoning, are appended after a brief statement of the facts, which seem to favor the below-named Benevenuta. Therefore, it must first be known that a certain person named Matthew, having two daughters from his first wife, named Lady Catherine, one of whom was called Benevenuta, who, after the death of her mother, remaining with her father and with his consent, having taken an oath and confessing herself to be over twelve years of age, ceded to the servant of Lord Angel, receiving on behalf of the said Lord Angel, all rights which she had, both present and future, in the goods and dowry of the said her mother, and in the goods of the said her father on account of the said her dowry, and by any other right, title, or cause, for the price of 165 florins, which she says she received at that time in the instrument. And on the following day, Cecharellus Zutii confessed to having received from the said Matthew for the dowry of the said Benevenuta, then future wife of the said Cecharellus, 200 florins. The other daughter born from the said first marriage is called Mascetta. Finally, while the said Matthew was still alive, the said marriage was consummated between the said Cecharellus and Benevenuta. However, this Matthew had already taken another wife, named Lady Maria, from whom he had two daughters during his lifetime, namely Bucciatella and Francisca. And after the death of the said husband, the said second wife gave birth to another daughter named Banna. But this Matthew, before he died, made a will, in which he left to Lady Mascetta, the maternal dowry being calculated, 250 florins; he also left to the said Bucciatella and Francisca 250 florins each, in which he instituted the said Mascetta, Bucciatella, and Francisca, and his said wife as heirs for their dowries. Furthermore, he bequeathed to his said wife 100 florins in addition to the dowry. Furthermore, he left to his daughter to be born 200 florins for her dowry. But if a male child were born, he made him universal heir, and he instituted all his daughters, namely the said Benevenuta, provided she received her dowry, and the aforesaid Mascetta, Bucciatella, and Francisca, and his said wife, and his said daughter to be born, for equal shares: and both in the said codicils and in the inheritance he made substitutions, but separately. It must be noted, however, that the aforesaid daughter to be born is none other than she who was called above Vanna, and no male child was born. And after this, the said Matthew died, and upon his death, the said Bucciatella, Mascetta, and Vanna were married with all the rights which they had in the paternal goods. And the said Francisca died in pupillary age, and the said second wife remarried, whence among the aforesaid heirs, on account of the aforesaid premises, several matters are brought into doubt. For the first doubt is,

Whether the statements of Benevenuta will be repelled, so that she may not succeed to her aforementioned father by the said testament, even if she brings in her dowry, notwithstanding the said cession. And because the opposing party says that she was moved to this, perhaps it is inquired into. § Si venditor, D. de edilitio edicto, where it is said that when actions are remitted, etc. But to this it is answered that this could apply when Benevenuta herself wished to return to the maternal goods, from which she had thus abdicated by ceding them; but not to the paternal goods, unless she had made a renunciation in his goods, according to c. 2, De pactis, lib. 6. But Benevenuta did not wish this simply and without legitimate cause, but through the testament of her said father. It should be known that the said chapter applies only because such a daughter, thus renouncing, wishes to succeed intestate. But this daughter wishes to succeed by testament, by the express will of her said father; therefore, if she had thus renounced, she would not be excluded; otherwise, the freedom of testating would be taken away from her father, which is disapproved by law, as in C. De pactis, l. Pactum, quod dotali, and there noted in the gloss. And Bartolus holds this opinion on l. Si, C. eodem. And if it is well observed, this cession does not contain such a renunciation, nor can it be said that the said cession extends to paternal goods, which, since it was made specifically and in detail concerning the maternal dowry, not in paternal goods on account of the said dowry, the general words that follow there...

† and by any other right, without title, the cause did not extend the cession itself, but it is restricted to those things which were specially ceded, and to their accessories, and not to the succession of the paternal goods, as in C. de transact. l. si decreta, and there noted by the doctors, and in l. si sub prętextu, eod. tit. And thus it is understood to have been made concerning the maternal dowry by reason of the said dowry, from the fact that the said cession extended to all things; nevertheless, because the parties confess that the said Matthew succeeded in all the goods of the said lord Angelo, for whom the cession was received, the opposing party vainly clings to the said cession, since the same Matthew instituted the said daughter with others: for that which the lord wished to do, he could do, as in l. 1. de sac. san. eccl., from which it is concluded that, notwithstanding the said cession, he succeeds to his father by the aforesaid testament.

Secondly, it is brought into doubt whether, in the collation to be made by the said Benevenuta, the price of the said cession should be brought into collation. And it is alleged that it should not, because only profecticia are brought into collation, not adventicia, as in C. de collationibus, l. si. But the said price did not come from the father, nor on his account, but in consideration of the mother's dowry: therefore it does not come to be brought into collation: for by no law can it be said that the said price came from the father, because it did not come out of his goods, as the instrument attests, nor did it come to the daughter on his account, therefore the opposing party is not to be heard, as in l. illam, C. de collationibus. Thirdly, it is brought into doubt,

Whether the dowry of 200 florins given to the future husband of the aforementioned Benevenuta is to be presumed to have been given precisely and in its entirety by the father, or whether the aforementioned 165 florins, which were the price of the said assignment, are presumed to have been converted into it. And regarding this, it is alleged that, although at first sight it seems that one should say that the said dowry was given without the said conversion, as in l. si, C. de dotis promissis, nevertheless the opposite seems to be held due to the strong presumptions occurring: the first is the shortness of time, because the said price was received on one day, and on the immediately following day the dowry was paid, and from the shortness of time a great presumption is drawn, as in l. si uentri, §. si, de priuilegiis creditorum; this is supported by what is noted by Doctor Bartolus in l. postcontractus, de donationibus. The second is the excessive reverence which the girl holds for her parent. For it is presumed that the father received from his daughter the price of the assignment in order to give it as her dowry. This is supported by l. 1, §. quae honorandae, ff. quarum rerum actio non datur. The third is that it is not to be presumed that the father intended that the said daughter should have so much more, since in his testament, when he left a legacy to another daughter, the sister of the said Benevenuta, he stated that the maternal dowry is to be counted. It seems without doubt to be held that, with the aforementioned presumptions concurring, the said price of the assignment is presumed to have been converted into the payment of the dowry. Fourthly, it is brought into doubt,

Whether the remaining daughters, wishing to renounce the said testament in favor of their father, are bound to collate their dowries, just as the said Benevenuta wishes to collate hers. It is alleged on behalf of the said Benevenuta that they are so bound, because since the said daughters succeed universally to their father, they will collate the legacy of the dowry, as stated in C. de collationibus, l. filiam cum fratribus. The opposing argument from l. a patre, eodem titulo, where it is said that a dowry left by will is not collated, does not apply, because that law speaks of a case where the daughter has a capital legacy of the dowry under another law, l. 1, and does not succeed to anything else from her father; but here the said daughters do succeed, hence the legacy of the dowry must be collated, as stated in the aforementioned l. filiam. And there is a glossa stating that another thing, which is not subject to collation, is collated to avoid inequality among the daughters, as noted in the glossa in l. illud, C. eodem titulo. It would be a great injustice if one daughter alone bore the burden of the testament to the benefit of the others, since there is no reason for predilection. Therefore, so that envy may not arise among siblings, parity must be maintained in collation, as stated in the aforementioned laws, and according to these principles l. filiae, eodem titulo, should be understood. Furthermore, a legacy might perhaps be said not to be collated when it remains within the limits of the legacy itself; but in our case, as is set forth in the present case, the said dowry legacies are due after the said daughters, while living, have been married; for the legacy of the dowry is purified with respect to all its effects upon the subsequent marriage, as when the day of the legacy has arrived, l. quod pupillae. Furthermore, if it were said that such a legacy of a dowry does not acquire the name and nature of a dowry unless marriage follows, by the same reasoning it would have to be said that the 200 florins paid to the husband of the said Benevenuta before he was her husband are not considered a dowry after the marriage has taken place; because the cause would be the same in both cases. Namely, because at the time appointed or designated for the dowry in the contract or in the testament, there was no marriage, taking the reason that a dowry cannot exist without marriage; where the reason is the same, we must follow the same law, as in l. illud ad legem Aquiliam. Hence, the father, by saying that Benevenuta collates the dowry, would have spoken in vain. And therefore, just as the others wish to say that they are not bound to collation, so could she say. But in truth, all are said to collate, because the subsequent marriage makes everything promised or given by legacy for a dowry to be considered as a dowry. In support of this is the matter of the law Titio centum, ver. sed cum ante nup., ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. Furthermore, does not the glossa in l. mulier, ff. de iure dotium, say that all the goods of a woman are presumed in doubt to be given as a dowry when the woman marries? Certainly so. Is it not the common and general usage of speech, and especially in the territory of Rieti, that even a virgin and any woman who does not yet have a husband is said to have a large or small dowry, according to the extent of her patrimony? Certainly so, because often the Lord Bartolus himself says in the aforementioned l. Titio that, according to the statutes of certain territories, daughters to whom something has been left by will are called "dowered"; the statute of Rieti, which is transmitted under the rubric de successionibus ab intestato, calls such daughters "dowered" to whom something has been left by will in the name of a dowry. Without doubt, therefore, it must be held that, since the father did not expressly forbid collation in the persons of the daughters, it must be made entirely, as in auth. ex testamento, C. eodem titulo. And such collation must be made with fruits and all increase, in order to maintain equality. And this collation, as has been concluded, is to be made among the daughters of the testator, excluding the said mother as coheir; because collation is not made to her, as noted in l. si emancipati, C. eodem titulo, and l. 1, C. de iudiciis utriusque iuris. And it suffices that in the division the said Benevenuta receives less by the amount of her dowry, so that it does not benefit her to repay the money into the common fund, as stated in the glossa in l. filiae, although cited above. And just as the dowry is collated, so must everything that has been received from the father's goods be collated, as stated in the aforementioned auth. ex testamento. The fifth doubt arises,

† How the surviving daughters and the mother succeeded the aforementioned Francisca, who died in pupillary age. It is alleged that, although at first sight it would seem to be said that, as regards the legitime and the Trebellian portion, the said Bucciarella and Vanna, her sisters related on the father’s side, succeeded, taking the substitution made as fideicommissary—because when the said Benevenuta was then of age and the others were minors, otherwise the substitution is understood to apply to that case in which it may equally comprehend all, and thus by virtue of the fideicommissum, as in l. 1, C. de militum testationibus, and l. quamvis, C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus—nevertheless, these do not apply in our case, for the said laws are understood where the substitution was made to all by one common word, e.g., “I substitute you to one another.” But in our case, in the first and last substitution, the testator spoke by distributed words, namely by saying, “and if one of them,” etc. The nature of the distributive is to attribute the disposition to each in solidum, and not simultaneously, as noted in l. hoc articulo, ff. de hereditate instituenda, and by those things which are noted there by Bartolus. Hence, the said substitution is to be taken in a disjunctive manner in the person of each, i.e., in the person of the adult as fideicommissary, and in the person of the minor as expressly pupillary. And with this division, it can also be understood that not even Bartolus himself in l. Lucius, ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, where he records that the same is held by the concise authorities, Master Giuliano da Cuneo and Master Raymond de Foris. Therefore, it is said that all the surviving daughters, substituted without preference, succeed together to the said Francisca, who died in pupillary age, to the exclusion of the mother, because she passed to second marriage without having requested a tutor. Moreover, within the year, neither did she accept the guardianship, nor administer it, nor renounce it, so as to make room for another legitimate or appointed guardian, as in l. sciant, C. de legitimis haeredibus, as fully noted by Bartolus in l. 1, ff. qui petere tutelam possunt. And if it is said by the mother that she was the nurse, nevertheless she did not make an inventory, and did not render an account before marrying a second time, and therefore she is deprived of all benefit of succession, as in l. omnem, C. ad Tertullianum. And insofar as succession takes place to the said Francisca, collation ceases, because the father, when he substituted to her, Bucciarella, and Mascetta, made no mention of collation, nor does the law provide that collation be made in fraternal succession, but only that the said collation be made in paternal succession. Sixthly, a doubt arises,

Whether the said testator Matthew, by bequeathing to the said Mascetta 250 florins of the common currency as her maternal dowry, could burden her with respect to her mother’s dowry. To this it is said: yes. The gloss is notable in the Institutes, *De singulis rebus per fideicommissum relictis*, and it is noted in the law *In ea*. And it is now useless to doubt this, because it is proposed in common points that the testament has been approved by her and by others. Therefore, it can be concluded in law that, since the said Matthew succeeded the said Angelo, in whose place the aforementioned cession was received, and the said Mascetta accepted the paternal testament, the dowry of her mother, just like the other goods of the said Matthew, come into the said succession to be adjudicated and divided, as has been said; so that the said mother derives no benefit from the said succession, and collation be made by all, lest envy be drawn among the daughters, but equality be preserved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A daughter is not excluded from testamentary succession by a renunciation of the right to succeed, even if accompanied by an oath.
2. The mother’s inheritance should not be collated when the father’s inheritance is at issue.
3. In case of doubt, it is presumed that the father provides a dowry from his own property, not from the wife’s patrimony.
4. When a dowry is subject to collation.
5. Whether a substitution made by the word “if he dies” is direct and excludes the mother, and whether one made by the word “succeed” operates differently.
6. Whether one may burden the mother’s dowry beyond the legitime.
body: Sper

† On the first point, it must be said that Benevenuta is not excluded from testamentary succession by the aforementioned cession, even though it was made with an oath; and this for several reasons. The first reason is that, although one may renounce a future succession with an oath according to canon law, as in c. *Quamvis*, de pace, lib. 6, nevertheless the right to a future succession cannot be ceded unless the person whose succession is at issue consents and persists in that consent, even with an oath; for an oath is contrary to good morals, because it induces a vow to seek death. C. de pace, l. *Si*; and see Bartolus, de verbis oblig., l. *Stipulatio hoc modo*. The second reason is that it does not appear that such a cession or renunciation of this right was contemplated; hence Spezzano says, de emptione et venditione, § 1, vers. *Pone, filius*, that legacies are not taken away by a renunciation inter vivos. The third reason is the form of the words of the contract, for the words state that she ceded to him all the right which she has and which belongs to her, and which may belong to her in the future, in the goods and over the goods of Matthew. These words signify all the right which belonged to her while Matthew was alive, not that which would belong to her after his death, as in ff. de negotiis gestis, l. 3, § *Haec verba*. The fourth reason is that the father does not appear to have consented, because he could not make a will, nor could he impose a law upon himself in this regard, as in the aforementioned l. *Si* and l. 1, de sacrosancta ecclesia, cum similibus. The fifth reason is that this daughter also does not appear to have contemplated that which would render her unworthy of succession. ff. de his qui ut indigni, l. 2, § *Si*; de donationibus, l. *Quidam in iure*, § *Si*. The sixth reason is that those words, "may belong in the future," are understood from a cause existing in the present, as noted by Bartolus, de verbis obligationum, l. *Qui Romae*, § *Si*, in the sixth and seventh questions. The seventh reason is that the word "hopes" is understood as referring to a legitimate hope, not to a blameworthy one. ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. *Cum ita legatum*, in principio. Finally, in support of this, the glossa in C. de pace, l. 1, in the third opposition, and this is the truth. Regarding the second pact, it must be said that

† Where the succession of the father is discussed, the succession of the mother, or the maternal dowry, ought not to be brought into account; for these are distinct inheritances and have nothing in common. And this is true, unless the father has imposed this burden in his will; for even beyond the legitime it is valid, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius Titius, in principio. Let us see whether, from the words of the testament, Benevenuta is bound to bring into account the dowry of her mother. The words of the testament state: “provided that the said Benevenuta is bound to bring into account the dowry of her mother.” Is the mother’s dowry therefore called the daughter’s dowry? For it was acquired by the daughter through the succession of the mother, and in common usage we call the patrimony of a girl her dowry. But the truth is that this peculium, whether paraphernal, is separate from her dowry. D. de donationibus, l. donationes in concubinam, § species. Therefore, the term “her dowry” includes the sum given to her by the father in respect of the mother; and thus the maternal patrimony need not be brought into account. And this concludes the second point. Regarding the third point, what is alleged is plausible, yet not conclusive; hence it must be said,

† that the father is presumed in doubt to have provided the dowry from his own property, not from the wife’s patrimony. C. de dotis promissione, l. si. And therefore Benevenuta must exercise her right of preemption over the paternal assets for the price derived from the said sale, if it is proven that it came to the father. Regarding the fourth point, it must be said,

† that prelegated dowries are to be received, not collated: and therefore the sisters of Benevento are not bound to collate the dowries prelegated to them, because the testator’s will must be observed in the division and collation; but if the testator had given the dowries inter vivos, and not prelegated them, they ought to be collated to the brothers according to the form of the last law of the Code, "Common to both laws." There are therefore three cases: sometimes the dowry is given, not prelegated; sometimes prelegated, not given. In the first case it is collated; in the second and third it is not. Digest, "On the action for the division of an inheritance," law Pomponius. Concerning the fifth point, it must be said,

† For when the substitution states, "when such one dies," and the ward has died, the mother is excluded: because the word "dies" is principally a direct term; since death is the immediate and final cause, the direct term signifies a direct succession, although it may sometimes be oblique through the father, as in cap. 1, de testamento, lib. 6. Therefore, since nothing else is required but death, and restitution of the inheritance is not required, the mother is excluded, as in l. precibus, C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus. And this is the truth with regard to the substitution of the first part of the will. But we are not in that first part, nor in the last substitution of the first part of the will, but in the last substitution. And the words say, "and if either of them shall die without children, the survivor shall succeed, and in the aforesaid inheritance." And some say that this substitution is reciprocal, and thus, since certain ones are of age, it cannot contain a pupillary substitution; therefore, succession is intestate according to the form of Auth. defuncto, and in Auth. post fratres. Others say that it is a fideicommissary substitution, because the condition of children does not fall in a pupillary substitution, but in a fideicommissary one, as noted in l. precibus with its material. And thus also succession is intestate: and so it is commonly held. However, because those who are joined to the nearest succeed, they hold the same nature; all these, because the first clause is direct, we consider direct. d. c. si pater, insofar as they agree with persons distinguished in the substitution, as prudently alleged by those words, "the aforesaid inheritance." Since he said, "in the right of direct inheritance to be taken," and afterwards added, "aforesaid": because the word "aforesaid" makes a relation and repetition, as it seems to me. To the last point

It was answered that above the legitime, the father may be burdened by a dowry stipulated to the mother; but in the legitime, no burden or any diminution may be imposed, as is stated in the Digest, title *De solutione matrimonii*, law *Si cum dotem*, section *Si pater*; and in the Digest, title *Ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, law *Lucius*, section *Maritus*.
