This is also held by Dynus in the Code, title *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Quoniam in prioribus*, and law *Sancti*. However, in the fourth part of the debt due by right of institution, he speaks. Digest, title *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Si debitor*. This is the truth. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the first will, in which an outsider is instituted as heir, is revoked by a second will that is less perfect and less solemn, in which those who would succeed intestate are instituted.
2. Whether a person related to, or closely connected with, the instituted heir may serve as a witness in the will. Likewise, what is the rule regarding a brother? Likewise, what is the rule regarding a woman?
body: The fact, concerning which counsel is sought, is as follows: Lord John Gentile of Todi made his will, in which, among other things, he instituted as his universal heir a certain person who would not have succeeded to him intestate; and he did not institute Francis, son of Giliolo Gilio, and Raynerius, son of Opposus Gilio, who would have succeeded to him intestate. Finally, after ten years had elapsed, he manifested his contrary will. And he said in the presence of five witnesses, three of whom were male and two female, that he wished to institute the aforementioned Francis and Raynerius as his heirs, and that he wished the will hitherto made by him not to be valid or to have effect. And he began to make another will, which he did not complete due to some impediment occurring, and he died, with the aforementioned Francis and Raynerius, who would succeed him intestate, still living. And the one whom he had instituted as his heir in the said will was also still living. It is true that one of the said five witnesses was the spurious son of the aforementioned Giliolo Gilio, and is the natural brother, although spurious, of the aforementioned Francis; nevertheless, it is now twenty years and more since they did not cohabit together.

† Now it is asked whether the aforementioned testament of the said John is valid in law or void, both on account of the said contrary will and on account of the lapse of ten years. And who are those who come to the succession of the said Lord John by right. Concerning which I say briefly that the said testament was and is void by the law itself, both on account of the manifestation of the said contrary will and on account of the passage of ten years. This is proved by the text in l. sancimus, and there also by the gloss and the doctors, C. de testamento instituendis, qui modis testamenta infirmantur, §. ex eo, and there noted around the beginning, the great gloss, concerning which fully by Bartolus in l. si iuste, ff. de legatis 3. For three witnesses suffice to prove the said contrary will, as noted in the aforementioned l. sancimus. Let the law hac consultissima, §. si quis autem, C. de testibus, be added, where it appears that a testament made in law, in which one is instituted who would not come intestate, is broken by an imperfect testament, in which those who come intestate appear to be instituted, concerning which fully by Bartolus in l. si is qui, ff. de testibus. But as it appears in the point in the aforementioned testament, one was instituted who did not come to the said Lord John intestate; and finally he declared that he wished the aforementioned Francis and Raynald to be his heirs, who succeeded him intestate, wherefore, etc.

† Nor does it matter that, as proposed above in the point, one of the said witnesses is the natural brother of the said Francis, even if he is illegitimate: for I say, according to the true opinion of the glossators and doctors, that not only an illegitimate brother, but also a legitimate brother, is admitted to testify for his brother in a civil case, unless he is repelled on account of domesticity, or because both are under the paternal power, according to the note by the gloss and Bartolus in *l. parentes*, Cod. de testibus, and Dig. eod. *l. 1*, § 1; or unless he is repelled on account of excessively intense friendship and goodwill, which is left to the discretion of the judge. On this matter, see also the note in the title *de testibus*, § 1, under the heading *sed nunquid frater*. Moreover

† To prove the aforementioned contrary will, there are, in addition to three male witnesses, two other female witnesses, whom I believe were admitted to prove said contrary will. For since the edict concerning witnesses is prohibitory, as stated in l. 1, ff. de testibus, all those are admitted to give testimony who are not expressly prohibited. But to prove said contrary will, it is not found expressly prohibited that a woman should not be admitted to testify; therefore, and so forth. For all things are permitted which are not found to be prohibited, as stated in l. 1, § 1, ff. de testibus; and l. necnon, § quod eis, ff. ex quibus causis maiores; and l. ab ea, ff. de probationibus; and l. multi, § cum quaeritur, ff. de procuratoribus, together with similar authorities. For a woman is only prohibited from testifying in wills according to the civil laws. l. qui testamento, § mulier, ff. de testamentis; and in the Institutes, ibid., § testes, and there by the gloss, on which see fully in the Speculum, de testibus, § 1, vers. item quod est, with the following versicles. These things being premised, it appears evident that the aforementioned Francis and Raynald, as being nearer in degree, come to the intestate succession of the aforementioned Lord John, to the exclusion of the aforementioned substitute in the above-mentioned will. Which is proved by l. secunda, § haereditas, ff. de suis et legitimis heredibus; and in the body of the Authenticae, de haereditate ab intestato venientibus, § si vero neque; and l. sive ingenua, at the end, ff. ad Tertullianum, together with similar authorities. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Another opinion on the same subject matter.
body: it was most wisely advised

† Three male witnesses, duly summoned to prove the aforementioned revocation, are sufficient, presupposing the passage of ten years, as stated in the cited law *Scimus*. And if any of the witnesses were in some way suspect, that suspicion can be removed by the aid of the testimony of women, just as if someone were to say that a witness should not be believed because he is an enemy. For friendship could be proved to the contrary by women, as shown in D. de edendo, l. *Si quis ex argentariis*, § 1. Nevertheless, in this case there is doubt, because it seems to refer to whether the testator revokes the first will simply wishing to die intestate; and then, if he could not make a will, the aforementioned revocatory clause seems to have no effect, as stated in D. de legatis 3, l. *Si iure*; and D. de testamento ex causa, l. *Fideicommissum*, § 1; and D. de testamento, l. *Si is qui*; and noted in C. de testamento, l. *Iubemus*; D. de administratione legatorum, l. *Ex parte*; D. de testamento militis, l. *Militis codicillis*, § *Veteranus*; and D. de testamento, l. *Lucius*. For the reason why he wished the first will not to be valid was that he wished the second to be valid; and when the cause ceases, etc., as in D. de his quae in testamento delentur, l. *Cancellaverat*; and D. de hereditate instituenda, l. *Si*. And if the first will had a derogatory clause regarding future wills, then there would be even greater doubt, as in D. de legatis 3, l. *Si quis in principio testamenti*; and noted in C. de testamento, auth. *Hoc inter liberos*. But certainly it cannot be denied that here there is the passage of ten years and a contrary will; therefore the first will is broken, because l. *Sancimus* requires only these two things. And similarly I say regarding a clause cancelling and invalidating: if the passage of ten years is assumed, the aforementioned clause is valid, even if the second will is not valid; otherwise, if ten years have not elapsed. And thus Bartolus is to be understood in l. *Si iure*. And although this passage is doubtful, it is not safe to interpret l. *Sancimus* otherwise than according to its plain meaning, namely, that the testator’s repentance, together with the passage of ten years, immediately revokes the first will, even if no one enters upon the inheritance, because the testator’s repentance requires no acceptance of the inheritance, since it produces its effect during the testator’s lifetime; which is contrary to Bartolus in the said l. *Si iure*. And these things are true, unless a derogatory clause appended to the first will shows that the first intention persists, as fully noted by Dynus and others in the said l. *Si quis in principio testamenti*. And this is a notable and useful matter for § *Si quis* in l. *Hac consultissima*. I say nothing, because there the second will was consummated, although not solemnized, and therefore the discussion of five witnesses does not apply here. Moreover, there must be five males, not females. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether that which is sought arises from a pupillary substitution in a fideicommissum.
body: Plora. et Nesutia

† They ought to have, in the first place, four hundred pounds, each of them. Moreover, they ought to have two hundred pounds for each, if satisfaction has not been made to them; and this because the will so states. D. de legatis 1, l. plane. Moreover, since they succeed intestate to their brother Francis, they ought to have the legitima and the Trebellianic portion in the person of Francis, and also the legitima and the Trebellianic portion of the speech, as in c. Rayn. et Raynal. de testibus. And according to some, the whole portion of John, because they say that what is taken from the pupillary substitution does not come from the fideicommissum; but according to others, it comes into the fideicommissum, and only the Trebellianic portion is deducted, as if the brother were requested by the brother. D. ad Trebellianum, l. ita tamen, §. qui suspectam. But according to others, two fourths are deducted, as if the minor were requested by the brother after his death, and the brothers to restore their portion, as is touched upon in D. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. ex tribus; D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, §. cum filiae. Because the fideicommissum begins from the heir of the minor brother, as in C. ut actio ab heredibus, et contra heredes, l. 1. And this opinion is commonly held, as if two substitutions were made to the minor: one pupillary, the other fideicommissary, because the father burdened all after the death of all. The matter is subtle, and there are various opinions, and much can be said for and against; nevertheless, I hold thus. Therefore, the legitima and the Trebellianic portion in the person of the brothers are due to the said sisters, but the remainder from the Trebellianic portion is to be restored. The cession, which is in question, was made before the death of Francis; and therefore the rights which are sought after the death of Francis do not come into the cession. D. de verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romae, §. duo fratres. I, Baldus. Defends his above counsel. Defends a certain counsel of his, and reproves those who reproved him.

Some are surprised, and it has seemed to them that this opinion is not good. And they allege childish matters, which those who are first-year students know: and they seem to philosophize, and they exult in error. Say then, I ask you, O critic, if the true guardian acts, and she herself were to bring a direct action in her own name, as in l. Cum quaeritur, De administratione tutorum, and alleged in her bill her own falsehood, would the bill proceed? But if she herself did not act, but he acted to whom the exercise of direct actions had been entrusted, even for his own benefit, would he be heard upon allegation of falsehood? I think no one doubts this point, about which you do not doubt, but you speak contrary to the truth of the law, and you rashly exult in this contradiction. Consider that this statute does not provide for anything other than the exercise of a direct action, as if a cession had been made. D. De mandato, l. Si procurator, §. Final. Hence, that which would repel the stipulator repels this procurator, even though he acts for his own benefit, as C. De procuratoribus, l. Qui stipendia. And especially when fraud appears through the confession of the plaintiff, where he who is in possession does not need any other restitution in integrum, of which l. 1, in the text and gloss, Quod factum est, De tutoribus, speaks. For the possessor does not need any other defense, since the bad faith of the party appears through his own confession, as Innocentius reads and notes in c. 1, De officio vicarii. For the office of the judge ought to provide for himself. Therefore, scrutinize my opinion, and do not criticize it, but hold it in veneration. Consider the equity of the case, and that if there had been falsehood here, it would have given cause to the contract: because there was no other contract, and he was about to pay the price. Hence, it is such as if you said, I sue on a contract to which you induced me by fraud, when otherwise you would not have contracted. Here the plaintiff is the enemy of his own bill, and contrary to his own conclusion, as any discrete man having some spark of intellect can see. This statute also requires that the promisor be bound, and he is not properly said to be bound whose execution is liquid. The words of the statute can act against the bound party. And if you are so arrogant that you do not believe, you will certainly believe Master Bartolus, who, in a decisive opinion, formally held this, which opinion I will produce in duplicate for the repulsion of slanderers, when it shall be expedient, because I have it. And laws which permit ratification are understood to allow action, when the ratifying party experiences utility from his own person, and when the contract was not celebrated by the fraud of the one giving him cause. And since ratification intervenes, which is not alleged here, and in truth does not exist, as is clear from other allegations by me, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a woman shall not succeed while a male is living, whether, upon his death, the woman succeeds by virtue of the benefit of the common law.
2. The signification of the word "until" (donec).
3. A mother who enters into a second marriage succeeds to her son’s estate together with the sons in the usufruct of the male line, but the daughter in the ownership.
body: All the pangrada [property] of the deceased Peter succeeded to Nico, his father, who had died intestate, for one-half.

† for a statute excluding a daughter does not exclude her absolutely, but only for a time, namely while a male heir survives. And therefore, upon the death of the male, she is restored to the status she holds under the common law, so that, upon the dowry being collated, she may succeed pro rata:

† as is evident from the temporal force of this word, until. C. de iure delib. l. si. §. until. instit. pro socio. §. remains. ff. fami. herc. l. inter haeredes. §. penulti. de tempo. ordi. c. dilectus filius. extra de spon. c. non est vobis. insti. de rerum diui. §. plene. ff. de dolo. l. si quis affir. §. fin. l. 2. ad Tertul. per Bart.

† The sister also succeeded her brother in the full ownership of the maternal goods, because the mother had entered into a second marriage. However, in the usufruct, the mother and the sister succeeded in equal shares, as stated in the Code, on second marriages, in the authority *Ex testamento*. But if the brother had possessed other goods besides those inherited from his father, then the mother and the sister would have succeeded in equal shares both in ownership and in usufruct, according to the same authority, namely in the other goods acquired. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The petition, the words of which are these: whether Titia, although she was not a guardian, gave and sold as if she were a guardian, is self-contradictory, on which matter see above.
2. Bartolus was not a phantom doctor, but a substantial doctor.
3. To exercise the action for recovery by means of negotiorum gestio, it is asked whether ratification is necessary.
4. Ratification requires three things.
5. He who suffers by the second decree is said to have the thing as abandoned.
body: This lord Christopher, friend of folly, is punished by his own future, as often happens, so to speak, from a small beginning. And he slanders me, and I him; yet I had neither said nor thought anything; he assumed the advocacy, and he deserves the due reward.

† I stated that the bill of complaint, the words of which are these, “Berta, as guardian, gave and sold,” although she was not a guardian, is self-contradictory in this narration, because one who narrates contraries in that which is the cause acts foolishly. That these are contraries is evident to all creditors: for if she gave, then she was a guardian; if she was not a guardian, then she did not give, as in *l. qui neque* and *l. iusiurandum quod ex conuen.*, § 1, D. de iureiur. He who denies this deserves to be rolled in mud, because falsehood is mixed with every contradiction. This was the first opinion I gave: against which opinion he, whose intellect is exceedingly sharp, and who flies so high to the stars that he is not in this world, having seen and scorned my opinion as unskilled and arrogant, advised the contrary. Nor is this surprising, because he flies without feathers like an owl, which is blinded by the light of day, and while those who see sleep, it flies, yet low with the darkness of the night. And presupposing this contradiction, nothing is consonant with or conformable to the conclusion; henceforth I shall not speak to myself, but to those who understand. And I divide the instrument into three principal parts. In the first, the sale by the guardian with the payment of the price; in the second, the solemn promise of the transfer of possession; in the third, the promise of the restitution of possession, upon the expiration of the fixed term. The parts are clear. From this contract, the transfer made is not proven, *de fin. instru. inter.*, c. *dilectus*, but rather the transfer promised. Here it must be considered, first, the common law, which holds that he who promises to transfer, if he derives an action from that transfer, must allege and prove the transfer, otherwise in one way or another: for if the transfer is as a cause, as it arises in named contracts, but an exception is raised, as in § *offerri*; but if the transfer is as a condition, the action does not arise, and it must be alleged in the bill. And so it is here, because the promise to restore the thing to be transferred contains the condition, if the transfer is made, if it shall be transferred, because when nature and natural reason require that something precede, and dispose under this order, it is necessary that this proceed, as in *l. qui pecuniam*, D. si cert. pe. Hence, if the instrument states that he promised to change, or to give in dowry, and the other promised restitution, it is understood as restitution having regard to the dowry: because law and nature look to this pact. And if, without having it, anyone were to sue for restitution, and did not allege the giving, he would be a beast of the herd, and not from the fold of Justinian. Secondly, it must be considered the municipal law, which provides that payment cannot be proven by witnesses, where the obligation consists in a confessed instrument, but this transfer would be the payment of that which was promised to be transferred, hence it cannot be proven by witnesses. And although one has promised to hold and preserve the thing promised to him, these are all understood as transferred, as any sane man sees and it is clear, C. de non num. pe., *l. si*. Then I divide the bill into two parts, in the first, the narration; in the second, the conclusion. The narration involves a contradiction, as I said. But furthermore it must be known that although one may sue for another with a mandate, and without a mandate with cession, and without cession in cases, as in deposit and similar, yet if anyone sues alleging a mandate, he is excluded by proof or confession of no mandate, and conversely if no mandate by proof or confession of mandate.

† Thus holds Bartolus, who was not a phantom doctor, but a substantial doctor in his consilia, and he begins with the incompatibility. Hence, one alleging both for and against cannot prevail first on account of the repugnance of the law. And consider: the libel states, “he gave, now six years ago,” and thus the libel is coherent as to place and time, as in the chapter *Abbate*, *de re iudicata*, book 6. This is impossible if she was not a guardian; nor can any fiction verify this word, “gave.” *Digestum*, *de manumissionibus*, law *Si pater ex provincia*. This word, “gave,” is a word of effect. And how can it be that “now six years ago he gave,” if she did not have administration? *Digestum*, *de solutionibus*, law *Filiae*. Consider, man of most wretched intellect, and do not write to the ear, but speak openly, because a true guardian validates the contract from the beginning; but if he is not a true one, he is not thereby feigned to have been a guardian, but it convalesces by special law and ratification. It is otherwise with a procurator; if you do not understand, see Bartolus in the law *Si tutor*, *in quibus causis in integrum restitutio non est necessaria*.

† and therefore there is another mode of instituting and acquiring: and perhaps you do not believe that ratification is necessary for exercising the action sought through a negotiorum gestor, and therefore Bartolus instructs you in the aforementioned law *Si tutor*, and it is expressly stated in the law *Inter quos*, § *Alienam*, on damage threatened, and in many other places. And the reason is that the consent of the ratifying party is required, so that ratification makes the transaction voluntary on his part, as stated in the law *Consensu* on actions and obligations, and in the law *Si pupilli*, § *Item quaeritur*, on negotiorum gestio. And if you do not believe this, observe how here there is no ratification:

† because ratification requires power in the person, consummation in the act: and that which is ratified must be ratifiable, you understand that power in the person is not present here: because a contract that may be penal to the principal cannot be ratified by a procurator without a special mandate. And thus Bartolus says that he has advised this a thousand times. On conditions and demonstrations. L. Si procurator. But this procurator did not have a mandate to ratify, and the contract contains a penalty, celebrated on both sides; consummation in the act is not present here for many reasons. First: because these goods, while males existed, belonged to the males alone, and it was their business alone according to the form of the statute: and therefore to consummate this contract, and to transfer to him the effect of enjoyment and possession, did not pertain to the women. Second: because this contract cannot be divided by one price, nor what follows from it or on account of it, by an added day. Quod si una, according to Bartolus. Third: because the thing did not intervene. For another possessed, that is, the person sent by the instrument, if clearly: as in §. Final, ff. L. Cum unus, through Bartolus, where he formally determines this. Fourth: because from the second decree, whereby possession was transferred, and the response of the pension, and the recognition admitted, possession cannot be restored to another than to him to whom the judge will adjudge it: because the right of the debtor was transferred to him totally, and from him must the possession be recognized. §. Item Praetore. And by law admitted, the action is lost. On conditions of theft. L. Sive manifestus. §. Tandiu.

† You do not know that he who suffers, according to the one put in possession by the second decree, is considered to hold the thing by virtue of the decree, as the ordinary gloss states in l. Praetor, de damno infecto. And because he cannot dispossess the one put in possession, it is required that the act be ratifiable; therefore, that it be ratified at such a time as to be ratifiable. l. Bonorum, and l. Final, de ratihabitione. And since the temporal opportunity of using and enjoying has been aborted and is not regarded retroactively, especially in law, how will it be ratified? ff. de usufructu legato, l. Si usufructu mihi in biennium; and for that part, since it is not established how much or where, ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. 1, § Incertam, de usucapione; si fur, § Final; l. Emptor, de usucapione pro emptore. And therefore the office of the judge must block the way to your foolishness. And you say: while I was saying that the formal power of acting proceeds from the tenor of the instrument and its force, you deny this. I do not answer you, but let the barber answer you, because he shaves it off. And while you say that fraud gives rise to an exception and does not render the libel foolish, you speak foolishly, if fraud is mentioned in the libel, as is fully noted in § Pactus ne petentem. You understood according to the argument; for I say that he who alleges that very thing which the instrument says, as here when it says "he gave," etc., admits it and affirms it: l. Optimam, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione. I affirm the person in the act; but you go on chattering, and I do not pursue other later foolishnesses, about which it is more convenient to be silent. And if you are so profoundly learned before the doctors of this city in alleging viva voce, where, God willing, your confusion will appear, I have not seen your foolishness regarding the recitation of the rescript, and therefore what has been said until now: let the doctors be sworn upon the altar. Baldus of Perugia, enemy of ignorance, most enemy of others' faults, ready to correct his own with any correction, and patiently enduring corrections with a willing and humble mind, because to be ignorant is not a vice, but nature. ff. de legatis tertio, l. Stichus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when acts performed by a minor are valid after he has reached majority.
2. A contract that is null because it is simulated does not give rise to a cause for prescription.
body: Sometimes

† Although the marriage was contracted by a minor, because no decree intervened, it is nevertheless just and celebrated in good faith. And such a contract is confirmed by five years' silence after reaching majority, as in C. si maior factus, l. si quando, because the cause of nullity was lacking solely because the solemnity introduced by the strict law had not been observed, and therefore equity provided for this in that law.

† Sometimes a contract is null because it is simulated; in such a case, that law has no application. But as you say that falsity does not give rise to a cause for prescription, so it must be said regarding simulation, as in C. de falsis, l. ex initio. And this is true, unless consent has been added after the attainment of lawful age, which is deemed to have intervened if they possessed the property for a long time as if it were divided, as noted in l. penultima, C. communi diviso. For in acts performed after lawful age, the fiction of the statute has no place, as in de legatis 2, l. Titia, § usuras, ff. de novatione; l. doli, § diversum. Therefore, the question of fact will be examined by the judge, as in C. plus valere, quod agitur, l. secunda. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution made in this manner to an underage son, if he should die without children, by which I substitute such a person in all my movable and immovable goods, is direct or oblique.
body: A certain Cola, having a wife pregnant in her final months, made a will, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows: namely, in all his movable and immovable goods, after the aforementioned legacies and bequests, he instituted as universal heir, both vulgarly and pupillarily and by fideicommissum, the son or daughter to be born from him and his wife, Lady Maria. And if his aforementioned heirs should die without legitimate children in any way, he wished all his movable and immovable goods to be handed over and restored to Cabuttio, his carnal brother; and he wished the said Cabuttio to succeed in all his movable and immovable goods, as stated above, etc. Finally, the said Cola died, while the said Lady Massia remained pregnant, from whom a certain girl named Vanarella was born after the death of her father, the said Cola. This girl died in pupillary age, while her mother, the said Massia, and her uncle, the said Cabuttio, her substitute, were living and remained. And while the said girl, his daughter, was living, the said Massia entered into a second marriage. The said Massia, after the aforementioned events, claimed against the said Cabuttio, the substitute, the legitime and the Trebellianic quarter of the goods and inheritance of the late Cola, her husband, and father of the said girl, her daughter, by virtue of the words contained in the above-written will. And on behalf of the said Cabuttio, it is said that the aforementioned [claims] are not due to the said mother of the said girl because of those words contained in the said will. And especially because of those words of the said will, namely "pupillarily," and also because of those words, "all," which are contained in the said will. It is asked whether the said mother of the girl is bound to receive or have anything in the goods of the inheritance of the late Cola, or not.

† A substitution made in this manner to an underage son, if he should die without children, whereby I substitute such a person in all my movable and immovable goods, is a fideicommissum and not a universal substitution, nor a direct one under the Trebellian law. See *l. cogi.*, § *generaliter*, ad hoc, D. de verb. signif.; *l. mouentium*, D. de usufr. leg.; *l. fin.*, D. de pecul.; *l. quam Tuberonis*, § *in peculio*. And therefore the legitime and the Falcidian portion, I do not say the Trebellian, belong to the mother, to whom the transition to second marriage does not prejudice, since no son survives, as is fully noted by the doctors, C. de sec. nup., auth. *ex testamento*. Nor do those words “vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum” stand in the way, because they were spoken among sons, in case more should be born, and thus they are not relevant to the present case. Moreover, the words of the fideicommissum were expressed, because the testator said “to be handed over and restored,” and then follows, as stated above. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How often may an arbitrator render a decision, when he has been given the power to make an award once, and more than once. Likewise, what if he issues a second award contrary to the first.
body: After

† Once a final award has been rendered, the arbitrator immediately ceases to exercise his office. D. de arbitris, l. qualem, §. final. And therefore he cannot render another award, unless it had been stated in the submission that he could award once and multiple times. For then the second award would be valid, because multiple submissions are deemed to have been made. D. de arbitris, l. quod tamen. Unless the second award were contrary to the first, for then the second would not be valid. It supports what is noted in D. pro socio, l. imposita. And therefore, since the award was null by operation of law, the judge’s precept ordering it to be paid was invalid, and consequently the promise was also erroneous, and although payment was made, it can be recovered on account of error, as noted in D. de condictione indebiti, l. Iul. And because the said promise was made under the judge’s actual compulsion and against the law, as in l. final, D. quod metus causa. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A renunciation made by a daughter concerning her father's estate does not prevent her sister from succeeding.
body: From the words

† No prejudice arises from the said renunciation in the succession of the sister, so that one sister succeeds to the other. And because the right of deliberation is transmitted in the succession to be made of Catherine by the person of Thomas, see D. de pactis, l. si vnus; §. ante omnia, de collatione; l. ante pactum, ad Velleiam; l. iubemus, de petitione hereditatis; l. hereditatis materterae. And although these goods were originally from the father’s estate, nevertheless it is true as stated, because they passed to another, as in C. de donationibus, l. si auia, and l. 1, C. de imponendis lucris describendis, lib. 10; D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. Paulus, §. fin. This certain donation, of which mention is made, does not include the succession of a living sister, C. de pactis, l. finalis; and what is noted in D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. idem respondet, and l. ea vero, §. de illo, although that §. cum glossa, l. posset allegari, pro and contra, D. de transactione, l. cum acquirendis, with similar authorities. And because those words “from the goods, etc.” are understood immediately, as in l. 1, §. nunc videamus, de coniugio cum emancipata libera, and it is as if expressly stated in D. de hereditate vendenda, l. secunda, §. illud. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A woman, who by statute does not succeed to her father together with her brothers, has her dowry as a preferential right, and it is immaterial whether she can freely make a will regarding her dowry.
body: Question

This is a point of the highest subtlety of law, and it is examined. C. de rei uxoriae actione, l. rem in praesenti, §. videamus, after the gloss, by Dynus in l. penultima, soluto matrimonio, by Dynus, and in l. post dotem, in the same title, by Bartolus. And here, if anyone wished to cite arguments for and against, many folios would not suffice; but conclusively and determinatively, this must be said: either this Thomasa succeeded with Ser Peter, together with her brothers, and then the dowry is common to all of them, and is not consolidated to her alone. C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. fin.; or she did not succeed, because perhaps the statute does not wish that a dowried daughter succeed when males are extant. And thus she is in a manner disinherited by the statute in consideration of the dowry, as in l. qui volebat, de heredibus instituendis. And now it is consolidated to this daughter, and she can dispose of it by will, as in the aforementioned §. videamus, and l. ultima, ff. de collatione dotis. And if this daughter were not given a dowry, her legitimate portion could not be denied to her: and she could have made a will, if the father gave a dowry for his daughter, and stipulated that it be returned to himself, or to his sons, if she should die without children. Thus, to this woman, upon the death of the father, it is computed in her legitimate portion, if the brothers are content to remit the stipulation for this purpose. l. 1, de collatione dotis. And thus it was in fact adjudged. These are the words of Jacobus de Arena in l. uxor, §. pater, de legatis secundo. But here the brothers remitted the stipulations willingly, and by consenting that it be imputed to the legitimate portion, as appears from another instrument, upon which I gave a second consultation. Therefore, the woman could dispose of this dowry by will. And this seems to me to be the very truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a shopkeeper or a clerk of an apothecary is a suitable witness.
2. Likewise, what is the rule regarding a relative? Likewise, what is the rule regarding a friend? What regarding a domestic scribe? What regarding a herald? What regarding another spokesperson or mediator between friends?
3. Whether on feast days one may be examined outside the articles.
4. Whether a witness testifying about a grant proves the article concerning payment.
body: It must be considered

First, concerning the witnesses, whether they are suitable. It is objected against Peter that he was a shop assistant in an apothecary and a manager of the said Nicholas, whence he does not appear to be a suitable witness, as in C. de testamentis, l. finalis; nor should faith be given to his writings, as if he were a witness and a domestic and familiar scribe. C. de testamentis, l. omnibus; de iure fisci, l. deferre, § idem decreuerunt, according to Bartolus and what we note in Inst. de testamentis, § si filius. For these witnesses do not appear suitable, because they are shop assistants, and also familiars and domestics, and especially in a case which is of grave weight, because it exceeds a pound of gold, as in C. si certum petatur, Auth. sed nouo iure. Philip also does not appear to be a suitable witness, because he is an affine, for affinity breeds excessive friendship, and therefore he is not an impartial witness, but rather contributes to some instruction than to full proof. D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. qui iurisdictioni; D. de probationibus, l. etiam; de excusatione tutorum, l. unanimi, with similar authorities.

But notwithstanding these objections, I say that the said shop assistants, insofar as it does not touch their contract or interest, can be admitted as witnesses: for in civil matters even blood relatives are admitted, let alone affines. It is certainly true that it is discretionary whether perfect and solid faith should be given to these witnesses, as we note in the second question, 5, cap. accusatores; Extra, vt lite non contestata, cap. accedens; and l. 2, D. de testamentis, l. 3, § tu magis; and l. lege Iulia. And since these apothecary shop assistants are throughout the world confident, as legal persons and industrious, faith ought rightly to be given to them. A domestic scribe is also not repelled from testifying; the text is notable, D. de testamentis militum, l. nuntius; nor a simple friend, D. de usuris, l. sciendum est; nor even a familiar, unless he is a dining companion, as noted by Innocentius, Extra, de officio delegati, cap. insinuante; and de testamentis, cap. in literis, according to Innocentius. And therefore I consider the said witnesses, in doubt, to be above all exception, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam, because those things which are objected against them are frivolous and empty, nor is it true that any of them is similar to a prosoneta, for prosonetae are commonly vile men, and prosonetae hope for [gain], whence they derive benefit. From these two joined together, the law has these [persons] as suspect, unless they are produced by the consent of both parties, as in cap. mediatores, de testibus, lib. 6. But these, who are not of this profession, although they are spokesmen between the parties, are not properly called prosonetae, but spokesmen and amicable negotiators, D. de argentariis, l. si de meis, § recepisse. And this I say concerning the said witnesses as regards their persons. Now I come to their statements, against which several objections are raised. First, that the party was not notified, but the contrary appears in the records. Second, that they were received by a judge not competent. For

† Since only the articles had been remitted for proof, they were received outside the articles, because an article pertains to the act of truth, and witnesses to the act of confession. But this allegation does not hold, because the judge questioned them on the articles.

And thus he questioned as he ought. And the witness, having been questioned, testified regarding the confession, by which the article is proved: therefore, he did not testify outside the article, but concerning matters pertinent or conducive to the article. Extra, de successione ab intestato, c. Cum dilectus; de deposito, c. Publia, §. fin.; de verbis obligatis, l. Si ita stipulatio, §. Grisogonus. For by the civil act of confession, the natural act is proved, although it is not induced, as stated in the aforementioned laws. And Codex, de falcidia, causa adiecta legato, l. Prima. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What a confession that someone possesses by a just title effects, when no other mention is made of the title.
2. Whether one confessing that someone possessed as his own confesses that he is the owner.
body: Whether to lady

† Petrucia the response made by her to the 15th chapter of Angnella's positions is prejudicial, in which chapter prescription from possession of twenty years with title is contained. It must be said that prescription is not established, even positing that no revocation of the error had been made. And the reason is that the article states that lady Angnella possessed by just title for the space of twenty years through herself and her predecessors, namely etc. And Petrucia responded that she does not believe it except regarding Petrus and the sons. For by this it does not appear for how much time out of that space of twenty years Petrus and the sons [possessed], since in the article Angnella does not separately intend the times of each possessor, but conjunctively, as in l. Papinianus § cum quis, de acqui. posses. Likewise, because those words, "by just title," are general words, because they do not state by what title; and an unjust title does not suffice for prescribing, ff. de publi. l. quaecunque § interdum, and

† even though it had been confessed or posited concerning possession per se or as one's own (pro suo), ownership is not confessed through this, but rather the manner or quality of possessing. Whence it is one thing to confess that someone possesses under the title pro suo, and another to confess that he is the owner. For it does not follow: "he possesses as his own, therefore he is the owner," as in ff. de solu. l. Titia, and l. liberis § fina. de libe. causa, [and] l. apud antiquos, de fur., unless from that title prescription has been completed, as in ff. pro suo throughout. And therefore, notwithstanding confessions of this kind, the arbiters ought to follow the path of truth; and what belonged to the father is presumed to belong to the sons, as in C. de probatione l. siue possidetis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A substitution by reason of the failure of a condition lapses.
2. Whether daughters and grandchildren through her are included by the term "children."
3. Whether one prohibited from alienating is deemed prohibited from making a will or transmitting by intestate succession.
body: Fictitious substitution, as is proposed in the theme, with respect to those who should die, leaving behind male children from their own body

† it perished by the defect of the condition. D. de legatis 1, l. filius; § cum quis erit; C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter; C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum auus; D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, § penultimo and final. And therefore, having examined such a substitution, there is no need to concern oneself further. Rather, it must be seen whether the prohibition of alienation applies solely to the said houses, which the testator wished to be preserved for his children; and if indeed it appears that the testator did not intend anything other than what the words of the writing signify,

Under the term "children" is included the daughter, and also the grandchildren through the daughter, as in C. de conditione inserta, l. 1. But if it were proven that the testator intended that the property could not be alienated outside the male line, because he wished it to remain perpetually among males, then it must be considered what the law provides.

† And it seems that the property should revert to the males, because one who is prohibited from alienating is prohibited from transmitting intestate, as stated in the Digest, *De legatis* (book 2), law *Codicillis*, § *penult*. And the reason is that he is considered to have been commanded to act and to ensure that the property does not come into the hands of the prohibited person, as noted in the Digest, *De verborum obligatione*, law *Si ita quis*, § *Ea lege*.

On the contrary, it seems that transmission to one’s own heirs does not constitute an alienation, since even during the father’s lifetime they are owners. See the Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*, law *In suis*; and *De usu pro haerede*, § *Nihil*; and the Code, *De impositione lucrativae descriptionis*, law 1, book 10. Hence, the rights of parents pass to their own heirs, even in respect of things from which alienation is prohibited: as in the Digest, *De non alienando*, § *Emphyteusis*; and *De soluto matrimonio*, law *Etiam*; the Digest, *De operis libertatis*, law *Ut iureiurando*, § 6; the Digest, *Ad Trebellianum*, law *Quia proinde*.

On this point, it must be considered that the division among the children themselves was upheld, because it was made among those permitted, as in the Code, *Familiae herciscundae*, law *Si familiae*, in the gloss. And the share of water that accrued to one remaining in another seems to have been capable of alienation, just as a purchased share, for exchange serves in place of purchase: Digest, *De legatis* (book 3), law *Pater*, § *Quindecim*.

Furthermore, it seems that the testator referred to alienation made by a person, not to that which occurs by operation of law. This is evident when he stated that a sale is made, etc., and thus he knew the fact: see law *Consilio*, § *Fin.*, *De curatore furiosi*. Legal alienation, however, is not a matter of fact, but of law and right. Moreover, these words sound more like alienation *inter vivos* than like transmission of an inheritance: see Digest, *De legatis* (book 3), law *Fundum*, where it is said, “the writing of the will [covers] every contract and action [and] obligation.” Although the term *actus* is general, it seems to be restricted by what follows, namely “obligation,” etc.: Digest, *De verborum significatione*, law *Verba gesserunt*; and law *Si cum fundum*. From these, it is inferred that both the share in the houses obtained by the coheir through exchange, and the hereditary share, are possessed as a matter of right by the daughters of Olufrus and the sisters of Francis. And that the said daughters transmitted [the property] to their sons, according to the aforementioned law 1, *De conditionibus insertis*; and the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law *Voluntas*. This is in accordance with what was consulted by the most prudent and excellent learned doctors, Master Bartolus of Sassoferrato. And it supports what is stated and noted in the Authenticum, *De restitutione fideicommissorum*, § *Manifestum*.

I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether that which is generally prohibited may be granted on account of some particular merit.
2. Whether a foreigner prohibited from acquiring immovable property in the city may be enabled to do so, if he has performed some notable service for the state of the city.
3. Likewise, what is the rule regarding the general prohibition of granting arms to the magistrates of the city.
body: 1. They provided and ordained that no officers of the commune of Perugia may at any time be given or granted weapons or anything else on behalf of the commune, except only that which they ought to have according to the form of the statute or according to the form of their election. And if anyone should propose or advise the contrary, he shall incur the penalty of one thousand pounds of denarii, to be taken from him de facto by any official of the commune of Perugia without any process. And the priors who are in office at the time when the aforementioned things are done shall be compelled to pay that penalty, which shall be taken from them de facto during their term of syndicate by the major syndic of the commune of Perugia.

† General provisions of statutes receive tacit exceptions on account of arising cases, in which it is necessary to provide specifically. Hence, a special cause prevailing, the general provision ceases. Therefore, on account of singular merits, there is a singular promise, which cannot be made according to general statutes, as in D. ad Sillaniam, l. 1, § hi quoque. And there Bartolus says.

† But if it is forbidden for a foreigner to acquire possession of the city, nevertheless, on account of singular merit, for example because he has labored greatly in the recovery of a certain rebelled castle, this may be granted and donated to him. Hence, with true and just merits supporting him, and obligating the community to gifts, a singular favor may be done to a lord in honor and power. To this effect, D. de donationibus, l. Aquil. regulus, and l. si pater.

† And therefore, if it is established to the Lords Priors and Camerlengos that the Lord Podesta has performed some notable deed in the preservation of the state, the recovery of castles, and the repulsion of rebels and traitors, they may grant him insignia. C. de statuis, et imaginibus, l. et virtutum praemia. For prohibitions are not issued against those who are highly deserving, as ff. de excusatione tutorum, l. sed reprobata, l. valde tantum. It is, however, safer if the Lords Priors and Camerlengos say, “We grant you these insignia,” and do not say “on behalf of the Commune of Perugia.” Nor is this to defraud the law. And because the Commune of Perugia is greater than these two colleges, as Inst. de iure naturali, §. plebs. I, Baldus. Addendum.

CONSILIVM LIIII

A statute provides that no official of the Commune may, at any time, be given or granted arms or anything else on behalf of the Commune, except that which he ought to have according to the form of the statutes or the form of his election, under a certain penalty. Now it is asked whether, upon the termination of office, arms of the Commune of Perugia, either simple or with some alteration, may be granted to an official who conducted himself well in office. And it seems to me that this has been done in the past, namely that certain arms were granted with something added or some alteration made, always preserving the truth. But whether it could or can be done is doubtful. And it must be known that, for a very great cause, such as the compulsion of enemies or the recovery of castles, this may well be done, according to Bartolus, who so notes infra, l. 1, §. hi quoque, ff. ad Sillam. But where that cause, on account of which it is permitted to transgress the laws, is not present, then it must be seen what is the law.

And first it seems that it cannot be done, because this prohibition is general as to persons, since it says “to no official”; as to time, since it says “at any time”; as to things, since it says “arms or anything else.” But the ordinance of a general law ought to be understood generally, as l. in fraudem, §. fin., ff. de militum testamento; ff. de publico, l. de proconsule; ff. de legatis praestandis, l. 1, §. et generaliter; and ff. de bonis auctore iudice possessis, l. in venditione, §. de tempore.

On the contrary, it seems that the statute says “to no official.” But it is certain that, upon the termination of office, one is not an official. Hence, if anything is then granted to him, it is not granted to an official, since it is granted at a time when he cannot be a ruler or official of the citizens. This is stated by the law in a similar case. For a provincial governor who gives earnest money for contracting marriage with a subject loses the earnest money. This is true during the office, but otherwise when it is finished, because he is no longer governor, as C. si rector provinciae, l. 1. Hence, this statute seems to speak during the magistracy, as ff. de officio proconsulis, l. solent, §. fin.

But against this is what is said about a guardian, who even after the termination of guardianship cannot contract marriage with his ward. C. de interdicto matrimonio, l. si patris. But there is another reason: during the magistracy, if this is sought ambitiously. It supports what is noted C. qui dare tutorem possint, auctore tutoris, in fin. But certainly it is not ambition to seek honors for virtues, as l. Barbarius Philosophus, ff. de officio praesidis. And therefore, since the statute speaks only of an official, it seems that after the deposition from magistracy, the donation of arms is not forbidden, at least if altered. Nor does it obstruct that the statute says “or anything else,” as if it were understood of something else of notable quantity or similar quality, and during the office, not when it is ended, and giving the reason of administration. Thus, between husband and wife, donation is forbidden, nor is marriage to be sold; yet, if a divorce is effected and a donation is made, it is valid, nor is it forbidden as incestuous, as ff. de donatione inter virum et uxorem, l. quae tantum, and l. cum hic statuit, §. si diuortium, and §. si mulier, cum si. And this I believe to be true, arg. ff. de noxa, l. in delictis, §. si extraneus; and ff. de testamento militis, l. Titius; ff. ad l. Falcidiam, l. si post missionem. And because, as I said, upon the termination of office, the cause of the law prohibiting ceases; and therefore it ends. l. auctoritas, ff. de divortio, l. fin.; and l. milites agrum, de re militari. I, Baldus.

It is provided by a statute that to no official of the commune of Perugia may arms or anything else be given or donated at any time on behalf of the commune, except only that which he ought to have by the form of the statutes or by the form of his election, under a certain penalty. Now it is asked whether, once his office is ended, to an official who conducted himself well in his office, the arms of the commune of Perugia may be granted simply, or with some modification. And it seems to me that this was done at other times, namely that certain arms were granted with something added or with some alteration made, saving always the truth. But whether this could or can be done is doubted. And it should be known that on account of a very great cause, such as the repelling of enemies or the recovery of castles, this could well be done, according to Barto., who notes thus below in l. 1. §. hi quoque. ff. ad Sille. But where that cause on account of which it is permissible to transgress the laws does not underlie the matter, then it must be seen what the law is. And first it seems that it cannot be done, because that prohibition is general: with respect to persons, because it says 'to no official'; with respect to times, because it says 'at any time'; and with respect to things, because it says 'arms, or anything else.' But a general provision of the law must be understood generally, as in l. in fraudem. §. fin. ff. de milita. testamen., ff. de publi. l. de procon., ff. de lega. praestand. l. 1. §. et generaliter., and ff. de bon. auth. iudc. pos. l. in venditione. §. de tempore. To the contrary it seems, because the statute says, 'to no official'; but it is certain that once his office is ended, he is not an official. Whence if anything is then granted to him, it is not granted to an official, since it is granted at a time when he cannot be a rector or official over the citizens. The law says this in a similar case: for a rector of a province who gives earnest-money for contracting marriage with a subject woman forfeits the earnest-money; this is true while the office lasts, but otherwise once it has ended, because he is no longer rector, as in C. si rector prouinciae. l. 1. Whence this statute seems to speak of the time during the magistracy, as in ff. de officio proconsu. l. solent. §. fi. But against this militates what is said concerning a tutor, who, even after the tutorship has ended, cannot contract marriage with the female ward, C. de interdicto matrimo. l. si patris; but there it is for another reason during the magistracy, if this is ambitiously procured; what is noted in C. qui dare tuto. pos. autho. tutoris. in fin. is relevant. But certainly it is not ambition to seek honors for virtues, as in l. Barbarius Philippus. ff. de officio praesi. And therefore, since the statute speaks only of an official, it seems that after the laying down of the magistracy a donation of arms, at least altered ones, is not forbidden. Nor does it stand in the way that the statute says 'or anything else,' for it is understood as of something else that is of notable quantity or of similar quality, and during the office, not once it is put to rest and the account of the administration has been rendered. Thus between husband and wife a donation is prohibited lest marriage become venal; nevertheless, once a divorce has taken place, if a donation is made, it is fully valid, for it is not forbidden as an incestuous thing, as in ff. de donatione inter virum, et vxorem. l. quae tentum. and l. cum hic status. §. si diuortium. and §. si mulier. with the following. And this I believe to be true, arguing from ff. de noxa. l. in delictis. §. si extraneus., and ff. de testa. mili. l. Titius., ff. ad l. Falcidiam. l. si post missionem., and because, as I have said, once the office is ended the cause of the prohibiting law ceases, and therefore it is brought to an end, l. autoritas. ff. de diuor. l. fin., and l. milites agrum. de re militari. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an instrument is valid without a place and without witnesses.
2. Whether a person who promises not to offend someone under a penalty to be applied by the local official incurs the penalty if he offends outside the territory of said official, or whether he incurs the penalty if he offends him while he is under ban.
3. What if I promise for myself and my three brothers that Titius will not be offended, and my sureties say that they have stood sure for me, but one of my brothers offends Titius, whether the sureties are bound.
4. A copy of the obligation extended literally, etc.
body: In the Year of Our Lord 1383, in the sixth indiction, during the pontificate of Pope Urban VI, on the last day of the month of July, Baldutius, formerly son of Gori of this cognomen, from the said borough, appeared before the noble man Nichelius de Stacriola, honorable vicar of the territory and borough of the Holy Sepulchre, acting for the magnificent and exalted Lord Galeotto de Malatestis, general lord of the said territory and borough. Baldutius, in his own and private name, and on behalf of and in the name of Griolus, son of Nicolai Bocchiani, and Guidonis, his brothers, and the sons of the aforementioned Gori, their father, by himself and their heirs, promised and agreed, and solemnly stipulated to the said Lord Vicar and to me, the notary Thadeus, written below, as a public person stipulating and receiving on behalf of the noble men of the house of Robertis of the said borough, and of all and each of the men of the said house of Robertis, not to offend, nor to cause to be offended, nor to consent to an offense, by himself or others, in air or person, by word, deed, or work, against any of the said house of Robertis, under the penalty and to the penalty of one hundred gold florins for each contravenor and for each offense. Which penalty in its entirety ought to come to the aforementioned magnificent Lord, our Lord Galeotto, and be applied to him by operation of law. Furthermore, on the above premises, the said Baldutius, by himself and his heirs, promised to the said Lord Vicar and to me, the notary written below, that he would do and see to it with effect that the said Griolus Boccognanus and Guido, and both of them, attend to and observe all and each of the things written below, under the said penalty named above. For which Baldutius, and his parts and mandates, the following sureties bound themselves: Master Nicolaus, Master Franciscus, Bartholomeus, Petri, Danielis, Ioinnis, Lugi. They renounced the benefit of the constitution of the law of surety, the privilege of the letter of the divine Adrian, the exception of bad faith, the condition of what is not due, and without cause, in facts, acts, and every other law and statute aid. I, Thadeus, son of the late Ioannes Lauren. of Marnia, notary by Imperial authority and ordinary judge, and now notary of the said community of the borough, because by edicts indeed, to the provision and obligation, as is contained above, as it is written, I intervened, and of these things I was requested to write, by mandate of the said Lord Vicar, I wrote and published, and appended my usual sign. After the aforementioned, Griolus, brother of the said Baldutius, with a certain company of armed men outside the district of the borough, killed Nicolaus, one of the said nobles excommunicated and condemned by the said community of the borough in person, namely to the penalty of the gallows, for which the Vicar of the borough, in the name of the sons of Lord Galeotto, demands from the said sureties the penalty of one hundred florins, which he says they have incurred by the death of the said Nicolaus, following the operation of the said Griolus. It is responded by the said sureties that they did not oblige themselves except solely for Baldutius, that he would not offend, nor cause to be offended, any of the said nobles, and that the said writings and promises are not to be believed: since there were no witnesses there, nor a place where it was made, nor was the said penalty stipulated for anyone for Lord Galeotto, or for another. And because there are no obligatory words by which the said sureties can be constrained to the payment of the said penalty, as will appear from the series of the words and the writing. Now it is asked, whether, seeing the form of the said writing, faith ought to be given to it. Furthermore, if faith is given to the said writing, whether, from the words inserted therein, and by its force, the said sureties can be compelled by law to pay the said penalty. Furthermore, if the said sureties can be compelled to pay the said penalty, whether each of them is bound pro rata, and what is the law regarding the dead and absent sureties, what is the law, etc.

† This writing is not formal, and therefore it does not prove: and first, because the place is not specified therein, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam; de probationibus, l. quoniam contra falsam; and in the chapter Abbate sane, de regulis iuris, book 6; and there noted in the gloss on the word "censeretur"; and in the Sextus, in the first gloss; and in the Speculum, de instrumentis, edition, §. instrumentum ergo, verse Quid si locus. Nor does it suffice to say that it was done in such a city, unless a specific place is understood from the fact that such things are accustomed to be done there, as in the proemium of Clementina and in Authent. quibus modis naturales efficiuntur, §. quantitas, column 6; and in the second question, 8, chapter of libelli, unless custom were otherwise, which must be observed in documents, as noted in Authent. ut praeponatur nomen Imperatoris, §. quo vero, column 7. Moreover, this instrument is invalid: because witnesses are not appended, as noted in C. de donatione, l. in donatione, in the gloss non ergo; and in Authent. de haereditatibus et falcidia, §. si vero absunt; and noted in C. de tabulis, l. generali. For this contract, of which the instrument speaks, is a simple extrajudicial contract. But let us assume, without prejudice to the truth, that the instrument would be valid as if it were a judicial instrument, as said in the law in this, first response.

† Nevertheless, in our case, the penalty does not appear to have been incurred, for several reasons. First, because the magistrate is not understood to be responsible for that which does not pertain to his care; namely, for that which is committed outside the territory, as in c. *Animarum*, de constitutionibus, lib. 6; and from the argument of D. de instructionibus, l. 1, § *Non autem omne*; and D. de nauigari cautius statuendo, l. 3, § *Certum*, si quid facit; c. *Quamquam*, de usu, in the Clementines; c. *Cum si*. Second, because the offender was excommunicated and an enemy of the republic, of which he held the magistracy; hence he is not understood to have stipulated in favor of an enemy. D. de dolo, l. 1, § *Non fuit*; D. de legatis 2, l. *Lucius*, § *Titius damna*; D. de manumissionibus testamentis, l. *Testamento Centurio*. For the safety of an enemy is not to be provided for. D. de religione, l. *Minime*; D. ad legem Corneliam de sicariis, l. 3, § *Transfugas*; D. de verbis obligatis, l. *Qui servum*. But let us assume, without prejudice to the truth, that these objections do not stand; nevertheless, the said sureties do not appear to be bound for another reason, because they gave surety for Baldutio. Baldutio, however, did not commit the offense; hence it must be considered what is meant by "for whom they gave surety for Baldutio," etc. For Baldutio promised for himself that he would not commit an offense; and for others, that they would not commit an offense, and gave security, etc. Hence this writing "for Baldutio" etc. can be understood in two ways. In one way, by referring the obligation of the sureties to the entire promise of Baldutio. D. locati conducti, l. *Quaero*. In another way, by referring it to the person of Baldutio, so that the sense is that if Baldutio commits an offense, they are bound; but not if another commits an offense. Just as the determination of a certain amount makes the surety not bound beyond it, so does the determination with respect to the person. D. de fideiussoribus, l. *Fideicommissum*, magistratus, § *Aurelio Romulo*. And because only one person is expressly mentioned, for he did not say "for whom" (in the plural), but said "for whom" in the singular number, as argued from D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. *Iulius Phebus*, in dubio. Therefore, whenever there is doubt about the understanding of a writing, it is considered that less has come into the obligation. D. de verbis obligatis, l. *Quicquid astringendae*. And in that which he owes in his own name, not in that which is due because of another's act, arg. D. ad municipalia, l. 2, § *Sed si filius*; and l. *Libenter*, § fin. Hence, considering all things, I think the said penalty is not due, especially because of what has been said about the ban. And if this opinion does not please my lords, let them at least take the path of equity in this doubt,

† That each surety be required to pay his proportional share. For the earliest laws maintained that each surety was bound for the whole amount; as stated in the Institutes, on sureties, §. But if several. However, equity introduced division by means of the rescript. But by renunciation of the rescript, one returns to that strictness. But in our case, it should be advised to the lords that the way of equity be chosen, as the Emperor does. D. on the institution of heirs, l. And this Tiberius. With similar cases. This I say concerning division, by way of persuasion. But as to what I said above, that they are not bound by reason of the ban: I hold that it is true in law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the legitimation of daughters, made at the instance of a party who has no sons but grandsons through a predeceased daughter, is valid even though no mention was made of the granddaughters.
body: Whether a father,

† He who legitimated his sons by imperial rescript, having no legitimate and natural sons, but having nephews through a daughter, without any mention being made of the nephews: is the legitimation by rescript vitiated? It seems that it is, because just as mention must be made of the offspring of sons, so likewise of nephews, who succeed in the place of their parents. On the contrary, that it is not vitiated: because the texts of the Authentica speak only of the offspring of sons. Now the question arises, what is the law? It appears to me that in the privilege of legitimation, mention or naming of the existence of nephews through a predeceased daughter was not necessary; because this is not provided for by any law, provided that the legitimating party has the power and authority to legitimate, even in the case of existing legitimated persons. Hence, the form of the privilege must be examined on this point. For this legitimation is a certain gift of the father and the prince, in which the consent of the legitimated is not required, when the father, by presenting petitions, obtains this from Caesar, or from him who holds his place in this matter. Just as anyone, using his right, or giving, or casting into the sea, according to the note in Cod. de inoff. testam. l. 1, and by this, Cod. de nat. lib. l. coniun. in fine. To the same effect is what is noted by Bartolus in l. Gallus, §. et quid si tantum, de lib. et posth. And this, in consulting, the venerable and memorable learned masters, Lord Federicus of Siena, and Lord Griffolus of Monte Polliciano, held. As appears in the work of the said Lord Federicus, consilium 54, which begins, "It seems to me." Nor is it said to deprive, because he uses his free and proper power, argument from Auth. de incest. nupt. §. fin. Furthermore, it does not obstruct. Cod. de nat. lib. auth. item si quis, because the form of the privilege to Caesar solves the contrary to that authentic by expressly derogating, as noted in Auth. qui mod. nat. effici. sui. §. fin. col. 7. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution made to someone, if he dies before having children, becomes void, or takes effect if he had children, but they died while the substitute was still alive.
2. Whether, and when, in the fulfillment of a condition, perseverance is required, or whether it suffices to fulfill it at a single moment.
3. Whether one not honored in the will, but taking by causa mortis, can be burdened by the testator.
4. Whether, and when, alienation is prohibited, and in the default of one degree another is substituted, so that the property always remains in the family, all members of the family appear to be successively instituted and substituted.
5. Chapter of the will of the late lady Agata Bucconadei.
body: I institute my daughter Antonia, daughter of the aforementioned lady Alienator, my sister, as my heir in my great hospice, in which I reside. And I will and command, however, on this condition: that if, by chance, before legitimate and natural sons are begotten and born from the said Antonia, the said Antonia should close her final day; then in that case, the said lady Alianora, her mother, shall succeed the said Antonia in the said great hospice, namely, if, God forbid, the said lady Alianora, my sister, should have died without leaving any sons legitimately descending from her own body. Then in that case, I will and command that Philippa, the girl, daughter and heir of the late Jacob Buccamodei, my brother, shall succeed the said lady Alianora in the same great hospice. And if the said lady Philippa should, by chance, die without sons legitimately begotten from her, as above, then in that case, I substitute for her in the said great hospice Manfred, the delicate son of the aforementioned lady Margaret Buccomedei, my sister, if he should then be living; and if he should not be living, let Ricarda, sister of the said Manfred, my niece, succeed in the said hospice, if she should then be living; and if she should not be living, let Machalda, another sister of the same Manfred, succeed in the same hospice, if she should be living. And in default of the sons of the said lady Margaret, let my nearest blood relatives pertaining to me in the male line succeed in my same great hospice, so that the male nearest to me, as above, in the said cases, shall be preferred and shall succeed in my said hospice, and shall have it, and shall be the true lord and true patron. And in default of the blood relatives of the male line, let the nearest blood relatives in the female line succeed in the same hospice. Nor do I prohibit all my heirs and successors in the said hospice from being able or ought to alienate, sell, or transfer under title of alienation my said great hospice to outsiders in perpetuity; but rather, from degree to degree, the hospice itself shall come and ought to come to my nearest blood relatives in the manner expressed and declared above, etc. Having seen a certain chapter of the testament of the late lady Agatha Buccamodei, in which is contained the singular institution of the daughter of lady Alianora in the great hospice, with substitutions made in a certain order, and having read its tenor; presupposing that from Antonia was born Antonellus, with William, his father and heir, surviving; hence it is doubted whether the said hospice pertains to the said William, or rather to lady Alianora, or to the nearest blood relatives of the testatrix. Therefore, that the truth may shine forth and be had, it must be considered,

Whether the substitution made to Antonio, if he dies before having children, takes effect if he has children and the children born die while the substitute is still alive. And it seems that the substitution takes effect, because it is the same not to have been born and not to have survived.

† All conditions, whether inclusive or exclusive, seem to require perseverance, as argued in the Digest, *de effectu tutorum*, l. 2, where it is stated: “it is necessary, however, that they be alive.” And in the Digest, *ad Trebellianum*, l. *ex facto*, § *pen.*, it is said that one who has lost his children is deemed to have died without children. To the contrary, it appears that this condition, “if he shall not have begotten children,” is excluded immediately and at once when children are born. And in momentary conditions, perseverance is not required. Codex, *de institutionibus et substitutionibus*, l. *ante pen.*; Digest, *de statu hominum*, l. *Aretusa*; Digest, *de verborum significatione*, l. *Enixa*. Therefore, as soon as Antonellus was born, the substitution made expressly and specifically to Antonia vanished, because the words of the will state: “if, before children are begotten from Antonia herself, Antonia herself dies, then, and in that case, Alianora shall succeed.” In these words, three things are to be considered. First, the form of the condition, namely: “if before children are begotten from Antonia herself”; for from such a form, especially when expressed conditionally, one cannot depart. Digest, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *qui heredi*, § *si*; l. *Meuius*. Second, the temporal adverb must be considered, which speaks specifically, namely the adverb “then,” as in Digest, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. 4, § *si*; Digest, *de usufructu legato*, l. *Vexori usumfructum villae*; Digest, *de vulgaribus substitutionibus*, l. *in substitutione filii*. Third, that word “and in that case” must be considered; for it restricts itself to one case. Hence, in this case, the argument from equivalents ceases, as discussed in l. *si mater*, Codex, *de institutionibus et substitutionibus*, and *de verbis obligatoris*, cum *servus*. And therefore, without doubt, this specific substitution made to Antonia from Alianora vanished, especially because Antonia died with a surviving son; hence, this is the case in the aforementioned l. *ex facto*, § *pen.*, and Codex, *de institutionibus et substitutionibus*, l. *generaliter*, in the beginning, and Digest, *de legatis* 1, l. *filius*, § *cum*. Secondly, it must be considered whether a substitution of conjuncts of the testatrix appears to have been made to Antonellus himself. And here it must be seen whether a substitution could have been made to Antonellus himself. And to know this

It is necessary to examine whether the aforementioned Antonellus is understood to have been honored by the testator. For a person is honored in two ways: in one way as a legatee, etc.; in another way as one taking by reason of death (causa mortis), and either may be burdened with a fideicommissum. C. de fideic. l. ab eo; and ff. de donat. causa mort. l. quod statu libere. But this Antonellus appears to take by reason of death, as noted by Bartolus in de verb. sign. l. mihi, et Titio. Therefore, he could have been burdened with the obligation of restitution; whereas he who is not honored cannot be burdened, according to l. 3, l. si fuerit, and l. sed si sic. What shall we say? Is Antonellus said to take by reason of death, and thus could he have been burdened? Yet, if the testator had said thus: “If Antonia should die without children, then the children shall take by reason of death,” ff. de haer. inst. l. Lucius, in the word “pretulit” [preferred]: which is understood not as disposing, but as giving an occasion for taking, as noted there. But the testator did not say thus: “if she shall not have procreated children.” Hence, even if she admitted children while living, the substitution nevertheless does not come into effect, because the children are not said to be placed in a taking by reason of death, but only in a certain event of fortune; and therefore it does not seem that they could have been burdened; and thus [the property] passes to the father, considering the first part of the testament and the specified substitution.

Now it is necessary to descend to the general clause. The testatrix said: “I prohibit all my heirs and successors in the said hospice from alienating the said hospice to outsiders, but let it always pass in perpetuity from degree to degree to my nearest blood relatives, in the manner expressed and declared above.” Now it is asked whether these blood relatives are admitted by this general provision, among whom the testator preferred Alianora, his sister. And on this point, a subtle argument has been alleged by the venerable doctor, Master Philip. For it seems that Alianora, having been excluded by the special provision, cannot be admitted by the general provision, according to the argument of ff. de leg. 2, l. legatorum, §. qui plures. For she was excluded by the contrary sense of the condition, as if the testator had expressly said: “If Antonia shall have procreated children, then let nothing be given to Alianora.” ff. de mil. test. l. si quis locuples; C. de cond. insert. l. 2. And to this effect is the entire maxim that the general is derogated by the specific, as in c. generi, with its material. To the same effect is the principle that a thing once legitimately alienated can afterwards be legitimately alienated to whomever, according to l. 3, l. pater, §. 15. To the same effect is that it can be alienated to a legitimate successor, as in §. Iul. Agrippa, with its authorities. Moreover, those words, “in the manner above,” seem to repeat everything specifically. C. de inst. et subst. l. poenae.

But the case appears contrary to the law: for whenever alienation is prohibited, another degree is substituted in default of one, and such persons seem to be substituted for one another and burdened; the text is in law 2, *Tales scio*, § *Seia*, and there also the gloss and Bartolus. And with this burden, the right of alienation passes to any member of the family written in the instrument, but it does not pass outside the family, not even to intestate successors. In law 2, *Codicillis*, § *Pe.*, there is the text.
