The words “in the manner aforesaid” do not obstruct this; rather, they support the opinion of Alianora, whom the testatrix preferred above all others, except Antonia and the children of Antonia. Therefore, upon their death, not only is William, who is an outsider and consequently prohibited, preferred to Alianora, but also the entire class of the testatrix’s relatives. In law *Cum ita legatur*, § *In fideicom.*, and law *Peto*, § *Fratre*, I think that even if it were true that Antonellus could not be burdened, this does not greatly affect the matter: for we are not speaking of a personal action arising from the will; rather, any possessor is immediately liable as possessor of the thing by vindication, which is granted for a thing bequeathed by the testator, as in the Code, *Communia de legatis*, laws 1 and 2. And therefore I hold for Lady Alianora, and I answer to § 15 as noted in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law *Voluntas*. And regarding the argument from genus and species, I say that they do not speak of this case, but of circumstances otherwise existing, namely, when the children are dead. And then the general clause prevails, since nothing is found to have been provided by the special clause, which the sorrowful testatrix extinguished, lest her blood relatives be deprived of the houses in which she had raised them, as in the Code, *De administratione tutorum*, law *Lex, quae tutores*. It is highly pertinent to human affection that hospices are notable, as noted by the gloss and Cynus in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law *Quotiens*, which gloss is very notable, although it is common. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The question, furthermore, whether it induces a claim for restitution.
2. When a specific item is left in place of a quantity, whether it appears to have been left with the intent of compensation.
3. Whether a legacy appears to have been left with the intent of compensation against a profit arising from a marital agreement.
4. Whether a bequest appears to have been made with the intent of compensation, yet doubt is raised by the disposition of the law.
5. A statute must be interpreted as far as possible in accordance with the common law.
6. How a statute providing for the maintenance of a widow is to be understood, and how such maintenance is to be provided within the husband’s house, and how outside the house.
7. If a woman is maintained by her brother, the heirs from whom maintenance was bequeathed are not thereby released.
8. Custom must be observed.
body:
In the restitution of the dowry, and of the donation made on account of marriage, the procedure is as follows and in this order: namely, that although it is contained in the dotal instrument that the dowry ought to be restored immediately upon the death of the husband, nevertheless the heirs of the husband are bound to the restitution of the said dowry with a term of one year for making the said restitution, even if the heirs and obligors have the things given in dowry. And if a single son, or several sons, remain from one deceased [husband] and a surviving wife, that wife does not gain the donation made on account of marriage if no daughter remains; she gains from the said donation whatever was written in the part concerning the gain. Which said donation is likewise to be paid within the said term of one year, notwithstanding that a shorter term was appended in the dotal contract. And the heirs of the husband and the obligors are bound to provide alimony to the said lady, even during the aforementioned period of one year, and until the dowry and donation have been fully satisfied. And if the marriage were dissolved by the death of the wife, etc.

The facts are as follows: First, Peter Contis confessed to having received from Niccolò Franci, paying for the dowry of Lady Joanna, sister of the said Niccolò and then future wife of the said Peter, 400 gold florins. And upon the restitution of the said dowry, he promised that in the case where the said lady survived the said Peter and no children remained, the said lady would gain from the donation propter nuptias 80 gold florins. Then, notwithstanding the said confession, the aforementioned Niccolò promised to the said Peter for the said dowry 400 florins. Second, John, brother of the said Peter, obligated himself to the restitution of the said dowry and donation. And in that second obligation, the said Niccolò paid 200 florins of the aforementioned sum, as appears from the instruments. Then, after the marriage was contracted between the said Peter and Lady Joanna, the said Peter, coming to death, made a testament, in which, among other things, he left by way of legacy to Lady Joanna, his wife, for her dowries, which he had from her at the time of the marriage contracted between them, for the restitution of the dowry, the aforementioned 300 florins. He also left the said lady, his wife, as usufructuary of the goods of the said testator, as long as she wished to remain in the house of the said testator, and observed and wished to observe a widowed, chaste, and honest life. He also left to the said lady the habitation of the house of the said testator, as long as she observed the aforementioned life and remained in the said house. He also left to the said lady the bed of the said testator, in which he lay, as it stands, and with the ornaments it has. He also left to the said lady one pair of shirts, which are in his chamber. He also left to the said lady all her garments made for her back, except pearls, gold, and silver. He also willed that the said lady might use all the household goods of the said testator necessary to the said lady, as long as she remained in the house of the said testator and observed the aforementioned life. Finally, after the death of the said Peter, the aforementioned Lady Joanna, his former wife, left the house of the said Peter and did not inhabit it, and remained in the house of the brothers of the said lady, and there received alimony from the said her brothers.

Now, from the aforementioned facts arise disputes between the said Lady Joanna on one part, and Lord John, in his own name and as heir of the said Peter, on the other. For first, the said lady says that she ought to have the aforementioned legacies made to her of the aforementioned things, namely the value of the bed, ornaments, shirts, and garments, except pearls, gold, and silver, notwithstanding that she did not remain in the said house. On the contrary, it is said on behalf of the said John, heir of the said Peter, that she ought not to have the said legacies, because they were left to her under a condition, namely, as long as she remained in the house, by virtue of the donation, etc.

Second, it is said on behalf of the said John that, insofar as the said things were purely bequeathed, the said things appear to have been left with the intent of compensating them with the said 80 florins which the said lady ought to gain by virtue of the statute and by virtue of the pact contained in the said dotal instrument, because he is a legal debtor. On the contrary, it is said on behalf of the said lady that it does not appear that he bequeathed with the intent of compensating, because he is a debtor by virtue of the promise contained in the said instrument, and not by legal disposition.

Third, it is said on behalf of the said lady that she ought to have alimony from the day of the death of the said Peter, for two years and beyond, since the dowry of the said lady was not restored, nor the donation paid, both by virtue of the common law and of the statute providing that the heirs of the husband and those obligated to the restitution of the dowry are bound to provide alimony, even within the year, and until the dowry and donation have been fully satisfied. On behalf of the said John, it is said that she ought not to have alimony, because she remained in the house of the brothers of the said lady, from whom she received alimony, where she worked. To which it is replied on behalf of the said lady that she ought to have alimony from the said John under the aforementioned titles and reasons, and especially because she alleges a custom that, notwithstanding that she remained outside the house of her husband after the death of the said husband, and has alimony from another, nevertheless she ought to have it from the heirs of the husband and those obligated to the restitution of the dowry. And because she says that she obligated herself to her brothers for the restitution of the alimonies received from the said her brothers, it is answered by John that the brothers appear to have donated such alimonies.

Fourth, insofar as she ought to have the said alimonies, how they ought to be granted: whether according to the mode and quantity of the dowry and the donation propter nuptias, or according to the quality and condition of the persons of the lady and the deceased husband, or according to the ability of those owing to pay the alimonies, or according to the custom of the place, which is alleged by the said lady.

Fifth, it is said on behalf of the said John that the said lady ought to restore the expressed quantity, namely for widow’s garments and other things delivered to the said lady for the death of her former husband, which quantity is said to have been 35 gold florins and more, or at least the said garments and other things, which he says are in her possession. On behalf of the lady, it is answered that she is not bound to the aforementioned, even assuming she had them; because the custom is for the wife to be clothed during the mourning of her husband by the heir with widow’s garments.

Now it is asked, what is the law in the aforementioned matters? Having seen the instrument of the dotal promise made by the said Niccolò, in the instrument of the promise of the said John, and of the payment of 100 florins, and the statutes, laws, and allegations of the parties, which are transmitted to your prudence: upon which it pleases you to give your counsel, proven in written laws and statutes, and sealed with your seal. Because the arbitrators elected by the parties to decide on the law and the fact intend to decide according to your counsel, and it pleases you first to declare what is the law in the aforementioned matters, and then whether the custom has any effect.

† On the first point concerning the force of the word "item," namely, whether it induces repetition when placed between legacies made to the same person. Some say that it does, by the law *In repetendis*, *De legatis* 3, and the Institution *De rebus diuisis*, § *Item lapilli*, especially since not only is the condition placed before, but also after, as if the extremes give understanding to the means, as in the Extravagant *De appellationibus*, chapter 2, *Requiris*. Others say the contrary, for sometimes there are several forms of legating, and each is perfect, and then the word "item" does not induce repetition, because when the sense of the sentence is perfect, nothing ought to be added to or taken from it. But when one sentence requires the aid of another due to imperfection, then a tacit and interpretative repetition is induced; but a sentence that is perfect and clear in itself does not require repetition, nor glossing, for it would have been easy for the testator to repeat if he had wished. And because in wills interpretation is broader, hence we ought not to imply a condition to restrict the favor of the legacy, and the same applies in contracts, as in the Digest *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Si ita stipulatus*, § *Griso*, at the end, and § *Et*, and in the Digest *De hereditate instituenda*, law *Si quis ita scripserit, Titius*, and this is held by Bartolus in the said law *In repetendis*, and thus he advised in the counsel which begins, *Visa facti narratione*. And therefore the legacies to which no condition is inserted, the said lady Pura ought to have, as she claims.

† On the second point, it must be said that they do not appear to have been left with the intention of compensating with 80 florins. And therefore the edict on the alternative ceases to apply, and this for three reasons. First, because where a quantity is owed, and a specific item is left, it does not appear to have been left with the intention of compensation, cf. D. 32.1.1 (l. plane).

Secondly, that which is legal but contractual, unless arising from a contract, and when there is a contrary agreement regarding the proportional acquisition of the dowry. C. de pact. convent. auth. æqualitas. It is certain, however, that every donation proceeding from a person and to a person is called a voluntary and liberal act, as ff. de leg. 3. l. 11. §. si rem and ff. de adim. leg. l. rem legatam. And liberality conferred in one will is not offset against another conferred in another will. ff. de probat. l. quinquaginta. The third reason rests on the understanding of the authenticum præterea. unde vir, et uxor, and l. si condotem. §. si pater. sol. matr.

† which laws speak, that the disposition of the law induces a debt without any act of man. For then a man is considered to bequeath, or give, with the intention of freeing himself from a purely legal burden. The example is in the father, who is bound to provide a dowry for his daughter, and in the legitime, in which the dowry is imputed, as in l. quoniam, Novella, de inofficioso testamento, and in the aforementioned auth. præterea. This is a special case: because that benefit was introduced as a substitute in the absence of human provision; but here we speak of a profit which arises from agreement, not from law, as noted in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali. And therefore, in case of doubt, it does not appear to have been left with the intention of compensation. C. de hereditate acquirenda, l. si adulta, de legatis 2, l. creditorem.

† On the third point, it must be considered that a statute, insofar as possible, ought to be understood in accordance with the common law, as is stated in C. de noxa, l. 2; de consuetudine, c. Cum dilectus. This is because the authority to enact statutes is granted by the common law, as set forth in l. Omnes populi, ff. de iustitia et iure. Therefore, a statute that is not expressly contrary to the common law refers back to the common law as its primary subject matter.

† And therefore it must be said that the statute providing for the maintenance of a widow is to be understood as applying provided that the widow can live honorably in her husband’s house and work for her husband’s heirs, as in the law *Sicut* in the title *De operis liberti*; but if she cannot honorably reside there, then she must be maintained outside the house, as in the law *Pe.* in the title *Ubi pupillus educari debeat*. Furthermore, if it is the custom of the country that upon the death of her husband without children, the widow leaves her husband’s house and goes to her parents’ house, then she must be maintained outside the house; because this does not depend on her will, but on custom, as argued from law 1 in the Code, title *De legibus*.

† On the fourth point, whether these alimony payments are to be made according to the capacity of the entire patrimony, or according to the capacity of the dowry and the donation. Response. Since she is supported in the husband’s household, she ought to be supported as she was during the husband’s lifetime, since she still bears his image and maintains his household, even if she had no dowry, because this operates to the benefit of the husband’s heirs. D. de comm. omn. l. in rebus; § possunt, D. de leg. 3; l. Item in legato; § parui, D. de sol. mat. l. si cum dotem; § si in seuissimo. But when alimony is provided outside the husband’s household, then it is due from the common fund according to the measure of the dowry: because the dowry is the final basis for the provision of alimony, and such alimony takes the place of a kind of interest. C. de rem in præsenti; § exact. And therefore they are to be provided according to the measure of the dowry, not of all the husband’s goods, arg. D. de alim. leg. cum unus; § alimentis; and l. qui filium, where it is said that a ward ought to be educated. And although the woman is supported by her brother, the husband’s heirs are not thereby released, because satisfaction has not been made in their name. C. de usuf. l. 1. Therefore, in our case, alimony is understood according to the quantity of the dowry and the donation. D. de ann. leg. l. liberto; § largius. Therefore, a woman having a dowry ought to be clothed and nourished from the dowry, namely from the fruits, insofar as they could be collected in an honest manner. Extr. de donat. inter virum et vxorem, cap. per vestras; l. ubi adhuc, D. de iure dotium; and d. auth. præterea, C. unde vir et vxor.

† On the fifth point, it must be said that custom is to be observed, as in l. venditor, §. si constat, of the title *de communibus praediorum*, together with similar authorities; for what has been done is done as custom requires. Finally, it must be known that the legacy of 400 florins is valid, as in l. cum scriptum, of the title *de dote praedicta*, and in the Code, title *de falsis causis adiectis*, l. l., l. si, §. si non designata, 2. responsio, and l. si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a father may burden his daughter in her dowry, so that the property thus burdened may not thereafter be disposed of by her by will.
body: On the second point,

Whether the lady Countess could make a will regarding her dowry, it must be said that she could undoubtedly make a will regarding her legitimate portion: because no substitution by fideicommissum could be made to her in that portion. But above the legitimate portion, the question arises whether a father can burden his daughter with a dowry which he gave to her inter vivos, and which in no way is to return to the father and his heirs. On this question, note the Digest, ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, § maritus. The solution is: if the dowry were to be returned to the father’s heirs by stipulation, then the daughter can be expressly burdened above the legitimate portion; otherwise, if the dowry is in no way to return to the father’s heir, because the father cannot make a will concerning another’s right, which does not pertain to him but to the daughter. Codex, de inofficioso testamento, Authentica unde si parens; Digest, familiae herciscundae, l. Pomponius; Philadelphus, l. finalis; Digest, de collatione dotis; Codex, communia utriusque iudicii, l. finalis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if a marriage has been contracted by words of the present tense between persons related in the fourth degree, and the Pope is unwilling to grant a dispensation, or one of the contracting parties is unwilling to await the dispensation, he may freely contract marriage with another.
body: The matter is discussed.

† Concerning the kinship between a certain pubescent girl and a certain pubescent youth, who are related to each other in the fourth degree of consanguinity according to the reckoning of canon law, and it is sought that a betrothal by exchange of rings (subarrhatio) take place, and it has taken place with the intervention of consent expressed by words of the present tense. It is certain that these betrothals can be ratified by the disposition of the Pope, as in the chapter *Literas*, *De restitutione spoliatorum*, because in this degree betrothals are not prohibited by divine law, but by the constitution of the Church, as in the chapter *Non debet*, *De consanguinitate et affinitate*. But let us suppose that the Pope does not wish to dispense, or one of the youths does not wish to await the dispensation; can he otherwise contract marriage? I answer: A marriage that is not binding does not create an impediment to marrying another, unless that other person is within the kinship or affinity of the first up to the fourth degree; for then, by the prohibition of public honesty, he would not be bound. All this is noted in the chapter *Non praestat impedimentum*, *De regulis iuris*, Book 6, and in Question 31, Cause 2, chapter *Si verum*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When one party contributes money and the other labor, what is the nature of this partnership, and how profit and loss are not to be divided.
2. Whether proof made after the conventional term is valid, and what applies to judicial proof.
3. Whether and when goods or other things are deemed to have been purchased with the common funds of the partnership.
4. Whether the testimony of witnesses stating that someone purchased something with another’s money, because they heard it from the purchaser himself, is valid.
5. Whether damage inflicted upon the partnership by one of the partners is common, and whether it is presumed to have been caused by that person’s fault.
1. Whether damage that befalls the partnership through robbery or other fortuitous event is common.
2. On all the above, see the following opinion.
body: In this question

I say, the partnership contracted between these parties is of this species: because one contributes capital, the other contributes labor and effort. For this John alone navigated, if necessary, he alone traveled abroad, he alone undertook the risks: as in *l. si non fuerit*, § *i.*, D. *pro socio*. Hence, the price contributed from the other side is the covering of the other’s labor and skill, as in *l. si duobus*, § *si in coeunda*, D. *pro socio*. In this species of partnership, if neither profit nor loss occurs, the entire capital is to be restored; if, however, profit occurs, the capital is to be restored together with half of the profit. If, however, there is a loss from the capital, a diminution is made to the extent that the loss covers it, and the labor of the other party is sterile and without fruit for him. This is proven in *l. 1*, through the gloss and doctrine, C. *pro socio*, and also from the pact of the partnership itself, according to *l. 1*, § *si convenerit*, D. *de deposito*. Therefore, in what manner the writ is to be executed according to the form of the statute cannot appear before the accounts are rendered. But after the accounts are rendered, if there is profit, let execution proceed against the capital and the half of the profit; if there is neither profit nor loss, [let it proceed] against the capital only. If, however, the loss absorbs it entirely, let no execution be made, or not. This is proven by the laws in *l. si cui libertas*, and *l. cum servus*, and *l. qui sub conditione*, D. *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, and in *l. statu liber ratione*, D. *de statu liberorum*, and *l. si ita fuerit*, in § *quod haec est*, D. *de manumissione testamento*, with similar authorities. Hence, before the accounts are rendered, there is no place for an exception, especially with respect to giving or paying; because it is not clear to the praetor, as in *l. haec autem*, § *fi.*, D. *quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur*. And because ignorance of that from which the form of jurisdiction arises impedes jurisdiction, as in *l. nullum*, and what is noted there by Bartolus, D. *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, hence it applies also *l. quæro*, D. *de eo qui pro tutore*, and *l. 3*, § *sed si cum tuto*, D. *iudicatum solvi*, and by Guillaume in *l. observare*, § *pro hoc ingressu*, D. *de officiis proconsulis*, and the law. Therefore, the judge acts well in wishing to be certified by granting a delay regarding that which might appear in the remainder, so that it may be seen in what execution could be made; since the other party asserts that in the remainder [the assets] remained due to the robbery, which the said John and Jacob alleged concerning the things of the aforementioned partnership. And from this it is answered to the statute on guarantee, which wishes that no exception be admitted against the execution of the writ, except an exception of payment to be proven in a certain form: because it is true that no exception is admitted against the execution of the writ, except an exception of payment, insofar as the said writ comprehends or restricts. But in our case, if the exception were true, the said writ would restrict or comprehend nothing; because there would be nothing in the remainder; therefore, hearing the common [claim], as if there were nothing in the remainder, is to act against the statute. Moreover, the statute, which prohibits proving any exception against the execution of the writ, presupposes a debt that is liquid, clear, and open; with this presupposition, no exception could be opposed or proven. But to liquidate the very debt, so that less other things may be seen, by whom and how much the debt is, or appears, the statute prohibits: as in *l. divus*, D. *de testamento militis*, *l. 1*, § *i.*, and what is noted there by the gloss, and what is noted by Bartolus, D. *quod vi aut clam*, and *l. ita pudor*, D. *de adulteriis*. And if it is said that he promised to return the said 100 florins with half the profit: and thus the debt is liquid. It is answered that this is true where profit arises, as in the instrument, not only if no loss arises; because although he promises to return the capital with half the profit, the capital remains in the obligation when profit ceases, as in *l. si cui servi omnes cum peculio*, D. *de legatis 1*. But where loss arises and is alleged to have occurred, the instrument says nothing, except that the accounts be rendered. We therefore remain with the disposition of the common law, by the virtue of which a diminution of the capital is made. Moreover, the promise, which is contracted over the partnership, is understood according to the nature of the contract itself, as in *l. stipulatus*, D. *de usu*, and *l. inter stipulantem*, in the beginning, D. *de verbis obligatorum*. And this concludes the first doubt.

The second doubt is as follows: since the said John promised that, if anything were lost from the said damage and loss, he would prove it within one month then next ensuing from the day of the damage and loss, by means of two or more suitable and credible witnesses; whether the said John should be heard, after the lapse of the said month, unwilling to show and prove the loss of the said damage, if the damage is alleged to have occurred by a fortuitous case, especially by a public theft and publicly done with contempt in the city. And regarding this point, I stand with the honest men and advocates of the parties, who hold that after the lapse of the conventional term, there is room for proof. First, from that foundation, because if a judge gives a term to one of the parties for something, and after the lapse of the term he is heard, if the right of the adversary is not made worse, for example, because his defenses are safe: as in *l. mancipiorum*, *de optione legati*; and what is said there by Doctor Bartolus and by Cynus in *auth. iubemus*, *C. de iudiciis*; and in *l. si ea*, *C. qui accusari non possunt*. Second, from another foundation, which was: rather, because the parties did not proceed to further steps by denying further hearing, or that the damage is to be considered as not having occurred, unless it is thus proved. This is stated by Innocentius in *c. cum tua*, *extra, qui matrimonium accusare possunt*; it is supported by *l. Titia*, *ff. de accusationibus*; and *l. sed et si per praetorem*, § *sed et si cum decreto praetoris*, *ff. quibus ex causis maiores*. And if it is said that these speak of a term assigned by a judge, whereas here we speak of a conventional term, because the act of a judge acting legitimately represents the act of a father, as in *C. de evictione*, *l. si ob causam*; and *l. 1*, § *haec verba*, and what is noted there, *ff. ne vis fiat ei*. Also, from a third foundation, from the nature of the purification of delay: for although days and penalty are added with respect to the penalty to be claimed, nevertheless no penalty is added with respect to the power of proving or not proving, as in *l. si insulam*, *ff. de verbis obligatis*. To this effect, one statement of Guillaume in the said *l. iubemus*, *C. de iudiciis*, is well suited, where he holds that, notwithstanding the term, a publicly known act can still be proved. It is supported by *l. 1*, *C. si, et adversus quos*. To this effect, what is noted by the gloss in the said *l. iubemus*, and the gloss in *Auth. ut sine prohibitione matres debitrices, et creditrices etc.*, § *quia multum*. Also, the proof of which the contract speaks was not required for any other purpose than that the said Lellus might be certain, not for the purpose that he should do something else. If, therefore, he had been publicly and tumultuously plundered in the same city, no other proof is expedient: because he who is certain need not be made more certain otherwise, as in *l. 1*, in fine, *ff. de actione empti*; and by Dyacinus in *c. eum, qui certus*, *extra, de re iudicata*, lib. 6. And in many similar laws, *l. emptorem*, *ff. de actione empti*, is well suited. Hence, regarding the present doubt, I do not insist further.

The third doubt is as follows: because, as appears from the instrument, the said Lellus gave power to the said John, with the said 200 florins, to trade, work, and do business in the art of bombazine and guarnelli, and in any other art he wished to engage in, sharing in profit and loss. And it is proved by the witnesses of the said John that, after receiving the said 100 florins, he had and kept a shop of guarnelli, bombazine, and other things pertaining to the said art; and that in the same shop there were such goods worth 200 florins and more, according to the form of *l. pro rata rerum*, *ad l. Falcidiam*; and *l. 2*, *C. de rescindenda venditione*; and what is noted in *l. unica*, *C. de senatusconsulto, quae pro eo, quod interest, proferuntur*. Also, some witnesses say that such goods were bought with the money of Lellus, assigning the cause of knowledge: because they heard it from the said John and from many others; and one assigns the cause, because he heard it from the said Lellus. And another, who saw the said Lellus settling accounts with the said John concerning such goods. And another also says that he heard from the said Lellus that they were of his money. And similarly, concerning the merchandise of beasts, he assigns the cause that he heard from the said John that the said beasts belonged to the said Lellus, John, and his brother. From this arise two doubts. And the first is, because the said John alleges that the said beasts were bought with the money of Lellus, and also with the moneys of the said John, according to *l. si adultero cum incestu*, § *idem Pollioni*, *ff. de adulteriis*.

† Whether the said goods are presumed to have been purchased in the common name and converted into common property, or not. In this doubt, it seems to be said that they are presumed to have been purchased in the common name of both. And I marvel that so many doctors do not allege this. For this seems to be the case that they were purchased in the common name, in the law *Quae negotiationem*, D. de administratione tutorum, thus inducing: if an uncle, as tutor of his nephew, conducts business in his own name, or if it is doubtful whether he acted for himself or jointly for himself and his ward, the nephew, even in doubt it is understood that he traded in his own name. And according to the common law, the profit would pertain to him alone. The law *Et magis*, D. de solutione doni, serves well. Bartolus holds this expressly in his own terms in the law *Titium et Mevium*, in § *Altero*, D. de administratione tutorum. And this is true, unless the father had mandated the tutor to conduct business in the ward's assets. For then, by reason of the preceding mandate, he seems to have conducted business also in the name of the wards; hence it is not the guardianship, but the preceding mandate that is the cause for which it is presumed that the business was conducted in the name of the ward. The tutor was bound to this, hence he acted for the ward and for his benefit, as in the law *Lutius*, in § *Tutorem*, D. de administratione tutorum. The law *Post dotem*, according to the reading of Decius, D. de solutione matrimonii, serves well. If therefore the preceding mandate is the cause of the presumption that the tutor seems to have traded for the ward and in the name of the ward, and not the guardianship itself, as I said above: therefore in our case it must be presumed thus, because the mandate preceded, accepted by the said John, as appears in the said public instrument. Moreover, it can be proved from the text and from what the learned Bartolus says there in the law *Qui in aliena*, § *Si is qui putabat*, D. de acquisitione haereditatis, where such a statement is collected, that when a mandate precedes from someone to do something, and you do it, although you do not express that you are acting in the name of that person, it is presumed that you acted in the name of that person, namely with respect to the mandator, but not with respect to the person with whom the contract is made, unless he knew. To this end, what we note in the law *Si pupilli*, § 1, D. de negotiorum gestione, serves well. If in the proposal the mandate preceded to trade with those 200 florins in the art of guarnellors, etc. And the business subsequently conducted, as regards the mandator, is presumed to have been conducted in his name, as by the said laws. Also to this end serves the law *I*, D. de solutione, and the law *Communis servus*, and what is said there by Jacobus de Arena, D. de acquisitione possessionis. To this also serves the law *Cum oportet*, C. de bonis quae liberis, and the authentic, C. de episcopis et clericis, and the law *Sed si lege*, § *Quod autem*, D. de petitione haereditatis, the law *Nesennius*, D. de negotiorum gestione.

† Furthermore, a doubt arises from this same factual scenario regarding the following question: whether the testimony of those witnesses is valid, who testify that the said John spent Lello’s money, because they heard it from John himself. For, although it is true that they do not strictly prove that Lello’s money was actually converted into those goods, since they did not see it being paid to him for the goods, nevertheless they clearly prove the intent and will of the said John, who wished and declared that those goods were purchased with that money. In support of this, it is noted that if one declared his intent and will to certain persons before the event, certainly, without doubt, the intent and will of the said John is declared. The gloss is to be noted in *l. Fulcinius*, § *Sed si is qui*, under the heading *de fundatione*, in the gloss on the word *animus* (intent), in the Digest, title *Quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur*. It is well supported by *l. Apud Celsum*, in the beginning, in the second gloss, in the Digest, title *De doli exceptione*. Now, just as the power and will to convert the aforementioned goods, even if they were his own, at the time of the said John, into the common cause, or into the cause of the said Lello, depended entirely on the power and intent of the said John; so too, if through the said witness the intent and will of John is proven, that he wished to bring the said goods into the common partnership, his will and declaration must be upheld. It is to be upheld, for not only to the living voice, but also to the dead voice of him upon whose will it depends, as is clear in *l. Nescennius*, and what is there stated by the doctors, in the Digest, title *De negotiis gestis*; and what is noted by the aforementioned Bartolus in *l. Nudatio*, in the Code, title *De donationibus*; and *l. Pro herede*, in the Digest, title *De acquisitione hereditatis*; and *l. Si quis a filio*, in § 1, in the Digest, title *De legibus*; and what is noted in the Institutes, title *De actionibus*, § *Aliæ*, with similar authorities. That his bare will could convert his own goods, not only those purchased later, into the cause of John by virtue of that subsequently arising partnership, is well proven in *l. Huiusmodi*, § *Qui servum*, in the Digest, title *De legibus*; and *l. Cui res*, in the Digest, title *De actione empti*; and *l. Fundo*, in the Digest, title *Ad legem Falcidiam*, with similar authorities. Hence, it seems to be concluded that, as far as the declaration of the said John is concerned, the said witnesses provide proof.

The fourth doubt is proven, although many witnesses, even for the greater part, state that the said robbery and plundering, or raid, occurred without the fault of John, but due to the fault of the plunderers, to whom it seems one should adhere, as if they had spoken more probable truths, as in *l. Ob carmen*, § *Finalis*, in the Digest, title *De testamento*; and because everyone is presumed good, etc., as in *l. Quidam*, in the Code, title *De legibus*; and *l. Non omnis*, in § *A barbaris*, in the Digest, title *De re militari*; and *l. Servos*, in the Digest, title *De testamento*. Nevertheless, because some said that it was due to his own cause, since he was on the side of the Lord Catalan, and a rebel against the city.

Whether such a deposit is prejudicial to him, inasmuch as this Lellus ought not to suffer damage arising from his own enmities, and the said John is bound to repair the damage to the said Lellus. Concerning which, many laws were said to favor the said Lellus. And first, it favors the said Lellus: because the tenant is bound, if the trees of the leased thing are cut down by enemies, and the gloss adds, even if the enmity was contracted without his fault, that the tenant is bound to repair the damage to his lord. So in the case at hand, since the said John had enemies by reason of his father, without his fault, who hate the partnership, he ought to repair the damage to the lord. For this, the case in the law *Siis, cum quo fundi*, D. de communi diviso, seems to apply. For this part, Master Bartolus seems to hold in the law *His*, in the principle, D. de solutione matrimonii, and the same author in the law *Stipulatio ista habete licere*, in the principle, D. de verbis obligatis, where, however, he distinguishes whether the depredators acted with the intent of hatred of the person, or for profit, for this is not certain. And therefore, I do not think that the said John is bound to make amends for this reason. Moreover, although he rebelled against the statute or the city, and was an enemy, individuals are not bound, as in the law *In tantum*, § *Universitatis*, D. de rerum divisione, and it is not to be granted to individuals, etc., as in the law *Non singulis*, D. de regulis iuris. And especially since, at the time of the said depredation, he was within the city, and was not under ban, nor was it established that he could be killed; and thus the city did not declare against him, Lellus, that he could be offended with impunity, as in the law *Admissionem*, § *Qui deficiunt*, D. de captivis et postliminio. And according to Innocentius in the chapter *Olim*, Extr. de restitutione spoliatorum, and according to Master Bartolus in the law *Hostes*, D. de captivis, and this notable word of Jacobus de Aretino, Master Bartolus places in the law *Ex facto*, D. ad Trebellianum, nor could his goods be depredated, since his person and that of the judge could be had, as noted in the chapter *1*, de militibus vassallis, who is contumacious, in the gloss. Moreover, that saying of Master Bartolus, that if my enemy causes damage to someone without my cause, that I am bound, I understand to be true if fault can be imputed, even slight fault, because he did not guard well, by the law *Ad eos*, D. de communi dividundo, and the law *Sed si de damno*, D. de locato, and by the law *In his*, by contrary reasoning, and there Peter holds, D. de solutione matrimonii. Otherwise, an absurdity would follow, that if he had been most diligent in custody, like any most diligent man, and in no slight or very slight fault, that he would be bound, which would be absurd. That his saying ought to be limited thus, the gloss holds in the said law *Si merces*, in § *Culpa*, D. de locato, where the gloss says: for since he has enmities, he ought to guard more cautiously; but against force and violence, which cannot be resisted, custody avails nothing, as in the law *Si ea res*, D. de aedilicio edicto, with similar authorities.

The fifth doubt is this: since it has been proven, as I stated above, that goods of this kind, purchased in the common name or solely in the name of Lello, were seized and plundered by force and violence during the time of the aforementioned novelty, whether such plundering results in a discharge of liability. And certainly I say that it does, both by the nature of partnership, as is the case in l. si duobus, in §. damna, and §. quidam sagariam, D. pro socio; whence is relevant the law quae fortuitis, C. de pign. actio, and l. 1, C. depositi, and l. contractus, D. de regulis iuris; and also by the nature of the thing: for he was a debtor of a genus with respect to a species, as in l. Titiae textores, in §. finali, D. de legatis 1, and l. naue saufelli, D. locati; and what is noted by Bartolus in l. si certos nummos, D. de verb. oblig., with similar authorities. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Another opinion, through conclusions, on the same subject matter.
body:
On another occasion, speaking theoretically and briefly to the consul:

The first conclusion is that when a partnership has been contracted with the express or tacit understanding that profit and loss are to be shared, if the capital is lost by chance, each party bears half the loss. For example, if I gave you two hundred [coins] to trade socially with this money, and it is taken from you by a fortuitous event, say by robbers, you must restore one hundred to me; thus, one hundred is lost to you and one hundred to me. I have fully cited authorities on this point and do not repeat them. Nor should your consideration of the labor be deemed valid, because the labor was in vain, and although I perhaps sweated greatly to acquire those two hundred, I plowed the sea.

The second conclusion is that when chance protects the defendant, the defendant must raise an exception based on this fortuitous event. And since exceptions were not invented in vain, but are weapons without which the defendant cannot defend himself, assuming the chance event is proven, if he did not raise the exception, it suffices for the defendant to be held liable, as stated in the *Institutiones* on replication, and in § *pactus ne peteret*, in the ordinary gloss, and according to Bartolus. This is true when a fortuitous event gives rise to an exception, as in § *quaesitum*. But when it frees the defendant by operation of law, as when a specific thing is owed and not a quantity, then it suffices to prove the loss, even if no exception is raised, according to the theory set forth in *l. ubi pactum*, C. de transactionibus. In our case, however, because a quantity was promised, liberation cannot occur except by means of an exception, ff. de solutionibus, *l. qui*, 10.

The third conclusion is that the exception must be so clearly proposed that, in its proper form, the plaintiff is truly repelled, as in *l. 1*, § *Labeo*, de fluminibus.

The fourth conclusion is that the articles of pleading must also be so framed that, upon their confession or admission, the effect follows conclusively and formally; otherwise, the articles are deemed irrelevant, as in *l. si quis libertatem*, § final, with similar cases, ff. de petitione hereditatis.

The fifth conclusion is that doubtful and uncertain proof does not avail. *Caput In praesentia*, de probationibus, because from uncertainty no certain conclusion follows. These are theoretical statements. Now I descend to practice, examining the records without going through ambiguities.

I begin with the petition produced on behalf of Lello, as appears from its form. The petition is most clear and the cause is established. 1. The contract is true, and nothing else is proven there. The obligation is also true, because if the cause is true, the obligation is presumed true, ff. de probationibus, *l. quinquaginta*.

I come to the exception of the defendants, and I say that it is most inept, because from the confessed cause nothing follows. The words of the exception state that he was robbed of all his goods, merchandise, and movable things. Note that it says "his," not "common merchandise." Hence this exception is inept and non-conclusive. C. de iure deliberandi, *l. si te bonis*. Consider well and read this exception, if you please.

I come to the articles and headings of the defendants. In the second article it is alleged that John practiced the art of dealing in silk and wool with the said two hundred florins. In the fifth article, however, it is contained that the said John practiced the art of trading in beasts with the said two hundred florins. Now a question arises: these articles are contradictory, because it is impossible that with the entire two hundred florins he did both this and that; and if he wishes to say that he did part in one way and part in another, an uncertain portion in "thus or thus" renders the article void and uncertain. Furthermore, this article, nor any other, states that the goods were bought in the common name, and consequently does not state that they were common. That they were bought in the common name is a matter of fact, and is not presumed unless it is alleged; for where there is a question of fact, even if the law presumes a quality regarding it, such fact must still be alleged, as in *l. si adulterium cum incestu*, verse *allegetur*, ff. de adulteriis.

Furthermore, in the fourth article it is contained that the goods which the said John had, etc., were stolen. These words, "John had," attribute the goods solely to John; for if they were common, John did not have them alone, but John and Lello together, as in *l. 2*, ff. pro socio, *l. Titii*, § 2, de legatis 2. Hence this article declares that the goods were solely John's, therefore they perished solely to John, if they perished, as in C. locati conducti, *l. damnum*.

Furthermore, in the ninth article it is expressly stated regarding the movable things and goods of the said John, therefore not common; for that which is common is not John's. This is a brocardic rule in *l. 2*, ff. de conditione instituta, and the gloss decides this.

I come to the statements of the witnesses, and because two things must be proven, first that the goods were bought with those 200 florins, second that those goods were stolen, I do not find that any witness says that the goods said to be stolen were purchased with that quantity of 200 florins, nor that this can be concluded by the reasoning of any witness. For sometimes the reasoning of a witness extends the statement of the witness, sometimes it restricts it, sometimes it confirms it; here it does none of these, and it does not prove that this is what results from that. *l. neque* and *l. non hoc*, C. unde cognoscitur. Rather, if they prove something was bought, neither with this money nor with another, from which he could have held this money in his purse, consumption is not presumed, as in *l. si a furioso*, si certum petatur.

Moreover, it must be known that the witnesses who attempt to say this contradict the positions of the defendant; for they refer only to the art of dealing in silk and wool, and the articles speak of the art of trading in beasts, and in this fifth article, secondly, please see this well for caution.

Furthermore, it must be known that sometimes enmity is the cause of damage, and then it is counted under § *culpa*; sometimes damage is the cause of enmity; for he who plunders me becomes my enemy, yet this is called a fortuitous event, as in *l. cum duobus*, in § *quidam sagariam*, and in § *damna fatalia*, ff. locati conducti. In our case, enmity was the cause of the damage: this appears from the destruction of houses, and expulsion from the city, and from the very odious name of partisanship, as is clear in a duel, according to the articles of the defendant.

Lastly, it must be noted that after delay, a fortuitous event does not free the debtor, as in *l. quod te*, si certum petatur. But he who owes an account to someone, under which are also included the remaining things to be performed if it pleases the creditor, is in delay by not rendering it at the appointed time, when time interpellates for the person, as in *l. magnam*, C. de contrahenda stipulatione, and *l. traiectitiae*, § *de illo*, ff. de actionibus et obligationibus. Since therefore John rendered no account in the half-years, he was in delay, and therefore the peril of destruction, even by a fortuitous event, harms the debtor. And to this, and to many things already said, no response can be made.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The successor of the creditor makes use of his rights.
2. The husband cannot alienate the goods of his wife.
3. The grandmother must have license, and the trebellianic portion is charged upon her from the person of the granddaughter.
body: † Heir of Gabriella

† The said Angela is owed 250 pounds; however, she must assign to herself the rights over the goods of Felice. L. Mulier, Qui potior in pignore habeatur. And from these assigned rights, the said Angela will be able to proceed against the goods assigned to the subsequent creditors, as stated in L. Assiduis, Qui potior in pignore habeatur, where it is said: "He who succeeds to the place of the prior creditor uses his right." C. De his, qui in priorum creditorum loco succedunt, L. 2, cum simili. And this concludes the first point.
† On the second point, it must be said that Felix could not alienate the property of his wife. Codex, De re vendicata, l. Mater.

† On the third point, it must be said that the aforementioned grandmother is entitled to her legitime and the Falcidian portion in the person of her granddaughter, as in the chapter *Ray* and the chapter *Raynal*, *de testamento*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that if anyone captures a banned person and presents him to the authority, he shall receive one hundred [units of currency]. Someone captured a banned person and handed him over to a soldier of the authority, who then led and presented him to the authority. Who ought to receive the one hundred? Is it the one who captured him, or the soldier who led him?
body: The facts are as follows. When several citizens of Casteillon, and those residing there, together with the soldiers of the Lord Podesta, having left the territory of Casteillon armed, went towards Montechiaro for the purpose of expelling certain persons standing in the territory of Casteillon who were making certain raids, and for the purpose of capturing certain outlaws present there. Afterwards, one of the aforementioned persons going forth began to capture a certain outlaw condemned by the Commune of Casteillon in person, at the time specified in a certain reform, which is transmitted to you. He who thus captured him, that is, the captor, presented the said captive to the said soldier of the Lord Podesta in the territory of the Castle, and the said soldier finally led the said captive and presented him alive to the said Lord Podesta. Now the question arises, what is the law, having regard to the reform, which states that if anyone leads, and not if anyone captures, he shall have 100 pounds from the said Commune. Whether the said 100 pounds contained in the said reform are due to the said soldier who thus led and presented him.

† Nothing is owed to the said soldier on account of the aforementioned matter, because although he apprehended and brought [the prisoner] to justice, he was obliged to do so gratuitously by reason of the office he held: as noted by Bartolus in l. si quis in graui, §. vtrum, ad Sillam. And because the soldier did not make the capture, nor is it alleged that he captured [the prisoner] by his own merit, hence he does not deserve a reward for having been preempted by another, arg. ff. ad Tertullianum, l. 2, §. si matri, vers. quid ergo, and vers. si forte. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the uncle is admitted to the succession, when the mother has been excluded from it because she did not apply for a tutor, although the uncle was likewise in default.
2. What effect a codicillary clause produces.
body: It is proposed that Potius Lueii, formerly a resident of Sottonio and of Chianciano, died many years ago, leaving behind as survivors Bartholomew and Antonia, who were minors, as well as Antonio Lucii, Fran. Lucii, his full brother, and the mother of the said minors. And that the said minors lived for several years thereafter and died while still in the age of minority, with no guardian having been appointed for them.

It is asked whether the aforementioned mother succeeds to them. I answer: no, as in the Institutes, ad Tertullianum, §. si, de legatis hereditatibus; l. sciant cuncti, cum sequentibus. But whether the aforementioned uncle succeeds to him: Bartolus says that he does not, because the uncle was also in default. But the glossa says the contrary, C. qui petant tutores, l. nepotibus. And so I hold by l. 2, §. uidendum, ff. ad Tertullianum. For he who from the beginning is not bound to request a guardian, is not bound to request one afterwards, and by fortuitous chance he is not bound to request it; because a privilege or exception ought to be perpetual. It supports what is noted in l. 1, C. quibus causis in integrum restituitur, that it is not necessary. Although this fails in a case which does not pertain to our case, and therefore I do not speak of it. And although the aforementioned uncle would not succeed, his sons succeed, who are paternal cousins and nearer to the aforementioned wards. But let us suppose that the mother had accepted the guardianship. It is now asked, since it is established by five witnesses that the aforementioned Potius instituted his sons and substituted to them the aforementioned Fran., and added a codicillary clause, "if it is not valid, etc.", whether the said substitution is valid. And it seems that it is not, by l. hac consultissima, §. ex imperfecto. Nor does the codicillary clause "if it is not valid, etc." obstruct, because this institution is valid among children; therefore the condition of the clause fails.

† On the contrary, it seems that if that clause is not valid, it is understood as valid to the extent that it is valid; but with regard to the substitution, not of the husband by the law of wills, therefore it is valid by the law of codicils, not intestate, but by the law of codicils made in addition to the will, and together with the will. Which I believe to be true, according to the noted Institutes on codicils in the beginning. And it is notable about this clause that it operates not only intestate, but also in relation to the will, and in all ways in which codicils are made. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a lessee may bring an action against a third-party possessor for fruits collected.
body: It is proposed that Odo, the brother of a certain Louis, and the sister of the said Louis, although not his heir, held and possessed the said thing for many years and collected its fruits; which fruits the said Peter wishes to claim from her by virtue of the said contract, by right of lease. The question is whether he can do so.

And I say that it is so, because what has come to the knowledge of the said lord concerning that which pertained to the said Master Peter, it is good and equitable that it be restored to the said Master Peter. D. si certum petatur, l. si me et Titium. The contrary is true, because the contract of lease does not bind a third-party possessor: as D. de pactis, l. si unus, § ante omnia. Moreover, a personal action does not follow the land, as C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. eum. Furthermore, it is expressly stated that a tenant cannot claim fruits collected by another. D. de fructibus, l. si servus, § locavit; and D. locati conducti, l. cum in plures, § messem. It supports what is noted by Cynus, C. de locato, l. si de fundo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the Pope commands that anyone be arrested from a certain place on account of the rebellion of that territory, and that they are not to be released without his special mandate: whether those who were outside at the time of the rebellion are included in such letters.
body: Lord

† The Pope does three things. First, he permits on grounds of reason. Second, he orders and commands capture, from which command he excepts only certain persons. Third, he prohibits in his consultation the release of those captured, and added a clause “notwithstanding.” The letters are clear: because of the crime of rebellion of all, the Pope orders the capture of each individual, prohibiting their release until he shall have given other orders. This is what the Pope intends in sum.

It is therefore asked concerning those who were not present at the time of the rebellion, but were exiles: whether the letters extend to them, and whether such persons, if captured, may be released without consulting the Pope.

It appears that they may be captured, because the form of the mandate must be diligently observed. D. de mandato, l. diligenter; D. de rescriptis, c. cum dilecta; D. de restitutione spoliatorum, c. Pisanis. But the form concerns universally all individuals; therefore, each individual may be captured without any exception of persons. For when something is said universally, it must be understood to include every species contained under the universal predicate. D. de rebus dubiis, l. si is, qui ducenta, § utrum; D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. si servitus.

Secondly, this is proven because the Pope excepts only certain persons; therefore, all others seem to be included. D. de functionibus instrumentorum, l. quaesitum, § idem respondet.

Thirdly, this is proven because this captor is a mere executor, and thus he had no duty to know who were to be captured and who were not, for no knowledge of legal causes pertains to a mere executor. He deals only with the fact itself, as in Extr. de appellationibus, c. novit ille; C. de excusationibus rei iudicatae, l. executorem; D. de officiis delegatorum, c. super quaestionum. Hence, he does not have the duty to know which sheep are from the fold and which are not, for this is difficult to discern and requires a higher inquiry, which does not pertain to a mere executor.

Fourthly, this is proven because the Pope has specially reserved this to himself, and therefore no one else may do this, since it is a matter of reservation. D. de postulando, l. 1, § de qua; D. de re iudicata, l. cum te.

Fifthly, because subjects are punished, interdicted, and suffer reprisals on account of the crime of those holding the city or territory, as is clear in the treatise on reprisals. And thus, on account of the sins of the lord, the subjects suffer, according to that of Horace: “Quicquid delirant reges, plectuntur Achivi” (Whatever the kings rave, the Achaeans suffer).

On the contrary, it seems for several reasons. First, because it is not the intention of the Lord Pope to order that the innocent be detained and imprisoned, as in C. de custodia reorum, l. 1.

Secondly, because if he had expressly ordered this, execution should be suspended until a second order is issued, as is fully stated in the law and noted in Auth. de mandato principis, § si quis autem cui, in the glossa ordinaria.

Thirdly, because the reason of the Pope’s letters should be attended to more than the literal wording. D. de administratione tutorum, l. ita autem, in principio; D. de remissione, l. milites agrum, and the note; D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. si is, qui animo; and D. de legibus 2, l. cum pater, § dulcissimis.

Fourthly, because the letters are letters directed against a certain class of men qualified in a certain manner; therefore, execution cannot exceed the limits of the mandate, and it must be clear to him, at least by information and reputation, that these persons belong to that class, D. de officiis delegatorum, c. 1, in Clementina.

Fifthly, it appears from the form, not only mental but verbal: because the words of the letters say, “We wishing that such rebels, etc.” Therefore, the words do not extend to those expelled, who were not against the city, but for it. No one hates his own partisans and accomplices. Only those who have deserved it are worthy of punishment, as in D. de legibus 2, l. cum pater, § rogo filia; D. de maiestate, l. testamento Centurio. And this is well supported by D. de magis conveniendo, l. 1, § 1; and D. de poenis, l. aut facta, § si; C. eodem, l. sancimus, cum si.

This question seems to be decided thus: either guilt is established, and then he cannot be released; or innocence is notoriously established, and then he must be released; or there is doubt, and then he must be detained until the assembly to be held discovers the truth, as in C. de custodia reorum, l. 2, in fine. And thus I hold, similarly noted in l. ex quacumque, D. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, when one brother is in partnership with another brother, or a partner, a debt arising from a wrongful act, or outside the scope of the partnership, should be common or solely personal.
body: The fact upon which counsel is requested is as follows, namely: Baldutius and Vitus, brothers and sons of the aforementioned well-intentioned Olio, after the death of their said father, who passed away eleven years ago or thereabouts, remained in partnership as brothers, the said Baldutius being over twenty-five years of age, and the said Vitus in the age of pupillage. And by means of a certain factor of theirs, the trade of cutting woolen cloth was exercised. And while they were thus in partnership, the said Baldutius was accused by Cola, husband of the lady Franca, of the rape of the said lady Franca, his wife, and of adultery committed by the said Baldutius with the said lady Franca; and the said Cola promised to pursue and prove the said accusation. And Barnabo acted as his surety. And because the said Cola renounced the said accusation, and the proceedings instituted against Baldutius were circunducted and cancelled, the said Barnabo, the surety, was compelled to pay to the treasurer of the great lord Galeotto 200 florins. And the said Baldutius paid to the lord treasurer for the cancellation and circunductio of the accusation instituted against him by the said Cola 50 florins. These 50 florins on the one hand, and the said 200 florins on the other hand, paid as above, were borne by the said Vitus, then a pupil, for one-half, and by the said Baldutius for the other half, as common money of the said brothers. Moreover, the said Baldutius borrowed from certain persons outside the business, which they carried on jointly and in common, 200 florins of gold.

† Now it is asked, since the said Baldus and Vitus wish to divide all their common goods, debts, and credits, whether the said Vitus, having become of age, can receive and have the value of the said quantities of florins of silver from the said Baldus out of the common money of the brothers, and also the 200 florins said to have been borrowed by the said Baldus, as is stated above, for which he received no security, nor did he borrow them for lost merchandise or for common utility. And what is the law in the aforementioned matters, let it be declared by your counsel with allegations. This Baldus can be considered as a brother; he can also be considered as one having common goods, and he can be considered as a partner, according to what is proposed, although a full partnership cannot be effectively contracted with a ward without the authority of the tutor, as in D. pro socio, l. ut conditionibus; D. de actionibus emptoris, l. Iul., §. si quis a pupillo. If he is considered in the first way, that is, as a brother, it is certain that whether he suffered damages justly or unjustly, he must impute the loss, that is, the damage, to himself, Baldus, and not to his brother, as in C. quibus res iudicata non nocet, l. 1, and l. fin. If he is considered in the second way, as one having common goods, the same must be said, that one of the co-owners cannot prejudice the other, and if he caused any damage to him, he is bound to make restitution, as in D. de communi dividundo, l. si is, cum quo. If he is considered in the third way, as a partner, this must be noted. And the first consideration begins with the person, the second deals with the cause. Regarding the person, it must be known that a ward is not bound by his partnership, except insofar as he has been enriched, as in D. de communi dividundo, l. sed mihi. Regarding the cause, it matters greatly between a partnership contracted in a determined manner for a certain type, for example, for the cutting of merchandise: and it does not extend beyond that, as in D. pro socio, l. societates contrahuntur. If, however, it is a general partnership, this must be noted, that such a partnership does not extend to wrongs, nor to the penalties of wrongs. And there is a threefold reason: first, because a partnership is not understood to be contracted on that which can bring nothing but damage, such as a wrong, as is clear in the definition of partnership. Second, because this agreement is dishonorable, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si a reo, §. fin. Third, because if one partner is damaged due to the fault of another, the injured partner recovers from the one at fault, as in D. de communi dividundo, l. si ut certo, §. sed ubi. Therefore, concluding to the point, it must be said that the said Baldus is bound to the said Vitus to restore to him as much of the money and portion of the said Vitus as he consumed or paid due to the fault of the said Baldus, as in D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. fin. Also, insofar as he borrowed from the portion touching the said Vitus out of the common money, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. Titium et Mevium, §. altero. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What these words placed in the will signify: "I wish this my last will to be valid by the law of wills, or at least by the law of codicils, or of any other kind of last will."
2. What the word "at least" signifies.
3. When an alternative confers a right of election, it distinguishes.
body: The facts are as follows. A certain person made a will, and at the end he says: and I wish this my last will to be valid by the law of wills, or at least by the law of codicils, or by any other law by which it may be more valid.

† Now it is asked how these words: “or at least by the law of codicils,” are to be understood, that is, whether, if it can be valid by the law of a will, it is valid by the law of a testament, and if it cannot, then it is valid by the law of codicils; or whether it should be understood that the instituted heir may choose according to the last law, C. de codicil. This creates doubt, because the testator did not speak conditionally by saying, “if it were not valid,” etc., for then it is certain that if it can be valid by the law of a testament, it is not drawn into a fideicommissum; for this clause is usually appended in default of a testament, as ff. de leg. 2. l. Lucius. §. filiam. and no. C. de codicil. I. 1. and C. de lib. praete. auth. ex causa. Moreover, he did not speak conjunctively by saying, “I wish it to be valid by the law of a testament and of codicils,” for then there would be an election of the heir, as ff. ad treb. l. recusare. §. Titius haeres. and ff. de manu. test. l. si quis seruo testamento; but he spoke disjunctively, when he said, “or at least.”

† For the word “at least” is, according to some, a disjunctive conjunction, or, according to others, an adversative; or it is a diminutive and subsidiary term, as is proved by these authorities: D. de acquisitione et usufructu empti, l. Si sterilis, §. Cum per venditorem; D. de foro competenti, c. Si diligenti; D. de procuratoribus, c. Cum iniuste; D. de privilegiis, c. Cum personae, §. Quod si talis. And see fully Archidamus in c. Statutum, on the word “at least,” D. de rescriptis, lib. 6. It must be considered what this disjunctive or adversative signifies. Sometimes it falls between powers, sometimes between final effects and considerations of the end itself. An example of the first is clear where the word “may” is placed in the conclusion of the sentence, as here, when it says, “or of another, whose [claim] may be stronger.” And note that the word “may” finds a valid principle, and then we examine the most favorable time, as in l. Si ita quis, D. de legibus, lib. 2. As for the second point, consider examples in a condition thus conceived: “If my inheritance does not devolve by right of testament, let it not devolve, or let it come, or be acquired by right of codicils.” Likewise in a copulative conjunction, if he said, “let it pertain by right of testament and codicils.” Likewise in a disjunction, if he said, “either let it come by right of testament, or at least by right of codicils.” And it is remarkable how these forms are in use due to the ignorance of men. In these forms, the final acquisition is examined, and therefore, if the heir did not transmit the inheritance, nevertheless he transmits a universal fideicommissum. D. ad Trebellianam, l. Cogi, §. Idem Metianus. Hence the clause would be very useful for this effect, and for certain others; but since we are in a case where power is examined, it must be known that

† Sometimes an alternative disjunction is placed between remedies. In such a case, the choice belongs to the party acting, in whose favor multiple remedies have been introduced. C. de furt. l. 1, with its subject matter. Sometimes it is placed between cases or contingencies, and then the outcome depends on the cause, and there the choice does not apply. de conditio. et demon. l. cum pupillus. §. disiunctiuo. ff. de condi. instit. l. si haeredi plures. In the present case, the testator [placed the disjunction] between cases of alienation: for, as he concluded that it should be valid in the better way, because a right decreed directly is better than one that is useful and oblique. And it appears that he wished that, if it can be valid with direct effect, that path should be taken; because the testator himself chose such a path through these words. And therefore I do not think that the heir has the option. This is the opinion of Baldus de Perusio, written to his father, the most excellent jurist Michael.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In an emphyteutic contract, in which someone received for himself and his heirs of both sexes down to the third generation descending from one to another, what those words mean. And number 4.
2. Whether the emphyteuta comes into a fideicommissum.
3. Who is included under the term "heir" in an emphyteutic contract.
body: Point. A certain testator, having certain goods, among which were certain enfiteutic goods granted to him and to his heirs of both sexes up to the third generation, died, leaving as his heirs his two sons, namely Palmerius and Herculanus. Palmerius and Herculanus, after the death of their father, divided the inheritance and agreed that each should be content with his share and that neither should claim anything more from the other. Then Palmerius died, leaving one son and one daughter, and he willed that his daughter should be content with a certain sum; he made his son his heir in all his goods and substituted the son of Herculanus, the aforementioned brother of Palmerius, to him. Then the son of Palmerius died without issue, and thus the son of Herculanus succeeded. The question now arises whether those goods, namely the enfiteutic ones, which fell to the share of Palmerius, the testator’s son, pass to this son of Herculanus. Concession

† A suit having been brought against James, formerly of Palmerius of the village of Loretoli, who stipulated and received for himself and his heirs, or to whom he wished to grant or concede his right, limited and completed in the third legitimate generation of both sexes, descending from one to another. These are the words of the instrument. From which James there remained two sons and heirs: as is proposed above; it is asked, what is the law? And it seems that these leasehold goods, which came to Palmerius in part, ought to pertain to his daughter alone: and this for several reasons. First, because the words of the instrument say, descending from one to another. Note that they say descending. In this degree, however, the daughter is descending, not the brother: as in the Institutes, on degrees, §. in the first degree. Moreover, Palmerius could not make a will concerning the emphyteusis to the prejudice of the daughter, to whom it devolves by agreement, as noted by Bartolus in l. ut iusiurandi, §. si liberi, on the works of freedmen.

† Moreover, since the said substitution made to the son of Palmerius was fiduciary, the ecclesiastical emphyteusis does not pass under the substitution; and the reason is that it does not pass to the heirs as heirs, but by the grace of the lord granting it, as noted in the Digest, title *Solutio matrimonii*, law *Etiam*. This is expressly held by Bartolus in the law *Si patroni*, in the beginning, in the Digest, title *Ad Trebellianum*. Nor does it avail to object that this daughter was instituted in a certain quantity, and prohibited from demanding or having more; for she holds this emphyteusis by the providence of her grandfather, not from her father, as in the Digest, title *De adoptionibus*, law *Si arrogator*, section *Sed an impuberi*. And because the heir in a certain thing, with regard to ecclesiastical emphyteusis, is called an heir, as in the law *Filius, vel nepos*, as noted in the Speculum, title *De testamentis*, section 1, at the words *Pone*, towards the end, where the Speculum expressly determines this. Furthermore, since the said substitution is fiduciary, the sister herself is the intestate heir of her brother; if of her brother, then of her father, because the heir of the heir, etc., as in the Code, title *De hereditatibus instituendis*, final law.

† Moreover, the term "heir" placed in such an emphyteutic contract must be understood strictly of the direct heir, not through a fideicommissum, as shown by the argument in the *ad Trebellianam* law *Quia proinde*, and in the *Si ager vectigalis* title, law 1, § *Qui in perpetuum*. For these reasons, it seems that judgment should be rendered entirely in favor of the daughter with respect to the emphyteutic goods. Furthermore, because in a fideicommissary substitution only the testator's goods are included (*De vulgari substitutione*, law *Cohaeredi*, § *Cum filiae*), but the said emphyteusis was not the testator's, except during his lifetime, whereby he could not make a will concerning it, as in the *Codex*, *De legatis*, law *Uxor patrui*. For in the person of the heir there is a new emphyteusis, just as there is a new usufruct (*De verbis obligatis*, law *Stipulatio ista*, § *Si quis ita*). For this occurs in all rights adhering to persons, as in the *Extra*, *De praebendis*, chapter *Dilecto*. And these reasons seem to decide the question. To the contrary, it seems on several grounds. And first, because the Dominus Dynus expressly determines in the aforementioned law *Si patroni* that in a universal fideicommissum the emphyteusis is included. For it comes into the petition of the inheritance not only directly, but also fideicommissarily; therefore, it comes into the fideicommissum (*De petitione hereditatis*, law *Item videndum*, at the end). Moreover, it comes into the action for the division of the inheritance as a hereditary corpus (*Familiae herciscundae*, law *Item predia*). Moreover, an emphyteutic thing can be specifically bequeathed; therefore, it can be left by fideicommissum (*De legatis* 1, law *Si domus*, at the end). For example, the substitute here is equally capable as the daughter, and therefore can rightly succeed to such an emphyteusis. This is expressly held by Johannes Andreae in his additions to the *Speculum*, under the title *De locatione*, § *Nunc aliqua*, words 167 and 168.

† Furthermore, in this matter, those words must be considered: “or to whom he wished to give or grant,” which are broad and comprehend every title; as in D. de edendo, l. quædam, § is autem; D. de publico, l. quæcunque, § in tertiam generationem, cited by Jacobus, who uttered these words. For it must be considered who is speaking, as in D. de usu et habitando, l. plenum, § æquitati. Nor do those words “descending from one to another” stand in the way, if you consider who is speaking, as I have said. And because these words are placed on account of the right of accretion, and in a subsidiary manner, i.e., that it revert from one to another; otherwise it would follow that even if no daughter survived, it would nevertheless not pertain to the son of Herculano, because the words say “descending,” but do not say “reverting,” which is false. Hence, these words must be understood in a certain simple and general manner. C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. si cum ante, according to Cynus. Since therefore the son of Herculano is among the permitted persons, he could rightly be left a legacy by fideicommissum. See C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntas. It should be noted, however, that sometimes one receives an emphyteusis from some ecclesiastical person for himself and his children, without adding “heirs”; and then the opinion of Bartolus is true. Sometimes “heirs” is added, and then the opinion of Decius is true, limited according to the opinion of Johannes Andreas. From these things, the solution of the question appears. Nevertheless, I greatly doubt here how this emphyteusis is to be divided between the daughter of Palmerius and the daughter of Herculano. For this daughter seems, in her own person, first to be entitled to one half, while the other half is to be divided as certain hereditary goods of the said Palmerius, namely into two parts: one part to be held by the said daughter in the person of her brother, the other part to be held by the son of Herculano by right of fideicommissum. C. Raynaldus and C. Raynaldus, Extra, de testamento. For when a male dies, a female succeeds: first, in her own person, to her father; second, in the person of her brother, to her brother. But to the first point, it is answered by the statutes, because a daughter dowered in a testament must observe her father’s testament. And if she is not heir to her father except in the portion left to her, nor is she heir to her grandfather, because she cannot be so except in the person of her father, who survived as heir to his grandfather, as in C. unde liberi, l. qui se patri. And therefore, in her own person as heir, she cannot come to this emphyteusis. It follows, therefore, that she shall have one half for her legitima and trebellianica portion, and the other half shall be held by the son of Herculano by right of fideicommissum.
