See what is noted by Bartolus in the said l. vt iusiurandum, § si liberi, de operibus libertorum. And thus this question seems to be decided, saving the substance of the truth.

Moreover, another doubt remains in my mind: whether, since the statute says that a daughter dowered in a testament is bound to inviolably observe her father’s testament, this prohibits her from deducting the trebellianica portion. I do not determine this doubt, because it does not arise in our case; for she does not deduct it in her own person, but in the person of her brother. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, while the mother is still living, and the uncle of the ward, who dies within a year from the day of the father’s death, the mother is deprived of the succession to the said ward, because she did not petition for a guardian, nor did she assume the guardianship itself.
body: Angelus Massioli of Turre Colla had two daughters, under the age of twelve. On account of a conspiracy and rebellion committed by him, he was beheaded, and all his goods were confiscated. After his death, the said two daughters remained as wards, along with Lady Lippa, wife of the said Angelus and mother of the said wards, and Nutus Massioli, the full brother of the said Angelus. Finally, the said two daughters died in their minority, seven or ten months after the death of their father, the said Angelus, and before a year had elapsed. The question now arises: who succeeds to the inheritance of the said wards, whether Lady Lippa, their mother, or the said Nutus, their uncle? It is presupposed that the said Lady Lippa did not petition for a guardian to be appointed for her ward daughters, nor did she accept the guardianship. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The common opinion is that the mother has one year to petition for a guardian, so that if she does not accept guardianship within the year, nor petitions for another, she is deprived of the succession; but if the child dies within the year, then she is not deprived of the succession. This is most true in our case. See that the mother is not excluded when an uncle exists, as in C. ad Tertullianam, l. Matres; de legatis hereditatibus, l. Sciant cuncti; and Inst. ad Tertullianam, §. Fin. And therefore I say that the said mother succeeds in all the rights of the said wards: although some say that if she does not petition immediately, she is at once excluded. D. ad Tertullianam, l. 2, §. Confestim. I say that the strictness of that § is mitigated today by the constitutions of the princes, and a year is granted to the mother and to all. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the disposition of a testator prohibiting his sons from dividing [the estate] until a certain time is valid, and what division is considered prohibited.
2. Whether a division may be revoked on account of minority of age or fraud exceeding half the just price.
3. Whether a prohibited division may be demanded when one of the partners is quarrelsome or wasteful.
body: The fact, upon which it is sought to have counsel, is as follows: Namely, the deceased testator made his nuncupative will without writing, in which he instituted Baldutius, Vitus, and three of his other sons as his universal heirs. And if any of them should die in pupillary age, or having become of age, he substituted for him and for those so dying the three other surviving sons of his, and the children of the predeceased in stirpes, and not in capita. He prohibited his said heirs that none of them should demand, or be able to demand, the division of the common goods of the said inheritance without the license of their mother, Lady Francischina, until they had completed the twenty-fifth year of their age. The said testator having died, the said three sons and their mother die; so that the whole inheritance of the said deceased came to the aforementioned Baldutius, who is over twenty-five years of age, and Vitus, who is a minor, being only over twenty-one years of age. Baldutius and Vitus, by common agreement, divided all the immovable goods of the said inheritance and the massarities, and proceeded to divide the merchandise and the names of debtors. Of this division there appears an instrument by Guar. It is true, although in the instrument there is no mention that this form was observed in the said division: namely, that they made two briefs stating, whoever receives such a brief, let him have such a part and share. The brief containing the better portion came to the said Vitus. And the instrument is clear, namely, that such goods the said Vitus chose of the will of the said Baldutius for his part, and Baldutius chose such goods of the will of the said Vitus for his part. From the said division arise these doubts: namely, because the said Baldutius, being of age, says that the said division is not valid, and could not have been made, because it was made against the prohibition of their aforementioned father. Also, because in the said division the said Vitus had a part worth two hundred florins more than the value of the part of the said Vitus [sic]. By the said Vitus it is answered, that after the said brothers divided by common agreement, that the said prohibition does not have the effect of impeding the said division, or making it invalid. And because in the prohibition no cause or penalty was appended. And because the consent of their deceased mother could not be obtained, because years have already passed. Also, it is not an obstacle that he said his part was worth more than the part of Baldutius: because he had and received the said part by the will of the said Baldutius; and because against the instrument of Guar. such exceptions cannot be opposed. Now it is asked, whether, considering the said words of the said testament, and the said prohibition, and the said statements by the said Baldutius, and the responses of the said [Vitus], and having seen the form of the instrument of Guar., the said division was valid, and is valid; and whether it can be retracted or annulled by the force of the said prohibition, because the part of Vitus is worth more, namely, than the part of the said Baldutius; it pleases you to declare in your counsel, in your manner.

† For clarity, it must be known that the aforementioned prohibition against demanding partition was valid in law until the age of majority; because such a prohibition may be established by agreement and by will at that time: as stated in D. de communi diuisione, l. in hoc iudicium § si conueniat, and § si inter socios. And this precept is presumed to have been made for a cause, so that minors might not be harmed by their own facility: as stated in C. de usucapione peremptoria, l. 2. And even if it were a bare precept, it would nevertheless be valid for raising an exception; because a cause is not required for securing a release or an exception. Hence, if partition is demanded, the defendant may raise the exception that the testator did not wish partition to be demanded: D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, in principio; D. pro socio, l. si conuenerit; D. de liberatione legata, l. non solum § si liberis. Although he cannot compel partition against the will of the other party, nevertheless the testator did not prohibit them from dividing, but prohibited them from demanding partition. Therefore, partition may be made between consenting parties; because consent was not prohibited, but the demand. These matters are indeed distinct, as stated in D. quae in fraudem creditorum, l. pupillus; D. de rebus ratione habendis, l. amplius; and D. de conditionibus furtivis, l. et ideo. I also hold that even if partition had been prohibited, nevertheless, because it frequently happens that partition is beneficial to both parties, it could be made: by argument from C. quoniam et quibus quarta pars debetur, l. 2; C. de fideicommissis, l. quotiens; because by their common consent they may depart from the prohibition: D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater § libertis. I therefore conclude that voluntary partition was not prohibited by the testator.

† Regarding the second point, it should be known that the division must stand, unless one party was deceived by more than one-half, or unless the benefit of age assists the other party, as provided in C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. maioribus. This applies even if lots are drawn or abbreviations made, as is customary. Although some might argue that fortune is similar to a game of chance, so that no relief is granted to the lesser share, in accordance with what is stated and noted in ff. de minoribus, l. si minor, this is not a good analogy: because in our case, fortune is equated with a good and equitable judge, as in C. communia de legatis, l. si duobus. However, it is necessary, and it appears, that the division did not hold for two reasons: first, on account of age, because the party was a minor; second, on account of the testator’s prohibition, as noted in C. communia dividundo, l. fin. The first point is resolved through the notes in ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § eam. As for the second point, it has been answered above, and therefore I hold that the division was valid, unless there was deception exceeding one-half: for then an action would lie to raise an exception, as I have said. Regarding the third point, I say that

† Division cannot be demanded: because the testator prohibited it, unless the other partner is quarrelsome or detrimental, as stated in the aforementioned law *Si convenit*, Digest, *Pro socio*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a compromise made to two persons with the power to choose a third is valid.
2. How execution of the award is to be sought before the ordinary judge, and whether a formal petition is necessary in such a request.
body: Against

† A *laudum* (arbitral award) rendered by a third party together with one arbitrator is valid, because the compromise made in favor of two persons with the power to choose an uncertain third party does not bind, as stated in D. de arbitris, l. Item si unus, §. Si in duos. And from these words, no authority is preferred regarding the election of the third party. Therefore, what is done by one of the arbitrators with that third party, not elected according to law, does not bind by operation of law: the text is there. Indeed, some say even more, that in this case, due to the defect in the form of the compromise, even the first two are not arbitrators, to such an extent that although they might agree in rendering the sentence, their *laudum* would nevertheless not be valid; because the text says, "I consider such a compromise not to be valid." This is noted in Speculum, de arbitris, §. Sequitur. And this is held by Guillaume Raynaud and Bartolus in the said §. Si in duos. But Franciscus Accursius, disputing, determined that the compromise in favor of those two is valid, and that they can pronounce judgment in concert, and can elect a third party in concert, as reported by Johannes Andreae in the said §. Sequitur, in the additions. And this is approved by the glossa in the said l. Si unus, §. Penult. Also, Cynus in the said §. Si duos, on the word "non valere" (not valid). But if they dissent in the sentence and in electing the third party, it is not valid; therefore, if they agree, it is valid. But the learned Johannes Monachus distinguishes: either we speak of *arbitri* (arbiters), and the compromise is not valid; or of *arbitratores* (arbitrators), and then it is valid. For if I can appoint a procurator to elect an arbiter in a cause, whoever he pleases: why can I not give this power to an *arbitrator*? No reason can be given to the contrary. Thus, general power to substitute can also be given to a procurator, as in C. 1, de procuratoribus, lib. 6. But it is otherwise with an *arbiter*: lest arbitrations be multiplied. D. de arbitris, l. Non distinguemus, §. De officio. Because one does not go to arbiters for the purpose of transferring lawsuits, but for deciding them. D. de arbitris, l. Quanvis. This opinion is held by Johannes Monachus in the rubric de arbitris, lib. 6.

You should consider that when a compromise is made in favor of two *arbitratores*, the election of a third party has no place, unless it was provided in the compromise for a third party to be elected, as in C. de contrahenda emptione, l. Si. For such a compromise does not consist in contradictory and necessary jurisdiction, nor is one forced unwillingly; and immediately upon their disagreement, the compromise ends; because they wish to arbitrate. It supports what is noted by Bartolus in D. de verbis oblig., l. Si quis arbitratu. But if a compromise is made in favor of two *arbitri*, then either no provision was made for electing a third party; and then, if they disagree, they are compelled by judicial authority to elect a third party, as in the said §. Principaliter. And therefore, although they disagree, the compromise does not end, but they are forced to elect a third party, whose authority must be obeyed. And because this descends from the tacit nature of the compromise, it is as if this third party were an arbiter elected by the parties, although strictly speaking he is not a compromise arbiter according to Speculum. Or there is a provision for electing a third party. And then either it is for a certain person, and the compromise is valid, and if they disagree, they are compelled to elect him. D. l. Item si unus, §. Sed si ita. Or it is for an uncertain person, and then if they are in agreement in rendering the sentence, the arbitration is valid; but if they are in disagreement in rendering the sentence, then it matters whether they are also in disagreement in electing the third party, and the compromise ends, because the praetor cannot compel them to elect a third party, because they had free power to elect anyone. Thus is understood §. Si in duos, when it says, "by assuming a third party they can dissent." Hence the praetor cannot force them to agree in sentence or election. And thus such a compromise is rendered futile, and for this reason the law considers it null. But if they agree in electing the third party, the reason for annulment ceases, and a confirming reason supervenes; therefore I consider it valid. And thus says the ordinary gloss. And this is especially true if the third party is elected according to the custom of the region; because it is customary to do and observe this. D. §. Principaliter, on the word "sed vsitatum est" (but it is customary). Or if he is elected in the presence and with the consent of the parties. L. 1, §. 3, on the word "litigatores consenserunt" (the litigants consented). I therefore say that the said compromise, and the election of the third party, and consequently the *laudum* itself, were valid.

It remains to be seen whether the judge, who pronounced that the arbitral award should be executed, pronounced correctly. On this point, careful consideration must be given to whether the arbitrator of the award deserves execution without any petition being presented before the executing judge. And it seems that he does not, because the law states that an action in factum must be brought for the execution of the arbitrator’s sentence. C. de arbitris, l. ne in arbitris; and l. cum antea; and noted by Bartolus, de re iudicata, l. miles, §. si. But in an action in factum, a petition or libellus is required, as ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. item veniunt, §. idem recte; and noted, de inofficioso testamento, l. qui de inofficioso testamento. But here no petition was drawn up containing what a libellus ought to contain; therefore, etc. And if it is said that the sentence is ordered for execution even ex officio iudicis, ff. de iudicibus, l. si praetor, I answer that this does not seem to apply to the sentence of an arbitrator: because this duty should be a mercenary one, which ought to arise from the exercise of jurisdiction in rendering judgment. But since the arbitrator had no jurisdiction, such a mercenary duty cannot arise from it. For jurisdiction is the mother of the judge’s duty. ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. 1. Nevertheless, I do not think one should insist on this point: because custom holds that execution takes place without another libellus. For when the arbitral award becomes res iudicata, it is equated to the sentence of a judge, and therefore deserves execution. Indeed, the production of the award in court, together with the petition for execution, has the force of a certain summary libellus, as ff. de re iudicata, l. a Diuo Pio, in principio, and §. 1. Hence, from the sentence of the arbitrator, once it has become res iudicata, arises the right of the party to invoke the office of the judge for execution, so that there may be an end to litigation. ff. de re iudicata, l. ait praetor, in principio. And in this case, this duty is noble, yet because the judge is not compelled to adjudicate, but only to execute what has been adjudicated, ordinary procedure is not required. In this manner and order, execution is ordered according to the ius commune, to which I refer myself, to avoid the doubts arising from the statute of Gualdo, which are set forth in l. a Diuo Pio. Since therefore it is to be executed, I advise that the judgment of Lord Anastasius was correct. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Things acquired jointly through the effort of two brothers belong to them equally.
2. Whether an uncle who ransomed his nephews from the enemy by means of money can recover that money.
body: Things jointly

† acquired by the industry of two brothers belong equally to them, without regard to the sons or nephews of either of the said brothers, and therefore they belong to each of the said brothers for a half share. C. de bon. quae lib. l. cum oportet makes for this, and in Spec. de iudi. §. sequitur.

† Likewise, if one of these brothers ransomed his nephews captured by enemies or taken by robbers out of common money, he can recover from them for his share through the action neg. gest., unless he did it out of regard for piety; which is presumed if the expense was small, but if it was large, a donation is not presumed, as noted in C. de neg. gest. l. Nesennius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How fraud is proven when a father makes a donation to another for the benefit of his illegitimate son.
2. Unusual precautions and an atypical manner of contracting render a completed act suspect.
body: To Spurius

† A father cannot make a donation through an interposed person, nor can he feign anything in fraud of the law, as is stated in C. de nat. lib. l. 1. siue itaque. However, such fraud is not presumed unless it is proven by evident indications, as in C. de dolo. l. dolum; and C. de distr. pign. l. et qui sub imagine, ver. si igitur; and C. de usur. l. eos, §. fin. In this matter, which cannot be proven clearly, arguments suffice, as in ff. de re milit. l. non omnes, §. a barbaris. Let us therefore examine whether fraud should be presumed from the preceding promise, which is inconsistent with the nature of a deposit, and from the subsequent cession made to a spurious child for a liberal and gratuitous cause, because the act finds a prohibited person, namely the spurious child. And it seems that this is so: because just as possession relates to temporal things, so does cession relate to rights, as noted in l. fi, C. quando fiscus, vel priuatus; and l. penul., C. de do. But if a father gives you a thing, and you give it to the spurious child of the giver, from the conjunction of these acts, and because the spurious child is found in possession, a simulation of fraud is presumed. For when a prohibited person is found in possession, especially gratuitously, it is likely that fraud has been committed, as argued in ff. qui mo. pig. vel hypo. sol. l. sicut, §. superuacuum; and C. de natu. lib. l. si quis feu. For paternal love is prone to such frauds, as in C. de dona. l. data iam pridem; ff. de bon. libe. l. nihil, §. facilior; ff. de probat. l. qui testamentum; ff. de lega. 3. l. cum quis decedens, §. Titia. Nor does any oath operate in this regard, as noted there. But against this, it is strongly argued what is noted in ff. de leg. 3. l. Lucius, §. in testamento, where the glossa says that from these arises such a kind of presumption, not full proof. Hence, Bartolus says in l. lti, de his, quibus vt indig., ff., that if a wife, instituted as heir by her husband and asked to restore to whomever she pleases, institutes a spurious son, fraud is not thereby sufficiently proven unless other conjectures intervene. Moreover, there is no doubt about this fraud, because the said instrument of deposit and the said cession are presumed by law to be simulated. To this effect, see extra de renun. c. si de praebenda, §. fina. But if there are not even other conjectures, then the question is doubtful; nevertheless, these acts strongly suggest simulation: because it is not likely that the depositor, if it had been a true deposit, would have considered the case of the death of the depositary; nor that he would later have donated gratuitously, and especially to a spurious child. See insti. de fideicom. hęredibus, in princi.

† For indeed, unusual precautions and an unaccustomed mode of contracting render the act suspect, as noted in l. 6, de conditionibus institutis. This much weighs heavily on my mind, that it was so in the truth of the facts. Therefore, a prudent advocate, when the time comes, should plead the aforementioned articles, once the litigation is joined, in a petition for rescission of this contract as being simulated, covering all matters that can inform the mind of a good man regarding the substance of the truth; because perhaps the mere assignment alone would not suffice to prove fraud, according to Bartolus. Nevertheless, it contributes significantly to proving what is sufficient, because he who donates an action appears to have acquired it for the benefit of the donee, not for his own. Likewise, this is supported by C. de repudianda hereditate, l. 2; ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. si is, qui bonis; and by what Bartolus notes in de donationibus, l. post contractum. I believe this to be true, because in the point at issue it is presupposed that he who received the instrument on the ground of deposit was not suitable for depositing such a large sum, de bonis quae libera, l. cum oportet, according to Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. He disputes certain statutes that prescribe the form for renouncing an inheritance, yet he does not set them forth.
2. Whether a renunciation made in accordance with the prescribed form is valid, even if those provisions added regarding the manner of selecting arbitrators and the satisfaction of creditors were not observed.
body: Form

† It is established by the statute concerning the repudiation of an inheritance to be made by public proclamation, and this was carefully observed in council, and the repudiation was approved in the general council of the campana. Hence, considering the statute, these ladies Milgla and Giotta are not heirs of their father, nor are they liable to creditors; but because by another statute certain provisions have been added to this statute, it must be considered,

† Whether those provisions regard the form, or not. For certain of these, such as the citation of creditors, seem rather to regard the manner to be observed in the election of arbitrators and in the satisfaction [of debts], as is clear up to the words “observed also and the rest.” For when it says “solemnities and the like,” it implies that the citation of arbitrators, the election, the satisfaction, and the like, of which I have spoken, are not of the solemnity of the repudiation, but only those things are of the solemnity which are contained in other statutes and ordinances to be observed for the substance of the form of repudiation. Equity also supports this, for since the repudiation appears public and not clandestine, it would be unjust to hold these ladies as heirs, as in the Institutes, *De hereditatum qualitate et differentia*, § *Sed his permittit praetor*. Moreover, since this repudiation was approved by those having authority, the statutes must be followed, as in the Institutes, *Qui manumitti non possunt*, § *Semel*. Nor does it obstruct that the statute says, “and if anything of the aforesaid is omitted, the repudiation shall not be valid,” because this is understood to refer to those things contained in that section *Observed also*, that is, as to the solemnity, and as the reference is to be made to the proximate matters, and not to those things said in other clauses. Otherwise it would follow, since it was said above that satisfaction must be made to creditors, that they could not renounce unless first the creditors had been satisfied from the goods, if any are found. And this is perverse and absurd, as in the Code, *De hereditatis actione*, law *Ut debitum*.

To the contrary it seems, and I premise that this statute is valid in law, as it formerly was by the law of the Twelve Tables. In the case of *sui heredes*, who were also necessary heirs by civil law, Institutes, *De hereditatum qualitate et differentia*, § *Sed sui*. Hence the statute could make them precisely necessary heirs, and if it could do so in every case, therefore also in some case. I also premise that the statute wishes that in this case truth should desire the support of words, just as the law desires it in the making of an inventory, in the Authenticum, *De hereditate et falcidia*, § *Si vero absunt*. Nor is it strange that creditors are to be cited, because their prejudice is at issue. For by such citation one finally arrives at the approval of the repudiation, after which immixtion could not be proved, as it could be if they were not cited. Digest, *De adoptionibus*, law *Nam ita divus*, with similar authorities. Moreover, the statute says “observed also,” for the word “also” implies and wishes that all things intervene. And below it clearly adds, “and if it were done otherwise, or anything of the aforesaid is omitted, etc.” Therefore nothing of the solemnities is to be omitted, as in the rule of law, and Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, § *Si praetor*. What shall we say about this point? I answer, if this statute was interpreted in a certain way and practiced for a long time, it must be observed, as Digest, *De legibus*, law *Si de interpretatione*. If, however, this does not appear, it must be considered that the statute gives the minor a year to repudiate, which year has here elapsed, and therefore the time for repudiating does not remain; for within the year it could be solemnly repudiated again, since it is an iterable act. Since therefore the year has elapsed, I doubt whether the statute requires the citation of creditors for the essence of the repudiation. Nevertheless, considering the words of the statute, truth always being reserved, it seems to be said that this is a harsh law, and this opinion is harsh. Nevertheless, even if very harsh, the law must be observed if it cannot be reduced to natural equity by sound interpretation: as in the law *Prospexit*, *Qui et a quibus*. And that which we have in a similar case supports this, Code, *De iure deliberandi*, law *Si*, § *Et si praefatam*, in the word *solidaverit*. I, as I said, doubt also on account of conscience: and because derogation was made to the statutes in the general council of Campania. But here it must be seen whether by another statute, or by custom, they had this power of derogating, and then the derogation is valid. Or whether they did not possess such power, and then they could not derogate from the general statutes; because an inferior cannot abrogate the law of a superior. Digest, *De maioribus et obsequiis*, chapter *Cum inferior*, with similar authorities. And then finally it seems to conclude against the said ladies, the opinion of the stronger authority always being reserved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If sons who have already been born are instituted as heirs and burdened with a fideicommissum on the condition that a posthumous heir is passed over, whether the fideicommissary substitution is valid by means of a codicillary clause.
body: A legacy to the said society is understood as a legacy to an approved college. And therefore it is valid, if nothing else stands in the way, as noted in l. 1, ff. quod cuiusque universitatis nomine.

But it must be considered that the sons who were born were instituted and burdened with a condition; whereas the posthumous son was passed over. Whether the fideicommissary substitution is valid by virtue of the codicillary clause? And it must be said that it is valid as regards the share of those born, but not as regards the share of the posthumous son, as in the law *Is qui*, *De iure codicillorum*. And therefore the share of the posthumous son pertains freely to the mother; but as regards the share of the agnate, the mother must have two quarters, because this partnership is lawful, although not pious; and the other two quarters pertain to the partnership. *Caput Raynu.* and *Caput Raynaldus*, *De testamento*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a curator appointed for the purpose of claiming and demanding can make a refutation, or provide authority for it. Likewise, if not, whether the oath of adults validates it.
body: It must be considered that in the instrument of curatorship these words are found: “so that from their goods she, Catharina Ferrarina, may be married.” Therefore, under this final cause, the curator was requested and appointed. This curator was appointed not for the purpose of confessing, but for demanding or authorizing the voluntary payment to be made by the aforementioned Baldus of the debt contracted on account of management, or from another cause. And therefore, these adults did not have curatorship for the purpose of confessing, unless it were truly proven that receipt had been taken, as in C. de novatione, l. non abstulit. Likewise, by those words, “of things managed and administered, and the rest,” it does not appear that the curator was appointed to release from the remainder, unless real and true satisfaction were made, as in ff. de liberatione legata, l. Aurelio, §. final. Moreover, this curator swore to act usefully; hence he could not authorize dissipation, l. qui fundum, §. si tutor, de usucapione pro empto. Hence, here there appears to have been manifest injury, with no account placed and no remainder restored, as in C. de transactione, l. praeses. Unless, therefore, it is proven that the remainder was returned and other things of the adults were restored, it is established that such restoration was made without a curator. It is true that the oath of the adults intervened, but because it was captious, it ought to be relaxed by the bishop. And sometimes statutes also provide for this, to which one must adhere, as noted by the doctors in Authen. sacramenta puberum, with similar authorities. Whether, however, in the division the matter came to an end? It must be said that it did not, as is clear from inspection of the instrument. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who confesses to a delict, but with a qualifying circumstance, is to be punished. Add the opinion of the co-consiliaries, beginning: “Suppose that a certain...” in the Sixth Part.
2. Either the whole must be approved, or the whole must be rejected.
3. He who swears concerning a fact is deemed to swear concerning the entire matter.
4. Whether those who are exempt and are not bound to pay anything ought at least to show the goods to the customs officer, or to notify him.
1. Whether a single confiscation may be imposed for multiple delicts, each of which individually induces the confiscation of goods.
2. Whether the license of the customs officer is proved by witnesses.
3. It suffices for the defendant that he destroys the plaintiff’s claim, or that he renders it doubtful.
4. Whether multiple delicts, which are finally ordered toward one final cause or fraud, are to be punished as multiple offenses.
5. If a colleague was joined to the first judge, may one alone judge?
body: Before you, wise and discreet man, etc., judge of the gabelle and so forth, appears P. and accuses B. and so forth, saying that the said B. brought and caused to be brought, in order to remove from the City, Countryside, and district of Arno, certain merchandise, goods, and so forth, of value and estimation, and so forth; which goods and merchandise, in the present year 1383 and in the present month of February, the said B. removed and caused to be removed outside to the warehouse or place where he had placed them, unloading and causing to be unloaded at the time of the said conveyance, without the license of the undersigned tax collector. And furthermore, the said B. removed and caused to be removed the said merchandise through the Porta Galliana, outside the City, Port, and district of Arno, without a bill of lading, without the license of the tax collector, official of such tax, and without paying what he ought to have paid within the time and term of the provision of Arno; all of which things, and each one of them, the said B. committed and caused to be done maliciously and deliberately, in order to defraud and commit fraud against the aforementioned tax, contrary to the form of the provision, to the damage and prejudice of the commune and of the said tax collector. And therefore, the said P., accuser, has demanded that the said B., accused and aforementioned defrauder, be punished and condemned by you, and by your sentence and office; and moreover, be subjected to the loss of the said goods according to the provision, modes, and custom of the said gabelle, and the other penalties according to the form of the said provisions, demanding the aforementioned things by way of simple petition and narration of fact. Here, B., the accused, responding and excusing himself, etc., said that he had brought the said goods and merchandise, and had extracted them outside the gate mentioned in the accusation, and had gone outside the gate with the license of the aforementioned tax collector, etc. In the first place, it must be seen,

Whether by this reasoning the punishable abstraction is proven, assuming that, given and having elapsed the terms for proving, nothing else has been proven on either side. And this is an ancient question. For some say that this response does not prove the wrongdoing: because the respondent expressly asserted the contrary, as noted in C. de except. l. si quidem; C. de don. ante nup. l. 2. For since this response contains two things with regard to the construction of the same speech joined together, so that the supposition cannot be separated from the apposition in the construction of the speech: it is necessary that the understanding follows the same inseparability, because the reason of correct speech must not be destroyed. l. Plautius, de auro et arg. leg.

And because either the whole must be approved, or the whole must be rejected. D. de deposito. L. publica. §. si. For concerning the same fact, or the same act, division is not admitted. D. de legatis 2. L. neminem. Nor variation. D. de procuratoribus. L. in causa. Nor concerning the fact and its quality. D. de manumissionibus. L. Gaius. Moreover, Innocentius seems expressly to determine this in C. status. de officio delegati. in 1. gloss. on the words “item si confiteatur manifestum,” where he says that he who says that he acted according to law does not confess a wrongful act. For then it would be notorious, and would pertain to that conservator of whom he speaks there. Hence, this question seems to be determined literally by Innocentius there. Furthermore, it is certain that one thing is the delict, another is the penalty, and one is separable from the other. Therefore, one being conceded, the other is not conceded. C. de infamibus. L. decuriones. C. arbitrium tutelae. L. cum interdictae.

† To the contrary it seems, just as he who swears an oath concerning a fact is deemed to swear concerning the whole, as in l. duobus, §. colonus, and l. si, de iureiurando, and noted in l. 1, §. 1, quarum rerum actio non datur. Likewise, he who confesses a fact is deemed to have confessed also the right, or the bond, which adheres to that fact; because the right is situated in the fact. ff. ad l. Aquiliam, l. si ex plagiis, §. in cliuo. And from the fact being established, the obligation is established, unless the contrary is proved. Moreover, although it were not proved by personal confession, it is nevertheless proved by legal presumption; because in delicts dolus is presumed. C. de sicariis, l. 1; C. de iniuriis, l. si non convitiis. Furthermore, by the confession the fact has become notorious; therefore the maleficium must be punished, and crimes ought not to be left unpunished, unless the judge wishes to suffer what he has allowed others to do by his dissimulation. l. nulli, C. ne sanctum baptisma. Moreover, indulgence ought not to be granted to defrauders of the treasury, in Auth. de manumis., in principio, §. oportet, and §. coges. Moreover, this response savors of a double affirmative, namely, of the fact and of the license. Therefore, the adversary of the respondent ought not to have to prove that the license was not given; because this would be to prove a negative, which is impossible. The negative is indeed proved by the very fact that the contrary is not proved. And thus the claim of the datiarius is founded in our case, not immediately in the response itself. And thus the first opinion ought to be understood. But when a term is given for proving, and the defense is not proved; and thus the second opinion ought to be understood. Therefore, if it is proved that the act was done with the will of the datiarius, it must be punished by the confession and the legal presumption joined together, as in ff. de furtis, l. inter omnes, §. recte. And this concludes the first point.

Secondly, it is asked whether those who are privileged and are not bound to pay anything incur this penalty of non-confession and exemption without observing the form of the statute. And I say that they do; because they ought not to declare the law for themselves by their own authority, but should instruct the praetor or the collector, and with his knowledge, so that collusion and fraud may not be committed against the tax by adding other goods: as in C. de sac. san. eccl. l. sacrosancta. For this matter requires some inquiry: as noted in c. fi. de cen. in cle. in 5. glo. ad Tur. l. 1. §. accusatus. versic. econtra mouet. And so I hold, lest the custom observed in similar cases were otherwise, as in ff. de publicanis. l. si publicanus. §. in omnibus.

Thirdly, it is doubted whether, for multiple offenses, each of which individually induces the confiscation of goods, only a single confiscation may be made. I answer: no, because that which is subject to confiscation is not singular; and the species has not admitted multiplication. D. de legatis 2, l. Lucius, § impuberem. Fourthly, it is asked,

Whether the license of the datiarius has been proved by witnesses having seen the acts. For it is certain that in a right being sought (ius quaerendo), the datiarius may oppose the fisc, and it would be applicable to himself. D. de publicanis, l. fin., § si quis professus. Otherwise, in a right already acquired by the fisc (ius quaesitum fisco), because the datiarius could then not prejudice the fisc. C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. fin. Although it appears that even in seeking a right he cannot prejudice the owner: as in l. qui Romae, § Calimacus, D. de verbis obligatis. But that is so because the messenger had a certain form of mandate. Hence, outside that form, he was not a messenger, but entirely another person. D. de pactis, l. si unus, § ante omnia. And in § si quis professus, he was a publican, and having the office in that manner and thing. And thus he resolves the contradiction of those two laws. Therefore, the witnesses and the chapters upon which they testified must be examined.

It must be known, however, that it suffices for the defendant to establish one of two things: either that he completely destroys the plaintiff’s claim, or that he renders it doubtful, so as to overthrow the plaintiff’s proof by causing the judge’s mind to waver, as stated in c. Cum partium, De regulis iuris, Book 6. For it suffices for the party raising an exception to make the matter doubtful where a delict may be presumed, and not where there is no delict, as in De novo operis nuntiatione, l. Non solum, § Sed ut probari, and there by Bartolus. But if the plaintiff’s proof is certain, it is not overthrown by the defendant’s doubtful and uncertain proof, as in Extra, De probationibus, c. In praesentia; and noted in c. Litteras, De rescriptis; in the Clementina; and in l. Eum actum and l. Matrem tuam, with similar authorities. And on this point, the matter has been most prudently alleged. And whatever can be said by the eminent doctor, Lord Ludovicus, if it is true that the witnesses do not prove the license, the defendant ought to be condemned. Therefore, I speak conditionally, because the statements of the witnesses were not transmitted to me; hence I could not examine them. This is certain: where it is established that the act is condemned by law, unless the defendant’s excuse is clearly proved, the defendant ought to be condemned, as in Extra, De testibus, c. Cum dilecti, in the text, noted.

† Fifth, it is doubted whether several delicts, which are finally ordered toward one final fraud, are punished as several. And in this, the words of the law must be considered, and whether they are distinct in place and time; and whether the law considers each one individually in punishing, as in the law *qui de crementis*, C. de accusationibus; the law *nunquam plura*, with similar authorities, de private delicts.

† Finally, it is asked whether, if a colleague has been joined to the first judge, one alone may judge. And it must be said that he may not, as in the Authentica *De differentia iudicum*, in the beginning, column 9. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a cleric may bind himself to the personal jurisdiction of a secular judge.
body: Cleric

† He cannot bind himself to the personal jurisdiction of a secular judge, as stated in the Decretals, *de foro competenti*, chapter *Si diligenter*, and in chapter 1, § *Et cum iusta*, *de clericis coniugatis*, Book 6. Rather, this must be done through the bishop, from whom he would be personally subject to jurisdiction, if the case had been brought before the bishop. And this would be said of a pact; otherwise, it would not, as stated in the Decretals, *de solutionibus*, chapter *Odoardus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How a mother, who has accepted the guardianship of her son and exercised it for some time, ought to request that a guardian be appointed for the same son if she wishes to enter into a second marriage. And whether the judge is bound to appoint the one whom the mother requested. Likewise, whether, upon her entering into a second marriage, there is room for a statutory or appointed guardian.
body: The case concerning which counsel is requested is as follows. A certain P. died intestate, leaving behind a certain daughter of his, who was a ward and an infant, and a certain Domina Catha., his wife and the mother of the said infant, who had legitimately and formally assumed the guardianship of her said daughter. Finally, wishing to enter into a second marriage, or to marry, she stated this before the judge, petitioned, and named a certain upright, wealthy, and sufficient man to be appointed guardian for her aforementioned daughter, and so forth. The judge, having conducted a diligent inquiry, and having summoned the agnates and cognates, and many good men, merchants, and neighbors, and having found that the person requested and named by the mother was good, suitable, and sufficient, appointed, decreed, and gave him as guardian to the said ward, who promised, swore, renounced, provided surety, and made an inventory, as is fully contained in the instrument of the said guardianship. Now it is asked: First, whether the said guardianship, in the aforementioned form, is valid in law. Second, whether the statute at the end prejudices the said guardianship in any way, such that it is not valid.

† To the first point, it must be said, without lengthy citations, that the instrument is valid. This is so, first, because the author of the specification places hope in the effect and substance of the instrument and its form, as stated in the *Speculum* in its treatise on tutors, in § *Si autem*, at the words *accedens*, by the same author. Furthermore, there is no doubt that when a mother goes to the judge, declares her intention to marry, and requests and nominates a tutor to be appointed for her son who is a ward, the appointment is one of *dativa* (appointed by authority) and not *legitima* (by operation of law). This is the opinion held by the said Bartolus in the *Authenticum Sacramentum*, C. *Quando mulier tutelam officium*, and in D. *De testamento tutorum*, l. *Si quis sub conditione*, at the words *quæro exclusa per transitum*, etc., in which passages he touches upon this point and recites the contrary opinions of those learned doctors, whose laws and opinions I do not cite here, because they are more than fully known to the consulting lord. And because these points are exceedingly clear, I shall not dwell further on them; but let the consulting lord write at length in his usual manner.

† To the second point, I say that the aforementioned statute does not prejudice the said guardianship: because our aforementioned case is totally different from the case of the aforementioned statute, although that statute, if carefully observed, intended to regulate and provide for the case in which the son would not have a guardian, so that the son would not be or remain without a guardian. But in the aforementioned case, he had a mother, and it can be said that there was no interval between the guardianship left by the mother and the aforementioned guardianship assumed by the said appointee. Indeed, it can be said that it continues from then on, and that the said ward had a guardian at all times. This is supported by the fact that when the mother declares her intention to marry, she does not immediately cease to be guardian by operation of law: as the glossa wishes in l. propter, C. in quibus causis tutela habetur, and in Inst. de cura, §. interdum, and as noted by Bartolus in the aforementioned auth. sacramentum, and l. si quis sub conditione, ff. de testamento tutorum. Therefore, when a guardian is requested and immediately accepts the guardianship without any interval, it appears that the ward is considered to have had a guardian at all times. This is supported by l. lecta, ver. dicebam, ff. si certum petatur. The opinions of the Monarch and of my excellent teacher, the renowned doctor of both laws, Lord Baldus de Ubaldis, in his repetition of l. praeterea, C. de pace quam boni fecerunt, are most apt. Furthermore, because the aforementioned statute, if carefully observed, speaks of the case in which the father dies and has not provided for his son with a testamentary guardian, and therefore it intends that provision be made for a legal guardian, which is consistent with the law: because when the testamentary guardian is lacking, there is room for the legal guardian, as in l. si quis sub conditione, ver. sicut, cum si, at the end. But in our case, after the father’s death, provision was made for the daughter according to the said statute, because the mother was appointed as the more proper legal guardian; and thus the said statute once had its application, and the disposition of the said statute was fulfilled. But in our case, we are in a different situation, where, after the said statute has already been satisfied by common law, provision for the guardianship of the said ward was subsequently made by law. This is supported by the fact that otherwise one would have to say that the common laws are entirely overridden in the aforementioned case: which should not be the case where they can be preserved and reconciled, as I have said. Ludovicus de Carminatis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that if a ward does not have a testamentary guardian, a guardian shall be appointed for him by the judge from among the nearest male relatives, or female relatives, etc.: If the mother has assumed guardianship of her son by operation of law, and wishes to enter into a second marriage and request a guardian, does she have the discretion to request whomever she wishes, or is she bound to request one of the statutory guardians? On this point, something is stated in the preceding and adjacent consilia.
2. In the appointment of any guardian, preference is given to the guardian requested by the mother acting as guardian.
body: Statute

† The aforementioned provision stipulates that if a ward does not have a testamentary guardian, a guardian shall be appointed for him by the judge from among the nearest male relatives, or even a female, if she is the mother, grandmother, sister, aunt, or stepmother, and even if she is under 25 years of age, provided she is of majority. The question arises: if the mother is the guardian and wishes to enter into a second marriage and request a guardian, does she have the discretion to request whomever she wishes, provided that she requests a suitable person? Or is she bound to request one of the statutory guardians, considering especially the aforementioned statute and weighing its rationale, which is that those who hope for the benefit of succession should not refuse the burden of guardianship? And it must be said briefly that by this statute all statutory guardians are reduced to the status of appointive guardians, as appears there, where the statute says that the nearest relatives ought to appoint a guardian for him. For this statute differs from the common law in many respects, and thus it is municipal law, and not common law. D. de iust. et iur. l. ius civile.

But it is so that the guardian appointed at the request of the mother, acting as guardian, is preferred to every appointed guardian, as in the Authentica *De nuptiis*, § *Si autem tutelam*, column 4. Moreover, this case of the mother is a case omitted by the statute; therefore, it is left to the disposition of the common law. L. *Cum dotem*, in the beginning, *De iure dotium*. A great question arises in the case of a statutory guardian, but in the case of an appointed guardian no one doubts, for example, that when the reason for the statute ceases, the statute ceases. D. *De administratione tutorum*, L. *Ita autem*, in the beginning, *De re militari*, L. *Milites agrum*, and L. *Adigere*, § *Quamvis*, *De iure patronatus*. But when the mother is in the middle, the reason for the statute ceases, because no one except the mother herself hopes for the benefit of succession, as in the Institutes *Ad Tertullianum* and the Digest, throughout the same title, and *De hereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Consequens*, unless the brothers are jointly related on both sides, and the sons of brothers. And thus it is concluded that the guardian requested by the mother and approved by the judge is the guardian. It supports this what is most excellently alleged by the same authority in *De interdictis*, and L. *Quis sub conditione*, and in the Authentica *Sacramentum*. I do not extend myself further, because in the allegations made by the same authority by Lord Ludovicus de Carminatis, the very truth is contained. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, when alienation is prohibited, the institution of an heir is also considered prohibited, and whether a thing prohibited from being alienated can be alienated together with the universality, is distinguished.
body: On the Prohibited

† Whether the institution of an heir is prohibited by the *ius aleraticum*, and whether true dominion passes irrevocably with the universality. And it seems that it does, if it is prohibited: because the institution of an heir is a transfer of dominion, as in D. de haered. instit. l. his verbis. Therefore, it is an alienation: as in l. 1. de fundo dotali, and it is clear from C. de secun. nuptiis. l. si quis prioris. §. certum. To the contrary, it seems that that which cannot pass by species passes by universality, from which it cannot be separated, since it is comprehensive of all, as in D. de acquir. rer. dom. l. quaedam. Solution: Distinguish, either the right, concerning whose disposition the question is, is not transmissible, because it receives its term and end by the death of the disposer, and in such a right the institution or legacy does not hold, as in C. de legib. l. vxor patrui, and D. de vsufruc. l. Sticho; or this right is transmissible, and then it matters whether the alienation is prohibited out of hatred for the person who was instituted heir, and then even if it passes with the universality, it is revoked, as in D. de verborum obligationibus. l. si ita quis. §. si ea; or the alienation is prohibited so that it may not be transferred through the fraud of the alienator to a more powerful party: and then the institution is valid with effect: D. de aliena. iudicii. l. ex hoc edicto. §. sed in hęredem; or it is prohibited so that the thing may be applied to another after death, and then it cannot be effectively alienated by institution, as in D. de leg. 2. l. peto. §. fratre. Hence, in the last will of the prohibitor, dominion is not transferred, but if the prohibition is by contract, it is claimed by condictio, as in d. §. ea; or it is prohibited so that provision may be made against the weakness of another, and then the prohibited institution is not forbidden, hence a minor prohibited from alienating may make a will, as in D. de lib. lega. l. Aurelio. §. fi; or it is prohibited so that the public interest may be provided for. Moreover, a statute prohibits that lands, from which the republic has collected a tax, be alienated to a *alibratus* [one bound by a perpetual obligation], or to one who can be compelled to pay. Then such alienation cannot be made with the universality, as in l. j. C. non licere habi. metro. lib. 11. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A testament in which a granddaughter is passed over is void by operation of law.
2. Whether a legacy made to be used as the legitime is said to have been made with the intention of compensating for the said legitime.
3. A legacy of another’s property made to a joint heir is valid, so that at least the value may be provided.
body: Testament

† the aforementioned [will] of Florence, due to the preterition of the said Duchess, her great-granddaughter, is null by operation of law; nevertheless, the Duchess does not succeed except to her legitime, which is one-sixth of the goods of Florence. And this is the effect of the codicillary clause, as is fully known through the authorities cited in C. de lib. pręteritis, Auth. ex causa. The statute, however, is irrelevant to the case at hand, because it speaks of a dowried woman; but this great-granddaughter was never dowried, nor does she succeed in the capacity of a dowried person through her great-grandmother, but in her own right; hence, the statute is of no avail for the purpose. Regarding the will of the aforementioned Agnelelli, it must be said that his will is valid without doubt:

But there are two doubts: first, whether the legacy made to the Duchess is deemed to have been made with the intention of compensating the said legacy with the said legitime. And Bartolus says that it is not, because the words of the testament state that the Duchess cannot claim more from the goods of Agnelellus; but this legitime is not from the goods of Agnelellus, but from the goods of Lady Florutia, C. de inoff. test. l. sancimus. Unless it were expressly stated in the testament that she could not claim more by reason of the legitime, and so forth. As noted by Bartolus in l. vt iureiu. §. si liberi. de ope. lib.

† On the third point, it must be said that when a thing belonging to another is bequeathed to a person jointly, the legacy is valid, so that at least the estimated value be paid, as in C. de legatis, l. cum alienam, and C. de fideicommissis, l. predia, cum si. And if it could be proven that the aforementioned sale of the said thing had been simulated, then the said legatee would proceed by the proper legal action against the possessor of the thing, by a vindicatio, as in l. tempore, de aqua pluviali. And if the heir possesses the thing, he may be sued by an action arising from the will, that he deliver possession. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether possession of movable or immovable property after the death of a testator gives rise to a presumption of acceptance of the inheritance.
2. The first dowry takes precedence over subsequent dowries.
body: A certain man named Autius had three sons, namely Bartolus, Vannucius, and Stephen. Bartolus took a wife named Titia, and the said Titia brought into the household an estimated dowry of 44 pounds of denarii, and Autius bound himself to its restitution. Vannucius also had a wife with a dowry, for the restitution of which Lucius assigned to his said daughter-in-law one piece of land. Then Autius sold another piece of land to Petrutius, his grandson. Then the said Autius died. Now, however, Blasius, son of the said Bartolus and of the lady Titia, intending to act as heir of the said Titia, seeks to recover the maternal dowry against the said Petrutius, and intends to bring a hypothecary action. The question is whether he can do so. The answer is: if the said sons of Autius have taken possession of their father's inheritance, then Titia's dowry must be recovered from the father's heirs, each for his hereditary share.

And they are considered to be heirs if, after the death of Autius, they possessed any movable or immovable property of Autius. L. gerit, D. de acquisitione hereditatis. But if they possessed nothing, nor are they heirs of Autius, then Blasius may bring an action hypothecaria against Petrucius or against Stephen, as he wishes; however, if he chooses to sue Petrucius, Petrucius may pay the dowry to them; and if he pays, the rights against every other possessor must be assigned to him. D., qui potiores in pignore habeantur, L. mulier. And then Petrucius, by virtue of the assigned right, could sue Stephen, just as the assignor himself, who is the prior creditor, could have done.
† For the first dowry is preferred to subsequent dowries, as is stated in the law *Assiduis*, in the title *Qui potiora in pignore habent*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, when, and in what manner alimony is to be provided to a widow, whether she remains in widowhood, whether she enters into a second marriage, whether the son is the heir or an outsider, and whether the dowry has been restored or not.
2. The mother succeeds to her deceased son in one-third of the usufruct.
body: Point. Angelo Petri Lunardoli of Castro di Poggio died intestate, leaving behind his sons Petruccio and John, and his wife, Lady Andreutia. The dowry of Lady Andreutia was 65 pounds. She was pregnant. Finally, this Andreutia gave birth to a daughter named Angelutia. Afterwards, for five years, Andreutia entered into a second marriage. The aforementioned sons of Angelo and Andreutia lived together with Andreutia and her husband for a period of ten years and more. Finally, Andreutia and her husband married off the aforementioned Angelutia and endowed her with the goods of the said Angelo. Finally, the aforementioned Peter died intestate, being over twenty and under twenty-five years of age, leaving behind Andreutia, his mother, and the aforementioned John, his brother. The said Andreutia and John, her son, came to the division of the estate after the death of the said Angelo, the father of the said John, for a period of fifteen years and more. Now it is asked whether the said Andreutia ought to have her dowry and maintenance for the period of the said fifteen years, and whether the said Andreutia succeeds in any part of the goods, and in the share falling to Petruccio, her son, now deceased.

† Regarding the alimony owed to a woman upon dissolution of marriage, it must be said as follows: either the woman remains a widow, and then she is entitled to receive alimony from the heirs of her husband, provided that it does not depend on her that they do not perform this duty; for in marriage a cause is feigned by which she preserves the honor and reputation of her husband through her widowhood. And thus is understood what is noted in C. de rei uxoriae actione, l. rem in praesenti, §. exactio. And this is true whether the heirs are sons or strangers. But if she has married a second time, then either she wishes to claim this alimony by custom after a year? Or as from her sons by natural law. For a son is bound by natural law to support his parents. In the first case, either the heir is such that he cannot incur delay, such as a minor under guardianship. And it does not seem that alimony is due, arg. de verbis obligatorum, l. cum filius, §. in hac; or at least restitution in integrum would be granted. Or the heir is such that he can incur delay, and in fact does so: and then, since a year interpellates, as in l. si mora, sol. matr., yet much more so if claimed in court, and then there are opinions. For Bartolus says that it would be usury, and cannot be claimed, sol. matr. l. insulam, §. vsuras, per Bartolus, unless, when she could not pay her second husband, she is bound to the second for usury, which she recovers from the heirs of her first husband as interest. And thus he advised. But it seems more correct, since the dowry is the woman’s own patrimony, and is given for this purpose, that she may also be supported from it. Moreover, since the action for dowry is one of good faith, that moderate interest be given, which the common people call alimony of the dowry, as noted in C. de sumptibus, l. 1. It supports extra de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, c. per vestras. But if she wishes to claim from her sons by natural law, then if her second husband has wherewith to support her, she cannot [claim from the sons], otherwise she can. C. de bonis quae liberis, l. si, §. ipsum autem filium. But here it must be observed, that in the preceding other case, if the stepfather had administered the stepson’s goods generally, and the wife together with him, neither could claim usury, because they ought to have paid and could have paid themselves, as ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. si quid possessor, and de negotiis gestis, l. divortio. Moreover, the creditor of minors under guardianship ought to be diligent in having a guardian appointed for them. And if he did not do so, some fault is imputed to him: the minors do not seem to be at fault. And therefore in this case it does not seem just that alimony of the unpaid dowry be owed to the mother: nevertheless the mother ought to recover her dowry. i. 25. lib. den.
† Moreover, the son succeeds to the deceased in one-third of the usufruct, as stated in the Code, *de secunda hypotecha*, in the authority *ex testamento*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether in a partnership, in which one contributes money and the other labor, upon the death of the one who was to contribute labor, before the time for the termination of the partnership, his right passes to his heir, or whether the partnership is said to be terminated by death.
body: The facts are as follows: Stidam entered into a partnership with Nicolaus on these terms and in this manner, that he [Stidam] was to contribute money to the partnership, and the said Nicolaus was to work with his own person in the said partnership. And the said Nicolaus was to receive one-fourth part of the profit that might accrue in the aforementioned partnership, and for the said fourth part to contribute to the loss, if any, that might occur in the said partnership. Afterwards, during the said partnership, the said Stidam, who was to contribute the money, purchased the fruits, revenues, and proceeds of a certain mill for five years next following, for the price of 200 florins, which purchase he made in his own name, and he paid the aforementioned sum of 200 florins in full from his own money. Finally, the said Nicolaus died after two years, or thereabouts, from the time of the acquisition of the said mill, and the said term not yet having expired. Now it is asked whether he who purchased the said fruits of the aforementioned mill is bound to share with the heirs of the said Nicolaus the fruits of the said mill after the death of the said Nicolaus, namely for the remainder of the time during which he must hold the said mill by virtue of the aforementioned term, or not. It is presupposed, as necessary, that it was the intention of the purchaser of the said mill to share the fruits of the said mill with the said Nicolaus, as profit or loss of other things that were in the partnership contracted between them. And he is prepared to share the profit for the time during which the said Nicolaus lived.

† For clarity, it must be known that profits accrued during the partnership are transmitted to the heirs of the partners, just as losses or damages incurred during the partnership: for what has passed is not extinguished by supervening death, as stated in D. 17.2.1.1 (actione, § 1). And therefore, if during the partnership, even for a single day, certain items were purchased in the common name, death after a thousand years does not sever past transactions, but new ones cannot be commenced in the name of the partnership after death, as stated in D. 17.2.2 (haeres socii), D. 17.2.1.2 (actione, § morte), D. 17.2.3 (adeo), D. 3.5.1.2 (nam et si servus, § si vivus), and D. 26.7.1.2 (Titium et Mevium, § altero). For this reason, it seems one should say that the fruits of the said mill ought to be common with the heirs of the said Nicolaus, because the beginning of the contract is considered, as stated in D. 50.17.1 (si filius) and D. 50.17.2 (si a colono). Nor does it matter that the said fruits were purchased in the name of only one person, because they ought to have been shared, and the right had arisen during his lifetime, as stated in D. 17.2.4 (si quis societatem contraxerit, in the final words: "if therefore the action had arisen"). Merely because the action had arisen, Nicolaus rightly transmitted it to his heirs, whereas conversely, they would be liable if any damage occurred, as stated in D. 17.2.5.1 (verum, § in haeredem), and as noted there.

To the contrary, it seems that, as stated in the case, this partnership was entered into with Nicolaus on account of the labor he was to contribute to the partnership. Just as, if he had never contributed labor regarding the mill, he could not demand anything to be shared with him, so too, if he died, since he cannot perform labor for the future portion, and thus there is a division of time, as stated in D. 45.1.11.2 (si servus communis meus, § si operae), especially since the heirs are uncertain, they are not the same as the labor of the deceased, as stated in D. 15.4.1.2 (si non sorte, § libertus). I say the same regarding losses. Suppose that after Nicolaus’s death, sterility supervened; this certainly does not harm the heirs of the deceased, who is not found named in the contract of purchase, but only in the contract of partnership, as stated in D. 17.2.1.3 (actione, § post), D. 17.2.6.2 (si id, § si filius, ver. duabus), D. 3.5.2 (eum actum), D. 3.5.3 (Pompo), D. 3.5.4.2 (at qui nam, § Scaevola), and D. 26.7.2 (tutorem, qui tutelam, praeterea si haeres). Moreover, if he does not demand that it be shared with him, he must fulfill his part. But here he cannot, because it is not the same labor. It is similar to the case of Caprarius, who did not keep the female slave for partnership purposes for more than one year, when he ought to have kept her for several years; only to that extent, and not beyond. Furthermore, he who purchased with his own money ought to have his capital preserved, as stated in D. 17.2.7.2 (cum duobus, § si in coeunda), and as noted there, and C. 8.1.1. Furthermore, profit, which is in part from the past and in part has its cause in future labor, must be divided, although it would be otherwise in instantaneous profit, where only the beginning is considered, whatever might subsequently happen in the future, as in the laws cited for this part. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, generality derogates from specificity, or not.
2. What those words, "all and each," signify when placed in papal letters.
1. Why a chaste man is so called.
body: It is asked whether this commission, individually granted by specifying the places, is derogated by a general commission subsequently made to another in Tuscany, with the clause revoking all and each of the collectors in the province of Tuscany, etc., since one of the aforementioned individually named territories is part of Tuscany.

And it is certain that a general commission does not derogate from a special one, as in the Digest, *De procuratoribus*, law *Itaque*, where one having a special mandate is preferred to one having a general mandate. To the same effect, in the Extravagant, *De officio delegati*, chapter *Studisti*, where the special delegate, not the general legate, knows the case. The species diminishes the signification of the genus. Digest, *De legatis* 2, law *Legatorum*; § *Qui plures*, *De vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, law *Cohaeredi*; § *Qui patrem*, *De alimentis legatis*, law *Alimenta*; § *Basilicae*, Code, *Familiae herciscundae*, law *Quotiens*, *De funerariis instrumentis*, law *Quaesitum*, in the last paragraph. Nor does it follow that that which is disposed of generally is considered to be disposed of individually by name, as in the Digest, *De legatis* 3, law *Si chorus*. For that is true, unless something singular is otherwise ordered by a person or by law, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Stipulationes commodissimum est ita componere*; and Digest, *De poenis*, law *Sanctio legum*. This is undoubtedly true, unless there were an express revocation in the letters. Therefore, that in which the weight of our question stands is,

† because in the revocatory clause these words are placed, "all and each." This term "each" is a mark not only of the species, but also of the individual, as if each one were expressed by name. Argument: Extra, de electione, c. et ut circa, in the word "all and each"; and in c. constitutionem, ut circa, de electione, in the gloss; and in c. grandi, de suppletione negligentiae praelatorum, there, "universally each, and singularly all," etc.; and ff., de legibus, l. iura, in the word "each person"; and Inst., de rerum divisione, § singulorum.

† Thus, a *syndicus* is so called, as if he were stating the cause of each individual: because each individual is deemed to be expressly included in the mandate; not that he pursues the acts of individual persons, as noted in l. 1, ff. *quod cuiusque universitatis nomine*. And below it follows, “as if they had been specially distinguished to you.” On account of these words, thus truncated and thus repeated, it appears that all other collectors appointed in Tuscany are revoked, whether in all of Tuscany or in one-third thereof. ff. *de iudicibus*, l. *insulae*; to this effect, ff. *de procuratoribus*, l. *si quis procurator*, § *si*. Notwithstanding these authorities, the first opinion seems to me more correct: because the Lord Abbot of Saint Peter was appointed collector, not to be a provincial collector, but for a certain place. And the revocation seems to refer to provincial collectors, not to those of a certain and designated place: because the words say “appointed in the province,” arg. d. c. *studuisti*. And on this point, the Lord Pope should be consulted, as noted in d. c. *generi*. This would be safer for both parties. However, as I said, a general mandate does not derogate from a special one, unless mention is made in the general mandate of the species derogating from the mandate, as in c. *dudum*, § *nos igitur*, and in c. *quamvis tibi*, *de praebendis*, lib. 6. And thus the question remains solely on that word, *singulos* [individuals]: whether by this it is understood that mention is made of the derogating species, or not. And it can sufficiently be persuaded that the Pope did not wish to revoke the Lord Abbot from some and not from others, as ff. *de procuratoribus*, l. *in causis*, in the beginning. This question is sufficiently arguable for both parties; nevertheless, I incline to the side of the Lord Abbot on account of the singularity of the mandate, and of his faith being chosen singularly and specifically by the Lord Pope. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the person providing the dowry stipulates that it be returned to him, or to whomsoever right and chance shall have given it, he distinguishes how those words are to be understood.
body: The words of the instrument are as follows: Colutius de Racaneto gave in dowry to Dominicus Vannis, future husband of the lady Belliflora, one piece of land, which Dominicus promised to render and restore to the said Colutius, or to the said Belliflora, or to the heirs of either, or to whomsoever right and chance shall have given it, the aforementioned piece of land constituting the said dowry, immediately and forthwith whenever, wherever, and however the marriage to be contracted between the said Dominicus and the lady Belliflora shall be divided, dissolved, or separated by death or divorce, without children born commonly from their bodies reaching the legitimate age of 25 years. Or with children of the said lady supervening, and in every way, case, and event concerning the restitution of the said dowry. Finally, the marriage was dissolved by the death of the woman, who died leaving a son surviving. This son died under the age of 25 years. It is asked whether the said donor can recover the said dowry. In these words, two things are principally provided for. First, provision is made for the restitution of the dowry, inasmuch as the marriage is separated by the death of the woman, or with children existing from that marriage, or without children existing; and if with children existing, either reaching the age of 25 years or not reaching it. If, however, it is dissolved by the death of the man, this is the second principal case, which is not subdivided. The case occurred that the marriage was separated by the death of the woman with a son surviving, who died in adult age. Hence, he who gave the dowry recovers the dowry; it is objected to him that she died with children; it is replied that the son did not reach the age of 25 years.

† It is asked, what right exists against the donor, contrary to the statement of Bartolus in l. Gaius, sol. matr., who says that if the donor of the dowry stipulates for himself, or for himself or to whom the event may give the return of the dowry, the action acquired belongs solely to the woman; because the law so gives and so disposes. l. rem in praesenti, §. accedit, C. de rei ux. act. Therefore it follows that the first part of the stipulation, by which he stipulated for himself, would be of no effect, which is certainly inequitable and contrary to law, because these words ought to have some effect. They can have effect, as is expressly stated in d. §. accedit, and C. de pact. conventis, l. ex morte, and C. de iur. dot., l. avia, and ff. sol. matr., l. quotiens, §. si quis, and ff. de pact. dot., l. ob res, §. si extraneus. It must therefore be known that stipulations of this kind are to be referred rather to the understanding than to the order of the words. The understanding, however, resides in the affection of the donor, as d. l. Gaius, in the word, propter affectionem, together with the nature of the dowry, because the dowry is annexed to the marriage and follows it, as C. de iur. dot., l. ubi adhuc, and l. pro oneribus. Consider therefore the affection of the donor, and the order of piety and charity: here, indeed, the donor wished the dowered woman to have it more than himself. And therefore if the donor died first, the woman surviving in marriage, or not in marriage. The first part of the words, by which he stipulated for himself, vanishes, and the whole right belongs to the woman, and thus the event assigns it to the woman, as ff. de leg. 3, l. uxorem, §. restitutio, and there noted. The same if the woman dies in marriage, with children. For children are part of their parents: as C. qui pot. in pig. hab., l. assiduis, and they enjoy the same privilege. l. est, sol. matr. And they are considered one person, as C. de impub. et aliis subst., l. si. And this donor loved the children of the woman more than himself. And therefore, while these children live, the donor cannot sue. But if the woman dies in marriage without children, the donor surviving, then in this case the donor loved himself more than the alien heir of the woman. And therefore the right and the event give to the donor the recovery of the dowry, as d. §. accedit, and arg. C. comm. utr. iud., l. si, and thus the said words ought to be understood. But let us suppose that children remained, but died during the lifetime of the donor. I answer, if nothing else had been done, the donor would have been excluded, but here something else has been done: because it was agreed that they should be excluded perpetually, when they reached the age of 25 years, otherwise not. Hence the stipulation remedies to the stipulator, and this gives the right and the event, as d. l. si, in princ. But let us suppose that the donor died first than the dowered daughters. I answer, the right of the stipulation transmitted to his heirs, as Inst. de verb. oblig., §. ex conditionali. And therefore, when those children died at 25 years, the dowry ought to be restored to the children and heirs of the stipulator: the woman, therefore, and her children born from that marriage are in the first degree of this contract; in the second degree, however, the donor and the heirs of the donor are as if substituted, which substitution is transmitted in contracts, as I said. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A mother is appointed as curator of the property of her absent son.
2. Whether a son absent for twenty years is presumed dead.
3. A mother is preferred to her son's consanguine brothers in succession.
4. A fiancé does not succeed to the property of his future wife.
body: Husband

†the daughter of that girl, formerly called Bartesi, has nothing in the inheritance of the said Vangutius; because the said Vangutius died survived by Venatio and John, his sons, to whom the inheritance of their father pertained.
