† Petrutius, also the third son, of whose life nothing has been known for already twenty years and more, is presumed dead, considering the accidents of the world; and even assuming that he were alive, nevertheless the said Dame Vangnola has the usufruct in the share of the said Vennatii and of John. And she can possess it, and she ought to be appointed guardian of the goods of her said son, if he were alive; and if not she, at least another, according to the chapter and the law *nec nos* on those who return from captivity and postliminium. And therefore it pertains to her to possess all the goods of her late sons, since no one makes a portion for himself.
† For the mother is preferred to consanguine brothers in succession, in the Authentica de haeredibus ab intestato, § consequens.

† Moreover, because the fiancé does not succeed intestate to the goods of his future wife. C. *Unde vir et uxor*, l. 1. From which it is concluded that the said Lady Vangnola has the right, and not the fiancé of the said girl. I, Baldus. Opinion on the matter of division, as above.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a division is to be rescinded if someone has been injured by more than half of the just price.
body:
The narration of the facts is as follows: Berrecordatus, coming to death, made a will; in which, among other things, he instituted Baldutius, Vitus, and several other sons of his as his heirs. And he prohibited his said heirs that none of them should demand, or be able to demand, the division of the goods, or of the inheritance, without the license of their mother, until they had completed 25 years of their age; as fully appears from the public will. Then, after the death of the said Berrecordatus, the testator, and of the said mother, and after the death of their other brothers, the said Baldutius and Vitus, the said Vitus being under 26 years and over 20 years, came unanimously and concordantly to the division of the goods and of the inheritance, concerning which a division was made between them, and the said Vitus swore not to contravene on account of minority of age, as appears in the instrument of division. Finally, execution of the said instrument of division was sought on behalf of the said Vitus against the said Baldutius according to the form of the statute de Guar. speaking. Now the said Baldutius, observing that the said division is damaging to him, wishes to apply remedies to oppose the said division, since the said Vitus wishes it to stand; concerning which the following doubts arise.

The first is whether the said Baldutius can say that the said division does not hold, notwithstanding the said prohibition made by the said Berrecordatus in the said instrument, since the said Vitus is under 25 years, and whether the said division, voluntarily made, stands in the way of Baldutius. And this is because execution of the said division was sought by virtue of the statute de Guar., in which it is provided that, when execution of instruments de Guar. is sought, the exception of nullity cannot be opposed, and the one opposing is not to be heard.

The second is that, in the portion of the said Vitus, two parcels of vineyard land came, which are worth double that for which they were estimated in the instrument of division: whether, for this cause, the said Baldutius can say that he was deceived with respect to the said things, and use the benefit of deception.

The third doubt is that, in the portion of the said Vitus, a certain holding came; whether the said house came into the portion of the said Vitus, or remained undivided.

On which matters, please give your counsel, having seen the aforesaid point, and the said will, instrument, and statute, and others which you may gather from the aforesaid.

† Division is considered a contract of good faith, because it contains an exchange within itself, and therefore relief is granted to the defrauded party when the injury exceeds one-half of the just price. Codex, De communi utriusque iudicii, l. Maioribus. But here it must be observed that this lesion, when a universitas is divided, must be assessed not with respect to a single thing, but with respect to the entire division of the universitas itself, by argument from those things which are read and noted in the Digest, De edicto, l. Labeo scribit. But this is true unless the individual items are estimated separately. For even then an action may be brought for each item individually. Digest, De edicto, l. Cum idem, and l. Si plura. Unless in the other things they have so much that it cannot be seen that he was defrauded: for from the same contract there is a compensation of one body to another body, as in the Digest, De actionibus emptoris, l. Si duorum, ver. Sed rectius est. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the provision of alimony for a widow, to be furnished within the household or outside the household, within the course of a year.
2. A woman acquires as her own the fruits of her daily clothing.
body: Heir

† The holder of the dowry is bound to provide the widow with maintenance from the dowry within the year, provided, however, that she works for the heirs of her husband, if she can reside with them without compromising her modesty, as stated in l. sicut, de operibus libertorum; l. rem in praesenti, § exactio, C. de rei uxoriae actione. But if she cannot reside honorably with the heir, and if she can indeed live honorably from her own work or from another source, then maintenance from the dowry consisting in money is not due within the year; otherwise, if she has no other means of support, the lady of these goods must then return the goods removed from her husband’s house. I do not say this by way of set-off, but rather that she is sued primarily for this purpose, according to l. penult., ff. de solutione matrimonii, through the authorities, and l. id vestimentum, de peculio, through Guillaume de Coucy.
† except for garments that are in daily use, which follow the woman, if they had been delivered to her. Bald.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legacy, or a donation causa mortis, is transmitted to the heirs while the condition is pending.
2. Whether a statute providing that a woman may not make a will without the presence of two relatives encompasses a woman's will for pious causes.
body: Having considered the aforementioned points, it must be said,

† Although a donation causa mortis is not transmitted to the heir while the condition of the donation is pending, just as a legacy is not transmitted, as is the text in C. de indicio vidui tollendo, l. 1, in fine; nevertheless, this is true unless the heir is named in the donation, as when I say, “I give causa mortis to Titius and to his heir”; for then it is transmitted, as in C. ut actiones ab haeredibus et contra haeredes, l. 1. And the term “heir” must here be understood most broadly, so that the donee may bequeath this hope, as in ff. de edendo, l. quaedam, § 1. For the legatee is in a sense an heir in the thing bequeathed, as in ff. de usucapione, l. id tempus, § si. And because it would be the heir’s own right, the testator may bequeath it, de legatis 2, l. unum ex familia, § si rem. And therefore, under the ius commune, the aforementioned legacy of 100 florins, assuming the capacity of the legatee, undoubtedly valid.

† But it is objected on the basis of the statute, which provides that a married woman must make her will in the presence of her husband, and so forth. I answer that this statute does not apply, because for pious causes we do not observe the common civil law or municipal law, but rather canon law, by which law it is undoubtedly valid, as stated in Extra, De sepultura, c. Licet, lib. 6, and in c. Cum esset and c. Relatum, De testamentis, with its glosses. And therefore the legacy made to Saint Louis for the augmentation of the church is undoubtedly valid. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a brother who has been instituted heir and mutually substituted for his other brothers is bound, upon the occurrence of the substitution, to restore to the surviving brothers the entire sum and everything that he received from the brothers who predeceased, or only a portion thereof.
2. What is the legitimate portion of the children if there are five, and whether they may deduct the trebellianic portion.
body: The point of the question, on which legal advice is requested, is as follows. Thebaldus, formerly of Mathias, having been in his last moments, made his last solemn testament: in which he instituted John, Odo, Richard, Mathias, and Henry, his sons, as universal heirs to all his goods in equal shares; and if any of the said sons, or their sons, should die in pupillary age, or later at any time without legitimate sons, the surviving male sons, born and posthumous, shall succeed him or them equally. After this, the said testator Thebaldus died, survived by the aforementioned sons, who were his instituted heirs. Then the said Henry, son and heir of the said Thebaldus for a fifth part, died an adult without sons, having accepted the paternal inheritance, and having made no testament himself, survived by the said John, Odo, Richard, and Mathias. Then the aforementioned Richard died an adult and without sons, having made a testament: in which he instituted John, Odo, and Mathias, his aforementioned brothers, as his universal heirs according to the mode and conditions written below, namely, that if any or some of the said brothers should die at any time without legitimate male sons born in lawful marriage, one shall die to the other in all his goods and rights without any diminution of right, institution, and the Trebellian share, nor in any other way, right, title, or cause, retaining nothing. And these are the words of the said testators punctually. Then the three surviving brothers, namely John, Odo, and Mathias, held and possessed the inheritance and hereditary goods of the aforementioned Thebaldus, their father, and of the said Henry and Richard, their brothers, as heirs of theirs, commonly and undividedly. Finally, the said John died, survived by Eustachius, his legitimate and natural son and heir, and by Odo and Mathias, his carnal brothers. Then the said Mathias died an adult without sons, having made a testament, in which he instituted the said Eustachius, his nephew, as his universal heir. Lastly, the aforementioned Odo died without sons, survived by the said Eustachius, his carnal nephew, and having made a testament, in which he instituted Martinus Petri de Urbe as his universal heir.

The question now arises, and is brought into doubt, between the aforementioned Eustachius, son of the said John, and his heir on the one part, and the above-named Martin, heir of the aforementioned Odo, on the other part: whether the said Eustachius, nephew of the aforesaid Theobald, the first testator, entirely excludes the said Martin, heir of Odo, from the inheritance and succession of the said Theobald and of his aforesaid deceased sons. And if he does not exclude him entirely, in what share and portion does the said Eustachius succeed, and in what share and portion does the said Martin succeed, in the person of the said Odo, to the said Theobald and to his other sons named above, and to their goods and inheritances? The words of the aforesaid testaments having been seen and examined, upon which your sound counsel is to be given in writing and under seal, as clearly as can be done. Let us assume.

That the entire inheritance of Theobald was worth 120 ounces of gold. In the first place, therefore, since he had five sons succeeding him, whose legitime among all is 60 ounces, which they divide equally among themselves, as in the Authentica *Novissima*, C. de inofficioso testamento, it follows that each has 12 ounces free from any burden of the testator’s noxious liabilities. These 12 ounces each transmits freely to his heir. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. *Si quis in suo*; and l. *Omnimodo*; and l. *Quia*; and l. *Sancimus*. Let us therefore say first in theory, that when the legitime amounts to up to one-half, the Trebellian portion is never deducted; even if the son is requested under a condition to restore, so that the one requested does not have more than the one honored. For no gloss of civil law, nor any text in the world permits this, but in the two quarters, i.e., the half, they are deemed to be. This is noted by Jacobus Beltramius in the Authentica *De restitutione*, and that which it generates, §. *Quamobrem*. For example, the testator can order that the Trebellian portion not be deducted, and especially since the legitime can be confused with it, as noted in C. ad legem Falcidiam, Authentica *Sed cum testator*; ff. ad Trebellianam, l. *Marcellus*, §. *Quod autem*; and what is noted by Dyaco in the same title, l. *Lucius*, §. *Maritus uxore*.

Secondly, in practice, and coming to the successions of this legitime, it is clear that the legitime of the first deceased, namely Henry, devolves by intestate law to his four brothers, namely to each for a quarter, and it devolves freely: because it was free and without the burden of a fideicommissum. Hence it is not included in the fideicommissum made among the brothers, because it is taken not by the benefit of Theobald, the first testator, but as from the goods of the deceased heir by a new and direct right. For the goods of the heir do not come into the fideicommissum. ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. *Coheredi*, §. *Cum filiae*, ver. *Nec fideicommissio*; de adoptionibus, l. *Si arrogator*. Similarly, the legitime of the second deceased went to the three surviving brothers, to each for a third by testamentary right, because the brother secondly deceased, Richard, made a testament in favor of all his brothers. And thus, since they were instituted equally, they must divide this legitime of the testator among those going. The third dying, namely John, died with a son, to whom he transmitted all his goods. This son is Eustace, concerning whom the question is asked, and in the person of John everything is free, because he died with a son. The fourth dying, namely Matthias, transmitted his entire legitime, and the quarter of Henry’s legitime, and the third of Richard’s legitime, to Eustace freely, because he instituted him heir in solidum. For the fifth dying, Odo, everything will be free, because he, dying last, had no substitute for himself, de legatis 2, l. *Peto*, §. *Fratre*. And although Eustace survived, nevertheless Eustace was not substituted, nor could John, his father, transmit to him the institution pending from the future deaths of Matthias and Odo, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. *Si in personam*; and fully noted in l. *Cum filio*, de legatis 1; and l. 1, C. de his qui ante apertas tabulas; and in sum, two portions are entirely free, namely the portion of John on account of Eustace, and the portion of Odo on account of the last dying.

But it is necessary to look at that which is not free, but subject to successive fideicommissa. It must be known, therefore, that the first fideicommissum comes into the subsequent one. ff. ad Trebellianam, l. *Marcellus*, §. *Quidam liberis*; and l. *Scaevola*. And therefore, excepting the first dying, to whom nothing accrued, by right of fideicommissum, whatever came to the second dying without children from the death of the first by right of fideicommissum. And the same in the fifth dying in the fideicommissary substitution together with him, in whom he could originally be burdened, it devolves. I declare from the beginning that the first dying was effectively burdened in 12 ounces, which came in equal parts to the four surviving brothers. Behold therefore, as regards the first, namely Henry, half of the 24 ounces, which were his share, which falls into the fideicommissum with its burden, was applied to the brothers, and the subsequent fideicommissum was augmented according to the prior, namely in three ounces for each. Thus therefore the second dying had 15 ounces burdenable and burdened, which by right of fideicommissum pertained to the brothers, to each for a third. And so also for the fifth dying, for the fourth dying, as I said, had 20 ounces burdenable and burdened. And in sum, whatever was burdenable, came down to the last, namely to Martin, heir of Odo, from the person of Odo, last dying. It therefore seems, saving error of calculation, dividing the inheritance of Theobald, as I said, into 120 ounces of gold, that Eustace has of these first 24 which were his father’s, and six of the ounces of Henry from the person of John, father of Eustace, and 8 of the 24 of Richard. And moreover one ounce of the three in which Richard succeeded Henry by right of fideicommissum, and 12 of the 24 of Matthias. The sum of ounces touching Eustace of the 120 is contrary to the law and one ounce, or about that. The whole remainder pertains to Martin, heir of Odo, last deceased. However, this calculation, insofar as it is a matter of fact, I commit to any better calculator. The process of law has been declared above by declaring in theory what comes in these substitutions, and what does not come, and what is free. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a marriage that is invalid by law constitutes an impediment to lawful wedlock.
2. Whether a bishop may declare papal letters, which are not addressed to him, to have been obtained by fraud.
body: The point of doubt and question, upon which it is requested that a legal opinion be rendered in writing and under seal, is as follows: whether, by virtue of the sentence inscribed below, the Magnificent John, son of the late Theobald of Saint Eustace, and the Lady Alouisia, daughter of the late John Caporei of the City, could lawfully contract marriage with others, such that the children subsequently born to the said John and to the Lady Berta, with whom the said John is said to have contracted marriage after the said sentence, ought to be considered legitimate according to civil and canon law, to such an extent that they may succeed the said John, their father, according to law. And on this matter, it is consulted what is the law, having regard to the sentence inscribed below, given between the aforementioned Alouisia and the aforementioned Magnificent John. There are two doubts.

First, whether a marriage that is invalid by law constitutes an impediment to lawful wedlock. And it must be said that it does not, if it is null by the law itself. And this is established in ecclesiastical law: and especially when it has been declared [null] and license has been granted to contract another marriage, as is read and noted in c. Non praestat, De rebus iudicatis, Book 6. Therefore, he who did not effectively contract prior wedlock marries lawfully and rightly. The text is in the Digest, De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Haec conditio. And this is true, unless the Pope had dispensed in the first marriage regarding the bond, thereby validating the substance of the marriage. c. Literas, De testamento sponsalium. For then it would have passed from non-being to being. And therefore another marriage could not be contracted afterwards, as in the Institutes, De nuptiis, § Affinitatis.

† The second doubt is whether the Bishop can declare that apostolic letters, which were not addressed to him, are obtained by suppression of truth, and in this way can invalidate or declare null an apostolic privilege. And I say that, incidentally cognizing the defense of the marriage, he can cognize and pronounce. And regarding the suppression of truth in the dispensation at hand, since the dispensation was obtained by suppression of truth, it did not hold by the law itself, as in c. Audientiam, de rescriptis, and in c. Ultima, de filiis presbyterorum, lib. 6. But the Bishop should not do this unless the suppression of truth is so manifest and public that it cannot be denied. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a will and the institution of an heir are valid, if the heir instituted was the son of a notary who had been requested to draw up the will.
2. If the testator ordered that the fruits of the goods be distributed each year by his executors to the poor, whether, after the lapse of a year and the execution not having been carried out, the bishop may endow those goods to nuns, so that they may receive the fruits therefrom each year for their sustenance.
3. A woman is more prone to poverty than a man, and is more wretched.
body: The fact is that Fls Cicolus Colae made a written will, drawn up in public form by Master Andrea Bartoli of Spello, public notary. In which, among other things, he disposed as follows: namely, in all his goods he instituted Cicculus Silvester, Iutius of Master Andrea Bartoli, and Lord Peter Putii as his heirs and fideicommissaries. In this manner and under this condition, that they may not sell the possessions, but are bound to collect the fruits every year, and to give and distribute them to the poor. Then, after the testator’s death, and after a year had passed, the Diocesan Bishop, considering that the pious intention of the testator was not being carried out,

† that the said Lutius was a son in the power of the said notary, whence the father could not enroll him: as in the Digest, *De falsis*, l. *De eo*, and l. *Impuberem*, § *Si ei filio*. Whence the writing of the father does not prove in favor of the son in power, just as neither does testimony; rather, according to some, although the testament is nuncupative, yet because the testator would not have made it otherwise unless it were written, the writing is considered adulterated, as noted in the Code, *De his qui sibi ascribunt*, l. 1, by Cynus.

† He granted these goods and these revenues to the poor nuns of the chapter and convent of the monastery of Saint Clare of Spello. The question is whether such a transfer is valid in law or not. And doubt arises because the distribution is not made from year to year, as the testator had willed. But it must be said that it makes no difference which of equivalent things is done: as in C. de inst. et subst. l. si mater. Hence the Bishop, to whom the power had devolved, as in C. de epi. et cler. l. nulli. And to whom the goods had devolved, could rightly donate them to the said nuns for their sustenance to be received each year in perpetuity: since nuns, who are and will be there at any time, are included under the appellation of the poor, as in Auth. de eccl. tit. §. si quis in nomine.

For a woman always tends more toward poverty than a man, and is more pitiable; nor can it be said that the Bishop lacked authority on account of other executors appointed in the will: for in the case of negligence no others were appointed, but only in the case of death, and therefore the case of negligence pertains to the Bishop. Moreover, many years had elapsed when the Bishop conferred [the office], and thus all executors had been removed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How the division is to be made among those who formed a confraternity.
body: John

† Pitius took as his wife Vannucia, the widow of Petrus, who had previously been the wife of Menecutius. And the said Vannucia had one son from her first husband, named Jacobus. And the said Johannes had one daughter from his first wife, named Lucia. And they were in agreement from the beginning that the said Lucia should be the future wife of the said Jacobus; however, this agreement lasted but a short time, and the said Johannes and the said Lucia went to live with the said Vannucia and the said Jacobus: and they purchased wheat and other things, which they consumed while living together. And afterwards they remained together for many years, and they gained little profit except for their sustenance. Jacobus says to the said Johannes that he wishes him to restore half of the consumed wheat, and he has justice on his side in this matter. However, the said Johannes says that he has borne other burdens and labors, and has done more work than the said Jacobus, so that one may be set off against the other. He has contributed even more of his labor to the household, especially by supporting a certain grandmother of the said Jacobus, who was of decrepit age. And in this the said Johannes has equity, that such consideration and compensation be made. And the said Jacobus says that he had eight florins and a half belonging to a certain youth in his possession, which remained with the said Jacobus and Johannes, to which were added five florins from the common fund, which were later found and sold for twenty-four florins. It is asked how these florins should be divided. And it seems that first thirteen florins and a half should be deducted as capital, of which two florins and a half belong to the said Johannes, and eleven florins to the said Jacobus; from then on, two parts and one part, i.e., five florins and a quarter of another florin, should be divided according to the proportionate casting of lots, and the other half should be divided equally between them; because both kept the oxen, l. cum duobus, §. si in coeunda, pro socio, C. de pactis, l. si pascenda pecora. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a document, in which it is stated that one hundred are owed according to a calculated account, proves that only that one hundred is owed.
2. Whether faith is to be given to documents made by a third party.
body: For they prove

† even if one hundred remained: for it does not follow that, because he produced an account of one hundred, only one hundred are due, as noted in C. de probat. l. rationes. To this it is answered that, when it is said that by a calculated reckoning on both sides, etc., it is clearly signified that nothing else remained but one hundred. l. publica. §. fi. ff. depo. C. de distrahen. pigno. l. si residuum. de pac. l. emptor. §. Lucius. unless an error in calculation were proved. C. de errore cal. l. 1. Moreover, since this can also be proved by witnesses and by the account which the plaintiff conceals, the oath of Nicholas is upheld, even with mere indicia, let alone manifest confession and calculation. C. de probat. l. si de possessione. C. de fi. iustr. l. fi.

† Moreover, great credence is given to the writings of merchants, because although the book belongs to Nicolaus, the entry was written by a certain third party, which constitutes half-proof. Indeed, it proves fully, because it has been proven that it was made by the command of both parties. For it is full proof when combined with other presumptions, as Bartolus expressly and elegantly holds in the Digest, *De donationibus*, in the law *Nuda ratio*. And therefore, the said Nicolaus has in this case not only the truth, but also the clearest right. Indeed, I say more: that even if the statute expressly stated that no credence should be given to the writing of a *fancelus* [clerk/scribe], it would nevertheless be believed, if it were established by proof that it was made by the command of both parties. And thus it must be limited, as is noted in the Digest, *De edendo*, in the law *Quaedam*, section *Nummularios*. Hence, those who write in the books in the presence of the parties, as is customary, appear to have written by the tacit command of both parties, as is noted by Jacobus de Belvisio in the first law of the Code, *De edendo*, which is notable and pertinent. See also the Code, *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, in the law *Optimam*, and the law *Cum ostendimus*, section *Finis*, *De fideiussoribus et tutoribus*, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a will made in the presence of six witnesses is valid as regards children, but not as regards strangers.
2. Whether a will, void due to the omission of a grandmother, is revived if the grandmother does not declare it void.
3. A dowry may be set off against a liquid debt, or one that can easily be liquidated.
4. A son burdened with a fideicommissum may make a will concerning his legitime and the Trebellian portion, excepting what is left to God, and number 5.
body: First, Nicolaus Cecchi had two wives, and the first was called Lanna, from whom John was born. The second wife is called Nicolosa, from whom, during the lifetime of the said Nicolaus, Francis and Anthony were born. And after the death of the said Nicolaus, a posthumous son named Louis was born. This Nicolaus died having made a will, with the said Francis and Anthony, who were infants, surviving him, and with the said Nicolosa, his wife, surviving him and pregnant with the said Louis, and with Guidutia, the mother of the said Nicolaus, also surviving. Then the said John, the son from the first wife, an adult, died having made a will, in which he effectively left the said Francis and Anthony, his full brothers, as universal heirs. And to the said Guidutia he made a simple legacy, and not by way of institution. Then Francis died at the age of four years or thereabouts. Then Anthony died at the age of two years or thereabouts. Then the said posthumous Louis was born. Then the said Guidutia, mother of Nicolaus and grandmother of these boys, died having made a will, in which she instituted her three nephews as heirs, namely the said Louis for one-third part, and Guidolina, daughter of the daughter of the said Guidutia, for another third part; Armelina and Guidolina are still alive. Then the said Louis died at the age of nineteen years or thereabouts, having made a will, in which testament he instituted the said Nicolosa, his mother, as universal heir. Therefore, having seen and examined the aforementioned wills, it is asked in what quantity or in what share the said Nicolosa succeeds to the said inheritances: presupposing that Conrad and John, substituted for a share in the will of the said Nicolaus, and the said Armelina, substituted for a share in the codicils of the said Nicolaus, are alive, and claim that the said inheritances of the said Nicolaus pertain to them, since all the sons of the said Nicolaus died without issue.

The testament of the said Nicholas was made in the presence of six witnesses, and it was valid as regards the sons and as regards the substitutions made among the sons, as established in C. de test., l. hac consultissima, § ex imperfecto. However, as regards the said Conrad and John, it was not valid. Therefore, the said Conrad and John have no greater right than that which is granted to them by the last codicils made by the said Nicholas, containing a fideicommissary substitution, as stated in l. diui, §§ licet, ff. de iure codicillorum; and I shall immediately declare what and how much right the said substitutes possess.

The testament of John, because it passed over his grandmother, was void from the beginning by operation of law; nevertheless, if the grandmother, living for a long time, did not declare it void, it was validated by the equity of the law, as stated in the number cited in the Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, in the law *Sancimus*, and in the law *Filio praeterito* in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*. Hence, Louis succeeded to it, and by possessing the goods of the said John, the said Louis acted as heir and became his heir, according to the law *Duo fratres* in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*. However, if she declared it void, it would not be valid unless it were proven that she had left something to her grandmother by way of institution, and even then, the said Louis would have succeeded, as stated above. The testament of the said Guidutia was valid; nevertheless, because she administered the guardianship of Louis, if her dowries are claimed back from the goods of Nicholas, heir of Cecchus, her father, who received the said dowry,

† compensation may be opposed, if the claim is liquid: or if it can easily be liquidated, that the said lady was indebted on that occasion, as noted in l. diuortio. §. ob donationes. sol. mat. cum si.

† The testament of Louis was valid. Moreover, Louis could freely make a will regarding one-third of all the goods of the said Nicolas, by reason of the legitime of the said children. And without doubt, this one-third part is free, and freely pertains to Nicolosa. C. de inoff. test. l. quam. in Auth. de trien. et semisse. §. 1. cum si.

† Moreover, Louis could have made a testamentary disposition regarding his Trebellianic share, which is one-fourth of the residue, namely two ounces out of eight, as stated in c. Ray. and c. Ray. de test. And thus, all things being computed, without any doubt, the said Nicolosa must effectively receive her legitime portion of all the goods of the said Cecchi, with the proviso that the Trebellianic share is not deducted from the third part bequeathed to God, in favor of the soul and the Church; therefore, the remainder pertains to the substitutes according to the form of the codicils of Nicolai. Hence, Nicolosa must receive, from the twelve ounces, first the four ounces that constituted the legitime of the children, which could not be burdened. From the remaining eight ounces, Nicolosa must receive two ounces less, by the amount that the Trebellianic share would be if it were deducted for God or the Church. Therefore, the younger brothers, on behalf of the Church, must receive one-third of the eight ounces, because they were substituted by fideicommissum for the third part, which amounts to two ounces; and two ounces for the third part. Armelina must receive two ounces, and John likewise two ounces, because they would receive no more than this, even if a half of the entire inheritance were deducted on account of the two fourths. Thus, in total, the said Nicolosa must receive four ounces and four third-parts of an ounce, i.e., one-third and one ounce. And so, having made the computation from the twelve ounces, Nicolosa must receive two ounces and one third-part of an ounce. Moreover, all goods purchased by Louis, and the fruits found in his inheritance at the time of his death, pertain freely and in full to the said lady Nicolosa. de vulg. subst. l. cohæredi. §. cum filiae. ver. nec fideicommisso.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What effect does a confession have, whereby he possesses by a just title, without any other mention being made of the title.
2. Whether one who confesses that another possessed as his own thereby confesses that the other is the owner.
body: To the lord

† The response made in favor of Petrucia prejudices the case concerning the 15th chapter posited by Angnella, in which chapter is contained the prescription arising from possession for twenty years with title. It must be said that the prescription has not been completed, even assuming that no revocation of error had been made. And the reason is that the article states that the lady Angnella, by herself and her ancestors, namely, etc., possessed with a just title for a period of twenty years. And Petrucia replied that she does not concede anything except regarding Peter and his sons. For by this it does not appear for how much time within this period of twenty years Peter and his sons possessed. In the article, Angnella does not allege the times of each possessor distinctly, but collectively, as in the law Papinianus, section Cum quis, On the Acquisition of Possession. Furthermore, because those words, "with a just title," are general words: for they do not state by what title; and a just title is not sufficient for prescribing. Digest, On Public Things, law Quaecunque, section Interdum. And

† Although it were confessed or alleged that he possessed as owner or for himself, by this he does not confess ownership, but rather the mode or quality of possessing. Hence, it is one thing to confess that someone possesses under a title as owner, and another to confess that he is the owner. For it does not follow: he possesses as owner; therefore, he is the owner, as in D. de solutionibus, l. Titia; and l. liberis, §. finalis, de liberalibus causis; l. apud antiquos, de furtis; unless from this title prescription has been completed, as in D. pro suo, per totum. And therefore, notwithstanding such confessions, arbitrators ought to follow the path of truth: and what belonged to the father is presumed to belong to the sons, as in C. de probationibus, l. siue possidetis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A son cannot be burdened in his legitime nor in the Falcidian or Trebellian shares; how this is to be considered.
2. Whether an infant transmits an unaccepted inheritance, whether he is a descendant or an outsider.
body: The point of the case is as follows: Petrus Trascianus had as his wife a certain Lady Vesucia, with a dowry of 250 livres, from whom he had two legitimate and natural sons, Francis and Christopher. Then the said Lady Vesucia died intestate, survived by her said sons and daughter. The said Petrus took another wife, from whom he had three legitimate and natural daughters, namely Margaret, Matthea, and Antonia. Then the said Petrus, father of all the aforementioned, died, having made a will in the form set forth above. Then, after the death of the said Petrus, his son and heir Francis made a will in the form set forth above. Then he died under the age of twenty-three years, and the said Antonia died ten days after the death of the said Francis, Antonia being two years of age. Her inheritance was accepted by her sisters, who were related to her on both sides, as you will see in her acceptance. Now the question arises: how should the inheritances of the said Petrus and Francis be divided among the said Christopher, and the sister related to the said Francis on both sides, and the said Margaret and Matthea, who are sisters of the said Francis on the father’s side only, and who are related to the deceased Antonia on both sides, as stated? Having examined the said wills of Petrus and Francis, and their form, and the form of the acceptance of the inheritance of the said Antonia, and having seen the statute concerning succession intestate. On these matters, it is requested that you give clear counsel, so that the arbitrators may understand the matter well and be able to render a decision that is well understood by the parties, because the parties are in agreement. And the arbitrators will abide by your counsel and declaration. For this counsel, they send you two florins as arbitrators’ fees, because the compromitting parties are poor. First, it must be considered to what extent Christopher, Margaret, Matthea, and Antonia succeeded under the will of Petrus, their father. And certainly, by virtue of the substitution, they succeeded per stirpes in the goods of Petrus left to Francis, except for the legitime of Francis, in which

† he could not be burdened, and with the Trebellian exception, as in c. Ray. and c. Ray. de testam. et legitima, in this case it is one-fifth of six ounces, dividing the entire inheritance into 12 ounces, considering the number of children, as in Auth. nouissima de inoff. testam. de trebell. It is true that it is one-fourth of the residue from the said legitime, i.e., one-fourth, having regard to the institution, not to the number of children. And the calculation should be set out thus: one ounce, and one-fifth of another ounce, touched Francis for his legitime, since there were five sons, who were to divide among themselves one-half for their legitime. For the Trebellian portion, however, there fell to Francis one-fourth of ten ounces, and one-fourth of one ounce, dividing what remained thereof. But one-fourth of 10 is two and a half, one-fourth of four parts of that ounce, and one is a portion of the four said portions remaining. And thus in total Francis could dispose by will of three ounces of the whole asse, and two parts of one ounce, and not of more. Therefore, the whole residue, of which he could not dispose by will, pertained to the four sisters virilely by the paternal will, and in all the right which competes to Antonia by the paternal will, and from wherever they succeeded Antonia, Margaret and Mathea, sisters united on both sides, excluding the sister Christophora, as in Auth. de consanguin. et uterin. fratribus in principio. And that Antonia, although an infant, transmitted the right of the paternal fideicommissum to her sisters, as C. de fideicom. l. si in personam; de leg. 1. l. cum filio per Dig. and also to their mother, as to the virile usufruct, as C. de sec. nup. Auth. ex testamento.

† I come to the testament of Francis. And I say that, because Antonia did not accept the inheritance of her brother Francis, and she died as an infant, her share accrued not only to Margaret and Matthew, but also to Christina for her hereditary portion, as stated in C. de caducis tollendis, §. his ita. Although Bartolus says that restitution in integrum may be sought in the name of the infant, nevertheless the common opinion adheres to the text of the law l. si insanti, C. de iure deliberandi, which holds that an infant transmits nothing regarding the inheritance of a stranger not accepted. This is supported by C. ad senatusconsultum Orphitianum, l. non pro numero. But Bartolus says that what is stated in l. si insanti is true according to the strict law; however, according to praetorian equity, by the benefit of restitution in integrum, it is otherwise, as in l. qui duos, de rebus dubiis, and c. 1, de restitutione militum. It can be said that either the minor was prevented from accepting by a fortuitous event, and restitution is granted, as when one perishes in a storm at sea, as in l. qui duos and in the aforementioned l. 1. Likewise, absence can be regarded as a fortuitous event in this regard; therefore, restitution is granted there. Or, it was due to the fault of the tutor, because something done with the minor is understood when the tutor commits fault against him, ff. de minoribus, l. ait praetor. Or, he was prevented naturally: for example, because he died as an infant by a natural, not fortuitous, event, and then he is not restored in integrum, as in the aforementioned l. si insanti. One thing, however, must be known: if he had had a tutor, he would have transmitted the right of deliberation through the knowledge of the tutor, according to Bartolus. But in our case, it is not alleged that the mother had assumed the guardianship of the said infant Antonia; and therefore her share, as if caducous, accrued to all three sisters, as I have said. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the consent of the fideicommissary to alienate, or otherwise to prejudice himself, affects a future fideicommissum.
2. The rule that he who consents loses his rights, and how it is to be understood.
3. In case of doubt, a donation is not presumed.
body: The point on which counsel is sought is as follows. Aguta, wife of Jacob Petrutius of Castro Copignano, made her will, in which she instituted as her universal heirs Jacob and John, her sons; and if either of them should die in pupillary age, or at any time without legitimate and natural children, she substituted Andrew, the flesh-and-blood brother of Jacob Petrutius, the said testator. The aforementioned testator died, with the said Jacob and John, her sons, and the said Andrew, her flesh-and-blood brother, surviving her. Then Jacob died, with the said John, his brother, and the said Andrew, his uncle, surviving him. The said John was then in his thirteenth or fourteenth year. He sold to Ser Laurentius, son of Lord Raynaldus, with the consent, presence, and will of Matiolus Vannutius, his curator, and of the aforementioned Andrew, Jacob, and the nearest blood relatives of the said John, one piece of land situated, etc., namely, from the goods of the inheritance of the said Aguta, his mother. The said Andrew, after the death of the said testator, his sister, cultivated the thing sold and rendered the fruits of the said thing to the said John, his nephew, up to the time of the sale of the said thing. After the time of the said sale, he rendered the fruits of the said thing to Ser Laurentius, the buyer, during the lifetime of the said John, and while the said John was living. Then the said John died intestate, having left no children, but with the said Andrew, his uncle, surviving him. Then the said Ser Laurentius, the buyer, died, while the said Andrew was holding, possessing, and occupying the said thing. The heirs of the said Ser Laurentius, the buyer, seek to compel the said Andrew to render to them the fruits of the said thing. The said Andrew refuses to render the fruits to them, on the ground that he held and possessed the said thing after the death of the aforementioned John, his flesh-and-blood nephew, and now holds and possesses it by right of fideicommissum and by virtue of the aforementioned will made by the said Aguta, formerly his flesh-and-blood sister. But it must be observed that the said John, before the sale of the said thing, sold several other goods from the said inheritance, which amount to his legitime. Now the question is: what right does the said Andrew have in the said thing? And whether the consent given to the said sale by him, as the nearest blood relative, prejudices his claim.

† The first question concerning consent, namely whether it prejudices the consenting party in a future fideicommissum, is thus determined by Bartolus: either the said consent impedes the existence of the condition of the fideicommissum, and then it prejudices the consenting party, as in D. 35.1.2, l. cum pater, § cum libertis, and D. 35.1.1, l. nihil, § omnibus, because by consenting he blocks his own path, so that he cannot revoke. And there is an example of this, since the condition “if he alienates” caused the day of the fideicommissum to arrive. For if alienation occurs with the consent of the fideicommissary, the alienation is valid and cannot be revoked perpetually. Or, by such consent, the existence of the condition of the fideicommissum is not impeded, for example because the fideicommissum was left under the condition that the person requested dies without children; and then this consent does not harm, so that upon the occurrence of the condition of the fideicommissum, the fideicommissum may be claimed. And Bartolus cites for this case D. 35.1.1, l. si a substituto, in principio, with its gloss. And thus this question is determined by him in D. 35.1, l. si fundum per fideicommissum.

† Moreover, the rule which states that he who consents loses his rights applies, unless on account of a conscience bound by some office decreed to him by the common law or by municipal law, as in C. de admi. tut. l. cum quaedam. But here he consented on account of an office decreed to him by municipal law, which requires the consent of relatives; therefore, etc. To this point contributes what is fully noted in ff. de pig. act. l. Gayus.

† Moreover, if it were to cause prejudice, a certain donation would be presumed; but in case of doubt, a donation is not presumed, especially in matters involving great prejudice, as is fully noted by Bartolus in *l. quae dotis*, D. *sol. mat.* Furthermore, the law provides that simple consent does not prejudice a right that supervenes, as in D. *quorum lega.*, *l. 1*, § *prodest autem*; nor does it prejudice, as in D. *de leg. 1*, *l. si fundum per fideicom.*, and D. *de leg. 2*, *l. codicil.*, § *i*, because there the discussion concerns a pure fideicommissum. And in the same way, one responds to what is noted in D. *de reg. iu.*, *l. aliud est vendere*, in the principle. Moreover, those words create doubt: because the sale was for holding in perpetuity. And thus this person consented to holding in perpetuity; therefore, it is never permissible to contravene this, otherwise what effect would the word “in perpetuity” have? Furthermore, the seller, with the consent of the fideicommissary, promised to deliver possession free, clear, and unencumbered; but this cannot be the case unless the fideicommissum, as regards the thing sold, is barred, as in C. *commun. de leg.*, *l. si*, § *sed quia nostra*. The Speculator, who sets forth the formula for how consent intervenes in this case, mixes consent and renunciation, as is evident in Spec. *de emp. et vend.*, § *1*, in the place near the end, there, “insuper,” etc. In this question, I say as follows: either mention of the fideicommissum was made in the consent, for example, “such fideicommissary,” etc., and then it prejudices, when not ex officio; otherwise not, according to the note in D. *de ver. ob.*, *l. qui Romae*, § *duo fratres*, and D. *de transac.*, *l. qui cum tutoribus*, because it does not appear that the conditional fideicommissum was contemplated, which could not be hoped for except through the sad event of the son’s death, nor was it permitted, as in D. *de condi. et demon.*, *l. tutelae*, in the principle, and D. *ad trebel.*, *l. ita tamen*, § *a patre*. And therefore, all things considered, I say that the said consent did not prejudice, because he did not consent as a fideicommissary, nor was mention made of the fideicommissum. The remaining points are clear. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the delict of the doer and of the one who causes it to be done is the same in number.
2. How a statute speaking of the doubling of the penalty is to be understood.
body: It is not.

† the penalty of death, unless in the event of failure to pay the money, if he is unwilling or unable to pay. But as regards the said John, who gave money to the assassins, the penalty is four thousand pounds; and a similar penalty applies to Peter Angeli. As for those who committed the murder, i.e., the assassins themselves, the penalty is hanging. And the reason for the aforementioned is, as regards John: because he who causes an act to be done is punished by the penalty of two thousand pounds, which is the simple penalty. And this is doubled by the money, thus making four thousand; and this according to the opinion of Master Bartolus. But certainly this question requires a more extensive investigation.

† First, the statute provided for a penalty of one thousand [librae] on the doer. Second, it provided for a penalty of two thousand [librae] on the one who causes it to be done, without money. Third, it established that penalties are to be doubled, namely, when he causes it to be done with money intervening. It is necessary to consider whether the offense of the doer and of the one who causes it to be done is the same wrong in number of the wrong itself, not to speak of the persons. And Dy. and Cyn. say that it is so, in l. 1, C. si reus, vel accusator mortuus fuerit. And if this is true, the penalty of two thousand pounds is a double penalty; because he who causes it to be done sins in himself and in another. Therefore, for the same homicide in number, he is punished with a double penalty than if he had done it himself, and thus this causing to be done is a qualified act. The penalty of one thousand pounds, however, is a simple penalty. And thus, by reason of the money given, the one thousand will be doubled. And there will be three thousand pounds of denarii, and not four thousand, as in l. si cum exe., §. quadruplatur, ff. quod mei causa. And although the statute does not speak in the first part by multiplicative names, because it does not say "in double," nevertheless it says the same thing, and it can be gathered from the words that it intended to be doubled, according to the note by Ia. and Cy. in l. 1, C. de sen. quae pro eo, quod interest. But if it is not the same offense in number, then for certain those two thousand are a simple penalty attached to a certain genus of offense, and thus the whole two thousand came to be doubled. But the assessors commonly do not care for anything else than to follow the opinion of Bartolus, and thus they practice. And of this fully noted by Bartolus, ff. de poenis, l. sanctio legum. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The statute declares that, if anyone dies intestate without children, the nearest blood relatives on the father’s side shall succeed to the patrimony, and those on the mother’s side to the dowry.
body: Eacttum et

† Ser Theus had two sons, namely Stephen and Peter Marcus: the said Theus dies, the said two legitimate and natural sons surviving. Then Peter Marcus dies, his legitimate and natural daughter, Lady Memma, and the said Stephen, his full brother, surviving. After this, Stephen dies, his legitimate and natural sons, Luca and Theus, and the said Lady, his niece, surviving. Finally, Luca and Theus die without children, their mother, Lady Melontania, and their cousin sister, the aforementioned Lady Memma, surviving. It is asked to whom, or to whom, the hereditary goods of the said Luca and Theus belong: whether to the mother or to the cousin sister, having regard to the words of the statute written below and the common laws. If anyone shall have died or has died leaving male offspring, the female sex shall not succeed, unless by the will of the deceased. And if any persons shall have died intestate without sons or daughters, the nearest blood relatives on the father’s side shall succeed in the patrimony: and the nearest on the mother’s side in the marriage portion: Provided, however, that males are preferred to females. The said Luca and Theus could have had a twofold patrimony, namely, the profectitious, which formerly belonged to their father or paternal grandfather. And in this patrimony Memma succeeds as the nearest relative on the father’s side. Likewise, they could have had adventitious patrimony acquired by them, or given or left to them by others. Likewise, they could also have had fruits acquired by them after the death of their father: and in these Lady Melontania succeeds: and the reason is, because these goods are not of that kind of which the statute speaks: for these goods are a third species in themselves distinct from those of which the statute speaks. And this distinction is proved by that which is found in the law and note, C. communia de success. aut. itaque. And a similar distinction is found not only there, but elsewhere, as in ff. de vulg. subst. l. sed si plures. §. in arrogato. and l. cohaeredi. §. cum filiae. ver. nec filiae cum missio. and C. de test. mili. l. 1. and ff. de pecu. l. hic quaeritur. §. potest. And for the declaration of the aforementioned matters, two heads of the statute must be considered, not connected, but separate. The first head is concerning succession in the patrimony, i.e., that which was derived into the successors from the paternal male line. The second in the marriage portion, i.e., that which was derived into the descendants from the maternal line: although afterwards the whole patrimony became one and the same in the person of the deceased, as in ff. de vul. sub. l. sed si plures. §. filio. If therefore the deceased has patrimonial goods understood in this manner, only the blood relatives on the father’s side succeed, whether the mother is in the middle or not: because it is not of the nature of this statute that there be a question concerning both goods, since it disposes of each separately. But if they are matrimonial goods, for example, because the maternal grandfather or grandmother had made these nephews heirs, their mother would succeed to them, however, according to the form of the statute simultaneously, as in C. de bonis quae lib. in l. quod satis. secundum bonum intellectum. If, however, they are goods of a third kind, we observe the common law in them, because a case omitted by the statute is deemed committed to the disposition of the common law, as in ff. sol. ma. l. si vero. §. de viro. and l. si cum dotem. in princ. And thus should be understood the opinions which I otherwise gave, and under this distinction should be saved the said opinions which I otherwise gave, both for the mother and for Lady Memma. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. On the succession of children to the property of a mother who had several husbands.
body: Certain

† Lady Ceccha had three husbands. The first was named Vannes, from whom she bore two daughters, namely Flora and Cia. The second was named Bartholomew, from whom she bore no children. Finally, the said husband, namely Bartholomew, died. Subsequently, Cia died. Then the said Lady Ceccha took a third husband, who is named John. Afterwards, the said Lady Ceccha made the aforementioned will and died, with John her husband and the said Flora surviving. It is asked, in which goods and to what extent the said Flora succeeds, and in which goods and to what extent the said John succeeds. Having seen and examined the said will, it must be known that the said Flora succeeds in all paternal goods and in all goods of Cia that devolved to her, and [in those of] Vannes. And in these, John has no share, as is provided in C. de secundis nuptiis, auth. Ex testamento, and l. Foeminae, §. Fin. It follows that we must consider the proper goods of the said Lady Ceccha. And it must be said that John cannot have more of them than Flora, as is provided in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. Hac edictali. And therefore, other legacies, which were left for the soul, ought first to be paid. Afterwards, the residue is to be divided equally between the said John, to whom his wife left half of her goods in the will, and the said Flora, so that it does not contravene the said l. Hac edictali, insofar as it disposes concerning plurality. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone has given a guarantee to pay the costs for the plaintiff, should he lose the case, whether the guarantor is bound if it has been declared that the instance is forfeited and the plaintiff is condemned in costs.
2. What is meant by "cause," and how it is to be understood.
body: It is proposed,

† Since a certain person had promised as a surety for a certain plaintiff that, if the plaintiff were to succumb in the case, he would reimburse the expenses, it was pronounced by the judge that the instance was peremptory, and the plaintiff was condemned in costs. The question is asked whether the surety is bound. The question turns on this point: whether the plaintiff is said to have lost the case, when it is certain that he can raise it again, as in D. de iudiciis, l. et post edictum, §. circunducto; and as noted in D. de dolo, l. arbitro, §. dolo cuius. And it is clear from an open reason, because such an interlocutory judgment, after another trial is hoped for, does not give rise to the exception of res iudicata; and thus it does not finally determine the case. C. de iudiciis, l. properandum; C. ut infra certum tempus criminalis quaestio terminetur, l. fin. And I say that the plaintiff is not said to have lost the case, nor is he said to have succumbed in the case, but to have omitted it. For it is one thing to omit by delaying, and another to lose, as the text and glossa state in C. de praescriptione longi temporis, l. 1.

But here it must be observed that the term *causa* is sometimes taken strictly and properly, and sometimes broadly and improperly. In the first mode, *causa* is taken for the fact, the obligation, or some other right which is put forward in court, as in C. *per quas personas nobis acquiritur*, l. 1, where the gloss says in this way that he is said to succumb in the *causa* from whom that right is taken away by an absolving sentence, or is declared not to appertain to him, as in D. *de exceptionibus rei iudicatae*, l. *et an eandem* and l. *conqueritur*. And in this sense *causa* is taken in innumerable places in the law, as is clear. C. *de transactionibus*, l. *causas*; and C. *ne liceat vna in eademque causa*, in the rubric and in the text; C. *vbi causa fiscalis*; and C. *causa statuta*, throughout; and note C. *de sponsalibus*, l. 1; C. *de actionibus*, l. *in causis*. And in the sum, he is said to lose the *causa* who loses the thing brought into court, i.e., the *causa* of the *causa*, or comprehensively both, as in C. *de paciscendis*, l. *postquam liti*, because the word simply uttered must be understood in its primary signification; hence one is not said to have succumbed in the principal *causa* unless he succumbed by a definitive judgment, or as it were by calculation. Sometimes *causa* is taken for judicial controversy, or the prosecution of the lawsuit, and then he who loses the prosecution, i.e., the *instantia*, is said to have lost the *causa*, i.e., the *instantia*: for *instantia* can be called *causa*, inasmuch as it is ordered to its effect, i.e., to the end of pronouncing judgment. C. *de iudiciis*, l. *properandum*, § *finis*, where it says: "and he has fallen from the *causa*." For "from the *causa*" is explained as "from the *instantia* of the judgment," not from the principal *causa*. But speaking properly, the *causa* is said to be finished when the lawsuit is entirely quelled, as in C. *de paciscendis*, l. *postquam liti*, in the words "finished *causa*"; and D. *de iure fisci*, l. *in fraudem*, § *neque*, in the words "the *causa* fails." And a good *causa* is said, having regard to the truth of that which is deduced in court, not to the order of the judgment itself, which is called *instantia*, because the parties stand upon the *instantia*, as in D. *de conditione ob turpem causam*, l. 2, in the words "but if I gave," in the phrase "in a good *causa*." It therefore matters greatly whether the surety of the plaintiff promised the expenses if the plaintiff should succumb in the prosecution of the lawsuit: and then, if the defendant is absolved from the observance of the judgment, he would be bound for them; or whether if he should succumb in the *causa*: and then he is not bound. A similar distinction is made in l. *grege*, § 2, *post litem*, D. *de fideiussoribus*. But if sometimes *causa* is put for judgment, i.e., for the prosecution of the lawsuit, this is when we speak having regard to the nature of such an act, as when we make a question whether a procurator is bound to pursue the *causa* of an appeal, whether it is the same as the principal one or not. C. *de procuratoribus*, l. *inuitus*; C. *ne liceat in vna, eademque causa*, l. 1; D. *iudicia solvuntur*, l. *pe*, cum si. But absolutely and simply, this name *causa* signifies not the emerging *causa*. Moreover, whether a delay is to be granted or not, whether the libel is aptly conceived or not: whether the times for proving some chapter are different or not: but the principal *causa* itself, as appears from what is read and noted in D. *de minoribus*, l. *intra utile tempus*; and C. *vbi, et apud quos*, l. *finis*, in the words "to decide such *causae*." And there are innumerable laws on this point. Since therefore fidejussio is of strict law, and words must be understood properly, it is clear that the said surety did not guarantee in this case, in which the plaintiff did not succumb in the principal *causa*, but in the emerging one concerning the *instantia*. And yet I readily admit that *causa* is sometimes put for *instantia*, as noted in D. *solutis matrimonii*, l. 1; and it is clear in C. *de iuramento calumniae*, l. 1 and 2; and C. *de iudiciis*, l. *rem non nouam*, with many similar cases. But where we speak of *causa* not with respect to the order or form, but with respect to the general outcome of the controversy, then it must be understood only of the principal *causa*. C. *de rebus creditis*, l. *generaliter*, after the principle, in the words "the *causa* or chapter is decided"; as in C. *de fructibus et litis expensis*, l. *terminato*, in the words "to the victor of the *causa*". I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation made to a church by someone of all his goods for the salvation of his soul and of his deceased, yet reserving to himself the usufruct and habitation of the house during his lifetime, and after his death remaining freely to the church, is to be called a donation inter vivos or causa mortis.
2. From what it may be known when a donation is causa mortis or inter vivos.
body:
In the year of our Lord 1465, in the 13th indiction, during the pontificate of Pope Gregory XI, on the 15th day of the month of January, acted in the village of Ponte Nuovo, before the house of me, the notary subscribed below, and so forth, present Blasio Vannoli, Peter of Villa Plani, etc. In the same year, on the 28th day of the month of January, acted in the church of Saint Mary of Roncione, district of Duca, present Paulutio, son of Master John of Drento, Petrutio Vdutii of Castro Geuentulae, county of Juderi, Mattheo Bartoli of Villa Sanctae Benorae, and Mattheo Vannutii of Castro Cassalinae, county of Perugia, witnesses called and requested for this purpose.

The chapter and convent of the church of Saint Mary of Roncione having been convened and assembled in the said church in open court, in which chapter was present Lord Peter, prior of the said church, and Lord Peter Andrioli of Bittoio, monk of the said church, there being present Cecchus Vannis, son of Cecchus of Castro Diruti, county of Perugia, and his wife, Lady Barthola, before the said Lord Peter, prior, and Lord Peter, and me, the notary, and the above-mentioned witnesses.

First, one house situated in Castro Diruti at the gate of Saint Salvator, with its roof and building, the boundaries of which are: on one side a road, on another the house of Pianutia, wife of Vannutius Cecchus, on another the heirs of Nicolaus, son of Master Angelus.

Also, one garden plot situated at the above-mentioned gate, bounded on two sides by roads, and on another by the common wall of the said Castle.

Also, one piece of land, partly vineyard and partly not, situated in the dependencies of the said Castle, in the locality called La Ripa, adjoining on one side Herculanus Petri, on another the heirs of Simonellus, on another Franciscus, son of Lord Orlandus, and on another a ditch.

Also, one piece of land, partly vineyard and partly not, situated in the said dependencies, in the locality called Versieri, bounded on two sides by the heirs of Petrus Gulielmi, and on another by the heirs of Colla Vannis.

Also, one piece of cultivated land situated in the said dependencies, in the locality [unnamed], its boundaries being: on one side a road, on another the heirs of Master Petrus, on another Vannutius Accursi, and on another Betulus Resticelli.

Also, one holding of cultivated land situated in the dependencies of the village of Sancti Angeli de Cole, its boundaries being: on one side a road, on another the heirs of Cellinus, and on another the heirs of Tudinus Neroli, and so forth, with accesses and egresses, and so forth, to have and to hold, and so forth.

Which donation and grant they made to the said prior for the salvation of the souls of the said donors and of all their dead, etc., always reserving the fruits of the said goods and the habitation of the said house during their lifetime; and after the death of the said Cecchus and Barthola, [the properties] shall remain to the said church, etc. Which

† That this donation was a donation causa mortis appears to be proven, because the words sound as though they were conferred after the death of the donors, as is clear there, when finally and conclusively the document states, “and after the death of the said Cecchi and Bartholutia, let it remain to the said church.” For these are words placed in the last position, which by their meaning and nature seem to indicate a donation causa mortis, as in l. Seya, de dote praelegata; and noted in l. quae dotis, sol. matr.; and C. de pac., l. fina.; and ff. de test., l. 1; ff. de leg. 2, l. legat. est; ff. de don. caus. mort., l. Seya, in fin. For the contemplation of death and the conferral in view of death indicate a donation causa mortis, as in Inst. de don. post princ.; ff. de don. caus. mort., l. 1. Hence there is no doubt that this is a donation causa mortis from the very form of the donation itself and its final cause: because it was made on account of death and conferred after death. Moreover, the word “remain” is appropriate to death, as in C. de don. ant. nup., l. si cum ante. Furthermore, where mention is made of the soul, it seems that one is contemplating death, as in c. dudum, § verum, de sepult. in 6; and noted in l. si quaestio, de leg. 3.

† On the contrary, it appears that it is a donation inter vivos, for three things are gathered from the tenor of the writing. First, the act of donating simply, up to the words “reserved.” Second, the reservation of habitation and usufruct, up to the words “and after death.” Third, the release of the thing from this servitude by another, from the words “and after death” to the end. From the first head, it was a simple donation, i.e., irrevocable, as in the Institutes, De donationibus, § Perficiuntur; and in the Code, Ut actiones ab haeredibus, et contra haeredes, l. 1. From the second head, the donor retained for himself the servitude of usufruct and habitation. Code, De donationibus, l. Quisquis; Digest, De actione empti, l. Fundum, where you will see. From the third head, it is expressed how that servitude ought to end. For if nothing had been expressed, the usufruct would end in many ways; but because it was provided that it should not end except by death, it does not end in other ways, as in l. Si cum in annos, Quibus modis ususfructus amittitur. And therefore those words, “and after death,” etc., are added to the release of the donated thing, so that it may be free from all servitude upon the death of the donors. Wherefore, since such death is not uncertain with respect to the donation of the ownership, but to the release of that servitude, the mention of death by no means makes the donation causa mortis. For it matters greatly to what death is added, and with what intent; because we ought rather to examine the cause of the words and the intent of the contracting parties than their mere letter, as noted in l. 1, Venditione, in fine, Digest, Communia praediorum. From the very imposition of the servitude, it also appears that the naked ownership was freely donated, as in Digest, De usufructu, l. Proculus. Hence, since from such conjecture it appears that he did not wish it to be donated, even the mention of death does not make it a donation causa mortis, as in l. Cum maritus, § Finis, Digest, De pactis dotalibus. Moreover, the formal retention of usufruct and habitation, and not causal, signifies that dominion is entirely transferred to the donee: for no one’s thing serves another. And although by a donation causa mortis, when delivered, dominion is transferred immediately; yet because it is in the power of the donor to revoke, and in a certain sense he is called owner. To what purpose, then, would the reservation of usufruct be made, when everything was in his power? Hence, because the reservation is in some respects, it is considered a transfer in others; and this ought to be judged as a simple and irrevocable donation with respect to ownership. Moreover, when there is doubt about the intent of the donor, and thus about the fact, or there is doubt about the law, because on both sides something can be probably alleged in law, it is rather to be judged that it is a donation inter vivos than causa mortis, as noted in the gloss, Institutes, De donationibus, post principium. And because the witnesses also say that it was said according to that word, “remain,” i.e., freely, hence they declare that death was added to the word “freely,” not to the word “donate,” so the principal word was simple, and without any mention of death. And thus, at least from the conjunction of the instrument and the witnesses declaring it, it appears that the donation was simple and inter vivos with respect to ownership, to which afterwards the usufruct and benefit are consolidated. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, etc. Justice and the reason of truth always reserved. I am also moved, because those words, “and after death,” etc., refer most immediately to the preceding, i.e., usufruct and habitation, as in Extra, De donationibus, c. Cum dilecti, which chapter serves well. But how is one to respond to the rule which says that the mention of death ought to operate something, and that it makes one presume the donation to be causa mortis; nor can the rules of law be broken? Solution: It has already been answered that death was not here added to the donation, but to the release of the donated things from the imposed servitudes. But against this it is objected, for that last clause ought to be referred to all the above. And thus also to the word “donate.” And thus to the determination of the word “donate.” It follows that it will be a donation causa mortis. The laws are common. But I answer, because the clause can, saving the intent of the speaker and the conjecture of law, be referred to all, then it is referred to all. Otherwise, if it cannot be referred, because the preceding are mutually contrary, as is the case here, for speaking of ownership, which was the first clause, ownership was donated. But speaking of usufruct and habitation, which was the second clause: these were not donated, but excepted. Then follows the third clause, cohering with the second, and not the first, and coming consequentially to the second, and not determinatively to the first. And the reason is, because the last clause was added to enlarge; but if a simple donation were reduced to a donation causa mortis, it would reduce the perpetual to the corruptible, and the irrevocable to the voidable, which is absurd, that a clause, which is added in favor of the donee, should restrict and diminish the benefit of the donation, as in l. Titio centum, in principio, De conditionibus et demonstrationibus; and Digest, De legatis, l. Nulla. To this also contribute those words, “to have, to hold, and to do whatever he pleases, perpetually,” which are decided under that “etc.,” having regard to customary formulas. This is also suggested by the favor of the Church, and the favor of the soul, hence the widest interpretation ought to be made, as in Digest, De usufructu, l. Locum, in principio; and Digest, De religiosis, l. Sunt personae; and in the Authentic, Constitutio, Quae de dignitatibus, § Illud. From the dignity also of the donee, who is the lord, the donation is presumed in the stronger and fuller sense. Digest, De iudiciis, l. Sed et si susceperit, § Libertis; and Digest, De usu et habitatione, l. Plenum, § Lubentius. Also, since the Church is our mother, it is probable that it was fully donated to her, as in Digest, De libertis legatis, l. Aurelius, § Titius testamento; and this was considered by the said chapter Cum dilecti. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a ward appears to die intestate.
body: In succession

† Regarding the children of Pillorus, who are not properly said to die intestate, I hold the common opinion of the doctors that this statute does not claim to apply, but that we should adhere to the common law, unless the father had made a pupillary substitution for them, or a summary substitution containing a pupillary one. For then, if the substitution lapsed, the ward is said to die intestate. And thus, in this case, the statute would apply, and the mother would not succeed except to one-eighth part, but according to the form of the statute, and the aunt would succeed to the residue. Others, such as Bartolus, say that although the ward is not properly called intestate, nevertheless his inheritance devolves intestate, and thus the statute always applies. So too do I myself in *l. in prima*, ff. *de suis et legitimis*. And this opinion is observed in many places: because excessive subtleties are not admitted by judges. And because that subtlety does not apply to laymen, hence the general intent of the statute. And the custom of speaking is also such, according to Bartolus. And presupposing this custom, if the poor substitutes repudiated, and the aunt succeeded in the substitution, but if they did not repudiate, then we would be in that other question, whether, considering the tenor of this summary substitution made until the twentieth year, it contains a pupillary substitution or not. And it seems to be the case regarding the poor ones that it does contain one, as *cap. si pater*, de test., lib. 6. And there are infinite opinions on this, and before it is known whether the said poor ones expressed in the substitution repudiate, one cannot advise on this with firm footing. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, upon the death of one brother who was a partner, the partnership remains between the father and the nephew through the brother.
2. Whether a tutor who purchases is deemed to purchase with his own money, or with the ward’s money, or with common money.
body: In this matter, it is necessary to proceed by stirpes.

† For when one of two brothers, partners in some business, dies, the partnership is terminated by death. Therefore, with regard to the new commencement of administration, there is no partnership between the minor son of the deceased brother and his uncle. D. 17,2,1, § morte. Nor can a partnership be commenced between the uncle and the minor even with the latter, since the guardian cannot authorize himself, as stated in D. 26,1,1. If, therefore, anything is acquired for the minor through the uncle, this does not occur by right of partnership, but it must occur by some other right. It can therefore occur in two ways. In the first way, because it was transacted in the common name; and thus it is acquired by the office of negotiorum gestio. In the second way, because the thing was purchased by the guardian from the minor’s money; and then it is acquired by the minor ratifying it by a special right, as noted in C. 4,55,1, si ut proponis. Nevertheless, it must be established that it was from the minor’s money.

† For in doubt it is presumed that the money belongs to the person in whose possession it is, who delivers it to another, namely, to the buyer himself. L. si defunctus, C. arbitrium tutelae. From these things the determination of the questions asked appears: because they were purchased in a common name. S. de communi pecunia. But if they were purchased in a personal name, they are not common, unless it is proved that they were purchased with common money, as in D. de admin. tu. L. Titium et Mevium, §. altero. The tutor, however, who denies that he has expended the ward’s money, is liable for interest, because he ought to have invested it in the purchase of lands, and thus to be diligent in the affairs of the ward as in his own. And if he had a good market for himself, he ought to have procured the same for the ward, whose money he held in his hands. This is good faith and diligence: to do for another what one wishes to be done for oneself, having undertaken his care. Likewise, if the uncle borrowed the ward’s money in his own name, the ward is not liable for the interest that could have been gained for him through lawful business. D. de neg. gest. L. qui sine usuris. And thus I answer the questions asked. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute, pact, or custom, by which a husband is to acquire half of the dowry upon the death of his wife, has application if the wife dies before the marriage is consummated.
body: Custom
