It was agreed by pact that the husband should gain half of the dowry upon the death of his wife. The question arises: if he did not marry her, nor bear the burdens of marriage, ought he to have said gain? Master Bartolus says that yes, in *l. nihil*, D. *de rerum amotione*; he cites D. *de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, *l. cum hic status*, § *si maritus*. Others say the contrary, because this gain has a tacit final reason, which, when it ceases, the gain also ceases, namely on account of the burdens of marriage, just as we say regarding the fruits of the dowry, D. *de iure dotium*, *l. dotis fructus*; D. *de solutionibus*, *l. de divisione*; and *l. si ante*. And it seems expressly stated in D. *quod falso testatus est*, *l. pater*, § *an in patrem*.

However, if it rested with the woman that she was not to be married, and then the husband gains, because the woman preferred to enter a monastery rather than consummate the marriage, C. *de episcopis et clericis*, *l. deo nobis*; or if for some other occasion she did not wish to adhere to the husband, without fault of the husband, or if it rested with the husband, or through the fault of the husband, then he ought not to gain, by argument from D. *de locato*, *l. quaero*, § *inter locatorem*; D. *de solutionibus matrimonii*, *l. ab hostibus*, § *si vir uxorem*; C. *de pactis conventis*, *l. aequalitas*, at the words *et quae nihil*; otherwise it is *l. aequalitas*, which begins *et quae nihil*.

But if it rests on chance, because the wife predeceases him without fault of the husband, then he ought to gain the dowry, because the condition was fulfilled, by argument from C. *de institutionibus et substitutionibus*, *l. antepenultima*. Moreover, it can be said that, by referring the pact to the marriage contract, it is a contract of dowry, or a donation, namely, "that you take me as your wife," so that the pact precedes the marriage. But if, on the contrary, the marriage precedes the pact, it is a contract of "I give," that is, a donation, because "you have taken me." Thus, the husband gains entirely, because he does not desire to fulfill the condition of the mode or cause for the future.

I do not depart from the aforementioned institution, because this pact is consequent to the dowry. But the husband, who would not wish to bear the burdens, could not demand the dowry, C. *de dotis promissione*, *l. ultima*, § *utramque*. Therefore, much less could he have it gratuitously and as a donation. Furthermore, this is aided by the fact that this donation is not here a title merely for gain, since it comes in consequence of an onerous title, D. *de conditione ob causam*, *l. si donaturus*, § *ultimus*, in the gloss.

From the foregoing, the solution of the question appears, that since it rested on the death [of the wife], the husband ought to gain said half of the dowry. This is aided by what we say in named contracts regarding the risk in a perfected contract, D. *de periculo et commodo rei venditae*, *l. necessario*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether there is a difference, whether it is said that women do not succeed while males are extant, or until, or as long as, males are extant.
2. What the phrase "quo ad" (as to) imports.
3. The statute of the Commune of Assisi.
4. That no woman may have recourse to the goods of the donor, whether dower-giver or not, nor may her son.
body: For the preservation of the sons of the city and community of Assisi, and so that inheritances and successions may not pass to others who are not of the house in the male line, they have decreed and ordained that if any woman, whether dowered by her father, mother, brother or brothers, grandfather, or grandmother, or by any other person, cannot or ought not herself, nor her son descending from her, to have recourse to or come to the inheritance or succession of any of the aforementioned dowers or non-dowers, nor to claim or hold anything from the goods, or over the goods of any of the aforementioned in any manner, as long as there shall be or remain a son, grandson, great-grandson, or male heir born of legitimate marriage, descending from the aforementioned or any of the aforementioned, and coming into the aforementioned succession together with such dowered woman; but she, the woman thus dowered, ought to be content with her dowry. And she indeed, or anyone proceeding from her, or succeeding and descending in the goods of any of the aforementioned, may not claim or hold anything by testament or last wills, donations, or concessions made or to be made, always saving and etc.

† To determine how this statute stands, one must consider the common law. For a statute sometimes impedes the transmission of an inheritance, and sometimes impedes the acceptance of an inheritance that has devolved. D. ad Sillenum, l. Si quis in graui, §. Si; cum l. seq. In the first case, a daughter dying while a male is alive does not transmit to the grandson: because she has no right which she can transmit. Hence the grandson cannot come by transmission, but he could come in his own person, if he were conceived while the grandfather was alive; otherwise not, as is noted. C. unde liberi, l. Qui se patris; C. de inoff. test., l. Si quis filium; D. de inoff. testam., l. Si quis filio; D. de suis et legit., l. Item praetor; because one not conceived had no rights of consanguinity with the grandfather, and thus does not succeed by the right of blood in his own person. In the second case, transmission occurs from children to children, not to strangers. l. 1, §. De his qui ante apert. tabul. And therefore, if indeed the statute were to stand in correcting the common law, insofar as the inheritance devolves upon the female together with the brother, the daughter dying while the brother is alive would not transmit to her own son. But if it stands not in correcting, but in suspending for a time, i.e., until, or as long as there is a male, then transmission would occur. For this part, the reason and the intent of the statute, and the cessation of the excluding cause, are favorable. For the first part, however, the strictness of the words is favorable: because it says, nor may she have anything. But she would have something, if she had the right to accept the devolved inheritance, for example if the male himself had this right, in the meantime he would not be heir in solidum: because if he were, he could not cease to be. But it could be said that this grandson succeeds by the contrary sense of the statute, and by the benefit of the statute, not by the force of transmission. For since the statute provided for her mother and for herself, because it said, nor descendants from her, it provides for herself by the contrary sense when they are lacking, arg. D. de off. eius cuius man. est iurisd., l. 1, §. Eius rei. And this opinion is friendly to nature and equity, although according to the strictness of the law one could very much doubt it because of the strictness of the words and the rules of law. But what I say, where the statute says, as long as, or until, I do not say the same if the statute said, the female shall not succeed while males exist: because this condition is interpreted, that is, if they shall exist. D. de usur., l. Euict.; D. de condit. et demonstr., l. A testatore. But when we speak of the preference of one over another, we inspect the time at which the succession is acquired: so much so that he who is then preferred becomes the perpetual successor, and transmits, and always excludes the other, as Inst. de legat., agn. success., §. Proximus; and l. Fin., D. de success. edict. Hence absolutes of the ablative are resolved into a momentary condition, and not into a successive condition, which namely momentary condition it suffices to have existed once. D. de testam. tutel., l. Penult., etiam sine perseverantia.

† but the word “quo ad” etc. requires perseverance. This is held by Bartolus, *Digestum*, ad Tertullianam, l. final. And thus the son of the lady Pacis succeeded in the third degree to his grandfather, who was called Cecche. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The nature of agreements is that they pass to heirs, even if no mention of them has been made. It fails, etc.
2. The nature of immunity is that it passes to subsequent successors. Hence it is inferred regarding the question whether nobles, who have immunity or exemption by agreement or concession, transmit it to their heirs.
3. Whether immunity extends to property acquired subsequently.
4. What these words or pronouns, "mine" and "theirs," signify.
5. Given a customary prescription that a levy not be paid, if the levy has been made a tax according to the form of the statute, whether it shall be payable.
6. What a tax is, and what a levy.
7. Bartolus rarely speaks well.
8. Whether, and for what period, a toll is prescribed.
casus:
CASE. The case upon which counsel is sought is as follows. Long ago, between the Commune of Genoa on one part, and the Marquises of Gavi, who then were, on the other part, a solemn convention was entered into, fortified by stipulation and obligatory on both sides, in which the said Marquises gave the Castle of Gavi with its borough, and with all its appurtenances and adherences: namely, with the whole territory and possessions, and with part of the toll of the said place, the other part being retained by themselves, and with others, of which no mention is made in the said convention. And of these they made a common remission and a pact not to sue further. And for this grant they received from the Commune three thousand eight hundred Genoese pounds, of which they were to buy houses and possessions in Genoa or its district, in which they were to come to dwell in the city of Genoa. Then the said Marquises promised to the said Commune, or to the one then presiding for the Commune, namely, the Lord Podesta of Genoa, to defend and warrant all and each of the aforesaid things, both by themselves and by their heirs, against every person, and to hold them firm and valid, and not to hinder, etc. The said Marquises promised certain other things in the convention, of which I do not care to make mention. And these are the things which the Marquises promised to the said Commune.

On the other hand, the said Commune, accepting the aforesaid things, or the said Lord Podesta, who then represented the whole Commune of Genoa, agreed, promised, and made a pact with the said Commune of Genoa to the said Marquises, that from the aforesaid moneys, namely, which the said Commune of Genoa gave them, and from the possessions acquired therefrom, and from the toll, and from their other goods, they shall not give any *collecta* (tax/assessment), except from the dowries of wives and daughters-in-law, or of their descendants, who were of Genoa, or whose dowries are from that stock from which other citizens are accustomed to give *collecta*. This is the promise made in effect by the Commune to the said Marquises. Note the words, namely, of the promise of the said Commune, from the word “on the other hand” (*versa vice*) upwards, just mentioned, downwards. Because the words taken materially from the said convention are those which create doubt in the question. And you will see below.

Finally, at the end of the instrument, one party promised to the other, and the other to the other, to attend to, fulfill, and observe the aforesaid things, etc. And thus they promised under a penalty of 20 Genoese pounds. And all these things appear in a public instrument written and published by the hand of Bartolus Alberti, notary, in the year 1200, on the 16th day of September, a copy of which we send you on a paper signed outside by A.

After the said convention, after a long time, a statute was made in the city of Genoa, namely, in the year 1389, on the 19th day of August, placed under the rubric “That every possession be assigned before for substituting burdens,” in which it is provided in effect that every possession situated in Genoa or its district, from such boundaries to such, be obligated and affixed for the *collecta* and burdens of the Commune of Genoa to be imposed henceforth. And whoever henceforth buys a possession in Genoa or its district, let him be bound to promise, or to give sureties, for paying the said impositions and *collecta* to be imposed for the said possessions; otherwise the said purchase shall not be valid nor binding by law itself, and shall be held imperfect, nor can dominion be transferred thereby to the buyer. Thus it appears in the said statute, which I send you signed and published by the hand of Francis de Vallella, notary, on a paper signed outside by B.

Finally, after the said statute, the descendants and heirs of the said deceased Marquises bought and acquired in the city of Genoa or its district certain houses and possessions, for which they made no promise to the Commune, nor gave satisfaction for paying the *collecta* to be imposed henceforth by the Commune according to the form of the aforesaid statute; because at that time they acted and treated themselves as free and immune, by virtue and according to the form of the aforesaid convention.

Now, from the theme of the said question thus posited, arises a question concerning the words of the said convention and their understanding, between the heir of the said Marquises and the descendant, namely, the nephew of the said aforesaid deceased Marquises, on one part, and the said Commune on the other; because the said heir of the said Marquises says that he ought to be immune by virtue and according to the form of the aforesaid convention, there where it says that in the convention the Commune promised to the said Marquises that they shall not give *collecta*, etc., to the *collecta* of the Commune of Genoa, both those which are imposed for movables, namely, for movable goods, and also from *collecta* which are imposed on possessions and immovable goods. By which he also says that he is immune by virtue of the said words from tolls and duties imposed and to be imposed by the Commune, both on revenues and on merchandise.

On the contrary, it will be said by the Commune that the said heir of the said Marquises ought not to be free nor immune from the aforesaid *collecta* and tolls. Now it is asked, what is the law.

From this theme arise the following points and doubts, upon which we ask that you give your legal counsel with prudent allegations and motives on each point.

The first is, whether such a contract of stipulation, or convention fortified by stipulation, passes to the heir, and to the heir of the heir of the said Marquises of Gavi, namely, the descendants in the male line of the said Marquises: namely, nephews or great-nephews of the said Marquises. And doubt is made, because in the promise made by the Commune of Genoa to the said Marquises there is no mention of their sons or heirs; but it is simply promised to the said Marquises, etc., without mention of heirs, descendants, or sons of them.

The second doubt is, whether those words added in the said convention in the promise made by the Commune of Genoa to the said Marquises, there where it says “on the other hand,” etc., where it is said that the Commune promises to the Marquises that from all the aforesaid moneys, and from the possessions acquired therefrom, and from the toll, and from all their other goods, they shall not give any *collecta*, etc., whether those words, “and from their other goods,” extend both to present goods which the said Marquises then had from the time of the said convention, and to future goods, that is, whether the said convention extends to goods then acquired, and to those to be acquired later, namely, to houses and possessions both acquired later by them and by their heirs. Assuming that the said contract passes to the heir, as above, and that the said convention extends even to goods to be acquired later, the words of the said convention make this very well, where it is said by indefinite words, “and from their other goods,” etc. And also those words, “except from the dowries of wives and daughters-in-law, or of their descendants,” etc., which are words of future time, and confirm the rule in things not excepted. And also those words, “from the toll,” which is collected annually. So that it could not be said in present goods, but in future goods.

The third doubt is, because the said possessions and houses acquired by the said heir of the said Marquises were acquired after the aforesaid statute made by the said Commune of Genoa, in which it is provided that every possession be affected and obligated to the Commune of Genoa for *collecta* to be imposed, etc. Whether by virtue of the said convention, from *collecta* imposed for the said possessions or houses acquired later, the said heir ought to be immune and exempt. And doubt is made by the said Bartolus in *l. Rescripto*, § final, *Digestum*, de mun. et hono., because by such a chapter the said possessions and houses seem to have been made tributary; which tribute is a merely real burden. But from merely real burdens it is said on behalf of the Commune that the said heir is not immune, but only from *collecta* by virtue of the said convention; which *collecta* is a mixed burden, and not merely real, which is imposed on the person for the things. Therefore, from such *collecta* imposed for the said possessions, the said heir will not be immune. For they understand the said convention, where it is said that they shall not give *collecta*, because they understand, namely, for movables and for movable goods. And in this the said convention operates, but not for immovable goods and possessions; because that would be a merely real burden by virtue of the said chapter.

On the contrary, concerning this, it is said on behalf of the heir that at the time of the convention made between the Commune and him, which was made before the said chapter by 88 years, *collecta*, both that which is imposed on movable goods and that which is imposed on immovable goods, namely, houses and estates, is properly and by law understood to be *collecta*, not tribute. According to the noted gloss, noted by Ioannes Andreas in *c. 1*, de immunitatibus ecclesiarum, lib. 6, in the gloss on the word “proponendum,” where the gloss also states that *collecta* is imposed on estates and possessions. Therefore, the heir says, I have that by common law that which is properly *collecta*, which is a mixed burden, which is imposed on the person for the things: thus is that which is imposed on possessions and immovable goods, just as that which is imposed also on movable goods. Therefore, I ought to be exempt both from *collecta* which are imposed on possessions and immovable goods, and from that *collecta* which is imposed on movable goods. Nor does the chapter alleged by you obstruct, because it is answered that the said chapter could not be made to the prejudice of the said heir and against his convention; because since he was immune from the said *collecta* by virtue of the said convention and pact, both those which were imposed for immovable goods and for movable goods: the chapter could not be made by the said Commune which would derogate or prejudice the convention made between them and fortified by oath; nor alter the nature by the said chapter, by which name of *collecta* from that nature and signification which it had at the time of the said convention and pact, and consequently he ought to be exempt from all *collecta* to be imposed both for movable and immovable goods, especially alleging the said heir that *collecta* which are imposed in Genoa on citizens and other inhabitants, are imposed both for movable and immovable: on the person for movable per centum. And it will be for possessions in 200. And he will pay as much for possessions as for the hundredth. And thus according to the order of Genoa, the said impositions, which are imposed on movable and immovable goods, are imposed on the person for the things. And thus they can properly be called *collecta*.

On this point, it pleases us to provide much care, because it is the principal point of this question: and to examine from there those words, “that they shall not give *collecta*,” what they import, and from what the said heir appears to be exempt under the name of *collecta*.

Also, it pleases us to weigh much concerning this point the words of the said convention, namely, there where it is said that from all the aforesaid moneys, and from the toll, and from their other goods, they shall not give *collecta*, etc., in that it said, “from the aforesaid moneys, and from the possessions acquired therefrom,” because of the word “other” (*alijs*) of their goods; because since mention was just made above of possessions, if the word “other” were implicating similars, it would be clear from the convention that even from *collecta* of possessions the heir was immune. Also, because it says, “and from their other goods,” because by the appellation of goods are comprehended both movables and immovables. And thus he would be immune from *collecta* of movables and immovables. Also, if the said words referred to the toll, and the toll they then had in their goods at the time of the convention, and the toll is considered immovable, the word “other,” implicating similars, would well imply also possessions.

Furthermore, it pleases us also to note this word, namely, the exception, which is in the said convention, where it is said, “except from the dowries of wives and daughters-in-law,” etc., which exception confirms the rule in things not excepted; because they are bound to pay only from the dowries of wives and daughters-in-law, etc. Therefore, from other goods, both movable and immovable, they are not bound to pay *collecta*.

The fourth doubt is, whether by virtue of the said words, “that they shall not give *collecta*,” etc., the said heir is exempt and immune from the tolls of the Commune of Genoa both on victuals and on merchandise imposed, which are imposed in this form: because whoever buys wine in the city of Genoa, pays three soldi by name of toll for one certain measure. And doubt is made, because the Commune says that no, because toll is a real burden, according to the note by Bartolus in *l. 2*, de privilegiis veteranorum, and in *l. 1*, noted by him, *Codex*, de mulieribus, and in which place, lib. 10. But the Commune says that the said heir is not exempt from real burdens, but from *collecta*, which is a mixed burden; therefore, from tolls, which are real burdens, he is not exempt, because the promise made by the Commune cannot be extended beyond the words contained in the said convention.

On the contrary, it is said by the said heir that he ought to be immune from the said tolls, because under this name of *collecta* the said tolls also fall; because they are collected from persons for the things which they buy and sell; so that the proper name of *collecta* is thus in tolls, as in these others; because whatever is collected from a person for a thing, is said to be *collecta*. But in tolls it is of this kind, etc. For by virtue of the said convention, as the said convention willed, that he ought not to give *collecta* from his goods: if he paid toll on that which he bought, it would follow that he paid toll from his goods; and thus it would be against the said convention, which ought not to be. From which the said heir concludes that he is also exempt from the said tolls.

And concerning this also, it pleases us to provide, and by your wholesome counsel to decide the said point with allegations of law, because it is one of the principal doubts of the said question. I, Baldus.
body: On the general

The nature of pacts is that they pass to the heir, even if the heir is not mentioned. D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium; § pactorum. D. de probationibus, l. si pactum. This is true if the form of the words permits it, and the nature of the contract, and the thing brought into the contract. For if the form of the words does not permit it, it is not effectively transmitted. D. de verbis oblig., l. eum qui ita, § 2, in the response. Likewise, if the nature of the contract does not permit it, as in D. pro loco, l. actione, § morte. Likewise, if an impediment arises from the nature of the thing brought into the contract, as in Inst. de usufructu, § finitur. For this reason it appears that the aforementioned pact, together with the right of immunity, the said Marquis transmitted to his heirs and descendants. D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, § si.

† For this immunity itself is of such a nature that it passes to successors. For nature is nothing other than a certain aptitude, and certain immunities possess this aptitude, even though they do not always pass. D. de iure immunitatis, l. 1, § personis; and see C. de excusationibus munerum, l. sordidorum, lib. 10. And properly, this immunity is not a privilege, but a certain pact, and thus faith must be observed. D. de iure immunitatis, l. 2. Since power is presupposed on the part of the contracting authority, and thus it does not obstruct what is noted in C. de decurionibus, l. vacuatis, lib. 10. On the contrary, such a contract also acquires the force of law, as in C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. penultima; D. de publicanis, l. Caesar; de decretis ab ordinariis faciendis, l. quod semel; D. quod vi aut clam, l. prohibere, § plane. To this add that the person was not the immediate cause of this immunity, but mutual performance, and thus it is not extinguished with the person, as in D. de in integrum restitutione, l. non solum; argument from C. de locato, l. viam veritatis. Nor is this a gratuity, since it comes from the rite of marriage, l. proxime; D. de hereditatibus institutis, l. si servo fideicommissaria. And at least by urbanity, the heir of the same blood is included. D. de aqua quotidiana, l. 1, § permittitur. For even if it is a benefit, it ought to be interpreted most broadly. D. de constitutionibus principum, l. beneficium. Moreover, certain words which are uttered by the recipient ought to be understood according to his probable intention, as noted by Bartolus in l. Gallus, § etiam, de liberis et postliminio. But it is certain that the stipulator is he who utters the words first, and subsequently the promisor. D. de verborum obligatione, l. 1. Hence, although the tenor of the writing presents words as if uttered by the authority of Genoa towards the recipient, yet since a stipulation was appended, the order of understanding is that the words were principally those of the stipulator, and consequently of the promisor. D. de pactis, l. veteribus. Moreover, if we consider this immunity, this immunity was granted concerning things. This appears from the fact that the office from which exemption is granted is the office of the collecta, which is imposed on possessors for their things. D. de muneribus et honoribus, l. rescripto, § final. But such things are transmitted to successors, provided they are such successors as were probably considered, as noted by Dynus in cap. privilegium personale, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Furthermore, from the conjunction of two transmissible natures, the transmission is more fitting; but here the nature of the pact is transmissible. C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. veteris, and there fully by Cynus; and the nature of the immunity concerning a real or mixed office. de censibus, l. forma, § quanquam. And the other extremity is perpetual, because granted to the city by the counts, it ought to reduce the other in case of doubt to the understanding of perpetuity; otherwise neither ought to be perpetual. D. de arbitris, l. sed interpellatur, § si ex altera. Moreover, from the quality of the person, and the expression of this quality as count, a real concession is presumed to all counts descending from them, and heirs. Otherwise, if they were not heirs, because they are not understood, as in the said l. si pactum; nor can it be understood, because in a reciprocal contract persons who do not participate in it cannot be included, as in Auth. de non alienando, § emphyteuta; and because he could not contract with a stranger even for receiving, as fully noted in D. de pactis, l. idem in duobus. Therefore two things are required: that he be of the genus, and that he be an heir. It supports what is noted in D. soluto matrimonio, l. etiam; and D. de servitutibus legatis, l. pater, per Bartolus. And thus he holds in this point that it is real as regards the counts, heirs from the root of the stipulator. We have seen the extension concerning persons; let us see the extension concerning things. Therefore, etc.

I come to the second point, and it appears that this pact, or immunity, does not extend to property subsequently acquired. For we see that words used simply in contracts are restricted to present property; hence, if I sell or give you all my goods, it is not understood to include future ones, as noted in the final law of the Code, *Quae res pignori obligari possunt*. And the same holds in judgments, when someone is condemned to the loss of his property, but with his person saved, as in the Digest, *Mandatum*, law *Si tibi mandaveris*, section *Is cuius bona*, because the present time is considered in contracts and similar matters. Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Ruptilia*, and law *In ea enim*; for those things which arise anew require a new stipulation and a new promise, as in the Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *Damnatum*, section *Si is qui vicinas*. And the same seems to be said regarding a toll, if the place where the toll was collected at that time is later changed, as in the Digest, *De aqua quotidiana et aestiva*, law *Hoc iure*, section *Si aqua*; or if the toll is increased, as in the Digest, *De rivis*, law 1, at the end, verse *Sed si eundem*. This is held by Peter in the Commentary on the Code, *De sacrosancta ecclesia*, law *Placet*, at the end. Moreover, a simple and pure disposition ought not to be reduced to a conditional understanding; but if it contained future things, it would be reduced to a conditional understanding. Law *Si ita acciderit*, Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*; and law 1, at the end, *Cum igitur cesserit*, in the beginning of the law on stipulations. Future things ought not to be included, lest the status of the obligation be changed, by argument from the Digest, *De verborum obligatione*, law *Insulam intra biennium*, in the reason of itself. Moreover, it is not probable that the sense extends to things which will be in the accusation at any time, by argument from the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Offilius*. For if this were so, the commune of Genoa could be deceived beyond half the just price; and this is not probable, by argument from the Code, *De transactionibus*, law *Si de certa*; Digest, same title, law *Cum Aquiliana*. It also supports the note in the Digest, *De superficie*, law 1, section 1; Digest, *De ex pacto*: certainly he who pays a debt confers no benefit. Digest, *Rebus dubiis*, law 1.

† To this is added the word "eorum," which is a possessive pronoun, just as is the word "meorum." D. de auro et argento legato, l. si ita. In the contrary, it is to be considered subtly what is present and what is future. And certainly, the present is the jurisdiction of him who granted the immunity from it. But to exact when the case has arisen is not jurisdiction, but is the fruit and accession of that jurisdiction, as Innocentius notes, D. de restitutione spoliatorum, c. in litteris, and in many other places. It is established, however, that fruits from the future come into a contract concerning a present thing. D. de actionibus emptoris, l. Iulia, § si fructibus. But this contract is concerning the present, namely, concerning jurisdiction not to be exercised in exacting; therefore, it comes into the contract, as stated in § si is, qui vicinas, v. si autem. Furthermore, the doctrine of Petrus supports this, that when that concerning which one contracts is universal, such as peculium and inheritance, future things come into it, as he notes in the said l. fin., quae res pignori obligari possunt, and it is expressed. D. de haerede vel actione vendita, l. venditio ex hereditate. It supports what is noted in I. Lucius, D. de fundo instrato. But jurisdiction is something universal. D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. solet and l. praetor. Therefore, when it is remitted, it is a universal remission, and it extends to things acquired, as D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. si servitus. Just as if a master grants his slave free administration of his peculium, it is understood to extend also to things which subsequently began to be in the peculium. D. de peculio, l. quam Tuberonis, § alia. But in the remission of patronage jurisdiction generally and in a single word, everything seems to be remitted. C. de bonis liberis, l. finalis. For liberation is presumed to be general, as noted in D. de pactis, l. emptor and l. Lucius. Moreover, this seems to be expressed explicitly in Extravagantes, de privilegiis, c. quia circa. Although one universality expressed does not bring in another connected and subordinate universality, as D. de haeredibus venditis, l. 2, § il lud, nevertheless, those which are parts of the same universality do come in, as if they adhere to the same universal subject, by argument from the said law si servitus. It supports what Petrus and Cynus note, C. de servitutibus, l. non modus. It can be said that the above-mentioned contract extends to goods acquired subsequently after the stipulation of immunity, but it does not extend to goods acquired by his heirs, as D. de pignoribus, l. Paulus. And thus I hold. And this is the second point. And this is true, unless the heirs have subsequently prescribed this immunity by custom. And then the prescription of liberty would benefit them. For although these prescriptions do not proceed against the fisc of Caesar, because he disposes by absolute and supreme Caesarean power, as C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. competit, nevertheless, it is otherwise in other cities, however illustrious, as noted by Innocentius, D. de postulando praediorum, c. bonae, and by Bartolus in l. publicanus, D. de publicanis.

† If, therefore, such a custom or prescription has intervened so that the *collectas* are not paid, and the *collecta* has been made into a tax according to the form of the statute, it is asked whether it ought to be paid or not. I will not omit the investigation of this point, even out of reverence for the consultation.

It must be known, therefore, that there is a certain office which is solemn and ordinary, introduced by perpetual law, or even by temporary law; for example, that any possessor shall pay in common one cup for every bushel of grain; or that any possessor shall pay the twentieth part, or shall pay ten solidi annually for every iugerum of land. And this is called a real tribute simply, as was the case in Rome with tributes, which were paid every five years, as noted in C. de indictionibus, in the rubric. And so it is also if it were said “up to five or ten years”; for in this case the force does not lie in the time, but in the form. Of this speaks the law *Omnes*, C. sine censu vel reliquis, de infinitis similibus.

There is a certain office which is sudden and extraordinary, because it varies according to the necessities of the time; and it is sometimes great, sometimes small, sometimes none. And this office is called by the Gloss a *collecta*. And it is mixed, which is imposed by permission of the common law on things, as noted in the said law *Rescripto*, §. fin., and C. de muneribus patrimoniorum, in the rubric, and in l. 1, of that title, lib. 10, and l. 1, §. quibus, quod cuiusque universitatis nomine, and by Innocentius in c. *Gravem*, de sententia excommunicationis, and by Bartolus in l. 2, actorum, ff. de re iudicata, and de privilegiis, c. *Cum et plantare*, and there by Innocentius. But in c. *Licet*, de censibus, Innocentius says that there is a certain personal *collecta*, and a certain real one. And thus the name *collecta* also includes tribute, as in Auth. de collationibus, in the rubric, and in the black letter. Of this also Innocentius touches upon in de praescriptionibus, c. *Si diligenti*, and it is the original Gloss related to the text, that tribute is called *collecta*, C. de apocis publicis, l. 1, on the word *inopes*.

But even assuming that it is not included, nevertheless a statute could not make the possessions of an exempt person subject to *collectae* to the prejudice of the exempt; rather, certainly, exempt persons are not included by general words. The Gloss is notable, C. de silentiariis, l. *Decurionibus*, lib. 12. Therefore, the power fails, and also the will. It follows from de bonis auctoris iudicis possessis, l. *Cum unus*, §. *Is qui*, cum si.

Moreover, this tribute was substituted in place of the *collecta*; therefore, it partakes of the nature of the *collecta*. ff. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. *Si donatae*, §. *Si sponsus*; de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. *Filiae*, §. *A Titia*.

Furthermore, a statute which affects possessions for offices and *collectae* does not make *collectae* ordinary offices, because they are not imposed by law, or by senatusconsulta, or by constitutions of princes, nor are they certain, as noted in C. de via publica numeris, l. 1, lib. 10, and ff. de vacuis muneribus, l. *In honoribus*, §. *Quod numerus*. And therefore, such offices imposed unexpectedly are, properly speaking, not tributes, although conversely every tribute is a *collecta*. And of many kinds of tributes, note de annonis et tributis, in the rubric.

And it is true that Bartolus says, that a statute and custom can make extraordinary *collectae* a mere real office, in the manner of a tribute. And by this, possessors are bound even for churches, as he notes in the said law *Rescripto*. For one must stand by custom. ff. de administratione tutorum, l. *Sive haeredum*, I. *Lucius*.

But he rarely speaks well who speaks against everyone. Hence the Church does not speak the truth: for even if it were a tribute, it must be understood as due after the assessment and specification, and not before. Such assessment cannot be made after the property has made full passage to the lord of the Church or to those exempt. Argument: the fragment *Qui potest* in the title *De pignoribus*; the law *Potior*; and in the chapter *Quia cunctis*, *De concessionibus praebendarum*, Book 6. And so it would be in the case at hand, assuming the exception of prescription: for prescription and sin are equated. Law *Nam satis*, section *Si ego*, *Quemadmodum servi amittuntur*; and note in law 1, Code *De servis et aqua*; and law *Hoc iure*, section *Ductus aquae*, *De aqua quotidiana et aestiva*. And therefore the caution which Bartolus gives there is worth not a straw, unless the assessment is certain.

† On the fourth point concerning tolls, it must be considered that tolls arise daily when the occasion presents itself. And although a certain form is given, nevertheless that form is not in the matter unless the occasion gives it; nor is it prescribed in the same way as immunity collected in respect of a real or mixed right; because that liberty concerns the liberty of the estate, which is more easily prescribed. D. de usucap. l. sequitur; D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, § si viam; D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, lege haec autem iura. But not so with these tolls, which have a cause entirely discontinuous and dependent on human act, as in D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. foramen. And therefore, for prescription, a time is required of whose beginning and contrary there would be no memory. And by the force of the pact, as I said in the beginning, this immunity does not fall, because it is not contained in the pact. D. de pactis, l. si unus; D. de annuis legibus, § si ante; D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. scio; D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. si viva. Moreover, the toll is paid for the contract, and before the thing is delivered, and thus not for the thing. For the contract precedes, and the obligation of the toll precedes the transfer of ownership to the receiving person; and thus it is not rendered on the part of the buyer, especially for his own thing; but he makes what is due to himself. D. de publicanis, l. licitatio, § mercato. And the exception confirms the rule under which it falls, but does not extend to other things which are not included by the nature of the words. D. de usufructu legato, l. in generali, § uxori. And thus it follows that these nobles are bound to the tolls. To this effect: C. de impositione lucrae descriptionis, l. prima, lib. decimo; and by Guillaume, D. de pactis, l. ab emptio, unless prescription helps; D. de verborum significatione, cap. super quibusdam. I, Baldus.

He cannot defend himself on the ground that he did not pay the common money which he owed; rather, the oxen were his own, and thus solely his, and the injury was done to his own property. C. loca. l. damnum. Nevertheless, the common entity, which took the oxen, caused damage and injury to its own internal interest, not to its destruction; and therefore the common entity must make amends. The said debtor, however, is bound to the creditor for the simple said amount; because it was not permitted to the debtor, out of hatred for the creditor, to retain the oxen, and thus the rule of l. non curabit de actione empt. cum si. does not stand in the way. I, Daldus,

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether daughters can be substituted in the dowry.
2. No one can be burdened with more than was left to him.
body: Dictae
The heir instituted succeeds Lella. From her, and not from the aforementioned Peter: except in 100 soldi. For in the dowry of Lella, and in her other goods, the substitution

† He did not hold, who could not be burdened with more than had been left to him in the will, according to the law Trebellian, the law Lucius, §. husband, Digest, on vulgar and pupillary substitution; the law coheir, §. last, Code, on fideicommissa; the law from him. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. Usury cannot be claimed.
body: Dictum

† The *coptunum* cannot be claimed by Paulellius from Petrutius, because it was promised over and above the principal, and thus it is usury, l. rogasti. §. si tibi. si certum peta., and whatever is added to the principal is usury, and usury cannot be claimed, extra de vsuris per totum; and whatever the creditor received from the said *coptunum* reduces the principal debt, ff. de solutio. l. Titiam. C. de pignoris actio. lege secunda, and similar laws. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a spurious child can be emancipated, and whether anything can be given to him.
body: Spurius

† He cannot be emancipated, because he is not in power. Likewise, nothing can be given to him by his father. C. de naturali. liber. l. 1. and Authen. licet. unless up to the level of sustenance, by canonical benevolence, as in extra de eo, qui duxit in matrimonium. c. cum haberet. when he has no other means from which to support himself: and in a case of necessity it is permitted, in another case it is not permitted. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How a tutor, or his heir, is bound to render an account to the ward concerning the administration of the ward's property.
2. A tutor is not bound to draw up public instruments for all matters.
body: Guardian, and

† The heir of the tutor is bound to render an account to the ward, and to the heirs of the ward, concerning the items recorded in the tutor’s inventory; for the inventory of the tutor must be upheld against the tutor and the heir of the tutor, as stated in C. arbitrium tutelae, l. final. And therefore immovable property is easily restored to the ward, because it shows and exhibits itself. C. quando, et quibus quarta pars de debetur, l. 2. But movable property, or property that moves, if it still exists, must be returned to the ward and the heirs of the ward. If, however, it does not exist, inquiry must be made as to what has been done with it. If they have been sold, the price must be paid to the wards and the heirs of the wards, and the accounts and writings drawn up therefrom, both public and private, must be brought forward. ff. de conditio. et demonstra., l. cum seruus; ff. de tutelis, et rationibus distra., l. 1. The duty of the judge, however, is to estimate whether the administration was conducted diligently and in good faith, after hearing both parties. ff. de administra. tuto., l. ad instruendum; C. de donatio., l. si quis pro redemptione; C. de iure deliberan., l. final., §. in computatione. It supports what is noted by Cynus in C. de episcopis, et cleri., l. nulli.

† Nor are costly and public instruments to be drawn up in all cases, neither by law nor by custom; and therefore simple and private writings must also be examined and considered, and whether they state things that are probable or not. D. de negotiis gestis, l. Necessarius Appolinarius ad examen ergo veritatis. And so, regarding these writings, the accountant or judge should resort to truth and conscience, approve what is probable, and not admit what is improbable into the calculation of the account. Extravagantes de accusatione, capitulo Qualiter, in the second gloss. Hence, one should not believe all reasons, nor none, but after examining the persons of those who wrote and produced them. D. de edendo, l. Si quis ex argentariis, § 1; D. de manumissis testamento, l. Qui filium. And before proceeding to sentence or to an award, delays should be granted for proof, and the proofs themselves should be placed before the court. C. de iudiciis, l. Properandum, § Cum autem haeremodicium. And in this case, proceedings have gone thus far, but not fully discussed. And therefore I cannot declare the case otherwise in my opinion, always concluding, however, that the account should be rendered according to the inventory, omitting the frivolous objections raised to the contrary. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One person filed a petition before a judge who was in his private chamber, another before the same judge sitting on the bench; who is said to have obtained prior registration (praevenire).
2. What matters a judge may adjudicate outside the formal court setting.
body: Point

† A certain Ser Nardus, curator of the dominions of Guilmina and Joanna, daughters and heirs of Venturutius, appeared before the judge in his chamber and produced a certain petition, by which he requested a document written by the hand of Peter and copied by Ser Iacobinus. In this document it is contained that the said Venturutius confessed to having received from Beneamato, by reason of deposit, 1451 [units], and promised to restore them to the said Beneamato after his death, and the said document produced was made in the form of a public instrument in the year 1361. Nevertheless, it is true that it is fictitious and simulated, and made in fraud of those coming intestate. And he had it committed in the said chamber to a messenger that he should summon Luca, who holds the rights of the said Beneamato, that he should appear that morning before the said judge to see the said petition produced, and all these things were done without the said Luca, who holds the said rights, as you will see contained in the acts. Then, immediately when the judge appeared at the bench, the said Luca produced the said instrument of donation made to him of the said debt, preserved to the said Ser Nardus as curator. And he requested that execution of the said instrument be made by the said judge, as you will also see in the acts. Afterwards, the said Ser Nardus produced his said petition, which he had first produced in the chamber by reason of the said citation. It is asked, now who has preempted, whether the said Ser Nardus, who had the aforementioned production made in the chamber and the commission of the action without the opposing party, or the said Luca, who requested execution of the said instrument. The acts having been seen, and the statute concerning fictitious instruments having been seen.

† Preparatory acts of judicial proceedings appear to be able to be expedited even in the judge’s chamber, as stated in the Digest, *De interdictis et actionibus*, law *Voluit*, § 1, and noted in the title rubric; especially since the first citation is made without knowledge of the case, because it precedes all knowledge of the case, as stated in the Institutes, *De poenis temere litigantium*, § final. And because the ordinary judge may administer justice in any honorable place within his territory, as stated in the Code, *Quomodo et quando iudex*, law *Si ut proponis praeses provinciae*, with certain places, and in the canon *Cum episcopus*, *De officio ordinarii*, Book 6.

To the contrary, it appears that this act cannot be performed except at the tribunal, according to the law *Nam mors maiorum servandus est*, as stated in the Digest, *De iustitia et iure*, law *Pe*. Therefore, it must be done in a place where, observing the custom of the ancestors, one may proceed, as noted in the Speculum, *De dilationibus*, § final, version *Sed cum a procedente*, unless the act is performed with the consent of the parties, according to the aforementioned law *Voluit*, because then it appears to be done by way of voluntary jurisdiction, and it is valid, as noted by Cynus and Petrus de Ancharano in the Code, *De confessionibus*, law 1, in the third question, and in the Speculum, *De sententiis*, § *Iustam*, version *Item quod non est nulla ratione loci*.

Furthermore, this citation, insofar as it resides in the judge, is part of contentious jurisdiction, and is the beginning of the lawsuit or case, according to the Code, *De transactionibus*, law *Causas, vel lites*; and therefore it must be done in a place where the entire judgment can be carried out, as stated in the Digest, *De iudicibus*, law *Ubi coeptum*, especially since in our case it is of great prejudice.

Furthermore, whether it is a definitive sentence or an interlocutory one, it must be done in a place where it is customary to pronounce it, as noted in the Code, *De sententiis et interlocutionibus*, law *Cum sententiam praesidis*; for the place of judgment must be a public place, and this is clear there. To this effect, it is noted by Cynus in the Code, *De contrahenda et communi stipulatione*, law *Optimam*, in the first opposition.

I conclude that unless the place of the ancestors is observed, the act does not hold, nor is prevention induced; because it is not understood as use, but as abuse of jurisdiction, for which the following authorities support: Digest, *Quando appellatio sit*, law 2, § *Edendi*; and Digest, *Si quis ordo in bonis possidendis servetur*, law 2, § *Dies*. And in one certain and determined place, fixed by custom for rendering justice, all other places are considered interdicted, as stated in the Digest, *De iudicibus*, law *Si locus*. But if, by custom, the place were arbitrary, then the act is valid, and prevention would be induced, and this applies to secular judges. In ecclesiastical judges, the aforementioned chapter *Cum episcopus* does not operate. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether fruits, damages, and interest must be specifically demanded in the libel.
2. An uncertain judgment is valid regarding accessories, and even if rendered under the condition of an oath.
1. Given a statute that nullity of a judgment cannot be opposed, if the judgment is null by operation of law, whether it must be put into execution.
2. In every invader and disturber, fraud is presumed, and title does not excuse unless he has possession.
3. Whether an office excuses a wrongful act.
4. Whether, with appeal prohibited, one may raise the issue of nullity from a judgment rendered on the occasion of a wrongful act, and whether one may appeal from the assessment of damages and expenses, or interest.
5. The term "on the occasion" and how it is to be understood.
6. What is properly called a cause.
7. Whether a surety given simply is bound for fruits, damages, and interest.
body: By one statute it is provided that whoever disturbs another in his possession shall be punished with a fine of one hundred pounds, and the Potestas shall cause all damages, fruits, interest, and injury suffered by the aggrieved party, which occurred on the occasion of the aforementioned disturbance, to be made good without delay, the amount of which shall be determined by the oath of the aggrieved party. By another statute it is provided that, since sometimes the Potestas, in the final days of his office, out of favor to someone, annuls proceedings and sentences, whereby the Commune of Perugia is defrauded and offenders escape punishment, we have enacted that the Potestas, the Captain, and the Major Syndic, or any one of them, may not hear or consider anyone who claims that any proceeding, condemnation, banishment, or sentence made against anyone by any officials of the Commune of Perugia for any felony, or on the occasion of any felony alleged to have been committed, is unjust or null, nor may they take cognizance thereof; and if they have taken cognizance, it shall be void by operation of law. By another statute it is provided that, so that felonies may be more effectively punished, we have enacted that if anyone has been condemned by the Potestas, or the Captain, or the Judge of Justice, for any felony to any penalty, no appeal may be taken from such sentence or condemnation, nor may recourse be had; and if an appeal is taken or recourse had, it shall be void by operation of law. And it is understood that by this chapter no derogation is made in any way to the jurisdiction and office of the Major Syndic and the Judge of Justice regarding civil causes. By another statute it is provided that from sentences, condemnations, and proceedings concerning and for felonies committed, no appeal may be taken, nor recourse had to the Judge of Justice, and the said Judge may not hear anyone, nor take cognizance of the aforesaid matters; and nevertheless, any sentence of acquittal, or of cassation and annulment, if made by him concerning or upon the aforesaid matters, shall be void and of no effect, and shall cause no prejudice to the Commune of Perugia, notwithstanding any statutes or ordinances speaking of the office of the said Judge and of recourse to be had or appeals to be interposed. And no other provision speaking to the contrary shall stand in the way. By another statute it is provided that a term of eight days shall be set for the accused to make his defense, and thereafter the judge may proceed to the reception of witnesses in the absence of the accuser, and without the accuser being summoned to be present; however, if the accuser is present, or if he is absent but has been summoned or cited to the reception of witnesses or to their publication, the judge may proceed to other acts, and upon these accusations he may receive all witnesses whom the accuser has listed in writing at the time of the said accusation, and no others, at the petition of the accuser; nevertheless, the Potestas may, ex officio, receive such witnesses as he wishes and believes know the truth about the felony, notwithstanding that the accuser did not list them. By another statute it is provided that if anyone wishes to produce witnesses concerning any felony, he may, at the time of production and accusation, and not afterwards, introduce such witnesses as he wishes and believes know of the felony; and concerning the accusation of a felony, he may not produce more than ten witnesses to take the said oaths. If, however, he wishes to introduce more than ten witnesses concerning any felony or accusation, he shall be bound to pay two solidi to the Commune of Perugia for each witness he introduces, before he swears to tell the truth; which if he does not pay, the judge shall not receive such witnesses to take their oaths, and if he does receive them, their testimony shall be void. Titius accused Gaius of disturbing him in a certain possession of his, and sets forth the qualities of the offense in the mention made of damages, expenses, fruits, and interest. And in conclusion, he requests that Gaius be punished and condemned according to the form of the law and the statutes of the Commune of Perugia. Gaius denied the aforesaid. Gaius was admonished by the judge to be present on each day and hour to hear the oaths of the witnesses and other acts to be performed until sentence; and the judge granted license to proceed until sentence, and assigned to him a term of eight days, for which Sempronius stood as surety. The witnesses swore to the said accusation after the said term of eight days, and beyond the number of ten, six more were sworn, with payment made for four, but confusedly. And some were received ex officio by the judge, without the said Gaius being otherwise consulted. And some deposed that the contents of the accusation were true, without being otherwise interrogated as to the cause of their knowledge. And the witnesses of the said Gaius say that the said Gaius stated that, at the time of entry into the possession of the said thing, he was entering as a testamentary fideicommissary of Martin. The judge condemned the said Gaius to one hundred pounds to the Commune of Perugia, and to damages, interest, fruits, and expenses to the said Titius. From this condemnation of the said damages, interest, expenses, and fruits, the said Sempronius, the surety, appealed to the Judge of Justice, and to the appeal, or at least appealed from the taxation thereof; in which taxation the said Titius swore concerning the aforesaid matters. Now it is asked: first, whether Gaius was justly condemned; second, whether the appeal interposed by the said surety from the said damages, interest, expenses, and fruits is valid; and whether the appellate judge ought to proceed in the aforesaid matters. And for the part of the said surety it is said that the sentence is void: partly because the witnesses swore after the term; partly because their proof is not as clear as noonday, since they do not give the reason for their testimony, which may be multiple, and thus it is opined, or because they heard it said, or because it is the subject of rumor, etc.; partly because the two solidi were not paid; partly because more witnesses were accepted than the jurisdiction requires; partly because the cause of the fideicommissum excuses him from dolus; partly because the said surety does not seem to have stood surety for the said damages, expenses, interest, and fruits; partly because this is a criminal matter; partly because this probatory oath should have been rendered before sentence; partly because the said fruits, damages, expenses, and interest were not claimed nor otherwise deduced. It is asked what is the law regarding each of the aforesaid points individually.

† As to the first point, whether fruits, damages, and interest must be specifically demanded in the libel: the ordinary glossa says that demanded damages are included when they occurred before the joinder of issue. Thus says the glossa in l. si quis missum, §. fin., ff. de damno infecto. Cynus says more, that if there are such damages whose quantity can be specified, it must be specified in the libel. C. si quis alteri, vel sibi; l. cum propria, per Cynus. Guillelmus de Cuneo says that interest, granted that it comes by the nature of the judgment, nevertheless does not come unless it has been demanded in the libel, by l. 4, §. hoc iudicium, de damno infecto; ff. de aedilicio edicto, l. ediles, §. Item sciendum. Thus notes Guillelmus in l. 2, ff. de eo quod certo loco, because thus he would supply by fact what he cannot. C. ut quae desunt advocatorum partium, l. 1. Much more strongly ought it to be demanded if it does not come by the nature of the judgment, but by the extraordinary disposition of a statute, as is in our case. But this is opposed by the fact that in criminal matters a demand, that is, a conclusion, is not required, as noted by Cynus, C. de falsis, l. nec exemplum, because the law concludes. Also, because where action is brought against a violent person, specification of fruits is not necessary, as noted by Innocentius in cap. gravis, de restitutione spoliorum. And when criminal penalty and reparation of damages come from the same law, the judge incidentally orders the damage to be made good from the same instance. ff. de calumniis, l. si ab eo; ff. de variis et extraordinariis cognitionibus, l. medicus. Nor does it appear from those laws that this was demanded in the libel. Moreover, it seems sufficient that it was demanded, since he demanded to be punished and condemned according to the form of the statute, just as if he said, I ask that justice be done, as in extra, de ordine cognitionum, c. cum dilectus. But I answer: even if it was not necessary to demand specifically by concluding, it was nevertheless necessary to allege, because they have occurred and consist in fact, and they relate to being, and not to non-being. And that this is true is shown, because one must prove them at least by oath: if one must prove, therefore one must also allege. Which certainly must be done before sentence, otherwise there would be need for a new judgment concerning interest and damages, and new proof with the party cited, as we say in l. 1, in principio, ff. de actione emptio venditionis; l. qui restituere. Or else the demand for them would be extinguished, as in l. terminato, C. de fructibus et litis expensis. The first is truer when they come by right of action; the second proceeds when they come only by mercenary office. l. Paulus, de re iudicata. For in all accessories, the same rule applies as in expenses, as noted, ff. de arbitris, l. quia arbiter. I return to the proposition, and I say that damages of the past ought to have been proved before sentence, at least by oath, as the statute provides. This is clear from the note, ff. de deposito, l. 1, §. si quis argentum, because the law says that the judge shall conclude the condemnation of the taxed quantity. C. de inutilibus stipulationibus, l. 3. Therefore, some proof ought to have been made beforehand regarding the interest.

But someone will say: it is true that the judge ought to have acted thus; nevertheless, if he rendered an uncertain judgment, it is valid in these accessory matters, as noted in the Institutes, *De actionibus*, § *Curare*. And he could also have adjudicated under the condition of an oath, because it is a condition according to the nature of the judgment, C. *De rebus creditis*, l. *Generaliter*, and as noted in C. *De sententiis*, l. *Cum iudex*. It seems to me that, since it was neither necessary, nor claimed, nor proven, the condemnation is null, because it was rendered on a matter that was neither debated nor pleaded, C. *De fideicommissis*, lib. 1, l. *Fin.*

† And although the statute prevents cognizance of nullity, yet when the nullity appears from the recitation of the sentence, and of the libel recited therein, this is not to cognize, but to have been cognized, nor to hear, but to have been heard. Since therefore the sentence has no being, nor the form of being, he who cannot hear on nullity, which requires proof of fact, nevertheless has his conscience informed concerning that which is patent of itself, and from such a sentence he cannot render justice. D. de feriis, l. si feriatis; D. de poenis, l. 2. This appears in the executor, because seeing the sentence null by the law itself, he ought not to execute it. D. de iudic., l. si praetor, § Marcellus. Sometimes he acts as a judge, sometimes he does not act as a judge cognizing, but as a good man. D. de quaestionibus, l. 1, § fina. It supports what is noted by Innocentius, D. de iudic., cap. de caetero. Moreover, when the sentence speaks, it seems to speak for both the victor and the vanquished: because it contains the confession, or assertion, of both parties. And therefore if it does not benefit the plaintiff, the plaintiff seems to confess that it does not benefit him. And whoever produces it, it is common, just like the statement of a witness. Hence, if the one acting on nullity is not heard as an actor, nevertheless the judge ought to read the sentence and examine its force, before whom the question is pending: as if the sentence itself had the force of the living voice of both parties, as C. de edendo, l. is, apud quem. If it is null, it will not be executed, and the judge to whom it is brought will pronounce that the act on nullity before him was superfluous, since he himself cannot judge on this. He will nevertheless add that by this he neither confirms nor invalidates it: because where judicial hearing is denied, whatever is proposed seems to be proposed outside the judgment, since it cannot pertain to the vigor of the judgment with the judge removed. Certainly it must be observed whether the sentence passed in a criminal case is founded on the statute, either directly or by analogy from similar cases: or whether it is not founded on it, for example because the judge says that since Titius was found going out at night, he is condemned to death. In the first case, appeal or recourse is not heard. In the second case, the actor is heard: because the judge who pronounced was in this respect private, and not a judge: because he did not have public authority, which arises from the statute. It supports what is noted in c. 1, de sequestris, pos. in Clem. porro. Another judge ought not to be the executor of the errors of others. D. de testamento tutoris, l. 1. It seems now that a new judge is a new condition. D. de iudic., l. edi. And noted in l. 1, de iuris et facti ignorantia, by Petrus and Cynus. Moreover, in this statute there is mention of injury and of oath: and from both the first and the second it seems that dolus is required. The first is clear. D. locat., l. si quis ignorans; D. de abigeis, l. 1, in fin.; D. de lib. causa. Therefore the second is clear. L. si quando, C. unde vi; c. fina., quod metus causa, per Innocentius; Inst. de verb. oblig., § penulti., per glossa; D. de in iur. iur., l. in actis. For against a culpable person, true or presumed dolus being absent, it is necessary that witnesses be present concerning the proof of interest and damages. D. ad legem Aquiliam, in l. Aquilia si delatum; D. de edendo, l. si quis ex argento. But since even by common law, turbative force is not seen to be punished except on account of dolus, as noted, D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. servus, on the word facinus. Therefore in all cases in this statute dolus is required, and a condemnation made where there is no dolus is not founded in common law, nor in the statute.

But against this it is objected, because in every invader and defender fraud is presumed. C. unde vi, l. fin. Nor does title excuse, unless he has possession. ff. de acquisitione possessionis, l. qui ex stipulatione. Nor does the office excuse, where the act includes a wrong: for certainly this does not seem to be a mandate, since a disgraceful and penal matter is not included in an indefinite mandate; for no one is considered to have appointed an executor or procurator for carrying out crimes, but only for those things which can be lawfully mandated. ff. de conditione indebita, l. si procurator.

But I answer that an office does not excuse a wrongful act, yet it gives rise to a presumption that there is no wrongful act, unless the contrary is clearly evident, as noted in D. de rei vindicatione, l. si rem, § tignum; D. de inofficioso testamento, l. athletae, § calumni; C. unde vi, l. meminerint, cum si.

† It is doubted, however, whether, when appeal is prohibited and there is a prohibition against appealing on grounds of nullity from a sentence rendered on account of a felony, one may appeal from the assessment of damages and costs, or interest. It must be considered here that sometimes an accusation is formed from the estimation, and the condemnation is moderated by it, as if someone who committed theft of more than ten pounds is to be flogged, and from such a sentence regarding the assessment of this sum no appeal can be taken, because the criminal penalty is founded upon it. Sometimes it comes incidentally, and it can be examined separately from the crime, because it is a question of calculation rather than of felony. D. de dolo, l. Sabinus. And it is incidental; then, that it may be appealed from as from an interlocutory judgment, so that we may say that the judge’s assessment is a kind of interlocutory judgment. This is stated in a similar case by Guillaume de Coulanges, D. de minoribus, l. Si ex causa, §. Nunc videndum. Similarly, after ten days no appeal is taken from the second sentence, which is the execution of the first, except on account of excess in the manner. According to the note, D. quod metus causa, l. Si cum excessu, §. Haec autem actio, this is relevant. D. de confessionibus, l. Cum fideicommissum. Nor does it obstruct, D. de rei venditione, l. Ex diverso, §. 1, where it is said that the same error applies to fruits; because that is true unless an appeal is taken, according to the note in l. Fin., C. quando provocatio non est necessaria. If one has confessed and been convicted, he does not appeal, unless the confessor merely persists in his confession, as in c. Romana, de appellationibus, lib. 6, except on account of excess in the manner. D. de verbis significatis, l. Aliud, §. Inter multum, and l. Si qua poena. Finally, the question of costs and damages is civil and incidental to the criminal charge, and therefore the appeal prohibited in favor of public discipline in the criminal matter does not seem to be prohibited in the civil matter; since even here a procurator intervenes, and it partakes of the nature of civil causes. C. ad legem Flaviam de plagio, l. Praeses.

But against this is the phrase "on the occasion of" and the like. For this phrase has the widest scope, hence the text says: "It happened not by reason of, but on the occasion of." D. 12.2.1 (Labeo). For everything that is directed toward something else, either directly or incidentally, or is directed by someone, either directly or incidentally, is called an occasion.

† Cause, however, is properly said to be that which is ordered to something by itself. L. verum est, D. de furtis; and L. si mulier, D. de rerum amotione. But I answer that there is a certain penalty proper to the offense, and there is a certain penalty of contumacy referred to the offense, and from neither of these can one appeal, although the second comes incidentally and not principally. But a certain matter does not concern punishability, but the prosecution of the thing, and if in this the judge, by error or injury, passes the bounds of reason, it is equitable that he be reduced to the proper measure, as is argued from D. de usuris, L. placuit. For, as I said, in this case the sentence is civil, and gives rise to a civil action in factum, as noted by Innocentius in C. fin., de dolo et contumacia; and if it were merely criminal, it would so ill serve the party as a pear serves a medlar. D. de pactis, L. si unus, § pactum ne peteret, vers. sed si pactum conventum. This sentence has equity and is civil, because in a possessory action one does not appeal; nevertheless, one will appeal from an inequitable taxation and oath: because one does not appeal from the condemnation, but from the excess of measure, as Innocentius notes in C. fin., quod metus causa, where he treats this matter fully. Here, however, it must be considered that the statute removes all recourse not only from the condemnation of the sentence, but also from the procedure. This taxation is such that the procedure, and as it were the procedure itself, is revoked by contrary authority if it is unjust. Innocentius says there, in C. fecit, de accusationibus, C. qualiter et quando, and L. 1. But there is a strong objection, because according to this the judge of the appeal could declare that there is no damage. For that which is nothing is less; if it is declared that the accusation of disturbed possession did not proceed, there is no damage. D. ad legem Aquiliam, L. si servus servum, § si olivam. But to this it suffices to say that the former speaks in a civil context, the latter in a criminal one; for it is sufficient against you if you do me injury by disturbing me. D. de iniuriis, L. iniuriam, § si. And thus, through this appeal, one does not come to the retraction of a criminal penalty.

† Regarding the last point, it must be considered whether the guarantor guaranteed specifically, or for every cause that could arise from the judgment. D. loca. l. quaero; D. de fideius. l. pro ea; §. si nummos; l. si; D. de in lit. iur.; and l. 1; D. de eo, quod cert. loco; l. centum capuae; and l. si; §. 1; D. ad municipales; l. libertus; §. fin., with many similar authorities. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution made by the word "accipiunt" is direct or oblique.
body: In the case proposed, it is stated that Thomas Lacobini of Trevi made his last will and testament, in which, among other things, he left to Rosa, his wife, and to Luca Vannis of Trevi, 25 gold florins. He also appointed as his executors Mascio Nic., resident of Petrutii, and the aforementioned Luca, and in all his other goods he instituted and made his daughter Margaret his universal heir. And if the said Margaret, his daughter, should die in pupillary age, or later at any time without legitimate children from lawful marriage, he left from his aforementioned goods to Mascio Nic., resident, and to Luca, as fideicommissaries, 100 gold florins for each of them by right of institution. And in these he instituted them, and each of them, as his heir, willing that they could not demand or have more from his goods. And all his other goods the said testator wished and ordered to be sold, given, and distributed among the poor of Christ of Trevi, or of its district, or part of them, and for pious places of the said district of Trevi, where it will seem best and be pleasing to the fideicommissaries. After these things, the said testator having died, the said Margaret died in pupillary age without surviving children. Rosa and the aforementioned Luca, her grandfather and grandmother, and those in the nearest degree, remain. Now it is asked whether the aforementioned Luca and Rosa, beyond the above-mentioned legacies made to them, can obtain and have anything from the goods and inheritance of the aforementioned Margaret. For the declaration of which, first it must be seen whether the aforementioned substitution made to the aforementioned Margaret by the said Thomas, her father, was pupillary or fideicommissary. And it seems

First, that the said substitution was, and is, pupillary: because in the words set forth above in the aforementioned substitution, it must be understood that the fiduciaries receive the said goods, and sell, give, and distribute them among the poor of Trevi, etc., as noted by the gloss in *l. alio*, at the end of the first gloss, *de alimentis et cibariis legatis*. But this word, "receive," is a direct verb; therefore, etc. Moreover, fiduciaries are considered in the place of the heir, as noted by the gloss in *l. si quis ad declinandam*, C. *de episcopis et clericis*, and in the *Speculum*, *de instrumentis editis*, § *nunc vero aliqua*, verse *item pone, quod aliquis*, with several following verses. Therefore, it appears that since the said fiduciaries take from their own hand, and not from the hand of another, the aforementioned substitution was, and is, pupillary. And this opinion is upheld by Master Bartolus in *l. fundi treba*, *de usufructu legato*, in the last question, and in *l. centurio*, ff. *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, in the second principal question.

On the contrary, it seems, and I believe this to be truer, namely, that the aforementioned substitution is fiduciary. This is proven by the text in *l. cohæredi*, § *cum filiae*, ff. *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, and there by Jacobus de Arena and by Cynus, C. *de impuberibus et aliis substitutis*, *l. precibus*, there: "If, however, this compendious [substitution] is made by a layman, whether by the words: 'I beg you to restore,' or if he says by these words: 'within the pupillary age,' or whenever he shall have died, it is fiduciary, and not direct," as ff. *eodem*, *l. cohaeredi*, § *cum filiae*, and there by him, etc. For the aforementioned substitution was made by mere oblique words, as appears above, there: "and all his other goods he wished and commanded the said testator, that they be sold, given, and distributed among the poor, etc." which are oblique words, per *l. 2*, C. *communium legatorum*, and *l. si quis legauerit*, ff. *de usufructu*, and *l. fundi treb.*, ff. *de usufructu legato*, and *l. eam, quam*, C. *de fideicommissis*, and what is noted in the said laws.

It is not an objection that it is said above that in the aforementioned substitution, the word "receive," etc., is understood, as noted in the aforementioned laws. For, granted but not conceded, that this were true: nevertheless, it is irrelevant to the matter, since the aforementioned fiduciaries do not receive for their own benefit, since they are mere executors, per *l. si quis Titio*, ff. *de legatis 2*, and in the *Speculum*, *de instrumentis editis*, § *nunc vero aliqua*, verse *item si testatori*. Moreover, granted that they receive, since they immediately restore to the poor, they are not said to have received, since a transaction is not said to be turned over unless it remains turned over, per *l. si pro patre*, § *versum*, ff. *de in rem verso*, and *l. qui sic soluit*, ff. *de solutionibus*. It is not an objection that it is said that the aforementioned fiduciaries are considered in the place of heirs. For I say that they are not considered in the place of heirs as to all things, as noted in the aforementioned *l. si quis Titio decem*, and *l. si quis ad declinandam*, § *licentiae*, C. *de episcopis et clericis*. For they are heirs in name, not in fact, and thus it does not obstruct the aforementioned ser. Lucas and Rosa, uncle and aunt of the aforementioned Margaret. Argument from *l. 2*, § *sed si sint*, ff. *ad Senatusconsultum Tertullianum*, there: "lest the bare name of heir should harm the mother," etc.

These things having been premised, I say briefly, in response to the questions of law to be answered, that since the aforementioned substitution made by the said Thomas to his daughter the aforementioned Margaret was, and is, fiduciary, the aforementioned ser. Lucas and Rosa ought to have the legitime of the aforementioned Margaret, due by natural law, in the goods formerly of the said Thomas, which is one-third part of all the goods formerly of the said Thomas. The remaining two parts ought to be sold, given, and distributed by the said fiduciaries among the poor of Trevi, according to the will of the aforementioned testator. These things are proven by *l. cohaeredi*, § *cum filiae*, ff. *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, and in *l. 2*, § *fin.*, ff. *de iure codicillorum*, and C. *de inofficioso testamento*, Auth. *nouissima*, and in the body of Auth. *de triennio et semestri*, § *singula singulis referendo*.

I, Baldus.
