consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A different time, but interest is claimed.
body: When the time appointed for the enjoyment of the usufruct has expired, no further period is granted for that purpose.

† as to the final cause of detention. That is, when the time has expired and he will no longer be held captive, the detainer ought not to remain in possession any longer. D. si certum petat, l. si quis nec causam, § finali; C. de usufructu legato, l. si usufruct. mihi biennium. And therefore, in the said detention, which has already been extinguished by the passage of time, he ought not to be reinstated; or he ought to be reinstated only for an instant, so that the statute may be satisfied. And if he were reinstated immediately and without delay, possession ought to be restored to the true possessor, namely, the said Lady Helen; as in c. cum ecclesia, de causa possessionis. And thus, with one hand he releases the agent, with the other he ejects him. By this, however, no prejudice is done to the heirs of the lessee, so that they may not claim from the lessor, or his heirs, what is due to them, if anything is due; but he cannot claim to be restored to possession for so long a time as was agreed, if the agreed time has already elapsed according to the said laws. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether in a matrimonial cause the referral of an oath has a place as a supplement to half-proof, and what if the cause is matrimonial.
body: Because

† One witness, testifying to the truth, introduces a certain inconsistency: for first he states that he said to the stepmother, if she wished the said John for her lawful husband; who responded and said that yes, and also said to the said Cech, if it pleased you to take the said stepmother as your lawful wife, who in response said that yes. Upon these words, the said Cech and Vanneta together touched each other’s hands and kissed. These words sound as though a marriage contract had been concluded, and afterwards he adds, promising each other, namely Cech to take the said Vanneta as wife, and the said lady Vanneta to take the said Cech as husband. These words sound like betrothals for a future marriage, and not for a present one. To this witness, as being incomplete and wavering, I do not give credence: and especially in so difficult a case, as is a matrimonial case. And because no annulment intervened, nor any customary rites were performed in the form of the Church, and therefore an oath ought not to be deferred, according to the noted authorities on oaths, l. 3, § quaecunque; and in the Extravagant, in the chapter Mulieri; and in the chapter Cum sunt partium, on the rules of law, book 6; in the Authenticum Qui, on the nature of legacies, § quantum, column 6. The truth, however, cannot be changed before God, and therefore license to marry ought not to be granted nor denied to the woman or the man, but left to their own conscience.

A patrimonial cause is arduous, and in it an oath is not admitted on the basis of a single witness, according to the noted provisions in Extra, De iure iurando, c. Mulieri and c. Finis; and in De regulis iuris, c. Cum sunt partium, lib. 6; and l. 3, § Quaecunque, ff. De iureiurando; and as noted in ff. De venditionibus in possessione mittendis, l. 1, § Si ea, where the glossa says “uxorem.” For it must be fully proven. However, Hostiensis says that if there is one witness of very honorable person and good reputation, and likewise the plaintiff, the oath may be tendered, in the said c. Mulieri, and there Johannes Andreae in his ancient additions. And because a consistent reputation is presumed true, and adds credibility to the testimony of the witness, and is a certain garment of it, and warms the testimony so that it bears some fruit, beyond what it would bear if it were naked by itself. l. Testium, § Eius debet quoque, ff. De testibus. The parity of the persons must also be considered, and other things which are called the external goods of marriage: namely, wealth, dowry, beauty, from which, if they mutually assist each other, the bishop, moved by his own impulse, may proceed to the tendering of the oath. And thus it is according to the discretion of Hostiensis: the bishop should scrutinize the secrets of his conscience, and follow the movement of his mind; because in matters of discretion it is permitted to him to supply from the fact in the aforementioned manner, and in certain other cases. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. I buy for myself and for Titius, and I buy on behalf of myself and Titius. These differ from one another.
body: All things done have the right,

† For it matters greatly how the words are framed. If they are framed thus: “I buy for myself and for Titius,” then the law speaks of that fund. D. de contrahenda emptione, per the previously cited authorities by you. Whether the words are framed thus: “I buy, receiving for myself and for Titius.” And then it is also valid in the person of Titius, if he ratifies it; because he made me his procurator. D. de actione empti, l. Iulius, § si procurator. On this, note D. de obligationibus et actionibus, l. quaecunque gerimus; D. de legatis 1, l. huiusmodi, in principio; in l. 1, D. de stipulationibus servorum; and in § alteri, with similar authorities. And thus the words were framed in our case. Hence the contract was valid in the person of both, and there is no simulation here, but rather the will of the brother advising his sister, to whom he could also expressly make a donation. And thus the objection does not hold, which we noted in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. uxor marito. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. He consulted on the law concerning a certain substitution, whether it is direct or oblique, but the form of the substitution does not appear.
body: BOO

† On this point, I wrote in *l. Centurio*, reciting Bartolus and holding that if the said distribution of times has been made, and other words allow that the substitution is direct: then it will be considered pupillary before the time of puberty. And to this effect, all the reasons put forward by Johannes Andreae in *c. Si pater*, *De testibus*, Book 6, may be adduced. And note that Cynus, in his additions to *l. Precibus*, formulating the question without distinction of times, holds it to be fideicommissary for many reasons. And because this question rests finally solely on the understanding of the chapter *Cum tibi*, *Extra*, *De testamentis*, where it is said that he who commits his will to another’s distributive disposition seems to have tacitly instituted him heir. This last will is called the distribution of the distributor to pious causes, interpreted according to Innocentius. And it is not called institution of an heir simply: because no benefit or detriment follows therefrom. And if he does not make an inventory, he is not therefore held liable in solidum to creditors and other legatees. However, it should be known that sometimes this executor is left with no other heir instituted, and then *c. Cum tibi* applies; sometimes with another universal heir instituted, and then certainly this one is not an heir, but a bare minister. *Digestum*, *De legatis*, 2, *l. Si quis Titio*, with similar cases. Thus it was here, because another universal heir was instituted, namely Margarita, daughter of the testator. Consider: it is true that in the first tablets another was instituted, but in the second tablets no one else was universally substituted: therefore the executors are understood to be instituted in the second tablets, and thus the substitution is direct, and the mother of the pupilla Margarita is excluded by this interpretative pupillary substitution, as in *l. Precibus*, *Codex*, *De impuberibus*. And because the distinction of times must have some effect, as noted there. But to this I respond: because I deny that he made second tablets here; for it does not appear that he wished to allow his son to make a will, nor concerning his son’s goods: although in an express direct substitution it is tacitly added, as noted in *l. 1*, *Digestum*, *De vulgari substitutione*, and *l. Si ita*, § *Si filio*, *De secundis tabulis*; nevertheless, in a doubtful substitution it is otherwise, especially when the mother is in the middle: to whom a legitime is due by natural law, and it is unjust to exclude her, and against all the spirit of piety. *Digestum*, *De inofficioso testamento*, *l. Nam et si parentibus*. Nor does the objection of the distribution of times hold, because it operates nothing in a fideicommissary substitution, but only in a direct doubtful one. Moreover, all words of partition or distribution of things or quantities suggest a fideicommissum. *Digestum*, *Ad Trebellianam*, *l. Cogi*, § *Generaliter*. Furthermore, if these legacies were understood to be left according to the second tablets, then if the pupillus had contracted debts, these legacies would be cut down, because they are not said to be given except after deducting the testator’s debts. But the pupillus himself is said to make a will, therefore the pupillus could also care for these legacies. On this, see *l. 1*, *Digestum*, *De tutoribus et rationibus distrabuendis*. Also, regarding the testator’s debts, suppose that these executors compromised: certainly it seems that they would retain for themselves as if by design. *Digestum*, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, *l. 3*. But it could be responded that these are bare ministers, and thus they benefit the poor. *Codex*, *De transactionibus*, *l. Si praeses*. Finally, I say thus: these cannot be heirs for the poor, to whom distribution must be made individually. *Codex*, *De hereditate instituenda*, *l. Quotiens*. Nor can they be heirs for themselves; therefore the substitution is not direct. But to this it is responded, because these distributors could distribute by shares of the inheritance. Indeed, even the whole inheritance could be given to one pious place, such as a church or hospital, by the Trebellian rule: therefore they are heirs not to retain, but to restore. Moreover, no one restores an inheritance by the Trebellian rule unless he is an heir. *Digestum*, *Ad Trebellianam*, *l. Mulier*, § *Finalis*. I respond: rather, a fideicommissary to a fideicommissary. *Digestum*, *Ad Trebellianam*, *l. 1*, § *De illo*, and § *Ille vero*. Thus also commissioners and fideicommissaries. I am also moved, because in our case the testator wished to use the word of institution, except in certain things and with respect to certain persons, and to whom he prohibited the right of accrual. *Digestum*, *De herede instituendo*, *l. Quo*, § *Si duo*; *De vulgari substitutione*, *l. Coheredi*, § *Finis*. From which, although this question is sufficiently doubtful, I judge this substitution to be fideicommissary. And so I hold, whatever is said on this point by Bartolus and some others. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An action on a hypothec is not brought unless excussion has been made.
2. Although the community of the poor is under the bishop, it does not draw the plaintiff to the bishop.
3. It may be argued from the cause to the person.
body: CXOV

† A plaintiff bringing a hypothecary action on account of a dowry, if he sues only a third-party possessor, ought not to be heard unless the husband’s assets in his possession have first been exhausted, as stated in the Authentica de fideiussoribus, § sed neque, and in the Authentica hoc si debitor, Codex de pignoribus cum suis. The Bishop, acting as the father of the poor, sold the property after issuing edicts and general proclamations. By this act, the woman is not prejudiced, especially regarding her dowry, because she was not specifically cited, and because she knew that her right would endure. Digestum de re iudicata, l. de unoquoque; de maioribus et obediencia, c. humilis, according to Innocentius; Codex si quis ut se ab hereditate abstineat; Authentica si omnes; in the Authentica de hereditatibus et falsis, § si vero absunt.

† The community of the poor is under the protection of the church and subject to ecclesiastical jurisdiction; nevertheless, if it is necessary for the community of the poor to appear in defense of the plaintiff, this case cannot be drawn to the bishop against the will of the plaintiff. D. de iudiciis, l. venditor; C. ubi in rem actio, l. 1. However, the defenders of the poor may attend the litigation to prevent collusion. But clerics cannot accept upon themselves the judgment with the intention of novating it; thus it is understood in D. 11, q. 1, c. clericum nullus; and in Speculum, de iudiciis, l. decreto, § restat, ver. quid si dominus clericus est, and the following verse; and it accords with what is touched upon by Bartolus in D. rem rabiendam habere, l. procurator ad exigendum, § 1.

† It is also said that the procurator of the poor may request that the exceptions, which he raises in the secular forum in his own interest, be remitted to be proved before the bishop; yet not that the bishop should pronounce by arguing the cause ad personam. De ordine cognitionis, cap. Tuam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether fruits diminish the dowry, or are in place of alimony, or are to be restored.
body: Since

† Whatever is added to the principal is interest. As stated in the law *rogasti*, section *si tibi*, in the title *de usuris*. And it was said that the custom of Cottum was established to circumvent the prohibition on usury. Certainly, whatever the aforementioned Paulellus received diminished the principal. For even in the restitution of a dowry, fruits received from pledges diminish the principal. Digest, *de solutionibus*, law *Titia*. But against this it is argued: because the wife and her children from the marriage claim certain items from the dowry, as in the Code, *de rei uxoriae actione*, law *rem in praesenti*, section *exactio*. And these are commonly called dowry allowances (*alimenta dotis*): and they are provided by custom. But this is true only during the subsistence of the marriage, in the case of the law *ubi adhuc*, Code, *de iure dotium*. Likewise, in the case of a dissolved marriage, if the wife and children had no other means of support; but where the son is robust and has means to support himself, Bartolus says in the law *insulam*, section *usuras*, in the title *de solutione matrimonii*, that interest or allowances are not due. Whatever the case may be regarding pledges, it reduces the debt; and if dowry allowances were due, they would first reduce the allowances, then the principal body of the dowry. But if they are not due, they reduce whatever they find to be reducible, namely the principal sum itself. In any case other than that of a dowry, there is no doubt that a reduction and compensation of fruits with the principal debt occurs. The laws are well-known. Moreover, in our case, the father is not in default, because before emancipation the father had full usufruct. Code, *de bonis, quae liberis*, law *cum oportet*, section *cum autem constantiniana*. And this is the same for all adventitious property, from whatever source it came to the son while he was under his father’s power. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether debtors of those expelled or under ban, by paying the treasury, are released from their creditors.
2. How it is to be understood that today novation is not presumed.
body: You propose the following facts, namely, that Bernard Blanci, a citizen of Montefiascone, was a creditor of Allegutius Salomonis on account of a loan in a certain quantity of florins, for which he held from the said Allegutius pledges in the said quantity, and more. It also happened that the said Bernard was content to restore the said pledges, and he did restore them because the said Allegutius arranged, with the consent of the said Bernard, that three citizens of Montefiascone, namely, Bartholomew the Master, John Bartholomew Cechi, and Antonius Iutii, should confess that they held in deposit from the said Bernard 150 gold florins on account of a deposit, and that they should promise to restore them to the said Bernard at every petition and will of the said Bernard. Bartholomew the Master, John Bartholomew Cechi, and Antonius Iutii, although they had received no deposit, entered into the promise, or any other payment or solution of money was made. And then, after the aforementioned promise had been made by the aforementioned Bartholomew the Master, John Bartholomew Cechi, and Antonius Iutii, the said Allegutius, being present, understanding, and hearing the said Bernard, acknowledged at their insistence that the debt of the said 115 florins was that of the said Allegutius, and that they had made the confession and provision concerning the said 115 florins for him, Allegutius, although no payment or solution of money had taken place between the said Bernard, Bartholomew, and Antonius either before or afterwards. After a month, or thereabouts, the aforementioned Bernard, who had previously been for many times, and then was, a resident of the city of Montefiascone, with the permission of the officials of the city of Montefiascone, departed from the said city and went to the said castle of Marta. In which castle he remained continuously for many years, even during the war between the Britons, the commune, the men, and the inhabitants of the castle of Marta, on the one part, and the Roman Church and the commune of Montefiascone, on the other part. Since the said Bernard, during the said war, did not return to Montefiascone, the place of his citizenship, but rather made continuous residence in the said rebellious castle of Marta, as is stated above, and held, as he did hold, for many years the rock of the said castle as castellan of the said castle of Marta, it is found that the same Bernard was condemned by the judge of malefices of the court of the General Patrimony, on account of the said rebellion and occupation of the said castle and rock, for the crime of lèse-majesté; and on account of the said condemnation and confiscation of the goods of Bernard, I hold, by the officials of the said court, that the said Allegutius was the principal and true debtor of the said Bernard, compelled, as appears in the instrument of discharge made to him.

† An ancient question is whether debtors of expelled or banned persons, compelled to pay the treasury, are released from their own creditor. And the truth is that if indeed the debtor’s goods had been confiscated, the debtor is released, whether he pays under compulsion or voluntarily; because the treasury had succeeded to the creditor’s right, and therefore payment was due to the treasury, since the treasury is regarded in the place of an heir, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si debitori deportato; and note in the same title, l. ubicunque; and D. de novazione, l. quo; and l. novatio; pro socio, l. actione, § publicatione; C. ad l. Iul. de vi publica, l. tutoris. But if the debtor’s goods had not been confiscated, then either he pays voluntarily, and is not released: D. de solutionibus, l. qui hominem, § si nullo; and l. si creditor; or the debtor pays under compulsion, and then either he was compelled by a private person, and is not released, but has recourse against the compeller: D. si quis cautio, l. 2, § fi; or he was compelled by the commune or public officials, and then he is released: D. de legatis 3, l. Paulo Calimacho, § fi; de annuis legatis, l. liber, § Lucius; D. de legato commissario, l. fi. And thus we hold, following Cynus, quod me causa, l. 2; and following Bartolus in the said l. creditor. And certainly there would be no doubt if anyone had paid the said Bern. or Ant., that they would be released from the said Bern. But the doubt arises because the obligors themselves did not pay, but Allegutius, formerly the principal debtor, whose debt the said two Bern. and Ant. had transferred onto themselves, by whose obligation and by the change of the cause of the debt a novation seems to have been made. Since the first cause was a loan, it was transferred into the cause of an alleged deposit, which could be done with the addition of a stipulation, C. si certum petatur, l. si ex pretio. Therefore, if Allegut., as the principal debtor among the promisors, had satisfied Bern., his creditor, D. de pignoribus actione, l. solutum, § satis factum. A sign also of the release was the delivery of the pledges, although this by itself alone would not release the debtor, as D. de pactis, l. postquam. If therefore Allegutius owed nothing to Bernar., the injury was done to Allegutio, not to Bern. And the official, who proceeded erroneously, is liable to Allegutio: D. de evictionibus, l. si pignora; D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. lectos. Or if the money had come into the treasury, the treasury would be liable: D. de administratione rerum ad civitatem pertinentium, l. 3, § gravi.

And if it is said that today novation is not presumed, as in C. de nov. l. si, I answer: it is true that the cause has not changed and the same form has been preserved; otherwise, tacit novation is presumed. D. loc. cond. l. cum in plures § lege in dicta; and D. de praes. stip. l. Valerianus; and note D. de nov. l. omnes. Therefore, if Allegutius was not a debtor, and those who were the true debtors paid nothing, they are not discharged. D. de cond. et dem. si peracta causa § 1. And consequently, Bernard, being restored to his former position, may be effectively sued. Consider that, because Allegutius was not a debtor, Bernard was a debtor of Bernard’s debtors, who had bound the goods of Bernard to the said three of the promisors, and under this hypothec was included the name of Allegutius, debtor of the debts, binding himself and his goods, as noted in C. de her. acq. l. haeredem; C. quae res pign. obl. poss. l. nomen. Thus, Allegutius was still bound to Bernard under a new head, namely, by the hypothec of the name. Wherefore, by paying, he discharged both himself and those whom he had brought in to promise, as in D. de neg. gest. l. si liber; D. de except. doli l. si opera. From which it is clearly concluded that the said Bernard has no justice in his petition, since the said Bartholomew and Anthony, as discharged, are in no way bound to him. And those things alleged for Bernard are worth not even a fly, since it was notorious that he was an enemy, and that compulsion to pay to the extent of the law was made, and the confiscation of goods cannot be denied. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son born to a woman living outside the household, who was not held as a concubine, is to be called natural, and whether legitimation made concerning him as a natural child by one having power is valid.
2. Caesar legitimates both in law and in fact, and grants this power and authority to another.
3. A son is called natural in two ways.
4. Who is to be called noble.
5. Whether a legitimated person, upon his instance, excludes agnates.
6. Whether from a donation of a large quantity it is presumed that someone is a spendthrift.
7. Whether a donation can be revoked on account of serious injuries and atrocious tortures inflicted upon the donor.
body: The facts of the case

It is proposed in the terms set forth below: Lord Peter, Lord of Reame, of the Salimbeni family and of Siena, being without a wife, attached himself to a certain unmarried woman, and from her he begot a son named Antonio. However, it is not established as a constant fact that he cohabited with the said woman and had an undoubted affection for her, such that she could be said to have been his concubine. For Lord Peter, in the course of time after the aforementioned events, took a certain noble woman as his wife. But for several years, before he took a wife, he had the said Antonio, his son, legitimated and restored to his birthrights by the honorable man Lord Francesco Banni of Florence, Count Palatine, who had the authority for this attributed to him by the Most Serene Lord Prince Charles IV, Roman Emperor, always Augustus. Later, after many years, the said Lord Peter died, with the said Antonio surviving him, and with no other son or descendant surviving him. The said Antonio, after the death of the said Peter, made a donation inter vivos to the noble man Lord Raymond of the Salimbeni family of certain castles and properties which had belonged to the said Lord Peter and remained in his inheritance. Of this donation, there is evidence in a public instrument drawn up by Ser Munelli, scribe of Ser James. The instrument of donation, and also the instrument of legitimation, are transmitted to the consultant. It is further proposed that the said Antonio had completed his twenty-fifth year at the time of the said donation, and that the goods donated exceeded the quantity and estimation of 1000 gold florins. First, the power or authority of the count who legitimated must be considered. Second, the condition or quality of the son himself. Third, the military service and nobility of the father. Fourth, the very form or act of legitimation. Fifth, the right of succession. Sixth, it must be considered whether such a donation, of such magnitude, was valid, and especially considering the statute of the commune of Siena, of which mention is made in the point I have seen and read.

† Regarding the first point, it must be known that the Emperor, by right, may and in fact is accustomed both to legitimize and to grant this power and authority to another, as is noted in the Authentica *Qui modo* (na. eff. sui), §. *Si*, Collatio 7, Extra, *Qui sint legitimi*, c. *Per venerabilem*. It accords with what is noted in l. 1, *De tutela et cura dandis ab his*, and yet the Count has the power to the extent that the tenor of the Imperial letters grants it, as in Extra, *De privilegiis*, c. *Porro*; ff., *De vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, l. *Ex facto*, in principio. We must serve the words of the rescript, and especially when they limit or modify the benefit of the Prince himself. ff., *Ne quid in loco publico*, l. 2, §. *Si quis a Principe*, and §. *Merito*; Extra, *De auctoritate et usu papae*, cap. *Ex tuarum*. Regarding the second point, it must be known

It is that a natural son is said in two ways: in one way legally, and then it is required that the concubine be undoubtfully retained in the household in the status of a concubine, differing little from a wife except in honor. D. de concubinis, l. in concubinatu; D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. in libertis; D. de legatis 3, l. item in legato, § patrui. And this was introduced in order to have certainty of the offspring; otherwise women could easily feign having sons by some great and noble man, and our successions would pass to strangers and others, arg. ad hanc rationem D. de his qui sui iuris sunt, l. filium; and C. de repudiis, l. consensu, § 1. In another way, a natural son is given according to the common custom of speaking, namely every bastard who is born of a free man and a free woman, even if he were born from a clandestine embrace, Extr. de electione, c. innotuit. For in the truth of the matter, without regard to legal fiction, this one is natural if both parents acknowledge that he is their son, and the father holds him as his son with undoubted effect, and pursues him with paternal charity, namely as far as God is concerned, who judges according to truth. Also, according to canonical equity, this one ought not to be called spurious, and he is legitimated by marriage. Inst. de nuptiis, § si; Extr. qui filii sint legitimi, c. tanta. Therefore, this other one, about whom the question is asked, according to the subtlety of civil law is not a natural son, but spurious, and according to true naturalness, and canonical equity, and common usage of speaking, he would be called natural. And therefore the father, who had him legitimated under the appellative name of natural son, is not understood to have concealed his effect, or to have deceived the praetor, but to have spoken the natural truth. And thus the legitimation is valid by will, power, and canonical form of the act.

† Regarding the third point, it should be noted that in certain privileges the sons of nobles are excepted, so that they cannot be legitimated. And then it may be disputed who are to be considered nobles: whether those who are commonly called nobles, or only those holding dignities, or those born from them. Nevertheless, I consider it sufficiently established that he is counted among the nobles who possesses jurisdiction and the mere and mixed empire by privilege or by non-tyrannical custom. But I do not pursue this matter, since this exception is not made in the present privilege. Regarding the fourth point, I say that the form and act of legitimation are in good order; thus, this young man has become a legitimate son by the gift of his father and Prince. C. de nat. lib. auth. si quis. Regarding the fifth point, I say,

The words of this privilege appear to be very different from those of similar customary privileges. For the prince here seems to have intended that, by such legitimation, prejudice should not be caused to the agnates, so that the nearest agnate would succeed together with the legitimated person; and thus it would happen that the legitimated person would have as a coheir a certain agnate of his father, even up to the tenth degree, if there were no other nearer agnate. This departs greatly from any intention of the father, since the son ought to exclude more distant relatives, as stated in the Authentica *De haeredibus ab intestato*, in the beginning: for the primary cause is that of children. But certainly, let it be far from us to say that the most holy and most religiously just Caesar erred. (Digest, *De legibus*, Book 2, Law *Unum ex familia*, § *Item pater Marchus*). For those who are around the Caesar are accustomed to be most wise, and in fact this is always the case.

Therefore, in order that we may understand the words of the rescript according to the manner in which its messenger, namely the Vice-Count, legitimated this person not only for the father but for the whole line of agnates, or as an agnate succeeding to other agnates together with agnates of equal degree: let him succeed to his own father together with his brothers' sons and their descendants, if there are any other legitimate heirs to his father; otherwise, let him succeed alone. And thus, under a correct grammatical construction, no absurdity follows. Therefore, this legitimated person succeeds to his father in full (*insolidum*) in paternal property, but he would not succeed in fiefs, nor in dignities, as stated in the gloss *Si de feudo fuerit controversia inter dominum et vassallum*. Natural dignities are rather retained by the grace of the Prince than by succession from a parent. And therefore, perhaps, he would not succeed in the Empire, whether pure or mixed; for every bastard is marked by a certain infamy of fact, and dignities do not wish to be polluted. But since jurisdictions, by custom, are patrimonial, they are certainly transmitted just like the rest of the patrimony.

† Now I come to the sixth point, namely, to the donation: and it appears that it is not valid as having been made by a notorious prodigal. For who is a greater prodigal than this one, who so recklessly squanders so much and such great things? By his own ruin of his patrimony, he consumes his entire substance and finds for himself a mad end; nor does the law permit anyone to misuse his own substance. But it may be answered that a donation of all goods is valid, as is noted in C. de pactis, l. si; C. de revocatione donationum, l. liqueat; and l. si totas. Nor is he thereby declared a prodigal and incapacitated from incurring loss, because his goods had not previously been interdicted by judicial sentence, as stated in the gloss to l. is cui bonis, under the heading de verborum obligationibus, together with its subject matter. And therefore, fraud and machination being absent, such a donation, made by a person of perfect age and sound mind, recorded before the acts of the praeses and insinuated in the records, was valid and held from the beginning.

† However, it must be noted that, on account of atrocious injuries or tortures inflicted upon the donee, the donation could be revoked, notwithstanding a pact not to revoke for ingratitude; because such a pact is not extended to the matter of delinquency. C. de reuo. dona. l. si. C. de decu. l. si ille. lib. 10. For a future atrocious injury cannot be remitted by pact, according to some. Others say otherwise. I do not say more on this point, because it does not pertain to the facts, nor was anything narrated to me viva voce. Furthermore, it must be noted, lest if this donor were to procreate children by a lawful wife, they might revoke [the donation] at some time, de reuo. don. l. si vnquam. And therefore, it is good in this case to reach a composition between these lords, the Magni of Salimbeni, because much can be said on both sides. Moreover, the statute does not apply to the proposition, because it speaks of one under 25 years of age; otherwise, therefore, for one older, as ff. de noua. l. doli. §. diuersum. And for now, let it suffice that I have said these things. And it seems to me that I was otherwise questioned, yet I do not well remember, nor could I find [it] in my memoranda. And it must be noted that, although the donation was valid, nevertheless, possession not having been transferred, the donee did not become owner, as C. de pac. l. traditionibus. Nevertheless, by iure cessio, i.e., by excess actions, action may be brought even without transfer, ff. de rei vend. l. si culpa, presupposing the validity of the donation. And this [is so] if the instrument makes mention of the cession of actions, or if in the donation the title suffices without cession, as noted, C. de act. et ob. l. 2. unless the cession, or donation, was made by a more powerful reason of office, as C. ne liceat potentioribus. l. 1. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, etc. Involved allegations of law without narration of fact.

A summary proceeding must be conducted for Lady Pluestra according to the form of reformation, since she has justice on her side, having purchased from an unworthy person and having held possession by virtue of a precarium. C. de rei vend. l. quotiens. And therefore, when a summary petition or statement of facts is presented, Francis ought to be compelled to relinquish possession, provided it is proven that Ardigus possessed the property at the time of the sale made to Lady Silvestra, unless Francis proves otherwise that it pertains to him. And I say the same regarding Ser John: because the aforementioned Silvestra had purchased earlier and had become the owner. ff. de pub. l. siue autem. §. si duobus; ff. de acq. emp. l. si ea res. §. fi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute extends its force to property situated in another territory. nos. 4 and 5.
2. Statutes may diminish the inheritance of children, but not abolish it entirely.
3. Whether grandchildren not yet in existence at the time of the other’s death may come to their own property.
4. A statute prohibiting a dowried daughter from succeeding does not apply to property located outside the territory.
5. Ascendants transmit the inheritance, not yet accepted, to their children.
body: With regard to the aforesaid, it must be considered

† First, concerning her own goods in the territory of Mount Saint Mary and in the aforementioned estates, I do not see by what right the sons of the said Bar. can claim anything. For they can claim nothing through the person of the mother, because she was excluded by the statute; for the statute that a dowried woman does not succeed, etc., is valid and binding within the jurisdiction and territory of the castle of the Mount, even if the dowries were less than the legitimate portion. And this was an ancient dispute, which is touched upon by Dy. in c. Indultum, Extra de re iudicata, lib. 6, and by Cyn. in C. de nuptiis, l. Sancimus.

And Bartolus in the law *Omnes populi*, Digest, *De iustitia et iure*, and all authorities hold that statutes may properly diminish the succession of children, but not abolish it entirely; because the laws sometimes fixed the legitime of children in a larger portion, and sometimes in a smaller one; yet they never entirely deprived children of everything, as is evident in the Authenticum *De triennio et semisse* and the Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, Authenticum *Novissima*. And the personal rights, which they themselves allege in the aforementioned places, which if I were to repeat, would be exceedingly long: and thus from the person of the mother who has received a dowry, they could claim nothing from the aforementioned goods, because the dowries given to the said Lady Barbara succeed in the place of the portion of the goods which she could have claimed in the goods situated in the territory of the castle of Montis, in which the statute has force, as in law 1, § *Haec actio locum*, at the end, Digest, *Si quis testamento liberum esse iussit*, and Digest, *Si quis cautionem*, law *Si eum*, § *Qui iniuriarum*. Nor do the words inserted in the statute, "until etc.," stand in the way, because this condition never existed during the lifetime of the said Lady Barbara, and therefore the action never accrued to her, and consequently it could not now be transmitted to the children.

† Moreover, the sons of the said Lady Barth. cannot come to the goods of Guidutius, their grandfather: because, although perhaps they, if contained under the disposition of the statute, as might be proved by law, cannot come to the goods with the mother excluded, since they were not in existence at the time of the death of the said Guidutius, they cannot come to his goods by any right, as in l. Titius, in fine, ff. de suis et legatis, and l. 1, § si quis proximior, ff. unde cognati, with its authorities; and the laws which are alleged to the contrary speak of sons, grandsons, and others who were in existence at the time of the death of the deceased, concerning whose property the matter is in question.

† Now I come to the goods of the said Guidutio situated outside the territory of the castle of Montis: and I say that in the aforementioned goods the statute does not hold; for statutes which prohibit, or make a prohibition odious, do not bind nor have effect outside the territory, as is stated in l. ex ea, ff. de posthumis, and what is noted there, and extra de sententia excommunicationis, c. si omnia, lib. 6. From which the learned Bartolus infers in l. 3, C. de summa trinitate, in the 6th principal question, in its proper terms,

† That statute, which provides that a dowried woman shall not succeed, does not apply to goods situated outside the territory of the city that enacted it: because such a prohibition and statute is odious, as stated in l. maximum, C. de lib. præt. and therefore it has no force outside the territory, according to the aforementioned laws. This is also held by Cynus, Petrus, and Jacobus de Arena in the aforementioned l. 2, C. de sum. tri., in a certain question beginning with "to treat how statutes bind in matters that are not delicts or contracts." And because all modern commentators hold this view, and thus the laws that might seem to speak to the contrary speak of a favorable, not an odious, prohibition, I conclude from the arguments that the said Lady Bartholomew succeeded intestate to one-half of all the goods of the said Guidutio, her father, situated outside the territory of the said castle of Montis, notwithstanding the said statute. And if it is said that the said Ioannes sold some of the aforementioned goods situated outside the said territory of the castle of Montis, I respond that if the said goods have not yet been acquired by prescription within ten or twenty years, the sons of the said Lady Bartholomew may claim the said goods from the possessors of the sold property, because she succeeded intestate to the said Guidutio in one-half of the said goods, as stated. This is proven in the Authentica In successione, C. de suis et leg., notwithstanding the aforementioned statute, by the laws cited above. And this succession

† And even though she was not acknowledged, the aforementioned Lady Barth. transmitted [the inheritance] to her sons, as in l. hereditatem, §. filius, ff. de castrensi peculio; in l. 1, C. de his qui ante apertionem tabularum. And therefore they could claim the said goods, if they are not prescribed. But if they were prescribed, then I say that the aforementioned sons of Lady Barth. can have the said sale ratified, and recover half the price from the heirs of the aforementioned John, as is the text and gloss, and the full matter in l. mater, C. de rei venditione. And thus it seems to me, Bonacursio Cechi of Sassoferrato, doctor of laws. And thus, as consulted by the aforementioned Lord Bonacursio, it seems to me, Ugo of Sassoferrato, the least of doctors of laws, in all things and in every way, with all due respect. And because he says that in the goods existing in the Monte Santa Maria the aforementioned sons of the said Barth. do not succeed, I think, considering the aforementioned statute and its words, that the sons of the aforementioned Lady Barth. are not excluded. And although the text in the aforementioned l. legibus, cited, and finally in l. si quis filio, ff. de iniuriis et iniuriosis, and irrito testamento, seems to imply the contrary, nevertheless, rightly understood, it does not say so: for there is a long difference. The words of the statute say, "as long as, and while, a male son exists, females do not succeed; while a male grandfather exists, they do not succeed." Thus, in the first case, the female is not totally excluded, but has a temporal impediment to coming to the succession; and therefore the statute does not totally deprive her of succession, arg. ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. Aurelio, in princ. ff. de pactis, l. epistola, §. si, ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. Titiae. Similarly, we have in our no. Barth., l. si sequitur, §. si maior, ff. de usucapione, where it is said that there is no difference: the statute says, "let him not be heard," or that the creditor is deprived by law by the lapse of a certain time: not arguing, as in the first case, that the natural nor civil obligation is removed. Secondly, thus, if in the proposal this Lady was not totally excluded from succession, but succession was removed by a temporal impediment, whence, the impediment being removed from the middle, the disposition of law is removed, arg. de iure patronatus, l. adigere, §. quamvis. Nor do the aforementioned laws alleged to the contrary stand in the way, because Dy. says in his own question, that even nephews born after the death of the grandfather we admit to succession, as he notes in l. Gallus, in fine, dig. ff. de liberis et posthumis. And this opinion was held by Cy. ff. de iniustis, ruptis et irritis testamentis, l. si quis filio, in princ. in additionibus. And the most excellent my Lord, do. Bal., asserted it by equity, tit. C. de his qui ante apertionem tabularum. And the same touches C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quis filium. This also reports that the said Barth. holds, ff. ad l. Iuliam, l. 2, §. sed videndum, and l. si. And it seems to me the truth with sounder judgment, in testimony of which I have subscribed myself, and sealed with my seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. On the threefold mode of succeeding, and when one comes in his own person, when in the person of another, and when an inheritance not entered upon is transmitted, or not, and it is a subtle opinion.
body:
Although the point has been prudently written about by others, for a more evident understanding it is necessary to state that there are three kinds of right: one is a right to come immediately in one’s own person; another is a right to come by virtue of the successor edict; and a third is a right to come by transmission made to him by another.

The right to come in one’s own person is that by which a person is called from the beginning, or afterwards upon the removal of some obstacle that had meanwhile stood in his way, as in D. 28,5,1 (*Qui posthumus*). And thus was the case of John Bartholomew, which is mentioned in the point: because there the males had died while the daughter was alive, having been passed over by the father, and thus she returned to her common right, the obstacle having been removed.

The successor edict applies whenever the preceding person has been extinguished and the next person is called; for example, if a son dies while his father is alive, the grandson comes by the successor edict, Inst. 3,1,1 (*Cum filius*); or if the prior agnate is removed by death or repudiation, the next in order or degree comes, Inst. 3,1,1 (*Placebat*); D. 28,5,1 (*Pater filium*) and D. 28,5,2 (*Si is qui*); C. 6,30,1 and 3, with similar authorities. And in this successor edict it must be known that grandsons born after the death of the grandfather are not included; because to them succession is not granted by the right of proximity, neither by civil law, nor by praetorian law, nor by the law of the forums, D. 28,2,1 (*Item praetor*) and D. 28,2,2 (*Lucius*); C. 6,25,1 (*Si quis filium*) in the principal part; C. 5,55,1 (*Qui se patris*); according to the doctrine in D. 28,5,1 (*Si quis filio exheredato*) in the principal part; because the extinction of the grandfather leaves nothing remaining in nature. He who did not have the beginning of birth while the grandfather was alive—which birth begins in conception—does not succeed to the grandfather by the successor head in the case of our question. The sons of the said Bartholomew cannot come by the successor order, which is taken from the prior person extinguished or removed, nor succeed to the grandfather, in whose life they were not conceived; and therefore they were not in the grandfather’s line at the time of the grandfather’s death; because a line is a certain quantity having a beginning and an end. But that which is nothing is not said to be a part of a line. It does not avail to be a quantity for the succession of an intestate.

It remains to consider the third, namely the transmissive edict: for the seeking of inheritances would not be restricted by reason, unless the laws of transmission, rights, and benefits had been found. And there is a twofold reason: first, because the soul, or mind, in which the substance of division consists, is not transmitted, or dies with the deceased, as in D. 19,2,4 (*Loca*); second, because by transmission it is necessary that the second heir be deemed to make the transmitting heir, and he feigns this in a subject already extinguished, C. 6,30,1 (*Fina*). And on these reasons is founded the rule which says that an inheritance not accepted is not transmitted, C. 6,52,1 (*Novissimo*). But the aforementioned rule fails in the case of an heir to whom the inheritance has been acquired by operation of law, as in the case of his own heir, D. 49,16,1 (*Ex militari*) § 1, with the following law, and in D. 49,15,1 (*Apud hostes*) with its material; for in the same way that inheritance is transmitted as a legacy, and it is acquired by operation of law according to the common opinion of the doctors, although the gloss says otherwise in D. 28,5,1 (*Si infanti*) and in many other places. For even in his own case the mind of mixing is required, D. 28,5,1 (*Cum bonis*). And this will is a certain power of his own soul, which no one can transmit; but jurists should not care about this natural subtlety; because excessive subtlety is not to be admitted by judges. Let us therefore be content that the law so provides, because it is good and equitable to me.

It also fails in other cases briefly noted by the gloss in D. 28,5,1 (*Ventre*), calculated there at length by Bartolus. But these exceptions do not apply here. For it must be known that sometimes an inheritance is not granted in any way, and then it is impossible for it to be transmitted. For it is absurd to transmit before having, and to transmit before being recognized by law. Hence this lady Bartholomew, who was recognized by municipal law, or rather, what is stronger, was prohibited from succeeding to a male who excluded her at all times, could not transmit what she did not have, because the consequence of transmission cannot exist without its antecedent. Therefore she did not transmit, because she had nothing transmissible. John, however, transmitted, and freely; and that transmission was made in a perpetual and inseparable thing, the lady Bartholomew being dead; for if she had made a part, the dead do not make a part, D. 28,5,1 (*Quo loco*) § 1. And if it be said very subtly that the daughter was suspended at the time from the act of accepting, but not from the habit of her existence as heir, and therefore she transmits, it is answered that that habit was either radically removed by the statute in the meantime, or was mortified and useless.

Observe what is the intention of the statute, when it excludes the female as long as a male survives. Certainly by "female" it signifies the rights of the female, which are two: namely, the right of succeeding and the right of transmitting; therefore the natural exclusion of the female excludes her in the meantime, even as to the right of transmitting. And thus she does not transmit; which is noted by Dynus in D. 38,1,1 (*Gallus*) in the final part of the great distinction. Moreover, as regards preventing transmission, a suspensive delay operates the same as a perpetual obstacle, D. 28,5,1 (*Si quis in gravi*) § 1, with the following law. Moreover, transmissions are either of acts or of powers, i.e., either of a right acquired in act, or of that which can be sought without any obstacle. But neither is present in this Bartholomew; and therefore it is impossible for her to have transmitted according to the strict reason of civil law. And of this strict and written law, as I said, it is noted in C. 6,61,1 (*Lib. prae*) § 3, where I examined this point, although not as fully as now; because only the sons of Bartholomew enter the maternal degree, and the mother was impeded by injury, i.e., by excessive favor of males, and not precisely excluded perpetually; for excessive favor of one generates hatred of the other, as in D. 50,17,1 (*Maximum vitium*). And because the statute, if it had considered this case, would likely have provided for the grandchildren and the daughter, and it would not have introduced a preference in equal nature and certainly female sex, it would be fitting that the arbiter, if it were to be compromised, so that they might decide on law and fact, and on truth and the equity of their own head, would somewhat remedy this disease; at least by supplying up to the legitime due by natural law to their mother. Nor do I believe that they would be reprehensible on this account, even in the way of conscience. For this purpose, it serves well in its own reason, D. 50,17,1 (*Paulo Calimaco*) § 1 (*Pompeo Euripide*). It can also be persuaded that the transmission of the legitime is easier, just as to become an heir, according to the note in D. 28,5,1 (*Pap.*) § 4, with the following. However, that which I said about the compromise, which is made in Perugia, consists in fact, not in law, according to the form of the statute, and therefore I do not found my argument on this.

In another point concerning statutes, I say that in different countries different statutes are to be observed, according to the matter, D. 1,4,1 (*Cunctos populos*), where it is placed. Otherwise I have also said fully elsewhere that if succession is immediately granted by the municipal law itself, because different statutes conferring succession are joined in place of different testaments, since everyone imposes law upon his own patrimony. But if someone had died having made a will, since the will of one man is unique and indivisible, it extends its force everywhere, assuming a valid principle, as I said there after other doctors.

From these things it appears that where the statute does not prevail, the daughter, i.e., the said Bartholomew, would have transmitted her right, as in C. 6,25,1 (*Sancimus*) § 1. But here it prevails in all places, and the cessation of the excluding cause does not cause the effect to revive, when it does not find a person to whom it can provide.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. In the name of the Lord, Amen. The municipal law provides that, due to a pronouncement or mandate of the judge made to the debtor regarding payment, if a party does not appear, the judge may from that time proceed to the granting of the tenement from the debtor's goods, provided that the party was summoned to come before the judge to pay, etc. It is therefore asked whether this constitutes a mandate, such that if the party did not appear and was declared in contempt, the judge may proceed to the granting of the tenement.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

A mandate shall be said to have been made, whether it is directed to a person present or to an absent person through a messenger or by letter. For this mandate is interlocutory, as is noted in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, in the law *Si debitor*; and in the Code, *De bonis quae liberis*, in the final law, section *Necessitatis*, in the great gloss. An interlocutory order may be directed through a messenger or by letter, although the contrary is true regarding a definitive judgment, as is noted in the Digest, *De officio proconsulis et legati*, in the law *Nec quicquam*, section *Nisi decretum*. Nor is it always true that it is interlocutory, but sometimes, as is noted in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, in the law *Vivam*; and sometimes it has the effect noted in the Digest, *De novo operis nuntiando*, in the law *De pupillo*, section *Meminisse*. Therefore, there is no doubt whether a mandate has been made, but there is doubt whether it is valid. Here it must be considered whether the person to whom it is made was a debtor by contract, or quasi by delict, or quasi by sentence, as in the law *Nam postea*, section final, *De iureiurando*. For those who are bound by a real action are not properly called debtors, as in the Institutes, *De actionibus*, section 1. It must also be considered whether this mandate was made following a confession or a sentence, or not. For a mandate pertaining to the expeditious solution of a matter by way of an interlocutory order cannot be made to an absent person, as in the Code, *Communi vel epistolariter*, in the final law, where the debt is liquid in one of three ways, namely, either by confession, or by oath, or by sentence. Then it can be made, because it is an executory mandate. And of such a mandate the statute must be understood, that is, what is a matter of law, as in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, law 4, section *Condemnatum*. And of this speaks the Digest, *De re iudicata*, in the law *Debitoribus*; argument from the Code, *De compensatione*, Authentico *Hoc autem*; Digest, *Quibus ex causis in possessionem*, in the law *Ea*. If, therefore, it is liquidated by the aforementioned modes, the mandate is valid, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, in the law *Ait praetor*, section *Praemittitur*. Otherwise, if it is not prohibited, the mandate is not valid, as is noted by Innocentius in the chapter *Solet*, at the end, *De sententia excommunicationis*. It is not doubtful that a contumacious person in paying and in compromising suffers a writ of sequestration, because this is one of the remedies of the praetor against contumacy, as in the Digest, *De in ius vocando*, in the law *Satis*; and as is noted in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, in the law *Non potest dolo carere*; Code, *De iudiciis*, in the law *Properam*, section *Si autem reus*, with its companions. To what I said, that this admonition is interlocutory, contributes what is noted in the Authenticum *De hereditate et falcidia*, section *Si quis autem non implens*. Elsewhere, however, presence is required, as in chapter 2, *De confessione*, Book 6. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the bishop ought to have canonical visitation over the fraternities of disciplines, or similar ones; and whether such places are subject to the bishop; and whether such legacies are said to be for pious causes.
body: The facts of the case

† Regarding the matter on which counsel is sought, it is as follows: Rale, son of Vagoli of Assisi, and the Prior of Saint Ruffin made their last will and testament; in which, among other things, they instituted, made, and willed their sons Francis and Angel to be their universal heirs in all their movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions. They ordered and commanded that if any of their said sons should die without a legitimate son or sons, as aforesaid, all his goods should devolve to the Prior and the Fraternity of Disciplinarians of Saint Vitalis of Costa of Saint Savino of the community of Assisi, who are now or shall be for the time being of the same fraternity; they left and bequeathed the said goods to them upon the occurrence of the aforementioned case. The aforementioned Francis and Angel died without sons, and the case of the aforementioned substitution occurred. A dispute arises between the Lord Diocesan Bishop and the said Prior and Subprior concerning the canonical fourth portion. It is said on behalf of the said Lord Bishop that from the said goods, concerning which the canonical portion is claimed, the canonical portion is due; and the said Prior and Subprior say that the fourth is not due from the said goods, nor is the canonical fourth due. On these points, having seen the aforesaid, it is requested that counsel be declared: whether the canonical fourth portion is due to the said Lord Bishop from the said goods, or not.

By reason of the aggregation of profits, this fraternity is not subject to the bishop, because it receives no spiritual rights from him. And the bishop did not institute their prior there, nor did he depose him. Since it is therefore not an ecclesiastical college, the fourth is not due to the bishop. To this effect it is noted in c. Per literas, de rescriptis, in the Clementines; de donationibus, c. Inter dilectos; by Innocentius, de sepultura, c. 2; by Bartholus, quaestio 4. It is not of episcopal right. But there the bishop does not have episcopal rights, since he exercises none there, as is noted by Archidiaconus, de consecratione, distinction 1, c. Nemo; by Federicus of Siena in his work, consilium 125, which begins: "Factum tale est. Quaedam domus, etc." And this legacy, although made out of a certain devotion, is nevertheless not for pious causes, ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Omnibus. And thus, neither by reason of the persons nor by reason of the cause, ought the bishop to have the fourth, although Carolus de Tuderto said the contrary, and wrongly, and it is noted by Federicus of Siena in his said work, consilium 145, which begins: "Cum aliqui boni viri." Nor does it avail what is made by mentioning the church of Saint Vitalis, because the prior of the fraternity does not govern that church, since he is a layman. And thus it is not a legacy to the rector of the church. And so I say and counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a second emphyteusis is valid during the existence of the first.
2. If the prelate refuses to accept the cession, whether it suffices to offer and deposit it upon the altar.
body: A certain Brother Crescentius, member of the church of Saint Michael of Can., and abbot of Saint Sani, gave and granted to a certain Vangolus of Camerio, for himself and his male and female heirs up to the third generation, by title of renewal in emphyteusis, a certain house adjacent to his own. This Vangolus possessed the said house for many and many years, beyond the space of 40 years. Finally, after the death of the said Brother Crescentius and Vangolus, with sons existing: a certain Brother Jacob, prior and successor of the said Lord Crescentius, by the same right and title, ceded and granted the said house to a certain Nutius Lolli of the said city, up to the third male and female generation of the said Nutius. However, the heir of Lord Vangolus protested many times and years to the said Brother Jacob that the census of the said house ought to be received into his hands; and thus he protested to other successors each year. Since they refused to receive it, the said heir placed the said census upon the altar of the said church, in the presence of a notary and witnesses, and also requesting the same that they draw up a public instrument concerning the aforementioned protests. Now the said Brother Jacob is dead; the heir of the said Vangolus is dead; and the said Nutius, to whom the said house was secondarily granted, is dead, from whom there is a nephew, namely the son of the son of the said Nutius, and heir. It is asked: whether the prior, who is now in office, can grant the said house to another; or whether the said nephew of the said Nutius can legally possess the said house, or not. Whether, if the rector of the church refuses to receive the census, it suffices for the emphyteuta to offer and deposit it.

† Here it must be considered that the first emphyteuticary held the useful dominion, which passed to the son. D. si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticus, l. 1; D. de superficie, l. 1, § quod ait. While this [useful dominion] endured, the second cession of the emphyteusis made to another did not hold against the prejudice of the Church, but it did hold against his own [prejudice]. For the administration of the rector of the Church does not extend to the goods which belong to the Church; yet the useful dominion did not exist at the time of the second emphyteusis, and therefore the second concession was null while the first was in force. D. de actionibus emptoris, l. si ea res; D. de publiciano, l. sive autem, § si duobus; C. de rei venditione, l. quod; and C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. si ante. For a useful right ceded to one cannot be ceded to another while the first cession endures. D. de legibus, l. non quocumque, § qui Gayus. From these it appears that if the said Serlac, heir of Vangoli, died first, the emphyteusis freely reverted to the Church, and therefore the new rector of the Church may grant the emphyteusis to whom he wishes. And this is expressly stated in Decretals, Collatio 10, Qui successores teneantur, cap. 1, illud constat.
† that the heir of Vangoli, who had offered and deposited each year, did not fall into emphyteusis, but his death extinguished it with him. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An unjust possessor, if dispossessed, ought to be restored.
2. A judge proceeding irregularly does not make one a true possessor.
3. Where there is no marriage, there is no dowry.
4. No judgment can be rendered for a debt due at a future date or subject to a condition.
5. A betrothed man, who is not yet a husband, if he bears the burdens, whether he can claim the dowry.
body: In the case of the medical doctor, Master Vernatiti, who brought a possessory action to recover possession, which he claimed he had earned by judicial decree:

It is to be noted for clarity that not only one who possesses most justly, but also one who possesses most unjustly, if he has been in fact dispossessed, ought to be restored to possession. And in this case the robber has an action: as in C. ad l. Iuliam de vi, l. si quis ad se fundum; and fully noted in ff. de iure, l. si vi; de furtis, l. itaque fullo; Dy. in c. qui ad agendum. Secondly, it is to be known that although the emperor, or any temporal or spiritual lord, had granted someone license, it is not valid: as in C. unde vi, l. meminerint; and noted in the same title, l. si quis in tantam; and C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. fi. Thirdly, however, it is to be known that

† that the authority of a judge who does not proceed properly does not constitute him the true possessor. D. 50.17.128 (Si cum nulla); D. 43.17.1 (Iuste); D. 43.16.1.1 § Hec verba. And therefore, in this case, the one who continues his possession is not said to have dispossessed the person admitted to tenure. D. 43.16.1.1 § Si quis ideo. For, in order that one may acquire possession through a judge, it is required that the decree of the judge be valid; and if it is not valid, and he has been sent in de facto to hold, he does not seem to possess, because he does not seem to have the intent to possess, except as one sent in. And thus he subordinates his will to reason. And a robber would possess more strongly than this person sent in. Fourthly, it is also to be known,

† For where there is no marriage, there is no dowry, nor an action for the dowry. D. de iure dotium, l. stipulationem; and l. tali; and l. promittendo. The dowry has an implied condition that the marriage shall follow.
† Fifth, it must be known that no judgment can be rendered for a debt payable at a future date or subject to a condition. D. 44.7.1 (Fulcinius), § si in diem.

Sixthly, and lastly, it must be known that after betrothals have been contracted, although the marriage is not perfected due to the impediment of defective age, nevertheless, if the husband or father-in-law bears the burdens of this marriage, this quasi-dowry may be claimed, if this was done so that it could be claimed beforehand, as noted in ff. de cond. et dem. l. Titio; §. Titio genero, ff. sol. mat. l. si ante. And since this is so in our case: because the said doctor, as father-in-law, supported the burdens of the marriage, as appears from the records, it seems that he supported and continues to support the burdens both by virtue of the award and by equity, and that he could have acted justly and deserved the judge’s decree, unless the dowry had been promised under duress, as in l. si mulier, §. si dos, quod met. causa; for then the judge’s decree granting possession would be void, because it was issued on the strength of a void and inane obligation. de fideicom. liber. l. cum vero subuentum; ff. ad Carbonia. l. 3, §. puberi; and note per Cy. C. de resti. mili. l. ignorare. But certainly, even if it was permitted under duress, which is not to be presumed in doubt: nevertheless, if it was later agreed upon, what was done becomes valid. ff. de condi. ob tur. causam. l. si ob turpem; C. quod me. causa. l. 2; extra. e. c.1. I, because I have not seen the records of both parties, cannot conclude anything else, except that if the said Master Venantius, in the names under which he acts, was lawfully made possessor, then, as one dispossessed, he is to be restored and reinstated in possession, as in ff. ne vis fiat ei. l. si quis; missum, ff. de acqui. pos. l. qui vniuersas, §. Item cum prętor. It pertains to the office of the judge to defend one placed in possession. ff. de iurei. l. 3, §. proderit, there: “lest he suffer violence in possession.” This text greatly favors the said Reverend Master, whose morals and life I have always known to be excellent. And in this case, notwithstanding the contrary rescript of the lord, he is to be reintegrated into possession. d. l. meminerit. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the wounded person dies after 20 days, and the assailant proves through a physician that the wound was not mortal, and that he was first assaulted, whether he is to be beheaded.
2. If the wounded person dies, whether it is presumed that the wound was mortal from the beginning, and when it is said to be mortal, and no. 5.
3. A non-mortal wound becomes mortal if it is not treated.
4. Whether, and when, in matters of expertise or judgment of art, the statement of one expert in that art is to be relied upon.
5. When the outcome is to be considered, and when the outcome falls into the cause.
body: It is proposed that Titus struck Seius with a single blow to the arm. The assailant was captured by the officials of the Podestà and detained, because the court doubted whether the wound was mortal. Nevertheless, physicians were not sent to examine the nature of the wound according to the form of the statute. Afterward, the said wounded man lived for nearly twenty days and finally died. It is said that the wounded man remained without a physician and without care for about sixteen days, and finally submitted himself to be treated by a physician. This physician testifies that the wound was not in itself mortal, but due to the negligence of the wounded man, it became putrid and induced a fever, which finally resulted in death. Another witness states that the assailant was first attacked by the wounded man, and thus, in his own defense, and in accordance with the form of the statute, he acted lawfully and without penalty. The court of the Podestà wishes to behead this Titus, because according to the form of the statute, the penalty for homicide is precisely the loss of the head. On the other hand, he claims that because he acted in defense, he should be absolved, or at least punished pecuniarily for a simple wound, according to other statutes speaking of wounds. The question is: what is the law?

† And it appears that he ought to be beheaded, because from the quality of the instrument a great and mortal wound is presumed, as in Extra, De homicidio, c. Significasti. From the quality of the instrument also the intent to kill is presumed. D. Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis, l. 1, § Sed si claua; C. Eodem, l. Si is, qui cum telo.

† From the subsequent death, it appears to be established that the wound inflicted by the principal was of such a nature as is declared by its effect. Arguing from the effect, as in the proemium; ff. §. penult., for the outcome reveals the acts. ff. de adul.; l. si quid a deo. For he is said to have been killed by legal interpretation when he was struck. ad l. Aquil.; l. huic scripturae. ff. de confes.; l. si is, qui stichum. From three things joined together, namely, from intent, the quality of the instrument, and the effect of the act, this person ought to be judged a murderer, because he should expect what he has done. C. de epis. au. l. 3. To the contrary is the truth itself, which is proven by general experience, by the rules of the art of medicine, which the sacred laws do not disdain to imitate in such indications. ff. de sta. homi.; l. septimo mense; in Auth. de resti. et ea, quae parit. §. unum, coll. 4; by a living witness, skilled in the art; and from the quality of the part of the body struck, since it was the arm. Regarding the first point, it must be known that experience produced art. Multa. Indeed, many experiments lead to the knowledge of truth. extra de elec.; cupientes; and c. qua sit. Hence the Emperor says, from the experience of things we find. in Auth. de appel. et intra quae tempora, in prin.

But it is established by experience that a wound which is not mortal becomes mortal if it is not treated, as stated in Distinction 29, chapter *Necesse*, and noted in the Digest, title *De locis*, law *Maritus*. The same is affirmed by the canons of medicine, namely that life is shortened if the disease is not cured, as in the chapter *Vita brevis*. And therefore the text says that antidotes ought to be prepared for diseases, as in the Authenticum *Haec constitutio innovat*, in the beginning, and in the Decretals, title *De iuramento calumniae*, chapter *Ceterum*. And therefore the Decree states that the experience of diseases compels us to discover many medicines, Dyonysius.

† that it be established by one expert physician, who expressly testifies to this effect. Similarly, it is proven that the wound was not mortal. And if it is said that, where testimony is given regarding the expertise of an art, as in the case of censuses, one witness is not sufficient, but several are required, as in the Authentica *De non alienando*, § *Ut neque*, in the word *architectus*; and in the law *Semel*, *De re militari*, Book 12, in the word *medicis*; Digest, *De ventre in suspicionem*, law 1, § 1, in the words *omnes, vel duae*; and Code, *De secundis nuptiis*, law *Hac edictali*, § *Mobilium*, in the word *arbitros*: I answer that this is true when several were appointed to judge such an act of expertise, for then it must be proven by several, because it can be proven by several. But where only one was appointed, and the judgment of another cannot be obtained, if that one is of known good faith, i.e., proven in his art, the judge may conform himself to the statement of that one, by argument from Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law 1, at the end. Indeed, certainly in our case the statute expressly provides that, unless physicians are appointed in the manner prescribed, it cannot be judged that the wound is mortal. And the words of the statute are clear. Moreover, the injured party should not deprive his adversary of the opportunity to prove [the matter] by appointing no physician, or only one. And therefore the wounded person is not bound to prove the impossible: because the means of defense could not be taken away from him, as in Code, *De postulando*, law *Prouidendum*, at the end. But so that we may proceed on the firmest footing, we weigh the statute concerning the manner. For first, the statute commands the judge not to proceed unless the judgment of physicians has preceded. Second, it is established that, without the preceding report, punishment cannot be inflicted, except in the case of the wounded person. Third, it sets forth who are to be sent and for what purpose. Fourth, it provides what is to be done if those sent were not admitted; nevertheless, punishment may be inflicted. Fifth, it treats of the salary of the physicians. Sixth, and lastly, a procedure carried out otherwise is annulled; the parts are clear in the letter of the statute. If, therefore, we consider the given order, without which a personal penalty cannot be imposed; if we consider the given witnesses, [who are] declarative. For the witnesses are the physicians put in the bag, who are appointed by the statute: just as in the customs of fiefs, peers of the court are appointed. So also it is. Code, *De advocatis diuersorum iudiciorum*, law *Nemini*, § *Iurisperitos*: without some, a penalty cannot be imposed. If we consider the conclusion of the statute, which concludes to presuming the simplicity of the wound, as if choosing leniency in doubt: undoubtedly, one must not proceed to corporal severity, but a more clement path must be followed. For it is holier and safer to condemn less than to change the limits by being severe. Digest, *De poenis*, and law *Interpretatione*. Especially where the life of a man is at stake. Code, *De appellationibus*, law *Additos*, where proofs clearer than light are required, which is called the light of truth. Digest, *De testibus*, law *Ob carmen*, § *Finis*; Code, *De probationibus*, law *Sciant cuncti*. Wherefore, there is no doubt at all that the penalty of the sword does not apply here. Also from the quality of the place, because the blow was made on the arm, a place that receives very great wounds, and yet one does not die from this: and it is a rare occurrence that one dies, if the sick person is well cared for, and from the great distance of time. For when the person struck lives for many days, not every wound is presumed mortal, as is noted in Code, *De emptione seruorum*, law 1. It must therefore be considered,

† That certain wounds do not require the advice of physicians, such as capital wounds, e.g., of the brain, or others from which one dies immediately. And these are punished with the penalty attached to death. Nor does the statute have application, because time does not permit deliberation for counsel. There are certain wounds that involve a prolongation of life, and these must be considered. D. ad l. Aquil. l. Item Mella, § Si plures; D. de trit. l. In hac. And I said, and I say, that where the testimony of one physician concurs with the length of life over some notable period in the court of the sick person, or elsewhere, which finds the said physician, as is the case here, without doubt the testimony of one physician is to be believed for the purpose of absolving. To this effect it is noted that Bartolus, D. de sic. l. Si in rixa, in fine, persuades that presumptions, together with one witness to the truth, conclude the judge, as noted in the Rosario, 6 q. 1, c. Ques pastorem. Nor do the allegations to the contrary, if there was intent, stand in the way; because in statutory penalties the blow is considered more than the intent. D. l. Is qui cum telo, through Cynus. Thus also holds Speculum and all. Moreover, the quality of the instrument, because this conjecture has been refuted and overthrown by many and other conjectures. For conjecture overthrows conjecture. D. de in integr. rest. l. Divus; D. de rit. nup. l. Non solum, cum si.

† Moreover, the outcome of the matter does not stand in the way, because there is an outcome that is beneficial to safety, and from this one draws an argument from the outcome. D. de poenis, l. aut facta, §. euentus. There is also an outcome that is harmful, and then either it proceeds from proximate and immediate causes, in which case the outcome is considered with respect to those causes. But if they are not immediate causes, but rather some occasion, then the outcome is not attributed to that remote principle, but to the more proximate causes, as in l. si mulier, D. rerum amotarum, and l. huic scripturae, D. ad legem Aquiliam. And therefore the argument from the outcome concludes only with immediate causes. Therefore, the acts should be called not from the outcome, but from the causes, since we have presumptions regarding the causes through the proof of one witness that he acted in defense, which I do not weigh, because it is insufficient. I therefore conclude that the one who inflicted the wound is to be punished, not for homicide, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, in a fief granted to someone for himself and his male and female heirs descending from him, the grandson through a daughter is preferred with respect to succession over the granddaughters through a son.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. Lord Jordan was invested with a certain fief by the person having the right of investiture in this form, namely, the said investor invested him for himself and his male and female heirs descending from him: so that if males fail, females shall succeed, etc. Here Jordan died, leaving three male sons, namely, Lord Bonfrancesco, Marco, and Vitaliano. It happened that Vitaliano died without any recognition being made, because it was not necessary. Likewise, Lord Bonfrancesco passed away in the course of time, also without any recognition being made. However, he left one male son named Jordan. Also one daughter named Joan. The said Jordan, together with his uncle Marco, recognized the said fief according to the terms before the court, because the time had come. It happens that the said Jordan dies: so that the fief remained entirely with his uncle Marco, since no other male from the male line survived. Afterwards, the said Joan was given in marriage to a husband, from whom she had a male son who is presently alive.
