Afterwards, it also happened that the said Marco, one of the three brothers in whom the entire fief was consolidated, died, leaving no male, but only two daughters, who are married, and with a male son surviving from the said Joan. It is doubted to whom the said fief ought to pertain, considering the form of the investiture, whether to the said daughters or to the said male son of the said Joan. In this case, this doubt arises, because it is certain that when the vassal to whom the fief came dies, the succession to the fief first goes to the sons. And if it comes to the nearest daughters, it goes to the daughters before going to other more remote ones, as in 10, col. de success. seu. c. 1, in principle, and § filia. And by this it seems that this fief, about which inquiry is made, upon the death of the said Jordan, came entirely to Marco, who died with two daughters surviving, who were nearer to that vassal. Hence, since this fief was feminine, because in the first investiture it was provided that if males failed, females should succeed, and no male survives the said Marco, it appears that the aforementioned daughters, as being nearer, should succeed in the said fief of the said Marco; but it should not come to the aforementioned son of Joan, daughter of Bonfrancesco, brother of the said Marco, for which supports the matter of degrees of succession in fiefs, chapter 1, verse mortuo. In the name of Christ, Amen.

† In law, I state that, from the time of the death of the said Mark, who was one of the sons of the Lord, the first investee, there survives a male son of Joan, the niece, from the sons of the said Lord, first investee, namely from Bonfrancesco, son of the first investee; whereas there survived to the said Mark daughters, the said male descendant of Joan, by reason of the feudal convention, ought to succeed to the entire fief and be preferred to the aforementioned daughters of Mark. And this is clear, because in feudal succession, proximity is not considered with respect to the person from whom the fief is vacant, but with respect to the proximity, or pact, or convention of the person from whom the fief began, as is gathered from Title 10, On Feudal Succession, § 1, there: “if he dies without a male heir, etc.” But, having regard to the convention and pact attached to the fief, by which it was agreed that, in default of males, females shall succeed, it is clear that the son of John, although he is descended through a female, is nevertheless among the descendants of the first investee. Therefore, although he is not more closely related to Mark, from whom the fief is vacant, but the daughters are more closely related to him, nevertheless, having regard to the pact of the investiture, the said male ought to be preferred to those daughters in this matter. And this is supported by the fact that feudal succession is rather made by the contract of investiture, or by pact, than by succession, as in Title 10, Whether an agnate or son of the deceased, Chapter 1. And thus, one ought not to consider who succeeds Mark, from whom the fief devolves; for it would be the daughters; but one ought to consider the pact made with the first investee, by which it is provided that, as long as any male survives, females shall not succeed. And that this opinion is true, namely that the male descendant of the said Joan is to be preferred in the succession to the entire fief, is proved by the fact that it is established that, where a fief from the beginning of the investiture was granted to oneself and to male and female heirs, or to oneself and to one’s male heirs, and, in default of these, to females, that whenever a fief, in default of males, has once come to females, and the condition of female succession has once existed, if afterwards those to whom the fief subsequently came die, one leaving a son, the other leaving a daughter or daughters, they do not succeed to the fief, even in the share of the father of the deceased, although they are more closely related to the deceased; but the male who survives from the other co-vassal succeeds, as in Title 10, On him who [holds] for himself and his male heirs, etc., Chapter 1. Therefore, much more ought the male, though more remote from the deceased than the daughters, to succeed, as if such a fief never came to females in any case, nor did the condition of female succession ever exist in the fief, which is the case in our matter: for, as is clear from the foregoing, although the fief was granted first to males, and, in default of these, to females, nevertheless, in no case did the fief become feminine; rather, it always remained masculine until the death of the last of the brothers, who died. Hence, if a fief granted for males and females had become feminine while a male existed, it could not, by remitting its nature, pass from succession to the more closely related females in the whole or in part to the deceased from whom the fief is vacant; rather, they are excluded by the surviving male, although he is more remote from the deceased. Therefore, much more in our case will it pass to the surviving male of Joan, although that male is more remote from Mark, from whom it is vacant, since in no case did it become feminine, nor did the condition of female succession ever exist. For this consequence, it is held that a thing more easily returns to a nature it has assumed than assumes a new one: as in Digest, On Pacts, Law 1, § Pactum, words “which in hope,” with similar authorities. For this, it is held that a thing more easily continues to be what it is than becomes something new: as in Law 1, words “but if one,” Digest, On Verbal Obligations, with similar authorities. Also for this, the gloss in the said Chapter 1 asks whether, in such a fief as is in our case and that chapter, a more remote male excludes a more closely related female to the one who first received the investiture. And it is answered that yes, which Jacobus de Belvisi understands to be true when the fief had not yet been acquired by the more closely related female, for example, the aunt, while the full brother and the aunt survived. This is directly applicable to our case. For in our case, at the time of the death of the said Mark, the fief had not yet been acquired by the daughters of Mark; therefore, it will pass to the male descendant of the aforementioned Joan, and by the foregoing, the question is evidently determined. Now, the contrary objection does not hold, because it has been removed by the premises. For here the question is not about the succession of Mark, from whom the fief is vacant, but about the succession of the first investee, and about succession by pact and convention of the fief, according to which any male, although more remote, is preferred to any female, however closely related, because it prevents the condition of female succession from existing. For this, it is held that whenever there is priority in sex or line, the more remote line or sex is preferred to any more closely related person of the subsequent line or sex; therefore, more remote descendants, namely great-grandchildren, who are in the third degree, are preferred to the father, who is more closely related in degree, because he is in the first degree, and the grandson in the third degree of ascendants, and the father and great-grandson in the third degree of descendants make a person. To this effect are the notes in Law “Nam et si parentibus,” Digest, On Undue Wills, and Institutes, On Intestate Succession, § 1, with similar authorities; and Digest, On Free Persons, On Legacies, On Cognates, and On the Edict Concerning Succession, Law 1, with similar authorities. And by this, the contrary arguments are removed. Thus advised the said Philip de Casatis de Regio, and beyond him, Document 16. And I subscribed, Gaspar de Caldarinis.

To the same effect. Regarding this question, which is the subject of inquiry, the case is, in my judgment, in Chapter 1, On brothers newly invested with a benefit, in Title 10, where it is expressly stated that the act of a new successor cannot alter the nature of an ancient fief. And this should be weighed, because it is the question for which a decision is sought. For although Francis de Caldeno renounced the fief, he did not thereby alter the nature of the fief, as is clear from the aforementioned text in the word “not paternal,” and others cited at length on this point. Let the prudence of the counselor supply the rest. And to the foregoing, it is pertinent that which is found in Title 10, On two brothers, from Chapter Invested, Chapter 1; and if there is a dispute about the fief between the lord and the agnate vassal, Chapter Natural; and in Chapter 1, Whether an agnate or son, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How those words, "let justice be done," are to be understood, namely, by whom it ought to be done.
1. That the parties are bound to compromise, if it is not expressly stated in whom and in what place, how this ought to be understood.
body: In the city of Venice, at the Office of Petitions, the Magnificent Lord Francesco Junior is acting against Milan of Malabambris, who has his domicile in Venice and in Lombardy, a familiar, subject, and follower of the Illustrious Prince and our most excellent Lord, in the peace treaty. On behalf of the said Lord, it is asked by chapters that the said lawsuit be removed from the jurisdiction of the Venetians and transferred to Genoa. The arbitrators pronounce in the first sentence, namely, that justice be done to Milan regarding the question raised against him by the said Lord Francesco in Venice. Later, in the second sentence, adding and correcting, they pronounced thus, namely: Also in that part of the article where it is said, and that justice be done to Milan regarding the question raised against him in Venice by the said Lord Francesco: and adding, we sentence and pronounce that regarding the said questions of Milan, each procurator is bound to choose common friends, to submit himself to their judgment and cognition, and to provide surety for standing by the law and for satisfying the judgment.

And if the aforementioned Milan is not satisfied with this, let him stand, and let the tenor of the aforementioned article be observed, which provides that justice be done to him. The Magnificent [Lord] daily responds to those who supplicate, "Let justice be done," and if he does not say by whom, it is understood that he refers the matter to the judge of the case. D. de iudiciis, l. ubi coeptum; D. de iudiciis omnibus, l. si; for we call even the law itself a judge. D. de iustitia et iure, l. si.

† If, however, he commands them to compromise, and does not specify where the compromise ought to be made in a fair and common place, by the argument of the last law, C. de fructibus et litis expensis, and de solutionibus, l. cum stichus, or the mandate is void due to uncertainty, ff. de arbitris, l. non distinguimus, §. de officio. But it seems that it should be in the place of the compromise and award, because there the contract was celebrated, ff. de iure, l. haeres absens, and in Auth. qua in provincia, C. ubi de crimine agi oportet, and de actionibus et obligationibus, l. contraxisse. Granted that he is bound to choose in the place, nevertheless, who will reconcile those discordant in choosing arbitrators? I ask about the compeller, who will appoint the third arbitrator. The Duke will not, because he is not one of the arbitrators. And if it is said that he is the lord of the place: therefore he executes the contract in the place, and this is quite pleasing in law: because the promise of the act submitted them to jurisdiction, nevertheless the third arbitrator ought to be a common friend, and of the confidence of the parties. However, it makes me doubtful, because it says, any procurator. Therefore, if there were no procurator, no one would be bound to choose. And if the procurator is appointed for a certain place, he cannot choose elsewhere: because he does not have a mandate. And therefore this chapter seems captious and equivocal. And it depends on the form of the mandate of the procurators. For that statement, that any procurator, is understood of present procurators, not future ones, as l. item eorum, §. 1, quod cuiusque, un. no. everywhere they ought to be compelled to compromise. Wherefore it is concluded, if the procurators had a general mandate to compromise in Genoa, otherwise they cannot compromise outside the place where they are situated, as ff. de verbis obligatis, l. qui Romae, §. Calimachus, and de arbitris, l. si cum dies, §. si arbiter iusserit. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute speaking of payment or satisfaction applies to a cession, and that the term "contract" is not properly understood to mean a donation. No. 4.
2. There is a great difference between saying, "I cede to you every action available to you by reason of the dowry," and saying, "I cede to you every action that I have against such a person."
3. How that clause, "I cede whatever right I have," is to be understood.
4. The term "contract" is not properly understood to mean a donation.
body:
The facts are as follows: After the death of B., the said A. remained a creditor in the inheritance and goods of the late B. for eight hundred pounds for her dowry. The father of the said lady, and the lady herself, with the consent and command of the daughter, confessed before a notary, stipulating and receiving in the name of the heirs of the said late B., that they, the father and the daughter, and each of them, had received and had certain things of value and estimation, by common agreement, of 344 pounds or thereabouts. And such a quantity of money the father and daughter confessed to have had and received as part payment of the dowry of the said lady. And after this, the said lady A. made a donation in this manner: that the said lady A., of her own free will and with certain knowledge, with the consent and decree of the lord consul of justice, by an express pact and solemn stipulation fortified, remitted and remits to C., her father, every action competent to her in any way for demanding the aforesaid dowry; ceding, transferring, and conveying to her said father by title of donation inter vivos, and by any other title by which she can do so more effectively, all and singular rights and actions, etc. Moreover, the said lady A., for the greater strengthening of the aforesaid, saying and protesting first that she is of the age of 18 years, swore on the Holy Gospels, with hands laid upon the scriptures, that all and singular the aforesaid are true, as promised above by her, to have and hold all parties rat and firm; and she swore, as above, that the said instrument of dowry is true and not fictitious or simulated; and that no solution, compensation, or estimation has been made thereof, but that in truth the said heirs of the late B. are true debtors. And the said C., the father, swore that he believes the aforesaid to be true; and they also swore that no money was given, counted, or to be given by virtue of the present donation; and they also swore in all things and in every way, as they are bound to swear according to the form of the statute of the commune of Perugia, etc.

Now E., heir of the said late B., asserts that the said A. committed perjury on account of the aforesaid oath, joined with the said confession of having received the said 344 pounds. And he accused the said A., intending the penalty of the statute concerning cessions to be made, the effect of which statute follows in this form: that a cession of rights by any title shall not otherwise be valid nor bind by the law itself, unless the cedent swears by his own oath that the debt, of which he makes cession, is true in whole or in part, when he cedes it; and that no solution or satisfaction has been made thereof; but that in truth the debtor, against whom he cedes, is a true debtor, etc. Finally, these words are added in the statute itself: and if at any time the contrary is found, or that the instrument, of which cession was made, was simulated or not true, or that the debt was paid or otherwise satisfied for it; and just as the contracting parties can be convicted of perjury, so that he who appears to be perjurious shall be punished in double the amount comprehended in the cession, one half of which shall go to the debtor, and the other half shall go to the commune.

It is also presupposed that the statute provides that a son under power and a person existing under the age of 25 years cannot obligate his goods to anyone in any contract or alienation, unless with the authority of his power, or of his judge, and two of his parents, etc. And that the aforesaid ceases in any contract which is made with the consent of his father or grandfather, etc. It is also presupposed that at the time of the contract this lady A. was under the power of her said father, and under 25 years of age, from which it is believed that the contract was not valid.

† From the aforesaid, it is asked whether the aforementioned lady is to be condemned to the penalty of the said statute, or not. It is alleged against the said lady that she swore that no payment or reduction had been made; yet from the said confession the contrary appears, namely, that part of the said debt has been paid, as above. And although the debt has not been paid in full, nevertheless some payment has been made, and at least on account of the said partial payment the debt was diminished: therefore it was reduced. Cf. *l. qui hominem*, D. de adiectis legibus. And even if the contract were null, nevertheless there was perjury, as noted in *l. si quis legis*, D. de falsis.

To the contrary, it is alleged for the said lady A. that she did not commit perjury, if the words of the aforementioned confession and oath are first examined. And first, considering that the aforementioned statute requires that the contrary be found, namely, that the debt was paid or satisfied. And thus an act of true payment and satisfaction is required, not of fictitious payment. *l. 3, § haec autem verba*, D. de negotiorum gestione. But from the said confession an act of true payment or satisfaction does not arise. *l. 1, § si mutuam*, D. si quid in fraudem patroni; and *l. finalis, in fine*, D. si certum petatur; and noted in many other places. Therefore, the penalty of the said statute ceases.

Moreover, the words of the statute say that the assignment is not valid unless the assignor swears by his own oath that the debt, of which he makes assignment, is true in whole or in part, and that no payment or satisfaction has been made thereof, but that the debtor, against whom the assignment is made, is truly a debtor. And if the contrary is found, or that the instrument, of which assignment was made, is simulated or not true, or that the debt was paid or otherwise satisfied therefor, and thus the contracting parties may justly be convicted of perjury, that he who appears to have committed perjury be punished in double the quantity of the assignment, one half of which shall go to the debtor, and the other half shall go to the common fund.

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that there is a great difference whether the assignment is made in this manner: “I assign to you every action competent to me by reason of the donation,” or in this manner: “I assign to you every action competent to me, which I have against such a person for one hundred, which is owed to me.” For if the quantity is not specified, only that right is deemed to be assigned which is truly owed. But if it is specified, then with regard to what is specified, it is necessary that the assignor prove that he is a creditor in the specific quantity stated, as in D. de haered. vel act. ven. l. si in venditione haered. and it is proved by those things which are read and noted in C. de falsa causa adiecta legata l. si non designata, and D. de leg. 2. l. mevio § a me. Unless the assignor was aware and the assignee was ignorant, and the assignor asserted that more was owed to him than was actually owed; in which case the assignor is liable on account of fraud, not because he assigned, but because he pretended or simulated that he was assigning, as in D. de haered. vend. l. quod si nulla. For he deceived the assignee by simulating that he had the entire right, when he did not have it; and what was truly not included in the assignment made by these words: “whatever right I have.” And therefore it must be weighed that the statute speaks of a simulated instrument, of which an assignment was made, not of the simulation of the assignment itself.

† Furthermore, it must be considered that in this assignment: “I assign whatever right I have,” the right which I do not have is not included, as in *l. si sic*, D. *de legatis* 1, according to Dyther. From this it follows in the question proposed that, although there was perjury in saying that nothing had been diminished, nevertheless that perjury was outside the assignment of rights and is not punished by virtue of the assignment, but on account of the malice committed externally, because he did not inform the assignee of that which he ought to have made certain to him, namely, the truth itself, as in D. *de dolo*, *l. eleganter*, § *non solum*. However, this cannot be said in our case, because the father was aware, and fraud is not imputed to one who is aware, as noted in *l. summa*, D. *de conditione indebiti*.

† Since, therefore, the words of the statute speak of perjury committed concerning the debt, of which cession has been made, and this is not perjury concerning the debt, of which cession has been made, because in the principal excessive word are these words: "all right which I have," which are resolved into a condition by the law *Si quod habeo*, although afterwards follow enunciative words, which refer to the execution, and those are false: because he swore that the instrument is true, and that no solution nor diminution has been made thereof. Nevertheless, to avoid the penalty of the statute, it suffices that the words immediately cease, since the statute disposes of a penalty extra-ordinary and beyond the common law, as in the Digest, *De acquirenda hereditate*, law *Si servum*, section *Non dixit*. From which it appears that, with respect to that from which cession has been made, it is valid in law that which he has, and there is no perjury thereon, although perjury was committed in the denunciatory words, which both the cedent and the cessionary knew to be untrue. And a false demonstration does not augment the principal disposition, where both parties know it to be false, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Si ita stipulatus fuero hanc summam*. Moreover, the statute seems to require a certain form of oath, in order that one may be punished. And therefore, that form being omitted, the statute ceases to apply; nor do those words stand in the way, "and also they swore in all things and by all things, as they are bound to swear according to the form of the statutes"; because in a woman, unless she is informed of the statute, these words do not prejudice her, as noted in the law *Sciendum*, Digest, *De verbis obligatis*. Also, these general words do not augment the special ones, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Stipulatio commodissimum est ita componere*; as in the law *Doli clausula*, Digest, *De peculio*; law *Sanctio legum*, Digest, *De legatis tertio*; law *Haeres meus*, section *Duae statuae*, Digest, *De alimentis legatis*; law *Alimenta*, section *Basilicae*; and law *Stichus nutrix*, Digest, *De verbis significandis*; law *Si non fraudem*, Digest, *De vulgari substitutione*; law *Veniendi*, section *Qui*. Moreover, it must be considered that the statute speaks of the penalty of the contracting parties,

† But by the term "contract" a donation is not properly understood, although it is included under a broad usage of the word; nevertheless, it is perhaps not included in penal statutes, as in D. de verb. sign. l. Labeo § contractum, and C. de praed. curial. l. fin. lib. 10, and this is accustomed to be noted in Auth. sacra publ. C. si advers. vend. However, this reasoning could be challenged by common usage of language. Another reason follows, namely that if the statute requires the authority of the father or of close relatives, and it does not intervene, the statute has no application, nor does its penalty, because the contracting parties have not reached a full act, as in D. quod quis iu. l. 1 § haec autem verba. And certainly the father cannot interpose his authority immediately for his son to contract with him, because there must be a distinction of persons between the father himself, the authority, and the contracting party, as in l. 1 D. de auth. tut. From these and other arguments that could be alleged, it is concluded that the penalty of the said statute does not apply in our case. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one may institute as universal heir his spurious brother, born of a blameworthy union.
2. Whether the children of a second marriage succeed in the mother’s inheritance together with the grandchildren of the son from the first marriage, and if so, whether they succeed per stirpes or per capita; and it concludes that they succeed per stirpes.
body: The case is as follows: Lady Dalia had two husbands. The first was namely Lord Laurentius, and from him were born Gualfredus and Dionysius, and five grandchildren born from the said Dionysius. Also, she had a second husband, namely one Lord John of Lista, from whom were born Bellus and Iafet. All the aforementioned are dead, as will appear below, namely because first the said Laurentius died, to whom Gualfredus and Dionysius succeeded equally. Second, Gualfredus died, to whom Dionysius succeeded, together with Lady Dalia, who is also admitted here to the succession together with the agnates by the form of municipal law. Third, Dionysius died, leaving five sons, who succeeded to him, and Lady Dalia with them. Fourth, Lord John of Lista died, to whom Bellus and Iafet succeeded. Fifth, Bellus died, to whom succeeded Iafet, his brother, and Lady Dalia, his mother. Sixth, Lady Dalia died, to whom succeeded Iafet, her son, and those five grandchildren born from Dionysius. Finally, Iafet died while the said five grandchildren, born and legitimate from the said Dionysius, were still living. And in the testament made by the said Iafet, he instituted as his universal heir a certain Lord William of Lista, the spurious son of the late Lord John and likewise the spurious brother of the said Iafet. Now it is asked, first, concerning the inheritance of Lady Dalia, in which the said Iafet, her son, and the five grandchildren born from the late Dionysius of the first marriage succeed; and whether they succeed per capita or per stirpes. Second, it is asked whether the said Iafet could institute as his universal heir Lord William, who was spurious and born from illicit intercourse, to the prejudice of the cognates or agnates of the legitimate progeny of the said Iafet, etc. On this matter,

† It is asked whether a legitimate brother may usefully institute his spurious brother, born of a condemned intercourse, as sole heir, so that the spurious brother may also acquire the paternal goods through the intermediary person of the legitimate brother who institutes the spurious brother, or not. At first sight, it would seem to be said that he cannot, because that which is prohibited by a direct path ought not to be granted by an indirect one, as in C. de nat. lib. l. 1, in the word “per interpositam personam”; C. quod met. cau. l. si per impressionem; and ff. de usucap. l. Labeo; ff. de bonis lib. l. quaeritur; ff. de auctor. l. si pupillus, §. si per interpositam personam. To the contrary, it seems, because that which I cannot do myself, I accomplish through another, when I am not prohibited on account of my own defect, as in ff. quae res pignori obligari possunt, l. Aristo, and the note in the aforementioned l. Labeo, de usucapione. But the spurious son is not prohibited by his own defect, but by his father’s, as in C. de nat. lib. l. final. Hence, although he cannot acquire from his father, nothing prevents him from being instituted by a stranger. For the legitimate brother is considered a stranger, and so that we do not delay in speech, this question is determined by the very case of the law: ff. de vulg. et praeleg. subst. l. si is, qui; and by the gloss in Auth. qui modis nat. efficiuntur iusti, §. ult., si quidem, in the great gloss, in the words “item a patre,” and in the heading “sed quid si pater.” And therefore, without doubt, the legitimate brother may institute the spurious brother as heir. Nor does it matter that the goods are paternal, for they ceased to be paternal upon the acceptance of the father’s inheritance, having been united with the son’s goods, and the whole has become one patrimony, as in ff. de vulg. et praeleg. subst. l. sed et si plures, §. filio. And to this point it is most aptly noted by Bartolus in l. final., ff. de his, qui ut indigni. And the reason is manifest, because this does not result from the tacit or express judgment of the father, but from the mere judgment of the brother, in which no legal prohibition is found. Nor is it true that he here seeks to act through an intermediary person, because the brother is not the agent of the other brother, but is properly and principally the testator himself. To this it is well supported by ff. de liberis et posth. legatis, l. si is, qui duos; and C. de donat. l. si aviae. From which I firmly conclude that the said testament is valid, unless it were proven that the legitimated son had tacitly pledged faith to the father to institute the spurious son, which is not to be presumed in doubt, as noted in ff. de leg. 1, l. Lucius, §. in testamento; and ff. de probat. l. cum tacitum; and l. qui testamentum. And the same applies to maternal goods, and to those of all ascendants, namely, those which had passed to the said testating brother.

† It is further asked whether, if there is one son from the first marriage and five grandchildren from the second, and the father having predeceased, the succession is to be divided per capita or per stirpes? And it must be said that it is divided per stirpes; hence the son has half of the mother’s goods, and the other five grandchildren have half of the grandmother’s goods, because they enter into the paternal place and are considered as one, as in the Institution on inheritances left by intestates, §. cum filius, and in the Authentica on intestate heirs, §. si quis igitur descendentium; nor does this transition to second marriages make any difference here, as in the Authentica on marriages, §. illud quoque, at the end of the title, column 4. And there is no doubt about this. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, in a fief granted simply to two brothers, one succeeds to the other, or whether the greater portion reverts to the granting bishop upon the death of one of them.
2. Whether a vassal of the church who kills a priest or utters insulting words against the bishop is deprived, or ought to be deprived, of his fief.
body: The following matter is submitted: The late Bishop Ugolino of Parma granted in fief, by way of honorific concession, to the absent Lord Antonio, son of the late Ilario of Arcilli, and to a certain procurator receiving on his behalf, and to Ilario, brother of the said Lord Antonio (son of the late Bogatto), who was present and received in the names of both, one piece of land. Subsequently, Lord Beltramo, also Bishop of Parma and successor of the said Bishop Ugolino, granted in fief to the said Lord Antonio, or confirmed the said fief, to him present and receiving for himself, and to the said Ilario, who was absent, for whom he promised ratification, in such a way and manner that each of them should hold the said fief. Then, after the death of the said Lord Antonio and while the said Ilario was still alive, Lord John, now Bishop of Parma, a few days later granted the said fief to Antonio de Ferro, citizen of Parma, as vacant, both on account of the death of the said Lord Antonio and also on account of the ingratitude or felonies committed by the said Ilario, as well as by his negligence in not making claim and not rendering the due oath within a year and a day, as he ought to have done. For the said Ilario never appeared before the present Bishop to acknowledge the said fief and to render the due oath. The said Bishop, in the grant made to the aforementioned Antonio de Ferro, declared the fief vacant for the aforementioned reasons, and treated it as vacant, and deprived the said Ilario of the said fief. And of that piece of land, the said Antonio de Ferro took possession. Here it is asked, which of them has the stronger right in the said fief. And so that this question may be clearly elucidated, I shall touch upon what is against Lord Ilario and in favor of Antonio de Ferro; then, conversely, what is to the contrary. Finally, I shall conclude what the law is in the present opinion.

† I answer the first point: because it must be observed on behalf of Anto. de Ferro that, since the fief was ancient and had been enfeoffed free to the said bishop, it was lawful for the said Anto. to sub-enfeoff it, as stated in Extra de feudis, chapter 2. Moreover, the said Ilarius did not appear to have any right in the fief from the last enfeoffment, especially because the said Anto. was constituted in sacerdotal dignity and was a prior; for a cleric cannot hold a fief, and indeed, if he holds one, he is effectively deprived of his clerical status, as stated in column 10 of the title "Si de feudo fuerit contentio inter dominum et agnatum," chapter "Qui clericus." Furthermore, because the said Anto. and also the said Ilarius are natural children, not born of a lawful marriage, nor are there any dotal instruments concerning them; for a natural child does not succeed to a fief, as stated in the same title, chapter "Naturales." Additionally, for another reason, namely that Ilarius committed such acts for which he was deprived of the said fief: assuming that the said fief could be obtained by him, he killed a priest, and thus inflicted a grievance of injuries upon the said bishop and the entire clergy, and detracted from the said bishop; for these reasons, the fief appears to have reverted to the said bishop. Nor is it without reason that he did not render homage nor take the oath of fidelity within one year, as he was required to do.

On the other hand, it may be alleged against the concession to Anto. de Ferro: first, that no one can be purely invested by right of the grantor in a fief which another holds, as is held in column 10 of the title "Qui successores teneantur." Moreover, it does not seem to be an obstacle to what is said, namely that the said Anto. could not hold the said fief, and because he was a cleric and constituted in dignity. For that appears to be true, inasmuch as on account of such a fief he is absent from divine services, or it is of such a nature that the vassal could not perform what is of the nature of the fief, namely, this is an honorific fief, and one which does not require such fidelity as could not be properly rendered by him. To the objection that they are natural children and cannot succeed to a fief, it is said that they are legitimated. Furthermore, assuming that they were not legitimated, although the said bishop could have refused the investiture, since he granted it to them, it appears to have been valid, as in column 10 of the title "Per quos fiat investitura," section "Personam." To the objection that Ilarius killed a priest and detracted from the said bishop, it appears to be denied; rather, even if it were true, he ought to have been deprived by sentence, this being proven, or he himself being joined in this matter, and sentence being passed with him cited; otherwise, it appears not to be valid, as in Codex, title "Quo et quando iudicium," law "Ea quae." Furthermore, to the objection that Ilarius did not render homage within the year, it is answered that the said bishop invested the said Anto. de Arcillibus receiving for himself and for Ilarius, and thus he was not negligent. And if it is said that he did not swear fidelity, it is answered that the said bishop was content with this, for since he could remit the oath entirely, as in the said title "Per quos fiat investitura," chapter "Si," much more could he accept it through another and admit him in this manner. Moreover, at least if he were not admitted by his own right, Ilarius appears to be admitted by the person of the deceased brother, since at the time of the last investiture he was within the year of the death of the aggrieved party.

† Finally, I concur. I consider it conclusively necessary to observe that a new fief of the *ius commune* granted simultaneously and simply to two persons, without the addition that one shall succeed the other, even if it had acquired firmness in their persons, does not devolve for the share of the deceased Antonio and his brother Ilario upon the same Ilario; rather, it reverts by operation of law to the Church, as is read and contained in the same column, *De duobus fratribus de novo beneficio investitis*, c. 1; and *De successione feudorum*, c. 1, in fine; and *De feudo marchiae*, c. 2; and *De beneficio fratris*, c. 1. Hence, if, as is alleged, the investiture was made to the said brothers without a pact that one should succeed the other, there is no doubt regarding the half-share of the fief: for it devolved to the Church, because it was accustomed to be enfeoffed, as I said, and the latest investiture made to Antonio de Ferro was lawfully effected. Indeed, it may fittingly be said that even the remaining half-share did not originate in the person of Ilario, especially because natural children, even if legitimated, if they can serve, do not succeed in a fief unless they were legitimated by that specific law so that they might succeed in the fief; as if the lord had not considered such successors, but only legitimate ones, as in the same title, cap. *Naturales*; and in the gloss, *Quasi ergo*, on account of the defect of the person, which was not known to the said bishop at the time of investiture, and the fief is to be considered as surreptitious and invalid, as in the title *Per quos fiat investitura*, § *Personam*, there: “unless ignorance is alleged,” etc. Moreover, a vassal is deprived of his fief on account of grave and dishonorable injuries inflicted upon the lord, as in the title *Quae sit causa beneficii amittendi*, § *Porro*. Therefore, Odofredus says in the title *Quibus modis feudum amittitur*, in the fifteenth cause, and in the thirtieth in the disputation, that a vassal is deprived of his fief even for verbal injury. Hence, if, as is asserted, he severely and dishonorably vilified not only the bishop but also the entire clergy for the homicide of a priest, and also detracted from the bishop with insulting words, he lost the benefice. It therefore follows that the fief could have been granted to another, even without summoning him, although Ilario held it in fact, although he was not to be deprived of possession unless the cause was known, by argument from *Extra*, *De praebendis*, cap. *Licet episcopus*, lib. 6. Furthermore, although the investiture and fidelity could have been legally demanded within a year and a day from the present bishop and others in the name of Ilario, and were requested and obtained by the brother, it is undoubted law that ratification was to be performed by Ilario, especially within the year, by argument from *Digestum*, *De rerum amissione*, l. *Bonorum*. Since this is not assumed to have been observed, he lost the fief. It therefore follows: because the possession was accustomed to be enfeoffed, the last concession made to Antonio de Ferro is to be upheld as conformable to law, notwithstanding the contrary allegations, as in *Extra*, *De feudis*, c. 2. I, Christopher de Castellione, have subscribed.

Regarding the said point, it must be briefly stated that the portion of the said Antonio, upon his death without an heir, reverted by operation of law to the said Bishop, as in column 10, *Qui feudum dare possunt*, c. 1, § *Cum vero Conradus*; and *De fratribus de novo beneficio investitis*, cap. 1. And therefore, the said bishop could, without any doubt, confer that part and make the investiture in the person of A. de Ferro, since such part of the fief was openly devolved to the said bishop, as in the title *Qui successores teneantur*, c. 1, col. 10.

† But there may be doubt concerning the parts of Ilarius. And if Ilarius, who is said to have killed a certain priest, was indeed condemned for the said homicide, he incurs the consequence of deprivation of the fief on account of the greatest diminution of status of the said Ilarius, as in c. Pastoralis, De iudiciis; and what Innocent notes in c. Verum, De foro competenti. For one thus condemned is considered as dead, as in D. De bonis libertorum, l. Si necesse, § Si deportatus; and C. De usufructu, l. Corruptionem. And then, even without another citation, possession can be taken from him, because this offering is a kind of execution of a definitive sentence, as Innocent notes in Extra, De appellationibus, c. Ex ratione. And it is clear from C. De bonis praescriptorum, l. Si quis post haec.

Or, if he was not condemned, but ought to be condemned and deprived, then, before he is deprived, the fief does not become vacant, by argument from D. De iudiciis, l. Qui se dicit. For the order of law is that first the vassal be convicted of fault and deprived, and then the fief be conferred, as in c. 1, De feudo sine culpa non amittendo. However, if the bishop first invested and then deprived, if it is the same bishop and not his successor, the investiture becomes valid, as in c. 1, Qui successores teneantur, same column. The same may apply if the homicide was notorious, because for such a sacrilege he was deprived by the law itself, as in c. Si quis suadente diabolo. Hence, he is not permitted to hold the fief of the church, by analogy to a heretic, 8. Dist., c. Quo iure; and in Auth. De privatione dotis, § 1. To this contributes what Innocent notes in De verborum significatione, c. Ex parte; and what Cynus notes in l. 1, C. Ne quis in sua causa.

Furthermore, since it was notorious that he had not sought investiture within a year and a day, he may also be deprived ex officio of the bishop on this ground, as in c. 1, Quo tempore miles, column 10. However, this must be done with Ilarius cited: because even in notorious cases, citation is necessary, as is clear in the aforementioned c. Pastoralis. Nevertheless, in excommunication by law, of which I spoke, since it is incurred by the very fact, citation is not necessary. And therefore, according to what is proposed, the said Ilarius has no right, but Antonio de Ferro has it, presupposing that the said fief was accustomed to be enfeoffed, as in c. 1, Episcopum vel abbatem, column 10. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Those exempted from the discharge of a certain burden during a specific description are not considered exempted upon the renewal of that description.
2. Whether an argument from the contrary sense is to be drawn from arbitraments.
3. Whether an argument from the contrary sense is a law.
body: A certain Lord Pasinus, acting as arbitrator between the parties set forth below, rendered an arbitral award which is valid, because he pronounced that certain brothers from Barbarica, during a certain assessment of hearths made in 1365 in the month of November, could not and ought not to be compelled or constrained by the said commune and inhabitants of Barbarica to pay or sustain with the said commune of Barbarica any burdens or levies; but they are to be understood as exempt, free, and discharged by operation of law during the aforementioned assessment. However, the said brothers are bound, in compensation for the aforesaid, to give and pay to the said commune of Barbarica, for the entire time that the said assessment of hearths, mentioned above, shall last, 36 plain livres, which the brothers paid for a certain period. Finally, it was decreed by the commune of Brescia that the valuation made for the communities of Brescia shall be considered as a new assessment of hearths. Hence arises the question whether the said brothers are bound, in the commune of Barbarica, from which land they are natives, to bear burdens by virtue of the said arbitral award or of the common law; and whether, because they did not observe the arbitral awards for a period of eight years, they are bound to pay and have incurred the penalty of the compromise.

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that a description of hearths is not said to endure if it does not endure in effect; just as a transaction is not said to be an *in rem verso* if it does not endure as such, as stated in l. pro parte, §. versum, D. de in rem verso. Nor is anything said to be done unless the act endures, as in D. quod cuiusque universi nomine, l. Item, §. quod si; and C. de his, qui ut indig., l. alium; and D. de fideiuss., l. stipul., in fine; and D. de hære. vend., l. 2, §. illud. And therefore, if something has been added to or subtracted from the ancient description of hearths, such that the form has been changed, then this constitutes a new description, as in D. de iur. et iur., l. ius civile; and D. loc., l. cum in plures, §. lege dictam. Or, if no new form has been given, then either the first description was temporary, and the time has expired. And I say that this second description is a new description, because it acquires its substance anew, although taken from the old one, as in D. de arbor., l. si cum dies, in principio; D. de damno infecto, l. si finita; C. loc., l. cum Hermes; D. de pret. stip., l. Valerianus; D. loc., l. item quæritur, §. qui impleto. For the arbitrator himself considered the temporary estimate which was then in force, and referred himself to it, as in D. de infamibus, l. quid ergo, in principio. And therefore the exception lasted until that time, and no further; because when the time of the privilege expires, the privilege expires, and any other temporary disposition, as in l. Fal., l. si postmissionem; and D. de pact., l. epist., §. si; and D. de excus. tutor., l. scire oportet, §. consequens; C. de temp. in integ. rest., l. supervacuam; D. de act. et obl., l. in honorariis, §. cum rescisse. But if the first estimate did not contain a fixed period of time, then by those words, "that it be considered a new estimate without any other novation," it appears that the old estimate is rather confirmed than that a novation is made, as in C. de novat., l. si; D. de verb. oblig., l. qui bis idem. Just as privileges are said to be renewed, yet true privileges endure, as noted in Auth. de hæred., and in Fal., in principio. And because a substitute also partakes of the nature of that in whose place it is substituted, as in D. de don. inter vir. et ux., l. si donatæ, §. sponsus; and D. de cond. et demonstr., l. si filiae, §. 1; and D. si quis testamento lib. esse iuss. fuerit, l. 1; and D. si quis cautio, l. si eum, §. qui iniuriarum; nevertheless, the contrary is true, namely, that the estimate is considered new, because the words of the law state that it is to be held as a new description, as noted in D. de verb. sig., l. mercis; and C. de novat., l. si.

† Subsequently, it must be premised for the sake of clarity whether an argument *a contrario sensu* is to be drawn from the arbitrator’s decision. For the words state “during the description of the hearths,” which implies that when this is not taking place, they are bound to pay simply, like the others of the said land. Or shall we say that this is an omitted case, so that we argue from an omitted case, not from a case tacitly disposed of by contrary understanding? And it is argued in favor of the first view that an argument *a contrario sensu* is to be drawn from the arbitrator’s decision.

† For the argument from the contrary sense appears to be valid, just as the text of the law and the contract, as is noted in D. de testamento, l. qui testamento, §. mulier; and C. de furtis, l. apud antiquos; D. de pactis dotalibus, l. inter socerum, §. cum inter patrem. To this effect is what is noted in C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. cum iudex, and l. cum eorum. To the contrary, it is said that this is an omitted case, so that the parties remain in the terms in which they were before the compromise. And this is established by D. soluto matrimonio, l. si cum dotem, in principio; and D. de conditione ob causam, l. si extraneus; D. de haeredibus institutis, l. ex facto, and l. Lucius. And it seems that the case is in the words beginning with a preceding negation, D. de manumissione testamento, l. Titia, §. si. But certainly here the mind of the arbitrator appears to be established, from which one must not depart, provided that it can be tacitly gathered from the interpretation of the words and the meaning of the words spoken, as in D. de appellationibus, l. ab executione; and as is noted in D. de arbitris, l. qualem, in principio. And this is proven in the same title, l. inter Castellianum. But here the intention of the arbitrator appears, who granted them the past and modified the future, until the description of the hearths made endures: and he willed that a certain thing be provided in recompense, by which it appears that he intended to exempt the said brothers from a certain exemption, not perpetual but modified, and therefore, when the time is finished, they remain in their former right, as in D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. 1, and there noted. Moreover, a temporal exemption signifies that the common law is to the contrary, as in D. de legibus, l. ius singulare. And it is supported by what is noted in the same title, l. cum lex in perpetuum, which can be most aptly adduced, and D. de legato secundo, l. statuliberam, §. Stichum. And therefore, considering that the said nobles are natives of the land of Barbarica, and there have their natural and civil domicile, they are compelled, for the things which they have there, to pay together with the inhabitants of the said place of Barbarica. L. 1, C. de mulieribus, et in quo loco, lib. 19. Nor do they have the benefits of the citizenship of Brescia, because they did not observe the statutes disposing concerning citizenship. D. de verborum significatione, l. aedificia, with the gloss. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether anyone is to be punished for insulting words.
1. The charges are irrelevant, from which no legal effect follows.
2. A natural son is so closely related a person that he may defend his father's possession.
3. Threats are sometimes just, sometimes reckless without malice, or with slight malice; sometimes with malice having in itself the atrocity of the offense.
4. In case of doubt, the charges are to be admitted with the clause, saving the right of those concerned, etc.
body: On the question at issue between Christopher and Anthony, brothers and sons of the late Raynald of Persico, on one side, and the said Hugolin of Cavalcabobbi and John, his natural son, on the other, on account of a certain rescript of commission and mandate issued by our Illustrious and Magnificent Prince, on account of the contents contained in the said rescript, the words of which appear, and especially on account of certain words which the said John is said to have spoken against a certain Castald of the opposing party: that unless he refrained from such things, he would make him suffer the rigors of his hands and throw him into the water of the Commessadio with his head. etc. Before the commissioner, chapters were presented on both sides, and on behalf of the said John it was argued that if the said John had spoken any words toward the said Castald, it was because the said Anthony of Persico had gone to the piece of land described in the said records, and had expelled the laborers of the said Lord Hugolin, and had used force against the said laborers in possession of the said piece of land belonging to the said Lord Hugolin and possessed by him.

† Moreover, that the said brothers committed certain other acts, which are mentioned in the said chapters against the said Lord Hugolin, and thereby they gave cause to the edict; for as Aristotle says, he does not begin who acts out of anger, but he who provokes to anger. And this is proved. D. de iudic. l. in tribus. For he is the principal author of the fault, from whom the malice begins, as C. de servis fugitivis l. quicunque. and C. de furtis l. si quis servo. On the contrary, it is said that the said chapters are irrelevant, because it does not follow that if one commits a wrong, therefore the other may commit a wrong, and say worse things: especially with regard to the fiscal penalty, where both ought to be punished for the wrongful act and the insult, as noted in C. ad legem Iuliam de vi l. si quis ad se fundum. D. soluto matrimonio l. viro, atque uxore. and l. cum mulier. unless one act was done for offense, and the other for defense with due moderation, as C. unde vi l. 1. D. ad legem Aquiliam l. scientiam §. qui cum aliter. and l. si ex plagiis §. si tabernarius. and l. quemadmodum §. si navis alteram. and D. si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicatur l. 1 §. cum arietes. These are common legal principles.

The said chapters are therefore irrelevant, from which no effect follows, as is stated in C. qui legitimam personam; l. momentaneae, ff. de iureiurando; l. si duo patroni, § idem Iulia, ff. de petitione hereditatis; l. si quis libertatem, § ult., with similar authorities. Since, therefore, the irrelevance appears from the reading of the chapters, as in C. de probationibus, l. ad probationem; and ff. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratus, § pro Aurelio, such chapters ought not to be admitted, nor should witnesses be received upon them. See also extra de officio delegati, c. cum contingat; and what is noted by Ioannes de Monachis in c. filii, de haereticis, lib. 6; and the argument from C. de appellationibus, l. ampliorem, § in refutatoriis; and C. de formulis, l. 2, a contrario sensu; and l. 1, de officio assessorum.

On the contrary, however, the truth of the matter appears. And let it be presupposed that the truth stands as is asserted to me, namely, that the said Lord Hugolinus possessed and possesses the said piece of land in the place called Commessadiis, in whose territory the said piece of land lies. And there, properly speaking, the said words were uttered, or otherwise I do not care, in order to prevent future force. For by cries, threats, and terrors, we can aid ourselves and our own. ff. ad Sillanum, l. cum dominus.

And I premise, for the sake of clarity, that a natural son is so closely united a person that he may defend his father’s possession both by deed and by word; and this for two reasons: first, by reason of natural affection, as noted in the Digest, *De iuramento et iureiurando*, in the law *Ut vim*; second, because by the right of familiarity he has a certain use or customary practice, as in the Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*, in the law *Qui iure familiaritatis*. And for both reasons it is lawful for him to defend his father’s possession against a disturber, as in the Code, *Si per vim vel aliter*, in the first law; since even other familiars of the father himself are permitted to do this. For a friend may lend aid in defense to a friend, even without request, as noted by Bartolus in the law *Prohibitum*, Code, *De iudiciis*, § *Libris*, Book X. Much more so may a son do this for his father, because between them there exists a friendship greater than which none is found, as noted in the Digest, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, in the law *Quidam cum filium*.

Furthermore, I premise that the said words may be considered in a twofold manner: in one way, insofar as they are directed toward the honor of our Magnificence; and in this manner they carry such weight as our Magnificence wishes, and according to his will he may take vengeance, by argument from the Code, *De summo imperio*, in the first law, at the end. In the second way, they may be considered with respect to those brothers or that castle; and in this manner those words do not deserve punishment, because one may resist both with threats and with arms against one who offers insult and disturbs possession, as is fully read and noted in the first law, § *Interdictum*, Digest, *Uti possidetis*, in the ordinary gloss and by Bartolus, and it is supported by the Digest, *De usufructu legato*, in the law *Heres in fundum*. For the said brothers or the said Castellan could not set foot in another’s property against the will of the said [owner], and especially by cutting down trees or doing something else, as in the Code, *De interdictis*, in the first law; Digest, *De servitutibus rusticorum praediorum*, in the law *Divus*; Digest, *Si servitus vendicetur*, in the law *Sicuti*, § *Aristo*; Code, *Quando liceat unicuique se sine iudice vindicare*, in the first and second laws; and to the Law Aquilia, in the law *Quemadmodum*, § 1, with many similar authorities. Thirdly, I premise,

† That threats are sometimes just, sometimes rash without malice, or with slight malice, and sometimes with malice possessing the atrocity of a crime: for in malice, just as in fault, there are degrees. For there is lesser malice, when it harms little or not at all. And there is grave malice, when it harms more. And there is most grave malice, from which public judgments arise, as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Servus non omnibus; D. de regulis iuris, l. Ad ea; D. de minoribus, l. Auxilium, §. In delictis. Which also clearly appears from the kinds of penalties, because there are lesser, greater, and greatest penalties, as in D. de infamibus, l. Quid ergo, §. Poena gravior; and D. de poenis, l. Respiciendum, in §. Delinquit.

Furthermore, I premise that one must consider not only the quality of the words, but the quality of the minds. For how something is said ought to be observed, as in D. ad exhibendum, l. Penultima; and with what mind something is done, as in D. de furtis, l. Verum; and l. Si quis ex dolo. According to that principle: "Intent and purpose distinguish crimes," in the same title, l. Qui iniuriae; and C. de iniuriis, l. Si non convitiis; and C. ad legem Corneliam de sicariis, l. 1; and D. de iniuriis, l. Eum qui nocentem, §. Si iniuria; and §. Si nupta; D. de adulteriis, l. Pe. And because it is probable and credible that the said words were not uttered with the intent to offend our Magnificent Lord, but solely to terrify the adversary, as it were admonishing him not to do a lawful thing, as in C. de adulteriis, auth. Si quis ei; and threatening not simply, but under the condition that he would do anything, those words had no effect. D. quod quisque iuris, l. 1, §. 1. By these words, it is certainly probable that the said Magnificent Lord, having information about the aforementioned matters, will not regard the arrogance of the said brothers as lesser pride and petulance, if it is true that Lord Hugolinus possesses what those words implied, since it savors of greater arrogance to do than to say, as in C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. Reprehendenda.

Hence, since it behooves the inquisitor to investigate all things, even those tacitly adjacent to the expressed, since otherwise he cannot write down the full and pure truth, as in D. de iure omnium iudicum, l. Cui iurisdictioni; and Extravagantes de accusatione, c. Cum dilectus; de testibus, c. Praesentium, lib. 6; de actionibus et obligationibus, l. 1; D. de testibus, l. Ob carmen, §. Si testes; and what our Innocentius says de probationibus, c. Quoniam contra falsam; because when the penalty is moderated according to the quality, it is necessary to inquire into that quality, as in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. Pomponius in negotiis; C. si quis Imperatori maledixerit, l. 1; and D. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. Famosi. Therefore, the said chapters ought to be admitted as pertinent: for even if they did not relieve from the whole, they relieve from so much, as is clear from the laws cited above.

† Moreover, even if it were doubtful whether the matters in question are pertinent in any way, they ought to have been admitted, namely with the usual protestation, that is, saving the right regarding impertinence, etc. (Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *Praetor*, § *Si controversia*). Hence, whatever, according to the subject matter, can pertain to the movement of the mind and the information of this prince, must be intimated to him, the fact being fully narrated. Note (Digest, *De infamibus*, law *Lucius*). And it is as if by reconvention in the same case to use pertinent matters, as (Code, *De sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum*, law *Cum Papinianus*). However, that which the note teaches in law *Si non convicii* does not apply to the present purpose, because there it speaks of an atrocious injury, as when one says to another, "You are a murderer" or "You are a gourd"; but to threaten is something light and not infamous, argument (Extra, *De re iudicata*, chapter *Cum testamento*). Indeed, it can be defended that it is not a private injury, because he deserves to hear such things, especially a person of low status, such as a Castaldus, as (Digest, *De dolo*, law *Non debet*). And although the Castaldus represents his lord, as (Digest, *De religione*, law *Ossa*, in the end), nevertheless in those things which he does wrongly, unless there is proof of a special mandate, otherwise (Extra, *De restitutione spoliorum*, chapter *Cum ad sedem*). Hence I conclude that on the whole of this matter the information should be received from both sides. Afterwards he will do what pleases him, having heard what is to be heard from both sides. (Code, *Si per vim vel alio modo*, law *Finis*). So that neither his majesty be contemptible, nor penal severity be extended beyond the fault, (Decretum, *De poenitentia*, distinction 1, chapter *Mensuram*). And it supports the above what is noted (Decretum, *De senatu*, chapter *Ea nascitur*, in the Novella; and chapter *Peruenit*, in the Novella). Moreover, there is a difference between some commotion and obstinate anger, (Extra, title, chapter *Universitatis*, in the Novella). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a daughter’s renunciation of her mother’s inheritance, with her father’s consent, is valid, and whether such renounced assets are acquired by the father.
2. In the renunciation of an inheritance, no cause is required.
body: Statute of the City. In Pavia it is provided that, upon the death of her first husband, a woman may marry a second husband, and that it is also lawful for the same woman, even if she has children from the first marriage, to give and transfer to the second husband the dowry given to her first husband, or which she had confessed to have received, and even a third part more, without thereby reserving anything for any of those children, or for any of them, to give or restore. And without anything being deferred or restored to any of them. And without anything being revoked by anyone on this account. Now it happens that a certain lady, after the death of her first husband, married a second husband, and from him she bore a daughter. Finally, this woman died in marriage, with her husband and the said daughter surviving. In the presence and with the consent of her father, the said daughter renounced her mother’s inheritance. Finally, the said daughter wishes to recover the said dowry.
† It is asked whether it is possible. The answer is that it is not, as in C. de repudiando hereditate, l. sicut; C. de iure et facto ignorantia, l. si emancipata.

And it is to be noted that in the renunciation of an inheritance no cause is required, as in the Digest, *ad Trebellianum*, law *Quia poterat*. Furthermore, it is to be noted that by such renunciation the inheritance itself devolved upon the father, as in the Code, *De bonis quae liberis*, law *Cum non solum*, in the principal part. Hence, the father could have taken possession of the said inheritance in his own name, as appears there, and this is true unless it were proven that acceptance had been made by the said daughter, because an inheritance once accepted cannot be renounced, as in the aforementioned law *Sicut*. Hence, according to the facts alleged in the petition of Lady Helena against Augustine regarding the common dowry, it seems to me that in the said petition, according to what is alleged, the said Lady Helena has no right, and especially on account of the pact not to molest and not to summon to court, etc. This pact would be valid even if the inheritance could not be renounced, because the notary, as a public person, received it for anyone having an interest, following the common opinion that a notary, as a public person, can acquire rights for another, especially the right of exception. And the foregoing are true, unless fraud or threats by the parent intervened, as noted in law *I*, section *Quae honorandae*, in the Digest, *Quarum actio non datur*; and especially on account of the oath that intervened, as noted in law *3*, section *Quid ergo*, in the Digest, *De contrario iudicio tutelae*. And these are the points in the case in which Advocate Dr. Adrilinus de Carona is involved. Add to the question of Dr. Augustinus de Magno, that by the aforementioned renunciation, even if a daughter from the first marriage existed, nothing would revert to her by such renunciation, because the right was acquired by the father, who steps into the place of the renouncing child, as noted in the aforementioned law *Cum non solum*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To what is he bound who is obliged to permit certain persons to enjoy such goods, etc.
2. To what is the one demanding from the exiles bound.
3. Whether the cancellation of the ban and of the condemnation has the force of restitution, or of a simple indulgence.
4. He who permits an instrument to be cancelled appears to have agreed not to sue.
5. To what are those persons bound who occupy the goods of the condemned.
6. Whether debtors of the condemned by contract can be sued on those contracts.
body: Given a certain chapter of peace concluded between the Illustrious Prince and our Magnificent Lord, the Count of Virtues and others, on one part, and the Magnificent Lord Francis Minor of Carara on the other, which contains the following: “Furthermore, we sentence and declare that the aforementioned Lord Francis of Carara shall permit the nobles of Scrovigni, etc., who have houses and possessions acquired by just title in Padua or in its district, as well as all clerics, subjects, and others holding any goods in Padua or its district by just title, to freely enjoy their said goods and rights situated in Padua, its territory, or the Paduan district, to the extent of the act of the said distinguished Lord of Padua, and to collect from any of their debtors any sums of money to which they are entitled; and that they shall be freely released and discharged from all bans, proceedings, and personal condemnations, as well as real condemnations, which have been or shall be made against the aforementioned persons or any of them, without any further payment of money, and within the specified time; and that they may alienate their goods and dispose of them at their own will and pleasure, etc.” Several diverse doubts arise. And first, to what is the said Magnificent Lord Francis bound by virtue of the said chapter?

And I say that he is bound to that which the word signifies with respect to his own act, or in which he himself is the cause: namely, to permit or suffer. In this word is virtually contained that neither by himself nor through another will he provide any impediment whereby the persons named in the said case might be prevented from obtaining the benefits agreed upon in the said contract, as in the Digest, *De servitutibus*, law *Quo*, and *De hominibus servitutibus*, section *Servitutium*. Hence, he cannot do anything, directly or indirectly, by which the prosecution of the rights of the persons named in the said contract is made more difficult, or by which they are disturbed in their possessions or revenues; for the said chapter must be observed in good faith and fully, as is fitting among such persons, as in the Digest, *De locato conducto*, law *Locationis*; and *De verbis obligatis*, law *Stipulatio ista habere licere*, section 1; and *De peculio*, law *Summa cum ratione*, in the beginning.

Secondly, it is asked, to what is the commune of Padua bound? Suppose, for instance, that it has collected the names of these debts that have been exacted; is the Paduan fiscus bound to restore the amounts exacted from the aforementioned debtors? And it must be said that either it exacted them unjustly or justly. In the first case, it is bound to restitution, because the fiscus ought not to enrich itself at the expense of another, as is stated in D. 50.17.127 (Si certum petatur, l. Si me et Titium); and in D. 12.3.1 (De condictione indebiti, l. Nam natura); and in D. 50.1.3 § gravissimum (De administrationibus rerum ad civitatem pertinentium, l. 3 § gravissimum). In the second case, however, it exacted them either before the peace was made, as from the goods of those whose property had been confiscated, or after: if indeed it exacted them before,

† Then it must be considered whether the cancellation of the ban and of the condemnation, etc., has the force of restitution in integrum, or whether it has the force of a simple indulgence. And if it is restitution in integrum, whether it is absolute or qualified. For even the word "I restore," when pronounced with an adjunct, does not operate except with respect to that adjunct, as is fully noted by Cynus in l. vlt. C. de sen. pas. On this point, I say that just as the cancellation of an instrument, when the debt has already been paid, does not give rise to the condictio indebiti, but when the debt has not been paid, it gives rise to the exceptio pacti, as in C. de cond. ob caus. l. dissolutae, and ff. de probat. l. si chirographum, unless something else was agreed upon; so I say in the case at hand that the words must be examined. For we are speaking either of goods still existing, or of those consumed or dispersed. In the first case, it is clear from the express pact that they are restored with respect to the said goods, and these can be reclaimed from any possessor, whether the fiscus possesses them or another, because the words state this; for it is expressly contained in the words that they are to be removed from all condemnations, both personal and real. Therefore, from the fact that it says "real," it is manifest that the things must be restored to them, namely those that exist and are not proven to have been consumed, arg. ff. si cert. pet. l. nam et si fur. with its gloss, provided it is established that they have come into the hands of some persons. For the fiscus would not be bound to restore what had not been incorporated into the fiscus, arg. ff. si cert. pet. l. ciuitas plena. Therefore, the restitution is deemed to have been made with respect to the things of which I spoke, and especially because the words say "to enjoy freely." Hence, they ought to be moderators and arbiters as if over their own things, as in C. man. l. in re mandata, and C. de contrah. empt. l. dudum, ff. de act. emp. l. si tibi liberum, de rest. spol. l. Pisanis, de statu hom. l. libertas. In the second case, if before the peace was made the money exacted from the debtors by the fiscus had been consumed, the words do not seem to be extended to this, because when the chapter speaks of quantities, it says "to which they were bound." This word is in the present tense, and does not include past things already perished, as in ff. de leg. 3. l. 11. § si rem, and ff. de verb. oblig. l. cum stipulamur § si a colono. However, those things which were exacted by the fiscus after the peace was made must be restored by the fiscus, even if they have been consumed; because they were exacted by virtue of the chirograph of the condemnations of the churches, and reduced to non causa. And especially because the fiscus itself knew this, since the compilers of the peace, who acted in its stead, knew it, as in ff. de trib. l. procuratoris in princ. But even without any knowledge, restitution in integrum draws its effect with it, as noted by Cynus in l. vlt. C. de sen. pas. Nor let anyone say that these were not cancelled, but were to be cancelled,

† because he who promises to cancel an instrument is deemed to have agreed not to demand performance, as is stated in the Digest, title *De pactis*, in the law *Labeo facit*; in the Digest, title *De legatis primo*, in the law *Servum filii*, section *Eum, qui chirographum*; and in the law *Huiusmodi*, section *Si cui*, and what is noted there; and in the Code, title *De donationibus*, law 1.

Thirdly, it is asked to what each of the persons who have occupied the goods of these late condemned individuals is bound. It seems to be said that if they indeed occupied them before the peace and the goods still exist, they must be restored to these parties. But if after the peace, whether the goods exist or not, because they could not consume the goods pertaining to these parties nor convert them to their own uses, as in C. unde vi, l. cum quaerebatur; and Inst. de vi bonorum raptorum, §. sed nec dum. Rather, it seems even more so that if they consumed them in bad faith before the peace was made and occupied them by their own authority, they are bound to make restitution, because although the thing does not exist, the obligation of its value remains, as in ff. de cond. fur., l. in re furtiva. And if it is said that at that time the things did not belong to these parties, and therefore the right was acquired by the fisc, it is answered that this right exists, and therefore they are restored to this right by the articles of the peace, unless they had occupied them by license of a superior and they had been consumed, as in cap. quamuis, extra de rescriptis, lib. sexto.

Fourthly, it is asked whether debtors, who were debtors by contract, can be sued on those contracts. And it must be said that either they paid the fisc before the goods were confiscated, and they were not released, at least if they paid voluntarily and not under compulsion; or they paid after the goods were confiscated, and then they were, and are, released. On this point, see fully the note in the Digest, De solutionibus, l. Credito. And what is noted in the Code, Quod metus causa, l. Cum te parti. I refer to the annotations there, submitting myself to the correction of such learned masters. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, given a statute that the nearest relative must be appointed guardian of a minor, the relative who is nearer through the female line is preferred to one who is more remote through the male line, or vice versa.
2. Whether a guardian appointed to authorize a division to be made is bound to make an inventory.
3. Whether an oath excludes adults, even if the oath is repeatedly repudiated.
4. Whether laws extend to matters not specifically enumerated.
5. Where a statute prescribes a certain form, if the form is not observed, what is done is invalid.
6. Whether a division among co-heirs is valid whereby one has all the immovables and the other has money or the names of debtors.
7. A testament of a usurer is invalid if caution (security) has not been given.
8. From the stipulation of a public notary, an action arises.
body: Premises are set forth from the words of a certain Statute of the community of Cumarum, the tenor of which is as follows. Item, it is statuted, that if anyone, etc. The case is proposed as follows: Ottonellus, Ioannellus, Stephanolus, and Marcolus, brothers, sons of the late Ser Bassanolus, formerly sons of Ioannes de Quadrio of Cumis, being over thirteen years of age for each of them, but under fifteen years, appearing before Lord Antonius, judge of causes, or of the said community of Palaetii, requested that Ser Massollus de Quadrio of Cumis, their present relative and willing to be curator, be given and constituted as their curator, to make a division and petition together with Ser Georgius de Quadrio and the son of the late Lord Ioannes de Quadrio, their uncle, to whom they were summoned by the said Ser Georgius, their uncle, concerning all and singular goods and movable and immovable things, rights and names of debts common among the said brothers on one part, and the said Ser Georgius on the other. And to consent to the said division to be made, and to receive and confess that they had received and had all those goods falling to their part in the said division to be made, according to their contingent part and portion of the said common goods, and the ratable part of the said goods, etc., as contained in the instrument of the said curatorship. It is proposed that the said Lord Ioannes de Quadrio, in his testament, instituted Bassanolus, Georgius, and Stephanolus, his sons, as universal heirs in equal portions. And in the case that any of the above-written heirs should die without male heirs, he substituted the other surviving male brothers, and male sons to be born from a legitimate marriage, in stirpes and not in capita, ordering that his inheritance should not pass to strangers. And that his said sons and heirs could not sell, alienate, or obstruct the said goods of the testator, unless with the consent of all. And if otherwise were done, it should devolve to those not alienating. Finally, it happened that while the said testator was living, Stephanolus, his son, died. Similarly, while the said testator was living, the above-written Bassanolus died, with the said brothers Ottonellus surviving him. Afterwards, the said Lord Ioannes died without changing his testament, with the said Georgius, his son, and Ottonellus and his brothers, his nephews under twenty-five years of age, surviving. This Georgius administered all the said common goods for eight years or so, and collected many fiefs and revenues ascending and amounting to the quantity of two thousand florins per year. And he also collected other quantities from hereditary debtors, which amount to the quantity of three thousand florins. After it came to a division between the said uncle and nephews with the authority of the said curator and by decree of the judge, the tenor of the division appears in the tenor of the public instrument, and it appears how almost all the immovable goods from the said division were assigned to the said Georgius; whereas the names of the debtors were assigned to the said adults. From the above, it is asked whether the said division was valid or not. And what is to be done regarding the eight thousand florins or so collected from fiefs and revenues, profits of possessions, and the other three thousand florins collected by the said Georgius from hereditary debtors.
