And because, first of all, the examination begins with the person, as stated in the Digest, *De iure codicillorum*, law *Quidam reserunt*, it must be examined by the curator whether the said curator was lawfully appointed to the said brothers, presupposing that the said minors had on their mother’s side a relative closer in degree and more suitable than the said Ser Masso.

It seems at first that the appointment of the curator was valid, because the minors themselves requested him and approved of him; therefore, they cannot disapprove of him, as stated in the Digest, *Qui satisdatio cogantur*, law *Ab arbitrio*. Furthermore, because the curator was entirely the closest relative on the father’s side and in the paternal line, he appears to be preferable as being more worthy, as argued by the law of the Twelve Tables, cited in the Digest, *De capitis deminutione*, law *Tutelas*.

I argue the contrary, namely that this curatorship was established by the statutes in the manner of a quasi-legal appointment: and the statute uses natural terms, not civil ones; for it speaks of “his nearest parents and kinsmen,” as stated in the aforementioned law *Tutelas* and in the Authenticum, *De hereditatibus ab intestato*, section *Si*. Moreover, the statute says “nearest,” and although it does not say “nearest in degree,” the sense is the same, because “nearest” is defined as one whom no one precedes, as stated in the Institutes, *De legitima agnatorum successione*, section *Proximus*, and in the Digest, *De verborum significatione*, law *Proximus*. I speak here when we are dealing with a reason for preferring proximity, as is the case here, since the statute speaks of a tutor and curator; thus, it intends that the tutorship or curatorship be granted according to the degree of proximity, similar to tutorship. This is true unless this statute has been interpreted differently by custom, as stated in the Digest, *De legibus*, law *Si interpretatione*. Furthermore, since this man was not among the nearest relatives, the praetor erred regarding the factual basis and the quality of the person; therefore, the decree is invalid, as stated in the Digest, *De tutoribus et curatoribus datis ab his*, law *Tutor si petitus*, and in the Digest, *De in ius vocando*, law *Sed si hac*, section *Paternum*.

But assuming that he was a curator, it would have to be seen whether he is a general curator appointed for the affairs, and thus, in order to oversee by way of voluntary jurisdiction or contract, is he bound to make an inventory, since those who have the duty to examine the estate, according to some, are bound to make an inventory, as noted in C. de episc. audi. l. de creationibus, so that it may appear whether they preserve the ward's property or not, as argued in ff. rem pupil. salu. fore. l. et si ad species. However, the contrary is commonly observed, because it pertains to the office of such curators to authorize or detain goods, and thus they do not intervene except in movable and immovable property, rights, and the names of debtors, which they, for example.

It follows to consider the third point, namely, assuming that he was not a curator, whether the oath excludes adults? And it seems that it does, as in the Authentica *Sacramenta puberum*, C. *Si adversus venditionem*. The contrary is the truth, because this statute expressly rejects the oath, as in D. *De legatis primis*, l. *Si quis inquilinos*, §. *Finis*; and D. *Qui satisdare cogantur*, l. *Qui iurato*. It follows to consider the fourth article,

† namely, whether, assuming that the said curatorship is valid, it extends to the said revenues, fictions, and profits of the common possessions, which were collected and advanced to him by the said George in the amount of the said thousand florins. And it seems that one should say no, because no mention was made of these. Cf. D. de pactis, l. emptor, § Lucius; and l. tres fratres; and D. de condictione indebita, l. si, § idem quaesivit. For these appear to have been deliberately concealed and done with intent, since the minors were not informed about them. And because the aforementioned matters pertain rather to the action for management of affairs (negotiorum gestorum) than to the division of the inheritance, as D. si certum petatur, l. eius qui in provinciam, § earum.

† And with regard to the consideration of all the aforesaid, it must be known that where a statute prescribes a certain form, if the form is not observed, what is done is invalid, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si praetor; D. ad municipalia, l. constitutionibus; C. de iure fisci, l. certa forma, lib. 10, and similar authorities. Furthermore, it must also be known that

† That this does not appear to have been a division, namely that one party should have almost all immovables and those which are in their entirety, and the other should have chirographs, and especially such as are, according to what I prescribe, usurious, which are not exacted without vexation, nor certainly assigned with effect, insofar as they partake of some wickedness, as in D. 10.2.12 (certe) § sed et si quid; and see the note by Guillaume in C. 10.2.1 (incerti iuris). Moreover, the outcome of lawsuits is uncertain, as in D. 33.6.1 (eo tempore). Hence this division seems to have been sufficiently excessive, as in D. 2.1.1 (maioribus). And the authority interposed thereon seems to have been ambitious, both by the curator and by the master ignorant of the quality of the claims and of his power, and believing that they were just claims; and therefore his authority does not seem to be valid, nor to confirm the act, as in D. 4.2.1 (prohibere) § plane. This number seems rather to be an error than the authority of the praetor.

It remains to be considered regarding the validity of the will. If the testator was a manifest usurer, there is no question, because it is not valid, if sufficient security has not been provided, as in c. *Quamquam*, *De usuris*, lib. 6, although perhaps all that is stated there is not of necessary form.

For if he is a public notary, from whose stipulation, according to the custom of the place, an action is acquired by others without assignment—for this custom is observed throughout almost all of Italy—then it is not necessary that such a notary stipulate by mandate of the bishop. For that statute was enacted so that an action might be acquired by an outsider; but once the effect is achieved, we do not concern ourselves with the mode, unless we were to say that there was another reason, namely that bishops wish to know these matters and have them notified to themselves; and therefore it was so statuted. And if this were the case, we would say that what is said there regarding the mandate of the ordinary is of the substance of the caution, and consequently of the validity of the will, unless perhaps such a notary could not be had with the bishop’s mandate; for necessity knows no law, as in l. 1, D. de officio consulis; and D. de mag. test., l. qui potuerunt; and D. de publicaniis, l. Caesar; and D. de muneribus et honoribus, l. ut gradatim, § et si lege; and Extr. de probat., c. quoniam contra falsam, where, due to the lack of a public notary, two honest men suffice. Copia. Punctus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It treats of the validity of a certain compromise, and of the sentence rendered by ten bailiffs of the commune of Florence between Count Orsini and a certain Lord Francis concerning the Castle of Cantiano.
body: There was a war and controversy between the Magnificent Commune of Florence on one part, and the Magnificent Lord Antonio, Count of Montferrat, on the other part. During which, the said Commune, having been pronounced guilty of certain injury, especially concerning the Castle of Cantiano of the County of Gubbio, of which the undersigned Lord Francis is said to have been dispossessed under the trust of the said Commune, and certain other affairs of the city of Gubbio having been variously attempted against the honor of the said Commune, rose up against the said Count to war, and the armed forces of the said Commune rode hostilely against the Count and his men. And while the war raged on both sides, the said Count Antonio, conscious of the committed acts, and remembering due gratitude, and remembering how much he was obliged to the said Commune for the immense benefits received, and grieving to have fallen into the indignation of the said Commune, and desiring to return to accustomed grace and love, and to be reconciled with the said Commune, through Master Lord Knight Lord Giberto, formerly born of the good memory of Lord Galasso de' Pii of Carpi, his suitable commissioner and mandatary, placing himself under the disposition of the said Commune as its father, and submitting himself, his persons, and his things to its every will, and granting a free remission and commission both of his person and of his status, his cities and lands, and of all other contents, solemnly made to the undersigned ten most prudent men, citizens of Florence, and to two parts of them, who were appointed by the said Commune to the war against the said Count, whatever and however they should be disposed by them, or by two parts of them, promising and offering to observe all things. It happened that the said Lord Giberto, commissioner and mandatary sent by the said Count to the presence of the Magnificent and powerful Lords, the Lord Prior of the Arts and the Standard-Bearer of Justice of the city of Florence, made the above-mentioned acts, and solemnly obliged the said Count for their observance, as is most fully demonstrated by the authentic instrument drawn up therefor. After this, the said ten declared many things of bailiwick, and among the other chapters of the same declaration, some chapters dispose concerning the exiles of Gubbio, and some are particular, disposing concerning the said Lord Francis and the Castle of Cantiano. Also there is a certain chapter disposing in this form, namely: "Item, that all and every doubt which might arise, and any obscurities or entanglements which might occur or arise in any way between the said Count, or the Commune of Gubbio, and the said exiles, or any or some of them, concerning the above-mentioned chapters disposing of the exiles, or concerning things omitted in the said chapters, or any of them; and also whether it should be said that the above-mentioned dispositions concerning the exiles are not observed in whole or in part, or that something contrary is done; and also whether any or some are exiles or are not; and also whatever other doubt might occur in the above-mentioned matters, remain and be placed under the disposition and declaration of the Magnificent Lords, the Lord Prior and the Standard-Bearer of Justice of the city of Florence, and their colleges, and the said ten of the bailiwick, and two parts of them, henceforth throughout the entire month of August next following; and from then on, only in the said ten of the bailiwick, or in two parts of them, even if others are absent, not requested, or dead, or impeded in any way; and that any disposition and declaration which shall be made de facto, and without the presence of anyone being requested, by the said Lords Priors and Standard-Bearer, and their colleges, and the ten of the bailiwick, or two parts of them, henceforth throughout the month of August, and also afterwards whatever is made by the said ten or two parts of them, notwithstanding that the officials are not, but are private persons, may and must be observed by anyone whom it might touch or concern, and be put into execution, all contradiction and opposition ceasing. Finally, it is contained in the same chapters that they are not to be understood, nor are they against the Roman Church, etc., the tenor of which chapter follows, as below, namely: 'Item, on account of the above-mentioned, or other things, the said Commune of Florence is not bound in any way, or to anything, to the said Count Antonio against the Roman Church, or the Emperor, or theirs, or any other of their counts, nor against the Roman Church or the Emperor, is any obligation understood or arising from the above-mentioned chapters, nor is any letter arising or to arise or to be understood to arise therefrom, notwithstanding anything. After which chapters, the same Magnificent Lord Count obtained from our present Lord Lord B. the Vicariate of the city of Gubbio and its County, in which, among other things, it is contained that the same Lord Count promises and swears to recover and maintain the rights of the church and the above-mentioned city. After which, certain discordances having arisen between the Magnificent Lord Lord Count Antonio, Count of Montferrat, etc., on one part, and the said Lord Francis de Gabrielibus on the other, the aforesaid Magnificent Lord Count and Lord Francis made a general compromise of all and every difference which turned or could turn, etc., in law and in fact, into the noble men John de Ungariis of Acto, of Saxto, and Abatteltorio de Simonictis of Exio, of which compromise it appears by public instrument, a copy of which is transmitted. Finally, the same Lord Francis, through his legitimate procurator, sold to the said Lord Count the Rock of Cantiano with all right and jurisdiction which the same Lord Francis had in the Castle of Cantiano; and he, being in the Castle of Montefloris, personally ratified the same sale, as appears from public instruments concerning the above-mentioned. After which, the same Lord Francis, then and now, and at the time of the undersigned declaration, having the power of the pure and mixed imperial sword and every mode of jurisdiction with full arbitrium as Captain of the Bailiwick of the city of Florence, offered a certain libel in the same city of Florence before the said ten of the former bailiwick against the said Lord Count Antonio, in which libel he narrates many things, and finally concludes in the undersigned form, namely: 'Wherefore, the same Lord Francis asks that you pronounce, decree, and declare that the said Lord Count Antonio could not, nor can, occupy the said Castle of Cantiano, the chapters of the said reconciliation standing in his way, and that the said Count Antonio is bound and ought to freely relax and restore it to the said Lord Francis, as and as the said Lord Francis possessed it at any time before the said month of November; and that he dismiss, relax, and restore to the said Lord Francis the said Castle of Cantiano free, vacant, and expedited; and that he allow and permit the said Castle, thus restored as is premised, to be restored, and that the said Lord Francis hold and possess it, and use and enjoy it freely and peacefully without any molestation; and also that you annul and invalidate the said sale and the donation of the said Rock, and the said pacts made between the said Count Antonio and the procurator of the said Lord Francis, and that the said Rock be restored and ought to be restored to the said Lord Francis; or if it should not seem to your donation that the said sale, donation, and pacts ought to be annulled, the same Lord Francis asks that you pronounce, decree, and declare that the said Lord Count Antonio did not pay to the said Lord Francis the above-mentioned price as he ought to have paid it, but that the declaration made by the said Lords Peter and Ser Peter, and the said penalty of 10,000 gold florins committed by the said Lord Count Antonio, is due, and that the said Lord Count Antonio incurred the said penalty of 10,000 gold florins, and that Lord Count Corrado ought to restore the said Rock to the said Lord Francis; and concerning all the above-mentioned doubts and controversies, as is premised, having arisen between the said Lord Count Antonio and Lord Francis, that you pronounce, decree, and declare, and pass a certain sentence.' And all the above-mentioned, the same Lord Francis narrates, proposes, and asks not by way of a libel, but of a simple petition and complaint; and in every mode, way, right, and form by which he best can, by virtue of the power and arbitrium granted to you and to each of you, asking that justice be administered to him, not binding himself to all the above-mentioned, but placing and puts them singly and distinctly, as is more expedient and useful for him in obtaining his right. On the part, however, of the said Magnificent Lord Count, exception was taken of the incompetence of the said ten, and especially of their suspicion, as well as of the place of Florence during the magistracy and office of the said Lord Francis, and by reason of his office; and that during the said magistracy, the above-mentioned ten could not cognize of the contempts in the said libel, nor impede themselves in any way. After which, the above-mentioned ten took, or made, a declaration of instrument, namely: 'Invoking the name of Christ, following the way of truth and justice, especially for the good of peace and concord of the above-mentioned parties; and so that to each we may faithfully administer what is due by reason and justice, as far as is possible to us, as we are bound and ought, moved by the above-mentioned reasons, and by many other just and reasonable causes, we pronounce, judge, arbitrate, and declare that the said Lord Count Antonio could not, nor can, occupy, hold, or cause to be occupied or held, the said Castle and Rock of Cantiano, the chapters of the said reconciliation standing in his way above all, and those of which mention has been made above. And that the said Lord Count Antonio is bound and ought to freely relax, and cause to be relaxed and restored, to the said Lord Francis, the said Castle and Rock of Cantiano, insofar as he holds them occupied and caused to be occupied by the said Lord Count Corrado, or any other person, free and expedited, and vacant and expedited, with its court, right, and whatever appurtenances; and that he allow and permit, and cause to be allowed and permitted, to the said Lord Francis, and that he allow the said Lord Francis to hold and possess them, and to use and enjoy them freely, expeditedly, and peacefully, and without any disturbance or molestation of the said Lord Francis, or of the said Count Corrado, or of any other person. And also we declare that the said Count Corrado, custodian or sequestrator of the said Rock of Cantiano, is bound and ought to restore and assign the said Rock to the said Lord Francis. And the above-mentioned we say, sentence, judge, arbitrate, and declare in every better mode, way, right, form, and cause by which we best can and ought. Now it is asked concerning two things: first, whether the said sentence, or declaration, is null by defect of jurisdiction of the said ten. Second, whether it is null by defect of exercise of jurisdiction, or cognition, of the same ten, especially considering the office of the said Lord Francis during its duration.'

† Regarding the first point, it appears to be the law, having regard to the reasons set forth below. First, having regard to the said compromise made lastly, by which it seems that every preceding compromise is removed. D. de arb. l. sed si in seruum. §. si. cum l. seq. et seq. and l. si quis rem. cum lege non distinguemus. §. compromissum. eo. tit. Second, having regard to the form of the said vicariate reserving the rights of the Roman Church; for the said declaration comes upon ecclesiastical matters, concerning which laymen cannot even dispose in favor, as in c. ecclesia sanctae Mariae. Third, having regard to the form of the same vicariate disposing of the said oath, so that the necessity of obedience removes the cognizance of the said ten, especially by the doctrine of l. non videtur. §. qui iussit. D. de re. iur. Fourth, considering that the novelty of Caetana occurred before the said declaration for two years, or thereabouts; hence any cognizance of the said ten seems to be removed. However, because the aforementioned parties, by not notifying the said ten of the aforementioned novelty by way of cognizance within a year, seem to recede from the said compromise, arg. c. plerunque. de rescrip. Moreover, the said ten, by not cognizing within the said time of a year, seem not to wish to arbitrate, or to accept the arbitration, in which case the compromise does not subsist, arg. l. si. §. sed et si quis. C. de communibus legibus. And thus Bartolus in l. si quis arbitratu. de verb. oblig. Fifth, because from the proemium of the said chapters placed above at the beginning, beginning "orta et c.", it appears that the said chapters were made by the impression of war imminent upon the said Lord Count by the commune of Florence. Cognizance given by impression is null by the law itself, as the laws wish. Sixth, having regard to the form of the said chapters, and especially the said chapter attributing cognizance, etc., because it is attributed upon doubts of the chapters disposing of exiles, or upon those contained in them. The chapters, as I said above, are some disposing of exiles in general and universally, and some particularly concerning Doctor Francesco and the Castle of Caetana. So that the said cognizance coming almost by way of a clause cannot be referred to the said Doctor Francesco and the Castle of Caetana, concerning whom special provision was made. l. doli clausula. de verb. oblig. cum sim. Moreover, in the matter of contracts, ambiguous language must be interpreted against the one inducing the contract, in favor of the other, l. veteribus. D. de pactis. Moreover, the aforementioned contract of the said chapters was of strict law, namely, confirmed by stipulation, in which interpretation must be made not broadly, but strictly, as l. quicquid astringendae. de verb. oblig. Seventh, and lastly, because the chapter disposing of the cognizance of the said ten disposes of doubts occurring upon the said chapters, or contained in them. The aforementioned chapters were not called into doubt by the said Doctor Francesco before the said ten. Moreover, concerning those contained in the same chapters, there is no doubt between the aforementioned parties, because the new fact of the contract of the sale of the said Castle of Caetana, and of the aforementioned ratification, is not contained in the chapters made before: and where the words of the law have place, there the disposition has place. l. ait praetor. §. docere. D. vi bon. rap. and l. si vero. §. de viro. sol. mat. And these things briefly concerning the first step.

The second point also seems established by the text placed in l. pars literarum. D. de iudic. cum sim. Second, from the cause of suspicion of the said ten subjects during the said office of the said Lord Francesco. arg. l. qui iurisditioni. D. de iuris. omn. iud. and de officio praesidis. l. senatusconsulto. Third, and lastly, because the place of Florence, during the said office, is returned to the said Lord Count, and by law can be rendered suspect, as is the text in c. pastoralis. de reg. iur.

It does not obstruct the aforementioned, if it is said that the same Doctor Francesco, at the time of the said chapters, was captain of the people of the city of Florence, because the present office is another in substance and quality, because that one was ordinary, and this one is absolute with bailiwick, etc., and the inference is not correct. l. naturaliter. §. nihil commune. D. de acquir. poss.

It does not obstruct that the commune of Florence is above the said ten, therefore it is not probable, etc., as l. non est verisimile. D. quod met. causa. I answer, because a delegate from the prince, and an ordinary having jurisdiction from a superior, are refused as suspects notwithstanding the aforementioned superiority, as l. apertissimi. and l. cum specialis. C. de iud.

It does not obstruct that the same Lord Count could have foreseen, or imagined, that the said office could correct the said Francesco, because such imagination by law does not remove the aforementioned exceptions, arg. legis pars literarum. cum sim. D. de iudiciis. because always the party could say, you could have imagined these things. Moreover, and holidays induced in honor of God, and also sudden ones, not only can be imagined, but are imagined, and yet exceptions belong to the defendant, therefore, etc. And these things for the information of fact, not of law; but let the most excellent and famous science of the one who ought to advise supply the law.

Proemium of the Sentence.

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of the Blessed and Glorious ever Virgin Mother Mary, and of the whole heavenly court, amen. And to the honor, exaltation, and augmentation of the state of the most holy and blessed in Christ father, and Lord Boniface, by divine providence Pope Ninth, and also of all and each of the parties subscribed below, and of any of the aforementioned parties, and to the tranquil state and pacific condition of the same, amen.

For human nature, constituted in the beginning of its beauty, instructed by divine prudence, fostered peace from the field of the Lord interwoven with flowers of peace, and nourished the concord of the human race in the bosom of tranquility with solicitous ministry. But reconciled by viperous cunning, machinations, and most wicked ambushes, and assailed by growing malice, it escapes its proper bounds, so that our fragility, drunk with errors for so long by diabolical snares, and wrapped in the darkness of sins, and also wandering from the straight path, has preferred the hatred of its neighbor to charity. Hence bodily discord, hence joined malice, hence the roar of wars; war has grown up, then the cruel slaughter of men, the streams of shed blood, and other horrible crimes in innumerable multitude, alas, woe is me, have flowed in and followed.

But our Creator coming, the spark and fountain of peace, and of humility, in the very birth of His nativity, raised up peace in its entirety, when He fulfilled that of Isaiah, beating their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks, and made all that peace hereditary to us as a portion in the eulogy of His death. And although sometimes wars and battles arise suddenly, which even divine justice sometimes permits against the obstinacy of sins, not to claim vengeance for Himself, but to correct and chastise those He loves, and to amend the wicked morals and corrupt customs of men by the scourges of war, nevertheless, by the splendor of His Spirit, often illuminating the minds of men, hostile right hands are often joined among the flashing common swords and flowing streams of blood, and sudden peace changes the rage of war.

Therefore, since in times past, with the adversary fabricating against human salvation, and the tongues of many detractors weaving inexorable strife back and forth, there has been vigor between the parties subscribed below, whose anger we wish to appease, whose fury to mix, and whose rage of war to extinguish, we, Richard Carozolus of Naples, by the grace of God general master of the sacred house of the hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem, and custodian of the poor of Christ, nuncio of the apostolic see; Antoniotus Adornus, by the grace of God Duke of Genoa, as a private person; as well as Petrus Ultramarinus, doctor of laws, Julianus de Castro, formerly of Larizatoli, Leonardus Gentilis, son of Obertus, and Iacobus de Carubio, formerly of Otinus, elected and constituted for the following by the community of Genoa, or by the representatives of the said community in place of the said community, as appears from our election public in the chancery of the ducal commune of Genoa by the hand of Antonius de Credentia, public notary and chancellor of the commune of Genoa, subscribed below, this year on the 29th day of December, Arbiters, arbitrators, amicable composers, and common friends, elected and assumed between the illustrious prince, and great and excellent Lord John Galeazzo, Viscount of Virtue, Lord of Milan, and imperial vicar general, or the respectable and eminent knights Lord Niccolò Spinelli of Naples, doctor of laws, Count of Ibia, and chancellor of the Kingdom of Sicily; and Lord Guglielmo de Bevilacqui, son of the late Lord Francesco, knight, counselors and procurators of the aforementioned illustrious and magnificent Lord John Galeazzo, Lord of Milan, etc., the said procurator for and on behalf of the illustrious and magnificent Lord John Galeazzo, his sons and heirs, and also in the name and on behalf of adherents, accomplices, supporters, and followers, recommendees, well-wishers, and subjects of the aforementioned Magnificent Lord John Galeazzo; and the illustrious and magnificent Lord Francesco de Gonzaga, Lord of Mantua, Imperial Vicar General, or the respectable and eminent knight Lord Filippo de la Molza, and the wise man Lord Giovanni de Bobio, doctor of both laws, procurators of the aforementioned illustrious Lord Francesco de Gonzaga, Lord of Mantua, in the said procuratorial name for the said Lord and his adherents, accomplices, allies, supporters, vassals, followers, recommendees, well-wishers, and subjects; and the magnificent community of men, people, and university of the magnificent city of Perugia, or the respectable knight Lord Niccolò de Balconibus, doctor of laws, and the noble and circumspect man Ser Hugolino Ecchini, honorable citizens of Perugia, syndics and procurators of the said great city of Perugia, in the syndical and procuratorial name of the said community, and in the name and on behalf of all and each of the adherents, accomplices, supporters, allies, well-wishers, followers, recommendees, vassals, and subjects of the said city of Perugia; and also the magnificent community of men, people, and university of the great city of Siena, or the noble and prudent man Bastiano de Piccolomini, citizen of Siena, syndic and procurator of the said great city of men, people, and university of the same great city of Siena, in the syndical and procuratorial name of the said community, and in the name and on behalf of all and each of the adherents, allies, well-wishers, accomplices, supporters, followers, recommendees, vassals, and subjects of the said city of Siena, on one or more parts; and the Magnificent and exalted Commune of Florence, or the eminent and respectable men Lord Filippo de Alimani, knight of Adimari, and Lord Ludovico de Francesco de Albergati, doctor of laws, and Guidone, formerly of Lord Tommaso, honorable citizens of Florence, syndics, procurators, and special nuncios of the said great and exalted Commune of Florence, in the syndical and procuratorial name of the said great people and Commune of Florence, and for the cities, castles, fortresses, lands, and places of the said Commune, or which are held or possessed by the said Commune, and their citizens and district inhabitants, and the same subjects of the Commune of Florence whatsoever, and also in the name and on behalf of all and each of the adherents, accomplices, and followers of the said Commune of Florence; and the Magnificent and powerful Commune of Bologna, or the eminent doctor of laws Lord Tommasino de Sancto Ioanne, and the wise man Hannibale Velandolo de Bentivoglii, honorable citizens of Bologna, syndics and procurators of the said great Commune of Bologna, in the syndical and procuratorial name of the said Commune of Bologna, and for its citizens and district inhabitants, and for the castles, fortresses, lands, and places of the said Commune, which are held or possessed by the said Commune by its subjects of the same Commune of Bologna whatsoever; and also in the gestorial and vicarious name and on behalf of all and each of the allies, adherents, accomplices, followers, and subjects of the aforementioned Commune; and the Magnificent and exalted Lord Francesco Junior de Carrara of Padua, etc., or the eminent men Lord Michele, formerly of Antonius de Rabata, citizen of Florence, valiant knight, and Lord Francesco de Consilii of Padua, doctor of laws, procurators and special nuncios of the aforementioned great Lord Francesco de Carrara Junior, in the procuratorial name of the said Lord Francesco, and for his civil, district, and territorial subjects, and for the castles, fortresses, lands, and places of the said Lord Francesco, or which are held or possessed by the said Lord Francesco, and his subjects of the said Lord Francesco whatsoever, and also in the vicarious and gestorial name of his adherents, accomplices, followers, and recommendees, or subjects; and also all the said syndics and procurators of the said Communes of Florence and Bologna, and of Lord Francesco de Carrara aforesaid, and in the name and on behalf of the illustrious and exalted Lord Alberto, Marquis of Este, for the said Marquis, and his lands, subjects, adherents, accomplices, allies, and auxiliaries; and the Magnificent Lords Astorgio de Mauffredi of Faenza, and Bernardino, and Eustachio, and their brothers de Polenta of Ravenna, etc., and Lord Ludovico de Aldobrandini of Imola, and their allies; and also in the name and on behalf of all other allies, adherents, and accomplices of the said Magnificent Communes of Florence and Bologna, and of Lord Francesco aforesaid, and of each of them, and for the said allies, adherents, and accomplices, and their lands, subjects, adherents, and followers, all together, syndics and procurators aforesaid, in the said modes and names, on one part and for the other part, as appears from the compromise made in us, contained in several public instruments of the same tenor, composed and requested by the public notaries subscribed below, namely: Niccolò Iacopo de Sportionibus, secretary of our said Master of the Hospital of Jerusalem, Catelano de Christianis, citizen of Cremona, and Lippo Nacelli, citizen of Florence, Giovanni Francesco Niccolò, citizen of Padua, and Antonius de Credentia, commissioner of our Lord Duke, public notaries, this year on the 26th day of the month of December, in the 12th indiction, according to the course of the year, at the fourth hour of the night, in the city of Genoa.

Having seen, and diligently inspected, by us the said compromise with the power attributed to us by virtue of the said compromise; having seen the rights of the said parties, and of each of them, petitioned and exposed before us by petitions and writings exhibited and produced, as well as responses and exceptions made on both sides; and all those things which the said parties, and each of them, wished to say, produce, and expose before us, once and many times, orally and in writing, without observing the order of law, and proceeding in an equitable and amicable manner, desiring to lead the said discordant parties to an amicable peace, and good and true concord, as in the present Sentence.

CASE.

Invoking the name of Christ, and always having God before our eyes and in our mind, we all three concordantly say, sentence, declare, arbitrate, and arbitrate, establish, order, and command, that below, namely, there be and ought to be good, true, and sincere peace between the said parties, and each of them, to last perpetually, and remission of injuries, wounds, burnings, damages, robberies, and any offenses whatsoever, and however made, given, or inflicted between the said parties, and each of them, and any of the said parties in their persons or things. And reserving the rights, if any, which the said illustrious Lord Count of Virtue has against the aforementioned Magnificent Lord Marquis of Este of Ferrara, etc., and conversely, reserving the rights, if any, which the said Lord Marquis has against the said Lord Count above: also remission of bans and forestations given and made, or given and made, by any magistrate of one of the parties against the subjects of the other party, secretly or openly, by any or some of them.

Moreover, we say, sentence, pronounce, declare, arbitrate, and arbitrate, establish, and order, that the city of Padua with the castles, lands, villages, and places which are held or possessed by the said Magnificent Lord Francesco Junior de Carrara, remain free to the said Lord Francesco in that state, degree, and condition in which it now is, or they are.

Moreover, we say, sentence, pronounce, declare, arbitrate, establish, and order, that all and each of the lands, cities, castles, and territories which are held and possessed by the aforementioned illustrious Lord Count of Virtue, both in the territory of Padua and in the March of Treviso, or elsewhere, whatever they may be, and of whatever origin, and wherever they may be, remain free to the aforementioned Lord Count.

Moreover, having regard that the aforementioned illustrious Lord Count of Virtue, at the time when he was in possession of the city of Padua, was dispossessed of the said city and other lands and castles which are held and possessed by the said Magnificent Lord Francesco, which remain to the said Lord Francesco by virtue of the present peace: we condemn, and pronounce condemned, the said Lord Francesco to give and pay to the aforementioned illustrious Lord Count, or his heirs, or legitimate person for him, or having or to have cause from him, for the damage and interest of the aforementioned dispossession, ten thousand gold florins each year on the day of the nativity of Saint John the Baptist, until the complete and entire quantity of five hundred thousand gold florins is reached; beginning the said time of the year from the day of the pronouncement of the present sentence. Which payments, if he does not make, or cause to be made, as above, he falls from the benefit of the present pact, nor can any of his allies swear to him in any manner that can be said or imagined, as above, under the penalty contained in the compromise. And furthermore, they are understood to have contravened, if in the said case they should give aid, counsel, or favor to the said Lord Francesco.

Moreover, we sentence, pronounce, declare, and arbitrate, establish, and command, that Lord Francesco de Carrara aforesaid permit the noble Lord Aliduxius de Monte Merlo, the nobles of Campo Sancti Petri, Master Marsilio de Sancta Sophia, and the sons of Ubertino de Grango of Parma, commissioner, and sons, and all others existing in the territory or in the service of the Lord Count, or who adhered to the said Lord Count, whether they are natives or inhabitants of Padua, and any other subjects of the aforementioned Lord Count, who have houses or possessions acquired by just title in Padua or its district; and especially Milanus de Malabardis, and father, and Lord Bonromeus de Bonromeis of Sancto Miniano, inhabitants of Padua, and all elected subjects, or adherents, or followers of the aforementioned Lord Count, who possessed any goods in Padua or its district by just title, to freely enjoy their said goods and rights existing in Padua or the Paduan territory, as far as the fact of the Magnificent Lord of Padua is concerned; and to collect from any of their debtors any quantities of money to which they were bound. That they be freely canceled and exempted from all bans, processes, and personal condemnations which were made or would be made against the aforementioned, or any or some of the aforementioned, without any payment of money. And that the aforementioned, and any of the aforementioned, may sell and extract fruits of any kind of their possessions, and lead them to any parts, as any citizen of Padua may; and that they may alienate their goods and dispose of them at their will. And that concerning the question of the said Milanus de Malabardis, which is moved against him in Venice by the said Lord Francesco, justice be done to him; however, that they may not go, nor be received in the Paduan lands which are held or possessed by the said Lord Count without the license of Lord Francesco.

Moreover, we sentence, pronounce, declare, arbitrate, arbitrate, order, establish, and command, that the aforementioned illustrious Lord Count and Magnificent Lord Francesco may not build, or cause to be built, in any territory not their own without the will of him to whom it belongs. In their own territories, however, each may cause to be built at his will.

Moreover, we say, sentence, and arbitrate, establish, and command, that the places of Correggio, and the lords of the said places, be returned and be with effect to the illustrious Lord Count of Virtue in that state, degree, and condition in which they were before they adhered to the Commune of Bologna. And that the said Lord Count receive and treat the said lords and place benignly, and admit them as dear and well-wishing, as he held and treated them before, and restore them to their goods, and remit to them any rancors and hatreds which he had hitherto taken against them in any way. And concerning the aforementioned place and lord, the Commune of Bologna shall henceforth not intermeddle.

Moreover, we say, sentence, pronounce, arbitrate, and arbitrate, establish, and command, that all lands, castles, fortresses, and places with their appurtenances taken, occupied, or invaded since the time of the league made in Pisa aforesaid by the Florentines, or their people, to the Commune of Siena, or its people, or their allies, or adherents, who ought to come into the present peace, be freely restored to the said Commune of Siena, or legitimate person or persons for the said Commune, or allies, or adherents aforesaid. And conversely, that all lands, castles, fortresses, and places with their appurtenances taken, occupied, or invaded since the time of the said league made in Pisa aforesaid by the Commune of Siena, or its people, to the Commune of Florence, or its people, or its allies, or adherents, who ought to come into the preceding peace, be freely restored to the said Commune of Florence, or its allies, or adherents aforesaid. And this within two months next coming. Excepting the place and land of Monte Publicano with its appurtenances; and the places and land of Lucignano of Arezzo, which shall not come, nor be understood to come, into the aforementioned restitution, but shall remain as they are, until provision is made by us, the aforementioned arbitrators, as to what is to be done concerning the said places and lands; to whose provision, deliberation, or declaration to be made concerning the said lands, each party, and each of the said parties, shall stand tacit and content, and tacit and content always and whenever it is made; notwithstanding that the term of the compromise had elapsed, and even if any of the said parties contradicted the present arbitration, or provision, and declaration to be made.

Moreover, we arbitrate, pronounce, sentence, and command, that all lands, fortresses, places, and castles taken or occupied since the time of the said league made in Pisa aforesaid by the Commune of Perugia, or its people, to the Commune of Florence and the Lord of Cortona, or their allies, or adherents, be restored to the said Commune of the Florentines and the Lord of Cortona within two months next coming. And conversely, let them be restored and relaxed.

Moreover, we arbitrate, pronounce, sentence, and command, that all castles, lands, fortresses, and places taken or occupied since the said time of the league aforesaid, as above, by the Commune of Florence, or its people, to the Lords of Petramala, or their people, be freely restored to the said Lords within two months next coming.

Moreover, we say, sentence, pronounce, arbitrate, arbitrate, establish, order, and command, that the Commune of Florence, or the Commune of Siena, or the Commune of Perugia, or the Lord of Cortona, or any or any of them, may not, nor ought to, receive, or cause to be received, or permit in their lands or places, or of their allies, or adherents, any exile of the adverse party, nor give them aid or favor to the prejudice, damage, or offense of the adverse party. The aforementioned communities and Lord, and each of them, are nevertheless bound to restore any of their exiles on account of the present war, as to possessions and movable goods which exist, and to absolve them from any bans and forestations, provided they do not go upon the territories from which they were banned or forested, or present themselves in the said lands and places, or of the said Lords' places.

Moreover, we sentence, arbitrate, pronounce, order, establish, and command, that the aforementioned Illustrious Lord Count may not intermeddle in the parts, or any part of Tuscany, namely: beyond the Frigidus River towards Tuscany, except as and as is contained in the said league made at Pisa aforesaid.

Moreover, that the Communes of Florence and Bologna may not, or either of them may, intermeddle otherwise or in another way in the parts of Lombardy or the March of Treviso, except as the said Lord Count in the parts of Tuscany by virtue of the preceding chapter, except in the territory of Bologna, or its district.

Moreover, we say, pronounce, and command, that each party shall cause the present peace to be published in their cities and lands on the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary next coming. From that day forward, let each abstain from offenses both at sea and on land.

Moreover, that if from the day of the compromise made in us aforesaid until the day of publishing the present peace in the cities and places of the said parties, it should happen, or has happened, that any of the said parties, or any of the said parties, has taken, or occupied, or takes, or occupies, any or some lands, castles, places, or fortresses of the other party, or of any of the other party, such lands, castles, fortresses, and places so taken or occupied, as above, shall be restored, and ought to be restored, the said spoils, and to each of them.

Moreover, we say, sentence, pronounce, establish, order, and command, that neither of the parties, nor any of the said parties, shall permit in their territories, to the best of their ability and in good faith, to gather any armed men in the manner of a society or company going out of their said territories into the territory of the other party, or of any of the said parties, against the will of the said other party, or of any of the said parties, to give passage or victuals to any armed men who wish to enter Lombardy or Italy, of whatever condition they may be; and especially by bridges, waters, and other passages which can be prohibited, but they are bound to prohibit the said passages to the said men to the best of their ability and in good faith. If anyone contravenes, he falls from the benefit of the present peace, nor can anyone of his allies aid him.

Moreover, since the city of Lucca is friendly and amicable to the aforementioned parties; and since the territory and district of the same city is contiguous to the territories and districts of the same, for which reason if the said city, or its territory, or district, were invaded or offended in any way, it could easily come to damage to the territories of the aforementioned parties, or of any of them, from which war and discord could arise between the said parties. Therefore, we sentence, arbitrate, pronounce, arbitrate, command, and declare, that the aforementioned city of Lucca with all its appurtenances be, and be understood to be, included in the present peace, so that it may enjoy and have all the immunities, graces, favors, prerogatives, and benefits of any kind of the said peace, with which any of the aforementioned parties may enjoy and have.

Moreover, because by the aforementioned syndics and procurators many things were petitioned on both sides before us, concerning which it was not possible for us to pronounce on account of the brevity of time, we condemn, and pronounce condemned, the said syndics and procurators of the said Magnificent Communes of Florence and Bologna, and of the said Magnificent Lord Francesco de Carrara, in the said syndical and procuratorial names, to give and pay to the said Lord Count one hundred thousand gold florins. Saved and reserved, if they, in the said names, have prorogated the term of the compromise made in us by one month next coming. And conversely, we condemn, and pronounce condemned, the aforementioned procurators of the aforementioned Lord Count, in the said procuratorial name, and by them the said Lord Count, and the said syndics and procurators of the Magnificent Communes of Perugia and Siena, and of the said Lord of Mantua, in the said syndical and procuratorial names, to give and pay to the said Communes of Florence and Bologna, and to Lord Francesco de Carrara aforesaid, one hundred thousand gold florins. Saved and reserved, as above, if they, in the said procuratorial and syndical names, have prorogated the term of the compromise made in us by one month next coming. And beyond the said penalties, we approve, admit, and accept any petitions of the prorogating party, and we reject and reprobate those parties who do not prorogue, or who have not prorogated. Reserving to ourselves the power and bailiwick to say, pronounce, sentence, cognize, and arbitrate, and arbitrate, correct and remedy, condemn and absolve, once and many times; and concerning those already pronounced, according to the bailiwick granted to us by virtue of the said compromise, and for the whole time of the said compromise. Commanding all and each of the aforementioned to be observed by the said parties, and each of them, and any of the said parties, under the penalty contained in the said compromise, and under the penalty of contravening the said peace. Commanding also that public instruments of the same tenor be made of all and each of the aforementioned by Iacopo de Sportonibus of Bergamo, secretary and notary of our said Master of the Hospital of Jerusalem, and by Antonius de Credentia, formerly of Corrado, chancellor of our said Lord Duke, public notaries subscribed above, and one of the same.

Laid down, given, and pronounced, and laid down, given, and pronounced were by the said Reverend and Magnificent Lords arbitrators and arbitrators sitting on the tribunal in the place subscribed below, and read, and published, and published by us, the said notaries, in the city of Genoa, and in the great new hall of the Ducal Palace of the Commune of Genoa, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1392, in the 14th indiction, according to the course of Genoa, on the 20th day of the month of January, before the third hour of the night, in the pontificate of the aforementioned most holy Lord our Lord Boniface, by divine providence Pope Ninth, in the year 3, present witnesses specially called and requested: the eminent man Lord Raphael Adorno, administrator of the Castle of the Kingdom, brother of the aforementioned Magnificent Lord Duke; the noble and wise man Lord Tommaso de Spina, doctor of laws; Lord Himerico de Illionibus, doctor of laws; Lord Giorgio Honesto, doctor of laws; Lord Benedetto de Viali, doctor of laws; Lord Master Andrea de Eptralita, physician; Martino Maruso; Nicolao Fatinaci, notary; Raphael de Laurentiis; Ioan de Pinis; Raphael Vatatio of Naples; Antonius de Fiesco; Tereliano Spinola; Clemente de Facio; Carolo Capitaneo; and Corrado Mazuro, notary and chancellor of the Commune of Genoa, all citizens of Genoa.

Furthermore, to all and each of the aforementioned, I say, on the day, hour, and place, and in the presence of the said witnesses, the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Brother Raymundus de Vinea of Capua, of the Order of Preachers, General Minister of the said Order, present there, having apostolic authority in and over all the aforementioned from the aforementioned most holy Lord our Pope, by virtue of certain apostolic letters granted to the said Lord Brother Raymundus, which we, the notaries subscribed below, saw, read, and inspected, sealed with the true and known public bull of our said Lord Pope, dated at Rome at Saint Peter, in the Kalends of June, in the second year of the pontificate of our said Lord Pope, interposed and interposes the said authority, and having premised canonical monition before us by him, he interdicts and interdicts from now on, and in this manner, the party not observing all and each of the aforementioned pronounced, commended, commanded, arbitrated, arbitrated, declared, and established by the said Lords arbitrators aforesaid: if it is a singular person, by excommunication; if communities, universities, or lords, by suspension and interdict in their lands, cities, and places, after fifteen days have passed, of which five for the first, five for the second, and the remaining five days for the third and peremptory term, he assigned. This canonical monition being premised after the said sentence, and if they have not observed any of the aforementioned, he promulgated the sentences, the absolution from which he reserved to himself and his superior only.

And thus I say and advise, I, Baldo de Perusio, doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the lessee is liable for a fire occurring in the leased premises.
2. When the lessee is liable for damage to the leased property.
body: The facts of the case are as follows: a fire occurred in a house that had been leased to Master Angelo, a lodger. The question is,

Whether the lessee is bound to make good the damage. And it seems that the lessee is not liable for an accident, as in *l. si quis fundum*, § *Imperator*, D. locati et conducti. But fault is not presumed unless it is proved, just as fraud is not, as in *l. quotiens*, § *qui dolo*, D. de probat. Therefore, etc. Moreover, wherever anyone uses a thing for its intended purpose, he is not liable for the peril, as in *l. eum qui*, in principio, D. comm. sed Angelus used this lodging for its intended purpose; indeed, he used it for the same purpose for which the owner used it. For he used that hearth for cooking, just as the owner had previously used it; therefore, by using it in the manner in which the owner did, Angelus is not at fault; therefore, he is not liable, as in the aforementioned § *Imperator*. Moreover, even if fault could be imputed, it would be very slight, because he was not diligent in seeing and ascertaining whether the hearth was sufficient for preparing food for the guest; and the lessee is not liable for very slight fault, as in D. comm., *l. si ut certo*, § *nunc videndum*. Therefore, etc. Moreover, this case seems to be addressed in *l. videamus*, § 1, D. locati et conducti, where, if it was agreed that he should not have fire, and he had fire, and subsequently a fire occurs, he is liable. This is presumed in doubt by a noble presumption of law, as in *l. merito*, D. pro socio.

Notwithstanding these arguments, it must be said without doubt the contrary. And for clarity, it should be known that the lessee is liable for the safekeeping of the thing, as in *l. itaque fullo*, in principio, D. de furt., and *l. si quis fundum*, § *Imperator*, D. locati et conducti. Now, Bartolus says in *l. si quis ex argentariis*, § *fi.*, D. de eden., that when it is established that a fire occurred in the leased house, and it does not appear how it happened—because this case does not easily occur without someone’s fault—and this is the ordinary gloss in *l. si modo nulla*, D. de leg. 1, and it is the text in *l. si vendita*, D. de peric. et comm. rei vend., and in *l. 3*, D. de off. praef. vigil.—if, therefore, the lessee, to whom safekeeping pertains, alleges this accident, the lessee’s fault is presumed to have caused it, unless he proves that it happened by chance. *l. 1*, D. de cust. et exhib. re., as in *l. si a bonae fidei*, § 1, D. de rei vend., and in *l. si quis fundum*, § *Imperator*, and there, *casus*, D. loc. et condu. Since, therefore, the lessee alleges that a fire occurred, and this is established, and it does not appear from where it arose, the lessee’s fault is presumed; therefore, he is liable to make good the damage, as in the aforementioned § *Imperator*, unless he proves chance.

There are certain accidents which regularly occur without anyone’s fault, such as the force of a river and the attack of enemies; then, unless it is established that an accident occurred, chance is presumed, unless fault is proved, as in *l. contractus*, D. de re iud., and *l. si merces*, D. loc. et condu. Moreover, the gloss says in *l. omnia*, § *species*, that if the lessee, or another to whom it pertains to keep the thing, alleges chance, he must prove the chance; otherwise, it is presumed to have happened through his fraud; it would be better to say that it happened through the fault of the custodian. And he cites *l. si quis fundum*, § *Imperator*, D. loc. et conducti, and *l. si*, § *fi.*, D. de cust. et exhib. re. Moreover, does the text not say in *l. 1*, D. de off. praef. urb., that although a fire occurs in a house, it is nevertheless presumed to have happened through the fault of the inhabitant?

† Hence I draw the following distinction, from which all the aforementioned arguments are derived. Either it is established that the fire occurred by fortuitous accident, and the lessee is not liable, as stated in the cited § Imperator and § Nunc videndum; or it is established that it occurred through the fraud or fault of the lessee, and he is liable to repair the damage; or it is doubtful, and it is presumed that it occurred through the fault of the lessee. And unless he proves fortuitous accident, he is liable, as stated in the cited § Imperator and the laws cited above, and in the gloss to § Species, and there noted by Bartolus in § Si modo. Now, I respond individually to the contrary objections: To the first, I admit that the lessee is not liable for accident, as in § Imperator; but he is liable for slight fault. But the fire is presumed to have occurred through the slight fault of the lessee, as in § Imperator. The objection from l. Quotiens, § Qui dolo, does not hold, because I say that it is true that fraud is not presumed; but because a fire does not usually occur easily without the fault of someone, it is presumed to have occurred through the slight fault of the lessee. Therefore, he is liable, as by the laws cited. Moreover, it is true that fault is not presumed, unless an external fact indicates fault, as argued from l. Si non convitiis, C. de iniuriis. Now, a fire occurring in a leased dwelling indicates the slight fault of the lessee, to whom the custody pertains; since a fire does not easily occur without the slight fault of the inhabitant, as by the laws cited above. Therefore, the fault of the lessee is presumed. The further objection, where one uses a thing for its intended purpose, that he is not liable for the peril of fortuitous accident, as in l. Eum qui, in principio, previously cited, is true if the user is in no fault; otherwise, the user is liable for the peril of fortuitous accident, as in the cited l. Eum qui, in principio. For if this lessee is presumed to have been in slight fault, since the fire occurred—which cannot easily happen without the slight fault of the inhabitants, by legal presumption—therefore the lessee is liable. The objection that he used fire in the same manner as the owner did, does not excuse him; for he ought to use it in the manner that diligent men do, and to guard the house as diligent men of his condition would do; otherwise, he is in slight fault, as in l. Quod natura, ff. de deposito. For it is not presumed that he acted without fault, since the fire occurred, which does not usually happen without the slight fault of the inhabitant. Moreover, either it appears that the fire arose from a defect in the hearth; yet he is presumed to be in slight fault, since the fire occurred, because he did not diligently guard whether the hearth was sufficient for the fire he was making or not, as any diligent person would have done. Nor does it follow that the owner made a fire on this hearth for a long time. This does not excuse the lessee from slight fault; for even assuming that the owner was not diligent, nevertheless this lessee must be diligent in the leased thing, as any other diligent person would have been; otherwise, he is in slight fault. For slight fault in another's things is thus defined: it is an inconsiderate deviation from that

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The fire whose fault is presumed to have occurred.
body: The diligence which careful men of that condition and profession exercise, as stated by Bartolus in *l. quod nerva*, D. de deposito. Therefore, the lessee is not excused from slight fault if he uses the thing as the owner did; rather, he must use it as any careful man of the same condition would use it. This is not presumed to have been done due to the fire that occurred, which does not usually happen without the slight fault of the inhabitants. Moreover, it appears that he used the leased thing in a different manner than the owner, because he made a larger fire than the owner. Also, it extended further beyond the hearth. Also, beneath the hearth this man placed a grate, which the owner did not have; indeed, the owner had only a stone. And it catches fire more easily in grates than if there had been no grate. And a careful man would not likely have done this. From these circumstances, not only is slight fault presumed against the lessee, but the slight fault of the lessee is also proven. Or, if it does not appear that it arose from a defect in the hearth, nor does it appear from elsewhere that the fire occurred, then the slight fault of the lessee is presumed, unless a fortuitous event is proven, according to the laws cited above. No other motive is objected. However, this man is in very slight fault, since he was merely negligent in not considering whether the beam was sufficient to bear the fire which the lessee made there daily. Solution,

† Since a fire does not usually occur without the slight fault of the inhabitant, it is presumed to have occurred through slight fault, unless a fortuitous event is proven, as stated in the cited § Imperator and there by Bartolus. Moreover, it does not appear that it arose from a defect in the fireplace, and since it does not appear from where it arose, the slight fault of the lessee is presumed. Furthermore, this negligence in not watching, etc., constitutes slight fault, because any diligent person would not have done so. Hence, it is slight fault, as is evident from the definition of slight fault. The last objection in § 1 of the law Videamus does not hold, because the text states that he made an innocent fire, and thus it is established there that the fire occurred without fault, but by a fortuitous accident. However, in doubt, since a fire has occurred, the slight fault of the lessee is presumed, in that he did not guard the leased thing as any diligent person would have. The objection from the law Merito, where in doubt one is not presumed to be at fault, is true, unless an external intervening fact induces a presumption to the contrary, which is the case here, as I have fully proven above. From all of which it clearly appears that the contrary determination has no foundation in law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Opinion of Master Signorini of the Homodei family, in support of the aforementioned opinion of Baldus.
2. Whether an action in rem hypothecaria may be brought against a third-party possessor.
3. When a lawsuit is said to be pending (lis mota).
4. Whether words uttered for another purpose serve as proof.
5. How the records of a case are to be proved.
6. Whether an erroneous confession by a procurator prejudices the principal.
7. Whether a negative may be proved.
8. Possession is lost after ten years.
9. Prescription does not run while the inheritance lies vacant.
body: A case actually arising in fact is as follows: For example, Titius, after a long time had elapsed, took a wife, namely Seia, and received from her a certain sum of money by way of dowry. Subsequently, by way of dowry, he delivered certain goods to one of his daughters, fictitiously constituting himself as holding them in the name of her husband, not truly. Then, after Titius died, and Seia left the aforementioned daughter and another son, the said daughter together with her husband truly gave the said goods, worth 400 florins, as a pledge to someone for the occasion of 80 florins, although a simulated sale had intervened between them, together with an agreement and license to repurchase within a certain time. And the said creditor, in place of usury, demands 116 florins or thereabouts successively. Without considering the aforementioned matters, he sold the said goods for the price of 100 florins to someone actually holding the said goods. After these things were thus done, the aforementioned son, observing the fraud committed against his sister, as heir of Seia, his mother, to whom the said goods were obligated on account of her dowry, filed a complaint in a real hypothecary action against the said external possessor. On the occasion of this complaint, the necessary proceedings were conducted in the process for the aforementioned case. Now it is brought into doubt what the duties of the judge should be in the aforementioned case. And it seems to be said that Titius ought to be absolved for the reasons set forth below.

† First, in a hypothecary action, the property of the principal debtor must first be exhausted before recourse is had to external possessors of the pledge, as stated in the law *ut autem hoc si debitor*, Codex, *De pignoribus*. Second, because it does not appear here that the litigation was formally joined (*litem contestatam*), it necessarily follows that there must be an absolution from the observance of the judgment, as stated in law 1, Codex, *De litis contestatione*; and law *prolatam*, Codex, *De sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum*; and chapter 1, *Ut litis non contestatae*. Third, because the defendant, together with those from whom he derives his title, held the property in good faith and with title for a period of ten years and more, he is protected by the aid of prescription, as stated in laws 1 and 2, Codex, *Si adversus creditorem*. Nevertheless, notwithstanding these points, the contrary is true in law, for the sake of which I will first found the plaintiff’s claim. Second, I will respond to the allegations raised in opposition to the opposing arguments.

I take the first point: for in the case assumed, there exists a dowry credit; the cause and possession on the part of the defendant were such that the properties in question were among the assets of the debtors at the time the obligation was contracted, which alone are sufficient to obtain success in the action brought, as stated in the law *et quae nondum*, section *quod dicitur*; and the law *si fundus*, section *in venditione*, Digest, *De pignoribus*; and the law *pignoris persecutio*, with the law *si ergo*, and others.

I take the second point, for the sake of which I assume as a fact that although the exhaustion of assets did not precede the filing of the libel, it nevertheless followed in a solemn and legitimate manner, with superfluous formalities omitted, as is evidently gathered from the proceedings. But it is doubtful to no one that when the right to sue supervenes, even after the litigation has been joined, provided it supervenes from a cause arising from the past within the same instance, condemnation may follow, and there is no need for a new interpellation, as stated in the law *si rem*, section *si*, Digest, *De pignoratitia actione*; and Digest, *Mandati*; the law *si mandauero tibi, vt actio*; and the law *si in diem*, Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*; and fully in the law *non potest*, Digest, *De iudiciis*. Therefore, much more strongly in this case, since the right to sue existed prior to the filing of the libel, the exercise of which right was not free, and becomes free after the judgment is accepted, and thus the first motive does not stand in the way. Moreover, the omission of the exhaustion of assets does not render the judgment null by operation of law, but the law grants the faculty of raising an exception, namely, if the judgment has not been commenced, to impede the proceedings in the manner of a dilatory exception; but if the judgment has been commenced, it operates as a peremptory exception to avoid a condemnatory sentence, according to the common opinion of all. But in this case, the exception was not raised before the litigation was joined, but afterwards, in the manner of a dilatory exception, and consequently it was raised ineptly. Therefore, it does not avail the one raising the exception, according to our note in law 1, Digest, *De exceptionibus*. Moreover, even if it had been raised as a peremptory exception, it was nevertheless raised after all the necessary acts of the case had been completed, and for caution, with no intervening act, legitimate execution was immediately sought after the exception was raised. Therefore, it is very admirable why there should be any doubt about this among persons of sound mind.

The second motive does not stand, for the sake of which I also assume as a fact that when the opposing party requested that the present question be committed to three good men according to the form of the decree then in force, they raised an exception proposing that the litigation had been initiated already after 57 days or thereabouts had elapsed, but between the parties the commission must be requested to be made within 20 useful days from the day the litigation was initiated, according to the form of the aforementioned decree, as appears from the proceedings.

† From which it appears that the opposing party confessed that the case had been litis contestatio before the positions and other necessary acts, since a case is said to be initiated only when the litigation is merely contested. The case is found in the chapter *Ex parte*, Extra, *De verborum significatione*, according to the letter. And the text joined with the gloss in *L. 1*, C., *De praescriptione longi temporis*. And it appears according to the sense: because the offering of the libellus is made to the judge, and for so much it can be done summarily and informally, as *L. Miles*, § *Lex*, ff., *De adulteriis*. Therefore, still between the parties the case is not initiated, nor anything demanded from the defendant, so much so that he is not constituted, as if interpellated, in delay, except by contumacy, but only by a preceding interrogation and the subsequent response of the defendant. Argument from *L. Amplius non peti*, ff., *Rem ratam habere*; *L. Denuntiasse*, in principle, ff., *De adulteriis*. Nor does it object that it is said, the case before the litis contestatio and after, as noted by the gloss in *L. Causas, vel lites*, C., *De transactionibus*, because it is true that the case is said, but it is not yet considered that the case is initiated between both parties, as was confessed from the opposite side by the laws alleged. And similarly it is responded to the statement of Bartolus alleged from the opposite side by making a difference, whether the word of litigation or question is pronounced by law or by man, etc., as noted by him in the aforementioned *L. Amplius non peti*. Also in the same act, and in many others, if the process is well examined, the opposing party confesses that the cause and question exist. And the cause is never said unless the litigation is contested, as holds the ordinary gloss in the aforementioned *L. Causas, vel lites*, especially because it is added, and the question. For the conjunction, and its nature, must be placed between different things, and it appears that the words were spoken to the effect of preventing the commission from being made to three good men, as if the term had elapsed, which did not begin except from the time of the litis contestatio.

† Nor does the objection hold, which is raised that the aforementioned enunciative words, uttered primarily for another purpose, do not induce a disposition, as in l. ex his verbis, C. de testamento militum, together with similar authorities. I concede that the preceding words do not induce a contestation of proof according to the time of the utterance of the contradiction made on the day mentioned in those narrative words; but rather a contestation of proof made retroactively during those days referred to in the records received, as argued in l. pub., §. fin., ff. de depositione. And this is so because those words were uttered narratively by way of cause, and upon these the entire contradiction then issued was founded, as argued strongly in the Clementina Literis, de probat. Although it would be otherwise if the enunciative words had been uttered merely demonstratively and for another purpose, as argued in the chapter Si Papa, de privilegiis, lib. 6.

† Likewise, it is not an objection that it is alleged that the acts of the case are proved only by written instrument, because rather they are also proved by other legitimate documents, for example by the confession of a party, as is gathered in the chapter *Quoniam contra falsam*, *de probat.*; especially according to Innocentius at the end of the said chapter, in the gloss at the end which begins, *legitimis documentis*; and according to the gloss in the chapter *Si*, *de probat.*, in the gloss *alioquin*, etc.

† Furthermore, it is not to the point that it is objected that an erroneous confession by a procurator does not prejudice the principal who proves the contrary, even if made in the manner of a contentious jurisdiction, as was the case in our matter, because it was made in the form of a contentious trial, and in a contentious trial, and by necessity causing the matter to be committed to three good men, as in l. non solum, in the beginning, in the gloss, ff. de procuratoribus, and l. certum, §. sed an ipso, ff. de confessionibus, etc., and the contrary is evidently asserted and proven from an inspection of the records,

† because the negative is sometimes rendered probable by an inspection of the written record, as is gathered in l. Titiae textores, D. de legatis 1, and there noted by the commentators. Moreover, the contrary is stated, unless the procurator is under a principal debtor, which depends on a future dominion, regarding which the procurator can claim ignorance. But in our case, the procurator was always in court, and he confesses regarding such an act, which depends on his own fact, regarding which he cannot claim ignorance; for example, if the litigation was initiated by him, or words importing this, it will prejudice the principal indiscriminately, and such confession must be adhered to. And thus it is understood in the passage moved by Signorinus de Homodeis in l. Titiae textores, D. de legatis 1, and more fully in l. Hoc iure, D. de verbis obligatis, and by Laurentius in l. 1, C. de erroribus advocatorum, etc. Which, responding briefly, I weigh, that where doubt would arise whether the act, according to the present time, is or is not a written *litis contestatio*, I admit that this is probable affirmatively and negatively from an inspection of the writing; but in this case, that is not brought into doubt; rather, it is asked whether, within the term fixed for the defendant to respond to the libel, a response was made or not, in which case the negative is not proven by an inspection of the writing: since, according to the present time, it is not found described in the acts, therefore the *lis* was not contested by the defendant. Therefore, it must be proven otherwise, indirectly, as in l. Optimam, C. de contrahenda stipulatione; otherwise, the confession of the procurator is adhered to, therefore also the *litis contestatio*.

Secondly, principally, the *litis contestatio* is collected from another point incontrovertibly, for the sake of which I suppose that a statute is in force in this city, which provides that, when a petition is offered to the judge, he shall give a copy to the present defendant, and shall fix a term of one useful day for responding to said libel, which having elapsed without a response following, the *lis* shall be held as contested. Therefore, since the form of said statute was totally observed, the *lis* is held as contested.

It does not obstruct that which is objected, that the plaintiff was a canon not subject to this statute; because, since the plaintiff has need to follow the forum of the defendant, in which case statutes ordering the judgment, which are in the place of the judgment, must be observed, and the judgment regulated according to them, without considering the person of the plaintiff. Therefore, the aforementioned motive does not obstruct.

It does not obstruct that the statute of this city specially provides that clerics shall have right rendered according to the mode and form according to which it is rendered to a layman against a cleric by the lord bishop or his vicar; for I admit that where the defendant, within the statutory term of one useful day, had immediately contradicted, alleging his benefit, then that motive would proceed; but in this case, he voluntarily accepted the term of one useful day, and consequently tacitly consented, arg. c. Si tibi absenti, in fine, de prebendis, lib. 6. And what is more, the defendant simply responded to the positions without any exception appended, which are not done unless there is *litis contestatio*, and consequently, by the consent of both plaintiff and defendant, renunciation was made to this statute. And it is doubtful to no one that, since this statute was devised in favor of the layman, it could be renounced by the layman, lest that which was introduced in favor of someone should redound to his detriment. Also, it was probable for the judge to be ignorant that the agent was a cleric; hence, licitly, according to the form of the aforementioned statute, the judgment could and ought to be terminated.

It does not obstruct, if it is said according to the foregoing, that by the lapse of forty days the instance was finished according to the form of the statutes of this city; because it must be noted that, when *litis contestatio* was sought on the part of the plaintiff, because the debt was to be committed to three good men according to the decree of the magnificient lords, our lords, it was opposed on the part of the defendant that he was a cleric, and consequently he could not use the benefit of the common statutes of Papal law against his will. Hence, immediately, by the benefit of the statute alleged above, the instance began to be regulated according to common law, according to which common law lasts for a space of three years, as in l. Properandum, C. de iudiciis. Moreover, since the exception of *litis contestatio* was opposed to the process, the judge could not proceed to the examination and decision of the principal cause, unless first these emerging exceptions were discussed and decided. Therefore, the forty useful days are not yet finished, since a useful day is considered to be that case in which the hands of the judge are not bound, and his power is free for the discussion and decision of the cause, therefore, etc.

Thirdly, principally, *litis contestatio* is collected from another point, because, upon the libel being offered, and the aforementioned term fixed, and the copy of the libel having been obtained, further positions were made by the plaintiff containing the whole tenor of the libel, and since the defendant responded simply, therefore, etc., as was well alleged orally in this passage before.

I take the third point, and first, since prescription of long time without positions does not proceed, as in l.
