Et sine positionibus, D. de usucapionibus, cum si, and since that position was not capitulated nor proven, the aid of prescription ceases. It does not obstruct that which is alleged, namely, that at the time the dowry was constituted for the daughter, Lord Albert possessed, as is proven by the witnesses of the plaintiff, and consequently, by the constitution, possession was transferred, as in l. Quod meo, in principio, D. de acquirenda possessione. For, granted that this were true, since there does not appear a new apprehension by the husband,

† the said possession, due to his negligence, was lost after being continued for ten years, as argued from l. furtum. §. 1. ff. de usucapionibus, and l. si de eo. §. si forte. de acquisitione possessionis, and notably by the great gloss at the end of l. 1. C. de servo fugitivo, and l. licet. C. de acquisitione possessionis. Nor does the objection hold if it is said that prescription could have been completed during this time, as in l. 1. and 2. C. si adversus creditorem. For it must be notably observed that, at the time the said dowry was delivered, while the father of the plaintiff was still alive, prescription could not run against the son with respect to the dotal rights pertaining to him through his mother’s succession, because one who cannot bring an action cannot be subject to prescription, etc. The case is literally covered in l. 1. at the end, C. de bonis maternis, and l. 1. at the end, C. de annua exceptione. And if one considers this carefully, the author infallibly removes the aid of prescription: for although it clearly appears from the proceedings that the lord Albert was dead, it does not appear that he died ten years prior to the initiation of the proceedings. Hence, although the continuous possession of ten years by the defendant and others from whom he derived title is apparent, nevertheless, since a person is presumed to live until the age of one hundred, l. final. C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, and it is not proven that the said lord Albert died ten years ago, it clearly appears that prescription could not run due to the absence of the person against whom prescription ought to have run. Moreover, even this response does not avail: although there is no defect on the part of the prescriber or the things to be prescribed, and prescription would not run, there nevertheless exists a defect impeding the aid of prescription with respect to the person against whom the prescription ought to have been completed.

† Since the aforesaid inheritance of the plaintiff’s mother was always lying open until the day the bill was presented, prescription cannot run against such a lying open inheritance, as stated in l. ea, quae and the gloss thereon, C. de temp. in integ. rest., and in l. si seruus haereditatem, ff. de stipulatione seruorum. And Cynus clearly holds this in a similar case in l. licet, C. de iure delicti. Therefore, etc.

It is not an objection to say that the statute of this city provides that, upon the death of the wife during marriage, the husband is the usufructuary of the dowry, while ownership is reserved for and passes by operation of law to the children, unless there is evidence of their contrary will. By this it is argued that here prescription does not run against a lying open inheritance, but against the son and so forth. For, first, it must be notably observed that that statute applies only where the dowry consists of land or other immovable property; otherwise, where the dowry consists of money, as in our case, since usufruct does not properly attach to money, as stated in l. 2, ff. de usufructu earum rerum, quae usu consumuntur. And the words of municipal law are to be understood strictly, and especially in their more proper sense, and from the stronger meaning. Therefore, etc.

Moreover, even if this statute were applicable in this case, since the gain from the dowry is still acquired by operation of law, albeit revocably, prescription does not run, just as in paternal goods which are acquired by operation of law by a son in power, albeit with the benefit of abstention, and yet prescription does not run, as Cynus clearly states in l. licet, C. de iure delicti. And note that the said l. licet speaks of a paternal inheritance. I, Baldus.

And thus it seems to me, and thus I advise, Philip of Casoli of Reggio, and in testimony of the aforesaid I have subscribed with my own hand, and I have ordered it to be strengthened by the authority of my seal. And the same seems to me, and thus I say and advise, John of Crispi of Cremona, doctor; and in testimony thereof I have subscribed and appended my secret seal. And thus I, John, the said ordinary judge of Homedeis, doctor of laws, say and advise; and in testimony of the aforesaid I have appended my seal and subscribed with my own hand. And thus I say and advise, I, John of Castiglione, doctor of both laws; and in testimony of the aforesaid I have subscribed and appended my seal. I, Signorinus of Homedeis, doctor of laws, have subscribed, and in sign of the aforesaid I have appended my seal. I, Walter of Zazii, doctor of both laws, thus say and advise that it is so in law; and in testimony of the aforesaid I have subscribed with my own hand and appended my signet ring. And likewise I say and advise, I, John of Castiglione, doctor of laws; and in testimony of the aforesaid I have appended my seal and subscribed with my own hand.

TO THE SAME EFFECT. The case upon which the opinion is requested follows in the terms inscribed below.

A certain Lord William of Saint Nazarius of Cigognola was alive, from whom were born and came into the light a certain Lord Simon and Zanone of Saint Nazarius of Cigognola, his legitimate and natural sons. Finally, while the said Lord William was living, the said Lord Zanone, his son, died, leaving a certain Zanoniano, his legitimate and natural son. Subsequently, the said Lord William died, having made a will, in which he instituted as his universal heirs the aforesaid Lord Simon, his son, and Zanoniano, his nephew and son of the said Lord Zanone, his predeceased son; and he substituted them for one another in case they should die without legitimate male children. Moreover, the said testator willed, ordered, and commanded in the same will that his universal heirs could not, nor should they be able, in any manner, case, or device, at any time to sell, donate, alienate, or in any other way transfer to another the parts belonging to the same testator in the Castle, village, place, and lands, and properties of Canevino, nor to grant the honors or jurisdictions of the said Castle of Canevino to any person; and if they should contravene this, that such donation, sale, alienation, or transfer to another should not be valid nor binding by operation of law. And in the said case of alienation, sale, donation, or transfer to another, the said parts of the Castle, lands, and properties, honors, and jurisdictions should pass to, and he gave and bequeathed them to a certain Lord Zanone of Petra, and to certain male children of a certain Lord Philippino of Petra, and to a certain Antonio and the male children of the latter.

Afterwards, the said Lord William, the testator, having died, the said Lord Simon, his son and heir as to one-half, died intestate, leaving behind him Lords Antonio, formerly consort of the excellent Lady Francisca of Vine, and Milan, his legitimate and natural sons and universal heirs. The said Lords Antonio and Milan, after the death of their father, came to a division of certain paternal hereditary goods, of certain others, namely, of the annual rents of the Castle and properties of Canevino, and of certain annual rents which were paid to them yearly in the land of Verona; which remained undivided and in common until the time of the death of the said Lord Antonio. The said Lord Antonio died about a year ago, having made a will, in which, among other things, he instituted the said Lady Francisca, his consort, as general usufructuary of all his goods and rights for the whole time of her life, provided she lived honorably in widowhood. And he willed, ordered, and granted and bequeathed to her the power to dispose of his goods in such quantity as she should see fit, both inter vivos and in his last will, for the soul of himself and his deceased ones; and he instituted as his universal heirs the said Lords Milan and his brother, and Zanoniano, his full blood relative.

After the death of the said Lord Antonio, the aforementioned Lady Francisca, the usufructuary, and the said Lord Milan came to a compromise in law and in fact, and to an amicable composition before the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, the Bishop Vincent, and Lord William of Belengeriis of Bassignana, doctor of both laws. Who, among other things, pronounced that the usufruct of all the goods and rights of the said late Lord Antonio pertained to the said Lady Francisca by virtue of the will of the said Lord Antonio; and they pronounced that she, as general usufructuary of those goods and rights, should be introduced and, having been introduced, maintained in the tenure and corporal possession of all the goods and rights of the said late Lord Antonio. And they condemned the said Lady to satisfy and give security for using and enjoying according to the discretion of a good man; and they condemned the said Milan to come to a division of all the common things and rights of himself and the said late Lord Antonio, with a curator appointed for those goods and the inheritance, so that the said Lady might know in specie which properties and goods she ought to use and enjoy. They reserved to the parties all their other rights. This sentence indeed passed into res judicata. And lest anything further might be attempted by any legal remedy, since the said Lady Francisca had provided the said security for using and enjoying according to the discretion of a good man for those goods in the inheritance according to the form of the said sentence, and by praetorian authority in the execution of the said sentence she was introduced, by herself or her legitimate procurator, into the tenure and corporal possession of those hereditary goods and rights of the said late Lord Antonio, and of the principal part pertaining to the said late Lord Antonio in the said Castle, lands, and properties, and honors of Canevino, and the rents of Verona, and certain other properties, all and undivided, of the said late Lord Antonio and of the said Lord Milan.

On account of this apprehension of possession, the said Lord Milan opposed himself, contradicting that the said entry and giving of possession were not valid, and should be revoked by the said Lord Vicar, especially because, first, with respect to the Castle, properties, rents, and rights of Canevino, he says that the usufruct is not due to the said Lady Francisca, especially in view of the will of the said late Lord William, his grandfather, by which every alienation, donation, sale, or transfer to another of their part of the said Castle, properties, rents, goods, and jurisdictions is prohibited to the aforesaid Lord Simon and Zanoniano, his universal heirs; therefore, similarly, the said usufruct [is prohibited], by the law *Si*, Code, *De rebus alienatis non alienandis*. Secondly, he says that the said entry should be revoked with respect to the rents of Verona, or of the brief, because he asserts that they are his in solidum, especially because he says that at the time when Lady Agnesina of Becharia, formerly his and the said late Lord Antonio’s mother, passed to second marriage with Lord Coradino of Monte Calvo of Becharia, the said Lords Antonio and Milan delivered the said rents of Verona, or of the brief, in solutum to the said Lord Coradino, as having the right ceded of the dowry of the said Lady Agnesina; which delivery in solutum, however, does not appear. And after the death of the said late Lord Coradino, he asserts that those rents were delivered in solutum to the said Lady Agnesina by the heirs of the said Lord Coradino, whom he asserts subsequently bequeathed them to the said Lord Milan by her will, and instituted him in those rents, as appears from the will of the said Lady Agnesina.

On the part of the said Lady Francisca, it is responded that the said entry ought to remain firm, and cannot be revoked, and that the said Lord Milan should be compelled to come to a division with a curator appointed for the goods and inheritance by the will of the parties, according to the form of the said sentence, regarding the said Castle, rents, and properties; notwithstanding the aforesaid. And first, with respect to the prohibition made in the will of the said late Lord William, it is responded that that instrument does not make faith, since it is not original, although authentic, taken from the original, and without those whose interest it is being cited, which makes no faith, argument *Autem si quis* in any document, Code, *De edendo*. Secondly, because, granted that it were original, it nevertheless makes nothing to the purpose of the said Lord Milan; because we are not in the case of alienation, or of the words of the will, because under the appellation of alienation, donation, or transfer to another is not contained the act of usufruct, by which the dominion of ownership is not transferred, since that which still remains in the dominion of someone is not said to be alienated, argument *Alienatum*, Digest, *De verborum significatione*. Thirdly, granted that we were in the words of the will, they still make nothing in favor of the said Lord Milan; because the words of the will do not embrace, except the universal heirs of the said late Lord William, namely, Lords Simon and Zanoniano. But they dispose of nothing regarding the heirs of the heirs, as in our case; therefore, it is left to the disposition of the common law. Fourthly, granted that the aforesaid did not obstruct, that at least with respect to his legitime, the same Lord Antonio could also make a will, and bequeath the usufruct to the said Lady Francisca, notwithstanding the will; since the legitime could not be burdened by the grandfather.

As to the fact of the rents of Verona, or of the brief, it is responded similarly that the will of the said Lady Agnesina, by which the said Lord Milan asserts that he was instituted by her, does not obstruct. First, because she could make a will over goods not her own. If, therefore, the delivery in solutum made first to the said Lord Coradino does not appear, those rents are still in the dominion of the said late Lord Simon and his heirs; therefore, no right is acquired to him by the will. Moreover, the said Lady could not deprive the said Lord Antonio of his legitime; therefore, etc.

Now it is asked, what is the law in the aforesaid? I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the nullity of certain proceedings.
2. The common form must be observed.
3. The order must not be inverted.
4. How many witnesses are required to impeach an instrument.
body: † Ipa

The case consists of two matters, namely, the proceedings and the inspection of the instruments. And because jurisdiction is the foundation of foundations of judgment, and it is presupposed that Lord Anselmus did not observe the form

† By mandate of our Magnificence, because the parties were not summoned, etc., the subdelegation of Lord Anselm was void by operation of law, as established in the rescripts: *Cum dilecta*, *De acquisitione hereditatis*; *Eum qui duobus*, § *Filius*. However, since it does not appear that this was known to Lord Prothasius, nor has anything been alleged by the parties regarding said nullity, Lord Prothasius is excused, because the error originated from the litigants, and it is a just error with respect to Lord Prothasius, being an error of fact, and concerning another’s fact, as stated in *L. ultima*, *Pro suo*; and *L. si res obligata*, *Cum si*. Now let us proceed to the remainder of the proceedings and to the instruments. And it is true,

† That, while the litigation was pending on a prejudicial and obstructive issue before the said Bishop, the order should not have been inverted, nor should a pronouncement have been made before the cause was clarified. D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. Dicimus. However, if a penalty was imminent by virtue of a rescript of the lord, a pronouncement could have been made under a condition, as noted by Jacobus de Belvisio, C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. Cum iudex. And on this account, Lord Prothasius, and also the other who judged, can be excused, because necessity knows no law. But assuming that he could have pronounced judgment, it is now asked whether he judged justly. For it is certain that Philippina has her instrument placed as constant. The only objection raised against it is that it is not a dowry instrument, because there was no marriage. Holy God! Even if there was no marriage, should she not have her debt? Does she not have an express hypothec? On this, D. de conditionibus ob causam, l. 1; D. de privilegiis creditorum, l. 2; D. solutione matrimonii, l. Si cum dotem, §. final; D. de deposito, l. Lucius; D. de conditione sine causa, l. Auunculo. Moreover, how could the right of dowry be infringed while the litigation was pending? And if it is said that this was due to a prior hypothec, do not many witnesses prove that the debt was simulated, made in fraud of future creditors, which is invalid? As noted, C. de donationibus ante nuptias, aut. Sed iam necesse. The response is that the judge cannot be blamed, but excused, and his sentence justified. Let us presuppose that the simulation was not proven. And in this the question finally stands, reducing it to the cause of the cause. And it is now settled that simulation is not proven by singular witnesses. Now it remains to consider those two concurrent witnesses. A statute is alleged to me, that liberation from an instrumental debt cannot be proven unless by five witnesses. Moreover, consider that these two witnesses, according to the point formulated to me, say nothing about simulation, but say that Lord Philip said, “I acknowledge that you are not bound.” These words imply liberation and a pact not to sue. D. de pactis, l. Tale pactum, §. final. If this is so, Lord Prothasius judged most correctly, considering the statute of Milan.

† Moreover, because to invalidate the tenor of an instrument, witnesses free from every exception are required, according to C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam, in fine; and the witnesses of Philip Pine do not appear to be of such weight and quality in so great a cause, and especially after the aforementioned testimonies have been given: nevertheless, I hear that in Milan the gloss of Accursius in l. per hanc, C. de tempore appellationis, is followed, because the judge ought to consider what credit should be given to the witnesses. It does not seem to me that the aforementioned instrument for 1000 florins is invalidated by the strict law, although in my conscience I believe that it was simulated, given all these indications. Finally, all these proceedings are null, and execution ought not to be carried out. Nevertheless, they are not null due to the fault of Lord Prothasius. And therefore he ought to be absolved from the contents of the petition. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute prohibiting the pronouncement of awards is deemed unjust, or is to be reduced to the discretion of a good man, unless fraud on the part of the arbitrator intervenes.
2. An action for supplementation has the character of a complaint.
3. Where there is enormity, fraud is presumed.
body: Statute

† That which prohibits an award from being declared inequitable, or referred to the discretion of an honest man, is understood by all the authorities unless fraud on the part of the arbitrator intervenes; but here fraud is presumed to have intervened: because he rendered judgment contrary to the form of the statute without any examination of the cause. Likewise contrary to the form of the testament. For

The action has the supplement of the place of the complaint of the officious heir, in which, if a sentence is passed against the will without any proofs being produced, such a sentence is not to be observed. D. de inoff. testa. l. si pars. Moreover, it is clear that the judge who admits no proofs is acting in bad faith. D. de eden. l. argentariis. §. cum autem.

† Moreover, that where there is enormity, fraud is presumed, Charles expressly states in l. si, ff. de pretio stipulato; hence such a sentence must be corrected according to the discretion of a good man. ff. ad trebellianam, l. servo invito, §. cum praetor; and note ff. de verborum significatione, l. si qua poena; and C. de dotis promissa, l. cum ea; and that there, through Cynus, I spoke fully on this matter, C. de arbitris, l. pe. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Certain persons purchased, for the duration of their own lives or that of one of them, a certain annuity from a certain university for 300 florins, such that the university was to pay 30 gold florins during their lifetimes. The purchasers lived only long enough to receive six hundred [florins]; whether the contract is presumed to be usurious.
2. Whether annuities can be purchased with a good conscience.
3. We consider the principle, if the intention is good.
body: The instrument states that certain persons purchased, during their lifetime or the lifetime of one of them, for 300 florins, a certain annuity from a certain university, namely that the said university would pay 30 gold florins during their lifetime. It is also presupposed that they received only six hundred. Now

† This university states that this contract was usurious, and that they truly intended to make, and did make, this contract in fraud of usury. The question arises, given these presuppositions, whether this contract should be presumed to have been made in fraud of usury.

And it seems that the answer is no, because annual revenues can be purchased with a clear conscience. C. de sac. san. eccle. l. iubemus. Moreover, this contract is not usurious by its form, nor ought it to be considered usurious by intention; for what if the buyer had lived for only one day? And thus this contract appears similar to one who buys a chance, i.e., a cast of the net. ff. de act. empt. l. si iactum.

† Moreover, if the intention was good from the beginning, we do not consider the outcome, but the beginning. D. de negotiorum gestione, l. sed an ultro, §. si. Moreover, the risk is considered. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si pater. Moreover, the mind is certain, except to God alone. X. de usuris, cap. in civitate. And noted in D. de pactis, l. iure gentium, §. pactorum. Moreover, to this effect: C. de usuris, l. si ea; D. de nautico faenore, l. periculi; D. pro socio, l. si non fuerit, §. 1. Moreover, this contract cannot be called a mutuum, because a mutuum is a loan repayable in kind, but here the principal is not due to be repaid; therefore, it is rather the price of a thing, where no distinction is made as to whether it is customary to lend at interest or not. C. de usuris, l. cum allegas.

To the contrary, it seems, for if this were true, the way would be open to all moneylenders to commit frauds: because they would buy these annuities individually, and would derive very great profits therefrom, beyond what they would if they converted the money into purchases of estates, and from the excess fraud is presumed. D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. modus. Moreover, the quality of the person is an increase of deceit. Ibid., §. in persona. Moreover, he was certain by legal presumption of superfluous profit, and of money to be gained over and above money, whence this contract is similar to usury, as in X. de usuris, c. in civitate, and c. naviganti. Moreover, that this contract is understood to exceed from the very beginning the sum of three hundred, nay, even today five hundred gold florins, seems expressly stated. C. de donationibus, l. sancimus, §. si.

Solution: From the quality of the persons, reputation, age, and other indications, I presume whether it was done or not done in fraud of usury. Arg. X. de pignoribus, c. illo vos; and de emptione et venditione, c. ad nostram. The conclusion is that this contract is not prohibited by its form, but by intention it could be illicit, provided, however, that the badness of the intention is not established by slight arguments, because in doubt consent is upheld. But if these were the arguments, namely, that he was accustomed to lend at interest, or to draw up instruments in fraud of usury, as in re. semel malus, and l. non omnes, §. a Barbaris, de re militari; that they were youths in law and in men, and by presumption would see much beyond the visible. D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. modus; D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. hereditatum; that if the thing had been put up to auction, it would have been sold for far more, for the quantity of the price is an argument of deceit. C. de mandato, l. per diversas. Moreover, that such contracts were not frequent, but were rather unusual in the region, as noted in D. de condictione institutoria, l. 3. Moreover, that such an annuity is in quantity partly a sale, partly a gift. C. de mandato, l. ab Anastasio. Moreover, with this clause he could not sell to his subjects. As D. de pactis, l. contra iuris civilis regulas, §. filios; D. quod vi aut clam, l. prohibere, §. plane. All these, and similar matters, require the discussion of the praetor. Arg. D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. praetor. The truth, which cannot be grasped to the nail, is committed to be examined by the subtlety of the judge: who ought not to judge on one argument, but on many. C. de quaestionibus, l. milites, §. oportet; C. de probationibus, l. iubemus; D. de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, §. 2; and what is noted in D. de excusatione tutoris, l. 2, §. aetas; D. ad Sillianam, l. excipiuntur. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when set-off may be raised or effected.
body: Omitting verbosity, which is of little use and very tedious,

I say that the aforementioned Zanonus is not bound to pay the said 100 florins: he had the right of set-off, since the debt owed to him is liquid, as appears from the documents. C. de compens. l. si; Inst. de acq. rer. dom. § bonae fidei. It should be known that although the last instrument contains the statement that this debt has not been paid nor satisfied, nevertheless Zanonus does not assert the contrary, but says that he now wishes to satisfy it by way of set-off, as in ff. qui potior in pign. hab. l. si debitor. But before the set-off is pleaded, it is not said that satisfaction has been made. And thus the instrument is true. Nevertheless, the modern set-off stands in his way by the aforementioned l. si debitor, where this is expressly stated. Moreover, because the cause of the last instrument, if it is not paid in this manner, is found to be entirely erroneous from the documents themselves, as noted by Bartolus in ff. de confess. l. non fatetur, at the end. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the codicillary clause operates in the case where the will is broken by the birth of a posthumous child.
2. Given a statute that, if agnates exist, the mother does not succeed to her son, whether in this case the inheritance not taken up by the son is transmitted to the mother by virtue of the mother’s privilege, as discussed in l. 1, C. de his, qui ante aper. tab.
3. Whether the mother is preferred to a brother united on both sides.
body: Clause

† A codicillary clause appended by these words: “If it does not, or would not, have effect by the law of wills, let it have effect by the law of codicils.” Whether it operates in the case where the will is found to be broken by the birth of a posthumous child. The authorities say that it does, by the law *Generaliter*, § *Testamento*, D. de fideicommissis liberis. Others say the contrary, and this is the opinion of the Gloss in the Authentica *Ex causa*, C. de libris praeteritis, and of Guido de Caylis in the law *Si quis agere*, C. de codicillis. And this is supported by the following reason and example: suppose the testator instituted his only son, who was already born, and without considering the posthumous child, appended a codicillary clause. A posthumous child is born. For if the said clause were to operate, the posthumous child would be compelled to restore to the born child half of his share, according to the chapters *Raynu.* and *Raynal.*, de testibus; or two-thirds of his share: because he does not appear to be burdened under a condition, since he is burdened immediately upon birth; but he is understood to be burdened purely, as in D. de liberis et posthumis. And thus, as one burdened purely, he will have only his legitime, and the son already born will have the residue of the entire inheritance, which is very inhumane and contrary to the presumed intention of the testator, according to the argument from C. de inofficioso testamento, law 3. Therefore, what is said to operate must be understood without prejudice to the omitted heir, as in D. de iure codicillorum, law *Is qui*, and D. de legatis 2, law *Cum pater*, § *Cum estimaret*. Hence, the instituted heir is rightly bound to the legacies left by him, even though the will is broken by the agnation of the posthumous child; but the posthumous child himself is not bound, because the testator did not consider burdening him, nor ought he to have considered it, as in C. de fideicommissis, law *Pe.*; and it supports what is noted in C. ad Trebellianam, law *Non iustam*. Bartolus says that either the testator considered the posthumous child, for example because he made mention of him in some part of the will, or he did not consider him. In the first case, either he burdened the posthumous child with special words, and he could not do so, since he was omitted, as in D. de legatis 2, law *Ex filio*; or with general words and words written in rem, and then he could burden him as any successor intestate, as in law 2, D. de iure codicillorum. But if he did not consider the posthumous child, he is not understood to have burdened him, as in the said law *Is qui*, because it is not probable that he would have burdened him with the restitution of the inheritance if he had known he would be born, as in D. de pactis, law *Tale pactum*, § *Si*. It would be different perhaps in a singular legacy left to the born son not by name, but by simple words. For he would have left it equally to any son, since there is not greater, but lesser affection for the one to be born than for the one already born. Hence, if the testator had considered it, he would have left it in the same manner. And to this reason it supports what is noted in D. de pactis, law *Tale pactum*, § *Si*. Considering therefore the above, because the interpretation of the said clause must be made according to the presumed will of the testator, and it is not probable that he wished his sons to be unequal in succeeding, since among children the cause should be equal, as in law *Cum pater*, § *Euic.*, D. de legatis 2, I would hold that the said codicillary clause operates for nothing, and that the posthumous brother is not understood to be condemned to restore his portion to the already born brother, so that absurdity may be avoided and natural charity preserved, which has great weight in the interpretation of the testator. And what I have written in various places, that the said clause operates in the omission of the posthumous child, I understand it as far as concerns what is left over by the instituted heir, not that the posthumous child is understood to be burdened, unless the legacies were left after the death of the sons, for example because the testator would say that he wishes his entire inheritance to be restored if it happens that any of those to be born from him dies without children. For then the will of the testator can be preserved without prejudice to the sons, as in D. de legatis 3, law *Paulo Calimacho*, § 1. Reflect upon this, for it is necessary to advise what is true.

† Now I come to another point: if a statute excludes the mother from the succession of her son on account of agnates, whether an unaccepted inheritance is transmitted to the mother by virtue of the mother’s privilege, i.e., by a certain singular prerogative derived from the title *De his qui ante apertas tabulas* or from the law *Apud hostes* with its gloss, and presupposing that the opinion of the gloss is observed by custom: nevertheless, it seems to me that one must say either that we assume that this custom is the common law, and it does not seem that the mother succeeds, because since the mother must come by transmission, and consequently as an heir, as is noted in the Code, *Unde liberi*, law *Qui se patris*, if she is excluded from the inheritance, it is impossible that she succeeds as an heir; or, if we presuppose that this custom is a custom, and that it has been introduced contrary to the common law in this singular case in favor of the mother, so that the custom dictates that it is not transmitted to anyone other than the mother, this would be a certain singular succession, not universal, in which the mother is preferred to the others by special right: just as we see that in certain goods some are considered to be preferred by common right, as in the Code, *De secundis nuptiis*, in the authenticum *Ex testamento*, and in the case of two brothers, one of whom is uterine, the other consanguineous; hence it matters greatly whether this custom has been introduced as an observance of the true or putative common law, or as a privilege of the mother. And this depends on the proofs.

It must also be considered that a statute which prefers agnates is understood to prefer them by that right which may pertain to the agnates: for to exclude the mother on account of agnates is to substitute the agnates in the place of the mother in a substitutable right; but in that right in which they cannot succeed to the mother, they ought not to be preferred, as in the Digest, *De contrariis tabulis*, law *Si post mortem*, section *Liberi*. Here, however, it must be considered that if they can be preferred by the right of accretion, they can obstruct the mother, just as we say elsewhere that he who is not admitted to a share makes a share, provided that he can be admitted by the right of retention, as in the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Plane*, first section, *Si duobus*, and in the Digest, *De legatis secundo*, law *Codicillis*, in the beginning. This is proved because the mother ought not to have a stronger right in seeking from the son than in what has already been acquired; since therefore the mother does not succeed in what has been acquired, much less does she succeed in what is to be sought. Moreover, the rule of law is that a pagan cannot have two inheritances; hence it cannot be said that the mother succeeds in one inheritance devolved to the son, and in other goods the agnates succeed, because it would be to say that the pagan died with two different inheritances, which is impossible, as is fully noted in law 1, Code, *De testamento militis*.

But here consider that, in our case, the infant had nothing else in goods except the right of mixing himself into the paternal inheritance, and thus he could only have the inheritance, since he had nothing else in goods. Hence the said rule does not seem to obstruct, because, this being given, no inconvenience follows that the mother succeeds, since no other can succeed. But from this it seems to follow a certain error, even with the statute favorable to the agnates being circumvented, that the mother succeeds and not the brother. Which the gloss rejects in law *Qui duos*, in the beginning, Digest, *De rebus dubiis*.

But that passage speaks of a brother related on both sides, not of a brother related by blood only. For under the common law, the mother is preferred to him, as in the Authentica Defuncto, Codex, ad Tertullianum. Hence you see that, because of the considerations for and against, this question is very difficult. Another doubt is added, because, assuming the custom, even if the agnate had the entire inheritance of the minor, nevertheless a separation of property should be made, and the mother ought to obtain at least by restitution made to her, namely, that which the custom grants her. But this is not well said, because the custom does not give a donation, but grants succession; therefore I do not believe that any foundation should be made from this custom according to what is now newly proposed to me in the facts, and according to different cases, different responses must be given. I have written the motives intricately, but you see and arrange them as you please. According to what is proposed, I think the mother has no right to claim, and consequently is not admitted to succeed except in the manner and form as the statute provides. Saving the special custom on this matter, if any were proven, then those concerning the form of proof of the custom itself would have to be examined. And the above are proven as to the first point: because succeeding in the person of another presupposes transmission, as in the law Cum antiquioribus, Codex, de iure deliberandi. As to the second, it is proven by what we noted in the law De quibus, de legibus. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws. Saving the faith, etc. And therefore I have subscribed and signed with the signs of my name. The above said regarding the statute, I say, and if there is any statute that provides on this matter.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is the effect of a grant of a thing made for a fictitious purpose, and of an emphyteutic lease.
2. In emphyteusis, within what time the delay may be cured, and how the words "speedily" are to be understood.
3. Add the opinion beginning "emphyteota ecclesię" in part 6.
body: †I am instructed by these words,

† which they say, regarding the fictitious and emphyteusis. It is established that the direct dominion was not transferred. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. cum manu sata, § nemo. And thus the contract was emphyteutic, whence the nature of the contract must be observed. But if the direct dominion had been granted in a census, then the thing would not fall into forfeiture, as is noted, D. de negotiis gestis, l. debitor, per William of Cuneo. And so it is to be understood, as is noted, In., in c. constitutus, de religiosis domibus. From these it is concluded that the said thing falls into forfeiture, if there has been a cessation in the payment of the canon of the church for two years, and provision has not been made by speedy satisfaction, as in cap. potuit, de locato.

† It is necessary, however, to purge the delay within two months by the word "speedily." ff. de iure fisci. l. aufertur. §. qui compensationem. Or, according to another opinion, within the time granted by the judge. Others say within three days. C. de iu. l. pe. But since in our case it is stated that four years and more have elapsed, there is no doubt that, considering the time, the period for purging the delay has expired. et c. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a single document is found not glued together with others in the files or protocols of one notary, but standing alone, whether it should be given credence.
2. Whether two witnesses suffice to prove that the notary wrote it.
3. In case of doubt, it is presumed that the notary was requested.
body: If it is found

Whether a document not glued to others in the codices or protocols, but standing by itself, ought to be believed. It must be said that, since faith is imposed on the said document by witnesses, the document must be relied upon, as in C. de fide instrumentorum, l. Si. For the testimony of living voices removes all presumption and stain. To this effect is Auth. de instrumentis cautelis et fide, § Si vero tale, and § Oportet. However, it is voluntary for the notary to place his sign at the beginning or at the end, provided that it is placed. Inst. de publicis iudiciis, § Item lex. Nevertheless, the notary observes this, who keeps the same form and sign, which was devised for the comparison of letters, as noted in the aforementioned § Oportet. And this faith can well be imposed by two witnesses described in the instrument. Moreover, it is credible if written in the testator’s own hand, and the notary could subscribe to it, as is clear from C. de testamento, l. Iubemus.

And that two witnesses suffice to prove that the notary, when requested, wrote the document, is proven by the fact that the witnesses testify concerning the handwriting, namely, that he wrote it. This is established in the note in l. 2, C. de bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas, where it was doubted. Here, the matter concerns only the handwriting, because the other elements are formalities and are all substantial to a public instrument. It would be otherwise if the notary’s book did not contain a sheet without any subscription of the notary, as noted in ff. de legatis 3, l. fideicommissum, § 1, and if it were in the testator’s hand, de testibus, l. si is qui, because it lacks the form of public solemnity and perfection, de edicto divi Adriani, Tol., l. edicto. Even among heirs, the mere hand of the testator, without other evidence added, would not suffice, although the gloss hints at the contrary in Auth. de testamento imperfecto, § 1. And from these points it is concluded that, according to what is alleged, the said writing must be reduced to public form by order of the judge. C. de testibus, l. publica; de fide instrumentorum, c. cum papa tabellione.
† And in case of doubt, it is presumed that the notary was requested, as stated in the number in the Authenticum de tabellis, § non autem, although others say the contrary, and wrongly. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and in what manner, one should proceed upon a petition by which someone seeks to be again enrolled in a society from which he was wrongfully struck, and concerning certain other matters.
2. If the submission of the libel and the joinder of issue are waived by statute, nevertheless a petition must intervene.
3. What the term "exinde" signifies.
4. The proemium declares the general church.
body: Elegantly.

† And it was copiously alleged in *narrat autem* [Saco]. But [in the case where] a certain Florentine had been struck off from his society, and he sought to be enrolled again, and he summoned those who had caused him to be struck off, and they did not appear, the plaintiff could not be put in possession of the goods of those summoned, because a debt did not precede. He says that one may proceed to a definitive judgment, and he reports that he has so advised. C. *Quoniam*, and *Quando iudex*. However, *Qui semel*, in his lecture. It appears, therefore, that this matter requires the pronouncement of a definitive sentence. And if the adversary appears, it also demands the joinder of issue. But if he does not appear, the case is held as quasi joined: and a definitive judgment may be rendered according to him.

And even if the submission of the libel and the joinder of issue are dispensed with by statute, nevertheless an intervention of the petition is required, at least in verbal form, in which it is concluded that a definitive pronouncement must be made concerning this reception to be carried out for the future. It would be prescribed to order rather than to pronounce, as in *l. nimis propere*, C. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, and ff. de re iudicata, *l. nullam*. The same is noted by Jacobus Butrigarius, that a definitive judgment is required, C. si quis ut se ab haerede abstineat, auth. si omnes. Therefore, a petition is also required, at least in verbal form, as in the decretal *Saepe*, de verbis significantibus, and *l. si*, de fideicommissis libertatibus. And thus, he who seeks execution, but does not seek a pronouncement, petitions ineptly, as noted by Bartolus in the said *l. 1*.

It is to be noted that an action arises from the decree of the Prince if it provides for the plaintiff, and an exception if the decree provides for the defendant, as noted in ff. quod metus causa, *l. extat*, in the major gloss, under the word "et est notandum." I understand "action" also to refer to the noble and principal office of the judge, in which a definition and the pronouncement of a definitive sentence are necessary, extra de officio iudicis, c. 2; ff. de minoribus, *l. Papinianus exulavit*. Although in the office of a mercenary judge, or a noble judge but not a principal one, as if a suit is brought against a contumacious party, a commission is not required, as noted in ff. de interrogationibus actionum, in the rubric. And the reason is that in those cases, the libel submitted in the principal case suffices. And this concludes the first point.

The sentence of the protectors, with the causes inserted therein, is certain, that it was valid before the latest decree of the Lord Duke, which formerly, and now, had acquired its force, notwithstanding that another Duke was deposed and annihilated: as in ff. de origine iudicii, *l. 2*, §. exactis deinde regibus. However, because by ducal law laws and sentences have become obsolete, this sentence is included under those, and even if it itself is annihilated, if it is not included, otherwise, as in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, *l. decernimus*.

The Ducal statute is divided into two parts: for in the first part it annuls and invalidates the decree of Lord Jacobus and all that followed from it; in the second part it restores to integrity the acts performed in the earlier time of the said Antonietus. I do not doubt regarding the first part that it does not touch our case.

† For that word, *exinde*, it signifies a substantial and immediate [effect], as is noted in *l. si mulier*, *rerum amotarum*, D. But this opinion is substantiated by another [ground], as appears from the causes expressed in the sentence. And one good and efficacious reason suffices; the sentence does not assist, as in C. *si ex falsis instrumentis*, *l. falsum quidem*, and there noted, D. *de iudiciis*, *l. si praetor*, § *Marcellus*. And without any rescript, the ordinary judges appointed by statute were pronouncing. D. *de officiis praesidis*, *l. saepe*. But I doubt even more on account of the reparatory and restorative clause, restoring the old sentences to that state, degree, and term in which they previously stood. For this clause is general. D. *de militibus testamento*, *l. in fraudem*, § *si*.

† If we say that the final cause, declared by the reward, restricts this generality, cf. D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Pacumeius; lest the hatred of Lord Jacob be extended to those who are not hateful, cf. D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si quis in suo, § legis. On this point, because the intent of the statute is doubtful to me, I remain undecided. And this is the second point; it is supported by what is noted in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. Si is, qui animo. Regarding the third doubt, there does not appear to be any doubt that the office of the *robaria* could not proceed by virtue of ordinary jurisdiction against the said [defendant], because that jurisdiction is written concerning the persons of robbers. But he is not alleged to be among them. Cf. D. de vi et vi armata, l. Cum a te. Because the *compari* are specially assigned to the office of the protectors and prohibited to others; hence no other person may intervene in the forbidden examination. Cf. C. de iure omnium iudicum, l. In criminali. Because this jurisdiction is more specially attributed than another, because it is a casual jurisdiction by reason of expression, according to l. In sacris, de proximis sacrorum scrineorum, lib. 12, and there by Bartolus, D. de legibus, l. Quod in rerum, § si quis, by Jacobus de Ravanis. Therefore, the sentence of the office of the *robaria* never had validity by any force of ordinary jurisdiction. Cf. D. de poenis, l. 2. And it does not merit right, nor fact, as is noted in c. 1, de sequestro possessionis, in the Clementines. Moreover, because it is expressly stated that through the office of the *robaria* no recourse may be had to the *compari*. For by these words all power and jurisdiction is denied. Cf. D. de alienationibus, l. 1, § autem. That text is the one properly adduced to this effect by Jacobus de Arena. And by these means also the response to the fourth and fifth doubts is clearly apparent. I conclude well for the said defendant, according to what is proposed, having seen the truth of the facts, as well as the statutes and allegations aforesaid. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a bill of complaint should proceed, in which the wife brings an action for the recovery of property, which was given as an estimated dowry. He concludes that it should.
2. The marriage being established, whether the woman has direct ownership, even if the dowry is in the case of consignation.
body: A libel

† that is contrary to law is inept: l. 1, ff. si mensor falsum modum dixerit. But this libel seems contrary to law, because the thing was appraised by a true appraisal, and thus has entirely become the husband's by title of purchase and sale: C. de iu. dot., l. quotiens. Hence the woman, who ought to have the value/quantity and instead claims the specific thing, not only sues ineptly, but also unjustly, because she claims one thing in place of another. Hence against the plaintiff two exceptions may be raised: namely, of ineptitude, and of claiming what is not owed: ff. ad l. Fal., l. 1, §. item qui ita. Indeed, there is no need for any exception, because the libel is non-conclusive, since the cause does not agree with the conclusion, as is noted in ff. de exce. doli, l. 2, §. circa, and by Innoc. in c. 1, de officio vicarii, and l. 1, ff. de offic. assessorum. Furthermore, the woman seeks to be declared the owner; therefore, she asserts direct ownership: ff. si ag. vect., l. 1, §. qui in perpetuum.

† But it is certain that during the marriage she does not have direct ownership, even if the dowry is in a case of consignment, for the administration is consigned to her, but ownership is not rooted out from the husband; otherwise she would become undowered and it would be a marriage without a dowry, according to Jac. de Are. in l. ubi adhuc, C. de iure do. Furthermore, at least an excussion ought to have preceded: C. de pig., auth. hoc si debitor. Therefore, it is wrongly brought, because it is done out of order, as in extra. de iu., cap. exhibita. To the contrary appears the case arising from the joinder of l. in rebus, C. de iur. dot., which says that upon dissolution of the marriage even appraised goods are vindicated, which is understood if the estate is not otherwise solvent, as is noted there; nevertheless the text in l. cum dotem seems to say by the very fact that the dowry—that is, the quantity/value—is not offered. Now l. ubi adhuc, at the verse sed ita, says the same thing if the marriage still endures, but the husband has been reduced to poverty (supply: or is still tending toward it by the newest law, supply: if he has begun to mishandle his property: C. de colla., auth. quod locum). Moreover, the opinion of Jac. de Are. is not true, because the dowry is not restored to her so that she ceases to be dowered, but so that she may be secure in her dowry, and for the sake of preserving the dowry, as is fully noted in l. si constante, in princip., ff. so. ma.; and this is the truth, that all remedies for recovering the dowry have a place in this case during the marriage, not so that it ceases to be a dowry, but so that it remains intact. And for that reason beneficial remedies introduced jointly in favor of both the parent and the children, not direct remedies, have a place. Now, returning to our case, since it is stated that the husband is banished, and therefore absent, and that the dowry is in a case of consignment and qualified restitution, and is literally not offered, it falls within the two said laws joined together. Nor do the arguments made to the contrary stand in the way. For to the first, the answer is that the property is deemed sold, but nevertheless let it be granted, not simply, but on account of the dowry, and therefore subsidiarily the woman vindicates by a beneficial in rem action. Furthermore, if the husband is banished, it is notorious that he is heading toward poverty, or at least is suspected under a burden of debt, wherefore excussion is not required: de verbo. oblig., l. decem, and as noted in l. fi., ff. si cer. pe. Likewise he is absent, therefore bringing an action against him is not required, as in de pig., auth. hoc si debitor. But certainly another reason is that either an order is prescribed by law, such that one person must be sued before another, and then the order must be observed if an exception is raised; or an order is not prescribed, but the law rests content with its own conditions, namely, that such person is insolvent, and therefore another may be sued: then an order is not necessary, but proof that the matter stands thus suffices: ff. si cer. pet., l. respiciendum. Furthermore, if it is said that direct ownership was claimed: that might be true if someone simply stated that she was the owner; but when she alleges the title/cause of ownership, she is deemed to set forth that ownership which arises from that title/cause; for one who sets forth the cause is deemed to set forth the action, as the doctors note on the said l. edicta, and in c. examinata, de iu., by Innoc. I conclude from the aforesaid that the libel proceeds, having regard to what it contains in truth, and that the order of excussion was not necessary, if those things were proved that tend toward the husband's poverty, or are probable. And so, retaining the other most learned arguments made in favor of this most just party, I hold, and especially because the words of the instrument state 'whatever a true husband [may do] concerning an appraised dotal property,' etc. Whence this contract was mixed: ff. solu. matri., l. si aestimatis; ff. de iure dotium, l. non solum. I, Baldus.

Four things are urged against us: the presumed tacit concession arising from long usage (l. Si quis diuturno); the present possession, whereby you ought to bring a negative action, since another is in possession of the convenience (in §. Aquaeducto, De actionibus); the most ancient custom (l. Hoc iure, §. Ductus aquae); and Bartolus in l. Quominus, in the 14th question, who raises a new and unresolved point, namely that when water is diverted elsewhere in a public river to the detriment of neighbors, it is not called an "immission of water" (l. Sicuti, §. Ariston, Si servitus vendi). And it is similar to what the noted doctor says concerning two mills. These four things seem to wound our natural liberty; therefore, you should consult wise men, and an agreement would be good. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is said to be a manifest usurer, and whether the wills of such persons are valid, and whether it is required that he be manifest at the time of death.
2. How "notorious" is to be understood.
3. How "manifest" is to be understood.
4. Who is said to be a manifest usurer.
5. Whether crimes are extinguished by death.
6. Whether it is necessary that the caution, mentioned in the chapter *Quanquam*, be provided before the will is made.
7. Likewise, whether the caution is vitiated if it is provided for a small sum, when a much larger sum had been extorted.
8. Whether the caution is vitiated because the surety is not suitable.
9. Likewise, whether it is vitiated if the caution is provided to other persons than those enumerated in the said chapter *Quanquam*.
1. Whether the archpriest of a parish church may receive the said caution.
2. In what matters a notary is to be believed.
3. Whether the caution is vitiated on the ground that the witnesses are not from the usurer's parish.
body: Case. The case on account of which counsel is sought is as follows, namely: D. made a will, against which it is objected that it is invalid, because it was made by a manifest usurer, and the form of the decree *c. Quanquam*, *De usuris*, lib. 6, was not observed. It is replied that he was not a manifest usurer, although he gave security at the time the will was made. Furthermore, that he observed the form of the said decree, because he gave suitable security, and he produces the security. But against the security it is objected: first, that it did not precede the will, at least that this is not established, because both were made on the same day. Second, that it is not suitable, because it is for a small amount, namely 10 florins, whereas more than 300 had been extorted by usurious wickedness. But to this the party supporting the will replies that an additional amount was included in the security, and if more appears. Third, that it is not sufficient, because the surety is not suitable. Fourth, because the one who demanded the security was not suitable, because he was not among the persons expressed in the decree *c. Quanquam*. Fifth, because the witnesses were not from the testator’s parish, but were unknown. Sixth, because the security was not given sufficiently for restitution. Having examined the said security alleged and the will. Regarding the first doubt, it must be noted,

† That the wills of those usurers who are manifest do not have legal force, as is stated in the decree *Quanquam*. And consequently it appears that this quality of being manifest must inhere in the person at the time of the will, and affect the person, so that the penalty enacted against such usurers may apply to them, as in *l. Praetor*, § *Docere*, D. *De vi bonorum raptorum*; *l. 1*, § *Non autem*, D. *Si quis testamento liberum*; *l. Ius esse*, D. 54; *c. Ex antiquis* and *c. Frequens*, D. *De rescriptis*; *c. Significante* and *c. Rodulfi*, D. *De vi et homine*; *c. Si*, D. *De senatu excommunicato religioso*, lib. 6. But it is presupposed that he was not called a usurer at the time the will was made, or it is not proven that he was a manifest usurer at the time the will was made; therefore it seems that the will is not invalid on this ground. However, the contrary must be said according to law, namely, that it suffices if he is now discovered to have been a manifest usurer at any time, and especially because this is established by his confession, which makes him manifest, or rather declares that he was such. This is the meaning of the gloss and all the commentators in the aforementioned decree *Quanquam*, explaining who is considered a manifest usurer. And although it might be said that he becomes manifest only from the time of the confession, nevertheless, because a will derives its force from the time of death, as in *De celebratione missae*, *c. Cum Marte*, § *Certum*, it suffices that he was a manifest usurer at that time. Otherwise, if we were to say otherwise, great fraud could be committed against the decree *Quanquam*, namely, that one intending to practice usury before actually doing so would make a will; thus the law would be imposed on words and not on things, contrary to *Decretum Quanto*, D. *De privilegiis de electione*, *c. Commissa*, § *Porro*, lib. 6. Hence, just as a confession made in court makes something notorious in law, *De cohabitatione clericorum et mulierum*, *c. Vestra*, so too a confession made before his priest, or even before witnesses, makes him manifest, which suffices to invalidate the will. And to distinguish between notorious and manifest, according to the notes in *2. q. 1*, *c. In summa*, and in the matter of notoriety in the decree *Vestra*, D. *De cohabitatione clericorum*, and immediately following, since in the caution given, the said defendant confesses that he lent money to some at usury, and after the said caution, the will followed, although made on the same day, it follows that the will was made by a manifest usurer. I say further, that if the said caution followed the will, and it were discovered today that he was a manifest usurer, although nothing was said about this during his life, we would still be in the case of the aforementioned decree *Quanquam*. And Federicus of Siena advised, as is found in his consilia, in his consilium 8, the words of which I set down literally below, which more clearly prove what I have said above regarding the question at issue, namely, how "manifest" is to be understood in the consilium of the Council of Lyon, decree *Vallet quanquam*, D. *De usuris*, lib. 6. The same Federicus responds literally as follows.

† It is certain that *poet* [notum] is taken for *notorium* [notorious], when it has the evidence of fact: or that which is notorious in law, for example, by confession, or by sentence, or by the judge’s publication, or by clear and undoubted proofs. *De verb. sign.*, c. *Olim*; and c. *Super quibusdam*. Moreover, *manifestum* [manifest] can be understood as that which is below notorious and above *famulum* [common report], inasmuch as it can be proved. And beyond customary proof is *lamosum* [gossiped] and *publicum* [public], although it cannot be called notorious. Of such a matter one may understand q. 3, c. *Eorum*; *De usu*, c. *Cum in tua*. *Publicum* does not necessarily include *notorium*; *De coh.*, c. *Tua*.
† Moreover, a manifest action may be brought, the proof of which lies in the thing itself being evident and manifest,

† Hence, the defect of Titius’s sight, or hearing, or knowledge is said to be manifest: yet, since it does not appear openly in all respects, and nevertheless, by subjecting him to examination, such defect is said to be evident and manifest. This is the case in *de electione*, c. *Si forte*, lib. 6; *de veritate sigilli*, c. 2, eod. lib. So, in the present case, if someone has not openly or notoriously practiced usury, nevertheless, if through a prompt and easy examination it will become manifest—for example, because his account books are inspected, concerning which there is no doubt that they are the books of the usurer himself—such proof may be called clear and manifest, as noted by Archidiaconus, *de usuris*, c. 2, lib. 6, to which saying the following accords: 27 q. 1, c. *Omnes feminae*; and *de non numero personarum*, l. *Generaliter*. Furthermore, beyond the aforementioned modes, William the Archdeacon and Johannes Andreas note in the same decree, *Quanquam*, that it is manifest when one publicly confesses before his priest and witnesses that he is a usurer, especially if he hands over his account books, and most especially if he makes such a confession at the point of death; for it is not to be presumed that he lies. To this effect: *praesumptiones*, *litteras*, 1 q. 2, c. *Sancimus*; and

It suffices that this is revealed after death, nor should anyone say of a usurer after death that proofs on this matter ought not to be received, as if crimes were extinguished by death. C. si reus, vel accu. l. 1. and 2. and de haereticis. c. accusatus. li. 6. For an action may be brought for goods after death. C. si ap. pen. l. quamuis. Likewise, wherever a penalty of exclusion from burial is imposed by caution, and someone has been buried contrary to such prohibition, and c. de sepu. c. sanctis. de haereticis. c. 2. cum si. lib. 6. And although certain modes are declared by which something is said to be manifest, nevertheless it may perhaps be said that if a synodal constitution had imposed some species of easier proof, so that one might be called a manifest usurer, this would not be disapproved, since the laws are accustomed to convict usurers by easier proofs, as appears de pig. c. illo vos. de emp. et vendi. c. nostram. cum si. And bishops may strengthen, and by the addition of penalties, the common laws, as noted doc. de officio archipr. c. vlt. These words of Federicus are to the letter. From which it is concluded, and that allegation does not hold, that the said person was not a manifest usurer at the time the testament was made.

It must be considered regarding the second point, namely whether the caution is valid as having observed the form of the said decree *Quanquam*, that is, whether the caution produced is sufficient or not. And first, against the caution itself, it is argued that it is not suitable, because it ought to precede the testament. But that it preceded is said not to appear, because it appears to have been given on the same day and the testament made. And on this article I will not insist: because from this head I do not think the caution is infringed, although the rubric *Testem quoque manifestorum usuriorum aliter facta etc.* seems at first sight to sound that the caution ought to precede, nevertheless I do not think that order is of the substance of the law. L. *Nec*, n. *Ordo*, ff. *De solutionibus*. For if they execute the mind of the law, the law is satisfied. *De verborum significatione*, L. *Intelligentia*; and c. *Praeterea*, *De regulis iuris*, lib. 6. And it would be easier to make restitution of usuries by the giving of the caution itself, whether it is given before the testament or after. Here the same effect seems to arise, therefore it suffices that it be given whenever before death, and this pleases the Gloss in the said decree *Quanquam*, and also Jo. And. in the *Novella* on the same Gloss, although he confesses that the legists perhaps follow the contrary opinion. Moreover, also from the tenor of the caution it appears that it preceded. It is established, namely, that assertions made by the notary in the accompanying instrument, such as the place and time of the making of the instrument, are to be believed. *De iudicibus*, c. *Abbate sane*, in fine, lib. 6, where it is rejected in *De falso*, *De probationibus*, c. *Postcessionem*, *De praescriptionibus*, c. *Ad audientiam*. And this case is about the time attested, indeed an instrument referred to another, therefore, etc.

Secondly, against the same opinion, because the security was given for a small amount, namely 16 imperial pounds. But to this the opposing party responds that if there is any defect, it was the fault of the notary, or of the recipient of the security himself for not providing caution: as if one ought not to be burdened by the fault of another. And no one ought to be punished without fault; rather, offenses remain with their authors, as the laws note, and especially in this case, since the testator, perhaps weighed down by illness and disturbed by the thought of death, could not make provision. Argument: Law *Hac consultissima*, § *At cum humana*, Code, *Qui testamento facere possint*. But this response would be of no value if the objection did not proceed from law. For a defect in the substantial form, whatever the fault, would invalidate the act, and consequently would also harm the one who was not at fault, *de electione*, chapter *Super eo*. A defect of place or time not specified in the instrument, although the fault of the notary vitiates the instrument itself, the same in similar cases. Therefore, the defense is better than the objection, if at the time the security was received it had been established that the sum of the extorted usuries was greater. For then that sum must always be expressed in the security. But where it is uncertain, as in this case, it is left to the discretion of the recipient, as the decree *Quanquam* expressly states. And in this case, although he may judge poorly and be liable to the injured party, nevertheless the security is not vitiated by this, as the text there implies. And if he acts otherwise, he is liable for satisfaction of the remainder. Behold, therefore, that although a penalty is imposed by law on the violator, and although the violator is punished by law, the act done against the law nevertheless stands, as noted by Dy., *de regulis iuris*, chapter *Quae poena*, book 6. Moreover, according to the gloss and other doctors, the security was also given for more, insofar as it will appear that he is liable for more by reason of usuries; and therefore, whatever is said, whether that clause refers to a small or a large amount, the law is entirely satisfied. And therefore I conclude from that point that the security is not defective.

Thirdly, it is argued that the caution is invalid because the surety provided is not suitable. This objection appears to be well-founded, for whenever satisfaction or caution has been given vitiously, it is not regarded as caution. See Digest, *Qui satisdare cogantur*, law *Quotiens*; Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Quamvis*, section *Si convenit*. For that which is null and that which is useless are equated. See Digest, *Quod cuiusque universitatis*, law 1, section *Pe*; Decretals, *De translatione*, chapter 2. And where there is a deficiency on both sides, the reason of the law is then lacking; therefore, the law has not been satisfied. See *De electione*, chapter *Commissa*, section *Porro*, Book 6. For if the reason is lacking, why is it provided by usurers? And what moves the legislator to enact regarding suitable caution to be provided is that those receiving usury may be more secure. This is rightly achieved through the giving of pledges or sureties. See Digest, *Qui satisdare cogantur*, law 1; and note in the aforementioned decree *Quanquam*, in the gloss. Therefore, since the surety is not suitable, the law is not satisfied. From the foregoing, it is concluded that the objection is valid in law.

Fourthly, it was objected against the caution that it is invalid, because the person who had received the caution was not among those persons who can receive a caution according to the form of the decree *Quanquam*. I say that this objection is valid in its own form. The rule is that no one can provide a caution for another, whether by contracting, by stating the law, or by stipulation. D. de regulis iuris, l. *Quae tutela*, § *Si*. Therefore, no one acquires for another through the power of the law by means of another person. Inst. *Per quas personas nobis acquiritur*, per totum. And therefore, the decretal *Quanquam*, wishing to acquire an action and easier restitution for those who had paid usury, requires the presence of those to whom restitution must be made, if they are present, or of those who can acquire for another by right: such as one’s own slaves, or those whom one possesses in good faith, or sons, as noted there. Beyond these, the decretal added the local ordinary, or his deputy acting as rector of the parish church of the testator, and a public slave or notary, however, by the mandate of the ordinary himself. Therefore, outside these persons, a caution otherwise provided does not bind. Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, § *Alteri*.

Let us therefore examine whether the person who received this caution was among those qualified to do so. It appears that he was: for in the caution it is stated that it was given to the venerable man, Master Bartholomew of Caselli, Archpriest of the major church of Parma, Vicar in spiritual matters, and Penitentiary in place of the said Bishop of Parma. By reason of the archpriestship, he seems to exercise the functions of the bishop, according to the office of the archpriest, Chapter 2. Therefore, he will be sufficient. Moreover, because he is called the Penitentiary, just as the rector of a parish church, so too he could thereby receive the caution. Thirdly, because it is stated that he was Vicar in spiritual matters, therefore he appears to be among those persons who can receive a caution. For the text says “to one exercising his functions,” and adds, “to whom indeed the ordinary, the Vicar, the rector, etc.” But I say that, unless it appears otherwise than through the aforementioned words of the notary that the said archpriest was Vicar or exercising functions in jurisdictional matters, the aforementioned caution is null, for those words are narrative, which is the same as if they were declarative, and therefore they do not prove. C. de testamentis, l. verba; and there, note on privileges, c. si Papa, lib. 11, tit. 6, as touched upon above.

† A notary is not believed, except concerning those matters which he was requested to record and which he perceived with some bodily sense: because he is, as it were, a kind of witness, therefore, etc. On witnesses, when the cause, which is between, etc. From this it is inferred that, since even a notary must stipulate by virtue of the mandate of the ordinary, otherwise he cannot do so, as in the same decree, *Quanquam*. That the archpriest, who is said to have mandated this to the notary, could not mandate it. Furthermore, even if this were conceded, proof of this mandate ought to be established otherwise than by the words of the same person, as noted by the doctors on proof, *c. Quam contra*. Moreover, even if it were granted that the said archpriest was a Vicar in spirituals, and this writing were upheld, or otherwise proven, nevertheless, perhaps in this case satisfaction would not be made to this decretal, *Quanquam*, because the cause of usury is not spiritual. And although it otherwise pertains to the ecclesiastical forum, as in the decretal *Dispendiosam*, on judges, and therefore also the secular judge cognizes it, and can compel usurers even to restitution, on usury, *c. Cum tu*, and *c. Quia in hominibus*, and *c. Post miserabilem*, and this is the opinion of the gloss on loan contracts, *c. Cum simili*, which gloss is also adduced for the other party. And we note this in the aforementioned decretal *Dispendiosam*, with its references. Although I think the aforementioned to be true, namely, that an action may be brought against a layman in both forums, when it comes into doubt whether there is a crime of usury or not, I do not doubt that this caution, which is a spiritual act, must be required. Therefore, it does not fall within the power of this vicar, even if he were a vicar, because that decretal, *Quanquam*, did not say "one exercising power in spirituals," or "Vicar in spirituals exercising vicarious functions," or "Vicar," as if referring to one who has general power, and who makes the same consistory with the bishop, and to whom recourse is had, except for exceptions. As is established in the Institutes, *c. 2*; on rules, *c. 2*; on frivolous and malicious appeals, *c. 1*; on appeals, *c. Romanus*, in the beginning, book 6. Because mandates are of strict law, on the office of delegates, *c. Praedictum*, and on rescripts, *c. Cum dilecta*, with similar cases. I say that a Vicar in spirituals does not make the same consistory with the bishop: and consequently he can be called a rural dean (foraneus), therefore he is not among the persons required for demanding this caution, according to the form of the decretal *Quanquam*. These things are clearly proven by the decretal *Et si principales*, on rescripts, joined with its two glosses. For since that Clementine wishes the principal Vicar, or Vicar, to be able to give delegation, but not the rural dean, the third gloss wishes that a Vicar in spirituals cannot be delegated. Likewise, the second gloss wishes that rural deans are those who are appointed for certain acts. Therefore, it follows well that this archpriest could not receive that caution, nor even the notary, in *c. De mandare*. Therefore, the caution is null. It does not object that he is said to be archpriest and penitentiary, because although the archpriest, by common law, officiates in divine services, or the celebration of divine offices, in the Decretals, 2, on the office of the archpriest, he does not do so in jurisdictional matters; rather, in these he is subject to the Archdeacon, as in the same Decretals, 1. Furthermore, it does not object that he is said to be penitentiary, because such power is not given to the penitentiary by the decretal *Quanquam*. And although the archpriest, by his own right, as a penitentiary, is a judge of individuals, at least of the city, regarding absolution of the penitential forum, i.e., of the soul, nevertheless not in this case; otherwise it would follow that in the same way any brother of the order of preachers or minors, who can hear confessions and absolve in the penitential forum, and thus are judges of souls, as in the Clementine *Dudum*, § *Statuimus*, on sepulture, could receive such cautions, which no one would say. Furthermore, it operates against the said caution,

† which does not hold, because the witnesses were not from the usurer’s parish. This seems to be required by the Decree *Quanquam*. Although the Archdeacon there says that this is rather a matter of due form (*de bene esse*) than of substance. Nevertheless, the contrary can be said with probability: because the text not only requires them to be credible, as is generally said about witnesses in other cases. 2 q. 7 c. *Testes*; and Cap. *Non potest* de Testibus; c. *Licet ex quadam*; and c. *Testimonium*. But the text adds “and from the parish.” Therefore, one should not depart from the words of the edict. L. *Non aliter*, ff. de Legatis 2; de Decimis, c. *Ad audientiam*; de Electionibus, c. *Qua propter*; Cum si. Lastly, that the caution was not sufficiently provided, although it is not stated in which respect it is deficient. Hence it must be observed that the form of the Decree *Quanquam*, in this regard, is simply that restitution shall be made by the usurious persons from whom the usuries were extorted, or to them, or to others who can acquire for them, or to the Ordinary, or to his deputy, or to the parish rector, or to a public servant by the mandate of the said Ordinary, and that they shall give sufficient caution for the restitution of the extorted usuries; and otherwise such a usurer cannot validly testify. And by the name of sufficient caution are understood pledges or sureties, as is noted in the said Decree. But in the caution which I saw, I do not find that he, the said [usurer], gave caution, either by promising to pay or to restore the extorted usuries; therefore the form of the law was not observed. Let the said caution or instrument be read and carefully examined. It is well stated therein to which persons restitution ought to be made, namely, to those from whom the usuries were extorted, or to their heirs. But it is not stated therein what ought to be restored, or what is promised to be returned, and therefore it is void. 32 q. 2, *Quod non*; de Poenitentia, Dist. 1, § *Hoc idem*, vers. *A mortuo*; de Desponsatione Impuberum, c. *Ad dissoluendum*; Cum si. Moreover, I also think that if anyone were to say, “I promise to him from whom I extorted usuries,” and said no more, such a promise does not bind, by argument from Inst. de Inutilis Stipulatione, § 1; and *Eius quod non*, ff. de Legatis 1, L. *Legati generaliter*. From which it is concluded that the said [usurer] must be considered a manifest usurer, as was deduced in the first article. And consequently, for his testament to be valid, he must adhere to the form of the Decree *Quanquam*, de Usuris, lib. 6. Also, that the first objection against the opposing caution is not valid, because the said caution preceded, which does not render the caution invalid. Similarly, the second is not valid, because it was given before the testament. Similarly, the third is not valid, because it was given for a small amount.
