But the other objections, thus declared and proved: as above, from which I conclude that the testament of the said [usurer] is void, and consequently that the heirs intestate ought to come to the inheritance. I, Baldus. I, Gaspar de Calderini, Doctor of Decrees and Knight, thus think it to be according to law, as the said Baldus has said. I, Laurentius, advise the same in all respects, as above. I, Petrus de Ancharia, as has been advised above, I say and advise.
The fact is held to be that a certain A. obtained a favor from the Supreme Pontiff, and it is found in part 5, consilium 77, beginning “casus talis” etc.
The case of Atancus of Aquis, by words of the present tense spoken in this manner, namely, etc., this opinion is found in part 5, consilium 78, beginning: "Case, Arancus of Aquis," and so forth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is required regarding the substance of marriage.
2. Whether, if a man is asked if he wants such a woman as his wife, and he answers, "I will, if she wills it," and she, when subsequently asked, answers that she wills what pleases her brother, a marriage is contracted between such parties.
3. Whether, in the case where the woman's brother had promised the said man, the man can proceed against him concerning the faith given, and summon him to a duel.
4. The duel is prohibited by civil and canon law.
5. Whether a woman is bound to appear personally in court.
6. If words of the present tense are exchanged between a man and a woman, and the woman immediately protests that whatever she did, she did by force or fear, whether the marriage is valid.
body:
The case is as follows: After several prior agreements had been made between the nobleman John the Notary on one part, and the nobleman Ambrose Scarapus on the other part, concerning the contracting of a marriage between the said Ambrose and the noblewoman Margaret, the uterine sister of the said John, it came to pass that the said Ambrose, personally present in the house of Antonio de Ponte, and the said Margaret being personally exhibited there and presented to the said Ambrose by the said John, her uterine brother, the matter was put to him in words of the present tense, asking whether the said Ambrose wished to take the said Margaret as his legitimate wife. The said Ambrose answered, “Yes, if she wishes the same.” And whether the said Margaret wished to take the said Ambrose as her husband and spouse, she answered that she wished to do so, which pleased her brother. And thus the parties departed from each other. Immediately after their departure, and subsequently thereafter, the said Margaret asserted and declared, and protested, that she had never consented to the said Ambrose as her husband, nor had she freely wished to consent. And that the words were uttered out of fear of bodily torture, which she feared would be inflicted upon her, and which she hoped would be inflicted through her said brother. This protestation of the said Margaret was made before the act of her presence, and of the said Ambrose’s presence, and of the aforementioned words exchanged between them, as she had done solemnly, inasmuch as she did not intend in any way to consent to the said Ambrose as her husband.

Later, however, the said noblewoman Margaret, through her procurator, brought the said Ambrose to suit before the Vicar of the Diocese of the said Bishop of Asti, petitioning that the said marriage be declared and pronounced null, as having been contracted through fear and without the consent of the said Margaret, and the said Margaret not being in her own liberty. This question is still pending before the judge, with no tacit or express ratification having followed, nor any intervention of conjugal cohabitation.

The said Ambrose, while the aforementioned litigation was pending in the episcopal court, brought the said John to suit before the secular judge of Asti, suing him for breach of faith regarding the said agreements, and asserting against him fraud and falsity. The said Ambrose offered himself ready to prove this by witnesses, and, should they fail, to prove it by combat. He petitioned that a place for combat or duel be granted between them. The opposing party, the said John, raised a declinatory plea regarding the forum on account of the person of the said John, who was not subject to the secular judge in that part of the matter due to the pendency of the litigation, which was being conducted before the ecclesiastical judge. It was interlocutorily decided that the secular judge was the competent judge, notwithstanding the said declinatory plea. From this interlocutory decision, an appeal was taken on behalf of the said John to the Apostolic See, and to the said Lord Bishop of Asti, and to whomever the said appeal might more properly devolve by right. And proceeding upon the said appeal, he was sent to the court. Now it is asked, what is the law?

On the first point, it must be premised for clarity, that it is a regular rule that

† That marriage requires the words of the bridegroom and the bride, as is stated in the extrajudicial collection *De Sponsalibus et Matrimonio*, chapter *Tuas*; and as noted in the last chapter of the title *De Coniugio Servorum*; and in chapter 1, section *Porro*, of the title *De Desponsatione Impuberum*, Book 6. Consent, however, is that which principally establishes marriage, as is stated in the Digest, *De Regulis Iuris*, law *Nuptias*. Therefore, in marriage, words and understanding, or consent, are required so that the marriage may have its substance and solemnity; nor is the mere form of words without consent sufficient; nor is tacit consent not expressed in words, according to what is noted in a similar case in the Digest, *De Actionibus et Obligationibus*, law *Non Figura*; and in the Code, *De Praescriptionibus Triginta Annorum*, law *Cum Notissimi*, in the beginning. Furthermore, an interrogation and response, or something equivalent, must intervene, as is noted in the Digest, *De Adoptionibus*, law 2, in the beginning; and as noted in the Decretum, Question 27, Cause 2, section 1, in the gloss beginning *Voluntarius Ius*. Therefore, it requires natural consent. But the Church and positive law require the aid of words, just as in a stipulation, as is stated in the Institutes, *De Verborum Obligationibus*, in the beginning. And this the Church has established, so that there could be no doubt about marriage. For no one can deny what he has clearly declared with his own voice, provided he has done so freely, with all deceit and fraud removed, as is stated in the Code, *De Non Numerata Pecunia*, law *Generaliter*; and in the extrajudicial collection *De Probationibus*, chapter *Per Tuas*; and in chapter 1 of the extrajudicial collection *Quod Metus Causa*; and in the extrajudicial collection *De Sponsalibus et Matrimonio*, chapter *Cum Locum*. Secondly, I premise that where words are required, there must be a probable conformity, nor should one speak of the present and the other of the future; nor should one, for example, speak under a condition and the other under no condition, nor one under one condition and the other under another, as is stated in the Digest, *De Verborum Obligationibus*, law 1, section *Cum Si Quis Simpliciter*; and section *Addicit*. From these premises, the weakening of the first point becomes apparent.

† For although a marriage may be contracted under a condition, so that it takes effect when the condition exists, as stated in the Decretals, De conditionibus appositis, chapter Super eo and chapter Finis; nevertheless, if the man responds under an intrinsic condition, such as “I will take Berta, if Berta wills,” and Berta responds under an extrinsic condition, such as “I will take you, if my brother wills,” no bond is contracted. And even less so if the male responds under a present condition, such as “I will take you, if you will me,” and the female under a future condition, because she says that she will do what pleases her brother; no obligation arises from such words. For a relative clause joined to a verb of the future tense makes a future condition, as in the Digest, De legatis primo, Stichum, “who will be mine.” Hence it is manifest that the words and the intent diverged, because the future is in a sense opposed to the present, as in the Digest, De in iustum testamentum, Cum in secundo; and De heredibus instituendis, Illa institutio and Illae autem institutiones. Therefore, the girl not only did not respond to the proposal, but responded to the opposite; and thus no conjugal bond was contracted, wherefore it is superfluous to inquire further about the girl.

Now let us consider the matter of the said Ioannonus, whether the said Ioannonus, because the marriage was not contracted, is said to have committed falsity or fraud against the said Ambrosius. And it must be said that he did not, for fraud is not committed against one who knows. For the said Ambrosius understood, or ought to have understood, the will of the woman, which was not conformable to his own will. But that which was substantial to the marriage, namely his consent, he directed toward another, which is impossible, as is noted by Accursius in the aforementioned law *Nuptias*, *De regulis iuris*. And although he is a nobleman, and perhaps illiterate, he is nevertheless not excused if he claims not to have understood the subtleties of the law, for if he had taken counsel with those more learned, he would easily have known, as in the Code, *De ingenuis manumissis*, law *Si auam tuam*. Moreover, the said Ioannonus, even if he had expressly promised a penalty, would not be bound to it, so that the free faculty of contracting marriage may not be impeded. For the marriage was not contracted, as has been shown above. To this effect: Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Titia*; and Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Haeres meus*, § *Ultimo*; and what is noted in the Code, *De sponsalibus*, law *Finis*, by Jacobus de Aretio and Cynus. For all who can provide an impediment or support concerning marriage cannot be bound to a penalty, nor punished thereby civilly or criminally. Furthermore, to treat here of a judicial duel is ridiculous: for since the law is apt against the said Ambrosius, there is no place for a duel; this holds true speaking of any law, even Lombard law, for the aforementioned reason.

† As to civil and canon law, there is no doubt: because dueling is prohibited, as in C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. negantes; and ff. ad legem Aquiliam, l. a qua actione, § si quis in colluctatione; and Inst. de haereditatibus quae ab intestato, § per contrarium. And it is also clear that this case is not a case of judicial combat, as shown in Collatio 10, de alienatione feudorum, pater, cap. non est consuetudo; and in the same Compilation, title de pace tenenda, cap. 1, § si quis hominem, where four cases are noted in which judicial combat is permitted, and this is not one of them; and in the same title, cap. si rusticus militem; and in Extra, de purificatione vulgari, throughout. For the vigor of judicial proceedings and the protection of public law are established precisely so that recourse to arms is not had indiscriminately, as in C. de iudiciis, l. nullus; and ff. de usufructu, l. aequissimum. Moreover, even if this were a case of judicial combat, since combat is an extraordinary remedy, it seems that one has receded from an extraordinary and odious remedy after having chosen the ordinary path of judicial process, as in ff. de minoribus, l. in causis; and fully noted by Dynus in ff. de novo operis nuntiatione, l. in provinciali.

† As to another point, namely whether a woman is bound to appear personally in court, it must be said that she is not, as stated in Auth. ut nulli iudicibus, § necessarium vero; and Codex, de custodia reorum, Auth. novo iure; and Codex, de officiis civilium iudicum, together with Auth. sed hodie. Hence, she ought not to be compelled to go personally before the judge, but it suffices for her to send a procurator. And let me be pardoned out of reverence for the said judge, who pronounced otherwise, because he does not seem to have duly weighed those texts and notes in Digestum, de iureiurando, l. ad personas egregias, according to the accurate interpretation.

But let us suppose that the words were, by their very nature, present-tense words suitable for contracting marriage; nevertheless, the woman made a public protest before honest persons, declaring that she in no way intended to consent to him as her husband, and that whatever she did, she did out of fear and under the impression of the said brother. It does not, however, appear that this protest came to the knowledge of the said Ambrosius. The question now arises whether the marriage was contracted or not. It seems that the marriage was contracted, because a protest made in the absence of the opposing party does not benefit the protesting party, except in matters that depend solely on the mind of the protesting party, such as the acceptance of an inheritance and similar cases, as is noted by the doctors in *l. qui aliena*, § *Celsus*, *de acquisitione hereditatis*; and in *ff. de negotiis gestis*, *l. Nesenius Appollinaris*; and in *ff. de religiosis et sumptibus funerum*, *l. At si quis*, § *Plerique*.

To the contrary, it seems, first, from the text of the said § *Celsus*, where it is stated that a preceding protest, which is contrary to the subsequent act, causes the subsequent act to have no effect, according to Dynus and according to the glossa placed there. Therefore, the protest is not invalidated: because, foreseeing that he would be compelled, he protested in order to avoid the injury of compulsion; hence, since there is a text and an ordinary glossa there, we must say that the said marriage was not a marriage, due to the lack of consent: as in *ff. de actionibus et obligationibus*, *l. Obligationum substantia*. For the said protest was legitimate and made in good faith, because one who resists fraud with fraud is not said to be fraudulent, but cautious. And the law permits this: as in *ff. de legibus 2*, *l. Cum pater*, § *Titio*.

Moreover, the brother’s fraud was shared with the said Ambrosius, and they agreed between themselves, by an unconditional pact, to the acts in question. And it is certain that a participant in fraud should not derive benefit from his own fraud: as in *ff. quae in fraudem creditorum*, *l. Ait praetor*, § *Actio haec*; and § *Si quis particeps*.

Furthermore, when dealing with such an act in which the will acts principally, indeed, in perfecting the matter in question, if the will is lacking, the act is not celebrated. This is so in marriage, because consent is of the substance of marriage, and free consent must not only be free from compulsion, but also from the suspicion of compulsion: as in *ff. quod falso testis autore*, *l. Nouissime*, § 1, where it says, “or that he would not be compelled by fear.” This text is very singular.

Also supporting this is *ff. de manumissionibus*, *l. Si pater*; and what is noted in *c. Unico*, *de renuntiis*, in the Clementines; and *extra*, *ut ecclesiastica beneficia*, *c. Ut nostram*; and *extra*, *de renuntiis*, *c. Super hoc*.

Moreover, it cannot be said that this protest was clandestine, since it was made before honest men. And therefore, both on account of its justice and natural equity, and also on account of the lack of substantial consent in contracting marriage, it must be said that no marriage was contracted: because words without consent effect nothing, as in *ff. de militum testamento*, *l. Diuus Traianus*, § *Ultimo*.

Furthermore, when the notification of the protesting party involves fear of the opposing party, it is not necessary that notification be made: as in *ff. de novi operis nuntiatione*, *l. De pupillo*, § *Ipsi praetori*; and *Codex*, *de his qui per metum iussu non appellant*, *l. Finalis*; and *extra*, *de appellationibus*, *ca. Si iustus metus*; and supporting this is *ff. quod metus causa*, *l. Si mulier*, § *Si dos*.

And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, if one of the four witnesses described in the instrument contradicts the instrument, the instrument is thereby rendered false, or so suspect that it does not constitute full proof.
2. Whether a single witness against an instrument constitutes grounds for torture.
3. A judgment rendered in a criminal case carries full faith in a civil case.
body: It is proposed that from a certain instrument drawn up in public form, in which instrument four witnesses are named. When it was produced in court, and the plaintiff wished to found his claim thereon, an exception of falsity was raised: and to prove the falsity, one witness described in the instrument was brought forward, who testified that the said instrument was false. Likewise, he produced certain other witnesses, who stated that the said notary had asked them whether they wished the said notary to describe them in the said instrument. Also, certain other witnesses testified that the notary is of bad reputation. And it is true that the said notary was arrested, and an inquisition for forgery was formed against him, and a most rigorous investigation was conducted, and the said notary was tortured, who always remained firm and constant in his instrument, declaring the instrument to be true. Whereupon the judge acquitted him of the criminal charge, and remitted him to the civil judge. Now the question arises, given these circumstances,

Whether the judge in a civil case ought to deem the said instrument false, or at least so suspect that, being otherwise uncorroborated by the instrument itself, it does not yield effective proof. And it seems one should say first that the said instrument ought to be deemed false, as in C. de probat. l. iubemus; or at least so suspect that it does not make full proof, as in ff. de edend. l. si quis ex argentariis, § 2; or at least that this remains in the discretion of the judge, as fully noted by Cynus, according to Jacobus de Arena and Petrus, in C. de fide instru. l. in exercendis, in the first question.

To the contrary it seems, because a public instrument is not reproved for the defect of falsity by one witness who is not of the substance of the instrument. This is held by Accursius in Inst. de inuti. stipu. § item verborum, and by Bartolus in l. 1, in fine, ff. quemad. testa. aperian., and by the Canonists in cap. cum Ioan. Haeremita, de fide instrumen. And because one witness is singular and unique, he does not make faith, especially in so arduous a case, as in extra de proba. ca. licet causam, § quanquam autem, and de causa pos. cap. cum ecclesia. And the text of the law requires testimony for the reprobation of an instrument, and the plurality of witnesses, and that they be above all exception. C. de contrahen. et commit. stipu. l. optimam, in fine; and noted in ff. de pac. l. iurisgentium, § pactorum. And this is the very truth, that an instrument is not reproved by one supernumerary witness; because the voice of one is the voice of no one, as in C. de testi. l. iusiurandi, with similar authorities.

It is nevertheless true that, although one good witness does not invalidate the instrument, he nevertheless provides grounds for torture, so that both must be tortured, namely the witness and the notary. Moreover, greater credence is given to the notary who stands by his instrument than to the witness who stands by his testimony, on account of the public authority of the notary. However, once the inquiry has been conducted and the notary has been definitively acquitted, it does not seem that the crime should be further debated, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on collusion, in the chapter *Si*, and it appears expressly in the Code, on the faith of instruments, in the law *Si*, at the end.

† For a judgment rendered in a criminal case creates faith in a civil case, as noted in C. quando ciuilis actio, l. 1; and C. ad I. Iul. de vi, l. si quis ad se fundum; and l. 2, ff. vi bono. rap. Moreover, the other aforementioned supporting arguments do not stand in the way: because good reputation has been proven against bad reputation, to which proof greater weight is given, since it is accompanied by a natural presumption to the same effect, ad idem, C. ne de statu defun., l. si mater. Furthermore, the supporting argument drawn from the statement of the notary made outside of court does not harm the party. ar. extra de testi., cap. sicut nobis. Moreover, it is more strongly presumed in favor of an acquittal than in favor of these remote indications, as in extra de renun., cap. in pręsentia; and C. de administ. tuto., l. si bonam. And by this, C. de prob., l. iubemus, does not stand in the way; because by the acquittal every stain on the notary has been purged: and consequently the notary’s credibility has been approved: and consequently the instrument must be upheld, as in C. de proba., l. cum precibus; and C. de edi. diui Adri. tol., l. edicto, cum si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When an heir dies during the lifetime of the testator, such an institution is called quasi caduca; and if there is no vulgar or coheir substitution, the institution vanishes, and all legacies and the like [fail].
2. Whether a codicillary clause operates in any way when the will is valid, or when it is invalid from the beginning.
3. A fideicommissary substitution made in default of the will seems to be made equally as if intestate.
4. The testator instituted his two sons as his heirs, and if either of them should die without children, he substituted the other in the whole; but if both should die without children, he willed that one half of his inheritance should devolve upon his two daughters, and the other half to the poor of Christ, with a codicillary clause appended in the will. Now, the aforementioned sons died during the lifetime of the testator. Then the testator died, leaving his daughters, who accepted the entire inheritance intestate. Whether one half of the said inheritance pertains to the poor of Christ.
body: The matter is proposed in these terms. Peter of Pignorio made his last will, in which he instituted as his universal heirs his two sons, namely Christatus and Florus, in equal shares, with this condition, however, that if one of his sons or heirs should die from this life without legitimate children, he substituted the other surviving one as his heir in the entirety. And if both should die without children born of a lawful marriage, he willed that one half of his entire inheritance should devolve upon his daughters Tecla and Margarita, and the other half be given and distributed to the poor of Christ for his soul and the remission of his sins. And he added a clause that, if it does not have effect by the law of wills, it should have effect by the law of codicils and by the law of any last will. The case occurred that both of the instituted heir sons died without surviving issue, while the said testator was still alive. Finally, the testator died, with his said daughters surviving, who entered upon the intestate inheritance of their said father; against whom the poor of Christ are proceeding, and they petition the Most Reverend Lord Bishop of Verona, to whom pertains the execution of the last will for pious causes, that the distribution of one half of the said inheritance be made to them. Now it is doubted whether the same executor can execute the last will, that is, distribute one half of the said inheritance among the poor of Christ, or not. For the sake of clarity, it must be premised,

† That when a named heir dies during the lifetime of the testator, such an institution is called as it were lapsed; if there is a vulgar substitute, the substitution is acquired. Likewise, if there is a surviving coheir, it accrues to him with his own burden. But if there is neither a coheir nor a substitute who is directly substituted, not only does the institution vanish, but also all legacies and fideicommissa dependent on the substitution, except those which are repeated ab intestato, as in C. de fideicom. l. ex testamento. Therefore, in two cases legacies and fideicommissa remain when the instituted heirs die during the lifetime of the testator: namely, when there is a vulgar substitute who has accepted, or a coheir to whom it accrues, or they are repeated ab intestato, as in C. de cadu. tol. l. 1. §. his ita and §. pro secundo; and fully noted in C. de fideicommissis l. eam, quam and C. de conditionibus l. fin.

Secondly, it must be premised that sometimes a will is valid from the beginning; and then the codicillary clause, "if it is not valid, etc.," has no effect, because it is false. Sometimes a will is not valid from the beginning, and then the clause has effect, because it is true, as is fully noted by Modus in l. 1, ff. de iure codicilli.

Thirdly, it must be premised that a fideicommissary substitution, which is made in the event of the failure of the will, appears to take effect equally as if intestate, as stated in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, *Lucius*, § *filiam*. Therefore, having thus clearly premised these three points, let us see in which case we are.

And if indeed the testator left something purely to the said daughters by way of institution, then it is certain that the will is valid; because the portion of the males accrues to them, as in D. de heredibus instituendis, l. 1, § si ex fundo, and fully noted by Mod. in C. de haeredibus instituendis, l. quotiens. And although these daughters should repudiate the inheritance under the will and accept it as intestate heirs, they would be bound to legacies and fideicommissa by virtue of the edict "si quis omissa causa testamenti," as in C. si quis omissa causa testamenti, l. 6, and D. eodem, per totum. But if nothing was left purely to the daughters, but they were merely substituted under a casual condition to a fideicommissum, the will was null, because they were passed over, as in Auth. ut cum de appellatione cogatur, § aliud quoque capitulum, and C. de liberis praeteritis, l. maximum vitium. I speak according to the ius commune. And then the codicillary clause operates well. Likewise, Auth. ex causa, as fully explained there by the doctors; and thus the fideicommissum is still due. But let us assume that, by the form of some statute, women could be passed over when males are extant; nevertheless, it must still be said that the said fideicommissum left to the poor is due. For those words, "if they should die without children," are pregnant words. For they can be understood whether they died during the lifetime of the testator or afterwards. Nor is there any reason why they should be restricted to the latter case. Thus, therefore, the sense of these words is twofold, namely, if they died during the father's lifetime, or afterwards. Now take the first time, and I argue thus: This fideicommissum is left under a condition quasi of caducity of the will; therefore, it is left in default of the will, and thus as intestate. Hence, that it is due, is a case in the aforementioned § filiam, and D. de heredibus instituendis, l. qui filio, § servus. Moreover, many doctors would say that the said substitution is direct, namely, vulgar in the aforementioned case; because it is concise, as fully noted by Ioan. Andr. and determined by disputing in c. si pater, de testibus, lib. 6, and by Cy. in l. precibus, C. de impuberibus, in additiones. Innocentius holds the same.

† Regarding the word “deueniat” [shall come]: because the addition of “de-” intensifies the meaning, as he himself noted in Extra, De testibus, c. Raynutius. Moreover, the testator’s will ought to be interpreted broadly, especially in favor of pious causes. Hence, although the testator said, “if it is not valid, etc.,” in favor of the pious cause, it appears that he also provided for a similar case, namely, “if it shall not be valid.” Argument: Codex, De posthumi heredes instituendi, l. fin. Whether the substitution is direct or not, the poor have a right not only by reason of piety and voluntary consideration, but also strictly by reason of law, and the distribution must be made according to the form of the will. For the testator preferred males alone to the poor, but placed women on an equal footing with them; and therefore the will must be observed as the mistress, as in Codex, De legatis, l. conquo, §. si. And to that rule which is stated in l. eam, quam and l. si nemo, the answer is given by what has been said above. And it is not an obstacle, De capite minuendo, l. si filius, and what is noted in Digest, De vulgari substitutione, l. lex Cornelia; because there it is a matter of pupillary substitution, whereas here it is a compendious or fideicommissary substitution. It also supports the above what has been prudently alleged, that legacies to pious causes do not await the acceptance of the inheritance. But to this it may be answered that this is true when there is no other defect than that of acceptance. But here we are in a case of caducity. Nevertheless, I conclude finally as I concluded above. Moreover, there is a gloss in l. praecibus, which says, and I do not consider this as compendious; because that text speaks when the instituted heir dies after the inheritance has been accepted. Moreover, even assuming it is fideicommissary, as I have said, it is a fideicommissum ab intestato in the case of caducity; because there cannot be caducity without a defect in the will. And it seems to me that it would be dangerous to advise the contrary in legacies to pious causes, since the testator expressly wished them to be performed. Argument: l. 1, Codex, Communia de legatis. In which legacies two witnesses suffice according to the best opinion, and all exceptions are greater, as in Extra, De testibus, c. cum esset, and cap. relatum. For if they were tainted by a slight blemish, they would not be believed. Argument: Codex, De fideiussoribus, l. quaestionem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, a citizen may or may not be a witness in a case of the city, or a townsman in a case of his town, or one of a corporation in a case of the corporation. And whether. 2.
2. A monk may give testimony in a case of his chapter.
body: Case. The men and commune of a certain place bring an action against Titius, stating that he is a burgess of the same place and requesting that he be compelled to bear real and personal burdens together with them; on the other hand, Titius denies that he is a burgess of the aforesaid place. The men and commune strive to prove that he is a burgess, and to prove this they produce men of the same place, whose depositions were received after a protestation was first made by the said Titius that his right of objecting both against the persons and against the statements would be reserved. This being done, Titius produces witnesses to rebut the statements of the prior witnesses. Finally, the men and commune of the aforesaid place produce witnesses to rebut the rebuttal witnesses of Titius, and to prove this they produce witnesses of the same place. From these facts it is asked whether the depositions of the witnesses of the place, both those first produced and those second produced, ought to be relied upon, and whether credit ought not to be given to them as deponents in their own cause.

† For the sake of clarity, it must be premised that certain causes belong to the community and not to individuals: as if the dispute were concerning the property of the fisc of that corporate body, or concerning mills and similar things pertaining by full right to the corporate body; and thus the dispute does not touch the individuals. And then individuals of the corporate body can testify, because what belongs to the corporate body does not belong to the individuals, as in ff. de in ius voc. l. sed si hac. §. qui manumittitur and ff. de re. diui. l. in tantum. §. vniuersitatis. However, how much credit is to be attached to the witnesses from other inferences is committed to the discretion of the judge, as in ff. de testi. l. 3. §. tu magis and l. ob carmen. §. fin. Certain matters, however, belong to individuals in such a way that they do not belong to the corporate body, as if certain distributions ought to be made among individual citizens; and then those whom the advantage and business touch cannot be witnesses insofar as it touches them, but insofar as it touches others, they can, as in C. de test. l. omnibus. Sometimes the question is mixed, for example because there is a dispute concerning the woods of the corporate body in which, by custom, individuals pasture animals and take advantage; and it seems that they are barred from giving testimony as if in a common cause. For although it is not their own cause simply, nevertheless it is their own cause qualifiedly, such that they could intervene in it as adversaries of the other party on behalf of their own interest; and if they are adversaries, therefore they cannot be witnesses, as in the said l. omnibus and ff. quando appe. sit. l. 2. §. et si alius. Now let us see what the law is in the proposed case.

† Whether this cause is said to be mixed, namely of the corporate body and of individuals. I say mixed principally, such that the witnesses are rejected as testifying concerning their own advantage. And it seems that it is, because the question is concerning a common burden; which question seems to be their own in part, because it affects each of them, as in extra de praescript. c. accedentes. 1. respons. But against this makes Inst. de test. §. legatariis and C. de testa. l. dictantibus; but there the witnesses do not depose concerning their own legacy, but concerning the institution of the heir; likewise to solemnity, not to specific truth. Likewise lex 1. ff. de autho. tuto. seems to stand against it, where one can authorize incidentally in one's own affair, although not principally. Wherefore it would seem that a distinction must be drawn: either they are introduced immediately to prove contribution, and then they are not fit witnesses; or to prove origin or residence, from which by an indirect inference of law, and not of the witnesses, contribution follows and is inferred; and then such testimony is received, because it is not principally concerning the bearing of a burden. And therefore citizenship can be proved by the citizens themselves, and especially when the dispute is between those who are of the same body. But Speculator says that they are admitted in default of others, and adds that in a cause of a corporate body a witness does not testify for any individual of the corporate body, and therefore not for himself; and therefore he concludes that in a cause of a corporate body or collegium, without distinction, anyone from the corporate body or collegium can testify, as he notes in Spec. de teste. §. 1. versic. sed nunquid in causa vniuersitatis, vel collegii. Innocent in c. 2. extra de testi. says without distinction that he who has an interest is not admitted as a witness. But here there is no doubt that they also have an individual interest and as to pecuniary advantage; whence, just as a partner is not admitted in an indivisible cause, so it seems in the present case that these are not admitted. On this point, these are the words of Odofredus: Note here that what belongs to the corporate body does not belong to individuals, and vice versa; whence what the corporate body owes, individuals do not owe, as in ff. quod cuius. vni. no. l. sicut. §. 1.

† Likewise you will gather that a monk can bear testimony in a cause of his chapter, and a citizen in a cause of his city; and this is supported by ff. de in ius voc. l. sed si has. §. qui manumittitur and infra de quaestio. l. 1. §. si seruus. Nevertheless, I have been accustomed to say thus: as to testimony on behalf of a city, I say that a citizen in one cause can bear testimony for the city, and in another cause he cannot. Whence distinguish: either the cause of the corporate body is purely of the corporate body, and individuals do not derive an individual benefit from it—as can be seen in the mills of the commune of Bologna; then, if litigation is about the mills, a citizen can bear testimony, because this cause is a purely corporate cause. But if individuals derive benefit from it, as you can see in a forest which has a certain wood that is common to the corporate body, so that anyone can go and carry wood from it; if these individuals litigated over the forest, they could not bear testimony, because then they would bear it in their own cause etc., as in C. de testi. l. omnib., and a cause is called one's own etc., as in infra quando appellatio. sit. l. 1. §. in propria. Odofredus. And so I, Baldus, hold.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a memorandum written in the hand of the testator’s father, among the children, even if witnesses are not described therein, is to be made public by order of the judge.
body: That

† the memorandum ought to be elevated and reduced into public form, for perpetual firmness, it is proved: as below. For it is necessary to premise for clarity, that sometimes, to prove a testament among children, only the writing of the father is introduced: in its own complete form as regards the act of disposition, but not with respect to solemnity as to the number of witnesses, at least two, in whose mouth every word regularly stands, as in Extra, de testamento, c. Cum esses, and c. Relatum. And then, when it appears that there is only the writing by the hand of the disposing father: some say that such writing is not sufficient; because no law provides that a testament among children is valid without two witnesses; just as a soldier’s testament is not valid unless two witnesses are present. Noted in C., de testamento militis, l. Milites in expeditione; and in ff., eodem, l. Lucius; and in C., de testamento, Auth. Quod sine, in the glossa ordinaria; and in C., de codicillis, l. Si quis agere, in the end. Hence, two witnesses are called indications among children, and not fewer, as noted in l. Ultima, C., familiae hereditatis. Since therefore the writing has no witness, and thus is a private writing, they say that no proof arises from such writing. It is certain. Noted by it, solemnity is not proved. They say the same that truth is not proved. It supports what is noted in l. 2, C., quemadmodum testamentum; in ff., de eodem, l. 2. For in a nuncupative testament, the writing must be read to the witnesses summoned to the testament, or at least present, where rogation is not required, as in C., qui testamento facere possint, l. Hac consultissima, §. At cum humana. Others say that the father’s writing alone suffices; because such undoubted writing ought to have the force of two witnesses; just as we say in contracts, in which truth suffices without other probatory solemnity, as in C., de non numerata pecunia, l. Generaliter; and in Extra, de probationibus, c. Per tuas; and in ff., de possessionibus, l. Publicia, in the end. And for this, the text and gloss seem to support it, as in Auth., de testamento imperfecto, §. Si nec dixit aliquis, that this testament is not promulgated, but retained in the mind. Rather, it is promulgated, since the memorandum was given to the notary to be published. To this it supports what is noted by Bartolus in l. Fideicommissa, §. 1, ff., de legatis tertio. But I leave this article, because it is not expedient to treat of it. Sometimes, however, witnesses are produced: because they heard and were present when the father made the testament among his children. And assuming that no writing in the world had intervened: nevertheless, the statements of these witnesses ought to be reduced into public writing for perpetual memory of the matter, as noted in C., de edicto divi Adriani tollendo, l. Ultima. Sometimes the writing by the hand of the father is produced, and given to the notary in the presence of two witnesses testifying both as to the writing and as to the reading and completion of the testament. And then there is no doubt that the said writing ought to be reduced into public and solemn form. As in C., de testamento, l. Publicati. To the effect that two witnesses among children operate the same as seven among others, the subscription of the testator at the end is not required, since the testator himself wrote the testament, as in C., de testamento, l. Cum antiquitas, §. Finis. Well, I concede that, since it is not subscribed by the notary, although the notary’s sign is there, it is not authentic writing; but it ought to be published by order of the magistrate, as in Extra, de fide instrumentorum, c. Cum P. tabellio. Especially since the notary attests at the beginning of the writing that the act is perfected. And to say the contrary would be very unjust, because it would be to subvert the true will of the testator among his children, among whom the law is content with will alone, as in the said §. Ultimo, in Auth., de testamento imperfecto. Nor do I omit that witnesses referring themselves to the memorandum prove fully, as if they made mention word for word of the contents of the memorandum, since it is one memorandum, and not several. As in Extra, de fide instrumentorum, c. Cum Ioanne heremita. This Bartolus holds, expressly proving by many laws and reasons. In ff., de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Si ita scripsero. Considering therefore the witnesses testifying so explicitly, as are Centurionus and Nassibene, as well as implicitly, as are many others, there ought to be no doubt in my judgment, that the writing, about which inquiry is made, having seen the acts and proceedings in the case, ought to be published for perpetual memory of the matter. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal may make a will or otherwise dispose of feudal things.
2. Whether the Knights of the Cross are capable of holding fiefs.
3. In the succession to a fief, who is to be preferred: brothers related on both sides, or those related through the maternal line.
body: For the sake of clarity, it must be premised that,

† In feudal fiefs, a vassal cannot make a will. For either he disposes of those goods in favor of the person succeeding to the fief, and it is not valid, because he left to himself that which is his, to whom he left it. I say that it is his after the death of the testator, for then the will takes effect, as in C. de leg. l. proprias, and ff. de condi. et demon. l. mea res. Or he left them to others: and then either entirely to an outsider, and it is not valid, as in c. 1. §. donare, quare olim feu. alie. pote., and in c. 1. §. 1. de alie. feu., and C. de leg. l. vxor patrui. Or he left them to an agnate, and then it matters whether to a more remote agnate, and it does not prejudice the closer ones even with the consent of the lord, as I fully noted in c. 1. de alie. feu. paterni. Or he left them to a closer agnate, and then the legacy is not valid, because it confers no benefit, since he would have succeeded anyway without the legacy. For the law says that a legacy which confers no benefit is not valid, as in ff. mandati. l. hęreditatem, and C. communia deleg. l. 1. §. penul., and the same applies to contracts: because although during the lifetime of the contracting parties alienation among agnates is valid, at death it is reduced to the common law of feudal custom, as in d. c. 1. de alie. feudi pater. Secondly, it must be premised for clarity,

† That these Crusaders are regulars: nevertheless, because they serve God in armed warfare against the infidels, perhaps they are not incapable of holding a fief, because they have not laid down arms of war, but have exchanged them for the better, that is, for a better form of military service. Argument: Digest, On Testaments of Soldiers, law *Quo dicitur*. Against this, however, it is argued, because they cannot serve their lord, as in chapter 1, *De eo qui arma bellica deposuit*. But in favor of the faith, it is perhaps not erroneous to say that those who fight against the infidels are understood to be serving their lord, and therefore they retain the fief during their lifetime. Argument: Digest, On Excuses from Guardianship, law *Sed et reprobari*, near the end, where it says, “contributing to his own benefit,” etc., provided that they do not behave negligently with regard to such military service, same title, law *Si duas*, § *Placet*. I, however, hold that according to the strict law of fiefs, the said Brother Francis is not capable of holding a fief, but that he can succeed in allodial property and is capable thereof. As in Codex, *De episcopis et clericis*, law *Deo nobis*. Although I have said that a fief cannot be bequeathed by will, this must be understood unless the local custom holds otherwise; because a special custom in a place derogates from the general custom of fiefs. For, as the rule of law dictates, the general is derogated by the specific. It supports this: Codex, *De aedificiis privatis*, law *An in totum* and law *Venditor*, § *Si constat*. Common law of fiefs, and *De feudi cognitione*, chapter *Obortus*, in the beginning.

† Moreover, it must be known that in the succession to a paternal fief, connection through the maternal line is not taken into account: because the maternal line is invalid and is regarded as if it did not exist; as I fully noted in c. 1, §. cum vero Coradus, qui feudum dare possunt. And thus holds Jacobus de Ardizone in his Summa. And this is the truth. However, until it is known whether the brothers are dead, those related on both sides are preferred: because the fruits of the fief pertain to them. For the fruits, once separated from the land or assigned to the vassal by custom, are allodial and not feudal, as in c. 1, an agnatus, vel filius, coll. 2. Therefore, in this doubt, those related on both sides are to be preferred in possession, or a curator of the goods should be appointed at their petition, and that of the other brothers: because it is in the interest of both parties; nevertheless, those related on both sides are more favored in this doubt, and it is established. C. de ca., l. nec nos. But if the said absentees left a procurator, the fruits ought to be assigned to that procurator. For in this case, the appointment of a curator does not take place, as in l. ab hostibus, in principio, ff. quibus ex causis maior. Moreover, death is not presumed unless it is proven at least by several indications, as noted in C. solum, matrim., l. si quidem, and ff. quemadmodum testamentum aperitur, l. 2, §. si dubitetur. But if death were proven, it is certain that the allodial goods pertain to the brothers related on both sides, and not to those related on only one side, as I said above, as noted in C. de legatis et hereditatibus, Authent. post fratres. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If an agreement was reached between the prince and the lord of a certain territory that the law shall be observed in said territory, whether a statute subsequently enacted by the inhabitants of said territory, providing that married women shall not succeed in the presence of males, is valid.
2. Whether a statute excluding women from succession is understood to also exclude their descendants.
body: To the most illustrious Prince, and the magnificient lord, the lord prince of Achaea and Morea, and the community of Sauiliani, which is a community specially subject to his principality and domain by grant: such is the agreement, that in intestate successions the laws are observed; and after this agreement the community of Sauiliani enacted under the heading that no woman may claim a share of her father’s or mother’s succession, in the form that follows, namely: Furthermore, that no woman, by herself or through another, in any manner, after she has been married, may claim anything, or raise any dispute, or bring any action against any of her brothers, or her nephews, on account of any succession of her father, or mother, or brotherhood, or for any other cause whatsoever: unless it had been expressly bequeathed to her, or given, or promised. Finally, it happened that a certain G. died intestate, survived by a married sister, and granddaughters through her, and also granddaughters through other sisters, and also grandsons through a certain brother of the said deceased. Now there is a dispute among the aforementioned concerning the succession. The question is asked, what is the law? And this question has several points.

† First, whether the said statute is valid. And it must be said that it is not, unless the authority of the said lord prince had intervened; because when it is enacted that the law be observed, it is understood to refer to the common law. But this statute is contrary to the common law, as in C. de legibus hereditatibus, Auth. Defuncto, and Auth. Post fratres, and in the Corpus from which it is derived. For when the name of law is simply uttered, it is understood to refer to the common and Roman law, as in Inst. de iure naturali, § 1. Since, therefore, this has been incorporated into an agreement, it has not only the force of law, but also that of a contract, as in ff. de publicis, l. Caesar.

But let us assume that the statute is valid, because the sovereign prince had granted it; if the daughter is excluded because she is married, are the other descendants through her also excluded? And some say that they are not. And they prove this by three reasons. First, because the statute does not speak of them. Cf. D. 24.3.10 (*Si vero*), § *De viro*. Second, because this quality of marriage is not present in every member of the lineage; therefore, it does not repel those who are unmarried. Cf. D. 35.1.10 (*Mulieri et Titio*); and D. 4.4.1 (*Tutelas*). Third, because the quality which is present in the one excluded by reason of marriage is not present in the unmarried woman; therefore, the unmarried woman ought not to be repelled. Cf. D. 28.2.1 (*Gallus*), § *Et quid si tantum*. But in this point there is much doubt. First, because the text says: if I exclude you, therefore I exclude any descendant through you, as in Collatio 10, *Qui feudum dare possunt*, c. 1, § *Cum vero Coradus*. Second, because a grandson ought not to have more right than a son, as in C. 5.55.1 (*Si viva matre*). Third, because a statute excluding a woman seems to provide that a male shall succeed, as fully noted by Bartolus in D. 38.2.2, § *Videndum* (*Ad Tertullianum*). On this point, many of the ancients said that if the law speaks of a daughter, a grandson is not included. And if it speaks of a sister, it is not understood to refer to the sister’s son; because this case is not provided for by the statute. Cf. D. 28.2.1 (*Commodissime*) and D. 28.2.1 (*Gallus*), § *Quid si tantum*. For since the statute operates by disinheriting, it does not comprehend any other person except that of which it speaks, being odious. Cf. C. 8.40.1 (*Illam*). Others said that if the daughter is excluded, therefore the descendant through her is excluded on account of the greater reason, although in wills tacit reason is not considered, but only words. Cf. D. 7.1.10 (*Si alii*). However, it is otherwise in a statute and custom. This is held by Cynus in D. 48.5.1 (*De adulteriis*) and C. 1.1 (*Quae sit longinqua consuetudo*). I believe it to be more true that if the married daughter is excluded in consideration of a certain person, the sons of the daughter are also excluded; because the exclusion of one is the inclusion of the other. Nevertheless, in the case which is proposed, according to what is proposed, I do not think the said statute is valid; because it has not been confirmed by a superior. The aforementioned succession takes place per stirpes. Florence, February 2. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It treats how a curator of the goods of an absent person is to be appointed.
body: Dinis

† In the law *Curato*, Digest, On the Curatorship of the Property of the Damned. If you take heed to your mind, because I have already seen several interlocutory sentences retracted, and someone is cited, and does not appear: the adversary is put into possession of his goods. From the first decree, afterwards, while he is still contumacious, it is asked how the sale of his goods ought to be made. And some say that a curator should be appointed for the goods, by whom the sale will be made. But they say this wrongly. For this rule holds, that to one who is present and sufficient for the defense of his own goods, although he does not appear, a curator is not appointed, unless he cedes his goods. For when he has ceded his goods, those goods then begin to be vacant, and a curator can properly be appointed. And thus the title *On the Curatorship of Property to be Given* speaks properly and principally, law 2, and note in the last law, and it helps, Digest, On the Curatorship of the Damned, law *Cuius bonis*. But the sale must be made by the judge, or by the creditors by the authority of the judge. And this is the case, Digest, On the Curatorship of the Damned, law *Cuius bonis*. But the aforementioned rule fails in the case of this law: because on account of the dignity of the senator, a curator is substituted for the goods of him who is present, so that the sale may be made more honorably. And note that the learned Doctor Dino speaks when a curator is appointed for the goods of one who is present. But if he is appointed for the goods of one who is absent, or who is in hiding, and a curator is not appointed: because it is not necessary, but one proceeds to the second decree against his contumacy, as in law *Fulcinius*, section 1, Digest, On the Causes for Which Possession is Given. Or he is not in hiding, but is absent for a just, necessary, or probable cause, or at least not for the purpose of fraud: and then a curator is appointed for the goods for the sake of selling the goods, or for granting satisfaction, as seems more expedient for the absent person, as in law 1, section 1, Digest, On the Curatorship of Property to be Given, and law 2, in the beginning, of the same title. From this principle, gather two things. First, that a curator can be requested to be appointed for an absent person, against whom an action is given. Concordant, law *Idem privilegium*, second response, Digest, On the Privileges of Creditors, and law 1, Digest, On the Duty and Honor, which is noted, Extra, On the Oath of Calumny, chapter *Caeterum*. Second, that when the debt is liquid, a curator is appointed for the goods to be sold, as is clear there. And the aforementioned law *Cuius bonis*, Digest, On the Curatorship of the Damned, a curator is also appointed where the debt is not liquid, or to be liquidated, so that it is necessary that a definitive judgment be rendered, and there is no one with whom litigation can be contested. Nor does anyone swear the oath of calumny, and thus one cannot otherwise arrive at a definitive judgment: because the absent person is undefended. But this must be established by the citation of friends and relatives, as is noted in law 2, Digest, On the Causes for Which Possession is Given, and Digest, On the Solution of Judgments, law 3, section last, and Digest, On the Causes for Which Majors, law *Ergo*. For as long as it is not established that the absent person is not defended, a curator for the goods should not be appointed; therefore, this must be established for the judge, as in Digest, On the Causes for Which Possession is Given, law *Haec autem*, section *Sin*. Therefore, a curator who is appointed for goods always seems to be appointed upon inquiry. Argument, Digest, On the Curatorship of the Damned, law *Observare*. But against this, the text in the same title, law *Bonorum*, works, where it is said that sometimes a curator for goods is appointed with inquiry, sometimes without. Nor is there any text which says that in this appointment relatives or friends are cited. And therefore, since this solemnity is not introduced by law, more should not be required than the law requires. But certainly, rather, it seems that when a curator is appointed for goods, he is appointed upon inquiry, as in Digest, On the Womb to be Put in Possession, law 1, section *Idcirco*. But there it does not speak of any other inquiry than the suitability of the person, nor does it expressly mention any citation of relatives or friends, although it would be safer to cite them. Bartolus says that they must be cited out of necessity, Extra, On Dolus and Contumacy, chapter *Causam*, which is between F. and especially, because one proceeds to an extraordinary judgment: because it is not of the nature of such a curator’s causes. It helps for this what is noted, Speculum, in the title On Citation, section *Sequitur videre*, verse *Sed nunquid sufficit denuntiare domi*. Hence, not only is this opinion safer, but it is truer. It helps what is noted, Bartolus, in the aforementioned law *Hoc autem*, section *Defendi*, Digest, On the Causes for Which Possession is Given. Others say, as Vincentius, that a curator for goods cannot be appointed unless the master cannot easily be approached, or it is not known where he is, as he notes in the said chapter *Centum*. But as is clear there, he speaks in another case, not so indistinctly: for he speaks when the procurator was in the case. But he did not have a mandate to swear the oath of calumny. For then a curator is appointed for the goods to explain a certain article. And this is what Vincentius says, which is true then, when the master cannot easily be approached, or it is not known where he is: for then it would be enjoined upon the procurator that he send to him at the master’s expense, as is noted in the aforementioned law 1, Digest, On the Causes for Which Possession is Given, by accusation. Consider whether a curator for the litigation or for the goods will be given for any absence whatsoever. The text speaks thus, as if they are given to those who cannot easily constitute a procurator. For when the ordinary and easy way is available, the extraordinary and subsidiary appointment of a curator ceases, as in law *Ab hostibus*, in the beginning, Digest, On the Causes for Which Majors, and Digest, On Posthumous, law *Item quibus*, and law *Qui negotiis*. Also, another law seems to weigh the word *diu* (long time). From the argument of which law it should be said that a curator is given in another case, if when the debtor was present for a long time, argument, law *Si diu*, Digest, On the Causes for Which Possession is Given. For such curators are not to be given suddenly, or abruptly: because one could easily collude with them. And therefore the rule is handed down, that a curator for goods is not given except in cases expressed in the law. Bartolus in the aforementioned law *Ab hostibus* thus says. Note, that a curator is constituted for the goods of absent persons. For this, Digest, On the Causes for Which Possession is Given, law *In possessio*, section last, and expressly noted, Code, On Captives and Postliminary Return, law *Cum cognatos*. I consider the reason of those things which the lord Dino says. For although he speaks of one who is present, yet not appearing in person or by a suitable procurator, nevertheless the same seems to me in one who is as it were present, that is, is not far off, and can easily be notified. Argument, Digest, On Infectious Damage, law 2, section *Si tam vicinum*. And if it is said, how will one arrive at a definitive judgment: I answer, even if the debtor were present, he would not be forced precisely to contest the litigation, as is noted, Code, How and When a Judge, law *Consentaneum*, and Authentic *Qui semel*, by the gloss and doctors, and by Jacobus de Arena, Digest, On the Womb in Possession, law 1, section *Denuntiari*, unless such were the case, in which no remedy was provided by law. It helps, Digest, If One Provides Security, law *Si eum*, section last. And these things are true, especially if in the appointment of the curator something was obtained by fraud from the praetor in the matter of fact: as in Digest, On the Appointment of Tutors and Curators, law *Tutor si petitus*, or if in the process conducted with the curator something was omitted or colluded. For then at least restitution in integrum would be given to the absent person, as is noted, Digest, On the Privilege of Creditors, law *Imperatores*, and Code, On Restitution of Minors, law *Ignorare*, and Digest, On Infectious Damage, law *Si finita*, section *Si forte*, and Digest, On the Causes for Which Possession is Given, law *Ad cognitionem*, last response, and last gloss. And although it is true that the cause of dowry is favorable, and one can proceed briefly and expeditiously in it, as is noted in law 1, Digest, On the Solution of Marriage, nevertheless the solemnities of judgments must be observed, and the dowry liquidated: as in Code, On Sentences Which Are Without a Certain Quantity, law last, where is a notable text. By these things, however, I say that no prejudice is done to the original dowry, nor to the donation: rather, it would remain in its primitive force, since all laws proclaim that dowries are to be preserved for women, as in the aforementioned law 1, Digest, On the Solution of Marriage, and Extra, On Pledge, chapter *Ex literis*, and Code, Who Has Priority in Pledge, law *Assiduis*, and Code, On the Right of Dowry, law *Ubi adhuc*, and law *In rebus*, and Digest, On the Solution of Marriage, law *Si constante*. But neither is that to be omitted, which pleases the Speculator, since this litigation regards the universality of the debtor’s goods: as in Digest, On Judges, law *Si fideicommissum*, section *Tracta*, and on that occasion a second missio can be made according to the form of the law from the divine Pius, it is necessary that such a curator make an inventory: otherwise the judicial proceeding with him is not valid, as in Code, On the Causes for Which Restitution in Integrum Is Not Necessary, law *Si tutor*. Others say the contrary, because this was not a curator appointed for all goods, but only for the litigation, as is noted, Code, On the Hearing of Bishops, law *De creationibus*. And this is the common opinion, and thus it is practiced. Nevertheless, it must be observed here, because this curatorship would not extend to the cause of appeal: as in Digest, What Is Named to Each Universal, law *Item eorum*, section *Sed si ita*, and Digest, On Tutelage, law *Quod dicitur*. And therefore, since the sentence passed in the cause of appeal was not passed with a legitimate contradictor, nor would it be valid, nor could its execution be requested, nevertheless this reason would not conclude in the first sentence, which would come to be executed with the appeal deserted, as is noted, Code, On Appeals, law *Eos*, in the beginning. But many great doctors say that one must first pronounce upon the desertion, and this is the opinion of Hostiensis, who promised eight arms of cloth in the month of April. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The appointment of a curator made to an absent person, who is not subject to the jurisdiction of the appointing party, is invalid.
2. If a foreigner, to whom a curator was appointed by the judge of the place, petitions for said appointment to be revoked, whereas the adversary, at whose instance the curator was appointed, petitions that it not be revoked, whether said cause ought to be committed to two good men according to the statute of the place, which provides that causes between a citizen and a foreigner shall be committed [to arbitration], the opinion is that it ought not.
1. A reconvention proceeds not only in separate libels, but also in contrary ones, and in a cause of appeal.
2. One who petitions that a compromise be made on a point of law ought not to be heard.
body: A certain Pattho de Saona, claiming to be a creditor of John de Ianua, who was absent from the city of Saona, petitioned the judge of Saona for a curator to be appointed for the goods of the said John. The judge, after issuing a public proclamation to see if anyone was a procurator or wished to defend the goods of the said absent John, appointed a certain curator. Against this curator, the aforementioned Bartholomew filed a petition concerning an action pro socio (as a partner). Finally, the aforementioned case was referred to good men under the pretext of certain statutes of the city of Saona. These good men condemned the said John, or his said curator, to pay a certain sum of money. Eventually, the aforementioned matters came to the knowledge of the said John, whereupon the procurator of the said John, before the said judge of Saona, on the grounds that he was neither a citizen of Saona nor a subject, nor did he have his forum in the city of Saona, petitioned for the revocation of the said appointed procurator and for the declaration that the curatorship and all its consequences were null. Subsequently, after many and various proceedings, the said Bartholomew filed a contrary petition, asking that the said appointment of the curator be declared valid, as well as all that followed from it. He requested that this question be referred to good men according to the form of the statute of the commune of Saona, which states that all cases arising between a citizen and a foreigner in the city of Saona must be referred to good men between the plaintiff and the defendant. On the other hand, the said John argues that the case should not be referred. The question is: what is the law? In the name of Christ.

† It must be premised for the sake of clarity that, since a curator is appointed for the property of an absent and undefended person, as provided in D. de curatoribus bonorum dandis, l. 1, and l. oportet, it is required that the person against whom the application is made be from the locality and forum of the judge granting the appointment, or at least from the forum by reason of the cause being litigated. Hence, it is necessary that he be such a person that, if present, he would be compelled to accept jurisdiction there; for an absent person is not declared contumacious by a declaratory judgment of forum, as stated in D. de iudiciis solutis, l. vir bonus. And this is more than manifest: an incompetent judge cannot appoint a curator, neither for the person, nor for the lawsuit, nor for the universal estate, as established in D. de tutoribus et curatoribus dandis ab his, l. 1, in fine; C. ubi per tutores et curatores, l. 1; and C. si a non competenti iudice, per totum. Therefore, whatever has been done with a curator not lawfully appointed is void by operation of law, as stated in D. quod falso tutoris auctoritate, l. 1. For lawsuits must be lawfully initiated, as in C. qui dari tutores possint, l. in universis. That the said appointment of the curator was null is apparent because the edicts did not come to the knowledge of the absent person, nor could they have done so, as in D. quae sententiae sine appellatione rescindantur, l. 1, § cum ex edicto. On the contrary, the citation of the absent person was defective, for he ought to have been cited in the city of Genoa, where he had his domicile. For this is the form handed down by law, from which one must not depart, as in Extr. de foro competenti, c. Romana, § contrahentes. Moreover, a mere house or possession does not constitute domicile, but rather household and custom, as in C. ubi senatus vel clarissimi, l. is; and D. ad municipalia, l. libertus, § sola. Furthermore, it is a rule of law that a curator is not appointed when a person can defend himself personally or through his own procurator. For the use of procurators is general, but the use of curators is special, and a curator is not appointed for one who is not in need and who is capable of managing his own affairs, as in D. qui ex causa maiestatis, l. ab hostibus, in principio; or when it is unknown where he is and creditors are pressing, as in C. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. cum cognatos, and the glosses thereto. And therefore, the said appointment of the curator was abusive, reckless, and void by operation of law; and in the same manner, the subsequent acts performed with such an abusive curator are void, as in C. de procuratoribus, l. licet. For where the person does not hold, neither does the judgment, as in C. qui legitimi personae, l. 1. It is therefore clear that the said proceedings were of no effect, according to what is alleged.

But now let us come to the principal question, whether the said case ought to be committed: and it seems that it should. For one who acts on the ground of nullity seems to be able to be sued on the ground of validity, just as we say the contrary. See the law and the note, Digest, De minoribus, l. Papi., § si filius, according to one reading.

For a reconvention proceeds not only on separate libels, but also on obstructive and contrary libels. Indeed, what is more, a reconvention has place even in an appeal, as if I seek that a sentence be confirmed, my adversary may seek that it be confirmed, as C. de appel. l. ampliorem in principio, and ff. quod cum eo l. Titianus. Nor is this surprising, because one petition contains another, that is, discussion; one of the contraries declares the remainder, as ff. de procu. l. Pompon. § si his. But the truth is to the contrary. For he who seeks that a decree be pronounced to be null in law is provoked to the cause by his adversary, and is called the defendant, and not the plaintiff, speaking properly. And even if he were the plaintiff, he would be a necessary plaintiff, compelled by the necessity of his adversary, as ff. de op. no. num. l. de pupillo § qui remissionem, and ff. de procu. l. non cogendum § fin. Then I argue thus: if this person is the defendant who seeks this, therefore he cannot be reconvened, as noted by Guillaume and others, ff. quod quisque iur. in alterum statuit l. si. The same applies if he is a necessary plaintiff provoked to the cause, as we say in the case of one to whom a new work has been notified, who seeks remission. For he cannot be reconvened, for it would be inequitable that the jurisdiction of the praetor should be in the power of my adversary, as ff. de iurisdi. omnium iudic. l. si idem in eodem § sed si mutuae, in the gloss which says that one ought not to be in the power of his adversary, as ff. de iudi. l. 2 § sed si agant. Moreover, this person who seeks that the decree be pronounced null seeks that the judge be pronounced to have had no jurisdiction; well, this petition comes to impugn jurisdiction, whence it seems that he consents against the judge. And thus the reason ceases, l. cum Papinia C. de sententiis et interlo. omn. iudic. Moreover, unless jurisdiction is first established, reconvention has no place, as in Authent. vt consequenter C. de interlo. omn. iudic. But here jurisdiction is established only as to revoking what was done improperly. For just as he proceeded abruptly upon lifting the veil, so he ought to revoke by contrary command, as noted ff. de euic. l. mino. in principio. Indeed, certainly this John seems to have been drawn into a prohibited examination, as C. de assertione tol. l. 1 in fine, C. de iurisditio. omn. iudic. l. in criminali, and noted by Peter and Cynus, C. de iudi. l. mili. Moreover, since there was long litigation over the petition of nullity, in which the judge acts ex officio, it does not seem that there is now place for arbitrators, as ff. de iud. l. sed si susceperit in principio. Moreover, this ex officio action of the judge regards an emerging article, and not the cause of the cause by reason of the emerging article; therefore reconvention has no place, nor is a libel properly said to be offered, as noted ff. de interro. actio. in rubric, although the nullity of proceedings comes accessorially by disposition of the law. Moreover, the petition of the said John is liquid. And that the appointment of a curator is not valid appears from the open nature of the business, nay, from the texts of the laws. And therefore the case is to be decided, not compromised, as C. de compen. l. fin. Certainly, nor can Bartholomew swear against calumny,

† and therefore he ought not to be heard, because it is established before the judge that his defense does not proceed from law. Hence, on a point of law, he ought not to be heard in requesting that a compromise be made, as noted by Petrus and Cynus in C. de rebus creditis, l. cum proponas. From which it is evidently concluded that the said delivery by the curator, and what followed therefrom, must be revoked as void. And thus it must also be pronounced by the judge, notwithstanding the contrary petition offered by the aforementioned Bartholomew. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a civil statute is valid, which provides that if damage or fire has been caused in any village, the village is bound to denounce the malefactor, otherwise it is bound to make amends for the damage. And whether the village is bound to make amends for said damage, where it does not appear how or by whom the fire was committed.
2. In how many ways fire arises, and when one may bring an action for fire.
3. Concealment is twofold.
body: The case is as follows: a certain hayloft full of hay, which was situated in the town of Rumelegi, in the district of Cremona. The said hayloft was surrounded by many public houses, and no one resided in that hayloft from whom fire could have been kindled. And by chance, at the fifth hour of the night, certain women and certain men perceived something burning; because of this burning, those women and those men, walking gradually, finally went and saw fire creeping over the hay, which was lying outside the said hayloft. The hayloft was finally entirely burned down before it could be aided. Who were present, or who were not present, is unknown.

† Furthermore, there is a certain statute in Cremona, which provides that if any damage or fire is caused in any village, those of the village are bound to denounce the malefactors; and if they do not denounce them, the village is liable for the restitution of the damage. Now the question arises whether those of the village are bound to make restitution of the said hay, on the ground that they did not denounce the malefactor.

It must be premised for clarity that a fire sometimes arises from the act of a man, sometimes from the act of nature, as by lightning, and thus by divine force; sometimes it is doubtful. In the first case, the aforementioned statute speaks, and there is no doubt, because the words of the statute are clear, not casting doubt on the force of the statute. For the statute is valid, as noted in *l. ne quid*, D. de incendio, ruina, et naufragio, and C. de decretis decemvirorum, in the rubric, *hoc igitur* and *dicto*. In the first case, either the plaintiff himself caused the fire, or another outsider. In the first case, he does not sue, because from his own fire he does not obtain an action, as in D. de furtis, *l. itaque fullo*. In the second case, a sub-distinction is made, because sometimes the fire is set by right, and then what is done by right does not deserve punishment, nor is the town bound to make reparation, as in D. quod vi aut clam, *l. si alius*, § *est et alia*. Sometimes the fire is set or caused by the act or negligence of a man. And in this case, the statute speaks, that the town is bound to make reparation. For this act contains injury, not right; and that which gives rise to an action under the Lex Aquilia against the doer, by the disposition of the common law, gives rise to a condictio ex lege and according to the form of the statute against the corporation itself, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, *l. si servus servum*, § *si fornicarius*, and *l. quemadmodum*, § *in hac quoque*. If, however, the fire proceeded by divine force, then there is no doubt that this should not be made good, as in D. de damno infecto, *l. fluminum*, § *servius*. The same applies if it proceeded by fortuitous accident without any fault, for from such a fortuitous accident no action lies against anyone; therefore, neither against the corporation; because there is no fault there, therefore there should be no penalty, as in C. de pignoratitia actione, *l. quae fortuitis*, and D. de regulis iuris, in *l. contractus*, and D. de locato, *l. videamus*, § *si fortuitus*, and D. de actionibus emptio, *l. si ea res*. For if the fire had been set by the incursion of enemies, the town would not be bound to make reparation for the damage, because custody against superior force is of no avail; hence the statute does not seem to have intended this fortuitous case, because it would be unjust to make good such damage, as in the said § *Servius*. Now there is another case, when it is doubtful whether the fire was set by a man. And whether fault intervened or not, and then recourse must be had to presumptions, if any can be found; because obscure and ambiguous cases are proved by indications, as in *l. non omnes*, § *a barbaris*, D. de re militari. But if presumptions do not appear, then although the fire may arise by fortuitous accident, as stated above, and is proved in D. pro socio, *l. cum duobus*, § *damna fatalia*, yet because it more frequently happens by the fault of a man, the legal presumption is adapted to those things which happen more frequently, which, as I said, is in this case: that the fault of some man preceded in the fire, as in D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, *l. si vendita*. Here, however, it must be considered: for either the owner inhabited the place, and the fault of the inhabitant himself would be presumed; or not, and the act of another rather than of the owner himself would be presumed; because no one is accustomed to burn or demolish his own things, arg. D. de probationibus, *l. cum de indebito*. Beware. The words of the statute say, "in damage given, done, or given"; therefore, it seems that it must be clearly proved, as in *l. 1*, § *item illud*, D. ad Syllam, and noted by Dy. in *l. 1*, D. quando ex facto tutorum, and by the doctors in *l. si quando*, C. unde vi. But to this it is answered that the words of the statute say that in damage given by fire, openly or secretly.

† Moreover, the hidden [act] is twofold: one which can be proven with difficulty, and another which cannot be proven at all. Nevertheless, because the statute speaks in simple terms, it must be understood simply, since the reason of the statute, being directed toward public security, is understood to bind even that which is entirely hidden. And the words here sound thus. Therefore, whether it is known or unknown who caused the damage, it matters not. Hence, it is not necessary here to impute the act to a certain person. It suffices that the act itself appears, even if it is unknown by whom it was done, as in D. quod metus causa, l. si cum exceptione, §. in hac actio; and D. de nau. cau. et sta., l. licet, §. possumus, where it must be proven by whom and by such a person as can obligate another; for there this is required because the nature of that edict demands it, and because we are there in the common law. But here we are in municipal and extraordinary law.
