And the nature of this statute does not require proof of by whom [the act was done]; and therefore, strictly according to the statute, after first examining those who ought to be examined and the presumptions, if any can be had, if indeed there are no other presumptions except the simple fact, as is alleged: the village shall be bound to repair such damage. Although this passage is sufficiently doubtful both in law and in fact.

Furthermore, in such hidden matters, reputation is a great aid, because those things which are done by night cannot be expressly known, as noted in C. de sicariis, l. furem, cum similibus. And if we were to say otherwise, it would follow that any wicked person could secretly set fire by night, and the village would not be held liable; which is contrary to the intent of the statute and contrary to public security, which the statute’s security regards. Therefore, the act is presumed to be that of a man, from the fact that the act is found; because it is, in a manner of speaking, a miracle that a fire occurs and is done by no one. D. de officio praefecti vigilum, l. 3. Unless it expressly appears and is proven that the fault of the owner preceded the accident. D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. si seruus seruum, §. si fornicarius. And the presumption of an accident, which is drawn from things commonly happening, as noted in C. de probat., l. valet nihil habuit, sed promisit, is not applicable. And pertinent to the foregoing are those things noted in q. 53, c. 8, c. libellorum, in the gloss beginning “ideo nomen.” And although that gloss speaks in reversed terms, when the name of the sufferer is unknown, nevertheless, as far as the village is concerned, it is the same as if the name of the doer were unknown, since the fact of the fire is established by the evidence of the thing itself. Because everything that is done is done by someone, just as everything that is moved is moved by someone. It should not be doubted that this fire was done by someone who applied it. I wonder how it could come into anyone’s mind that this fire proceeded without the act of a man. It could well be that it proceeded without malice. But that is beside the point. On the contrary, considering that it was by night, and considering the circumstances, according to the prudence of every good and natural man, malice ought rather to be presumed than fault. Nevertheless, the statute does not require this, nor ought we to require it.

And although under the common law a corporation ought not to be punished for another’s delinquency, nevertheless the statute rightly decreed otherwise, especially regarding fire, as in D. de incendio, ruina et naufragio, l. ne quid, where the words of the statute are clear, the cavils of advocates ought not to have place, even if the law is harsh. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the Pope sold the immovable property of a certain church, together with its fruits and revenues, whether the buyer is not bound to abide by the lease made concerning said property by the prelate of the aforementioned church.
2. Whether the buyer is bound to abide by the lease made by the seller.
3. Whether the lessee, just as he has a right of retention for expenses, likewise has such a right for the rent already paid.
body: Pope,

Whether the Roman Church sold certain properties of certain monasteries to a certain nobleman for the evident necessities incumbent upon the said Roman Church, with these words added, namely, with all revenues, profits, and emoluments, etc., promising that the aforementioned goods were not sold, donated, given, obligated, or ceded, conditioned, or in any other way alienated to any other person, using the term alienation in its broad sense, nor was any contract made or will appear concerning them, in whole or in part, to the prejudice of the present contract and sale; and that the said goods and possessions, both movable and immovable, fruits, revenues, profits, yields, and emoluments, with all their appurtenances, are free and exempt from every bond of obligation, and thus intended the said nobleman to hold them. Now it has happened by chance that the prelates had leased the said things for nine years; this nobleman does not wish to abide by the lease, but rather wishes to have the fruits free and unencumbered for the time to come. It is asked whether he may do so.

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that sometimes both the buyer and the tenant hold their title from the fisc, or from him to whom the fisc succeeds by universal succession, as in C. ad l. Iul. de vi, l. tutoris. For instance, because the person whose goods were confiscated had previously leased them to another, as in ff. loc., l. si fundus, so that the fisc is found to be bound to both by its own contract. And then either something is expressed in the contract regarding the reservation of the rights of the lessee, and the agreement must be observed, as in ff. de act. em., l. si mercedem, in princ. and §. si habitatoribus; or nothing is expressed: and then the right of the tenants is tacitly excepted, and this in favor of the fisc, as in ff. de iur. fis., l. Valerius, ver. Papae, and ver. Trisonio suggerente. Or the buyer alone holds his title from the fisc, while the tenant holds his title from another, who by his own contract could not bind the fisc: and then the one holding title from the fisc is not bound to allow the tenant to remain, because it is not in the interest of the fisc. And therefore we are then not in the privilege of the fisc, but in the mere common law, by which law it is lawful for a singular successor to expel the tenant, even during the term of the lease, as in C. loc., l. emptorem, and ff. de le. i., l. nihil proponitur. For the personal obligation arising from the contract of lease does not affect the thing, nor does it extend to the singular successor, as in ff. de contrah. emp., l. si, §. si, according to the general rule stated in de act. et obl., l. eum. On this point, fully noted by Dy. in l. diuortio, and l. si filio, §. si, ff. so. ma. In the prelate of the church, noted in c. vlt., ne prę. vi. suas., and by Arch. 11. q. 2, c. alienationes, and by Gul. de Cu. ff. de eden., l. prętor, §. sed et si seruus. It supports this, eo. tit., l. quędam, §. is autem, where it is said that the singular successor is not the successor of the right, i.e., personal actions do not accompany him, as in ff. ad Tre., l. 1, §. si haeres, and C. si cer. pet., l. 1, and ff. de iud., l. si fideicommissum, §. tractatum. This is also clear, because if such personal rights followed, there would be no need for their assignment, which is false, as in leg. and no. ff. de act. emp., l. Iul., §. si fructibus, and ff. quod vi, aut clam, l. is, qui in puteum, §. si postea. From these, it clearly appears that the said nobleman is not bound to allow the tenants to remain. But so that this may appear more clearly, it must again be premised for the sake of clarity that the term of this lease does not endure, but is suspended. This is proven thus: when the right of the grantor is resolved, the right of the grantee is resolved, as in ff. de pig., l. lex vecti., and ff. lo., l. si quis domum, §. hic subiungi potest. Since therefore the prelate, who is reduced to the status of a usufructuary, is deprived of this usufruct, and not only he, but the church by the supreme authority of the Supreme Pontiff, who can make such alienations, as in C. de quadrien praescri., l. omnis, and l. bene a Zenone, and it is expressed in the said l. Valerius, and expressly noted by Io. And. extra de iud., c. cum venisset, in nouel., it is rightly necessary to say that the term of the said lease is finished, since it no longer depends on his successor, as in io. col. qui. mo. feu. amit., c. 1, §. rursus. And supporting the above is that question concerning a donation which a prince makes of another’s thing, of which note in princ. digestorum, and ff. de rei ven., l. item si verberatus, ff. de le. 2, l. qui solutum, §. 1, ff. de euic., l. Lucius. Moreover, the Lord Pope here did not sell another’s thing, but his own. For all things of the churches are his with regard to full and free disposition, and no prelate in the world can do anything without at least the tacit authority of the Pope, who, as the father of fathers, concurs with every prelate in the power of jurisdiction, as noted in c. si eo tempore, de ele., lib. 6, per Io. Mo. Moreover, the Pope here expressly granted the fruits, and there is no doubt that hanging fruits are fruits; indeed, they are part of the dominion, since they are not separated from the fief, as in ff. quae in frau. cre., l. si, §. pe. Moreover, the lessee cannot make the fruits his by gathering them against the will of the owner, because the patience of the owner is required, as elegantly noted in ff. de fur., l. si seruus communis vni., §. locaui. Since therefore the said noble buyer is in possession, the tenant cannot enter, nor export the fruits, by his prohibition. I understand this in the tenant who cultivates less, arg. ff. de don., l. qui saxum, and ff. de actio. em., l. qui pendentem, ff. de vsufr., le. l. hae. res in fundum. But against this it is argued: for although the singular successor is not bound, nevertheless the exception which hindered the actor hinders him, as in ff. de actio. em., l. in venditione, and ff. de dam. in se., l. fluminum, §. adijcitur, and ff. de iureiur., l. etiam, cum si, and there by Gul. For since he paid the pension, and rightly contracted from the beginning, it seems injurious to rescind.

† Moreover, we observe that he has a right of retention on account of expenses incurred, as stated in the Digest, *De vi et vi armata*, law *Colonus*; and in the Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Plane*. Therefore, the same should apply on account of unpaid rent. However, it is replied to this that these cases are not similar. For if the expenses were not reimbursed, the new owner would be enriched at another’s loss, which is inequitable. This reasoning does not apply to rent, which is a portion of the fruits. Indeed, elsewhere the law establishes a great difference between price and expenses, as in the Digest, *De condictionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Quibus diebus*, section *Quidam ita*. What, then, is the outcome? Would this tenant lose the expenses paid as if by a fortuitous event? To equate this fact with a fortuitous event would certainly be a poor analogy, because a fortuitous event should not harm either the tenant or the owner, as is fully noted in the Digest, *De locato conducto*, law *Si uno*, section *Cum quidam*; and in the Code, *De societatibus*, law *Damnum*. And thus it appears that he recovers from the one from whom he originally derived the cause, by means of the action for something given without cause. See the argument in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Inde*, law 2, and law *Nec novum est*. But that law is well explained by Zeno, if one says that when the prince takes away someone’s right, action must be brought against the treasury. And the law *Lucius* in the Digest, *De evictionibus*, says that against no other person, but whatever the case may be, this has nothing to do with our present fact. It suffices to have concluded that the said buyer-owner has full right over the things and the fruits, and is not bound to stand by the tenant. Nor does it matter that the goods were pledged by the lease instrument; for when the principal obligation is removed, the accessory pledge is also removed, as is fully noted in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Si tibi*, section *De pignore*. Furthermore, it does not matter that the Pope cannot derogate from the rights of laymen; for this right rather extinguishes by its own nature, being accessory, than by his own act. Moreover, because the Pope’s freedom in ecclesiastical matters cannot be impeded by anyone, as stated in the Extravagantes, *De constitutionibus*, chapter *Ecclesia sanctae Mariae*. And thus the objection based on the aforementioned law *Si filio*, section *Fin.*, in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, does not hold. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What the creditor bringing a hypothecary action against a third-party possessor ought to prove.
body: It must be premised and is evident,

† That the plaintiff bringing a hypothecary action against a third-party possessor is bound to prove that the thing was in the debtor’s assets at the time of the obligation, or afterwards, or before: so that it is inferred afterwards, as in D. de pign. l. et qui nondum sunt, §. quod dicitur; and D. de probat. l. ante omnia; and C. si aliena res pign. data sit, l. cum res; and see Inst. de act. §. item serviana, with its glosses. And that which would exclude the debtor in the rei vindicatio or the Publician action, that excludes the creditor bringing a hypothecary action against a third-party possessor. And that which would assist the debtor assists the creditor. This doctrine is taught in D. de pign. l. si ab eo. But in our case, such a right of the debtor, which would suffice for him to bring a rei vindicatio or a Publician action, is not proven. Therefore, that which ought to have been proven for the substance, for the assets, is not proven, and consequently the defendant ought to be absolved: as in C. de eden. l. qui accusare. That this is not proven appears because, for proving this, the confession, or rather the response of the defendant, is introduced; and if the adversary wishes to use it, he must use it as the response was made, as noted in C. de except. l. si quidam; and l. 2, C. de donat. ante nup. But from the response it appears that, although the sale proceeded, the price was not paid. And therefore, the seller and his heir have the right of retention for the unpaid price, as in D. de act. empt. l. Iul., §. offerri. Moreover, it does not appear that the said contract, received in another’s name, was expressly or tacitly ratified; since knowledge, which is of the substance of ratification, is not established, as noted in C. de rei vend. l. cum a matre. Furthermore, the interrogation was ambiguous and tricky, whence it was lawful for the respondent to qualify his response, as in the law and note in D. de iureiur. l. iusiurandum et ad pecunias, §. si de qualitate. Furthermore, the said interrogation was not to be answered simply; and therefore it ought to be considered as not answered, since a protestation preceded regarding not answering, unless it was legally required to answer, as in the law and note in Extr. de off. deleg. c. cum contingat. From all these things, according to what is alleged, it appears that either the said response is null, or one must adhere to it as it stands. By this, the defendant, the facts being thus, ought to be absolved from the hypothecary action, or at least not compelled, unless the price is offered or paid. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What is required in order that someone be said to be legitimately imprisoned, and consequently the jailer and his sureties are bound either to produce the debtor or to pay the sum for which he was imprisoned, and in the following opinion.
body: In that

† The arrest, from which the obligation of the guards depends, requires that four things be considered in certain arrests, namely: the cause, the jurisdiction, the order, and the form of the recommendation made in prison. Regarding the first, I say that the arrest was just on account of the cause: because there existed a true debt, namely arising from a deposit, and a dowry, or at least from a deposit, as appears from the confession of the debtor made in the presence of the creditor and in the presence of the lords Antiani; as is evident from the form of the writings, to which one must adhere, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. in contractibus, §. sed quoniam; and ff. depositi, l. publica, §. fin.; and in l. 2, C. de servis reipublicae manumittendis. Regarding the second, namely the jurisdiction, I similarly say that the arrest was possible in law, because those Antiani possess that jurisdiction which custom grants them. And it suffices that they are in quasi-possession of that jurisdiction, as in l. 1, C. de emancipatis liberis; and noted in ff. de iurisdictio omnium iudicum, l. more maiorum; and C. de diversis rescriptis, l. 1. Since, therefore, the lords Antiani are in quasi-possession of jurisdiction and of causing others to be imprisoned for delicts and debts, there is no doubt that they can exercise that jurisdiction. For, since this has been granted to them, not only by the tacit consent of the people, but by an express statute, they can exercise such jurisdiction and that authority, especially since imprisonment is an execution of jurisdiction, as in ff. de origine iuris, l. 2, §. exacte deinde regibus. Regarding the third, namely the order, when pressed by the burden of a large debt, or even without the burden of such a large debt, if suspected of flight, one may be imprisoned for custody, so that his flight may be prevented, as in l. ait praetor, §. si debitorem, quae in fraudem creditorum; and noted in l. si, C. de fideiussoribus; and ff. de pignoribus, l. quaesitum. Moreover, it does not differ from fraud and delict not to repay a deposit, as in ff. de dolo, l. dolus. Regarding the fourth, according to what is proposed, it appears in two ways that the imprisonment was made. First, in general concerning money and person, as in Auth. de armis, circa medium. Second, it was specific for the said deposit, and therefore the prison guards ought to guard well and diligently, so that this debtor would not escape to the damage of the creditor, as in C. de custodiendo reo, l. ad commentariensem. Thus, both the guards and their sureties are bound to produce the debtor or to pay, as in ff. de in ius vocando, l. eum, pro quo.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. He treats the proximate matter, namely concerning those in prison, and whether the *antiani* or the priors may have someone imprisoned.
body: In the present matter, two points are principally to be investigated. First, concerning capture and imprisonment. Second, concerning custody and the obligation of custodians and sureties.

† Regarding the first point, four matters must be considered, namely jurisdiction, cause, order, and the form of the imprisonment itself, which are to be examined in order. And first, with regard to jurisdiction, it is argued that the priors were not competent judges: because they do not possess contentious jurisdiction, except in the absence of the magistrate. For Innocentius says that rectors appointed by universities have jurisdiction, but the universities themselves do not, as he notes in the extrajudicial collection, in the title "De Constitutionibus," chapter "Cum accessissent." To this effect, in the extrajudicial collection, in the title "De Foro Competenti," chapter "Conquestus," where it says, "power," and the commune of Bologna; and the argument from the Digest, in the title "De Tutoribus et Curatoribus Datis ab His," law "Ubi absunt." Furthermore, the priors do not have greater jurisdiction than that granted to them by custom or statute. Argument from the Digest, in the title "Quod vi aut clam," law "Prohibere," section "Plane," and in law 1, Code, in the title "De Emancipatis Liberi," and noted in the Digest, in the title "De Pactis," law 1, "Item magistri." Moreover, to imprison someone is a species of mere, or at least mixed, imperium. And no one has this power unless it is permitted to him expressly, or by necessary consequence, as in the Digest, in the title "De Origine Iuris," law 2, section "Exactis deinde regibus." Therefore, if they cause someone to be arrested, in this respect they are reduced to the status of private individuals, and the defendant, before being imprisoned as a matter of fact, must be released; nor does it benefit the creditor to have him detained in prison, nor is the defendant liable for flight on the ground that he fled from prison, by argument from the Digest, in the title "De Negotiorum Gestione," law "Nam et servis," in the principal part. On the contrary, the adversary who brought the defendant before a non-judge is said to have brought him to a prohibited examination, as in the Code, in the title "De Iurisdictione Omnium Iudicum," law "In criminali." And it supports what is noted in the Digest, in the title "Quoties Metus Causa," law "Ex tatis," in the first major gloss. To the contrary, it seems that in the statute of the commune of Bologna, in the chapter "De Officio Custodum Carcerum," it is provided that the jailers are bound to guard well and diligently those imprisoned in the said prisons who are consigned to them on behalf of the said lords priors of the commune of Bologna. Therefore, it appears that the lords priors have this power. Furthermore, in the statute under the rubric "De Iurisdictione," it is expressly provided that they may detain and cause to be detained any persons whatsoever. Therefore, they expressly have this power of imprisonment, as in the aforementioned law 2, Digest, in the title "De Origine Iuris." Moreover, the said priors are in quasi-possession of this jurisdiction, which suffices for its exercise, as in the Digest, in the title "De Officio Praetoris," law "Barbarius." And this is clear from the facts, as proposed. And thus I conclude that the lords priors, for cause, may cause someone to be imprisoned, and that this pertains to good governance, over which they also have discretion, according to the note by Bartolus in law "Ambitiosa," Digest, in the title "De Decretis Ab Ordine Factis." Now I come

† As to the second point. Regarding the cause, it appears that the cause was not established, or at least was not determined in the proper manner, and thus the seizure ought to have been revoked by contrary imperial authority, as noted in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, l. *Si cum nulla*; and in the Digest, *De evictionibus*, l. *Minor*, in the beginning. The contrary is true, as it appears that the debtor, by confession made before the said *antiani* or magistrates. Hence, whether we consider the confession simply, it has ready execution as a matter of legal notoriety, as in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, l. *Si debitori*; or whether we consider it with its circumstances, namely, because it was made before the consuls or *antiani*, and thus before many standing by, it possesses in itself legal notoriety and is effective, so that no other legal procedure is required, according to the notes on the cohabitation of clerics and women, c. *Ultimo*. And thus I conclude that this seizure held good on account of a notorious and true cause.

And from this arises the third conclusion, which he held in order. This also appears to be the case, because the person apprehended was a fugitive, and had fled, as is evident from the acts described above. Indeed, in the case where someone is a fugitive, if this appears summarily, or in some such manner, so that the judge’s motion concurs with this suspicion: he may first be apprehended, and afterwards the matter must be clarified, lest the flight be used as evidence; if we were to say otherwise, as noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in *l. consentaneum*, C. *quomodo et quando iudic*. Moreover, the creditor himself could apprehend him and present him to the judge, if the judge is not readily available, as stated in *l. ait praetor*, § *si debitorem*, *quae in fraudem creditorum*, and as noted by C. in *de iudicibus*, *l. nullus*. This is also confirmed by the award rendered, which is also mentioned in the acts. Now I come to the form of the imprisonment. And it seems that the form was incongruous,

† because the cause was not specified by the messenger, nor does it suffice that it was committed by the judge, since it was not executed by the messenger, as noted in c. 2, in the gloss, ff. ut lit. pen. in cle. I say the contrary, because I find in the records the cause and the amount specified, as appears in the above-written documents. From these it follows, according to the proposed statutes, namely concerning the custodians and their sureties, namely, that they are bound to keep the creditor indemnified, and either to produce the fugitive or to pay the debt. And this is by the form of the statute, and also by the form of the contract celebrated by the said custodians with the commune of Bologna, and when the notary received the stipulation for those whose interest it was, as ff. de adop. l. his verbis, and l. 1, §. exigere, ff. de magistratibus conueniendis, and in c. quanquam, de vsu, lib. 6, and ff. de vsur. l. Gayus, to this effect ff. de in ius voc. l. eum, pro quo. And thus it seems to me that Bal. should say the following as a matter of law, according to what is proposed in the documents, after which I subscribe myself. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If an outsider provides a dowry for a woman and stipulates that it be returned to him, yet it does not appear whether the stipulation was made at an interval or immediately, what is the law?
2. What the terms "plus" and "ante" signify.
3. An instrument is presumed to be true and formal.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that an outsider who gives a dowry cannot effectively stipulate it for himself unless immediately, that is, at the time of the giving itself, as in C. de pactis conventis, l. ex morte; and fully noted in ff. solutione matrimonii, l. quo; and C. de rei uxoriae actione, l. rem in praesenti, § accedit. Therefore, either it is established that it was immediate, and his stipulation is effective; or it is established that there was an interval, and the stipulation is effective, because the right has been acquired by the woman, and it appears that the promisor promised to the stipulator while being deceived by an error of law. Argument: ff. de exceptione doli, l. 2, § circa. But sometimes it is doubted whether it was immediate or with an interval, for example, because two documents dated the same day appear, one attesting to the woman, namely the payment, and the other to the stipulation. And in this doubt, it is better to respond in favor of dowries, i.e., in favor of the woman regarding the dowry, as in ff. de regulis iuris, l. in ambiguis, pro dotibus. And according to this understanding, Dynus posits a similar case in l. 1, ff. solutione matrimonii, unless there is another presumption that it was immediate. And this is the point of our question. For those words, “but before this contract, etc.,” can be understood as with an interval, previously, and they can be understood as immediately before. For if they are understood as with an interval, the right is acquired by the woman; but if they are understood as immediately before, the right is acquired by the stipulator. What, therefore, shall we say in this doubt? Shall we judge in favor of the woman regarding the dowry, or shall we judge in favor of the stipulator? And strongly in favor of the woman is the aforementioned l. in ambiguis. But in favor of the stipulator is that which the aforementioned Dynus says.

† On the words “before” and “after,” or on eviction, before and after. For the said Doctor says that these words are to be understood in such a way that the act in question is not vitiated, as he himself noted. D. 24,3, De divisione. Therefore, in case of doubt, these words are to be interpreted in favor of the stipulator, so that the stipulation may be valid and not fail. Argument: D. 35,2, Titia cum testamento, § 1. Moreover, even if the interval before these words signifies that the payment was made previously for the purpose of fulfilling a future payment, it does not simply benefit the woman. For this is a certain confession of the contracting parties, which must be adapted to the act in question and strengthen it, as in D. 45,1, Si ita stipulatus fuero. For a defect in stipulations is not presumed if the penalty can be derived without defect, as in D. 50,16, Si ita stipulatus, § Grisogonus. This also supports the point, because when two subordinate acts are mentioned in the same instrument, they are presumed to have been performed in the proper order. And because the time expressed in the instrument should not be understood, but only the time of the instrument itself, in matters that could have been done at that time, as noted by Innocentius, Extra, De probat., Quoniam contra falsam; and Extra, De officio delegati, Cum in iure; and the modern doctors in D. 24,3, Post dotem. From these, I conclude in favor of the stipulator, and in case of doubt, I adhere to the instrument.

† because an instrument is presumed not only to be true, but also to be formal in form and in cause, as in C. de prob. l. cum precibus. and note ff. de pac. l. iurisgentium. §. quod fere. and in l. 1. C. de vsur. and in l. sciendum est. ff. de verb. oblig. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A. promised B. to pay such a quantity of money, from which he could purchase as many places from the places of Janua, from which he will perpetually receive five hundred each year. Since there are three places, from each of which five hundred are received: but one place is more convenient than another, and safer, and therefore worth more. Of which is the aforementioned promise to be understood. And nu. 4.
2. When in disputes the choice is of the debtor, and when of the creditor.
3. The promisor in general is deemed to refer to the medium.
4. When the indefinite is equivalent to the universal.
5. In doubt, one must not depart from the words of the contract.
body: To the evidence
† it must be noted, moreover, that in contracts words are added which imply uncertainty:

† Sometimes the choice belongs to the debtor, as in alternative obligations, as stated in l. plerunque, §. si, D. de iure dotium; likewise in an obligation of a genus, as when a man is promised in general, as noted in D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. et si generaliter; and in D. de conditione indebiti, l. cum his, §. si; and in D. de familia erciscunda, l. haeredis, §. si incerto; and in Inst. de actionibus, §. praeterea. The same applies when an uncertain thing is promised out of certain things, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. comprehensum, and l. si in emptione fundi, in principio. Sometimes the choice belongs to the creditor, as when this is expressly or tacitly agreed upon, because the words of execution are placed in the power of the claimant, as noted by Iacobus de Arena in l. si ita distrahatur, D. de contrahenda emptione; and the same is stated there by Cynus, who says that either the acceptance is alternative, and the choice belongs to the creditor; or the performance is alternative, and the choice belongs to the debtor. Similar words are placed by the gloss in last wills, in l. Lucio, D. de legatis secundis. But sometimes the law states that what is moderate must be performed, as in C. de donationibus, in l. sancimus, post principium, where it is said that if someone promised a certain income from his possessions, and did not specify from which possessions, he is obliged to transfer lands from his own substance capable of yielding the income, to the extent he specified in the donation, namely in such lands as are neither better nor worse, but moderate. For extremes are to be considered defective; but that which holds the middle seems more commendable and expedient for both parties, as in D. de edicto, edictum, l. si quis venditor.

† Wherefore, since when one promises in general terms, he is deemed to refer to the average and common manner, and not to a singular one. But there the matter concerns uncertainty of quality. Elsewhere, however, it is said that in case of doubt, interpretation should be made against the stipulator, because he ought to have stipulated for something certain. And he who has a certain claim must conclude his proofs, or make it certain by the debtor’s election, as in D. de pactis, l. veteribus, with its accompanying material. Having thus laid down these premises, let us proceed to our case.

The words of the contract state that Antonius shall deliver, or cause to be delivered, by himself or his messenger, to Percivallus such a quantity of money as will enable Percivallus to purchase, and to be able to purchase, so many places among the places of Genoa, from which he shall have and receive in perpetuity, every year and each year, an annual revenue of five hundred Genoese florins of good gold and just weight, etc. Since there are three places in the city of Genoa from which the said annual revenues are collected, yet one place is more advantageous and more secure than another, but that which is worth more in price appears to be the minimum in the obligation; for the quantity is here in the obligation, whence it is understood to be the lesser sum, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussorem. But here it must be considered that the quantity in the obligation, with respect to the species, is for the purpose of attaining the species, that is, the place, and therefore it seems that, as in species, the moderate one ought to be due, as in D. si quis argentum, and C. de communi delegatione, l. fin., §. sed si quis emptionem, and D. de auro et argento legato, l. qui lanceam. And for and against this is what is noted by Dy. in c. in obscuris, minimum est sequendum, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. It seems to me that this case is not doubtful:

† because sometimes it is taken indefinitely from a certain whole, and then what has been said about election applies. Sometimes it is taken from the whole, and then it is equivalent to a universal: and so it is here. For those words, “from the places of Genoa, and from those same places,” are in the plural number and stated indefinitely, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. si. Hence, the buyer or seller cannot choose from one place, but from all these places. Hence, if there are three places, one-third will be purchased in one, one-third in another, and so with the remaining third, unless it were proven that the contracting parties had a different intention. For, according to the strict meaning of the words, what I have said is true, just as we say in another matter that the Falcidian deduction is not made from one thing, but from all things, as fully noted in C. ad legem Falcidiam, l. 2, which supports this. D. de solutionibus, l. cum Stichus, 1. responsio. Against this, however, it is argued, namely, that if the parties are not in agreement, the judge arbitrates, as in D. de legatis 1, l. non amplius, § cum bonorum. Moreover, the heir may and must arbitrate regarding the moderate amount, as in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, auth. hoc ius porrectum, responsio, penultimate; and D. l. si quis argenteum, post principium; and D. de legatis 1, l. legato generaliter. But whether we adhere to the words of the instrument, as I have said above, the words signify that from all,

And in case of doubt, it is safer not to depart from the words of the contract, as in the Digest, under the title "On the Rules of Law," in the law *Semper in stipulationibus*; and in the law *Quicquid astringendae*, under the title "On Verbal Obligations"; and in the Digest, under the title "On Fidejussions," in the law *Fideiussores magistratuum*, section *

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How those words are to be understood, if the castellan of the mountain of Baruc were to impose forced labor for the affairs of Lord the Marquis, the men of the mountain of Baruc. Let it be known that the castellan is to lead stones, and wood, and other things, and the castellan would do these at his own expense, nor does he wish that the men of the mountain of Baruc be compelled in all these matters.
body: The words state that, if the castellan of the mountain of Barucio were to act as a steward for the affairs of the Lord Marquis, the men of the mountain of Barucio would assist the castellan of the Lord Marquis in transporting stones, wood, and other materials, and the castellan would bear the expenses himself; nor does he wish to compel the men of the mountain of Barucio to provide any of these things by force.

† It is asked what these words, so broad and material, import: for this writing appears to contain a contradiction within itself. Namely, that the men of Monte Baruccio are bound, and yet that they cannot be compelled, i.e., forced; therefore, the writing is invalid, as in l. ubi repugnantia, D. de regulis iuris. But it must be said that these words are to be understood in such a way that they do not introduce a contradiction, as is proven in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. non ad ea; D. de legibus 2, l. legatorum, § qui plures. Thus, the sense is that they cannot be compelled regarding all these things, namely, apart from conveying stones and wood. But they are indeed bound so that stones and wood be carried or borne when Ubertino de Guttuariis is firing his kilns for his business: because it is stated in the superior part of the instrument that the men of the corteselas are bound to something else for the nobles of Guttuarii, to which the men of Monte Baruccio are bound to the said Marquis: because these words introduce a similarity. Argument: D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. in testamento.

But here it must be considered that this obligation is very uncertain: because it does not state for what portion they ought to help in leading stones and wood, and thus, on account of the uncertainty, it seems invalid: because that which cannot be understood is held as not promised, as in D. de iudiciis fideicommissorum, l. ita fidei. But I answer that, rather, it can be understood, because those words, “they help the castellan of Monte Baruccio to lead stones and wood, and the castellan does other things at his own expense,” have this sense: that the stones and wood are borne by the said men, but the castellan is bound for the other expenses. Nor could the men of Monte Baruccio be compelled beyond the corvée of carrying wood and stones, but they are bound to these two things. Argument: C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. nemini; and D. de verborum significatione, l. ferre dicimus. And it is probable that this was the intention of the legislator, who wished the said men of Monte Baruccio to be exempt in other matters, but not in the carrying of stones and wood for firing. Nor do the words sound otherwise. Therefore, the said noble has similar power for firing for the business of the said noble; the said men are bound to carry to the kiln the stones and wood necessary for the kiln; but the said noble will do other things at his own expense, nor can he compel the said men to other things.

Nor does it avail if it is said that the men of Monte Baruccio did not render such aid: because the Lord Marquis, who did not need it, was not bound to require such aid, nor was he in delay or negligence: according to that rule, “if necessity does not demand, nevertheless the patria does not remit,” as in C. de decuriis, l. in filiis, lib. 10. Furthermore, because prescription does not run against the statute of the law, except by contrary desuetude: because laws remain in force by perpetual observance, as in C. de haereticis, l. Arriani. Nor can negligence be imputed to the law, and therefore it is not removed by prescription.

As to the other point, it must be said that they are bound to dig, and nothing else, according to the tenor of the writing, which is clear, as noted in D. de pactis, l. veteribus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Which of two expectants has the stronger claim to a benefice, namely, he who holds expectatives.
body: To the evidence

It must be known that, when there are two petitioners under expectation, and one is prior in date and first received, he is undoubtedly preferred to the other petitioner: as in c. Duobus, De rescriptis, Book 6. For the benefice which the second petitioner obtained does not become vacant; and therefore it is impossible for it to be conferred upon the second: as in c. Nulla, De concessionibus praebendarum. Since, therefore, Francis first obtained letters and was first received, the petition of Lord Ubert did not take effect by operation of law. And although he possessed it for a long time, nevertheless, since he did not have canonical entry, his possession was vitious, and therefore it does not become valid by the passage of time: as in c. T., De regulis iuris, Book 6. It follows, therefore, that another person, who petitioned after the death of the said Ubert, petitioned invalidly. Moreover, the subrogation in place of the said Lord Ubert did not take effect, since one cannot be subrogated in place of someone who had no right. From this it is concluded that the said John had a right by virtue of his own and original supplication, not by virtue of the subrogation obtained by the second petitioner. I speak with regard to the prebend formerly of the said Francis, for this is the prebend concerning which the petitioner speaks. As to which prebend was that of the said Francis, it appears not only from the body [of the document], but from the law itself. For if the prebend which was conferred upon him was taken away by virtue of opinion, another prebend, which is subrogated in its place, is considered to be governed by the same law: as in D. De donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Si donante, § Si sponsus; and D. De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Filiae actitiae. Hence, according to what is alleged, the said Lord John has justice on his side. Furthermore, in the case where Ubert had had a right, the subrogation made in favor of the said Lord John was valid and remains valid during the pendency of the litigation; therefore, the said expectants could not accept, nor can they: as in c. 1 and 2, Ut lite pendente, Book 6. Nor can the said expectants disturb the said Lord John in his possession. I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one born in the Riparia of Verona is said to be born in the territory of Verona, so as to enjoy the benefit of the statute favoring those born in the city or territory of Verona.
2. The common appellation is held to be according to law.
body: The statute of the city provides that no one shall henceforth be received, admitted, or be able to belong to the college of judges of Verona, unless he is a native, or his predecessors were from the city or territory of Verona. It has now happened that a certain person named F. from the city of Vicenza, together with his wife, about thirty years ago or thereabouts, transferred himself to reside both in the city of Verona and in its diocese, and from then until now has lived there almost continuously, and at present resides there, and has acquired citizenship there. Finally, after a certain period, in the riperia of the said city of Verona, in the place called Turre, which, as is alleged, has its own rector and a right of judging separate from the judge of Verona, he begot a son by the said wife named R., who has reached the degree of a master of law and wishes to be enrolled in the college of judges of the said city. It is objected against him that he is not a native of the city or territory of Verona, because the said riperia has its own president and is entirely separate from the presidency of Verona, and therefore the territory is not the same: as in D. de assess. l. si eadem.

† To the contrary, it is said, because the Riperia of Verona, from its very name, shows itself to be among the villages of the City of Verona, as C. de epis. et cle. l. nulli. §. quod si in vico, and l. quod si in vico, ff. ad muni. 50. It must be said, however, that if the said Riperia, or its inhabitants, perform any subjection to the city of Verona, by which they can be compelled and therefore drawn to the forum of Verona, then the said Riperia is understood to be part of the territory of Verona, as noted in Auth. qui mo. nat. eff. sui. §. si quis igitur ex qualibet. Nor does it matter if it is said that it is not part of the territory simply, but in a certain respect. For it must be considered that sometimes the question concerns separate headings, and then one must assign each thing to its proper heading; sometimes the question concerns a certain undivided heading, as in our case regarding admission into the register, or into the college of judges: and then I say that the statement is verified in a certain respect. Arg. ff. de lega. 1. l. Titiae textores. Especially because this statute is ambitious and odious. Arg. in l. 1. C. de monopo. and extra de pręben. c. pe. It must also be considered whether the division of territories has been authorized or prescribed, or not. For if indeed it has been authorized or prescribed, then from one bishopric two bishoprics have been made. l. 1. C. de metropoli. berito. lib. 11. But if such a division does not appear to be juridical or prescribed, one territory remains as before, as ff. de leg. 2. l. Gayus. §. 1.

† Furthermore, the common opinion must be considered, and how the common people designate things: for the designation of the common people is held as law, as in l. cum delationis, §. asinam, de fundo instrato, and noted in ff. de legatis 3, l. librorum, §. quod tamen Cassius, and ff. de flumine, l. 1, §. 1. Hence, if the said riperia is commonly called the riperia of the city of Verona, these words signify a certain dominion, as in ff. de relictis, l. 2, §. in locum; at least as regards its origin, it retains the name of Verona, and it is not understood that something has been entirely changed from its origin, even though accidents have changed, as in ff. de legatis 2, l. cum filius, §. haeres meus. And therefore, although strictly speaking, men born in the said riperia would not be said to be born in the territory of Verona, yet broadly speaking, and considering the speech of the said common people, it can sufficiently be said that he was born in the Veronese territory, if not in fact, at least in name. Moreover, the quality of the thing is known from its very name, as in ff. de officio praefecti urbis, l. 1, and C. de defensoribus civitatum, l. defensiones nihil. All these things being considered, and because in this matter one ought to act benignly and not rigidly, since in that matriculation no one’s detriment is at stake, it must be said that the said d. R. ought to be received, that is, matriculated, in the said Veronese college. For in that which harms no one, the more benign path is to be followed, as in ff. de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. 2, §. Item Varus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In the alienation of a minor's property, what and how many things are necessary.
2. Where a decree is found to have been appended, whether everything is presumed to have been done with due solemnity.
3. A perpetual emphyteusis, or a perpetual leasehold, is a true alienation of the useful domain.
4. Whether a ratification made during majority validates a contract made during minority.
5. Whether ratification is deemed to have occurred through the acceptance of a census.
body: For the understanding of the questions proposed by me in the following, it must be premised,

† That in the sale of the property of wards, neither the guardian nor the praetor is permitted to have free discretion to dispose of it, but the alienation is valid only if a debt is pressing and this is established before the judge, as in D. de rebus eorum, l. magis puto, § si aes, and § in primis; and many other things are necessary, as is said there. Indeed, even a public auction is necessary according to the common opinion of the doctors, as in D. de minoribus, l. et si sine, in principio, because the ward is equated with the church, whose movable property cannot be alienated without a public auction, as in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, auth. hoc ius porrectum.

It is true, as the Speculum states, that where a decree is found appended, everything is presumed to have been done solemnly, as I noted in the Speculum on Sales, §. nunc videndum. But this statement is not true without qualification: for a decree is not presumed unless it is established that the form required by law was observed, as I noted in l. actor, D. de rerum vindicationibus, and l. 1, C. de praediis curiae, lib. 10, and D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. praetor. Nevertheless, a certain glossa says that all these things are presumed if the notary makes mention of them, as I noted in l. 1, C. de fide instrumentorum, and iure hastae fisci, lib. 10.

Secondly, I premise that perpetual emphyteusis, or a perpetual leasehold, is a true alienation of the useful domain; and therefore, when alienation is prohibited, such a leasehold or investiture is rightly prohibited, as in the Authentica de non alienando, § emphyteosim. Thirdly, I premise that although a contract in which the aforementioned formalities have not been observed is void from the beginning, nevertheless, if it is ratified by the minor himself after reaching majority, or by his heir of legitimate age, whether the ratification is express or tacit, such contract is confirmed, as in the Codex, Si maior factus sine decreto, etc., l. fin. Now I come to the point, and I say,
† that this contract was ratified by the guardian, namely, by the aforementioned person, who succeeded to the place of the said ward and received the annuity.

† For through the acceptance of the census, approval of the contract is induced. Cf. D. de contrah. emptione, l. si praeteritus; and Inst. de rerum qualitate et differentia, §. si; and D. de inofficioso testamento, l. si proponas, §. 1. Wherefore it follows that the said contract cannot be infringed according to what is alleged, as in l. 1, C. de furtis; and in l. 1, C. si servus extraneo; and D. de acquisitione per emptorem, l. bona fides. It is also alleged that the creditors sold a certain portion by virtue of their creditor’s right, observing the solemnities of the statutes. Such a sale is also tolerated by an undistributed inheritance, and even by a ward on account of his father’s debt, as in D. de negotiorum gestione, l. debitor; and D. qui ex causa in possessionem eant, l. apud Iuliam. And therefore the lawful contract made by the ward should not be revoked, unless recourse were had to the remedy of restitution in integrum in that case where restitution could be sought, as in l. 1, C. si adversus venditionem pignoris; and D. de negotiorum gestione, l. nam et servus, §. qui negotia; and C. de restitutione in integrum, l. quae a patre. As for the claim that the property had been barren on account of war, I do not consider this a foundation: because it is not a just cause for selling the ward’s property, since such barrenness does not have a perpetual cause, as in D. de rebus eorum, l. si fundus sit sterilis. Moreover, although the said girl did not have the right at the time of the contract, she subsequently acquired it and ratified the contract, and they acquire force by subsequent act, as in D. de rei vindicatione, l. si a Titio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A settlement may be made concerning past usury, but not concerning future usury.
body: Considered

† At the point concerning Blasius, I say that the transaction must be upheld, and it cannot be called into doubt on the ground of usury or reduction of the principal, merely because of fruits received before the transaction, as is stated in l. Titia, ff. de solutionibus. For a transaction may lawfully be made regarding past usuries: as in ff. de pactis, l. si unus, §. illud. As for future usuries after the transaction has been concluded, there is no need to inquire, because those fruits belong to Blasius, or to his successor, by virtue of supervening ownership, not by right of pledge: C. de transactionibus, l. si pro fundo; and ff. de re vendita, l. si a Titio; ff. de exceptione doli, l. apud Celsum, §. si a Titio; and ff. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. 1, §. si a Titio. And I do not think there is any room for doubt on this matter. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a mandate is terminated by death.
2. If someone confesses that he has been duly paid, whether those words imply a donation.
3. Whether anyone is to be apprehended personally unless the cause of apprehension is first established by citation.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that sometimes a mandate is directed after death by the nature of the act, for example, when a testator in his last will mandates something to his heir; and then it is not revoked by death, but confirmed, as in D. de legatis 2, l. Cum pater, §. Mando filia. This is because, by the nature of the thing, as when a testator mandates that he be buried. For even if he mandates it while living, nevertheless the nature of the thing confers that mandate after death, and the mandate is not revoked by death: as in D. de mandato, l. Si vero non remunerandi, §. Si quandoque mandatum. It is conferred after death by the form of the words; and then similarly it endures after death, until it is revoked by the heir, as can be gathered from those things noted in C. de mandato, l. Mandatum, in the first opposition. And although a testator cannot appoint a curator of his future inheritance, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, §. Mevia, according to the understanding of the glossa there placed, nevertheless the mandate can endure after death, not by way of curatorship of goods, but by the way of a simple mandate, if it began in the life of the mandator. For in many cases we see the mandate endure after death, as in D. de procuratoribus, l. Si defunctus; D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. Fundi; and what is noted in D. de legatis 2, l. Cum pater, §. Mevio.

Secondly, it must be premised for clarity, that if a procurator sells the thing of the master and receives the price in the name of the master, the dominion of the money is immediately acquired by the master himself, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Si ego. Thus the gestor is liable for the restitution of the money by two actions: namely, by the action on mandate, as in D. de institoria, l. Quicunque, §. Si rei; D. de procuratoribus, l. Qui proprio, §. Procurator, as in the others. Also by the vindication of the thing, since he possesses another’s money, as is noted in a similar case in D. si certum petatur, l. Cum fundus, §. Servum tuum imprudens; and l. Nam et si fur.

Thirdly, I premise and weigh that one absolved from rendering an account of things to be done in the future must nevertheless observe good faith, as in D. de mandato, l. Creditor, §. Lucius. For fraud is not included in a general permission, as in l. Si pater, D. de privatis creditoribus. And although he has been released from accounting in a contract or last will, nevertheless he is not released from dolus (fraud), as is fully read and noted in D. de liberis legatis, l. Non solum, §. Si haeres; and l. Aurelio; and C. de transactionibus, l. Actionem. And although he were released from personal obligation, he is not released from vindication of the thing, by which he can be sued as any possessor, as is elegantly noted in D. de liberis legatis, l. Aurelius, §. Mevia, in the glossa which begins “Quondam.” Also, although he were released from what he did during the mandate, nevertheless after he has performed his office and is no longer procurator, because he sold and received the price: if he subsequently commits dolus, he is liable for such dolus. Just as we say in another matter that someone is liable under a new condictio, who was not liable under the first, as is fully noted in D. de furtis, in l. Si dominium; and D. de condictione furtiva, l. Sed nec legatarius. And these are the things that can be considered for the part of the plaintiff, that he can act and vindicate the said money. But for the part of the defendant, that he can use the exception of dolus, it is thus proven.

It is certain that if an express pact of non-petendo (not to sue) was appended here regarding that which will be demanded by virtue of the procuration. Hence, whether action is brought personally or realiter, the exception of the pact of non-petendo stands in the way. For in personal actions it removes natural obligation and defeats civil obligation. It also defeats the action itself, as in l. Si unus, §. Pactus ne peteret, D. de pactis. But in real actions it does not remove obligation, which is not present in real actions, as in Inst. de actionibus, §. 1. But it well defeats the action itself, as these things prove: D. de pactis, l. Emptor, §. Lucius; and C. de transactionibus, l. Ut responsum; and C. de furtis, l. Post decisionem. And if it is said that this administrator commits dolus by not returning the money: it is answered by interpretation. For he does not commit dolus who retains the thing by the will of the master, as in D. de donationibus, l. Si tibi dederim. Also, future dolus can be tacitly remitted, namely by remitting the action: D. de pactis, l. Si unus, §. Illud nulla, 2. responso.

Moreover, since the procurator is constituted in such a way that he manages the business rather for himself than for the master, such a procurator is a procurator in rem suam (for his own interest), as in D. de fideicommissariis hereditatibus, l. Plane. Which procuration savors of a donation, as in C. de donationibus, l. Illam; D. de procuratoribus, l. Si quis in rem suam procurator. But here it must be observed what kind of donation it savors. For between the living it savors a donation, and insofar as it is beyond the legitimate sum, insinuatio (official registration) is required, as in C. de donationibus, l. Sancimus. But insofar as it is conferred after death, because mention of death is made, it savors a donation causa mortis (in contemplation of death), as in D. de donationibus causa mortis, l. Seya; and D. de dote praegata, l. Seya; and what is noted in D. de solutionibus, l. Quae dotis. Nor is insinuatio required, but five witnesses are required, otherwise it is not valid. And these are the considerations for and against this captious procuration.

But it seems to be said that in this procuration the words emitted by this woman do not savor a donation between the living, nor causa mortis; but rather the mere faith of the procurator chosen, and fullest confidence had in him, and in his mere and pure conscience.

† How could she have been able to free herself from a well-paid obligation regarding that which was not in existence, nor was it brought into any formal existence during her lifetime? These matters involve contradictions. As stated in the Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations, Titia usufruct; and in the Digest, On Verbal Obligations, law 10. This occurs because the nature of women is most avaricious, as stated in the Digest, On Donations Between Husband and Wife, If she stipulated. Moreover, one who confesses to having received something is moved by a cause other than the intent to donate; hence, it is not a donation. Code, On Non-Nullity of Penalties, In contracts. Unless this confession is made between those prohibited from donating to each other, or to another. Digest, On Legacies, Book 3, When someone dying; § Titia. Digest, On Proof, He who makes a will. On Antenuptial Donations, law 1. It is established that if these individuals were procurators for their own benefit, or if they were to derive some advantage from the procuratorship itself, such persons would not be called procurators in the proper sense, but abusively: as is read and noted in the Digest, On Procurators, law 1, in the beginning. The statute, which speaks of procurators using these words, would not apply to them: because the words of a statute must be taken in their proper sense, and not abusively or improperly: especially when the statute disposes contrary to, or beyond, the common law, as in the Digest, On Negotiorum Gestio, law 3, § These words. Furthermore, we have certain cases, and let us see if they are pertinent to the proposition. If I hand over a thing to you to sell, and you use the price by way of a loan, you are bound to repay the money by a certain action on loan, not as a procurator. As in the Digest, If a Certain Thing is Demanded, If anyone without cause; and law Certain action; § If; and law You requested. Therefore, if the intention was that I should donate the money to you, it ought not to be recoverable, as in the Digest, On Prescriptions, If you sell a thing. But it seems that a response has already been given to this: for it is true where there is an intent to donate. But in our case, a donation is not expressed. Moreover, prudent interpretation has broken down captious liberality, as in the Digest, On Transactions, When the Aquilian action. Also, another presumption excludes a presumed donation, as in the Digest, On Stipulations, If with gold. And concerning these, whether a reason should be given or not: since it seems contrary to the nature of a mandate that the remainder not be returned, and that the procurator enriches himself at another’s loss, although the nature of the words is open to the contrary, much can be disputed, and by what mind this was said and agreed upon must be proven before the judge. Argument from the Code, On Fidejussio, Will. In this ambiguous and unclear situation, it does not seem reasonable to begin with a seizure without prior citation: the statute ought to be understood, since it is so clear on the part of the plaintiff that a denial does not make the matter probably doubtful, as in the Digest, On Transactions, After the matter; and Code, On Falsehood, Sufficiently clearly; and Code, On the Order of Cognitions, If.

† Moreover, the statute that permits arrest does not state that citation is unnecessary. And it is expressly contrary to the laws that one who was not first cited verbally may be cited in rem, as expressly noted in C. quomodo et quando iudices, l. consentaneum. Likewise, the common laws support this: ff. de regulis iuris, l. si cum nulla; de executione rei iudicatae, l. nimis propere; and C. de exhibendis reis, l. 2. Furthermore, citation is made for the purpose of defense, which is a matter of natural law; and therefore it ought not to be omitted, as in c. pastoralis, de re iudicata. For these reasons, I conclude that, upon examination of the words of the statute, in which there is no mention of the absence of citation, at least one verbal citation is required before proceeding to the actual arrest of the person; because all judicial proceedings ought to begin with citation, as in Inst. de poena temere litigantium, §. sin. It therefore appears from the foregoing that the question is sufficiently doubtful regarding whether a reason should be given or not; and this is a doubt in law, requiring intellectual speculation. And although some say that a point of law is always certain, they do not speak the truth when the point of law depends on a dispute of fact or on the quality of the parties’ claims, as in C. de rebus creditis, l. cum proponatis. And this is the sole reason, considering that the party producing an instrument must abide by its tenor, as noted by Innocentius, extra de censibus, cap. olim. This seems sufficient to prevent arrest, because whether something is due or not is a question of legal subtleties. But there is another reason due to the order of citation not being observed; because citation is the necessary beginning in every judicial proceeding, as in the aforementioned §. sin., Inst. de poena temere litigantium. And therefore, I believe that the said procurators, even with the veil lifted and without preliminary citation, cannot be personally arrested according to law. To this are added the common laws: ff. de adoptionibus, l. nam ita divus; and ff. de re iudicata, l. de unoquoque. It is not the case that this is a mere executor, but a judge, to whom it must be clearly established the right to arrest, as in l. hoc autem, post principium, ff. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur. And this supports the aforementioned, extra de rescriptis, c. 2. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. On the interpretation of statutes prohibiting the filing of complaints, appeals, or claims of nullity against arbitral awards, or the seeking of any form of reduction to the judgment of a good man. See here the beautiful [treatments].
body: Three things are to be considered in the present case.

† First, in this case it must be considered the statute which provides that, once arbitrary precepts and arbitral awards have been made between ascendants and descendants, or agnates, or cognates, or relatives by affinity, whether present or past, or neighbors of the same parish, they may no longer be declared inequitable; nor may one appeal from them, file a complaint, or petition for relief, but they must be put into execution with all legal remedies. And regarding this statute, it was advised that if an arbitrator, through fraud or through an intolerably biased sentence, disposed of something, a reduction to the judgment of a good man may be sought, namely, to the extent that fraud is found; because fraud is not included in any breadth of power: as in D. de manum. l. creditor. §. Luc. which is especially apparent from the fact that in every compromise these words are placed, as if by a good man, or equivalent words, whence tacitly, by contrary reasoning, it is understood that if the award is rendered through fraudulent machination or intolerable bias, a reduction may be sought, as in D. pro socio. l. unde si Neruae. and D. de oper. lib. l. si libertus. Thus, therefore, it comes from the tacit agreement of the parties, as in D. de appel. l. ex consensu. The statute does not oppose this. As in D. de re iud. l. si convenerit. And to this effect is D. de manumis. testa. l. si quis locuples. and Extr. de iureiu. c. Quintauallis. And Bartolus says that when there is an immoderate quantity of damage, and no cause clearly appears, fraud is presumed, as he notes in D. pro socio. l. si societatem. §. arbitrorum. and D. de pręto. stipu. l. si. This is manifest by natural reason. For those who compromise do not compromise in order to squander or dissipate their property: but rather their intention is to win, as in D. ad leg. falc. l. in ratione. §. cum quidam. For if anyone had the intention of squandering his property, he would do this without an arbitrator, as in D. de condi. et dem. l. Męuius. And statutes, although they speak indistinctly, must nevertheless be referred to the intention of the contracting parties, arg. D. de vsu. l. si stipulatus. And the said advice was true, juridical, and sound, nor should it be thought that the mind of the advisor was otherwise: because by laws which punish fraud, the way should not be opened to frauds, as in C. de in dicta vidui. toll. l. 2. and C. vnde vi. l. meminerint. It adds to the foregoing that even if one does not appeal, restitution in integrum may be sought on that ground, because it seems to be a just cause. As elegantly noted in D. ad Tre. l. seruo inuito. §. cum praetor. And there is an express law that where there is fraud in a perpetual arbitrator, the exception of fraud is available. As in C. de arbi. l. non distinguemus. §. cum quidam. Now, the consultant, who was consulted on this point, which consists in law, pronounced that the said award was fraudulent and inequitable: from these things, namely, which appear from the records, namely, from the paternal testament, from the form of the statute, the consultant advised that it should not be reduced to the judgment of a good man, and the judge so pronounced, and thus pronounced on an article of fact, and not on an article of law. And this is the first pronouncement: because on this article of law it was never pronounced, except once. And now a complaint is made from this pronouncement. But against this complaint it is objected from another statute, which provides that in all precepts, arbitrations, and arbitral awards, which have been declared inequitable or unjust, within the time comprehended in the statute of the commune, and on which it has been pronounced in favor of those precepts, arbitrations, or arbitral awards, it is presumed, and they may no longer be declared inequitable, nor may one appeal from them, complain, or petition for relief: but they must be put into execution with all legal remedies. Therefore, the complaint ceases: because statutes can remove appeal and every kind of complaint, as in C. si de momen. poss. l. 1. But to this it is clearly answered that it is not true that a sentence has been passed on the arbitration or arbitral award: but it has been passed on a mere article of law, namely, that it should not be reduced to the judgment of a good man, that is, that it is not reducible. For this is the sense of these words. For if another sense were intended, namely, that inequity was a weakness of intellect, as in D. de vsur. l. placuit. Therefore, the consultant wished to say that by the first statute the reduction is impeded, not however that from the quality and justice of the arbitration itself it should not be reduced, because it is equitable. Hence it appears that the statute in question does not touch our case: because no advice has been given, and a sentence following the advice has not been passed on the arbitration and for the confirmation of the arbitration, but only on an article of municipal law. But what if we suppose that all these things cease, nevertheless the decree of the lord follows, which is thus contained. We will, however, that by this present decree derogation be made, and be understood to have been made, to the statutes of our cities and lands, which entirely remove the remedies of appeal, nullity, and complaint. From which decree it clearly appears that the prince opens the way to those complaining, notwithstanding municipal statutes, as in Extr. de iureiu. c. Venientes. Hence, statutes which say that appeal is removed do not prevent appealing to the prince himself, to whom subjects cannot impose law, as in l. 1. D. quis, et a quo appellet. and no. C. de iudic. l. apertissime. That is also well to be noted, that in the first statute it does not speak of nullity, although it uses the word "complain": because to declare a sentence null is not properly a complaint: as appears in the matter of testators. For one thing is to propose a complaint, another to declare null, as in D. de his, quibs vt indig. l. postlegatum. The second statute, however, speaks well of nullity. And this, namely, this statute is properly that statute of which the lord's decree speaks. For because it is more absurd not to be able to complain of nullity than of inequity, as noted in ca. 1. de seque. poss. et fructuum. and in c. ut calumniis. de re iud. in Clem. ideo, the lord was moved to make the said decree, as in D. de app. l. si expressum. From which it is clearly concluded that the complaint, which is in question, ought to be admitted, and judgment introduced, and especially by virtue of the said decree. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, it is permitted to princes or private individuals to build, or not to build, out of emulation on land, or in waters and rivers. And see below, consilium 195.
2. There are three kinds of buildings.
3. Certain rivers are public and navigable, etc.
4. Corrupted air more readily infects children and the innocent than the culpable and the wicked.
5. The shedding of blood is sometimes permitted.
body: It is said.

† The ninth work, which pertains to the emulation of another city and provides material for sedition, is not permitted to be undertaken by anyone, as stated in the Digest, *De operibus publicis*, law *Opus nouum*; and it is noted in the Code, *De fundis limitosis*, law *Quicunque castrorum*. For emulations are prohibited by law, as in the Digest, *De iustitia et iure*, law *Ut vim*; and especially those from which the slaughter of many innocent people may result. The text states: "Let no people or cities make sedition against one another." But let there be peace for all cities, while equity is preserved for our subjects here, and the passions of any cause do not incline toward any of the parties, as in the Authenticum, *De mandatis principum*, section *Deinde conueniens*. I consider, however, that there are three kinds of buildings.

† For certain things are done principally for emulation; others for construction or habitation principally, without any other consideration. Others, however, are done for defense. The first are prohibited if the aptness or act of harming concurs with the intention of the builder. The second, however, are permitted, and by law, one may build on his own property, as in C. de servitutibus et aqua, l. si manifestae, and l. altius. The third kind of buildings, for defense, is lawful, both in constructing and destroying, and this if done on one’s own property. By “one’s own” I call even one’s own territory, as in C. de officiis praefecti et praetoris Africae, l. 2, in the penultimate column, in the words “interes vero si quas civitates, seu castella.” Therefore, secondly, I premise for clarity that one must always return to the principal motive of the intention. For if something can be done for recession and emulation, what is more principal must be considered, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. rogasti, and l. si quis nec causam. Thirdly, it must be premised for clarity,

† That certain rivers are public and navigable, and such rivers are called royal, as in c. 1, *Quae sint regalia*, Col. 10. And these are reserved to Emperors and Kings in their territories, nor is it lawful for anyone, without the prince’s consent, to divert them into another bed, as in D. *De fluminibus*, l. *Quominus*. Some, however, are public but not navigable: and this is irrelevant to the present matter. Nevertheless, even in these, no one may build unless custom grants the right to build, as in D. *De damno infecto*, l. *Fluminum*, in princ., and there noted; and D. *Ne quid in flumine publico*, in the rubric, black and red, where the text states that nothing shall be done in a public river or on its banks whereby the water flows otherwise than it flowed in former times. Therefore, from the foregoing it appears that in navigable rivers nothing may be done whereby the usual navigation is impeded. This is publicly proclaimed by interdict, as in D. *De novo operis nuntiatione*, l. *In provincia*, § *Si*, together with l. *Si*; and D. *De interdictis*, l. 2, § 1. Hence neither the riverbed nor a ditch may be altered, nor dried up to the injury of the inhabitants, D. *Ne quid in loco publico*, l. 1, § *Sunt qui putant*. Indeed, even without injury, if the river is public, l. 1, § *Hoc interdic.*, D. *De aqua quotannis et aestiva*; and D. *Ut in flumine publico navigari liceat*, l. 1, in princ. And all the above are true, especially when the alteration of the riverbed would corrupt the air or cause pestilence.

For corrupted air more readily infects children and the innocent, due to the tenderness of their age, than the culpable and the guilty, when a pestilential sky threatens ruin; on account of which even streams are forbidden to be corrupted, as in D. de rivis, l. si, and l. 1, D. de cloacis. And these statements are true, unless such things can be done for the sake of common utility, D. de servitutibus rusticorum praediorum, l. si. Moreover, if they were done for the purpose of avoiding hostility or for repelling enemies, because nothing is blameworthy in the way of defense, as in D. de iustitia et iure, l. ut vim, and D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. si ex plagiis, § tabernarius.

For if the shedding of blood is permitted on account of defense, as is fully read and noted in Extra, De homicidio, c. Significasti; and wars are permitted by the same cause, as in Digest, De iustitia et iure, l. Ex hoc iure gentium; and in 23 q. 1, c. Noli estimare; as in c. Quis culpatur; and c. Militari; and c. Summa militiae laus; therefore, much more strongly, other things are permitted. As noted by Innocentius in Extra, De restitutione spoliorum, c. Olim; and Extra, De iureiurando, c. Sicut; and Extra, De voto, c. Quod super. Nevertheless, whatever may be the law regarding building, there is no doubt that our Lord does not thereby break the peace; because he introduces nothing into another’s domain. I say this of him to whom he is bound by the pact of peace, since our Magnificent Lord has promised nothing; hence nothing of this pertains to the Lords, because it was not adhering to them: the chapters of peace do not contain this, Digest, De verbis obligatis, l. Si stipulatus, §. Grisogonus. And those who are not included in the chapters of peace do not enjoy the privileges of peace, as in c. 1, §. Nomina vero, De pace constantia, col. 11.

Moreover, the said M. is he who began a novelty by exercising new power in an emulative manner; from which suspicion may arise for the illustrious Lord, and therefore he may look out for himself in return. Codex, De sicca, l. 2; and l. Si ut allegas. Thus art is deceived by art, Digest, De legibus, l. Cum pater, §. Titio. And necessity makes lawful what it does, Digest, De manumissione testamento, l. Qui non potuerunt. And it pertains to the Lord to consult not only for himself, but for his subjects, because their status is connected, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, De appellationibus, c. Dilecti, sicut. Just as subjects are bound to defend the status of their Lord, so conversely, as in c. 1, §. Finis, De foro et fide; and in the said c. Domino guerram faciente, in the title Hic finitur lex. Then the customs of the kingdom begin. 1 Distinctio, c. Ius gentium; and c. Ius militare. 24 q. 3, §. Quid non; and c. Fortuito. 2 q. 1, c. Noli estimare; and c. Militia; and c. Apud vos; and c. Dominus vester; and c. Notandum, eadem causa. 2 q. 2, with infinite similar cases.

Furthermore, our Magnificent Lord holds regalia from the Emperor, and performs his office in all things. Argumentum from Digest, Quod vi aut clam, l. Prohibere, §. Plane; Codex, Et ubi et apud quos, l. Finis, cum si.

It is further to be known that some emulate, yet do not act improperly. And of these speaks the law Opus, Digest, De operibus publicis; and Extra, De restitutione spoliorum, c. Pisanis. Some emulate, yet do not act improperly, but for the terror of one meditating against them. And this is our case. For it is lawful to extinguish the fire of great thought with water, Digest, Quod vi aut clam, l. Si alius, §. Est et alia flumina. Therefore, either they were anciently so, and thus they are done, and no novelty is made by any party with any capacity for harm, as was granted to the Lombards in the Peace of Constance, as in c. §. Nos Romanorum, De pace constantia, col. 11, where the text thus says: “We grant to you cities and persons of societies in perpetuity, that within bridges, waters, and mills, as you have been accustomed to hold from ancient times, and hold.” Or if one party does not wish to acquiesce to antiquity, let him know that the cause of the provocator is the worse in law, Digest, Ne quid in loco publico, l. 2, §. Idem ait. And that whatever law one establishes for another, he should use the same law, as is written throughout. “All things whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you even so to them,” Matthew 7; and 1 Distinctio, c. Humanum genus.

Moreover, the Magnificent Lord has not yet altered the navigable river or its bank, and thus if we go to strict law, he can say, “I build on my own,” Digest, De damno infecto, l.
