Proculus; and Digest, De aqua pluviali, l. 2, §. Idem autem. It makes the same point, Codex, De nihil aggeribus non rumpendis, l. 1; Digest, De extraordinariis criminibus, l. Sacularii, §. In Aegypto; and §. Si quis arbores sicomorum.

Furthermore, it was agreed in the peace that anyone may build on his own, which pact is valid between them, Digest, Communia praedio, l. Venditor, in principio, where it is expressed.

In waters, three things are to be considered: law, pact or privilege, nature of the place, and antiquity, Digest, De aqua pluviali, l. Secunda, in principio. And it is lawful to kill an enemy with poison, as Vegetius teaches in De re militari. I say this by forum law, not by heavenly law. But piety and natural reason of the mind do not revoke the intention, Codex, Qui accusari non possunt, l. Propter insidias, with moderation, however, Codex, Unde vi, l. 1.

I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a confession or a pact of non-petendo made by the paternal creditor in favor of the son, who abstained from his father's inheritance, benefits the grandson possessing some of the grandfather's goods, and number 3.
2. The son abstaining from the inheritance is not bound to the father, unless he possesses, because he can be sued hypothecarily.
body: Creditor

† Since the son, who had abstained from his father’s inheritance, made such a confession, namely, that he confessed that, in his own name and in the name of the paternal inheritance, he owed nothing to the said son, either with cause or without, purely or under condition. And he confessed that if any instruments should be found against the said father or son, either under a general or special condition, by himself or with others, that they are without cause; and he promised to return those instruments cut and cancelled. Now what is the case? The son of the said son possesses certain ancestral goods, and therefore he is sued by a hypothecary action on account of a certain fiction. It is asked whether the said pact and confession hinder the said plaintiff, or not, assuming a statute which says that anyone may stipulate and make agreements in the name of another.

And I premise for clarity that a son who has abstained from his father’s inheritance is bound by no law to pay his father’s debts. Therefore, it is true to say that he is not liable, neither in his own name nor in the name of the heir: as in C. si minor se ab hereditate abstinuerit, l. 1; and Inst. de haeredum qualitate et differentia, §. sed et his permittit praetor; and D. de gulis et pupillari substitutione, l. filius, qui patri; and fully noted in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. necessarius. Nevertheless, if he possesses any of his father’s goods, he may be sued hypothecarily, like any other possessor, as in D. de pignori, l. si fundus, §. in venditione.

Secondly, I premise for the sake of clarity that the said confession made against the said son is expressed in conjunctive terms, namely, that if any instrument is found in which it is contained that the said father and son ought to give, that such instrument is without cause. But if there were any instrument that spoke of the father alone, or of the son alone, the confession does not speak of such an instrument. As stated in D. 12.3.1 (Si haeredi plures) and D. 16.1.1 (Reus), § Cum tabulis. Therefore, what is not provided for in the instrument, we also cannot assert, as stated in D. 46.1.1 (Fideiussores), § Pro Aurelio. I therefore consider in the present point, first, D. 2.14.1 (Si tibi decem), § Cum possessor. Secondly, I consider the nature of the real action: because under the remission of debt it is not contained that it cannot be vindicated. This is the text of D. 40.12.1 (Aurelius), § Mevia, with its gloss. Thirdly, I consider the form and nature of conjunctive words, which speak of a common debt, not of the father’s debt alone. And therefore, under one, the other is not contained, as stated in D. 35.1.1 (Hoc legatum). Wherefore it does not seem to me that the hypothecary right, which is in question, has been extinguished. Nor do those words “by himself, or with others” stand in the way; because that word “by himself” is to signify the father and the son, and those words “with others” are to signify others; hence our case is not present, as stated in D. 33.1.1 (Titiae textores). Moreover, in the said writing a cause is appended, which is not true; because neither in the past nor at any time was a cause appended in the said instruments, at least one that would be true. This is manifestly proven by the contrary instruments. And therefore, although a pact not to sue does not require a cause, nevertheless if a false cause is expressed, the pact is not valid, unless we were to say that it is a certain donation, which is not presumed. Rather, error is presumed, as stated in D. 2.14.1 (Si cum te) and D. 13.5.1 (Si). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether letters of exchange, which are made daily by merchants, whereby such a person pays B. one hundred for the same amount which he received from him, and his partners prove the receipt to be true against the writer of the said letter, and for which part it is for B. and for which for the partners.
2. How these words, "held and received from Seius, etc.," are to be understood.
3. Against a confession of law, and as a matter of law, proof to the contrary is admitted regarding the confession.
4. One suing on a natural loan, if he proves it to be civil, does not found his claim.
body: Sempronius Manfredi wrote a certain letter to Titius, a merchant, on his return to Venice, a private one in his own hand, of the following tenor, namely: “In the name of God, Amen. On the first day of February 1381. Pay by this first letter, according to your custom, 43 pounds of grossi. These are in exchange for 440 ducats which I have received from Seyo and his partners. Otherwise, pay them.” Titius refused to accept this writing, nor to pay anything on its pretext. Wherefore, the said Seyo brought an action in court against the said Sempronius, stating that the said Sempronius is indebted to the said Seyo and his partners in the amount of 430 gold ducats, received and accepted in Bologna from the said Seyo and his partners; and which the said Sempronius lawfully confessed to have received from the said Seyo and his partners, and this in exchange, and by reason of the exchange, of 44 pounds of Venetian grossi, which the said Sempronius lawfully agreed with the said Seyo and his partners to pay to the said Seyo and his partners, or to have paid in Venice by Titius, a merchant residing in Venice, as is most clearly shown by a certain writing, or bill of exchange, written by the hand of Sempronius in the said month of February of the said year, and delivered to the said Seyo by the said Sempronius to be sent to the said Titius in the said city of Venice, as is contained above in the registered letter. The said Seyo also stated that one-half of the said money belongs and pertains to him by virtue and on account of the said writing and bill, and also of the partnership. Therefore, he concludes that the said writing, acknowledged by the said Sempronius, be put into execution against and to the prejudice of the said Sempronius, requesting that proceedings follow the form of the statutes, and especially the statute placed under the rubric “Concerning the writings of merchants and money-changers,” and by the force of any other statute bearing on the matter. Finally, in the course of the proceedings, the said Seyo confessed in court that he had not personally paid any sum of money to the said Sempronius; but he believes that a certain Jacob and John paid it as partners of the said Seyo, and for the said Seyo, and in the name of the partnership.

† And according to what appears in the document produced in the said case, and it is presupposed that the said Jac. and Ioan. and Seyus were partners, nevertheless the principal name of the partnership was that of Seyus. It is also presupposed that the said Jac. and Io. testified in court regarding non-payment, yet one of them is an outlaw, the other is an odious actor of the plaintiff, and the defendant is suspected. From these matters, therefore, the question of law arises. And omitting verbal subtleties, it can be said in one word that the said Sempronius ought to be absolved from the claims: and this for the following reason, because in the libel mention is made of the said Seyus as the one making payment, there where it says, "received and accepted in Bologna from the said Seyus and partners," which words have this meaning, namely, from Seyus for one half, and from the partners for the other half, as in D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. 4; and D. de duobus reis, l. reos, § cum tabulis; D. de re iudicata, l. Paulus; C. si plures una sententia, l. 1. Where it must be considered that by the word "partners," Seyus is not comprehended, who is separated from the others by his own proper name; just as it is written, "say to his disciples, and to Peter." For although all were disciples, nevertheless Peter is named principally by himself. To this effect: D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, § qui discretas. And this is clear, because if Seyus were included under the general name of partners, he would be named twice. Moreover, since there were three partners, he ought not to sue alone for one half, but for his proportional share; because unless otherwise appears, partners are presumed to be partners in equal parts, not in unequal parts, as in D. pro socio, l. si non fuerit. Or, which is absurd, he would have one half for the first, as named by himself, and one third for the second, as named among the others: which is contrary to the nature of partnership, and contrary to good faith, because a partnership ought not to be a lion's share. I therefore return to the point, and say,

† that those words, “received and taken from Seyus,” signify that Seyus paid personally and truly. Cf. D. de sicer. peta. l. si. §. fin. And although, according to the custom of merchants, one partner sometimes writes the name of the other, nevertheless this abuse does not apply in drafting the writ and in bringing the action, because one must not depart from the words of the writ, as C. de fideic. lib. l. si. and C. de lib. causa l. cum precum. Moreover, this private letter does not prove true payment, but rather a confession, as noted in C. de non nu. pe. l. si ex cautione, unless the defendant confesses the payment, or at least does not deny it, as D. si cer. pet. l. lecta. and D. de ver. ob. l. si ita stipulatus. §. grisogonus. And although, by the form of the statute, the exception of non-payment of money cannot be raised, nevertheless it does not follow that payment was made; on the contrary, whatever the statute says, the non-payment may be proved by the plaintiff’s confession.

†because even against a presumption of law, the contrary is proved as a matter of law by confession, as is shown in the Authentica *De aequalitate dotis*, § *Aliud*. For through confession the malice of the actor appears, whence he ought to be repelled by the office of the judge, as noted by Innocentius in c. 1, *De officio vicarii*, and in c. *Constitutus*, *De filiis presbyterorum*.

† Moreover, the Speculum expressly determines that a plaintiff suing on a natural loan, who proves a civil loan, that is, a confession, does not confuse his own claim; and therefore the defendant ought to be absolved. Thus elegantly noted in the Speculum, De testibus, § 1, verso “Sed pone, egi.” Furthermore, the words of the bill of complaint are very worthy of consideration, namely, “which the said Sempronius agreed to pay lawfully to the said Serus and partners.” For the understanding of this, it must be premised that when a counting out, a stipulation, or a confession intervenes, an action arises not from the counting out or the confession, but from the stipulation, as in D. De nova operis nuntiatio, l. Si ita fuero stipulatus, § 1, and the following law; and fully noted in D. Si certum petatur, l. Certi condictio, § Si nummos. It is necessary for the stipulation to be proved; otherwise the plaintiff fails, as in l. 1, in principio, D. De edendo, and l. An eadem, § Actiones, D. De exceptione rei iudicatae. But here a stipulation of the said Serus was alleged, and the exact contrary appears, because Serus was not present, as in l. Prima, in principio, D. De verbis obligatis, and l. Stipulatio ista, § Alteri. And therefore, because the cause is not proved, nor the action, the plaintiff fails, as in C. De edendo, l. Qui accusare, and C. De probationibus, l. Actor quod asseverat. For these are the most substantial matters which must be proved, as is clear to any intelligent jurist. Moreover, no one sues without an action, as in D. De negotiis gestis, l. Si pupilli, § Videamus. But this Serus has no direct action, nor any useful, natural, or ceded action; therefore he cannot sue, as noted in l. 3, D. Pro socio, and D. De actionibus et obligationibus, l. 2, and D. De locato, l. Cum in plures, § Messem. Otherwise it would follow that cessions of actions were introduced in vain: which is false. And it must be considered that this was not a mute contract, but a contract of exchange, because payment must be made in the same kind, as in D. De solutionibus, l. Pauius. In which contract, if the prerequisites are not observed, one sues for restitution by the condictio ob causam, which does not arise from the writing itself, but from a quasi-contract, in which the writing does not merit execution; because one does not sue according to the tenor of the writing, but from a new cause. Then the petition for execution of the writing would have place when one sues to fulfill it; because then one sues from a cause which existed at the time of the contract. But the condictio ob causam did not exist at the time of the contract, nor was it considered by the contracting parties. Wherefore it is something coming from outside and emerging, in which, as in a case of unforeseen accident, it does not follow. Hence one cannot sue to execute either from the words or from the intent of the writing, but one would have to sue merely by the provision of the law, as in D. De condictione indebiti, l. Fina, § Fina. Finally, it must be concluded that, since the writing has two parts, one concerning Serus, the other concerning the partners, namely, according as the word sounds, Serus counted out part, the partners part. And since it is established that there was no counting out, the said plaintiff, who said one thing in the bill and the contrary in the responses, being repelled as contradictory, as in l. 1, C. De furtis, and l. Prima, C. Si servus externo. That also must not be omitted, that if the said witnesses did not fully prove, nevertheless, joined with the said response of the plaintiff, by which it appears that the writing, as regards the plaintiff himself, is simulated, they aid the defense of the defendant. For that which is simulated, although it has the appearance of being, does not have true and substantial being, as in D. De regulis iuris, l. Imaginaria. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one may proceed against a division by virtue of the nature of a simple division, even if a general settlement is annexed to the division.
2. A compromise is a species of settlement.
3. Whether, among brothers instituted as heirs and mutually substituted by fideicommissum, if they die without children, the claim for the fideicommissum is impeded upon the occurrence of the case of substitution, if before the case they divided the inheritance among themselves and compromised.
body: In the will of Roland of Scarampi, certain institutions and substitutions were made after the death of those who would die without children. One of the instituted heirs died during the lifetime of the testator, and then the testator died. A question therefore arose among the surviving instituted heirs as to how that lapsed share should be divided: finally, they came to a certain general compromise between them in this form. And also concerning all lawsuits, controversies, questions, and causes hitherto arisen between the said parties, and which might arise in the future for any cause, and especially on account of the inheritance of Roland Scarampi, and of all and each of the matters dependent, emerging, and connected therewith. Finally, the arbiter gave his award and made a division of the goods of the said Roland. And the parties ratified the said division by word and deed, and each possessed the part adjudicated to him. Finally, some of the said instituted heirs died without heirs. The survivors therefore wish to claim the fideicommissum. It is objected to them on the grounds of the said compromise, award, division, and ratification. Now the question is asked, what is the law.

† And first, that the said fideicommissum cannot be claimed, because it is contrary to the division; although it may be admitted by the nature of a simple division, as in D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, § haereditatem; nevertheless, the case is different if a general transaction is annexed to the division. D. de verbis oblig., l. qui Romae, § duo fratres, according to the interpretation of Decius and his followers. And the reason is that a general transaction ought to operate generally, as is fully read and noted in D. de pace, l. tres fratres, and C. de transactionibus, l. sub praetextu.

But a compromise of arbitrators is a certain species of transaction, or at least of agreement, as in Auth. ut differentes iud. § 1. Therefore, one must not depart from the generality of the words, as noted in D. de pactis l. emptor § Lucius. Nor is this surprising, because all things are included in a general word, as in D. de verbis oblig. l. quicquid astringendae secundo responso, and D. de serv. urb. praed. l. si servus.

† To the contrary is the truth, if the words of the compromise are carefully observed, and more carefully the words of the award, and of the inheritance itself. For I return to the first point, namely, to the words of the compromise. For the compromise has two clauses: one concerning questions that have arisen. And there is no doubt about this clause. The second concerns those matters which may arise in the future between the compromitting parties; no question can arise regarding a fideicommissum left after their death, because the condition is pending in the meantime, as stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Haeres meus*. Hence, restitution under the Trebellian law could not be made before death, as noted in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law *Post mortem*, and in the Digest, *Ad Trebellianum*, law *Si ante*. Moreover, that word "may arise" is understood in terms of a power which exists in law, not of an injurious power. For future injury does not seem to have been considered, nor ought it to have been considered, according to the note by Cynus in the Code, *De accusationibus*, law *Si quis*. Therefore, this word "may" must be understood in a civil sense, as in the Digest, *De servitutibus*, law *Si cui*, and in the Digest, *De verbis obligationum*, law *Nepos Proculo*. Added to this is the word "although," with the occasion or cause. For these words denote something which is in the occasion or cause of the past, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Demonstratio*, section *Quod autem*. But in a fideicommissum left after death, no cause has yet been caused, nor is there any principal thing. And where there is no principal, there cannot be anything dependent, emerging, or connected, as in the Digest, *De fundo instrato*, law *Sicut*. And this is held by Bartolus in the aforementioned section *Duo fratres*, although he does not speak so fully. But let us assume, without prejudice to the truth, that this would fall within the compromise: nevertheless, it must be considered that it does not fall within the award, because the award remained within the limits of a simple division. And one cause is for dividing, another is the latest cause for claiming the fideicommissum, as in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Qui cum tutoribus*, in the principle, and in the aforementioned section *Haereditatis*. But certainly, a third principal point must also be considered, because they divided the inheritance among themselves, whence it appears that it was divided with its burdens, and consequently with the burden of the fideicommissum, as in the Digest, *De hereditate vel actione vendita*, law 1, section *Si quis debitori*. From these reasons, I say and conclude that the fideicommissum, whose condition has occurred, can be claimed after the death of the compromitting parties, notwithstanding whatever may be alleged to the contrary. Nor does the Code, *De pactis*, law *Prima*, stand in the way, because there a pact was specifically and expressly appended concerning a future compromise, which was not the case in our situation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statute that an appeal shall be made from the *potestas* to the *capitaneus*, if it subsequently happens that the same person is both *potestas* and *capitaneus*, whether an appeal may be taken from a sentence rendered by the vicar of that *potestas* to the same *capitaneus*.
2. If the judge of the first instance has become the appellate judge, whether an appeal may be taken to him.
3. Whether an appeal may be taken from a sentence that a judge pronounced nullly, or where the procedure was conducted improperly against the possessors of goods without first exhausting the remedies against the principal debtor or his heir.
4. In which cases exhaustion of remedies (*excussio*) is not required.
5. If a person’s goods have been confiscated, whether an action may be brought against the principal possessors of the goods under an express hypothec, if no prior action has been brought against the fisc concerning the confiscated and unexhausted goods. And at number 7.
6. The crime of usury is an ecclesiastical crime.
7. The interpretation of the statute which provides that a public instrument shall prevail over a private one and a chirograph.
8. How it is proved that someone is a usurer.
body: It is proposed,

† Where a statute was in force in a certain city, providing that an appeal should be made from the *potestas* to the *capitaneus*, it was finally ordered that the same person should be both *potestas* and *capitaneus*, so that he should exercise both offices. It happens that the vicar of this *potestas* rendered a sentence, from which sentence an appeal was made to the *capitaneus*. The question is whether the said appeal proceeds according to law, or not. And it seems that it does not proceed. For there is an injustice in that the ordinary judge does not cognize through the way of appeal from his vicar, as is stated in the extrajudicial collection on custom, chapter *Non putamus*, book 6, because it is the same court, as is said there.

I say the contrary, that this man was not the vicar of the *capitaneus*, but of the *potestas*. For these are separate offices, and what is done by one office can also be reformed by the strength of the greater office, even by the same person, as in the Digest, *Quando appellatio sit*, law 1, section *Solent*, verse *Sed si praeses*.

But I oppose this, for it would follow that if the same person had pronounced judgment as *potestas*, it would afterwards be returned to him as *capitaneus*, which seems false, as in the Code, *De appellationibus*, law *Eos*, in the beginning. Moreover, no one can exercise two contrary offices, as in the Digest, *De procuratoribus*, law *Licet*, section *Si plures*, and fully noted by the doctors in the Digest, *De adoptionibus*, law *Si consul*.

But to this it seems a response is open, because when a sentence is rendered by a vicar, no injustice is found in the ordinary judge himself. Hence the reason why the ordinary judge does not cognize is not suspicion, but because it is the same consistory. But here it is not the same consistory of the vicar of the *potestas* and the *capitaneus*; therefore, the reason prohibiting appeal to the same person ceases, and the reason permitting it subsists: because when two jurisdictions and two rights concur in the same person, it is the same as if they pertained to different persons, as in the Digest, *De his quibus ut indignis*, law *Tutorum*, and in the Digest, *De auctoritate tutorum*, law *Accipien*.

† A question similar to this one is whether, if the judge of the first instance has become the appellate judge, an appeal may be made to him. And the standard gloss determines that it may. D. de inoffic. testam. l. filius, in the final gloss. But the contrary seems to be noted. C. de appellat. l. eos, in the beginning. But these glosses are not contradictory: for either you ask whether an appeal may be made to him, and I say that it may; or you ask whether he ought to hear the case himself or delegate it to another, and I say that he ought to delegate it to another, so that all suspicion may cease. Nevertheless, if he does not delegate, the proceedings are not thereby null, as D. de iur. om. iud. l. praetor. And this is the truth.

† The second doubt is whether a sentence, by which the judge pronounced that the proceedings against the possessors of the goods were null or improperly conducted, without first exhausting the remedies against the principal debtor or his heir, may be appealed. And it seems that it may not, because this sentence is rendered on the basis of written law and in accordance with written law; and if a contrary sentence were rendered, it would be void by operation of law, because an error would be expressed in the sentence, as in D. de appellationibus recipiendis, l. si, in the penultimate paragraph, in the response. But I say the contrary, because an appeal may be taken from a sentence rendered on a declinatory exception, as in C. de procuratoribus, l. ita demum; and see the note in Auth. habita, C. ne filius pro patre; l. cum Titia, D. de accusationibus. And this appeal may be justified:

† because there are certain cases in which excussion is not required. The first is when the principal debtor cannot be subjected to excussion due to his power, as noted by Bartolus in l. si, ff. si certum petatur and ff. de verbis obligatis, book 10. The second is if it is notorious that he is insolvent, as noted by Accursius in the aforementioned two laws. The third is if his goods cannot be possessed without great difficulty. For such a person is not understood to be solvent, as l. 2, ff. qui satisdare coguntur. Therefore, if any of these is proven, excussion is not necessary. And it should be known that this proof may be made during the pendency of the action on the hypothecary claim, even if it was not made previously, as ff. de pignoris actione, l. si rem, §. fin. And it supports the foregoing that what is noted by Cynus in C. de pignoris, auth. hoc si debitor, in the last question.

† The third question is, if the goods of someone have been published, whether an action can be brought against the principal possessors of the goods under an express hypothec, if the fisc is not first sued, and the fisc is not excused on the goods of the confiscated. And it seems that yes, because it is in the creditor's discretion against which possessor and on which thing he will bring a hypothecary action, which discretion should not be able to be taken away from the creditor by the debtor's act, otherwise there would be an open way to frauds, because the debtor would alienate fertile estates to himself, reserving or retaining sterile and almost useless things, on which creditors would have to go, which seems absurd, as ff. de distr. pig. l. creditoris arbitrium. On the contrary, it seems, because the fisc is in the place of the heir, as C. ad l. Iuliam de vi. l. si tutoris. and ff. de noua. l. nouatio. and there note. Therefore, it is the principal debtor. And thus first to be excused, as C. de pignor. auth. hoc si debitor. although some great doctors formerly understood that authentic in tacit hypothec, not in express, as ff. de iu. fis. l. moscis. and touched in Auth. de fideius. §. 1. but that opinion is commonly not held, which therefore our stands in another point, namely whether when the goods of our contemporaries' banished are confiscated, the fisc is bound by personal actions. For in the deported there is no question. But these banished are not in all respects equated to deported. as no. insti. quibus mo. ius patrię potestatis soluitur. §. relegati. I say that it is bound as a successor of the goods by personal action, insofar as the goods suffice, if the goods are incorporated into the fisc. For if it is bound only because it is a possessor, hypothecary discussion would not be necessary, just as for other possessors. and therefore if not all goods were confiscated, but a single thing, discussion of the fisc would not be necessary: because it would not be in the place of the heir. ar. eorum, quę plene no. ff. de transa. l. controuersia. from these the above question is solved, that discussion is necessary, if the fisc is a universal successor, otherwise not, as ff. de iu. fis. l. 1. §. diuus. and this considering the common law. But let us come to a certain statute, on which the plaintiff bases himself, in which another mode of proceeding is given more expeditiously, when any of the creditors is put in possession. and although that statute speaks of putting in possession. s. ventris nomine, nevertheless, he who buys from him should not be in a better condition than his author, as ff. si mulier in possessionem missa. l. 1. §. necessaria. and C. vt in poss. leg. l. certa forma. and arg. extra de iu. c. quia 5. But this is not expeditious, because the statute does not speak, except of the one put in possession, and not of another who buys justly and in good faith. And therefore it does not seem that the said statute makes much to the case, unless we say that the said statute receives an extensive interpretation to the singular successor: because the statute is equitable, and the office of the judge, which arises from the statute itself, is based on equity. And as written in rem it should be extended to the buyer. ar. ff. de eden. l. quędam §. is autem. and ff. de no. ope. nun. l. fi. and ff. de aq. plu. arc. l. post venditionem. and since this judgment is based on the office of the judge, discussion is not necessary, because hypothecary is not intended here by way of acting, but by way of proof to show the priority of rights. But certainly he does not have better rights, unless discussion is made. and therefore whatever is considered, discussion seems necessary: unless in one of the three cases, which he placed above. and this seems to me truer. But it should be known that Bart. holds that when goods are confiscated, the guarantor of the confiscated can be sued without discussion: therefore the same in pledges. this he holds. ff. si cer. pet. l. fin. and ff. de verb. obli. li. 10. But the contrary is held by Host. and Ioan. Andr. extra de pigno. c. ex literis. which I believe is truer. Moreover, the determination of this question depends on what has been said, namely, that if the fisc, which is a harsh adversary, could not easily be sued, or it were notorious that the goods which the fisc holds are not suitable for payment: that then discussion of the fisc is not necessary, otherwise yes, as I said, since it is in the place of the heir, and confiscation is evident. and these are true, if the debt is a true debt. But if it is usurious, and of double the true principal, and the principal is paid, then the hypothecary action is removed, because the debt is extinguished, as ff. de solut. l. Titia. which proof if it is easy, and can be proved plainly, can also be done before the secular judge,
† Although regularly the crime of usury is an ecclesiastical crime, as noted by the Moderators in the Digest, title *Solutis Matrimonii*, law *Titia*.

From all of which it is thus concluded: either it is established that the instrument is for double the amount, and because the lot has been resolved, the hypothecary action ceases; for the plaintiff received the things unpaid, which amounted to the true quantity of the debt, as stated in C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. libera quidem Theodora, and in D. de pignoris actione, l. eleganter, in principio. Or it is not established that it is for double the amount, and then it is presumed to be a chirograph subscribed by three witnesses, as if it were a public instrument, as stated in C. qui potestatem in pignus habent, l. scripturas. And this holds if the adversary confesses the subscriptions to be true. For such a confession has the effect of liquidating the chirograph. And this is according to the common law.

But it remains to be seen what is the law regarding the municipal law, which provides that a public instrument prevails over a chirograph, namely, whether this statute is to be understood according to the distinction of the aforementioned law concerning writings, or indiscriminately. And that they are distinguished by the common law is proved by the common laws: C. de noxa, l. si serui vestri; and Extra de consuetudine, c. cum dilectus. But I say the contrary, that this statute can have a civil and natural reason indiscriminately. Therefore, it must be understood indiscriminately, as in ff. de publiciana, l. de pretio. The contrary authorities do not stand in the way, because in those cases a simple understanding would be contrary to reason. However, as I said, if such a chirograph is approved by the confession of the adversary, such a confession is equal to, indeed greater than, any public instrument and any depositions of witnesses, as noted in ff. de iureiurando, l. sed et si possessori, §. pe., since it has the force of a sentence, as in l. 1, C. de confessis. But if the adversary does not confess to the writing, then one must adhere to the statute indiscriminately, as I said, because the statute must have the force of a statute. If it were restricted by the common law, it would not have the force of a statute, but would be mere common law in its content and effect, as noted in Extra de constitutionibus, in c. 1, lib. 6, and it would accomplish nothing, which is absurd, as in l. si quando, de inofficioso testamento; l. si quando, ff. de legatis 1; and l. 1, ff. ad municipalia, and similar cases. Consider that the words of the statute say that on account of writings made by one’s own hand, etc. But when it is subscribed by the own hand of three witnesses, strengthened by the aid of another, it is not simply one’s own hand. Argument: C. qui testamento facere possunt, l. hac consultissima, §. fi.; and C. de testamento, l. iube; ff. de legatis 3, l. hoc legatum; ff. si certum petatur, l. certi conditio, §. quoniam; ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 1, §. item quaeritur. And a private writing noted by three witnesses has acquired this right, that a publicly made writing establishes the right, and therefore the said Lord Nicolaus has truth and justice regarding the substance of the debt and the mortgage, namely, up to that sum for which it does not appear that satisfaction has been made. And no other doubt remains except concerning the order, that is, concerning the discussion [of assets]. However, since the discussion was made during the pendency of the lawsuit, and it does not appear that there is anything else in the goods not distributed except a certain house, which it is not expedient for the creditor to have, because it was inhabited by the stipendiaries of the lord for the said agent, it must be pronounced against the possessors, except, however, if the house can be sold for present money and there remains a surplus from the price. By how much it remains, he cannot act, because insofar as it can be collected from the things of the principal debtor, one does not proceed to alien possessors by the mortgage action, nor should any part consider this onerous to itself, since by this both parties are consulted, and justice and truth are also satisfied, as in ff. de solutionibus, l. quod Stichus. Nor does that which was touched upon above concerning usage obstruct the said Lord Nicolaus, because a change of conduct over a long time excludes the presumption of that rule, semel malus. Likewise, a subsequent good reputation removes a preceding bad reputation, as in c. 1, ne de statu defunctorum; l. si mater.

† Moreover, although with regard to proving someone to be a usurer in general, the constitution of the Patriarch concerning singular witnesses and reputation may suffice, it is otherwise when proving someone to be a usurer in particular, i.e., in a specific contract, because such a statute is expressly contrary to the law, which provides that the voice of one is the voice of none. Hence, such a statute is odious and contrary to the right of the party. And if a definitive judgment of a man were unjust, the same seems to be said of the judgment of a statute: as in D. de decretis ab ordinariis faciendis, l. ambitiosa. Although in many places such statutes are observed rather by usurpation than by right, unless the usurer were manifest; but then the witnesses would not properly be called singular, because they concur to prove the same thing. Cf. D. de accusationibus, l. ea quidem; and 2 q. 1, c. de manifesto, with similar authorities. And it supports what is noted in c. ultima, de appellationibus, lib. 6, in the Novellae. Therefore, the said possessors must either remove the claim by offering, as has been declared above, as in D. qui potior in pignore habeatur, l. mulier; and D. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur, l. Paulus, § qui pignoris, where those rights have passed to them; or else relinquish possession to the said lord Niccolò, the prior creditor and one with the earlier time, as in D. de pignore, l. si fundus, where in the vindication they have ten florins. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute speaking of a true felony, or felon, applies to one condemned for a felony by contumacy, given a statute providing that an inquisitor, if summoned and failing to appear, shall be deemed to have confessed, etc., and the opinion is that it does apply; which is noteworthy, because it is a matter of daily occurrence, and perhaps many would say the contrary.
2. Who is said to be truly condemned of a felony.
3. In criminal cases, whether a procurator or defender is admitted.
4. An example of a condemnation made for a certain felony against someone, if taken from the public archive, proves and makes faith.
body: The statute of the city of Alexandria provides that those who are banned or condemned for a felony, which is truly a felony in their cases, shall not be heard. It also provides that every injury, damage, wounding, homicide, whether given, said, or done by words or deed against the person or property of anyone banned for a felony, which is truly a felony, shall remain forever unpunished, so that in no way shall any proceeding be taken against such an offender in any manner, whether in a civil or criminal case, provided that the ban or condemnation appears, with proof of the ban given by the principal himself or by his procurator. Another statute provides that if someone summoned does not appear within a certain term, he shall be deemed confessed and punished accordingly, as if he had committed that felony, so that mere contumacy makes him convicted or confessed. Now it is proposed that a certain Antonio, together with two associates, made an assault against a certain Peter and wounded him with several blows, concerning which proceedings are being taken in court against the said offenders. Against this proceeding, their procurator raises the objection of the ban and produces evidence, namely that a copy made by a public notary was exemplified from the public archive.

It is asked whether the said exception, and whether the said document proves, and whether a procurator is admitted, considering a certain fourth statute, which provides that in a criminal case a procurator or defender is not admitted before the contestation of the lawsuit by the principal. Now I come to the responses in order.

† And it seems that this outlawed person is not said to be outlawed for a true felony. For the authorities commonly say that one is condemned for a true felony when he was present and made his defenses, and yet was condemned; but not when he was contumacious and condemned in contumacy; because then he is said to be condemned for a fictitious or presumed felony, by a presumption of law and by right, as in D. 48.3 (De his qui non infamantur), l. quoniam. But the contrary is true, because if someone were placed under outlawry on account of contumacy, and if he were not present in court, it would follow that no outlawed person could be harmed with impunity; which is contrary to the text of the statute. Therefore, a true felony is understood to be one that is verified even by tacit confession, as in C. 5.18 (De interdicto matrimonio), l. si tutor. And that this person is condemned for a true felony appears from the fact that the guilt is punished by such condemnation and purged by satisfaction; for if it were a penalty for contumacy, the principal offense would still remain to be punished, as in D. 4.8 (De arbitris), l. si quis rem, which is false. Consider therefore that here flight or contumacy is treated as a crime, because otherwise it would not be a true felony, but as proof of the crime, from which proof the true felony becomes clear, as elegantly noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. 9.13 (De raptu virginis). For the presumptions of the law are the clearest proofs, as in D. 22.5 (De legibus), l. licet Imperator; see also C. 5.70 (De periculo tutelae), l. si tutor. Regarding the second point, whether a procurator ought to be admitted or not, there is no question, but it is a case covered by the statute. And therefore there is no room for doubt, as in C. 4.2 (De furtis), l. ancillae.

† Nor does another statute, which excludes the attorney before the joinder of issue, apply here, because it is true that if the case is to be joined, the principal must appear. But here the case cannot be joined, because in no way can proceedings be taken. And Jacobus de Arena disputed this question and held that if proceedings were taken, the process would be null by operation of law; so that we would always be before the joinder of issue, and consequently the attorney would never be admitted, which is ridiculous to say. To the same effect is what we find in Jacobus Butrigarius in the question on the Ravagese, which he also places in l. 1, C. quomodo et quando iudices. This is also supported by the fact that the statute concerning banished persons is a special statute and cannot coexist with another general statute, and therefore it derogates from the general one, as in ff. de poenis, l. sanctio legum, and in c. generali, with its subject matter.

† On another point concerning proof, I say that one must adhere to the example taken from the public archive, as stated in the Code, *De fide instrumentorum*, in the authenticum *Ad haec*. And if the judge should doubt the original, he should look to what is said in the Extravagantes, *De accusationibus*, chapter *Qualiter et quando*; and in the Digest, *De finitis regundis*, law *Si irruptione*, section *Ad officium*; and in the Digest, *De edendo*, law 1, after the principium. From these authorities it is clearly concluded that proceedings may be taken against those denounced, inquired into, or accused, notwithstanding any municipal public law containing a hatred that is rational in a certain respect (secundum quid), not simply and absolutely, as in the Digest, *De publicis*, law *Licitatio*, section *Quod illicite*; and in the Code, *De Iudaeis*, law *Nullus*; and in the Digest, *De calumniatoribus*, law 1, section *Quod autem*. For these individuals, thus banned and considered as deserters, are regarded as public enemies, against whom war is rightly declared, as in the Digest, *Ad legem Corneli de sicariis*, law 3, section *Transfugas*; and in the Code, *Quando liceat se sine iudice vindicare*, law *Opprimendorum*. And thus I, Baldus, hold.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that an official or rector of any territory or place may not, during his term of office, receive anything either personally or through an interposed person, whether a royal or princely counselor is included under the term "official" or "rector," and whether an admiral of ships or galleys, or otherwise a master of a ship, is included. And number 3.
2. Whether ambassadors who have received gifts or presents from the emperor are bound to restore them to the sender.
3. Add consilium 378 in part 5.
body: The words of the statutes of the undersigned, set forth below under the heading, having been premised.

† That rectors or officials may not receive gifts or presents, the tenor of which is as follows. No official or rector of any territory or place may, during the term of his office, accept anything for himself or through an interposed person. The fact of such content and tenor is presupposed, namely: In the name of the Lord, Amen. The case of the present question, etc.

I premise, for the sake of clarity, that an ancient question arose concerning the ambassadors of Milan, who received gifts or presents from the Emperor of Constantinople, namely whether they were bound to restore them to the common good of Milan. Regarding this question, see the gloss in ff. 22.1.1, *Si vero*, § *Item quicquid*; and in l. *Qui proprio*, § *Procura*, *Ut inter caetera*, ff. 3.38, *De procuratoribus*; and there, Guillaume de Cuy; and by the gloss in l. *Si plures*, § *In arrogato*, ff. 28.6, *De vulgari et pupillari substitutione*; and by the notes of Cynus in C. 4.18, *De furtis*, l. *Manifestissimi*; and in it, the doctors commonly said thus: either the gift was made in consideration of the community, and then it is sought for the community; or in consideration of the ambassadors themselves, and then it is sought for them, as here; or there is doubt, and then either the Emperor knew them personally, and then it seems given in their consideration, as ff. 49.16, *De castrensi peculio*, l. *Si forte*, and l. *Miles*, and l. *Dotem filio*, § *Finis*, and l. *Heredi*, in the beginning; or he did not otherwise know them, and then it matters whether he promised by proper names or by appellative terms, as ff. 40.12, *De stipulationibus servorum*, l. *Si servus communis*, § 1; and ff. 15.1, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *Cum ita datur*; and ff. 28.5, *De iure deliberandi*, l. *Cum aliquis*. Others say: either the gifts are fitting for them, or not, and therefore according to the quality, etc., as above, ff. 24.1, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, l. *Utrum*; and ff. 47.18, *Communi dividundo*, l. *In rebus*, § *Possunt*. But Bartolus says that in no way are the ambassadors bound to restore the gifts, unless it was expressly given to them that they should be rendered to the community. And by this is the case, if it is well considered, ff. 17.2, *Pro socio*, l. *Socius*, *Qui in eo*, at the end. The same is held by Petrus and Jacobus de Radulphis, saying that although the gifts were granted to them in consideration of the community, nevertheless they are granted to them so that they may have them for themselves. To this effect, ff. 9.2, *De bonis damnatorum*, l. *Divus*, at the end. Also, because it is customary to do so, and this is especially to be considered, as l. *Iuris gentium*, § *Pactorum*, D. 2.14. Also, a gift is given to one in honor of another, as infra, D. 35.2, *De legatis secundis*, l. *Cum filius*, § *Pater*. Furthermore, that no regard was had here to the community of Genoa appears, because the king was moved by the singularity of the person: for he did not give to the principal ambassador, nor to other counselors, but to Lord Damian alone; and from singular affection the intent is to be understood, as ff. 35.2, *De legatis secundis*, l. *Si quis servum*, § *Si inter duos*; and argument from C. 6.24, *De institutionibus et substitutionibus*, l. *Reprehendenda*. And certainly, according to the common law, there is no doubt that the royal donation was valid, because in his kingdom it had the force of law, as C. 5.13, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, l. *Ultima*; and ff. 47.12, *De publiciano*, l. *Cessat*; and much more so in the case of remuneration, as ff. 39.5, *De donationibus*, l. *Aquilius regulus*, and l. *Si pater*. And certainly, that which is given to a well-deserving person is not considered given in consideration of office, but as to a stranger, as noted in C. 6.25, *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Autem unde si parens*; and C. 8.53, *De collationibus*, l. *Si donatione*. And I do not think that a question should not be made of this, having regard to the common law, nor even having regard to natural equity: because the good are to be rewarded, as C. 11.30, *De statuis et imaginibus*, l. *Et virtutum*, and l. 1 post principem; ff. 1.1, *De iustitia et iure*; and especially by kings and nobles, as ff. 39.5, *De donationibus*, l. *Aquilius*. And in this I say nothing else, except that I hold thus.

But now it is necessary to descend to the statutes of the commune of Genoa, and the words state that no official, or ruler of any land or place, may receive anything during his term of office, etc. It is alleged against Lord Damian that he was an official in the island of Cyprus. But this allegation does not appear true, because being a counselor without any authority, and without any weight of his own endowment, is not to hold office: because he presides over no administration, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. quidam decedens, and l. Titium et Mevium in principio; and D. de mutatione et huiusmodi, l. honor in principio. It supports what is noted in D. de inofficioso testamento, l. ob haec verba. Moreover, this statute proceeds further, stating that what has been received shall be restored. These words necessarily signify that it must be returned to the giver, or his heir: because that which is prohibited from being received must be restored to the payer, as long as he himself, or his successor, exists, and not to another, as is noted in C. statutum, § insuper ut gratis, de rescriptis, lib. 6; and as noted in C. quamquam, de usuris, in the same book, by Johannes Andreae and by Johannes de Monarchia. And therefore, by this statute, nothing ought to be applied to the commune of Genoa. But another statute follows, which says that no power, or consul, or ruler, who has been in any Empire, kingdom, city, or place of any dominion, may receive any reward or grace. And it adds that what has been received shall be converted to public utility. And this statute is more doubtful, and seems expressly to determine against Lord Damian, because since Lord Damian was admiral of two galleys, there is no doubt that he served as a soldier in those galleys, and as a master of soldiers he had jurisdiction over those whom he commanded, as in D. de bonis possidendis ex testamento militis, l. 1; and C. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. magisteria. Furthermore, considering the nature of the office, he also had the power of the sword over his enemies, at least de facto, by the commission made to him, as noted by Cynus in l. 4, D. de officiis praesidis. To the contrary, it seems that the words say: any power, or consul, or ruler: these words must be understood according to common usage of speech, as noted in D. de legibus, l. librorum, § quod tamen Cassius. But Lord Damian held neither of these offices: because he was simply a master of a ship, and a private person. Nor does it appear that any jurisdiction was entrusted to him. Moreover, mere imperium could not be delegated to him, as in D. de officio eius, cui mandata est iurisdictio, l. 1 in principio; and D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. Imperium. Certainly, nor according to what is proposed, does it appear that any jurisdictional commission was made to him. And therefore it is presumed that he did not have it, although a certain bare ministry was committed to him, as in C. de mandato principis, l. 1; and C. de iure fisci, l. prohibitum; C. de diversis officiis, l. probatorias, lib. 10; D. 106, c. nobilissimus. And therefore, since he was a mere private person, he is not called a power, as noted in l. ultima, C. de praescriptione longi temporis; nor a consul, because consuls must at least have voluntary jurisdiction, as in D. de officiis consulum, l. 1, and there fully by Cynus. Furthermore, he is not called a ruler: because a ruler is properly said to be so from jurisdiction, or with some jurisdictional power, as in C. de officio rectoris provinciae, throughout, with many similar cases. And therefore the said statute does not seem to speak, nor ought it to be understood, in the case of Lord Damian. There is another reason: because, granted that he had an office with jurisdiction, nevertheless he did not receive [the money] on that pretext. And thus this question is determined by the argument of D. de adoptionibus, l. si pater, § qui duos; and l. si consul; and D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. tutor petitus, § quae tutoribus, where the case of this question appears. It also supports Lord Damian, because things that are different in name are not the same, as in C. de feriis, l. a nullo; and C. de codicillis, l. si idem. But it is certain that an admiral of a galley in vulgar usage is not called a ruler: but has a name appropriate to himself, and by itself, whence he is not contained by a general term. Argument: D. de legibus, l. haeres meus, § duae statuae; and D. de alimentis et cibariis, l. alimenta, § Basilicae; and l. Stichus nutricis; and in C. generi, with its material. It also supports the foregoing: because different qualities have different reasons, as in D. de annuis legatis, l. quo Marco homini doctus; and l. 2, D. de stipulationibus servorum. To this also well applies what is fully noted by Johannes Andreae in C. cum olim, de re iudicata, by Innocentius; and D. de his qui veluti indigentes, l. tutorem; and D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papius, § sed nec impuberes; and what is noted by Cynus in C. qui testamento facere possunt, l. senium; and in C. si gratiose, de rescriptis, lib. 6; and Extra de praebendis, nisi esset. And although many subtle arguments have been alleged to the contrary against the said Lord Damian, nevertheless I believe that justice favors him: especially because, as I said above, the donation of the king has the force of law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, it is permitted, or not permitted, to build out of emulation, concerning which it was said above in counsel 188.
2. When water, or a river, is said to be part of the territory.
3. There are two kinds of peace.
4. When peace is said to be broken.
5. If two parties made peace, and one offended the other, and it does not appear who was first, whether one may accuse the other.
6. When peace is said to be broken. And no. 13.
7. Those things which are extinguished specifically are not included in a general statement.
8. Peace, and statutes concerning peace, are of strict law.
9. Whether a general statement admits of restitution.
10. When it is permitted to build, or to do something, in a public or private river, and no. 14.
11. These words “at the will of” are not reduced to the discretion of a good man.
12. The word “however” restricts all preceding matters.
13. He who kills the brother of him with whom I made peace is said to break the peace.
body: To praise and commend what you have said is not expedient, because they show themselves. Nevertheless, the associates with whom you conferred are surprised, because you say that on the points which you touch upon, nothing was seen nor alleged by your associates. For, as you know, since it is the truth, that two matters were chewed over between us and them, namely, whether it was lawful under our magnificent law to have the building in question constructed. Secondly, whether it was lawful or not, whether the lord is understood to act against the peace. And on both points you brought forward all the laws and allegations which are made for and against: and we repeat them now, for they act against our lord. L. Opus, D. de operibus publicis. And the twofold interdict of the praetor, either that nothing be done in a navigable river, as L. Quominus; and that nothing be done in a public river, even if it is not navigable, as D. Ne quid in flumine publico, per totum. The responses, however, are these. First, that our said lord has regalia granted by the Emperor, or at least entrusted to him; therefore he has the power to divert the river; otherwise an absurdity would follow, namely, that in his own territory he could not divert any public water, which is as much against the liberty of power as against the custom of his dominion and of other lords. For we see that regarding public waters which are in their territory, and even regarding navigable rivers, they do whatever they wish, and now they send [waters] to one castle, and now to another, upon which they also make the strongest and impregnable fortifications and castles on the rivers themselves, which is by custom and by common law: and it is implied in contracts, as if it were expressed in the contracts themselves, as D. De edilit. edict. L. Quod si nolit, §. Quia assidua, where the text thus says: "But those things which are of custom and usage in good faith actions ought to be included." The same is said by the text D. De aqua pluv. arc. L. Si prius, §. Recte placuit, there where it says: "But those things which are almost in custom may be done." This also the Lord of Mantua confesses by his very act: because he made a work upon a public and navigable river. Moreover, these buildings which are said to be made out of emulation are made, but then only because the work itself is the beginning and cause of emulation. But when it comes to repelling the emulation of adversaries, it is not said to be made out of emulation; rather, this is lawful by natural and civil law, as D. Quod quisque iuris in alterius statu, in rubro et nigro. And it is expressed in L. Si, eod. tit. This also we see in the construction of castles.

† For the King of France builds fortresses on the borders of his territory in emulation of the King of England, and vice versa; and indeed all lords of the world do the same. For since jurisdictions and territories are distinct, each one may fortify himself and encamp within his own territory, and this is not contrary to the law. For the law *opus* speaks according to ancient times, when the jurisdiction of the Roman people and of the Emperor was united in the same person; but here, as I have said, territories and jurisdictions are divided, so that one lord has no power over another. And it is read and noted in the Digest, *de manumissionibus*, in the law *apud eum*; and in the Digest, *de acquisitione possessionis*, in law 1, § *veteres*; and in the Digest, *de arbitris*, in the law *nam magistratus*; and noted in the law *si*, Codex, *de praescriptione longi temporis*; and it is clear in the Peace of Constance. Moreover, that which is done to prevent harm is done because it is within the power of my adversary, to whom one ought not to concede that which he has the power to do against me, as noted in the Digest, *de iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, in the law *si idem cum eodem*, § *si mutuae*. Nor is anyone bound to open a way so that a reconciled friend may be able to offend him, as in the Extravagant, *ut lite non contestata*, chapter *accedens*. And although you ought not to dispute on this point in law, nor bind yourselves to it, because it is not certain, nevertheless in the way of disputation you could sufficiently defend that our lord may build the said structure; yet I do not advise that he do so, lest many innocent people perish on account of the house, as in the Codex, *de poenis*, law *sancimus*; and in the Digest, *de statu hominum*, law *Imperator*. For the lord himself is not the beginning of the motion, but is the mover being moved, or moved by those emulating him: as in the Codex, *de servis fugitivis*, law *mancipium*, § *si*; and in the Codex, *de furtis*, law *si quis servum*. But whatever may be said about power, whether he can or cannot, let us suppose, without prejudice to the truth, that he could not. Law *ut sicuti*, § *Aristo*, Digest, *si servitus vendi*. Nevertheless, it must be said without doubt that our lord does not act against the peace; for the aforementioned building is not in the act of harming, although it is in the potentiality of harm. Hence, just as a posthumous child before birth does not break a will, although it is in the potentiality of harm, so damage that is in the potentiality of harm, before it actually harms, does not break the peace. For potentiality, before it is reduced to act, is assimilated to a condition, hence in the meantime no obligation arises. As in the Digest, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law 1, at the end; Digest, *de verbis obligatorum*, law *interdum*; Digest, *de statu hominum*, law *Aretusa*. Moreover, granted that the damage were in actual fact, nevertheless nothing would have been done against the peace, for peace is nothing other than the articles of peace, as in the Digest, *de pactis*, law 1, § 1. But the articles of peace do not state this, nor was this considered; hence, whether we consider the substance of the obligation, which arises from consent, those things are not included about which there was no consideration, as in the Digest, *de transactionibus*, law *cum Aquiliana*; and in the Digest, *de contrahenda emptione*, law *lege* and law *Rutilia Polla*; and in chapter 1, *de eo qui interfecit fratrem domini sui*, column 10. Or whether we consider the form of the obligation, it is contained in no article. Therefore it is not included, as in the Digest, *de verbis obligatorum*, law *quicquid astringendae*; Digest, *de fideiussoribus*, law *fideiussores magistratuum*, § *pro Aurelio*. But against this it is objected, as you write, because in the first article of the peace it is thus contained: "We establish, ordain, and command that there be and ought to be a good, true, and sincere peace between the said parties, and each of them, to last perpetually," for these words imply that peace is to be observed according to the judgment of a good man, i.e., good concord, which cannot exist without justice, as in the Extravagant, *de summa Trinitate*, chapter *Rex pacificus*. And it is said that an offense is anything done from which an action for injury may be brought, i.e., anything that can be drawn to maleficence, as in the Extravagant, *de verborum significatione*, chapter *Ex parte in Christo*. But this disturbance, which arises on account of navigation, which is partly interrupted, seems to pertain to the action for injuries, as in the Digest, *de iniuriis*, law *iniuriarum*, § *si*. Therefore such a building cannot be made. But to this you have given a response, and you can respond even more clearly, because these general words do not include cases unless they are similar to those expressly mentioned, about which the peace was made, per law *fin.*, § *cui dulcia*, Digest, *de vino legato*. And because in the said peace the genus precedes and the species follows, and therefore the genus is restricted. Moreover, it is contained in the articles of peace that in their territories, where they could build, they may do so according to their free will.

† It is certain, however, that this territory belongs to the Lord Count both on land and in water, as established in the Digest, to the law *Rhodii* on jettison, in the law *Deprecatio*, and as noted in the gloss to the chapter *Ubi periculum* on elections, Book 6. And although the water is on the surface, the territory is in the soil. Therefore, since the said chapter expressly permits that, even if the said pact were not valid under the common law, it is nevertheless valid as far as excluding this case of breach of the peace, as is clearly proven if it is carefully deduced, in the Digest, on the legacy of a peculium, in the law *Cum dominus*, § *Finis*. Moreover, because whatever may be the case regarding public law, between the parties to the peace this private agreement must be observed in fact, as in the Digest, on the signification of words, in the law *Si cum fundum*. Those words, therefore, "given or inflicted," restrict the most general genus of the predicate to things similar to the past damages and injuries, namely to cavalry raids, arson, and the like, which is the common doctrine of the jurists, in the Digest, on obligations from words, in the law *Quidam cum filium*, and in the law *Venditor*, in the Digest, on the action concerning a predial servitude, and by argument from the Digest, on conditions and demonstrations, in the law *Meuius*, and in the Digest, on the action for restitution, in the law *Mulier*, § *Si quis haereditarium*. But since you touch upon something concerning the peace and its nature, stating that it was not deliberated upon between them.

It must be known that peace is twofold: one kind is perfected in the present, as concerning past injuries; the other is successive, by which form is given to the future time. There is no question regarding the first, because it gives form to past injuries and does not pertain to the future, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. cum stipulamur and l. si a colono, and D. de leg. 2, l. si ita scripsisset. Successive peace, however, requires the perseverance of tranquility, as in D. de arbitris l. inter Castellanum, as in C. de publicis l. Titiae, or C. de consulis l. 1, and D. lib. 12, C. de caducis tollendis l. unica, near the beginning, so that recourse to arms is not again had for recurring injuries, as in D. de usufructu l. aequissimum, and D. si servi ven. l. harum. And peace is usually made concerning those matters concerning which a truce and forbearance are usually made in the first manner, as noted in D. de captivis l. hostes and l. postliminii, and it is provided in Extravagantes de treuga et pace c. 1, and Extravagantes de iudiciis c. novit.

† Who, and when, is said to infringe this peace? The words of Bartolus state in l. facta, § causa, ff. de poenis. I ask: since you and I were enemies, we made peace; finally, I struck you. It is asked whether the peace is considered broken. I answer that this must be considered from the cause: for just as we say in a certain transaction by which we withdraw from litigation, as in l. fratris, C. de transac., and in res iudicata, which is the end of lawsuits, as in l. 1, de re iud., a person is considered to act against the judgment and the transaction when he acts from a cause that was decided and determined, as in l. cum quaeritur, de re iud., l. si de certa, de transa. But if he were to act from a new cause, he would not be said to act against the transaction or the judgment, as stated in the aforementioned laws. So, in the case at hand, if I struck you from an antecedent cause, by which I had been your enemy, concerning which enmity peace had been made, then I break the peace. But if I were to strike you from a cause supervening anew: because anew between you and me a quarrel supervened from jest, or drunkenness, then I do not break the peace. For this it is helpful that it is said here that in maleficia the cause must be considered. The same applies to this in ff. de condi. sine causa, l. si fullo.

And it is noted by Johannes Andreae in the final chapter of the title *De immunitatibus ecclesiarum*: two parties made peace together, afterwards they offended each other, and it does not appear who did so first and who second. The question is asked whether one can accuse the other of breaking the peace. And the text seems to indicate that not, as in the Digest, *De legibus*, title 2, law *Cum pater*, section *Libertis*, because they broke the peace simultaneously. But if one did so first and the other second, then the second can accuse the first of breaking the peace, but not the first the second, as in the aforementioned section *Libertis*, and there by Bartolus. In support of this is what is noted in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Qui fidem*; and law 1, section *Cum arietes*, in the Digest, *Si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicatur*; and in the Code, *De appellationibus*, law 1.

Furthermore, it is certain that our lord is not obliged to maintain navigation outside his territory for the said Marquis, especially by virtue of any peace treaty. Nor is he bound to ensure that the said Marquis obtains profit from navigation at Mantua, as in the Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *Proculus*; and in the Digest, *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law 1, section *Idem aiunt aquam*. Hence the said Marquis cannot bring any claim against our lord, because in stipulations, not only when words are lacking, but even when they are obscure, interpretation is made against the party who offered them, as in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Veteribus*; and in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *Semper in stipulationibus*. Hence you can clearly and most openly defend our lord.

Moreover, he is worthy of praise who has the good intention of providing security not to alter the bed of the said river, in the case where the other party is content within its own boundaries, as in the Code, *De novo operis nuntiando*, final law; and in the Extravagantes, *De novo operis nuntiando*, final chapter. This is reasonable, as in the Code, *De finium regundorum*, law *Si constiterit*; and in the Code, *De iudicibus*, law *Nullus*; and in the Digest, *Quod metus causa*, law *Extat*. For thereby our lord shows that he does not wish to do anything that does not benefit himself and harms another, as in the Digest, *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law 2, section *Item Varus*. However, he does not intend to procure others’ advantages, nor to endure traps laid against himself, nor to place others’ conveniences before his own, as in the Digest, *Ad Trebellianum*, law *Postulante Sticho*, section *Si*; and in the Code, *De testamento*, law *Si quando*, where it says that he would find difficulties in others’ advantages. It must be known that

That public peace, nor even private peace, is not said to be broken by judicial controversies, as appears from the Digest, On the Interpretation of Words, in the law *Venditores*. Nor is it broken by any slight occasion, nor even by grave suspicion, unless it has been reduced to an act, as appears in Chapter 1, section *Si quis enim*, of the title *In which cases a fief is lost*; and in the Digest, On Restitution to the Original State, in the law *Scio*; and in the title *Here the Law Ends*, section 1, column 10. For the fact that provision has been made concerning injuries does not mean that the actions and rights of the parties are extinguished, as appears in the Extravagant Decretals, On Injuries, in the chapter *In nostra*.

Furthermore, it must be known that he who is named in a contract is not bound by it, except insofar as he is named, as in the aforementioned section *Pro Aurelio*; and in the Digest, On the Interpretation of Words, in the law *Si ita stipulatus*, section *Grisogonus*; and in law 3; and fully noted in the Digest, On That Which Is Certain, in the law *Centum Capuae*. But the said Marquis of Ferrara was named in this peace with a reservation of the rights of both parties, both of our Illustrious Lord and of the said Magnificent Ferrara. Therefore, as far as their rights are concerned, which pertain to the right of forum, nothing on either side is included in the peace, as appears in the Digest, If One Provides Security, in law 2, after the principal. But the rights concerning rivers pertain to the judicial right of forum, as appears in the Institutes, On Interdicts, section *Si*. Therefore, no transaction was made concerning them, nor was anything agreed upon.

† Because those things which are excepted by a special provision are not included in a general statement, as is fully noted by Dyonisius in the chapter *Generale*, and it is clear from the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, in the law *Haeres meus*, section *Duae statuae*; and from the Digest, *De legatis secundo*, in the law *Legatorum*, section *Qui plures*; and from the Digest, *De alimentis et cibariis legatis*, in the law *Alimenta*, section *Basilicae*; and in the law *Stichus nutricis*; and from the Code, *Familiae erciscundae*, in the law *Quotiens*; and from the Extravagant, *De officio delegati*, in the chapter *Studuisti*. Moreover, just as a private person stands in relation to another private person, so does a magistrate stand in relation to another magistrate. But a private person is not bound to permit to another private person the flow of private water; on the contrary, he may intercept the water. Therefore, the same applies between public persons, such as the aforementioned two Magnificent Lords. But, as has been said, one ought not to dispute concerning the river, but concerning the peace, which is not broken with regard to the Lord of Mantua, because our Lord owes him nothing; nor is it broken with regard to the Marquis, because this is not found in the articles of the peace, which is of strict law, just like a contract of compromise, as in the law *In summa*, in the beginning, *De conditionibus indebiti*; and in the Digest, *De pace*, in the law *Conventionum*.

† And regarding peace, and the statute on peace, that they are of strict law. Also, from canon law, there is a text in the cited chapter *Iniuria*, in the title *De iniuriis*. Moreover, what is omitted is held to be omitted, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Ex ea parte*, section *In insulam*; and in the Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Fistulas*, section *Frumenta*; and in the Digest, *Solutis matrimonii*, law *Sic cum dotem*, in the principal part. And from these, you can respond to the first chapter *De pace firmanda*. Because there the legislator proceeds further to aggravate certain crimes even of individual persons against individual persons, which individual persons cannot break the peace: nevertheless, during the time of peace, their malefices are more serious, as is held in the title *De pace*, in the cited chapter *Federicus*, section *Si quis advocativa*. Otherwise, it is certain in itself. And it supports what is noted in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *Aliud*, section *Refertur*.

But also, that which is contained in the chapters of peace must not be omitted, namely that none of the said parties, nor any from the said parties, may give passage or provisions to any armed peoples who wish to enter Lombardy or Italy, and especially by bridges or waters, etc. And he who made a new bridge provided material for travel and passage, and therefore makes armed peoples stronger, more capable, and bolder than they were previously; and thus no one doubts that such an act is not comprehended in the benefit of peace: because he not only thinks, but acts and perfects the aptitude from the occasion given against those things which are of peace, as in the Digest, *Si ususfructus petatur*, law 1, section 1, and section *Utrum*; and expressly noted in the Code, *De re militari*, law *Si quis barbarius*, book 12. Who then will support him in peace, who breaks the bonds of peace? as in the Digest, *Locati conducti*, law *Quaero*, section *Inter locatorem*. And the law does not aid him who falls into the law, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, law *Auxilium*, section *In delictis*.

It is also to be known that he who does something justly is not said to offend; but he who suffers something justly is said to have been offended, as in the Digest, *De manumissione testamento*, law *Testamento caetero*; Code, *De adulteriis*, law *Gravis*; Code, *De his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt*, law *Sed servus*; Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Quid ergo*, section *Si haeres*; Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Qui servum*; Code, *De liberis et eo loco*, law 2; and Digest, *De conditionibus obligatorum*, law *Qui damni cum filium*. The allegations of my lord Baldus of Perugia, who always urges and desires true peace, and as far as I am concerned, cordially urges it for the public good.

It is to be known that lords sometimes wish to change the public riverbed from their territory into their own territory, and they can, and thus it is observed in law and in fact; sometimes from another’s into another’s, and they cannot; sometimes from their own into another’s, and they cannot; sometimes from another’s into their own, and they cannot, unless after the water has entered their territory, as these are proven in the Digest, *Si servitus vindicetur*, law *Sicuti*, section *Aristo*, with the *si*.

It is also to be considered that the territory of our lord, or our lord himself, ought not to owe the Marchioness of Ferrara a servitude of not building higher, or not building in the territory of our lord, just as neither does the converse, since those territories are free, as in the Code, *De servitutibus et aqua*, law *Altius*. Nor even by the way of personal obligation, which is different from servitudes, as in the Digest, *De servitutibus rusticorum praediorum*, law *Pecoris*; and Digest, *De servitutibus*, law *Ut pomum*; and Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Si*, section *Si*; and Digest, *De servitutibus legatis*, as is clear. In the Extravagant, *De praebendis*, chapter *Nisi esset*, it can be said that some bond contracted from here or there comes to impede the freedom of discretion from here or there in one’s own territory, because it is said that words limit the contract and restrict it to their form, as noted in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Emptor*, section *Lucius*. And in verbal obligations, words are desired, as fully noted by the doctors in the Digest, *Si certum petatur*, law *Cum quid*.

Finally, it is to be considered that our lord does not introduce, nor wishes to introduce, anything into the territory of the Marchioness, because the river, about which inquiry is made, enters the Po before it reaches the territory of the Marchioness; and especially since therefore the river Po does not change its quality. Since therefore nothing is changed from his territory, he complains in vain in law or of another’s injury, as in the Digest, *Si servitus vindicetur*, law *Loci corpus*, section *Competit*, where is a notable rule that he alone is said to be offended who obtains the right of action in his own name from such, nor is affection considered, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Si ita stipulatus*, section *Griseogonus*, at the end. It supports what is noted by Innocentius in the Extravagant, *De appellationibus*, chapter *Dilectus*.

That which is not to be omitted is that the interest of profit, which the Marchioness claims, ought not to be considered here, because it is interest outside the thing, i.e., from work, not from the thing, as in the Code, *De senatusconsulto, quod pro eo*, law *Unica*, section *Quae in aliis*; and Digest, *De actione empti*, law *Si sterilis*, section *Cum per venditorem*; and Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Si haeres*.
