Moreover, since the said Marchioness consented to that clause that each one may build in his own territory at the will of his liberty, it follows that he cannot complain of such building. For under this generality of words, which refers to free will, nothing comes to be restricted, because it matters much whether the word of will is placed between contracting parties, or whether by this speech power is given to some third party. In the first case, even if someone judges unjustly with respect to common law, nevertheless he does not judge unjustly with respect to the law of the convention, because to one who wills and consents, no injury nor fraud is done. And this is clear in the Digest, *De legatis secundo*, law *Cum quidam*; and Digest, *De legatis secundo*, law *Fideicomissa*, section *Quamquam*. In the second case, it well received the restriction of the discretion of a good man according to some, according to others not, as noted by Cynus in the Code, *De dote promissa*, in law *Si cum ea*.

Since therefore the award was homologated, those words were spoken between those parties: therefore they are understood not only of just, but also of mere and unjust will, by the said section *Quamquam*. And by the aforementioned, the response appears to law *Creditor*, section *Lucius*, in the Digest, *Mandati*. And it supports what is noted in the Code, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *In ementis*, and law *Si*, and in law 1 in the Digest, *De legatis secundo*.

It is also to be considered that the clause of peace, when an unforeseen case supervenes, for the existence of which it is necessary to provide for the public good of the subjects, does not exclude appropriate remedies, even if something were done contrary to the effect of peace, not principally, but consequentially. Argument from the Digest, *Quod vi aut clam*, law *Si alius*, section *Est et alia*. And what is noted in law *Si mulier* in the Digest, *Rerum amotarum*.

From all these arise such conclusions for the first, that our lord can build with respect to the Marchioness; and especially because of the said general words: because effusive speech is accustomed to prejudice generally, as in the Code, *De dote promissa*, law *Si*, section *Si*.

And it should be noted that a general term, which serves to expand the power granted by common law, admits of no restriction. And note this through Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus in l. 1, § item nuntiatio, D. de novi operis nuntiatione, and most fully through Bartolus in his repetition of l. 1, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis. Second conclusion: that our lord, not only in fact, but also in deed, and through the acts of the building in question, the question now being posed in dry land situated in water and in the course of a river, is not, nor can he be said to be, a breaker of the peace, considering what has been said above.

† Regarding this, there are four cases. For sometimes harm is done to the public by the act of a man from the public domain, and this cannot be done. D. de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. si autem. Sometimes harm is done to a private party from a private domain: and then it may be done, unless he who suffers the harm has some benefit assigned to him by law, or by agreement, or by prescription: as D. de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. si in meo. Or say in one word, that he prevails who has the stronger rights. As l. praeses, C. de servitute et aqua, according to Cynus. Sometimes harm is done to a private party from the public domain, i.e., from that which is in the public domain: and this cannot be done if a right has been acquired by the private party. Sometimes harm is done to the public from a private domain, for example by navigation: and this cannot be done: as l. quominus. And these statements are true according to the common law. But we are not under the common law, but under an agreement. And I say that, considering the agreement, it is not contrary to peace: as l. quamvis, D. de in ius vocando; l. 3, § si quis volentem, D. de libero homine exhibendo. And this [is so] for four reasons.

First, by reason of the words “at the will of the testator.” For, by the nature of language, these words are not referred to the discretion of a reasonable man: as in *l. fideicommissum*, § *quamquam*, *De legatis* 3; and in *D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, *l. quia poterat*; and in *C. de institutione haeredum*, *l. cum proponas*. Second, by the nature of the adversative term. For the word “nevertheless” is an adversative term, and therefore it also coheres with the first chapter of the peace, i.e., “I make peace,” *tamen*, etc., *D. ad Trebellianum*, *l. Lucius*, which had.

Thirdly, also from the nature of the restrictive term, for this word, “however,” restricts all that precedes. Likewise, those words “make peace” import, as below, i.e., “saving,” as I shall say below: as C. de inst. et substitu. l. pe. and l. item labeo. §. 1. ff. fa. hęr. There is also a fourth reason, namely, the change of condition and quality of things. For a new bridge, which gave occasion for injuring the lands of the lord, certainly gives the lord counsel to resist. As ff. de le. 2. l. cum pater. §. titia. Finally, these words, “however he may be able,” etc., do not admit of restriction. Likewise, it suffices that we are outside a penal case: as ff. de condit. et demon. l. in testamento. and l. et i. mulcta. in prin. and there by Bartolus. Likewise, what is not permitted per se is permitted per accidens, as ff. de verb. obl. l. qui sermo. For when the antecedent is not prohibited, neither is the consequent, as noted in l. iurisdictio. ff. de iuris. om. iudi. Likewise, as I said above, no account should be taken of profit which is not assigned by law, custom, or pact. For even if I remove the profit which is sought by another with the aid of my territory, I am not said to break the peace with him, when I remove it for a cause, being unable otherwise to defend myself from ambushes. ar. ff. quod vi, aut clam. l. si alius. §. est et alia. Likewise, a pact must have some effect. As in l. si quando. de le. 1. Likewise, as an agreement between private persons stands, so stands an agreement between lords, which, if reduced to the manner of private persons, pertains to the aforesaid, because the immediate cause is considered, not the remote one, as l. verum. de fur. and l. si mulier. rerum amotarum. And these things I say, retaining the allegations otherwise made. Likewise, he who does justly does not incur a penalty. As ff. de uerb. ob. quidam cum filium. Likewise, a penalty requires a completed act. As in c. perpetue. de elec. in nouella. unless it is added to a present act and future damage. l. labeo. de statu lib.

† Moreover, it must be known that sometimes a personal enmity precedes, and peace is made concerning it, and such peace is not broken except by a personal offense; because war and peace are relatively opposed, and what is affirmed of one is denied of the other. This is supported by what is noted by Bartolus in l. 4, de verb. oblig., §. catho. Sometimes an enmity precedes that is both personal and real, as in the war that exists between lords and communities, and then, whether an offense is committed against the person or against property, the peace is broken, as noted by Bartolus in ff. de publicanis, l. illicitatio, §. quod licite. This is true if the offense committed is similar to the previous one, for example, by waging war, or acting in a hostile manner, or by devastating the statute or honor of the other party, such as by capturing a castle or fortress, or by sending ruins through secret passages onto the territory of the other. However, if the offense is not of the same kind, i.e., is not similar to the previous one, then the peace is not said to be broken. For peace is a kind of transaction, and therefore it refers to lawsuits that are of the same kind, and not to others: as in C. de transactionibus, l. si certa. For the cause and the intent of the words must be considered as restricting indefinite and ambiguous words, as is read and noted in ff. communia praediorum, l. si in venditione, 14 ne, in fine.

† Moreover, it must be premised that something is in the river, by reason of which the river itself becomes more harmful to those passing publicly. Sometimes by rescript to another river, and this occurs in four ways, nor are there others navigable, and thus from public to public: as in D. de fluminibus, l. quominus, and l. si autem; de aqua pluviae arcendae, de private to private: as in C. de servitutibus et aqua, l. praeses, and de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. si in meo; from public to private, and from private to public. And because these do not pertain to our matter, I do not pursue them, nor does the illustrious Lord Count seek to know or be informed about this under the common law: on which point the doctors, if asked, would well speak the truth when questioned. But he only wishes to know this: whether by the said buildings, not only if the water is removed from its usual course, or even if it should happen to be removed through preceding fault, machination, or ambushes of the Lord of Mantua, the peace made with Janua is broken, since he says and protests that he intends to observe the peace, and not to divert the river except for his evident and necessary defense, for example if the Lord of Mantua through the new bridge, which he had made or permitted, allowed the enemies of the said Lord Count to pass. And certainly on this point, although perhaps in counsel of natural equity another thing might be advised to the Lord for many reasons that may occur according to the strict reason of law, the said Lord Count does not break the peace. And for clarity I premise that in this question two things are to be considered. First, the present state of the thing by presence is reducible to the former state. Also by desistance from the work. Hence the convention is not yet consummated, and consequently it has not yet come to a breach: as in D. quod quisque iuris in se possidet, l. 1, § haec verba, and C. si mancipium ita fuerit alienatum, l. ea quidem. And this appears manifestly: because from those things which have been done hitherto, no one is injured, and no one can act as one injured. Also, the course of future time does not pertain to the judge, unless where this is expressly provided by law: as in l. 1, in principio, D. de usu. Nor is it true that in civil cases that which is about to happen is held as done, as is noted in l. si quis non dicam rapere. And the reason is: because the adversary’s interest has not yet arisen. It supports what is noted in c. perpetuae, de electione, lib. 6, in the Novella. But since the Lord Count does not make a preparatory act except for the end, let us see whether, following the end, he breaks the peace. And this can be considered in three ways: in one way, that he breaks the peace with the Lord of Mantua. And it must be said that he does not, because with him no contract of peace was celebrated: and where there is no prior possession, there is no deprivation to be given: as in D. de verbis obligatis, l. decem, and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titia usufructu. Secondly, it must be considered whether, on account of the Lord of Mantua, who is offended, or would be offended, the peace is understood to be broken with the Lord Marquis. And I say that it is not, even if they were natural brothers.

† For thus it is settled in law, that if there were two brothers, and one were my enemy, and the other not, and I make peace with the enemy, and then I kill his brother, that on account of such an offense the peace is not broken. D. 45.1.127 § Grisogonus (De verbis obligatis). And there by Dy. and Bar. And it is expressed in c. 1, De eo qui interfecit fratrem domini sui, col. 10. And this is clear from an argument from the contrary: because if he, with whom I do not have peace, were to kill me, he would not be bound to the penalty for breaking the peace; for contracts ought to be compatible, as D. 18.1.1 § Emptor (De empto vendito); and l. ult. D. 46.4 (De acceptilationibus); and l. ult. C. 5.61 (De indebita uiduitate tollenda); and D. 50.17.107 (De regulis iuris); and C. 9.1.1 § Sed cum in secunda (De furtis). Thirdly, the Marquis can be considered principally for himself: because he says that his river, the Po, in his territory is made narrower or wider to the detriment of navigators, or of those circumnavigating the art of navigation, which is reckoned as damage to the Marquis himself: as C. 10.35.1 in fine (De caducis tollendis), where it is in the interest of the state to have wealthy subjects. It supports what Inn. notes in Extr. De appellat., c. Dilectus. For although this were true, which is denied in the case, yet this would be a small matter. Arg. D. 4.6.1 (De in integrum restitutione). Moreover, granted that there were a great interest, nevertheless the peace is not broken for the causes and reasons set forth above, namely on account of the emergence of a new case, on account of the provision granted for one’s own safety, on account of the words and intent of the contracting parties, on account of intolerable ambushes, and on account of remedies to be applied, where the matter does not admit of delay. And because the matter has come to a new case, for which other provision would have been made if it had been considered, since a dangerous calamity is imminent: all of which have been most perfectly declared in the foregoing, from these it appears what is the law in the disputation of the forum. But because these disputations could be dangerous for the state of all Italy: and because such laws, as Blessed Bernard says, are rather lawsuits than laws, I advise that all matter of suspicion be removed on both sides, and that peace be kept without ambushes, which may please Almighty God, so that Paradise, Italy, may not be dissolved on account of wars, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It treats of a certain confiscation of goods, and whether dotal property is subject to it.
2. To what a judge who makes the case his own is liable.
body: Having seen the sentence passed by Lord Mure, Vice-Captain, and his colleagues against Marcus the painter, in which it is contained that the said Marcus was proceeded against by way of inquisition, as well as upon the intimation of the Provisors of the Commune of Trieste, because whereas the said Marcus was residing in the city of Trieste, a certain foreign priest, Georgius, came into the said city and acquired from Meuio certain goods, the damages to which were recorded in the aforesaid inquisition; the said goods the said priest Georgius acquired from the said Meuio by right of succession. After this succession, the said priest came into the said city of Trieste and married his daughter, Lady Gilia, to the said Marcus the painter, then residing in Trieste. The said goods the said priest Georgius gave to the said Marcus as dowry and in the name of dowry. The said goods, thus held by the said Marcus as dowry and in the name of dowry from the said priest Georgius, the said Marcus held, possessed, worked, and enjoyed the fruits of for many and many years peacefully and quietly. And then, after the acquisition of the said goods given to him in the said name, the said Marcus departed from the city of Trieste and from the habitation of the said city together with the said Lady Gilia, and went outside the district of the said city; and immediately after the said departure he dwelt outside the district of the said city; and likewise the said priest Georgius departed from the habitation of the said city after the said acquisition, and continuously remained outside the said city and its district. And therefore the said Vice-Captain condemned the said Marcus in florins, and that he lose the said goods according to the form of the statutes of the Commune of Trieste. Which goods were afterwards sold by the Commune by virtue of the said sentence of the said Lord Vice-Captain, notwithstanding the protestation of the said priest Georgius, against whom Lord Mure acted, and a complaint was lodged, as appears in the records. It is asked, what is the law? And it must be said that the said Lord Mure and his court erred in four ways. First, because they formed the said inquisition invalidly by confiscating the said goods. Second, because they proceeded unskillfully, disregarding the protestation of the said priest. Third, because they pronounced judgment wrongly. Fourth, because they carried out an injurious execution. And for the evidence of the first and third errors, it must be premised,

† That on account of the husband’s delict the dowry cannot be confiscated: rather, it ought to be restored to the woman, both by civil law and by canon law, as in D. 23.3.10 (Si marito publico iudicio damnato). And not D. 9.2.1 (Quandoque in legibus). And Extravagantes, De pignoribus, c. Ex literis. And it supports this, L. 1, C. 9.48 (Fiscales creditores praeferri). L. 10, and C. 7.47.1 (Si quis post haec). And C. 5.13.1 (Donationes inter virum et uxorem). Hence, since in the inquisition mention is made that the things were dowry property, and the same is alleged in the sentence: it appears evidently that the inquisition was unjust as regards the conclusion of confiscating the goods, and therefore the said D. Muxe conducted his case improperly. I also say that the said D. Muxe proceeded wrongly: for if he had carefully weighed his inquisition, it would have been clear to him that if the goods were those of the said priest, they were presumed to remain his, unless alienation were proved, as in C. 4.19.1 (Sive possidetis). Hence, since alienation, i.e., the giving and delivery into dowry, was not proved by the attestation in the said inquisition by the said inquisitor, the protestation of the said priest is well-founded, as in D. 42.1.1 (A Diuo), § Si super rebus. I said fourthly that it was wrongly proceeded to execution: because the sentence did not deserve execution, as in D. 18.6.1 (Lectos). And D. 21.2.1 (Si pignora). And D. 50.17.2 (Quod quisque iuris in alterum statuit). And there noted. Therefore, the said Lord Muxe ought to be condemned on account of his incompetence, namely, that he either see to it that the possessions be restored to the dispossessed priest, and furthermore in other damages and expenses according to the form of the libel presented against him: because by so proceeding he wrongfully dispossessed the said priest. Or, if he cannot restore the possessions, let him be condemned for whatever is more in the interest of the said priest to possess than to claim from the occupants, i.e., in the estimation of the possession. For the said priest did not lose any dominion, but only possession, and therefore only the possession is estimated at the judge’s discretion, as in D. 4.2.1 (Si mulier), § Possessionem. And D. 43.17.1 (Si duo), § Fin. And furthermore, he is to be condemned in expenses and damages arising from the occasion of the litigation, as in C. 7.61.1 (Non ignoret). It supports this, D. 3.5.1 (Si iudex). And Inst. 3.13 (De obligationibus ex quasi delicto), in principio. And in 10, col. De pace iuramento firmata et servanda, § Iudices vero. But it must not be omitted that, since the aforementioned execution was injurious, the said judges to whom recourse is had, if their office extends to this, can revoke the said execution as void, as being wrongly done, as in C. 4.2.1 (Meminerint). And in L. 3, De administratione rerum ad civitatem pertinentium. And noted in L. Minor, in principio, D. 21.2. And Extravagantes, De purgatione vulgaris, c. Significantibus. And if they did this, it would greatly benefit the said Lord Muxe: because the said priest would recover his possession, as in L. 1, C. 7.45 (De re iudicata). However, the damages and expenses the said Lord Muxe cannot avoid in any case, as in C. 5.59.1 (Severiter). And to the aforementioned, what is noted by Cynus, C. 5.12.1 (Ne uxor pro marito), L. Ob maritorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the interpretation of a statute ordering that wine be sold at a certain measure, and prohibiting its sale anywhere other than in a tavern.
2. Where certain measures are appointed, it ought not to be sold by other measures, otherwise fraud is committed.
3. What falls under the appellation of a tavern.
body: Statute

† It is provided that sworn wine measurers shall be bound by oath to exercise their office without fraud, and to measure for any persons who request them, provided that such measurers must possess a *urna*, a half-*urna*, a *conzium*, and a half-*conzium*. Another statute provides that the great *datium* (tax) on wine sold in taverns must be publicly proclaimed, etc., and that any person selling wine in a tavern is bound to pay to the commune, or to the appointed tax collector, a certain quantity; and he must sell using the aforementioned measures under penalty of 25 pounds for each offense. Subsequently, an addition was made to this statute, namely, that if anyone sells wine by the *furatula*, he shall incur the penalty of one pound and make restitution of the damage to the tax collector. Recently, proceedings were brought against a certain woman, who sold wine secretly elsewhere than in a tavern, to the detriment of the tax collectors. The woman excused herself, stating that she sold by a certain measure called a *scutella*; and it is the custom of the place that wine may be sold with the said *scutella* elsewhere than in a tavern without payment of any *datium*. Nevertheless, the judge condemned the said woman to one pound by virtue of the aforementioned addition. The judge is now sued in the *syndicatum* (action for damages against a public official), on the ground that he made the case his own (i.e., acted arbitrarily). The question is: what is the law?

And for clarity, it must be premised that where certain measures have been appointed, sale must not be made according to other measures, lest fraud be committed to the prejudice of the tax collectors, since laws and statutes ought not to be defrauded. As is stated in the Code, *De legibus*, in the law *Non dubium*; and in the Digest, *De legibus*, in the law *Fraus*; and in the Digest, *De iure patronatus*, in the law *Si libertus minorem*. And therefore, lest fraud be committed from one measure to another. Moreover, because it makes no difference what is done with equivalent things; and because small units are reduced to large ones, and conversely. Moreover, so that the occasion for defrauding and offending may be removed, and so that the *datium*, which was established for public utility, may not be defrauded, I, the undersigned Bartolus, say that she was reasonably condemned by virtue of the addition of the said statute.

† For a tavern may be called broadly, wherever wine is sold by the measure: whether we consider the disposition of the law, or the common usage of speech, which ought to be considered: as in D. de funer. instr. l. tabernae, and l. cum delationis, §. Asinam, and D. de leg. 3, l. liberorum, §. quod tamen Cassius. Although this name, tavern, has many meanings: as in D. de pign. l. cum taberna, and D. ad l. Aquil. l. si ex plagiis, §. tabernarius. And because the official swore to observe the statutes, and not customs: it suffices that he observed the statutes: and especially because the custom with its essential elements was not proven: as in D. de legib. l. de quibus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute that punishes a citizen or inhabitant of any place who brings wine produced outside the district of that place to its port, who is to be considered an inhabitant in this case.
2. Whoever alleges that someone is a citizen or inhabitant must prove it.
3. Who is properly considered an inhabitant.
4. Whether priests fall under the category of inhabitants and whether they are covered by the statute, etc.
5. If someone brings wine to a prohibited place due to stormy weather, whether they should be punished.
body: Statute

† of the city of Trieste, among other things, we prohibit that any person may not transport into the city of Trieste any wine produced outside the district of Trieste beyond one urn: under penalty of 10 pounds seized, and added under penalty of 200 pounds. And subsequently follows in the said statute a clause which says: Furthermore, we prohibit that any person, whether a citizen or inhabitant of Trieste, may not, for any cause, in any manner or by any device, by land or by sea, transport any wine produced outside the district of Trieste, under penalty of 300 pounds and forfeiture of the wine. Now it has happened that the lord Muxe etc. instituted an inquiry against Peter Bocco, whom he alleged to be a citizen or inhabitant of Trieste, concerning the condition of a certain boat loaded with wine produced outside the district of Trieste, which boat he alleged the said Peter had transported into the port of Trieste etc. Who, Peter, in responding to the said inquiry, denied it. And among other things, as appears in the proceedings, he stated that he was not, nor is he now, a citizen of Trieste, but a Venetian both by origin and because he was so regarded, treated, and considered, and that the said Peter at the aforementioned time was not an inhabitant of Trieste, but dwelt in Cremona. And therefore the statute does not apply to him, for it has only two headings, one of which speaks of a citizen, the other of an inhabitant: and the said statute does not comprehend other persons: as C. non liceat habitatoribus metropolita. l. 1. ff. sol. ma. l. si vero. §. de viro.

† And for clarity it must be known that he who alleges someone to be a citizen or inhabitant must prove whether this quality pertains to some offense or some penalty. Likewise, whether it pertains to the forum or jurisdiction. And if he does not prove it, the judge may not proceed, nor condemn. And the reason is: because these are matters of fact; and facts are not presumed unless they are proven, as noted by Innocentius in the Extravagant Decretals, De rescriptis, c. Super literis. And it is proven in l. Quaecunque, §. Finis, ff. De publiciana actione; and in l. Praetor, §. Docere, ff. De vi bonorum raptorum; and in l. 1, §. Occisorum, ff. Ad legem Silanianam. Likewise it is

It must be known that he is properly said to dwell who dwells with his household, and makes there a hearth, and other things which dwellers are accustomed to do: as L. 2, C. *Ubi senatus vel clarissimi*; and C. *De agricolis et censitis*, L. *Cum simus*; and L. *Mulieri*, D. *Quibus modis ususfructus amittitur*. Furthermore, it must be premised that this dwelling can be changed at the will of the dweller himself, provided that it is changed by act and by intent, as D. *Ad municipalia*, L. *Domicilium*. From these it appears that the decision of this question rests on whether it is established that he was a citizen or a dweller, or not, namely at the time set forth in the inquisition. For that time is examined, as D. *De noxa*, L. *In delictis*, § *Si extraneus*. And on behalf of the said inquisit certain letters have been produced, which letters, however, prove little, as D. *De testibus*, L. 3, § *Idem divus Adrianus*. Also, certain witnesses have been produced to prove that the said inquisit was a Venetian. But this benefits the said inquisit nothing, because it suffices that he was a dweller at the time of the offense. For this alone is to be considered, and on behalf of the said Lord Muxe this seems to be proven by several witnesses, namely by Master Valentine, Lady Clara, and by other witnesses. From which it follows that the said inquisit was legitimately condemned in 300 livres of denari and in the forfeiture of the wine, if he had any right in the wine.

For if it belonged to a priest, it could not be confiscated: as in C. de sac. san. ecc. l. sac. sanc. thessalonicen. ecclesia. Nor is one excused by acting against the prohibition of the statute on the ground that he transports another’s wine to the port: as in ff. loc. et conducti. l. placet. §. nauem. Nor does it avail to say that this carrier ought to be excused by ecclesiastical privilege, just as the household members of priests are excused: as in C. de episc. et cle. l. 1; for this person was not transporting the wine as a household member, but by reason of hire: as in ff. de publ. l. licitatio. §. mercatores. But rather it works against the opinion of Master Muxa, because it is not true that goods brought into the port must immediately be removed from there: as in ff. de publ. l. Caesar.

But I answer that this occurred there due to the cause of a storm, not by design. Moreover, because the statute speaks in simple terms, and although it is harsh, it must be observed; thus it is established. L. *prospexit*, *Qui et a quibus*. Furthermore, it seems to oppose the statement of Muxa more strongly, because the statute speaks conjunctively of the penalty of three hundred pounds and of forfeiting the wine: as if it were speaking of one’s own wine, not another’s, by the nature of this conjunction. Cf. C. *De senatu et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum*, L. 2; and C. *De impuberibus et aliis sub tutela*, L. *quamvis*; and D. *De liberis et posthumis*, L. *si ita*, § *regula*. But I answer: the words of the statute speak generally, nor is the concurrence of the conjunctive elements required, but the crime ought to be punished in the manner in which it can be punished. Cf. C. *De incestis nuptiis*, L. *cum ancillis*. And therefore the sentence of the said Lord Muxa and his officials, considering the said proofs and the reasons of the laws, was justly rendered, without prejudice, however, to the said priest. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute speaking of delinquents and punishing them, although it does not mention the district or territory, is nevertheless understood in case of doubt to apply to delinquents within the territory.
body: Three statutes are found in the city of Trieste, in two of which, under the rubric concerning those who violate women and virgins, it is contained: first, that if anyone detains any woman who is a citizen or inhabitant of the city of Trieste or its district, he shall be punished with a penalty of two hundred pounds. In the other statute, however, these words “in the city of Trieste or its district” are not present. Hence, Lord Muxe condemned a man who detained a woman from Trieste against her father’s will to two hundred pounds, although he did not detain her within the city of Trieste or its district.

† It is asked whether he judged correctly. And it seems that he did, on the basis of the general provision of that indefinite statute existing in the communal loggia. To the contrary, it seems that one should readily conform to statutes, as in l. 1, C. de inofficiosis donationibus. Moreover, because in case of doubt we ought to choose the milder penalty or the milder law, as in ff. de legibus 2, l. Sempronius Proculus; and l. Si praeses, ff. de poenis. Furthermore, because the force of a statute in case of doubt does not extend to acts committed outside the territory of the enacting authority, as in c. Ut animarum, extra de constitutionibus, lib. 6; and in l. Extra territorium, with its accompanying material. This is the truth, and therefore the sentence of the said Lord Muxe was rendered contrary to law, and he made his case frivolous. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a notary may stipulate for another in conventional matters, just as in judicial ones.
2. Whether a notary may acquire for another by a contract of the law of nations.
3. In the case where a notary may seek for another, by what method he may stipulate.
4. What if the person for whom the notary has stipulated does not wish to acquire for himself, but refuses.
5. Whether an heir may bring an action from a stipulation made by a deceased person.
6. The inheritance holds the place of the deceased in acquired right.
body: The words of the Code and in the reading of the Digest, on adoption, say thus.

† Question 1: Whether a notary may stipulate for another in conventional stipulations. The aforementioned authorities said that he may not, but only in praetorian and judicial stipulations. But our modern jurists say better, and that he may. And they prove this, because the law intends to introduce something special in the person of the notary by reason of his public office. But if he could not stipulate in any act other than a judicial one, there would be no speciality, because any private person may stipulate in such judicial matters, as in the cited law *in omnibus*, and in D. 45.1, *Si quis cautionem*, l. *pen.* For this also stands D. 19.1, *De usuris*, l. *Gallus*. And this is proved in Auth. *De haereditatibus quae ab intestato deferuntur*, § *Ex his*, col. 9, because there a replication is acquired through the notary, which is a remedy of an action; as in Inst. 4.13, *De replicatione*. Therefore, etc. And this is held by the gloss, and rightly so, in Inst. 3.19, *De inutilibus stipulationibus*, § *Si quis aliis*.

Secondly, it is asked in this regard whether a notary can acquire for another from a contract under the law of nations. And it seems that he cannot, because the authority of a notary is of civil law, just as the authority of a magistrate: as in *De origine iuris*, l. 2. And therefore, after its origin, he can do nothing concerning those matters which are of the law of nations. Argument: D. *De capitis diminutione*, l. *Tutelas*; and Inst. *De iure naturali*, §. *Si*. Moreover, in contracts under the law of nations, obligation arises on both sides: as below, D. *De verborum significatione*, l. *Labeo*. But if a notary could acquire in a contract under the law of nations, then there would be obligation for only one party, because he would acquire for an absent person, but would not bind the absent person, since no one contracts while ignorant, as D. *De actionibus et obligationibus*, l. *Ex maleficiis*, §. 1. Therefore, to avoid the limping nature of the contract, it must be said that he cannot acquire. On the contrary, it seems that he can: because guardianship is of civil law: as D. *De tutoribus*, l. 1. And yet a guardian acquires for a ward from a contract under the law of nations, as C. *Quando ex facto tutoris*, l. *Penultima*. Moreover, a judge is of civil law, as in the cited §. *Post originem*. And yet he acquires from a contract under the law of nations: as D. *De evictionibus*, l. *Si plus*, §. *Si visu*. Moreover, a stipulation cannot be made between absent persons, as D. *De verbis obligatis*, l. 1, §. *Ex consensu*. Therefore, if in a contract of the stipulator he acquires, where greater solemnity is required, much more will he acquire from a contract under the law of nations, argument: D. *De stipulatione servi*, l. *Si ex te*, §. 1. This is the truth. The objection that there cannot be a contract under the law of nations unless obligation arises from both sides does not stand; because it can be answered, as D. *De actione empti*, l. *Iulianus*, §. *Si a pupillo*. Or better, it should be said that here obligation arises, because when the absent person wishes to have a right acquired for himself from such a contract, he immediately becomes bound to the price: as in the cited l. *Iulianus*, §. *Offerri*. Argument for this is what is said in a contract celebrated by oath: D. *De iureiurando*, l. *Si duo patroni*, §. *Si quis iuraverit*, and §. *Marcellus*.

Thirdly, it is asked, since through a notary one acquires for another from every contract, in what manner he ought to stipulate: whether he must frame the obligation and the giving in himself, or whether he may confer the giving upon another, as in “you promise to me that you will give to him.” Some say that both must be framed in his own person on behalf of another, as in D. 16.3, l. eum, § Iul. Others say that he may confer the giving upon another, just as a tutor and an agent may, as in the same l. eum, § Iul. And I consider this latter view to be true; otherwise, a case might arise in which, by framing both in his own person, the stipulation would be void, as in D. 45.1, l. antepenult., and D. 40.12, l. si servus.

Fourthly, it is asked: suppose that he stipulated, the notary does not wish to acquire for himself, and thus refuses; will it remain acquired to the notary himself? It seems that it will, as is said elsewhere. C. si certum petatur, l. absentis; pro hoc, ff. de legatis 2, l. si Titio. But it must be said that it will not, because when the notary stipulates, he does not wish to acquire for himself, but, acting as the minister of another, he wishes to acquire for him; and therefore it ought not to remain with him. Argument: ff. de legatis 2, l. Lucius, § si a te; and infra, ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, § filia. Moreover, by stipulating, he did not have the intention of acquiring for himself, nor did the promisor have the intention of giving to him; therefore, he is repelled by an exception. Argument: infra, de solutionibus, l. si debitor tuus, which is highly pertinent; otherwise, it would be a detrimental donation. Argument: ff. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquiliana. And it appears to be the text in a similar argument: infra, de acquisitione rei donatae, l. homo liber, in principio. From these things, the doubt concerning the cession of direct mandates is resolved. The objections from C. si certum petatur, l. si absentis, and l. cum quaeritur, de administratione tutorum, do not hold, because there the contract was at the risk of the gestor, and something was performed by him. Here, therefore, nothing remains to be considered except solely the first point,

† Whether the stipulation is valid. And it seems that it is not, because there is no person to whom it can be acquired, which is of the substance of the stipulation, as in D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. Ususfructus. Moreover, just as a legacy cannot be left to a dead person: as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. Et cum triplici, and l. Quidam referunt, de iure codicillorum; and the reason is given there, that there must be a person, and so forth; likewise, one cannot stipulate or make an agreement, because this is to stipulate or make an agreement for another, but for no one: as in D. de operis liberti, l. Qui libertus, §. Posthumus. Furthermore, the law is explicit. D. si certum petatur, l. Eius, qui in provincia, vers. Quod si stipulatus, there: "if expressly named," etc.; and D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. Si servus communis, §. Servus capti. Moreover, it is one thing to act in the name of the deceased, another in the name of the inheritance: as in D. de negotiorum gestione, l. 3, §. Haec verba. Moreover, a rescript of the prince is not valid, nor is a benefit, if the prince grants it as to a living person, and he was then dead. D. de regulis iuris, l. Inde Neratius. Moreover

† The heir occupies the place of the deceased in a right already acquired, not in a right to be acquired. As stated in D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. fin.; and D. de fideiussoribus, l. mortuo. Moreover, it is a special rule regarding liberty that a decree is transferred to the heir, as in D. de fideicommissis libertatis, l. cum quasi. Therefore, the common law is to the contrary, as noted by Petrus and Cynus in D. qui satius cogantur, l. si decesserit. Furthermore, arguing from judgments to contracts: just as a judgment is not valid, so too a contract ought not to be valid; as in D. de in ius vocando, l. de qua re, §. cum absentem; and D. quae sententiae sine appellatione rescindantur, l. Paulus. To the contrary, it seems from the glossa placed there, which states that the rule is different in a pact than in a judgment. For it says that a pact is transferred to the heir, even if it was concluded in the person of the deceased. Moreover, this is supported by the fact that the heir and the deceased are considered as one and the same person: as in C. de hereditate instituenda, l. fin. Moreover, this is supported by the fact that we are dealing with a contract of good faith, where it is not appropriate to dispute on technical points of law, but only on natural equity: as in D. de mandato, l. si fideiussor, §. quaedam. Moreover, this was based on the presumed intention of the contracting parties, which ought to be regarded as express: as in D. de probationibus, l. si pactum; and D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. fin. Moreover, lest he who received the goods be enriched at another’s loss: as in D. de condictione indebiti, l. nam natura. Moreover, the agreement does not have two parts, one of confession and the other of disposition; therefore, at least the confession should be upheld, because it was made with cause: as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter; and as stated there by Petrus and Cynus. Solution: Although this second part is very equitable, yet according to the subtlety of the law, the said agreement was no proof of the things possessed; because by it one does not contract as such, but only a testimony of the truth arises. This testimony is transferred to the heir, as stated above by the singular theory of Petrus and Cynus in the aforementioned l. si decesserit. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a subject of the king or prince can prescribe royal prerogatives, or those things which are reserved to the prince.
2. Whether a subject can prescribe against his superior prince, for example, the king, the right of creating notaries.
body: The case is as follows: the reverend father, the Lord Bishop of Beloech, and the Church of Beloech have, and have had for a time of which there is no memory to the contrary, full and mixed jurisdiction, and all manner of jurisdiction. And for the said time, and still are, in quasi-possession of appointing notaries, or public scribes, who have drawn up, and do draw up, instruments and public acts between parties, which are regarded as public. And in the public writings of those notaries they affix the seal of the bishop and of the Church of Beloech, and a certain fee for the seal is received in the name of the bishop and of the Church of Beloech. And no notaries appointed by the king have, for the said time, drawn up acts or public instruments in the said city and diocese, nor has the king’s seal been affixed by royal officials, nor has any profit accrued to the king’s court; rather, by the court of the Lord Bishop they were compelled to observe the contents of the instruments and public acts in which the seal of the bishop and of the Church of Beloech had been affixed, and to the bishop and to the Church of Beloech belongs the profit derived therefrom. And this has been the case for the said time without any contradiction or impediment on the part of the king or his officials. Now certain royal officials wish that notaries appointed by the king should go to the city of Beloech and there draw up public instruments and acts, just as the bishop’s notaries do, and affix the royal seal, and that the royal officials should receive the profit, just as those of the bishop do; and this on the ground of the superiority which the king has in the city of Beloech and its diocese in temporal matters. On behalf of the bishop and of the Church of Beloech it is said that this cannot be done, because he has never exercised his superiority in this case, and this would entirely undermine in this respect the utility and rights of the Church of Beloech, because everyone would resort to the notaries appointed by the king and have the king’s seal affixed, since exceptions can be raised more quickly and more favorably, and it must be presupposed that the king has the power to appoint notaries in his kingdom. From these facts it is asked whether the Lord King can, in the said city and diocese of Beloech, appoint notaries, or send those appointed by him elsewhere, to draw up instruments and to affix the royal seal and to obtain the profit in the said Church of Beloech; and it seems that he can, for the reasons set forth below.

First, because by law, competencies belonging to superiors by reason of superiority are not extinguished by prescription, even if the superior has not exercised those rights among his subjects for a thousand years. Argument: Extra, de praescriptionibus, chapter Cum non liceat and chapter Cum ex officiis, with concordances. Since therefore the right to create notaries in the city and diocese of Beauvais and in the whole kingdom of France pertains to the king by reason of superiority, it follows that it will not be extinguished by prescription. Second, because rights belonging to someone by way of faculty and natural liberty cannot be taken away from anyone by prescription of time alone. But it is necessary that the one wishing to use his liberty be once prohibited, to whose prohibition he acquiesced, and afterwards, out of fear of the prohibition, refrained for a long time from using his liberty. For then, by that prohibition, the quasi-possession of liberty is lost and transferred to the prohibitor, and consequently prescription begins to run from that time, as all these things are proven in those things noted by the doctors, Extra, de appellationibus, chapter Significante; de verbis significatis, chapter Abbate, in the gloss; and Codex, de servis, law 1, by the gloss with its concordances. Since, however, it pertains to the king by way of a certain faculty to create notaries in any place of his kingdom, and it is not found anywhere that he was prohibited in the city or diocese of Beauvais, except in this manner: it follows that no prescription can be said to have run against him. Third, because although the power to create notaries pertains to the bishop of Beauvais by legitimate custom or prescription, this does not prevent the same power from pertaining to the king by another right, namely, the right of superiority. Just as in a similar case we see that although the power to excommunicate, visit, correct, and do similar things pertains to the bishop in his whole diocese and each of its churches, nevertheless the same power can pertain by another right to the Archdeacon and Archpriest in the church of their archdeaconry and archpriesthood in the same diocese. Nor does one power impede the other; rather, they concur simultaneously, as all these things are proven when joined together, Extra, de officiis archipresbyterorum, chapter 1; Extra, de officiis archidiaconorum, chapter 1 and chapter Ad haec; and Extra, de officiis ordinarii, chapter 1 and chapter Cum ab ecclesiarum and chapter Conquerente, with concordances.

† Notwithstanding the foregoing, the contrary must be said, namely: that after the bishop and the Church of Belvezer have legitimately acquired the mere and mixed empire, and all jurisdiction and power to create notaries by custom or prescription of time, the memory of whose beginning does not exist, the Lord King can no longer by right create notaries in the said city and diocese of Belvezer, nor send any notaries created elsewhere to exercise the office of notary there, thereby indirectly depriving the bishop and the Church of Belvezer of the benefits which they receive from the impression of the seal. This is declared as follows: it is certain that, although this right to create notaries began to pertain to the Church of Belvezer, it also pertained to the King as prince in his kingdom, recognizing no superior, and by right it could not pertain to any other person, according to the noted opinion of Innocentius in Extra, De fide instrumentorum, chapter Cum P. tabellio. But after the Church of Belvezer began to use this right with the knowledge and patience of the royal majesty, and with no one contradicting in any way, immediately by such patience the King lost the quasi-possession of the said right, and it was transferred entirely to the Church. And thus, consequently, the Church, by using the said right without contradiction of the king for so long a time, the memory of whose beginning does not exist, legitimately prescribed that entire right, and the Lord King lost not only the possession but also the ownership of the same right. And all these things are proven by: Digestum, De publicanis, law Si ego, § 1; Digestum, De servitutibus, law Quotiens; Digestum, Si servus vendicetur, law Et si forte, § 1; and Extra, De praescriptionibus, chapter Audientia, and there by Innocentius; and more fully by the same author in Extra, De restitutione spoliorum, chapter Olim, n. 3; and De capitulo monachorum, chapter Dilecti. And if we were to say that the Church of Belvezer always had this right, even before that city was part of the Kingdom of France, and thus the King never had that power there—which is rightly presumed in doubt, both on account of possession and the antiquity of so much time, and on account of the favor of the Church—then it would be clear and without doubt. Nor does the above objection hold, if it is said that the right to create notaries, which cannot pertain to any inferior from the prince except by privilege of the prince, according to the noted opinion of Innocentius in the said chapter Cum P. tabellio, could not be prescribed by the Church. Argument: Distinction 93, chapter Illud; and noted in Extra, De praescriptionibus, chapter Tanti temporis, cuius in contrarium non est memoria. For royal rights and even all rights which cannot be prescribed without the privilege of the prince are well prescribed, Extra, De verborum significatione, chapter Super quibusdam; and De praescriptionibus, chapter 1, lib. 6; Digestum, De aqua quotannis et aestivo, law Hoc iure. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person succeeding to another in a certain territory, or in the jurisdiction of a certain territory, is called a singular successor or a universal successor.
2. Whether the right to collect a toll is called a servitude, and conversely, whether the right not to collect a toll is called liberty.
3. Whether and when it is permitted to build bridges over rivers.
body: To make the matter evident, it must be premised, as has been said, that the bridge, the chain, and the castle be removed and taken away entirely; so that at no time whatsoever anything may be demanded or be capable of being demanded from merchants or other persons, or concerning other goods ascending or descending therefrom, by any means or device, on account of that place or castle, whether on land or in water, there or elsewhere. Moreover, the tower, which is on the other side of the Adige directly opposite the said castle, must be demolished, as both the words and the intent demonstrate a perpetual and infinite duration, as in D. de iudiciis solutis, l. nouissime; and D. de servitutibus rusticorum praediorum, l. si seruitus and l. eum debere. And therefore it must remain demolished in perpetuity, as argued in D. de arboribus, l. inter Castellianum; and expressly noted by Cynus in C. de poenis, l. seruus.

But let us see who is bound to observe the said pact. For the commune of Venice builds nothing, and therefore it is not bound to the commune of Padua by its own act; it made no promise, so it does not violate the pact. Moreover, they are not partners, such that the act of one would bind the other, as touched upon in one question in D. de arbitris, l. si duo; and in D. de alienatione iudicio mutata causa faciente, l. 3, § opus, which does not clearly determine anything. But the truth is that the commune of Venice is bound by the act of its singular successor, as in D. de novi operis nuntiatione, l. fi, and there by Decius; and in D. de verbis oblig., l. stipulatio ista, § sed si se, and § sicut; and in D. de damno infecto, l. fluminum, § adijcitur. For the commune of Venice ought to have seen to it with the Paduan, to whom it granted by right, that the same things be observed, according to the noted rule in D. de pactis, l. non impossibile puto; and in D. de verbis oblig., l. si ita quis, § si ea lege; and in D. de locato, l. in lege, and l. si fundus. And thus all the doctors writing on this point determine, as well as Albertus Papiensis and the Speculum, as noted in Spec. de emptione et venditione, § scienti, vers. sed pone Petrus. Nor can it be said that any prescription stands in the way: for since it was never proceeded against except now, the right of action never began to effectively accrue except now, and thus prescription never runs: for before, as I said, the action was not born; as in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi; and in C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus, § fi; and in C. de annali exceptione, l. 1, § fin. Moreover, because the commune of Verona was in quasi-possession of this quasi-servitude by virtue of this pact, and against the possessor, or quasi-possessor, no prescription runs, as in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. male agitur; and in D. quibus ex causis maioribus res iudicata esse desinit, l. si is, cuius.

Secondly, it must be premised for the sake of clarity and investigation, whether this pact pertains to the royalty of some established servitude, so that the territory is thus affected, and the direct way may be prohibited by the Paduan commune through a notice of new work and an action in the nature of a negatory action. And it seems that it does not, because this is not a pact, but rather something akin to the common law, as is fully noted in the Speculum, De causa possessionis et proprietatis; and specifically, § Quia vero, under the words “quid de colligentibus pedagia.” For when a thing returns to its natural state, it is not called prescription; nor can it be said that the common law is prescribed by its observance, but rather that it is fostered. Argument: Digest, De usucapione, L. Sequitur, § Lana. But to the contrary, it seems that this is a servitude not to build, so as not to prejudice the navigation of the Veronese and the public. For there are certain real servitudes, although unnameable; and the real nature is recognized by reference to the place, the unaltered enjoyment of which the inhabitants enjoy, as is noted in the Speculum, under the same words; but see Petrus at the end of the verse, where he elegantly determines this. And it supports what is noted in the small gloss, Digest, De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, L. Quibus diebus, in the beginning. Also, because servitudes cause a quasi-possession; and if it is perpetual, it is necessary that it be real, as in Digest, De servitutibus, L. 4. Therefore, the territory owes a servitude to the territory, and consequently, anyone who violates it can be sued by a negatory action, as in Institutes, De actionibus, § Aeque; L. Interdicto, Quod vi aut clam; and Digest, De novo operis nuntiatione, L. De pupillo, § Impositiva. And also by other remedies, as in Digest, De iniuriis, L. In iniuriam, § Si. Bartolus, in L. Publicanus, § Fin., Digest, De publicanis, says that the right to collect tolls is a certain servitude, and consequently its opposite is liberty; from which saying it is verified that such rights are attached to territories, just as jurisdictions are, as in Code, Ubi et apud quos, L. Fin. Although the contrary seems to be noted in L. Ultima, Digest, Uti possidetis. The Speculum says that the right to collect tolls is induced rather by custom than by prescription; yet from this it does not follow that it does not adhere to the soil, just as other benefits are received by reason of the soil. It also supports what is noted by Innocentius, Extra, De separatione, C. Certificari; and what is noted in the Speculum, under the same title, De causa possessionis et proprietatis, § In retinendo, under the words “porro.” From this it appears that from the said pact arose a custom of not collecting tolls. This custom concerns both the liberty of the community of Verona and the liberty also of each individual passing by and navigating, to whom a right has been acquired from the pact itself and the custom, indeed even from the common law: for these are royal rights, which do not pertain to the treasuries of cities, but to the prince, as in C. 1, Quae sint regalia, Collatio 10.

Furthermore, it is to be observed more subtly that the successor of the territory and jurisdiction is not called a singular successor, but a universal one. And therefore he succeeds to it with its causes, qualities, and defects. For this is the nature of universal succession, whether direct or oblique, and especially when succeeding to the treasury, as in Code, De hereditate vel actione venditionis, L. Quod autem castrum. And that the jurisdiction thereof is something universal, it appears because the delegates there are said to be delegates to the universality of causes, as in Digest, De iurisdictione omnium iudicum, L. Solet and L. Praetor. Also, the castle itself is called a universitas, as is noted in L. 1, Digest, Quod cuiusque universitatis nomine. Also, because jurisdiction is a certain collection, which is taken from the whole and consists in law, just as an inheritance and a peculium; and therefore its rights, both active and passive, pass with it, and for these rights the rectors thereof act and are sued, as is noted by Bartolus in the said L. Si publicanus, § Fin.

From these things it clearly seems that it is not permitted for the Paduan commune to make any building, by which the said liberty might be disturbed; and especially to build a bridge, because it would be difficult to place a chain there which would impede those passing by. For not only that which offends, but that which can offend, must be considered, as in Digest, De statu liberorum, L. Labeo; and Extra, De restitutione spoliorum, C. Pisanis.

But the foregoing is opposed by the fact that in the pact of the new peace made with our magnificent lord it was agreed that anyone could freely build in his own territory; therefore, one must depart from the old pact, as in Digest, De novi operis nuntiatione, L. 1, § Inde quaeritur; and Digest, De aqua pluviae arcendae, L. In summa, in the beginning. For since this pact regards the liberation of an obligatory bond, it is valid and must be understood generally, as is noted in Digest, De pactis, L. Emptor, § Lucius. And to this effect are the common laws: Code, De transactionibus, L. Sub praetextu specierum; and noted in the same title, L. Actione in ordinario apparatu. And by Cynus: for from general words nothing is to be detracted, as in Digest, De verbis obligatorum, L. Quicquid astringendae, 3. However.

This opposition seems harsh to me, because it has an allegation made by us in another case, and he who alleges the contrary ought not to be heard. But if some response can be given, it can be said that the power to build freely does not take away the rights of a special convention made to the contrary, of which no mention is made in the pact. And this by the rule that the general is derogated by the specific, as in C. Generi, with its matter; and Digest, De legatis 2, L. Legatorum, § Qui plures; and Code, Familiae erciscundae, L. Quot.

Moreover, it is not entirely his own territory, which serves another. It must be considered that jurisdiction, with respect to which a territory is said, is divided into its species, namely, into the cognizance of the castle, into the perception of tolls. If, therefore, it does not perceive tolls as regards this article, it is not its own territory, because the jurisdiction is not its own. It supports De officio archidiaconi, C. Dilecto; and what is noted by Bartolus in the said L. Ultima, Digest, Uti possidetis.

Furthermore, this pact is reciprocal, whence it must be understood in that case in which the terms on both sides are equal and suitable, as in Code, De impuberibus et aliis substantibus, L. Quamvis.

Furthermore, the custom of not collecting tolls regards not only the community, but individuals with the rights of individuals, and a public convention does not derogate, because they are different species, as in Digest, De pactis, L. Conventionum. It supports Extra, De iniuriis, C. In nostra; and what is noted by Innocentius, Extra, De appellationibus, C. Dilectus; and the ordinary gloss in L. 2, Quae sit longa consuetudo; and Digest, De pactis, L. Si; and De locato, L. Si cum Hermene.

It is established that public rivers are free up to the heavens, as in Institutes, De rerum divisione, § 1.

And therefore, it is not permitted to build private bridges over them, even according to the common law, just as it is not permitted over a public road: as stated in the Digest, title "Ne quid in loco publico," law 1, section "Tractatum," and there by Bartolus. Either the Paduans wish to build the said bridge over the navigable river according to the common law, and they cannot; or according to custom, and then either they allege a custom, which has been abolished by the pact of the Venetians; or a new one, and this is impossible, because they presuppose a contrary term. If there were no pact made by the magnificient [lord], this question would be easily resolved, by those things which have been said in the first point, which are true and undoubted; but the pact made in the city of Genoa makes me doubt greatly, especially because of the allegations made in Florence on behalf of our lord, although the cases are not entirely similar, because our lord owes no servitude to anyone. Moreover, the city of Verona, which has been grievously injured, must be restored. Moreover, the lord count, or any administrator, cannot remit the liquid rights of cities: as noted in the Code, title "De transactionibus," law "Praeses," and in the Code, title "De pactis," law "Pactum curatoris," etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, in actions that are popular by the form of the statute, if one person has brought an action against someone, and a judgment has been rendered against the defendant, although not in accordance with the statute, another person may nevertheless bring an action against the same defendant on the same grounds.
body: Caution is observed

† Formerly, by a statute concerning the clearing of ways, wells, places, roads, and sewers, it was provided that if they are obstructed, they must be restored to their former state by those causing the obstruction, under a certain penalty, and with a popular action instituted. And in the same statute it is provided that the official must, at least once each month, inquire, inspect, and compel the neighbors to perform the aforementioned duties, etc. On this same matter there is another statute, similarly prohibitory and restorative. It is added that a certain person acted against the said statute, and therefore, being sued, suffered a sentence, although not one formally conforming to the aforementioned statute. Now another neighbor, whose interest is affected, brings suit anew and invokes the said statute. It is opposed to him that a sentence has already been rendered, and that he knew the case was being litigated; and therefore the popular action cannot be invoked anew by him: as in D. 3.3.1 (de procuratoribus), l. non cogendum, §. qui ita. For it is established that the prejudice first raised was first occupied, and in such popular actions the condition of the occupant is better, provided that he subsequently prosecutes the case in good faith: as in D. 12.2.1 (de iureiurando), l. eum qui, §. in popularibus. And to this effect: D. 43.8.1 (de sepulchro violato), l. sepulchri violati actio in primis; and what is noted in D. 48.2.1 (de accusationibus), l. si cui, §. eiusdem.

On the contrary, it seems that since the said sentence was not rendered according to the form of the statute, the statute has not been satisfied, nor the utility of the neighbors, whose interest is affected. Therefore, until the statute is satisfied by a condemnatory judgment, or common law by an absolving judgment, anyone whose interest is affected may sue: as in D. 40.4.3 (de libero homine exhibendo), l. 3, §. si tamen plures, at the words "si tamen reus condemnatus"; and it is expressly noted in the sentence in the aforementioned §. in popularibus. And the reason is that a sentence rendered not according to the form of law, but by compromise or by the pronouncement of an arbitrator, does not create law among all, just as neither does a transaction or agreement, as noted in the aforementioned §. in popularibus, in the gloss of the Ordinarius; and argue from D. 2.14.1 (de pactis), l. iure gentium, §. si paciscar; and D. 21.3.1 (de evictione), l. si dictum, §. si compromisero; and C. 2.4.1 (de transactionibus), l. praeses.

Moreover, the statute provides that inquiry be made every month, and permits inquiry to be made multiple times. For although this is one continuous delict, the statute provides that, so to speak, from the present, the action be reborn every month: as in D. 7.5.1 (de usufructu accrescundo), l. 1, in fine; although otherwise it would be different: as in D. 12.2.1 (de iureiurando), l. qui iurasse, §. si pater. And it is reasonable that, until the wrong is purged, one may be compelled to purge it. I do not speak of the popular penalty; for it suffices that that penalty was imposed once.

I therefore conclude, according to what is proposed, that suit may be brought, or the statute be observed; because the law precisely wills that those things by which the air is disturbed be removed, as in l. 1, §. 1, D. 43.28 (de cloacis). And thus I, Baldus, hold in law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a count, having the power to legitimize any illegitimate persons, both present and absent, can legitimize an infant.
2. In the legitimation of a spurious child, whether the blood relatives must be cited, both during the father's lifetime and after his death.
3. Whether a legitimated person can succeed to a parent according to the father's will, and how the will should be ordered when there is a legitimate daughter and a natural daughter.
4. By the authority of the Emperor, even incestuous offspring can be legitimized.
body: Concerning

† the first article, in which it is asked whether an infant can be legitimated by a count having the power to legitimate any illegitimate persons whatsoever, whether present or absent, it seems at first sight that it should be said no, because through this the legitimated person, not consenting, would be brought under paternal power, as in § generaliter in auth. qui. mo. na. filii effi. sui. col. 7. To the contrary, it seems that it must be said that it is done and can be done by authority of the prince, as in C. de eman. libe. l. iubemus. in fi. Likewise, this tends toward the utility of the infant, and therefore he is understood to consent, arg. C. de iure delibe. l. si infanti. with its following law. With this presupposed—namely that it is expedient for the infant—I hold that the legitimation is valid, after the manner of an absent person, to whom he is equated; therefore, even a madman can be legitimated through such a rescript, although in him there is no true consent, as in ff. de reg. iur. l. furiosi. and arg. ff. sol. mat. l. 2. § voluntate.

† Nor are any blood relatives of the father to be cited in that legitimation which the father makes or petitions for, because they would shamelessly allege a hope of future succession during the lifetime of him concerning whose succession it is treated, as in ff. ad Treb. l. 1. And to this effect is ff. de ventre inspi. l. 1. in fin. and noted by the Moderns in l. Gallus. de libe. et posthu.

† Concerning the second point, whether the legitimated person can succeed the father according to the paternal testament. I reply yes, to a virile portion, because the words of the rescript say so, namely: “yet in such manner, as I have said, that they obtain an equal portion just as other legitimate children.” Whence if the virile portion should exceed the legitimate portion, the legitimate and natural daughter ought not to remain content with the legitimate portion; rather, it ought to be supplemented up to the virile portion, the dowry having been computed, similarly to that which I have said regarding the virile portion, C. vnde vir, et vxor. auth. praeterea. Others nevertheless say that it suffices if the legitimate and natural daughter has the legitimate portion, nor could she claim more against the judgment of the father, as in C. ne filius pro patre. Auth. nouissima. For just as the legitimated ought to be content with the legitimate portion, so also the legitimately born, since they have been made equal by the rescript. But the first opinion is safer. Concerning the third doubt, on the method to be observed so that the said legitimate daughter may be content with the dowry, an answer has already been given. Likewise concerning the fourth point, on the method to be observed in drawing up the testament, the answer is similarly clear: because the testament ought to be made in such a way that the said daughter has the legitimate virile portion, the dowry having been computed; and if less should be left, a supplement would be made. Concerning the fifth and last point, it must be said that the mother can renounce such succession under oath, as in extra de pac. c. 2. and most fully noted by the More Modern Authors in l. pactum. C. de col. Lastly, it is to be known that the said rescript is valid, and the legitimation followed thereupon, as noted in Auth. qui. mo. natu. effi. sui. § fi. col. 7. and in c. naturales. si de feu. fue. contro. col. 10. and there most fully by the More Modern Authors.
† For by imperial authority even incestuous persons can be legitimated, as in ff. de ritu nuptia. l. qui in prouinc. § diuus. and there by Dyn. in the additions. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the modesty of the price, together with a pact of repurchase, if the buyer was accustomed to usury, gives rise to a presumption of a usurious contract, or rather of a pledge, rather than of a sale.
2. Whether it is necessary to prove that the buyer was a usurer at the time of the contract, or whether it suffices that he was so before, or after, or at any other time.
body: James

† As is reported by Cynus, C. *plus valere quod agitur*, l. 3, held that, granted that these three things are established, namely that the usurious buyer did not intervene with a just price, and that there was an agreement to resell, a pledge is not presumed thereby. And he responds to the decree *Illo nos* on pledge, stating that there a pledge is presumed because an agreement regarding the estimation of the principal was appended, which is of the nature of a pledge. But Johannes Andreae, in the said chapter *Illo vos* in the Novella, reproaches this opinion, saying that this opinion does not accord with the decree *Ad nostram* on sale and purchase, and adds that the opinion of Iacobo de Arena is erroneous. I therefore say that it must be considered that when only one thing is proved, namely that the purchase was made at less than a just price; yet no promise to resell intervened, nor was the buyer accustomed to lend at interest, and then a usurious contract is presumed, but the law 2, C. on rescission of sale, and Extra on sale and purchase, c. *Cum dilectus*, applies. Sometimes two things are proved, namely that the thing is said to have been sold at less than a just price, and an agreement to repurchase at the same price intervened, whenever the thing is offered, or until a certain time. And then, if the thing is bought at a low price, and must be resold at a low price, fraud is presumed: because the lowness of the price is an increase of deceit: as in the said chapter *Ad nostram*, according to Bartolus and Innocentius. But others contradict this by means of l. 2, C. on agreements between buyer and seller, where it is expressly determined that this contract is valid, and is not a fictitious contract. And therefore others say that not only must the quantity of the price be examined, but also whether he who claims to have bought was accustomed to lend at interest or not. For if indeed he was accustomed to lend at interest, a lending contract is presumed, and the title of purchase is fabricated in fraud of usury. For the person is an argument of deceit, together with the other coherences mentioned above: as in D. on transactions, l. *Cum his*, § *Sed personarum contemplatio*; and argument from D. on proof, l. *Qui testamento*. I therefore say that where three things are proved, namely both the unjust price at which it is bought, and the unjust price at which it must be resold, and that he who promised to resell was a usurer, such a contract is to be considered a lending contract.

But it is doubtful whether it is necessary that the thing was accustomed to be lent at interest at the time of the contract, or whether it suffices that it was so afterwards, or simply, without proving a certain time, it does not seem to be said that the time of the contract is to be considered. For when the condition of a person varies according to time, similarly those things which are done by a person vary, as in D. de negotiorum gestione, l. eum actum; and C. ne de statu defunctorum, l. si mater. Moreover, the life of a person is estimated from what precedes, as in D. de re militari, l. non omnis, §. Bar. On the other hand, the contrary seems to hold, because from later events we also know earlier ones, as in C. de adulteriis, l. si qui; and l. quicunque; C. de apocrisis pupillorum, lib. 10; and in Auth. de restitutionibus, et ea quae parit, §. fi. Sol. Considering the above-mentioned case, I believe that the said contract is to be considered usurious; and this is confirmed also by the renunciation mentioned in the said contract. See the arguments read and noted in l. 6, D. de conditione instituta; and C. de mandato, l. per diversas; and l. ab Anastasio; and what is noted by Guillaume de Coucy in D. de pactis, l. si tibi decem millia. For a small excess of value, and much more if the price were appropriate according to such agreements, the contract would not be considered usurious. In the said l. 2, C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem. Nor is he who is bad in one thing always bad in all things; because contracts are distinguished. For one may be bad in lending at interest, and not bad in buying; hence, the reason for separated things is separate. D. de calumniis, l. fi.; and C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si maritus. But when there is a great excess of the common value of the thing in relation to the agreed price, there: because it is not likely that the contracting parties on both sides would throw away their own interest; and from other conjectures mentioned above, fraud is presumed, as I said above. And this is what the text says in the said c. ad nostram, where it says that they amounted to half the just price. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How are those words to be understood, “under this condition, however, if it should happen that Titius dies without a lawful heir born from him”: namely, whether they are to be understood as meaning that he was lawfully born at the time of birth, or that he is lawful at the time of death, even if he was not lawfully born from the beginning. The latter opinion is held. It would be otherwise if he had said, “without an heir lawfully born from him.”
body: Let us see.

†What sense those words should have, under this condition, namely, if it should happen that Sempronius dies without a legitimate heir born of him: whether they are to be understood strictly, that he be legitimately born at the time of birth, or legitimate at the time of the testator’s death, even if he was not legitimately born from the beginning, provided he is born of him. For if the said words were understood in the first manner, legitimation made by the prince would not prejudice the donee; because he would not be of that species, or of that form, of which the extinguishing or impeding condition of the donation speaks, as C. de his, qui veniam aetatis impetra, l. fin.; ff. de legatis 2, l. si ita quis, §. is cui; ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, si fideicommissum; ff. de iure fisci, l. Statius Florus Cornelio; ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. ex ea parte, §. in insulam. But if those words are understood in the second manner, then the donee would be excluded; because the donor dies with a legitimate heir. Moreover, he dies with an heir born of himself. And that he dies with a legitimate heir is apparent; because these words are civil, as ff. de verbis significandis, l. lege obvenire hereditatem; and ff. de suis et legitimis, per totum; and C. de legitimis haeredibus, per totum; and ff. de capitis diminutione, l. tutelas; and ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. 2 and 3. But it is certain that, considering civil law, which is concerned with legitimation itself, this legitimated person is a legitimate heir, as noted in Auth. quibus modis naturales efficiantur sui, §. 1, Coll. 7. That he is born of himself, nature itself teaches, as the text says in the Decree, c. nasci, de adulterinis; and in the said Auth. quibus modis naturales efficiantur legitimi, Coll. 6; and in the said Auth. quibus modis naturales efficiantur sui. Furthermore, it must be considered that the words of the said condition do not speak by an adverb, because they do not say “without an heir legitimately born of him.” For an adverb joined to the time of birth would signify the time of origin, ff. de verbis obligationum, l. si a colono; and ff. de noxa, l. in delictis, §. si extraneus. But they speak by a noun; because they say “legitimate heir,” and thus refer to the time of death, as ff. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. fin.; and l. antepenultima; ff. de testamentis tutorum; and l. si cognatis; ff. de rebus dubiis. Furthermore, this is demonstrated by evident reason. For let it be granted that the same donor dies intestate, and let this proposition be formed: “He dies with a legitimate heir born of him.” Certainly this proposition is true and necessary; therefore, its contrary is impossible, as noted in l. 1, ff. de conditionibus et institutionibus. Furthermore, it can be more strongly persuaded that even if the said condition had not been added, the said universal donation would be invalidated as by a sort of agnation of a posthumous child, as C. de revocatione donationum, l. si unquam; and argumentum ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. fin. For Bartolus and the Moderns call these legitimated persons posthumous, as appears from them in l. Gallus. Furthermore, we say that affection is to be considered, as ff. de testamentis tutorum, l. si quis ita; whence the father’s affection, expressed by the words of the condition, causes the donation to fail, by argumentum ff. ad Trebellianum, l. haeredibus, §. fin. From which it is evidently concluded that, if it should happen that the said donor dies with his said son born of a freedwoman, and finally legally legitimated by him through petitions presented: such donation fails by virtue of the condition. Moreover, if the condition had not been added, it would be broken by the agnation of the posthumous. Therefore, I distinguish these cases, because by the added condition it appears that the donor was not undutiful in giving, since he expressly provided for his children, as ff. de haeredibus instituendis, l. Lucius. Which if he had not done, the law would rescind it, as in the said l. si unquam.
