From which is inferred another conclusion, namely, that if he had said it by an adverb, the donation would be rescinded then as undutiful by the provision of the law, not by the nature of the inserted condition. But it is not expedient to treat this here, but let it be left to the disputation of the prudent. But we only have to conclude that the condition failed, and that the donation is not said to be rescinded, but to cease, that is, to be deemed not made, as ff. de manumissionibus testamentorum, l. si quis locuples; and ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. non solum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a spurious child succeeds to a fief, of which someone has been invested with this agreement, that he may leave it to the heirs he wishes.
2. The tenor of the investiture is to be considered.
3. What these words, placed in any person in the investiture of a fief, signify.
4. Whether a spurious child is infamous, and a dishonorable person. and no. 6.
5. Whether a fief is something hereditary.
6. It does not seem that a dishonorable person was considered.
body: The question is whether Spurius, the son of a certain priest, was instituted as universal heir by his uncle or paternal uncle in an inheritance, which includes a certain castle held in fief from the King. This fief is honorable and was newly acquired by the said deceased for his heirs, whom he wished to leave it to.

† Now it is asked whether the said spurious child ought to be admitted to the succession of the said fief together with the other goods, or whether those who succeed intestate come into it? And it seems that he should be admitted. For, granted that such a spurious child is capable of succeeding his father, he is not, however, capable of succeeding his uncle, as noted by the gloss in Auth. quibus modis naturalis efficiuntur sui, §. fin. But this fief was not held from the father, but from the uncle; therefore, etc. To the contrary, it seems from the text with the gloss in c. naturales, col. 10, if there is a dispute about fiefs, and from Johannes Andreae in c. lator and c. per venerabilem, who are legitimate children. Moreover, there is a certain gloss in the Visirico of Catalonia concerning intestates, which states that it is the custom in Catalonia that a spurious child does not succeed his brother in a fief. The tenor of this gloss is as follows: "What if the intestate has only a spurious brother? Does he succeed him in the fief, or is our lord preferred, who shall succeed him?" See ff. unde cognati, l. si spurius. Understand this if he was born of the same mother, as will be said there; otherwise, the lord will succeed: see C. de vacando, l. 1, lib. 10. Nevertheless, I do not believe, from the aforementioned laws and from what is said here, that the spurious child succeeds, but rather the lord. And thus stands the custom of Catalonia, extra de feudis, §. idem quoque.

There is also another gloss in the said Visirico, stating that where someone acquired for himself and for whomever he wished a certain fief, the vassal who acquired the fief in the aforementioned manner may alienate the fief to suitable persons and not to prohibited ones. The tenor of the said gloss is as follows: "But suppose that the testator acquired the fief for himself and for whomever he wished: then, if he dies without children, he may leave it to suitable persons and not to prohibited ones." See C. de iure emphyteuticario, l. ultima, because even if he dies without children, it does not revert to the lord, and this on account of the appended pact: see infra de feudis, §. si quis sine filio.

There is also a certain constitution issued by the learned King, of the following tenor, adding that it is lawful for a vassal to dispose of his fief inter vivos or in his last will to an incapable person; and that the nearest relative of the vassal, though capable, may succeed intestate in the fief, just as he may succeed in other goods. But where the vassal has alienated or left the fief inter vivos or in his last will to any church, or religious house, or chapel, or cleric, or has received it for his soul, or otherwise disposed of the fief to an incapable person, he must then alienate the same fief within a year to a capable person. From this constitution, the said spurious child argues that, although he is not capable of retaining the said fief by virtue of the general institution, at least the power of alienating the said fief within a year is granted to him, and thus that the price of the said fief is sought for him by virtue of the said constitution.

It is opposed against the said spurious child that, by virtue of the said constitution, the power of alienating the fief is attributed solely and exclusively to the capable person, where the fief has been disposed of to one who is incapable of retaining it, but capable of acquiring it, such as a church and others expressly mentioned in the said constitution, and to these, and l. sed et si quia, §. quaesitum, with its subject matter, si quis cautio. For, although they are incapable of retaining, because they cannot perform the service due to the lord for the said fief, nevertheless they are capable of acquiring. And indeed, if these have the faculty of alienating, this cannot be said of the said spurious child here, since he is capable of both capacities, both of acquiring and of retaining: see d. c. naturales in the gloss, and the aforementioned glosses cited above.

Moreover, the said deceased did not dispose of the said fief, since he made no mention of it. For a fief does not come under a general disposition: c. in generali, if there is a dispute about fiefs, no. Jacobus de Ardizzone in his Summa, §. quaedam, and pertransit. And this is what the said constitution of Catalonia wishes to say there, when it says, "disposed of the same." Also, it is said that the fief is an honor, and in honors spurious children do not succeed, except in subsidium: see l. generaliter, §. spurios, ff. de decurtatione; therefore, etc.

From the foregoing, it is asked what the law is. First, recourse must be had to the tenor of the investiture. For, as is newly proposed regarding a new fief, someone was invested for himself and his heirs, to whom he wished to leave it. It is doubtful what the sense of these words is, whether, by this breadth of power, because it says "to whom he wished to leave," strangers are included. And it seems that they are not, because these words, thus absolutely pronounced, must be understood according to the matter of fiefs, arg. ff. de usuris, l. si stipulatus, and ff. locati conducti, l. si unum. But in the matter of fiefs, the name of heir is placed for descendants: see in c. si clientulus, §. et si clientulus, de alienatione feudorum, and note ff. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. fin.

To the contrary, it seems. For this fief does not have the nature of a fief, because according to the nature of a fief, no disposition of the deceased is valid in the fief: see in c. unico, de successionibus feudorum, in principio. Also, it does not have the nature of a fief for another reason: because the words say, "and to heirs, to whom he wished." These words are extensive, so that the fief could be disposed of at the pleasure of the vassal to any external person: see in c. 1, de feudo non habente proprii feudi naturam. For this, it is noted by Cynus, C. de operibus libertorum, l. liberti, libertaeque.

For the agreement, or the tenor of the investiture, is rather inspected than the general nature of the fief. Indeed, because nature is a genus, whereas the agreement is a species, and therefore the species derogates from the genus. Moreover, it is permitted by agreement that which is not permitted by law, as in c. j. de duobus fratribus, regarding those invested by the captain; and in c. 1, §. cum vero Corradus, there: "unless expressly named"; and in c. qui feudum dare possunt, in the same column; and in the title de quibusdam aliis extraordinariis capitulis feudorum, c. si cui militi, where it is said that the rules of fiefs are overcome by the wording of the investiture, as well as by the force of the words and the intent of the contracting parties.

† What, therefore, is the conclusion? Certainly, the vassal could, by these words, also make a testament in favor of any person whatsoever. But consider in what sense “any person whatsoever” is understood: for these words are restricted to a suitable person, just as we say, “let each one have [it] if he is capable”: as in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. 1; and ff. de muneribus et honoribus, l. ut gradatim, §. et si lege. Therefore, he could not transfer [the fief] to a prohibited person, for example, to his spurious son, as in c. naturales, si de feudo feudalis controversia; or to another who was not his equal, for example, a knight to a rustic: as in c. 1, §. ex eadem lege, de lege Corradi; or a robust man to one vitiated in body: as in c. 1, an mutus vel surdus. For prohibited and incapable persons are not said to be admitted to such transactions, as noted in ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. si ita quis, §. si ea lege. Even the church [is excluded], because the church ought to be a cultivator and promoter of justice, and ought not to suffer anything contrary to justice to be or to be done in itself or in another, as in c. 1, de feudi alienatione. Thus, therefore, such a conclusion may be formed: that by the aforementioned words, “and to the heirs whom he wished,” persons prohibited by law, or by custom, or by nature incapable, are not included. Argument: ff. de iudicibus, l. cum praetor, §. pe. et fi. And these things have been said with regard to the tenor of the investiture, considering it simply and in itself. And from these, the infeodator...

† Since the aforementioned illegitimate son of the priest is not possessed of honor and dignity by the feudal tenant and lord of the fief; on the contrary, illegitimate sons are considered infamous with respect to such acts. For as Azo says, to be illegitimate is a certain infamy, as he notes in the Summa, Codex, On Infamy. It follows that he is not suitable for an honorable fief, especially that of the king; because in fiefs reputation is greatly considered on account of the purity of the fief and its nobility: as in the title Here the law ends, then the customs of the kingdom begin, chapter To the Lord War. Hence it is said that fief and reputation embrace each other, and conversely fief and infamy abhor each other. But against what has been said, this is opposed: it is certain that this illegitimate son can be instituted as general heir by his uncle; because the prohibition of the illegitimate son is only from descendant to ascendant, as Codex, On Natural Children, law Final; and as noted in the Authentic Who May Become His Own, section Finally. If this is so, therefore, the fief passes with the universality, as Digest, On Acquiring Ownership, law Certain.

But to this I respond that a fief is not simply an heritable corporeal thing, but is a certain thing which is sometimes in the inheritance, sometimes outside the inheritance: as is noted in the Digest, De petitione hereditatis, in the law Item videndum, § Si; and in the Decretals, chapter 1, An filius vel agnatus, Collatio 10. Likewise, it is sometimes among the assets, sometimes not, as argued from the law in the Digest, De usufructu legato. Therefore, it does not pass with the universality [of the estate], nor is it found to be included therein, because its nature and condition do not permit it. See the arguments noted in the Digest, Ad Trebellianum, in the law Quia perinde; in the Digest, De operis libertatis, in the law Si operarum.

Having considered the matters concerning the investiture, let us examine the royal constitution, which provides that it is lawful for a vassal to dispose of his fief, either inter vivos or by last will, to a capable person. And this is sufficiently determined by the foregoing: for I do not consider capable him whom reason repels. Hence, it is necessary to descend to another part of the constitution, which states: "But if a vassal has alienated or bequeathed his fief inter vivos or by last will to any church, religious house, chapel, or clerk, or has received it for his soul, or has otherwise disposed of the fief to one not capable thereof, he shall then, within a year, alienate the same fief to a capable person."

But I hold that the said constitution does not touch our case: for the said bastard is not repelled because he is not capable, but because it does not appear that the king, who made the investiture, had such a base person in mind: as in the Digest, Ad Trebellianum, in the law Ex facto, § Si quis rogatus.

† But that a spurious child is a person of infamous character, is the text of the Institutes, On Inofficious Wills, §. soror, unless he has been legitimated by the prince, or by his constitution: as is noted in Collation 10, If there was a dispute concerning a fief, c. 2.

† Moreover, regarding the fact that no consideration appears to have been given to a person of base character, this is held by Marinus de Fano in his treatise on emphyteutic law in question 23, question 1, and he cites the statement in § si quis rogatus, and the laws utrum and licet, under the title On donations between husband and wife. He concludes that even in the case of an emphyteusis of a most noble castle and of honorable standing, it is not understood that any noble person invested thereby should be considered as having taken into account persons of base origin. For such persons degenerate. C. de natura liberorum. l. si. This matter is also touched upon in Speculum, de locato, § nunc aliqua, verse 67, where it is asked concerning the first degree down to the last, concluding that the son of a priest, being a spurious child, is not included in the investiture, neither directly nor incidentally; and consequently, since it does not devolve upon him, it cannot pass to another: as stated in l. alienatio, de acquisitione rerum dominii. Nor is he understood to be contained within the words of the edict or constitution, namely, he who is totally alien to the contract; because the constitution is founded upon the contract, and where there is no consent, there is no contract: as stated in l. 1, ff. de pactis; and ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligationum substantia; and l. non figura; and ff. si certum petatur, l. non omnis; and l. si ego. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether he who is bound to give or pay something, if he comes to a more affluent fortune, is obliged, if he becomes a bishop, to pay from the revenues of the bishopric.
2. What is meant by a more affluent fortune.
body: On the aforementioned point, I answer simply,

And I say that, having become a bishop, he cannot pay anything from the fruits of the bishopric, neither in the forum of conscience nor in the forum of judgments, unless this was expressly granted to him by the Pope. The text is in c. Si propter tua, de rescriptis, lib. 6, where it is expressly stated that a bishop, on account of his debts, cannot pay anything from the goods of churches even subject to him, unless this has been granted to him by special grace of the Pope. How, therefore, are those words "from a more abundant fortune" to be understood?

I answer that they are understood to be liable if he were to gain something with their connivance. For then, first, debts must be deducted, and the remainder accrues to the episcopal see. 18. qu. 1. c. statutum. And in the Extravagantes, de solutionibus, c. si quorundam. And there, noted by Johannes Andreae. For it would be absurd to say that the Pope wished to bind the episcopal see for the delicts of the bishop, and especially those committed before he was bishop, as in c. delictum personae, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. And it supports what Innocentius notes in the Extravagantes, de testamentis, c. cum in officiis. And in the Extravagantes, de praebendis, c. nisi esset. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a murderer, or another malefactor, who flees from the territory where the crime was committed to another, if he is subsequently forcibly brought back to the first territory, where he committed the crime, can be punished there, or rather should be restored to his liberty, in which he was in the alien territory.
body: A certain subject of the said Count of Savoy killed a certain subject of the same prince, and the killer fled to the territory of the said Count of Virtues. Finally, while there, he was violently captured by some of his neighbors, subjects of the aforementioned Lord Count of Savoy; who grievously wounded the same killer, so that he was weakened in some of his limbs and rendered useless, and, violently extracting him from the aforementioned territory of the said Count of Virtues, they returned him to the power and bailiwick of the magistrate of Bugella, acting in the name of the Count of Savoy. Now, since the said magistrate of Bugella, often requested by the magistrate of Vercelli, from whose jurisdiction the said killer was violently extracted, to release him and restore him to his former state, refused to release him. It is now asked, what is the law regarding the aforementioned matter, namely whether the said magistrate of Bugella is bound to release the alleged killer and restore him at the request of the magistrate of Vercelli, assuming, however without conceding, that the magistrate of Bugella has clear knowledge of the crime, etc.

† On this point, it seems that at first glance one should say that, since the aforementioned person was violently captured, albeit outside the territory, he is in any manner under the power of the judge, and where he committed the offense, there he ought to be punished. For in whatever province a person commits an offense, he ought to be punished in that province, all privileges ceasing: as in C. *Ubi de crimine agi oportet*; Auth. *Qua in provincia*. And if it is said that the judge in whose territory he was captured may demand his return, this does not seem true for two reasons. First, because he is not his citizen nor an inhabitant, and thus he has no right of vindication: D. *Ad municipalia*, l. *De iure*. Secondly, because in demanding him back, he acts with fraud (*dolo facit*). For, as is stated immediately in Auth. *Ut nullus iudex*, §. *Si quis vero comprehensorum*, he commits a wrong when he demands back someone whom he will immediately restore, according to the rule *Dolo facit*.

Nevertheless, despite these arguments, the truth lies to the contrary: because it was not lawful to capture him in alien territory, where he cannot be cited by the thing itself or by effect, that is, by capture: as in D. *De bonis*, Auth. *Iudicis possessio*, l. *Cum unus*, §. *Is qui*. Moreover, a form has been established by law, that a remission be requested and that he be remitted, as stated in the aforementioned §. *Si quis vero comprehensorum*; D. *De acquisitione*, l. *Si cui*, §. *Si qua forma non servata*. If this form is not observed, the captured person, as one spoliated of his own liberty, ought to be restored to the same liberty: as in D. *De aedilicio edicto*, l. *Quis sit fugitivus*, §. *Idem Celsus*. And this is expressed in Extravagant *De verborum significatione*, c. *Ex parte*, in the beginning.

Furthermore, a certain form has been given by law, that if against such a form there is only a word, it is not valid by the law itself; but if there is some act being executed, it ought to be revoked by a contrary act: as in l. *Prima*, §. 1, D. *De feriis*. But here a certain form has been established, as I said above, and this is not true merely by law, but by written custom, as is clear in 10th column, *De pace tenenda*, c. *Et eius*, this one as necessary, as is clear there in the word *postmodum*. Nor does the rule *Dolo facis* oppose this; because that rule has no place in those who have been spoliated, especially of their own liberty, as noted in l. *Extat*, *Quod metus causa*; D. *De iudiciis*, l. *Si de vi et possessione*.

Moreover, because such remissions are not made by the custom of modern times, and therefore, since he is not bound to remit, the aforementioned exception has no place, as noted in c. *Pastoralis*, *De re iudicata*, in the Clementines. And the aforementioned points are confirmed by what is noted by Bartolus in d. §. *Cum sacrilegium*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son, who merely mentions in the narrative clauses of the compromise that he has his father’s mandate to compromise, but not in the operative clauses, appears to have compromised in his father’s name or by his father’s mandate.
2. Whether the award is understood to have been rendered in the same names as those in which the compromise was made.
3. Whether the son, by protesting in his father’s name, appears to have acceded.
body: The question is,

Whether a son, who, by mandate from his father to compromise on behalf of the father himself, makes mention of the mandate in the compromise in words of narration, and does not repeat the same wording in the words importing the compromise, namely, in the word “I compromise”: but simply says, “I, Francischinus, son of such-and-such, compromise”: is to be understood as having done everything not only in his own person, which he expressly assumed in the compromise, but also in his capacity as agent. And it is to be said that he acted even in his capacity as agent; because what is said in the preambles is deemed to be repeated in the subsequent parts. As in D. de verb. oblig. l. Titia, § idem respondit. And because such are the subjects as the predicates demonstrate. As in D. de interrog. act. l. si defensor. And it is clearly proved by D. de institoria, l. Lucius, and D. de verb. oblig. l. si ita stipulatus, § Grisogonus.

Secondly, it is asked regarding the award, whether it is understood that the award is rendered by the same persons by whom the compromise was made. And it must be said that it is so, since the award refers back to the compromise, as in C. de diversis rescriptis, l. Si libellum. And this applies in that which concerns both father and son in common. Otherwise, if it concerns only the son: for then the name of the son would not include the father, as in Extra de rescriptis, c. Edoceri.

Thirdly, it is asked whether, by the protestation which Antonio made in the procuratorial name of his father, the said Antonio appears to have accepted the inheritance. It must be said that he did not: because he protested in his own name, but rather Jerome himself seems to have accepted the inheritance, because he subjected himself to the hereditary debt, as in l. 2, C. de iure delictorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the conjunction "and" or another conjunction placed between clauses induces a verbal conjunction, from which arises the right of accretion.
2. How many types of conjunction there are.
3. The plurality of clauses causes the verbal conjunction to cease, insofar as it pertains to the right of accretion.
body: The question is
†ame, whether the conjunction "and" or some other conjunction placed between clauses induces a verbal conjunction, from which arises the right of accretion. And it must be premised,

† That certain conjunctions are of words: certain of sentences: certain of expressions, as noted in D. de peculio legato, l. quidam in testamento. Conjunction of words is when one verbal act governs two different words: as “I bequeath to Titius and Seius such a fund.” Conjunction of sentences is when there are two sentences with a copula: as “To Titius the fund, likewise to Seius I bequeath the same fund.” Conjunction of expressions is also of different things, or persons: as “I bequeath to Titius the fund. Likewise to Seius the house.” I also premise that sometimes one determination determines several determinables: as “I bequeath to Titius and Seius the fund.” For “I bequeath” determines, but the determinables are Titius and Seius: then, on account of the unity of speech, the legatees are conjoined by words and by thing, which is the same as saying by the unity of speech. As in C. de caducis tollendis, §. hæc ita tam varie. And this is when the testator did not speak distributively; for if he had added shares, on account of the distribution of shares they would not be conjoined by thing, but nevertheless by words, as in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. interdum. For where there is division of the will distributing shares, there is said to be a real distinction, while the verbal conjunction remains. And both proceed from you by virtue, and the testator’s will, as in D. de legatis tertio, l. re coniuncti. In the 1st and 2nd responses.

Question: Therefore, although there are two sentences coupled, nevertheless each stands by itself, such a copula does not make a verbal conjunction; because there are different terminations determining different determinables, as noted in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. liber homo, §. Titius. And where there is distribution of shares, there is no conjunction by thing; and this is clear from the argument from effect, because it does not produce the right of not diminishing. Also, because the testator’s speech does not attribute its virtue to each in solidum. From which it is thus concluded that distribution of parts removes real [conjunction], but distribution of sentences removes verbal conjunction; and this is the very truth.

And two principal words make two sentences, which dialecticians call categorical, because each of them has a subject and a predicate, and the principal parts are per se. Hence there is no copulative here; because it couples neither sense nor words, since each by itself has its own construction, and therefore it is a union. And just as distribution of parts relates to real distinction, so distribution of sentences relates to verbal disjunction. These are proved expressly in Inst. de legatis, §. si coniunctim. In the 2nd response.

† What I said, that the plurality of clauses causes the verbal conjunction to cease, insofar as it pertains to the right of accretion, is true, if each clause is perfect in both noun and verb: "I bequeath the estate to Titius, and I bequeath the same estate to Seius." But if one clause is perfect in noun and verb, while the other is even without a verb, as in "I bequeath the estate to Titius, and to Seius the same estate," then there is a verbal conjunction. This is because the verb "I bequeath," placed once, is common and flows over the whole. As stated in D. 34.2.1 (*Cum pater*), § *Cum imperfecta*, the verb is taken to apply to the commonality. And thus the opinion of Master Raynerius could be understood, who says that there is a verbal conjunction in coupled clauses. In this way, the opinion of Bartolus in l. *Triplici*, D. 50.16, can be reconciled with the opinion of Raynerius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A donation made on the condition of providing maintenance, if the maintenance is not provided, is revoked. And no. 3.
2. One who fails to provide maintenance cannot purge the delay, unless within a few days.
3. Whether a donation between prohibited persons is valid when the affinity ceases or is dissolved.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that if a donation is made on the condition of providing maintenance, and such maintenance is not provided, the donation is revoked, and the repetition of the donated thing is available, as well as a useful vindication of the thing, as stated in the Codex, On donations made on condition, law 1.

Secondly, it must be premised that he who has not provided alimony cannot purge the delay unless within a few days, as noted by Cynus in the Digest, title 1, and is proven in the Digest on verbal obligations, in the law "If anyone," section "Seia." Nor would a biennium be considered a certain period within a few days, nor a year in the case of alimony, as in the Digest on leases, in the law "The day," section "Between the lessor." For alimony does not require delay, but rather support, as in the Digest on holidays, law 2. And therefore this donee, concerning whom the question arises, if he was interpellated and did not provide alimony for a long time after the interpellation, cannot purge the delay, but has fallen from the donation.

† A doubt, however, occurs to me, whether those words, that the said serf Modestus ought to have food and clothing, constitute a delay. And I say that they do, as in the Digest, On Manumission, Testate, l. Mevia. Hence, if the donee neglected to give him food and clothing by virtue of the pact, to which ingratitude is also annexed, he may be deprived of the donation, as in the Code, On Revocation of Donations, l. si.

It is also doubted whether a donation may be made between the persons in question. And it seems to be said that, after the affinity was dissolved, as noted in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Sed hoc*, it could thus be done; but say that, since the said donation subsequently became void, as has been stated, the doubt has expired. Nevertheless, I do not omit that which is subtly alleged by the last law of the Code, *De pactis*, that a donation of present and all future things, where there is a mere donation, was not valid. And let the subtly made allegations suffice on this point. Finally, however, I say that he who did not provide alimony ought not to have the benefits of the donation. This is supported by the Digest, *De conditionibus appositis*, chapter *Verum*, and by the Digest, *De donationibus*, law 3. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Under a statute providing that a son under paternal power cannot obligate himself without the consent and permission (parabola) of the father, whether he can obligate himself for the redemption of the father himself with his consent.
2. What a parabola is.
3. Under a statute providing that contracts made with a son under paternal power, even with an oath, without the father's consent, are presumed to be simulated, how it is to be understood.
4. In proving age, conjectures suffice.
body: There occurs

† a doubt: if a statute states that a son under paternal power cannot obligate himself without the father's consent, whether he can obligate himself for the sake of redeeming the father himself with that father's consent. And it seems that he cannot, because consent is here in the place of authority; and therefore a father cannot grant it in his own matter, as is noted in l. 1, ff. de auto. tuto., and this is true,

† because that word, "without word/permission" (sine parabola), according to the common understanding of the populace, seems to sound in the granting of authority; arg. ff. man. l. si vero non remuneram. §. interdicta. But assuming that he could obligate himself having considered the cause—namely, in redeeming the father, as in ff. solu. matri. l. quamuis, for this cause is pious and necessary—the question remains whether the statute ought to be understood indiscriminately, or whether this case ought to be excepted from the statute as if by natural reason, as in Auth. si captiui. And it must be said that either the statute provides a mode or form, and must be observed without distinction, as in ff. ad muni. l. quaestionibus; or it disposes something that natural reason abhors, and then it is understood according to the common law, as in C. de nox. l. si serui vestri, [and] de consue. c. cum dilectus.

† And this as to the first statute. There follows another statute, in which it is provided that contracts made with a son under paternal power, even with an oath, without the father's consent, are understood to be simulated. Concerning this, I say that if the father consents in any manner whatsoever, even if the consent is not valid, nevertheless the fiction of the statute ceases on account of the father's consent, as is noted in C. de his, qui. vt indi. l. polla; and therefore a doubt remains regarding the oath, because this statute does not seem to derogate from the common law in a case where the father's consent intervenes, but certainly it does in the case of minors, as the statute openly states. Consider therefore that this statute was made in hatred of creditors, for no other reason can be assigned; as in ff. de condi. inde. l. qui exceptionem; and an oath is of no effect with respect to that law which cannot be renounced, as in ff. de legat. 1. l. si quis inquilinos. §. fi. Since therefore the statute expressly reproves the oath, such an oath neither validates the action, as is noted in ff. de iu. pa. l. adigere. §. fi., nor impedes the proof of minority by witnesses, because the statute expressly provides this. Nor is this statute contrary to natural law in this regard, but rather contrary to positive law, as in C. si minor se maiorem dixerit. l. si alterius; and therefore the statute is valid. Consider that to swear concerning age is not to swear concerning a future giving or doing of a thing, but concerning the past; and these are very different things, as is noted in ff. de infa. l. Lucius. Furthermore, the mode of proof does not tend to the detriment of eternal salvation, because he did not swear that he would not prove it—namely, that he was of age—so that the authority of the statute can permit this, as is fully noted by the Moderns in l. si quis pro eo, de fideius., and more fully by the More Modern writers on C. de legibus. l. non dubium. In point of law, however, I do not doubt that minority has been proved, because one is not presumed to have been born after the marriage by the argument from what commonly happens, and because illicit intercourse is not presumed.
† And in proving age, not only evident proofs but also conjectures suffice, on account of the passage of a long time; as in ff. de probat. l. cum de aetate. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a natural or spurious son, while a legitimate and natural daughter is living, can be legitimated so as to succeed both in fiefs and in any other goods, notwithstanding the daughter. And number 2.
body: The case is as follows. A certain man has a wife, and a daughter by her. He also has a natural or spurious son by a certain woman.

† Now it is asked whether the aforementioned person can be legitimated, so that he may succeed both in fiefs, whatever their condition, and in other goods, notwithstanding that a legitimate daughter is still alive, etc. Regarding fiefs, we have such a text: "natural sons, even if they later become legitimate, are not called to the succession of a fief, either alone or with others." And there we have such a gloss: "What is said here about natural sons, I understand thus: unless these become legitimate so that they succeed in the fief, and this has been expressly stated by the Emperor, and thus by exception and privilege what would otherwise not be permitted is allowed, as in C. de precibus imperialibus offerendis, l. quotiens." And thus it happened in fact in Modena in the case of a certain Hugo against the Passamontes, as was reported. Whether, however, what the gloss says about natural sons applies to spurious sons, I answer: either the legitimation is by the aforementioned serene Emperor, or by another who has a sufficient mandate from the Emperor himself for this purpose; then it is the same as in the case of natural sons. Or another has a mandate from the Emperor to legitimize natural sons, and that does not extend to spurious sons, because they are not worthy of the name of sons: as in Auth. quomodo et quando, §. finalis, col. 7, and C. de natura liberorum, l. ultima. If, however, the question is whether a female daughter obstructs this legitimation, a distinction must be made: either it is a regular fief, in which females do not succeed, as in Io. Colla, qui feuda possideant, c. 1, §. hoc autem notandum; and then the legitimate female is not objected against. Or it is an irregular fief, because perhaps by pact it passes to a female; and then by the authority of the Lord Emperor the male succeeds together with the female, yet he does not exclude the female from making her portion: as appears from the common style of Imperial privileges, from which argument is to be drawn, as in ff. de peculio legato, l. si peculium, §. sicut. And what I said about the legitimation by the aforementioned Emperor, or by a count having power for this, is true in a secular fief; otherwise in an ecclesiastical one: because the Emperor cannot legitimize for this if the Church is the owner; because the jurisdictions of the Emperors and the Supreme Pontiffs are not only separate, but also obstructive: nor are they usurpable: as in extra, qui filii sint legitimi, cap. per venerabilem, and C. de testamentis, l. consulta diualia.

† Now it remains to consider allodial goods: and it must be said that the Emperor is accustomed to legitimize either by himself or through his commissioner, saving the right of the legitimate heirs in part. And the customs of princes, unless something else appears from their intent, ought to be regarded as constitutions, as in l. 3. §. fina. ff. de supel. leg. This is true when the legitimation takes place during the father’s lifetime, or after his death, before the daughter has intervened in the inheritance; otherwise, if by intervention she had acquired an irrevocable right: unless this was expressly disposed to her by the prince, the legitimation would not extend to goods which are not properly part of the inheritance: but are the daughter’s own goods, as ff. si certum peta. l. eius, qui in prouincia. §. penulti. and what is noted there, ff. de vulga. substi. l. sed et si plures. §. filio. ff. de separa. bon. l. 1. §. sciendum. de rescrip. cap. quamuis. lib. 6. de libe. et posthu. l. Gallus. §. et quidsi tantum. and there by the Moderators. And it supports what is said in leg. and no. C. de sen. pas. l. in quaestione testamenti. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, if the great-grandfather and the preceding ancestors received the fief for themselves and their descendants, both male and female, in perpetuity, the daughter is excluded from the succession to the said fief, whose father and grandfather received investiture only for themselves and their male children.
2. Whether the vassal, by renouncing the fief, prejudices the son to whom the succession belonged.
3. Whether the vassal, selling the fief to someone with an agreement to repurchase, forfeits his right if he did so without requesting the lord: and whether he prejudices
4. another succeeding to the said fief.
5. Whether by new investitures it is said that there has been a departure from the nature and quality of the old investitures.
6. Whether the resignation of the fief and the investiture made to another can be proved by witnesses.
body: It is proposed that the ancient investitures, dating back fifty years, were granted to sons and descendants, both male and female, in perpetuity. However, for the past fifty years, they have been granted to males only. From the last of these, namely Bartholomew de Saratico, was born and came into the world the lady Isolda, who is now living. She claims that, notwithstanding the investiture of her father and grandfather, which was limited to males only, she derives her right from the investiture of her great-grandfather and the ancients, from whose investitures the right was acquired for all their posterity and for both sexes. The question is asked whether the investiture of the ancients benefits her, or rather the investiture of the moderns, or more recent ones, i.e., of her grandfather and father, which was restricted to males only. And whether the custom, having gained strength over such a long time, should generate prejudice against the said lady Isolda. And this point is very doubtful.

For the nature of fiefs appears to be such that, on account of the father’s fault, prejudice arises to the son, as noted in c. 1, §. autem qui dominum, under the heading “What is the first cause of losing a benefice?” and in c. vassalli feudum, under the heading “If a vassal is deprived of his fief, to whom is it to be deferred?” where this is discussed at column 10. But a certain fault consists in neglecting one’s own rights and those of one’s children, abandoning the provision of the ancients, departing from it, and making new prejudicial contracts, as in D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. si quis ante, and C. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima. To the contrary, it is argued that in no chapter of the feudal law is it expressly stated that a father’s agreement can derogate from what a son holds by descent from his lineage, and not from his father; therefore, in this matter we must adhere to the written law, as in c. Albertus de orto, §. strenuus, under the heading “On the cognizance of fiefs,” column 10. But according to the common law, a father cannot deprive his children of a right acquired for posterity by privilege or antiquity, as in D. de interdictis et relegationibus, l. 3, and D. de contrahenda emptione, l. non tantum, §. si emancipatus. Moreover, this fief is permissive to both males and females, and it is an ancient fief; therefore, it ought not to change its former status by reason of the persons of the ancient successors, as in D. de verbis obligandis, l. 2, §. ex his, and C. de restitutione militum, l. qua parte, and in c. 1, §. si vero, under the heading “On investiture made of another’s property,” in the reason of itself, and by argument from D. de diuersis et temporibus praescriptionum, l. an vitium, §. ex facto. Furthermore, a female in fiefs appears to be appointed in default of males, and as a substitute after their death in their place. For the place of a female in the succession to a fief does not open as long as a male survives, since the one who was first invested with this fief, in c. qui sibi, under the heading “He who received investiture for himself and his male and female heirs,” column 10. It is certain, however, that a prior degree cannot generate prejudice to a substitute, nor can one transfer to another what is not purely in his own goods, as in C. comm. de legatis, l. si, §. si autem sub conditione, and Auth. res, quae. Moreover, custom does not avail, if any is said to have been introduced; for it is not true that this is a custom, but it would rather be a prescription, which cannot prejudice a woman to whom the place has not yet opened, as in C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus, §. si, and C. de annali exceptione, l. 1, §. ult. Moreover, these last investitures appear to have been made by error or by the imposition of bishops; which investitures indeed do not harm, as noted in c. 1, on the word “defend,” under the heading “On the fief of guardianship and castaldy,” column 10. And in doubt, error is presumed when someone does what he is not bound to do, unless certain knowledge appears, as in D. si quis cautio, l. sed et si quis, §. fin., and D. de probationibus, l. cum deinde. And if it is said that the son does not succeed to the fief unless he is an heir, as in c. 1, under the heading “Whether the son or agnate,” column 10, and if he is an heir, therefore he cannot come against his father’s contract, it is answered in three ways: first, because it is not to be simply conceded that in an ancient fief it is necessary that one be an heir, unless in the fief itself with its burdens, as noted in c. 1, §. haec quoque, under the heading “On the succession of fiefs,” column, unless the investiture speaks of heir-sons and not of descendants simply, as noted by Cynus, C. de operibus libris, l. liberti, libertaeque. Secondly, it is answered that one thing is the case with a female, another with a male. For a female does not come by the edict of succession, but precisely by agreement, as in c. 1, §. hoc autem notandum, under the heading “Who can give a fief,” from which agreement a useful action is acquired by virtue of a contract between living persons, as in D. de verbis obligandis, l. quodcunque, and D. de solutionibus, l. stichum, §. quaesitum. Thirdly, it is answered: because even an heir can come against the act of the deceased when it tends to defraud the heir of the benefit of the law, as noted in l. 1 and 2, C. si quid in fraudem patris. From which it is concluded that the said lady Isolda can come to the said fief by the investitures of her ancestors, and beyond. For in these it is not considered that she was conceived while that parent who was the beginning was alive, since it certainly passes to infinity, as in c. 1, §. hoc autem sciendum, under the heading “Who can give a fief,” and in c. vassalli feudum, under the heading “If a vassal is deprived of his fief, to whom is it to be deferred?” there where it says, “and even to infinity.” The second article of the question is this.

† Because it is alleged that the said Bartholomew, father of the lady Isolda, renounced the fief, and it is doubted whether the said renunciation would prejudice the said lady Isolda. And it must be said that a renunciation does not prejudice anyone other than the renouncing party himself. For him to whom the right is transferred by the death of the renouncing party, the refusal of the fief does not prejudice, as in c. 1, de alienatione feudorum, pars. For just as one extinguished by death does not prejudice another, so neither does one quasi-extinguished by refusal, as in c. 1, de vassallo decrepitaetatis. Where it is said that, notwithstanding the refusal, the fief is paternal. But to the refusing party himself, while he lives, the refusal does indeed prejudice, as in c. tres erant agnati, de eo qui finem fecit agnato de feudo. There it says, unless he refused the fief to the lord. Now follows the third doubt, and a very doubtful one is proposed,

† That the aforementioned Bartholomew, father of the said Lady Isolda, made a certain sale to a certain cortesía of the right of fief, with a pact of repurchase, without requesting the consent of the lord bishop. Whether by such a sale the fief reverted to the lord, even though sons were still living. And it seems expressly stated that it did, for the text says that if a vassal sins against his lord so grievously that he ought to forfeit the fief: the benefit shall not go to his nearest relatives, but shall revert to the lord, so that he may have at least this vengeance for his injury, as in c. 1, § denique, Quae fuit causa beneficii amittendi. And immediately it adds: If a vassal alienates a benefice contrary to the constitution of the Emperor Lothair of good memory, because he seems to despise his lord, the benefice pertains to the lord, it is written, so that he may acknowledge that he is depriving himself of the price and the benefice. And this appears to be one case in which one can prejudice his descendants and those of his ancestors, as in the title De prohibitione feudorum alienationis, per Federic, c. 1, § habito consilio, and § nos autem, and § callidis, where it says, they shall forfeit the fief, and it shall freely revert to the lord. And note, because it says freely, i.e., without any obstacle.

On the contrary, it seems that the said cortesía was in possession by the authority of the bishop, although invalidly; hence the said Bartholomew did nothing in contempt of the bishop, but rather for the confirmation of what had been done by the bishop; and therefore, although he prejudiced himself, he did not act against the nature of the fief; wherefore he did not prejudice his daughter after his death. Moreover, since he had renounced the fief, which renunciation harmed only himself and not his daughter, it immediately appears that he was not a vassal, and thus the sale was not made by a vassal. Hence the penalty of the said chapters, which speak of alienation made by a vassal, ceases to apply, by argument from ff. De militum testamento, l. Titius, and ff. De noxa, l. in delicto, § si extraneus. Also, he did not transfer any possession, as in ff. De verborum significatione, l. alienatum. Also, the pact of repurchase perhaps ought to have some effect, as in l. 2, C. De pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, and ff. De alienatione iudiciaria, l. ex hoc edicto, so that it may seem that he sold rather the advantages than the inseparable right itself, as is subtly noted in l. 1, C. Si pignus pignori datum sit. And these points are approved by the Papal privilege, which has the power to supply if there were any defect, l. 1, ff. Ad municipalia. And thus I say and advise.

As for the question whether the said fief is feminine, i.e., whether it descends to females in default of males, it seems to be answered that it is, considering the original and authentic documents. By argument drawn from the form of the contract: because the letter of the ancient investiture dictates this, hence there is no question about ancient investitures; for where there is the case of the instruments, as we say, there is the case of the law. C. De probationibus, l. cum precibus, and C. De surrogatione, l. ancillae, and ff. De publiciano, l. Caesar.

But the question is whether, through the new investitures, which are said to constitute a departure from the nature and quality of the old investitures in favor of males only, such a departure has occurred. And it seems that it has. For whenever something is added to or taken away from old agreements, a new agreement is created, and that which is confirmed by the new agreement must be observed, as stated in D. loc. cond. l. Cum in plures, § Legem dictam; and D. de praet. stip. l. Valerianus; D. de nov. oper. nunt. l. Omnes; C. de pact. l. Pacta novissima. Again, agreements that detract from or diminish obligations are believed to exist at least by way of exception, as in D. de contrah. empt. l. Pacta conventa. Therefore, since the person of the daughter was removed from the new investitures, they assumed a new form and cast off the old one, by the power and will of the contracting parties concurring, as in D. de acqu. poss. l. Si quis ante; and C. de nov. oper. nunt. l. Finis. And this appears to be true by argument from the contrary. For, on the contrary, if the first fief had been paternal, women could have been added in the new agreement; therefore, just as the new agreement is valid for adding, so it is for diminishing, as in D. de vulg. et pup. sub. l. Et si contra. Note that the understanding lies here. Suppose, for instance, that the ancient investiture stated "in males only"; I say that the new investiture could not state "in males and females simultaneously," but it could well state "in males, and in females upon the failure of males." For no one ought to have his right taken away, as in D. de pact. l. Finis; and C. loc. cond. l. Si cum heres; and D. de const. poss. l. Unde salsum; and D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. 2. Moreover, the father, who is the legitimate administrator of his children, cannot alienate the rights pertaining or to pertain to him with respect to immovable property, as in C. de bon. mat. l. 1; nor can any prescription run against them while they are in his power, as in C. de ann. exc. l. 1; and D. de acq. vel amitt. poss. l. 1. Furthermore, since there is no place for a woman in the fief while a male exists, therefore in the meantime prescription does not run against the women, as in C. cod. de del. l. Finis, § Si autem sub cond. From which it is concluded that the father could not depart, to the prejudice of the women, from the provision of the ancient parents, whereby a right of hope had been acquired for the daughters, as in D. de iur. patr. l. Divi fratres; and D. de contrah. empt. l. 3, § Si emancipatus; D. de interd. et rel. l. 3; and the argument in D. de bon. lib. l. Si in libertinum; D. de pact. l. Si unus, § Ante omnia; D. de iur. iur. l. 3, § Peculium; D. sol. matr. l. 2; and l. Non solum. Moreover, it must be considered whether the writing was obtained by suppression of truth (obreption). For an investiture partakes of the nature of grace, according to which I do not say simply, as in D. de obsequ. l. Titius; and noted in D. de aqua quot. et aest. l. 1, § Permittitur. And therefore, if there was any suppression of truth, this suppression should not harm the daughters, as in D. de in ius voc. l. Sed si hac, § Patronus.

† Subsequently, it must be considered whether the resignation of a fief and the investiture made to another can be proved by witnesses. Regarding resignation, we do not have a fully explicit rule; but concerning new investiture, it is certain that it cannot be proved except by peers of the court or by a tested writ, unless it were truly tested in a case of deditio, as in Collation 10, "What is investiture," ch. 1, in the beginning; and ch. 1, "Who are the witnesses necessary to prove a new investiture," same Collation; and in ch. 1, "On feudal castles"; and in ch. 1, "On controversy of investiture," in the gloss beginning "Who ought to be present." Beware: for this is false in the investiture of clerics, as in ch. 1, § "In the case of clerics," "If a dispute arises between lord and vassal regarding investiture," Coll. 10, where it is said that in the investiture of clerics peers of the court are not necessary; nevertheless, many suitable witnesses, free from all exception, are required, because great prejudice arises to the Church. In emphyteusis, however, an instrument is required; and therefore it is surprising that it is not so required in a fief, yet one cannot give a reason for customs.

Again, it is doubted: if a father sold a fief which, after his death, ought to come to his daughter, whether the daughter loses the fief upon the father’s death. For the gloss generally asks whether the father’s fault harms the son, in ch. 1, § 1, and § "Also, he who has the lord," which was the first cause of losing a benefice. And in this, it must be considered that some fault is purged by the law of contract; some, by the law of delict. If indeed it is purged by the law of contract, it harms the son who comes from that contract, namely, that of the offender; otherwise, if he comes from the contract of an innocent person; because the son coming in this case is not the successor of the defects from the father’s contractual fault; because he does not have his cause from him, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. Quocunque; and D. de divers. et temp. praescrip. l. An vitium, § Ex facto; and D. de senatu, l. Emancipa, § Final; and D. de adop. l. Si arrogator, § Sed an impuberi. But if the fault is purged by the law of delict, a distinction is made whether the delinquent is the lord himself or not, as in ch. 1, § "Finally," which was the first cause of losing a benefice.

The above is not obstructed by the same chapter, § "If the vassal," because from what is said there, "for a price," it appears that he speaks of a new fief; and perhaps of a fief that is not gentile, because a gentile fief is not given for a price. But it is acquired by the love and honor of the lord, as in ch. 1, "On a fief given in place of a commissory law," Coll. 10, Strenuus. Therefore, let the expert in the law retain the rigid customs of pacts within their terms, so that he does not go further; but where a case has arisen which is not comprehended by feudal custom, let him use the written law without calumny, as in ch. Obertus de Orto, § Strenuus, "On feudal cognizance," Coll. 10.

Concluding, I say that, considering the ancient investitures, the said lady has justice; since new investitures could not prejudice her; as in D. de pact. l. Si unus, § Ante omnia. Also, those who could not prejudice Lady Isolda by contract could not prejudice her by alienation; because he who cannot alienate by consenting cannot prejudice by offending, as noted in C. unde vi, l. Si quis in tantam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a spoliator is bound to make restitution to the one who was spoliated, if after a short interval he himself was also violently ejected or spoliated, and whether the spoliated party may sell the thing of which he was spoliated.
2. In the instrument of donation, there is not contained an action appropriate for damages and interest.
3. The sale is not void by operation of law, even though deception exceeding one-half intervenes.
4. Whether a donation made by a father of a certain thing to one or two of his sons, while others are still living, is valid.
1. Whether a donation of a certain thing made to sons is valid after a sale of the same thing has been made to another.
2. Whether, and when, if there is a controversy concerning a feudal thing, whether in the possessory or in the petitory, the ordinary judge of the place or the lord of the fief has cognizance.
body: A certain most noble man, named Jac. de Spinolis, lord of one half of the Castle of Saravalle, the town, and so forth, was called. It is said that he was dispossessed of this half by Lord Hannibal and his brothers; then, after a short interval, Lord Hannibal was, as is said, deposed and dispossessed of the said possession by Lord Ant. Spinola. It happened that Lord Ioan. sold his half to the said Lord Ant. for a certain price received therefrom, yet not descending to the due quantity of the price, but below half the just price. Furthermore, after the said sale, the said Lord Ioan. emancipated three of his sons, to whom, as a reward for emancipation, he donated the said half of the said place of Saravalle. Moreover, I say that after the death of the said Ioan., G. and R., who were the aforementioned donees of the said Ioan., and the said Lord Ant. Spinola compromised themselves to the said Philippus de Regio, who, at the command of the said Ant., by his award, paid to the said G. and R. a certain sum, and the said Castle and its possession remained with the said Lord Ant. From the foregoing, several doubts arise. First, whether the said Hannibal can be sued by the said G. and A. for the restitution of possession of the said Castle. Second, whether he can be sued by the same parties for damages and interest. Third, whether the said sale made to Ant. was valid, considering that a certain rescissory sentence was issued regarding the said sale in favor of the said G. and R. against the said Lord Ant., with the price not at all restored to the said Lord Ant. Fourth, whether the said emancipation and donation were valid, since the said Lord Ioan. had several sons and made the said donation after the aforementioned sale; and also, what effect the said donation could produce, assuming it was valid. Fifth, whether, by the compromise made with the said Lord Ant. and the subsequent award, and the satisfaction made to the said G. and R., who are now acting against the said Hannibal, any right of defense is prepared or acquired for the said Hannibal. Furthermore, it is asked what is the law if the said Castle were a fief of the Roman Empire and were entirely outside the jurisdiction of the commune of Genoa, namely, whether the statutes of Genoa have any effect in this matter, and whether the Genoese have any jurisdiction or cognizance in this matter against the said Spinolas, who are natives and have their domicile in the city of Genoa, who, however, are said to have left in a place more than exempt, namely, in a Genoese place entirely free to them, from which place they have no interruption, as in the law extra territorium, de iudiciis omnium iudicum. Now I come in order to the solution of the questions.

† Regarding the first point, it appears that the said Hannibal cannot be sued for restitution: because he is not liable for that which did not come into his possession, except within a useful year, as stated in the Digest, *De vi et vi armata*, law 1, in the beginning. But that which did not endure is not said to have come into his possession, as in the law *Si pro parte*, § *In rem versum*, Digest, *De in rem verso*. Furthermore, since the said Hannibal does not have the ability to restore the thing, he is therefore not bound to do the impossible, as in the Digest, *De rei venditione*, law *Si autem*, § *Possidere*. Moreover, he lost possession by fortuitous event or force majeure; therefore, he is discharged on account of the accident. On the contrary, it appears that a supervening accident does not discharge the wrongdoer: because he is liable for the accident due to his own fraud, even if the thing would have perished in the same manner in the hands of the plaintiff, by argument from law 1, § *Rectissime*, Digest, *De vi et vi armata*. Furthermore, it suffices that it came into his possession for a moment, although it subsequently ceased, unless perhaps he lost possession immediately and without any interval, as in the Digest, *Quod mei causa*, law *Si ipsa*; and thus, at the moment of acquisition, the right of obligation becomes perpetual. I come to the second point, and briefly say,

† That the action appropriate for damages and interest is not contained in the deed of donation, but only the right to one-half of the said Castle. And therefore it is certain that by virtue of the donation one cannot sue for damages or fruits concerning and relating to the time past before the donation itself, as in D. de actionibus, l. Iulius, § si fructibus, and it is expressly stated in D. quod vi aut clam, l. is qui in puteum, § si postea. It supports what is noted in D. de usufructu, l. defuncta, in principio.

† On the third point, it seems to be said that, although there has been deception exceeding one-half of the just price, nevertheless the sale is not void by operation of law, as l. 2, C. de rescind. vend. seems to indicate. It seems, however, to be said that an appeal should be taken from the rescissory sentence, as in Extra, de emptione et venditione, cap. Cum dilectus. But in this matter, it is necessary to examine the procedure and the sentence; otherwise, counsel cannot be properly given.

† Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that the existence of other children does not render the donation null, although it could sometimes be declared inofficious, as in l. Titia, §. Imperator, D. de legatis 2, and l. 1, C. de officiosa donatione. As for the passage concerning the fact that he made the donation after the sale, it must be said that the rights arising from the cause of the sale, which the aforementioned Doctor Antonius had ceded, could not be ceded again to the said donees, as in ff. de legatis 1, l. non quaecunque, §. qui Cayum. And therefore, the said donees, by virtue of the said cessions, remain in their position despite the aforementioned sale, nor does it seem that they can bring an action against the said Hannibal, because although the interdict unde vi may be ceded according to some authorities, it nevertheless cannot be ceded more than once, as in the aforementioned §. qui Cayum, because useful rights are entirely eradicated from the cedent by cession, as noted in ff. ad trebellianum, l. ex asse.

† On the fifth point, it seems to be said that if, by the law cited by the aforementioned Doctor Philip, it was fully satisfied for the said G. and R., they cannot further act, as in the law *illicite*, concerning their things. To the contrary, it seems, because this would be true if possession were restored to them; otherwise, if not restored, as fully in the law and notes in the law *nec ullam*, § *pe.*, D. de petitione hereditatis. On the sixth and last point, however, consideration should be given to the fief.

† First, concerning jurisdiction, whether the ordinary judge could take cognizance of a possessory action: which is affirmed, as noted in Extra, De iudiciis, chapter Certum. There, Bertolus states that a possessory action may be cognized by the ordinary judge. Others say that it cannot be cognized except by the said lord of the fief. And this question is not easily determined. I, however, say thus: either the dispute is between feudatories, and the lord of the fief takes cognizance, who can and must judge between them according to the laws of the fief, even if the action is brought by interdict for recovery of possession; because on both counts the feudatory is subject to his lord. Or the dispute is between a feudatory and a non-feudatory, and then, whatever possessory action is brought, and whether the feudatory is dispossessed by a non-feudatory or vice versa, cognizance does not pertain to the lord of the fief; because he has no jurisdiction over either party, and because the laws of fiefs do not apply to non-feudatories, and therefore the ordinary judge takes cognizance, namely the local authority, as in Codex, Ubi de possessione agi oportet, law 1. Note, however, that even if a criminal action were brought between feudatories, the lord would not take cognizance as lord of the fief, unless he otherwise possessed *merum imperium* (full jurisdiction), but the ordinary judge would take cognizance. Digest, De iudiciis, law Solemus, section Latrunculator. In a petitory action, however, either both claim to be feudatories, and the lord takes cognizance; because it is a matter of fief. Or only one claims to be a feudatory, and then the ordinary judge takes cognizance, and this is the truth. However, as I hear, in the city of Genoa it has often been observed and pronounced that cognizance cannot be taken except by the lord of the fief; hence, one must adhere to custom. As for alienations, it would be necessary to examine them. But since they were made between co-heirs, or between the agnates themselves, it suffices to refer to what is stated and noted in the 10th Collation, in Chapter 1, De alienatione feudi paterni, where it is said that they may alienate among themselves. Which, indeed, is to be understood as fully noted in my latest lecture. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the libel is to be drawn up in matters of spoliation.
2. The word "then," what it signifies.
3. No interdict is sworn in, nor any condition.
4. By how many remedies one may proceed against the invader.
5. How the word "occupy" is to be understood.
6. When a son under paternal power is sued on account of a delict, whether he may be in court without the consent of his father.
7. Whether an oath excuses from the reimbursement of expenses.
8. Whether a probable error excuses from the reimbursement of expenses in the principal cause and in the appeal.
9. Whether, and when, an appeal may or may not be taken from a sentence rendered in a possessory action.
body: The words of the libel presented before the learned man, Master John Bernat of Braid, by Andrea and John, son of the late Antonio Richi of Cherio, against and opposed to Antonio, son of the late Giacomo Vachii, and Daniel, son of the aforementioned Antonio, are substantially as follows: Although the said Andrea and John had been in possession of certain lands for long periods, and had also held and peacefully possessed the same from the year of our Lord 1388, in the month of October of that year, both before and after, and although they pertained and belonged to them by right, nevertheless the aforementioned Antonio and Daniel, to whom no right pertained, rashly and in fact invaded and occupied the said lands and trees, and ordered and caused them to be occupied and invaded, and hold them occupied, and also uprooted them. And it is added that, with their presumptuous audacity against God and justice, they held them despoiled, etc. And the conclusion of the libel is as follows: Wherefore they ask that it be pronounced and declared that the said plots of land, and their possession, pertained and belonged during the current year of our Lord 1388, and before and after, and also now pertain and belong by right to the aforementioned Andrea and John, the plaintiffs; and that the said Antonio and Daniel had no right, nor do they have any right, in and upon the said plots of land, and that they ought to be removed from the detention, occupation, and possession of the said plots of land. And that the said Andrea and John ought to be admitted, restored, and reintegrated into the possession of the said plots of land; and not only that, but that the aforementioned Antonio and Daniel, as each of them is concerned, be condemned to restore, etc.

† On this petition, therefore, it is doubted whether this petition is properly or improperly framed as regards the possessory judgment. And it seems that it is properly framed: because in the said petition it is contained that the said Anto. and Daniel temerarily and by force invaded and occupied; and also commanded to be occupied and invaded, and hold occupied, the lands and places aforesaid, and that they held the said Andreonum and Ioannonum despoiled against God and justice. Moreover, the despoiled party is to be restored immediately, as the law and note, ff. de vi, et vi armata, l. 1, § 1, in the gloss which begins, est. n. spoliatus statim restituendus. and C. ad l. Iul. de vi publica vel privata, l. si quis ad se fundum. and de agris et censibus, l. si coloni. and C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si maritus. and C. locato, l. si quis conditionis. and C. unde vi, l. inuasor. and l. non ab re. And the reason is, because the despoiler always sins until he restores the thing; and therefore, unless he purges his fault and crime, he ought not to be heard on the property or any other right of his, as the law and note, 2 q. 1, c. in primis and in c. frequens, de restitutione spoliatorum, lib. 6. Furthermore, against despoilers a simple complaint suffices: as is the notable gloss, 1 q. 4, c. quia praesulatus. If, therefore, the spoliation is proved, the judge rightly ordered the possession to be restored. To this effect, ff. de officio praesidis, l. illicitas, § ne potentiores. and what is noted, C. de servo fugitivo, l. cum servum quis. That the possession and spoliation are proved is shown by the fact that it says the actors proved that they possessed before the spoliation. Also that the occupation followed: from which it is presumed that they possessed up to the time of occupation, as ff. de acquisitione possessionis, l. clam possidere, § qui ad nundinas. For no one is presumed to renounce possession or otherwise cease to possess, unless it is proved, or unless the former possessor himself alleges it, as fully noted by the Moderns, C. de probationibus, l. sive possidetis. Certainly possession has something of right in itself, as ff. uti possidetis, l. 1, in fine, plurimum ex iure possessio mutatur, as ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. possessio quoque, in principio. and note, ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. 1, in principio. although it consists principally in fact, as ff. si servus venditus, l. 2. and is noted, ff. de verbis obligatis, l. stipulatio ista, § hoc quoque. Moreover, possession has many benefits in itself, Inst. de interdictis, § commodum. to which rights and benefits no one of sound mind is presumed to renounce or yield, as extra de renuntiatione, l. super hoc. It is made by what is noted, 16 q. 4, c. volumus. and by Dynus, ff. de manumissione testamento, l. mea. and l. 1, ff. soluto matrimonio, per Dynus and others. Since, therefore, the despoiler is not to be supported in his crime, the said petition ought to be considered valid, and is especially supplied in a declaratory manner by the proofs made and conclusive. Argument, C. de iudicibus, l. licet. and what is noted, ff. de deposito, l. 1, § si quis argentum. But to the contrary, that the said petition was improper, as regards the possessory recovery, or any canon for reintegrating possession, or even in the triticaria action, as ff. de conditione triticaria, l. 1 and 2, it seems clearly proved, because by any of these modes violence is alleged at least from the beginning, and the judgment must be founded upon it. But the law provides that when violence is alleged, fraud is alleged, as the law and note, ff. de vi, et vi armata, l. 1, § ad solam autem. Therefore, the place and time must be alleged in the petition. i.e., the time when the plaintiff was ejected. Also that he possessed at that time, as ff. de vi, et vi armata, l. 1, § rectissime. and there by Bartolus, whose words are these: Note that you must allege in the petition the time when you were ejected, and that you had the lost things there at the time of ejection. and by Innocentius in c. qualiter, de accusatione, Bartolus. But in the said petition no certain time of ejection is alleged, although the time of possession is alleged. Therefore the said petition is improper: because it lacks the substantial elements of the form. Argument, ff. de accusationibus, l. libellorum, § quod si libelli. and what is noted by Innocentius, extra de privilegio, c. ex parte abbatissae. Furthermore, those words, "held despoiled," are not sufficient for the propriety of the petition: because I can hold someone despoiled, and not have despoiled him, as ff. de usucapione, l. fur, § fundi. Also spoliation happens in many ways. Moreover, the beginning of the spoliation must be examined, as ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. clam possidere, in principio. and from that beginning the action arises, not from the continuation of the crime, as ff. de furtis, l. inficiando, § infans. and ff. de iureiurando, l. qui iurasse, § si pater. and note, eadem titulus, l. eum qui, § in popularibus. This petition, therefore, was defective, because it does not contain in which month the spoliation was made; indeed, the text seems to require that the day be expressed.

† This number signifies the *dictio*, which is then placed in the edict of the praetor. Argument: D. de vi, et vi armata, l. 1, §. interdum autem hoc. Certainly, if the libellus (complaint) is defective, it can never be supplied by the adequacy of the proofs, from which point the exception of defectiveness was appended. In this number, it is beneficial to append it, so that the remainder of the procedure may not be valid as being entirely defective, as noted by Innocentius in c. 1, X. de officio vicarii, and according to the Speculum and the noted authorities in X. de iudiciis, c. examinata, in the Novellae. For such proofs appear to have been received before the joinder of issue (*litis contestatio*), since the joinder of issue does not appear to hold, because the libellus is defective, as D. de officio assessoris, l. 1; C. de formulis, l. 2. Nor do I find that mention is made therein of a specific time, i.e., of the spoliation, but I do find that mention is made of time in general, i.e., in the cloud, and during the times of possession. Likewise, I find that the time was appended during which the occupied property is detained, i.e., the time of the libellus. But because this is not the time of spoliation, the preceding allegation of defectiveness remains. The form of libelli must be observed, and if it is not observed, the libellus is null. D. de dolo, l. item exigit; and D. de iniuriis, l. praetor edixit. And even assuming there were some defect, it ought to be rejected by the judge; hence, if the judge pronounced the libellus adequate, one could rightly appeal to the superior as from a grievance, as D. de minoribus, l. ait praetor, §. permittitur, and as from a right disapproved, because all imprudence of law in a judge giving an interlocutory decision is held to be a grievance. The text is there noted. And although one could not appeal from a mere possessory action, nevertheless this article of the defectiveness of the libellus is separate from the cause of possession, because it is not a question of possession, but of procedure. Hence, we adhere to the common rule, which is that one can appeal from a sentence passed on the text of a defective libellus, as X. de emptione et venditione, c. cum dilectus. Nor is it new that one does not appeal from a possessory action. And yet, from certain interlocutory decisions passed in the instance of a possessory judgment, one can appeal, as noted by Guillaume in D. de minoribus, l. si ex causa, §. nunc videndum. And this is clear from what is said and noted in l. 1, C. de appellationibus. Hence, although one does not appeal from a sentence passed in the cause of the appeal, nevertheless one appeals from a sentence passed in the mode of proceeding, as D. de liberali causa, l. liberis, §. si; and D. de iudiciis, l. si de vi. Many other things are also alleged, that the said libellus is defective, notwithstanding that the words "invaded" and "occupied" are appended in the said libellus; because from this it does not follow that it was by violence, as C. unde vi, l. cum quaerebatur. Likewise, he who pronounced the sentence seems to have spoken quite defectively concerning the said libellus, saying that the said libellus could conclude in various actions and remedies, and he named certain actions and remedies which seem to have little bearing on the proposal, nor do I pursue the multiple allegations made on this point, although they were very subtle and prudent. Solution: Here it must be observed that, although it seems that the month should be stated in the said libellus as in a criminal case, because dolus (fraud) is alleged, argument in c. praesentium, X. de testibus, lib. 6, and the aforementioned l. item exigit, nevertheless the ancient drafters of libelli, such as Rosfredus and the Speculator, intend nothing else in the libellus than what suffices to say: "I complain of such a one, who violently and rashly deprived me of the possession of such a vineyard or place, which place and vineyard he detains as occupied. Wherefore I ask, etc." As is clear in Spec. de restitutione spoliorum, §. spoliatus, near the beginning. It is supported by X. de restitutione spoliorum, c. cum ad sedem, and c. saepe, and 2 q. 7 c. notum, and X. de probationibus, c. licet causam. And afterwards in the procedure, the specific time of spoliation and the possession at that time will be proved. And those things which have always had a certain custom of drafting libelli must not be changed.

And because no interdict brings infamy, as noted in C. de interdictis, l. incerti, and l. 3 de vi, et viarum; nor does any action on a stipulation, as in ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Caesar, and the note in l. certi conditio, in principio, ff. si certum petatur; therefore, it is not necessary to say anything else, except that he was dispossessed of the possession of the thing which he then possessed. The laws which speak of the insertion of a month in the libel speak in a criminal or infamous case, and thus they do not stand in the way. And this is the more equitable and just opinion: because we ought to consider the reality of the matter rather than excessive subtlety, notwithstanding the most prudent allegations made to the contrary.

† Furthermore, it should be known that a direct interdict *unde vi* is granted against an invader who acts with dolus (fraud). However, if the invasion is without dolus, the invader is bound to restore possession, as noted in the gloss beginning *quod est* on § 1 of l. 1, ff. *de vi et vi armata*. Moreover, a *condictio triticaria* is granted, and indeed any condictio degenerates against the defendant by analogy to a thief, as stated in l. *si*, ff. *de usufructu quemadmodum caveatur*, and as noted in § *rex si pignori* of l. *si quis nec causam*, ff. *si certum petatur*. And by this means, certain allegations made against the libel are removed.

† It is also to be noted that the word *occupare* sometimes refers to vacant possession; and then it does not imply violence, unless perhaps in resisting, so that possession is not taken away by force.
