Sometimes it concerns non-vacant possession, but which the plaintiff says he held at the time of occupation; and then it directly signifies expulsive violence in movable property, and abductive violence in movable property, as in D. de vi et vi armata, l. 1, § item Labeo, in the gloss beginning *cum dominus*. It is therefore concluded from the above that the said libel, as regards its aptness, can be sustained, that it was aptly conceived. To this effect is the doctrine of Bartolus in l. haeredibus, § in hac, de dolo, whose words are these, to be noted very diligently: that when a civil action is brought, which is infamous, the month must be stated, just as when a criminal action is brought, as in X. de procuratoribus, c. tuae, and de iniuriis, l. praetor. But if it were an action arising from a civil delict, which does not bring infamy, this would not be necessary, as is said there in metu, and is proved in l. Neratius, § si, ad l. Aquiliam. These are the words of Bartolus. Also, as I said, temerity suffices; therefore, in a civil action, it is not necessary to state the place and time in the libel, as noted in c. Abbate, de re iudicata, lib. 6.

Secondly, the principal doubt arises because the son of a free man was a party in this lawsuit, and it is said that he did not have his father’s consent, and thus the judgment did not hold, as stated in l. si, §. necessitate, C. de bonis quae liberis. Whether this is true: and it can be said that the father’s consent is not necessary when the son is sued for a delict, according to the common opinion of the Doctors. Moreover, it is special in the case of momentary possession, at least in the interdict for recovery, in which exceptions based on mere technicalities of law are not admitted, because the dispossessed party must be immediately restored, and one should not proceed through evasive, dilatory, and frivolous exceptions, as in C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. 1, and C. qui legitimam personam, l. momentaneae. Furthermore, he had his father’s consent, who gave him consent and mandate for conducting the common lawsuit, as in ff. qui in rem suam, pig. vel hypo. sol., l. si Titius, in the word “consensu mutuo.” It is therefore established that the parties were legitimate. Now it remains to come to the merits of the case, presupposing as true in fact that the plaintiffs were dispossessed of their possession. For due to the multitude of documents and various occupations, it was not possible to fully examine the testimonies and allegations of both parties. They seem to presuppose this as true: and therefore the dispossessed must first of all be restored, as has been said; nor does it matter that the defendants claim to have had title and just cause, because they did not have a cause from anyone by whom possession could be taken from them without their being named and cited, as noted by Innocentius, extra, ut litis non contestatae, c. quoniam frequenter. And therefore those who were wrongfully dispossessed must be restored to their possession, as in C. unde vi, l. meminerint, and noted in l. si quis in tantam, in the large gloss, and C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. si, and 2 q. 1, c. in primis. And therefore the judgment was rightly given, and the appeal wrongly made, presupposing, as I have said, that it was proven that the plaintiffs were dispossessed and the defendants occupied. For even if such a cause excused them from dolus, it does not excuse them from the restitution of another’s possession, as has been said.

† Another point is touched upon, namely whether an oath excuses one from the reimbursement of expenses. The glossators commonly say that it does, for the reasons set forth in D. de iureiurando, l. 3, § proderitque. But William of Cunaeus and Butrigarius hold the contrary: because when an oath follows a judgment, the oath vanishes, as in D. de iureiurando, l. nam postea, § si damnatur. And so the modern authors commonly hold, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. generaliter, and C. de iudiciis, l. properandum, § siue autem. But it must be said in this matter that it is a question of discretion depending on the quality of the case. For if indeed the defendant persisted in good faith, or at least was not in bad faith, because the case was doubtful in law or in fact, certainly he ought not to have left his right undiscussed, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. illud. But nevertheless this does not apply to the invader, in whom fraud or gross negligence is presumed, as in C. unde vi, l. meminerint. But if someone did not invade from the beginning, but succeeded the invader, and he believed himself to possess justly, just ignorance excuses him until the cognition of the truth is found to have been agitated, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. qui alterius. And concerning this reimbursement of expenses in our case, I say that which the ordinary gloss says in c. ignorantia, de regulis iuris, lib. 6, and according to that gloss in this part I give my advice. The words of the gloss are these.

† Although in the principal cause a probable error excuses one from the reimbursement of expenses, in the cause of appeal the loser is indiscriminately condemned to pay the expenses to the winner. But Accursius says otherwise. C. de reb. cred. l. generaliter. §. 1. But that gloss of Johannes Andreae must be understood as applying to expenses incurred in the cause of appeal. Note

† However, it is to be noted that in our case the appeal was frivolous, as established in C. si de momen. pos. l. 1, and this is so according to the second rule, ll. idem secundum cano., unless a reasonable cause for appealing was expressly stated in the appeal. And this rule of canon law is much more equitable, and in accordance with the strictness of civil law; indeed, if it were permissible to speak of mitigating injustice, where a definitive pronouncement is made in a possessory action against the plaintiff, or against the defendant who has no other remedy, nevertheless the letter of the law and authority dictate otherwise, to which we must adhere. And on this point, see extra de resti. spo. c. cum ad sedem, and in c. Ro. §. si autem, de appel. li. 6. Therefore, I conclude by saying that the appeal from the sentence rendered in the aforementioned possessory action was frivolous; yet in one case the appeal would be justified, and indeed restitution would be granted, namely, when the sentence was rendered out of enmity, or through the fraud of the judge, or his gross negligence; because such matters are worthy of correction and should not remain unexamined and uncorrected, as noted in ff. ad treb. l. seruo inuito, §. cum pretor, and there the singular gloss. Finally, I beg you that next time you do not send me so many sheets of paper; for I am not occupied so much by the reading of a larger book, i.e., an old one, as by the writing of your letters. But send me points and legal doubts, and I offer myself ready to all that pleases you. Commend me most highly to the Magnificent and Illustrious Prince, and my most singular lord, the Lord Prince of Achaea. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the term "paternal uncle" includes only the uterine brother of the father, and thus on the side of cognates; and what applies in a statute excluding the mother from the succession of her son when a paternal uncle exists. See nos. 4 and 5.
2. In a statute, the reason is always presumed.
3. The word "or," and what it signifies.
body: The statute of the city of Florence, placed under the rubric “how a woman succeeds intestate,” provides as follows: No woman may succeed intestate to her deceased sons or daughters, if there exist from the person of the deceased any natural and legitimate son, grandson, or great-grandson, or father, paternal grandfather, paternal uncle, brother, sister, or nephew through a full brother; nevertheless, she may receive and obtain maintenance from the goods of such deceased, if she had no other means by which to support herself suitably. Now it has happened that there were two half-brothers related only through the mother; from one of whom there remained a son under puberty, who died, his mother and the aforementioned uterine brother of his father surviving. Now the question of succession arises between the said uterine brother and the mother, and it is asked who is to be preferred intestate. And presupposing, without prejudice to the truth, that the said statute applies to a person under puberty, on which point I am now asked for my opinion, it remains only to see

Whether the aforementioned statute, which speaks of an uncle, should be understood, considering its words and intent, to refer to the said carnal brother of the father, who is a maternal brother and not a paternal one. And the question rests on this: whether an uncle can properly be called one who is of the line of cognates and not of agnates. Placentinus said that he cannot; whose opinion is held by Cynus. But Johannes and the ordinary gloss say the contrary, not only in the case of a nearest uncle, but also in the case of a great-uncle. This is held by the gloss in C. de successionibus edictis, l. si mater. And certainly regarding this, in him who is commonly called Zius, of whom in Auth. de haereditatibus ab intestato, § 1, who is a third-degree collateral nephew, there does not seem to be any doubt, because uncle, i.e., father’s brother, is to be understood in two ways, from the father or from the mother, as in ff. de gradibus, l. iurisconsultus, § 3, gradu. For an uncle is the brother of the father, whether he is the father’s brother united on both sides, or consanguineous only, or uterine only. And this is true when it is stated simply, and not under the reason of agnation. Now therefore it remains to be seen whether preference would be given under the reason of agnation expressly stated, or presumed by law. And by those things noted by Cynus, according to Jacobus de Arena, in l. 1, C. de adulteriis, such statutes seem to be founded on the presumed privilege of agnates, or of the male line, by which the dignity of families is preserved, as in l. 1, ff. de venditionibus insipientibus. Moreover

† In a statute, the reason is always presumed, as noted in the last chapter of *de regulis iuris*, book 6, according to Dynus. But to exclude the mother on account of such an uncle, no reason can exist, neither natural equity nor civil; therefore, it is not understood that the statute provides for what lacks reason, by argument from the Digest, *de pactis*, law *tale pactum*, § *si*, and what is noted there. Moreover, the words say, "paternal or maternal grandfather," from which it is tacitly understood that it refers to a similar uncle, i.e., one who is on the side of the agnates, by argument from the Digest, *de vi legum*, law *si*, § *cui dulcia*. To this effect is that common principle, which provides that one altar should not be covered and another left uncovered, as noted in the Code, *qui potestatem pignoris habent*, law *assiduis*, § *acceptis*. For since both are merely cognates and not agnates, the mother ought to be preferred by the strongest reason, as in the Digest, *de inofficioso testamento*, law *nam et si parentibus*. Furthermore, another section of the statute contains that what has been said about the mother applies to all and each of those related or connected to any person, whether male or female, dying through the maternal line, or from the mother's side. For

† If the word "or" is used in an expansive sense: since this uncle is related through his mother's line, he does not succeed. But if it is used in an explanatory sense, that is, then it does not touch our case. Regarding this, it must be said that when the word "or" is placed between different things, it is used in an expansive sense, as in the Digest, De auro et argento legato, l. Si quis ita legaverit. But when it is placed between things, one of which comes under the position of the other, then it is used restrictively, or at least declaratively, as noted there. But if it can be used in both ways according to the text of that law, l. Si quis ita, it is used in an expansive sense, and so it seems in our case. Therefore, the statute appears to consider only the male progeny and to grant principal favors. This

† The question is highly doubtful, because the word "patruus" (paternal uncle) is ambiguous. And if you say that this person is a maternal uncle, not a paternal one, certainly, on the contrary, he is a paternal uncle: because the father's brother, considered with respect to the nearest root, is paternal, although considered with respect to the more remote root he is maternal. Nevertheless, I am more inclined to the opinion that he does not exclude the mother, on account of the intent of the statute: because the statute, although it does not specify which uncles are meant, nevertheless all the words above and below in the said statute refer to agnates. See the argument from the Digest, l. si, §. cui dulcia, de vi legum. And because the statute does not wish to grant a prerogative to the genus of cognation: therefore, cognates are left to each other according to the common law. See the argument from the Digest, de excusationibus tutorum, l. sed et milites, in principio. Thirdly, moreover, in the heading of the said statute it is provided as follows: "But uterine brothers, or others born from the female line, cannot succeed, etc." But that provision does not operate against the mother, because the mother is not born from the female line, but is the principle of generation. And therefore it seems to me that in the said succession the said mother is preferred. That which must not be omitted is that if a brother does not succeed a uterine brother, therefore neither does he succeed any descendant of him, as in the tenth column, qui feudum dare possunt, §. hoc autem notandum. And this reasoning decides the question against the said uncle. Whether

† That the brother uterine of the father is included under the term "paternal uncle," as far as the interpretation of words is concerned, is prudently alleged. For even in the mere line of cognates a paternal uncle is found, and not only the immediate one, but also the distant one, as in the noted case, C. de success. edict. l. si mater. Although Placentinus there wished to assert the contrary, saying that in the mere line of agnates one is not properly called a paternal uncle, but a maternal uncle: or by some general name of his, namely Zius, as in Auth. de haered. ab intesta. § 2. But the opinion of Placentinus is not true, although Cynus holds it there; for the contrary would be against the intent of the speaker. For the interpretation of words never has such force that it should prevail over the better sense, as in C. de lib. praet. vel exh. l. 3, and ff. de excus. tut. l. scire oportet, § et si maxime. This chapter of the statute provides as follows: "But uterine brothers, or others born from the female line, cannot succeed to any one or several of their uterine brothers, if there exist any or several relatives on the father's side, at least up to the fourth degree inclusive." Therefore, those who are agnates beyond the fourth degree do not exclude closer cognates; and this is due to the restrictive wording "up to," and also because, since the said agnates up to the fourth degree exclude closer cognates contrary to the common law, certainly in the case omitted in the said statute we must follow the common law, as in § de viro, and l. si cum dotem, and in Auth. de haer. ab intesta, § ex his. From which it is concluded that the said Peter is preferred to agnates more remote than the fourth degree, on account of the prerogative of degree, as in Auth. post fratres. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a universal fideicommissary may cede or donate the right of fideicommissum before restitution has been made to him; and whether he may bring an action for things alienated before restitution has been made to him.
2. A son who has alienated some property is presumed to have alienated it for his legitimate portion.
3. The son deducts two fourths.
4. Things alienated for paying debts, or usury, or things wrongly taken away are not imputed to the son in his legitimate portion.
5. These words, "under the condition," when they make a condition; and when they make a mode.
body: Pepus Nicolutii made a will, in which he instituted as his universal heirs John Petrutii and Pepus Ciuelli, his nephews. And if any of the aforementioned nephews should die in pupillary age, or at any time without legitimate and natural children: that then the goods of the deceased should devolve to the other survivor: and he substituted them mutually. And if both should die without children legitimately descending from them, he willed and left that all his aforesaid goods, each and every one, should remain and ought to remain to the lady Philippa, and the lady Jacoba, and the lady Joanna, his daughters, in equal portions. And he substituted them mutually to each other in the said case: provided that the said his daughters are bound and ought to build one hospital, where it seemed to them convenient, and to give and pay for the said hospital being made 5000 li. This will was made on the 27th day of the month of March, 1337. After this, the testator died, the said his nephews and the said his daughters surviving him. Finally, Pepus Ciuelli, nephew of the said testator, died without children, the said John Petrutii, his cousin brother, surviving him. Finally, the aforementioned ladies Philippa and Jacoba, daughters of the testator, died. Finally, the aforementioned John Petrutii died without children, the aforementioned Joanna, daughter of the aforementioned testator, surviving him. Finally, the said lady Joanna, saying that the inheritance of the said testator pertained to her by virtue of the aforementioned substitution by title of donation, and inter vivos: donated with the burden of building the hospital to Nicholas Toldoli, her son, all her rights and actions which she had in the said inheritance of the said Pepus the testator, and of the said his nephews. Finally, the said John made a will, in which he instituted the hospital of mercy as universal heir. And in codicils he bequeathed to Peter Carlucii, his cousin brother, one house, with a certain tower, etc. Now the heirs of the said Nicholas demand the said house and other goods of the said inheritance. It is asked, whether they can.

It must be premised for the sake of clarity that a universal fideicommissum cannot be restored to anyone other than the universal fideicommissary. Therefore, it cannot be assigned, nor can this right be donated, since the donation in question was impossible and void by operation of law. The text is literal: D. de iure dotium, l. Si mulier, §. Ex asse, where it is expressly stated that a universal fideicommissum cannot be restored to a procurator appointed for his own interest. Since, therefore, the fideicommissum in question is universal, it follows that before the restoration made to the said Dame Jacoba, it could not be donated or assigned, as is noted in D. ad Trebellianam, l. Qui ita, §. 1, according to the gloss and Dynus. It is established that the universal fideicommissary, before the inheritance has been restored under the Trebellian law, has no real action for claiming the hereditary property, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. Facta and l. Restitutam, and C. eod., l. Penultima. And if it is said that property alienated by the heir can be claimed by the universal fideicommissary without restoration having been made, as noted in D. ad Trebellianam, l. Marcellus, §. Res quae, let the discerning reader observe that it is true that restoration of those specific things is not required, but rather universal restoration is required in order to obtain certain particular things; yet he would not thereby assume the hereditary burdens. This is ridiculous and contrary to the will of the testator and the dispositions of the law, because restoration under the Trebellian law is not divisible, nor is the Trebellian succession itself, as in d. l. Restituta, in principio. Moreover, these things were not alienated at the time of the concession, nor was there any hope of claiming any thing from future alienations; and therefore such a right is not included in the assignment, because those words, “all his rights and actions which he has,” speak of rights that were then in existence, and not of those arising from a future and unknown cause, as noted in C. quae res pignori obligatae poni possunt, l. Ultima, and D. de legatis 2, l. Si ita scripsisset, and D. de verbis obligatis, l. Si a colono. For those words, “which he had,” are in the present tense. Likewise, those words, “saying that the inheritance pertains to him,” are in the present tense and do not include the future, as in the aforementioned laws. Moreover, the said donation was universal and void; therefore, it produces no effect, because it had an impossible and vitiated beginning, as in the rule, Quod ab initio, with similar authorities. Furthermore, it must be considered that the testator did not make a substitution simply and purely, but conditionally, or at least subject to a mode, in the fulfillment of which there was a preceding delay, and it ceased to be possible to fulfill. And then I argue thus: when the fulfillment of a mode is prevented by a preceding delay, the legacy is vitiated, as in C. de conditionibus insertis, l. Ultima. But here it formally ceased to be possible to fulfill due to the death of all the daughters; because they cannot choose a place, nor agree on a place after death, as required by the words of the testament, as in D. de manumissionibus testamenti, l. Si ita. Moreover, even if the mode fails by chance, the legacy fails, if it appears that the testator would not have left it otherwise. This is presumed if the mode was for pious causes; because the place is presumed to have been inserted in place of the final cause. This is the same as saying that the testator would not otherwise have left it, as in D. de donationibus, l. 2, §. Si. But when the precise mind of the testator is apparent, who inserted that mode into the substance of the substitution; because he said, “I substitute, provided that,” i.e., “not otherwise,” D. de manumissionibus testamenti, l. Mevia. For the word “I substitute” is the substantial root, upon which the mode is founded. Moreover, it must be known that it is absurd for the praetor to give more to him who claims the fideicommissum than the testator willed, D. ad Trebellianam, l. Facta, §. Si praetor, vers. Plus. Hence, one ought not to claim more than the testator willed. Hence, it must be noted first that “not to claim” implies a condition. But whether “not to claim” itself carries a mode. Whatever, therefore, it is, whether a condition, and this has failed, as in C. de conditionibus insertis, l. Legatum, or a mode, and then its nature is final and executory, the legacy is without effect, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, in rubrica. Moreover, when the testator orders a hospital to be built, it seems that a year is appointed, as in Auth. de ecclesiis et titulis, §. Si quis aedificatorem. Hence, after the year has elapsed, he is repelled from the judgment of the deceased, as noted in Auth. de hereditate et falcidia, §. Si quis autem non implens, and Extr. de testamentis, c. Nos quidem and c. Si heredes, and C. de episcopis et clericis, l. Nulli. For he seems to have invited them to the fideicommissum who use their judgment, not the contrary, as in D. de legatis 2, l. Cum pater, §. Libertis, vers. Eos, and C. de fideicommissis, l. Quaestionem, in fine. There remains another article,

† namely, that the son, or grandson, or his heir is presumed to have alienated for his legitimate portion, which he may deduct in a single thing, if such deduction concurs with the discretion of a good man: just as a creditor has the discretion to be paid or to choose, as in Auth. de restitutione et ea, quae parit. §. quamobrem. And thus it has often been consulted. Hence, since the hospital was the universal heir, it could sell up to the legitimate and Trebellianic portions in a single thing: as in ff. de legatis 1. l. non amplius. §. si. cum l. seq. Moreover, the heir of the heir could effectively alienate the universal fideicommissum, although he himself is bound to the price, as in l. si. §. si. ff. de legatis 2. because the price in universals succeeds in place of the thing, as in ff. de petitione hereditatis l. si ad rem, et precium. And fully noted, C. de rei venditione l. mater. But it must not be omitted, that if the condition could still be fulfilled, it should be fully fulfilled, and therefore it should be fulfilled; and by paying interest to the poor at the discretion of the bishop, it should be declared, because it does not have a certain quantity or nature of itself, as in C. de senatu l. 1. For delay is committed to the poor by the thing itself, just as to minors, as in ff. de legatis 2. l. Titia Seyo. §. usuras. For the poor are considered uncertain in place of minors, indeed in place of infants, who do not have understanding, as in C. de episcopis et clericis l. orphanotrophos. And hospitals are of the same decree, therefore it follows what follows from the premises. Furthermore

† Nor should it be called into doubt whether the Falcidian or Trebellian deduction may be made; for on this point there is today no controversy, since it is a case determined by the decretals resolving this ancient question, now decided in the chapter *Ray. et Raynaldus* and the chapter *Si pater*, which the whole world observes, *extra de testamento*. Moreover

† There is no doubt that property alienated to pay off debts, or usury, or uncertain sums wrongly taken, or for other legacies, is not imputed to the heir in respect of the legitime or the trebellianic portion, as noted in the Digest, *ad Trebellianum*, l. *Marcellus*, § *res, quae*. Moreover, it is presumed that the heir alienated in these cases if the creditors or legatees did not raise litigation for a long time, because the presumption is that they would have done so if they had not been satisfied, since they are not presumed to have forfeited their rights, as in the Digest, *de probationibus*, l. *cum de indebito*. However, this presumption is not entirely conclusive, but only probable, if nothing else similar appears. See the Code, *ad Macedonianam*, l. *fin.*, and the Code, *de pignoribus*, l. *ult.* Therefore, with regard to this point, the words of the will must be examined if alienation is proven. But if it is not proven, nothing is presumed to have been diminished, because facts are not presumed. As for those words *sub modo*

It must be known that whenever they impose a modus, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. cum ab eo. And this is presumed from the order of performance, because if the order is such that the principal disposition is to be executed before the burden, it creates a modus; but if the order is reversed, it creates a condition, as when I say, “I bequeath to you 10, when the ship arrives from Asia.” For consent is lacking unless the ship arrives. As in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. non solum. Nor can provision be made by a caution: because it is not within the power of the cautioner for the ship to arrive or not to arrive. But if it were conceived entirely in the negative, as if it were said, “provided that the ship does not arrive from Asia,” the Mutian caution would have place, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Mutianae, and l. cum tale, §. Lucius.

Let us now consider whether the said lady Joan, if admitted to the fourth part, would be admitted after deducting the legitima and the trebellianica. And certainly she would not be admitted except for a third, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. in testamento, and l. tales conditiones. For the right of accretion, upon failure of a condition or modus in the person of those who have predeceased, cannot possibly have place. The case is in the aforementioned l. tales. Indeed, as we have said, the modus has been consumed by delay, and the force of the fideicommissum has vanished, because since Joan is excluded, nothing can accrue to her, as in D. de usufructu, l. si quis Titio, §. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. And if there are several partners or co-owners in one toll-house, having the right to collect the revenues of the said toll-house, can each one sell or alienate the right of his portion without the consent and request of the others?
body: The question is,

Whether Lord Spineta can demand that the division of the said toll be made against the will of his partners, so that, as regards his share, he can appoint a collector and sell the said toll for his portion at the proper time. Lord Spineta does not have jurisdiction, but for the convenience of receiving the fruits, he can place his own collector or attendant there at his own expense, so that he may not be defrauded in that which concerns him. And because this question is formed similarly in Speculum, title De decimis, §. Finis, where it is most fully alleged, I do not extend myself in alleging. And his partners cannot sell to his prejudice without his knowledge, because he is in possession of the convenience for his part, inasmuch as he has received those conveniences. However, division does not apply, because the convenience itself, not the shares, is divided. Moreover, it does not solely pertain to Lord Spineta, as in Digestum, De contrahenda emptione, Law 1, §. Finis, by Christopher de Castellione. To the same effect, the subscription by Baldus: The Noble and Magnificent Lord Spineta, who has the convenience of receiving the fruits of the toll, etc., can place his own collector there, who, together with the others, shall describe the consortium of his partners and see what is collected, because it is in his interest, since the convenience of his share is involved, as noted in Speculum, De decimis, §. Finis, and there is copious allegation in this matter; and therefore I do not extend myself in alleging. Also, when the toll is sold, he can always have his own procurator there, or attend personally, if he wishes, so that fraud may not be committed. And for this, he must be required, as in Codex, De distractione pignorum, Law Creditor hypotecas. For he who does not require him whose interest it is, seems to act secretly and in bad faith. There is a notable text. Hence I conclude that the partners cannot sell the toll to his prejudice without his knowledge and consent, as in Digestum, De aqua pluviali arcenda, Law In concedendo, with the following law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and in which cases, a husband shall or shall not forfeit the dowry on account of his wife’s adultery. And whether a singular successor or an extraneous heir of the husband shall forfeit the dowry, and may set up the wife’s adultery as a defense.
body: For

† For when a wife has been repudiated by her husband, accused, and condemned for adultery truly committed, the husband immediately profits from the dowry, as in Auth. ut liceat matri, et aviae, §. quia vero, and C. de repudiis, l. consensu. And this right passes to the heir, because it has already been reduced to judgment, whether the heir is his own or an outsider, as in l. 3, C. si per mortem intervenit. The exception also passes in this case to the singular successor having title from the husband, as in l. etiam, ff. de iureiurando, and as noted by Dy. in l. fluminum, §. adijcitur, de damno infecto.

The second case is when the woman was repudiated by the husband, but was not accused and condemned; and then the husband properly has the exception, but his outsider heir does not have it, as in leg. et nota, ff. soluto matrimonio, l. rei iudicatae, per Dy. and Bar., and it is touched upon by the doctors in l. ultima, C. de adulteriis. And in the same way it does not pass to the singular successor upon the husband’s death, because the singular successor is equated with an outsider heir. However, in the decretal it is said that an adulterous woman does not recover the dowry, as in extra de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, in c. plerumque. But it speaks of two cases: namely, when separation of bed has been made by the Church, or when she herself withdrew by her own will, spurning the husband’s bed. In the first case, when she is separated by the judgment of the Church, she is sufficiently in a manner condemned of adultery, as in extra de processu, c. tuae, §. si vero. In the second case, the reason is that she sinned in two ways: namely, by committing adultery, and by dispossessing the husband, as it were, of the possession of the bed. But when the husband repudiated her by his own authority, the woman sinned only in one way, namely, by committing adultery. And therefore, upon the husband’s death, the outsider heir or singular successor does not have the exception of adultery. The Speculum, however, holds indistinctly that unless the woman is condemned, the husband does not profit from the dowry, nor can the heir, she not being condemned, plead the exception of adultery, in spec. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, §. fin., versi. quid si mulier agit ad dotem contra haeredes, and in spec. de exceptionibus, §. dicto, versi. item quaeritur, eccles. Ioan. And. in d. c. plerumque refers to the Speculator as being content with his decision.

The third case is when the husband neither repudiated nor accused; then it cannot be opposed, as in C. de revocatione donationum, l. si, and C. de decurionibus, l. si ille, lib. 10, and noted by the gloss in d. l. rei iudicatae, §. 1. From which it appears that either she was condemned, or she was separated by the judgment of the Church. Buyers of goods can oppose the exception of the dowry received or not received, and therefore, outside the aforementioned two cases, possessors of goods can be sued hypothecarily for restitution. That third case, which I touched upon, namely, when she withdrew of her own free will, seems to require limitation. If the husband accused the morals of his wife. And this pleases, and according to the aforementioned distinction it must be understood, as noted by Iaco. de Bel. in the question disputed by him, which he places in l. unica, C. de rei uxoriae actione. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, the master is liable for the delict of a slave, servant, or pupil who steals pledged goods, or other things deposited with him or otherwise in his possession.
body: These

† The question is formed in a similar case. D. de comm. naut. l. eum, qui. §. si rem. together with l. se. and l. si mei causa. §. 1. and l. argen. and briefly the glossators say that the quality of the persons must be considered. For if the pupil was a man known to himself and to others, and held to be trustworthy, who afterwards fled after breaking open the granaries: it is still regarded as a fortuitous event, and the lender is not liable for the pledge. But if he was an unknown and disreputable man, then he who placed trust in him, in whom men of ordinary diligence ought not to have placed confidence, would be at fault, at least with slight fault. As according to the case which is proposed, namely, that he was otherwise experienced, and the lawful lender is not liable for the things taken away by him, as in the aforementioned l. argentum. And it helps, D. si cert. pet. l. si quis nec causam. and l. rogasti. and D. de comm. naut. l. si ut certo. §. nunc videndum. Nor can it be said that this man was employing the services of bad men: because he was not accustomed to be bad otherwise, hence there ought not to have been a bad presumption or sinister suspicion against him, as in the aforementioned l. argentum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A decree cannot be valid in part and invalid in part.
2. Whether a payment of an unsatisfied debt made by a judge to one of the heirs, who claimed that a certain debt had fallen to him in the division of the inheritance, is valid, if this was not established before the judge; and, assuming it is not, whether the ratification by the co-heirs validates the aforementioned payment. Number 3.
3. Whether one can ratify the act of a manager even for his own benefit.
body: It is proposed to you that one of the heirs asserts that a certain entire credit of two thousand florins fell to his share at the time of the division. He brought an action before the judge and obtained both the first and second decree for the full amount, without any proof being made that the said credit had fallen to his share. Now, subsequent creditors seek to have these matters, as having been done in fact, revoked, and the fruits collected to be counted toward the principal, because he was put in possession on account of a false claim.

And they say that the said *missio* cannot be divided so that it is valid in part and invalid in part, since he sued in his own name for the entire amount, as in D. de cond. indeb. l. si non sortem § si centum, where Bartolus speaks thus.

† Hold therefore in mind this §. pro dationibus insolutum, which states that dations in satisfaction made throughout the day are such that if the dation in satisfaction is vitiated in any part, the whole is vitiated. Likewise, a decree cannot be valid in part and invalid in part, as stated in l. in hoc iudicio, D. de familiae herciscundae. But on the contrary, it is said that the coheirs, although they ratified the aforementioned second decree some time later, and asserted that the truth of the matter was that the said credit had accrued to the share of the said claimant, and notwithstanding that the rights had been assigned, whereby the ratification ought to be drawn back retroactively, as in c. rati. and l. si, C. ad Macedonianam, D. de iudiciis, l. licet. But to this it is replied, first, that the ratification does not appear, although the coheirs assert it to be true that the said credit had accrued to the share. For one thing is to confess, another to ratify. Likewise, it is said that the subsequent assignment operates to no effect, as D. de iudiciis, l. non potest videri. Likewise, it is alleged that even the ratification could not be made to the prejudice of a third party, namely, the other creditors, to whom a hypothecary right was due, and to whom also the right of compensating fruits against the principal was due, as D. de solutionibus, l. Titij. For this is the rule, that no one can ratify to the prejudice of a third party, as D. de pignoribus, l. si fundus, §. 1. In support of this side, it may also be alleged that these decrees cannot be interposed unless the debt has been liquidated, as D. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur, l. hoc autem, §. 1, where it says, it must be established, it must be clear to the praetor, etc. Since therefore the credit was not proven, the dation in satisfaction did not hold. It supports this what is noted in Extra, de constitutionibus, c. Ecclesia Sanctae Mariae, where the glossa says that when proof is entirely omitted, the sentence is null by operation of law. In support of this also is the fact that it is a lesser matter for a spiritual person to ratify what was done nullly by an illegitimate tutor; therefore, the contrary is the common law, as noted in l. si tutor, C. in quibus causis in integrum restitutio non est necessaria, according to the glossa of Petrus and Cynus. To this also supports what is noted in the species, de defensione, §. 1, vers. sed pone. For by ratification the defect of false petition, which has the effect of impeding the second decree, does not seem to be purged, as D. ne vis fiat ei qui in iudicio vocatus est, l. 1, §. haec verba. Just as the defect of false impetration. For letters are said to be false because they were obtained by a false procurator, as c. Ex parte decani. Likewise, this plaintiff seems to have brought useful actions in his own name, as C. de procuratoribus, l. qui stipendia. Therefore, the other coheirs cannot ratify what was not done in their name, as in the rule ratum and l. si servus, D. de precario. And to this supports C. de condictione indebiti, l. creditoris. Likewise, because the said proceeding does not seem to have any foundation of truth. Likewise, because the said bare assertion of the coheirs seems to have been made in fraud of the creditors, as C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si cui, and D. de iureiurando, l. nam et postea, §. sed et si quis, and c.

† Now it is asked, what is the law in light of the aforementioned allegations, and others that may be made for and against. The solution is that the common opinion holds that anyone may ratify the act of a gestor, even to his own detriment, as noted in ff. de cond. ob cau. l. si procuratori falso. There is less doubt regarding this in the case of a simple procurator, and in the interposition of decrees, as in ff. rem ra. ha. l. bonorum, and ff. de procu. l. mutus, §. is, qui. Hence, although there was deception of the praetor, nevertheless ratification reconciles the matter, as in ff. de neg. ges. l. si autem, §. item si fundum, and as noted in ff. de excep. rei iu. l. si mater, §. hoc iniure. Therefore, the first creditor may ratify and confirm the act of a non-procurator, notwithstanding the second creditor, because ratification is deemed to operate retroactively, and the first creditor may exercise his right and prejudice the second creditor by virtue of the priority in time, as in ff. de excep. rei iu. l. ex sextante, §. latinus. The objection based on l. si fundus, §. 1, ff. de pig. does not hold, because a debtor cannot prejudice the right acquired by a creditor, as stated in the second response there. But a prior creditor may well prejudice a subsequent one, as in l. pupillus, quam in frau. cre. And therefore, if ratification appears, the aforementioned proceedings of the agent are reconciled as if from the beginning, and thus they are counted toward the principal as if received from his own property. However, I do not weigh the new cession, because it effects nothing toward the validation of the proceedings, as in ff. qui satis. cog. l. Iul. I weigh the ratification, because it verifies the act as retroactive; and in support of this is ff. de fur. l. si uendidero, §. si Titius, ver. quod si pecunia, where if the owner ratifies the payment made even to a false procurator, the procurator’s fraud is purged, because the debtor is released. How much more so in our case, where it is to be believed that he was a true procurator, because the owners so assert, and credit is to be given to their intent and actions, as in ff. de procu. l. si procuratorem absentem. Moreover, there is no doubt that by such ratification the debtors are released from the said coheirs; therefore, the ratification is valid. Furthermore, this datio in solutum is valid, as in C. de euic. l. si ob causam, and l. a diuo pio, ff. de re iud. Moreover, it must be considered that he who acted did not express that he was acting by useful actions, nor by direct actions, nor was it demanded by him that it be declared. Hence, it is understood that he cumulated both avenues, since in effect these two avenues tend toward the same end, argu. C. de annu. excep. l. fi. Therefore, since it appears that he acted in a procuratorial capacity, ratification reconciles the act, as in ff. de neg. gest. l. 1, and as noted in the same title, l. si pupilli, §. pe. Moreover, he also acts in the image of the cedent by a useful action, as in d. l. qui stipendia, and ff. fa. hęr. l. plane. Hence, from the beginning to the end, it must be concluded that since the debt was true, and consequently there was no deception of the praetor regarding the substance of the debt, and the mandate in rem suam was verified and also ratified, the aforementioned datio in solutum assumed force, either from the beginning or ex post facto, so that it is drawn back retroactively, as in ff. de solu. l. si quis offerenti, §. 1, and §. si duo. The objection based on what is noted in l. 2, C. de iure fis. lib. 10, does not hold, because there was a defect of jurisdiction, as noted by Innocentius, extra de offi. dele. c. prudentiam. And thus it seems to me, Baldus de Perusio, saving the substance of the truth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What are the acts by which someone is deemed to have accepted an inheritance.
body: On

† As to the question whether the lady Simona, by compromising, ratifying the award, and executing it, appears to have accepted the inheritance of John Boia, it must be considered that either she performed some act transferring a thing of the said John Boia to another: and then she appears to have accepted the inheritance. For there are four ways of accepting an inheritance: namely, by an acquisitive act, by a translative act in favor of another, by a possessory act, and by word. For these acts cannot be performed without the right and name of heir, as stated in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. pro herede, § Papiam; and l. gerit; and l. cum bonis; and l. duo fratres; and Inst. de qualitate et differentia hereditatum, § final; D. de hereditate instituta, l. iam dubitari. But if someone performs some act which does not touch the right and name of heir, he does not appear to accept, because acceptance is a matter of fact and intent, as C. de iure deliberandi, l. potuit; and C. unde leges, l. nam hoc; and C. de repudianda hereditate, l. 1. But if it is an act which can be performed in two ways, namely, as heir and as non-heir, in case of doubt it is not presumed that one accepts, as noted in D. de conditionibus ob causam, l. 1, § si parendi. It remains therefore to see whether, by compromising over hereditary bodies and hereditary rights, one appears to accept; and if someone raises a question as heir, or it is raised against him as heir, he is understood to accept the inheritance, unless there is doubt whether the inheritance was devolved upon him or not, as noted in D. de transactionibus, l. controversia; and l. 3, in principio. Hence this question, which is asked, is one of fact rather than of law, as D. de statu hominum, l. idem erit. And because the said acts do not appear to have been able to be performed perfectly without acting as heir of the said John, if I am not mistaken in the facts, I say that she appears to have accepted the inheritance of the said John, on account of the transfer of dominion and the release made over the whole, as Inst. de qualitate et differentia hereditatum, § final; and D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. duo fratres. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a minor who, having given promises to the arbitrators to ratify and not to contravene, may nevertheless seek restitution against the award. And whether he who promised to abide by the sentence of the arbitrator in any case under a penalty of one thousand, if the arbitrator sentenced that two hundred be paid to someone within certain terms, provided, however, that the entire payment be made within two years, incurs the penalty if the payment was not made in the first term: and if so, whether he incurs the entire penalty. And in number 1.
body: The words state, and the aforementioned contracting parties promised to us, the above-named, by solemn stipulation, to stand by, obey, and submit to every sentence, award, and arbitration; and never to contravene or come against it, whether by themselves or another, in law or in fact, for any reason or cause, nor to appeal, nor to supplicate, nor to petition for the sentence to be reduced to the arbitration of a good man; nor to perform any act, in law or in fact, by which the sentence, award, arbitration, or friendly composition might be rendered void or annulled in any way, or could be rendered void or annulled, under a penalty of one thousand in each case in which there was a breach. Moreover, certain A., B., and D. promised in their own proper name that they would cause the principals, upon reaching majority, to praise, approve, ratify, and confirm the said compromise, and all and singular things contained therein; and that they would stand by and obey the sentence, award, arbitration, and arbitrament of the said arbitrators and friendly composers, and of all friends, when they shall have become of age. In the sentence of the said arbitrators and arbitraments it is contained thus, that six hundred ducats ought to be paid at certain terms; and it adds, so that the entire payment be made within two years, etc. Now, in the first of the said terms, payment was not made. It is asked whether the said guardians, who bound themselves for the minors to the said penalty, can be sued. On this point

† Lord Di. thus wrote in his consilium: that if a minor compromises into arbitration and promises a penalty if he does not comply with the sentence, that by seeking restitution in integrum against the sentence of the arbitrator he does not incur the penalty. For it seems that the question is about his own facility, not about the sentence of the arbitrator; and therefore the text advised that it be added in the form of the compromise that he shall not come against the sentence, nor seek restitution in integrum. Di. reports the same from Bartolus after Di. in l. cum minor, in the beginning, ff. rem rai. hab. Moreover, the words say that this penalty is incurred in each individual chapter. But one chapter of 600 florins seems to exist; for the division of payments is not a chapter, but is part of a chapter; therefore, unless all performances have elapsed, the penalty cannot be demanded, as ff. de pi. act. l. si necessarias, §. si annua. Moreover, these expromissores deferred their promise to the time of the legitimate age of the wards, namely, that if they then did not obey, they themselves would be bound; therefore, they cannot be sued before that time. It supports what is noted, ff. de cond. ind. l. si procurator, §. fi., with the following law.

On the contrary, it seems that the said penalty is incurred, and with effect, with respect to the said expromissores. For it is certain that by the restitution of the minor they are not relieved from the effect of the promise, as C. de fideius. minorum, l. 1 and 2, and noted, ff. de procu. l. minor 25. an. Also, it is certain that they did not stand within the limits of the promise as ratified; but they promised that the said minors would comply and obey every arbitration. But it cannot be denied that compliance with the arbitration has not occurred. For the arbitration has two parts. For one part, or chapter, has that which is to be paid; the other part, or chapter, has that to which it is to be paid, as ff. de arb. l. celsus, §. idem ait. Since therefore it has not been paid on the day, the penalty seems to be incurred, as ff. de pe. leg. l. 1, in the end. Nor can it be said that the said penalty seems to be inserted into the quantity; rather, it is inserted into the fact with respect to the said promisors, who promised to do and to see to it, as ff. si cer. pe. l. fi., §. fi., and the law, and noted, ff. de ver. ob. l. stipulationum aliae, §. si sortem. Also, there is no doubt that penalties appended in arbitrations and in arbitraments can be imposed on account of contempt, as ff. de arb. l. cum pęna and l. si quis rem, and C. de arb. l. 1 and l. pluribus; otherwise they would be appended in vain, which is ridiculous to say, as ff. de arb. l. 3. And here consider that those words, "when they shall have become of age," seem to refer to ratification, and not to payment. For payment has a certain time, and therefore it is not deferred by an uncertain time of age, as ff. de leg. 1. l. talis scriptura. Also consider that division by times seems to induce a division of chapters with regard to the penalty, as ff. si cer. pe. l. lecta, and it serves well. ff. de mino. l. emilius largianus. It might be doubted,

† Assuming that the penalty was incurred with effect, whether it was incurred as to the part by reason of the part of the share, or in its entirety: and it seems that it was incurred in its entirety, as in D. 26.5.1 (*heredes*), § *in illa*. To the contrary, it seems that in discretionary penalties they are reduced to the manner of praetorian penalties, in which division is made, as in D. 45.3.1 (*si seruus*), § *si plurium*. Regarding which, say as in the aforementioned § *si sortem*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the heirs of an infant can seek restitution in order to accept an inheritance that has been offered, before it has been accepted during his lifetime. And what if the four-year period has elapsed.
body: Question and

Whether, since the infant did not accept the inheritance during his lifetime, the infant’s heirs can seek restitution in integrum in order to accept it. Some say yes, by the law *Qui duos* in the title *De regulis iuris*, according to the exposition of that text by Jacobus de Arena, and by the arguments in the title *De acquirenda hereditate*, the law *Pantonius*, and in the Code, in the title *De testamento militis*, the law *Si Valerianus*. Others say the contrary, by the law *Si infanti*, § 1, in the title *De iudiciis delictorum*, and this opinion is held by Jacobus de Belvis. But whatever the case may be, assuming without prejudice to the truth that restitution in integrum can be sought by the heir of the infant on behalf of the infant: nevertheless, it cannot be sought here, because the four-year period has elapsed since the death of the infant; indeed, if it were granted, the restitution would be void by operation of law, according to Dino, in the Institutes, in the title *De actionibus*, § *Rursus*. Moreover, those who say that the guardians were negligent, for they ought to have accepted the inheritance while the infants were alive, are correct; hence, they should not be aided to their own advantage. Rather, they make themselves strangers to the succession, who did not accept the legitimate guardianship nor make an inventory, as stated in the law and notes in the Digest, in the title *Ad Senatusconsultum Tertullianum*, law 2, § *Quid ergo si petiit*, in the gloss on the word *quod potuit*. It is certain that a guardian who did not make an inventory nor receive administration by decree of the judges cannot bind the infants, nor give authority to an older infant in any act, and especially in the acceptance of an inheritance, which is a solemn and highly binding act, as stated in the Code, in the title *De tutela et cura*, in the law *Qui satisdatio cogatur non dedit*, the last law, and the law *In dubium*, and in the Code, in the title *Arbitrio tutoris*, the law *Veteris*. Therefore, the guardian, who does not have the right to administer the inheritance, could not accept it on behalf of the infant. Nor could he seek restitution in integrum, especially since the time limits do not favor him, as stated in the Code, in the title *De tempore intra quod integrum restitutio petatur*, the last law. However, a doubt arises for me, because the time for seeking restitution on behalf of the infant does not seem to run against the infant’s heir before the infant’s inheritance was accepted, as stated in the Code, in the title *De tempore intra quod integrum restitutio petatur*, the law *Ea quae*, § *Si*. And thus, perhaps the time for seeking restitution would not have elapsed, because it is valid with respect to its starting point; and so we would remain only at that point, whether restitution in integrum can be sought on behalf of the infant, who suffered much difficulty: and there are opinions for and against among the moderns, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If one of several guardians administered the estate, may another, who did not administer, ratify the judgment rendered against the administering guardian, so that it may prejudice him?
2. If he who did not administer promised that he would do and see to it that no means be found to challenge the judgment, may he, if an appeal is taken or restitution is sought, be sued on the basis of such a promise?
body: It is proposed that a certain tutor, who did not manage the guardianship, but whose co-tutor administered it well, against whom a judgment for one thousand had been rendered, settled with the former ward for five hundred pounds. And since he had no means from which to pay, he brought with him a certain money-lender with money, and feigned that he was paying the said five hundred, making it appear in the instrument: and he acknowledged that he held the said money from the said former ward on account of a partnership. Upon this being done, the said money-lender took the said money away with him. This former tutor is sued for this money. It is objected that the said money did not in truth intervene, but was a certain fiction. The question is asked: what is the law?

† It is answered that if the said tutor was bound, his release is considered as payment, and he is bound to pay, as in l. si mulier, ff. de cond. ob caus. But if he was not bound, the simulated acts being treated as void, nothing is considered to have been contracted, as in C. si cert. pet. l. si ex pretio. This is touched upon by Bartolus in ff. si cert. pet. l. singularia, when he discusses the practice of that law. Secondly, it is asked,

† Because the said tutor, who did not administer, approved the sentence passed against the co-tutor who administered: whether this sentence prejudices him. And it must be said that, although he confesses the sentence to have been rightly passed, nevertheless he does not confess that it prejudices him, because a matter acted upon between others, etc., as in C. qui res iud. non not. per totum. Thirdly, it is asked, because this tutor, who did not administer, promised that he would do and see to it that no means would be used to challenge the sentence, and if it were challenged, that he would keep the said late girl indemnified. Whether, if an appeal is made, or restitution in integrum is sought, this person can be sued on the basis of such a promise. And it must be said that he cannot: if fraud on the part of the judges is proven, which was not known to the promisor, as in ff. man. l. creditor. §. Luc. The same applies if gross negligence, which is compared to fraud, is proven, as noted in ff. ad Tre. l. seruo inuito. §. cum praetor. But the opposing and true view is that, even if fraud had occurred in the sentence, nevertheless, since he promised to do and see to it, he is bound in this regard absolutely, because a pact and agreement regarding past fraud is valid, as in ff. de pact. l. iuregentium. §. si paciscar. and noted in C. de transa. l. actione. Moreover, that which was done through fraud can be ratified, as in ff. de neg. gest. l. Pomp. and ff. de condi. ob tur. causam. l. si ob turpem. But I respond that between knowledgeable parties the pact would be valid; otherwise, however, if the promisor erred, even through ignorance of the law: since it concerns avoiding damage, as in ff. de condi. inde. l. si me putem. in princ. and l. in summa. And the instrument executed for this purpose must be relaxed, as in ff. de ope. lib. l. si libertus. Here it must be observed that if this co-tutor proves that the guardianship was conducted well and legitimately: according to what is asserted to me verbally. So that the tutors, according to the truth of the matter, were not obliged to pay the said moneys to the said ward, nor any of them under the said impulsive promise: and all promises must lack the firmness of force, as in l. illicitas. in prin. ff. de off. praesi. Hence, in this matter, not only does law operate, but the truth of the fact holds the principate. Furthermore, it must be noted that the said co-tutor could not ratify the sentence against the acting party: because nothing was done in his name in court. Therefore, ratification did not make the judgment his own, as in ff. de neg. ge. l. pup. §. si ego. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, if out of five witnesses described in the instrument two were present and three were not, the instrument is to be declared false.
2. Whether an instrument containing several chapters, if one is false, is to be declared false in its entirety. On the first point, see also above.
body: In a certain

† public instrument, five witnesses are recorded, of whom two were present, and three were not present. It is asked whether the instrument is valid. And it seems that it is not: because it is false in its solemnity; which falsity concerns the whole instrument, as noted by Innocent in extra de hære. c. fraternitatis. To the contrary it seems: because since a sufficient number of witnesses remains, the instrument is not vitiated, as read and noted in ff. quemad. test. ape. l. 1. §. fi. And this is true if, through the two witnesses who pertain to the solemnity of the instrument, credit is given to the contract of which the instrument speaks. For in doubt it is otherwise, because the presumption that in doubt operates in favor of the notary has been blackened and rebutted, as in C. de proba. l. iubemus. Secondly, it is asked,

† if an instrument contains several separate chapters, and in one chapter the instrument is false by reason of the place, or even in its entire substance, whether another separate chapter is vitiated. I say that it is not vitiated in the other chapter, provided that credit is attached to the true chapter, namely through witnesses deposing, or if the adversary does not deny that that chapter is true, but only says that the other chapter is false, as in ff. de fal. l. filius. §. sequens, and as is fully read in C. de transa. l. si ex falsis, and C. de fal. l. satis aperte. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A usurer, providing security, stated that he wished to be believed regarding the amount of usury by the oath of any person requesting it, provided that person is worthy of belief. As to whether the person is worthy of belief, he wished that the decision rest with the discretion of the diocesan bishop, or his vicar, and three lay executors of his last will: provided that some person worthy of belief appears and wishes to be admitted to swear an oath concerning the usurious amount. One of the three executors has renounced his role; another is absent; the third objects. What will be the share of the diocesan bishop? Furthermore, what if all were present: would the diocesan bishop have a fourth part, or a half, in the votes?
2. Matters that cannot be fully proven are established by arguments and documentary evidence.
3. A moneylender is not presumed to lend gratuitously.
4. The general custom of the moneylenders of the city must be examined.
body: V. On the words

They state in a certain clause of a usurer, namely, adding that he wishes to be believed regarding the amount of usury by the oath of any person requesting it, if that person is credible: but whether such a person would be credible, he disposed to stand by the judgment of the diocesan, or his vicar, and of three other certain laymen, and executors of his last will: one of whom renounced the execution. Now a certain credible person demands usury, producing also account books and indications, and offering to swear separately. One of the said executors contradicts; another is contumacious; the diocesan, seeing the credibility of the claimant and the indications sufficiently clear, wishes to defer to the oath by virtue of the said clause, adding that he wishes, etc. The question is, what is the law. And it seems to me that he cannot: because that which is committed to several simultaneously cannot be carried out by one, or fewer, as in the Digest, On Arbitrators, l. Pedius, § 1. And the conjunction placed between several persons for one effect seems to be placed collectively, as in the Code, On Conditions Inserted, l. Si plures, and l. Si ita scriptum, On the Manumission of Testators. Especially because offices and judgments partake of the nature of an indivisible thing, as in the Digest, On Arbitrators, l. Quod tamen. Moreover, this one seems to have been omitted in the stipulation; therefore, he must be considered as omitted, as in the Digest, On Contracting Sale, l. Si. This question is very doubtful because of the textual rules, which say that in contracts one does not depart from the person, unless when he judges badly, as in the said l. Si, and in the Digest, On Verbal Obligations, l. Si quis arbitratu, and in the Digest, Who May Be Compelled to Give Security, l. Ab arbitro, according to one reading. On the contrary, it seems: because the lender spoke to these as to good men, and also as to executors of the last will; nor did he express that all should judge simultaneously; therefore, if one dies, or acts from afar, or refuses to execute, the judgment remains with the other who wishes to fulfill the office; especially where the favor of the soul is concerned. Argument in c. Religiosus, § Sane, On Wills, Book 6. Furthermore, this judgment is uncertain not to induce an obligation, but to execute an obligation already induced, which should not be vitiated by the act or negligence of the commissioners: as noted by the Moderns, in the Digest, On Verbal Obligations, l. Si quis arbitratu. Furthermore, by common law, the diocesan has judgment over these declarations, as in the Extravagants, On Judges, c. Cum sit, which judgment the lender cannot modify, because no one can impose a law on a law, nor on a superior, as in the Digest, On Legacies, Title 1, l. Nemo potest. Furthermore, according to what is proposed, the credibility and integrity of this claimant are notorious; and in notorious matters, such discussion is not necessary, as in the Digest, Who May Be Compelled to Give Security, l. Si vero, § Qui pro rei qualitate. And therefore, notwithstanding the allegation of one executor, according to what is proposed, the diocesan, or his Vicar, with certain indications, may defer to the oath of the said most credible person. Indeed

† because elsewhere it is held that matters which cannot be clearly proven are established by arguments; and with these arguments supporting the case, an oath is administered, as in C. de donationibus, l. si quis pro redemptione, and l. non omnes, §. a Barbaris, ff. de testamento militis. In support of this position, it is argued that these are two clauses in one: the first clause provides that the oath shall be relied upon if the petitioners are worthy persons; the second clause states, "and whether such petitioners, etc." Therefore, even if the second clause were deficient, the first clause should not fail, by argument from ff. de legatis primo, l. quidam testamento, and ff. de arbitris, l. Celsus, §. idem ait. And this position seems to me more just and more true, without prejudice to the substance of the truth. For I hold that this contract is no less favorable, in favor of the soul, than a last will, in which one departs from the person, as in l. 1, in fine, ff. de legato secundo, especially since the caution itself was interposed at the point of death, and thus the execution of this caution devolves upon the bishop, who performs the office of a good man, ff. familiae herciscundae, l. certe, §. 1, ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. continuus, §. cum ita, and in c. cum ab uno, de re iudicata, lib. 6. Moreover, because the association of others does not diminish the faith of the diocesan, who, even if others disagree, could adhere to whichever of them he wished and supply the deficiency, by argument from what is noted in ff. de re iudicata, l. duo iudices dati. And this supports the foregoing, ff. de dote praelegata, l. Theopompus, and what is noted in Inst. de verbis obligatorum, §. penultimus. Here it must be considered whether the whole constitutes one clause or two; and the truth is that, although there are two, the second is for the declaration of the first and is accessory to it; and the arbitration was appended to the accessory, in which case, if those appointed to arbitrate do not arbitrate, one departs from the person and proceeds to the good man. For as Bartolus says, when arbitration is appended to something already done, even if it be an accessory, the good man succeeds in place of the declaratory arbitrator, as in l. officio, ff. de contrahenda emptione; thus he says in l. si quis arbitratu. Furthermore, it is established that he who contradicts seems to arbitrate badly, as noted by Innocentius, extra de testaments, cap. Raynaldus. Therefore, recourse must be had to the arbitration of a good man, as in ff. pro socio, l. unde si Nervae. And it must be observed that in this matter judgments appear according to the quality of the persons. What, then, if at times he lent at interest above the rate, at times below, and at times lent gratuitously? I answer that it must be considered in which activity he was more engaged, i.e., what was more customary for him, by argument from ff. de pignoris actione, l. universorum, and ff. de statu hominum, l. quaeritur.

Furthermore, in the case of a moneylender, it is not to be presumed that he lends gratuitously, as in the rule *semel malus*; nor does the noble presumption, mentioned in *l. merito*, D. *pro socio*, apply to him, because his customs indicate the contrary, indeed they clearly demonstrate it. *l. non omnes*, § *a Barbaris*, D. *de re militari*; and Extravagant *de pignore*, c. *illo vos*. This is certain: not only does one who renounces, but also one who has continued to be absent from his office, make himself an outsider, as in C. *de procuratoribus*, *l. eum qui res agit hereditatis*; and D. *de fideicommissis libertatis*, *l. si liberta*; *l. si legatario*, § 1; and *l. Lucius*. Nor should their cessation impede a just judgment; nor does the present writing. Moreover, if all four had accepted, the bishop would not have a fourth voice, but half of all the voices. And with one voice added to his, he would make the majority, according to the noted doctrine in Auth. *causam quam fit cum monachis*, D. *de episcopis et clericis*. Others, however, say the contrary. But it is not expedient to see what the law is on this point, because it does not pertain to our case.

And according to this, the singular custom of the father himself is examined; or say that the general custom of the moneylenders of the city, who engage in a similar practice, is examined. Argument: Digest, *De funerariis impensis*, law *Cum delationis*, § 1. Or, a certain middle course should be observed. Argument: Digest, *Ad Trebellianum*, law *Titius*; and Extravagant, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, chapter *Ut super*; and Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Sed si lege*, § *Quod autem*. And this is an argument that the bishop may set a rate, and then an oath may be taken. Digest, *De in iure iurando*, law *In actionibus*, in the principal part. But there it speaks of an oath of affection; otherwise in an oath of truth and obligation. As there, law *Verum plane*; and law *Cum furti*; and *De iureiurando admonendo*; and note, Institutes, *De verbis obligatorum*, § *Pecunia*. For it is well known that the testator did not entrust to these declarations anything but a declaration of faith, not a declaration of debt or quantity. And therefore, if faith is established by the notoriety of the fact, as is proposed in the case, it seems that one should adhere to the truth. Distinction 97, chapter *Nobilissimus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The testator, having instituted several heirs, made a legacy to one of them of the remainder of what the testator himself was owed by Titius. Moreover, the legatee claims this remainder by right of legacy. The debtor says he is ready to pay, but wishes to receive a release from all the heirs regarding what he paid to the testator; the heirs refuse. The question is what the law is: whether the heirs can be compelled to grant a release for payment made to the deceased. No. 2.
body: A certain nobleman of Ast, Loysius, had made a legacy to one of his heirs of the remainder which he was owed by Messer James and Bartholomew, brothers of Scaram. Finally, the said Loysius, by virtue of the legacy made to him, demanded from the aforementioned Messer James and Bartholomew the remainder which they were bound to pay to the said testator; but those debtors offered themselves ready to pay, provided that a discharge be made to them by all the heirs for what they had paid to the said testator. One of the heirs, however, did not wish to make the said discharge.

† It is asked whether the claim of the said legatee is thereby impeded. I answer that the said legatee has two rights in making his claim, namely, direct actions for the hereditary action, and useful actions for the share of the coheirs, as in D. 26.5.1 (Plane) and C. 6.30.1 (Ex legato nominis). Nor is he prohibited from using his right, even if the coheirs are unwilling to make restitution of the moneys paid to the testator. But the plaintiff, having received the residue, ought properly to make a discharge in this manner, namely, with respect to all and the whole of that which he could claim as heir, or as legatee by name and on account of the said residue, by confessing that he has been fully and entirely satisfied with respect to all and the whole of the said residue. As in D. 2.15.1 (Emptor), § Lucius, and C. 8.1.1 (Si residuum), and note the opinion of Bartolus in D. 2.15.1 (Cum Aquiliana); and this suffices for the person making payment, as in C. 4.18.1.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether heirs can be compelled to make a discharge of what was paid to the deceased. And it must be said that debtors who have paid can demand that an instrument of discharge be made for them. And if any instruments appear concerning debts that have been paid, these should be returned to them voided and cancelled: as in C. de cond. sine causa, l. dissolutae; C. de lib. causa, l. sicut datam; C. de fide instru., l. plures apochis; C. de discuss., l. ne casu, li. 10; and l. chirographis, ff. de adm. tut. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the quantity is determined by a public instrument or by the truth of the matter.
body: In the case of the noble men Hentici and Ioam de Tunchis, it must be said as follows.

† But if an error of calculation is proved, one must adhere to the truth, and rather to the writing. As in C. de errore calculi, l. 1. Or if an error of calculation is not proved, then one must adhere to public instruments. As in C. de prob., l. cum precibus. No one is presumed to err in his own act. As in l. ult., ff. suo, and l. quamquam, ad Vellei. However, when two things concur, namely, that there is a dispute concerning the avoidance of damage, and that he proves the matter to be otherwise, even in his own act an error is presumed: as is read and clearly proved by the gloss and others, ff. de condi. indeb., l. sed et si me putem, in princ., and l. cum is, in princ. And it supports what is noted, ff. de leg. 1, l. si res obligata, where there is a good gloss: more words are not necessary, because in these cases the truth stands. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What if certain goods are given or bequeathed to the brothers of St. Mary of Mount Carmel to have and to hold: whether the donation or legacy is valid, and whether at least they may hold them so as to sell them; and what is the case with the brothers of the Order of Preachers, likewise and with the Minorites.
2. Whether, in a donation of all movable and immovable goods, debts owed by others (nomina debitorum) are included.
body: Having pondered the following doubts, whether the brothers and the chapter of Saint Mary

† from Mount Carmel may acquire, at least as regards selling. On the second doubt, whether if a mother having a son donating in this manner, namely: all movable and immovable goods, the names of debtors are included, since the said son is a debtor of the said mother, and if they were included, the donation would be called inofficious in fact and in counsel. On the first point, the words of Jac. de Are. in l. deo nobis. C. de ep. et cler. are as follows, namely: because of the younger brother, whose order cannot have property, whether he succeeds to the father or another blood relative. And it seems that he does not. ff. de iu. fis. l. in metallum. de his quae pro non scriptis. l. si in metallum. But it could be said, since the order has a father, namely the Roman Church, he seeks for it by reason of the Church; just as I see in the case of a filiusfamilias who has a son under the power of his grandfather, who cannot seek for his father, seeks for his grandfather. C. de bonis quae liberis. l. quod scitis. Hence, by order of the Pope, he approached, and it is sought for the Roman Church, as is the case with a common slave, which cannot be sought for one of the masters, the other seeks for the whole. ff. de auth. tut. l. si seruus communis. And although it is sought for the Roman Church, nevertheless the brother will have provisions therefrom. ut ff. de ali. et ci. leg. l. seruus. and for this sup. eo. l. seruos. and of this C. de epi. et cle. l. raptores. Others say that the order will have it, so that it may sell: which I hold in the case of the Preachers, who have movables, and for this they have, so that they may sell. est ff. de lega. 1. l. caetera. §. si duobus. and l. si seruo. § si cui. eo. ti. and de leg. 3. l. fideicommissa. §. si seruo. But the words of Cy. in d. l. deo nobis. in uersi. quid ergo in aliis, who neither in the universal nor in the singular can have goods: whether they will be admitted to succession, or legacy of those goods which according to the rule they cannot have: some, as Jac. de Bel. and Pet. and others teach, say that they can in no way have such succession or bequest, as ff. de his, qui pro non scrip. habentur. l. in metallum. infra de haere. insti. l. j. Others say that yes. as that they do not possess, but that they sell, and convert the money into clothes, books, and food. ar. ff. de leg. i. l. caetera. §. si duobus. and l. filius. §. si quid. and d. l. fideicommissa. §. si seruo. de leg. 3. which they say has place in those who can have movables, such as Preachers. Jac. de Aret. seems to agree, that if anything of this kind were left to regulars, it is valid, and is acquired by them for the Roman Church, which as head is inherent in the order, just as the father in the son, and the master in the slave, as ff. de optione legat. l. si Pamphilo. ff. de dam. infec. l. si seruus. and de insti. ser. l. 1. §. 2. and §. proinde. and from these the brothers will be supported. arg. supra eo. l. raptores. and de ali. et cib. leg. l. seruus according to him. The brothers would not rejoice much in this, if the Roman Church had it. It appears that Master Cyn. does not recite Jac. de Are. in total. Glo. Io. And. in c. 1. de reli. do. lib. 6. on the word, domum uterem. says, that it can be bequeathed to them, so that they may sell: for they must live from alms, and by this the rule or constitution is not infringed, which says that they cannot possess immovables, and thus it seems to agree with Jac. de Are. Also Clementina dudum. §. uerum. de sepul. seems to permit that for the use of the church they may acquire, so that they may repair churches from the price, or from the quantity left to them.
