Also since they can receive money for pious uses: therefore also other things to be converted into money, as ff. de fideiuss. l. si ita fideiussorem accepero. e C. de consti. pec. l. fi. Nor do the words of the donation, which they say, to hold and possess, stand in the way: because these words are said to be held as not appended. ut ff. de pec. leg. l. si pecu. in prin. or they say to be understood, as long as they sell. to sell, however, they say, since they are mendicants, and cannot possess goods, except movables. it is made by that no. in d. c. 1. de reli. do. in gl. caeterorum. and thus I have seen commonly observed in other mendicants, except in the Friars Minor. And even they today, because the charity of alms grows cold, they too much withdraw. and relax their reins. as we see in the province of Blessed Francis. and especially in the city of Assisi. But rights inseparable from the person, namely, inheritance, these mendicants cannot acquire. Some, however, say that neither possessions: as if they did not have commerce. ut ff. de uer. obli. l. multum in terest. for and against it is made by that no. ff. de leg. 1. l. sed si res. Finally, on account of custom, I do not depart from the saying of Jac. de Aret. saving the substance of the truth, considering also the necessity of the church in need, so that they may be expended in its restoration or construction according to what the brothers report to me by word. arg. ff. de exercitoria. l. Lucius.

† Now I come to the second point, on which point the words of Bartolus in l. mouentium, de verborum significatione, are thus stated. The gloss asks whether the names of debts ought to be counted among movables or immovables. And it says, as is held in the gloss. But the law which the gloss cites, C. quoniam et qui, pars 4, debe., speaks of a fourth part, whereas we are speaking of the right of obligation. But Dyonisius in l. post, ff. de auctoritate tutorum, says: either the action contains movables, and then it will be movable; and this is the opinion of the gloss in Auth. de non alienando, § 1, col. 2, and C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus, and l. 1, C. si adversus transactionem. Jacobus de Arena says better that, speaking properly, names are not contained among movables or immovables, but there is also a third species by itself; for what is movable or immobile is judged with respect to the place which it occupies, but names and actions, since they are incorporeal, do not occupy a place. Therefore they cannot be counted among movables or immovables. Hence the jurist makes of these a third species, as in l. a Diuo Pio, § in venditione, and l. quam Tuberonis, § pen., ff. de peculio. Hence it is not necessary that this third species be numbered among movables or immovables; it retains its species by itself, as in the said laws. But when it is necessary that it be assigned to one of these, then the definition of these glosses applies, as by William in l. 1, ff. de statu hominum. What shall we say? I say that names are movable or immovable. And this is not because they are tangible, but it is a genus by itself, as in l. a Diuo Pio, § in venditione, de re iudicata, and l. quam Tuberonis, § pe., ff. de peculio, de fructibus et interesse. Nevertheless, although it is not movable or immovable, yet when we have to judge whether it is movable or immovable, the statement of Dyonisius and the gloss has place, because it is judged according to the nature of those things which come into it. Johannes Andreas in the title de fructibus et interesse says that it is not to be held according to the usage of speech; see there. If we observe the words of the donation, because they speak of things circumscribed by place, it is certain that names are not contained, as in l. Gayus, in principio, ff. de legatis 2. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute prohibiting alienation inter vivos, or mortis causa without certain solemnity, appears to prohibit the making of a will.
2. A donation mortis causa pertains more to a contract than to a last will.
3. Where there is mention of a curator, we never speak in the context of a last will.
4. [Continuation of point 3]
5. Whether codicils are revoked by a subsequent will.
body: V. On the words

† The statute thus states: minors under 25 years of age, beyond the payment of the Papal solidi in the year, cannot even with a tutor or curator, or by oath, be bound, nor can their immovable goods be sold, given in dowry, or for the sake of marriage between the living, or by reason of death, exchanged, or alienated under any other title, nor can contracts be made or disposed of on their goods: unless certain solemnity is observed, which is mentioned in the statute itself. If this is not observed, the statute annuls what is done. It is asked whether the said statute annuls the last will, for example, a testament or codicils. And it seems that it does: for one who makes a testament or codicils is also said to alienate. As in C. de rebus alienatis, l. si, and C. de conditionibus ob causam, l. ea, l. and there fully noted. The contrary is true: because the words of the statute do not say this. For they only make mention of contracts by reason of death.

† as is the donation causa mortis, which accedes more to the contract of last will. As noted in l. 2, de dote praelegata. And therefore it does not contain a mere last will. As in ff. de legatis 3, l. pater filium, in principio.

† Moreover, wherever mention is made of a curator, we never speak in the context of a last will, which does not require a curator. The text and the gloss are in *l. ab Aurelio*, § *si*, *de lib. leg.* And therefore, by way of a codicillary clause, it undoubtedly had effect, what the said Ubertus did in favor of his sister.

But now it must be considered whether the codicillary disposition has been revoked by the subsequent will. And it is to be said that it has not: because, since a derogatory clause was included in the codicils, the restoration is not understood to be confirmed; for no clause revoking the codicils was included in the will. Hence, it is presumed that the same intention endures, as in D. de leg. 3, l. si quis in principio; and D. de leg. 1, l. si mihi et tibi, § in lege; and D. de iure codicillorum, l. diui, § licet; and D. de probat., l. cum tacit, and l. quinquaginta; and Inst. de codicillis, § sed cum ante. From these it is concluded that the codicils made in favor of the aforementioned Georgia are valid in law: saving, however, the Falcidian portion, which is due to the instituted heir, namely the aforementioned posthumous child, and the aforementioned Antonius, as in C. ad leg. Falcid., l. imponendas, and l. quamquam pater. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that during the marriage husbands are usufructuaries, possessors, and administrators of all the goods of their wives, both those given in dowry and those acquired from other sources, and that upon the death of the husbands all the goods of the said wives are to be restored to them forthwith, whether by this statute the restitution of the dowry money is to be made immediately, or whether the lapse of a year is to be awaited according to the disposition of the common law.
2. The term "goods" includes the names of debtors.
body: It is established and provided that the husbands of Terzi, while the marriage subsists, shall be usufructuaries of the women's goods, possessors, and administrators of said goods, both those given in dowry and those acquired. And upon the death of the husbands of said women, all the goods of said women shall immediately revert to the aforesaid women.

† Now it is asked, whether from what is said concerning dowries, and immediately added, that a dowry given to the husband in ready money can be demanded at once, or whether a year ought to be awaited according to the disposition of the common law, as in C. de rei uxoria actione, l. rem in praesenti, §. exactio. And it seems that it can be recovered immediately, without awaiting the year. For the statute says, all the goods of those women: but it is certain that it is the woman’s own property, as in ff. de minoribus, l. denique, §. sed utrum; and ff. fideicommissis hereditatibus, l. Pomponius, Philadelphus; and C. de collationibus, auth. quod locum. Moreover, it is certain that

† That the term "goods" includes debts. Hence the law states that if anyone bequeaths the usufruct of his goods, it is understood that he also bequeaths the usufruct of the debts, even those owed in money. This is our text in l. 1, C. de usufr. And thus this term "usufruct" is taken broadly, meaning those things which are consumed by use, as in ff. de iureiur. l. sed et si possessori, §. sed si rerum. Moreover, the statute says "all," which is to be understood without diminution, as fully noted in C. sine censu vel reliquis, l. omnes, cum si. Hence, concluding from the first to the last point, both from the nature of the dowry and from the generality of the language, it appears that this statute was granted to the woman for the benefit of representation; otherwise, the statute would accomplish nothing. And we may argue from the statute to the legacy, which is valid on account of the benefit of representation, as in Inst. de legat. §. si quis uxori.

To the contrary is the truth, and this consists in a certain subtlety of law. For actions are properly said to be in the goods only when they have arisen. Before they have arisen, actions are not said to be in the goods, but rather a hope of suing, as in Inst. de verb. oblig. §. ex conditionali, and ff. de donat. l. spen. But it is so in the action for the dowry that the action does not arise until after one year. The text is in ff. de pact. l. iuregentium, and indeed in the final §. secundum Gul. de Cu. and many other great doctors. Therefore, the words of the statute, which say "all the goods of the women," cease to apply, as in ff. de verb. sign. l. cedere diem. In the meantime, they are in the husband's hereditary goods. See ff. de usufr. leg. l. Sempronius atalus.

Furthermore, even if the action had arisen, it is nevertheless not enforceable, and therefore it is not purely said to be in the woman's goods, but subject to a time condition. Wherefore, in the meantime, the woman cannot bring an action, as in C. de iud. fi. l. iusta, lib. 10, and Inst. de except. §. temporales, and l. certi condictio, ff. si cert. pet., and C. de cond. ex lege, l. 1, primo responso. The statute intends to remove the delay in restitution, but it does not intend to introduce the representation of a claim where there is no claim that can be substantively made, or at least where it is not in exercise. I could say more words, but those which I have said are those which pertain to the substance of the law, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that whatever the husband acquires during the marriage shall be common to the wife, and vice versa, saving the usufruct, which belongs to the husband alone; and another statute providing that the husband may sell and alienate, as he pleases, the goods acquired during the marriage without the wife’s consent, it is asked whether the husband may entirely donate the acquired goods by an inter vivos donation without the wife’s consent.
body: Statute

† In Trieste it is provided that whatever a husband acquires with his wife during the subsistence of the marriage, or the wife with her husband, is common to both: saving that the husband ought to have the usufruct during the subsistence of the marriage. Another statute provides that husbands of Trieste may and can sell and alienate the goods acquired with their wife, while they are standing in marriage, at their will, without the consent and will of the said wife. It is also proposed that by general custom this statute is simply interpreted and understood, namely, that husbands, the goods which they acquired during the time of marriage, alienated and disposed of under any title between living persons at the pleasure of their will, without any requirement of the wife. And that it was so practiced in long times past. Now it is asked, whether the husband, without requiring and with the wife ignorant, can entirely donate the goods which he acquired during the subsistence of the marriage by donation between living persons. And for clarity it must be premised that the said permissive words, that the husband may sell and alienate the said goods at his will, are understood of any donation between living persons, provided that the donation is made for good merit and not by fraud of the woman. As in D. 39.5 (Quae in fraudem creditorum), l. Si pater; and l. Si unus; D. 39.5 (Si quid in fraudem patroni). Or it is better to say that the alienation permitted to the husband is not understood except of his part, as in C. 4.38 (De contrahenda emptione), l. Dudum; and D. 32.1 (De legatis 1), l. Servorum electione, § Cum fundus; and C. 4.39 (De rei venditione), l. Mater; and l. Is qui; D. 7.1 (De usufructu legato). And this would be true, considering only the statute speaking of union. As noted in D. 17.2 (Si certum petatur), l. Si socius; and D. 18.1 (De actione empti), l. Iulianus, § Idem Celsus. Furthermore, it is evident that statutes should be reconciled with statutes, as in X. 1.12 (De consuetudinibus), c. Cum dilectus; and X. 1.6 (De electione), c. Cum expediat; and l. 1, C. 5.13 (De inofficiosis dotibus). Furthermore, it is not likely that a statute which does not apply in one part, should take away in another, lest it be a mockery. Arg. D. 35.1 (De conditionibus et demonstrationibus), l. Non ad ea. Nevertheless, these not withstanding, thus custom has interpreted the statute, and reduces the statute to the common law, which provides that husbands do not acquire for wives, but wives for husbands, and that the husband can dispose of his acquisitions at the pleasure of his will. There is no way to doubt that the said donation made by the husband was valid, since the power of the law and the will of the husband make it valid. As in C. 5.18 (De donationibus ante nuptias), l. Cum te sponsae; and l. Si filiae; and l. Si ante. It seems expedient to me that custom be proved without observance. For if it were not proved, I doubt greatly: because the words of the statute are ambiguous, and in doubt correction of laws is not presumed. For what is said, that the husband may alienate, seems to be understood of his part, not of the wife’s part. For also conversely, the wife could not alienate the husband’s part. And it is equitable that equality be observed between husband and wife. Arg. C. 5.17 (De indicio vidui), l. Fin. And because the donation, of which we speak, is a dissipative title. Hence this does not seem to be granted to the prejudice of the wife, since she already had acquired a right of dominion for her part. Finally concluding, if custom interpreting the statute appears, custom must be followed. But if it does not appear, you, who have understanding, look at the arguments for and against. But I do not omit one thing, that this statute does not speak of goods acquired with the wife by common industry, but from inheritance or legacy, as in D. 17.2 (Pro socio), l. Nec adiecit. Because the wife ought to assist the husband, and not conversely. As noted in l. Sicut, D. 39.4 (De operis liberto); and by Innocentius in X. 3.26 (De testamento), c. Cum inofficiosus. Namely, if the husband can alienate, since all such things ought to be his. But if they were acquired from common money, then otherwise. As noted in C. 4.21 (De fidei instrumentis), l. Scripturae. But as I said above, as it was practiced in ancient times, so let it be kept: if custom is established. And it supports what is noted in X. 1.12 (De consuetudine), c. Ex parte vestra; and X. 3.23 (De pignoribus), cap. Ex literis; and C. 5.27 (Ne uxor pro marito), l. Ob maritorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It treats of the fourth part, which is owed to the parish church on account of a burial place chosen elsewhere.
2. If the deceased leaves 30 to the Minorites or Preachers and 10 to his own church, whether the fourth part is due from the 30.
3. If the deceased leaves a legacy to a certain brother on account of kinship or devotion, or familiarity: for example, because he was his confessor, whether the fourth part is due from this legacy.
4. Whether the parish church ought to impute to itself, in satisfaction of the fourth part, what was left to it by the same testator.
5. Whether the fourth part is due from a legacy left to a brother on account of kinship or friendship, if otherwise he would not have left anything.
6. Whether the fourth part is due from legacies left to the Minorite brothers, even if it happens that the deceased is not buried there.
body: †This is an example of a certain opinion, of the tenor and content following, namely: we order that the brothers of the said orders [shall be subject to the rule] regarding all acquisitions and c. [et cetera], simply according to the gloss.

But if the deceased, who chose to be buried in the church of the said brothers, ordered those items in his last will, the fourth part is due, whether they are tapers, candles, oblations, or any other funeral expenses; and if he did not order them, the fourth part is not due. See Extravagantes, De sepultura, cap. 1 and the following chapter; Caput de his etiam; Caput Cum super; and Caput In nostra presentia. And this is clear in the same decretal, Super caput Ea tamen, which speaks of all acquisitions, and then determines, continuing, and says, “whatever and in whatever manner left,” where it is understood, “in the last will,” as is apparent to the observer. But if the deceased leaves a legacy and is not buried with them, the fourth part is not due. See Extravagantes, De sepultura, in the gloss beginning “S. Quod te reliquit.” Furthermore, if someone makes a testament before an illness, or during an illness from which he does not die, and leaves twenty to the brothers, and later, as time passes, falls ill and chooses burial with the Minorites or Preachers, the fourth part of the aforementioned twenty is not due. This is clear from the cited chapters, Relatum, in the gloss beginning “In ægritudine tamen,” and from the cited chapter, Super cathedra, where it is said, “in the article of death, or in the illness from which he died.”

But suppose that the deceased left 30 to minors or to preachers, and 10 to his church. I ask whether a fourth is due from the 30. I answer that it is not, but rather from the entire adjudicated amount, as in *Extra*, *De sepultura*, c. *L.* and c. *Cum super*, where it is said that a fourth is due from the whole testament, namely that which is left for the one who is buried and for his church, as is sufficiently understood. See also *Extra*, *Eodem titulo*, c. *Relatum*. Otherwise, the parish priest would have more than a fourth, which he ought not to have from the aforementioned religious, as is clear from the same decree, *Super cathedra*, and *Extra*, *De sepultura*, c. *Verum infra quartam*, if there is a custom, as expressly appears in *Extra*, *Eodem titulo*, c. *Certificari*. And therefore nothing of the 30 ought to be given to the priest, but his own 10 suffice for him. But if he had bequeathed 8 to the priest and 30 to the brothers, it must be said that the 8 and the 30 make 38, and from this entire sum a fourth is due, and so with other amounts.

But suppose that the deceased left something to a certain brother by reason of kinship, or devotion, or familiarity, because he was his confessor. I ask whether the fourth part is due from this legacy. I answer: no, because the fourth part is due from legacies made by reason of burial, as is clear in the Extravagant Decretals, on Burial, in the chapter *Caeterum* and the chapter *Nam damus*, together with their concordant authorities. As for all those things which friends offer of their own purse, who come spontaneously to honor the deceased, or place upon the altar, or for private masses, the fourth part is not due, for the first reason mentioned above. But if it is left to the work of the brothers’ church, either with mention made of the brothers, or with regard had to the brothers, I do not see that the fourth part ought to be given; because the church is not under the jurisdiction of the brothers, but of the Roman Church, to which special dedications are made, and because it is assigned to the special use of the people; therefore, even if the brothers withdraw, the church remains consecrated to divine worship. Moreover, the fourth part ought not to be given from legacies concerning matters acquired without observing the proper order. First, I shall discuss the point,

Whether the parish church ought to impute to its fourth part that which has been left to it by the same testator. And although there have been various opinions, I hold the part that it ought to be imputed: first, because the text says that the parish church ought to have the fourth part of its judgment *de sepulcro*, c. 1. and c. 2. there *omnium rerum*. and c. *de his*. there *de bonis suis*. and c. *cum super*. there *de testamento*. c. *eo*. tit. lib. 6. there *canonica portio*. 13. q. 2. *aliud* there *quae testamento*. Therefore, if the testator, before his death, following the precept of the first decretal *de sepulcro*, intended to leave the fourth part to the parish church, he ought not to ask for anything further, unless perhaps a supplement, if it has less than is due. Moreover, the parish church is held in the place of a son. *de probat.* in *praesentia* tit. q. 2. c. *si alia* ad fin. and c. seq. 15. q. 4. §. *fin*. But if a son has less than a fourth, he does not bring an action of querela. But he brings an action on the condition from l. *ad supplementum*. C. *de inofficiosa testatione*. l. *cum quaeritur*. and l. *omnino*. and l. *sancimus*. §. *si quando*. and §. *generaliter*. and l. *si quis iudicium defuncti approbasse videtur*. ff. *de inofficiosa testatione*. l. *si pars*. §. 1. and l. seq. and l. *pen*. and l. *Papin*. and l. *conditioni*. §. *condictioni*. Thus, therefore, the parish church will sue for a supplement, having computed the legacy. If, therefore, you equate the church with a son, as was concluded above. If you equate it with a father, or mother, *de summa trinitatis* c. 2. in fin. *de privilegiis* c. 2. lib. 6. still the same as above, because since they did not sue for any legacy, the querela which they could have brought if they were disinherited sons ceases. C. *de inofficiosa testatione*. l. *cum filii*. eo. tit. l. *pater filii*. and l. seq. Moreover, if you equate the church with a patron, or patrons: because it can also be said, that through it we are regenerated by the sacrament of baptism, *de consecratione* dist. 3. c. 1. 2. and 3. still the same as above, otherwise, as above, because if the patron has obtained his portion in the goods of the freedman, the action *contrabulas* ceases: and if he has obtained less, that does not have precedence, but he imputes it to the fourth. ff. *de iure patronatus*. l. *suam*. §. *excludere*. ff. *de bonis liberti*. l. *contra*. §. *totiens*. and §. *si data*. and l. *fin*. in fin. and l. seq. ff. *de bonis possessionibus contra tabulas*. lib. 1. l. 2. But if he does not succeed in any of the said ways, he succeeds by another right of the people, for example, if a wife is deprived of her dowry, and suing, who is admitted together with free children up to the fourth part in the goods of the husband, still legacies and fideicommissa are computed in the fourth. C. *unde vir et uxor*. l. 1. and auth. there *quae est in corpore* *de exhibendo* and *introducere* ad fin. Moreover, if it is said that this fourth is due to the parish church, on account of the burdens which it sustained in the life of the deceased, in compensation of burdens: and in law no one ought, that for the other part, for which satisfaction has been made to this injury, cannot further sue: because by the solution of that which is due, every obligation is removed. *Institutiones* *quibus modis tollitur obligatio* in princ. But that this fourth is due in compensation of injury, is proved: because if anyone is buried in the parish church, and leaves nothing there, and leaves much to other churches, the parish church asks for nothing of what is left elsewhere, as noted by Ray. in the *Summa* *de sepulcro*. and *pen*. and ab. eo. tit. c. *de his*. Therefore, the injury is removed by a transaction allowed by law, just as a transaction would be removed. Moreover, and by the pact of a man. ff. *de iniuriis*. l. *non solum*. §. 1. Moreover, although this fourth is asked for as a debt: nevertheless, the testator, bequeathing to the parish church for a concurrent quantity, seems rather to have paid than to have given: lest the heir be burdened with a double prestation at the same time. ff. *solutis matrimonii*. l. *si cum dotem* §. *si pater*. and l. *non solum* and l. *pater*. ff. *de legatis* 2. l. *cum pater*. §. *qui dotalem*. ff. *de dote praelegata*. l. 3. in princ. and l. *pen*. Moreover, in doubt it is presumed that one would rather contract a loan than give, because in doubt no one is presumed to wish to throw away his money. ff. *de probationibus*. l. *cum de indebito*. ff. *si certum petatur* *de alimentis legatis*. l. *Lucius*. This part is held by Hostiensis in the *Summa* *de sepulcro*. §. *an sit licitum*. although the gloss and Io. And. in clem. *super cathedra* *super libro integre*. And that this point may shine more clearly, it is expedient to see the motives of the adverse party. Behold, they are moved: because clem. *dudum* says that the fourth is due entirely: not distinguishing, it is induced. c. 1. *de sepulcro*. with all its explanations. The chapter *officii* is induced, and the chapter *requisisti*. *de testamento*. where the case seems to be. Moreover, because if churches come as daughters, they do not come into the division of prelegata. C. *de oblationibus*. l. *filia*. and l. *a patre*. Moreover, if the *leuciarii* do not confirm in the fourth that which they receive beyond the burden of the militia from the militia. C. *de inofficiosa testatione*. l. *omnimodo*. Holding the first conclusion, it can be solved regarding clem. *dudum*. by that newest law, it is understood also with the supplementation of ancient laws, and reasons. s. with the parish church the fourth was not promised. Nor is this new, that later laws are determined by earlier ones. ff. *de legibus*. l. *non est nouum*. with l. seq. Thus it is answered to the explanations placed there adding *officii*, and to the chapter *requisisti*, it can be answered in two ways. First, according to one opinion noted there by Innocentius, namely, that action is brought for a supplement, by l. *si quando*. C. *de inofficiosa testatione*. Secondly, it says that the bishop, as regards the testator, is a stranger, wherefore on account of the legacy left the bishop does not have to impede the execution of the right, which is between the bishop, and the chapels, since the testator said nothing. But the parish church has a right in the goods of the deceased. as one joined and coming intestate. Hence, by leaving something to the parish church, he seems to have wished to compensate in the fourth. As to the others, which speak of collation not being made. Say, that this is not a good consequence, these are not conferred, therefore they are not computed in the fourth. For prelegata are not conferred, nevertheless they are computed in the fourth, as l. *pen*. C. *de collatione*. To that which is said regarding the *silentiarii*, say, that it is a special privilege of theirs, which ought not to be drawn to a consequence. *de regulis iuris*. l. *quae a iure*. 7. *questio*. c. *petisti*. And thus the decision of this strong and doubtful matter is concluded.

The second doubt is whether a fourth part is due to a brother left a legacy on account of kinship, friendship, and affection, if he would not otherwise have been left anything. And it seems that it is not due. For the text states that a fourth part is due to the parochial church from those things which anyone leaves to Christ, to churches, or to pious places for the remedy of his soul. 13 q. 2, § sed aliud, towards the end, de sepultura; c. 2; and c. in nostra. And Innocent notes this in the same title. From this, l. 1, § ad municipium, ff. ad legem Falcidiam, is made to apply, namely that here it was not left in such a manner. de verbis significandis, ex parte, 3, there: "which persons specially"; and c. pro hoc faciebat formerly the Extravagant of Benedict: likewise, regarding legacies left to individual persons, as proposed in the case, according to the ancient laws, a fourth part is not due, as has been proved above. But by the Clementina dudum, de sepultura, § huiusmodi, the ancient law is not changed; therefore, one is not forbidden to adhere to it. C. de appellationibus, l. praecipimus. That it has not been changed is evident. For by the name "brothers" is understood the convent, or the universality of brothers, not individual persons. ff. de rebus dubiis, l. civibus; ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. municipibus; ff. de legatis 2, l. Lucius, § civibus; ff. quod cuiusque universitatis, l. municipes. Likewise, regarding the Clementina dudum, § huiusmodi. And the ancient laws state that the fourth part is due in compensation for labor for the satisfaction of the injury which the parochial church suffers, because the parishioner is buried among the brothers; but this brother, being a blood relative or friend, committed no injury; therefore, no fourth part is due from the legacy, especially since it was not left to him on account of burial, for even if he had been buried elsewhere, he would nevertheless have been left the legacy. C. de legatis, l. cum aliena. Moreover, the fourth part due to the parochial church is similar to the Falcidian share due to the heir. And just as it is in the goods of heirs, so this fourth part is in the goods of rectors and curators. The first is proved by C. ad legem Falcidiam, l. pe; ff. in the same title, l. si haeres. The second is proved by a certain commission of Boniface VIII, and noted in the Clementina dudum. Then it is argued thus: if the heir does not take the Falcidian share from a mortis causa acquisition contrary to the will of the deceased, as C. ad legem Falcidiam, l. mortis; ff. de donationibus causa mortis, l. qui precio; therefore, neither does the parochial church draw this fourth part on account of the will of the deceased. Although therefore this legacy is sought by the monastery, it is not to be weighed, but rather on whose account it is left, and where the will of the deceased is directed, is what matters. ff. de bonis possessionibus contra tabulas, l. pen., § hoc solum, where we do not inquire to whom it is sought, but to whom honor is due. It applies. ff. de donationibus causa mortis, l. filio; C. de usufructu, l. si; ff. de aditione legati, l. legatum; ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. qui liberis, § haec verba; ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. qui heredi in paterno; ff. de operis liberti, l. campanus, § cum libertus. Moreover, the last will of the deceased is to be observed. 3 q. 2, c. ultima voluntas, de testamentis; c. tua; C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. pe. First, to this, the will of the deceased is not observed; but so that from the legacy left to the brother on account of kinship, he might deduct for the purchase of vestments or books. And thus it is concluded regarding this legacy. And thus I conclude that the fourth part is not to be deducted. This was the opinion of Oldradus and of many his followers, which savors of equity; although others are against it. It was also the opinion of Stephanus, where he does not leave in fraud.

The third doubt is whether the fourth part [of the estate] is due from the goods left behind by the Minor brothers, even if it happens that he is not buried there, either because he chose that place but could not be buried there, or because he changed his will. That which makes this doubtful is that the fourth part is due, which is declared in the gloss on c. 2, §. verum, De sepultura, where the aforementioned confession is explained. For this, Paulus cites the work of Hostiensis, which states that the fourth part is due to the parochial church from all goods left to all churches, according to that opinion; if that were the case, there would be no question. But that opinion is commonly rejected. This was the opinion of Hostiensis, Petrus de Ancharano, Egidius, Innocentius, and the Abbreviator, against Johannes de Monasterio in c. Super cathedra, contra, and against Ioannes Andreae there, and against almost all the glossators. Therefore, the question proceeds on the basis that the fourth part is due only to the church where he chose burial. And assuming this, I say that the fourth part is not due from the goods left by the brothers if he is not buried there, even if he had chosen burial there. For that fourth part is due in satisfaction for the injury done to the parochial church, c. 1, De sepultura. But the convent of the Minor brothers does no injury to the parochial church, since he is not buried there. Moreover, the fourth part is due from the goods left to the church of burial, which must be understood as burial with effect; therefore, choice alone is not sufficient unless it achieves effect. D. Quod quis iuraverit, l. 1, in fine. Otherwise, it would follow that if he successively chose burial in twenty churches, the fourth part would be due from all the goods left: which is absurd. For only the last choice, put into execution, is entitled to the fourth part. 13 q. 2, c. Ultima voluntas. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, the wounding party is liable for the ensuing death.
2. Whether, and when, it is permitted, or not, to injure someone in self-defense.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that sometimes a wound and death stand in the relation of cause and immediate effect: for example, because the wound was mortal and incurable, whereupon the wounded person died immediately or within three days. And then it is doubtful whether the wounding party is liable for homicide. He killed, because he separated the soul from the body. As stated in D. ad l. Aquil. l. It a vulneratus, §. Nec mirum; and l. Huic scripturae; and noted in l. 1, C. de emenda servorum; and ad l. Corneliam de sicariis throughout. And this is true not only if he died within three days, but also within five or more days, provided it is established that the wound was mortal and incurable, on which point the judgment of physicians must be relied upon. As stated in l. Semel, De re militari, lib. 12. For one who is expert in his art ought to be believed. As noted in l. 1, in principio, D. de venditionibus inspicendis.

Sometimes a wound and death stand in the relation of cause and mediated effect: because someone was wounded in such a part of the body that many days later a spasm supervened, and then death. And the same applies, that he is liable for homicide: for since there are two causes, and one is subordinated to the other, the whole is attributed to the primary cause. As is read and noted in D. locati, l. Martius; and D. de damno infecto, l. Damni, §. Sabino. And this is true when the causes alternate in natural order. But sometimes a wound and death do not stand in the relation of cause and effect, but are entirely disparate, so that the wound does not influence the death, nor does the death depend in any way on the wound through an intrinsic cause. For example, someone is wounded in the foot, and dies from an abscess under the armpit. These two causes are not of the same nature, nor does the wound influence the abscess in any way, and then the wounding party is not liable for homicide: because he did not kill, nor did he have the intent to kill, but [is liable] for the wounding, however. The same applies if he did not employ physicians, or employed bad ones, or did not guard himself against deadly things: for then the penalty of the Cornelian law on sicarii is not imposed, but he is punished only for the wounding: because the text says, "If the slave was not mortally wounded, but perished through negligence, there will be an action for wounding, not for homicide." D. ad l. Aquil. l. Qui occidit, §. Fin. And elsewhere it says, "If the slave died from blows, that is, wounds or strikes, and it did not happen through the negligence of the physician or master, rightly an action for negligence will be brought." Therefore, otherwise, if the fault of the sick person, or of the physician, or of those present, intervenes. As in D. ad leg. Aquil. l. Si ex plagis, in principio. Another law says, "If it is alleged that someone died, it will come within the discretion of the judge as to how he died." D. de edicto edilitio, l. Quod si noluit, §. Si mancipium. And as I said above, the assessor, who does not know medicine, if it is doubtful how he died, ought to consult those more expert in the art, that is, physicians. As in D. de statu hominum, l. Septimo mense; and D. de solutionibus, l. Si pater. Unless the law itself were expressed on this point, as is the case in Extra, De homicidio, c. Significasti. For where the law interprets, we do not require another interpreter. And the foregoing are confirmed by what is read and noted in D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Ab hostibus; l. Si vir uxorem.

And certainly in our case, the magistrate proceeded prudently and with excellent reason, because he caused the said experts, who examined the wound with their own eyes, to be brought in. Optimal argument. D. de usufructuario quemadmodum caveatur, l. Prima, §. Recte. Moreover, from these it is concluded, and necessarily follows, that the said John is not to be condemned for homicide. Because squinantia, which is a disease of the throat, has nothing in common with a wound of the hand, nor is it its consequence: as nature itself makes most manifest. As in D. de verbis obligatis, l. Ubi autem non apparent, §. Ipsi enim medici hoc attestantur per regulas medicinae. To which rules one must adhere, as the glossa says, that the Bononienses [said] to Carocio. D. de regulis iuris, l. Omnis definitio. For the art of medicine is the truest art, and its rules arose from experience: as Aristotle says in the proemium of the Metaphysics.

I now proceed to another point. Whether it can be defended that he acted in his own defense, considering the statements of the witnesses. And it seems that it cannot: because he himself began the brawl, and of his own accord rushed at him, intending to seize Bartholomew; and it was lawful for Bartholomew to resist, even with a sword in hand: because John appeared stronger than he in personal strength, as in D. quod metus causa, l. non est verisimile, §. si iusto metu. For that text presupposes that this seizure is unjust; therefore it cannot be carried out by a private individual, as in l. ut vim, de iustitia et iure. Since this capture is a kind of summons, it cannot be made except by order of a judge, as in C. de exhibendis reis, l. neminem. This John, therefore, who rushed from place to place, is called an aggressor, and consequently, although the brawl increased, and he later made his defense, such defense was unjust: because he had previously engaged in an illicit act, as in D. si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dixeris, l. 1, §. cum arietes; and D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. si ex plagiis, §. tabernarius; and l. quemadmodum, §. si navium alteram; and C. de his qui ad ecclesias confugiunt, l. si servus. Therefore, he should not be excused: because he placed himself in necessity, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. idem iuris, §. finalis. He should complain of himself, and not of another, as in the same title, l. item mella, in principio.

On the contrary, it seems: because even if it was lawful for the said Bartholomew to resist, so that he would not be led to the magistrate, this was not permitted absolutely, but with the moderation of unblamable defense, as in l. prima, C. unde vi. Hence, if violence was being done to him without arms, he should not have laid hand on the sword: as is proved there. Unless it is proved that he could not otherwise escape the injury of the aggressor. And this is stated by the notable gloss, which is in the said l. 1. Moreover, it even seems that he could lawfully be seized and led to the judge, since he was preparing himself for flight. Argument from D. de furtis, l. interdum, §. qui furem; and D. de adulteriis, l. capite quinto. And it seems expressly stated in C. de maleficiis et maleficis, l. finalis. And if this is what it means that he could lawfully be seized, he could not resist, as in the said l. si servus; and D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. quemadmodum, §. pe., there: "if, however, the magistrate etc." Briefly, I cannot base myself on this, because the cause for which he could justly be seized does not appear. The same therefore seems to apply in the present case as in two persons attacking each other, of whom we note in l. si servum, §. sequitur, de verbis obligatis, according to Bartolus. Finally, concluding, I hold that he is not excused from the penalty for the wound. However, because he is not a murderer, as I have clearly proved above, let him be excused from the penalty for homicide. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the libel should proceed, in which it is alleged that such a person, with the intent to steal and to appropriate, etc., removed and concealed so many items and goods, which amount to an estimation of two hundred ducats, subject to error of calculation.
2. Whether a procurator is admitted to raise the exception of an incompetent libel in criminal cases.
3. Whether a manager, even if acting with malicious intent, commits theft by removing goods which he received from his principal.
4. What statute is to be considered in offenses.
body: The words of the accusation state: 9. That Antonius Cotta, with the knowledge and intent of Bernard, and by means of the agreements and promises contained and specified in the instruments, and to the great damage and detriment of the said Bernard, knowingly and fraudulently, with the intent and purpose of committing theft of the aforementioned moneys, pledges, and things, and of converting them to his own use, and of concealing them and each of them: from the said house he removed and took away, or caused to be removed and taken away, and from their place he transported them to a place of his choosing, namely, so many and such pledges, things, and moneys from the aforementioned things consigned to him, which amount to the sum of 1247 pounds, 17 shillings, saving any error of calculation. Which moneys, things, and pledges, and each of them, he concealed and conceals, knowingly and fraudulently, and with the intent of concealing them, he transported and transports, the said Antonius and others. Now it is asked whether the said accusation proceeds, or whether it is indeed inept.

† And it must be said without doubt that the said accusation does not proceed: because it is entirely uncertain and obscure, whether we consider the things themselves or the estimation of the things. For no things are specified, as required by the nature of libels, as in Extra, de libellis oblationis, c. significantibus; Digest, de re vendicata, l. si ob rem agat aliquis; Digest, de furtis, l. in actione; Digest, de deposito, l. 1, § si quis argentum, and § si cista; and as noted by Innocentius in c. ultima, Extra, de sepultura; and c. certificari; and as expressly noted by Speculum in the title de libelli conceptione, § iuxta propositionis, under the words "quid si peto"; finally, that the things, and that a libel without enumeration of the things is uncertain, is an express law, Digest, de iure dotium, l. si ego, § dotis, under the word "plane"; and it is supported by Codex, unde vi, l. si quando. Moreover, this libel is uncertain as to the estimation, and this for two reasons. First, because of the words "salvo errore calculi" [saving error in calculation]. For these words imply a condition, namely, unless there is an error in the calculation, as in Digest, familiae herciscundae, l. item Labeo, § 1. Hence, such wording leaves us in doubt or ambiguity, for it may be that, upon calculation, nothing is owed, or less is owed; and a libel that is obscure and general, especially in criminal matters, does not proceed, as in l. vulgari, Digest, de iniuriis, l. praetor dixi; and Digest, de dolo, l. item exigit. Moreover, a libel must be so conceived that the plaintiff cannot be reproved for calumny. For the utility of defense and reproof cannot be taken away from the defendant, as in Digest, de eo quod certo loco, l. arbitraria, § 2; and as noted in the said l. si rem, § ultimo; and argumentum, Digest, de contrahenda et communi stipulatione, l. optimam, in fine. Furthermore, it must be considered that no one can be certain of the estimation of things unless he is certain of the things themselves; but conversely, one can well be certain of the things, but not of the estimation; and therefore the uncertainty of the libel is sometimes tolerated with respect to the estimation, but not with respect to the things to be estimated; because it is impossible to estimate things that do not appear, as noted in the said § si quis argentum; and it is expressed in Digest, de in litem iurando, l. in actionibus, § plane. Furthermore, in the said libel of accusation, money and other things are mixed. It is established, however, that a manager [institor] is not said to contract money, since he may consume it by reason of business and alienate it. Goods [merces] are also of this kind, as in Digest, de pignoris actione, l. cum tabernam. For this is the natural use of trade; nor is that said to be contracted which is according to the natural use of the thing, as in Digest, de usufructu, l. arboribus, § navis. Hence, from these and other reasons, it is most certainly concluded that the accusation is inept, general, ambiguous, and to be repelled by the office of the judge, even if no one opposes it, as in l. 1, Digest, de officio assessorum; and Extra, de postulatio praeparatorum, c. bonae; and Digest, de iniuriis, l. praetor, § praeterea.

Secondly, it is asked whether a procurator is admitted to oppose the said libel. And it must be said that, since ineptitude appears from the form of the libel, the procurator is undoubtedly admitted. And as Innocentius elegantly states in c. Cum inter, Extra, De electionibus, wherever it can be established without proof of fact, that is, by law alone, that there is some exception, so that the parties may not be wearied by labors and expenses, judgment should immediately be given on that exception. To the same effect is what Innocentius notes, Extra, De accusationibus, c. Veniens. For wherever the matter left behind is not re-chewed, but there is a separate question, there the procurator is admitted; because this article does not touch the crime nor impunity, but the procedure. Although there was formerly a great question, when it touched both mixedly, whether the procurator is admitted, as was the case in the question of ravagese. But there is no doubt about the first point, that the procurator is admitted to dispute over procedures, as C., De adulteriis, l. Quoniam Alexandrum; and C., Ad legem Flaviam, De plagiariis, l. Praeses. And thus is the truth. And it supports what Cyriacus notes, C., De accusationibus, l. Reus.

† On the third main point, whether an institor, even with malice and for the purpose of disturbing or hindering the accounts, commits theft by removing the goods, it matters greatly whether he received goods that were valued or goods that were not valued. For where he received valued goods, he cannot have the intent to gain: since the valuation was made for the purpose that condemnation be made in the valuation itself when the goods themselves are not present, as in D. de comm. div. l. si ut certo § commoda; and C. de iure dot. l. si inter; and D. de aestimatoria actione l. 1. Since therefore he cannot have the intent to gain, from such a contract he does not commit theft. And if it is perhaps said that those goods are worth more than they were valued at: certainly this should have been expressed in the libel, which was done here, nor is it probable, nor should the judge hear him unless he declared that there is an interest beyond what was agreed, that the goods would be worth as much as the said accusation claims: because therefore theft requires the intent to gain, which cannot be present here, it is manifest that the accusation of theft does not proceed. Moreover, the rule of law must be considered, for the text of Scaevola says that theft is committed of possession, not of ownership: because no one subtracts from another that which always remains with the owner: as in D. de cond. furt. l. 1; but possession is subtracted: because he takes it away from the owner, as in D. de acq. poss. l. rem quae nobis. Wherefore we say that theft is not committed except in respect of possession, as in D. de usuc. l. si homo; and D. de cond. furt. l. sed nec legatarius; and D. si quis testamento liber esse iussus fuerit l. 1 § Scaevola. Furthermore, the accuser does not claim possession: therefore he cannot claim theft. This also appears from the very uncertainty: because no one can possess an uncertain thing, as in D. de acq. poss. l. 3 § in certam; and l. locus.

† On the last point, that the statute is to be considered in delicts, no estimation arises: because the place of the delict is considered, where the action is first formed, and the condemnation is moderated: as the doctors fully note in l. cunctos populos, just as regarding the status of the person the time of the delict is considered in delicts: as l. prima. ff. de poenis. and regarding the place, arguing from time to place. And we say the same also of unwritten custom, by l. quam semper soleo allegare post Iacobum de Aret. ff. de extraordinariis delictis. l. secularii. §. sunt quaedam. and especially in ordinary penalties, which are formal penalties, or formed from the very beginning of the delict. and place, time of the delict accompany it, as necessary concomitants, and cannot be separated from it. as in cap. abbate sane. de re iudic. lib. 6. and arg. ff. de euic. l. si fundus. and ff. de iudi. l. omnem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a wife, who has made an agreement with her husband that, should she die during the marriage without issue, those from whom the husband has acknowledged receiving the dowry may dispose of the dotal goods as if they were their own, may nevertheless make a will notwithstanding said agreement; and it distinguishes three cases, as at nos. 2 and 3.
body: Laurentius confessed that he had received from the lords Ubertino and Francisco, by way and on account of the dowry of their cousin Margaret, daughter of a certain Squartia, son of a natural father, and others, certain sums of money, movable goods appraised, and unappraised immovable goods. He promised to restore this dowry in the event specified to the said Margaret and her heirs, under the pacts and conditions set forth below, namely, that if the said lady Margaret should die before the said Laurentius without heirs born of her body, it should be lawful for the said Ubertino and Francisco to take corporeal possession by their own authority and to dispose of the said immovables as their own in perpetuity. Finally, the said event occurred, because the said Margaret died, having made a will. Now it is asked whether the said lady Margaret could make a will, notwithstanding the said pact.

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that either the aforementioned goods belonged to the said lady, or to the said nobles, or it is in doubt to whom they belonged. If, indeed, the goods belonged to the said lady, then the question is quite doubtful. It hinges on whether the said pact resembles a donation causa mortis or a donation inter vivos. For in the first case, it would be revocable; in the second, it would not. And that it is not a donation causa mortis but rather inter vivos seems to be proven by the word "perpetually," which signifies precisely and absolutely, as in D. de don. cau. mort. l. vbi ita donatur. But against this stands the rule handed down by the glossators and by Master Dino, for they say that where mention is made of death by way of a final cause, i.e., that she would not otherwise have made the donation, it is a donation causa mortis and can be revoked, as in D. de don. cau. mort. l. Seya and l. Seya de dote praelegata, and noted by Cynus in l. 2 C. de iu. dotium. And it is clear from D. de leg. 3 l. cum quis decedens § nuptura, and most fully noted in D. solu. mat. l. quae dotis. I believe that since this pact was appended with death added as a final cause—for it is evident that this woman did not intend to make a donation unless the marriage preceded—it is to be understood as a donation causa mortis and could have been revoked in a will, provided that in the will mention was made of the revocation by special words or general words importing this. Nor does the word "perpetually" stand in the way, because that word contains within itself a condition of death. Nor does l. vbi ita donatur stand in the way, because there she donated irrevocably.

† Now the second case is considered. What if the goods belonged to the nobles themselves? And this admits of no doubt, because the things ought to be restored to them, according to the form of the agreement, as in D. 24.3.10 (quotiens) and C. 5.13.1 (auia). For in this case the woman makes no donation; and therefore she cannot make a will to the prejudice of the nobles, unless the nobles themselves approved the will. For the property of the instituted heir may well be bequeathed and left to another, as in D. 34.1.1 (vnum ex familia) § si rem, and D. 34.1.2 (cum filius) § dominus, unless he had made an inventory; for then he could not be burdened more than he was benefited. Moreover, he would deduct the Falcidian share, if it had been disposed of by way of legacy, as in Auth. sed cum testator, and fully noted in C. 4.20.1 (cum a matre) and C. 6.59.1 (fi) § in computatione. Nevertheless, I do not believe that a general institution is to be understood in this sense; rather, the goods of the heir ought to be separated from the goods of the testator, especially because in wills those words are placed: “wishing to make a will of his own goods,” etc., as in X. 3.26.1 (filius). Furthermore, agreements made concerning the husband’s profit are valid and could not be revoked by will, as noted in D. 23.2.1 (l. 1), because they are dotal agreements, as in C. 1.3.1 (deo nobis). Also, on account of the burdens of marriage which the husband sustained, as noted in D. 19.5.1 (si donaturus) § fin.

I come to the third case, namely, in doubt whether it is understood that she was endowed from her own goods or from those of outsiders, and since these outsiders were administrators, it is more probable that it was from the woman's goods, as is fully noted in l. si, C. de dotis promissa; and see the argument of l. ultima, ff. de petitione hereditatis; and especially because this tends in favor of the woman herself. It must also be considered that if this Margaret died intestate, the aforementioned relatives would not succeed to her intestate estate, because she was born of a natural son, as ff. unde cognati, l. hac parte; and as noted in Inst. ad orf., § nouissima. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute that imposes a penalty on one who sells the same thing to two persons, if a husband and wife first sold the husband’s property to one person, and then, after the husband’s death, with their common children surviving, the wife, as mother and guardian of those children, and in her own name, sold the same property to the person who had been the notary of the first contract, is she deemed to have incurred the penalty?
body: Given the statute of the consistory of Piacenza, which provides that if anyone sells or in any way alienates any immovable property which he had previously sold or alienated to others, he shall be condemned in each case to 25 pounds of Piacenza currency, and that every sale or alienation after the first sale or alienation shall be void by operation of law; and that the podestà and judges thereof shall be bound to place and defend the first buyer in possession of the said property, as the true and legitimate buyer, even though the said property had not previously been delivered by the seller or alienator; and nevertheless the seller shall be bound to restore to the second buyer the price received by him, etc. It is presupposed that Antonius and Berta, husband and wife, for a certain price sold certain lands, which belonged to the said Antonius, to Sempronius, their son-in-law. And afterwards they received the said lands from the same Sempronius on a fictitious lease, as appears from the hand of the notary Georgius. It happened afterwards that, after the death of the said Antonius, with his children surviving, the said Berta, as guardian of the said children of Antonius and in her own name, sold the same lands after a year to the said Georgius the notary, who was absent, although he asserted that he had been agreed with the said Berta, because the said Berta was sufficient for the payment of the said fictitious lease. And from the foregoing it is asked: first, whether the said Berta is to be condemned in 15 pounds, as having sold the same thing to two persons; secondly, it is asked, if the said Sempronius ratifies and approves, whether the said Berta is bound to the said Georgius for the restitution of the price, damages, and interest, by virtue of the said statute.

† In brief, I resolve that she is not bound to restore the price: because the ratification reconciles and confirms the said second sale. The said second buyer knew the quality of the thing, as is stated in D. de pignoribus, l. si fundus, § 1; C. de evictionibus, l. si fundum sciens; C. comm. de legatis, l. si, § si; and D. de furtis, l. si vendidero, § si Titius; D. si certum petatur, l. proinde. For since the second buyer’s interest ceases, because the contract is confirmed, therefore his action to recover the price ceases. Moreover, he ought not to rescind the contract which he approved with certain knowledge, and which the first buyer’s will made valid. As for the penalty of the fisc, into which he fell by selling to two persons and thus completing the offense in one sum, it is more doubtful whether they are excused: because the matter has passed to a completed delict. Nevertheless, I believe that he is excused: because he is a woman, and because he did not commit stellionatus by selling to one who knew; for as the rule of law says, there is no fraud against one who wills it, nor deceit against one who knows, as D. de regulis iuris, l. nemo videtur fraudare eos. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether it is permitted for private individuals to divert the course of water.
2. If water flows into my territory, am I permitted to do with it as I wish, and to lead it wherever I please?
3. Whether one who has an upper mill may retain the water for the use of his mill, and prevent it from flowing for the use of one who has a lower mill.
body:
And it seems that, once water has been diverted into one’s own territory, the owner of the territory may divert it wherever he wishes; provided, however, that he does so in order to provide for his own needs, not to harm his neighbor, as stated in D. 39.3.1 (*Si in meo fundo*) and D. 39.3.1 § *Item aquam* (Digest, *De aqua pluviae arcendae*), and in D. 39.1.1 (*Proculus*) (Digest, *De damno infecto*). The reason is that water follows the nature of the bed and assumes its condition. If the bed is public, the river is public; if it is private, the water is private. The text establishes this doctrine concerning the bed in D. 43.12.1 § *Ille etiam alveus* (Digest, *De fluminibus*). Bartolus holds this opinion in D. 39.3.1 § *Sicut* (Digest, *De aqua pluviae arcendae*).

But the contrary view appears to hold. For it is impossible to alter the course of water whose contrary course is not remembered, as stated in D. 43.20.1 § *Ductus aquae* (Digest, *De aqua quotidiana et aestiva*). The ordinary gloss simply states that it is not permitted to divert water elsewhere, as noted in D. 41.1.31 (*Item lapilli*) (Digest, *De rerum divisione*). Moreover, water is common with respect to the convenience of the neighbor, and they are in a sense partners. Therefore, one cannot usurp the entire flow of water for himself, as stated in D. 8.5.1 (*Imperatoris*) (Digest, *De servitutibus rusticorum praediorum*) and in D. 3.3.1 (*De usu aquae*) (Digest, *De variis et extraordinariis cognitionibus*). This is the view held by Cynus in D. 41.1.3 (*Quaedam*) (Digest, *De rerum divisione*), where he says: “The fifth question is: what if someone uses that which is common or public so continuously that he appropriates the use of others? Certainly, he can be compelled to use it pro rata.” As in D. 10.3.1 (*Communi dividundo*) (Digest, *Communi dividundo*), as occurs among several persons having a water servitude, where the division is not of the servitude or the servient land, but of the water, by measure or time, as in D. 7.1.1 (*Arbor*) and D. 10.3.1 § *Cum usufructu* (Digest, *Communi dividundo*). This is almost expressly stated in D. 8.2.1 (*Imperatores*) (Digest, *De servitutibus urbanorum praediorum*). And thus we see in Bologna water divided between the Friars Preachers and the Minorites. Cynus. From this it is gathered that one cannot preempt the entire use of things that are in common use, but must divide it pro rata with others.

Furthermore, custom makes this division, which operates in the same way as a privilege of the prince, as stated in D. 39.3.2 (Digest, *De aqua pluviae arcendae*) and in X 1.2.1 § *Praeterea* (*Super quibusdam*) (Decretals, *De verbis significatis*). Bartolus distinguishes in Question 14, saying: “The fourteenth question: suppose one has a mill above, another below. The one who has the mill above, in the summer time of drought, wishes to make a collection of water; the one who has the mill below objects, because his mill is rendered useless or of little use. The question is what is the law. It seems that he cannot make a collection of water; for it is not permitted to make a work by which the river dries up and is desiccated, as stated in D. 43.8.1 § 1 (Digest, *Ne quid in flumine publico*). But by this the river is desiccated, at least for a time. Therefore, etc. On the contrary, that he can. For the formula is his, as has been said above. But once the water has lawfully entered his property, he may do with it whatever he wishes, as stated in D. 43.20.1 § *Illud Labeo* (Digest, *De aqua quotidiana et aestiva*). I answer: either when the said buildings were constructed, something was agreed upon regarding this, and that is observed, as stated in D. 43.20.1 § *Si quis* (Digest, *De aqua quotidiana*). Or no pact was added, and the same follows if an ancient custom has proceeded regarding this, which has the force of a pact, as stated in D. 39.3.1 § 1 (Digest, *De aqua pluviae arcendae*). Here add that custom can also exist among certain private persons, as stated in D. 10.3.2 § *Si constat* (*Venditor*) (Digest, *Communia praediorum*).

The other member of Bartolus’s distinction follows: or no pact or custom has proceeded, for example, because the buildings are newly made. And then either the one who has the lower building was prior in time in holding it, and thus the superior owner cannot retain the water for himself; or he was posterior, and then the water can be retained for utility, not for mere detriment to the inferior possessor, according to Bartolus. And thus it is true:

But the question now arises: what if the mill of the lower possessor was destroyed and remained in that state of destruction for a long time? Can it be repaired before the owner of the upper mill collects the said water for the newly constructed third mill? It seems that it cannot, because the servitude is lost by lapse of time, as stated in the Digest, *De servitutibus rusticis praediorum*, in the law *Attilicinus*. The contrary is true, because this is not a servitude, but rather a certain faculty, against which prescription does not run during a period of non-use, namely before the neighbor is in possession of the third mill. For without possession, nothing is prescribed, as in the legal rule *Sine possessione*, neither corporeal nor incorporeal things, except only the exception against a personal action, as in the chapter *Sine possessione*, *De regulis iuris*, Book 6, and in the Digest, *De servitutibus urbanorum praediorum*, in the law *Servitutes quae in superficie*. From these considerations, I conclude that, according to the facts proposed, it was not permitted to change the course of the water; and this not because anything is introduced into another’s property, for nothing is introduced, but because something is taken from another’s property and another’s benefit is usurped. For these cases are equivalent, as in the Digest, *Si servus vindicetur*, in the law *Sicuti*, section *Aristo*, and in the Code, *De finium regundorum*, in the law *Si constiterit*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether revenues can be acquired by prescription, or whether anyone can acquire by custom the right to collect a toll, as a revenue, and what is the case with other royal prerogatives.
2. In corporeal things, a twofold quasi-possession is found.
body: Since the ancient

The question is whether tolls can be prescribed, or whether a custom regarding ancient tolls can be established, which Lord Dynus raises in the Digest, *De publicanis*, in the law *Si publicanus*, § *In omnibus*. The words of which are these: “It has been a question whether the collection of a toll can be prescribed, for example, if someone collects tolls for a very long time and wishes to continue collecting them, precisely because he has been collecting them, and does not claim any other title. And it seems that it cannot [be prescribed]: because he collected them knowingly, and contrary to law, as in the law *Non solent*, Code, *Nova vectigalia institui non posse*. And therefore it is not prescribed, as in the Authenticum *Ut nulli iudicibus*, § *Nulli vero*, Collatio 9. On the contrary, because it is prescribed, is this § *In omnibus*: because the rule is the same for opposites. For just as one can prescribe the freedom from a toll, so one ought to be able to prescribe that it is owed there. Argument, Digest, *De publicanis*, law *Licitatio*, § *Earum*; and Code, *De aquae ductu*, law *Usu*, which begins *Aliis incipit veterem*, in Book 11. But say that it is not prescribed, unless for such a time of which there is no memory of the contrary, as in the Digest, *De publicanis*, law *Imperatoris*, § *Idem scripserunt*. But in the last law, Code, *Nova vectigalia*, the text seems to say that two things are required, namely, the command of the Emperor, and ancient custom. Dynus and Bartolus say that ancient custom suffices, provided that the knowledge of the prince intervenes, which is required in incorporeal rights that pertain to the prince. These regal rights, therefore, cannot be prescribed unless it is shown that the prince was aware. As in the Code, *De servis et aqua*, law 2. Speculator says that a custom is required of which there is no memory of the contrary, in Speculator, *De causa possidendi et proprietatis*, § *Quia vero*, under the words *Quid de colligentibus pedagium*. This gloss, which is in the law *Minus*, Digest, *De verborum significatione*, in the second gloss, holds similarly that both are required, namely, a privilege and custom. Nor will one suffice without the other. Cynus, in the law 2, Code, *Nova vectigalia*, holds that one of these suffices, namely, that the prince has suffered it for a very long time, or that he has expressly granted a privilege. As in the Extravagant, *De verborum significatione*, and *Super quibusdam*.

Furthermore, it must be said that if you begin with a privilege, either the privilege is solemn, and the privilege alone suffices, because it induces whatever is necessary; or it merely gives cause for prescription due to some just error, and then both are required conjunctively, namely, privilege and prescription, or custom; and then a period of 40 years suffices. But if you begin with custom, and there is no privilege there, then such regal rights are not prescribed without the knowledge of the prince, unless for such a time of which there is no memory of the contrary. Argument, Code, *De praescriptione triginta annorum*, law *Comperit*. But with his knowledge and patience, a period of 40 years suffices, as if the prince had tacitly remitted his prohibition, according to the work of Cynus.

But here it must be noted that in our case, the confirmation of the statutes was made first by the Commune of Novara, which seems to have held these regal rights in its territory by virtue of the Peace of Constance, as in chapter 1, § *Nos Romanorum*, at the beginning, *De pace Constantiae*, column 10. But one could doubt this, because the Emperor does not grant his regal rights there except insofar as it was previously customary. And this is difficult to prove due to the antiquity of time. But the following supports the same point more strongly: because our lord, who holds regal rights by his privileges, which he has from the Emperor, confirmed the statute, whose confirmation has the force of a privilege, unless it was obtained by obreption. Of which obreption, however, no one can judge except the prince himself, because this is a privilege. It is otherwise when the prince writes for the observance of the common law, because then even an inferior judge can rule on surreption, as in the Extravagant, *De rescriptis*, chapter *Super literis*. And it supports what we note in the Extravagant, *De iudiciis*, in the chapter *Cum venisset*, in the Novella. Since, therefore, the confirmation of statutes has the force of law and privilege, the said confirmation creates a right, and indeed among all, because it is a universal right as regards all those passing through, unless they prove themselves exempt. As in the Code, *Sine censu vel reliquis*, law *Omnes*, and what we note in the Extravagant, *De censibus*, chapter *Peruenit*, in the Novella. For he can make a law for all who enter his territory, who enters the territory; because such a law is given to the property, by analogy to the confessoria and negatoria, in which it is not distinguished from where they arise, because they are real actions. As in the Institutes, *De actionibus*, § *Aeque*, and the Digest, *Si servus venditus*, law *Si qui diuturno*, § 1.

It must also be considered that from the quasi-possession of these rights, at least once established by confirmation or privilege, no one can be expelled, nor disturbed in using the said custom, until judgment is rendered on the petitory. As in the Extravagant, *De electione*, chapter *Querelam*, and argument, Code, *De agris et censibus*, law *Si coloni*, Book 11. From which I conclude that, unless I saw otherwise by proof of fact, that the said passersby, like others, are bound to pay. Nor is there a right that they are under one power, because they are different universitates, and therefore they can be considered under different law. As what we note in Innocentius, in the chapter *Dilecta*, *De excessibus praeparatorum*. I do say, however, that if it were notorious that the collector was acting without right, that his possession would not hold him, as Innocentius elegantly notes in the Extravagant, *De filiis presbyterorum*, chapter *Constitutus*.

† For I consider that in corporeal things there is a twofold quasi-possession: namely, active, and of this I speak; and passive, which is for defense, not for attack: and the latter the praetor always protects during pending litigation. As in the Institutes, On Interdicts, §. commodum; and l. chirographis, §. 1, D. de administratione tutorum. Consider also that those who collect new tolls are doing something doubtful, namely, in a public place or on public bridges. I say something obstructive to liberty, namely, to impede and to act, to trade, and the like, which pertain to public utility, because the use of merchants, and especially concerning foodstuffs and clothing, is very necessary to all men, wherever they are. Hence, even if the praetor’s edict does not speak on this point, recourse must nevertheless be had to the office of the judge, as noted in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. quibus diebus, in principio; and by argument from D. de religiosis, l. si quis sepultura; D. de aqua pluvia arcenda, l. 2, §. idem Varrus. Moreover, the praetor ought of his own office to prohibit illicit exactions. As in l. illicitas, in principio, D. de officio praesidis; and in the case where it is established that the exaction is illicit, otherwise say what I have said above. And it supports its own reasoning in D. ne quid in loco publico, l. 2, §. idem ait si in publico; and D. de communi dividundo, l. communi dividundo, §. inter praedones, where it is said that the possession of a robber does not pertain to the force of a judgment that savors of law. And thus I say, I, Baldus. And thus, as above, I say and advise, I, Johannes Zanobius de Ubaldis, of Perugia, knight and doctor of laws, counselor of the illustrious Lord Duke of Milan.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a father in his will instituted A. and B., his daughters by a predeceased wife, and C., his son by a surviving wife, for what share are the daughters heirs, and for what share is the son?

2. And what if he subsequently added, “I nevertheless wish that my said daughters shall have 400 pounds for each one who contracts a carnal marriage, and one hundred for each one who contracts a spiritual marriage”: does it thereby appear that he receded from the prior institution, and are the daughters said not to be instituted beyond that, but in a certain sum, and can they deduct two fourths? And no. 2.

3. Likewise, what if it is added in the will, “And if my said son should die in pupillary age, or afterwards without children, or without a will, I wish that my said brother shall have one-half of all my goods and rights, all my legacies and debts being paid, and I bequeath that one-half to him; but the other one-half is to be distributed among the poor”: what is the law concerning such substitutions upon the death of the said son in pupillary age?
body: Gregory in his will thus says: I institute as my heirs Margaret and Joan, daughters of a certain lady Baldina, formerly my wife, and John, my son, by Lady Joan, now my wife, etc. I wish, however, that the said Margaret and Joan, my daughters, be content with 400 pounds for each of them who shall enter into carnal marriage, and with 100 pounds for each of them who shall enter into spiritual marriage; and in the meantime they ought to have maintenance from my goods. Now the question arises, what pertains to the male, and what pertains to the females.

And it appears that the daughters were instituted in one half, and the male in the other half, as in D. de haered. inst. l. liber homo § Titius. For he said “Margarita and Joanna, formerly of the lady Bladina,” and then he said “and John of the lady Joanna.” To the same effect: C. de impub. et aliis substitutionibus l. si. On the contrary, it appears that each is entitled to a third, because he spoke thus not by way of conjunction, but by way of demonstration, as in D. de haered. inst. l. si ita quis haeredes. Therefore, the rapidity of speech applied to the females, not conjunction. And thus, if one of the daughters were to die, given the composition of the sentence, the share would not accrue more to the daughters than to the son; and this seems more correct, because there was a single sentence, i.e., the word governs the entire sentence, as in C. de cad. tol. § his ita. But against this it is objected, and truly, that the said daughters do not appear to have been instituted universally, because the testator subsequently proceeds as if derogating, when he says that the daughters are to be satisfied and content with four hundred pounds, etc. For it is certain that later words derogate from earlier ones, as in D. de leg. 1 l. si mihi et tibi § in legatis, and l. diui § licet de iure codicillorum. Hence, the said daughters do not appear to have been instituted as universal heirs, but in a certain quantity. Also to this effect: D. de haered. inst. l. qui nolebat. On the contrary, it appears, and is more correct, that on account of the express institution, which preceded these words “satisfied and content,” they signify a fideicommissum, as in D. de leg. 2 l. peto § quid ergo, and § idem dicemus. Nor does it avail to the contrary, under that title, l. cum pater § pater qui filio, as noted there.

† Now it remains to be seen whether the daughters thus burdened may deduct the two fourths. And it seems that they may, by c. Ray. and Ray. and c. Si pater with its subject matter. But the contrary must be said, because they were requested purely, as appears from the word “interim.” And therefore they ought to be content with the legitime, according to what is noted in the said chapters and in many other common laws. And this concludes the first and principal part of the will. Now follows in the said will: “And if my said son should die in pupillary age, or afterwards without a son or without a will: then I wish that John, my brother, shall have half of all my goods, and I bequeath said half to him, after all my legacies and debts have been paid. The other half shall be distributed among the poor.” The son therefore died in pupillary age.

It is asked what is the law regarding the said substitutions in favor of the brother and the poor, and it seems that the said substitutions are direct pupillary substitutions by the nature of that condition, if he should die in pupillary age, as in *l. precibus*, C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus; and thus the said substitutes would come to all the goods of the minor, even to the maternal dowry, as in D. de vulgari substitutione, *l. sed et si plures*, § *ad substitutos*. Nor does the word "I bequeath" (*lego*) obstruct this, for according to the law of the Twelve Tables, that word is applied even to direct substitution, as in D. de verborum significatione, *l. verbis legis*. But I say the contrary, considering the words of this will: because the testator substituted in pure marriage, abstracted from all debt, and thus in certain goods, and not in all. Hence the said word "I bequeath" cannot imply a direct substitution, from which nothing alien can be excepted, as in D. de heredibus instituendis, *l. ex facto*.
