Furthermore, because the testator spoke in a varied manner, and did not place this word "I bequeath" except in this case, and thus he seems to have intended the proper meaning of this word, which signifies a certain distinction between a legacy and an institution or direct substitution, as is clear from the diversity of the titles *de vulgari substitutione* and *de legatis* 1. I say therefore that the said substitution made to the son was fiduciary, or legatine, so to speak. And from this it follows that, since the son was burdened under a condition, half of the entire legitime is deducted for the poor, and no more, but half of the entire legitime and half of the Trebellian portion are deducted for the brother, and what remains comes into the fideicommissum. Divide therefore the inheritance into 12 ounces: in 6 ounces the poor were instituted, from which two ounces are deducted for them, and thus they will have 4 ounces. Now 6 ounces remain for the brother of the testator, from which three ounces are deducted for him on account of the legitime and the Trebellian portion; therefore 5 ounces remain, which do not come into the substitution, but pertain to the intestate heirs of the son himself. Or if we say that the said substitution was not universal, neither to the poor nor to the brother is anything deducted except the sole legitime. And thus from the person of the son there would be deducted from the fideicommissa only four ounces, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, *l. lex Falcidia*, § *nunquam*; and note D. ad Trebellianam, *l. 1*, § *inde Neratius*.

But it is opposed, and it seems that neither the poor nor the brother ought to have anything: because an uncertain condition in a will, namely, if they should die in pupillary age, or afterwards without children, or without a will, etc., requires these two conjunctively, as in C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, *l. generaliter*, in the beginning. But a minor is not said to die without a will, as in D. de suis et legitimis heredibus, *l. 1*, in the beginning. But this opposition is of no avail: because the law speaks generally when the substitution is made to a person of age. But when it is made to a minor, it is manifest by nature that he dies without children; and it is manifest by nature that he dies without a will, as in C. de testamento militis, *l. si*. Therefore both conditions are true.

From these things it appears conclusively that the paternal substitution is not to be infringed, and that the brother of the said testator comes to at least three ounces of the 12 ounces, and the poor come to four ounces of the 12 ounces, and that 5 ounces of the 12 ounces remain for the nearest relatives coming intestate from the minor himself. And I speak of what was left to the minor. But the maternal dowry is not contained in the fideicommissum, because it is not among the goods left to the minor, but depends on the inheritance of the mother, D. de vulgari substitutione, *l. cohaeredi*, § *cum filiae*, ver. *nec fideicommissum*. And because the testator expressly disposed that debts should first be deducted. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute concerning matters to be submitted to arbitration, whether the plea of res judicata bars the arbitration agreement.
2. Whether one who ratifies an arbitral award is thereby deemed to have waived the collusion of his procurator.
3. Whether an appeal may be taken from an interlocutory judgment rendered on the execution of a res judicata, namely that it does not prevent the case from being submitted to arbitration.
body: It is proposed that the twelfth sentence was rendered through collusion of the procurator, which the lord subsequently ratified on account of a certain promise. The ratifying party brings the first ancient action. The exception of res judicata is opposed. It is replied on the ground of collusion, as well as on the ground of the promise, or undertaking, by which the ratifying party was induced by fraud, and would otherwise not have acted. And a compromise is requested according to the form of statute 1.

† It is asked whether the said exception of res iudicata and acknowledged matter impedes the compromise. And for clarity, it must be premised that when such a definitive sentence is rendered, which cannot be challenged by any remedy, and then either it is clear from it, or it can immediately be proven, and it impedes the proceeding both of the judge and also the compromise; because one ought not to transact concerning that upon which such a sentence has been rendered. As in D. de cond. indeb. l. eleganter, § si post. Or it is obscure whether it has been pronounced. And then such an exception does not impede the proceeding, nor the compromise; but the compromise ought to be made with the exception reserved. As is read and noted in D. de iureiur. l. nam postea, in princ. Sometimes there is such a sentence, against which one can challenge by some remedy. For example, if it were said that it was rendered through the collusion of the procurator. As in D. de dolo, l. eleganter, § penult. Or if it were said that the sentence was rendered through some obreption in the final cause. As in D. quando actio de peculio est annal., § quaesitum. Or through the fraud of the arbitrator. As in D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, § cum quidam. In which cases, if one pleads the exception of the sentence, a replication of fraud is made. As in D. de dolo, l. cum a te. And then, on account of the doubtful and uncertain outcome of the litigation, the compromise ought to be made, the plaintiff being admitted in the meantime on account of the ambiguity. As in the said laws. Those who, however, allege such qualities, must prove them. As in D. de re iud. l. diuus, and Extr. de probat. c. licet causam, in its proper time, and before the arbitrator. Therefore, the interdict and the exception of res iudicata is prejudicial to the proceeding, sometimes not. For, as I said, if the res iudicata could not be challenged by any remedy, such an exception ought not to be reserved for the morrow, but should immediately obstruct. As in D. de cond. indeb. l. eleganter, § si quis post. But if it can be challenged by remedies of law, then it does not impede the imminent proceeding; but it is reserved: as I said above.

But here it may be doubted whether one who ratifies a judgment is understood to remit collusion. And it must be said that he is not, if he was ignorant of the collusion; otherwise, the contrary holds. As in the Digest, On Pacts, l. Tres fratres. Concerning the aforementioned promise, it should be known that this promise is something extrinsic. And by this means the judgment would not be rescinded, but an action would lie for the performance of what was promised, if it was a formal promise; unless it was expressly stated that, if the pact were not observed, the judgment would have no effect; because a judgment is stronger than a named contract, in which place is not given to repentance. As in l. Si pecuniam, in principio, Digest, On Conditions on Account. Consider that here there was fraud in two respects: first, in the collusion; second, in the non-observance of the pact. And therefore recourse must be had to l. 1, in fine, Code, On Excessive Claims. From these things it appears, according to what is proposed, that the compromise, with the petition thus qualified as proposed above, ought to be made, because the exception of res judicata does not avail; because the action is brought on a new cause, since no action was previously brought. As in the Digest, On the Exception of Res Judicata, l. Si mater, § Eadem; and l. Si fullo, Digest, On Conditions Without Cause.

† It is further asked whether an appeal may be taken from an interlocutory judgment rendered on the exception of res judicata, namely, that it does not stand in the way of the case being compromised, or of proceeding to further steps. And it is certain that it may not, if the appeal contains an express error of law. But if the appeal contains a cause of such a kind that, being true and just, and from which a grievance appears, since such a grievance touches the principal fact, it may well be appealed against according to the common doctrine handed down. D. de minoribus, l. intra utile; and D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. arbitro, with its most recent material. And it is expressly stated in c. ult. in the first response, de appellationibus, lib. 6, where it openly presupposes that an appeal may be taken from such an interlocutory judgment. Although it could be said that such an interlocutory judgment, rendered against the authority of a definitive judgment, of which there is proof, is void by operation of law. As in l. 1, C. quando provocare non est necessarium; and l. 1, C. sententiam rescindere non posse. Since, therefore, in an appeal from an interlocutory judgment the cause must be expressed, recourse must be had to causes. And if they are approved in law, the appeal holds; if they are rejected, the appeal does not hold. Moreover, what constitutes reasonable causes is sometimes committed to the discretion of the judge. As in D. de legibus, l. non possunt; and in c. cordi, de appellationibus, lib. 6. And although deciding on causes pertains to the judge ad quem, nevertheless something also pertains to the judge a quo: because it pertains to him to grant or not grant the appeal. As noted in c. si ante, de dolo et contumacia, in the Clementines. Here one thing is especially to be considered, that the parties, by order of the praetor, had compromised the case regarding the aforementioned arbitral sentence first rendered, from which order no appeal was taken. And by the said compromissaries a pronouncement was made. And yet afterwards it was declared that their pronouncement was void by operation of law. I now say that the aforementioned order still deserves its execution: hence, what was brought into the compromise by the order, although it was not considered to constitute a compromise, must be compromised again: because the said interlocutory judgment has passed into res judicata as regards the parties, and has not been suspended. As in C. quomodo et quando iudex, l. si ut proponis; and C. de senatu ex periculo recipiendo, l. 1; and D. de iureiurando, l. qui per salutem; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. haec conditio, in principio; and what Innocentius notes in de officio delegati, c. in literis. And by this reason, among others not omitted, it seems to me that the said case is to be compromised notwithstanding the appeal: because from the said order, the execution of which is sought, no appeal was taken in time. And therefore, from the execution of that order, no appeal can be taken. It supports this what is noted in D. de novo operis nuntiatione, l. cum procuratore, by Bartolus; D. quod metus causa, l. si cum exceptione, §. haec autem actio. Moreover, I do not find that the judge ad quem has made any inhibition to the judge a quo. And thus the judge a quo is not prohibited from proceeding to the execution of his interlocutory judgment. As noted in c. non solum, §. illa vero, de appellationibus, lib. 6. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who disregards a notice of new work served upon him is bound to demolish the work.
2. Whether a notice given to the builders and craftsmen is valid, or not, to the prejudice of the owner of the work.
3. Whether a withdrawal from a notice given by the throwing of a stone is deemed to have occurred by a second notice given by order of the praetor.
4. Whether in a notice given by the throwing of a stone, an express statement of the place is necessary.
body: It is alleged that there were two denunciations. The first was made by the throwing of a small stone, for the purpose of preserving, as the denouncers asserted, their right. The second denunciation, however, was made by the praetor. And concerning both denunciations, a judgment was sought, and it finally appears that the denouncers had no right. Nevertheless, due to the contempt shown to the first denunciation, it is requested that the work done be destroyed and restored to its former state. It is also alleged that the said denunciation made by the throwing of a stone was made to the craftsmen and laborers at the work itself; yet it does not appear determinately in which part of the work the hollows were, and the work is long and extended. From this case, it is asked, first, whether the denunciation made to the said craftsmen is valid or not to the prejudice of the owner of the work. Second, if it is valid, whether there has been a departure from it by the subsequent denunciation made by order of the praetor, and thus there has been no departure. Third, it is asked, since the place or places where the said protestation by the throwing of a stone was made do not appear, what effect the said protestation has. Fourth, whether the said denunciation is nullified by a certain response made to a certain position, in which the denouncer said that he did not intend to disturb the said possessors.

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that the person who disregards the interdict of new work, that is, the one who scorns it, is bound to demolish the work at his own expense, unless the interdict is manifestly frivolous. As stated in l. 1, in principio, ff. de novi operis nuntiatione. Furthermore, it may be issued for the purpose of preserving a right and averting damage. As stated in ff. de novi operis nuntiatione, l. 1, § nuntiatio. Moreover, it may be issued against artisans working on the project. As stated in ff. de novi operis nuntiatione, l. de pupillo, § si quis forte. From these reasons, it would appear that the said work ought to be restored to its former state and demolished at the expense and to the detriment of the party proceeding with the work. But in opposition, other considerations regarding the nature of the interdict of new work must be taken into account.

† And first, it must be considered regarding the general nature of all protests: for they do not harm the ignorant. Hence the glossa says in the aforementioned § si quis forte: artisans take the best counsel for the lord if they do not notify him; because the lord is not bound to destroy the work done at his own expense. Nor, if the work was constructed at his own expense, ought he to suffer damage by losing the expenditure. But Jacobus de Radineis and many others say that he ought to show patience and loses the expenses incurred, but he is not bound to make them. The opinion of the glossa is sufficiently equitable. And I add that if it is not established that there was a mandate from the lord, that the work was done on his property, the lord ought not to demolish, nor suffer it to be demolished; because the building accedes to the soil, whoever may have made it. As in the Digest, De conditione indebiti, l. si in area, unless it was done with the knowledge of the lord. Nevertheless, this knowledge must be proven. Secondly, I premise that the nature of our operation is that the work done is revoked by way of an attentatum. It must be known, however, that those things which are revoked by way of an attentatum ought to be revoked before the one seeking this contests the litigation regarding the right of the principal cause. But if he has contested the litigation, it is never revoked by way of an attentatum, but it is necessary that a reasonable cause be proven. As Speculum says in the matter of those things which are innovated after an appeal is pending. For after the judge begins to cognize the merits of the principal cause, it is necessary that he pronounce on the whole, and not merely on the attentatum. And thus it certainly is in our case. Hence, if after the litigation is contested, the right of the protesting party appears, that which was not built by right ought not to be revoked by way of an attentatum, since it appears afterwards in full examination regarding the right to build; otherwise, if the right not to build appears; for then not only from the attentatum, but from what is proven, ought that which was lawfully made to be demolished. As in l. 1, Quod vi aut clam.

Thirdly, it must be premised whether it is permissible to pursue two protests. On this point I do not insist, but refer to *l. cu procu.* in the title *de novi operis nuntiatione*. And finally, I hold that if those building have the right to build, and this is established, since the matter is subject to inquiry and is not immediately at the boundaries, the work ought not to be demolished. Nor is it necessary to allege uncertainty, because the laws are well-known, as in *D. de novi operis nuntiatione*, *l. non solum*, § *sed ut probari*. It must be conceded, however, that it is not necessary to give notice in every single clod of earth, as in *D. de acquisitione possessionis*, *l. possideri*, § 1. And therefore no foundation could be made on this point. And this supports what I said above: because the dispossessed party must be restored before all else. However, if he contests the lawsuit regarding the right, and the lack of right is apparent, he is not to be restored; because he is deemed to have renounced his benefit, who has chosen another course, as in *X. de restitutione spoliorum*, c. 1. It would be otherwise if he had pursued the mere benefit of restitution. Our question depends greatly on the records. For if it is established by the records that there is a right to build, and if the owner was admitted by the judge of causes to prove his right, for certain no demolition ought to take place; because every demolition is by way of an attentatum against the edict of the praetor. And just as if it had been clear from the beginning, so also now, when it has reached that state through the legitimate order of judicial proceedings, from which the interdict of new work cannot begin; otherwise, the force of the judgment, and its authority, and the examination of causes, and the entire procedure in the case would accomplish nothing in favor of the owner, which is most absurd. As in *D. de iudiciis*, *l. de qua re*. Therefore, I say that the truth must be followed. Moreover, regarding what has been built after security has been given, there is no doubt: as in *C. de novi operis nuntiatione*, *l. unica*, and *X. de novi operis nuntiatione*, c. *si cum*. Spezzano says two things in this matter, and I will say a third. First, he says that if it is certain that someone has given notice calumniously, which I understand even if less temerarious, the building erected after the notice ought not to be demolished, according to Roffredus. Second, he says that if notice is given to the craftsmen and workers, it does not harm the ignorant owner. And he cites the aforementioned *l. de pupillo*, § *si quis forte*.

And I say thirdly, that it is not sufficient that the notice be made otherwise legitimately, unless it be made in the work and in the place about which there is dispute; for example, if the question is whether a work can be made in a river by drawing water from the river itself, the notice must be made in that place, that is, when one separates to draw from the river. And therefore all the laws which speak on this matter speak by the expression "in the place." As is stated in l. in loco, as cited in § si forte. But because a ditch made in one's own place and free land cannot be the subject of a notice of new work before one arrives at the river, since this notice is founded on that provision, namely, that nothing be done in a public river or its bank, as stated in ff. de fluminibus, l. 1, § in flumine. And therefore many doctors of this city advised that the notice of new work did not impede the ditch, because the ditch was being made in free land, over which no servitude is claimed. And this is precisely our case. From which it is concluded that the said notices of new work could not have been made to the prejudice of the said nobles of the counts, considering all that ought to be considered, and also the uncertainty of the places. For it must be clear as to how much, where, and what. As stated in l. non solum, § sed ut probari. And this is also stated by the Speculum, as cited above, and it is evident from this reasoning: because the notice of new work is equivalent to a libel, as noted in l. 1, in principio, ff. de novi operis nuntiatione. And from it, when it is formal, libels for demolition arise. Therefore, it must be certain, and the matter certain. As noted in l. 1, in principio, de edendo, in the great gloss. Here it must also be considered that the order of the praetor, justified by the clause "if you feel yourself aggrieved," resolves into an alternative, namely, that he shall not build, or he shall come to answer. As is noted in the ordinary gloss in l. de pupillo, § meminisse. And thus I have seen it to be held and observed by the curiales of the Roman Curia. I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It treats the matter. L. *admonendi*. And when an oath should be deferred in supplement of proof, and see there one beautiful statement regarding private writing.
body: Committed

† This article was submitted to the consultant, so that by virtue of the aforementioned rights and the proofs made by Albert the notary, it might be legally proven that the said Albert had expended or placed into the partnership those posts, or some of them, etc. The consultant advised that it was sufficient that this was half-proven, and that an oath should be tendered to the said Albert concerning the said posts. And it must be said without doubt that, in so advising, he either did not advise on the article, or he advised on what was not proven. And the reason for this is: because full proof and half-proof differ in species; indeed, they are almost opposite species. For half-proof introduces a certain privation in a qualified sense, though not absolutely. Moreover, since an oath is tendered in default of proof, he who says that an oath should be tendered asserts that there is a defect regarding full proof. This is the text: D. de iureiurando, l. admonendi, at the words "in dubiis causis." For if there is doubt, then it is not proven. Moreover, this law openly states that this oath is not proof, but rather a relief from the burden of proof: D. de iureiur., l. eum qui, in principio. But nothing was committed to the consultant regarding relief from the burden of proof; therefore, he exceeded the limits of his mandate. Just as we say elsewhere that the proof of one witness is not proof, although the tendering of an oath follows from it: as noted in c. 1, de electione, lib. 6. For by the term "proof," full proof is understood, as is read and noted in D. de condictionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Lucius, and D. de verbis oblig., l. qui Romae, §. Augerius. Moreover, he was to advise according to the acts and proven facts. But this oath was not yet among the acts, nor among the proven facts, because it did not exist in reality: as in D. de verbis oblig., l. cum stipulamur, and l. si a colono. For these words, "acts and proven facts," signify the perfect past tense, not the future: as in D. quod quisque iurat, l. 1, §. haec verba. Hence, if it is well considered, this consultant rather advised on what was not fully proven than on what was proven. And since the article was formed by the will of the parties, one should not depart from the article itself: as in D. de re iudicata, l. si convenerit. Wherefore it follows that the arbitrators, who, proceeding through error arising from their ignorance, tendered the oath, should not follow the error, since they have not yet rendered a definitive judgment; but they should, by interlocutory pronouncement, declare that such tendering did not effectively stand. And to this it contributes that what is noted in the aforementioned l. admonendi, according to one reading which states that no definitive sentence had been passed there, and therefore the oath is not upheld, which reading decides our question. And Bartolus holds this among others there.

Furthermore, if it is asked what is the law in common law, whether an oath should be tendered or not, it must be said that whenever presumptions strongly favor the plaintiff, the oath should be tendered to the plaintiff, and not to the defendant: as in Auth. de consuetudine recti feudi, §. sed sacramentum, col. 10, and in l. in bonae fidei with its material. I say "strongly favor" when they are vehemently alleged: as in c. cum dilectus, de successionibus ab intestato. But whenever there is less than half-proof, it is certain that an oath is not tendered. If, however, there is half-proof, then if the case is major or troublesome, the oath should not be tendered; otherwise, it is at the discretion of the judge to whom of the litigants he shall tender it. These are common principles, and therefore let the acts speak. Nevertheless, one thing must be known: that although a private writing sometimes makes half-proof, it must nevertheless be established that it is a writing in the hand of a solemn and trustworthy person. For if there is doubt as to whose hand it is, it creates no credibility: as in C. de fide instrumentorum, l. sicut iniquum, and what is noted by Bartolus in l. quaedam, §. nummularios, D. de edendo. Hence, one present at the acts, although as regards the rough equity of the conscience of a learned man and a master in theology, nevertheless as regards the justice of the forum, does not lack right, but proof in certain posts, as appears in the reading of the writings, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether it is lawful for a creditor to enslave his debtor, and whether a contract, promise, or oath made in prison is binding.
2. Whether it is necessary for one who claims to have done something out of fear of imprisonment to prove that he was in prison at that specific point or hour when he did or promised it.
3. Whether a debtor detained by a creditor in private prisons, after being subsequently released, may challenge the same creditor to a duel on account of this injury.
body: It is proposed

† That John was imprisoned in a certain castle of certain nobles who claimed that he had stolen certain sums of money, while he was their factor in the art of usury and at their stations; on account of which said John made a certain promise for the sake of his liberation, and swore to return to said castle, unless he paid. And he promised therefore not to complain, nor to raise the defense of fear, nor to harass, nor to demand a duel, and he confirmed this by his oath. However, in truth he was then under the power of said nobles, and could not depart without their consent, and after said deed, he still remained in the strongholds of said nobles for six months, or thereabouts. Now it is asked, since this John did not return by the term, nor did he pay, whether he is to be judged a malefactor and perjurer, and what should be decided concerning him. I answer, the truth of law arises from the truth of fact. As in D. ad leg. Aquil. l. si ex plagiis, § in cliuo. And therefore if it is true as is alleged, this man is not a perjurer: because it was not lawful for said nobles to retain him in private prison. Indeed, by the strictness of law, if they had any right, they lost it. As noted in D. quod metus causa, l. extat, and l. si. Nor did the oath bind said John. As in D. quod metus causa, l. qui in carcere; D. de verborum significatione, l. qui neque sequantur; and noted in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. nam et servus, in principio; and D. de testibus, l. qui alatronibus.

But the said Lo. doubts whether he ought to prove that he was in prison. And it is to be said that if before the said contract he was in prison, and also afterwards, it is presumed that in the intervening time he was not in his liberty. Hence it is not necessary to prove, as to the hour and moment when the instrument was executed, that at that time he was not in his liberty; because the middle is inferred from the extremes, as we say in *pos.* and in every act which admits of continuity, as no. 18, dist. *quia sunt culpae*. And in *Spec.* de probat. § 2, ver. *sed quaeritur*, how, as has been said, he will not be bound to return to prison, as no. in the said law *nam et servus*.

† On this point, the question is asked whether the said John could challenge the said nobles to a duel, and it must be said that he cannot, according to Roman law, nor is it among the cases in which, according to Lombard law, which is like a municipal law and does not have the authority of general law, and consequently should not be extended from similar cases to similar ones, it is lawful to make such a request. As is clear in my work, in the Usages of Fiefs, on keeping the peace, c. 1, §. si quis hominem, col. 10. And this is proven by C. de ac. et obl. l. negantes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the reservation of certain goods impedes the efficacy of the rule of monastic profession.
2. Whether one prohibited from alienating may alienate himself by transferring to religion, or by dedicating himself.
3. Whether a statute prohibiting alienations whereby public functions are diminished, confirmed by a superior prince, encompasses alienations made to churches.
body: It is asked,

† whether the reservation of certain goods impedes the efficacy of one professing a monastic rule; and it must be said that it does not, unless the person professing expressly protests that he does not intend to profess unless the reservation is valid. And then perhaps the profession is still valid, either because the pact is not valid against the force of religion, as noted in ff. de pac. l. in traditionibus, or because it is understood of a reservation as to the use of fact, which can be made with the permission of the Abbot. Concerning this, it is fully noted by the doctors on C. de sac. san. eccle. aut. ingressi, and there by Cy. in the question that begins "ulterius procedo." And because a pact does not hold against prohibiting rules of law, as in ff. de pact. l. contra iuris. in prin., for the rule of Blessed Augustine and of Blessed Benedict, and other approved rules, are public law in authority and utility, and therefore cannot be abrogated by a pact, as in ff. de pac. l. ius publicum. Moreover, a pact made against the force and authority of laws is not valid, as in ff. de leg. 1. l. si quis inquilinos. §. fi. and C. de agri. et censi. l. quemadmodum. lib. 10.

† But it is asked whether one prohibited from alienating can alienate by dedicating himself; and it must be said that he can, because he does not alienate himself, but the law does. Whence an adult, by professing, transfers all movables and immovables to the monastery, although without his person he could not alienate immovable goods, even to a church, as noted by Cy. in the said aut. ingressi, in the third question.

† It is asked, moreover, whether a statute confirmed by the decree of the lord prohibiting alienations through which public burdens are diminished includes churches, so that an alienation cannot be made to them. I do not decide otherwise, because there are opinions as to whether the fiscus or the church should be looked to. For the fiscus can impose a law upon its own things, that is, upon the territory that belongs to the fiscus as to fiscal matters, as noted by Accur. in ff. de verb. obli. l. ita quis. §. ea lege. Others say that the liberty of the church is so great that the fiscus cannot impose a law over this, unless it were done in fraud of the fiscus. And this opinion is commonly approved, and it was the opinion of Dy., as I have stated, on C. de sac. san. eccle. l. fi. Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It treats of the paternal and the avuncular fief, and how they are recognized, and in what they differ.
body: The words of the investiture are as follows: He confirmed, in the name of the aforesaid fief, Solomon present and receiving in his own name, and Jacob his brother for the remaining half, in the said castle, lands, foundations, rights, and things, and also the tenth which they hold and have been accustomed to hold by an honorable paternal, avuncular, ancient, and most ancient fief; and having received them for the parts and names mentioned above, he invested them with all the aforesaid things by means of his ring, which the said Lord Abbot held in his hands, to them, however, and to their male heirs descending from them in the male line, succeeding one another, in the name of an ancient paternal, avuncular, familial, and legal fief, and of an ancient and most ancient fief, in perpetuity, in them and their legitimate heirs aforesaid descending from them or any of them in the male line, according to the form of prior instruments and investitures, and according to the custom and usage of the said monastery, those present and consenting, etc. Moreover, the aforesaid Solomon, under his own name and that of his brother Jacob, confessed that they, and their aforementioned predecessors, held and had been accustomed to hold from the said Monastery, by an ancient and most ancient fief, certain plots of land, etc. From the words of which investiture, it is rightly doubted what kind of fief this is, whether paternal or avuncular. I call it paternal, i.e., one which took its beginning in the person of Solomon and Jacob, and was derived to their sons, namely, to Gaspar and the said Jacob, sons of Solomon, and to Antonello and Stephaninus, sons of the late said Jacob, brother of the said testator. For if indeed the said fief is avuncular and ancient, upon the death of Antonello and Stephaninus, it would have reverted to the said Jacob, son of the said Solomon, who now lives, and would have been excluded from the Lord Bartolini; as in c. 1, § hoc autem sciendum, qui feud. dare possunt, column 10; and in c. 1, de gradibus succedendi in feudum; and in c. 1, de natura successionis feudi, same column. But if the said fief was paternal, i.e., of Solomon and Jacob: for it is certain that one thing is a paternal fief, another is one acquired from ancient predecessors, as is noted in c. 1, de successione feudi, in the gloss quid igitur, near the end; then, upon the death of Antonello and Stephen, the portion of their father Jacob would have reverted to the monastery, and would have opened up to the Abbot himself, notwithstanding the testament of Stephaninus and Antonello; because in a fief, no testamentary disposition has effect, if only the disposition of the investiture is considered; as in the said c. 1, ver. nulla ordinatione, de successione feudi. Namely, because a fief is not transmitted by hereditary right except to children; as in c. 1, an agnatus, vel filius, same column. Now let us argue for and against.

† And first it seems to be said that the said fief is ancestral and ancient; and thus it pertains to the said Jacob by right of agnation. For the words of the writing say so, and the parties assert so. Therefore, one must adhere to the writing. As in C. de probat. l. cum precibus; and C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione l. optimam; and D. de legibus 3, l. ille aut ille § cum in verbis; and D. de fideiussoribus l. fideiusso magistratus § pro Aurelio.

To the contrary it seems: because on account of the new tenor of the said investiture, it appears that there was a departure from the nature of the ancient fief, and a new fief was constituted in the person of the said Solomon and Jacob. D. de pactis l. pacta novissima; D. de locato l. cum in plures § lege dicta; D. de praetoria stipulatione l. Valerianus; and argument from c. tres erant agnati, de eo qui fecit finem agnato. For granted that Solomon and his son could have succeeded in the place of Antonello and Stephen in the said case: nevertheless, because they consented that the investiture be made to each individually for himself and his male heirs, such a pact is valid as a new contract. Argument from D. de pactis l. ab emptione. Moreover, each one seems to have provided for himself and his heirs, and successively: as in c. 1, de duobus fratribus a capitaneo investitis. But it does not seem that one brother provided for another: especially since it is of the nature of a contract that one does not contract for another. As in c. 1 § si autem unus, de his qui feudum dare possunt; and D. de verbis obligatoribus l. si quis ita stipulatus § Grisygonus, where it says, "the person, however, never etc."; and l. stipulatio ista § alteri.

What shall we say? Was the party of Jacob open to the monastery, or not? The question is doubtful, on account of the ambiguous language; in doubt, words are to be interpreted against the proferens, i.e., against the recipient who intends to extend the obligation, and thus against the feudatory. As in D. de pactis l. veteribus; and note in D. de transactionibus l. qui fidem. I doubt on account of those words, "according to the custom of the Monastery." Also on account of those words, "according to the ancient investitures." For these words have the import of a certain relation to something else, of which I am certain. As in Extr. de verbis significandis c. Abbate; and C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus l. pe. If those words, "succeeding one another," had not been there, for by this he made a substitution, both among the recipients themselves and among their descendants. The first is clear in the word "themselves," namely, those named in the instrument. The second is clear in the word "their heirs." For substitution can undoubtedly be made even in contracts. As in D. de legibus 3, l. haeredibus. The consequence is clear from l. cohaeredi § qui discretas, D. de vulgari substitutione; and D. de legibus 2, l. Titia Seio § Seia.

But further it follows to see that the said lady Beatrice, together with her husbands, possessed the said fief for a period of 30 years and more. Hence there should be no doubt that against the said agnates, if they had any right, it was prescribed: as in c. si quis per 30, si de feudo fuerit controversia. Where it is to be considered that by this prescription made in good faith, useful dominion is acquired, especially with title: as in C. de praescriptione 30 annorum l. si quis emptionis. And therefore, if any useful dominion had belonged to the agnates, it would have been eradicated from them. As noted in l. ut certo § si duobus vehiculum, D. communi dividundo. And therefore, although it ends with the death of the prescriber, nevertheless it does not return to the agnates, in whom no causal principle of successorial right is found: because it is once extinguished. As in D. de colonis l. qui res § aream; C. de remissionibus pietatis l. solida providentia. But it would revert to its perpetual ownership, and thus to the church, whose ownership does not die. As in c. 1 § inde, potest feudi alienatio. Many things are said by the doctors that if the agnates remain silent for a year from when they knew that the right of retraction belonged to them, and remained silent, it is as if they had consented: as in c. Titius, si de feudo fuerit controversia. Consider whether this has place when the agnates come by a successorial pact, or not. Moreover, there is no doubt that consent prejudices. As in c. 1 § praeterea, qui modis feudum amittatur.

From these things, therefore, concluding: I am of the opinion for the monastery that the fief was apt for the monastery, and by this it is concluded for Master John de Trecio. Saving, however, the substance of the truth, both in law and in fact. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, by the renunciation of the fief made by the vassal in the hands of the lord, prejudice is caused to the agnates in the succession to the said fief.
2. Whether prejudice is caused to the agnates by felony or other injury committed against the lord.
3. A vassal who contracts friendship with the enemies of the lord ought to be deprived of the fief.
1. He who causes himself to be enfeoffed by two opposing parties sins more gravely than he who denies the fief.
2. A fief cannot be enfeoffed to the prejudice of the agnates in the daughter’s son, unless by custom it pertained to women.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that a vassal may renounce a fief into the hands of his lord, as in c. 1, § rursus si fidelis, Qui modis feudum amittatur, and in c. 1, De vassallo decrepitae aetatis. However, this is not to the prejudice of the agnates, to whom, by the nature of the ancient fief, the fief ought to revert after the death of the renouncing party; for an inequitable condition ought not to be imposed on one person through another. D. De iuris et facti ignorantia, l. Iniquissimum; D. De pactis, l. Si unus, § Ante omnia; and l. Si. C. De locato, l. Si cum Hermene. And therefore, the said fief remains paternal, or ancient, with respect to the agnates, as in the aforementioned c. 1, De vassallo decrepitae aetatis. Therefore, when the said renouncing party dies without an heir, the investiture made in the son of his sister becomes void, and the agnates are called, as in c. 1, De natura successionis feudorum.

Secondly, it must be premised that, on account of the felony of the offense committed against the lord, the fief is forfeited to the lord, as in c. 1, *An ille qui interfecit fratrem domini sui*, so that at least this vengeance for his injury may be had. But if one does not grievously offend against the lord, but against another, it does not prejudice the agnates, as in c. 1, § *Denique*, and § *Si vassallus*, which was the first cause of losing the benefice; and in c. *Si vassallus culpam*, *Si de feudis fuerint controversiae*.

Thirdly, it must be premised that if a vassal has conspired with the enemies of his lord against the lord, or has joined his friendship with them in a manner tending to the prejudice of the lord, and especially contrary to the statute or the interest of the lord, he is to be deprived of his fief. As is stated in the law and noted in the Digest, On the Duties of the Prefect of the City; in Law 1, at the end, On Inofficious Wills; and in the Code, Liberi, at the end.

Fourthly, it must be premised that he who causes himself to be enfeoffed by two opposing parties commits a greater offense than he who merely denies the fief, although the latter is nevertheless to be deprived of the fief, as in the chapter *Vassallus feudum*, under the title *Si de feudo fuerit controversia*. Therefore, he ought to be considered a tergiversator both in the affirmative and in the negative, as in the Digest, under the title *De his qui non in fideiussione*, in the law *Athletas*, section *Calumniator*. And he from whom he first held possession may divest him of the possession which he has betrayed, as in the Code, under the title *De acquisitione possessionis*, in the law *Si*.

† From these premises thus laid down, the decision of the questions asked is clear, namely, that the said fief could not be enfeoffed to the son of the sister to the prejudice of the agnates, unless it were such a fief as, by custom, pertained to women: because a woman does not succeed to a fief, nor does her heir, unless the fief is promiscuous, that is, open to both men and women, as in c. 1, §. hoc autem nondum, de his qui feuda possident. Hence, in this case, the son of the sister would rightly be capable [of inheriting], because he has the right of agnation, as in C. de legitimis heredibus, lege, l. 12 tabularum. But if the fief is simply paternal, although the son of the sister obtains the right of agnation in other matters, nevertheless in the fief it is otherwise, on account of the nature of the fief itself, as in c. 1, de feudo feminino, and what is noted there, and in §. ff. de eo qui sibi, et heredibus suis maribus, et feminis investituram accepit. But if the fief were new, in which case agnates do not come into it, it would revert to the Church, and [the Church] could enfeoff whomever it wished, as in c. 1, §. femina quoque, per quos fiat investitura, et per quos recipiatur. And from these things appears the determination regarding that son of the sister.

Now let us come to the fact concerning the agnates: and I say that, presupposing that the investiture was first made to them by one having the power, it was valid in law; nevertheless, what is it that, on account of subsequent fraud or gross negligence, the said agnates may be deprived [of the fief] and it granted to others, as it pleased the Church? This requires, however, prior deprivation by sentence, or, if the matter is notorious, no sentence is required; because in notorious cases the order of judicial proceedings is not required, but in others, as in tit. de pace tenenda, c. quicunque advocati, and l. emptorem, de actione empti. It is true that the lord may spare them, and the fief remains with them by virtue of the old grant, as in ff. de peculio, l. peculium, §. si ere alieno, and l. fi., C. de revocandis donationibus. Thus, concluding from first to last, this fief is open to the lord, if he wishes. But if he wishes to remit the felony, he may do so; I speak, as I said, assuming the power, or quasi-possession of power. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the question of whether several persons are to be admitted when emphyteusis was granted to them from the beginning.
2. Whether the right of accretion has application in fiefs.
3. What the term *altero* signifies.
body: To be considered

It is established that when an emphyteusis is granted to several persons from the outset, if nothing else is declared, it is deemed to have been granted to each person for a share. As stated in D. de duobus reis, l. reos, § cum tabulas; and by argument from C. si certum petatur, l. si non singulari; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cui fundus, § si; and C. si plures una sententia, l. 1; and D. de regulis iuris, l. Pau. In these laws it is said that the nature of the conjunction among persons assigns to each a virile portion. And if one considers the matter closely, it is not one contract made simply, but rather, as one might say, one-half to Titius and one-half to Seius. For even in legacies these would be two legacies, not one legacy. So too in contracts, there are two contracts in number.

† And if the question arises concerning the right of accretion, if indeed we are speaking in the context of a last will, the right of accretion has place: as in D. de legibus 3, l. re coniuncti; and this is due to the force of conjunction and the extensive favor of the last will: as in C. de caducis tollendis, § is ita. But in contracts we do not say so. For what is omitted is held as omitted: as in D. de verbis oblig., l. quicquid astringendae, and in l. si mihi et Titio; and therefore, since the contracting parties did not provide for themselves regarding the right of accretion, the right of accretion ceases, and it fails in mere usufruct, as in D. de usufructu accresc., l. 1, § interdum. These points are proven in fiefs, which are similar to the emphyteusis of the Church: as in col. 10, qui feudum dare possunt, c. 1, § cum vero Corradus, ver. quod si communiter; and in c. 1, de duobus fratribus, a capite inue. quibus inspectis. Indeed, it must be said that the fief is reverted to the Church in part. For, as I said, since there are two contracts, one of them is extinguished, and the case is one of caducity. But on the contrary, regarding the tenor of the words of the contract. For the tenor of the investiture is stronger than any tacit natural rule: as in the aforementioned laws cited above. But the tenor of the writing says, "for himself." And this word would imply "for the Church," as in D. de pactis, l. qui futurum, § si ex altero, and l. auus; and it adds, "and their heirs." This word is also understood tacitly: as in D. de verbis oblig., l. stipulatio ista, post principium; and D. de probationibus, l. si pactum. And it adds, "from them," namely, when heirs remain from both. And it adds, "or from one of them," by which word "one," it clearly appears that even if one survives, it ought not revert to the Church; because this has been consolidated in the person of one. And thus, one survivor excludes the Church. Argument from C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. si; and D. ad Trebellianum, l. haeredes mei, § cum ita. And it works well in its own reason. D. de herede instituendo, l. Lucius, where it says, "the imprudent counsel of the testator is observed." For he did not name only the brother, but the heir, and also his children. We have a similar case. D. de legato secundo, l. Titia Seio, § Seia. Consider.

† For this term "the other" is taken from "some." And therefore, for the truth of the proposition and the continuation of the entire contract, it suffices that something [be the case], as in D. 22.6.1 (*Si qui ducenta*), § *Utrum*. This is supported by the principle that words must have some effect, as in D. 45.1.1 (*Si stipulatus*). But if this term "the other" did not have this sense, namely that one should have the whole in default of the others, this addition would have no effect, which ought not to be the case, as in l. 1, D. 50.4 (*Ad municipium solutio*). The question turns on this term "the other," how it is to be referred: whether to what both contracting parties received, even for the other; or rather to what each received separately for himself and his heir. But considering the affection of the persons and the generality of the words, I hold that the common provision is directed even to the other. Argument: D. 2.14.1 (*Tale pactum*), § *Si*. And thus I opine that the portion of the dying person without an heir is not reverted to the church, on account of the tenor, as I said, of the investiture or contract. This tenor is not to be strictly construed, but interpreted indefinitely, as the words sound, as in the cited c. 1, X. 2.26 (*De duobus fratribus*), from the chapter *Inuestitura*. And it is supported by D. 36.1.1 (*Iulia fideicommissa*), where it says "to him or to them," as in l. *Haeredibus*, in principio. I, Baldus. Consilium of those from Camagna of Montferrat, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given an arbitration agreement in which there has been a waiver of appeal, reduction of complaint, rescript, privilege, exception, restitution in integrum, etc., may the arbitral award be sought to be revoked, where no fraud on the part of the arbitrator is alleged, but only injustice? Likewise, does such a waiver extend to an arbitral award in which there is an express error? Likewise, does it extend to an arbitral award in which the arbitrator has exceeded the scope of the arbitration agreement, or has rendered an award on a matter not submitted to arbitration?
body: 71. In a certain arbitration by Niccolò de Tileo, etc., and a compromise made in his favor, and after viewing the petition presented to the Illustrious Prince, the Lord Marquis, by the men of Camagna, it may be doubted: whether, as a matter of law, the said award can be invalidated, annulled, or reformed, without alleging fraud on the part of the arbitrator, but merely simple injustice.

And this doubt arises from the words of the compromise, in which there was a renunciation of appeal, reduction, rescript, and privilege, exception, and restitution in integrum, as is more fully contained in the said compromise. And briefly, it would seem to be said that the answer is no, on account of the aforementioned renunciations. This question is ancient and common. And the doctors commonly say that unless the arbitrator is acting in bad faith, others add or with gross negligence, a reduction cannot be sought. But if there is bad faith, or gross negligence, a reduction may be sought: and especially by the universitas, which can be aided by the remedy of restitution in integrum. And for this, the ordinary gloss in D. ad leg. Trebellianam, l. servo invito, §. cum praetor, sets forth the doctors. D. puts it in C. scienti, de regulis iuris, lib. 6, and in D. quidam cum filium, de verbis obligatis. And this is also pleasing to Nicolaus de Matarea. But these things are true, unless the error is expressed in the sentence of the arbitrator; because a sentence or award where error is expressed is not valid: as in D. de appellationibus, l. si expressim. The same is true if the arbitrator goes beyond the matter of the compromise. For if the compromise is about controversies, he cannot order that I sell my property, so that I may obtain the price: for there is no compromise on this point, and in this case the time for declaring it null does not run. This is expressly stated by Bartolus in D. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquiliana. And from this it clearly appears that the said sentence, as regards the sediment, is null by operation of law, because it was rendered beyond and outside the compromise. This appears from the fact that the words of the sentence say, "we pronounce that the said plain ought to remain to the said Antonio," and adds, "Furthermore, we pronounce in compensation of the price and value of the said plain, etc." From which it clearly appears that the said arbitrator confesses that the said plain belongs to the said men of Camagna, yet he wants them to sell, or that it be considered sold; because the name of price signifies sale: as in l. ultima, C. de praediis curialibus, lib. 10. But this the arbitrator cannot do: as in C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. sicut. It is supported by what is noted in l. 1, C. de episcopis audiendis, by Cyriacus and others. And this is expressly noted by Bartolus in the aforementioned l. cum Aquiliana.

Regarding the other chapters, I say that customs, from which law arises, must be observed. I say observed, on both sides: as in D. communia praediorum, l. venditor, §. si constat. For those things are tolerable which ancient custom has approved: as in D. de pollutione, l. Imperatores, and D. de publicanis, l. si publicanus, §. in omnibus vectigalibus. For the text in the Usus Feudorum says that the authority of the Roman laws is not insignificant. But they do not extend their force so far as to overcome usage or customs: as in C. Ubertus, de feudorum cognitione, col. 10. And therefore the said award must be reduced to the equity of ancient customs, notwithstanding the general renunciation; because there was no renunciation of customs, to which it is not understood that derogation is made by general words: as in D. de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. si prius, §. recte placuit. My conclusion is that truth and custom must be observed, where they are established. And if it is said that rather there was a renunciation by the syndics, I say that they did not have a mandate for this, by those things which they saw. And thus it does not prejudice the said universitas: as in C. de pactis, l. pactum curatoris, and C. de transactionibus, l. praeses, and D. de pactis, l. Imperator Severus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A daughter leading a shameful and luxurious life may be disinherited by her father; it is doubted how it is to be proven that she leads a shameful and luxurious life. Also, whether such a daughter may claim her legitime or its supplement.
body: Fillafamilias

† If a daughter has chosen a life of luxury, she may be disinherited by her father: as in Auth. ut cum de appel. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum, vers. si alicui ex prędictis. Nevertheless, the heirs must prove this against the disinherited daughter. And if they do not prove it, the daughter prevails in the querela inofficiosi brought against her father’s will: as C. de inof. test. l. omnimodo. That she has chosen a life of luxury is proved by the argument from what commonly happens, which is the strongest in law in doubtful cases: as leg. et no. C. de proba. l. neque natales. By this argument from what commonly happens, it is proved, because the young man frequently approached the young woman, when public reputation sufficiently proves a life of luxury, nor is she excused on the ground that she says she could not be known [sexually]: because she was narrow. For although rape [stuprum] is not consummated, it suffices that the act proximate thereto, or the attempt, has been reached, as C. de epi. et cle. l. si non dicam rapere, with its material. To which c. 1. §. item si fidelis, in the words vel concumbere se exercuerit, is most apt. quibus mo. feu. amit. col. 10. Moreover, even without a contract of bodily intercourse, a life of luxury, indecency, and dishonesty may intervene: as ff. de contratab. l. non tamen. §. si emancipatus. This appears in her who commits prostitution: as ff. de his qui notantur infa. l. athletas. §. Pomponius. I conclude, therefore, that if such a shameful and disgraceful life is proved, the said daughter could legitimately be disinherited. And since a legitime is not due to one disinherited, which otherwise is due by natural law, because the disinherited is held as dead: as ff. de coniung. cum eman. lib. l. 1. §. si pater emancipatus, and it is customary to note, ff. de vul. sub. l. cum ex filio, in the beginning, it follows that the said daughter, legitimately disinherited, cannot demand a supplement of the legitime. And these things are true in the ius commune. Nor does it avail that the father afterwards left her something by way of institution; because that institution is considered in law as a legacy, since we assume her expressly disinherited. To this effect C. de hęre. insti. l. quoriens. And by this the gloss is answered, which is in Auth. nouissima, C. de inof. test. and C. ad treb. l. si quis precio. For it is not presumed that the testator corrected himself: as ff. de condi. et demon. l. non ad ea. One might doubt against the said daughter whether the legacy is valid, when it was made with insult and infamy of her: as noted in l. 3. C. quemad. test. ape. as ff. de leg. 1. l. turpia. and ff. de haeredi. insti. l. quotiens. §. si quis nomen. But I think it more humane that what was left to her is valid, out of regard for humanity, and compassion, and paternal love. For these are just motives of the testator. arg. ff. de infami. l. furti. §. pactus. and what is noted there. and C. qui ac. non pos. l. propter. insidias. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether by public outcry and reputation, and by the indication of flight, and by a confession made out of court to a certain private person, all joined together, it is proven that the husband killed his wife, so that he may and ought to be excluded from the profit of the dowry.
body: It is alleged that the wife of Peter Ferraris, who is called Peter Merlinus of Aquae, was found dead in the morning from certain blows inflicted upon her,

† And that the husband took to flight. Nevertheless, it is not established that the husband killed her, except by public outcry and rumor, and by the indication of flight, and by the indication of a certain confession made out of court to a private person. And since the intestate heir of the said woman was claiming the dowry, the husband opposes this by means of the pact for gain. It is replied that the said [pact] is not understood to have been made in the case in which the husband killed his wife. Rather, even if he did not kill her, nevertheless the wife perished through the negligence of the husband: because he perhaps did not employ a physician in her care, or employed a bad one: as in D. 24.2.22 (Si ab hostibus), § Si vir uxorem occiderit. And there, note that the husband ought not to be induced by a pact to commit a delict, but rather ought to be punished. And from the same cause, one ought not to obtain both punishment and reward, as in D. 3.5.1 (Sive hereditaria). And truly, this is not a replication, but is an exclusion of gain by the law itself: because this tacit condition is inherent, namely, if he did not kill her, or did not contribute fault to her death. Where, therefore, it were established that there was killing, or notable fault regarding the death of the wife, this question would have no doubt. But let us now see whether it is established in such a manner regarding the homicide, or the fault of the husband, that the husband ought not to gain the dowry. And truly, it is not: because rumor is not sufficient to prove a crime. For rumor, speaking properly, is not a species of proof, nor even a presumption of law: as fully in the law and notes, according to the modern interpretation, D. 48.18.1 (De minore), § Tormenta. Likewise, flight alone does not prove a delict. As in D. 48.12.1 (Divus), and noted fully by Cynus in C. 9.13.1 (De raptu virorum). Likewise, a confession made before a private person does not even prove [the fact], although it makes some indication. As in D. 47.1.1 (Quaero), § Si; and noted in D. 48.10.1 (Ictus fustium); and D. 48.5.5 (Capite quinto). And by Innocentius, X. 1.6.1 (Per inquisitionem); and X. 2.24.1 (Cum super). Hence, confessions ought to be made in the records: as in C. 9.22.2. From which it appears that by the aforementioned means the homicide, or something of that sort, has not been proven, which would repel the gain of the dowry. From this follows another point, that if the judge expressed in his sentence that it was proven by these means, he expressed an error of law in the sentence: and thus the sentence is void on account of the expressed error of law.

On the contrary, it seems to be said for several reasons. And first, because where a wrong cannot be proven clearly, it is proven by argument. As in D. 4.8.1 (Non omnes), § A barbaris. Likewise, by the argument from what commonly happens, as in C. 4.20.1 (Neque natales). Likewise, there is no doubt that these witnesses are strongly corroborative. As in X. 3.20.1 (Cum dilectus). Likewise, the judge could not pass sentence, saving his conscience, otherwise than he did. As in X. 2.27.1 (Cum aeterni), Book 6. Likewise, the judge rather expressed his motives than that he bound himself. As in D. 36.1.1 (Qui filium), § Sabinus, at the end, there "and certain other things etc." Likewise, it is presumed that he who lived alone with the woman killed her, especially since he also took to flight: as in D. 19.2.1 (Dominus horreorum); and in Auth. 4.13.1 (Si vero etiam quidam). Likewise, it suffices that the judge could have been moved by other causes than those expressed. As in C. 4.1.3. Hence Innocentius says that if the judge says thus, that it is proven by A and B, therefore I condemn: although it is not proven by A and B, nevertheless the sentence is valid. As he notes, X. 2.20.1 (Quoniam contra falsam), at the end. He says the same, that if one cause is false, and another can be true, the sentence is valid. As he notes, X. 6.35.1 (In praesentia). Likewise, the said Peter treats of gain to be obtained with the injury of another, namely, with the killing of the wife. To exclude the gain, it seems sufficient that the husband does not avenge the death of his wife, if she was killed by another: as in D. 49.14.1 (Ei qui). Since, therefore, she was killed either by another, and the husband ought to have denounced it; or by himself, and then we have the proposition. Likewise, such exact proofs are not required to exclude gain as to inflict damage. Thus, although the said judge had expressed an error of law in some respects, nevertheless he said that he was moved by several other reasons. Regarding which, as far as presuming in favor of the sentence, the word of the judge is accepted: unless appeal has been taken from the sentence, as elegantly noted in D. 2.1.1 (Si praetor), § Marcellus. And thus I hold, especially by this reason, and by the statement of Innocentius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the payment of a legacy made from the revenues of grain and wine ought to be effected, and whether the heir is required to send the grain and wine to the legatee’s house, or vice versa.
2. A legacy for alimony is not presumed in the case of a woman possessing a large dowry.
body: Confirming my opinion, always subject to the correction of my brother Lord Angel and other experts.

I say that, in my opinion, the said payment should be made from the revenues of wheat and wine, and the testator is understood to have intended the wheat and wine that is harvested from his estate, namely: in the place of Mons Magnus, where the said wheat and wine is harvested. And this for four reasons. First, by analogy: because if the testator orders a house to be provided, it is understood to refer to those he has in his estate. Likewise, therefore, if he orders a revenue to be provided. As in D. 32.1.1 (*Si domus*), in the beginning. Therefore, the performance must take place in the place where the thing is, or nearby, or conveniently. The second reason is that, even if the place of Mons Magnus is contiguous, nevertheless the toll and burdens pertaining to the heir, but not to the legatee, must be paid; because they are burdens of the collection of fruits: as in D. 7.1.1 (*Si pendentes*), § *Si quid cloacarii*. Thirdly, by D. 32.1.1 (*De legatis*), in the section *Haeres* according to Julius, where the heir is not bound to pay for a future purchaser; therefore, neither for the burden of collection; because that burden arises after the legacy is perfected. Fourthly, by the general rule. For an heir burdened with one obligation is not bound to the risks that could occur to the carrier; and therefore, if the legatee wants the legacy to be provided from the estates, he should go to the place, or at least to the domicile of the heir. However, if the heir committed fraud, he would incur the penalty of *laudemium*. As in D. 13.6.1 (*Si legatarius*). Therefore, let him send, and the heir shall pay in good faith. To this also contribute the general rules, which are noted in D. 16.3.1 (*Item illa*). Also another rule, because in obligations we look to the minimum, as in D. 46.1.1 (*Fideiussorem*) and D. 32.1.3 (*Sempronius Proculo*). But if the thing were to be carried to the house of the legatee at the expense and cost of the heir, it would not be the minimum in the obligation, but the maximum. Nor do I dispute further on this point: because much could be alleged for and against. But also, as I alleged in another opinion, there is the ordinary gloss in D. 2.15.1 (*Cum hi*), § *In causa*, D. 2.15 (*De transactionibus*). This is my opinion.

† I do not omit this: because a woman having a large dowry is not presumed to have a legacy for alimony, unless perhaps in that case in which the restitution of the dowry is pending: as in the sole law, § exactio, Cod. de rei uxoriae actione. And there is no doubt that a dowry of 100 florins is a large dowry in fact and in name. It is established in Cod. unde vir et uxor, Authent. praeterea, and there Accursius notes. On a certain statute of Milan concerning assassins. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Who is called an assassin, and what it means to assent with the head or shoulders, and whether they signify a similar consent or command.
body: Although the aforementioned allegations are sufficiently sufficient for the confirmation of the same,

I say that, according to the matters alleged, a personal or corporal penalty in no way applies, because no assassination has occurred; for neither does the *ius commune* provide for it, as is evident in c. 1, *De homicidiis*, lib. 6, nor does the statute; therefore, we ought not to assert it, as in D. *De aqua pluviae arcendae*, l. *Si servus*, § *Non dixit*. And even if it were proven that an express command of the father intervened, and why the son ought not to have been obedient, as in D. *De actionibus et obligationibus*, l. *Servus non omnibus*, nevertheless, for this reason alone the son would not be called an assassin; because he acted neither for a reward nor for the hope of a reward, but out of reverence and paternal friendship. Argument: D. *De negotiorum gestis*, l. *Si pupilli*, § *Sed si ego*. And since the father is not an assassin, the son is not an assassin; therefore, the father does not offend through an assassin, as in D. *De furtis*, l. *Si is qui rem*, § *Si tu Titium*. And I do not believe that this should be done. But a doubt remains regarding pecuniary condemnation, namely whether the father, who is said to have assented, should be tortured. And let us see what it means to assent with the head or shoulders, whether it implies consent or a command. And the *glossa ordinaria* says that it implies consent, D. *De pactis*, l. *Item quia*. But since one commits the offense and the other consents, he who consents is not liable unless the offender would not otherwise have committed the act; as in D. *De verborum significatione*, l. *Saepenumero*, in fine. And nothing has been proven on this point. Therefore, the father should be absolved due to lack of proof. Moreover, if the father were subjected to torture and confessed that he simply assented, unless he confessed that the son did so for his sake and that he ratified it, he should not be punished without other proof. Furthermore, he could not be questioned on this point, because nothing has been proven on this matter. Also, this case is not covered by the statute, which speaks of torture. Also, here multiple indications do not concur, and one indication is much less than half-proof, as noted in D. *De probationibus*, l. *Comprobatio*. Hence, concluding from the first point to the last, I do not think the father should be tortured, but rather absolved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It treats of the prescription of the right to impose fiscal burdens and of the prescription of liberty against such imposition.
body: The question arises between the Count and the inhabitants of the Castle of Rocher, and Do. Margaret and others.

† To make the matter evident, it must first be premised that villages or castles cannot impose fiscal burdens, unless they have done so by virtue of the longest custom, namely, a period of time of which there is no memory to the contrary: as is noted in ff. de publicanis, l. si publicanus, §. in vectigalibus; and these are royal prerogatives, as in c. 1, quae sint regalia, col. 10; and Princes reserve these to themselves, as in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. perit; and in Auth. de mancipiis principum, §. publicorum, col. 3. And this longest time, whether it be called prescription or custom, is not force; because it is held as truth: as in ff. de aqua quotidiана et aestiva, l. hoc iure, §. ductus aquae; and as noted in I. 1, C. de servitutibus et aqua, at least as a solemn privilege, as in extra de verborum significatione, c. super quibusdam, §. praeterea. Secondly, it must be premised that although a village or castle has prescribed such a right, and although immunity cannot be prescribed against the Imperial fisc, nevertheless it can well be prescribed against a village or castle. For the rights of a village or castle are prescribed within a period of 40 years, except in certain cases, as is noted in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. si. Thirdly, it must be premised that custom or prescription does not bind those against whom the prescribers or those invoking custom have never used prescription or custom: as in extra de officio archiepiscopi, c. diiecto. These persons are therefore immune: not because they have prescribed immunity; but because the imposition of the burden has not been prescribed against them: as in ff. de itinere actuque privato, l. 1, §. Iul. From the premises, it follows manifestly that against the said Lady Margaret and her predecessors, the said Castle of Rocherii never acquired any right: neither by common law nor by custom. For even from the universal, a certain species can be excepted by non-use, or more accurately, is not included: argument from ff. de legibus, l. ab omnibus, in principio; because custom and prescription are matters of fact and consist in fact; and therefore they do not receive execution regarding persons or acts: text in the said c. cum dilecto. Moreover, when someone has a right by privilege or custom, and I wish to prescribe against it, a forty-year prescription is sufficient: as expressly noted by Bartolus in the said §. in vectigalibus. It is not necessary here to dispute l. vacuatis, §. 1, C. de decimis, nor l. privilegio, C. de incolis, nor l. cum de in rem verso, de usuris; because these do not properly touch the matter. Having considered these points, I say that the said Lady Margaret ought to be absolved, and perpetual silence imposed upon the common body of the Castle of Rocherii. Nor do I exclude the most solemn allegations made by others for this party; indeed, I praise them, because they are very good and subtle. And it helps to prove that, by common law, villages and castles do not impose collections, but rather bear them: as in Auth. qui monasteria efficiunt sua, §. si quis igitur, col. 7. Also, that against the prescriber, fiscal rights are prescribed within a period of 40 years, is well supported by what Innocentius notes in extra de postulatio praeparatoria, c. bonae, el. 2. Also, liberty is prescribed even by one who knows himself to be bound: as in ff. de usucapione, l. sequitur, §. si vero. And therefore I remain in the aforementioned conclusion of the absolution of the said Lady Margaret. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If I overcome the one who overcomes you, I all the more overcome you.
body: Because in the case at hand no maternal grandmother was left. The question is whether the statute concerning those who succeed intestate, § “If, however, he dies intestate, having left behind, etc.,” applies. And the answer is that it does not: because that statute speaks of a maternal grandmother being left, and also of a male son of the father’s brother or of a sister, etc. For, since the said statute departs from the common law, it appears to require the presence of a maternal grandmother, who is very effective in excluding uterine sisters, as is shown in the Authentica “Defuncto” and in the following Authenticae. Therefore, if the grandmother is not found, it is not said that uterine sisters are excluded by others who are more remote. On the contrary, it seems that the said statute mentions the grandmother in order to grant a share to the son of a sister, which is demonstrated as follows: the son of a sister takes a share from the grandmother and prevails over the grandmother in that share; therefore, all the more strongly does he prevail over her than the grandmother herself prevailed, according to that rule,

† If I defeat the one who defeats you, I defeat you. As in D. 3.5.1 (*Aequissimum*) and D. 20.1.1 (*Aequissimum*) with its companion texts. And I believe that this is the intention of the statute. But whether this statute is understood to dispose of goods in another territory is a sufficiently much-debated question, in which I say nothing other than what I wrote after Cynus and Bartolus in *l. Cunctos populos*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the contract of a notoriously prodigal and dissipator of goods, to whom, however, administration of his property had not been interdicted by a judge, is valid.
2. Whether such an oath, or another rashly taken, can be relaxed by the bishop without the other party being summoned.
body: It is asked whether the contract of a notoriously prodigal and dissipator of goods is valid, even though he had not been interdicted from his goods by a judge, who was not only a prodigal but also an adult. Secondly, it is asked whether an oath rashly taken can be relaxed by the bishop, the other party not being cited.

† And the first point is very common. For the gloss in *l. is cui bonis*, D. de verb. oblig., holds that unless he has been interdicted from administering his property, contracts entered into with him are valid. Likewise, the gloss in *l. 1*, near the beginning, D. de cura fur., notes the contrary rule regarding wills, citing *l. is cui bonis*. Peter follows that gloss, because one cannot be seen to contract in good faith with him, as stated in D. de usucap. pro empt., *l. si quis cum sciret*. Bartolus holds that a judicial interdiction is required, pursuant to *l. Iul.*, D. de cura fur. And if you say that what is notorious is considered equivalent to a sentence, this is true only with regard to making a matter certain, but not with regard to further disposing of or prohibiting something; see D. de contrah. empt., *l. si quis sciens*. But in support of Peter’s opinion it is argued that a madman and a spendthrift do not appear to have consent, as in D. de reg. iur., *l. furiosi*. It will be said that a spendthrift is, as it were, far from governance (*procul a regimine*), and therefore cannot have the power to alienate things, especially immovables. Otherwise he does not have it, especially when two defects concur, namely prodigality and minority. However, there is an argument to the contrary in D. de tutel., *l. qui habet*. And it is supported by what is noted in D. de cond. indeb., *l. interdum*, and D. de fideiuss., *l. Marcellus*. Therefore, either the spendthrift is doubtful, and a judicial interdiction is required; or he is certain and notorious, especially when contracting with himself, and a judicial interdiction is not required. Reason and natural equity greatly applaud Peter’s opinion. Nevertheless, the common doctrine holds, as I said, that this notoriety is not equivalent to a sentence. But here arises a doubt: granted that the contract is valid, whether this spendthrift can be restored under the general clause “if it shall seem to me that there is a just cause,” by proving enormous lesion, even if not beyond half the just price. But since this passage has been left untouched by others, I omit it for the present.

It remains to be considered regarding the oath of a notorious prodigal. For, granting the oath, it appears to be rash, and therefore to be relaxed: because it seems to be at the expense of the eternal salvation of the buyer himself. This question is resolved by the foregoing. For, if one can effectively contract with such a prodigal, then the said oath could not be relaxed. But if fraud had intervened, it could: because the oath is rash, and because fraud has intervened. Argument: Authentica "Sacramenta puberum," Codex, "Si adversus venditionem." And immediately it is asked, in the case of relaxation, whether the said oath can be relaxed without the buyer being cited. I say that it cannot, because this act requires knowledge of the cause. As in Digestum, "De adoptionibus," law "Non ita divus," with similar authorities. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When contracts entered into by an adult or a spendthrift are validated by an oath, and number 3.
2. In notorious matters, a declaratory judgment is not required except as a precaution.
body:
