William, the adult, requested that a general curator be appointed for him, and the judge appointed a curator for him in these words: “Considering and knowing that the said William is an adult who is dissolute and prodigal, and such a person as spends what ought to be spent and what ought not to be spent, and who would easily be induced to alienate his goods and to bind himself to all and each thing that any cunning man might wish; and because it is better to prevent the wound than to seek a remedy after the cause has been wounded, and lest the said William be reduced to want and poverty and have a sad outcome, in every manner, way, right, and form, I have given, constituted, and decreed Francis as curator to the said William, thus saying: ‘Concerning the general administration of the said adult William, I hereby grant and decree to you, Master Francis, present and willing, the care and governance of his person, things, rights, goods, and all assets of the said William; and I will and command that you give security, take an oath, and make an inventory of the goods of the said William, and do all other things and each thing that must be done in such a case, the form of law being observed; in such a way and so that the said William may in no manner, nor by any form of right or cause, be able nor validly sell, donate, or alienate his goods, nor in any way bind himself or his goods to anyone, without the license, authority, and consent of the said Master Francis, his curator. And whatever shall be done by the said William without the license of his said curator shall be null and void, and of no effect by any right or cause.’”

It is also alleged that the said William was manifestly a prodigal. It is also alleged that the said curator gave no oath, although this was commanded to him by the judge and is also imposed by law. And in the same way he made no inventory, and thus he lacked administration by operation of law, as we note in the law Legitimos, Digest, On Legitimate Tutors, in the beginning. It is also alleged that the said adult William, being a prodigal, with the authority of such a curator as he was, made many contracts, whereby he was reduced from his entire patrimony to nothing; in some cases a judicial decree intervened, in others it did not. An oath also intervened, in which he swore not to contravene in any way or for any cause. It is also alleged that he prodigally consumed all the money which he received from the said contracts, so that at the present time of the trial he is found richer in nothing.

The question is therefore whether his legitimate heir can validly claim the goods thus and so alienated.

† And for the clarity of what is to be said, it must be premised that sometimes a person is merely an adult, and in such case contracts celebrated by him are validated by oath, provided fear and fraud are absent, and this effect, namely the validation of the contract, passes to his successors. For such an oath solemnly represents him as being of full age: as in the Authentica *Sacramenta puberum*, C. *Si adversus venditionem*; and this is taken from that source and by the same authority: as noted in l. 2, C. *De rescindenda venditione*. Sometimes a person is merely a prodigal, and in such case there are three situations. The first is when he has been so declared by sentence and a curator has been appointed to him as to a prodigal. The second is when he has been declared a prodigal and his property has been interdicted; yet no curator has been appointed, or one appointed is less suitable, or one appointed is suitable but has not given security, has not sworn, or has not made an inventory. For these circumstances are equivalent, and in these two cases, if we inquire whether support is given to the contract by oath, it must be said that it is not; because the oath of a prodigal is equated to the oath of a minor under tutelage: as noted by Jacobus de Arena in l. *Qui habet*, ff. *De tutela*; and by Bartolus in ff. *De verbis obligatorum*, l. *Is cui bonis*. For the oath does not remove prodigality. Indeed, even the decree appended in such alienations is null by operation of law; because in the interposition of such a decree many solemnities are required, which have not intervened: as in ff. *De rebus eorum qui in cura sunt*, l. *Magis puto*, § *Non passim*; and in ff. *De transactionibus*, l. *Cum hi*, § *Si praetor*; and l. 1, C. *De praetoria curia*, lib. 10. The third case is when he has not been declared a prodigal, nor has his property been interdicted by a judge, nor has a curator been appointed; and then it matters whether he is a notorious prodigal by the notoriety of the fact. In such case there are differing opinions: for some say that this notoriety is equated to a sentence: as noted by Guido and Petrus in ff. *De testamentis*, l. *Is curbonis*; because one cannot be seen to contract in good faith with one whom he knows will squander his assets on nefarious or reckless uses: as in ff. *De usucapione pro emptore*, l. *Si quis cum sciret*. But the contrary is held by Guido and Bartolus in ff. *De verbis obligatorum*, l. *Is cui bonis*, citing l. *Iulia*, ff. *De cura furiosi*; and noted in the same title, l. 1. For notoriety is not equated to a sentence, but to proof, according to Bartolus.

But commonly, in matters of notoriety, the following rule is given: that in notorious cases a declaratory judgment is not required, except as a precaution. See *l. emptorem*, in the beginning, D. de actione empti; and the glosses in *l. at qui natura*, § *cum me absente*, D. de negotiorum gestione; and *l. 1*, C. qui et adversus quos. To this effect is that general principle: to add a demonstration to a thing already demonstrated is futile; see *l. 1*, at the end, D. de dote praelegata. This is clear there by the converse case. Suppose, for instance, that someone is interdicted from managing his property, and he notoriously returns to sound and upright conduct, without any decree, just as a madman who has returned to his senses does not need a curator, even during lucid intervals; see C. de curatore furiosi, *l. cum alijs*. But if he is a prodigal who is not manifestly so, contracts entered into with him are valid, unless he was induced to contract by fraud; because neither the law nor the minister of the law, nor any natural or civil reason, otherwise forbids it; for otherwise the law would vainly mention the interdiction by the judge and the appointment of a curator. Yet it would be rash to say this, according to the aforementioned *l. Iulianus*, D. de curatore furiosi, and according to *l. sciens*, D. de contrahenda emptione.

† It remains now to come to the third principal case, namely when someone is an adult and a prodigal. And it is certain that a curator must be appointed for him, as for a minor, because this is an ordinary curatorship. But not as for a prodigal, because nature is considered rather than accident: as in l. qui habet, ff. de tutel., and there by Dynus and others. Therefore, it may be doubted whether, since he contracts as an adult and not as a prodigal, his oath should confirm the contract. And for clarity, it must be premised that although he has a curator only as a minor, nevertheless the judge can prohibit administration and alienation for two reasons, namely on account of age and on account of prodigality. Therefore, the oath is not valid, because if the oath of one who suffers only from the vice of prodigality is not valid, much less is it valid if he suffers from a double defect, namely age and prodigality. Moreover, if the written document is carefully observed, the superior judge wisely appointed a curator as for a minor, but he interdicted the goods, not only as for a minor, but as for a prodigal, because so the document says, which must be followed, and thus concluding from the first to the last, the said oaths are void by law itself. For a contract is made against good morals by contracting with one to whom goods are interdicted. And therefore the oath is not valid: as in c. non est obligatorium, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Nor could the contracting parties claim ignorance, because one who contracts with someone as such is presumed to know his quality: as in ff. de regulis iuris, l. qui cum alio. Nor must it be omitted that the contracts of those who are not legally elected or created are not valid: as in ff. de iureiurando, l. iusiurandum quod ex conventione, §. pupillus, and ff. de negotiis gestis, l. qui aliena, §. quanquam. And from the foregoing it is concluded that the said contracts and obligations are void by law itself, the oath being in no way valid, neither by civil law nor by canon law, because a prodigal is not understood to consent: as in ff. de conditionibus indebiti, l. interdum, and ff. de fideiussoribus, l. Marcellus, and ff. de iureiurando, l. tutor, §. prodigus, and ff. si certum petatur, l. certi conditionis, §. quoniam, and Inst. de cura furiosi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a recognition or confession made by someone before a public notary, that a certain thing belongs to Titius and not to another, is valid.
2. Whether a cession made before the notary in favor of the said Titius on the occasion of the said recognition is valid for the purpose that the said Titius may claim the right, and concludes that both are valid.
body: A certain Laurentius, merchant, and others, appeared before a public notary receiving in the name and on behalf of Hillarius, and in truth acknowledged that all those sums of money, and everything and the whole thereof, in which the said Laurentius and Francis had been condemned and are bound to Guidatius and John, formerly partners in the city of Pisa, by virtue of a certain arbitral sentence rendered by Justus de Merinis and others, pertained and belonged to the said Hillarius; namely, that the novation and sale of wine, of which mention is made in the said sentence, pertained and belongs to the said Hillarius, although this is not contained in the said sentence and in the instrument of the said novation and sale. Wherefore, wishing to acknowledge good faith, by way of recognition, he ceded the said rights to the said notary receiving, as above. Now it is asked whether the said recognition is valid, and this is the first question. Secondly, whether the said cession is valid, so that an action may be brought thereon:

And it seems that the said acknowledgment is not valid: because a confession made before a notary does not have the authority of res iudicata, as noted in C. de lib. cau. l. iubemus, unless the notary has been appointed for this purpose by a judge, as stated in cap. quanquam, de vsu, lib. 6, and as noted by Innocentius in c. dudum, de contro. coniuga. On the contrary, it seems that the notary is a public person through whom we acquire rights, as noted in Inst. de inuti. stipu. in §. si quis alij, and in ff. de ado. l. his verbis. And this second opinion is approved by common usage.

Secondly, it is asked whether the aforementioned assignment is valid. And it seems that it is not: because the said assignment does not contain a certain title. As in C. man. l. per diuersas, and l. ab anastasio, and as noted in l. 1 and 2, C. ne liceat potentioribus. Furthermore, because in the assignment of actions, confession is not sufficient, but the truth must be established. As stated in the aforementioned l. per diuersas, and as noted by Jacobus de Belvisio in Auth. de quali. dotium, §. aliud. To the contrary, it seems. Suppose, for instance, that someone sold my wine in his own name and thereby acted in the name of the sellers. Could he not acknowledge this in good faith and consequently assign the rights to me? Certainly, no one doubts that he could. First, from the general rule: because acknowledging good faith is not prohibited. As in ff. de admi. tu. l. quotiens, §. sicut, and ff. manda. l. quintus. Second, from a special rule: because one who manages another’s business may assign the rights to the person to whom the business principally pertains. As in ff. de nego. gest. l. pe, and as noted there. Moreover, this assignment is necessary and follows from the management of the business. And in such a necessary, or quasi-necessary, assignment, confession suffices. As in the aforementioned l. per diuersas, §. excep, and ff. de solu. l. Modestinus. And it should be observed here that it is not true that the title is lacking; because the title is the same as the cause. But here the cause is not lacking: because the preceding management is the cause of this assignment, which management is proven by the assertion of the parties, and it is not only a cause, but a necessary cause. As in ff. de proc. l. si qui in rem. And therefore, concluding, I say that the said acknowledgment and assignment are valid. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When collection or assembly is prohibited by an edict, or a decree of the Prince, or by a statute, what falls under the term "assembly," and what assembly is understood to be prohibited, and whether. 2.
1. When a penalty is imposed on having [something] and on the person, whether it is considered a capital penalty, or how those words are to be understood, and what if the penalty is reserved to the discretion of the superior, how he ought to exercise his discretion. number 4.
body:
The Decree provides that no one shall dare or presume, openly or secretly, directly or indirectly, or under any feigned pretext, to contract, form, or in any manner celebrate among themselves any league, union, confederation, pact, or agreement, nor any association or conspiracy, under penalty of excommunication and a penalty to be imposed at the discretion of the same lord, which penalty shall also be incurred by all and each of the supporters and participants, as well as those providing aid, counsel, and favor in the aforementioned matters, in any way whatsoever.

It finally happened that Zenardus and Ruffinus, fearing that their friends from the lineage of the House of Flaganario might be divided among themselves, at the instigation of certain nobles of Gambarini, went to a certain place where they summoned and gathered many people. And among them, they uttered these words: “You know your friends, and we know the instigations and cunning of those from Gambarini, who wish to divide you; and because united strength is stronger than dispersed strength, we beg you not to believe them, nor in any way adhere to them, but rather, according to your usual custom, in defenses and offenses, where you wish to be offended, you should stand together as one; otherwise, you could easily fall into final destruction.”

It is also stated that no pact or agreement was concluded, but only the aforementioned gathering took place, and the aforementioned words were spoken. Now the question arises: since an inquiry has been made against all the aforementioned assembled persons, and also against those who uttered the said words, and nothing else has been proven other than what has been stated, what penalty should be imposed?

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that the word “congregation” is the most general genus. As stated in the Digest, *De pactis*, l. 1, § *conventionis*, where it says: “they are gathered and come together in one place.” It applies to a bare congregation, in which nothing is established by agreements, such as a gathering to hear a sermon, a harangue, or some parliament. It also applies to a congregation in which something is established by agreements or statutes, which has various names, depending on what the assembled persons impose upon it, or what the law imposes. For sometimes it is called a union, sometimes a confederation, sometimes a sect, sometimes a conventicle, sometimes a conspiracy, sometimes a conspiracy. For all these signify a certain consent among themselves, confirmed by the interposition of faith. But words merely spoken, without the effect of a conclusion, are said, not promised. As stated in the Digest, *De edicto edilitio*, l. *sciendum*, § *dictum*; and see the note in l. *eleganter*, after the principal part, Digest, *De conditione indebiti*.

Secondly, it must be premised for the sake of clarity that, in punishing, or not punishing, or more mildly chastising such assemblies, regard must be had to the quality of the persons and of the cause. As to the quality of the persons, this is evident, because we judge such matters from the persons of the men: as in C. si quis Imperatori maledixerit, l. 1; and ff. ad l. Iul. maie., l. famosi, § 1; ff. de actio. et obli., l. fi. As to the second point, namely the cause, this is evident, because when there is private enmity, it is not presumed that such acts are done against the Prince or the commonwealth, but only that a private person defends himself against another private person. The text is notable in ff. de capti. et postli. reuer., l. si quis ingenuam, § 1, in ciuilibus. And this is induced by nature; for, as Aristotle says, common fear gathers together those who are most separated. Moreover, this has become established by custom, as in the title de pa. iura. fir., § conuenticulas, coll. 10, and there noted. Furthermore, if anyone wishes to divide some kinship, resistance should be offered to him, at least by advising and persuading; because the division of relatives is harsh and absurd: as in C. conia utriusque iud., l. possessionum. Moreover, the law says that it is fitting to consider with what mind something is done: as in ff. ad exhib., l. pe. Therefore, the counsel that was offered was principally out of the charity of friendship; because a friend wishes good things for a friend: as in C. de nego. gest., l. officio.

Third, it must be premised for clarity what is meant by "in the thing" and "in the person." For it is not understood strictly as referring to the penalty of death; because this term "in the person" is equivocal. As noted by Cynus in the Code, *De episcopis et clericis*, in the law *Si quis*: "I do not say 'to seize,' unless the enormity of the offense suggests it, or the law proceeding further declares it to be a capital penalty, especially." As noted in the Authenticum *De armis*, § *Oportet*. Therefore, in the small gloss, which states: "This is what we say 'in the thing' and 'in the person.'"

Fourthly, it must be premised, and herein lies the substance of the question: because the text of the decree states, "under penalties to be imposed at our discretion on anyone acting contrary thereto," the ablative phrase "at our discretion to be imposed" signifies a condition, that is, if we shall impose, or in such manner as we shall impose. As in D. de cond. et demonstr. l. a testatore; and C. de contrah. empt. l. si. Moreover, when the Prince reserves this to himself, he undoubtedly denies it to any inferior, whether ordinary or delegated: unless the Prince commits this power and the movement of his will to another. And then that other ought not to judge otherwise, even though the Prince would have judged. As in X. de rescript. cap. super literis; and l. 1, D. de off. praef. praet. It is probable, and indeed it should be so advised to the Prince, that the penalty should not be capital, nor of all goods, but a more lenient penalty: because when someone is punished solely by reason, lest the matter pass into a bad example, he ought to be punished more leniently. As in D. de poenis, l. si quis aliquid, § qui abortionis. I conclude that the mode of this penalty is not fixed by the form of the decree, but reserved to the Prince, who is to declare it according to the movement of his own will, to whom nothing can be done other than to persuade him to impose a penalty according to the movement and piety of his own mind, in accordance with the slightness or mediocrity of the offense: because this offense is not enormous. The law says that a crowd is not placed, but an act in a crowd, as in l. praetor, D. vi bonorum rapt.; and l. metum, post princ., D. quod metus causa. But this allegation does not conclude against the Prince, who, by reserving the sentence to himself, appears to have reserved to himself what, how much, and of what kind, and by what genre of penalty. As in D. de infa. l. quid ergo, § poena gravior, with its material; and C. de summa Trinitate, l. cunctos populos, in fine. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether something is presumed to be new or old, and how it is to be proved.
body: Three judgments have been rendered here, two of which are clear and liquid, concerning which there is no dispute. The third judgment, however, was rendered in favor of the defendant, on the ground that it was not clear and liquid what ought to be paid. For it is said that no part of the pleadings contains the assertion that this acquisition was void. Hence it could be that these goods were acquired at the time of the second judgment. Likewise, it could be that these goods were acquired at the time of the third judgment, or during the third trial. Therefore, in this ambiguity, whether anything should be presumed in favor of the plaintiff or the defendant, the matter remains sub iudice lis est (under judicial dispute).

† For the gloss in c. *Literas*, de rescriptis, in the Clementines, states that that which is not proven to be new is presumed to be old; and this is fully discussed there. But the gloss of the civil law argues that it must be proven clearly and openly what is old and what is new; otherwise, acquittal follows regarding the whole matter. As is noted in D. 47.2 (*De negotiorum gestione*), l. *Eum actum*. However, another gloss states that the intention of the plaintiff is founded on present possession. D. 12.2 (*De iureiurando*), l. *Qui iurasse*, § *Si pater*; and l. *Eum qui*, § *In popularibus*. For this action arises from present possession, as D. 42.1 (*De iudiciis*), l. *Non quicquid iudicis*. Moreover, he who claims to be exempt must prove both the thing and the time; because no one is presumed exempt unless he proves it, since the common law is against him. C. 4.20 (*De probationibus*), l. *Actor*. Furthermore, one must resort to an estimation, whether it concerns all things or certain ones. Arg. D. 22.5 (*De probationibus*), l. *Cum de lege*; and see l. *Incola*, D. 50.4 (*Ad municipalia*). Also to domestic witnesses, as the gloss elegantly notes in C. 4.36 (*De usuris*), c. *Quando et quibus quarta pars debetur*. Also to instruments of sale, since they contain the time. D. 10.1 (*De finium regundorum*), l. *Eos*. Also to reputation. C. 4.44 (*De rei venditione*), l. *Indicia*. Also to neighbors. D. 43.12 (*De flumine*), l. 1, § 1. And it supports what is noted in D. 18.1 (*De rei venditione*), l. *Si rem agat aliquid*; and according to Dynus in D. 33.1 (*De legatis primo*), l. *Si sic*, § 1. And from what Dynus notes there, this question is rendered sufficiently doubtful due to uncertainty; hence this question is one of fact rather than of law. In this doubt, however, I say that the community and the inhabitants of Santa Julia are bound to pay what has hitherto been customary. D. 47.2 (*De furtis*), l. *Cum de in rem verso*. For doubt is resolved by established custom. C. 11.48 (*De agris et censibus*), l. *Finem litibus*, lib. 11; and in c. *Querelam*, X. 1.6 (*De electione*). And it supports the foregoing: D. 43.24 (*De novo operis nuntiatione*), l. 1, in principio, there: “hitherto, insofar as”; and l. *Non solum*, § *Sed et probari*, in the same title. And what is noted in C. 7.32 (*Uti possidetis*), l. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the plaintiff fails to prove his case, the defendant must be absolved from the claim, and the judge must not condemn him moved by any natural reason, but only according to what is alleged and proven.
2. The exception of compensation may be raised in an appeal.
3. Whether an episcopal constitution can make someone a usurer.
4. An episcopal constitution cannot derogate from the common law.
body: Several points are touched upon, and may be touched upon, and it is not expedient to discuss them in detail: because the libel of the plaintiff contains the cause of deposit. By reference to the protestation made to the alleged creditor. Now it must be considered, that in the point it is said,

† Since nothing has been proven regarding the deposit, from which presupposition it necessarily follows that the defendant ought to have been absolved from the claim, as in C. de eden. l. qui accusare. And if the judge condemned him, perhaps moved by some natural equity, this did not pertain to the judge, because he must follow the acts and the proven facts. And therefore, since an appeal is brought, the appellate judge must pronounce that the judgment was wrongly given and the appeal well taken. Nor can the said condemnatory sentence be aided by instruments making mention of another cause, as is fully noted in l. 1. in prin. ff. de eden. with its general subject matter. Moreover, even if the cause of deposit had been proven, nevertheless the payment of usury has been proven, which diminishes the principal by the law itself, as in extra de pig. ca. illo vos. and ff. de solu. l. Titia. For indeed it must be observed that, if it did not diminish the debt as usury, it would diminish it as a partial payment of the principal, as in ff. si cer. pet. l. lecta.
† Regarding the question whether the exception of compensation may be raised in an appeal, it is to be said thus: as in C. de temp. app. l. per hanc.

† On another article, which asks whether he is called a manifest usurer whom the bishop’s constitution declares manifest, it must be said that he is not: insofar as this means that he cannot make a will. For the common law does not bend to the bishop’s statute, since the bishop cannot make anyone intestate. Wherever the common law permits making a will, which it does precisely by not prohibiting it.

† A statute of the bishop cannot derogate from the common law, because the capacity to make a will is a matter of public authority. As stated in the Digest, *De testamento*, law *Testamenti factio*. And thus, in effect, I respond to the questions asked. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How identity is proved.
2. Whether a fictitious party is required to produce the properties.
3. How it is said that something is established.
4. Add the opinion of the following.
body: Words

† Having heard the arguments, we declare that the possessions described in such an ancient instrument pertain to the Church of Tasem, and we condemn B. to restitution of whatever things he possesses from them. Finally, execution was sought, and many witnesses testify that the said B. possessed certain estates which were the same body as the said ancient bodies. However, because the boundaries had been changed, he cannot testify except by reputation. The judge referred the oath of proof regarding the identity of the bodies to the long opinion of the people and public fame, and regarding the property of the church, namely, that for the entire period of the recollection of the said ancient witnesses, the church has received the fruits as its own properties. If it thus appears that there is civil possession and identity due to the remoteness of time and the change of boundaries, see D. 10.1.17 (finium regundorum), l. eos. The judge of the case, considering the difficulty of proof and the continuous payment of the tax up to the time of a certain war, referred the oath in default of proof. And it was administered to the more favored party, namely the church, and because it had been dispossessed, whence it is presumed to be the owner, see C. 7.31.1 (de praescriptione triginta annorum), l. si quis emptor, § vel per quem. § videtur determinari ista quaestio. Moreover, because common opinion in such ancient facts makes law, see D. 44.7.1 (de fundo instrato), l. cum delationis, § 1.

† Moreover, there is no doubt that, if the action were brought against the fictuaries, and they did not produce the properties, they ought to release all of them according to the opinion of Speculum, although others say the contrary. Nevertheless, the opinion of Speculum is the more correct one, where the properties are entangled and confused during the times of the fictuaries. And it supports this what is noted in the Digest, *De re vendita*, in the law *Si in rem*, in the beginning. And I say that the judge could lawfully tender an oath, as in the Code, *De re vendita*, in the law *Si indicia*. And what is noted in the Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, in the law *At qui natura*, § *Cum me*, because it is as if against a notorious absent party; and up to this point the judge has proceeded correctly and properly. Because such matters can be certified in the executions of sentences, as in the law *Facultas*, Code, *De iudiciis*, Book 10. And what is noted in the law 1, in the beginning, Digest, *De edendo*.

† Then the judge of the execution of the cause committed this question of the commission to the counsel of a wise man, who advised that if it is established regarding the possession, execution should be carried out. But concerning this word "if it is established," there can be a question whether it is established. I answer that the word of the present tense retains its truth. It will sufficiently be established in the future, since it is established. As in D. 45.1.11 (Si iam facta) from the Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations. And although the consultant says that it was not established for him, this is true in that the oath sworn and tendered in default of proof was not produced to him. Thus, such counsel ought to be rescinded, as if it were a semi-full report, and notwithstanding this, that arbitral award should be committed to execution. Here it must be observed. For here there are three doubts. The first is concerning the dominion of the church. But this is settled by the arbitral sentence in the things described in the said instrument. The second is concerning the identity of the bodies, and on this point it has already been alleged. The third is whether B. possesses. And the identity of the bodies being established, the possession is clear. And therefore, according to what is proposed, I stand by the aforesaid conclusion, which I believe to be true in fact and in law. And therefore, if it is proven that the opinion of the common people has firmly and unshakably held and holds concerning the identity of the bodies, this is not only fame, but is as if notorious. And on this point the judge could sufficiently ground himself in executing, with the aid of the said oath; otherwise, if it were not so, the case is arduous; and especially since it can be doubted whether the truth is known to the plaintiff, that condition "if it was established" has not been satisfied; because it is understood, i.e., if it will sufficiently be established. As in D. 45.1.11 (Lucius) from the Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations. The conclusion stands thus: either there is an unshakable ancient opinion proven by witnesses concerning the identity of the bodies, joined with the aid of the said oath, and execution of the said counsel must be carried out notwithstanding. And this by the said law At qui natura, § Cum me absente, and the law Emptor, in principio, from the Digest, On Purchase. I, Baldus.

Having seen the instruments mentioned therein, and having seen the witnesses who are corroborated by the conjunction of the instruments, and having seen the oath administered by the judge, which is more than half-proof, and having seen the confessions to which no contradiction can be made: I say that the sentence pronounced in favor of the church of St. Vincent is to be executed, even against the goods which the adversary denies possessing. By the law *Non alienum*, Digest, On Interrogatory Actions; and notably in the law *Si a te*, § 1, Digest, On the Exception of Matter Adjudicated; and by those things which another consultant said: because he did not see the records, one should not depart from my opinion, because it is true and removes every cavil. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a son under paternal power cannot bind himself without the consent and advice of his father, whether he may bind himself on behalf of the father himself in redeeming something, with the father’s consent.
2. What is meant by “advice” (parabola).
3. Given a statute providing that contracts made with a son under paternal power, even under oath, without the father’s consent are presumed to be simulated, how this is to be understood.
4. In the age of discretion, presumptions (conjectures) suffice.
body: The question can be manifold. One can be in respect of the legal opinion (consilium) rendered. And because the opinion contains these words, "having considered the things shown, etc.," it is certain that if, from other things shown together with things not shown, the arbitral sentence has been liquidated, the said sentence ought to be ordered into execution, notwithstanding the said opinion, and notwithstanding the interlocutory judgment rendered according to the form of the said opinion: because by a reference made to the rendered opinion, it is deemed to repeat that same thing, as in l. haec sententia, with its subject matter, C. de sen. quae sine certa quant. If, however, from the things proved a certain conjecture cannot be made as to what those things are upon which execution ought to be carried out, then execution is to be stayed until it is proved, at least through indications and conjectures, since proof of the identity of specific bodies is difficult on account of antiquity. But now let us see whether ancient reputation and the common opinion of those dwelling around are among the said conjectures. And it must be said that they are, as in C. de rei vendi. l. indicia, and C. de fluminibus, l. 1. §. 1. But it must be said still better that, according to the things which are proposed, an ancient possession and perception of quitrents up to the time of the war having been proved, the said church, which does not now possess, is presumed to have been despoiled and ought to be restored to its status, whoever may possess, as in extra de restit. spolia. capitu. saepe, and C. de praescrip. l. si quis emp. §. vlti., and C. de agri. et censi. l. si coloni; and therefore the arbitral sentence is to be ordered into execution, because between the compromising parties themselves it is held as truth. I say this having considered the customs providing for the execution of arbitral awards. Likewise, since the property once belonged to the church, it is always presumed to be its own, as in C. de proba. l. siue possidetis. Likewise, the difficulty of proofs cast by the adversary of the church since the time of the war ought not to harm the church; nor is this properly an oath in default of proofs, but it is another species of oath, as in C. vnde vi. l. si quando. And therefore the lord judge of the case ought to draw conjectures from various grounds, and, these being joined together, to execute the arbitral sentence as to the unliquidated part, both from the joinder of ancient possession proved and also because the new possessor does not show a title (whence he is presumed a despoiler, in the said capitu. saepe), as well as from the corroboration of the said oath. And this is according to the things proposed in the premise, because otherwise the acts are not seen. These and other things, however, ought to be left to the conscience of the one judging, as in ff. de test. l. 3. §. tu magis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal who offends the adherents of his lord is deprived of the fief.
2. The fief is to be taken away, the cause being known, with the judicial order preserved.
body: A fief has nothing in common with adherentia.

† And therefore, a vassal who offends those adhering to his lord is not deprived of the fief, which is proven by the following argument: It is certain that natural brothers adhere to one another by the bond of nature, as stated in l. 2 and l. 3, ff. de lib. caus. And yet, if a vassal offends the brother of his lord, he is not deprived of the fief, because in fiefs the person is not understood to be extrinsically implicated, as in the title "An he who killed the brother of his lord," cap. 1, col. 10. And this is true, unless he offended out of hatred for the lord, and would not have done so otherwise; for then he is deemed to have sinned against the lord himself, as in ff. de relig., l. ossa, §. si; and as noted by Bartolus in ff. de cap., l. hostes; and by the gloss of Accursius according to one interpretation in ff. de dolo, l. arbitrio, §. fina. How it is to be proven that he acted out of hatred for the lord, and that he would not have done so otherwise, is set forth notably by the gloss in l. apud Celsum, in princip., ff. de except. doli. Nevertheless, it must not be omitted that if such an offender could be outlawed by the lord, in such a way that he cannot remain in the lord’s protection due to the lord’s negligence, and is therefore outlawed, then the lord may lawfully seize the fief in execution of the criminal sentence, as is read and noted in the aforementioned cap. 1, "An he who killed," etc.

† It is also to be known that a fief ought not to be arbitrarily taken away, but only after the cause has been examined and the judicial order observed: unless, as I have said, it is taken away in execution of a sentence: as in the chapter *Quicunque advocatus*, otherwise in § *Sub titulo de pace tenenda*, column 10. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the value of the currency should be assessed at the time of entering office, or at the time of the payments to be made each month.
body: On

† As to the question raised, whether the value of the currency is to be assessed at the time of entering office, or rather at the time of the payments to be made each month, I say that one must adhere to custom: for so state the letters of the Illustrious Prince, the Lord Marquis. If, therefore, the custom were to look to the beginning, then we ought to consider that. But if the custom were that the emerging custom be observed with respect to each individual payment, then the times of payment would have to be considered. And that custom is to be observed in such salaries, even if nothing is said about it, is proven by C. loca, l. licet, and there by Jacobus de Arena. But let us suppose that no custom appears; what then is the law? I answer: either the currency has been abolished, or its valuation has been increased or diminished. In the first case, the value of the old currency is considered, as in Extra, de censu, cap. olim. In the second case, either the change occurred before the debtor’s default, and this harms the creditor; or after the debtor’s default, and this harms the debtor. On this matter, the doctors fully note ff. si certum petatur, l. cum quid, and l. vinum, and thus holds Jacobus de Arena in the said l. cum quid, because valuation is an extrinsic quality, and therefore the time of payment is considered. And from this it appears that whether the valuation has been increased or diminished, the time of payment is always to be considered. On the matter, see the note in cap. ult., de decimis, in Clem., and in many others. But the truth is what I said, that the time of payment is to be considered, as is asserted by the common practice of the said city of Alba. Such would be the law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donor, who has given all his property inter vivos while reserving to himself the usufruct, and with the addition that after his death the donee shall distribute one half of the said property among the poor, may revoke the donation by a subsequent testament made by him, and thus whether it is considered a donation inter vivos or causa mortis.
2. Add consilium 375 in part 5.
body: Certain

A wife gave her property inter vivos, reserving to herself the usufruct, on the condition, however, that after her death the donee should give half of it, or its value, to the poor of Christ and to maids to be married, as it should seem best to the said donee, for the soul of the said donor, in remission of her sins. Finally, the said donor made a will and revoked the said donation. Now the bishop says that by the lapse of a year the execution has devolved upon him; the donee says that the bishop has nothing to do with it. For if this clause, a donation inter vivos made to the poor, declaring performance after death, it is certain that it cannot be revoked, as in D. de don. causa mort. l. vbi ita. Moreover, the bishop cannot intervene in contracts, although he may intervene in last wills, because no law provides that he should interpose himself in contracts. Therefore, etc., as in D. de ver. sig. l. verba gesserunt, et contraxerunt. But if it is said that the said clause is a last will or a donation causa mortis, it has been revoked, as in l. j. C. de sac. san. ec. and l. non omnis. D. si cer. pet. For in this case it cannot be alleged, because the said clause has the character of a donation causa mortis, l. cum pater. §. medio. D. de leg. 2. Nor should the benefit of the said half remain with the said donee, because as regards the said half he was chosen as a minister, and with the burden absorbing the said half, and not as one receiving a benefit. Briefly, it must be said that the donation was principally a donation inter vivos and irrevocable. And all the clauses which were added, although they speak of performance after death, are irrevocable, because they are clothed with the contract inter vivos. And therefore, the said clauses are perpetual, and repentance has no place, as in D. de dona. causa mortis. l. vbi. and l. Seya. and C. de dona. quę sub modo. l. perfecta. And therefore, what was contained in the contract of donation must be observed, because repentance has no place. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person condemned to decapitation and confiscation of all his goods, because he refused to go to the boundaries assigned to him by the Prince, is considered condemned for the crime of lèse-majesté.
2. What is the penalty for violating or not observing the boundaries assigned to him, and what is the penalty for disobeying the command of the Prince.
3. If an inquiry were conducted against someone for the crime of lèse-majesté, could he be condemned due to contumacy.
body: The question is

† Fifth, those who have deserved the indignation and severe sentence of the Prince on account of the crime of disobedience, because they refused to go to the boundaries assigned by the lord, and therefore, a process having been formed therefrom, were condemned to amputation of the head and loss of goods, are to be understood as having all their goods confiscated, and are condemned for the crime of lèse-majesté. And it seems that this is so, because by this very fact they are rebels: as in C. de servis et occultis eorum, l. si desertores, lib. 12. Moreover, because it is written that he who does not obey the Prince shall die the death: as in Extra de maiestate et obedientia, cap. 2. Moreover, the mandate of the Prince is law: as in l. 1, ff. de constitutionibus Principum. And thus the contemner of this mandate, as one who violates the law, deserves to be punished capitally: as in C. de veteris numismatis potestate, l. universos, lib. 11. Moreover, there is no doubt that this disobedient person incurs the crime of sacrilege: as in C. de diversis rescriptis, l. sacrilegii, and de crimine sacrilegii, l. 1 and 2, and C. ut dignitatum ordo servetur, l. 1, lib. 12. Furthermore, often for contempt and neglect of so great a precept, capital punishment is imposed. Hence, if those deported by the Prince depart from the island, they are punished with capital penalty: as in ff. de poenis, l. capitalium, § in exulibus, and l. omne delictum, § qui propositum, and § contumaciae, and C. de errore militum, l. annonae, l. 2, 13, and l. 1, C. de commeatu, eodem titulo. On the contrary, it seems that in the crime of lèse-majesté, the cause is considered, namely that something was attempted against the Prince and his statute, or that it falls under other enumerated cases: as in ff. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. 1, where it says that it is committed against his security; and in Institutiones de haereditatibus ab intestato, § per contrarium. Otherwise it would follow that all those who were exiled capitally were condemned for the crime of lèse-majesté, which is not true, unless they are exiled on account of the crime of lèse-majesté, which cause must be alleged and appear from the records; otherwise it is presumed rather from the motion of the Prince than from the crime of treason.

And therefore the ancients said that a contemner of the Prince’s mandate is punished by an extraordinary penalty, at the Prince’s will. L. 1, in fine, C. de primicerio, lib. 12; and D. ad l. Iul. peculatus. Unless, therefore, the omission of the act is joined with a crime, mere contumacy does not constitute the offense of lèse-majesty, although it is a capital offense; because the title of such a crime is not found to have been imposed on contumacy alone. Therefore, neither ought we nor can we impose it. As noted, D. de extraordinariis criminibus, in the rubric. And thus I hold in law on this point, and thus I find it determined at length in the writings of the ancients. And I know this to be expedited for many reasons. D. de accusationibus, L. iudiciorum; C. ad l. Iul. maiestatis, L. et quisquis.

† However, there is no doubt that if someone were prosecuted for the crime of lèse-majesté, he could be convicted of the crime on account of contumacy. This is a special rule, as stated in the Extravagant of Emperor Henry, which Bartolus abridged. And these statements are made subject to the correction of any wise person. Moreover, if one examines the matter correctly, this is a case covered in the aforementioned § In exulibus, and likewise in the Authentica Damnum, § Quisquis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pupillary substitution made to an alien minor, upon his dying during the age of minority, is to be considered direct, and thus invalid; or fideicommissary, and thus valid.
2. The word "substitute" is a direct term.
3. By what words a fideicommissary substitution is made.
4. These words, "I substitute to myself," signify a direct substitution.
body: The case is as follows: A certain testator, making his will, said thus: “By naming him with my own mouth, I institute Titius as my universal heir, under the conditions set forth below, and subject to the orders set forth below; and in the event that it should happen that my heir Titius dies in pupillary age, then, and in that case occurring, I substitute to myself Sempronius as universal heir; and in the case that it should happen that the said Titius dies outside of pupillary age, then, and in that case occurring, I substitute to myself the said Sempronius as universal heir.” The case occurs that the said Titius, an outsider instituted by the testator, died in pupillary age, and the testator’s will was annulled on account of omission, with regard to the institution, according to the form of the Authentica *Ex causa*, Codex, *De libris praeteritis*.

† It is now asked whether the substitution made in favor of Sempronius is valid by virtue of the Authentica *ex causa*, as a fideicommissary substitution; or whether it does not stand as valid, being a second substitution made by the said testator, especially through the words “I substitute Sempronius to myself.” And in the aforementioned matters, it is to be seen and stated what is the law.

That the said substitution is valid as a fideicommissum appears from the glossa ordinaria to the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, in the law *verbis civilibus*, where this doctrine is given: that when a pupillary substitution cannot be valid on account of the substituting party—for example, because he is an outsider—it is valid insofar as it can be valid, that is, as a fideicommissum, notwithstanding that, on the surface of the words, it appears to be a pupillary substitution. For in wills a more liberal interpretation is to be made, as in the Digest, *de regulis iuris*, in the law *in testamentis*; and so that the thing may be valid and not perish, direct words are made oblique, as in the Digest, *ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, in the law *ex facto*, in the beginning. And that gloss in the law *verbis civilibus* is held by many learned men as a notable theoretical point, and the opinion of Cynus is with them, as I wrote there.

On the contrary, we have the glossa ordinaria to the Institutes, *de pupillari substitutione*, § *extranea*, which, referred to the text, says that wherever a substitution has been made to an outsider, whether of age or under age, by the words “let him be heir,” it is not valid, nor is it drawn into a fideicommissum. And for this view the text seems explicit in the said § *extraneo*, where it says: “But to an outsider, or to a son of age instituted as heir, no one can so substitute that, if the heir has existed and has died within a certain time, another may be heir to him.”

But someone will say that those words, “if he shall be heir,” were not used here. But I answer that in a pupillary substitution they are tacitly contained, solely by the institution of an underage heir. And if it is said that this is not a pupillary substitution, I answer that it is so as regards the will, although not as regards the power; for that is what the addition “if he shall die in pupillary age” signifies. And the civil and direct word “heir” confirms this, as by the text in the said law *verbis civilibus*, where such a testamentary institution is not valid on account of the impossibility of law. For it is impossible that a pagan should directly substitute an outsider after the inheritance has been accepted. Likewise, it is expressed in the law *centurio*, Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*. Also, the gloss which says the contrary, Codex, *de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus*, in the law *precibus*, in the great gloss, under the rubric *si vera*, “thus he substitutes, if the son,” in the word “he shall be heir,” is rejected by all as false.

Someone will say that that gloss is rejected only when the substitution could at some time be valid directly; for then the law is satisfied that it be valid according to the rules of civil law for as long as it can be valid. But if it can be valid at no time, as the word sounds, let it be valid as the understanding sounds, according to equity. Argument from those things noted in the Codex, *de familiae erciscundae*, in the law *quotiens*. But this response does not remove the contrary argument; for this substitution could at some time be valid directly, namely, before the inheritance is accepted; for it contains a vulgar substitution. For, speaking properly, this is not a pupillary substitution, but one made for a pupillus; for it does not have those things which are not of a pupillary substitution, as in the said § *extraneo*, and the laws *2*, *iam hoc iure*, and *qui plures haeredes*, *de vulgari substitutione*.

What, therefore, is to be said in so doubtful a point, where the gloss in § *extraneo*, which was the last gloss of Accursius in this matter, expressly determines that the substitution is not valid? Nor is it true that, if what I do is not valid, I do it as I can, when it can be valid in a contrary manner. But finally, when it can be valid in a similar manner, as in the Codex, *de testamentis*, in the law *non codicillum*, and Codex, *de fideicommissis*, in the law *si quis agere*. It is certain, however, that direct and oblique are not of the same species, but they are confused and have the reason of contrariety in themselves, as in the Digest, *ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, in the law *si haeres*, where the direct absorbs the oblique by confusing it.

It seems to me that our case is outside the dispute of the gloss and the doctors. And therefore I divide the will into three parts. In the first is placed the institution of the heir. In the second is placed the direct substitution. In the third is placed the substitution of puberty: another substitution after the times, in the same speech, but diversified by the same words. Of the institution there is no doubt. But of the first substitution I say that it is more truly direct.

† And for the sake of clarity, I premise that the word "instituo" is necessarily direct, as noted by Bartolus in the law *Centurio*, and this is evident from the name itself, as shown throughout the Digest and the Code on the institution of heirs. Nor is there any term devised by law so direct as the word "instituo." And thus also did Bartolus advise.

Secondly, it must be premised that every fideicommissary substitution is made either by the word "restituas" (you shall restore) or by a word that is reduced to the meaning of "restituam" (I shall restore), as established in C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter; in the aforementioned § extraneo, 2. responso; and in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. restituta and l. ex facto, in principio. For let us now see whether those words, "I substitute to myself Sempronius as universal heir," can be reduced to this understanding: "I substitute, i.e., I restore." And it is certain that they cannot; because a testator cannot restore to himself, nor burden himself with the obligation of restoring. Therefore, it must be explained that "substitute" means "I institute in the second place, either in order or by subrogation, Sempronius as my universal heir." Moreover, this dative "mihi" (to myself) is of such a nature that it rejects an intermediate person, as stated in ff. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. qui liberis, § hæc verba. Furthermore, the law provides that when a testator divides substitutions, one of which is adapted to an oblique (fideicommissary) form, the remaining one must be adapted to a direct (institutional) form, as in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. recusare, § Titius.

† Moreover, that the term "mihi" signifies a direct substitution is expressly stated in l. si ita §. qui filio, ff. de secundis tabulis, and is noted by the gloss and by Dino in l. 1. §. 1, ff. de vulgari substitutione. From these it follows that, according to the subtlety and truth of the law, since the said substitution is purely direct and not pupillary, but impossible—because it was made in favor of an outsider after the inheritance had been accepted—the authenticum on account of this rescinds it and renders it invalid. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that, upon the death of a wife during marriage without common children, the husband shall acquire the entire dowry, always subject to the rights of the children of the first marriage, what portion shall the aforementioned children of the first marriage have in the goods of their mother, who is also the wife, if they compete with the husband of the second marriage?
body: Assuming a statute in force to the following effect: if there are no common children, the husband shall acquire by way of gain the dowry given, and certain goods which the said lady had from the house of her husband or their father-in-law, or by reason of either of them, even before the marriage; provided that by this statute no derogation is made to the right of the children of another marriage. The facts are as follows. Lady Helena, having both movable and immovable goods valued at 200 pounds, married Antonio, and gave to him as dowry those same goods, estimated at that value, and from that marriage she bore four sons. Then, after the death of the said Antonio, she married a second time to Francis, and the same Francis gave her as dowry in Valencia 500, or 600, or thereabouts. And leaving no children from that marriage, she died, whereby it comes about that the aforementioned sons from the first marriage, on the one hand, concur to the goods of the same Lady Helena, claiming that they ought to have both the dowry given to the said Francis and the other goods of their mother. And the said Francis, the husband, on the other hand, claims to have acquired the entire dowry given to him, and all the other goods of the same Lady Helena, except the legitime of the aforementioned sons born from the first marriage, or at least the fifth part of all the dowry and other goods. Therefore, the question arises from the premises. First, whether the said Francis acquired by law the said dowry and the aforementioned goods, or whether he did not.

Having considered the said statute and its wording, the husband must have a virile portion of the dowry and of the other things comprehended in the said statute, since the children of the first marriage have a virile portion, that is, a fifth part; because the statute refers to the law, namely this edictal one. C. de secun. nup. and therefore it must be understood according to that law. For a statute that refers to the common law must be understood according to the common law. ut extra de consue. c. cum dilectus. and C. de noxa. l. si serui uestri. and C. de iure deli. l. fi. §. in computatione. And this advantage he has from the form of the said statute, even against the will of the woman. ar. ff. de adop. l. si arrogator. §. sed an impuberi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To what extent a general remission or release extends.
2. What is to be presumed as prior and what as posterior if two instruments appear to have been executed on the same day.
body: †ACetu the allegations are notable and subtle for proving,

† That all matters pertaining to the reckoning of accounts appear to have been remitted by a general and most comprehensive refutation. As stated in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Emptor*, section *Lucius*. Nevertheless, it appears that those things which can be claimed by vindication are not considered to have been granted by a general release. The text with the gloss is found in the Digest, *De liberatione legis*, law *Aurelius*, section *Meuia*. Furthermore, a debt already extinguished by payment is not included under the term "debt," as stated in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Fideicom*, section *Si rem*. Moreover, that which can be vindicated is not included under the term "debt," because he who is liable to a real action for vindication is not called a debtor, as stated in the Institutes, *De actionibus*, section *Actionum*. It is, however, true that specifically and expressly these matters can properly be brought into a pact and into an acceptilation, as stated in the Code, *De transactionibus*, law *Ut responsum*, and in the Digest, *De acceptilatione*, law *Et uno*, section 1. Furthermore, the chirographs of purchases could be returned cancelled, and then no action could be brought on them, as is noted masterfully and fully in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Ab emptione*.

It is proposed that on the same day two instruments appear to have been executed: one of release in favor of the debtor, and another of assignment in favor of a certain outsider. It is called into doubt which of these instruments is presumed to have preceded the other. Although it is impossible [to determine this from the text alone], and it depends on the facts, nevertheless, when such doubts arise, the cause of the possessor is stronger: as is noted in C. de edicto diui Adriani tolerato, l. edicto; and in ff. de testamento militis, l. codicillis, §. ueteranus, according to the legal rule which states that what is unclear is to be decided in favor of the defendant, as is stated and noted in ff. de arbitris, l. si de meis, §. si, where this doctrine is expounded by the glossators, Odofredus, and others. Thus, in the case at hand, the condition of the possessor is stronger than that of the assignee. And so the second point, namely regarding the time, has been fully explained. And because the matter has been argued very fully and at length by the most excellent doctor, Master Ugolinus, I do not extend myself further, lest I become verbose and tedious. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal may make a will concerning feudal goods, and what if he makes a will simultaneously concerning his own proper goods and the feudal ones.
2. Whether by the custom of the kingdom or province it may be established that a vassal may make a will concerning a fief.
3. What and of what kind is the nature of the succession of royal dignities, for example, a county or a marchioness.
4. Whether custom may provide that in three royal dignities women succeed. Likewise, the firstborn son or firstborn daughter.
5. Given such a custom, whether the firstborn daughter is preferred to her uncle, the second-born son. Likewise, whether a male descendant of the firstborn daughter excludes the aunts. And number 6.
6. Whether a monk, made a count by papal dispensation, succeeds in the fief opened to him after he was made a count.
7. Whether the Pope succeeds in the fief of a county, or another fief opened to him after the papacy.
8. Whether a fief is part of the law of nations.
body: What is handed down as a rule in fiefs is called the nature of the fief; but what is established by individual agreement or individual custom is not called the nature of fiefs, but an accident, or an impropriety, or a certain alteration of the fief, as is clear in c. 1. de natura feudi and in c. unico de feudo non habente propriam naturam.

† It is well known, however, that in a fief the disposition of a will is not observed; rather, nature, agreement, or custom prevails, as in c. 1, in the beginning, de successione feudorum. Hence, neither an institution of an heir nor a legacy has any effect in fiefs, as in c. 1, § donare, qualiter olim feuda possint alienari. And whenever a fief is extinguished by death, even an estimation is not due, as in C. de legatis, l. uxor patrui, and ff. de usufructu legato, l. Sticho. And if a vassal makes a will simultaneously concerning his own goods and his vassalage goods, it is valid as to the former, but not as to the latter, as in ff. de adoptionibus, l. sed arrogator, § impuberi.

But whether by a special custom of a fief or province it can be granted to a vassal that he may make a will, bequeath, and transmit his right to any successor. I answer: yes, because custom operates in the same way as an agreement. D. de pactis, l. non in possessione; and note D. de regulis iuris, l. nec ex pretorio; and C. de decretis decurionum, l. 10, as in c. Ubertus de Orto, de feudis cognoscendis. Indeed, even in dignitary fiefs, transmissive custom is strengthened by law: as in c. 1, § in feudo comitatus, de feudis alienandis. And if custom can do this in royal fiefs, much more so in lesser ones. If, therefore, custom permits making a will, one must follow the custom, as C. de testamento, l. si, because solemn custom has the force of a privilege granted to the country, and consequently to all of the country, as C. de testamento, l. si non speciali, according to one reading. However, the will must be perfect as regards its disposition and legitimate as regards its solemnity, and also such that it can be proved. The first is proved by C. de testamento, iubemus; D. eodem, sed his qui; D. de legatis 3, l. fideicommissum, § 1, and there the gloss. And it is the notable text in l. Lucius, D. de testamento militis. The second is proved by D. de inofficioso testamento, l. sed quando; and D. de legatis 1, l. nemo potest; and D. de legatis 2, l. codicillis, § si. The gloss, however, says that in doubt solemnity is presumed: as that witnesses were summoned, and a notary, as noted in C. de iure et facto ignorantia, l. si post divisionem. The third is proved in this way: because if it is a private writing of the testator, or of another writer even subscribed by witnesses, it does not prove the will, unless a public notary was also present together with the witnesses. For if a notary was summoned, it must be reduced to public form and authentic writing, as noted in l. 2, in principio, in the gloss beginning "ut ei credatis," D. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri; and C. eodem, l. 2. And if the notary is dead, the form will be preserved: c. cum P. tabellio, de fide instrumentorum. And these things have been said concerning the first point. Concerning the second point, however,

† Whereupon it is asked, what is the nature and quality of the succession to royal dignities, such as a county or a march, it must be said that which is stated in the text in c. 1 de feudo marchiae. Where the text thus says: concerning a march, or a duchy, or a county, or any royal dignity, if anyone has been invested by the Emperor by way of benefice, he alone must hold it; for the heir does not succeed in any manner, unless he has acquired it from the Emperor through investiture. And the reason can be assigned here, because such fiefs are granted with great deliberation, and not to persons other than those to whom this is suitable on account of their singular industry, their faith being tested, and their gravity, and for the light of their wisdom. Arg. ff. de officiis praefecti praetori, l. 1, §. his annalibus. That which therefore is granted and retained on account of singular industry is not transmissible by its nature, nor ought it to be extended. Arg. ff. de curatore furiosi, l. cuius bonis; and ff. de tutelis, l. tutela; and ff. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus; §. de officiis; and C. de caducis tollendis, §. ne autem; and de officiis delegatis, c. quodam abbas; and ff. de minoribus, l. 3, §. si quid minori. Therefore, according to the proper and original nature of these royal fiefs, such fiefs are not acquired by succession, but by investiture. But today this has been usurped, considering the general custom, because they pass by succession. This is what the text says in feudo comitatus, vel marchiae, vel aliarum dignitatum, that it is not succession according to reasonable usage. But today this has been usurped, as in c. 1, §. in feudo, de feudis alienis.

But it is asked whether custom can provide that in such royal matters women succeed. And it must be said that yes, not only descendants, but also collaterals, as in Extra, De rescriptis, c. Significavit nobis comitissa. For there it speaks according to the Gallican custom. It supports this, De foro competenti, c. Ex parte B. Therefore, custom could provide for the succession of such dignities, and this custom is observed both in fact and in law. Moreover, it can provide that the firstborn son or firstborn daughter succeeds: so that this privilege of primogeniture is claimed for itself, as in c. Licet, Extra, De voto. And there fully by Hostiensis, and note, 7 q. 1, c. Quam periculosum. Although in Jacob and Esau the contrary was observed, Genesis 25 and 27, because it is written by the Prophet Malachi, the word of God saying, "Jacob I loved, Esau I hated." But if we were not in the terms of divine disposition, the law would be to say that the testament of Isaac would not have been valid, as noted, De testamento, l. Haeredes palam, and ff. De hereditatibus instituendis, l. Quotiens. But in those days there was no dominion, neither direct nor otherwise. I therefore conclude in this that custom is to be observed. But concerning this, it happens to doubt about two questions, one of which is common, and yet it consists rather in the quality of ingenuity, than that it can be determined for or against the truth. So that to assert with certainty is rather superstitious than discreet, etc.

† The question being thus posed, given the aforementioned custom, whether the daughter of a predeceased firstborn daughter is preferred to her aunt, the second-born daughter. In this question, I have set forth arguments at considerable length. See C. de iure delib. l. cum antiquioribus, in my writings. And in favor of the daughter of the firstborn, it is argued: First, because succession is a right of blood, as is noted in ff. de pactis, l. ius agnationis; but rights of blood pass to descendants, as in l. 4, ff. de interdictis et relegationibus, and l. 1, C. de privilegiis eorum qui in sacro palatio militant, lib. 12. Second, because the daughter enters the maternal degree, as in Inst. de successionibus ab intestato, §. cum filius. Third, because the privilege of primogeniture is not principally for the person, but for the cause of primogeniture; and therefore it passes to her bloodline. Fourth, because this privilege of primogeniture has become a right of nature, which descends upon the offspring of the parent, and in a certain sense substitutes for them the immortality of the propagator. And it is essentially one and the same, not simply, but in a certain respect, as outside the case of a duke, see ff. quod metus causa, l. isti quidem, in fine, and C. de impuberibus et aliis sub tutela, l. finalis. Fifth, because the grandson comes through the person of the father, not through his own. This is clear, because he formally succeeds in the right in which the father stood, as in Auth. de haereditatibus ab intestato, §. reliquum. Sixth, because those things which are of nature are transmitted through the organ of true and identical descent; and the same applies if they are graces imitating nature. Moreover, contracts are transmitted in infinitum; therefore, so too are customs. Moreover, this is not properly a transmission, but a certain prerogative of natural seed. Moreover, those things which are transmitted against one’s will are transmitted while the condition is pending, as in ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. qui patri heres extitit. But a kingdom and dominion are transmitted whether one wills it or not, by the majesty of the root, which always takes root.

To the contrary, it is argued: Because the mother died before she could transmit, therefore she transmitted nothing, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quis filium. Moreover, because one ought not to honor the daughter of the deceased and grant to the grandson, as in C. de bonis matri, l. si viva matre. And thus it was observed in fact in King Robert regarding the succession to the fiefs of the Kingdom of Apulia. In certain other provinces, however, the contrary is observed, as appears in the Kingdom of England.

Because, as I said, this question is ancient and very common, it can nevertheless be persuaded that rights of primogeniture are extinguished by death, since primogeniture could not exist when its proper subject is extinguished, see ff. de operis liberti, l. qui libertinus, §. posthumus; and ff. de bonis liberti, l. si libertus; and ff. de legatis et tutoribus, l. tutela, §. si duo; and what is noted in C. si in fraudem patroni, l. defuncto.

† Now follows another doubt. Suppose the firstborn daughter died leaving a male issue; whether that male excludes the aunts or stepmothers from the succession to these feudal dignities. This question is likewise to me sufficiently obscure: nevertheless, on account of the magnitude of the case in which we are; for it is in a certain sense to put one’s mouth in the sky; yet also on account of the reasons and laws turning hither and thither. For the rule of fiefs is this, that no place is open to a woman in the succession to a fief, so long as a male remains from the successible stock, from him who was first invested with this fief, as in c. 1, *de eo, qui sibi, et suis haeredibus maribus, et foeminis inuestituram accepit*. And all the commentaries and the summae of the doctors seem to accord with this opinion, and both from the ordinary summa and from the extraneous summae. For all proclaim this with one voice and one speech. But let us see whether our case is very different. And for clarity I premise that some rights are divisible, some indivisible. Moreover, of the indivisible, some are communicable, some not. For if two are counts, the county is well common between them according to the common law, but not partible; because dignities do not admit of division, as in *extra de pręben.*, c. *maioribus*, and l. 1, ff. *de officio consulis*, and in ca. 1, §. *praeterea Marchia*, *de prohibita feudi alienatione per Federicum*. But by custom, as said above, the firstborn alone is count, and bears the title of administrator of the dignity. And the same applies to the countess, when by custom a woman succeeds. Secondly, it must be considered that the daughter is prior in degree, and that feudal successions are deferred according to degree, and the texts of the fiefs, when they make mention of children, always name sons first, as in c. 1, *de gradibus succedendi in feudo*. If therefore the fief cannot be held except by reason of one proximity, it ought to belong rather to the daughter of the vassal than to anyone more remote in degree; for the immediate cause is stronger than the remote cause, as noted in l. *si mulier*, ff. *rerum amotarum*. Moreover, it is absurd that a nephew, disturbing the order, should exclude a daughter, speaking according to equity and natural reason, which has place in those fiefs in which custom does not determine, as in c. *Vbertus*, *de ortu*. Moreover, it is not true that the nephew comes through the person of the mother, if you suppose the mother to have renounced; but it is necessary that he come through his own person and his own order, as C. *de inofficiosa testamento*, l. *si quis filium*, ff. *eodem*, l. *si is, qui*, and C. *unde liberi*, l. *qui se patris*, and in c. 1, §. *praeterea*, *qui modus feudum amittitur*. And therefore it must be observed that if in the investiture there were the word *primogenitus*, the said c. 1, *de eo, qui sibi, et suis haeredibus*, would not have place; because here primogeniture is weighed from the form of the investiture rather than a male of a more remote degree; for *primogenitus* signifies son, *secundo genitus* signifies nephew, not the year or month of birth. For *primogenitus* is understood, i.e., first in the degree of generation. The same is therefore true in a custom speaking thus. Thirdly, I consider that the son of my daughter is not my agnate; because agnation is not contracted through a woman. And therefore, since the son was male, it does not pertain to the nature of fiefs for a woman, unless this nature is altered by pact. And thus speaks c. 1, *de eo, qui sibi, et suis haeredibus maribus, et fęminis inuestituram accepit*. And here it must be observed, because that which is said there, *tandem pro masculo iudicatum*, seems to stand in the virtue of that clause, *et his deficientibus foeminae*. For a male does not fail, considering the virtue of this indefinite clause, as l. 1, C. *de conditionibus insertis*. Moreover, successions which proceed from laws, i.e., customs, are not regulated according to contracts, but according to intestate successions; and therefore these universal intestate successions are not transmitted by him who is prevented by death, as ff. *de liberis et posthumis*, l. *Gallus*, §. *et quid si tantum*, and ff. *de inofficiosis testamentis*, l. *posthumorum*. And all natural reasons of the world, unless approved by civil law, could not confer one obol of succession to the living by civil law, as ff. *de verborum significatione*, l. *lege obuenire haereditatem*. Whence no one is so prudent that, from the motion of his own mind and reason, however subtle, he can infringe the liberty of the laws, to which supreme authority belongs, as C. *de legibus*, l. *fin*. But if reason arises from laws or from customs, just as the law or custom itself ought to be observed as the soul and spirit thereof, as C. *quae sit longa consuetudo*, l. 1 and 2, ff. *de legibus*, l. *de quibus*. For Aristotle says in the *Secreta* that interpretation is the spirit of the writing, 7. *Secretorum*, and noted by Dy. *extra de regulis iuris*, cap. *in argumentum*. Against this it is objected. For it is true that, just as a male stands in relation to a male, so a woman to a woman; nevertheless, this would not be proportional, just as the fact stands in relation to a woman, so a male to a woman, unless the woman were in equal succession by the form of the investiture, as in c. *si cui militi*, §. 1, *de quibusdam aliis extraordinariis capitulis feudorum*. That chapter is extraneous. But to this I answer, because the tenor of the investiture will be sufficiently said to be the tenor of the custom, and its natural interpretation, and the affection of the parent, as ff. *de pactis*, l. *tale pactum*, §. *fi*. For every natural man loves his daughter more than a nephew from another daughter. Considering therefore in the aforesaid the degree, and the agnation, and that here the pact fails, and only custom has place, I cannot conclude anything else than that the custom be observed, which failing, in the place or province the fief would be open to the lord of the fief, as in ca. 1, §. *notandum*, *qui feudum dare possunt*, and also c. 1, *de gradibus succedendi in feudum*, and in cap. 1, §. *profecta*, *de lege Corradi*, in that verse, *quod intelligitur de solis masculis*, and not the word *solis*. But assuming the custom itself that women succeed, the eldest of the women ought to succeed, unless she consented to the younger being invested, as in c. 1, §. *praeterea*, *si ille, qui modus feudum amittitur*. I add also concerning the aforesaid, that even if the custom permits testating of the fief, or alienating in another manner, this is understood according to the nature of the thing itself, as ff. *de usuris*, l. *si stipulatus*. Whence the quality of the right cannot be changed by such alienation, in §. *ex eadem*, l. *de lege Corradi*, and ff. *de actione empti*, l. *vt in venditione*. That also I do not pass over in silence, concerning a fact known to me, even if it were not expressed to me in the point. For it is held in the statutes or, in the texts of the fiefs, that a knight who has assumed the habit of religion cannot retain it, so long as an agnate or lord remains. And I note the word *agnatus* of the masculine gender, as in cap. 1, *de eo, qui arma bellica deposuit*. And if afterwards he has laid aside this habit, as in c. 1, §. 1, *de feudo foeminae*. For it comes to my doubt,

† Suppose that a monk, by papal dispensation, became a count; does this person succeed to an open fief after having become a count? And I hold without doubt that he does. For, as if returned by postliminium, or restored in full, and made capable of succeeding, indeed as if a new man, grace has been restored to him and capacity opened up, as in D. de manumissionibus testamento (Digest, On Manumissions by Will), l. Aristo; and C. de sententiis passionum (Code, On Sentences of Passions), l. in quaestione testamenti; and D. de legatis tertio (Digest, On Legacies, Third Title), l. si deportati servo; D. de in iustum testamentum (Digest, On Invalid Wills), l. si quis filio, §. pen.; and D. de legatis praestandis (Digest, On Legacies to be Performed), l. inter; and D. de hereditatibus institutis (Digest, On Instituted Heirs), l. si alienum, §. in extraneis. For always in the subject his own day is considered, as in D. de stipulationibus servorum (Digest, On Stipulations of Slaves), l. si usufructu; and l. si servus communis me; and l. castrensis peculii, §. ult.
