† What, therefore, is to be said of the Pope, who finds himself Pope at the time when his brother, the Count, dies? For this is certain: he does not acquire [the inheritance] for the Roman Church, because it is contrary to the nature of the thing itself, and the Church, as the guardian and promoter of justice, does not wish for anything contrary to the observance of law, and especially contrary to the law of nations or its character.

† For if fiefs are not of the law of nations, nevertheless their quality: since both servitudes and all things pertaining to a villa are of the law of nations, I would not say this if there existed a male descendant from the first-born daughter, who was in fact and in law the first-born. But because I do not consider him to be the first-born in law, who died before the fief became vacant, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. pen., vers. si quis autem suscepit. Therefore, where custom weighs primogeniture, one born from her cannot obtain a share: because the right in her is not yet formed, nor materialized. For the Pope and also for clerics, it must not be omitted that they are not bound by customs which are against the liberty of the Church. For although they are not among the first inventions of the law of nations, they are nevertheless among those new forms which nature always hastens to produce and deduces, as it were from offspring to offspring, from some principle given towards a consistent effect, as in c. 1, §. sed quia natura nouas, which was the first cause for the loss of a benefice. Hence, although the emphyteutic contract is not in itself of the law of nations, it is entirely so according to part, that is, according to consent and tradition, according to nature and equity; fiefs are distinguished by natural and good customs, as in c. Ubertus, §. si quis, in qui causae feudum amittitur. Let us therefore see in the Pope if anything resists him while living. For after death there is nothing, as in Auth. de nuptiis, §. disponit. So that upon his death there is no doubt that the fief reverts to the lord, if there is no other agnate; otherwise there is no other custom extending transmission. Moreover, custom is public law. Someone might say that the Pope is exempt from laws, but this is nothing to say, because the nature of contracts is certain elements for them, and therefore just as the Pope is not the master of the elements, so he is not the master of contracts which began with his predecessor, as in C. de restitutione militum, l. quae a patre; otherwise it would smack of tyranny. But certainly another reason supports the Pope, because while he is Pope, he is a soldier of heaven, and can declare war on the world, and has both swords; the earth is his and its fullness, therefore he has not ceased to be a soldier of the world. Furthermore, it is unjust to say that the Pope is not capable: since he is the vicar of Jesus Christ. I speak of the Pope, of whom the saying in c. 1, de eo qui arma bellica gerit, does not speak, because the reason of that chapter is that he ceased to be a soldier of the world. And this reason is false in the case of the Pope. Furthermore, a second reason is that the benefice does not pertain to him who ought not to exercise the office. And this reason is false in the case of the Pope, or inapt, because insofar as the Pope serves through a substitute, for this is permitted to the majesty of God, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. quisquis, and also C. de iniuriis, l. si. Furthermore, if this fief passes to a woman, who can serve through a substitute, much more so to the Pope, indeed and to any cleric, as noted by Innocentius, extra de probationibus, c. in praesentia, and extra de fide instrumentorum, c. inter dilectos. But certainly the Pope has the sword as Pope, not as Robert. Moreover, he comes as R., not as Pope, and thus nothing pertains to the matter of the Papacy, as in D. de adoptionibus, l. si pater, §. qui duos. Always saving the right of the lord Count of Savoy, who is the lord of the fief, and to whom it seems to pertain to have cognizance, when there is a question between vassals of such a fief. Upon this, however, I impose a guard upon my mouth, and a door of circumspection upon my lips, intending nothing to conclude or opine concerning the rights of the lord Count of Savoy. These things being saved, and the aforementioned custom being supposed, and that she is called first-born who is first in the nature of things at the time when the fief becomes vacant, as in Inst. de legibus agnaticae successionis, §. proximus, and for the lady Catherine two reasons stand: because first she is an existing daughter, and because she is an agnate. And that the condition enables women can sufficiently incline towards the said illustrious lady Catherine, or towards the sister, if the said lady Catherine would permit her to be invested. Furthermore, consider, because the text spoke on this question, therefore it has regard to the tenor of the investiture. Moreover, in custom nothing ought to be supplied beyond the usual observance. And therefore if the custom does not provide for the son of a woman, neither can we provide, as in D. de solutione matrimonii, l. si vero, §. de viro, and D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si servum, §. non dixit. If therefore the son of a woman wishes to succeed by irregular custom, it is necessary that he prove that it speaks of him: because since this irregular custom comes to correct the common law of fiefs, it ought not to be extended, as noted in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, auth. quas actiones, which is noted in Auth. de restitutione fideicommissi, §. manifestum. Wherefore I say that it is against the common law, because the son of a woman is a cognate, and not an agnate, and it is a double extension from degree to degree, from head to head, that is, from daughter to grandson, and from agnate to cognate. For although the son of a sister has the rights of agnates, he is nevertheless not an agnate, as in C. de legitimis haeredibus, l. meminimus. Then the text says: the place is not open to a woman in feudal succession. Where it is to be noted that in a royal fief the word used signifies that it is a certain tacit creation of a fief, especially in the person of a woman: for custom takes away from the lord of the fief and gives to the woman: so that this is not properly succession, but a new creation, as elegantly noted by Bartolus in a similar case, D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in quartam. Finally, the letter succeeds concerning this fief, the word "of this" being to be weighed: because if by creation, therefore it is not of that same fief: as in D. de verbis obligationum, l. stipulatio ista, §. si quis ita, and extra de praebendis, capitulo dilecto. But this is not well secured, as I said, because it would follow that it was a new fief, and not an ancient one, hence the word used is placed correctively with regard to the continuation of succession. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a depositary is preferred to other creditors.
body: On

† In the case of Master Beltraminus concerning the false claim, on which the council was convened by the aforementioned R. and N. de Diversis, and Lord R. responded without his seal and subscription, in the form that follows. Master Beltraminus cannot demand the said sum unless against the inheritance of Ioannolus de Meda: because Ioannolus was finally bound, the obligation having been transferred, as stated in the Digest, title *Manus*, law *Inter causas*, section *Abesse*. This Master Beltraminus holds a written instrument in the form of a deposit, and in a deposit, the depositor is preferred to other creditors, unless the debt were usurious, as stated in the Digest, title *Depositum*, law *Si hominem*, section *Quotiens*; for then he is on equal footing with other creditors, as stated in the Digest, title *De privilegiis creditorum*, law *Si ventri*, section *In bonis*. And therefore, if the debt is not usurious, he may proceed against the heirs of the said Ioannolus, and is preferred to other creditors, whom the heirs are bound to satisfy, as stated in the law *In omnibus*, Digest, title *De iudiciis*, saving the benefit of inventory. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether those who have the faculty of seeking alms in a certain diocese under the name and title of a certain saint may prohibit others wishing to beg for another church, yet under the name of the same saint, is distinguished.
body: In a certain diocese there is the hospital of St. Dobon, in which great hospitality is observed, and great devotion is shown in giving alms and leaving legacies. This hospital, for a time beyond the memory of the contrary, received certain collections and an annual sum under the aforementioned name in the regions of Italy. In the same diocese, however, there is the church of St. Bobon, which for some time past has been accustomed to collect the said revenue. The question is whether the said church can be prohibited from doing so. Three cases must be considered.

† For either the rectors and collectors of the church gather under the name of the hospital, and are bound to restore to the hospital if it ratifies; and if it does not ratify, they are bound to pay for theft to those who have paid. They also incur the crime of falsity, whence they are liable for damages, as in C. de fur. l. falsus; ff. de conditio. ob cau. l. si procuratori falso; ff. de fal. l. qui nomine; ff. ad muni. l. Titio. Or they gather under the name of the church, expressing this in their collection and collecting activity, and then it is lawful for them, even under the name of one saint, because they cannot be prohibited from seeking alms, unless an ancient custom of the hospital derogates from these new collectors: for then they can altogether be prohibited, since they thrust the sickle into another’s harvest; yet until sentence is passed in the petitory action, they are not to be removed from possession of this act of collecting, as in extra de ele. c. querelam; and extra de ap. c. significante. In the petitory action, however, long and temerarious possession does not favor the said church, since it is not permitted to diminish another’s right by concurrence, as in ff. de aqua plu. arc. l. in concedendo; and C. de ser. et aqua. l. pręses; and l. si manifestę. Nor can it be said that the rectors of the church were thus in quasi-possession in good faith: since both the proximity and the continuous act of the hospital ought to have removed the said rectors from presumptuous daring by the sting of conscience. ar. ff. loc. l. dominus horreorum; and l. 1. §. 1. ff. de flumi. And this case is similar to that of the Mill, when a second mill is built in a public place in derogation of the revenues of the first mill: for that which was previously acquired for another is preferred by the prerogative of time. For these collections are in a certain sense public and have the occasion of divine law. Yet I do not say that those who, out of certain knowledge and certain devotion, wished of their own motion to offer to the church, and not by the way of placing collectors, could be prevented, for this is mere and pious liberality, which cannot be denied to anyone, as in ff. de pact. l. pe. The third case is when the church, which is later in time, or its rector, sells, leases, or grants collections in the name of a saint without mention of the church, and this it cannot do, lest the hospital be circumvented. The same applies conversely if the church were earlier; therefore they must be specified, so that neither party falls into a trap due to uncertainty. And this a superior can order, so that women and simple persons are not deceived; he should order that one bear one insignia and the other another, in the case where both may bear and sell or lease collections, so that the difference is understood clearly and openly, even by simple people: for although Jacob supplanted Esau under a false skin, with an unchangeable voice, as is written by the prophet Malachi at the beginning and in Genesis 25 and 17, yet this was not lawful according to law, but only by divine mercy, as noted in ff. de test. l. haeredes palam; and ff. de haere. insti. l. quotiens. in prin. And therefore it is not lawful to supplant another. And where there is greater and older devotion, it is believed in doubt that the preaching is made. Indeed, even where there is greater poverty and fruitfulness, which is not squandered but distributed among the poor, as in Authenti. de ecclesiasticis titulis. §. si quis autem vniuersorum. col. 9. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The plaintiff in a hypothecary action must effect excussion.
body: In the case of Lord Amonet and Lady Isoldina, citizens of Asti, it must be considered that, according to the common law, in the execution of a personal action brought, although the first creditor holds a hypothec, if he has not asserted it, the second creditor, who holds a hypothec and possesses such execution, excludes [the first]. For the method of proceeding against the second hypothecary possessor is to assert the first hypothec. For a personal [action] does not exclude one’s own hypothecary [right].

And this hypothecary action, which ought to be brought, requires the prior exhaustion of the debtor’s assets, as stated in the Authentica de fideiussoribus, § sed neque. It is true that by statute another form has been established among creditors, namely another form of priority, as above, under the heading de rebus dandis in solutum, c. unico, in principio. By this statute, in personal execution, nothing else is considered except who is truly prior. However, since the first creditor is not truly prior unless exhaustion has been carried out, the statute adds, under the heading that principal debtors must be subjected to exhaustion, that whoever acts out of order without this prerequisite being observed is repelled, the defendant is absolved from the suit, and the plaintiff, being temerarious regarding the order of law, is condemned in costs, as in the Digest, de iudiciis, l. eum qui temere. And thus, Lady Isoldina ought to be absolved from observing the judgment, according to what is alleged. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A debtor of someone for five hundred florins on account of a purchase at a just price, as appears in the instrument, subsequently made another instrument, in which he states that he had sold to the aforementioned first seller of his, and on account of the sale had promised to give and pay to the same person 40 florins by way of an annual annuity, and this for the price and in the name of the price of the said five hundred florins in which he was indebted by virtue of the prior contract. What these words signify, and how such an instrument is to be understood.
2. Whether a judgment rendered against a principal in a case in which a procurator intervened after the litigation had begun until the end of the case is valid.
body: Sacinus gave to Sinodonus half of a certain house for the price of five hundred florins, which price he confessed to have received. After this, another instrument was made between the said contracting parties, in which it is contained that, notwithstanding the aforementioned confession of the said five hundred florins, which florins the said Sinodonus truly owed and owes to the said Sacinus, the said Sinodonus sold and, by reason of the sale, promised to give and pay to the said Sacinus 40 florins as an annual rent, and at this price and under the name of the price of the said five hundred florins, for which the said Sinodonus was bound and obligated to the said Sacinus by reason of the aforementioned sale. This is the tenor of the said two instruments. Now there is no question regarding the first instrument, because the words are clear and do not require interpretation, as in D. de legibus 3, l. ille, aut ille, § cum verbis.

But regarding the second instrument, the question arises: from the very words it appears that Sinodonus, who in the first instrument was the buyer of this casana, in the second was the buyer of the price which he owed for the casana, i.e., the buyer of the release from the said price. In this way it is asked, what did this Sacinus sell? For in a sale there must be a thing and a price, as in l. 1, D. de contrahenda emptione and l. 1, D. de rerum mutatione and D. de praescriptionibus verbis, l. naturalis, §. at cum do. I do not know how to understand what else could be considered as the thing, other than the obligation of five hundred florins itself, or the very thing deducted in the obligation, and the very five hundred florins which were sold for a perpetual annual income of forty florins, a contract much frequent among moneylenders in this country in similar effects: because they buy an annual income of 40 florins for a price of 50 florins. Thus, in the case at hand, for the price of five hundred florins remitted to the said Sinodonus, the said Sinodonus agreed with the said Sacinus to provide the said annual income. So that henceforth the said Sinodonus is not bound to the said five hundred from the first contract, but to the forty annually from the second contract: since the first contract is novated, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. pacta conventa, §. Paulus. How then the claim is founded on the said five hundred florins against the said Sinodonus I do not perceive, because the price of the casana was transferred into an annual income, arg. in l. 1, D. de penus legato. But these seem to be wondrous words, because the second instrument says that Sinodonus sold. What he sold, however, I cannot understand, and if the contract cannot be understood, no action arises from it, because that which cannot be understood is held as nothing, as in D. de deposito, l. Publia, in fine, and D. de iure fisci, l. ita fidei. This second contract therefore accomplishes nothing with itself, except a retroactive confession of the unpaid price, and thus the said annual income could not be claimed, because promised without cause, as in l. 2, §. circa, D. de exceptione doli. Moreover, this contract, unless understood as I said in the first way, is a usurious contract, and expressly usury cannot be claimed. Nor can the secular judge condemn to their payment, as in c. ultima, de exceptionibus, lib. 6, and a sentence on usury to be paid is null by law itself, and does not merit execution. Someone will say that rather the seller is owed interest formally fixed by convention, but as it interests according to the truth of the matter. Moreover, here it was not acted in the name of interest, and thus nothing to the point. Now it follows to see about another point, because this Sinodonus was condemned in five hundred florins in the name of the said price of the casana, and the procurator who was in the case after the joinder of issue until the end of the case was not condemned.

† It is asked whether the sentence is valid. And it must be said that, according to civil law, it is void by the law itself, as C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. 1. But according to canon law, there is a dispute among canonists, as may be read and noted at length in Extra de electione, c. Querelam, and there is an excellent gloss by Bernardus. We, however, are in the forum of Justinian, and thus in civil law; and thus the said sentence is void by the law itself on account of an evident defect: because it appears from the reading of the records, according to what is alleged, that it ought not to be committed to execution, as is read and noted at length in D. de re iudicata, l. 4, §. Condemnatus, according to the Moderns. It is no objection that another certain procurator was condemned, because he was a procurator for another matter, not for the suit of five hundred florins; and thus he was an incompetent procurator in this case, as noted in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Si ergo, and in D. de restitutione in integrum, c. Suscitata. But Bartolus holds indiscriminately that the sentence is void, but if the principal was absent at the time of the sentence: as he notes in D. de verbis obligatis, l. Stipulatio ista, §. Si stipuler vero. From the foregoing, the reason appears; nor is it an objection that the said principal was cited to the sentence, because the citation does not bind him to appear, and consequently he is not a true or fictitious contumacious party, since the procurator had abandoned him, as in D. de nova operis nuntiatione, l. Edendum, §. 1, and in D. de procuratoribus, l. 1, §. Usus. But if the principal had been present, the sentence would validly stand due to the procurator’s absence; indeed, even if both were present, as in Inst. de satisdationibus, §. Si vero aliquis, and arg. D. de verbis obligatis, l. Si procuratori praesentis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that no citizen may alienate his property unless the taxes and levies are paid at all times, even if he is a cleric or an ecclesiastical entity. What is the rule regarding clerics who hold patrimonial goods, or other property acquired by succession or contract, as to whether they are bound to pay levies imposed by the commune after such acquisition? And there are many points concerning the college of clerics, and the opinion of Bartolus in the law *Rescriptum*.
body: Given the statute of the citizens, confirmed by oath, that no citizen may sell or alienate his property without always paying the *datium* and the *collecta*, even if he were a cleric or an ecclesiastical place.

† It is asked, what is the rule regarding clerics who have and possess patrimonial goods, or other goods from succession or contract: whether they are bound to pay *collectae* (levies) imposed by the commune after the said acquisition. And it seems that they are not, because clerics in their own things have that privilege which the church has in the things of the church, as is noted in c. *Si*, de vita et honestate clericorum. Bartolus touches upon this question fully in Speculum, in Spec. de clericis coniugatis, and there he holds expressly that clerics are not bound to pay *collectae*, but they are indeed bound to pay *tributa* (taxes). And he adds that *collectae* differ from *tributa* because *tributa* are perpetual and certain, but *collectae* change and vary according to the variety of imminent affairs. However, Speculum speaks when we are merely in the *ius commune*. But when citizens make a statute among themselves, or a pact with the Syndic of the community, that it may not be transferred to the prejudice of the fisc, Speculum touches upon nothing of this. Bartolus, however, touches upon it, and first he says that *collectae* are imposed on persons for things, whence they ought not to be imposed on clerics, because they are not subjects, as l. *Rescripto*, §. *Sciendum*, de muneribus et honoribus. But he says that this may be a remedy, that citizens make a statute, because all estates are tributary for the payment of *daticae* and *collectae*. For from this, the goods are hypothecated to the commune and affected, so that whosoever they pass to, they pass with their burden and with their quality, as C. de restitutione militum, l. *Cum a patre*. For this is a hereditary debt, and therefore it passes to any heir; nor is anyone freed from hereditary burdens because he is a cleric, as ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. 2, §. *Ex his*. For even to clerics things pass with their cause and their vices, as ff. de acquisitione possessionis, l. *Pomponius*, §. *Cum quis*. Nor does the authority *Item nulla communitas*, C. de episcopis et clericis, oppose this, because that authority must be understood unless the goods were previously affected by a pact, or quasi-pact, as by an estimation made in common with a perpetual promise for oneself and one’s successors to pay *collectae* and general functions, as is noted in ff. ad municipalia, l. *Incola*. For if something were specially imposed on clerics, such imposition would be against the liberty of the church, and thus would not be valid. But when a *collecta* is imposed on estates according to an estimation made in common, this is not against the liberty of clerics. Nor are the estates free, because they are already hypothecated. And this is the case in which a hypothec produces a similar personal obligation, C. de bonis quae libera, l. *Cum oportet*, §. *Sed cum tacitos*. And elsewhere a hypothec is found without a personal obligation, as ff. de publiciana, l. *Commissa*, and C. de usucapione, l. *Usucapio*. This opinion of Bartolus gained usage, so that clerics through their bishop ought to be compelled to pay these burdens, which by their nature are mixed. However, by the consent of ancient lords, they have been reduced to the likeness of real burdens. Moreover, in many places the laymen themselves have the right to seize by hand in the very estates, causing the revenues to be taken from both lords and tenants. For when, before the things came to the clerics, they could be disposed of by laymen as their own proper things, and thus the preamble of the hour of the clerics’ acquisition was affected, albeit under some uncertainty of future designation, rightly the statute must be stood by; because, inspecting the beginning, they were valid, nor can clerics complain, because nothing of their right is lost; for they could not acquire what was not. I.e., they could not acquire liberty where there was perpetual servitude, as ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. *Alienatio*, and ff. de servis rusticis praediis, l. *Viam constitui*, §. *Si fundus*. It is wonderful, however, that by this caution the whole liberty of clerics is infringed, because in effect it is the same to say that clerics are subject to laymen, which is impossible, as in c. *Ultima*, de censibus et clericis, and in c. *Si diligenti*, de foro competenti, with all its glosses, unless it be said that it is not true that they are subject, but the things are well subject; for with this burden they came to the clerics, just as if an emphyteutic or censual thing came to them, which ought to render sense to a private person, for the fisc ought not to be in a worse place than other singular persons, but rather in a better one. And the opinion of Bartolus, for the sake of public utility and public necessities, is in use, and otherwise it would be to damn the whole world. But Iacobus Butrigarius in the said Auth. *Item nulla communitas*, in the lecture, does not firmly adhere, but sufficiently gives to understand that before the *collecta* is imposed, the goods are not hypothecated; as if this were impossible, and thus the beginning of the acquisition of dominion will be free and not affected. And from this it follows immediately that clerics are not bound to new *collectae*, because their estates, in this respect, do not seem to be of the territory or district of laymen. And this is the safer opinion, because it is dangerous to speak against churches and clerics in these matters. However, the opinion of Bartolus is observed in fact, unless there is another mode, where by the obligations of predecessors, clerics, being wealthy, are bound for patrimonial goods, together with their neighbors, to contribute to those things which expedite the republic, in which the salvation and safety of all is provided. And certainly in cases of necessity, they ought to offer themselves; for what touches all, let it be felt by all. By this, however, I do not say that laymen make statutes; otherwise they would not make them except out of hatred for clerics. For then, made in fraud of ecclesiastical liberty, I would believe them not to be valid. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Twenty inquisitors, accused of poor custody because they had not apprehended two malefactors, stated in court that they had been negligent but had done all they could. How such words are to be understood.
2. If in a notarial instrument it is found that witnesses said the inquisition to be true, and two witnesses attest that they never said so. How this is to be understood.
3. The presumption favors the notary rather than the witnesses.
4. A witness who does not testify regarding the inquisition to what he knows commits perjury.
5. Whether a procurator may be admitted when falsehood is alleged criminally, or civilly, or by an action arising from a quasi-maleficium.
6. One condemned by public judgment, or who has confessed, cannot be a procurator, although the rule is otherwise for other infamous persons.
7. On the question of whether torture and an oath in lieu of proof are applicable.
body: The judge

† He formed an inquisition of negligence against the said custodians, because they did not apprehend two malefactors, who in court uttered these words, namely, that they had been negligent, but had done all they could. The question arises, since these statements appear contradictory, whether one should adhere to the confession; or whether it should be understood that they immediately corrected themselves before turning to other matters; or whether the entire document is vitiated, as being perplexed, self-contradictory, and repugnant, such that no faith is to be given to it, as in D. de testibus, l. qui falsa, vel varia; and D. de re iudicata, l. ubi repugnantia; and l. 1, C. de errore advocatorum. Likewise, if someone were to say, “I thus confess, but I deny,” the latter part of the statement should be examined, when in the same context an adversative conjunction is appended, as noted in D. si certum petatur, l. si tibi. That he who does all he can is not negligent is clear in C. fin., de feudis, sine culpa non admittendo, col. 10. Here it must be observed that negligence is attributed to the group as a whole, whereas “they did all they could” is attributed to each individual, because one person could not apprehend two malefactors, but twenty could, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. ita vulneratus. And thus the statement is saved, and the confession of negligence remains; because all together, not each individually, were negligent, and thus the judge could fine them, as in D. de accusationibus, l. levia.

Next follows another step, because it is written in the notary’s book that the witnesses declared the inquisition to be true, but two of the said witnesses say that they never said this. Now the question arises whether the said witnesses should be believed, at least as regards the most rigorous examination. And it seems that they should, because two witnesses make two presumptions, even if they are singular, provided that one witness does not instigate the other witness, as noted in the Digest, De quaestionibus, l. Maritus. On the contrary, it seems that they should not be believed, because these witnesses are singular and assert a pure negation; hence, by reason of their singularity, they prove less legitimately, as in the Extravagantes, De testibus, c. Licet causam. And by reason of the negative, even less faith should be given, as in the Extravagantes, De causa possessionis et proprietatis, c. Cum ecclesia Sutrina, and as noted in the Digest, De arbitris, l. Diem proferre, § Si plures. Moreover, the notary is held in the place of witnesses, as fully noted in the Institutes, De inutilibus stipulationibus, § Item verborum. And two affirming witnesses overcome two denying witnesses.

† Moreover, greater weight is presumed for a notary of deeds than for witnesses, as stated in the extrajudicial decretal *Ad audientiam* on prescriptions. Furthermore, the aforementioned witnesses, when examined regarding the inquiry, ought to have testified to something.

† And by not testifying what they knew from someone, they commit perjury, since they have been interrogated by the judge, as in C. de episc. et cler. l. presbiteri. And note this through Innocentius, extra de falsariis, c. 1. Therefore, by saying that they did not testify, they tacitly include their own wrongdoing: they ought therefore to say, we testified thus, and not thus. And speaking principally in the affirmative. Jacobus de Arena places this in the discretion of the judge, as is stated by Cynus, C. de falsis, l. si quis decurio.

† For otherwise it would be impossible to prove the falsehood committed by the notary concerning the reception of witnesses. Thus, it must be observed that one must examine whether the crime of falsehood is alleged in the libel criminally, or civilly, or indeed as an action arising from quasi-maleficium, since fraud is not expressly stated in the libel. If falsehood is not alleged criminally, the procurator ought not, nor could he, be admitted, and especially if ensnared in the same species of crime, as provided in l. placet, §. at crimen, de publicis iudiciis, and Codex, de libellis criminalibus, l. si filium. And since the exception of the procurator has always been raised, and he has always protested, the rule of l. quamuis indubitati, Codex, de advocatis, ceases to apply. Moreover, because he ought to have subjected himself to the penalty of talion, as stated in Codex, qui accusare non possunt, l. dixit. Furthermore, according to what is alleged, if true, he is most infamous and most wicked, and therefore is barred by public crime, both under civil law and under canon law.

† Moreover, one condemned by public judgment or having confessed cannot be a procurator, although the contrary holds for other infamous persons, as in l. 1. in princ. ff. de posthumis, according to Guillaume and Cynus, and in the Institutes, de exceptionibus, §. si.

† If, however, the issue of forgery is raised in a civil action, torture has no place. And therefore, by singular witnesses nothing is proved, nor can an oath be deferred in the defect of proof where the question is grave and involves fraud, as noted in l. 3, § quacumque, ff. de iureiurando. If, however, it is a matter of ignorance, even then torture has no place, nor does an oath seem to me appropriate, having regard to the point, because otherwise I have not seen the acts, that it was acted criminally, although in consequence interest was claimed, as noted in C. de falsis, l. nec exemplum. And because the accuser was not legitimate, the accused shall not be harassed by this principal reason, and by the others aforementioned, as in extra de accusationibus, c. 1. It is also proposed that the witnesses are humble or base persons, and that they spoke with the party: hence there is a certain presumption of subornation, and if we were to say otherwise, they could always rescind what they deposed, saying, I did not say so. And on this pretext even a res iudicata would be rescinded, although no appeal was taken from it, as in l. diuus, and ff. de exceptionibus, l. qui agnatus. Which would be very absurd, and would give material to witnesses to commit false subornation. These things are true when the writer of the acts is of unblemished reputation: but if he were considered here suspect, because he otherwise made false writings, then he would rightly admit false witnesses in a case of forgery, provided it was raised by a legitimate person and in a legitimate manner, otherwise not, as in C. qui accusare non possunt, l. si cautiones, and fully noted in C. de his quibus uti indiciis, l. polla, and l. si, de fidei instrumentis. I have said these things, reconciling with the consilia of other doctors, having also inspected the quality of the judge, because he is a simple man, and not acting for any interest of his own, and this by l. si, de dolo, l. quod si ut scires, with its gloss, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a minor, who divided property with his brothers without the authority of a curator or judge, and having reached majority, persisted in such division until the age of 40 years, can now claim the division to be unjust, because he was prejudiced, and void, because it was not formal.
body: It is proposed,

That a minor divided property with his brothers without the authority of a curator or judge, and having reached majority, persisted until the age of 40 years. Now he claims the division is unjust, because he was prejudiced; and void, because it was not formal. The question is whether he can do so. And it seems that he cannot, because he remained silent for five years after reaching majority: as in C. si maior factus, l. vlti. in principio. But because various doctors interpret that law in different ways, I turn to another division, and I firmly say that he should not be heard, because possession held as divided for a long time after reaching majority has in itself the force of a tacit and formal division, and since it was done between adults, because 15 years have passed since minority, there is no doubt that the tacit division presumed from possession as divided must be upheld. This is the gloss of the original text, true and commonly approved in l. placet, C. communi diuidundo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A father, having instituted his two daughters as his heirs, prohibited them, and each of them individually, from alienating anything from the goods of his inheritance, adding that he wished his goods to pass to the heirs of his said daughters; and in the event that they should alienate them, he wished the goods to pass to the Confraternity of the Holy Spirit. The question is whether the goods alienated by one of the said sisters, who died without issue, pass to the surviving sister or to the Confraternity. The opinion is that they pass to the sister. Furthermore, whether the last surviving sister, dying without issue, may make a will and institute an outsider as her heir, and whether this is considered an alienation, such that the said goods would pass to the Confraternity.
2. Who is included under the term "heir."
body: The words of the will state as follows: I wish and command that my daughters, for the entire duration of their lives, may not sell or alienate anything from my goods, because I wish all my goods and inheritance to pass to the heirs of my daughters. And if it should happen that my said daughters, or any one of them, sell or alienate anything from my said goods and inheritance: I wish those goods which were sold or alienated to pass to the consortium of the Holy Spirit.

† It is now asked, since one of these daughters has died without leaving any children, and the other, who survived, has no children, whether the said survivor may make a will regarding the said goods or not; and whether, upon the making of a will, the Brotherhood of the Holy Spirit has a right or not. And it seems to be said that she may not make a will in favor of an heir who is an outsider: for he who is prohibited from alienating is prohibited from instituting an heir. For the testator wished the goods to be preserved for the heirs of his blood. For it is not probable that he understood it to apply to others entirely, whom the affection of the testator does not embrace, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si. Therefore, when the testator wishes the goods to be reserved for the heirs of his blood, that daughter who died while her sister survived does not seem to have been able to alienate in favor of her sister, who was the testator’s daughter: and if she had alienated, it pertains to the surviving sister, who is among the children of the testator, as if they had been substituted for one another. Argument: D. de legatis 2, l. Titia Seio, §. Seia libera. But if the sister fails without children, the Brotherhood succeeds to the outsider instituted, as if substituted in the second degree. It seems to me that the Brotherhood is not substituted except in the case of alienation inter vivos. For the law provides, etc. Briefly, I consider those words, “during their lifetime.” For these words signify nothing but a prohibition of alienation, which is made inter vivos, by which the making of a will is not prohibited, even in favor of outsiders. The text is: D. de legatis 3, l. pater filium, §. fundum. Nor does it avail to object that afterwards the word “to sell” or “to alienate” is placed simply: for the preceding words restrict the subsequent ones. And although in the prefaces they are said, they seem to be repeated in the subsequent parts, as in D. de verbis obligatis, l. Titia, §. idem respondit. For one part of the writing explains another, as in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. qui non militabat, §. Lucio.

† And therefore these daughters, having no children, may make a will in favor of outsiders: nor ought the consortium of the Holy Spirit to have any claim, because it was placed in a condition prohibiting alienation, not granting it: and thus it was added as a penalty: which penalty is not incurred if one does not act against the will. And this suffices for the decision of the question. But if anyone wishes to inquire further, what is said, “I wish to come to the heirs of the daughters,” I answer that it is interpreted as referring to children who may come by the sole provision of the testator, not to extraneous heirs who could not recover alienated property: because he who is liable for eviction is expelled by the exception when he brings the action, as in D. de evictionibus, l. vendicantem; and D. de verbis obligationum, l. qui Romae, § duo fratres. Therefore, it is not probable that the testator intended an accidental and extraneous heir, because it matters greatly whether the term “heir” is used in a preferential sense, understood as an heir of blood, or in an indifferent sense, consisting solely in the legal right of inheritance, and then generally, as in C. de duobus fratribus, de bonis inventis, c. 1; and C. de feudis alienatis, c. 1, § et si clientulus; and D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, § si. Moreover, if it is asked whether the surviving sister succeeds the predeceased sister, if perhaps the predeceased sister alienated something inter vivos, it may be plausibly said that she does, as if the testator also intended her to be substituted, since she was his daughter. Arg. C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntatis. And this is based on the conjecture of the testator’s will. Arg. D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Lucius. And thus the word “heirs” also comprehends the sister, who is the nearest heir by right of blood and agnation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What if a father bequeathed to his son, who intended to study law, the law books that he then possessed, and subsequently purchased new ones for the same son while he was studying law: whether these newly purchased books are considered bequeathed. Likewise, whether they are considered given as a gift. And number 2.
2. If a father bequeaths to his son, who is preparing himself for legal study, law books, and medical books for medical study, and he, who studied medicine, after obtaining a degree in it, declared that he wished to study law: whether the law books are to be communicated to him.
3. If a father bequeaths books to his son who is studying: whether he acquires the books before the completion of his studies, and whether he is bound to furnish security.
body: To obey

† Having disposed of himself for the study of the laws, he bequeathed to his son the legal books which he then possessed; afterwards, while the son was studying, he purchased new ones. The question is whether the newly purchased ones are to be regarded as bequeathed. I answer: no, as in D. 33.7 (de libris legatis), l. Aurelius, § testamento; and D. 32.1 (de legatis secundis), l. si ita scripsisset; and D. 31.1 (de legatis primis), l. stichum, qui meus erit.

Secondly, I ask whether it appears that they are making a gift. I answer: no, if he had other sons; so that envy may not arise among the brothers, as in law 2, *Cum pater*, § *Euict.*, and in the Digest, *De peculio legatorum*, law *Ita filii*; unless it appeared from certain signs that the father wished them to be preferred on account of the preeminence of their studies: for such liberality of the father, or the military service of the son, is confirmed, as in the Digest, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Quae pater*.

Thirdly, it is asked: if a father, disposing of himself for legal studies, left legal books to those studying law, and medical books to those studying medicine, and one of the sons is a doctor of laws, another of arts, and wishes to return to the study of law, whether the legal books should be communicated to him. I answer: yes, if he gives security for studying law; otherwise not, as in D. de leg. 3, l. si tibi. Nor is he understood to be studying or disposing himself unless he does so effectively and with intent; because the testator considered the purpose and invited the sons to good. Nor does it avail to object: l. iube, C. ad trebellianum; because there it speaks of another kind of security, not of the occasion in which we are, as in C. ut in possessionem legatorum, l. cum Archimedoram. Also, the purpose and aptitude must be considered; for if he is not apt for studying law, the books should not be communicated to him, as in D. de leg. 3, l. Stichus. And especially because to migrate from arts to laws is to vary from the first purpose, and perhaps the testator is not understood to have intended anything but the first purpose; as in D. de verb. sign., l. boves, § hoc sermone. Since in this first purpose he persevered for a long time, earned the insignia of doctorate, and the testator did not wish that he should have two rewards. But his knowledge, to which he disposed himself, which I understand principally and primarily, this however I do not affirm, because one can be perfect in several sciences with the intellect assisting. The other things, however, which I said, I well affirm.

† The words of the testator state: “Provided, however, that if any of his sons were inclined to study legal science or canon law, as is currently the case with G., his son, who is studying civil law, or if in the future any other of the said sons were so inclined, as above, and wished to go to university for the aforementioned purpose, the said books shall be kept for him, so that he may study upon them and acquire the said science. And if the said son should successfully complete his studies, he has bequeathed the said books to him; otherwise, and in no other way.” The question now arises: if one says that he wishes to study, what is the law?

Solution: Before the completion of his studies, he ought not to have ownership of the books, but rather the use of half of them, upon providing security to G., who previously completed his studies, for the restitution of the said books if he does not complete his studies. Moreover, he must have studied for at least five years in order to be able to acquire half of the books. And if he should die in the meantime, he would lose the use, and would not transmit the said books to his heir. For, since books are not entirely consumed by use, but rather provide their utility without consumption, as noted in the Digest, *De pactis*, l. *Postquam certe*, the right of use properly applies to books. Furthermore, I do not care whether it is a right of use or a usufruct, because caution (security) must always be provided.

That the aforementioned is true is evident from the conditional words of the testament regarding ownership, and the modal words regarding use. It is also to be noted that in the testament are the words “as is currently the case with G., his son, etc.” Hence, it is not sufficient that another son is in some way inclined and apt for legal science, as in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, l. *Stichus*. From these things, the response to the second point appears, as well as to the third and also to the fourth; for one must adhere to the testament. Therefore, it is necessary to take care that he study for at least five years, because before that time no one is considered able to complete legal studies, as in the first constitution of the forums, § *Quibus*. If they have studied well, etc. However, I do not think that it should be detrimental to one wishing to study the laws that he is a master in the arts; for this greatly contributes to legal science. And of this we have examples in John and Jacob of Ravenna. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It treats of a certain proceeding conducted in the episcopal court, and of many objections that were raised.
2. The purchaser of an inheritance cannot claim individual items unless he proves delivery.
3. By the cession of rights, ownership is not transferred.
4. The custom of the forum of execution must be observed.
body: Chaste

† Before the Right Reverend Lord, Bishop of Trent, Leonard, son of a certain Ser Nigri, brought an action against Bertoldus for the vindication of a certain house, which he alleged had been usurped by the said Bertoldus to the prejudice of his soul, stating that the said house belonged to and pertained to him, Leonard, by right of useful dominion, or quasi. And finally, the litigation being contested on the said libel, the said plaintiff made many positions, and in one asserted that the said house was the property of the said Bishop of Trent by right of direct dominion; in other positions he deduced certain matters which imply that the said house pertains to the said plaintiff by succession, for another part by virtue of a purchased inheritance. But from the opposite side, to exclude the succession, a certain division is produced, from which it appears that the said plaintiff was excluded from the thing claimed in the division. Furthermore, it is alleged against him that the said purchase of the inheritance profits him nothing, because it does not appear that he ever had any possession or detention of the said thing; therefore, he could not have any dominion, as in the Digest, *De rei vindicatione*, law *Si ager nec publicianam*; and in the Institutes, *De acquisitione*, section *Aliæ*. Moreover, no investiture made to him by the Bishop is proven, nor did he capitulate on it, and the right of emphyteusis is not required without corporal investiture, as in the law *Si*, Code, *De iure emphyteuticario*; nor even the useful dominion of a fief, as in chapter *Quid sit investitura*, column 10. It is therefore asked, what is the law? I answer: It is manifest that the defendant ought to be absolved when the plaintiff does not prove his case, as in the Code, *De edendo*, law *Qui accusare*; even if the defendant were a robber, as in the Code, *De rei vindicatione*, law *Si*; and in the Institutes, *De interdictis*, section *Commodum*. And this is most certain. No one doubts that the defendant is to be absolved when the plaintiff does not prove his case, even if he has proved nothing, as in the Extravagant, *De probationibus*, chapter *Ex literis*, section *Si ambarum partium*. Now, although we proceed abundantly to the laws of the defendant, it is certain that Bertoldus has the investiture of the Bishop. But he came to it in a certain order, about which there is doubt in individual cases. And first, I begin with the instrument of debt, which instrument speaks rather ambiguously regarding the oath; nevertheless, in doubt, it is presumed to be over the entire oath, as noted in the law *J.*, Digest, *Quarum rerum actio non datur*. And to this effect is what is noted in the Code, *De rescindenda venditione*, law 2. It seems that by reason of the oath, action may be brought before the Bishop so that it be observed, not, I say, so that he be punished, because that would not have place unless there had been a violation of the oath, as in chapter *Cum contingat*, *De iureiurando*; in chapter *Quamvis*, *De pace*, Book 6; and in chapter *Ultima*, *De fideiussione compromissoria*, same Book. And assuming, without prejudice to the truth, that this allegation were not sufficient, nevertheless the said Bishop would be competent for another reason, because the contract was celebrated, which is of his temporal jurisdiction, and thus by reason of the contract one acquires the forum, as in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Heres absens*, and law *Omnem*. But from the opposite side, the other party says that the oath does not bind, because the one swearing was a minor, because it is asserted that he had a guardian. But I answer, because at the end of the instrument it is said that he was of age, and thus more regard is had to what is said at the end than at the beginning, as noted in the Digest, *Si certum petatur*, law *Si tibi*. Also, because it seems said through ignorance regarding the guardian, and improperly, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Pater Severinam*, section *Conditionem*. Also, because in doubt one must stand by the last statement, and laws *Novissima* and *Non ad ea*, Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*. Also, assuming that there were a repugnancy regarding age, nevertheless as to the substance of the debt there is no repugnancy, but rather total consonance. Moreover, a decree was appended. Moreover, the procurator confirmed by confessing in the form of judgment. Moreover, the exception of non-payment of money was never appended, so that from the confession true payment is presumed, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Si ita stipulatus*, section *Grigolonus*, and there by Bartolus; and to this effect is what is noted by Cynus in the law *J.*, Code, *De confessionibus*, and law *Non solum*, in the beginning, Digest, *De procuratoribus*. Then I proceed further, because it is objected against the process that it was not made in the place of the elders: because sometimes it was in the place of the abbot, sometimes in the audience of the Bishop. But that does not object against the vicar of the Bishop, as in chapter *Cum episcopus*, *De officio ordinarii*, Book 6. Also, it is objected that the said process could not be made in the church, because it is a *truffa* [trick/fraud]: because this would be true in a secular judge, otherwise in an ecclesiastical one, as in chapter *Docet*, *De immunitate ecclesiarum*, Book 6. Also, it is objected regarding holidays. But this does not object, because the protestation regarding holidays was removed by the process and the consent of both parties, as in the law *J.*, Digest, *De feriis*. Also, it is objected that the principal instrument contains a repugnancy. But to this the answer is, that it is not a repugnancy of perplexity, but of conception, which does not vitiate, as in the Digest, *De manumissionibus testamento*, law *Stichum imo*. Also, it is objected that the thing was estimated at a higher price than it was sold. But this does not obstruct, because we do not care about the estimation of the estimators, but only about how much the thing can be sold at a public auction, as in the Code, *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, Authentic *Hoc ius porrectum*; and in the Code, *De executione rei iudicatae*, law *Otto*; and in the Authentic *De fideiussoribus*, section *Quod autem*. Also, it is presumed in favor of the decree, from which it was interposed, as noted in the law *J.*, Code, *De fidei instrumentis et iusta hastatione fiscalis*, Book 10; and in Speculum, *De emptione et venditione*, section *Nunc videndum*. Also, it is objected that the thing was specially obligated, therefore one should not descend to other things. But this objection is of no value, because this would have place when there is contention between creditors, prior and posterior, as in the Code, *De pignoribus*, law 2; otherwise, it is in the election of the creditor which thing he chooses, as in the Digest, *De distractione pignorum*, law *Creditor*. And thus the answer to the motives of the opposing party appears, and it remains clearly concluded that the said Bertoldus ought to be absolved definitively: both because the plaintiff proved nothing of his right, and because the defendant justified his possession.
† And that which is not to be omitted is, that the purchaser of an inheritance cannot claim individual items, unless he proves delivery, as is stated in l. 1. §. 1. ff. de usucapione dotis.

† Certainly, ownership is not transferred by cession of action unless possession is transferred, as stated in D. 27.3.1 (Plane). Nor can an action be ceded unless it appears that the true payment of the price has been made, as stated in C. 4.21.1 (Per diversas) and C. 4.21.2 (Ab Anastasio), and expressly noted by Jacobus de Belvisis in Auth. de aequalitate dotis, § Aliud. And it should be observed that it is objected against the proceeding that the party is a filiusfamilias, because the father did not consent, as stated in D. 4.4.11 (§ Necessitate). But to this it is answered that he had the father’s consent; and a general consent suffices, as stated in C. 10.30.1 (Quod locum) and D. 50.16.1 (§ Si). And because the father was absent, in which case the son may be in court without the father, as stated in D. 4.8.1 (Si filius) and D. 2.11.1 (§ Si).

† That which must not be omitted is that, when a case is litigated in the bishop’s forum concerning a sale and execution, the law of that forum must be observed, and not that of the secular forum; because the custom of the forum of execution must be observed, as in C. de exact. trib. l. missi opinatores, lib. 10, where the text is notable. It must be considered, however, that if anyone declares that he holds possession for another who does not possess, the declaration is of no effect, as in ff. de acq. poss. l. quod meo, in principio. And to support what has been said above, that ownership, neither useful nor direct, is transferred by cession, the authorities adduce for the case l. si sponfalibus, in principio, ff. de iure dotis. And this is confirmed by the following reason: because the thing was held in emphyteusis, ownership of which could not be transferred by reason of the sale without the consent of the owner; indeed, he would forfeit whatever right he had, as in l. si, C. de iure emph. From which it conclusively appears that the said Bertoldus ought to be definitively absolved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the boundaries of a certain territory are proved by witnesses, public reputation, or instruments, and which of these is the stronger proof.
2. Whether boundaries are proved by instruments made for another purpose that incidentally mention the boundaries.
3. How witnesses testify regarding boundaries, and how they testify regarding a matter that is more perceived by the intellect than by the senses.
4. A witness who gives false testimony concerning boundaries is rejected entirely.
body: The matter is proposed as follows: Since D. Lizan. of Castro Novo sold wine mixed with water in a certain tavern of his, in which he resided, a certain Jo. Bu., an excise officer or tax collector of the bread and wine tax, which is levied on goods sold in bulk and in retail in Dargina and beyond the Adda, denounced and accused him before the judge of the excises of the city and bishopric, and of Piacenza, alleging that the said B. had sold wine and bread in retail to many and various persons without the seal and license of the excise officers or their officials, and against their knowledge and will, in the said house or tavern, which they assert is located in the territory of the bishopric of Piacenza. However, A. Pillizarius appeared as procurator on behalf of Biondili, as stated above, declining the jurisdiction of the judge, especially because the said house is situated in the territory of Castro Novo, which is entirely exempt from the jurisdiction of the city of Piacenza. On these points, both parties produced instruments and witnesses to establish the truth regarding the said territories. Here it is asked what the judge’s course of action should be in the said proceedings, so that this question may be more clearly elucidated. First, an argument will be made in favor of the jurisdiction; second, an argument to the contrary; finally, by what right the matter should be resolved. I therefore take up the first point.

And first, it seems to be concluded in favor of the said tax collector, since when there is a dispute concerning the boundaries of a territory, in such cases one must proceed according to the Digest, through ancient books, or in another manner by which they may be better proved; likewise by witnesses, reputation, and any other supporting evidence, as is read and found literally in the Extravagant Decretals, *De probat.*, c. *Cum causam*. And the term "books" comprehends all volumes, whether on paper or in parchment, and thus public documents, as in the Digest, *De legibus*, l. *Librorum*. Thus, the legislator also states elsewhere that boundaries are to be proved by monuments, i.e., public instruments which contain the boundaries, Codex, *De finibus regundis*, l. 2, and there most clearly in the gloss, and l. 1, and Digest, *Eodem*, l. *In finalibus*. To the same effect is what is said and noted in the Codex, *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, l. *Optimam*, in the gloss *Si servus*. And thus it is argued that the boundaries of a plebate or territory are not proved by instruments; for such division is proved by ancient witnesses, 16 q. 1, c. *Plures*. Moreover, credence is given to rustics, especially elders and ancient persons, Digest, *De legibus*, l. *Si chorus*. And thus reputation is valid in such matters, especially when memory is not available, Digest, *De probat.*, l. *Si arbiter*; Digest, *De aqua pluviali*, l. *In summa*, § *Idem Labeo*. For ancient instruments prove the common opinion of men, which is presumed to be true, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *In testamento*; *De fundo instrato*, l. *Cum delationis*, § *Asinam*; and Digest, *De fluminibus*, l. 1, § 1, *Cum si*. In the present case, however, instruments are found to have been exhibited to the judge, in which it is affirmatively contained that the contract regarding the *arimagnis*, in which the aforementioned tavern is situated, is of the territory of Sancino. Therefore, by the force of those instruments, jurisdiction appears to be founded, and it is further proved by 12 witnesses that the tavern itself is of the said territory, and by reputation and public voice. Therefore, prima facie, it seems to be concluded in favor of the jurisdiction.

I respond to the second point, where it must first be observed concerning defective proofs that they are entirely lacking on the part of the accuser, and subsequently on the part of the accused. And if he had provided nothing for the solution, as in the Codex, *De rei venditione*, l. *Si*; Digest, *De probat.*, l. *Ei qui*; and Codex, *Eodem*, l. *Actor*; Codex, *De edendo*, l. *Qui accusare*; Extravagant Decretals, *De causa possessionis et proprietatis*, c. *Cum ecclesia*, *Cum si*. Then it will be declared most evidently that the accused has proved abundantly that that tavern was and is of the territory of Castro Novo, which first uproots the foundation of the instruments: because even if faith is given to the narrative words of the instrument and the affirmative acts, which at that time could not be, to the prejudice of those who ordered or requested the instrument to be made, as in the Codex, *De fidei instrumentis et iuramento hastae*, l. 1, li. 11; Codex, *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, l. *Optimam*, nevertheless, such words do not thereby make proof between other persons; rather, it must be proved originally, Codex, *De iure deliberandi*, l. *Cum aliquis*. Therefore, the gloss there determines that the boundaries of a plebate or territories are not proved between others by such narrative words of uncertain public documents. And it supports this in the Extravagant Decretals, *De probat.*, c. *Quoniam contra*, and there fully read and noted according to Innocentius and the other commentators, as in the Extravagant Decretals, *De officio delegati*, c. *Cum in iure peritus*; *De posthumis*, c. *Bonae memoriae*; Authenticum, *Ut sponsalia*, § *Ad hoc*, col. 9. Nor is this surprising, for it pertains to the office of the notary only to draw up instruments in those matters which are done in their presence at the time of the mandate accepted; otherwise, it is not a public document, but testimonial letters, to which no credence is given, says Innocentius in the said c. *Quoniam contra*. However, they prejudice the parties present to full proof, not of the instrument, but of the tacit confession resulting from the mandate imposed on the notary to draw up the instrument, to which tacit confession it is necessary to adhere for full proof, to such an extent that it would avail nothing to prove the contrary, according to Innocentius in the Extravagant Decretals, *De censibus*, c. *Cum olim*.

† Therefore, it is clear that the words of the determination must be followed in that doubt, which asks whether proof of the boundary is fully understood to be established by instruments made for another purpose and incidentally mentioning the boundaries: to which it must be answered that full proof is established between the contracting parties, or those by whose command the instruments are drawn up; however, between others who are strangers, although they induce something with respect to them, this is not sufficient in itself without other arguments, as in a similar case regarding reputation, as in the cited chapter *Cum causam*, where the glossator, citing many authorities which I omit because they can be seen there, stated. This opinion is followed by Dynus, Petrus de Iano, Butrius, Cynus, and Marsilius in the cited law *Cum aliquis*, and it is the common opinion, which is brought into harmony, and thus all the instruments produced are sufficiently nullified, which were drawn up between others and for another purpose, not principally to prove the boundaries; for true proof of the boundary would be induced by instruments found principally concerning the boundaries, or by ancient books produced from the public archive, as in the cited chapter *Cum causam*, and what the glossator notes there with the concordances cited above, which must be understood in this case. True proof would suffice in a question of boundaries, as in the Code, *De fundis limitibus*, laws 1 and 2, book 11. Moreover, it is the case that such instruments produced by the accuser are ambiguous and reducible to the proposition of the accused, and thus they favor the accused rather than against him; they merely assert that the Armagnacs are of the territory of the Seneschal, which can, indeed must, be understood according to the statements of the accuser in the instruments themselves, rather than those of the accused; and consequently, whatever is of the territory of the New Castle could rightly and ought to be of the jurisdiction of the river. Hence, those instruments are irrelevant, even if they had been made principally for the cause of the boundary, or drawn up between the litigants; because doubtful proof is irrelevant, as in the Extravagant, *De probationibus*, chapter *In praesentia*; Code, *Eodem*, law *Neque natales*; and law *Non epistolis*; Code, *Unde legitimi*, law *Non hoc*. This is especially so since the accused has produced several instruments against the assertion that the Armagnacs are of the territory of the New Castle, to which a correct interpretation is given; the remaining instruments of the accuser, the witnesses, and other documents, in order to avoid the sinister suspicion of falsehood, must be reduced to consonance, as in the Extravagant, *De testibus*, chapter *Cum tu*; and Code, *De fidei instrumentis*, law *Diversa*. For those instruments are not so numerous, nor were they drawn up publicly among all, or the greater part, from which some popular opinion would result in favor of the jurisdiction or territory of the Plebatus; since it appears that there are several instruments redundantly supporting the opposite certain opinion in favor of the territory of the New Castle. Hence, the popular opinion alleged to the contrary favors the accused more than it does against him. From these things, the foundation of the instruments of the opposing party is clearly removed.

† It remains, therefore, to respond in various ways to the witnesses produced by the accuser. For this purpose, it must be known that where a witness testifies concerning matters of law, which are perceived immediately by the intellect and not by bodily sense—for example, if he testifies that a certain thing belongs to another, or to a certain jurisdiction and territory—no faith is given to such a witness unless, when questioned, he also provides the reason based on a fact immediately perceptible to bodily sense. C. de usur. l. 1; Extra de testib. c. Cum causam, according to Innocentius, who speaks elegantly on the point. And in this respect, the statement of the witness differs, because it deals with law, from that which deals with fact, which is rather sensed than understood. For if he testifies truthfully concerning such a fact, it is not expedient for that testimony to be supported by a witness, unless he has first been compelled by the judge to do so; otherwise, he would be considered a suspect witness. C. de testib. l. Solam, and what is noted in the gloss there. To state the reason is easy, because the office of the witness consists in informing the judge of matters of fact, whereas the judge has the duty to determine what is the law. C. de testib. l. Testium; ff. de testib. l. Qui testamento, §. Si; ff. de his quae in testamento delentur, l. 1, near the beginning. And Innocentius says, in the place cited above.

Insofar, therefore, as the witnesses say that that tavern is within the territory of Senio, they prove nothing; rather, one must resort to the cause of their statement. This cause is found, almost in all their attestations, to be only one, namely, that the Magnificent Lord Lauro de Aptanis, then Captain of the Bishopric of Piacenza, made a division of those territories in the presence of many persons from both Castro Nuovo and Senio. In that division, it is asserted that a certain ditch was left as a boundary between Castro Nuovo and Senio, according to which boundary, the said tavern would be of the territory of Senio. This reasoning fails in various ways: first, because the division of territories does not pertain to the office of the Captain, but rather to custody, according to the decree. Second, because those individual persons did not have mandates from those communities, nor did they otherwise represent the community. On the contrary, on the part of the accused, several witnesses are found who mention that division, stating that in their presence the boundary of the territories was in the stream of Senio, which is indeed more probable, since boundaries are usually distinguished by water streams, according to the Gloss, whom Johannes reports and follows in the cited chapter Cum causam. According to that stream, the said tavern is situated beyond it, in the territory of Castro Nuovo. What more is needed? The very same witnesses of the accuser are contradictory to one another. Moreover, the witnesses of the accuser testified that all the said taverns adjoin the parish of Florenzola on one side, which has been clearly proven to be false. That, however, is not in doubt,

† That a witness who gives false testimony in matters connected with the case is rejected entirely. Extra, De haereticis, c. Fraternitatis. According to Innocentius, and Extra, De regulis iuris, c. Defleat peccator, in the gloss; and 3 q. 9, the reason of this is evident: for he swears to tell the truth in the case, or in the articles, and their circumstances; therefore, in matters connected therewith, or others pertaining to the case or article, if he gives false testimony, he is guilty of perjury. Certainly, the testimony of a perjurer is rejected by law, even after repentance, as Extra, De testibus, c. Testimonium; 22 q. 5, c. Parvuli. Therefore, etc.

I therefore return to the second point, and beyond the foregoing, it must also be observed that the accused witnesses clearly prove that the tavern itself is within the territory of Castrum Novum: for they state the reasons of fact concluding the boundaries of the territory, especially because they say that up to the stream of Senio, in long-past and most ancient times, whatever lands were used were tithed from the territory of Castrum Novum, not only by the factors of the spectable and eminent knight, Lord Niccolò de’ Terzi, but also by his predecessors. Likewise, during the time of litanies, as is customary in such matters, they were visited up to the bridge of Strata Rupta of the aforementioned stream of Senio. Similarly, concerning damages or any offenses committed beyond the stream, it was known of these by the consuls of Castrum Novum, as some of the witnesses say; and what is more, all depose that now, forty-five years having elapsed, or thereabouts, by a certain person named, it was sworn in the same place where wine is currently sold, that wine was also sold there in those days for several years by license of the vicomte then lord of the same Castrum Novum. By which acts indeed is proved the most ancient quasi-possession of the territory of Castrum Novum up to that stream, arg. ff. De verborum significatione, l. Si pupillus, §. Territorium. For such quasi-possession is said to be proved by such acts of fact, and consisting in fact, arg. Extra, De praescriptionibus, c. Audi, ad finem; Extra, De officio ordinarii, c. Conquerente; and d. c. Cum ecclesia.

From such quasi-possession, continued for so long a time, and although before the boundaries of the territory of Castrum Novum did not extend, nevertheless at least the boundaries were prescribed without doubt up to that stream, and it was common opinion at that time regarding the regulation of boundaries. Indeed, a time of merely thirty years suffices, as C. De finium regundorum, l. Si.

Furthermore, much weight must be given to the fact that in the present judgment the question of boundaries does not principally arise, but the question of jurisdiction arises incidentally; and since at present the commune of Castrum Novum is in quasi-possession of Castrum Novum up to that stream itself, from the present quasi-possession is presumed dominion over the territory, as ff. Si servitus vindicetur, l. Sicuti, §. Si quaeratur; and leg. and not. ff. De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Quidam in suo, per Laurentius de Arena, and there also Bartolus refers.

The conclusion therefore clearly follows from these things: it is and ought to be the part of the judge to declare that the said tavern is within the territory of Castrum Novum, and consequently that he is not the competent judge in the case of the said cause. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If one of three arbitrators orders that 10 be given tomorrow, another 8 the day after tomorrow, and the third 5 on the third day, whether such a sentence is valid.
body: Even if to premise

† the words of the text is in some way superfluous, nevertheless, for a clearer understanding, I premise them. The text states in l. diem proferre. §. si plures. at the word inde quaeritur. ff. de recept. arb. that if of three arbitrators one condemns in 15, another in 10, and the third in five, Julian writes that 5 ought to be paid, because all consented to this sum. The text says the same in c. 1. de arb. li. 6. at the word licet cum, and assigns the same reason. Secondly, I premise that there is a difference between a smaller sum and a shorter delay (dilatio). For a smaller sum makes a smaller obligation, but a shorter delay makes a greater obligation; whence the obligation of him who owes 5 within a month is greater than of him who owes 10 within a year, as in Inst. de act. §. plus autem; and similarly the obligation of him who owes unconditionally is greater than that of him who owes with a term, as in ff. mand. l. si tibi mandavero, ut pro me fideiubeas. Thirdly, I premise that it must be considered that sometimes a lesser amount in quantity is appointed, sometimes less in time, and sometimes these two are mixed together: for example, there are three arbitrators; one orders 10 to be given tomorrow, the second eight the day after tomorrow, the third five on the third day. For if anyone should say that the award of the shorter time is valid because the lesser is included in the greater, he would not speak correctly, because less in time is more in reality. Whence it would follow that he who condemned in less would be condemning in more, which is false, as in the said §. si plures. Wherefore, not lingering in much discourse and coming to the case proposed, I say that the award of the said arbitrators was by no means valid, because they cannot be reduced to harmony. And to this points ff. locat. l. si decem, and ff. de contrah. empt. l. in venditionibus. If, however, two were to agree in sum and in time, the award of the two would be valid, even though the third disagreed, and note this in said c. 1. de arb. in 6. And for the confirmation of the aforesaid there is an express law in ff. de verb. obl. l. si ita stipulatus fuero decem aut quindecim. Likewise, §. si plures considers not only the natural reason, which is that the lesser sum is contained in the greater, but also considers the presumption that the arbitrators appear to agree. And therefore, if there were another difference that did not allow of such an interpretation, the award would not be valid. And so it is in our case, on account of the mixed differences and entanglements. And it supports this in its rationale: ff. sol. matr. l. si constante. §. quotiens. And the aforesaid are confirmed because different due dates have different demands (interpellationes), and therefore there is no conformity, as in ff. de praetor. stipul. l. Valerianus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a pregnant mother, who, after the death of her husband, did not request that a curator be appointed for the womb, is deprived of the inheritance of her son already born; or, if, after the birth of a posthumous child, the mother did not immediately, but rather in the eleventh month thereafter, and thus within a year, assume the guardianship of her son, she is nevertheless deprived of the inheritance of her son.
body: A certain man died, leaving behind a pregnant wife, who remained so for about four months and did not seek a curator for the womb. Finally, when the posthumous child was born in the eleventh month, she assumed guardianship, made an inventory, and proceeded formally, doing everything required for guardianship. Then the posthumous child died.

† It is asked whether the succession of the minor child pertains to this mother, or whether she is deprived of the succession for two reasons. First, because she did not petition for a curator for the womb, nor for the estate. Second, because she did not immediately accept guardianship upon the birth of the posthumous child. And there is no true doubt regarding this question, because it is a case covered by statute. D. ad Tert. l. 2. §. quod si cum praegnans, where the text formally states that if, while pregnant, she did not petition for a curator for the estate, I say she falls under the sentence [of deprivation]. And there Bartolus says that this text is very notable.
