Furthermore, there is another reason, because she did not immediately petition for a guardian for the born minor, as in D. ad Tert. l. 2. §. confestim, where the text formally states that "immediately" is to be understood as when she first could, i.e., when she had access to the praetor sitting for this matter. But this mother did not petition immediately; therefore, she falls from the inheritance, and thus she is deprived of her son's inheritance by two reasons, as being unworthy to receive the legitimate inheritance, as in D. qui petant tuto. l. 2. §. mater. To the same effect in Auth. de haere. ab intesta. §. ex his, and what is noted in D. de reg. iur. l. quo tutela.

However, the contrary seems to be the case, for the law from the father states that if the mother accepted guardianship of the minor within a year from the day of the father's death, she succeeds, as in Inst. ad Tertul. §. si. Where the text seems to be against Bartolus, who says that l. sciant. C. de legi. haeredibus does not apply to the mother, but to others in whom the duty of petitioning for a guardian is imminent. Since, therefore, this mother made use of the benefit of the law, she does not lose the inheritance. That §. confestim, which says that she must petition immediately, provided she does not exceed the year, has no place in the new law, because it suffices that she petitions within the year, unless perhaps a causative necessity for prior petitioning arose, for example, because creditors were pressing, or there was danger, or a penalty would be incurred, or the assets were being squandered, and similar matters. Then, indeed, the mother must perform diligent office, as in C. qui petant. tut. l. cum a matribus. And the common opinion, and in a sense the vulgar one, is that the mother must have a year. And thus it is commonly practiced.

Therefore, the remaining point is that she did not petition for a curator for the womb, and it is added in the facts that the mother was very ill due to an epidemic. For illness seems to excuse her, as in the aforementioned §. confestim. But the contrary seems to be the case, because she could have appointed a procurator to petition for a curator, as appears there, hence another consideration is required. For the law states that a curator is given for the estate at the petition of creditors, or of him who hopes for the succession of the unborn posthumous child, as in D. de ven. in pos. mit. l. 1. §. quotiens, or when some other just cause is imminent, as in D. de hęr. insti. l. si quis instituatur. But here it is not alleged that any just cause was imminent; therefore, the mother is not said to have neglected her duty. Moreover, she is not said to have neglected her duty, because the child remained in the womb for only a few months, i.e., less than four. Hence, from the fact that she did not petition for a curator for the womb, she should not be deprived, arg. C. de epis. et cle. auth. presbyteros. Furthermore, by subsequently accepting guardianship within the year, she purged the delay, as by the aforementioned laws. Moreover, the succession of children is owed to parents as by natural law, as in D. de inoff. testa. l. nam et si parentib. in prin., by which persuasions it can be said that the mother ought to be admitted to the burdensome inheritance of her son, and not excluded from it.

Proceeding more clearly in this matter, I say that the text, "if pregnant, she did not petition for a curator for the estate," must be understood, i.e., if she was in delay in petitioning. For it is understood in the same way in petitioning for a guardian for the already born child: because that text proceeds from the words of the law to its meaning taken by analogy. Since, therefore, the mother would not be repelled by the lapse of a shorter time of four months according to Bartolus by the aforementioned auth. presbyteros. la 2, I say that this mother did not lose the succession due to not petitioning for a curator for the womb, and especially because of her illness, as in the aforementioned §. confestim, where it says, "unless perhaps hindered by illness," etc. Furthermore, she is not excluded, because after 11 months she accepted guardianship, because she has this from the benefit of the new law, as I said above. Wherefore, I think the mother should by no means be excluded from the burdensome inheritance of her son, although this passage is doubtful because of the strict letter of the aforementioned §. quod si cum praegnans. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, the giving of an unpaid debt in dowry extinguishes the personal or hypothecary action; and whether, and when, the giving of an unpaid debt has the force of a sale.
body: Antonia Maiis, former wife of the late Jacob Durgi, having her husband’s goods hypothecated for 84 livres on account of her dowry, made a cession and gave in law all rights competent to her in the goods of her said late husband on account of the aforesaid dowry to John Helias. By this cession thus made, acting as guardian and in the name of the tutorship of Girardin, her son and heir of the said late husband, and wishing to free her said son from the burden of the said obligation, she gave in satisfaction and in payment of the said 82 livres 23 perches of cultivated land, which belonged to the aforesaid late Jacob, to the said John; the said 82 livres being compensated by the said 23 perches. Nevertheless, the said John reserved, in case of eviction of the said perches, all right competent to him in the goods of the said late Jacob. It happened that the said 23 perches of land were not delivered to the said John, nor was notice given to the said guardian or to the heir of the said guardian, that the same 23 perches of land should be delivered to them, the said lands being held and possessed by another against an alien possessor detaining and possessing 9 perches which were among the goods of the aforesaid late Jacob. A hypothecary action was brought by the said John on account of the rights ceded to him by the aforesaid Antonia on account of the aforesaid dowry against the alien possessor.

† It is objected that a hypothecary action cannot be brought against him, first, because the debt has been extinguished by the alleged *datio in solutum*. L. *Eleganter*, D. *De pignoribus et hypothecis*, as there, and the gloss in L. *Libera quidem Theodora*, C. *De senatus consulto Velleiano et interloquendo omnium iudicum*. Moreover, a *datio in solutum* made with things for money is a sale and purchase, as in the laws themselves. And if the thing given in *solutum* is not delivered, an action for damages (*ad interesse*) lies. L. 1 and L. *Iulianus*, D. *De actionibus emptoris et venditoris*, and the delivery of the said thing must be demanded. D. § *Offerri*. And the perception, or quantity, or estimation of the fruits perceived, can be demanded. L. *Curabit*, D. *De actionibus emptoris et venditoris*. And if the thing is evicted, an action for eviction then lies, which eviction requires a judgment. L. 3, C. *De evictione*. The original action does not have place unless a judgment has followed. And therefore, since this was agreed, the original action does not revive unless eviction has followed. And eviction must follow by judgment, L. 3, C. *De evictione*. It follows that the original action cannot be brought when the thing is not delivered. But if it were said that a thing which cannot be delivered is considered as evicted, so that an action *ex empto* has place, as noted in the said L. 3, I say that a distinction must be made. Either we ask whether an action *ex empto* can be brought if the thing cannot be delivered, so that the non-delivering party is liable for damages, and I say yes. D. L. 1, D. *De actionibus emptoris et venditoris*. Or I ask whether, from the fact that it cannot be delivered, or is not delivered, the action once extinguished by *datio in solutum* is revived. I say no, because in its proper meaning, eviction requires a judgment. D. L. 3, C. *De evictione*. But relief is provided by the remedies set forth in L. 1, in the beginning, D. *De actionibus emptoris et venditoris*, especially since it was agreed that, upon eviction following, the first action remains firm, and it was not otherwise stated that the thing is considered evicted: for what is omitted is considered as omitted, and left to the disposition of the common law. L. *Commodissime*, D. *De liberis et posthumis*. The law *Veteribus*, D. *De pactis*, supports this. And especially since a pact and a municipal law are equivalent, gloss in the rubric, C. *De decretis decurionum*. But a statute would not be extended to a fictitious eviction; therefore, neither would a pact, L. *Quicquid astringendae*, D. *De verbis obligatorum*. From which it is said that a hypothecary action cannot be brought by the aforementioned John, the cessionary, against the said external possessor. But John can bring an action for damages against the party making the *datio in solutum*, or his heirs, if the thing or property given in *solutum* is not delivered. To the same effect. Having seen the beautiful allegations made above: since, however, they do not touch the marrow of the question, I say in one word that there is a case and an ordinary gloss in L. *Qui res*, in the beginning, D. *De solutionibus*. For in the case of a dowry, in order for the first hypothecary action to be removed, it is necessary that the thing accepted in *solutum* remain with the recipient; otherwise, the first action, both personal and hypothecary, continues. And this is the singular case there, which is not found elsewhere according to Bartolus. Against the aforementioned opinion, two points are alleged. First, it is not true that L. *Qui res* establishes something special regarding a dowry. To this allegation, I respond in no other way than that the truth of the matter is to the contrary, and I speak to those who understand. Second, it is alleged that if this privilege were special, it would not pass to the cessionary. From this it would follow that a woman could not cede the hypothecary right she has from a tacit hypothec. Which is ridiculous. And consider that a woman can cede a personal hypothecary right. And again consider that if, after the cession, she did something such that the personal and hypothecary rights were not extinguished in the person of the woman, that does not extinguish the right ceded in the person of the cessionary, nor can it extinguish it, as in C. *De hereditate vel actione vendita*, L. *Si*. And much more does the prior cession endure, as in C. *De actionibus et obligationibus*, L. *Si a creditore* and L. *Si insolutum*. And on this point, there is no intelligent person who would doubt: for it is one thing to cede an action, another to cede a privilege, as in L. 1, C. *De privilegio dotis*, and L. 1, D. *De solutione matrimonii*, and L. *Assiduis*, D. *Qui potior in pignore habeatur*, with its most common material. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, a tenant farmer or emphyteuta may be evicted for non-payment of the pension or canon, or for abusive enjoyment, for example because trees are being cut down. And number 2.
2. Whether a husband and a usufructuary may cut down fruit-bearing trees.
body: Vulgar

And that the tenant, who has not paid the rent for two years, may be expelled from the dotal use of the thing, because he does not comply with the tacit condition of the contract, as stated in the Digest, Title "Locatio Conductio," Law "Quaero," Section "Inter locatorem." This is also expressly provided by the Statute of Pavia, which declares and adds that, by operation of law and fact, ownership with all improvements made is vested in the landlord. It speaks generally, saying that if anyone is a fictual tenant, although from the preceding and following provisions the said statute appears to speak of an emphyteuta; nevertheless, if this applies to an emphyteuta, it applies all the more to a simple tenant, because he has neither dominion nor possession, as stated in the Digest, Title "De vi et vi armata," Law "Colonus." Certainly, it is better not to rely on the said statute because of the words "with all improvements," which properly refer to an emphyteuta, as stated in the aforementioned Law "Colonus" and in the Code, Title "De iure emphyteutico," Law "Contra." And thus we are solely in the common law, namely, in the case, the aforementioned Section "Inter locatorem." It should be noted, however, that this lessee paid part for one year, and for the following year nothing; I say that the payment of that part does not help with regard to the avoidance of the penalty and expulsion, as stated in the Digest, Title "Familiae herciscundae," Law "Haeredes," Section "In illa." For this matter is very strict: so much so that for one coin less paid, the thing falls into forfeiture; because it is true that the rents have not been claimed. And this is with regard to the point of delayed payment.

† Now it remains to consider the second point, namely, the abuse of enjoyment. And on this I say that the tenant farmer may rightfully be evicted, because he has cut down fruit-bearing trees, and other large, non-germinating ones. For by this the substance of the thing is deteriorated, and greatly, wherefore even an emphyteuta could be evicted, as in C. de sacr. san. eccl. auth. qui res iam dictas.

† and the husband, who is the owner of the dotal property, could not cut down these trees, because they are not in the fruits, but in the ownership, as in D. 24.3.10 § si fundum. Likewise, neither can the usufructuary cut them down from the trunk: although he may use the foliage and the fruits, as in D. 7.1.17 and D. 7.1.18 and D. 7.1.19. And it is expressly stated in D. 12.2.1 § colonus. Therefore, according to what is proposed, the said tenant can undoubtedly be expelled. I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is Ligium, and at number 9, and why is it called a Ligius man, at number 10.
1. What is ligietas.
2. What is homage, and how manyfold it is.
3. In what way homage differs from fidelity.
4. What is fidelity, and how manyfold it is, at number 6.
5. What the word Ligium, or ligietas, imports in law.
6. Whether a vassal can be a Ligius man of several lords by reason of different fiefs.
7. Whether the contract of fiefs is a named or unnamed contract, and whether repentance has place in it, and what in a Ligius fief, at number 14.
8. Where there is an oath, there repentance has no place.
9. Whether the goods of a Ligius vassal are liable and affected on account of the Ligius oath.
10. Whether a vassal can make a will concerning feudal goods.
body: To make the matter clear, it must be premised that in the tenth column of the *Usus feudorum*, this term,

† Ligium is not found expressed by the word itself. Nevertheless, under this term its effect and the reality of this fief can be comprehended, having knowledge of the aforementioned fiefs, if anyone rightly looks into it, as I will say there. But what is this fief named, which is called the Ligium fief? We have the text in two places. One text is in c. Pastoralis, de re iudicata, in the Clementines, 1, §. denique, where it says: "The King himself, our Lord, and of the Roman Church, by reason of the aforementioned Kingdom, is notoriously subject, a Ligius man, and a vassal." Another text is in the title De quibusdam aliis extraordinariis capitulis feudorum: these chapters are extraneous and are not in the body of the Decretals, yet they are notable and true, and he who was the principal commentator on the matter of fiefs, namely, Lord Jacobus de Ardizone of Verona, cites them as solemn and legitimate chapters. The text of the said chapter is formally as follows: "If anyone invested with a Ligium fief, for which he owes fidelity to his lord against all men, having instituted Lucius and Titius, his sons descending from him, as his heirs, should die after a division has been made, and if the fief should come to Titius alone, it was reasonably pleasing that he alone should be bound by the oaths of fidelity, to whom the entire right of the fief had passed. But if Lucius, another lord, afterwards acquired the fief by investiture, for which he similarly made fidelity to him against all men, and Titius dies without children, to whom the fief which he had by division devolves: whether to Lucius, his brother, or to the lord, may be questioned. And since it is pleasing that a Ligius man cannot be of two [lords], it seems that the fief pertains to the lord; but it was seen more correctly that the fief which he acquired by investiture is not an impediment to him, and that it is permitted for him to serve the former lord through a substitute acceptable to him." From which text it appears what a Ligium fief is. For a Ligium fief is one for which the vassal, invested with the fief, owes fidelity to his lord against all men. And this, if it be asked, is what this fief is.
But the question is definitively asked, what is this ligeance? I answer, it is nothing other than supreme fidelity, or supreme homage, against every man, with none excepted.
† And again, if it is asked, what is homage? I answer that homage is the same as the oath of fidelity, which is made for a certain fief, as is noted in the last chapter, extra, on the rules of law.
† However, homage differs from fidelity: for homage is that act of rendering an oath with its due solemnity, and it takes place at the beginning:

† but fidelity is a permanent obligation, having perseverance and a duration of time; just as the contract, with regard to the utterance of words, passes in an instant, as to buy, but the purchase and sale remain perpetually, as subtly noted by Guillaume de Cuyck, D. de iustitia et iure, l. ex hoc iure facere. Therefore, it does not endure in the course of time, but the fact has been continuously persevering, as C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. sicut; and D. de commodato, l. in commodato, § sicut; and D. de captivis, l. in libello, § factae. It is therefore apparent from the foregoing what homage is and what fidelity is,

† And fidelity is twofold: one superior, as in a Liege fief, and one inferior. For a Liege fief consists in superior fidelity, which is owed to the Pope, the Emperor, or the King, or to any other person who acknowledges no superior, or who acknowledges one only in a qualified sense and not absolutely. Know, therefore, that the following doctrine may be given here: every fief, even if it is not expressly stated to be Liege, is Liege if fidelity is sworn to the prince; because it is of the nature of the predominant prince that no person be excepted, as C. de legibus, l. si; and in c. 1, de natura feudi, col. 10; and in c. Imperialem, §. si, de prohibitione feudorum alienationis, per Federicum, especially when the prince grants regalia, such as all things pertaining to the status of the Empire, and tributes, and similar matters. Likewise, whether it is a March, a County, a Duchy, or other similar dignities, however they are named by customary usage. For we look rather to the reality than to the bare names of things, as C. de libellis praeteritis, l. 3; C. de testibus, l. quam indignum. For example, if the name of the dignity is Dauphiné, or if it is called a Ban, as in Hungary, for there is no force in this. But if anyone were to receive a fief from some vassal, and even if he swore fidelity de facto against every man, such a fief is not Liege. Consider. Note that the text says that fidelity must be owed against all men. Weigh, therefore, the word "must." But this person does not owe fidelity against every man, because he swears an impossibility; therefore the fief is not Liege, because an impossible oath has no force, as ff. de legibus, l. si quis inquilinos, §. si. Moreover, the prince is always deemed to be excepted, so that the oath is not unjust, as in the cited chapter and §. de prohibitione feudorum alienationis, per Federicum. Or we can say that it is a Liege fief, in a qualified sense, against all others, except the prince, nor is this new. For some things are not true absolutely, and yet are true in a qualified sense, as ff. qui satiationem cogunt, l. sciendum, §. creditor. Thus, having declared what and how a Liege fief and liege fidelity are, it is sufficiently apparent from the nature of the obligation what kind of contract it is considered to be, and of what name. For just as the name of the contract denotes the obligation, so conversely, as ff. de praescriptionibus verbalibus, l. insulam. And let these things be said for the declaration of the first point. And I conclude that a Liege fief is nothing other than homage against every man. Wherefore, since homage is owed to the King, while he is subject to the Caesar, I answer: although he is subject to the Caesar according to law, as God on earth, it is not said that the general rule is infringed; because God and the Caesar do not cause the rule to fail, but they give it the understanding of law and justice. Argument: ff. de legibus, l. apud Iulium, §. si; and extra de iureiurando, c. quemadmodum. And therefore all princes can have Liege vassals in the midst of the Caesar, whatever name they are called, as parts of his own body. C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. quisquis.

† Now I come to the second point, which asks what the word "Ligium" or "ligietas" means in law, beyond the condition and nature of the other fiefs designated in column 10. Regarding this, it must be said that there are certain general natures of fiefs, and certain singular natures. Some arise from pacts, some arise from another source as regards the general natures of fiefs, such as acquiring by investiture given, or equivalent: and I call equivalent a fictitious tradition in cases approved by the custom of fiefs, as in c. 1, "what is investiture," col. 10, and in Auth. "on the custom of a rightful fief," § "know," in the beginning. Also, such as retaining what is acquired, and transmitting it to sons, if they are heirs, because this is an undoubted case, as in c. 1, "whether the son, or agnate," col. 10. Also, losing it by felony contracted, and by felony declared, as in c. 1, "what was the first cause of losing a benefice," and in c. 1, "who, how, fief, loses." Also, it is of the general nature of fiefs to have a singular possessory action, which is not in other contracts, as extra de iud. c. "ceterum," namely, that if there is a dispute about a fief between two vassals, the lord has cognizance; but if between the lord and the vassal, the peers of the court judge, as in the said c. "Emperor Frederick," § "if about a fief." And where there is contention between those who are properly called captains, such as Dukes, Marquises, Counts, and Barons, and their like, the Emperor, or King, from whom he judges, as in c. 1, "against whom, or whom," and in c. 1, "de l. cor. radi." fully by Jacobus de Belvis, and by me after him in c. 1, "on investiture made to a husband." And many other general natures, both affirmative and negative, are in fiefs. But there is a certain consistency attributed to fiefs in their nature, beyond the nature of other contracts. The law says similarly in emphyteusis, as C. de iure emphyt. l. 1. I therefore say that in the common nature, a Ligium fief does not differ from a simple fief, but it differs well in homage: because fidelity is sworn against every man. Also, it differs in dignity and nobility, as in c. 1, "who is called Duke, Marquis, Count," col. 10. Also, perhaps it differs in this, that a Ligius vassal cannot say to his prior lord, "you contend unjustly with my other lord"; rather, he is precisely compelled to aid the prior lord, because as he swore, so let it be the law, since he swore to the prince; but to a vassal who is not Ligius, a distinction is applied in c. "domino guerram," in the beginning, in the title "here the law ends, then the customs of the kingdom begin." Therefore, the prince can say, "he who is not with me is against me," as noted C. de Iud. l. "celicolarum." Also, there is a manifest dignity, which the text of the aforementioned extraordinary chapter makes:

† because a man cannot be a Ligius vassal of two lords for different fiefs, unless this occurs by reason of succession. And thus not from the principal purpose, as the aforementioned notable chapter states, and by this means the third point is also answered. Nevertheless, one matter remains to be declared, namely that in a simple fief one may hold many fiefs, and all under an oath of fidelity; yet he must aid the older lord, for he is to be preferred to all others, as in c. *contra omnes*, in the title cited. Here the law ends, where the text thus says: “The vassal must aid his lord against all, even against his brother, son, and father, unless against another older lord; for this one is to be preferred to all.” These are the words of the text.

Suppose therefore that Titius holds from the Marquis the Castle of Saint Stephen in fief, and from the Count the Castle of Baldus; must he aid only the older lord? I answer that, as regards his person, he must aid only the older lord, and this with his personal presence. For properly speaking, the person is more honorable, more gracious, and more acceptable in law to his lords than if he sent a substitute, in whom the insignia of nobility and the praises of virtue cannot be so well recognized, without which there is also usually greater diligence and superior experience in the principals themselves, whence they can more quickly respond and come to aid, especially in matters of arms, in which counsel is taken up into arms, and this is naturally evident.

And if, because necessity, which has no law, compels him to send a substitute, he will send the best one he can. To the first lord he will serve with his person; to the second lord he will serve with his castle, that is, according to the usual custom, by sending men and money in proportion to the resources of that castle; for in such matters custom is always observed. And therefore the use of fiefs is called *usus feudorum*, as in c. *Obertus*, de feudis cognoscendis, column 10; and see the argument in l. *venditor*, § *si constat*, ff. de communibus prœdiorum, where the text says that the custom of the quarries must be observed.

Someone might ask: By what law do you prove this distinction between the person and pecuniary resources? I answer that this is clear, because the person is something indivisible, and therefore both lords have an interest in it, but the proper lord is preferred first, ff. de locato, l. *in operis*. But it is not so with things, because the first lord alone and the second lord alone have interests, not concerning the same thing. For the reason of separated things is separate, as in ff. de calumniis, l. *hæc actio*, and C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. *si maritus*. Just as in this example, one donates to me a fief, another a house; here there is no priority or posteriority, because these are names of relative order concerning the same subject or the same effect, as in l. *qui duos*, ff. de rebus dubiis, and in the first constitution of the Forum, where it says that what is first cannot have anything before it. And note that *relativum* is relative to the same substance, not in l. 1, C. de senatu, quæ pro eo, at the end.

Now let us see if it is so in a Ligius fief, and I say that it is not, for he must serve the first lord in such a way that he must in no way serve his adversary, that is, the second lord. Therefore, since he cannot serve the second, he must relinquish the fief; for it is against nature that he should enjoy the benefit who cannot render the service, as in c. 1, de eo qui arma bellica deposuit, and C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. *qui sub prœtextu*. And let him impute to himself that he binds himself to this perplexity by a Ligius oath, see ff. de falsis, l. *qui duobus*. Nor is the lord bound in this case to accept a substitute; for he must not be the author of perjury. For this is permitted only when the Ligius vassal incidentally and without his fault falls into this necessity by reason of succession, as the author of the text elegantly teaches us in the aforementioned extraordinary chapter. As for who the name of that author was, I do not know; certainly it was not Obertus, because he puts his own name; therefore I think it was Gerardus Gagapisti, or another authentic and great man.

One can also be Ligius to one and simple to another, that is, not Ligius, as in the said c. *grandi*, there: “To the King, or to any other.” One can also simultaneously receive fiefs from several, and then the cause of all is equal, as in ff. de pignoratitia actione, l. *aliena*, § *si pluribus*. In this case therefore, as regards his person, he has the choice of whom to serve; and if he chooses one, he must serve the other by a substitute. Nor does it seem that in serving thus he acts against his own right, because he does this from the nature of lawful contracts and for the purpose of preserving his own right. Where it is a matter of preserving a right, it does not matter by whom it is done, provided it is done according to the effect of the contract, as in ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. *cum servus*.

I say the same regarding serving by a substitute, whether simultaneously or not, since the same body cannot be in different places at the same time, as in ff. de communibus, l. *si ut certo*, § *si duobus vehiculum*. To the first lord he will serve with his person, personally and properly; to the second lord he will serve perfunctorily or imaginatively, that is, by a substitute, who is his image, but does not have the truth of nature, as in ff. de religione, l. *ossa*, § *si*, and C. de caducis tollendis, l. *unica*, § *ne autem*, and ff. de conditione indebiti, l. *si non sortem*, § *libertus*. And thus, what cannot be done in the same person, will be done in a similar one, as in ff. de constitutione peculii, l. *qui autem*, § *sed et si quis*, where it says: “another person not less suitable.” And this is an argument to this effect, ff. in ius vocandi, vt eant, l. 2 and 3, and what is noted there, it is presumed that the substitute is suitable if he is of the same kinship, by that notable law, and see C. de agris et censibus, lib. 11, l. *nescimus*.

Furthermore, it is well known and a common saying of the Speculator in the title de feudis, § *quoniam*, verb. *et nota*, where he thus says, and note, that a Ligius homage is that which is made to the Most Serene Lord Emperor or King, saving the fidelity of no other. But that which is made to others is not called Ligius, because it is made or sworn saving the authority of the Lord Emperor or King, as in the Liber Feudorum, de prohibita feudi alienatione, c. *Imperiale*, at the end.

† Many, however, consider Ligium homage to be that whereby the vassal places his hands within the hands of the lord, renders him homage, and promises fidelity, and is received by him with a kiss; which, however, is not true, as I have said. Others say that there is a twofold homage: one is called Ligium, in which no exception is made as regards the words; nevertheless, in the minds of those who possess supreme and general jurisdiction, namely the said Emperor or King, they are understood to be excepted, as in the extrajudicial title *De iureiurando*, chapter *Venientes*, against whom one is not bound to aid his lord, as in verse 15. Another, however, is non-Ligium, when, namely, someone is excepted, for example, "I render you homage excepting the fidelity by which I am bound to such my Ligium lord," or "saving that I may constitute whomsoever I wish as my Ligium lord," as in verse 12, or "saving that I wish to aid you against such a person." But the former statement is more correct, although this latter usage is approved by common speech, and according to this latter mode we speak almost throughout the present section. §.

† A man is called a Ligius, as if bound to his lord: or legius, as if containing legality; whereas what in Italy and elsewhere is called vassalage, in France is called homage; we provincials, however, commonly call nobles who hold fiefs vassals, and our commoners simply men. That a man can belong to two [lords] is proven in the Extravagantes, De supplemento praesentationis, chapter Grandi, there: "or to any other person, etc." These are the words of the Speculator verbatim. Moreover, that subtle noble doctor John of Blanosco, in his treatise on fiefs and homages compiled [therefrom], from which the aforementioned Speculator took these words in his Summa in the second chartula under the rubric "viso igitur," thus says: 11

† It must be noted that homage is twofold: one kind is *ligium* (fealty), which carries with it a quasi-legal obligation, that is, fidelity; for a *ligius* man owes fidelity to his lord against all. And thus in *ligium* homage no one is excepted as regards the words; but as regards the sense, those who possess general jurisdiction are understood to be excepted, for they are not bound to aid their lord against them, as noted above. And by this it appears that the law cannot permit a man to render *ligium* homage to two lords, because one cannot owe such simple fidelity, in which no one is understood to be excepted save the superior, to two persons. This is clear.

Homage is not *ligium* when someone is excepted; for example, “I render you homage excepting the fidelity which I owe to my *ligius* lord,” or “I render you homage on this condition, that I may constitute for myself a *ligius* lord against whom I am not bound to aid you.” It would be the same if another person were excepted, for instance, “I render you homage on this condition, that I do not wish to aid you against such-and-such a noble.” This man is not *ligius*, because he is not bound to owe fidelity against all; for he excepts certain persons against whom he is not bound to render fidelity or aid. These are the literal words of the aforementioned John of Blanosco, etc.

And it is similar to what we say regarding manual obedience. Moreover, “hand” signifies power, as in D. de iust. et iure, l. manumissiones; and discretion, as noted in D. de arbitris, l. pen.; and see what is noted in l. 2, C. quando decreto opus non est. Furthermore, to give someone one’s right hand signifies firmness and solidity, as noted in Inst. de verbis obligationibus, in princ. Therefore, if a *ligius* man places himself within the hands of the prince, he becomes his subject, and there is no place for repentance, as in D. de iure omnium iudiciorum, l. est receptum.

Therefore, retaining the statements of the aforementioned great jurists, namely John of Blanosco and the Speculum, as well as Master Martin of Fano, from whose opinions one must not depart, it conclusively appears that whether fidelity is said to be a servitude, as in X. de accusationibus, c. veniens, or whether it is said to be a kind of service, because the vassal is not diminished in status, nevertheless the *ligius* man is bound by a stricter tie, because he owes fidelity against every man, except God in heaven and God on earth, that is, the Emperor, or he who is monarch in his own kingdom, such as the King of the French, and any others who enjoy free imperial authority. However, I think the same applies to free peoples, according to the notes in D. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. hostes. But let us see whether there is a difference in what follows.

† For the customs of fiefs state that a vassal may renounce the fief, and the fief returns to the lord, and he may do so even against the lord’s will, provided that the lord is never offended, as in c. unicus, §. ult., de vassallo, qui contra constitutionem Lotharii. Hence it is not without reason that doubt arises whether the same holds for a Ligian fief. For the understanding of this question, it must be known whether the first assumption is true, and it seems that it is not: because a fief, according to almost all doctors, is a proper name of a contract and gives rise to an action, but in named contracts, because repentance has place, as C. de act. et ob. l. sicut. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that from a fief arises a condition ex moribus, or a condition ex lege Federici, or Corradi, because from a donation arises a condition ex lege, and yet today it is a named contract, as noted in l. si, ff. de condit. ob cau. Likewise, a compromise is a named contract, and yet if the compromise is made by a bare pact, a condition arises ex lege, as C. de arb. l. pe. The sign, however, that it is a named contract is that repentance does not have place, but rather a penalty is incurred. Secondly, it is argued thus: whether we say that this is an innominated contract, or a named one, or an anomalous one: because there are more transactions than words, nevertheless equality must be observed on both sides. ff. de arbi. l. sed interpellatur, §. si ab altera. But it is so that the lord cannot withdraw from the vassal, as in c. 1, de forma fidelitatis. Therefore, neither can the vassal withdraw from his promises. Moreover, even if it were a named contract, he has fulfilled his part by corporal investiture, for the lord has nothing else to do, so much so that the lord’s forbearance is no longer in obligation, but comes by the office of a mercenary judge, as l. 1, ff. de ser. ru. prae. Since, therefore, the obligation has perfectly arisen, and the action is rooted in the lord, it cannot be taken away by the will of one party: as ff. de neg. ge. l. Pompo. writes. Moreover, it is a serious matter to break faith, as ff. de constit. pecu. l. 1, in princ. Hence infamy often pursues where there is no faith, as ff. 13 de infami, §. fur, l. mandati.

† Moreover, where there is an oath, repentance has no place: because it is equivalent to a stipulation, as is noted in l. si pecuniam, in principio, ff. de conditionibus ob causam; nor is a custom valid which induces perjury, because it is neither reasonable nor honest, as ff. de pactis, l. iure gentium, and generally. This opinion is held by the gloss, extra de constitutionibus, c. quae in ecclesiarum. To the contrary is the text in the said c. 1, de vassallo, etc. I say that either we are speaking of an ecclesiastic fief, which the church grants, or of a singular fief. In the first case, it matters whether the words say, “we grant to you a fief,” l. feudorum, or simply, if the gloss speaks simply, customs of fiefs do not prejudice churches, unless the church approves: because customs burdensome to churches are not valid. But if those words, “by the law of fiefs,” or words of equivalent meaning, are added: then the same applies in an ecclesiastic fief as in a lay fief, where I subdistinguish, either it is a fief granted for a certain service, and repentance has no place: and the reason is, because the status of the obligation is certain, and therefore it cannot be changed by a subsequent act: as ff. de verbis oblig., l. intra insulam; or it is simply granted, and then it can be renounced: because this condition is tacitly implied, if it is not renounced. And this tacit condition is introduced by custom: as in the said c. 1, vassallo, which is against the constitution of Lothair, and c. Thus the gloss distinguishes in c. ult., de capitaneo, qui curiam vendidit. And the reason is: because when the thing fails, the burden of the thing fails, as ff. de usufructu, l. cum usufructuarius.

† Now follows whether this has place in a Ligian fief. And I hold that it does not, because such a contract has the force of law, as C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. pen. and ff. de publicaniis, l. Caesar. And the inferior cannot abrogate the law of the superior, especially of the prince, as C. de legibus, l. pe. And by these means another difference of ours between a Ligian and a non-Ligian fief is made clear. 15

The fourth point follows, whether the other goods of the Ligius vassal are affected by the ligium oath. And it must be said that they are not, but rather they are free, just as castrensia and non-castrensia goods receive division with respect to the burdens of creditors: as C. de testamento militis, l. 1; and ff. eodem, l. si certarum; and peculia diversi generis; ff. de pactis, l. hic quaeritur, §. potest; ff. de minoribus, l. denique, §. sed utrum. Hence, the Ligius and the non-Ligius do not differ in this respect, because all things are free which are not subject to servitude, as C. de servitutibus et aqua, l. altius; and ff. de servis rusticis praediis, l. servo generi. Moreover, they have free testamentary power over their freehold property, for their status itself is free, as noted in Inst. de iure personarum, in the gloss.

But they cannot make a will concerning fiefs, as in c. 1, § ad hoc, de pace iuramento firmata; although some say that if the fief were free, they can make a will in favor of the church, as among free persons, saving the lord’s ownership and the due services. On this point it is customary to note extra de fidei instrumentis, c. inter dilectos, which does not please me, unless custom granted this, because it would offer the lord hope of consolidation, since the church does not cease to be heir: as in cap. si clientulus, de feudi alienatione. For this, gloss ff. de verbis obligatis, l. si quis ita, § ea lege. Moreover, it seems contrary to the nature of a fief that the church, succeeding by reason of monastic profession, should deposit the fief and not acquire it for the church: as in c. 1, de eo qui arma bellica deposuit. Nevertheless, this should be understood when it is such a fief that it cannot be served by a substitute; otherwise, while the vassal lives naturally, the church has the benefit of the fief, not the root, but after his death there is nothing. ff. de pignoribus, l. lex vectigalis; extra de probationibus, c. in praesentia. And what is noteworthy, the doctor teaches C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, authentic ingressi. I do not deny either that, on account of the delayed performance of services, or on account of the reckless enjoyment of the fief itself, if anything is owed by way of penalty or damage, the lord could have recourse to certain goods, just as any creditor. C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, auth. qui res iam dictas; ff. solutione matrimonii, l. diuortium, § si fundum ad instar fructuarii. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a city subject to a certain lord may enact statutes without the license of the same.
2. What is contained in the term of law.
3. When a pact and agreement is special, and a statute follows the general rule, whether one derogates from the other, and which of them prevails.
4. Whether a statute excluding a daughter also excludes a granddaughter through her.
body: The words of the Pacts state: Furthermore, it has been agreed between the aforementioned parties in the manner and form set forth above, that in intestate successions of those who die, civil law shall be observed, notwithstanding the pact written below, or above, or any custom whatsoever. In another chapter of the pacts, there is such a chapter, that the council of the commune may sometimes, at its free will, make, diminish, increase, and change chapters and ordinances according to its own will, impose, diminish, increase, annul, and invalidate penalties once and many times at its own will: and whatever they have done shall be valid and binding, as long as it pleases the council. These are the chapters by which the community must live. Finally, there follows a certain statute of the said community in this form: Furthermore, that no woman, by herself or another, in any way, after she has been married, may claim anything, or bring any action, or raise any issue against any of her brothers, or nephews, on account of any succession of her father, or mother, or brotherhood, or any other cause whatsoever, unless a legacy had been expressly made to her. Finally, it happened that a certain G. died intestate, survived by a married sister, and nephews through her, and also nephews through other predeceased sisters, and also nephews, and a certain brother of the said deceased. Now, there is a dispute among the aforementioned regarding the succession. It is asked, what is the law.

† And it must be premised for the sake of clarity, whether the said statute is valid or not. And it seems that it is valid, as in D. de iust. et iur., l. omnes populi. To the contrary, it seems that it is not valid, because this community is proper and peculiar to the said Prince of Achaea, or to one holding title from him, and peculiar peoples cannot make statutes unless they have the license of their own lord; but other peoples, who live by their own customs and laws and are in quasi-possession of this liberty, can well make statutes, and their statute has the force of a statute and of confirmation, as these things are proven from those which are read and noted in l. 1, § 1, quod quisque iur., and in the aforementioned l. omnes populi, according to the ancient and modern commentators. Since, therefore, the community in question is without any power of liberty to make statutes by itself, it can make nothing, except insofar as the agreements of the said lords determine that the said community can make statutes; of this there is nothing, neither in law nor in fact. Having seen, therefore, the chapters of the said lords, it can be alleged that the said statute is valid by the said chapter which begins, “Item quod consilium comunis,” where it is said: “and what they shall have done, shall be valid and binding,” and thus free power is granted to them even in those matters which are of mere and mixed Empire. Hence, it should not be called into doubt that which is expressly granted, as in D. de procur., l. procurator, cui libera, and l. 1, C. de thesauro, lib. 10. To the contrary, it seems by the chapter which begins, “Item conventum est,” which provides that in intestate successions the laws shall be precisely observed, notwithstanding any of the above- or below-written agreements or custom. In this chapter two things are to be noted. First, that it says, “the laws shall be observed.”

† This is understood in civil law for three reasons. First, by reason of excellence and authority, as in the Institutes, De iure naturali, § Ius autem. Second, by reason of natural justice, which is administered by the common law in intestate successions: as in the Authenticum, De hereditatibus ab intestato, l. Nullam vero. Third, because statutes are more matters of fact than of law; hence they are not understood to apply to statutory rights: as in c. 1, De constitutionibus, lib. 6. Secondly, the derogatory words must be noted. For where derogatory words are added, that which is first in the order of speech is last in the determination, as in l. Si ita, ff. De legibus, 3; l. Si quis, in principio, ff. De testibus solvendis. The said statute of the said community is invalid, because that chapter which begins “Item conventum” is a special chapter concerning intestate successions.

But the said chapter, which begins “Item, that the counsel of the commune,” is a general chapter; and where the genus and the species are incomparable or contrary, the species always derogates from the genus, even if there were no derogatory or contrary words, whether the species precedes the genus or follows it: as in the rule that the genus is derogated by the species. From which it is concluded that to each of the aforementioned persons, concerning whom the question is asked, his portion is due intestate, as in the Authentica “Defuncto” and in the Corpus, from which it is taken. For the common law so provides, and the said chapter “Item, that it was agreed” so wishes to be observed, and this is the truth. However, another point was narrated to me the day before, but it was not narrated as it ought to have been narrated; and therefore, according to what was then proposed, I wrote at that time, but now I write with the point reformed, rather ordered: because at first it was not well ordered. Hence Scævola always says, according to what is proposed; for the law depends on the fact, as in § “In cliuo Capitolino.”

† I do not omit that point, namely that if the said statute were valid, it would exclude the granddaughter, and according to the opinion of Cynus, which he sets forth in l. 1, in the penultimate paragraph, C. quæ sit longa consuetudo, it would also exclude the son of the said granddaughter, because it appears to be the intent of the law that this applies to grandsons and granddaughters of those who have predeceased, to whom that addition, "if she has been married," does not apply. These words are understood with reference to the time of death of the person whose inheritance is in question. I formerly said in my lectures, and I now say, that they are not excluded: although Bartolus argues to the contrary on account of a certain inclusive force, which is nothing as regards our case; rather, from the contrary sense, if she who is married is excluded, then the rule is different for one who is not married. For those words, "if she has been married," have the force of a condition, i.e., "if she has been married," that is, at the time of death, as I said, or, if you wish to say more, say "at some time." Nevertheless, this exclusive quality excludes her or those to whom the said quality does not pertain. And if it does not exclude those, therefore it does not include the contrary, because, so to speak, the successive edict of the statute has no place, assuming that the person is in a prior degree and in effect is antecedent, as in C. de successionibus edictis, l. si a me frater. Moreover, if anyone carefully considers Bartolus in l. 2, ff. ad Tertullianam, he will find that he does not contradict my opinion, because he speaks in different terms. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. He treats beautifully the manner and order of succeeding to fiefs.
2. The first dictum, and then the further dicta: what they signify.
body: First

I shall speak of feudal goods, and briefly. Therefore, when a vassal who held a fief dies, the first cause [of succession] is that of children. But if the vassal has no children, and the fief is paternal or ancient, the brother succeeds first, together with the children of predeceased brothers; for the children of brothers succeed together with the brother of the deceased, namely per stirpes. For several children of one predeceased brother occupy one share; and if there were ten children from one predeceased brother, and five from another predeceased brother, and they come to the succession of the deceased without children together with the brother of the deceased, that brother has one-third part, those ten another third part, and those five the other third, as in c. 2 de gradibus successionis in feudum. For the succession to fiefs is considered in the same manner as regards the degree of succession as are other successions introduced by the common law, since the same reason applies, whether natural, civil, or customary. And there is no doubt about this, because it is the case of the said chapter, and it is also a rule in the matter of fiefs that in cases where custom does not provide otherwise, the common law must be observed, as in the said § strenuus de feudi cognitione. From this it follows that in the feudal portion of Anthony, the children of Anthony’s brothers succeed together with Peter. Now it remains to see, since afterwards one of the children of the said brothers, namely of Stephen, who was called Henry, died, and it is asked whether the paternal cousins of the said Henry are excluded by the said Peter, the uncle of the said Henry. And it must be said that they are, because the said uncle is in the third degree to the said Henry, and the said paternal cousins are in the fourth, and it is certain that the third degree excludes the fourth. C. de legatis hereditatibus, auth. cessante. And thus the text in the said c. de gradibus should be understood, where it says, “then the more distant agnates.”

† For that term “deinde” (then) and that term “ulteriores” (more remote) also signify the order of degrees, namely, that first the nearest relatives succeed, then the more remote ones, and so on up to the third degree of collateral relatives, or according to others, in infinitum. [See] the law “quidquid extat” (whatever exists), i.e., as long as there is anyone of that lineage through the male line, or according to others, in infinitum. [See] the law “in tempus longissimum” (for a very long time), i.e., up to the tenth generation. But it is not necessary to dispute these matters here; it suffices to refer to chapter 1, § “hoc autem,” in the title “Qui feudum dare potest.” Moreover, that the above statements are true is proven, because it is certain that intestate successions are governed by the right of proximity; therefore, the nearer relative is preferred, as stated in the Code, Title “De Successorio Edicto,” law 1, and law “Si auia.” This is also evident from the rubric itself “De gradibus succedentium in feudis” (On the degrees of those succeeding in fiefs), for where there are degrees, there is preference. And by this, the law regarding fiefs is determined. I say the same concerning other non-feudal goods, because the text is found in the aforementioned authenticum “Cessante” and in the authenticum “Post fratres,” and where the case of the law applies, there is no doubt. [See] the Code, Title “De Furtis,” law “Ancillae.” I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Just as a manifest usurer is prohibited from making a will, unless the form of the chapter *Quanquam*, *De usuris*, Book 6, is observed, so too is he prohibited from making a codicil and from making a donation *causa mortis*, but not so *inter vivos*. And number 3.
2. Whether a donation *causa mortis* accedes more to a contract than to a last will.
3. Add below, opinion 298, where, regarding a donation *causa mortis*, he holds the contrary.
body: The question is,

Whether a manifest usurer, without having provided security, may make a donation causa mortis. And I do not speak of the donation causa mortis made in a will or codicils; for there is no doubt about that, that he cannot, because no one who is intestabilis may make codicils, as L. 2, D. de legatis 1, and D. de iure codicillorum, L. diui, § codicillos. And on this point all the doctors agree in C. quamquam, § fin., de usuris, lib. 6. But I speak of the donation causa mortis which passes into a contract of stipulation, so that action lies on the contract, or passes into a naked pact, on which action lies by condictio, as L. si quis argentum, as noted, D. de legatis 2; L. cum pater, § mevio; and by Cynus in L. fin., C. de donationibus causa mortis. Of these two types of donation causa mortis, see L. legata est, D. de legatis 2, and L. ut haeredibus.

It seems that this contract is not prohibited, as D. de verbis significandis, L. verba gesserunt. For this donation is a species of contract, and an obligation and action arise from the contract; therefore it is not a last will, as D. de verbis obligandis, L. verba gesserunt. Likewise, it is not a legacy, although it has the force of a legacy, as noted in C. de collationibus, Authent. ex testamento. But I say the contrary, for he who is intestabilis by his own fault cannot make a donation causa mortis, as L. 1, D. si quid in fraudem patroni. Moreover, since some form is required in a last will, the same is required in a donation causa mortis, as D. de transactionibus, L. cum hi. Moreover, if a will is rescinded by contrary tablets, a donation causa mortis is rescinded, as L. 1, D. de legatis praestandis. Moreover, just as a pupil cannot make a will, so he cannot make a donation causa mortis, as L. 1, § 1, D. de tutelae et rationum distrahendarum.

† And although in contracting more weight is given to the contract than to the last will, as noted in l. 2, ff. de donationibus prælegatis, nevertheless the rule is different with regard to the acquisition to be made therefrom, which is only sought after death, and the obligation begins with the heir, as noted in l. 1, C. de donationibus causa mortis; dominion passes therefrom without delivery, just as in legacies, as in l. 3 and 4, ff. de publicis. And although a condition arises, nevertheless an action arises from the will according to the gloss and Bartolus, and it is supported by what is noted in Inst. de donationibus. Moreover, if we were to say the contrary, an absurdity would follow, namely, that fraud would be committed by transferring from a contract to a last will. Moreover, a donation causa mortis is a mixed thing; therefore, we take that which is prejudicial on account of the donor’s delict. And I believe this opinion to be the more correct, although this question is disputable, and it is supported by what is noted in l. 1, ff. de testibus, where the gloss equates codicils, letters, donations causa mortis, and gratuitous permissions made after death. Moreover, it is supported by what is noted in C. de pactis, l. si.

† However, they may validly make donations inter vivos: for this is not prohibited by the decretal, nor does its rationale, as it seems, forbid certain contracts, nor the appointment of procurators and managers, as in l. eius, qui in provincia, in principio, and l. lecta, ff. si certum petatur, cum suis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a city statute providing that a mother and the maternal line shall not succeed when male agnates are present, whether, if a mother and an aunt are present, the said agnates exclude the aunt. And he concludes that they do not, and he refutes the opinion of Bartolus in l. 2, ff. ad Tertull. with many arguments.
body: The Statute of the City of Parma provides that the mother and the maternal line shall not succeed when male agnates are extant.

† Now it is asked, if the mother and the grandmother exist, whether the aforementioned agnates exclude the aunt. And it seems that they do, so that the sense of the statute is this: male agnates, and not the mother, so that the statute has a double sense, one conferring upon male agnates, because a condition appended by law tacitly induces a disposition, as Bartolus holds in l. 2, ff. ad Tertullianam, with many laws and sufficiently notable reasons, which it would be futile to describe here. For two things are to be weighed: namely, the favor of the line of agnates, and the favor of males. For often the condition of women is worse than that of males, as l. in multis, ff. de statu hominum, with the common matter.

To the contrary, it seems, because if Bartolus’s reasoning were true, similarly, considering only this statute, the sister united on both sides to the deceased, or the daughter of the brother, would be excluded. But this consequence is absurd and unjust, that agnates who are in the 10th degree would exclude the carnal sister, or the daughter of the brother, who is in the 3rd degree of agnation; and the opinion itself suffers from the same disease of absurdity in saying that the aunt is excluded. For these cases are omitted by the statute. We must avoid injustice and absurdity, as Inst. de legibus agnatorum successionibus, §. sed quia sancitum. And the aforementioned example concerning the sister is clearly shown in Inst. ad Tertullianam, §. soror autem. And if it is said that one thing applies to the sister, another to the aunt, this opinion is of no avail if Bartolus’s reasoning is true. Moreover, if one is excluded, another is not excluded unless found to be excluded; hence it is not a good consequence: the line of cognates is excluded on account of the favor of male agnates; therefore, the line of female agnates, or women of the line of agnation, is excluded. For neither the reasoning of the statute nor the words can support males in this matter. And where the words of the statute fail, the statute fails, as ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. si cum servum, §. non dixi. For since the words of the statute cannot in any way be drawn to this, it would be absurd to say that the statute corrects the common law. And this is gathered from the theory of Cynus, C. quae sit longa consuetudo, l. 1, in the last question, where he distinguishes whether the words of the statute can be drawn, albeit improperly, and then they are drawn. Hence I distinguish thus: Either from the inclusive force, of which Bartolus speaks, absurdity and correction of the law would follow; then no inclusion is made. C. de conditionibus insertis, l. cum patrem. Or absurdity would not follow, and then there is inclusion; for example, if the sister or aunt renounced, or died, and did not transmit, in which case Bartolus’s opinion may proceed. But if absurdity, correction of laws, and inversion of degrees would follow, then I say that Bartolus’s opinion is not true, because this case is omitted by the statute.

And therefore, concluding, I say that in the aforementioned case the aunt succeeds, not that she could of herself exclude the mother. But because she finds the mother excluded by the statute through the person of male agnates; just as one has through an excluding intermediate person what one does not have by oneself, as ff. ad Tertullianam, l. aequissimum. It is true that the Moderns follow Bartolus’s opinion greatly. However, in this they err, as I think, or rather, not condemning Bartolus, but saving him, I understand him with the aforementioned distinction. And if it is said, what favor then does the male have? Certainly this does not move me, because the statute requires two things conjunctively: one on the part of the excluding person, that he be a male agnate; the other on the part of the excluded, that they be of the maternal kindred, or cognates. Also, the response is that the way is potentially open to him; for it is possible for him to succeed where there is no other person in the middle of the maternal kindred. For if the paternal kindred is opposed to him, I do not think even the feminine is excluded, because it is not from that natural reason, equity, and also law, upon examining subtlety, and the ancient doctors before Bartolus would have held this point as undoubted. And I say this, saving the counsel of anyone who thinks better, to whom I also submit myself. To truth and justice. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a thing was given as security for money with the reservation that, if the thing were lost, the original action would remain intact, and it happens that the thing was not fully delivered, nor can it be delivered, whether the original action can be brought.
body: The question is,

The thing was given in satisfaction for money in this manner, and with this reservation, namely, that if the thing were evicted, the first action would remain. The case occurred that the thing was not fully delivered, nor can it be delivered. Now it is asked whether, by virtue of the reservation, one may sue by the original action. And the reason for doubt is that what is evicted is considered as not delivered, as in D. 35.1, *Non quacunque*, in the beginning. Moreover, a fiction ought to operate more strongly than truth, as in D. 6.2, *Si filius*. Therefore, if a fictitious non-delivery preserves the right, much more strongly does a true non-delivery preserve the right. Furthermore, what is expressed in one case operates in its similar case. Hence the law says that an outsider who stipulates for the dowry to be returned to himself, if the marriage is not contracted, is considered to have stipulated the same: as in D. 19.1, *Si extraneus*. But these cases are similar, indeed they are one and the same case at different times, namely, at the beginning, where it is not delivered, and afterwards, where it is evicted. Hence the legal rule rightly states that what is evicted is not in our goods. Moreover, in ambiguous matters we must look to what is probable, as noted in D. 2.15, *Veteribus*. But it is probable that he intended to provide for himself in both cases, since in both cases the identity of reason is found, for which this is provided. Argument from D. 46.3, *Qui rem*, in the beginning, there: "unless from the event, etc." And the same seems to be said if someone delivered, but perfunctorily, that is, neither fully nor with effect; because that which is not effectively delivered is not said to be delivered, as in D. 2.15, *Emptione*. Moreover, for this view there seems to be a law almost expressly stating it: D. 7.5, *L. 3*, § *Desinere*.

To the contrary it seems, because the law provides that an exception or reservation for one case does not comprehend another, because it is not found to be reserved, as in D. 18.6, *Si vina emerim*. Just as an excluded case cannot include, so a sole excluded case ought not to be included. Moreover, whenever the general ordinance of the law disposes one thing generally, and the special provision of a person disposes another thing specially, such a specified case is not extended to other cases which are included under the rule, as in D. 46.1, *Sed et si quia*, § *Quaesitum*, and D. 38.1, *Quaesitum*, § *Idem respondit*. But here the general ordinance of the law proceeds, that when a thing is given for money, the first action is extinguished and the second is contracted, as fully in the law and note, C. 4.26, *Libera quaedam Theodora*. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, this case is not understood to be reserved. Moreover, these cases, namely, the thing not being delivered, delivered, and evicted, are cases contrary in their terms: as in D. 21.2, *Habere licere*. This is also shown by the types of actions: because before delivery one sues for delivery, but after delivery one sues for double, which is not incurred when the thing is not delivered: as in D. 19.1, *L. 1*, in the beginning, unless it were considered as delivered: as in D. 21.2, *Si rem*, in the beginning.

The question is doubtful. For, having examined the cause of the words and the intent of the contracting parties, which is to be examined, as noted in D. 10.3, *L. 1*, § *Si venditione*, the first opinion seems truer. I, according to the subtlety of the law and the true opinion, hold this by that which is read and noted in D. 14.4, *Valerianus*, and D. 19.2, *Cum in plures*, § *1*, *Dicta*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if the testator ordered through his trustees or executors that something, even a pious work, be done when it shall seem good or please them or the majority of them, the said bishop may intervene in such execution after the lapse of a year if they do not carry it out within that year. And he holds that he may not, on account of the suspensive clause placed in the will.
body: The testator, by his will, disposed that a certain portion of the goods should go to the poor of Christ, adding these words: “In the aforementioned matters, however, he made G., M., and D. his fideicommissaries, each of them jointly and severally, with the power to substitute and convert [the bequests] into other causes, as it shall please all three or the majority.” And he added these words: “Yet the testator himself wishes that his said fideicommissaries may be bound, or ought to be, to carry out the execution of the said legacies within a certain time.” And he added that the execution should not devolve upon any other person by the passage of any time, but should remain solely with his said fideicommissaries. Now the question arises, without calling into doubt the substance of the bequest,

Whether, after one year, execution devolves to the said bishop. And it seems that it does, because the bishop’s execution is of public law, as in C. de episc. et cler. l. nulli. And therefore it cannot be derogated from by the testator: as in the Auth. cited there. To the contrary it seems, for this fideicommissum appears to have been deferred to the time of the death of the executors, unless during their lifetime they have otherwise chosen to declare it, as in ff. de leg. 3. l. fideic. §. sic fidei. For it matters greatly whether suspensive words are appended by the testator, and then the said bishop can do nothing to the contrary: because he ought not to exceed the limits of the mandate, nor can the said bishops rescind testaments: as in C. de testa. l. consulta diualia. Or the words are not suspensive of the legacy or disposition, but pure, or purified, and then, on account of the negligence of the executors, it devolves to the said bishop. The conclusion, therefore, is this: where there is no negligence, there is no devolution; and therefore, if the testator wishes the legacies to be performed then and when it pleases the executors, the said bishop cannot compel them to make the execution prematurely, because he cannot impose upon the testament, and he cannot anticipate a delay placed in the testament, as in ff. ad Trebell. l. sed si ante. The law, therefore, speaks of those things which pertain to the necessity of the executors, not of those by which the testament would be rescinded or changed into another form, because, as I said there, the times designated in the testament must be awaited. ff. de vsu. l. in fideicom. §. cum polidius. Or by which a greater obligation would be induced upon the persons of the heirs than the testator intended. arg. ff. de ver. ob. l. stip. illa. §. inter certam. and C. de fideic. l. post mortem. and ff. de leg. 2. l. vnum ex samilia. in princ. And thus I said in l. 1. ff. de leg. 2. in rep. and in my reading. This disposition, when the phrase “when he shall have wished” is appended to the burdened party or executor, or to both, extends until the day of his life: as in d. l. fideicommissa. §. sic fidei. And the bishop cannot compel or execute beforehand: because the form of the testament opposes it. argu. ff. man. l. si tibi mandauero, vt pro me. in prin. Otherwise, those suspensive words of time would accomplish nothing. This point: that the bishop does not intervene, as now, is not on account of the mere prohibition of the testator, but on account of the suspensive nature of his disposition. And by this, a response is given to c. haeredes. and to c. nos quidem. extra de testa. Thus a response is given to §. si quis autem non implens. in Auth. de hęre. et falc. and in Auth. de ecclesia. tit. §. si quis. Because there he did not wish to fulfill the testator’s vow, here he does, but at the proper time. And by this also, the constitution of the said bishop does not obstruct: because only the Pope can dispose, and not without cause against the will of the testator, as noted in c. quamquam. de vsur. lib. 6. Also, because the said constitution is made for the execution of the will, not for derogation, hence the benefit of delay is to be taken from no one, as in l. iustas. C. de iu. fis. lib. 10. Or changed into another form: because, as I said, the times designated in the testament must be awaited, as in ff. de fur. l. in fideic. §. cum pollidius. I say, therefore, that by appending a time to the legacy, namely by saying “when it pleases the executors,” that this “when” the said bishop cannot take from the hands of the executors for that reason, because beforehand they are not negligent. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a manifest usurer can bind himself by title and cause of a donation causa mortis; and take note that the contrary was held above in consilium 294.
1. What is included in an appeal from a testament.
2. Whether the disposition in the chapter *Quamquam* on usury, Book 6, is favorable or odious, and whether it applies to donations causa mortis.
body: The question is,

Whether a manifest usurer, without having provided security, can bind himself by title and cause of a donation causa mortis, or not: the text of the decree *Quamquam* on testaments speaks of cases in which the testator is in no way bound; but nothing is expressed there concerning donations causa mortis, if we take the term properly.

† This word, namely *testamentum*, signifies in the strict sense a universal disposition with the institution of an heir, as stated in the law *proxime*, D. de his, quae in testamento delegantur. If, however, it is taken in the broad sense, it signifies the final declaration of one’s mind, that is, also codicils made by an intestate, or a letter, or even something left without writing, as noted in D. de testamento, l. 1. Nevertheless, codicils made by an intestate are improperly called a testament, and therefore a direct action on the testament does not arise from them, but only a useful action: as noted in the said l. 1, in the final gloss. And this is not for any other reason than because it is used improperly. For according to its proper meaning, a direct action would be available, nor is there any law which states that there is a third mode. In the most improper sense, namely so as to include a stipulation causa mortis. Although the gloss holds this view in l. 1, C. de donationibus causa mortis, it holds otherwise, and more correctly, in l. *legatum est*, D. de legatis 2, and in l. *cum pater*, § *Meuvia*, and in l. *vt haeredibus*. Therefore, according to the proper meaning, and also according to the improper and broad meaning, a stipulation is not included under the name of testament; but we ought not to employ an abusive interpretation and the most improper one, especially when we are engaged in the correction of laws.

† It is certain. Note that the chapter *Quamquam* corrects both civil and canonical laws: for, according to the provision of the old law, one could make a will regarding one’s goods, saving the rights of one’s creditors, as in D. 34.5, *Eius qui in provincia*, in the beginning. But that decree *Quamquam* was issued in favor of souls; however, this favor is not without disapproval: for it ought to be lawful for everyone to make a will regarding their own goods, since this is permitted even to robbers, pirates, and public prostitutes, although their shameful profits are to be extorted from the heirs, as in D. 36.1, *Sed et qui magna*, and D. 49.14, *In heredem*. Nor do they accrue to the bishops, but to the fisc, as in D. 28.5, *Papinianus*, § *Meminisse*. Therefore, the canonical law remains due to the frequency of the crime of usury: for it is practiced more frequently because of the sweetness of usury, and because one sins with impunity, and charity grows cold. And unless a remedy were applied, infinite souls would be damned. It was specially established in the wills of usurers that, the caution being omitted, they should be invalid by the law itself; and it does not speak of contracts; therefore, it has no place in contracts, as in D. 50.17, *Verba gesserunt*. For no law provides that a manifest usurer cannot bind himself, both during life and after death, as in C. 4.7, l. 1, and C. 8.38, l. *Veteris*, and now in C. 8.50, l. *Ultima*.

But against this it is objected: for the law provides that the term "will" contains any last will. Also, the law provides that a donation *causa mortis* accedes to the last will, considering the effect, as in Inst. 2.7, § 1. For this is not a good argument, that where the correction of laws is concerned, an argument from analogy does not proceed, as noted in C. 1.3, *Quas aedes*. Moreover, these are not analogous cases: as noted in C. 6.24, l. *Semini*. Furthermore, just as we ought not to be more lenient than the law, so neither should we be more severe, as in D. 28.2, *Si servum*, § *Non dixit*, and C. 10.10, l. *Illam*. Moreover, it was easy for the legislator to declare that the same rule applied to donations *causa mortis*; for when the law intends this, it expresses it, as appears in C. 5.18, l. *Unica*, near the end. Moreover, no one would say in statutes that a statute stating that no one could make a will without the presence of relatives meant that one could not make a donation *causa mortis*; for why would they be called by different names if they did not differ? as in C. 6.23, l. *Si idem*. Since therefore the statute does not say this, neither should we say it: as in D. 28.1, l. 1, and D. 24.3, *Si vero*, § *De viro*. I therefore conclude that the disposition of the canon should not be extended to the disposition of laws in a case omitted by the canon.

It follows that we must say that the said stipulation *causa mortis* is valid; nor is it new that greater capacity is required in the act of making a will than in a donation *causa mortis*, and greater solemnity, as in D. 39.6, *Tam his*. Moreover, a donation *causa mortis* rests on the consent of two witnesses, yet the will of one. It is established that that which is confirmed by the consent of two is firmer, as in law, and noted in C. 8.50, l. 1. I know well that many laws could be alleged to the contrary, and one natural reason, lest fraud be committed against the caution, unless it be answered that it is not fraud to take a path conceded by law. That, however, is not doubtful, that a donation *causa mortis* accedes to an innominate contract, and repentance has place, and a condictio *ob causam* is given, as in D. 39.6, *Senatus*. Nor did the Cassians doubt, as in D. 34.5, *Non omnis*, and l. *Cum quis*, D. 13.3. And therefore it was rightly said that a donation *causa mortis* accedes more to a contract than to a last will, as in D. 23.3, l. 2, and D. 35.1, l. 2, and it is touched upon in C. 10.10, *Ex testamento*.

Concluding therefore from the above, I say that according to the proper, strict, or broad signification, the said chapter *Quamquam* does not speak of, or is understood to refer to, a stipulation *causa mortis*; nor did the lawgiver think more carefully of it, and if he did, it is not clear to us. Moreover, if there are laws that extend the name of "legacy" to a donation *causa mortis*, they do not signify identity, but an extensive interpretation, which I think has no place in the case of the said chapter. To this also I am moved to say by the authority of many moderns, who hold the same, and especially of the Illustrious College of Milan, which, as is reported to me, has advised this both previously and now, and many great wise men of that college advise thus, and therefore I do not deviate from them. And it is confirmed, for it would follow that a manifest usurer could not donate to his son in his power, since such a donation has the force of a legacy, unless the Gregorian caution is given: which I know no one has reported. Let this be added to the above, that public law, which consists in the making of a will, can more easily be denied on account of a delict than proper and private law, for the law denies you its aid, not yours, as noted in a similar case in C. 11.39, l. *Assiduis*. And we see that a deportee can contract, but not make a will, D. 35.1, *Si deportati servo*; the same I say of an excommunicated person, that he can, for he could not make a will according to Hostiensis; nevertheless, he could donate, and bind himself to a capable stipulator: for it is lawful for him to stipulate, as in § *Alteri*. And if anyone says the contrary, let him, if we are to believe him, allege a text or an ordinary gloss fortified by laws, although at first sight, because of the broad words of the gloss, chapter *Quamquam* is held and spoken of by Johannes Andreas and the Archdeacon; many have moved towards the contrary opinion. The law says that it is unjust that free men should not have free alienation of their things, D. 40.12, *Non usque adeo*.
