However, the opinion, to the ultimate confusion of manifest usurers, establishes that no one should interfere with their wills, so that their wills are void. But this opinion plants its feet firmly in wills; but they have successors intestate, and no law forbids them to contract, for not being able to bind themselves, both during life and after death, would not be so detestable to them as not being able to make a will. And let this be the conclusion, where the law plants its feet; nor is it our part to extend the law; there we must plant our feet, as noted in a similar case in D. 17.2, *Si non fuerit*, and it appears expressly in C. 10.10, l. *Ultima*, lib. 10, according to that of Horace: "There is a measure in things, there are certain limits, beyond which and short of which right cannot stand." As noted in Inst. 2.20, in the rubric. And by this response is given to D. 46.4, l. *Cum hi*, § *Idem erit*, for there it is mere favor, and therefore to be extended, as in D. 38.1, l. 1, § *Si vero*; nor does it matter that there prejudice to a third party is involved, here not, nor does conscience press: and because by this no one is enriched with another's injury, but we are only outside the penalty of that chapter.

But how will you answer D. 26.7, l. 1, § 1, with its gloss, which says that he who cannot make a will cannot donate *causa mortis*? I answer, that rule is true when no other disposition of law precedes, premising a donation *causa mortis*. But here a general disposition of laws precedes, which is not found corrected except in wills. Moreover, in permissive matter, to whom it is permitted to make a will, it is permitted to donate *causa mortis*, for it is a favor, as in D. 36.2, *Sed si mortis*. And to the above contribute two laws, which make an open difference between a donation *causa mortis* and a legacy. For in a donation *causa mortis*, fruits perceived during the donor's life come into it; otherwise in a legacy, as in D. 32.1, *Si mulier*, § *Sed si habenti*, joined with l. *Uxor patrui*, C. 6.24. Also, the law expressly says that by deportation the last will is interrupted, but a donation *causa mortis* is confirmed, as in D. 24.1, *Sed et si mors*, which makes much for the decision of our question. And it makes that which is noted in D. 35.1, l. *Talis scriptura*, in the last gloss.

For now it remains to answer, although touched upon above. For it is certain that that which is prohibited by one way should not be permitted by another, lest the law be circumvented, and the disposition of the law be rendered derisive. But if a donation *causa mortis* were permitted, then that chapter *Quamquam* would not be worth a fly, for usurers would provide for themselves, that is, by the way of a donation *causa mortis*. But I answer, three things are to be considered here. First, that which is greatest, namely, the institution of an heir; as to this, that decretal cannot be circumvented, for in a donation *causa mortis* no one is instituted heir. It fails in the case of a soldier, as in C. 8.50, l. *Licet*. Secondly, it can be considered as to codicils made to a will, and the same applies, as in l. *Proxima*; for a donation *causa mortis* is not properly made to a will, nor to intestacy, nor does it require the acceptance of the inheritance to be confirmed, but the donee has someone against whom to sue on the stipulation or pact, like other creditors, as I said in D. 35.1, l. 2. Thirdly, we can consider codicils made intestate; for if a usurer could provide for himself by another way than by the Gregorian caution, it does not seem a great inconvenience. For what if he wished to donate to the poor or pious places, towards whom and which he cannot make a codicil, and therefore does not wish to give caution, lest he be excommunicated while alive? Is this great injustice? Certainly this is unjust by natural or divine dictate. Also, this is another way, but it is not similar, nor equal, therefore not prohibited. It makes that which is noted by Dy. in D. 35.1, l. *Servum filii*, § *Qui chirographum*.

From the first therefore to the last, concluding, always saving the determination of the Holy Mother Church, I conclude that a donation *causa mortis* is not condemned, but possible; and given the possible, that which is given is possible in quality. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if a debtor who promised to pay at the place of the contract and wherever he might be found is summoned in another place than that of the contract because he was found there, the prescription is said to be interrupted by this summons.
body: It is proposed that about four or eight years ago, a certain A. of San Nazario lent to a certain B. of San Nazario 120 florins, which he promised to pay at the place of the contract and wherever he might be found. Since the latter was by chance found in Pavia after about twenty-five years, he was summoned at the creditor’s request and placed under a ban; however, this does not appear except from the report of the messenger, who says that he summoned him on the aforementioned occasion, and he does not declare otherwise, nor does any commission appear. It is true that the statute of Pavia provides that the report of the messenger shall be believed.

† Now it is asked whether the prescription has been interrupted. It is said that this person was a stranger to Pavia, and thus could not be summoned, as stated in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Haeres absens*, because one who is about to depart immediately is not considered to have come, as stated in the Digest, *De publicanis*, law *Caesar*. Furthermore, it is not apparent that there was a commission from the judge, as stated in the Code, *De exhibendis reis*, law *Neminem*. Moreover, the words of the messenger are vague and uncertain, and thus do not carry credibility, as stated in the Digest, *De iure fisci*, law *Ita fidei*.

On the contrary, it appears that the said prescription has been interrupted. This is proven as follows: the forum is competent, and the summons was issued; therefore, the prescription is interrupted, as stated in the Code, *De praescriptione triginta annorum*, law *Sicut* and law *Cum notissimi*.

The first point is proven by the law *Contraxisse* in the Digest, *De actionibus et obligationibus*. It is no objection that he is a stranger, for the rule that a stranger cannot be sued unless he has promised to pay there, as noted in the aforementioned law *Haeres absens*, is true only in that specific context.

Secondly, that he was summoned is proven by the report of the messenger, combined with the statute of the commune of Pavia, which provides that the report of the messenger shall be believed. It is no objection to say that this person is not from Pavia, because we are here in an ordinary judicial proceeding, and thus the law of the judicial forum is considered, not the law of the forum where the contract was celebrated, as stated in law 1 of the Code, *De emancipatis liberis*, and as noted in the law *Cunctos populos*.

Furthermore, it is no objection that it does not appear that he was summoned lawfully, for it is presumed in favor of the official that he performed his act lawfully, since the mandate is apparent, as stated in the Digest, *De evictionibus*, law *Herennius*, section 1.

Moreover, it is no objection that the summons is general and vague, for speciality is not required in a summons for the purpose of interrupting prescription. For the one who summons is considered to have asserted all his rights in the summons; by "the one who summons," I mean the one who causes the summons to be issued, as stated in the Code, *De annali exceptione*, law *Si ex multis*, and as noted in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Si quis intentione ambigua*.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal may refuse his portion of his paternal fief to another of his co-brothers, or agnate, or may not donate it to them without the consent of the lord. And whether. 3.
2. Whether a donation made by a vassal in the manner described above requires insinuation.
3. A donation by a prince does not require insinuation.
4. A notary, as soon as he is created, may draw up instruments.
5. Whether a division prejudices the fief with regard to the donated things.
6. What is required by a subscription of a very long time.
body: Textus I de alienatione feudi paterni. Itaque dicit.

† The alienation of a paternal fief is not valid even with the lord’s consent, unless the agnates consent. And afterwards he adds, and although the alienation of a benefice is prohibited among agnates, nevertheless if it is paternal, it is permitted. Hence it is expressly stated there that a brother may donate his share to his cognate brothers even without the lord’s consent, just as he may renounce his share of the fief into the hands of his agnates, as in c. unicus, De eo qui fecit finem agnato de feudo paterno. And the reason for the concession among agnates is that that which is preserved in the body or line of the agnates does not appear to be alienated, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntas, and l. 1, C. de imponenda lucra, descriptio, lib. 10. It should be noted, however, that the text states that the said donation is valid as a renunciation. For by renunciation the person renouncing is released. For he who does not wish to have his share makes himself alien to the fief. And that which, by renouncing, he has relinquished pertains by a certain hereditary right to those to whom he has relinquished it, and not to the lord. And I hold this as firm, that the donation was valid as a renunciation. And this concludes the first point.

† Now it remains to be seen whether the said donation requires insinuation, being above the lawful sum. And it is certain that a donation by princes does not require insinuation, because it has the force of law, as C. de don. inter virum, et vx. l. penu. On this ground, Master Bartolus of Sasso Ferrato advised that a certain donation of a castle, which one Prince of the Ursini had made to another prince, his consort, did not require insinuation, because where there is a prince, insinuation is not required, as C. de testamentis. l. omnium. And since insinuation is an act of voluntary jurisdiction, the same person may both make the donation and insinuate it before himself, as ff. de adop. l. si consul. and l. an apud. ff. de manumis. vindicta. But I do not know whether those about whom the question is asked can be called princes. And I believe they cannot; nevertheless, in a fief, this donation seems valid: because it is not properly a donation, but a renunciation, as the text says. Just as having a thing as abandoned does not require insinuation, so neither does the renunciation of a benefice. Moreover, this is rather a matter of the nature of a fief than a contract of donation. And that which proceeds from the nature of a fief does not require insinuation; otherwise it would follow that a vassal could not renounce even in the hands of his lord unless insinuation had intervened, which I think would be ridiculous, as in c. 1. de vassallo, qui contra constitutionem Lotharii. Moreover, it would follow that if a vassal consents that the lord make investiture to one to whom the fief does not pass by succession, such investiture would not hold without insinuation, which is false: because in the usages of fiefs you will never find mention made of insinuation, as in c. 1. §. Praeterea. quibus modis feudum amittitur. But of his own property, a vassal cannot make a donation without insinuation, unless up to five hundred gold coins, as C. de donat. l. sancimus. and l. si quis argentum. From these things follows immediately the solution of the third principal question,

† namely, that the said donor could not sell to another, nor pledge as security, that which he could not subsequently donate to another from his fiefs, because it did not belong to the agnates; as stated in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Lex vectigali*; and in the Code, *De donationibus ante nuptias*, law *Si ante*; and law *De rebus*. And it must be known that, by reserving to himself the usufruct, he is deemed to have transferred possession; as stated in the Code, *De donationibus*, law *Quisquis*. However, non-feudal property, insofar as it exceeds the legitimate portion, he could rightly sell and encumber, because, since alienation was not permitted by law, it had not been alienated and remained in the donor’s assets; as stated in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Et quae nondum*, section *Quod dicitur*.

† On another point, it must be said that as soon as a notary is appointed, he may draw up any instruments, and thus the first instrument is as valid as the thousandth: as in D. de officio praetoris, l. Barbarius Philippus.

† On another point, namely whether the division prejudices the fief with regard to the donated properties, it is answered that it does not, because it is presumed that the division was made due to an error of law, as stated in l. si filia, in the beginning, ff. de familia erciscunda; and in C. de collationibus, l. qui soror; and as noted in ff. de verbis obligatis, l. qui Romae, § duo fratres; and in ff. de pactis, l. tres fratres.

† On another point, whether long silence is prejudicial to him, it must be said that it is not, because in matters in which there was error, the brothers do not have the title required for prescription of ten or twenty years: as in C. de praescrip. longi temp. l. si; and C. de praescrip. 30 ann. l. si quis emptionis; and ff. de usucap. l. cum solus; and l. Celsus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the synodal constitution, which provides that executors of wills for pious causes must, within a year computed from the testator’s death, fully carry out the testator’s will without any further admonition; otherwise, they shall be deprived of the office of execution. And the said Bishop, etc. What if the testator, having instituted the poor as beneficiaries, commanded the executors to carry out the execution as and when it seemed good to them, and that the said discretion should not devolve upon any other person by the lapse of time? Whether, by the lapse of a year, the executors are deprived of their office, and whether the testator may grant his executors the power to commute the legacy made by him for pious causes, as they see fit. And number 4.
2. What this word, “as” (prout), signifies.
3. What these words, “when it is convenient for you, etc.,” placed in the testator’s disposition regarding execution, signify.
4. A disposition made with captatory intent is not valid for pious causes, and what is meant by a captatory disposition.
5. Whether a testator may extend the time for execution granted by law or by synodal constitution.
body: Constitution

† The Patriarchal, or synodal, decree which states that it is understood to have been transferred to the diocesan level, both according to the form of law and according to the synodal constitutions of the Lord Patriarch, is sufficiently consonant with the common law, and adds something even beyond it. We establish that executors of wills for pious causes must, within one year computed from the death of the testator, fully fulfill the will and execution of the testator without any further admonition; otherwise, they shall be deprived of the office of execution. Nevertheless, I base my argument on the aforementioned constitution, because it is equitable and reasonable, as stated in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. nulli; and Extra de testaments, c. nos quidem; and D. eo, l. si haeredes; and what is noted in Auth. de haereditatibus et fideicommissis, §. si quis autem non implens; and in Auth. de ecclesiis, tit. l. si quis.

However, the words of the said constitution must be considered, for the constitution states that one is bound to execute fully, within one year from the day of the testator’s death and without further admonition, the will and disposition of the testator, namely the disposition of that will. Therefore, the disposition of the testator must necessarily precede. Regarding the will of the testator, one must consider not only what the testator disposes to be done, but also when, because the time is the extreme point from which the year of the constitution begins. For the year of the constitution does not begin before the time fixed by the testator for the performance of the legacy, because neither can nor should execution take place, since the executor must observe the form of the mandate, as in D. de mandato, l. si mandauero tibi, ut pro me in diem fideiubeas, in principio; and D. de legatis 2, l. si ita sit, §. sub conditione; as in D. de usufructu, l. in fideicommissi, §. cum Pollidius. And this applies when a certain day is appointed for execution, and even more so if the day is conditional, as in D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. sed si ante, and l. sed si alia, §. finis. And this applies when the time is precisely determined. In these terms, our question does not arise.

But for the clarity of what is to be said, it must be premised: what if the time is not fixed, but left to discretion? For example, if the testator says, “I command my heir to build a hospital for my soul, as and when he sees fit,” or “that for my soul he endow so many girls, when he sees fit,” does the common law or the bishop’s constitution apply, requiring that he declare his will within one year? It seems that it does, as in l. finis, §. 1, C. communia de legatis. On the contrary, it seems that these words are extensive to the time of the death of the person burdened: because the law states that this legacy, when he wishes, has a duration as long as the person from whom the fideicommissum is left lives; but if he dies before giving it, his heir performs it, as in D. de legatis 3, l. fideicommissa, §. hoc autem legatum. But there the word “voluerit” (wishes) was added. It would be otherwise if he had said “cum arbitratus fuerit” (when he shall have decided). For then it does not have a duration, except as it ought to seem to a good man, as in D. de fideicommissis libertatibus, l. Thais ancilla, §. sorore; and in l. 1, D. de legatis 2.

Solution: One must refer to the words of the testament, for that must be done which the testator willed and placed in necessity. But if he placed something not in necessity, but so that the heir should perform it when he preferred to perform it,

† or as he shall prefer, because this word, "as," properly signifies time and quality, as in C. de eden. l. edita actio. Then the testator's will must be observed, and the reason is that the testator so willed, as in C. de necessariis servis. l. cum quidam. in fi. and ff. de ver. sig. l. nepos proculo. ver. Nam qui ambigue loquitur. and C. de fideicom. l. voluntas. For once the testament is confirmed by death, no one can add to or change it, says the law: as it is written, so let the law be, as in ff. de ver. sig. l. verbis. For the will of a sane person ought to be regarded as legitimate law, as in ff. de leg. 2. l. codicillis. §. ult. Nor ought the heir to be compelled to pay legacies or fideicommissa before the time, because the testator, who appointed a time, is deemed to have tacitly forbidden payment before that time, arg. ff. de leg. 2. l. statuliberum. §. Stichum. and ff. de verb. oblig. l. stipulatio ista. §. inter certam. and ff. de verb. signific. l. cedere diem. Because, these things being premised, in our question it must be considered whether a time was appointed to the bequest. Or whether the bequest has vested, and the day has arrived, so that the time was appointed only to the execution. And it seems that the time was appointed only to the execution, that is, to the office thereof. For a testament has several parts; it has indeed the institution of the poor for a fourth part, and it is of the nature of an institution that it does not admit of a day or condition, as in ff. de her. inst. l. hereditas ex die. Therefore, the institution of the poor is pure and present, and the right is acquired for the poor immediately upon the testator's death. For just as a legacy is acquired, so too is the inheritance, in favor of the poor. For in this case, the inheritance is said to be subject to the deduction of debts, and thus they hope for benefit, not detriment: hence the same reason applies as in legacies, as in C. de sac. san. eccl. l. ut inter divinum. Behold, therefore, that we have a pure institution, but the designation of the poor, which is mere execution, is that which is committed to the executors to fulfill according to their conscience within the term of a year, as in d. l. nulli. There are therefore two precepts of the testament, because the clauses are separated, as in ff. de condi. et demon. l. haec scriptura. ff. de leg. 1. l. quidam testamento. C. quando dies leg. cedat. l. ex his verbis. Moreover, either the testator disposes of the power of the executors, or of his own goods. In the first case, the disposition of the law ought to be observed rather than the will of the testator, as in the gloss licet posita super d. l. nulli. In the second case, the will of the testator must be observed, because he can impose upon his things whatever law he wishes until death, as in C. de sac. san. eccl. l. 1. And that which he disposes concerning the prince or God, he may alter, revoke, or commute, or suspend to a day or condition, whether in the same will or in another, and whether in the same clause of the testament or in another, as in ff. de alimentis leg. l. 3. §. conditio. ff. de condi. et demon. l. quibus diebus. §. quidam titio. and not ff. de act. et ob. l. obligationum fere. §. conditio. In the solution of the contrary from the said §. quidam. in the gloss ord. That God or the prince do not differ from others in this matter is proved, as in C. de testamentis. l. omnium. ver. nec sane. and C. qui testamenta facere possunt. l. si quis Imperatorem. It must therefore be seen whether the testator limited his disposition as to the office of the executors only, or as to the words which are directed to the poor themselves. For words which are directed to the mere executor regard the office, but words which are directed to the burdened party regard the bequest. Let us therefore weigh the words of the testament, and omitting the legacies, because the legatees have been satisfied, I come to the institution of the heirs. The words of the testament say that in the fourth part he instituted the poor of Christ to be maintained by his other heirs. Note this, and if the testator had not proceeded further, there would be no doubt that if they were not elected within a year from the testator's death, computed from the fictitious notification of the constitution, the bishop would have the right to this fourth part for distribution, on account of the devotion of the coheirs, and the force and authority of the law or constitution, as in l. 1. in fi. ff. de pen. leg. But the testator proceeded further, and ordered his mind to be such, namely, because he said, wishing also that his said fideicommissaries, in whom he fully confides, should distribute and dispense the parts of the inheritance hereinafter described, according as it shall seem best to them, and as it shall please them. And make a point here. And thus far the same, which I said. What if there were no further words? We would be in the case of the constitution of the year, and the mandate transferred to the executor. For this speech refers to the quality of the poor, not to the time, thus far, as in ff. loc. l. si in lege. ver. ideoque arbitrium. But it must be seen what follows, because the sentence is imperfect unless the whole law is considered, as in ff. de leg. l. in civile. and the following declare the preceding, as in ff. de leg. 1. l. si servus plurium. §. fi. and ff. de test. l. heredes palam. §. sed si notam. for neighboring parts of the writing declare each other, as in C. de inst. et subst. l. si testamento. and extra de app. c. 2. requiris. Therefore, the following word in the said testament is "for their benefit," and on this I insist greatly.

† Because these words, "when it shall be convenient for you," are interpreted as meaning "when difficulties and impediments have ceased," as in D. de verborum significatione, l. Nepos Proculo; and D. de fideicommissis liberis, l. Thais ancilla, § 1; and especially considering the affection for the daughter, whom the testator does not wish to force into a hasty sale of the property, as in D. de negotiorum gestione, l. Divortio; and l. 1, C. de praediis curialium, lib. 10.

But that which is more to be weighed in the said testament is that which follows. He adds the power and authority to convert the said legacies into another pious cause, as he shall prefer to convert them at his will, and likewise the said parts of the inheritance, etc. And it is doubted here whether this power can be given to executors. For Jacobus Butrigarius says that it cannot. C. de testamento militis, l. captatorias.

† because he says that a captatory disposition is not valid for pious causes. But Bartolus says the contrary by c. Cum tibi, Extra, De testibus. Moreover, since this can be done with knowledge of the cause, as in ff. De usu et legato, l. Legatum civitati, therefore much more strongly the testator can dispose of these things, and it is not called a captatory disposition, with due respect to the Butrican, because that disposition is not called captatory which cannot fail in its substance, as in l. Utrum, § 1, ff. De rebus dubiis. But this disposition cannot fail in its substance, because, with alteration or commutation ceasing, it remains in its being, namely, in the institution of the poor themselves. However, such alteration should be made from similar to similar, or to better things, because the words of the testament should be commuted for the better, as it would seem more expedient to be done for the soul of the testator; because the confidence which the testator had tends more to burden than to relieve the heirs, as in ff. De legatis 3, l. Unum ex familia, § Imperator Marcus. And if you make a point here, all these do not pass within the year; afterwards they pass to the Bishop with a certain quality of power to alter, with another not being able to alter, unless the Pope alone, as in c. Quia contingit, De relictis donationibus, in the Clementines. But what is it? Other words follow, which are decisive of the question, namely, "willing, however, the testator himself that his fideicommissaries be bound, or ought, within some time, to commit the said legacies to execution, and not to distribute and dispense the said underwritten parts of the inheritance, as above." But what is this particle? It does not dispose except of compulsion, and granted that they could not be compelled, it does not follow, therefore, that the Bishop cannot execute. For it is certain that if they do not accept the office, they could not be compelled, as noted in l. 1, ff. De legatis 2. And yet the Bishop succeeds in the execution to those who repudiate, just as the legitimate tutor succeeds to the excluded testamentary tutor, and if there were not more words, the execution would pertain to the Bishop. But other words follow, both declaratory and dispositive, namely these: "And he ordered that the execution of the said legacies, or the dispensation of the said inheritance, not devolve to any other person by the course of any time, but remain entirely in his said commissioners, or fideicommissaries, as above." Hence arises the question,

Whether a testator may dispense beyond the course of a year, and extend this time for executors. And it seems that he may not, for two reasons: first, because the year is within the power of the law, and not of the testator, as stated in the aforementioned authority *Licet*. Second, because where the poor are instituted directly, the nominator of the poor is not an executor, but rather a certain declarer. For the poor, once declared, take possession by themselves, because this is the nature of an heir, that he takes directly, not through an intermediary person, as in D. 28, 5, *Sed si conditione*, § *Si*.

On the contrary, it seems that he may, because he who can grant an office can also extend it, as in D. 3, 1, *Vel in perpetuum ita repetere*. For example, if an executor were dismissed by the lapse of the first year, I would reinstate the same executor in the second year, and so individually for each year, as in D. 7, 1, *Sicut in annos*. Just as if the testator said, "I wish that their office lasts for ten years." For no law prohibits this; therefore, it is permitted, as in C. 1, 3, 1. The authority *Licet* does not obstruct this, which is true in that the testator cannot prohibit that an account be rendered to the Bishop. But it does not say that the testator cannot appoint to the execution of the will, as he pleases, the Bishop. And to this effect, D. 19, 2, *Si in lege*, at the end of the beginning.

Moreover, as I said, this is more a certain declaration of persons than an execution, in which case Bartolus says that delay can be purged up to the litis contestatio. And this unless the power of choosing whenever they wish has been granted; and then they can nominate and choose until death, according to Cynus, as I refer in my lecture there. And it is proven by D. 28, 5, *Unum ex familia*, in the beginning; and C. 5, 17, *Foeminae*, § *Si*.

Furthermore, it seems absurd that if the testator has more confidence in the executors than in the diocesan bishop, which often happens in fact, though not among good and grave bishops, that the testator cannot find for himself an appropriate provision. Moreover, could the testator not say thus: "I choose such an executor, and if he does not choose within a year, I substitute such another, and if such another does not choose, I substitute another?" I do not believe anyone would doubt that the testator could order this, as in D. 35, 2, *Ut heredibus*. Just as therefore he can substitute John for Peter, and Peter for Martin, and so for each individual, so he can substitute the same person for himself on account of a change, because it is not the same office, but a new one, and divided in time from the first, as in D. 35, 1, *Pater Severinam*, § *Conditione*; and D. 35, 2, *Si*, § *Si*; D. 36, 1.

From which it appears that, since the common law and the constitution of the Bishop dictate that the will of the testator is to be observed, that Bishops should dismiss testamentary executors. But that they can assist them, lest they abuse the office, in which the testator placed fuller confidence, and they are bound to render an account every year; because they themselves cannot embezzle the goods of the poor. X. 3, 27, *Qui Christi pecunias*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What is included under the term "children" and what under the term "offspring."
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that the term “son” sometimes includes only a son of the first degree; because sons and daughters properly are those who exist first in the order of those born from someone. Hence, my son properly is he who was born from me and my wife, as in D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. Filium. But a grandson changes the name with respect to another, because he is properly called a grandson, as in D. de lib. et posthum., l. Gallus, in principio. And therefore the law says that there is a great difference whether the name “son” is expressed, or the name “children”; because by the name of children all descendants are included, as in D. de excus. tutor., l. 2, § Haec autem. And from this it could be inferred that when the name “son” is used in a privilege, such a privilege is personal and is not to be extended to other children, as in the legal rule Privilegium personale, and D. de iure immunitatis, l. 1, § Personis. For this purpose, so that it may pass to all, it must be granted generally, as in l. Immunitates generaliter, eodem titulo. Elsewhere it is also provided that a disposition concerning a son is not extended beyond to other degrees, as in l. Legi, and noted in Auth. de restitutione fideicommissi, § Manifestum. Likewise, if a father instituted sons or disinherited them, grandsons are not comprehended, as in D. de inoff. testam., l. Posthumorum. It supports this: Inst. qui de tutela possunt, § Si.

On the contrary, it seems: because by the term “sons” we understand all children, as in D. de verb. sign., l. Filii appellatione, and D. de verb. sign., l. Liberi, § Sed et Papinianus, and § Praeterea. For this should be so from natural affection, as the text says there. The common usage of speech also supports this, because commonly people understand by the name of sons all their descendants; because this name, “son,” is a denominative name, not a proper one, because all are sons by derivation of blood. And this appears in the usages of fiefs, because although the text says that by the name of heir a son is included, yet elsewhere it says that this name “son” includes all children in infinitum. And this is the true nature of this vocabulary in favors and benefits, as in col. 10, de feud. alien., § Et si clientulus fecit, and in c. 1, § Hoc autem, qui feudum dare possunt, eadem columna. Likewise, divine scripture says that all Hebrews are sons of Abraham, and thus we have divine scripture as a witness. Likewise, this is not an extension, but a certain broad mode of signifying. Therefore, that a grandson is not included, it seems to be said, is a matter of strict law; hence an extension of words is not to be made, D. de verb. oblig., l. Quicquid.

It also seems to be equated to a pact not to sue. For I make a pact that I will not sue you or your son; the pact is made with you two, excepted from others, D. de pactis, l. Avus, and l. Idem in duobus, § Personale, and l. Qui in futurum, § Ex altera. Likewise, this seems to be granted for two ages, namely, of the father and the son, not in perpetuity, that is, as long as they live, it seems to be granted, arg. D. de pactis, l. Episcopus, l. Si. Likewise, a signification taken from someone, that is, from a son, should not comprehend the entire progeny, but then only comprehends when it is taken from the whole, D. de pign. act., l. Si necessarias, § Si avus; D. de leg. praet., l. 1, § Et generale, verborum significatio continetur. As in D. de verb. sign., l. Si proprie.

Because briefly, all the laws that are alleged for or against, both the aforementioned and those similar to them, do not sufficiently serve our purpose; because we are not here in a privilege or concession, but in a reservation of liberty; because the words say so: “let him remain free.” For these words, uttered enunciatively by way of cause, at least prove and create an exception, as in D. de rei vend., l. Emptor, § Ancilla. But it is certain that one transmits his liberty to all posterity; hence, whoever frees a father frees all who will proceed from him in whatever degree; because the liberty of parents descends to posterity. For when the lord Francis and his sons remained emancipated from the republic and sui iuris, it necessarily follows that those born afterwards from them partake of the benefits of their progenitors in whatever degree; just as if I emancipate a son, a grandson conceived from him after his emancipation is not bound by the ties of my paternal power, as in Inst. de patria potestate, § 1.

Therefore, the words which say that the said lord Francis and his children, etc., do not make a personal arbitration, but designate with whom the arbitration is made, as in D. de pactis, l. Iure gentium, § Pactorum, and D. de probat., l. Si pactum. And this clearly appears, because the said great noble lord Francis was lord of the city, and by the nature of lordship and preeminence he was free, and to reserve liberty for someone is not a privilege; and therefore the laws that are alleged concerning privileges to the contrary do not touch the point, nor do the laws that restrict the interpretation of “son”; because here, by the nature of liberty reserved, not as newly given, an extension is made to all children of whatever degree. Moreover, the cause of this reservation is real, perpetual, and transmissible; hence, even if it were said to be a concession, it would nevertheless be in rem with respect to the entire lineage of children. Likewise, benefits which fathers have acquired by their good conduct are transmissible, as in l. 3, D. de interdict. et relegat. Likewise, this general interpretation accords with many laws, and therefore is not to be restricted by consideration of the outstanding merits, which were worthy of this reward and a greater one, as in D. de donat., l. Si pater. And because in doubt both blood and the reasoning of the grant make the favor even broader, as in D. de lib. leg., l. Aurelius, § Titius testamento. Likewise, this is a benign interpretation; hence, concluding from the first to the last, all posterity enjoy the said liberty, existing in whatever degree, and also future ones, because all seem to be one body, as in C. de impub. et aliis substit., l. Si, and l. Cum scimus, C. de agr. et cens. lib. 10. And all arguments made to the contrary speak of the strictest and most rigorous interpretation, not of a benign interpretation. Likewise, they speak when it is a matter of a new status or benefit being sought, not when it is a matter of preserving what has been acquired, and especially in favor of liberty. Arg. D. quarum rerum actio non datur, l. 1, § Honorandae. The aforementioned difference between acquiring anew and preserving is proved by an argument from similarity. D. de procurat., l. Procuratorem non semper; D. de peculio, l. Peculium, l. 1, Si aere alieno; D. de aqua quot. et aest., l. 1, § Permittitur; and C. de acqui. poss., l. Si.

I, Baldus. To the same effect in the declaration of nobilities passing to descendants. Part of a certain privilege of Charles IV tending to the above. Charles IV, by the favoring clemency of God, Roman Emperor, always Augustus, and King of Bohemia. The other part of the said bull of the holy city of Rome, in whose circumference are these legible letters with a Cross placed before: “Rome, head of the world, guides the reins of the round orb.” And above the said city are these legible letters: “Golden Rome.” By me, Nicholas of Bellignano, notary and chancellor of the commune of Genoa, the undersigned, having seen and read it, not abolished, not canceled, not erased, not vitiated, nor suspect in any part of it, but entirely free from every defect and suspicion. The tenor of which privilege is as follows: In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, happily, amen. Charles IV, by the favoring clemency of God, Roman Emperor, always Augustus, and King of Bohemia, for perpetual memory, to the noble Andrea and Antonius de Fisco, brothers, sons of the late Benedict, sons of the late Elianus, brother of the said Andrea and Antonius, Luchus and Vincentius de Fisco, brothers, sons of the late Albertus, Bartholomew and Nicolaus de Casanova, brothers, sons of the late Ugolinus, Branchaleonus, brothers of Branchaleonus of Louvain, as well as counts of the sacred Lateran palace, our faithful of the Holy Empire, dearly beloved, our grace and every good. The scepter-bearing sublimity of Caesar’s dignity, just as it is preferred by the election of office and dignity to inferior powers, so that it may govern the faithful committed to it with the support of desired consolation, that the throne of the emperor may be strengthened more fruitfully and advance with more abundant prosperity, inasmuch as it has poured the gifts of its indefatigable virtue upon its subjects with a more generous gift of benignity; thus, from the flashing splendor of the imperial throne, other nobilities, as if rays proceeding from the sun, so illuminate the standing and conditions of the faithful, that the integrity of the primal light suffers no detriment of diminished luminosity. In the month of January, on the first day.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who is of unsound mind may make a donation, and who must prove the alienation of the mind.
2. Whether the lord of the territory from which the offender originates, or the lord of the territory where the offense was committed, shall punish the offender.
3. Whether in the succession to a fief, one related on both sides is preferred to one related only on the male side.
body: The donation which Antonius made of a part of his fief to his brother Godofredus, although it was made without the consent of their co-heir Georgius, and although the fief was ancient and paternal, was valid and remains valid in law; because this is permitted by the custom of fiefs, as in c. 1, de alienatione feudorum, paragraph, column 10. And this is true, unless the said Antonius was of unsound mind; because one who is of unsound mind, or insane, cannot make a donation, nor any contract, nor even a last will, as in ff. de regulis iuris, l. in negotiis. It is necessary, however, that the said Georgius, who alleges that the said Antonius was then of unsound mind, prove this; for everyone is presumed to be of sound mind until the contrary is proved, as in C. de codicillis, l. nec codicillos; extra de successionibus ab intestato, c. cum dilectus.

† On another point, namely whether the ban and the condemnation of Martin, who is a subject of the said Godfrey, ought to pertain to Godfrey alone, considering that the said delinquent is his man only; or whether it ought to be common to the said three brothers, because the offense was committed in the castle of Osegna or its territory, which is held in common by the said three brothers as undivided: it must be said that the place from which the delinquent comes is not considered, but rather the place where the offense was consummated; because by reason of the offense he becomes a subject of that place, and there he ought to be punished, as in C. *Ubi de crimine agi oporteat*, aut. *Qua in provincia*. This is the truth. Now follows the third point, which asks that, since there were four brothers, two from the first marriage and two from the second, and after the father died, when one of the said brothers subsequently died, they divided the inheritance into thirds.

† Now it is asked, what would be the law if one of the aforementioned three were to die: for example, Antonius. Whether George and Godfrey would succeed him intestate in Antonius’s share in equal portions, or not. It must be said that although they made of the said division what pleased them, this does not prevent the following: if the aforementioned Antonius were to die, either we are speaking of feudal goods, and both would succeed pro virili; or of allodial goods, and only Godfrey would succeed: because he is related through both the paternal and maternal lines, whereas George is related only through the paternal line. And double relationship is stronger, as in the Authentica Defuncto, Codex, Ad senatusconsultum Tertullianum, and in the Corpus, from which the following Authenticae are taken. But why is it so varied, such that what applies to allodial goods does not apply to fiefs? I answer: because in fiefs the maternal line is not considered, but only blood. And this is due to the nature of fiefs, and thus is the common opinion and the truth of the great doctors. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute that the village is bound to make restitution for the robbery, but if within 30 days it presents the malefactor or malefactors, it is not bound, provided that there were four malefactors, and the village presents one, whether it is bound, and in what manner.
body: Statute

† It is provided that if any robbery has been committed in the County of Milan, those dwelling nearby are held liable for the restitution of the stolen goods; but if they have surrendered the malefactor, or malefactors, within thirty days after the robbery was committed, the village is not held liable for the aforementioned restitution. It happened that there were four robbers, and one of them was surrendered. The question is asked: what is the law? And it appears that the village is in no way released, as in the Digest, *De his qui deiecerunt vel effuderunt*, l. 1, § *si plures*. To the contrary, it seems, for when one pays, the others are released, since it is a mere action for the recovery of property, as in l. 1, Cod., *De conditione furtiva*. It would seem to be said that the assets of the one who is in prison should be examined, and if he were to pay, or if his assets were sufficient to pay, the village should not be pursued; because the one who suffered the damage has been sufficiently compensated. But to the extent that he is not able to pay, to that extent the village is held liable. Equity supports this: because the fiscus in a manner bears upon the pledge. Also, for this reason, the law *Moschis*, Digest, *De iure fisci*. Also, the intent of the statute sufficiently dictates this through the alternative liability of the village, or as expressed in the words of the statute; for that it is not sufficient to have presented one for all, is sufficiently proven by l. *Necessarias*, § *Si annuatim*, Digest, *De pigneraticia actione*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an emperor, or one having from him the power of legitimation, can legitimize a child born of a nun and a man having a lawful wife, from whom he had before the legitimation legitimate and natural children, and afterwards also had.
2. Whether children born afterwards rescind such legitimation, or at least whether it is not considered to be to their prejudice.
3. Whether at the time of such legitimation the legitimate [children] are to be cited. And no. 4.
4. Whether legitimation extends to property existing outside the lands of the empire.
body: The case in question is as follows. A married man, lawfully wedded, begot a certain son named B. by a certain professed nun. Seeing that he was honest and discreet, he had him legitimated by someone having power over such matters from the Roman Prince, and subsequently obtained a caution from the Roman Pontiff. Upon the death of the father, a dispute arose concerning the paternal inheritance between the said B. and the legitimate and natural brothers born and procreated by the said A. and the wife whom he had at the time when he begot the said B. For the said B. wishes to succeed to his father equally with the said legitimate and natural brothers, without distinction as to whether they were born before or after him, nor as to whether they were born before or after the said legitimations. And this he claims by virtue of the said legitimations, by which he says he was restored to his birthrights and placed in the status, rank, and right in which he would have been if he had been born legitimate. The said brothers, however, contradicting and totally opposing him, deny that the said legitimations could have been made to their prejudice, and consequently strive to totally exclude the said B. from the paternal succession.

† Now it is asked, what is the law regarding the knots and points that can be drawn from the aforementioned case, keeping God and justice in view, so that the one who has to judge does not have to give an account to God or the world. The words of the Commentary on C. de incest. nup. Aut. ex complexu are these: It is asked whether the Emperor can legitimize a spurious child. The glossa says yes. Some understand this as far as temporal matters are concerned, not as far as spiritual matters. But in the person it is the opposite, so that as far as spiritual matters are concerned he can, not temporal matters, except in lands subject to him temporally. Commentary. Also, the words of ff. de ritu nup. l. qui in provincia are these, and note that the benefit of the prince legitimizes incestuous children, and thus there is no question whether the Emperor can legitimize spurious children. Commentary. The words of the glossa in Authen. quibus modis na. effici. sui. §. si. col. 8 are these: I ask, however, whether the prince can make them legitimate if he says notwithstanding such a law. I think yes. Accursus says the same in 10. col. si de feudis fuerit controversia. c. naturales. The form of the privilege must be sufficient and encompassing the case about which it is asked. For this case of ours is one of the rare occurrences. Also, he is spurious, and according to some also incestuous. Also, so to speak, he is born of sacrilege. Also, of a slave, because a nun is a slave of her profession, whence it could be argued that the prince would not seem to have thought of such a detestable child. But against this is the truth because of the words of the privilege, which say spurious bastards, and incestuously coupled, conjunctively or disjunctively, and whatsoever begotten from illicit and condemned intercourse, to restore to all legitimate rights, to abolish entirely the stain of birth, and to restore to all and each right of succession, etc., and the necessary non obstante clauses are appended, so that the privilege is solemn and most splendid. Nevertheless, two doubts remain. The first doubt is whether it makes any difference that the nun is a cleric and a spiritual person, but this does not matter, because the Emperor has not established anything concerning the person of the nun, but concerning the succession of temporal goods, which is a matter of civil law, and to which succession even a spurious child can be called by the prince, and he who has this power from the prince, and in the lands of the empire, there is no doubt, as I note, Ia. But. in l. 1. C. de iure annul. aureo. and there I wrote fully after him. For just as the prince can dispose concerning a blood relative, so can he concerning a nun, especially if it is forbidden by divine law, and yet in conferring succession there is no doubt that he can, because such rights are introduced by civil law, as ff. de ver. sig. l. lege obvenire hereditatem. But by the term civil law, praetorian law is also included, as ff. unde cog. l. si spurius.

Second motive and doubt, whether children subsequently born rescind this legitimation of a spurious child. And the question was raised by Dy. in l. ex facto, ff. de vul. et pup. substi. But the truth is that it is not rescinded, since the father does not, by presenting petitions, cause the son to be legitimated, especially in our case, where both the father and the prince’s lieutenant considered the children, nor is it provided by any law that a right acquired by imperial benefit is taken away by children subsequently born, since the legitimation was not made to the detriment of the children, but to concur with them. And this is clear from the tenor of the legitimation. Notwithstanding C. de reuo. do. l. si vnquam, because there the father did not consider the children in any way, and the question was not between the children, but with a certain stranger.

The third motive is more doubtful, because in this legitimation the children born were not cited, nor could the others yet to be born be cited, since they were not yet in existence. Therefore, since the matter concerns the prejudice of the legitimated, the decree should not harm those not cited, as stated in D. 25.5.1 (nam ita diuus) and D. 38.16.1 (si). But Bartolus in this question determines that when a father legitimizes his son, because he says the law of his own thing, i.e., his succession, the legitimation is valid even for children not cited, just as he can alienate his goods and make a will regarding them. For since he can legitimize against the will of the legitimate children, and they have no right to object, therefore it holds even if they are ignorant, as he maintains in D. 28.2.1 (Gallus). But if the legitimation were made after the father's death, it would not be valid in the rescript, whether it said cited or not cited. The conclusion therefore is that, notwithstanding that no citation was made, the said William, spurious and most spurious, can nevertheless succeed pro rata with the other legitimate children born before or after. These are the words of Cynus in the said law non ita diuus.

† In this connection, it is doubted whether, in a rescript or privilege of legitimation obtained from the emperor, or from those who grant it in the name of the prince, blood relatives ought to be summoned. And it seems that they should, as in this law, and in the law *Divus* concerning the annulment of gold coins, and in the law *J.* concerning the cause of liberty. On the contrary, it seems that they should not, as above in the same title, in the law *Cum adoptio*. Moreover, since such an emperor may order what he pleases regarding property, he ought not to be hindered by others, as in the law *Dudum*, Codex, on contracting purchase. And this seems true to me, Cynus.

† Moreover, if this legitimated person had property in the lands of the Church, the legitimated person would in no way succeed to them: because the words of the Pope state, without prejudice to others, which in such matters etc. And thus I hold, and thus is the truth according to God and conscience, and your reverence may and ought to judge thus, and will be judged neither by God nor by the world: because no one knows more than you. What I said concerning property existing in the lands of the Church, I say likewise if it were in the kingdom of France, or in the lands of infidels, in which our Roman Emperor is today regarded as nothing. It is provided in the Extravagant, *Qui filii sint legitimi*, c. *Per venerabilem*. And that we know in l. *Cunctos populos*. I speak of intestate succession. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when it suffices, or does not suffice, for something to be done by anyone.
body: Words

† When it is asked whether it suffices that something be done by anyone, either when it concerns the preservation of my right, and then it suffices that it be done by anyone: as in the case of water, both in summer and winter, L. 1, § quaesitum. Or when it concerns my exemption from a penalty, and then the same applies: as in C. si mancipium ita fuerit alienatum, L. si puella. Or when it concerns binding another to me, and then it is necessary that it be done by me or through my agency: as in L. 2, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, and thus is understood what is noted in ff. de verbis obligatorum, L. cum servus. Dy. From this it seems to be said in favor of Mark, who was captured and presented. Those good men, concerning whom the question arises, are not bound, but the other three are bound for three parts: because this distinction is applied to obligations to appear in court or to present someone: as in ff. si quis cautionem, L. si servus, § si plurium. But the truth is that even for this Mark they are not released: because it is true that it suffices for it to be done by anyone when the same effect follows. Otherwise, if the same effect does not follow, as in ff. de legatis 1, L. non quocumque modo. Hence, since the said Mark was not presented by the one from whom he ought to have been, nor to the benefit of the injured party, so that he could be imposed upon him as a kind of pledge while in prison. But rather to the contrary, hence he was thrust into a place from which no benefit can arise for the injured party, it rightly follows that the said good men, concerning whom the question arises, are bound to make full restitution, as in L. Pedius and L. ne quid, ff. de incendio, ruina, et naufragio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a father appointed four testamentary guardians for his underage son, with the addition that one could not act without the others, and upon the death of one of them, while the mother and grandmother still survive, whether the guardianship pertains to the other three co-guardians, or to the mother herself, or to the grandmother.
2. Whether a testator may deprive the mother of the legal guardianship of her son.
body: The testator, by will, appointed four guardians for his son who was under the age of puberty, with the addition that one could not act or administer without the others. Finally, the testator died, and immediately thereafter one of the said guardians died, the mother and grandmother of the ward being still alive, as well as the three guardians named in the will.

It is asked to whom the guardianship pertains, and it seems to pertain to the three aforementioned persons named in the will: because as long as any one of the testamentary guardians survives, all others are excluded, both the mother and the grandmother, as well as the statutory guardians; but in the place of the deceased, a dativus guardian ought to be substituted: because dativus guardianship, having taken the place of testamentary guardianship, concurs with testamentary guardianship, as in D. de testamento tutoribus, l. si quis sub conditione. From which it follows that the mother, who was one of the said three guardians, comes together with them, and not alone.

On the contrary, it seems that the said mother comes as a guardian ab intestato: because with regard to guardianship, the father died entirely intestate on account of those words of the will that one cannot act or administer without the other. For in this case, testamentary guardianship ceases in all respects, so that there are no remnants of testamentary guardianship. For where the said comprehensive clause is appended, no one has the right of guardianship upon the death of the other, as in c. si, §. sanae, extra de testamento, lib. 6, and there the ordinary gloss, by analogy, introduces the office of guardians and executors for pious causes.

From this it follows that the mother is admitted if she wishes; if she does not wish, the grandmother is admitted, as in Auth. matri, et aviae, C. quando mulier tutelae officium fungi potest. Nor is it necessary that they excuse themselves; it suffices that they do not wish: because their guardianship is voluntary, anomalous, and, so to speak, extraneous. If therefore both renounce, recourse is had to the statutory guardians, who are the nearest in degree, as in Auth. de haereditate ab intestato, §. ex his. And this is the truth.

† Notwithstanding. If it is said that, since the father did not wish the mother to administer alone, this must be rejected, by what is stated by Dy. and Bar. in ff. de adulteriis, l. miles, § sexaginta. For this is false: for although he forbade her as testamentary guardian, he did not thereby deprive himself of the legitimate guardianship. Moreover, I say further, that even if he expressly wished to deprive her, he could not do so, except indirectly by providing for the ward with a testamentary guardian. And the reason is: because the testator does not grant the legitimate guardianship, therefore he cannot take it away, as in ff. de legitimis tutoribus, l. legitimos, in principio. And I marvel at Bartolus, who cast this into doubt. It is therefore concluded, as above, first in favor of the mother. Second, in favor of the grandmother. Third, in favor of other legitimate guardians. And this is the substance of the truth, because where no remnants of testamentary guardianship remain, as is the case here: since testamentary guardianship never had effect, one rightly proceeds to the guardianships in the aforementioned order. Nor should it be said that testamentary guardians are excluded, but rather that they are not included, nor appointed by will on account of the aforementioned clause, which could be inserted according to law, as in l. Titium et Mevium, in principio, and ff. de administratione tutorum. And therefore the treatises examined regarding the guardian cannot be adapted to this case. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an adult, without the authority of a curator and having been notified by the judge of the benefit of age, may appoint litigation attorneys with an oath not to contravene.
2. Whether, after the case has been referred to the counsel of a wise man, it appears to be concluded, and whether public instruments may be produced before the judge or the consultant.
3. Whether a prescription that begins to run against a person of full age runs against his universal successor who is an adult.
4. Whether, after the referral to the counsel of a wise man has been made, an exception may be raised regarding expenses incurred for the permanent utility of the matter. Likewise, whether expenses are offset against fruits.
body: It is asked,

† Whether a female minor who has reached puberty, acting without the authority of a curator and a judge, having been informed about the benefit of age, can appoint procurators for litigation under an oath of not contravening. And it seems that she can, as in Auth. sacramenta puberum. But the truth is to the contrary: because that authentic speaks of those things that are done by the consent of both parties, whereas a procurator's mandate consists solely in the will of the principal alone. And therefore the principal can change their mind, as noted in c. ulti. de procu. li. 6. Furthermore, that oath would limp. For if the adversary accepted it, it would be valid, but if he did not accept it, it would not be valid. Indeed, this is the opinion of some, and it is false, because it ought not to limp. Likewise, the gloss that is in Auth. sacramenta puberum does not stand in the way, because that gloss is understood when it is sworn upon a contract made in court, an example being in the stipulation iudicatum solvi. But in our case nothing was contracted with the adversary, and thus that gloss does not stand in the way. Likewise, judicial proceedings pertain to law. And therefore it is not within the power of someone who does not possess a legitimate standing to legitimize themselves or another: because it ought not to limp. For even if a contract is sometimes found to limp in favor of a minor, it never limps to their detriment, as in C. de procu. l. non eo minus. Furthermore, giving a mandate is not a contract except between the procurator and the principal, as in ff. de procu. l. licet. §. ea obligatio. Hence, a procuratorship with respect to an adversary is not a contract, nor a quasi-delict, or similar; and therefore Auth. sacramenta puberum has no application. From these points I conclude that the said procuratorship is not valid, as in C. de in inte. rest. mino. l. si curatorem habens, and as noted in §. item sacramenta. de pace tenen. col. 10. Likewise, a minor cannot legitimize themselves in court, therefore neither another, such as a procurator or a messenger, according to Cy. and well stated on Auth. sacramenta. Likewise, this is expressly proved: because it is certain that a tutor takes an oath, and by taking the oath binds himself, and nevertheless through that oath, if the tutor is under 25 years of age, he is not legitimized, as in C. de legi. tute. l. fi. For the acts of the court require a formal person, not a perfunctory one, as in C. qui dari tu. pos. l. in universis.

† Now I come to the second point, whether, once a case has been committed to the counsel of a wise man, public instruments can be produced. And it seems that they cannot, because they cannot be produced before the judge, since the case seems to be concluded, as in C. de rela. l. j. together with what Inn. notes on de causa pos. c. pastoralis. Likewise, neither before the legal assessor: because in the production itself a certain examination of the case is required, but with the legal advisor there is no examination of the case, namely whether the production is to be admitted or not, as in C. de dilatio. l. cum, a nobis. Solution: I say that if there was not an express conclusion in the cause, clear instruments can be produced; it is otherwise if they are not clear: because clear instruments are fully established proof. And especially if it is sworn that one could not produce them before because one had no knowledge of the instruments, arg. extra de excep. c. pastoralis and extra de fide instru. c. cum dilectus, and what is noted in c. saepe. extra de verb. sig. in Cle., and what is noted in l. fi. ff. de fer.

† On the third point, by which it is asked whether a prescription that begins against an adult runs against a minor over puberty who is his universal successor: it must be said that it does. But if the time limits for restitution in integrum are granted, restitution in integrum is given to the minor over puberty. And I speak of the time provided for the running of prescription of a thing, or of ownership, or of another action. This is fully noted by the gloss and all the doctors in l. sancimus. C. in quibus causis in inte. resti. non est necessa.

† On the fourth and last point, by which it is asked whether, after the said commission, one can except on the grounds of expenses incurred for the perpetual utility of the thing: I answer, it can be excepted, and even if it were not excepted, nevertheless it ought to be provided for by the office of the judge. Furthermore, this allegation is admitted even in the execution of the judgment, as in ff. de confes. l. cum fideicommissum and ff. de peti. haere. Clearly, however, proofs must be offered readily, and they must be clear, which will be weighed from the quality of the thing itself, as Bart. elegantly notes on ff. de ver. obli. l. cum servus. One thing I do not omit, that they are set off against the fruits consumed, as in ff. de rei ven. l. sumptus, which is notable according to Accur., whose words these are in ff. de rei ven. l. in fundum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the procedure conducted against a procurator appointed for a minor, with the intervention of an oath, is valid. And this matter appears to be the same as that in the first point of the preceding opinion above.
2. Whether a quasi-contract is formed in judicial proceedings, and how this is to be understood.
3. The joinder of issue (litis contestatio) made with an adult without a curator is void by the law itself, although if he were subsequently to confess in the course of the proceedings, it would be valid, but he would be entitled to restitution.
body: On

† As to the point in question, namely whether a proceeding conducted with the procurator of a minor, who was appointed with an oath to ratify and confirm, etc., and with the notary intervening as a public person receiving this promise, etc., is valid or not, such that this procurator may contest the suit and carry it through as if he had been appointed by a major; 25. it appears that the opinions of the doctors are diverse. For the glossa says that the oath operates in the same way in judicial proceedings as in contracts, and the reason is given: because in judicial proceedings one contracts as it were. Thus, our glossa in Auth. sacramenta puberum and in Auth. de pace tenenda, §. item sacramenta, Coll. 10. Others say precisely that such an oath does not make the minor a legitimate person in the appointment of the said procurator, because Auth. sacramenta puberum does not speak of judicial proceedings, but of contracts, and it is an odious constitution, not a favorable one. And therefore it should not be extended: because if the benefit of minors is favorable, its contrary is odious. Also, because the said constitution comes to correct ancient law, although not simply, as C. de legibus, l. non dubium, and ff. de pace, l. iure gentium, and §. generaliter. Therefore, it is not extended from similar cases to similar cases, as noted in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, Auth. quas actiones. Also, this oath is interposed against the force and authority of the laws, therefore it is not valid, as ff. de legibus 1, l. si quis inquilinos, §. fi, and C. de arbitris, Auth. decernimus. Also, in one word, namely by oath, the rule and form of judicial proceedings would be abolished, which is that a legitimate person must be in court, or legitimately appointed, and not merely an adult, as C. de auctoritate praestanda, l. clarum. The third opinion is that of Jacobus de Ravenna and Gulielmus de Cuneo, who say that after such an oath has been given, if the minor or his procurator is admitted by the judge against the adversary, the judgment is valid; however, if the adversary does not wish to admit him, then he is not to be admitted. Therefore, it is valid after the fact, which could have been impeded before the fact. Thus holds Gulielmus de Cuneo, ff. de procuratoribus, l. minor, 25. an., and Jacobus de Ravenna in Auth. sacramenta, consider more subtly.

† And first state that in judgments, a quasi-contract is formed at that time when the judgment is not void by operation of law. It is otherwise if it is void by operation of law, as in D. 14.3.3 § idem scribit. And therefore, when a judgment is void by operation of law, if the principal act is invalid, the oath is also invalid, as in D. 43.26.1 § si quis inquilinos § fin. and by argument from D. 40.1.1 si minor. This is not objected to by Auth. sacramenta puberum, because there it speaks of contracts, where a natural obligation arises from consent. And therefore, the reinforcement of an oath can attach to it; but in judgments, a natural obligation does not arise, as in D. 12.6.1 Iul. because they are rendered against one’s will, as in D. 50.17.1 inter stipulantem § sacramenta.

Secondly, consider that when an adult without a curator enters into the joinder of issue (litis contestatio), it is void by operation of law, even if he subsequently confesses during the proceedings, such confession would be valid; yet he would be restored to his original position (restitutio in integrum), according to Nicolaus de Matarello and Cynus, C. de confessionibus, l. 1; de auctoritate praestanda, I. clarum. Therefore, regarding the foundations of the judgment, the aforementioned oath produces no effect; and if the foundation does not hold, subsequent confessions do not hold either, because they were not made in a valid judicial proceeding, and the procurator did not have a mandate to confess outright (de plano). But rather, they were made in a judicial form which is void, since the judgment itself is void by operation of law. And this is evident from the records; therefore, it must be said that the acts performed by the said procurator, constituted by an incompetent person, or rather by a non-procurator, since the mandate is void by operation of law, are invalid. And just as in a dead lawsuit (lite mortua), so much less do they bind if the judgment was always void by operation of law, as in ff. si quis cautionem, l. si servus, in principio. And because we are in a matter of nullity, not in a matter of restitutio in integrum. And we are in those cases which proceed by way of public clamor (via strepitus), and not by consent, the authority sacramenta puberum has no application. Nor does the reasoning of that authority apply, and thus I hold. Furthermore, the objection from ff. de confessionibus, l. certum, §. minorem, where a minor is restored against his own confession, does not prevail; because it has already been answered according to the distinction of Nicolaus de Matarello. Moreover, because that §. aliter must be understood as stated above, when the confession was valid by operation of law; otherwise, restitutio in integrum is not necessary: against which the oath would operate well, as if a minor had confessed with the authority or assistance of a curator, as noted there; or if it were a case in which he had a legitimate representative: as in momentary possession. From these things it appears that an oath does not revive a dead matter, but rather provides the patronage of incommutability to a matter already revived. And thus I say, and I advise. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the will of a usurer is valid, or not, and whether he can make a pupillary substitution.
2. What must be proved to challenge the will of a usurer.
3. How it is proved that someone is a usurer, and what proof is required. nu. 5.
4. Before which judge it must be proved that someone is a manifest usurer.
5. Whether the exception that the testator was a manifest usurer prevents the grant of possession under the edict of the divine Hadrian.
6. Whether the challenger of the will can receive a legacy.
7. Whether a constitution of a bishop, or of the Emperor, or of the Pope can change anything from the disposition of c. quamquam, and thus make someone testable, or not.
body: A certain Thomas de Laude made a will, which appears in public, solemn, and undisputed writing, not disparaged, obliterated, or canceled in any part by the hand of the public notary. In which said will, among other things, he instituted as his universal heir a certain infant, his legitimate and natural son; and if he should die in pupillary age, he substituted for himself the testator’s own brother, and the uncle of the said pupil; thereupon he dowered his daughters, and also left tutors to the said underage son. Finally, this testator died, survived by his wife, Lady Catherine, and mother of the said pupil and of the said conjugal daughters. After his death, the said mother remained for ten months, or thereabouts, without assuming guardianship. Finally, claiming that the said will was null, she petitioned to be separated as the legitimate or anomalous guardian of the said son and daughters, but did not obtain this. Afterwards, within a year, the said infant died; upon whose death the said substituted uncle produced the said will before the judge, in which prima facie no defect appears, neither regarding the person nor the writing; and he petitioned before the judge to be put in possession under the law *Edicto*, from the Edict of the Divine Adrian. To this petition the said mother contradicts and opposes by objection, that the said putting in possession ought not to be made for this reason, because the said testator was a manifest usurer, and that he died without having provided security. Hence, she says his will is void by the law itself, and in chapter *Quamquam*, on Usury, Book 6. Now it is asked: First, whether the said will is of any effect or not. Second, what ought to be proved so that it may be null. Third, before which judge it ought to be proved. Fourth, whether the said exception impedes the putting in possession. Fifth, and lastly, whether a manifest usurer can make a will for his son, i.e., make a pupillary substitution, or not. And what of the codicillary clause. Furthermore, it is asked: if this woman impugns the will, ought she to have a legacy? And what comes under these words, “lady of the farmstead and usufructuary of all his goods”: And note that this infant died without having entered upon the inheritance, nor in any way instituted heir; and also see the archiepiscopal constitution, which speaks of manifest usurers. Whether the said constitution ought to be understood according to the said decretal *Quamquam*, and whether by a constitution of one other than the Pope, that decretal can be altered in any way.

† On the first point, it must be said that either the said testator was a manifest usurer at the time of the testament or during his life, and then his testament was not valid, neither as regards the institution of heirs nor as regards the pupillary substitution: because he who cannot make a testament for himself cannot make a testament for his underage son. As stated in D. 36.2.2 (ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione). All legacies and fideicommissa are also void, even for pious causes. Likewise, the testamentary guardianship is void: because he died intestate without having provided security, as in c. Quamquam, § Si, de usuris, lib. 6. But if he was not a manifest usurer, then his testament is valid, as in D. 34.5.1 (ff. si certum petatur), l. Eius, qui in provincia, in principio. And the reason for the difference is this: a manifest usurer is infamous both by law and by fact, and since he is criminal, but a non-manifest usurer is not infamous. Moreover, what is hidden is tolerable, whereas what is done openly is not. Hence, he who sins openly is punished more severely than he who sins secretly, as is clear in the case of a manifest thief and a non-manifest thief. For things done secretly are not brought to public example, as are things done openly, as appears in D. 47.2.2 and 3 (ff. de furtis) and l. Sive manifestus, de conditionibus furtivis. And the analogy from thief to usurer is sound, although not in all respects. For the decretal states that a usurer is a thief in a broad sense. From these considerations, therefore, the solution to the ancient doubts appears, namely, concerning the testament, the legacy of guardianship, and concerning the pupillary substitution; nor is it necessary to repeat this further in the following points.

I come to the second point, and I say that it must be proven that he was a manifest usurer, because one is not presumed to be a usurer unless it is proven: for everyone is naturally presumed to be good, and not evil, as stated in D. de probat. l. quotiens, § qui dolo, and C. de inofficiosa test. l. omnimodo. Moreover, it is not sufficient to prove that he was a usurer, unless this quality, namely, that he was manifest, is also proven. For qualities which aggravate the offense are not presumed, unless they are proven, as stated in D. vi bono rap. l. praetor, § docere.

But how will this be proved? I answer: because it was notorious, inasmuch as he held the altar ready, or held it at some time; for since this is more than manifest, it is therefore manifest. See Extra, De cohabitatione, c. Si quis. But even without notoriety, it can be proved that he was manifest, by proving that he practiced usury, and that he was publicly held and considered a usurer by all who knew him and associated with him. See L. 4, ff. Ad Macedonianam; and the argument in Extra, De probationibus, c. Per tuas; and Codex, Ad Macedonianam, L. Zenodorus. For life and morals make one manifest, and even association operates something, both for ill and for good. See L. Non omnes, § A barbaris, ff. De re militari. Likewise, a usury ledger seen by many witnesses, or produced in court during his lifetime, proves him to be a manifest usurer. See the note of the Archdeacon, Dist. 45, c. Qui sincera. Also, a confession made before many persons outside of court. Argument from ff. De edictis edilitibus, L. Quaero, § Si. For if it had been made in court, it would not only establish manifestness, but notoriety, just as a judgment does. See the notes in the aforementioned places. For it would be notorious in law, or manifest, as already explained, so that it passes into notoriety: which is the same as the highest proof, which cannot be higher or more evident, although civil law uses this term improperly. See Codex, De probationibus, L. Ea quidem. This notoriety is the preamble of the canonists. From these things it appears what and of what kind are the matters to be proved; and concerning some of these, although not all, it is noted in c. 1, De usuris, lib. 6. And it supports what is noted in Dist. 47, c. De Petro.

† I come to the third point, and I say that this clamor, whether someone is a usurer or not: or whether this controversy pertains to the ecclesiastical forum.
