Hence the secular judge must remit this article to the ecclesiastical forum, because the case of usury is an ecclesiastical case, nor does this dispute pertain to the secular judge where there is need for disputation: because the matter becomes doubtful, as noted in 11 q. 1 c. in the Summa. For ecclesiastical cases are cognized in this manner, because whenever the ecclesiastical judge does not have to follow the sentence of the secular judge, it is a sign that that case is of the ecclesiastical forum, as in c. ult. de except. lib. 6.

I come to the fourth point. And I premise, for the sake of clarity, that in proving usury, half-proof never suffices; so that, with this consideration in mind, proof is difficult and not perfunctory, but requires exact and deeper investigation; because, as in criminal matters, proofs must be clearer than light, with the exception of those which are supported by canonical presumptions, as in Extra, De pignoribus, chapter *Illo vos*; and Extra, De emptione et venditione, chapter *Ad nostram*; and Codex, De probationibus, law *Sciant*. Hence, in this case also, both proving and impeaching witnesses must be received, and the execution requires a lengthy process.

† Having thus assumed this as true, it appears that the exception of usury, unless proven, and unless by public documents, does not have the power to impede the seizure under the edict of the divine Adrian. As stated in C. de edicto divi Adriani, title 2, because this is a special privilege of that edict in favor of testaments, for which a public document is evident; and because one proceeds as from what is notorious, and there is no proportion from the obscure to the notorious, as in l. ultima, C. de compensatione; and because he who seeks the execution of the edict is more properly said to be requesting execution than bringing an action. Hence, exceptions, unless they are liquid or suitable, do not easily impede the seizure, because a prudent judge can see and consider them. However, as I said, this exception does not pertain to the secular judge for examination. Nevertheless, by this, he should not remit his office of legal execution. I admit, however, that if this exception is later proven before the bishop, which should be reserved in the seizure itself, whatever has been done will be revoked, as in ff. de evictione, l. minor, in principio, as the cause of the seizure being detected as invalid, or reduced to the cause. Argument in l. si fullo, ff. de conditione sine causa. I come to the fifth point, and I answer as I answered above.

† From these it appears what is the law regarding the mother: for if he was a manifest usurer, the mother succeeds the impubes intestate. Nevertheless, while the question of usury is pending, the instituted heir must possess the goods with suitable security, as in D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. inter omnes. But if he was not manifest, then the mother being perpetually excluded, the pupillary substitute succeeds, as in C. si pater, de testamento, lib. 6, and D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papiæ, § sed nec impuberis, and C. de impuberibus et aliis sub tutela, l. precibus.

† The constitution of the archbishop must be understood in accordance with what has been said: because the archbishop cannot make anyone testable or intestable, but only the Pope or the Emperor, as stated in l. ff. and l. ex imperfecto, C. de testa. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a minor, having been circumvented by a superior through ignorance of fact, may nevertheless bring an action so as not to be deceived, but rather be kept unharmed, notwithstanding the oath.
body: If it is so as is proposed,

† That the minor was deceived by ignorance of fact by those of greater age, I say that, notwithstanding the oath, he may bring an action so that he may not be defrauded and may be preserved from damages. And this for several reasons: because division is a kind of exchange, as fully set forth in the law and notes, ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. qui Romae, §. duo fratres; and thus it is a contract of good faith, as in the Institutes, de actionibus, §. actionem. In which contract, if anyone is deceived by the temerity of his adversary, such deception ought to be removed, as in C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. maioribus; and fully in the law and notes in l. eleganter, in principio, ff. de dolo. The second reason is, because one who is ignorant does not seem to swear, as in ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. ex actionibus, §. longe; and C. de donationibus, l. nec ignorans; and C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si; and ff. de pactis, l. tres fratres. The third reason is, that consent is required in an oath, as in C. de nuptiis, auth. quod eis; but nothing is so contrary to consent as error, which reveals ignorance, as in ff. de iurisdictio omnium iudicum, l. si per errorem; and ff. de iudicibus, l. 2; ff. de confessione, l. non fatetur. The fourth reason is, because auth. sacramenta publica expressly states that where fraud intervenes, the oath is not valid, as being repudiated by law. For civil law can well repudiate an oath by natural reason, or by reason of public utility; especially when the oath otherwise is valid by special law against the common law, as is in the said auth. sacramenta publica; and ff. de legibus, l. 1, l. si quis inquilinos, §. si; and C. de legibus, l. non dubium; and notes in l. adigere, §. si, ff. de iure patronatus. The fifth reason is, because illicit transactions the president of the province ought to rescind, as in l. illicitas, in principio, ff. de officiis praesidis; from which it is concluded that, if the facts alleged are true, the remedy is ready for the said minor, by which he ought to be preserved indemnified against the said injury; because it is unjust that they should enrich themselves by their own fraud. For sagacity, which is committed against a minor of tender age and counsel, is a species of malice fraud. There is another reason, because it is alleged that this adversary of the minor administers the patrimony of the minor, whence he cannot plead ignorance of the goods of the said minor, as in C. arbitrio tutoris, l. si; and therefore from presumed fraud, or great temerity, which is compared to fraud, he cannot be excused with probability. Argument: ff. unde cognoscitur, l. optavi; and l. si ita, ff. de funerariis instrumentis, with many similar cases. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the movable or immovable property of clerics can in any way pass to their blood relatives by will or intestate succession, and what is the rule regarding fruits collected by the cleric from both benefices and patrimony, and number 2.
2. Whether rectors of churches are usucaptors or usufructuaries.
3. Fruits consumed by clerics are presumed to have been consumed rather from the fruits of the church than from the patrimony.
body: It must be premised for the sake of clarity,

†by which no one of the clergy, nor of the lay population, can usurp ecclesiastical goods by right of consanguinity, as stated in Extra, De praebendis, c. 1. I understand this to apply to ecclesiastical goods, as the text says, or to those acquired in consideration of the Church. Such goods pass neither by will nor intestate to blood relatives, whether they are movable or immovable. Other goods, however, which came to clerics in consideration of the person, or from the inheritance of someone, pass to their blood relatives intestate, or by will according to the disposition of the clerics, as in c. 1, and c. Cum in officiis, and c. Ad haec, and c. Relatum, Extra, De testibus. These are the words of Bartolus ad litteram, and in the aforementioned c. 1, De praebendis. And these statements are made regarding goods. But it is not to be considered regarding fruits.

† And in this regard, one must refer to the glossa ordinaria found in the last chapter of the title "De Officio Ordinariorum" in Book 6, which distinguishes between those who have administration, such as rectors of churches, and those who do not, such as prebendaries or holders of benefices without cure of souls, as noted by Innocentius in the final chapter of the title "Ne Praelati Vices Suas."

† For if they indeed have administration while they are alive and in good health, they are equated with usufructuaries; but if they are in the illness from which they die, they are equated with usurers. Nevertheless, in either case, if they make no disposition of the fruits, the fruits must be reserved for the successor of the church. This is therefore the case in question, because this person held the governance of several churches and made no disposition of the fruits during his lifetime, nor was he able to make one at death. It is certain, therefore, that the fruits of the churches must be reserved for the churches themselves and their successors. But here, a twofold division must be made: because the heirs must have the fruits collected from his patrimonial goods. The clerics of the churches, however, must have the fruits collected and remaining from the ecclesiastical goods. The same applies to pensions, as in D. de usufr. l. de fun. To this division, a discerning judge ought to arrive, namely, to the division of the fruits collected and received, either by agreement among the new rectors among themselves, or according to the quality of the ecclesiastical goods. There is no doubt regarding pensions: because the instruments of the pensions state from which goods they are to be taken; thus, the conjecture, as I said, is drawn from the qualities of the goods, as noted in l. 2, C. de rescind. vend. Similarly, the fruits must be considered according to the quality of the patrimonial goods.

† However, it must be noted that fruits found to have been consumed are rather to be deemed consumed from the fruits of the church than from those of the patrimony; because one is permitted to live on ecclesiastical fruits, as stated in the Decretals, *De praebendis*, chapter *Cum secundum*. And patrimonial fruits are free and exempt, as stated in the Code, *De episcopis et clericis*, law 2. Therefore, by the subtlety of the judge, these matters are to be determined and each item returned to its respective owner, as it affects them, as has been said, and fully noted by Innocentius in the Decretals, *De praebendis*, chapter *Episcopus*. And it is supported by the Code, *De episcopis et clericis*, authentic *Licentia*. And it is noted in the Decretals, *De successionibus ab intestato*, chapter *Cum dilectus*. And we have a similar case regarding fruits in the Digest, *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, law *Centurio*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How witnesses intending to prove that Titius died thirty years ago, or that thirty years have already passed, ought to give their testimony.
2. Whether the statement of a witness is to be referred to the entire period of time or to a part of the time, and whether it constitutes proof.
3. What interpretation the statements of witnesses are to receive.
body: Titius died thirty years ago. Witnesses were produced to verify the said chapter and stated that the matters contained therein are true. When asked how and in what manner they know the aforementioned facts, they answered: because they were present at the death of the said Titius and at his burial; and that he died on a certain vigil of Saint Peter. Moreover, one of the said witnesses adds: and because I have a certain son who was born in the said year in which the said Titius died. It is therefore asked whether the number of years of the death of the said Titius is fully or semi-fully proven, or whether only the death itself is proven, and not the time of his death.

† I answer that it seems to be said that the time has been proved; because when the witnesses stated that the facts were true, they fully testified regarding the time. And when they subsequently add the reason of bodily presence,

† The time is tacitly considered to have been repeated, namely, it is already thirty years and more, because the reason is understood to have been given regarding the whole, just as we say that it is presumed that an oath was taken concerning the whole. As in l. 1, § 1, ff. quarum rerum actio non datur. Furthermore, because what is said in preceding matters appears to be repeated in subsequent ones, as in ff. de verbis oblig., l. Titia, § idem respondit; and ff. de pactis, l. item quia. Furthermore, because preceding matters declare subsequent ones. As in ff. de legatis 1, l. si servus plurium, § fin. Furthermore, that which is said simply is referred to the whole. As in ff. de verbis oblig., l. 1, § si quis simpliciter; and ff. de aedilicio edicto, l. quæro, § fin. Furthermore, because indefinite terms are equivalent to universal ones: as in ff. de rebus dubiis, l. si is, qui ducenta, § utrum; and according to Dynus in the rubric de regulis iuris, book 6; and ff. de servis urbanis prædiis, l. si servitus; and Codex, quæ res pignori obligari possunt, l. fi. Furthermore, because there is a reason why it is more properly referred to a part of the time than to the whole time, as in l. 1, Codex de liberto præterito vel exheredato. Furthermore, because the statements of witnesses ought to be understood as it is probable that the witnesses intended, as in ff. de probationibus, l. cum de ætate. Furthermore, because the words of witnesses are not to be distorted, as in l. penultima, ff. ad exhibendum. To the contrary, it seems: because when the reason of a witness is doubtful, we do not adhere to the statement of the witness, as in Extra, de probationibus, c. in præsentia. Hence, the statement of a witness is drawn to the reason, and not vice versa, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, de testibus, c. causam. Furthermore, the statements of witnesses are not to be supplemented with regard to the efficacy of completing proof, although sometimes they are supplemented with regard to completing the presumption of the crime of falsehood, as in Extra, de testibus, c. cum tu; and noted by Innocentius in Extra, de rescriptis, c. cum causam. Furthermore, the statements of witnesses do not receive interpretation other than an explanatory or declaratory one that is plain and clear, unless the witnesses themselves explain themselves, and immediately; because only the witness can interpret his own statement and his own mind, as noted in Authentica de testibus, § quia vero. Solution, notwithstanding these points:

The first part is the more correct one, by the reasons first alleged. For there are two kinds of interpretation: one which is proved by laws, and this is received by testimonial statements which consist in fact, and this is not received by the statements of witnesses. Since, therefore, the first opinion is confirmed by reasons and arguments of the laws, therefore it is true. As in D. ad Trebellianum, l. qui filium, §. si. I conclude, therefore, that the said witnesses seem to prove that the time about which they testified is true: so that the reason may be conformable to the statement, and not discordant; because in a witness discordance is not presumed, nor variation, nor vacillation. I hear that the said witnesses are contrary, although it is not alleged in the point; but if so, it is certain that they do not prove either fully or half; because adverse testimonies derogate from each other, as is fully read and noted. C. de fide instrumentorum, l. scripturae; and D. de testibus, l. ob carmen, §. final. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a contumacious party who fails to respond to the positions within the allotted time should be deemed to have confessed.
body: The statute shall be upheld, which provides that a certain order be observed in lawsuits, controversies, and disputes; and among other things it provides that within certain delays each party may, is bound to, and ought to make and produce whatever positions and interrogatories, pertinent and impertinent, simple and complex, and any others whatsoever; and chapters and intentions of whatever condition they may have been, so that by the party against whom such positions and interrogatories are made, it is required that he must altogether answer the same positions and interrogatories, except those which depend on explanations or interrogatories already denied, or unless they concern another’s fact, about which the defendant could reasonably be entirely uncertain, in which case it is at the discretion of the judge whether one should at least answer according to belief, or not according to belief, having regard to the position and interrogatory, and the person to whom such position or interrogatory is made. And chapters, positions, and articles of whatever condition, whether pertinent or not pertinent, are admitted, saving the right regarding impertinences, and not admitting them, with a time granted to both parties for the definitive sentence; and if positions or interrogatories have been made, it is understood that a certain delay is granted for obtaining copies and deliberating; and then another delay for answering clearly and openly, which delay is understood to be established by law. And if it has been personally commanded to the principal or procurator that within a certain term he ought to answer what he believes or estimates regarding those positions or interrogatories: and if he does not answer, or refuses to answer, or contumaciously absents himself within the term or terms above written and given to him: and the adversary appears within the term or terms above written, and accuses his contumacy, he shall be held as having confessed or denied, to the benefit and will of the party making the positions and interrogatories. And although on these positions or interrogatories he has not at any time been asked by any judge what he believes regarding them, and although the said positions or interrogatories have not been read to him, he may, nor ought, the positions and interrogatories to which no answer has been given, upon the request of the adversary, be pronounced and declared as confessed or denied, as above. Another statute provides that anyone wishing to sell and obtain the benefit of public notices (cridae) shall appear before the judge, etc., in which statute three months are established for the opposing party to show his right, and for the absent party a term of six months is established. Now, having made the opposition, the positions were made within the said term, which were shown by the judge to the party against whom proceedings are taken; it is ordered that he ought to answer with the assignment of a certain term, who then was contumacious and did not answer, but answered afterwards after 16 days, or thereabouts.

† It is asked whether a judge ought to deem a contumacious party as having confessed, either by virtue of the first statute or by virtue of the common law. On this point, I answer that, according to the matters proposed, he ought to deem him as having confessed, both under the common law and under the municipal law. And I premise, for the sake of clarity, that the trimester and semester ordained with respect to the entire case do not prevent intermediate delays from being assigned, and indeed ought to be assigned, for each individual act to be performed. For individual acts require individual delays, especially regarding those matters which depend on the judge’s discretion as to the assignment of said delays, as in C. de dila. l. siue pars. and ff. de fer. l. oratione. and l. fina. And we have it in the common law that in a case of appeal a year is established, and from the cause two years: may not certain positions (pleadings) be made in the meantime? No one doubts that they may, as in C. de appel. l. ampliorem. §. 1. And if one is contumacious in responding, will he not be deemed to have confessed? Certainly so, regarding positions read to him or otherwise served, because they have been delivered; for these are equivalent, as in ff. de eden. l. 1. §. 1. And commanded to respond, unless he has a just cause for not responding within the term, and this by the general rule which the gloss places in ff. de confes. l. certum. and by the special text which we have in c. et si post praestitum. de confes. lib. 6. and by the masterly statements of the doctors, as elegantly noted by Iac. de Aret. in l. 1. §. quid ergo. ff. de ventre inspi. Certainly, and that which is not to be omitted is that if a term were set by the law itself, it would be no less peremptory than the term of the judge; for from such a term one becomes truly contumacious, as noted in c. si ante. de dolo, et contu. in cle. Furthermore, it is not to be omitted that if the statute made an ordinary cause summary, or vice versa, the law would be the same as regards positions; because to state a position and to respond is an act perfect in itself, as noted in c. saepe. de verbo. sig. in cle. And therefore I do not care whether the procedure is otherwise regarding other acts, provided that in the positions themselves the proper form required therein is observed. Wherefore it is concluded, and necessarily follows, that the said positions are to be deemed confessed. And thus the judge is to rule, unless the respondent had a probable cause or impediment, as in C. de appellatio. l. praeses. Nor does it avail the said respondent that he responded long after the term; for to relieve a contumacious party, the judge ought not to admit such a response in his favor, by argument from ff. de in integrum resti. l. diuus. and ff. de verbo. obli. l. si ita quis. §. Seia. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How the children of the first marriage succeed together with the children of the second.
body: Pilia

† The daughter of the first marriage succeeds to the male portion of the mother’s estate; because there are four children, one from the first marriage and three from the second, as stated in the Authentica de nuptiis, § illud, verse si enim, towards the end, Title of Collation 4. Nor does the preceding statute contradict this in any way. This is reasonable, because the daughter of the first marriage ought to receive her share from the maternal goods, and not be entirely deprived thereof. Her share is the male portion, as established in the Institutes de haeredibus quae ab intestato succedunt, § cum filius, and in the Authentica de haeredibus ab intestato, in the beginning. Lord Dynus states that if a statute intended to deprive her entirely, it could not do so, as he notes in chapter Indultum. For a dowry given from paternal goods is not excluded from the maternal estate in the case proposed; because it is not to be considered as subject to collation in any manner, as provided in the Code de collatione, laws Ut liberis, Illa, and Illud. And just as it is not collated, so it is not imputed to her; because the accounts of separated deceased persons are separate, as stated in the Digest de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, law Si maritus. The statute also supports this in the words “but of the maternal goods,” namely, when they do not originate from the same marriage. Hence, the conclusion in the first point: considering the number of children, she succeeds to one-fourth part, neither more nor less; because the shares of the daughters of the second marriage accrue to the male heir, with the burden of providing dowries if they were not dowered, or with the burden of paying the dowry left in the will, as stated in law Cum plures, § penult., Digest de administratione tutorum. And from this it appears how the son and the children of the second marriage come into their shares among themselves: namely, according to the form of the statute, those two daughters of the second marriage receive their dowries, and the brother receives the remainder. And this is the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Within what period of time must an inheritance be entered upon after the death of the testator, and whether such period runs against one who is ignorant.
2. Whether prescription runs while the inheritance lies unclaimed.
body: The widow was entitled to receive a certain sum of money; it has now been forty years and more. The said lady died thirty years and more ago, leaving a certain grandson through a predeceased son. Because the grandson learned of his grandmother’s death twenty-eight years ago, which knowledge, however, has not been proven, the grandson acknowledged the inheritance before the judge one year ago.

† It is asked whether the said acknowledgment of the inheritance is valid or not. I answer that the time for acknowledging possession of goods does not run against one who is ignorant, as in l. 2, §. dies, D. si quis ordo in bonorum possessione servetur. And from the head of children he has a useful year, and from the head of cognates he also has one hundred days to be computed from the day of knowledge. Therefore, if from the day of knowledge the year and one hundred useful days had not elapsed, the said acknowledgment of the inheritance made before the judge, as an acknowledgment of possession of goods, is valid. But if the said time had elapsed, it must be seen what is the law according to civil law, whether the time of thirty years, which is given for entering upon an inheritance, according to civil law, begins from the day of knowledge of the death of him whose inheritance is in question, or whether it runs against one who is ignorant. And it seems to be said that it does not run against one who is ignorant: because one who is ignorant can neither in law nor in fact enter upon the inheritance: and it is certain that when there is an impediment, the prescription does not begin to run, as in l. 1, in fine, C. de annua exceptione. Just as we say in the time for deliberation, that it does not run against those who are ignorant, as in C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum antiquioribus. And everyone who has the right of deliberation can enter upon the inheritance, therefore the said entry is valid. Hence, if there were no question about anything other than the right of entering upon the inheritance, the said avuncular debt could be claimed.

But there is doubt: because it is prescribed against the said debt, as in C. de praescr. 30. ann. l. sicut. which prescription began during the lifetime of the grandmother, and therefore even while the grandmother's inheritance was lying unclaimed, it completed its course, wherefore the said nephew can be repelled by the aid of the prescription of the debt, not to mention the prescription of the right to succeed, which prescription of the debt runs against all, both those who know and those who do not know, and therefore unless the said prescription was interrupted, the said debt could not be claimed, according to the said l. sicut. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether custom can establish that a vassal may alienate a fief.
body: A certain nobleman, holding a hereditary fief from the Illustrious Prince and Lord, the Count of Savoy, in a certain noble valley called the Secusa Valley, in the County of Savona beyond the mountains, in which fief there were innumerable and fertile possessions, not being accustomed to attend to the agriculture of the nobles, leased certain of the said possessions to certain rustics in perpetual emphyteusis, to be held in perpetuity under the name of emphyteusis, and as they call it, albergamenti, for a certain annual pension, as well as for the intrata, or entry fee, receiving a certain quantity, and furthermore for the right confessed to him. Now, by the official of the said Illustrious Prince, it is said that the aforementioned contracts were not valid, because they were made without the license of the principal lord of the fief, and his regalia were not given, nor was one grosso given for each florin to the Lord Count of Savoy, nor to his officials, whom the Lord Count ought to have been notified of, i.e., informed of the aforementioned matters, and from whom investiture should have been requested within a year. Hence, since these things were not observed, it is said that this fief, in this part, has become forfeit, and the said emphyteutic contract is invalid, and the things should revert to the chamber, or fisc, of the Lord Count. And upon this, an inquiry has been formed, and a complaint has also been presented by the procurator of the Lord Count. On the other hand, it is said that the noble feudatories of the said Valley have, by privileged custom, the same power in granting as those receiving from them have in receiving, i.e., they can do the aforementioned freely, lawfully, and without penalty, and this custom has been proven notorious, so that it could not have been hidden from the conscience of the prince for the longest times, and by witnesses of great length. Now, the question is, what is the law?

† If the question is raised concerning the general and proper nature of fiefs, the text in *Callidis insuper machinationibus*, in order to counteract the cunning machinations of certain persons who, having received a price, as if under the color of investiture, which they claim to be permitted, sell fiefs and transfer them to others, so that such a fiction or any other may not be devised in fraud of our constitution, of which it is stated in that constitution in § *Habito consilio*, we prohibit in every way, under the penalty of our imminent authority, that the buyer and the seller, because they have been found to have contracted such illicit alienations, lose the fief and it returns freely to the lord, col. 10, *De prohibitione feudorum alienationis* per Federicum, c. *Imperiale*, § *Habito*, and § *Calidus*, and § *Nos autem*, states: we render all illicit alienations void, notwithstanding prescription of any length of time. From this text, it would seem to be said that the intention of the Lord Count was well-founded, notwithstanding any contrary custom of whatever time. But against this is the very truth, that an established custom is held as an express pact, by which and through which the aforementioned alienation may be permitted. And first, from the general rule, both among the naturalists, who say that what is customary is as if innate, and among the jurists, who say that custom is a kind of pact, as noted in l. 2, *Quae sit longa consuetudo*, and that it exists among any discrete good men; because custom, especially in fiefs, which derive their force from custom, which is the greatest part of the law, as in Inst. *De iure naturali*, § *Ex non scripto*, is held as ordinary and solemn law, as in c. 1, *In quibus causis feudum amittitur*, and in c. *Obertus*, *De ordine*, § *Strenuus*, Auth. *De feudis cognoscendis*, coll. 10. And it is most expressly stated in its own terms in c. *Nos Romanorum*, § *Libellariae*, *De pace constantia*, where the text says: let libellary and precary constitutions regarding fiefs remain in their own state according to the custom of each city, notwithstanding our law, which is called that of Emperor Frederick. And therefore there is no doubt, since ancient custom has been proven. For he who does not observe the custom of the ancients does not observe their honor, from which the greatest princes and successors say one must beware, and I say, beware greatly. For to custom, as to its mother, reverence must be shown; for all law by which the world is governed is divided into two parts, and the greatest part is custom, as in Inst. *De iure naturali*, § *Ex non scripto*, to such an extent that it is equivalent to natural law, which is now immutable. And here it must also be noted, because if one considers § *Callidis*, this proceeding must be founded against feudatories, not against peasants, who cannot lose their right unless the sword is placed at the root of the gladiator, as in l. 2, C. *Ubi in rem actio*. Certainly, against the said nobles and ancient feudatories, the inquiry dictates nothing, no accusation having been brought against them, and therefore without doubt the said proceeding is incompetent and unjust, and the said peasants ought to be absolved, and perpetual silence imposed upon the opposing party. That the said custom is proven appears from the instruments and the statements of witnesses seen and examined by me. Notwithstanding the argument from prescription, because custom has more power than prescription; because in custom there is the tacit consent of the lord, the law is known. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If leagues, factions, conspiracies, and secret meetings, as well as assemblies, are prohibited under penalty, do those who assemble to apprehend malefactors incur that penalty?
2. Whether four men are said to form an assembly.
body: By the decree *ut cautum est*, lest leagues, unions, confederations, sects, conventicles, conspiracies, or combinations be formed, under penalty of fine and corporal punishment to be inflicted at the discretion of the lord. The case occurred that certain brigands from the city of Genoa came one night upon the district of a certain castle, and there committed homicides and thefts; finally they were outlawed in both fine and person. Moreover, certain nobles, who had an interest in the matter, approached the local authority and obtained permission that they might make a gathering of people to capture the said malefactors, should they return, which authority indeed granted them license, saying however to them that under this pretext they commit nothing else. These nobles made the aforementioned gathering, and since the said outlaws did not return, they could not capture them. But four of these nobles, turning from lawful to unlawful conduct during the same gathering, withdrew apart and went to drain a certain stream, for which draining there is a very well-known penalty.

† Now it is inquired against the said nobles concerning two crimes, namely, concerning the gathering of people and concerning the river. They are not concerned with the latter, but they defend themselves against the charge of gathering, because this gathering was lawful and for a licit and permitted purpose. The question is: what is the law? I answer that these men should not be punished for the gathering, because this gathering could lawfully have been made for the purpose of capturing the said robbers. And this is called good fraud, as is expressly noted by the commentators on the Genoese in l. 1, § dolum, and there the gloss in the word deseruiunt, ff. de dolo. Moreover, there is an express law that it is permitted to all and each to capture such persons as public enemies, as C. de mathe. l. si. And if it is permitted to capture them, then consequently everything by which one arrives at that end is permitted, such as gathering friends and well-wishers to exterminate these condemned beasts who harm the region, as the commentators note in l. 3, ff. de vi, et vi armata. It therefore appears that the gathering was lawful under the common law, for there was just fear of return, while the matter was still in the flagrant crime, as we said concerning the one struck, who fears being struck again, as in l. 1, C. unde vi, with its material. It therefore appears that the gathering had a lawful beginning, and although some afterwards committed offenses, the gathering itself was not bad, nor is it bad, because the principal cause must be considered, as in l. si mulier, rerum amotarum, and in l. 2, § 1, ff. de vi bono rapto. For indeed there were not all those four who pertain to the mind of the decree of the lord,

† Because four individual men, without other aids, cannot make such conspiracies as those of which the decree speaks, although Bartolus says that four men make a people, in l. 1, C. de proba., which law says nothing about this, because there "people" is put for "knee," not for a collection of a multitude. And we must adapt the words of the decree to the words of the Lord, who by four men would not make a new decree: and that four men are not called a multitude is clear in l. si, C. de testa. Therefore, it must be said without doubt that this is not the case for which, by the form of the decree, any penalty should be imposed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the appointment of guardians is valid in such a manner that all must administer jointly, and that one cannot act without the other, nor two without the third.
2. Whether the guardianship is terminated upon the death of one of them.
3. Furthermore, by what action the remaining two are held liable after the death of the first one.
body: Three tutors were appointed in the will with the clause that all of them together, and not one without the other, nor two without the third, etc., were to administer the estate upon the death of the testator. All of them administered it together for a certain time; after one died, the two administered it; after two died, the one administered it. Then that last one died, and an action is brought generally and indifferently against the heirs of one of them, that they render an account of the administration and the rest for the entire time during which their ancestors administered and neglected to administer, and also restore the rest. The question is, what is the law?

† And first, whether the said tutors could be appointed in the will in such a way that one cannot administer without the other. And it must be said that they can, as is stated in the Digest, *De administratione tutorum*, law *Titium et Mevium*, in the beginning.

Secondly, it is asked whether the guardianship is terminated with respect to all upon the death of one of them, and it must be said that it is so, as is stated in the Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Pedius*, § *fin.*, and as noted in the last chapter of the Sixth Book of the Decretals, *De testibus*.

Thirdly, it is asked by what action the other two were liable after the death of the first. I answer: you should say that certain acts are performed in the preliminaries of guardianship, and he speaks of these. D. de negotiorum gest. l. cum pater. And this is not our case: certain acts are performed in the guardianship itself, and these undoubtedly fall under the action on guardianship; certain acts are performed in the remnants of guardianship, for example, in connected affairs. And the same applies so that the guardian may be present for the case after puberty. D. de negotiorum gest. l. nam et ser. §. si viuo. Certain acts are performed outside all remnants of guardianship under a new office of management, and these do not fall under the action on guardianship, but under the action on negotiorum gestorum, as D. de suspectis tutoribus l. 3. §. quaeri potest. From the diversity of all times and ages, the type of action is diversified. D. de negotiorum gest. l. Pomponius in negotiis. D. de administratione tutorum l. tutorum, qui tutelam. Furthermore, as is proposed, the action is brought against the heirs of one of the guardians, and it is not stated in what respect, and thus the libel is uncertain, as D. de negotiorum gest. l. cum alieni. From these it appears that the said libel is ambiguous and confused, and does not proceed, since the defendant objects to the ineptitude of the libel, as D. de negotiorum gest. l. eum actum, provided that the plaintiff can declare this. For if it is uncertain due to the act of the adversary, the cumulative and ambiguous libel proceeds well, as noted in D. de tributoria actione l. quod in haeredem. §. eligere. Moreover, I say that if the action on guardianship is brought for the entire time, the libel is inept, because the action expressed in the libel is inept, incompetent, and untrue. For the action on negotiorum gestorum and the action on guardianship differ in genus, as D. de negotiorum gest. l. diuortio. For the legists hold this, that expressed matters harm, unexpressed matters do not harm. That is, an expressed incompetent action harms, but silence does not harm; because a competent action is understood to be proposed tacitly, as fully noted in l. 1. in principio, in fine, magna glossa, D. de edendo. And it is clear in l. 1. §. 1. D. si mensor falsum modum dixerit. And this proceeded from the origin of civil law, as is clear. D. de origine iuris l. 2. §. deinde. Although Innocentius, following canonical equity, says the contrary regarding the proposition of an action, but not in the other points touched upon above. Extr. de iudiciis c. examinata. But you in Lombardy must observe the opinion of the legists, because we are in the lands of the Empire. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the testator instituted his son and daughter as universal heirs, yet willed that the daughter should be content with a certain dowry, and that his goods, or possession thereof, should not pass to the daughter, but to the male heir, whether the daughter is a universal heir for one-half: and what pertains to her.
body: The testator made this. First, he instituted his son and daughter as universal heirs. Second, he ordered that the daughter should be content with a certain dowry. Third, he established and ordered that his goods, or possession of them, could in no way come to the said daughter, but ought to remain with the above-mentioned male.

† Now it is asked whether the said daughter is the universal heir before she marries. And it seems that she is, by virtue of the first clause of the will. Nevertheless, upon the occurrence of marriage, she must be content with the dowry, if it suffices for the legitime. For what is said, that a son, when requested under a condition, deducts two-fourths, as in c. Rayn. and c. Rayn., is true only as often as the testator has not provided for the legitime, or has provided for it, but less fully, as in C. de inoff. test. l. quam in prioribus, and l. scimus, §. cum autem. Wherefore, if the legitime is deducted according to the testator’s will, the son never deducts two-fourths, according to the true understanding of the laws. And the reason is: because the son is not burdened beyond what he ought to be burdened, since the father has provided for his own legitime, as in C. ad Treb. l. iubemus, and in Auth. de resti. et ea, quae parit, §. quamobrem.

To the contrary, it seems that the last clause of the will appears to revoke the first. And it is certain that the later writing prevails over the earlier one, as in ff. de leg. 1, l. si mihi, et tibi, §. in leg.

Solution. I do not believe that the later writing revokes the earlier one, but rather distinguishes it. For this seems to have been the testator’s intention: that the possession and administration of the goods should be entirely in the hands of the male, taking this interpretation from the word “in the hands of” (penes), as in ff. de leg. 2, l. Titia, §. Gaius, and from the fact that the male is more worthy, arg. ff. de leg. 2, l. cum pater, §. pater pluribus.

From these, it is inferred that this daughter, having married, must be content with the dowry, if the dowry contains as much or more than the legitime; otherwise, she will have the legitime, with the dowry counted towards it, as in the aforementioned laws. For those words, that she must be content with the dowry, carry the force of a fideicommissum, as in ff. de leg. 2, l. peto, in princ. For these words occupy the place of taxation. ff. de haer. insti. l. qui volebat, and ff. de leg. 3, l. cum quis decedens, §. nupturam.

It is not an obstacle, ff. de leg. 2, l. cum pater, §. pater, qui filio, because there the father’s will was not in limiting, but in demonstrating, as noted there.

From these, the conclusion appears: that the said daughter is in the meantime heir for one-half, but she must not possess and administer the goods, but the male; nevertheless, she will not in the meantime be without benefit, at least up to the legitime. As to what is the law when the condition of marriage exists, it is apparent from the above, and therefore I do not recapitulate. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A widow, for the restitution of her dowry, received certain things *in solutum* (in satisfaction) from the heirs of her first husband, without the judge observing the form prescribed by the statute. Subsequently, she married a second time and gave the said things as dowry. The heirs of the first husband ratified the said donation of the said things as dowry to the second husband, with the agreement that they would obtain release from the first action. Before the ratification, they had already received from the said property fruits equal in amount to the valuation of the dowry. It is asked whether the said *datio in solutum* was valid. And, assuming it was not, whether it could have been ratified. See no. 3.
2. Whether, by virtue of the *datio in solutum*, the heirs of the first husband are released, or by virtue of the receipt of the fruits.
3. Whether the dowry instrument ought to remain in the possession of the woman herself.
body: A widow sought restitution of her dowry against the heirs of her husband and received certain things unpaid by the judge. However, the form of the statute of Milan was not observed: so that it is presupposed that the giving was null by law itself. I presuppose, however, that I do not know whether that statute was stipulated. But considering the words of that statute, I believe true that which I have premised. Finally, the said widow married a second husband, and gave the said things as dowry with the agreement that it be permitted to her to choose the things, or their estimation, in the case of the dowry to be restored. Finally, the heirs of the said first husband ratified the aforesaid donation of dowry made to the second husband on the condition that, if and insofar as they obtain, or have obtained, release from the first action for dowry. And this ratification was made after as many times as the fruits received from the said thing given unpaid in fact amounted to the quantity of the entire dowry to be estimated. Now the heirs of the said first husband wish to claim the aforesaid thing given unpaid notwithstanding the said ratification. The question is, what is the law.

† And first it is asked whether the said *datio in solutum* could have been ratified. And it seems that it could, as noted in l. 2, C. communia utriusque iuris. For that which is not valid as a judgment is valid as an agreement; for since it was done subsequently, it appears to have been submitted by tacit delivery, as in ff. de rei vend. l. quaedam mulier; ff. de aqua pluv. arc. l. praedia. For the will of the owner acceding to the possessor is regarded as delivery, as in C. de acquirenda possessione l. 2. Moreover, one may ratify to one’s own prejudice, even that which was not transacted in one’s own name, but contracted concerning one’s own thing, so that one may be repelled by an exception. The text is in ff. de pignoribus l. si fundus § 1. It is not objected, C. de rei vend. l. mater, because that law speaks in the matter of bringing an action, not in the matter of pleading an exception. To the contrary, it seems that the said ratification was made under the condition that, consequently, liberation would follow; but liberation had already been induced previously by the estimation of the fruits, as in ff. de solutionibus l. Titia. And thus the condition is false. Furthermore, what weighs more heavily is that it seems to have been made through error of law; for the one ratifying did not know that he was liberating the fruits by computation, otherwise he would not have done it. And the words indicate this, and in ratification this is notable, that it requires knowledge of both law and fact, otherwise it is not valid, as noted in the said l. mater. And the reason is clear in ff. de regulis iuris l. in totum omnia. Insofar, therefore, as the fruits diminish the dowry and the interest on the unpaid dowry, the debt has been consumed together with its accessory; therefore, concluding from the first to the last, the condition of the ratification fails, and consequently the ratification itself. Moreover, one who is able to set off is similar to one who pays; as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus l. Iul. Although set-off does not occur unless opposed by a person, nevertheless this exception is perpetual, as in Inst. de actionibus § in bonae fidei. By which reasoning it can be said that the said ratification is not valid; because it does not seem that the one erring intended anything other than the deliberation which would arise from the ratification itself, not that which arises externally from set-off. This question is doubtful to me; for the woman erring in the solemnity of the law gained the fruits, but they do not come into set-off, as noted in ff. de petitione hereditatis l. sed si lege § scire. Moreover, she herself did not receive them, but the second husband did, for the burdens of the marriage. Furthermore, the dowry after default should not be sterile, and therefore unless the debt of the first dowry is offered to the possessor, who has a cause from the woman, the thing cannot be recovered, as in l. si rem § fin. ff. de pignoribus actione; and ff. de exceptione rei iudicatae l. ex sextante § latinus. And this holds, setting aside all ratification. And even assuming that it was not in existence, it is certain that the *datio in solutum*, which did not hold against the action on the dowry, did not extinguish it, as in ff. de solutionibus l. qui res in principio. It is also certain that from the same ratification one cannot obtain both liberation and recovery of the thing, as in ff. de solutionibus l. qui hominem § ult.; and l. cum his in principio ff. de condictione indebiti.

† Therefore, concluding from the first point to the last, I say that the thing given in lieu of payment can be vindicated, the substance of the dowry being preserved. It is also certain that if the heirs of the second husband restore the estimated value to the said woman, it is considered that satisfaction has been made to her both for the first and the second dowry by a single payment alone, as in D. de distr. pign. l. Rescriptum § 1. And then the heirs of the second husband, as purchasers, succeed to the place of the woman, as in C. de iure dot. l. Si inter virum, and the right to raise the exception of the pledge is granted to them by virtue of the woman’s person; and yet it would not be granted to the woman, to whom satisfaction has been made, as in l. Fin. in princ. C. de iure dot.; D. de solut. l. Modestinus; D. de iure iur. l. Etiam; D. de act. empt. l. In venditione. We would have you advise that the giving in lieu of payment did not hold. On this point I say that the giving in lieu of payment did not hold, because the statute requires that what and how much was given in lieu of payment be described in the dowry instrument. And although under the common law there was no difference whether it was in the same document or another, as noted in a similar case in C. de testib. l. Publicati, nevertheless, because the statute goes further by annulling, what is done is not valid, as in C. de legib. l. Non dubium. And the tacit reason of the statute seems to be founded on avoiding the frauds of dowries being repeatedly claimed, as in C. de discuss. l. Ne casu, lib. 10.

Secondly, if you wish to know that the ratification is invalid, I say that it is invalid, because the woman did not consent to her ratification; therefore, a transaction between others does not prejudice the said woman, as in D. de pactis, l. si unus, § ante omnia.

Thirdly, you wish to know whether the dowry instrument ought to remain with the woman herself. I answer: yes, because since the delivery did not hold, the unpaid obligation of the dowry remained in its full force, nor was it extinguished by operation of law or by means of an exception, as stated in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, in the law *Qui res*, in the beginning. Therefore, if the instrument of credit ought to be with the creditor, as is noted in the law *Praetor*, in the beginning, in the Digest, *De edendo*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a lord may by force expel a vassal from the fief.
2. Whether another may be invested in a fief that has not been opened.
3. By what means action is brought against the real successor of a vitiated party.
4. How judgment is rendered concerning fruits.
5. Fruits are proven by presumptions.
body: It is stated,

† that the lord de facto despoiled his vassal of the possession of a feudal castle. Moreover, that this which is stated is true is proved by the notoriety of the fact. For this is a great deed, which cannot be other than notorious. For the spoliation was committed by the illustrious lord, the Lord Marquis, concerning a notable and great castle; and he who was despoiled was a notable man, whence this notoriety filled the eyes of all, and passed into the public notice of all his fellow-countrymen, so that it can be concealed by no evasion, as in Extra, de colla. cle. c. pe. et fi. For in a notorious matter we do not need witnesses, because it reveals itself, 2. q. i. c. de manifesta; ff. de act. em. l. emptorem; ff. de neg. ge. l. atqui natura. §. cum me; ff. de do. praele. l. j. in fi.; C. quoniam, et qui. quarta pars debi. l. 2; de offi. dele. c. statuimus. Most of all, however, it could not escape the notice of connected persons that he was despoiled, as in C. de resti. mino. l. de tutela; ff. vnde cog. l. octaui; and especially since they were neighbours, who cannot be ignorant of what is done publicly, as in C. de nup. l. si vicinis; ff. de fun. instr. l. si ita; ff. lo. l. dominus horreorum. It is true, therefore, as I presupposed, that the lord de facto despoiled the vassal. Secondly, I premise that the lord despoiled the vassal in an unlawful order: whence the vassal ought to have been restored immediately, as in C. vnde vi. l. inuasor, and fully noted under the same title in l. si quis in tantam, and in c. 1. §. 1. de mili. uas. qui contu. est colla. 10. That it was in an unlawful order appears because no fault of the vassal was proven, nor declared by the peers of the court, before whom the lord, if he had any cause, ought to have pursued and proved it, and not with an upright neck leap forth to an injury, as in ff. quod metus causa. l. extat, and l. fin. §. 1; and as noted in c. 1. quae fuerit prima causa benefi. amit. §. porro; and de prohi. alie. seu. per Fede. §. insuper; and in c. si quis. si de feu. fue. controuer. For on this account the vigour of judicial proceedings and the protection of public law were established in our midst, lest anyone be able to take vengeance for himself, as in C. de Iudae. l. nullus; and thus you shall judge the great and the small, nor shall there be respect of persons with you, as in C. de iudi. l. rem non nouam; and the general custom of fiefs is greater than any individual prince, and so binds him that he cannot go against it, as in c. 1. de natura feudi; and these are the first foundations for the search for truth.

† Thirdly, it is to be premised that others cannot be invested with a fief that is not open, except with the consent of the first feudatory, as in c. 1. §. rursus. quibus modis feu. amit., and in c. 1. qui succes. teneantur, in both the rubric and the black letter. For a benefice that is not vacant cannot be conferred, and it is exceedingly contrary to good morals and induces a wish to catch another's death, as in C. de pact. l. fin. Fourthly, I premise that although the interdict unde vi is personal, because it takes its origin from a person's own wrongdoing, as in ff. de ui, et ui arma. l. cum a te—and this is signified by the words of the edict, because it says 'unde vi', as in ff. de ui, et uiarma. l. i. in princ.—nevertheless other remedies are not lacking against one who succeeds into the vice, as in c. saepe. de restitutio. spolia.; 3. q. 1. c. reintegranda; and C. de agri. et cen. l. si coloni; and ff. quod metus cau. l. metus. §. in hac. Likewise, it is established that he who derives his title from a violent party is a robber and a possessor in bad faith, as in Extra, de iudi. c. quia; and C. de fru. et lit. expen. l. 2.

† Then it must be known that an abusive title, obtained through fraud and deceit, does not excuse one succeeding into a real defect on account of his own fraud from restoring the fruits that ought to have been gathered, as is noted in ff. quod metus causa. l. sed et partus. in princip., and in Specu. de fructi. et interesse. §. 1. uersi. etut praescripta. For violence is a vice affecting the property and prohibiting title and alienation, as in C. de acquir. posses. l. uitia, just as is the taint of theft, as in ff. de contrah. emptio. l. si in emptione. §. item si empttr. Likewise, it is to be premised that he who was always a robber, by building anew, is deemed to have abandoned his expenses, as is fully noted in ff. de rei uen. l. in fundo; and ff. de conditio. indebi. l. si in area; ff. communi diui. l. in hoc iudicium; ff. de nego. gest. l. si pupilli. §. sed et si quis; and noted in Specu. de expen. §. 1. But expenses that are incurred for the sake of the fruits are properly deducted from the restitution of the fruits, because the meaning of this word 'fruits' is derived from utility, not from the standing crop: ff. de usufructu. l. fundi trebaciani; ff. fami. ercisc. l. fundus; ff. solu. matrimo. l. fructus; C. de fructi. et lit. expen. l. 1. Now, with these premises laid down, the solution to the doubts will appear.

† And first, as to the first doubt, I say that so far as concerns the restitution of possession and quasi-possession, the sentence was justly rendered, as in C. ad l. iul. de ui. l. si quis ad se fundum. Secondly, I say that as to the restitution of gathered fruits, the sentence was justly rendered, saving the deduction of expenses; because that which is collected after deducting expenses is contained under the name of fruit. Thirdly, I say that with respect to the fruits to be gathered, the sentence was justly rendered for the whole time during which Usnardus possessed, but not for the time during which the ward possessed; because a ward is not bound except in so far as he has been enriched, as in ff. de regu. iur. l. neque interdicto. Fourthly, I say that upon the liquidated fruits, the sentence held good as being liquidated by reference to the acts of the proceedings, as noted in C. de sent. quae sine certa quantitate. l. 3., and by Bartolus in l. ait prętor. ff. de re iud.; but upon the unliquidated fruits, considering that we are in the interdict for recovery, and that proof is difficult, the judge—by the oath of the plaintiff, after inspecting the condition of the persons and the place—will be able to tender the oath to the plaintiff himself, and upon its taking, he will be able to declare the said sentence. For this will happen on account of the difficulty of proof, as in C. vnde vi. l. si quando; and ff. quod vi, aut clam. l. semper. §. in hoc interdicto; and what is noted in Inst. de verb. oblig. §. penul.; and by Innocent in c. fi. Extra, quod metus causa; unless perhaps as to the time during which the ward possessed, because a ward is not held except in so far as he is enriched. But concerning the time of Usnardus, I think it was rightly judged. And if it be said that this sentence was uncertain, I reply: upon these accessory matters it holds good according to the opinion of the gloss if they were not yet clear to the judge on account of the difficulty of proof, as in Inst. de acti. §. curare; and because when restitution of a castle with territory and jurisdiction is sought, the action is deemed universal, as in Extra, de ordi. cogna. c. cum dilectus, where the specification of particular items can be made in execution, as noted in l. 1. ff. de edem., by Innocent in Extra, de resti. spo. c. grauis, and de sepul. c. certificari, and C. de iur. fisci. l. facultas. lib. 10, with many similar texts. Concerning the confession of the female guardian acting as actor, I do not attach great weight to it, except in so far as it agrees with the witnesses; for since she confesses everything to the letter, it is sufficiently noted with suspicion, and regarding the said responses, the ward can be said to be undefended. Concerning the judge who pronounced sentence, as to whether he contradicted himself, it is not to be worried about, because I think the things I stated above are true; and ff. de confes. l. certum. §. sed an ipso is relevant. Likewise, relevant to what I said concerning the oath is what is noted in Spec. de fur. §. 1. ver. quid sit res, with the four following verses. But which witnesses prove and which do not prove, let the acts of the proceedings speak, because the judge, in assessing, ought to examine and approve according to the conviction of his own mind, as in ff. de testa. l. ob carmen. §. fi., and l. 3. §. tu magis; and

† one thing must not be omitted: that fruits are proved by conjectures, as noted in l. 2. C. de rescin. vend.; and just as from the fruits we infer conjecturally the value of the property, so on the other hand a proportion of the fruits, such as is involved in management, is presumed from the value of the property. And Iacobus de Arena says that that is presumed to be gathered which is commonly accustomed to be gathered according to the custom of our regions. And although he adds, and does not believe this to be true, it must be understood unless the action is against a robber, against whom a presumption suffices alongside an oath. On this, see what is noted by Iacobus on C. de rei ven. l. si feudum; and yet know that Iacobus alleges nothing of value. Bartolus says that expenses are proved by conjectures, therefore also fruits: ff. de verb. obl. l. cum seruus. That also is certain: that depositions are accounts, because witnesses swear for both parties; therefore, I can use your witnesses just as I use mine. We say this same thing in the case of written instruments, as is noted in l. 1. §. editionis. ff. de edend., in the fine notable gloss. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How are those words to be understood, that in a feudal contract the vassal shall hold [the fief] in honor of the command and service of his lord, one good horse, etc., or shall give to the said lord so many measures of wine at the time of the vintage, if it shall please the said lord more; and granted that the vassal for many years does neither, and the lord demands neither, whether the vassal has fallen from his right.
body: Among the other agreements which the vassal of the Church made with the Lord Bishop, there is such an agreement, namely: and henceforth he shall hold by the hand to the honor of the precept, and the service of the same Lord Bishop, and his successors, and of the See of Pavia, according to the custom of good and faithful vassals, one good horse, or he shall give and pay to the said Lord Bishop, and his successors, in the name of the said Bishopric, in the place of the stratella, six Piacentese congii of good and pure wine every year at the time of the vintage, if it shall please the said Lord Bishop more that the said vassal give and pay the said wine, than that he maintain the aforementioned horse. Now the said vassal has neither maintained the horse nor given the wine for many years already. And this is because he was never demanded by the said Lord Bishop, but rather, with the knowledge and tolerance of the latter, he held and possessed the said fief without any complaint or interpellation, peacefully and quietly. It is said on behalf of the said Lord Bishop that the said vassal did not observe the agreement. On the contrary, it is said that this agreement did not deserve to be observed, because the case of the agreement did not occur.

For there are two clauses, one concerning the maintenance of a horse for honor and service, and the word “command” placed in the middle refers to all, as is required in *Extra*, *de appellationibus*, c. 2. And therefore, since the bishop gave no command, the vassal is not bound, because obedience presupposes a command, as in *Digestum*, *de acquisitione haereditatis*, l. *si quis mihi bona*, §. *iussum*; and it is similar in the case of the services of freedmen, because he is not bound to offer his services unless they are indicated to him nominatively and expressly, as is fully read and noted in *Digestum*, *de conditione indebiti*, l. *si non sortem*, §. *libertus*. For the services of vassals are similar to the services of freedmen. And in the *Usus Feudorum* it is expressly provided that a vassal does not fall from his right unless he is required by the lord. Hence, in the oath of fidelity, those words are placed: “if I shall be required,” in c. 1, *de nova forma fidelitatis*. Moreover, this clause has a tacit condition, if it shall be to the lord’s interest, but here it was not to the lord’s interest, as in c. 1, *de feudo sine culpa non amittendo*. The second clause, however, is concerning the furnishing of wine. And this clause is conceived under a potestative condition: “but if it shall please the lord bishop,” which the lord bishop ought to have fulfilled at a congruous time, namely, at the time of the vintage; as in *Digestum*, *quando dies legati cedat*, l. *nec semel*, §. *si in habitatione*, and l. *firmo*. Moreover, the day does not precede the declaration of the bishop’s will, as in *Digestum*, *de legatis 1*, l. *si ita legatum*, §. *illi si volet*. And thus the bishop will lack both on account of his negligence. For this is what the text says elsewhere: “it ought not to be offered, but to make delay to the one asking,” *Digestum*, *quorum legatum*, l. *fi*, §. 1.

On the contrary, it seems that since the vassal ceased to be able to furnish the horse and the wine, he is bound to the furnishing of the wine without any other declaration. For the law provides that if a stipulation is thus conceived, “if I shall not give Stichus, I will give 10,” upon the death of Stichus, 10 are immediately due, as in *Digestum*, *de verbis obligationum*, l. *ita stipulatus*, *la grande*. Since, therefore, it ceased to be possible to do this, because flowing causes cannot be held as non-flowing, it seems sufficiently said that the wine is substituted in place of the service, as in *Digestum*, *de usufructu legato*, l. *si usus fructus mihi in biennium*. And for this, *Digestum*, *de verbis obligationum*, l. *si ita stipulatus fuero, si Titius*, §. *ult*. Moreover, according to an option bequeathed, if all the slaves have died except one, the option is not necessary, as in l. *si optio*, *Digestum*, *de optione legata*. Moreover, it seems special in the case of a debtor to the church, that he is bound to offer, even if not asked; for the church is equated to a minor, to whom irregular delay occurs, as in *Digestum*, *de legatis 2*, l. *Titia Seyo*, §. *usuras*, and l. *in minorum*, *in quibus causis in integrum restitutio est necessaria*.

This question is very doubtful. For if the words had said that he would maintain one horse for honor and services, this vassal ought to have offered; because a vassal of the church is bound to maintain. But because the word “for honor and command” is added, which signifies that the church ought to command for itself, it seems that there is a departure by pact from the privilege of the church, and we are in the common law, namely, that the debtor must be interpellated, if this is the sense, that to command is of the substance. But it seems more to be said the opposite, namely, that the word “will maintain” is obligatory, and that word “command” is not suspensive of the obligation, but consecutive, as if it said, for the purpose of obeying the command. Therefore, the vassal, who, having maintained the horse for the service to be exhibited whenever it was commanded, does not seem to have complied with the convention. Hence Jacobus de Aretio says that those who are bound to keep a horse for riding must always keep the horse ready, so that when it is commanded, without any delay, he may execute what is commanded.

Nevertheless, it must be considered that it does not seem that on account of this first head the thing falls into forfeiture, unless the second head is also not observed, which seems to be observed by the bishop declaring his will. And for the future time there is no doubt, but it is doubtful whether he wishes to ask for the wine of the preceding vintage time, when nothing was paid. For a potestative condition is not drawn back, as in *Digestum*, *qui potiores in pignore habeantur*, l. *potior*, and l. *qui balneum*, and *Digestum*, *de legatis 1*, l. *si ita legatum*, §. *ita valet*. Unless it is said that he seems tacitly to choose the wine from the perishing of the fact, for necessity itself makes the election, as in *Digestum*, *de legatis 1*, l. *cum res*, §. *si Stichus*, where it is said that if one thing of the alternatives perishes, the other, which did not perish, is due. Concurring, *Digestum*, *de solutionibus*, l. *Stichum, aut Pamphilum*, in the beginning.

Assuming therefore both possibilities, a declaration of will was necessary, as in *Digestum*, *de eo quod certo loco*, l. 3, §. *non utique*. But the fact having flowed, and the other extreme, namely, the wine, having succeeded in the obligation by the law itself, nevertheless, because the question is doubtful, not that it is such a fault by which the vassal falls from the fief, for not every occasion by which the faithful one seems ungrateful for the accepted benefit suffices for this, as in c. *Ubertus*, *de ortu*, §. *si quis*, *in quibus causis feudum amittatur*, col. 10. It must be considered that the law provides that the condition “if it displease” must be declared within 60 days. And if it is not declared, it seems to please. This is the case. *Digestum*, *de aedilicio edicto*, l. *quod si nolit*, §. *si quid ita*, and noted by Bartolus, *Digestum*, *de verborum obligatione*, l. *si quis arbitratu*, in the question which begins: “I ask, within what time.” By whose words our question seems expressly determined for the part of the episcopate; because the arbitrium of choosing was granted upon substantial matters, as in emphyteusis and lease, the pension is of the substance. Those words, therefore, “if it shall rather please,” which is the same as saying “if it shall more please,” seem sufficiently declared by the lapse of two months, and thus concerning the wine to be asked, or if this is the sense, if the service of the horse displeases, after two months have elapsed, the service seems to have pleased. But this does not seem to have been offered, nor placed in the figure of the service. For if this had been the case, it ought to have been intimated to the same lord bishop by the things noted by the same Lord Bartolus there, and *Digestum*, *de constitutione peculii*, l. *item ille*.

If, therefore, by the lapse of two months it does not seem that this displeased, but pleased, and nothing was observed, therefore the thing falls into forfeiture. Moreover, since from any head the thing falls into forfeiture, therefore the thing falls into forfeiture, although it cannot be said distinctly and clearly from which head; for it is necessary that one head be observed, as in *Digestum*, *de liberis et posthumis*, l. *Gallus*, §. *si eius*. Hence it seems to be said that the feudatory did not have good counsel; for since he ought to omit nothing of contingencies, he seems to have omitted everything. Moreover, this helps: *Digestum*, *de verborum obligatione*, l. *cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo*, in the end of the beginning, in the reason of itself.

From these, the way is open through the inquisition of truth; for things can be alleged for and against. Moreover, it can be alleged for the promisor: for if anyone stipulated alternatively, whichever he wishes, he will ask for what he chose; therefore, before the election, he will not ask, as in *Digestum*, *de verborum obligatione*, l. *si quis stipulatus sit Stichum*. Moreover, a condition added to rescind or to transfer must exist, as in *Digestum*, *de in diem adiectione*, l. 2. And similarly a condition added to declare something, as in *Codex*, *de contrahenda emptio*, l. *fi*; or to modify something, as in *Digestum*, *de contrahenda emptio*, l. *haec venditio*; or to show the will, as in *Digestum*, *de legatis 3*, l. *fideicommissum*, §. *quanquam*.

But these not standing in the way, I consider that this obligation is not alternative, but disjunctive, because both are not in the obligation, but the service is in the principal obligation, and the wine in the secondary obligation, and in the power of the second’s good pleasure a novation was made against the will of the creditor, since he has the election; therefore the first head of the obligation is not novated, even if the legal penalty had been incurred; for the legal penalty does not induce novation, as in l. 2, *Codex*, *de iure emphyteuticario*. We seem finally to reduce the understanding of the said §. *si quid*, so that since the service is understood to have pleased the lord of this contract, and if it is not performed, the thing falls into forfeiture. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, when an action for the recovery of an inheritance is brought, the defendant is to be interrogated as to whether he has the ability to restore the property. And whether he is to be interrogated as to whether he holds possession by virtue of a will or intestacy, and whether the will is valid and solemn, or not. And number 2. And add the following opinion.
body: In the procedure for bringing a petition for inheritance, the inquiry is conducted for the purpose of expediting the trial, namely whether the prospective putative defendant possesses or holds the property, as in any real action, as stated in D. de interrogatione actionis, l. qui servum, § in iure. Furthermore, it must be inquired whether he possesses the whole or a part, as there, and in the same title, l. non alienum. Moreover, he must be asked whether he possesses as heir; and if he says no, he must be asked whether he possesses as possessor, as C. de petitione hereditatis, l. cogi. And if he says that he does not possess as heir or possessor, but by a just title, he must be asked by what and what kind of title, as there, noted, and D. de petitione hereditatis, l. qui interrogatus. But whether he ought to be asked whether he has the ability to restore the thing, I answer: no, for either this inquiry is superfluous, as if he says that he possesses, or if he says that he has ceased to possess through fraud or fault. Or it is irrelevant: because although someone has the ability to restore the thing, if nevertheless he does not possess, or quasi-possess, nor has he ceased to possess through fraud or fault, he cannot be sued, as D. de usucapione, l. servi nomine. Moreover, whether if he says that he possesses by testament, the solemnity or non-solemnity of the testament should be disputed here. I answer: this inquiry is premature, and he is not bound to respond as to whether it is solemn or not: because this requires a deeper investigation, since it concerns the decisive issue of the case, and does not pertain to interrogatories, but to positions, which are made after joinder of issue, and pertain more to the title on confessions than to the title on interrogatory actions, as noted in D. de interrogatione actionis, l. 1, in the gloss beginning "scilicet circa." Moreover, because no law provides that he is to be asked about this before joinder of issue, or that the judge ought to ask about this ex sua aequitate (by his own equity), therefore there is no need for this inquiry to be answered, otherwise certain enumerated cases would be in vain. For argument from enumeration of parts is valid in law, as D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. patre furioso. I concede, however, that the person interrogated must respond from which testament, and whence he has his cause, just as he is compelled to respond about the title and its quality by the aforementioned l. cogi. And this concludes the first part of the interrogatory. Now it remains to see

† On the second part: because the plaintiff demands an answer on this point, namely, whether the will is solemn, and if it is solemn, he intends to bring an action for the restitution of the inheritance on the ground of a fideicommissum, and thus he demands an answer in the disjunctive, and he passes from a direct claim for the intestate inheritance to an action based on the will. And I say that this interrogation cannot be made, because neither should this alternative libel be admitted, since the plaintiff is contradicting himself, as in C. de codicillis, l. si, and l. 1, C. de furtis, and ff. de tributoria, l. quod in heredem, §. eligere. Therefore, let him who is about to act make the choice himself, and not demand to be informed by the defendant on this choice. But let him consider it himself, as in C. de edendo, l. ipse dispice. Moreover, no law provides that an interrogation should be made in this way; nor is there any equity that the defendant should inform the plaintiff which action he should bring, for interrogations are made to establish the defendant in court, so that he may make himself an adversary, as in C. de alienatione iudiciaria, l. 1, not to instruct the plaintiff which action he should choose, because no one is bound to instruct his adversary, except in cases expressly stated in law, as in l. 1, C. de liberatione agnatorum, and there by Jacobus de Arena. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What interrogatories may be posed by one intending to bring an action for the recovery of an inheritance, and to which the defendant is bound to respond; on which matter also see the preceding opinion above. And some elegant remarks concerning protestation.
2. What is contained in an appeal by a party in a judicial proceeding.
body: Acturuis

† In a petition for inheritance intestate, the plaintiff first requests that the future defendant be interrogated as follows: namely, first, whether he holds or possesses the said inheritance, or at least has the ability to restore it. The question arises whether this interrogation must be answered. I answer: either the one who requests the interrogation takes an oath against calumny, stating what he believes, or he does not. If he does not take such an oath, the gloss in l. 1, C. de confessis, at the end of the great gloss, states that the interrogation need not be answered if it concerns matters of calumny or cruelty. In that case, three articles of the said interrogation must be considered. The first is whether he ought to restore it; to this he must answer, as stated in D. de rei vend., l. officium. The second is whether he possesses it; to this he must answer that the petition for inheritance is principally an action in rem, although it is called mixed due to the conjunction of personal obligations, as stated in D. de in integrum restitutione, l. qui servum, § in iure; and D. de re iudicata, l. 1; and D. si pars hereditatis petatur, l. 1, in principio; and C. in quibus causis cessat longi temporis praescriptio, l. hereditatem; and C. de petitione hereditatis, l. hereditatis. The third article is whether he has the ability to restore it; and regarding this, doubt may arise.
