For since one who has the ability to restore is bound to undergo judgment, as stated in D. de exhibendis, l. de eo, § 1, therefore he ought to be interrogated on this point. To the contrary, it seems that if he is not bound and does not possess, mere ability does not make him an adversary, nor can judgment be founded against him. For the law is not so, as stated in D. de usucapione, l. servi nomine. The interrogation continues: also, whether he holds it in solidum or pro parte, etc. I answer that just as he ought to be interrogated about the whole, so also about the part, as stated in the aforementioned § iniuriae.

† Item, and concerning a certain part, nevertheless the name of part contains a half, if it is stated without an addition, although a certain gloss says that the name of part uttered in court is simply obscure, as in D. de procuratoribus, l. Pomponius, §. sed criminis. Therefore, so that one does not proceed in equivocation, one must be asked for which part; there follows an interrogation. Item, whether with a title or without a title. And of this one must be asked, because the defendant must instruct the plaintiff, so that the plaintiff may found the libel from the person of the defendant, that is, from the fact of the defendant: and all interrogatory actions, that is, interrogatory articles, were invented for this purpose. For if the defendant intends to make himself a defendant, and to found the judgment, he must be inquired from what head he makes himself an adversary, as in C. de petitione hereditatis, l. cogi. and noted in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. qui interrogatus. There follows an interrogation, and if he answers that he is asked with a title, with what title? This can be understood of a title in general, for example, for a gift, or for a buyer. And in this a certain gloss says words little intelligible: unless by diminution. And therefore the gloss says that they are dreams; it can also be understood whether he is bound to say in hope, namely, from such or such, so that it may appear whether the title is held as no title. And the glosses commonly say that he is to be asked. Understand this to the effect that the future plaintiff may deliberate whether he ought to sue or not; he is not bound to produce the title in which consists the peremptory exception, or the joinder of issue, as in C. de probationibus, l. siue possidetis. There follows an interrogation. If, however, he answers that he did not possess, he is asked whether he ceased to possess through fraud. The doctors say that an interrogation must always be made, even if it were made by way of a challenge [postae], it would not be answered. For he who asks does not allege a crime, but he who alleges alleges more easily; therefore one is compelled to answer an interrogation by way of a challenge, because by interrogation a crime is not imputed, as in D. de noxa, l. quotiens, §. praetor. But it seems that by civil law even a challenge must be answered, as in D. rerum amotarum, l. Marcellus. And there by Bartolus. But Bartolus says badly, as noted by Innocentius in c. dudum, de electione. For one is not bound to confess a crime, nor even to deny it; for perhaps he would be perjurious in denying. Nor does l. Marcellus stand in the way, because there it speaks when an oath was tendered to the respondent, as a term of the lawsuit for its decision, not to relieve the adversary from the burden of proof, as in C. de edendo, l. qui accusare. And therefore one is not compelled to answer concerning an alleged crime, except at two times, namely, the time when the issue is joined; for one must answer upon the libel, and the time of torture, and whatever Bartolus says. There follows a certain protestation in this form, with a protestation that he does not intend to prejudice himself in his other rights, if it should happen that A. made a valid testament, upon which article I say that a protestation contrary to law is not valid. And therefore whenever there are remedies, a protestation operates nothing, as in l. 1, C. de furtis; D. de petitione hereditatis, l. postquam; C. de inofficioso testamento, l. contra maiores; C. de codicillis, l. fin. Just as we say in a similar manner concerning that protestation saving the right to add and subtract; because against laws a statute does not validate a protestation, de re iudicata, c. abbate. Item, in prejudicial matters a protestation does not avail, as noted in Clem. gratiae, de rescriptis. We see a similar thing in alimony, if a father protests that he supports his son with the intention of recovering. For a protestation is of no effect, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Nesennius Appollinarius. Item, in the interdict of new work a protestation contrary to law is not valid, as in D. de novi operis nuntiatione, l. de pupillo, §. si quis riuos. There follows an interrogation, if, however, it should happen that a valid testament is found, it is asked whether he is an heir by testament, since he is about to act by fideicommissum. This is in effect, and this interrogation is well among the permitted ones, if it is made in due order, namely, that the heir is bound to answer concerning his own fact, not another's, as in D. de interrogatione actionum, l. 1. and C. de iure deliberandi, l. si curatoris. But here it is not made in due order. For since first the contrary way was placed, namely, intestate, and now a transition is made to the way of testate, these are contrary ways from the origin, that is, from the source, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. ius nostrum. There it says that naturally there is a conflict between testate and intestate. Hence it appears that this digression is foolish, where even variation is not permitted, at least in the meantime, as in d. l. fi, C. de codicillis. And therefore this interrogatory from the words "If, however, it should happen to be found" to the end, as contrary to law and reason, must be rejected; indeed, also because the actor is contrary to himself, at least in the meantime; nor can two contraries coexist simultaneously, he destroys himself, as I said at the beginning. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. But if the thing to be sold is common property, and it is added that it shall be given to the highest bidder, is the second-to-last bidder compelled to accept it, even though the last bidder offered something more, but was absent at the time of the sale of the said thing, or otherwise does not pay, or cannot provide suitable sureties? And this is a most excellent opinion.
body: The method and form of the auction of *datia* in the city of Ancona is as follows. For, first, a *datium* is set at a certain sum of money without any obligation of an overbid. Then it is said thus: such a *datium* is set at so great a quantity, for example, one thousand; if anyone promises more, he shall have such a quantity of money by way of overbid for every pound of money which he promises in excess. And thus the bidding proceeds successively for a certain time, before the *datium* is sold freely and awarded to the offeror, or to the one wishing to offer. It happens that within the said time several have bid for the *datium* of the merchants with an obligation of money for the overbid, and the second-to-last bidder promised three thousand pounds, or offered it by the customary words in such auctions, namely by saying to the notary appointed for this purpose, “Write down for me such a *datium* at three thousand pounds,” and this was done; but the last bidder offered a greater quantity by similar customary words. Finally, before the time for selling the *datium* and awarding it arrived, this last promisor departed from the country without bidding farewell to his host; so that neither he nor another on his behalf was found at the time of the sale of the *datium*, nor was he solvent, nor had he provided a surety, since sureties are not provided for the departure from the country unless by the buyer at the time of the sale, to whom the *datium* is sold freely. Now the question arises whether, by law, the second-to-last bidder is compelled to receive the *datium* for the quantity promised by him, the last bidder not being found, who had promised such or a greater quantity.

† And it is argued that the said penultimate bidder is not bound, because he appears to have been displaced by another offering more. For in the auction it is not stated that the contract shall be awarded to the more suitable person, but to the higher bidder; and since a higher amount was offered, therefore, by the force of the words, he withdrew from the penultimate bidder. For the law provides that he who promised to give a surety is deemed to have observed what he promised, even if he gives one not suitable in terms of assets, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. qui satisdare plane. Hence, it is not necessary to care whether he is solvent or not, provided he is such a person as can be bound. But notwithstanding these arguments to the contrary, the truth is otherwise. And this is proved by the same law. For it is required that he be such a person as can be bound and sued, as in that law, l. primo responso. But this person, who has left his country, cannot be sued; therefore, he is not suitable, as in D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. sciendum; and note in Auth. de exhibendis reis, §. suscepto; and D. de procuratoribus, l. neque foemina. It is also proved by the aforementioned l. qui satisdare, at the end, by the reason of itself: there, “because he who admitted etc.,” from the contrary sense. For this last bidder was not proved suitable, nor was there a contract with him, as clearly appears from the facts of the case. Certainly, this is also proved by another reason. For, in order for someone to be said to offer more, there is required suitability of assets, a greater promise, utility, and ease of suing, as in D. de in diem additione, l. vbi autem, §. pen. and fin. But here is the exact opposite, because neither ease of suing, nor equal utility, nor equal quantity can exist where someone is not solvent. For he who has nothing from which to pay is similar to one having an exception, as noted in D. de procuratoribus, l. Litius. And thus, with regard to the obligation, he is not considered suitable when compared to one who is solvent. Moreover, the words of the auction must be understood with effect, as noted in the common gloss in the aforementioned l. qui satisdare; as in l. 1, in princ., D. qui satisdare cogantur; and l. 1, D. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit. Moreover, one is not understood to have offered unless he also observed the certain conditions which he ought to observe; but this person did not observe the certain conditions: because he did not proceed to a perfect contract, nor did he provide suitable sureties; and therefore he should not be approved, as in D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. arbitro. Moreover, in the case of the fiscus there is no doubt: because the fiscus can choose the more suitable person, since this is also permitted to a private person, as in D. de in diem additione, l. Sabinus. Moreover, a higher bid is admitted only if the person who won the auction is ready to provide suitable sureties as security, as in D. de publicanis, l. licitatio, in princ. Considering therefore both the common law and the law of the fiscus, it must be said without doubt that the said penultimate bidder is bound by his bid as the stronger one, indeed as the last one. For the last is that after which nothing valid follows; and he is compelled according to the form of his bid, the last bid being held insufficient and null to the prejudice of the fiscus. This is also manifest, because the said bid is made in favor of the fiscus, and therefore that which is more useful to the fiscus must be accepted. Moreover, otherwise it would follow that fraud could be devised, because he who bid improperly could cause someone else to permit a non-suitable person, in order to free himself from the obligation. Which is absurd, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. si cum lis. Moreover, the fiscus does not accept unless the debtors are sufficient and the goods sufficient, as in D. de iure fisci, l. 1, §. an bona. Moreover, it applies to the reason of itself: D. de lege Iulia, l. si seruus plurium, §. si quis ante. And in this conclusion I rest, that the said penultimate bidder is entirely bound, and is not freed from the obligation by another who permits a fraudulent person. Certainly, the republic does not seem to have given this in its instructions to the auctioneers, that they may dismiss a suitable person and accept a non-suitable one, as in D. de pactis, l. si in personam, §. si pecuniam; and D. de usuris, l. si bene; and devised in fraud of the fiscus. And all transactions devised in fraud of the fiscus are rejected by the law, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and how, it is to be proven that a wound is mortal or not; and whether, and how, it is to be proven that someone died from the wound, or from another cause, or from poor custody, or from a combination thereof. And this is a fine opinion for instructing a judge as to how he ought to inquire into the truth in such hidden matters.
body: Whether a wound

† Was mortal or not, and whether someone died from the wound, or from bad care, or from a mixture of both, is a question of fact rather than of law, as in ff. de sta. ho. l. idem erit. and ff. ad l. aqui. l. si ex plagiis. §. in cliuo; nevertheless, it is determined by arguments and reasons. For every doubtful question is determined either by arguments or by reasons, as in ff. ad trebel. l. qui filium. in fi. In the proposed question, moreover, arguments are drawn from three things: first from nature, second from experience, third from the art and testimony of physicians. I say that arguments are drawn first from nature: for if the person struck died immediately, that is, within three days, nature itself in a certain way shows that he died from the wound, unless the contrary were proved from evident reasons, for instance, from an infection in the groin, or from a mortal plague, as noted in l. 1. C. de emen. seruorum. But if someone died after long intervals of time, then he would not be presumed to have died from the wound, because things that occur after a long interval do not seem to be inherent, unless it were openly proved that it was from the wound, as because he was struck with a poisoned arrow that could not be cured. And this is proved by the same gloss on C. de emenda. seruorum. And the reason for the difference is that nature defers terminal suffering very little. If, however, it is apparent for a long time, the suffering was weak from the beginning; whence death did not proceed principally from the wound, but on account of the fault of the sick person, which ought not to be imputed to the one who inflicted the wound, as in ff. ad l. aquil. l. qui occidit. §. fina., and there is an ordinary gloss in ff. solu. matri. l. ab hostibus. §. si vir vxorem. Secondly, I said that arguments are drawn from experience. For we experience that the location is either mortal, as in the brain, the throat, the chest, the intestines, and the like: then one dies from the wound. But if in non-lethal locations, as in the buttock, which can withstand great wounds, as we see in men and in beasts of burden, from which one does not usually die. If, therefore, a defect on the part of the sick person is proved, the fault of the sick person outweighs, because the blow was not directed toward the danger of death. Likewise, the instrument with which someone was struck must also be considered, as in extra de homi. ca. significasti. and ff. ad l. Corne. de sica. l. 1. §. sed si claua. Likewise also the magnitude of the wound. Likewise whether a spasm supervened on account of the wound, because he was struck in nervous locations; and, in short, the judge ought to contemplate everything pro and contra, and in doubt always adhere to the more benign side: the text is in ff. ad l. aquil. l. Item mella. §. si plures. Thirdly, he said that an argument is drawn from the art of physicians: for everywhere every expert must be believed in his art, especially when someone is a doctor or a licentiate, and thus approved by public authority, or one who has long been reputed suitable through wholesome practices and experiences, or because he assigns reasons according to the canons of medicine from his own sight and touch, as in l. semel. C. de re mili. lib. 10. and de aduo. diuer. iudic. l. nemini. §. iurisperitos. and in l. vlti. C. de ponderatoribus auri. and de verbo. obli. l. 1. §. fin. Indeed, this testimony of skilled physicians, who were present from the beginning of the disease and afterward, the judge ought to embrace, because they know and can truly testify, and they are presumed to speak the truth, because truth is always presumed in a sworn witness, just as in instruments, as in C. de probationibus. l. cum precibus. If, therefore, the physicians prove this, and the location was not of itself mortal, and the fault of the wounded man is proved, it is certain that he did not die from the wound, or that it is at least doubtful; and therefore the mind of the judge ought to incline to the milder side: because where the life of a human being is at stake, doubtful proofs do not suffice to inflict death, but they ought to be clearer than the midday light, as in C. de probatio. l. fi. Therefore, although a question of fact is in the discretion of the one judging, ff. ad turpillia. l. 1. §. calumniatoribus, nevertheless he ought to look at all things, and according to the signs that preponderate pass sentence, which I think ought to be absolutory regarding the homicide, and condemnatory regarding the wound, according to those things that are set forth in the case. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. On the change of the riverbed, the flood, and whether in such cases prescription is more beneficial.
body: The following facts have occurred: A community constructed a mill some forty years ago and more, by diverting water to the said mill, which it drew from the river Grana. And thus they held and possessed it for the said period of forty years. It is true that for some fifteen years, or thereabouts, the said community widened the channel leading water to the said mill, and made it broader than before, through certain lands of the said community, which it purchased from the men of Camagna; nevertheless, the said lands are not within the district of the community of Camagna, but within the district of the community of Lu. Or let us even suppose that they are within the district of the said community of Camagna. Recently, however, a bill of complaint was filed against the said community of Lu. by a certain nobleman holding the said land of Camagna in fief from the Lord Marquis, both in his own name and in the name of the said community of Camagna. In this bill it is contained that the said community and the men of the place of Lu., on the bank of the river Grana, which river is subject to their control, and which bank it is, is thus stated in and concerning the power of Camagna in the place where it is said to be at the fountain of Grana, to which bank they adjoin, etc. The men of Camagna constructed a certain waterwork, which they call a "bale," a diversion of the water of the said river, on account of which work the course and flow of the said river is said to become worse and more deteriorated, and the flow of the water of the same river lower, to the damage of the said plaintiffs. They therefore demand that the said work be destroyed, and other matters contained in the bill. It is true that the illustrious Lord Marquis, in the year of our Lord 1355, granted to the said community of Lu. the faculty of constructing one or more mills on the stream of Grana, before the said noble plaintiff had any right in Camagna, but it belonged freely to the Lord Marquis. These things being thus presupposed, the question is asked: what is the law?

And it is held that the said work, being manual, could not have been made, if it is proved that the place is within the territory of Camagna; because one cannot intrude into another’s jurisdiction, as in D. 8.5 (Si servitus vendicetur), l. Sicuti, § Arist. Moreover, because the banks of public rivers belong to those who possess lands near the bank, therefore nothing can be built there against their will, as in Inst. 2.1 (De rerum divisione), § Riparum. Furthermore, interdicts have been granted so that nothing may be done in a public river or its bank: as in D. 43.12 (Ne quid in flumine publico), in the rubric and in the text. But the contrary seems true: because the Prince, i.e., the Marquis, granted this; because he could do so in his free territory, as in D. 43.8 (De fluminibus), l. Quo minus. Here it must be considered that prescription was not raised against the said faculty: because no one was in contrary or obstructive possession, and since no one prescribed, therefore the one having the right did not lose his right, as in D. 41.2 (Quibus ex causis maiores), l. Sciendum and l. Denique, together with the following law. Moreover, because he who uses part of a faculty, while not being hindered in the other part of the entire faculty, retains quasi-possession, as in D. 7.6 (Quemadmodum servitus amittitur), l. Si in partem. Furthermore, there is no doubt that a work which was made for 40 years is prescribed in favor of the doer, as in C. 7.33 (De praescriptione 40 annorum), l. Omnes. It also seems sufficiently manifest that this is a prescription of a certain use, in which 10 years between present parties suffice, even without title; because prescription runs only against an adversary, so that he cannot prohibit, as in D. 8.5 (Si servitus vendicetur), l. Si quis diuturno, and fully noted in D. 7.1 (De usu), l. Cum de in rem verso. It is also said on behalf of the said community of Lucca that the said river of Grana is not in the possession of Camagna, but in the possession and permissive use of both communities, and that what is common is not mine: as in D. 10.3 (Communi dividundo), l. Sabinus. Moreover, by the same law it appears that, since the work was done by one partner with the other suffering it, especially for a long time, the work ought not to be destroyed. It seems to me, having considered the aforesaid arguments for and against, that the said prescription of 40 years undoubtedly stands in the way regarding that which was attempted and possessed for 40 years. But regarding that which was made afterwards and stood for a long time, it is not so clear, if it were proved that it was made in the possession and district of Camagna. But if this is not proved, the lord of Camagna would not have justice, nor would the men who possess lands near the bank, unless they proved something else, unless from present possession; similarly, they would not have a founded claim. Moreover, because they suffered it for a long time, and thus it seems prescribed, or at least a certain custom was introduced, as in l. Venditor, § Si constat, D. 10.3 (Communia prœdiorum). However, this article is not entirely settled, as I said. But the article of 40 years has no doubt. Likewise, there was no doubt that the said Marquis could grant, since he holds the place of a Prince, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a notary who cancels records should be punished for falsification, and what if he annulled a condemnation.
body: A certain notary wrote in the book of condemnations that a certain condemnation made for three pounds was made for one pound and five shillings, and he canceled the word "three pounds." He also drew his pen twice across it, intending to show that the said condemnation had been satisfied. And it is true that the said notary was not a notary authorized to write the said satisfaction; therefore, so that he may not be condemned for forgery, he claims that his writing was invalid. The question is, what is the law? I answer,

† That the said writing and cancellation do not constitute proof of payment and of the cancellation, and from this it could be argued in favor of the said notary, because the writing appears to be rather private than public: as in *l. si quis privatum*, D. de falsis. Nevertheless, I see no response to the point regarding the cancellation: because whoever he may be who cancels public records, he falsifies them and causes the truth not to appear: as in D. de falsis, *l. 1*, § *qui rationibus*. And therefore he is liable: *l. Cor.*, D. de falsis; as in C. de test., *l. si unus*. Also, by the decree of the Lord. And although the offense of words is sometimes excused, as noted by Cynus in *l. 1*, C. de sepulcro violato; D. de falsis, *l. si quis legatum*, nevertheless I do not see how the cancellation, which is an act, and regardless of by whom it is made, can remain without being punished by the penalty for falsification, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a private document lacking a date or the name of the consul proves anything, at least in favor of the Church.
2. Whether a document is valid in which it does not appear what quantity is owed by way of a livery (livellum).
3. Whether a document is contrary in which someone states that he holds a certain territory by right of livery.
4. Whether someone may lease his own property by way of livery.
5. Whether a confession made out of court before worthy persons is valid.
6. Whether census books prove.
body: The Reverend Vetus alleges a memorandum written in the hand of Lord John, and the words of the memorandum are as follows: I

† Ioan. Algardus de Feltro legum doctor, assero me teneri episcopatui Feltri nomine census iure liuelli pro quodam meo Fologono, quod consueuit esse Molendinum positum in Sancto Vocato. iuxta ecclesiam Sanctae Mariae. non scribitis mihi, quod in schedula contineatur aliquid plus. et videtur, quod dicta schedula non valeat: quia non continet diem, et consulem, vt in Auth. vt praeponatur nomen Imperatoris. in prin. et no. C. de tabulis. l. generali. lib. 10. In contrarium quod valeat, videtur tex. ff. de pig. l. cum tabernam. §. idem quaesiit. Secundo

It appears that the said document is invalid, because it does not specify what quality is to be understood by the term "livello," as stated in the Digest, under the title "On Obligations Arising from Words," in the law *Triticum*, and in the law *Certum*, under the title "On Confessions." But to this it is replied that the said document is authenticated by the payments of the censuses, because such things are as their subjects declare them to be, as stated in the Digest, under the title "On Legacies," in the law *Si servus plurium*, § *Finis*. Thirdly, it appears that the said document is invalid, because it states "for a certain my Fologono." For the word "my" signifies ownership, as stated in the Digest, under the title "On Legacies," in the law *Stichum*, which will be mine.

† Hence this document, as being self-contradictory, is invalid: for first he said “by right of enfiteusis,” and secondly he said “my own.” For since an enfiteusis is a kind of lease, as in Inst. De loc. cond. §. adeo, no one can lease his own property: as in C. De loc. cond. l. qui rem

† But to this it is answered by the statement of Bartolus, who says that, on the contrary, one may take his own property from the church by leasehold (livello); for it is understood that the church grants him the ownership, as he beautifully notes in the Digest, De acquisitione possessionis, l. Si aliquam rem.

Secondly, your reverence alleges the confession of the said Lord John, made out of court before worthy persons. But it seems that the said confession is not valid, as in C. de iur. et facti igno. l. cum falsa, and noted in ff. de interro. act. l. 1. On the contrary, it seems that the said confession is strongly supported in favor of the church, as in extra de succes. ab intest. c. cum dilectus. Likewise

† First, for the episcopal see, the censal books were alleged. But it seems that they do not prove, because they are domestic books, as C. de probat. l. rationes. On the contrary, it seems that they prove, if they are written by hand, as in c. ad evidentiam, de praescript. de censu; c. cum olim; and noted extra de probat. c. cum causam. From which it is concluded that the episcopal see has justice. For the said Lord John could not bequeath more right than he had, as C. de legat. l. uxor patrui; and ff. de pactis l. lex vectigalis; and ff. de contrahenda empt. l. qui tabernas; and ff. de legat. 1. l. qui domus, §. si. Moreover, it is certain that the emphyteusis of the church does not pass to an alien heir, as noted in l. etiam, ff. sol. matr.; nor even to another church upon the death of the emphyteuta, as noted by Innocentius de probat. c. in praesentia. This is not obstructed by a certain instrument of sale produced by the opposing party; because a transaction between others does not prejudice the church; otherwise, ecclesiastical rights could easily be overturned, as ff. de pactis l. si unus, §. ante omnia; and noted by Cynus C. de locat. l. desiderium; and it is expressly clear, C. de aqua pluv. arcend. l. ex liberis; and it applies in Auth. de alienat. et empt. §. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, concerning the same controversies and causes, one may repeatedly submit to arbitration and have awards rendered.
2. What difference there is between a null sentence and one rendered by a judge lacking jurisdiction.
body: It is alleged that a certain arbitral award was rendered between partners, in which certain names of debts were adjudicated to one, and certain others to the other; and one of them was ordered to produce the consignments, and afterwards the account books. Finally, a controversy arose concerning the said assigned debtors; and because the account books were alleged to be corrupted, and certain other matters, a new compromise was made regarding the said controversies, and any others whatsoever. The second arbitrators exchanged the said adjudications of the names to one of them for a certain sum of money. Ultimately, the said award was declared unjust and null. Afterwards, the judge of reduction confirmed it. Now it is again declared null. The question is, what is the law, having regard to the decree of the lord. And

It seems that one must first say that the sentence of the said second arbitrators was not valid by operation of law. And this for a twofold reason. First, because there could not be a compromise regarding that matter, and upon that matter, upon which judgment had been given and which had passed into res iudicata, as in D. de transactionibus, l. post rem. For even with the consent of the parties, it cannot be done that a sentence be valid against a sentence, as noted in C. de transactionibus, l. si diuersa. And according to Cynus in l. 1, C. quando prouocare non est necesse, in the second objection. The second reason is that a sentence which has passed into res iudicata cannot be amended nor changed, as in l. 1, C. sententia resendi non posse. The third reason is that it is not probable that there was a compromise concerning matters decided, nor that the parties wished to novate the sentence, unless it had been stated specially and expressly. See D. de nouatione, l. aliam. Notwithstanding the decree of the Lord: because the words of the decree say that the sentence was confirmed. But just as a sentence passed by a judge incompetent neither in fact nor in name is a sentence, as in l. si, C. si a non competenti iudice, and l. 2, §. eum, D. de pęnis, so too a sentence passed by no arbitrator, or by an incompetent arbitrator, and especially when it exceeds the limits of the mandate, as in D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, §. quaesitum, and l. qui tamen. Moreover, there is a difference:

† Because when a sentence is null, yet it has the name of a sentence before it is declared null, as noted in l. si, C. de ordi. cogni. But when it is from an incompetent judge, it is never considered as anything, nor by name, nor by presumption of law, as noted in cle. 1. de sequestra. pos. and facit. ff. de proba. l. cum precibus, there, nor to etc. Moreover, a judge cannot confirm a sentence issued by someone entirely deprived and lacking all power, as ff. de ac. et ob. l. obligationes, which do not consist in their own strength etc. In the contrary, the truth seems to be. For it is certain that due to a new doubt, a new judgment can be instituted, and a new sentence is valid, and similarly a new compromise, as ff. de condi. indeb. l. eleganter. §. si post. But here arises a new doubt, which is said, that the code of accounts was adulterated. It is certain that for this cause restitution in integrum would be granted, as ff. de re iudi. l. diuus. and ff. de exceptio. l. quis agnitis. Similarly, the law says that action is taken for money taken away, even though it has been settled, as ff. de pac. l. tres fratres. I do not make force, whether restitution in integrum can be compromised or not, because since the statute disposes of the execution of the sentence of arbitrators, therefore it makes delegated judges, I do not say ordinary: because they are not for the universality of causes, as C. de iudi. l. cum specialis. ver. et executorie. and there noted, this clearly appears: because the sentence issued through fraud still remains the first action, about which compromise can be made, as ff. de dolo. l. cum a te. Also, there is a tacit clause in compromises. s. malice to be absent, obstructive, as ff. de arbi. l. ita demum. Also, when after the sentence arises a question of nullity, there is no doubt that this question must be known and pronounced, and the sentence is valid, as noted ff. de appel. l. si expressim. and fully noted in I. 1. C. quando prouocare non est necesse. Also, the award of the arbitrator is more similar to a transaction than definitive. And it is certain that the last transaction prevails, as C. de pac. l. pacta nouissima. And therefore there is no doubt in the proposed theme, that both the second sentence and the third are valid in law. I say more, that the word, first sentence, which is in the decree of the lord, is understood broadly, with s. having made mention of nullity, thus. ff. quęmadmodum testamenta aperiantur. l. 2. And therefore there is no doubt that the last confirmatory sentence was valid, which by the decree of the lord imposed silence on all further controversy. And thus is the response clearly to the doubt, which is asked, namely, that the last sentence deserves execution, and that the decree of the lord speaks of it notwithstanding in another part alleged, by which it clearly appears responded. In the same fact. To the same. Of this same matter.

Considering the second compromise, since in it the compromise was made regarding every cause that could be raised and conceived, I say without doubt that the second award should be upheld. For no reasonable doubts could arise against the first award, nor could any be raised without some injury to the first arbitrators. For the first arbitrators could have erred in fact, for example, in the calculation of accounts, as in C. de errore calculi, l. 1. And although if this were the case it would be lawful for the contracting parties to deceive themselves and for the victor to claim the palm, nevertheless this does not accord with a good man, as noted in ff. de reg. iur., l. semper in conventionibus. And therefore, that the matter be reviewed and calculated anew, the reason will not deviate from equity, and the compromise is valid. Secondly, it may be that the account books did not make full faith in law: and if they were written legally, as it were, like the Gospel, as in C. de probat., l. exemplo, and l. si, C. de conveniendis fisci debitoribus, lib. 10, whence this doubt could have been raised in law. Also, it may be that in the accounts themselves there was some suspicion, not due to the fault of the writer, but from an external source, as in C. de testam., l. si unus. Also, it may be that the arbitrators did not know the quality of the names adjudicated, such that they adjudicated bad names for good names: as in ff. si certum petatur, l. periculum. Since therefore these things are possible, and the compromise was made regarding all possibilities, the second compromise was valid; because a compromise regarding a possible doubt is well valid. And by this very fact it is understood that there was a doubt, which the arbitrator declared, as in ff. de peculio, l. quod debetur, and l. super servis, C. qui militibus non possunt. Moreover, this conclusion must be firmly held, that if it is cognized again and anew by the will of the parties, the sentence is well valid; otherwise, if nothing is cognized anew: the first is proved expressly in ff. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. duobus; the second is proved in C. de transactionibus, l. si diversa. And it is induced to this that, since the arbitrator and umpire pronounced, it is presumed that he cognized; although otherwise in a true judge and mere arbitrator, and the reason is, because in the umpire his faith is elected, and it is necessary that he receive proofs, unless he wishes, as noted by Dynus in his consilia, in the consilium which begins Ptholomeus manentis. Whence it appears that the second award was valid. But why more? Suppose that the second had not been valid, the sentence of the judge confirming it followed. Now I say that the sentence of the confirming judge passes from nothing to something: as noted in ff. de appellationibus, l. si expressim, and C. quoniam provocationes non est necesse, l. 1. Thus therefore the second award was confirmed. And here it must be observed, that according to Bartolus and Innocentius, from this sentence one cannot appeal, as noted by Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de legatis 2. Although I am not of this opinion in common law, nevertheless by the form of the decree of our lord, I do not doubt that one can appeal further, or that it cannot be declared null. And if the second award is well considered, it was not contrary to the first, not by the permutation of names for quantity, but it is rather a certain diversity, such that he who did not make the names should have money for them, as in ff. de administratione tutorum, l. ita cum quaeritur, and l. ita constante, ff. de iure dotium. Finally, whether he made or did not make the names, I do not care, because everything passed with the matter expedited, such that henceforth nothing can be retracted. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. He who says that the crime of usury is lawful is a heretic.
2. Whether one who believes that a manifest usurer can make a will, even contrary to the form of the chapter *Quanquam*, is to be judged a heretic.
3. Whether it is lawful for a Prince to make a statute contrary to that decree.
4. Whether a sentence passed against an heir instituted in the will of a manifest usurer prejudices his sons in the substitutions, when the case of the said substitutions occurs, without them having been cited.
5. Whether the sentences passed on the *apodissa* are to be upheld.
body: It must be premised

† It is evident that he who says the crime of usury is lawful is an adversary of divine law. And he asserts two contradictories to be true at the same time, namely, crime and lawful. But he who believes that it is lawful is a heretic, because he errs in an article of faith, since he does not believe the Gospel nor the Old Testament. And if this person were Emperor, he ought to be reproved more for the article of faith, which is to believe the Gospel. But concerning this a doubt arises,

Whether one who believes that a manifest usurer can make a testament may likewise be considered a heretic. And I say that he is not: because this negative proposition pertains to voluntary canon law, not to that which is necessary for salvation.

† Hence, even if a certain lord were to enact a statute that a manifest usurer might make a will, by this he would not be a heretic nor a schismatic; nevertheless, his statute would not be valid: because no temporal prince can enact anything contrary to what has been enacted by the council of the chapter, as is stated in *de usu*, book 6. For the crime of usury is ecclesiastical, and therefore the Pope can punish the offender and render him intestate: because in ecclesiastical crimes, the principate of the Church is greater than the principate of Caesar. From this it follows that the aforementioned Magnificent and Illustrious [lord], not only from an impulse of mind that clouds the eye of human reason, but also with all deliberation and counsel of his nobles, although he is said to have fullness of power in this matter, yet having no power at all, much less with the fullness of his power, could not rescind the sentences pronounced against the memory of the usurer, by which the will also appeared to be null as having been made by a manifest usurer, as stated in *extra de iu.*, c. *at si clerici*, and *de foro compe.*, c. *si diligenti*. From this follows the conclusion that the sentence of the Bishop of Pergamo and the sentence of the Archbishop of Milan prevailed over the arguments of the said Magnificent [lord]. But here a doubt arises, because the record states that the aforementioned sentences are not found, and therefore it must be said here that some things are true and not presumed: hence, although it is true that the said sentences were pronounced, they are presumed not to have been pronounced if they do not appear. Moreover, no one is presumed to be incapacitated unless it is proven. *C. de codicil.*, l. *nec codicillos*; and *ff. de prob.*, l. *ab ea parte*. And therefore, if it does not appear by proof that the said testator was a manifest usurer, nor does it appear by sentence, we presume in doubt that the will is valid, as noted in *C. de iuris, et fac. igno.*, l. *post diuisionem*. But here

It is asked, assuming that the sentences were apparent, whether the sentence pronounced against the testator’s brother prejudices his sons, who were not cited, in the event of the occurrence of the said substitutions. And it seems that it does, as in the Digest, *De venditionibus*, *In principio*, l. 1, § *Denuntiari*. To this effect it is said: because a sentence pronounced against an instituted heir concerning the intestate estate of the deceased prejudices legatees and fideicommissaries who rely on the will, as in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Papinianus*, § *Si eadem*. By the same reasoning, if a sentence were pronounced against a pupillary substitute, it would prejudice the legatees of both wills; because, when the head of the will is rescinded, the legacies are also rescinded, even if the legatees were not cited, provided that the heir defended the case in good faith and was present at the time of the sentence, as in the Digest, *De condictione indebiti*, l. 2 and 3; and fully noted by Cynus and other doctors in the *Extra* in l. *Ingenuum*, Digest, *De statu hominum*, and in other places.

But the truth seems to be to the contrary: because the said laws speak when the sentence is pronounced with the heir. But when it is pronounced with a substitute by fideicommissum, it does not prejudice other substitutes, nor legatees, unless they are cited; because he against whom the sentence is pronounced is not the head of the will, by argument from the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Circa*. And therefore, in law, I say that, assuming that the said sentences were apparent, the substitution made in favor of the sons of the said brother is not prejudiced.

But if the witnesses survived, or the instruments by which it could be proved that the testator was a manifest usurer, then undoubtedly the daughter of the testator would have a right by reason of intestacy. Also, the sentences of the bishop and archbishop would make a strong indication, as in the Digest, *De iureiurando*, l. *Si duo patroni*, in the beginning. From these things it is concluded that, the matter being thus situated, the will must stand, subject to what is said below; for in the second place

† The principal question concerns a certain judgment rendered against the said brother of the testator, by virtue of a certain *apodissa* (judgment roll), in which the said brother is found condemned as a debtor of the said daughters, as heirs of the father intestate. For by this it was necessarily pronounced that the said brother was not an heir, as in C. de haere. acq. l. vt debitum. And I answer that the secular judge cannot invalidate the testament of one who is said to be a usurer; because, as I have said, the cause is ecclesiastical and assigned to bishops, as noted in 11. q. 1. in the Summa. Nevertheless, since the judgment was rendered upon the said *apodissa*, and not upon the validity of the testament, the judgment must stand; and although the original does not appear by the original, it appears by transcript through the records, as in C. de test. l. publicati, and C. de re iud. l. gesta. And although it somewhat implies a tacit contradiction, that the true heir by testament is condemned to someone as an heir intestate, it suffices that the judge believed that the testamentary heir was not the true heir. For if the judgment displeased him, he ought to have appealed, as noted in C. si saepius in integrum restitutio postuletur, l. 1; ff. de falc. haer. l. cum putarem; ff. de pec. l. eo tempore. This is what is said: the judge makes law, even when he decides unjustly; as in ff. de iud. et iur. l. pe., and noted in ff. de cond. indeb. l. si non sortem, §. haer. From these it is concluded that the judgment rendered upon the said *apodissa* must stand, whatever may be the case regarding the residue of the goods of the said testator. Nor is it surprising if what I have said seems to involve a certain contradiction with respect to different persons; because a matter acted upon between others often results in contrary judgments, as in ff. de adul. l. denuntiasse, §. quaeritur. One thing I do not omit, that the said schedule ought not to be produced, since it does not exist; provided, however, that an oath of purgation is taken thereon according to the form of the last law, C. de fide instrum. And this is the response, which I give with the counsel of the Magnificent, saving the better opinion, as in l. Claudius Felix. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. One thing is to be absolved simply, another is to be absolved from the observance of the judgment.
body: The opinion was in this form: that the parties were to be absolved on account of the observance of the judgment, and certain reasons existing in the fact were inserted, some containing allegations of laws, about which I do not dispute. Upon seeing this opinion, the judge pronounced by these words, namely, he said, he sentenced, he pronounced, he declared, and he absolved by words of the present tense in all things and in every respect, as above. This is clearly apparent in the said opinion. And it is proposed that the action which had been brought was an action of guardianship against the heirs of the testamentary guardian, and that it did not appear that the inheritance had been accepted by the ward. Now it is asked,

Whether, if they are sued by an action for management of affairs, those who managed them, without the action being simply expressed by name, so that they render an account, whether the exception of res judicata will be a bar to them. To which I answer and say that it will not, because by the said sentence they have not been absolved from the debt; because the reason assigned in the aforementioned absolute release from the observance of the judgment does not concern the liberation of the debt: as in l. 1, § 1, ff. si messor falcem dixerit. Hence, by this it appears that the mind of the judge pronouncing does not touch this case; because they do not say that by this the administrator is not bound to render an account. For rather he is bound, whether he is a tutor, or pro tutor, or manager of affairs. But they say that the libel was not properly drawn up. Moreover, the words of the sentence say that the acceptance of the inheritance was not proven, but about this there is a very great question, which I do not touch. For whatever it may be, purely the administrator ought to render an account, and his heir, and their heirs. Furthermore, that the libel would not proceed on account of obscurity, multiplicity, and the non-declaration of times, I was and am of the opinion that it does not proceed otherwise than if the libel had not been declared when it ought to have been declared; but now, if the action is properly brought and the libel is correctly formed, the case must proceed, although in the cause the things to be proven must be proven, and the effect of the litigation will depend on future proofs. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What those words appended in the papal legitimation signify, insofar as the public interest is concerned.
body: Words

† The words of the first privilege of legitimation state thus: “you may succeed,” etc. But the words of the second privilege state thus: “that you may freely and lawfully provide for, retain, and possess the same inheritance, insofar as it concerns the public interest, as if sufficient dispensation had otherwise been granted to you in this regard.” Now the question arises whether the said second privilege operates in any way with respect to the effect of acquiring the said succession by the legitimated person, and of depriving the other legitimate successors thereof. And I answer that it is manifest from those words, “insofar as it concerns the public interest,” that the Pope did not intend to derogate from the rights of private persons, to whom dominion had been acquired by the acceptance of the inheritance: as in C. de emancipatis liberis, l. nec auus; and l. ex facto; and cap. ex tuarum, de auctoritate et usu pallii. Indeed, it appears expressly from the contrary sense of the words that the Pope did not wish to derogate from the right acquired by another: as in ff. de manumissionibus testamento, l. si quis locuplex. And if he had wished to do so, he could not have done so in the affairs of the Church, because the Emperor has divided the empire with Jove. And even assuming that he could have done so, he nevertheless did not wish to do so; hence the said legitimation is, according to the terms proposed, void, empty, and of no effect. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a surety who has guaranteed someone who was to be punished capitally is bound if that person flees.
2. Whether such a promise or suretyship can be made through a messenger or by letter.
3. Whether a surety can intervene where a capital penalty is to be imposed.
body: When servants of a certain captain were fighting each other in the custody of a castle, one mortally wounded the other. The captain seized him and held him in good custody until they were reconciled. It is true that this captain did not have *merum imperium* in the castle, but there was another person to whom the illustrious lord had given the power to punish those who shed blood in the castle: and the penalty for wounding was death. This superior sent for the delinquent and ordered the captain to send him to him. The captain delayed for some days in sending him, but finally sent him under faithful custody. Finally, it happened that, upon the report of a certain alleged messenger, this malefactor was remitted to the said captain as a surety for him. After the said wounded man died from the said wound, the said malefactor fled. Now the question is whether the said captain should be punished for this.

† To which I respond that if he indeed did not act as a surety, he ought not to be punished; for it is sufficient that he returned him to his superior within a few days, as stated in D. si quis cau. l. et si post tres. But if he acted as a surety for him, or by stipulation, he ought to be punished with a fine; as stated in D. de custod. reor. l. si quis reum, and note 23, question 5, c. cum homo.

† Or if he gave surety through a messenger or by letter, the suretyship is invalid; and therefore he is not bound, nor is he liable under the said suretyship; because a stipulation is not contracted through a messenger, as stated in l. 1, in principio, ff. de verbis obligatorum; and a surety is not bound unless a stipulation intervenes, or unless he is present and allows himself to be recorded in the acts as giving surety, as in C. de fideiussoribus, l. blanditus; ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. 5, §. satis exceptio; and noted in ff. de fideiussoribus, l. tuto; l. cum ostendimus, §. ultimo. Hence, what was done incautiously should not be imputed to him, unless he again undertook to keep him in custody, as in C. de custodiendo reo, l. ad commentariensem. That

† It is also certain that where the case is capital, one ought not to be released even by a thousand sureties, as in D. de custodia rei, l. Divus, there: "but so great a crime," etc., and noted by Petrus and Cynus in C. de appellationibus, l. Aeos, § 2, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a father, who, having made a will, instituted his daughter as his universal heir and promised under oath never to alter the will, may nevertheless alter it and institute another heir.
body: To obey

† He made a will, in which he instituted his daughter as heir, and he swore to her, present and not accepting, that he would not revoke it, and he decreed that he could not revoke it; and if he should revoke it, he gave and delivered; and he expressly renounced all laws permitting revocation, and specifically the last law of the Code on pacts and the law "Stipulation conceived in this way, with if." It happened that afterwards the testator revoked it and instituted another heir. The question is asked: what is the law?

Solution: This question is most ancient. Some say that he cannot revoke it by reason of the oath, lest he fall into perjury, and because the oath cannot be kept without the loss of eternal salvation. Also, because by thus making a will the father paid a debt according to natural law. Also, because the will was fortified by contract and delivery; otherwise, the glossa would say in vain that a will can pass into a contract, as is noted in the Digest on wills, law "Heirs openly," section "If." And the canonists hold this opinion by reason of the oath, and Dominus Dynus holds it by reason of the contract. And for this supports the law "Although" of the Code on pacts.

Others say that it can be revoked notwithstanding the oath, because the making of a will is of public law, to which derogation cannot be made by the will of a private person. Also, the contract was not celebrated under a lawful agreement, but under an unlawful one. Moreover, a donation between father and son can be revoked just as a will can, as in law 2 of the Code on inofficious donations.

Solution: The ancients commonly said that the oath was to be observed, and that one cannot proceed against the oath of the deceased by anyone who claims to be his heir, on account of the favor of the testator's soul. The moderns commonly hold the contrary. Code on sacred churches, law 1; and Digest on fidejussio, law "If anyone for him." Nor can one renounce obstructive laws. And Code on laws, law "No doubt"; and law 2 of the Code that fidejussors should not be given for dowries. Because renunciation is against good morals and induces a vow to capture death. And this opinion is safer. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, when a son receives a dowry from his wife, and both the father and the son bind themselves to its restitution, the agreement is valid whereby the father is not held liable beyond the portion that may fall to the son in his [the father's] goods.
2. Whether there has been a departure from the prior agreement by the subsequent solidary obligation, and the obligation of all goods by way of a subsequent security.
body: The father and the son bound themselves to the restitution of the dowry, yet by these words, namely, obligating themselves and their goods only up to the portion of all goods that could pertain and belong to the said son from the goods of the said father, and not beyond. Afterwards, however, the father used these words together with the daughter, namely, obligating each of them jointly and severally all their present and future goods. From this case arise two doubts. First, whether the pact is valid that the father is not bound beyond the portion falling to the son. Second, whether there has been a departure from the said pact by the subsequent obligation, which is solidary in enforcement and obligates all goods. And I return to the first,

† And it appears that the said modification of the obligation did not hold to the prejudice of the woman’s dowry: because when a dowry is given to a son, the father ought to bind himself in solidum for the restitution of the dowry, as noted by Dy. in ff. sol. ma. l. si cum dotem. §. trans. grediamur. Moreover, a pact made to the prejudice of the dowry is not valid, as ff. de pac. dotalibus. l. 2. Furthermore, the pact is impossible: because as long as the father lives, the son ought not to have any legitime, as noted by Dyn. and others in l. vlti. ff. de lib. agno. Moreover, pacts concerning future succession are not valid, as C. de colla. l. pactum. On the contrary, it appears that this pact is not contrary to good morals, nor is it disapproved by law, but is a certain modification of the obligation, as ff. de pac. l. si quis pecuniam. Moreover, at the time when the dowry is given, any pacts may be opposed, provided that civil law is not impugned, as ff. de pac. dotalibus. l. cum dos. Therefore, the father is not bound more than up to the resources which fall to the son from the father’s substance, for example, if there are two sons, up to one-half; if three, up to one-third. Otherwise, the said words could also be interpreted as “up to the legitime,” as C. de inof. testa. auth. nouissima. But the first interpretation is more humane, in favor of the dowry. However, I hold this opinion, that the pact is valid, in which the father binds himself in the manner aforesaid, and the son in solidum; and consequently, the father is not bound beyond what he has obligated himself, as ff. de fideius. l. fideiussores magistratuum. §. 1. Now I come to the second point,

And it seems that one must first say that there was a departure from the aforementioned pact by means of the subsequent writing, as in *l. lecta*, D. *si certum petatur*. To the contrary, it appears: because the limitation made in the beginning seems to be repeated in the following provisions, as in D. *de pactis dotalibus*, *l. cum pater dotem*. For the subsequent words can be joined with the preceding ones, so that the sense is that, insofar as he promised by personal obligation, he bound himself for the whole amount with all his goods. To this effect are all the laws stating that the subsequent writing is determined by the first, as in D. *de legatis* 2, *l. legatorum*; § *qui plures*, C. *familiae herciscundae*, *l. quotiens*; and Extravagant *de appellationibus*, c. 2, *requiris*. For in the latter part of the contract it is not said that each bound himself personally for the whole amount of the dowry, but that his goods are bound for the whole amount, words which concern only the hypothecary obligation. And this seems to me more correct, notwithstanding *l. lecta*, D. *si certum petatur*, because there the preceding writing could not be confirmed by the subsequent writing; here, however, it can, even preserving the reason of correct speech. Furthermore, the statement of Doctorus in § *transgrediamur* does not obstruct, that if the father ought to have been compelled, nevertheless this necessity was not reduced to an action of promise, but was modified, in which modification the time of the contract is considered, as Butrintus elegantly notes in the said *l. pactum*, C. *de collationibus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A grant of possession by decree is invalid if those who ought to be cited are not cited,
body: There are three,

† For which reasons, principally, the aforementioned procedure of the said judge did not hold, namely, the *datio insolutum* and the introduction into possession. First, because the person to be cited, or who had been cited, had died in the meantime, wherefore the citation was voided by operation of law, as in *l. Paulus*, D. *quae sententiae sine appellatione rescindantur*. Second, because an adult son succeeded his father. For when a son succeeds his father, the inheritance is not said to be lying vacant due to the existence of his heir, as in C. *de usucapione pro herede*, *l. nihil*. And therefore he ought to have been cited by name, as in *l. 1, § denuntiari*, D. *de venditione inspicienda*. Moreover, because the said son was a cleric, against whom one cannot proceed unless he is cited before his own judge, as in Extravagant *de foro competenti*, c. *si diligenti*, unless one were to say that this allegation is not true when the judgment was commenced against a layman and a cleric succeeds him, as in D. *de iudiciis*, *l. heres absens*, in the beginning. But even then, another reason remains: because he was a son and heir, he ought to have been cited by name, as stated above, and a procedure carried out where there is no legitimate citation does not hold, as noted in C. *de accusationibus*, *l. si accusatoribus*. It is also alleged that the time for making an inventory was pending, as in C. *de iure deliberandi*, *l. si, § donec tamen*. I do not dwell much on this allegation: because the benefit of inventory ought to have been alleged before the judge. Moreover, because the son had not yet intermeddled, and therefore we were not within the time for inventory, but before it, as noted in *l. finalis*, in the first part, C. *de iure deliberandi*. It is also alleged in Auth. *ut cum de appellatione cogantur*, § *penes*. But I also think that this ought to be alleged, or at least be clear to the judge, arguing from D. *de re iudicata*, *l. quaesitum*. Finally, I hold that the *datio insolutum* did not hold by operation of law: because it requires concealment, and a dead man cannot conceal himself. Moreover, from the contumacy of the second procurator, the principal does not suffer according to the decree, as noted by Bartolus in *l. hoc amplius, § finalis*, D. *de damno infecto*. Furthermore, the mandate of the procurator was revoked by death, because the principal died while the litigation was neither contested nor quasi-contested, as noted in D. *de iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, *l. et quia*. Moreover, the son, who was also the heir by disposition of law, was not cited. For when it is to his advantage to be an heir, then he is an heir, as in Inst. *de hereditatibus ab intestato*, § *sui*, and if someone omits the cause, *l. 1, § si proponatur*, and D. *de vulgari substitutione*, *l. si filius, qui patri*, in the reason of *sui*. Moreover, when he is not an adult, agnates and cognates ought to be cited in court: as in D. *quibus ex causis maior*, *l. ergo*. Otherwise, the procedure does not hold. And thus, concluding from the first to the last, it clearly appears that the said second decree and the corporal immission were, and are, null and void by operation of law. To the same effect it is also made, because an appeal was pending: for an appeal, which suspends the pronouncement, suspends the acts consequent to the pronouncement, as in D. *de minoribus*, *l. infra utile tempus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. See also below, in the second charter, at the end.
2. One who alienates a fief without the lord's consent forfeits his right.
3. Whether a vassal who alienates part of a fief forfeits the whole. And see below, in opinion 349.
body: He who was prosecuting a lawsuit concerning tithes, which were claimed for him by the Bishop of Vercelli, while he was litigating over them against a certain possessor, made a contract of the following tenor, by which contract he granted to the party sharing in the costs of the litigation a portion of these feudal goods. Now

† It is asked whether the aforementioned donor, as an alienator of the said fief, has forfeited his right. And it is certain that he who alienates a fief without the request of the lord, whether by donation or in any other manner, forfeits the fief by operation of law: as in cap. 1, §. denique, which was the first cause for the loss of a benefice, col. 10; and in cap. 1, §. donare, under the heading "How formerly a fief could be alienated," as in cap. Imperator, Fed., §. calidis, under the heading "On the prohibition of alienating fiefs," according to Fedine. But it is doubtful whether he who alienates a part loses the whole. And it seems that he does not: as in cap. 1, in the beginning, under the heading "On the vassal who acts against the constitution of Lothair," in the same column. Others say that he loses the whole according to the newest law, by the aforementioned §. calidis. But they incline to the first opinion, namely, that he loses only the part alienated, as all the ancient authorities commonly teach, because that which has not been alienated ought not to revert to the lord. For even usufruct is extinguished by alienation and reverts to the lord, but not to a greater extent than was alienated, as in Inst., De usufructu, §. finitur. But some modern authorities hold that he loses the whole, because the vassal sins against the person of the lord: for he scorns the lord, and this contempt, regarding the person, is something indivisible; because one cannot sin against a person except in solidum (as a whole): as in cap. 1, §. similiter, under the heading "In what ways a fief is lost," col. 10. Nevertheless, in our case, there is no need to dispute this point: because the alienation begins with the whole, and therefore the whole has reverted to the church, although a pact concerning a share of the litigation costs in case of victory was made contrary to good morals, as in D., De pactis, l. sumptus. Nor let anyone say that delivery did not intervene: because in corporeal things, the assignment of the action is held in place of delivery, as noted in C., Qui fiscus vel privatus, l. si; and in D., De donationibus, l. ad eum. Therefore, the alienator is not excused because he made the pact at a certain time: because this serves to increase, not diminish, the offense, since he has sinned in several respects. This question is doubtful. But this opinion seems defensible, and therefore the vicar of the bishop seems to have pronounced correctly. It is supported by C., Ne liceat potentioribus, l. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legitime is due to grandsons or granddaughters through a daughter, and whether they can bring an action for supplementation.
2. If the matter concerns the legitime of paternal grandsons, how the division among them is made, and what their legitime is.
1. Whether a mother's dowry is counted in the legitime of her children.
2. Whether a mother transmits the inheritance of her mother or grandmother, not yet accepted, to her grandchildren.
body: The case, for which a legal opinion is requested, is as follows. Jacobus, a citizen of Asti, son of the late Petrus de Ecclesia, of sound mind although afflicted in body, made a nuncupative testament without writing. In it, he instituted as his heirs, in 500 florins of good gold and weight, Henricus, Petrina, Isabella, Augustina, and Damasia, sons and daughters of Antonia, late wife of the said testator, and son and daughters of Gulielmus Zabertus, husband of the said Antonia; commanding that the said Henricus and the said Petrina, Isabella, Augustina, and Damasia be silent and content with the said 500 florins of gold, and that they could not demand anything else in the goods and inheritance of the said testator. In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, accounts, and actions whatsoever, wherever they might be and could be found, he instituted as his universal heir Georgius de Ecclesia, his brother; and if the said Georgius should at any time die without children born to him from a legitimate marriage, and in that case he willed that each of the daughters of the said Gulielmus Zabertus and Antonia, late wife of the said testator, should have for each of them 100 florins of gold, and the said Henricus, son of the same Gulielmus Zabertus and the said late Antonia, wife of the said testator, should have in that same case 200 florins of gold. But if the said Georgius should die leaving behind him a son or sons male, or one or more males, and afterwards the said male sons, one or more, should all die, none of them leaving behind a son or sons male, or a son, born from a legitimate marriage: then, and in that case, he willed that each of the daughters of the said Gulielmus Zabertus and the aforesaid Antonia should have 100 florins, and the said Henricus, son of the said Gulielmus and the said Antonia, should have 200 florins of gold. The said Jacobus de Ecclesia, the aforesaid testator, died after making the said testament, the said Georgius, his brother and heir by the aforesaid testament, being alive, and who Georgius accepted the inheritance of the said Jacobus by the aforesaid testament, and with the said son and all the daughters of the said Antonia, daughter of the said testator and of the said Gulielmus Zabertus, being alive. Now it is asked whether the said nephew and nieces of the said Jacobus, and the son and daughters of the said Antonia and the said Gulielmus Zabertus, can sue for the supplement of the legitime due to them in the goods and inheritance of the said Jacobus, their maternal grandfather, notwithstanding the words appended in the said institution; because he says that they cannot demand anything else in the goods of the said testator, and notwithstanding other ordinances made by the said testator in the said testament, as above, in which he ordained that if the said Georgius should die without one or more male sons, and if he should leave one or more sons, and the said sons should die without one or more male sons born from a legitimate marriage, that then, and in that case, he willed that the said daughters of the said Gulielmus and the said Antonia should have 200 florins, as contained in the said testament. Furthermore, it is asked that the said Antonia was the only daughter of the said testator; and the said sons and daughters of the said Antonia, nephews and nieces of the said testator, were five after the death of the said Jacobus, the testator. Now there are only four, because one of the said daughters of the said Antonia died after the death of the said Jacobus, as stated above, in the case where they can sue for the supplement of their legitime of the inheritance of the said Jacobus, their maternal grandfather, with respect to the half, because at the time of death and after the death of the said Jacobus there were five nephews and nieces; or with respect to the third part, because the said mother of theirs was the only daughter of the said Jacobus, the testator, and his said son and daughters are now only four, because one of the said daughters died after the death of the said Jacobus, the testator, as above. Furthermore, it is asked if the said sons can sue for the supplement of their legitime, as above, and whether and whether the dowry given by Jacobus to his father, Gulielmus Zabertus, husband of the said Antonia and father of the said children of the said Antonia, in the name of the said Antonia, his daughter and wife of the said Gulielmus, can and should be computed in their said legitime. Furthermore, it is asked whether the said Antonia could transmit the inheritance of her mother, wife of the said Jacobus, predeceased by the said Jacobus and not accepted by the said Antonia, to her said son and to her said daughters, and whether the son of the daughter of the said Antonia can demand the dowry of their maternal grandmother, who died before the death of the said Antonia. And on all the aforesaid points, step by step and successively, it is asked what is the law. On the first point, it must be said that

† Although the said nephews are nephews through a daughter, nevertheless the legitimate portion is due to them by natural law, because the distinction between agnation and cognation has been abolished, as stated in C. de liberis praeteritis, l. maximum vitium, and in Authen. de heredibus ab intestato, §. nullam vero. This legitimate portion the testator cannot prohibit or diminish, as the text states in Authen. ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur, §. ceterum. In this legitimate portion, a conditional substitution made after the death of the instituted heir is not imputed, because they must have their legitimate portion without any delay or condition, as stated in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. quoniam in prioribus, and l. scimus. And nevertheless, if the condition of the substitution should subsequently occur, they could bring an action on the ground of a fideicommissum, and to that which was to be restored according to the said laws. For one who seeks a supplement to the legitimate portion is not said to impugn the will, as stated in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omnimodo.

† On the second point, it seems to be said that, however many grandchildren there are from one son or daughter, they are all considered in the place of one, and the legitime of all of them is one-third part, as is established in the Institutiones, De heredibus ab intestato, §. et quia placuit. But this seems to be contradicted, namely, that upon the death of a son or daughter, the number of grandchildren is to be considered, as if they were held in the place of sons: for it matters greatly whether they come with an uncle, and then they come per stirpes; or whether they come alone, and then their number is inspected. This seems to be what the text says in the Authentica, De triennio et semestri, §. prohibemus, where the text thus says: "And we say all these things not only in the case of a father, but also of a mother, and of a grandfather, and in the place of a grandfather, and in the place of a grandmother." The gloss also seems to hold this view in the verse "hoc servando in omnibus personis," where the gloss says, namely, sons and grandchildren. Moreover, natural reason supports this. For just as a grandfather is bound to provide maintenance, so too does the law provide assistance through the debt of the supplement of goods, lest the inconvenience mentioned in the text in the verse "pauperes erunt filii" ensue. For although mention is made there of sons, the law proceeds further, extending to grandchildren, as appears there; and according to this, grandchildren would be in a better condition than their father, which seems absurd, by argument from the Codex, De bonis matri, l. si viva matre. This passage is doubtful, because the text does not clarify whether it speaks of grandchildren from one son or from several sons. But certainly the text seems to be rightly understood as meaning the same as in the case of sons, namely, their shares, because they enter into the place of the father. Consider that grandchildren do not pertain to the grandfather except through the root or stock, and the root is one, and the stock is single, and therefore they cannot have more than their stock would have had. And this opinion is safer and more probable, although the question is sufficiently doubtful in this regard, as in the Digest, De colonis, l. dedit dotem, in the reason of itself.

On this point, a distinction seems necessary: for either the legitime is formed in one son and devolves from him to several grandchildren, say five or six; or it is not formed in one son, because he predeceased the living father. In the first case, it is not increased by the number of grandchildren, even if they come in their own person with their father repudiating; otherwise it would follow that one son, who had five sons, could cause his sons to have one-half as their legitime under the more full edict of succession, which is absurd, because at the time of death the father of their father would not have been bound except to one-third. In the second case, the number of grandchildren is considered, not the father or their father, who is no longer in existence, nor do the grandchildren then succeed in his place, but in their own right; and therefore the legitime is formed and the condemnation moderated according to the number of those who succeed primarily and principally. Hence, if from two predeceased sons there remain from one two grandchildren and from the other three, they will have one-half to be divided among the grandchildren according to the number of persons, because if it were divided per stirpes, there would not be five, but two; nevertheless, in succeeding, they are like their shares.

Consider this, for this mode of succeeding according to number is contrary to the case of the said §. et quia placuit. If therefore you have reference to the stirp, according to what that §. says, it necessarily follows that even a thousand grandchildren succeeding in the place of the father should not be reckoned as more than one person, because they enter into the place of the father. And just as in the querela there is room for the right of accretion, as in the Digest, De inofficioso testamento, l. qui repudiant, in the beginning, so too in the right of action for the supplement, which succeeds in the place of the querela, although there are various opinions of the moderns on this, as in the Digest, De inofficioso testamento, l. pater filium, and by Dynus in the Digest, De legatis 1, l. plane, §. si coniunctim. The gloss, however, hints at the contrary in the verse in the Authentica, De triennio et semestri, in the beginning, and there Ioachimus de Belvis. You, however, hold that when the legitime is formed according to number, that same form is preserved in the right of accretion, by argument from l. 1, Codex, De impositione lucris descriptione, book 10. And thus one-half formed in five can remain entirely in one by the right of accretion. And I hold this opinion. On the third point

I say that, according to Bartolus, the mother’s dowry is counted toward the legitime of her children, because they succeed in the place of the mother: as in C. de collationibus, l. illam. But according to Jacobus de Belvisio, it is not counted with them, except under the right and title of heir of the mother; and even if they repudiate the maternal inheritance, the legitime is still due to them. Therefore, the mother’s dowry is adventitious, as is well argued in ff. de legatis tertio, l. sed si sic. What is adventitious is not imputed to the legitime: as in C. de collationibus, l. finalis. Nor does it matter that they succeed in the place of the mother, because this is not true in all respects; for it is not true with regard to the burden of imputation, since this is expressly provided for by law. Nor does it matter that it must be collated to the other children, because no collation is made to strangers: as noted in C. de collationibus, l. si emancipati.
