I distinguish in this matter as follows: either the children come together with other children, and then they impute the maternal dowry to their legitime: C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. finalis; or they come together with strangers, and then they do not impute it. And this is our case, although the dowried daughter herself, if she were to come to the succession, would indiscriminately count her dowry toward her legitime, because she receives it immediately from her father: as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. quoniam novella. On the fourth and last point, I say,

† That the mother of these sons transmits the inheritance of her mother, and likewise that of her grandmother, to the grandchildren, even though it has not been accepted; because it is a special favor for descendants and ascendants that an unaccepted inheritance be transmitted, as in C. de caducis tollendis, § in novissimo, and l. unica, C. de his qui ante apertas tabulas. And from this it follows that these grandchildren can claim the dowry by right by virtue of the transmission. And if they do not wish to accept the maternal inheritance, they could claim it under the successor edict; but there is this difference: because when they can claim by transmission, even those conceived after the death of the grandmother can do so, but under the successor edict they cannot, unless they were conceived during the lifetime of the grandmother. Thus it is understood in leg. et no. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quis filium, in principio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a duel is permitted, and in what cases it is or is not permitted, and whether it is permitted for the cause of a denied debt.
2. Whether a person released from prison under a sworn caution, if he has not observed his promises, ought to return to prison.
body: †Illustrious Lord, you have asked me two questions. First, whether, having seen the documents sent to me in the French language, which I had translated and explained to me word for word, the case concerns a fight between the noble knights Ubert and Raul, as contained in the aforementioned letters. The said Lord Raul claims that Lord Ubert owes him two thousand florins. Furthermore, he claims that Ubert promised him not to hand over the Castle of Velleis to anyone until provision had been made for a certain benefice. Lord Ubert denied this. Therefore, the said Lord Raul, in response, said to the said Lord Ubert that he would take his vengeance upon the person of the said Lord Ubert and upon his goods, unless he fulfilled the aforementioned obligations.

And it is certain from Roman law that a duel should not be initiated, as stated in the Codex, Title "On Actions and Obligations," law "Negating." Likewise, it is certain from customary law that a duel should not be initiated, because it is lawful for the said Lord Uberto to defend himself by denying, especially outside of court. Moreover, a duel must be a last resort, as in the Tenth Collection, Title "On Military Vassals Who Contumaciously Refuse," Chapter Unique, § Final. Nor is this the case under Lombard law: for if it is found in Lombard law that a duel ought to be fought on account of any denied debt, except for a denied deposit, if it amounts to 20 solidi, as in Lombardy, how one ought to defend oneself, law "If anyone by himself." Furthermore, to challenge to a duel is a certain frenzy against all humanity and against all natural reason, and it is not permitted except in the few cases contained in law, as noted in the Institutes, Title "On Intestate Succession," § "On the Contrary"; and in the Codex, Title "On the Use of Arms," law 1, Book 11; and in the Digest, Title "On What is Done Through Fear," law "There Exists" and law "So That Violence"; and in the Digest, Title "On Justice and Law." And therefore, on this point, the said Lord Raul should not be heard: because neither by any law nor by equity should his rash desire be embraced by the judge. And this concludes the first question, namely, concerning the duel. Now I come to the second point, which asks whether

† Francischinus and Aymo ought, by law, to be prisoners of that lord Raul. And it must be said that in this matter the general custom is to be observed, which provides that those who are released under a sworn bail, if they do not keep their promises, ought to be brought back and return to prison. For this agreement is called a pact of war, if someone was lawfully captured in war: as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. nam et servus, in principio. Therefore, in this point I say that the promises ought to be kept: because they were in prison not for a pecuniary debt, but through the misfortunes of war, as they confessed before the Illustrious and Magnificent Prince and the said lord Duke of Burgundy. However, since this was committed to him, if time permits, I say that his declaration ought to be awaited before they are bound to return to prison, as in C. de excusatione rei iudicatae, l. nimis propere. I, Baldus. He treats of two instruments made at different times, and of a certain protestation.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In all matters and causes that can be brought before a judge, it is generally considered more important what is claimed than what has been contracted, done, or otherwise established as a right.
2. If two documents and two promises are made regarding the same debt, the second has reference to the first, and whoever claims the second also claims the first.
body: To the evidence

† It must be premised that in judicial proceedings, that which is not pleaded has no effect, as in D. de institoria, l. habebat. Likewise, in protests, that which is not pleaded has no effect, as in D. de adulteriis, l. denuntiasse. And generally, in all matters and causes that can be brought before a judge, greater regard is given to what is pleaded than to whether a contract was made or a right otherwise accrued, as in C. de petitione hereditatis, l. haereditas materterae. Therefore, one must specify the day when one bases one’s case on the day of the contract. Nor can one prevail on any day other than that which is pleaded. The text is in Cap. Abbate, de re iudicata, libro 6. And therefore, at first glance, it would seem to be said that a protest which states that that instrument, or instruments, obliges and condemns to one effect of two thousand florins of good, just weight and alloy, concerning which Messer Lazolus and Marianus, brothers, sons of the late Messer Venturini de Caputiis, citizens and merchants of the parish of Saint Anthony, and each of them bound and condemned in solidum, are read as written by Ser Gabriel de Raymundis on account of business transactions handed over and written by Iannollus de Procellis, citizen and then notary of the markets, son of the late Ser Jacopo, in the year of our Lord 1370, on Monday, the 10th day of the month of June, under the eighth indiction, and which accrued to the said Messer Nicolaus in part of the principal in the division, etc., as obreptitious, cannot found the plaintiff’s claim based on the said division and indication of name; rather, the entire proceeding ought to be judged obreptitious, and consequently no proceeding is valid extra ordinem for execution, as in D. de fideicommissis, libro 1, cum vero, § subuentum; D. ne vis fiat ei, l. 1, § haec verba; D. de carborum edicto, l. 3, § puberi. This appears because under the true day the right to sue remains, even if it had fallen under a false day; therefore, the judgment is not pleaded. From this follows another conclusion, that he who obtained by obreption is not understood to be a possessor in good faith, since on this account he ought to be punished, not to profit; as in D. de falsis, l. si quis obrepserit; and D. de his qui notantur infamia, l. debuit. And therefore, on account of presumed fraud, he ought not to profit from the fruits; rather, he is liable for those received and to be received, as in C. de fructibus et litis expensis, l. litigator.

† But to the contrary, it must be premised for clarity that if two instruments and promises are made regarding the same debt, the second instrument has a tacit reference to the first, and that he who invokes the second instrument also invokes the first, in which consists the root and principle of the obligation, as in D. de verb. oblig. qui bis idem. Hence, in the case at hand, given that two instruments appear, one for 60 and another for 70, and granted that the act is repeatable, nevertheless both instruments appear on account of one fact and one cause; hence there, two for one, there is only one case in each instance, in the said law qui bis idem, and in the same title, l. si dari stipuler. And therefore, either only one instrument was drawn up, or two. If one, the protesting party has a right based on unity, as in X. de fide instrumen. cap. cum Ioan. Heremita. If, however, two, since the unity of the cause, both conventional and judicial, is established, the plurality of instruments does not induce a plurality, except as regards interrupting prescription, and this in favor of the creditor. Wherefore, since there is one true debt, although the proofs by instruments are multiple, the creditor’s right in proving is not diminished thereby, but increased, as in l. 2. de discussoribus, lib. 10. Since, therefore, we must adhere to the truth and not proceed by cavils, and since the debt is true, and whether there is one instrument or two, the creditor has a right from the original instrument, the protestation is founded upon the substance of the truth. And to make this even more manifest, I premise for clarity that regarding the same rogation, a notary can draw up several instruments and deliver them at different times, and it does not matter whether the time is short or long; hence, the notary who was requested for 60 could well deliver and write instruments, as delivering and writing are acts that can be done at any time. This is the ordinary gloss in D. de iud. l. exigere dotem, in principio. And therefore, let him who weighs words take note: for the protestation does not say that the instrument was not drawn up and written in 1370, but that it was delivered and written in 1370; these words do not say that it was requested at that time. Moreover, it is one thing to request, another to deliver and write, as in the said law exigere. And therefore, if it is well considered, the protesting party here does not restrict himself to the time; hence the protestation is verified by other acts. Indeed, I say that it is verified in all respects, even as to time. For what can be reduced to the truth cannot be considered an error; hence it appears that it is one thing to say, “he wrote in such year and day,” and another to say, “he wrote under such year and day.” And this is manifestly apparent to any literate man, not to mention a jurist. And therefore, since there is no error in the protestation, the said protestation is valid, and consequently the entire proceeding is free from the defect of obreption, and consequently the whole question is decided as to all points. I do not touch upon the other matter of ratification, which is also a kind of verification, as noted by Butrius in l. Iulia, D. qui satisda. cogantur, because it is not expedient to treat it, since we have a preceding cause that is clear and true and does not need ratification. Furthermore, it is certain that in the same debt I can be the first and third creditor, and I am preferred to the intermediate creditor by the conjunction of two obligations. For the origin must be examined, as in D. qui pot. in pign. hab. l. 3. For an obligation added to an obligation does not make the creditor’s condition worse. Furthermore, the debtor is not presumed to have thrown away his own interest, and therefore it is presumed that there is one credit and one debt, and not several, C. de novat. l. fina., and D. de probat. l. cum de in debito, unless plurality appears. Furthermore, the sentence spoken of here is a non-repeatable act, as noted by Butrius in l. secunda, C. de erro. advoc. And by this, if there were an error in the time, nevertheless the assignment would be vitiated, and it refers more to the cause than to the time. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether interest is to be proved by oath.
2. An oath may be tendered, considering the quality of the person, and to whom it ought to be tendered, preceded by an assessment.
3. Whether a judge, who did not expressly tender an oath, but accepted the oath of a party, is deemed to have tendered it.
4. Whether a judge who did not tender an oath may tender it anew after all probatory terms have elapsed, and whether an oath may be tendered even after the expiration of the probatory term up to the conclusion of the case.
5. The subject matter of the following opinion,
body:
It follows to inquire about the article of proof concerning interest on money not paid, on which I briefly say that, having regard to the quality of the persons and the places where such things commonly occur, it is a matter of discretion whether an oath is to be admitted or not; because one must distinguish between a true contumacious debtor in non-payment, and to what extent and in what manner, having regard to the quality of the persons and the common opinion of the merchants who are in the region, of which the judge may inform himself as of a matter of notoriety, even outside the formal course of the trial. D. de in ius iur. l. nummis; Inst. de verb. oblig. §. po; D. de eo quod certo loco, l. 113, §. si. For it cannot be anything but notorious that which is daily frequent among the hands of merchants, because it is common knowledge.

It is proposed that a certain debt of two thousand florins arises from a contract of good faith, and that the debtor was ordered to pay and did not pay, but rather was in default; the creditor claims interest. It must be presupposed that the creditor is a businessman and merchant, who is accustomed to make profit from merchandise, or even if he is not a merchant, he nevertheless claims interest to the extent that it is commonly received from the purchase of real estate. Furthermore, it is presupposed that he swore an oath regarding his interest, namely to the extent that it is commonly received from the purchase of real estate, for example 5 per centum, the judge, however, not admitting it otherwise, except because he accepted the oath, if and insofar as he is bound by law, and not otherwise. Furthermore, it is presupposed that all periods for proof have elapsed.

Now it is asked whether the said interest is proved by the oath. Secondly, it is asked whether the judge, who accepted it, is thereby understood to have tacitly admitted the oath. Thirdly, it is asked whether the said oath can be newly admitted, all periods for proof having elapsed. Furthermore, it must be observed whether, if the party was summoned to see the oath taken on one day, and if the oath was not taken on that day, it can be taken on another day.

† All these questions appear doubtful. For interest is not proven by oath, but by witnesses. This is a general rule, unless it were half-proven, and an oath were deferred in default of proof, considering what ought to be considered, as in C. de sen. quae pro eo, quod interest, l. 1, §. in alijs. To the contrary it seems: because these three concur, namely, a contract of good faith, contumacy, and fraud; because obedience was not rendered to the judge, as in ff. de in lit. iura, l. nummis; ff. de rei ven., l. qui restituere; and as noted in inst. de verb. obli., §. pen.

† On this point, I say that from the quality of the persons arise presumptions, from which an oath may be tendered to the creditor against the said debtor. For the quality of the person is a very strong presumption, as is noted in l. 133, § final, D. de eo quod certo loco, and noted in C. unde vi, l. si quando. Therefore, having regard to the quality of the person and the quality of the contract, because it is one of good faith, and to the judicial order, and to the contumacy, and to the fraud, at least presumed, of the debtor, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. non dolo carere, I say that the oath ought to have been tendered, subject to the judge’s discretion in its assessment. However, by the new law, which is C. de iudicibus, aut. tamen, it seems to require that the assessment precede. But it seems to be said that if it was not assessed, it can be assessed after the oath. But if the judge’s motion concurs with the oath, assessment is not necessary, as is the brief conclusion. And considering the said concurrent circumstances for the oath, it ought to have been tendered on the said interest: for, as I said, we are in a contract of good faith, and a command has already been made by the judge, and not obeyed. As in D. de in litem iurando, l. in actionibus. The assessment will be made according to the note by Cynus in the said aut. tamen, and this regarding the oath.

† As to the second point, it seems to be said that accepting, and being bound to accept, is equivalent to having tendered it. Argument: Digest, On Fideiussors, Title, l. cum ostendimus, § ult. For to accept is the same as to approve, and although the judge does not say "tender," an equivalent suffices; although it would be safer to adhere to the words of the law, which state that he swore after the condition had been tendered, as in l. iii, in princ., Digest, On Oaths. And therefore it is safer to tender the oath anew and to observe the words of the praetor's edict.

But it is doubtful that all the terms for proof have elapsed. Hence, after the term has passed, he does not seem to be heard: as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. in contractibus, § illo. But there, against the one swearing, there was a presumption of law from the lapse of the term. And therefore it seems to be said that either it is a legal term, which binds the judge and the litigants, and cannot be deferred. Or it is a judicial term, which does not bind the judge, so that he can always supply it by the benignity of his office up to the sentence, as in ff. de interrogationibus et responsionibus, l. ubicunque, and extra de fide instrumentorum, c. cum Io. heremita. Then the judge can, as it were, by supplying it, or even by setting a new term for swearing anew immediately, defer and receive the oath by the said laws. And this, considering the quality of the contract: because it is one of good faith, and the command of the judge, and the delay of the debtor, and the quality of the persons: because they are merchants, and by common course interest arises both in the purchase of properties and in others, I think there is room for the deferral of the oath, and it can be deferred up to the conclusion in the case, just as instruments can be produced and interrogations made, as in extra de fide instrumentorum, c. cum Io. heremita. For the publication of witnesses, or the term for producing witnesses, does not obstruct the deferral of the oath, as in ff. de iureiurando, l. admonendi. And the above are proven by l. nummis, with its matter, ff. de in litis iurando, and ff. de rei venditione, l. qui restituere, in fine. And this is true wherever interest comes accessorially, and the above-mentioned circumstances concur, or several, namely, the difficulty of proof should concur. But then there would be no speciality in contracts of good faith, and arbitrations, nor in the command of the judge, which is false. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a fief can be given as dowry.
body: Although

† The points must be carefully considered, for it is true that the said daughters legitimately have a right to the said fief; but the husband, by virtue of the custom of acquiring the dowry upon the predecease of his wife, has no right in the dotal goods. The case is found in c. j. §. fi. de investitura de re aliena facta, col. x. Nor does the objection based on the investiture by the Lord Bishop hold, first, because the Lord Bishop reserved the right of another; second, because the said fief was not disclosed to the said Lord Bishop, and therefore he could not make an investiture of it, as in c. j. qui suc. te. col. x. Nor does the objection hold that a wife may grant fiefs in dowry for herself. Moreover, because things which are prohibited from being alienated may nevertheless be given in dowry, as C. communia deleg. aut. res, quę; but since that authority does not apply to a fief, certainly a fief cannot be given in dowry, except for as long as it remains with the woman; hence, with the death of the woman, the fief terminates and reverts to the lord or to the agnates, as in c. j. an maritus succedat uxori in beneficio, col. x. and ar. ff. de leg. j. l. si domus. §. fi. and C. de leg. l. vxor patrui. and ff. de pig. l. lex uectigal. ff. de le. ij. l. peto. §. praedium. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son, for whom his father incurred expenses both in his studies and in obtaining his doctorate, upon succeeding to his father’s estate together with his brothers, is bound to deduct said expenses from his share; and whether, if a son was sent to study by his father, the brothers are bound after the father’s death to bear the expenses from the common fund.
2. Whether that which a brother earns from the practice of medicine or from the advocacy of cases is required to be shared with his brothers after the father’s death.
3. Whether, in the division of paternal goods, dowries ought to be deducted beforehand from the share as a debt.
4. Whether brothers who have improved the common possessions may recover their expenses pro rata from the absent brother.
body: The question is asked.

† A father sent his son to study, and he incurred great expenses both during the studies and in obtaining the doctorate. Then the father died. Whether this son, succeeding to his father’s estate together with his brothers, is bound to reckon these expenses against his own share.

Answer: The words of Cynus in l. ex parte, § filius, ff. de familia erciscunda, in the version “et pater” say: if, therefore, the father makes his son a soldier, provides him with a wife, and celebrates the marriage, such a son is not bound to contribute to his brother, who did the same, for such expenses after the father’s death. From this it appears that he for whom the expenses were made profits by them, especially because they no longer exist.

Moreover, in the same §, Jacobus de Belvisi says these words: the argument of this § determined this question. A certain man had two sons who were lawyers, and for one, who had studied more deeply, he paid 100 pounds for the convocation. Later, having instituted his sons as heirs, it was decided that the other son could not deduct another 100 from the common inheritance on account of receiving the convocation.

Argument: supra, in the same title, l. si filia, § Neratius. But Doctor Dynerius says there that the brothers are bound to buy books and make expenses from the common fund for the son sent to study by the father, and this by that text and the said l. ex parte, § filius.

But briefly, this conclusion, that the son does not reckon the expenses made for him by the father in his studies against his share, but profits by them, is made by the gloss and others, ff. de muneribus et honoribus, l. et qui originem, § suis. And therefore also, because these expenses are not in existence, and therefore, as I said, they cannot be reckoned in his share or legitime.

† As to the second point, I say that he ought not to share with his brothers that which he earns from medicine, especially after the death of their father, unless they had entered into a partnership among themselves. This is not alleged in our case, as is shown by D. 17.2.14 (*Cum duobus*), § *Si fratres*; and C. 10.32.1 (*Sed indivisa*). Nevertheless, if the father had promised to give to the other sons the amount he had spent on the medical education, these other sons ought to be made equal to the physician; because the father, by speaking thus, appears to have intended to confer this benefit upon his sons. The final judgment and the last will of the father among his children are valid in the presence of two witnesses, C. 5.61.1 (*Filii patris*). And therefore, this being proven, all the sons ought to be equal. As to the third point, there is no room for doubt,

† That in the division of paternal goods, dowries ought to be claimed first as a part, like a debt owed: because it is a paternal debt, as in the Digest, *De hereditatibus*, law *Si maritus*. And this is certain if the wives are alive. The same applies to the dowry of the first wife, especially since from her there remained an infant son, who died before his father, to whom the maternal dowry had come, as in the Code, *De iudiciis delatorum*, law *Si infanti*; and in the Code, *De bonis quae liberales*, law *Cum non solum*, in the beginning.

† On the fourth point, because these brothers who remained at home improved the possession, it must be said that if they incurred expenses for the permanent utility of the thing: for example, because they planted a vineyard, or built houses, or, when the lands were sterile, made a great expenditure and rendered them fruitful, such expenses, which they made from their own purse, not from their labor—for while the father is alive they are bound to work for the father, since they are supported by him, as in l. sicut, de operis libertorum, and ff. communis dividundo, l. in rebus, §. possunt, versi. nam cibariorum, and c. possent—they could recover them, as in ff. de negotiorum gestis, l. ex duobus. But if they principally incurred expenses for the sake of fruits, by plowing and cultivating well, although the possessions incidentally become better, I say that even then they recover, insofar as that physician has been enriched after the father’s death; because they appear to have managed a common affair, and therefore, with respect to that physician, they have a right of recovery of fruits, or retention up to the corresponding amount, as in ff. communis dividundo, l. in hoc iudicio. But if the father had restored the other sons by making them equal, the said expenses made for the perception of fruits cannot be recovered. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, one may build on a common wall; and there are three reasons for which it is permitted to differ.
2. When one may use a common thing, he distinguishes.
3. Whether one may build on his own land next to a common wall.
4. Whether he who is permitted to build may construct pilasters and other supports for the building.
5. Declaration of the law *Maeuiana*.
6. Whether the term *solarium* includes a wooden or stone structure.
7. Whenever there is doubt about interpretation, recourse must be had to the good man in the law *vel contractus*.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that there are three grounds on account of which it is permitted to build on a common wall: namely, agreement, acquiescence, and the nature of the thing. Regarding the first two, it is stated in the law *Sabinus*, under the title *De communi diviso*; regarding the third, an example is found in the case of a common thing that requires rebuilding or support, as in the Digest, *Pro socio*, law *Cum duobus*, section *Idem respondit*, and in the Code, *De aedificiis privatis*, law *Si ut proponis*. Another example is when several persons have a common tower that requires fortification for guard purposes, so that something is built there. For what is done for the sake of guard is done out of necessity, because such buildings require guarding in order to avoid damages and injuries, and to place oneself in safety, as is manifest from nature and from many laws.

However, it must be premised for clarity that, although under common law a partner does not have the right to build against the will of his co-partner, as in the Digest, *De servitutibus urbanorum praediorum*, law *Si inter me*, section *Si*, nevertheless, if the wall was acquired jointly so that a partner could insert structures into it, there is no doubt that each one may insert structures into the common wall. For what can be done in another’s property by right of servitude, can be done in a common thing by right of agreement, as is clear in the aforementioned law *Sabinus*. The words of Jacobus de Belvisi are there.

These are the points. It is asked whether anyone may use a common thing, and when not; thus distinguish: either he wishes to use it for the purpose for which it was established, or for another purpose. In the first case, against the will of the co-owner, as in the Digest, *De rerum divisione*, law *In tantum*, § *Pe*, and noted in the same law *Sabinus*. If for another use, subdistinguish: either from such use the thing becomes better, and he may; but if worse, he may not. If, however, neither better nor worse, subdistinguish: either such use benefits the user, and then he may rightly; or not, and then he may not. To these points: Digest, *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law 2, § *Item Varrus*. On this, noted by Dytherius, Extravagant, *De re iudicata*, chapter *In re communi*. It is relevant: Digest, *De usufructu*, law *Arboribus*, § *Navis*, where it speaks of natural use; and Digest, *Pro socio*, law *Cum duobus*, § *Item mella scribit*, where it speaks of conventional common use.

† Finally, I premise that one may build on his own land next to a common wall, provided that he does not harm the wall, as in D. de serv. ut. pr. l. quidam hiberus; because, since one’s own property does not serve another, it is free by natural law, as in C. de serv. et aqua l. altius, and there noted, and D. de op. nov. n. l. si prius, and there by the gloss and Doctor, D. de serv. urb. praed. l. cum eo.

Fourth, it is premised for the sake of clarity that he who is permitted to build is permitted to construct pilasters and other supports for the building, because when one thing is granted, that which follows from it is also deemed to be granted, as in the Digest, *De servitutibus praediorum rusticorum*, law *Servitutes quae in superficie*, section *Si domo*.

† Finally, it must be premised that the law *Męuiana*, C. *de aedificiis privatis*, speaks of private buildings, not public ones; likewise, it speaks of the province, not of Italy, as is evident in the text there. Moreover, it does not hold by general custom, as is noted in the ordinary gloss there. Therefore, that law has no place in our question, neither by law nor by custom. Indeed, Jacobus Butrigarius says that even the Greek law translated into Latin, D. *fin. regund.*, l. *fin.*, has been abolished by general custom, and thus is not valid at least simply as regards building. From which it appears that the said pilasters can be made, as well as other supports.

† A solarium constructed of stone, because according to its sense and meaning it contains both wooden and stone elements, as appears in no. in d. l. fin. ff. finium regundorum; nor is there any law in the law that makes a distinction. Provided, however, that doors and windows are not obstructed from the use of passage and light, with “light” being understood according to the discretion of a good man. See ff. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. qui luminibus, and l. binas aedes.

† For whenever there is doubt concerning the interpretation of a law or a contract, we must always have recourse to the good man, as in D. pro socio, l. societatem, §. si; and D. de eo quod certo loco, l. ideo and l. quod si; and D. de operis lib., l. si libertus ita; and Extr. de iureiur., c. quintauall. And thus the question is answered affirmatively, that the said community may construct pillars and a vaulted arch, whether of stone or wood, as it wishes, for perpetual use, without thereby violating the agreements, that is, by not making it excessively low, but leaving sufficient air space, so that the house may be suitably inhabited. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a vassal is said to alienate by the cession of his right, and thus to forfeit his right, as above in opinion 332.
body: Who brings a lawsuit

† He had tithes assigned to him by donation between spouses, and he made a certain assignment in these words: “I have assigned, transferred, and donated to Titius, constituting him as procurator and placing him in my stead.” This assignment was made to a certain procurator with whom he had entered into a pactum de quota litis, and he swore not to contravene it. The Church, which is the lord of the fief, says that this man has forfeited his right. The latter contradicts this, arguing that he did not deliver possession, or quasi-possession, which is acquired through the patience of the lord, as noted in C. de usufr. l. corrup. and l. 2 de serv. et aqua. Furthermore, because the assignment was invalid due to the defect of litigiosity, the vicar of the bishop pronounced that he had forfeited his right, because a feudatory cannot alienate either the right or the corpus without the request of the lord; hence, if he alienates the right, he forfeits his right, and it reverts to the lord. I advised that the sentence of the vicar could be defended in law, for he who is prohibited from alienating a thing is prohibited from assigning the action, as fully noted by Dy. and others in ff. de auc. tu. l. pup. and ff. de iure deli. l. ait praetor. Moreover, if the action could be assigned, the assignee could demand that possession be delivered to him, as in ff. de rei vend. l. si culpa. Furthermore, all those who could not alienate the thing could assign the action, in which assignment no delivery is required, as noted in C. de haer. vend. l. fi. The glossators also say that by the assignment of a thing sold, useful dominion is acquired; therefore, it is an alienation, as noted in ff. de eden. l. 1 in princ. Moreover, the law states that he who has useful dominion, if he credits the useful thing sold, retains nothing, as noted in ff. ad Teb. l. ex asse. Therefore, it cannot be denied that it is an alienation; but he who alienates the fief without the request of the lord makes himself alien to the fief, as in c. 1 § donare, in quibus causis feudum amittatur, col. 10. And it is wonderful how this abusive term, namely, “Amen,” a legal evasion of property, is commonly placed in notarial instruments, because property is with the Church; but it should be explained as property, i.e., useful property, in which the license to use is considered as quasi-delivery. For this is so in incorporeal rights, and the right to collect tithes is an incorporeal right; and therefore, from the first to the last, it seems to me that the sentence was juridical, notwithstanding the objection regarding the defect of litigiosity, because in prohibitions the effect of law is not required. Moreover, the defect of litigiosity does not appear. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What effect a codicillary clause produces.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This question appears doubtful on the ground that this clause, “if it is not valid, etc.,” seems to have been added in the event of the invalidity of the will, i.e., when intestate succession applies, as in D. de legatis 2, l. Lucius § filiam. But here the will is valid: l. hac consultissima § ex imperfecto, C. de testibus. Therefore, the said clause seems to have no effect. However, the contrary view seems correct to me, because the clause “if it is not valid, etc.” is understood to mean “insofar as it is not valid,” as noted in D. de transactionibus, l. controversia. If, therefore, with respect to legacies made to strangers, the will is not valid by the law of wills, because seven male witnesses were not present, it is nevertheless valid by the law of codicils, if five male witnesses, or women, were present, as in C. de codicillis, l. si in fine. I say that it is valid by the law of codicils made in addition to the will, because the institution of heir, which is the head of the will, is valid. It is certain that a legacy made to a father after the death of his children becomes void if the father dies before the children, as in C. de caducis tollendis, § si autem sub conditione. It is also certain that the legitimate heir of the said children must receive the legitime and the Trebellianic portion, c. si pater, de testamentis, lib. 6. And therefore the opinion of the most excellent Doctor Peter is entirely correct. And so I hold, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that anyone is to be punished for each blow struck,
2. if someone struck Titius with a single blow, from which blood flowed from three parts, whether he is to be punished for one blow or for three.
body: In the Name of Christ.

† The statute provides that anyone is to be punished with 10 [units] for any blow resulting in blood. Titius was accused in the following form, namely, that he struck Seius with a single blow, by which single blow blood issued from three places on the face. The question arises whether the judge should punish him as for a single blow with 10 [units], or as for three blows with 30 [units]. It seems that he should be punished as for three, because there are three wounds. And I argue thus: the rule is the same for contraries. But whenever several ends tend toward one end, it is considered nevertheless a single offense. L. illud, in fine, ad leg. Aquiliam. Therefore, conversely, if one [act] tends toward several ends, it ought to be punished as multiple offenses. Secondly, this is proven because we ought rather to look at the terminus in illicit acts, which is in the patient and the recipient, because he receives multiple harms, and if multiple injuries, then multiple punishments. D. de privatis delictis, L. nunquam plura; C. de sepulchro violato, L. qui se pulchra. Thirdly, it is proven because a blow is called, as it were, a cutting of the skin, but here there are multiple cuttings of the skin; therefore, multiple crimes, even if born from one strike, as if someone with one strike amputated two legs from another, he would be punished because he disabled, or rather rendered useless, two limbs. So too if two eyes, and similar cases. And this is held by Bartolus. But the ancient doctors said the contrary, for either the statute says for every wound, and then he is punished as for multiple offenses; or for every blow, and then as for one. And the reason is: because striker and stricken are names of persons, but a blow is a verbal noun, and verbal nouns are sometimes used actively, sometimes passively. In doubt, they ought to be used actively here, as in D. de poenis, L. interpretatione. In the city of Perugia, it was practiced both for and against, and the question is quite doubtful. However, when in the inquisition or accusation those words are placed, “with a single blow,” and the procedure is founded thus, since the places on the body can be so close and contiguous that it is almost considered a single continuous act, yet only a single punishment ought to be imposed for the whole act, an absurdity would follow: since always one baked stone breaks into many minimal particles, and punishments would be imposed for all of them. To this contributes what is noted in Inst. de actionibus, § ferrum, just as one thing is the work, another the thing worked upon. And thus I say, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation causa mortis, even if made in a fixed portion, is converted into a cause of forfeiture if the donee dies before the donor; and what is the rule in donations between husband and wife.
2. Whether a petition containing multiple grounds for nullity is said to be properly formulated.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A donation causa mortis is converted into the category of a lapsed legacy if the donee dies before the donor, as established in D. de caducis tollendis, l. 1, in fine; and D. si certum petatur, l. Non omnis; and the fruits of the intervening period must be restored, according to D. de conditione ob causam datum, l. Cum quis, and in other laws cited above. Nor does the oath constitute an obstacle, for a donation causa mortis is reduced to the nature of a last will, which, although sworn, is manifestly considered by its very nature to be subject to lapse. A donation between husband and wife proceeds in a similar manner, because if the donee predeceases the donor, the law revokes it and converts it into the category of a lapsed legacy; and therefore there is no perjury here, because this results not from human action, but from the law. C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. 1, § Marito. The exception regarding the incapacity of persons is not understood to be removed, even though the statute states that no exception may be raised against the instrument, because it is understood to apply to all persons, as in l. Gradatim, § Et si lex, and similar authorities.
A petition containing several grounds for nullity is properly framed, and it suffices to prove one of them, as is read and noted in the law on contracts of sale, l. si mater tua. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a petition, in which the facts are narrated without a conclusion, is to be upheld.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Concerning the libel, there can be sufficient doubt, because in the libel not only is the fact substantial to the conclusion of the libel narrated, since the promise is narrated, where the conclusion ought to be that the promisor be kept indemnified, not that the quantity not yet paid be given to him, unless the plaintiff were already condemned. D. 3.5.1 (Si quis mandato). And therefore there is sufficient doubt about the ineptitude of the libel, without disputing about the subtleties of law in the action of mandate, which is one of good faith. D. 17.1.1 (Si fideiussor), § 1 (Quandam), from which it is premised, and paid for the liberation of captives. Nor can it be disputed with Boldrinus de Bono, and the equitable, unless according to the use of arms this one, who liberated the souls of captives, can recover what he paid. D. 4.2.1 (Metum), § 1 (Sed licet); and D. 3.5.1 (Nesen); D. 3.5.1 (Quamuis); D. 23.3.1 (Cum simi.).

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How a statute prohibiting appeals is to be understood, and which appeals are deemed permitted.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† Whether the aforesaid statute can remove an appeal from a sentence that is rendered by the vicar of the lord. It seems it must be said that either an appeal is taken before the definitive sentence, and this removal is valid, C. de sententiis, et inter. om. iud. l. fi. and what is noted there in the last gloss, which is very singular; or an appeal is taken from that definitive sentence, and it is certain that by law of the prince's power the statute holds, otherwise not, de iureiu. c. venient. But it does not seem to me fitting to dispute about this, because the vicar of the lord ought to presuppose that the statute which the lord and the citizens use is valid, nor can he exceed the form of the statute according to which the form of swearing was given to him, just as he cannot exceed the form of a mandate, de resc. c. cum dilecta. Whence it is to be seen whether, the statute standing, an appeal can be made. And it is to be known that from a major vicar to the lord an appeal is not made, c. 1. de consue. li. 6. Yet from a commissioner of a single cause committed through a rescript, an appeal is indeed made to the one committing it, because there is no force in the name that he is called a vicar in the quality of the office; whence he to whom a special cause is committed is a delegate, and from him to the delegator an appeal is properly made, l. 1. §. ab eo. ff. quis, et a quo. But it is to be known that a statute prohibiting an appeal, since it is against the ius commune, has no place, but another way the form handed down by the statute itself [must be observed], because when the form is changed, both the substance and the effect of the judgment are changed, de restit. spol. c. Pisanus. Thirdly, it is to be known that from a sentence rendered pursuant to a rescript of the prince an appeal can be made on account of the inequity of the report, ff. de appell. l. 1. §. quaesitum. The same holds in the case proposed: on account of an improperly calculated accounting an appeal can be made, not on account of the inequity of the judge, who, as far as in him lies by following the report—if nevertheless he ought to have followed it—did nothing unjustly. Besides, such accountings can be corrected through the office of the superior, ff. qui satis. cog. l. arbitrio, and from a sentence rendered through an error of calculation an appeal is made, as is noted in C. de errore cal. l. 1. And at times an appeal is made from an interlocutory sentence, although it is prohibited to appeal from a definitive sentence, as noted by Guilielmus in ff. de mino. l. si ex causae. §. nunc videndum. Furthermore, sometimes an appeal is removed by law on account of a trifling prejudice, and then an appeal cannot be made, C. si de momen. pos. l. 1; sometimes on account of a grave excess, and the same if the truth is most evidently established, de aper. l. constitutiones; sometimes for the abbreviation of lawsuits, and then an appeal can be made once a cause approved by the law is expressed, as in a cause of alimony or of promises, and a cause expressed in law is that it is not established to have been proved, l. j. quandoque. ff. de proba.; [sometimes] on account of the exceptional authority of the judges, and an appeal cannot be made, but a supplication, l. 1. de offic. praefe. praeto. But in our case, the judge ad quem ought to consider the causes set forth, which are very pregnant; and if they are relevant, they say they prove that they hold apostles as granted; and it seems to me that they are relevant and are just, if they are true, and therefore let the truth be examined, ff. de in integ. rest. l. omnes. Sometimes an appeal is removed by a rescript, and then, because rescripts elicited against the law are not valid, that clause is understood solely of a frivolous appeal, about which many say many things in c. vt debi. de appel. I, Baldus.

In the name of God. Marinus, who made a will, in which he left by way of institution his daughter Marina as heir to his goods, and to his wife 50 gold florins, which the same Marinus claimed he had given to Marina as dowry, and in the name of dowry for the marriage contracted between Baldus and Marina, with the hand of Ser Matthew the notary. And also by the same right of institution he left to the said Marina from his goods 47 and a half gold florins: and also one piece of land, etc. In all his other goods, however, he instituted his daughters Margaret and Bartola as universal heirs in equal shares, and if any of his said daughters and universal heirs should die at any time without legitimate sons or daughters, he wished and ordered that the shares of such deceased person should devolve and ought to devolve upon the other surviving daughter, or upon her legitimate and natural sons. This Marinus, having made his will, died, leaving and surviving him the said Marina and Bartola, his daughters, and Mutia, the wife of the said testator and stepmother of the said Marina, Bartola, and Margaret. Afterwards, the said Bartola died intestate, without children, aged 14 years and more, leaving and surviving her the said Marina, her sister, and the said Margaret, her sister and substitute heir, also surviving. Afterwards, the said Margaret died, having accepted the inheritance of the said Bartola, leaving and surviving her Baldus, her legitimate son, and the said Mutia, her mother, and the said Marina, her sister. Finally, the said Mutia died, having not accepted the inheritance of the said Bartola, leaving and surviving her the said Marina, her daughter and universal heir.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a mother transmits an unaccepted inheritance to her infant children, and a son to his father.
2. What is the quantum of the legitime and the trebellianic portion, which is owed to those burdened on account of a fideicommissum.
body: In the Name of Christ.

† The sale of the fideicommissary substitution made to Bartola by her father concerning her sister Margarita, and co-heir universal, is void, on account of those words of the substitution of universal heirs, and he adds “to the other surviving sister.” And thus this substitution operates solely between the two sisters instituted as universal heirs. D. ad Trebellianum, l. Iulius Phebus. And this fideicommissum was transmitted by Margarita to her infant son, and this son to his father Phebus. C. de iudiciis delegatis, l. si infanti; C. de fideicommissis, l. si in personam. But it must be examined regarding the residue, namely the legacies and the Trebellian portion, which pertain freely to Bartola, to whom they have devolved. And it is certain that they devolved to Margarita and Marina as intestate heirs of Bartola, since Bartola’s mother did not accept the inheritance, as stated in Auth. Defuncta. Therefore, in this legitime and Trebellian portion, Marina and Margarita succeeded equally, and this is certain. But what is the quantity of this legitime and Trebellian portion of Bartola, this is doubtful at this point, namely, what portion Bartola had as dowry, of which her husband profited one-third according to the form of the statute, which one-third is imputed into the legitime of the said Bartola as an alienated asset, as in Auth. Res quae, C. communia de legatis. And therefore, what remained to be seen, namely between these sisters Marina and Margarita, is very clear, because there is only the Trebellian portion. Suppose an example: if one believed that Bartola’s legitime portion was one hundred, Margarita’s portion is one-fourth of two hundred, that is fifty, of which at most twenty-five are affected, and no more. This is true, if one rightly considers how these fourths are calculated and from where. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. One who does not reside in a benefice on account of notorious peril is deemed to be residing, and the sentence of deprivation of the benefice pronounced against him is null, and he ought to be restored as one who has been despoiled.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This deprivation was most unjust and utterly void, since the Arezzo disaster and the danger, not to mention the disgrace, of residing in the city itself were certain. Hence, Baptista was not bound to return to a place that was unsafe and notoriously suspect, as stated in the chapter *Accedens*, *De re iudicata*, and in the chapter *Pastor*, in the gloss *Loquor*, if these events occurred within the walls of the city of Arezzo and among the partners residing there. For one is considered a resident if he does not stand in the way of his own residence, as noted by Johannes Andreae in chapter 1, *De clericis non residentibus*, Book 6, in the *Novella*, where he explicitly states this in cases of devastation of lands and determines that such persons are to be regarded as residents. And since the judge knew this, the sentence of deprivation issued by him is void, *De re iudicata*, chapter *Quæsitum*. It therefore follows that, as one unjustly dispossessed, he ought to be restored to his benefice, as is read and noted in question 1, chapter *In primis*. And it is highly pertinent to the foregoing that which is noted by Cynus in the Code, *De iure emphyteutico*, law 1, near the end. And even assuming that the group of those partners was not in the city, the city was under siege, and notorious dangers threatened those returning and remaining. I say the same: this cannot be imputed to fault, but to the adverse fortune of the city, and thus they ought not to have been deprived of their benefices, in which no fault is found.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who has sworn to return into the hands of the enemy is bound to do so, if the enemy is cruel.
2. Whether comrades-in-arms and deserters may mutually betray and betray one another.
3. Things unjustly and illicitly acquired are not to be shared.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† Although good faith is not to be kept with bandits, even if they swear to promise on account of a disgraceful cause, they disgracefully receive. ff. de ver. ob. l. si plagii; ff. de pac. l. iure gentium, §. si ob maleficium; supra me. cau. l. qui in carcere; ff. de dolo, l. 1, §. cum fuit. If, however, the war was lawful there, both spoils and agreements are lawful. ff. de cap. et post. reuer. l. si quid bella. For this belongs to military law. i. discriminis. C. de do. §. quis pro redemptione; ff. de iustit. et iu. l. manu.; ff. de sta. hom. l. libertas. Therefore, good faith is to be kept with such an enemy, from 22. qu. 2. c. noli aestimare, and an oath at least out of honor and the custom of arms. ff. de capt. et postli. reuer. l. ius, §. fin. Whence he is not said to be liberated who is bound to return even out of simple honor. arg. ff. de verb. signi. l. nepos proculo; ff. de condi. inser. l. filius; although no one is compelled to return to enemies, so that through this he can in a broad sense be said to have escaped. ff. de cap. l. nihil; ff. de condit. ob causam, l. si pecuniam, in the small gloss; ff. de acqui. re. dom. l. in laqueum; ff. de nego. gest. l. nam et seruus, in princi. Certainly, nor is it to be thought that he who substituted his own flesh as a hostage wished to have had the intention of not returning; for it is not probable that he would abandon a necessary person ensnared. l. 3. ff. ne quis eum. For such an intention ought to have existed, as in said l. nam et seruus. And therefore he is not said to be liberated from the enemy who owes a pledge, according to the note at the end in l. litigatores, §. quid ergo, ff. de arb. For he alone is said to be liberated who is liberated fully in law and in fact. ff. de sol. l. et et l. cum quis, §. qui hoiem. For he is not free from me over whom I have the right of claim, even if he has escaped my custody. ff. de acq. poss. l. 3, §. si seruus quoque, and §. non va. filios; and ff. de sol. l. fugitiuus. Likewise, even if he were free, according to what is noted by Inn. in c. sicut. de iureiu., nevertheless on account of his deceit he will be made to return concerning deceit. ff. de dolo, l. eleganter, §. seruus pactionis. I conclude, therefore, that he is not said to be liberated, as one who, so to speak, can be made to return. ff. de sol. l. si creditor fundum. And this as to the first point, unless on account of the cruelty of the enemy he fears death. ff. de his, qui sunt sui, vel alie. iu. l. 2, §. dominorum; because one is permitted to redeem his blood even by craft. ff. de bon. eor. qui sibi mor. consci. l. 1, and what is noted in c. pastor. de reiud. in cle. supports this.

† On the second point, it is by no means to be doubted that fellow soldiers of a just campaign can contract a partnership between themselves and enter into agreements. C. de pac. l. licet; otherwise in private robbers. ff. de fideius. l. si a reo, §. id, quod vulgo. It being supposed, therefore, that the war is just, prisoners of burden are to be shared, just like the rest of the plunder. For a man who is captured in war becomes a thing from a person, and is deemed in the place of a donkey or of any movable property; and in doubt between kings it is to be presumed that war is waged by the law of nations, as sovereignty and justice are contended for on both sides. ff. de iusti. et iu. l. ex hoc iure. And even if it were not just at the head, that is, as to things, nevertheless necessity causes that to be lawful for subjects which otherwise would not be lawful. ff. de act. et ob. l. seruus. Not in all things, which have a place when the master was a private person, but a king is a public person, who must publicly be obeyed; for what is commanded must of necessity be done. And this as to the second point, and in the forum of the courts; although in the forum of con-
† -science it would be otherwise, if the subjects had a wounded conscience.

† That must be known, that things ill-acquired are therefore not divided, as in l. caeterę. fa. hęr., l. quod autem, ff. pro socio, because they do not fear, nor do they proceed to the force of a judgment. l. communi diuidundo, §. inter prędones, ff. communi diui., nor are they said to be acquired. ff. de acque pos. l. quod seruus. Therefore, the words having been considered and weighed even better: because the words do not say 'liberated from obligation', but 'liberated from captivity'; and it being supposed that on account of the cruelty of the enemy he is not bound to return to captivity, and since he is not the owner of his own limbs, he is not bound to submit himself to swords. ff. ad leg. aquil. l. liber ho., nor to give another the occasion for wrongdoing. I say that he was liberated from captivity: for he is not detained in prison, nor is he bound to return on account of cruelty; and that which is noted in §. ex qui. cau. na. l. in eadem. ff. de ver. sig. l. liberationes, and l. qui neque sequantur, and l. sequantur, and l. solutum non intelligimus, otherwise is, §. does not stand in the way. Therefore, this noble knight the lord Florimond ought to be considered as liberated. And it does not matter how he was liberated, especially so far as relates to the effect of the exercise of his rights. ff. de ver. ob. l. cum seruus fugitiuus, who would commit a theft of himself; but he ought to be called freeborn, returned by postliminy, as in the laws cited above.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What effect do those words, "I request that justice be done," have?
2. By proceeding in the case, one is not understood to have waived those exceptions which do not impede the process.
3. Whether a statute concerning those holding land in fief is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ.

† It is most true that by these words they requested that justice be done; it is not understood as concluded. And the reason is that the state of the case did not permit it. Then it is concluded, because the protestation and reservation would benefit Lord Florimond, as in l. si fideiussor, in the beginning, qui sat. cog. fa. hær.; likewise l. Item Labeo, § 1. And that justice may be done at any time, not only at the end of the case, but during the proceedings and in order toward the conclusion. Hence these words, “I request that justice be done,” are rightly understood and ought to be understood as proceeding or occurring, as reason dictates. For at the beginning of the case it is understood as proceeding, but in all proofs of the agreement it is understood. In deciding, the words are to be understood civilly. ff. de serv. l. si cui. And justice being done is represented in any act and in any state of the case. ff. de iust. et iur. l. pen. de cond. indeb. l. eleganter, § si quis post, according to Jacobus de Belvisis. And a procurator appointed for the conduct of the case cannot conclude in the case in the preludes of the judgments, just as he cannot renounce. ff. de nov. l. si quis delegatus, according to Bartolus. For he would act fraudulently and contrary to the form of the mandate. de proc. l. qui procurator; ff. de pact. l. sed si tamen; ff. de fideiuss. l. contra te, § post litem, as in l. non contest. c. 1, according to Innocentius.

† proceeding even in the case is not understood to constitute a waiver of those exceptions which did not impede the process. C. de probat. l. exceptionem; C. de except. l. si quidem; lit. contest. It appears that the way of examining them is not precluded, as noted in ff. de rei vend. l. officium. It should be known that those exceptions which impede the process by their ineptness are those arising from a preceding decision of the case, if, however, they are proved immediately; otherwise, they are to be examined after the joinder of issue, as noted in ff. de iureiur. l. nam et postea, in the beginning. Some say that all notorious exceptions impede, as noted in Io. And. in c. 1, de lit. contest., lib. 6. It is, however, more cautious to invoke the office of the judge at that time than to attempt [to proceed], arg. ff. de pet. haer. l. plane; and l. pe. de bonis lit. l. qui cum maior, § si patris, in the gloss, for the case is joined on the ground of notoriety, as noted in de neg. gest. l. at qui natura, § qui me absente. That little note is irrelevant to the matter at hand, because there the notoriety was for the plaintiff, not for the defendant; nevertheless, what I said does not hold due to the exception taken from the definition of the exceptions themselves. How much

† To another point, whether the statute concerning those holding land in fief is valid, it must be said that if it regards public utility, for example so that the land may be better held, which perhaps has bad air, such as Sarema, and few farmers, it induces inhabitants. D. de edil. edict. l. quid sit fugitivus, §. eadem cesso. And it supports what is noted in Auth. de mandato, princ., §. sed et suscipientes, col. 3, which states that he has useful dominion, and therefore he can impose a law on his thing. D. de superf. l. 1, §. quod ait. But if it were made out of emulation of superiors, it is not valid. D. de oper. publ. l. opus publicum; otherwise, by bad faith. D. de doli except. l. 1, in fine; D. de poen. lib. l. eorum; and l. si privatus. D. qui et a quibus. These, however, were deceived in their time. But now it is concluded that in the case at hand, one should proceed as the expert, Lord Florimond, has done, provided that the exception of prescription does not stand in the way.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone makes a gift to a certain woman and her heirs, whether this constitutes a dowry or a donation, and whether the children of the first marriage succeed in it.
2. A custom that grants something notable to primogenitures is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† As regards the point set forth below, which states that the said Guitard granted the place of Bartholomew Aquilino and Toserius Bartholomew, and to the heirs descending from them, and promised and swore to uphold this donation, a doubt arises whether this is a dowry, or a donation, or something mixed of dowry and donation. Namely, that during the marriage it is a dowry, but afterwards it is a donation collated to the children of that marriage, so that children born from another marriage in no way succeed beforehand, but the second donation belongs solely to the daughter, whereas the second dowry belongs to the husband. And this doubt arose from the word "donation." And if it is a donation with respect to the daughter, whether it was valid immediately or not. And I say that this is not a simple donation, but a donation causa dotis (by reason of dowry), and it is valid immediately, as C. de fideicommissis hereditatibus, l. Pomponius; Philadelphus; and ff. quod in fraudem creditorum, l. si; ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio centum, §. Titio genero. And therefore, when the daughter becomes widowed, the dowry reverts to her. C. de rei vindicatione, l. sed quamvis; ff. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. pater certam; ff. de dote praestanda, l. 1, in principio. And it is noteworthy that mention was made of the children of the first marriage not simply, but as heirs, and therefore it encompasses all children, provided they are heirs, whosoever the marriage from which they were begotten. ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. placet; ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si licet. Although the father did not intend this, nevertheless the disposition of the law makes it so, as ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. continuus, §. si. The objection from ff. de pactis dotalibus, l. inter socerum, §. cum inter patrem, does not hold, because there the mother died in the same first marriage; and thus it is of no effect.

† Regarding the other point concerning the custom that grants precedence to the firstborn, it must be said that this custom holds force on account of the honor of families, and because it grants something distinctive to firstborns, which ought not to be taken away from them; for this is a benefit of the law, not of the father. D. de adoptionibus, l. si augeatur, § sed impuberi. This right also passes derivatively in this manner; and therefore the lord Florus, who succeeded Aquilinus and Anebimus in the said right, has a stronger right to the castle in dispute. C. de donationibus, l. si auia. And once spoliation is proven, restitution must be made, according to L. Iul. de vi, l. si quis ad se fundum, de restitutione spoliatorum, c. saepe, and c. frequens, lib. 6, together with countless others. From the foregoing it follows that the children of the second marriage are excluded by custom from the said castle, as in other matters pertaining to the common law. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether women excluded by males regain the right of succession upon the death of the males.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the matter inserted, the facts are as follows. A certain person dies having made a will, from which there remain four legitimate and natural children, of whom two are males and two are females; these females are married and have been dowered by their father. Now, however, one of these two male sons dies intestate, with his other brother and the two aforementioned sisters, who are married and dowered, as stated above, surviving him. Now the question is asked whether the said two sisters succeed to a share of the inheritance of the deceased together with the surviving brother, or not, notwithstanding the form of the aforementioned statute, which reads thus, namely: "Furthermore, we establish and ordain that if any woman has been dowered by her father, mother, or full brother, she may not come, either directly or indirectly, to the succession of her father, mother, or full brother intestate, if legitimate sons remain from the said persons or any of the aforementioned, whether sons or sons of sons. But if no sons remain from them, such a woman shall succeed as the order of law requires. We do, however, will that a woman dowered and married to a foreigner may not succeed in the paternal or maternal goods, or those of other blood relatives, if there are extant from them sons, daughters, or other blood relatives up to the third degree. But if there are no other blood relatives obtaining in the third degree, or of the nearest, such a woman may succeed to a woman, according as the order of law requires." In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Since there remains a male son of the woman who brought the dowry, the female heirs of the dowager do not succeed, on account of those words of the statute, “or any of them,” i.e., of the donors; it is not stated, “or any of them,” i.e., of those whose inheritance is being discussed. This is also shown by the following clause; I do not cite the laws, because it is not expedient. But this second brother died without male sons; whether the females resume the right of succession. Some say that they do, but Bartolus says that they do not, because the statute does not say “as long as,” etc., but “if sons,” etc. He places this in l. si, and 2, ff. ad Tertium; he was doubtful, nevertheless I adhere to Bartolus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a statute provides that if anyone manages the affairs of another, and on account of such management a lawsuit is brought, that the case be submitted to arbitration, it must first be established summarily that something was indeed managed.
2. What must be proven from the outset so that the judgment may be valid, or so that it may be initiated.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It matters greatly whether the statute states that if anyone has managed the affairs of another, and by reason of such management any litigation that might arise is to be submitted to arbitration. In that case, it must first be established summarily that some management has taken place, because the law speaks under this condition: if anyone has managed. Hence, the management is introduced by the arbitration agreement. I do not say that it must be valid or of a certain quality, but of any quality whatsoever; nor do I say that it must be fully proven, because it ought to be fully examined later. Hence, wherever the preamble, which introduces the action, is to be more fully ventilated subsequently, summary proof suffices to introduce it, as in D. ad exhibenda, l. thesaurum. And unless the action is summarily proven, the subsequent proceeding ought not to be introduced, as in D. de libellis criminalibus, l. liberis, §. si. Hence, if the statute were to say that if anyone were a minor and injured, and sought the aid of restitution in integrum, he ought to submit to arbitration, it would first be necessary to prove summarily the minority and the injury, according to the noted opinion of Bartolus and others in D. de iureiurando, l. nam et postea, §. si minor, prius. It must first be established for the judge regarding the cause, which is the final and precise cause of the mandate to order something outside the common law, namely that he ought to mandate something to the parties. Since civil matters fall under civil matters in a certain order, the act of the ordering party must be known before the ordered act, as in C. de ordine iudiciorum, l. pe. And if the statute were to say that the causes of widows ought to be submitted to arbitration, it must be clear that she is a widow, as in C. qui accusare non possunt, l. non ignorat.

But whether the statute states that the same arbitration applies to causes arising from managed affairs, and then it suffices to allege them, because for the introduction of actions, in general, what is alleged is in the middle, what is proven is at the end, what is proven is in the execution, and what is adjudicated is the judgment, as in D. de iure omnium iudiciorum, l. cum quaedam, §. si. And it would be perverse to found proof before the action, since the law has placed proofs in their proper place and has ordered all acts legitimately, and they ought not to be mixed or entangled. And in X. de iudicibus, c. exhibita. Nor ought we to wait until the litigation is contested and the matter is liquidated; because by the same reasoning we ought to wait until the proofs are concluded. And then the arbitration would proceed under a liquidated matter, nor would it be expedient to submit the cause to arbitration unless the parties have a disputed cause, or one fabricated from false allegations, as in C. de iudicibus, l. rem non novam, §. patroni.

Therefore, recourse must be had to the words of the statute. The statute says that arbitration shall be made regarding the administration of guardianship. Certainly, above all, it must be established that there was a guardian; otherwise, he is not compelled to submit to arbitration, just as if the statute were to say: causes of appeal shall be submitted to arbitration. For above all, it must be established that there is an appeal, as in c. Roma, de appellationibus, lib. 6. Nor ought it to be proven immediately, as in the introductory beginning, from whom the appeal was taken; because this is to be proven later.

It must therefore be known that certain matters regard the order of one act in relation to another; and then the matter is to be ordered, as I have said. Certain matters do not concern the order, but consist in points to be debated from the facts narrated, such as the jurisdictions of judges. And then the law speaks when certain [matters arise]. Certain matters regard the decision of the case, and in these [the party] has no right, because he does not prove what he ought to prove. On the testament of a soldier, l. Diuus; as noted by Innocentius, Extra, de priv., c. Ex parte abbatissae. And therefore, in our case, if the management of the gestor is denied under the Pisan statute, it must be proved summarily regarding the person of the gestor, for example, that Titius managed [the affairs]; nor is the heir bound to submit to arbitration, because he is not sued concerning the administration; for the word "cause" signifies the immediate person, not by way of derivation to another, and the statute is contrary to the common law, therefore it must be construed strictly. D. de coniug., cum eman. lib., l. 1, § Nunc videamus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether substitutes are excluded from the succession of a ward, if they have not requested a guardian, just as the mother would be excluded, and whether succession then takes place by the express vulgar substitution or by the fideicommissary substitution. And no. 2.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows: A certain Andreas of Saxo Ferrato made his will, in which, among other things, he instituted his children yet to be born as his universal heirs, to whom he made a substitution, vulgar, pupillary, and by fideicommissum. The testator then had a wife. And after she died, he took another, from whom a male child was born. And in the said will, he appointed several tutors for the said son: finally, the testator died; then some of the testamentary tutors died. Then, after many years, the ward died, with no tutor having been requested for him by the said substitutes, nor the guardianship administered by one of the testamentary tutors, who now lives.

† It is asked whether the aforementioned male or female substitutes are deprived of the said substitution. And in this question, one must consider several points due to the multiple substitutions involved. And here there is a certain subtlety of the law. First, however, it must be known that the substitutes are not required to petition for a guardian: just as they are not required to do so in law, as is noted in C. ad Ter. l. matres. And if only one guardian had been left in the will, and he were alive, nor had he been removed or excused: this would be clear, whether he administered or not, as is noted by Cy. C. de admi. tut. l. si. But because several guardians were left, and some have died, and no guardian was petitioned in place of those who descended, nor did the survivor administer: and thus the ward lacked a guardian due to this defect, the substitutes are deprived of the inheritance, just as the mother is deprived: as ff. ad Ter. l. 2. §. quod si decesserit quidam. And this must be presupposed as true with regard to pupillary substitution. But with regard to vulgar substitution it seems otherwise, and with regard to fideicommissary substitution: as ff. qui petat tut. l. credendum. although some understand that law in a singular fideicommissum, not a universal one. Nevertheless, the truth is that neither from the vulgar substitution nor from the fideicommissum is one excluded, for the reason of that text, which says that from another’s judgment etc. It must be seen

Therefore, the question remains whether, since the ward did not have a tutor authorizing him, succession takes place under the vulgar substitution expressly made from all the goods of the testator—because the express vulgar substitution precludes the existence of a *sui heres*—or whether it should be said that succession takes place under the fideicommissary substitution, which is confirmed by the existence of a *sui heres*; or whether it should be said that he is altogether unworthy to succeed. And I hold that the substitute comes in under the fideicommissary substitution, and that substitution is to be considered which is confirmed by the existence [of the heir]; and therefore the substitutes, by virtue of the fideicommissum, come in after deducting the legitime and the Trebellian portion, which legitime and Trebellian portion pertain to the legitimate successors of the ward; and this person, who succeeds intestate, is the step-aunt, who is said to hold the nearer place and degree.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the debtor who pays the depositor is discharged, if a cession of actions has been made.
2. The debtor, having notice of the cession, may pay the cessionary.
3. What the words "transferred" and "granted" signify.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be said that the person who paid the aforementioned depositor is discharged, for three reasons. First, on account of the nature of the obligation arising from deposit: the thing deposited ought to be restored to the depositor, unless another person having stronger rights pursues them in court. D. de deposito, l. bona fides; C. eod., l. pe.; and Auth. sed in cautum. Moreover, the depositary is not liable except for fraud and gross negligence. But there is no fraud nor gross negligence in satisfying the depositor: for in the case of one who is ignorant, no fault is found. D. comm. div. her., l. argentum. Furthermore, he was obliged to pay him out of necessity. For he had no exception to raise; therefore, he is discharged, as D. de solutionibus, l. si stipulatus, § si lancen.; and C. de deposito, l. si. Second,

† on account of the general nature of assigned actions: for if the debtor is certain of the assignment, he may pay the assignor. C. quae res obligari possunt; l. nomen; ff. de transactionibus; l. si; C. de nova; l. 3; and the note, ff. de pactis; l. si cum emptor. Thirdly, on account of the nature of the retention of the usufruct. For he who has the usufruct of a claim may lawfully receive payment. As C. de bonis maternis; l. 1. But this donor reserved to himself generally the fruits of all things given, therefore also of the claim. C. de usufructu; l. 1. Although it is said that here there is no question of payment, but of confession, which does not harm anyone other than the confessor, as C. de nova; l. non abstulit. I respond in three ways: first, because it does not matter in what manner satisfaction has been rendered. ff. de solutionibus; l. solutum; §. satisfactum. Secondly, because confession in a deposit proves true payment, nor can the exception of non-payment be opposed. ff. de deposito; l. publicus; in fine; C. de non numero pecuniae; l. in contractibus. Thirdly, because the confession of him to whom the business principally pertains harms those who derive their title from him. ff. de pignori; l. si superatus. From which it is concluded that the said depositary is discharged. Nevertheless, the depositor is then said to restore this money to the assignee. ff. de exceptione doli; l. apud Celsum; §. quod si alicui. And these statements are concerning the depositor who assigned his rights, and afterwards confessed that he had been paid, whether this prejudices the assignee. And it determines that it does not. And it should be known that I speak of the confession of a debt paid after the assignment, if the assignor were to confess that he did not have the right to assign, and thus would act against his own assignment. This is another matter, concerning which see the note in l. si non actor malitiosus, and in other laws prudently cited by you. It should be known that a donation is a title, an assignment is a quasi-delivery, and a mandate is a commission of direct actions. And to these three are adapted all the words which notaries multiply:
