† And the word "transferred" is properly referred to the word "granted," and to direct [grants]. D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem; and noted in C. quoniam fiscus vel privatus; D. de manumis; D. de procuratoribus, in the end; C. de procuratoribus; D. qui stipulatus est; D. de fideicommissis hereditatibus; D. plane. And thus I say, and I advise, following Baldus.

A certain man named Raynerius Geppi of the city of Cortona had as his wife the lady Miranda, daughter of Vannius of the said city, endowed with a certain sum of money. During the said marriage, the brother of the said lady Miranda died, and his inheritance came to and belonged to the said lady Miranda. After the death of the aforementioned brother of lady Miranda, the said Raynerius received the pensions, fruits, and revenues of the goods of the said inheritance pertaining to the said lady Miranda. It does not appear whether lady Miranda was willing or dissenting. Finally, the said Raynerius died. Now the said lady Miranda demands from the heir of the said Raynerius that an account be rendered to her regarding the said fruits, and that the said fruits be restored to her. It is alleged on behalf of the said heir that the said fruits ought not to be restored, because the said Raynerius consumed them in the household and family together with the said lady Miranda; and also because he provided the said lady Miranda with suitable medicines for her sustenance. On behalf of the said lady Miranda it is said that this is not true; and even assuming it were so, it is nevertheless said that the said fruits ought to be restored to her, because the said goods are not, nor were they, dotal, nor paraphernal; and that the said heir also received a certain quantity of fruits from the said goods after the death of the said Raynerius, which he also demands be restored. The question now arises: what is the law?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A woman has threefold patrimony.
2. The husband profits from the fruits of the dotal goods, and what is said regarding paraphernalia at number 3, and what in the third genus of the wife's goods, whether the husband profits from the fruits, at number 4.
3. To give is to lose.
4. Whether a woman, remaining silent when the husband receives the fruits, is deemed to have made a gift such that she cannot recover them.
5. Whether the husband may set off the maintenance provided to the wife against the fruits of the dowry or of the paraphernal goods or of others, and in the following opinion, at number 1.
body: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

† To make clear what is to be said, I premise that a married woman may have a patrimony, that is, her own goods, of three kinds. For some are dowry goods given in dowry, and the husband is the owner of these goods. L. Dote, C. de rei vend. et non vend.; fully in L. In rebus, C. de iure dotis; and in these the husband acts in court, I say, as owner. But how he ought to manage such goods, not in L. Si constante, § Si maritus, Sol. Ma. The woman has certain goods not given in dowry, but handed over to the husband and prepared by him in the husband’s house; and these are called paraphernal goods, and of these the husband is then bound to keep safe, and he is always deemed to have a mandate in these. L. Si, C. de pactis conventis. The woman has certain other goods not given in dowry, nor handed over to the husband; but they are outside the aforementioned species: as is rightly proved by looking at L. Si ego, § Dotis, ff. de iure dotis, where these two last members are proved. This division of patrimonies was perceived by the Gloss in the said L. Si, C. de pactis conventis, in L. 2 and 3, Gloss. More clearly did Bartolus set it forth in L. Si maritus, C. de procuratoribus.

† Now, to the point, I say that in the first category of dowry goods, the husband indisputably enjoys the fruits. L. pro oneribus, C. de iure dotium; and fully noted in L. diuortio, ff. sol. matr., even if a contrary agreement were made. L. si conuenerit, ff. de pactis dotalibus; and there is nothing to the contrary regarding these.

† In the second category of fruits, the gloss in the aforementioned law *Si*, Codex, *De pactis conventis*, distinguishes between industrial and natural fruits. Cynus disputes this; Marianus recites [authorities] in this matter. Bartolus, coming later, reduced this matter to two cases in the law *Maritus*, in the principle, Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*: namely, either they are perceived against the will of the wife in natural fruits, or they are great, or small. He says that great ones are to be restored insofar as [the husband] is enriched; small ones he is not bound to restore. But let us see for God’s sake: because if we did not see well, the goods of which we speak are not of this category, but of the third category, because in truth it is posited that administration was not granted to the husband. Nevertheless, whatever it may be, let us find the reason how the husband profits from the fruits of paraphernal property, and the reason is, as the gloss says in the aforementioned law *Si*, Codex, *De pactis conventis*, on account of the labor which the husband sustained. Another reason I find given by my lord, the learned Baldus, namely, because the husband is bound to custody, and is obligated for the custody of the said goods, therefore in compensation for the said burden the husband profits from part of the fruits, as in the aforementioned law *Si*, Codex, *De pactis conventis*. Hence, if you look carefully at these goods, one must consider, according to Bartolus, the will of the woman regarding the perception and consumption of the fruits. But according to the gloss and Baldus, we consider the will of the wife regarding the delivery of the aforementioned goods: because immediately upon losing [them], the law obligated the husband to custody, and gives him in compensation for the said burden part of the fruits. Therefore, to understand myself, it is not to look at the will of the wife at the time of the perception made by the husband, as it seems Bartolus wished.

† Because, in the third category of property, the husband is not bound to the aforementioned custody, the said reason ceases, and so too does the disposition of the law. L. adigere, § quis, de iure pat.; ff. de ali. leg.; L. Seyo, in principio. Since, therefore, in our case it is not alleged that she granted the administration, these goods are thus of the third category. Nevertheless, I find that in this matter my aforementioned lord, Lord Baldo, in his consultation in a certain question concerning a ward, in the question of a certain Catherine, daughter of John called Sacro de Pupio, a consultation which begins: “Certain things are those which are in the dominion of the husband, etc.,” reproaches Bartolus, as he is reproached elsewhere, as is the Gaul. See in the enumeration of cases, as in L. Gallus, § idem credendum, de lib. et posthu. And because he left the more difficult case untouched, as is said elsewhere in § ille casus in the said L. Gallus, namely, because Bartolus distinguished only two certain cases, i.e., where the wife’s will is clearly apparent, or because where her will does not appear, Bartolus says nothing, and thus he failed in the enumeration of cases. And in this, after much discussion, he concludes that the fruits must in no way be acquired by the husband, but that the property must be restored by the husband’s heirs to the wife, unless it were a case of poverty into which the husband has fallen without her fault; for then the wife must provide for the necessities of the husband. He himself cites Extra, de consuet., c. ex parte. I will uphold this opinion with certain laws and reasons. And first, by proving, I will respond to one objection that might be raised. And I argue thus: the common nature of both sexes is such that no one is presumed in doubt to squander his money. L. cum in debito, ff. de prob.

But to give is to lose, as stated in the law *contra iuris*, Digest, *De pactis*. Therefore, it should not be presumed that there was a donation. Moreover, this is proven by the special nature of the female sex, which is such that all women are extremely avaricious, to the extent that they are not presumed to make donations. See the law *si ego*, Digest, *Ad Velleianum*; Code, *De donationibus ante nuptias*; the law *si asponso*. And it should not be presumed that this lady would differ from her kind, by argument from the law *eleganter*, § *non solum in ratione sui*, Digest, *De dolo*. From these authorities, one may well respond that it cannot be said that it is presumed that she made a donation. Furthermore, even if it were said that a donation was made, since a donation between spouses is not valid unless confirmed by death, and this woman survived, such a donation would have no effect. See the law *si stipulata*, at the end, Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*. Thirdly, this is proven by the unusual and incongruous nature of marital relations: for it is incongruous and monstrous for a woman to make a donation to her husband; rather, it is the husband who ought to make a donation to his wife. See the law *si stipulata*, cited above. Therefore, it should not be presumed. See the law *apud Iulium*, at the end, *De legibus* 1; and the law *continuus*, § *cum quis*, *De verbis obligatorum*, cum sequentibus.

† Nor does it avail to say that the said lady remained silent while the said Rayner was collecting the said fruits, and therefore she appears to have consented: Extra, de regulis iuris, c. Qui tacet, and the following chapter, lib. 6; and l. Qui patitur, ff. de manumissionibus. Therefore, since they were collected with her consent, the heir of her husband is not bound, as is noted in the aforementioned l. Maritus, ff. ad legem Falcidiam, according to Bartolus; and this is supported by l. Si servus and l. Utrum, with the gloss, ff. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem.

Setting aside many things said by Dino in the aforementioned c. Qui tacet and the following chapter, and those said by the doctors in l. Filius, §. Inuiti, ff. de procuratoribus, and l. Inuitus, Cod. eodem titulo, and l. Gayus, ff. de pignoratitia actione, I say that because we are dealing with a disform act, namely taking from another’s goods or entering into someone’s possession, where no contract proceeds from whose nature one may or must do such a thing, dissent is presumed: l. 2, Cod. de acquisitione possessionis; and see Bartolus in l. Quae dotis, in the last column, ff. de solutione matrimonii. The same applies to a formal act, so that one does not appear to consent to those who prepare prejudice for themselves; for this is removed, because when I remain silent while someone acts in my property or right, to which I owe reverence, I do not appear to consent, and reverence removes such presumption: l. 1, §. Quae onerandae, quarum rerum actio non datur, and l. Pe, ff. de furtis; and Bartolus expressly holds this in the aforementioned l. Quae dotis. And this supports what is noted in a similar case in l. In eadem, ff. quibus ex causis maior. Thus it is clear that the gloss cited above does not speak well at all.

Therefore, it remains to conclude that in the case where the wife’s will does not appear expressly, it is presumed in doubt that the fruits were collected against her will, as is clear from the above. And thus the heirs of the husband are bound to restitution of them. And so I find that the aforementioned learned Doctor Baldus concluded in the said consilium; and I find that the Eminent Doctor of Laws, Doctor Franciscus de Albergotis of Arezzo, held the same opinion in concluding the aforementioned question. Therefore, it must be concluded that these goods were not paraphernal. And thus, for the reason stated above, the husband ought in no way to have the fruits. And it seems to be the case, if the letter is not violated, in the aforementioned l. Maritus. And even if it were posited that they were paraphernal, nevertheless, since they were collected against the will of the said lady Mirada, and against her will is presumed by law, they must still be restored. This is well supported by the gloss in the aforementioned l. Ubi, Cod. de iure dotium; and by l. De his, Cod. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem.

† nor the defense which the aforementioned heir introduces, namely that the said lady was supported with great delicacy; for on this account he cannot retain [the fruits]. The text is in § taceat, C. de rei uxoria actione, and l. quod in uxorem, C. de negotiorum gestis, and especially since the husband himself did not protest when he intended to recover from the said lady Miranda, as in l. alia, C. de negotiorum gestis, and l. Nescio, ff. eodem, and as noted in the said l. quod in uxorem. Moreover, this man had a dowry, by means of which he was bound to support and nourish her. l. dotis, ff. de iure dotium, and l. pro oneribus, C. eodem titulo. Indeed, even without a dowry he must maintain her. l. si cum dotem, § si autem in severissimo, ff. eodem, and l. quod si nulla, ff. de religiosis et sumptibus funerum. Hence in Auth. de nuptiis, § sic itaque, ver. quis enim, col. 4, and in Auth. qui matrimonium efficax, § quodam, col. 6. Therefore he will not be able to say that he consumed the said fruits in supporting the said lady Miranda. It remains therefore, both from the aforementioned reasons and also from the authority of the aforementioned doctors, that it must be concluded that the aforementioned heir ought to render an account of the said fruits and is bound to their restitution. As for those perceived under the title of soluto matrimonio, there is no doubt: for he must absolutely restore them, as is noted in l. divortio, ff. soluto matrimonio. Always reserving, however, the sounder opinion, according to l. Claudius, ff. qui potiores in pignore habentur. And thus I say and advise, I, Andreas Alpheus de Cort., the humblest doctor of laws. And to the truth I have subscribed and appended my usual seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether fruits of the dowry, or of paraphernal property, consumed by the husband are to be recovered by the wife.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The most learned Doctor, Master Andreas, alleged all that could be alleged. And I am of the same opinion as he, except with regard to things consumed in common use: which, even if consumed with friends or shield-bearers, would not be recoverable from them. This is held by the gloss in l. si stipulata, §. si vxor, on the word "factus est." Argument to this effect: ff. de communi dividundo, l. in rebus, §. possunt; and ff. de usu et habitatione, l. caeterum, §. multa, together with the following law. And thus counseled Master Recuperus and Doctor Bartolus, that one is not liable for what has been consumed, but only for what remained with the husband, or for the remainder. And thus is understood l. pen. ad leg. Falcidiam, de donationibus inter virum et uxorem; l. si id, quod, §. si quis. And this is the truth. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the Year of Our Lord 1360. Indiction 13. during the time of Lord Pope Innocent VI, on the 12th day of the month of January. Blaxius, son of the late John, son of Peter, of Viso, with the presence, consent, and will of Peter, son of Peter, and through John, his blood relative, for himself and his heirs, gave and bound, ceded and granted by way of pledge to Ser Vannus Berretutius of the said place, present, stipulating and receiving for himself and his heirs, one piece of land, both vineyard and non-vineyard, situated in the district of the land of Nissi, in the locality called Col. Next to the heir of Cambi Præterpellis, and the heir of Vannus Berta, and on the other side, with its entrances and exits up to the public road: with all its right and action, use, or claim, which and what the said piece of land has upon itself and in itself, to have, hold, possess, and enjoy, for one hundred Florins of good and pure gold, and of just weight; which Florins the said Blaxius, in the presence of me, the notary, and witnesses, confessed and acknowledged to have had and received in his possession from the said brother of Vannus: and to have been given, paid, delivered, and counted to him by the said Ser Vannus. The said land, the said Blaxius, for himself and his heirs, promised and agreed with the said Ser Vannus, the writer and recipient, to redeem from the said Ser Vannus for the aforementioned 100 Florins, and to restore the same Florins to him. However, by an express pact made and agreed between them, that the fruits to be collected from the said piece by the lord Ser Vannus for that time during which the said land shall remain pledged, shall not be computed, nor ought to be computed, into the principal. The said Blaxius promising to defend the said land for the said Ser Vannus, and to whom he shall have given right, legitimately against every man, community, and person, and not to raise any lawsuit or dispute against it for him, the said Ser Vannus, or to whom he shall have given right, etc. Renunciation of minority of age, and of non-delivery, and of the pledge, and of the non-receipt of the said Florins, as if not delivered, and not counted, of the said Florins, and of the non-making of the said pact, etc. And for greater caution of all the aforesaid, at the prayers and commands of the said Blaxius, Master Nicolaus acted as surety, and bound himself principally to the said Ser Vannus for the said Blaxius, and promised that he would so act and see to it, that the said Blaxius would observe all and each of the aforesaid things promised, done, and agreed by him, otherwise the said Master Nicolaus promised to observe them from his own property, etc., shall have promised, etc. Response, etc. Done at Viso in the house of the said Master Nicolaus, present Ser Hugolinus Todini of Misso, and Cronellus of Antiquo, community chamber, witnesses to these things. 1361. Indiction 13. and on the 10th day of the month of April, present Lord Jacobus, son of Peter, Riccintus Vannus, Jacobus Redis. and re-gratification of part of the pact of the said year, month, day, and place, present the said witnesses, Lord Jacobus, son of Peter, one of the nearest blood relatives of Blaxius, son of John, son of Peter. And there present, and willing, the said Blaxius, the sale made by the said Blaxius to Ser Vannus Seretutius of Misso of a certain piece of land, vineyard and non-vineyard, situated at Redis. Viso, locality Col. next to its sides. Of this sale it is established by the hand of me, the above-named notary, he ratified, approved, and likewise consented, etc. Now it is asked, since the said Blaxius at the time of the celebration of the said pledge contract was under 14 years of age and lacked a tutor, and the said contract, because it was celebrated and bound without the authority of a tutor and a judicial decree, is null and void among the fideicommissaries. And whether the said ratification made by the said Lord Jacobus of the sale, since in truth no sale was made, nor is found to have been made, prejudices the aforementioned Blaxius. And in the case that the said Blaxius wishes to recover the said piece of land above pledged, whether he can recover it. Whether the fruits collected from the said piece of land, vineyard and non-vineyard, diminish the principal and the main debt, notwithstanding the pacts entered into in the contract itself. And whatever the law may be concerning the premises, please declare, and give your counsel in writing, sealed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A pupillary contract without a tutor and a judge is null, but whether the surety is bound.
2. An agreement to gain fruits is not valid, because it is usury.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the first question, the case is as follows: C. de praediis minorum, l. et si his; and note C. de legatis, l. non dubium, according to the gloss and Cynus, because it is not valid with respect to the ward. But whether the surety is bound is not to be inquired into here, because the document states that Master Nico bound himself principally.

† Nevertheless, there is no doubt that fruits are estimated as principal, nor is an agreement to gain fruits valid: because whatever is added to the principal is usury. And see. ff. si cert. pet. l. rogasti. §. si tibi. cum si. And thus I say, and I advise. I, Baldus de Perusio. V. l. Doctor.

A certain man had two sons, whom in his last will he instituted as his universal heirs, as legitimate and natural sons, yet in equal shares, with the condition appended that if either of them should die without legitimate children, the share of the deceased would devolve upon the survivor. The testator, having not otherwise altered his will, dies. The elder of these two sons, having taken a wife, begat children; the other, the younger, became a brother of the Order of Saint Dominic. Some time later, after the younger had entered the aforementioned order, the elder dies, leaving behind some small children, with their mother remaining as their guardian. The younger, after the death of the elder, and with the consent and will of the entire chapter, made a certain composition and transaction with the aforementioned minors, the mother receiving for them as their guardian. The composition was as follows, namely, that the said guardian, or another person for the said minors, was bound to give to the said brother annually a certain quantity of money at certain terms; and if the said guardian, or another person for the said minors, did not pay the said quantity of money to the said brother at the said terms, as was contained in the instrument of composition and transaction, that the said composition and transaction should be held now, as from then, as not made; and that the said parties should remain ipso facto in that state in which they first were before the aforementioned contract of composition and transaction. Now neither the said guardian nor another person for the said minors has paid to the said brother the said quantity of money at the said terms, as was contained in the said instrument. On account of this non-payment made to the said brother, the Church of Saint Dominic seeks to be remitted into tenure and corporal possession of one-half of all the goods of the father of this brother, by virtue of the institution made by him in his last will; on the ground that the agreements were not observed by them, and the Church, as injured in the said composition beyond one-half of the just price, seeks restitution in integrum as holding the place of the minors; notwithstanding that it has to act with the minors.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The Church, after the lapse of four years, cannot seek the benefit of restitution in integrum, nor can it claim to have been injured beyond half of the just price.
2. The party against whom the agreements were not observed ought to be put into possession.
3. Whether the Order of Saint Dominic is capable of inheriting.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† If four years have elapsed from the day of the composition, the church cannot seek the benefit of full restitution, as in c. ult. de restitutione in integrum, lib. 6. Nor can it allege in the contract of transaction that it was injured beyond half the just price. ff. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. Lucius, §. si.

But because the agreements were not observed, the church ought to be put in possession of the aforementioned goods. C. de edicto diuini Adriani, l. si; C. de pactis, l. cum proponas; C. de transactionibus, l. cum proponas, and l. ut rursum.

† And I assume that the brothers of the Order of Preachers are capable, by virtue of the general custom of the entire Order, which cannot be unknown to the Pope’s knowledge, or by apostolic privileges, and thus it is no objection that their Order is said to be “healing.” Moreover, by law they may acquire [property] so as to sell it, although the contrary holds for the Minor Friars (de episcopis et clericis, l. Deo nobis, according to Jacobus de Arena and Cynus), because the Decretals *Exiit* and *Exiit* do not speak of the Preachers nor of their rule, but only of the Minor Friars; and therefore they have no application to the Preachers, nor to the Hermits, nor to the Carmelites, although they are mendicants. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio. See l. Doctor.

In the name of Christ, Amen. The case is stated as follows: A certain Paulus Paulutii of Perugia had two wives. From the first he had a son named Martin, who became a brother and professed member of the Hermits of St. Augustine. From the second, named Simonella, he had other sons. Finally, the said Paulus died, survived by the said brother Martin, his son Ramus from his own wife, and the said sons from the second wife. Finally, a certain Thomasius, acting as syndic and procurator of the brothers, chapter, and convent of St. Augustine of Perugia, having a cause on behalf of the said brother Martin against the said sons of Paul from the second marriage, [acted]. Finally, the said brothers, chapter, and convent ratified, confirmed, and approved all and singular things done and performed by the said Thomasius as syndic and procurator of the said brothers, chapter, and convent in the aforementioned matter. Finally, the said brother Martin, asserting himself to be the syndic and procurator of the said brothers, chapter, and convent on one side—whose instrument of syndicate is transmitted to you in public form—and the said lady Simonella, guardian of the said sons, on the other side, came to a certain contract by name and occasion of six hundred pounds of denarii, which the said Paul had confessed to have received as dowry from the lady Hugolina, formerly his wife and mother of the said brother Martin, and by name and occasion of one hundred pounds of small denarii in the hands of the said Paul from the goods of the said lady Hugolina; and by name and occasion of a certain legacy made to the said brother Martin by the said Paul of two bushels of grain and two measures of wine during the life of the said Martin; and by name and occasion of the supplement of the legitime, and several other causes; and for the cause of transaction, composition, and pact, they agreed, namely: that the said lady Simonella, guardian of her sons of the said Paul, delivered and granted to the said brother Martin, in his own name and as syndic and procurator of the said brothers, chapter, and convent, a certain piece of land situated in the county of Perugia within its boundaries, to have, hold, possess, and enjoy the fruits of during the life, and while the said brother named Martin lived. And this the said guardian did because the said brother Martin, in his own name and in the syndical name of the said chapter, promised the said guardian not to demand the said six hundred pounds of denarii in one hand, the said six hundred pounds of denarii in one hand, the said one hundred pounds in the other hand, nor the said legacy, nor the said supplement of the legitime, during the life of the said brother Martin, and while the said brother Martin lived. And he promised not to sue, nor molest, nor raise controversy against the said wards and heirs of the said Paul, and their goods, for the said money and supplement of the legitime, nor for possession of the said goods, during the life of the said brother Martin. With this pact, that if the said lady Simonella should pay therefrom to two, or within five hundred pounds of denarii to the said brother Martin as syndic having sufficient mandate to refund: or that a deposit of the said five hundred pounds be made, that the said brother Martin as the aforementioned syndic was bound and ought to leave and release to the said guardian and the said wards the said piece of land; otherwise it would be lawful to re-enter possession of the said piece of land by one’s own authority. Of which transaction, composition, and pact appears a public instrument, which is transmitted to you in public form. Finally, after the lapse of the said two years, the said brother Martin and the aforementioned syndic sold the said piece of land for a certain price. Now the heirs of the said Paul wish to recover and claim the said piece of land from the buyer thereof. It is opposed on behalf of the said buyer that the said piece of land is prescribed by prescription of 30 years and more. It is replied on behalf of the said heirs that the price was not, nor is, fully paid, and thus the sale does not hold. And thus the said buyer can be said to have been, and to be, a possessor in bad faith; and because he knew the condition of the said piece of land, that it was for enjoyment of fruits during the life of the said brother Martin; and the said heirs at the time of the said sale were wards, and thus as a possessor in bad faith he does not prescribe at any time. Also, because he bought from a non-owner; for brother Martin was not the owner, and it does not avail that he had a legitimate mandate to sell. And even if he had a mandate, nevertheless the chapter was not the owner; for brother Martin, by virtue of the said transaction, had the said piece of land for enjoyment of fruits during his life only, as appears from the transaction itself. Also, it is necessary to have the guardianship and inventory of the said lady Simonella, guardian. Now it is asked, having seen the above, whether the said heirs of the said Paul can recover and claim the said piece of land; and if they can, by what way action should be brought.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The law concerning tutors applies to transactions.
2. A contract entered into by a minor, although void ab initio, even if it has effect after the minor has reached the age of majority, is considered valid and binding for the benefit of the contracting parties.
3. What these words mean: "to have, to hold, and to enjoy the usufruct."
4. Prescription does not run against one who is unwilling to sue, nor does it run during minority.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be considered in the first place whether this contract was valid from the beginning. The jurist states in the law *Si quis a pupillo sine tutoris auctoritate emerit*: it is established from one side that the contract is valid. D. de actionibus emptoris, l. Iulius, § Si quis a pupillo. The same applies if there was the authority of the tutor, yet the decree of the judge did not intervene, where the substance lies. C. de administratione tutorum, l. Lex quae tutores. This law also applies in the case of a transaction, as is noted in C. si adversus transactionem, l. 1.

† However, it must be considered here that the ward is on one side, and the church on the other, which is equated with a ward. Thus, by its nature, the contract was established from the beginning. Nevertheless, because in fact it had effect even after the attainment of lawful age, and provided utility to the contracting parties, it ought to be regarded as valid. As stated in the Digest, *De auctoritate tutorum*, law *Pupillus obligari*, section *Sane*. Hence, there is no need to insist upon the validity of the contract, which both parties have utilized; for it has been confirmed, although it did not hold previously.

† Let us therefore consider what this contract entails. The words state that he delivered and granted to have, hold, and enjoy the usufruct of a certain piece of land during the lifetime of Brother Martin. The force of these words appears to be such that, during the lifetime of Brother Martin, not only the usufruct but also the ownership was transferred, as noted in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § sed si pluribus. And the case seems expressly provided for in D. de donationibus, l. donatione in concubina, § species. And see the commentary of Cynus in C. de iure dotium, l. si mulier dotem, and of Bartolus in l. 4, D. de alimentis legatis. Thus, therefore, during the lifetime of Brother Martin, no ownership of the said thing remained with the said sons; but upon the death of the said Brother Martin, the ownership, which had been temporarily relinquished, reverted to them, as in C. de legatis, l. si.

From this follows the manifest conclusion that, while brother Martin was alive, prescription did not run in favor of the said sons, because they were not owners and could not bring an action. C. de annali exceptione, l. 1, in fine; C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus; C. communia de legibus, l. si, §. penultimo. However, after the death of brother Martin, so much time had not elapsed as would have allowed prescription to be completed. Moreover, even assuming that the contract had never been valid, it is certain that prescription did not run against the said sons during their minority. C. in quibus causis in integrum restitutio non est necessaria, l. si. After reaching majority, since the possessor in bad faith had alienated the property, thirty years would have been required, as stated in the Authentica malaefidei, which years have not here elapsed. Therefore, it is concluded that the said property can be vindicated by the possessor, since it is presumed that the wards also were ignorant of their right and of the alienation made; and even if they had known, the result would be the same due to the bad faith of the purchaser. C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. si quis emptionis. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio. V. l. D.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a woman may succeed to the inheritance of a pubescent son, even though she did not petition for guardianship, and number 2.
2. Whether a minor may accept an inheritance without the authority of a curator.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because the deceased was over the age of fourteen, this does not prevent the mother from succeeding to him without the appointment of a guardian, as stated in the law *Matres*, Codex, *Ad Tertullianam*. However, because the said deceased has a full sister, Mathia, not to mention a mother, the mother shall succeed together with Mathia, the sister, each taking one-half; if the said Mathia is a sister of the deceased on both sides. Otherwise, that is, if she were a sister on only one side, the mother would succeed to the whole, excluding her, as in the authenticum *Defuncto*, Codex, *Ad Tertullianam*, and in the Corpus, *Unde vir et uxor*, and in the authenticum *De Nuptiis*, § *Si vero filii*, column 4, according to the gloss.

† As regards the male child who died in pupillary age, if his mother did not assume his guardianship within a year from the day of his father’s death, she is excluded from his succession, and the aforementioned sister Matilda succeeds, as provided in l. sciant, C. de leg. hae. Nor is the sister prejudiced by the fact that she herself did not petition for a guardian; for since she was preceded in degree, as for example by the mother, she was not bound to petition, as stated in l. nepotibus, C. qui pet. tu. Likewise, it does not benefit the mother, even though it is alleged that the aforementioned son’s goods were in her possession. Since she did not assume the guardianship lawfully, as she ought to have done, as provided in l. 2, § si mater, ff. ad tertul. Nor does the redemption of the aforementioned goods, if made by the aforementioned party of Nicolaus Mascius, avail the aforementioned persons in any way.

† As for the last question, namely whether the aforementioned sister Matilda ought to take possession of the portion of the inheritance due to her with the authority of a curator, I say that she does not, because an inheritance is acquired by the mind alone, as stated in the Institutes, *De haereditatibus quaerendis et differendis*, § *fin*. And so I say and advise, I, Francis, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a person who owns a house, part of which is his own property and part of which is held under a life lease, pays the annual rent for the entire house, does he prejudice himself by having paid it?
body: In the case where someone held one possession, which in truth was burdened with a census for one-third part, and for the other two parts was free, M. paid one hundred simply, and having regard to the boundaries of the said property, it appears that the census was paid for the whole property, as if the whole had been subject to census; because in the payment it is stated how he paid the census for such a property, whose boundaries are such and such. And he describes the boundaries of the whole property, not only of the part subject to census, because whether he prejudices himself, so that henceforth the whole is considered subject to census, especially because he who paid confessed that it was subject to census. In the Name of Christ Amen. 1.

† When the formal origin of the emphyteutic contract is established, from which it appears what and how much is the emphyteutic payment of the census, if the caution is understood simply as to what and how much, as it appears in the origin, because the payment is to be referred to what is due, not to what is not due. D. de solutionibus, l. 1; C. eodem, l. 1, with its subject matter. And because if anyone pays the canon for his own property, he does not prejudice himself. C. de locato et conducto, l. qui rem; and fully noted D. de acquirenda possessione, l. si aliquam rem. And therefore, notwithstanding the said payment, the original truth, as the primary cause and foundation, must be inspected. D. de donationibus, l. qui id, quod. And the description of boundaries shows the body of the thing, but not the quality of the thing: because it must be understood according to the principal instrument to which it refers. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. qui tabernas; D. de legibus 1, l. si domus, §. si. However, confession must be adhered to, unless the contrary is proved by the original instrument, i.e., by the reaffirmation, to which adherence is due. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether in statutes the masculine gender comprehends the feminine.
body: In the Name of Christ, and of His glorious Virgin Mother, amen.

† The statute states that whoever shall have killed or captured any of our traitors, or shall have led any of them into the fortress of the commune, shall have and ought to have from the commune 26 gold florins in money, and from the right of the said commune, etc. Now, a certain person captured a certain woman, a traitress and rebel against the commune, and led her into the fortress of the commune, and claimed for himself the said 25 florins according to the form of the statute. The question is now, what is the law? Having considered the aforementioned reform, it seems to me that one should say that in statutes the concept of genera applies; because since the masculine is used in the law and in a matter indifferent to both sexes, and in the case proposed, then the masculine contains the feminine, and vice versa, according to Cynus in l. Quicunque, C. de servis fugitivis et nobilium, and Extra de electione, c. Generali, lib. 6, and in Speculum de disputationibus et allegationibus, § Post haec, under the words "or masculine," under the words "the same holds," Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de verborum significationibus, even if the statute contains odium, provided it is reasonable, as in l. Si quis id quod, de iuris et facti ignorantia. Moreover, this statute, according to the captor, contains favor, and therefore should be extended, as in the aforementioned l. 1, de verborum significationibus, and l. Si quis ita, de testamento tutorum. From which it seems to be concluded that the reward of the aforementioned reform ought to be due to the one who captured the said woman and led her into the fortress of the commune. Franciscus Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A woman claiming to be pregnant by someone is not believed unless she proves it according to the form of law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If a woman asserts that she is pregnant by someone, she is not believed unless she proves it according to the form of the law, as stated in no. ff. de lib. agno. l. 1. §. mariti and the following §, and similarly in I. §. si, and there fully by the doctors, what kind of proof this should be. Since therefore nothing appears, they prove that she ought not to be disturbed, things being thus, nor does it suffice to prove that this man used to visit the house with the blood relatives of the said woman, unless other indications are also proven. Francis, from the lords Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the Hospitallers are bound to the defense of the city.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† Gillius [Andrucii], a citizen of Perugia, prior of the hospital of Saint Mary Magdalene of Marsciano, although he resides there for the custody of the hospital, is not bound to perform guard duty, because he is similar to a guardian of a ward who resides there on account of the affairs of the ward, C. de epis. et cleri. l. orphanotrophos. And because hospitalers ought to attend to the care of the poor, they ought not to be called to another personal burden; for they are appointed to the service of the Prince, that is, of God, and therefore they have exemption from personal duties. I, Baldus de Perusio.

In the name of Christ, Amen. [The inheritance] of Francisca belongs to the maternal aunt alone, to the exclusion of the uterine brother, as in auth. defuncto. C. ad tertul. and in the body of the law from which it is taken, and through the gloss in Auth. de nup. §. filij si vero col. Bald. CONSILIUM CCCLXXX. Otherwise, the case is as follows. This is a certain inquest which the aforesaid lord podestà has made, and perhaps intends to pursue, by virtue of his own office and that of his court, by his discretion and edict, against and concerning Simon, [son] of Andruccio, otherwise called Rui, of the village and locality of Santa Maria. In, of, and upon the matter that, with public fame preceding and a clamorous notification reporting—not indeed from malicious and suspect persons, but rather from truthful and trustworthy ones—it has come by report to the ear and notice of the said lord podestà that the said Simon, the aforesaid accused, in the year immediately past, went to the house of Vulgutia, daughter of the late Angnolo [son] of Iacopo, of the locality of San Giovanni; which house, situated in the said locality adjacent to the property of Pucio [son] of Vanni of Spello, and the property of Russino [son] of Pucio, the public road, and other boundaries; into which said house the said Simon entered, and with her had carnal intercourse, knowing her and committing adultery with the said Vulgutia; from which intercourse had by the said Simon, the said Vulgutia became pregnant by the said Simon, and was and is full by the said Simon; and the said Vulgutia now at present has given birth and is delivered, and there was born one male child, whom the mother of the said child says under her oath to be the said Simon's, and that she was and is impregnated by the said Simon; and the aforesaid Vulgutia was delivered in this year and in the month of February of the said year; and the aforesaid acts were committed and perpetrated by the said Simon in the said year and the months immediately past in the house of the aforesaid Vulgutia, against the form of the statutes and ordinances of the commune of Castro con. and the common law, rendered, pronounced, etc. At the end of the note of this trial, it is said that this woman is a prostitute.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when sexual intercourse with a virgin widow who is married, or with an unchaste woman, is illicit and punishable.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised that sometimes a man knows a woman by force; and then such knowledge never goes unpunished, although some say that it is not punished in the case of a prostitute, according to the law *Verum*, in the Digest, *De furtis*. On this point, see fully the note by Cynus in the law *1*, in the Code, *De raptu virginum*. Sometimes force does not intervene, but rather the consent of the man and the woman; and then, if she is married, adultery is committed. If she is a virgin, or a widow of honest condition, rape (*stuprum*) is committed, as stated in the Digest, *De quibusus*, in the law *Si quis vidua*, and in the note in the Code, *De adulteriis*, in the laws *Si ea* and *Si mulier*. But if she is a widow, or unmarried, otherwise of ill life and reputation, and given to lusts, then there is no penalty, according to the Code, *De adulteriis*, in the law *Quae adulteram*, and in the note by Bartolus in the Digest, *De adulteriis*, in the law *Si uxor*, in the principal part. It is certain regarding a concubine, because concubinary intercourse is not punished, as stated in the Digest, *De concubinis*, in the law *In concubinatu*, and in the note in the Code, *Ad officianum*, in the law *Si qua illustris*. Considering, therefore, that the inquisition does not state that she was known against her will, nor that she was married, nor that she was of honest life, but rather that she was a prostitute, it appears from the indications, the assertion, and the point formed by me, that Simon Andrucii, inquired into by the lord power of the commune, should be entirely absolved from the contents of the inquisition. I, Baldus. For the lord Francesco, son of the lord Baldus, and for the other citizens, referring each thing to its respective person.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An arbitration granted to two citizens does not include the lands of the church without the express license of the Lord Pope.
2. A publication does not bind except with respect to those things which are done after the publication, and how it is to be made.
3. Everyone is understood to have an arbitration according to custom.
body: Arbitrium

It is clear that two citizens did not include the lands of the church in the pact, which cannot be subjected, nor confederated, nor obligated without the express license of the Pope, as appears in the chapters of the Peace of Bologna, and in the chapters subsequently issued with Pope Urban VI, because it includes what is impossible, illicit, and penal. L. 3, § si procurator, Quod quisque iur. The purchasers of the tax, since nothing appears that the city of Assisi was subject, seem to have purchased that which appeared, just as that which was not; for because they were not informed of all things, they entered into the contract. L. 1, § fi., ff. de acquisitione emptionis. Hence this right does not pertain in the common manner. I paid the aforementioned purchasers 10 florins, and I served the remainder, if I remember correctly, which amounts to 15 florins, whence I am released, because the commune, which is represented by them, ought not to collect the tax on account of the bride and the widow, nor be contrary to itself. De conditionibus et de titulis. And having chosen one of the contraries, another cannot be chosen. C. de iure, L. 1, cum si. And it pleases me to send for the tax collectors, and Ser Rugrindo, so that he may know the truth:

† The ordinance was not proclaimed by public crier, and therefore it does not bind; for only those things which are done after publication bind: as in the Authentica "Ut factae novae constitutiones." Publication, however, must be made in the usual manner by a herald, and in the customary places. L. iubemus, C. de defensoribus civitatis.

† The Prior and the Camerarius did not have the discretion to cause the money to come into the common fund; this is understood according to the custom of the commune or of the lord, not in that which was never heard of, regarding pledges, l. obligatione generali, de pign. l. universorum. Bartolus in l. ambitiosa, ver. Item an ex virtute, in the word, de more populi. Otherwise, infinite absurdities, injustices, and scandals would follow. This ordinance does not apply to those elected, except to those who were elected by the commune of Perugia, as is clear there in the word, communis. And afterwards follows the conjunction, for the word, seu, although it distributes between election and sack, nevertheless the word, et, by its own force repeats the antecedent, and that, and there when it says, ff. de fun. instr. l. seiae, §. gayo. But Fran., my son, was not elected by the commune of Perugia, nor named by the commune of Perugia in anything. The reason for the difference: because he whom I do not honor, I do not burden. C. de fideic. l. ab eo. ff. de adop. l. si arrogato, §. sed an impuberi. If any Perugian should come to the government or lordship of any city, land, or place outside the district of Perugia and outside the lands subject to it, he pays in the name of a toll 6 denari for each pound. Because the city of Assisi is not of our district, nor is it subject to us, but to the Roman Church; because it is of the duchy, and no one can subject it to us except the Pope. And because the sins did not appear, but were secret: it was by Lord Fran., son of Baldus, that he was burdened and invited to satisfy the buyers of the toll, and justly, because they held the place of the commune, and therefore he ought not to be vexed further. And many others are in the same case. I, Baldus, 1350. In the month of April.

Lady Agatella, widow of the late Cecholilunta of Pizichellis, heir of the said Cecholi by testament, donated certain goods to Brindozio, her son, with this condition, that if the said Brindozio should die without legitimate natural male children, that the donated goods should come to the said Brindozio: provided that both of them, in the said case, if he had a daughter, could dowry her in a certain quantity. In the same year, day, and month, the said Brindozio and Baldutius made a general release between themselves. With this added, that the said release should not prejudice anyone as to anything contained in the records of the said donations. After this, in 1386, in the month of December, Lady Agatella freed and absolved the said Brindozio from the condition appended in the said donation, and willed that he could make a will and dispose of the donated things at the will of his pleasure. Now it is asked, whether from the pacts appended in the said donation made by the said Lady Agatella to the said Brindozio, a right was acquired by the said Baldutio: so much so that it cannot be taken away from him without his act, and especially considering the words appended in the said general release made between Brindozio and Baldutio, from which they seem to tacitly confirm the pacts and conditions of the said donations.

In 1350, in the month of April, immediately after the said donation, the said Brindozio and Baldutius, and each of them for an equal share, promised to the said Lady Agatella, their mother, to give her annually a certain quantity of grain and wine for alimony. In 1375, in the month of January, the said Lady Agatella, by title of sale, gave and ceded to the said Baldutio all the right that she had against the said Brindozio and his goods, by name and occasion of the debt of the said alimony, for a certain price which the said Baldutio then gave and counted to her. Then in 1376, in the month of December, the said Lady Agatella, notwithstanding the said cession of right, settled, released, and remitted to the said Brindozio all that she could demand from him by reason of the obligation of the said alimony. Now it is asked, whether the said release and remission made by the said Lady Agatella obstructs the said Baldutio, the cessionary: especially since the said Brindozio, before the said release and remission, knew of the said cession of right and made by the said Lady Agatella to the said Baldutio. An elegant counsel.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone makes a donation to another on the condition that, if he dies without sons, the donated property shall pass to another, whether the donor can release the donee from such a condition to the prejudice of the son for whose benefit it was attached.
2. Whether a debtor can make payment to the assignor to the prejudice of the assignee, when the debtor was aware of the assignment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That the said Agatella could not release and absolve Brindozio from the aforementioned condition appended to the inter vivos donation made to Brindozio, in which it was stipulated that if the said Brindozio should die without children, the goods would devolve upon Baldutio. This is proven because from such a contract a right in hope was acquired by the said Baldutio, and this contract is a named contract; hence, repentance has no place against the will of Baldutio, as in D. de pactis, l. si; D. comm. div., §. sicut; D. de iure dotium, l. si ego, §. 1; D. de contrahenda emptione, l. si post mortem, §. si. This is supported by what is noted in Speculum, de locatio, §. nunc aliqua, ver. 75.

To the contrary, the case seems expressly stated in D. de servorum expositione, l. si quis hac; and D. de conditione ob causam, l. si petitam, §. si servum. And this is expressly held by Bartolus in D. de verborum obligatione, l. qui Romae, §. Flavius Hermes. For latest pacts are to be observed between the same parties, C. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima. Moreover, with regard to Baldutio, this appears to be a donation mortis causa or a capture mortis causa: as in C. de donationibus causa mortis, l. nec fratres. Therefore, repentance has place, l. non omnis, si certum petatur; D. de donationibus causa mortis, l. senatus.

Observe that sometimes a pact is opposed for the cause of one contracting party only; and then that one may repent, and not the other, D. de pactis, l. si cum fundum. When, however, a pact is appended for the cause of both contracting parties, and not of a third party, then it is lawful to rescind by common consent what has been done, as in D. de locatio, l. cum in plures, §. si. When, however, a pact is appended for the benefit of a contracting party, and this is our case, and according to the rule of the gloss in the aforementioned l. si quis hac, it seems that when for the benefit of two, one is not sufficient in resolving, especially in a named contract, as noted in the same title, l. quaesitum; just as is today the contract of donation according to the opinion of the gloss in l. ult., D. de conditione ob causam.

Consider that the donor to that third party with whom he contracted is not obligated; therefore, he seems to have free power to repent: D. de obligationibus, n. inuitis non nudis beneficiis ligamur; Inst. de obligationibus, in principio. Also, because, as I said, such a pact accedes to a donation mortis causa, l. seya, D. de donationibus causa mortis; and D. de dote praestanda, l. seya. At present, I do not resolve this doubt, but leave it unresolved without conclusion. However, whoever considers the aforementioned has the light of understanding transmitted by the said authorities, the gloss and Bartolus joined together, and by me.

† On the second point, there are contrary glosses. One says that the debtor’s consent is not sufficient, but a certain prevention by the denunciation of the cessionary is required, where the cession is liquid; but where it is not liquid, litis contestatio is required. The perception of part of the claim, however, induces prevention in every case. C. de novis actionibus, l. 3. Thus says the gloss in l. nomen, quae res pignori obligatae possunt, namely, that denunciation is required, because the direct right is preferred to the useful one, unless the one having the useful right ceded prevents it. The gloss in voluntary cession, ff. de pactis, l. si cum emptore, holds the same opinion. But in restitution under the Trebellian trust, the laws proceed more strongly by the authority of the Senate. Hence there prevention is not required, but mere knowledge suffices. Thus holds that gloss. But the gloss in l. ultima, ff. de transactionibus, says indistinctly that a debtor, knowing, cannot pay the cedent, and that gloss is held by Petrus and Cynus in the said l. 3 and l. nomen, and by Ricardus Maior, principally the gloss which is in l. nomen. It supports what is noted in C. de evictione, l. emptor. The same supports the contrary, because knowledge is not sufficient unless with prevention according to law. Moreover, it is in the interest of the debtor to pay rather the cedent, who would deny the cession if payment were made to the cessionary. Also, this faculty is acquired by the debtor from the beginning. Also, payment made to the cessionary, although it does not liberate by the law itself, but by means of an exception, it is in the interest of the debtor to be liberated by the law itself. C. de exceptionibus, l. 1. Also, l. 3, C. de novis actionibus, lays down a rule, and does not except unless three cases: first, because the case is contested by the debtor denying; second, when part of the debt is recovered; third, when denunciation is made by prohibiting, or certifying. Hence, to add a fourth case is not safe. Thus holds Johannes Andreae in Speculum, de cessione actionum, at the end. But Iacutus de Arena, Raymundus, and Bartolus say that either the cession is made for the benefit of the cedent and the cessionary, so that it is in the interest of the cedent to pay the cessionary; and then mere knowledge suffices, as if the cedent and the cessionary were in a manner two parties to the cession. Hence, payment can be made to the cedent, not prevented by the cessionary; or for the benefit of the cessionary alone: then he alone is considered the party to whom credit is due, constituted of the cession; and thereafter payment cannot be made to the cedent. Thus say they, Iacobus in l. 1, ad Trebellianum; Bartolus in l. facta, eodem titulo; Raymundus in the said l. si, de transactionibus. Since the creditor has the power to cede against the will of the debtor, and to bind him, as we read in C. de haereditate vendenda, l. 2, it is not surprising if, by cession, the debtor is bound to the cessionary, at least usefully: of which in l. 1, ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, per Bartolus, when the words of the cession do not restrict themselves to the action, but are of broad law; because all right is ceded, etc., as was in our case. Or the name of the debtor is ceded; because this word, "name," is common to action and obligation, de actionibus et obligationibus, l. si insolutum. Note in l. 3, C. de novis actionibus, an action was granted, or ceded insolutum for a preceding debt, explaining the letter there "solutionis causa," i.e., insolutum. Or explain, as in l. Modestinus, de solutionibus, because the creditor ceded rights to the one paying. And in the same title, l. Stichum, § si mandato. Or explain "solutionis causa," i.e., to the end, that payment might be made to the mandatary, or cessionary. According to the first explanations, the title of the cession was well for the benefit of both, as in purchase and sale, l. si ut certo, § nunc videndum, common. But the utility of collection belonged to the cessionary alone, and therefore that law joined with its gloss, which says the same in cession as in procreation, contradicts Iacutus, Raymundus, and Bartolus. Hence I consider principally the text of the said l. 3, l. ultima, de transactionibus, which, however, adds a fourth case, namely, of knowledge. And in the understanding of these two laws, this passage stands. And I say that in a mandate in rem suam without cession, that law 3 speaks without doubt, and the reason is: because in equal matter the mandate is preferred, because the actions remained totally with him, nor was a useful action acquired by the procurator. This says the text there in the word "remanserunt." In cession, however, I subdistinguish: either only the action is ceded, and the same, as noted there, and the reason is, because the whole obligation remained with the cedent: and to him alone the debtor is bound. And thus speaks the gloss and C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. 1, and ff. de edendo, l. 1. Or the obligation is ceded, or it is a universal contract, in which all right is ceded: as when an inheritance is sold, or it is a universal restitution: as under the Trebellian trust. Or it is an indefinite and common name, as in the said l. si insolutum. And then that law 3 does not speak, but that law ultima, de transactionibus. For the eyes of the debtor look to the obligation. Or it is not properly a cession: but an obligation of the name, and then our law speaks. And de pignoribus acceptis, l. si convenit, and l. ultima, de loco communi. In our case, therefore, because all right was ceded, the debtor, knowing, could not pay to the prejudice of the cessionary, since it was not in his interest. ff. solutionibus et liberationibus, l. 2, in principio. From these it appears to you that our ancestors did not have the knowledge of all things. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is to be preferred in guardianship, whether the maternal grandfather or the mother.
2. Whether the mother is excused if she did not petition for guardianship within a year, provided that another legitimate guardian has petitioned for it.
casus:
CONSILIVM CCCLXXXIIII.
Otherwise, it is a case. The facts are as follows: A certain woman had a certain daughter from her husband. The husband dies, the said daughter surviving him from the wife. After the passage of time, the father of the wife, within two months from the death of the said husband, assumed the guardianship of the said daughter, his own granddaughter, before the said wife passed to second marriage. Later, the said daughter dies, her said mother surviving her. After whose death, the said mother sells certain goods formerly belonging to her said daughter. Now it is asked whether she could sell them or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† According to those who say that the maternal grandfather is preferred to the mother in guardianship, there is no doubt that the mother succeeds to the inheritance. L. *quot tutela*, *de regulis iuris*. For the mother is excused, since she is preceded in degree. As in L. *nepotibus*, *qui dari tutores possunt*. And this opinion is quite equitable: because the counsel of men is stronger than the frail counsel of women. And this is held by Marcus Sylvius in the *Authentica* *matri et aviae*.

But according to the opinion of Cynus, who says that the mother is preferred in guardianship, I say that if the grandfather, with the mother’s knowledge and acquiescence, assumed guardianship within the year, the mother is excused; because the legitimate guardian excuses her, as is noted in the Code, *ad Tertullianum*, law 3. And therefore the mother succeeds in the inheritance, and the sale made by her is confirmed. Digest, *de rei venditione*, law *Si a Titio*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In a kingdom, who is to be preferred, whether the uncle to the nephew, or the nephew to the uncle.
1. Add below, opinion 386.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In a free kingdom, which is subject to the dominion of no one except the royal majesty alone,

† It was long debated who should be preferred. Whether the son of the firstborn, when the king was alive. Or the firstborn son of the king, having regard to the firstborn brother. And in this question I will allege for and against. And first, for the uncle against the nephew, namely, that the uncle should be preferred. It is argued thus: nothing stands in the way of the uncle being preferred; therefore, the uncle succeeds. The consequent is true; the antecedent is proved. For if anything stands in the way of the uncle, it is the nephew himself; but I prove that the nephew himself is not objected against the uncle. For if he were objected against him, a double absurdity would follow, namely: because the son would be in a worse condition than the nephew, which is contrary to natural and civil reason, as in C. de bonis maternis, l. si viva matre. For although there, according to Rizzardus Maior and Cynus, another absurdity would be that the one prior in degree would be posterior in succeeding. And thus the order of law would pervert the order of nature: which is absurd, because the rights of blood proceed by degrees, and begin with the prior, not the posterior. Inst. de haeredibus ab intestato, §. cum filius; ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. pater filium. Secondly, it is proved: if this nephew has any right, he has it either as an heir by blood: and this is inconvenient, as has been proved. Or by transmission, or transaction made by his father into him; and this is impossible, because by the death of the firstborn, the hope of succeeding to the kingdom was taken from him. ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. posthumorum. There is nothing that he can transmit: for either we say that the right in act is transmitted, and this is false: because the firstborn, while his father was alive, did not have the actual right of the royal dignity. Or we say that the power is transmitted: and this is impossible, because such power has become caducous due to the obstacle of death. It supports what is noted, Inst. de verbis obligatorum, §. ex conditionali; and C. de caducis tollendis, §. in novissimo. And it is also certain that while the father is alive, the son has no right in the inheritance, as is proved there. ff. de liberis agnoscendis, l. si; and noted in Auth. de haeredibus et falcidia, §. si quis non implens. Thirdly, the same is proved: because this firstborn, let it be considered as prime and original matter with regard to his son; nevertheless, while the king was alive, in this matter, or in this subject, the royal form was not impressed. Hence neither the name of king nor any royal authority belonged to him. That which was not in him is united with forms and perfect things. Nor can anyone transmit a right which is recognized as not having, as noted, C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quis filium. And it is confirmed: because through a medium that is incapable and imperfect, a perfect transition cannot be made to any of the extremes: as ff. de servitutibus rusticarum praediorum, l. qui sella, §. rusticis. But the firstborn is a medium that is incapable and imperfect for such transition; therefore, he cannot found himself on his own person, because he is more remote in degree and the prerogative of the order of birth. Felicitas. For this kind of succession proceeds from the order of birth, as appears from the terms of the custom described above, which states that the firstborn son of the king succeeds. Moreover, the father of the nephew, while the king was alive, was extinguished by nature. Hence from his person no aid should be derived. ff. de operis liberto, l. qui libertinus, §. posthumus. Furthermore, the non-privileged succeeded to the non-privileged, because the privilege was not consummated; hence a supervening case stood in the way of the origin of the privilege. And thus the privilege ceases, as ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. pluribus, §. et si placet; and l. inter stipulantem, §. sacramentum; and C. de tempore in integrum restitutionis, l. ea quae. Furthermore, the nephew cannot found himself on a caducous foundation. Hence the nephew cannot found himself on the father, who is cut off, according to Aretinus. For before he was founded in the right of succeeding. For when the foundation is destroyed, all things are destroyed, as ff. quod vi aut clam, l. nam origo; and de pignoribus, l. lex vectigalis. Also, this first one who died did not have royal power in himself, by which he could pass into any royal act; therefore, he cannot operate it in another. And certainly the second should produce its effect by the virtue of the first cause, as ff. de fideiussoribus, l. tutor; and ff. de donationibus, l. id quod. For from the beginning of the title, the subsequent event is formed. C. de impositione lucrae descriptionis, l. 1, lib. 10. And every derivation presupposes the virtue of the deriving person in another, without which there is no derivation, as l. 2, §. 1, ff. de stipulatione servo. Also, imperfect virtues do not generate anything perfect of the same species: and this is clear naturally. Est. For a valid argument is that which is taken from the nature of the things themselves, as ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. ubi aut non apparet, §. illud dubitationem recipit, where it says "it is manifest from nature itself." Also, every disposition of law should agree with natural things, as ff. de interrogatione actionis, l. confessionibus. And art should rather imitate nature than nature art, as ff. de liberis et postumis, l. filio quem pater. And causes that are bereft or imperfect generate only equivocally, as is clear through Aristotle in the second book of De Anima. From these, therefore, it is clear that the influence of succeeding did not arise from the father of the nephew, and that the order of birth stands in the way of the nephew; therefore, it is evidently concluded in favor of the son of the king. Given that the nephew draws honor from the father, nevertheless he does not seem to draw the vigor of succession from him; therefore, since he has neither the vigor of succession through another nor through himself, he will be posterior in the order of preference. To the contrary, it holds that the nephew supports justice and entirely repels the uncle; thus it is proved. Presupposing, namely, as true, that this virtue of succeeding is in the privileged root, and I argue thus. The nephew, born from the privileged root, assumes the same nature that the father had: and this nature is not indivisible to others, but of the whole generation; therefore, the nephew is preferred. The consequence is noted. The major is proved, because the form and origin, which is believed to come from the root, is found in any derivative, as ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in ratione, §. si filio, ver. ut. For. Also, the right of nature and that dignity are here one and the same, or at least inseparably connected, like the sun and its splendor. Since, therefore, the nephew is the splendor of glory and the figure of the substance of his father, as appears in the first Epistle to the Hebrews, and from the root of the father, the right is one flesh with him. Just as we are all one flesh with Adam, since we are derived from him as from the source of generation, and as from a certain mass. Just as that which is of the mass, namely, its part, is not really distinct from it, so the nephew is not understood as something really distinct from his father, as C. de impubibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. si. Here, we are not dealing with the distinct form of man, which is the soul, but with communicable matter, because the nature of the father and the son is almost the same: and we are here in the matter of generation; therefore, let him commit those things which are of the primogeniture, just as from the same vine is the vine and the shoot, or germ. From which it is concluded that this nephew should be called firstborn in the virtue of generation, which is derived from the father into the nephew. And this is the natural reason. Secondly, it is proved, because the nephew enters the place of the uncle, although, namely, the father is placed on one slip of paper depicted in the tree of consanguinity, and his son on another, nevertheless the father and son make only one degree, namely, the first. And they are two as one, just as there is one window from two angles, as noted, Inst. de gradibus, after the beginning. Then I argue thus: the father and son are in the first degree between themselves, as ff. de gradibus, l. iurisconsultus. Therefore, if both are in the first, it follows that both are in the right of primogeniture. Thirdly, thus: the dignity created from the principles of nature is like flesh and blood, which passes to posterity: because it is born from the marrow and bones, and hence has substantial transmission and natural derivation, which derivation is privileged, because derivation is made with its cause, and virtue, and habit, and disposition, just as water flowing through. For emanation is not cut off, but extended by extensive virtue, and into the flux of generation such as the generator itself is. And therefore the son enjoys the privilege of the father: because if the son did not enjoy it, the father's prerogative would be diminished: and it would be a personal privilege, not natural, and written into nature itself, which is false: this fails, however, in taxed cases: as C. ad Trebellianam, l. iubemus, in principio; and fully noted, ff. de verborum significatione, l. liberorum. Fourthly, thus: the successive edict of men from the head of the firstborn to the head of the secondborn should have place whenever the successive edict ceases in the line of the firstborn, and not otherwise: because the direct line is preferred to the collateral; therefore, so here. ff. si testamentum ex parte, l. 1, in principio. Fifthly, this is proved: because the firstborn is not simply a son, but a royal son; therefore, the nephew, from him, is a royal nephew, and thus his kingdom should be by the habit generated previously. And we are not in transmission, properly speaking, of any simple inheritance, but in the subrogation of a person: because the nephew is subrogated in the place of the father as an heir by blood: and by this many things alleged to the contrary are solved. King Robert wanted the kingdom for himself, but the more common opinion is for the nephew, and so I hold in a natural kingdom, and not one adventitious by fief, as was the case of the aforementioned king. And it is confirmed by the saying of the Apostle, if a son, therefore an heir. As noted, de acquisitione hereditatis, l. necessariis. And just as the nephew makes a part with the uncle in common things: because he enters the right, habit, and paternal status; so arguing from the conclusion of the part to the conclusion of the whole. If such, what is it that cannot belong to only one? Amen. The nephew, drawing root, principle, and order from the father, should exclude his collateral, i.e., the uncle: because the descending line defeats the collateral. In Auth. ut fratrum filii, §. 1. Baldus.

CONSILIVM
Also, it is a case. CCCLXXXVII.
In the name of God. Amen.
The case is such: Lady Angela had a husband named John, and a mother named Margaret, and three daughters, namely, Richabella, Ursulina, and Epiphania, who were underage. She made a testament: in which she left 25 to the mother, and to each of the daughters she left 1. And in these, she instituted them, and any of their heirs, as heirs; commanding that they could not ask for more of her goods. In all her other goods, she instituted John, her husband, as universal heir, and made him so during his life. And after the death of the said John, she substituted the aforementioned her daughters as universal heirs in equal portions. And if any of them should die without sons or daughters, she substituted the survivor. And if all should die at any time without sons or daughters, she ordered, willed, left, and commanded that her said inheritance and goods be distributed and given by her trustees, etc. Finally, it happened that the testatrix died. Afterwards John died, and all the daughters died before puberty: because none reached the age of 12 years. Margaret, the mother of the testatrix, survived, who claims the legitime of the said daughters, and the legacies made to them. It is asked whether the said Margaret should have the legitime and the aforementioned legacies. By the trustees, it is said that she should have nothing at all, by virtue of a certain statute, the tenor of which is such: Although it is furthermore useful to speak of substitutions, insofar as by various interpretations, contrary to the mind and purpose of the testator, successions of goods and inheritances are transferred to others than is equitable, or otherwise, and especially favoring parents or ascendants of the testator, to whom it most fittingly belongs to perform the offices of firmness: we decree that every and any substitution, conceived and made, or even to be made in the future, by any words truly or doubtfully acted, to substitute directly, and under any form or conception, or proof of words, except by the word "to restore," shall always be understood. And if they are not considered oblique, nor fiduciary, but direct, so that all goods, or things, are without prejudice to the restitution of the disposer, and the substitution of the prudent, integrally and without any deduction or diminution to be made in the process of any legitime or Trebellianic portion, shall come: not by some medium, or by the direct way, to the substitute, one or more; notwithstanding that by common law the words do not agree in institutions, unless an evident contrary will of the disposer, or testator, or leaver, appears, namely, by the word of restitution, or restoring, as has been expressed in the substitution conceived. And what is more, if indeed sons, or male or female children, who are underage, to whose persons direct substitution by law is very much suitable, should happen to die in their pupillary age, one or more, we consider that not only paternal goods, but also the substitutes of the underage children themselves, one or more, shall come without diminution in any of the aforementioned cases, unless the substitution was made by the said word of restitution.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A statute may abrogate the rule that no deduction is made for the Falcidian or Trebellian portion.
body: In the Name of Christ.

This statute is greatly contrary to the common law, and especially in the substitution which a mother or an outsider makes, who cannot regularly substitute directly after the inheritance has been accepted. And therefore, under the common law, the legitime is deducted from the fideicommissum. But this statute provides that it shall not be deducted, unless the word precisely signifies the restitution of the inheritance; and this statute is valid. And therefore, in our case, I hold that Margarella, in the name of the minors, does not deduct the legitime from the goods of the testatrix, but that the executors of the will may distribute everything according to the form of the will. For they are substitutes for the poor, and they appear to be substitutes by the word "substitute." For in this word, as in a common word, every substitution in words is resolved, *de vulgari substitutione*, law *Iam hoc iure*, section *Sed si alter*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a grandson through the firstborn son is preferred to his uncle. And number 9.
2. If the firstborn renounces the kingdom, or becomes a younger brother after having begotten a son, whether we shall exclude the grandson and give the kingdom to the uncle. Likewise, what if the firstborn becomes insane, whether we shall take it away from the son and give it to the uncle. Number 3. Likewise, what if both the firstborn and the second-born had children, yet the second-born first, because he first took a wife. Number 4.
3. Whether an appeal lies against kings, and whether they can impose taxes without cause, and take from the patrimony of each individual.
