4. Whether the firstborn can make a donation, or defer to the third-born.
5. If one of the co-kings dies with a son, whether that son will be co-king with his uncle.
6. Whether the right of primogeniture is transmitted, so that the son of the firstborn excludes the uncle.
7. A king who is a ward must be governed by a guardian, and what the guardian is then bound to do.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is a custom in certain kingdoms, and it is reasonable and prescribed, that the firstborn succeeds to the kingdom. It happens that a king begot two legitimate and natural sons, of whom the first, dying while his father was alive, left behind a legitimate and natural son. Now the king dies, and there is a contest for the kingdom between the surviving son of the king and the grandson of the king born of the said firstborn son. The grandson claims that he is king by right and by the privilege of his father. But the son of the king arises to the contrary, saying that he is the son, and also born earlier than the grandson would be. The question is asked: what is the law? And the question is posed in a free kingdom, and not only where civil laws are observed, but also in kingdoms which are ruled today as they were ruled when only nature and the dictate of natural reason sanctioned things for men. In this question, it is necessary to allege arguments for both sides. And this question is a common one, yet nothing is so firmly opined that it closes off understanding for posterity. First, therefore, I will allege for the grandson against the uncle. Second, I will allege to the contrary for the uncle against the grandson. Third, I will state what I think, always reserving the sounder opinion. That the grandson should be preferred is proved by many reasons. And first thus: the grandson is born from that root which was preferred, as appears from the terms; therefore he assumes for himself the nature from that source and from that root, which is considered the original form and cause. And because everything that is decided through a medium partakes of the nature of that medium, if that medium is natural and not merely instrumental; for through the medium it is specified and naturalized, and this is manifest in nature, because a graft produces fruit of its own species, not fruit of the root, as in D. de donis, l. qui id, quod; and D. de fideiussoribus, l. tutor; and D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in ratione, §. si filio, in the words "famam, et originem." This is from the law of nature, because each thing generates such as itself is. And in this God fertilizes human nature, so that it may be preserved through successive offspring, as noted in Auth. de nuptiis, in principio, column 4. Second, this is proved because the firstborn son is the splendor of glory and the figure of the substance of his father, and essentially the same. And he is also considered lesser, at least as some part of his parent by legal fiction, as in C. de impub. et aliis substituendis, l. si; C. de agris et censibus, l. cum scimus. Hence, in burdens and honors, they are reduced to the understanding of one person, as noted in l. 2, C. qui aetatem, lib. 10. Third, it is proved because the grandson enters the paternal degree, as in Inst. de hereditatibus ab intestato, §. cum filius; and in Auth. ut fratres filii, in the rubric and text. Fourth, it is proved because the natural cause passes to the grandson; he is produced from the seed of his father, and in him the name of the father is perpetuated. Here we take the firstborn as he is from the root of the parent and from his mass, as in D. de verborum significatione, l. pronuntiatio. Fifth, it is proved because the firstborn, while the father is alive, is understood to have had dominion over the kingdom, with administration excepted, as in D. de liberis et postumis, l. in suis. Sixth, it is proved because the succession edict prefers succession from degree to degree, as from head to head, for example, from the old law: the second degree is preferred even to the last of the agnates over the first degree of cognates; because succession passes more easily, or goes, to those having the symbol, as in D. si tabulae testamenti nullae extant, l. 1, in principio. For where there is greater difference, there is greater difficulty, as in C. de adoptionibus, l. cum in adoptivis. Since therefore there are two heads of custom, namely, the head of the firstborn included, and the head of the second-born excluded, the head of the firstborn never passes to the head of the second-born unless the subject persons coming from the first head are extinct; but here they are not extinct, but they claim. Seventh, because the father is not said to be extinct, from whom the grandson lives, as in C. de fideiussoribus, l. cum acutissimi; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum avus; C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter; D. de hereditatis institutione, l. Lucius. Since therefore the second-born seems to be substituted in place of the first failing, said substitution is understood to have in itself the condition tacitly, if the first should die without children. Wherefore children prior exclude the hope of the posterior. Eighth, it is proved thus: that which induces the preference of succession is the precedence of dignity of the firstborn; but the dignity of the father, already communicated to the son by the dictate of reason, benefits the son, as in C. de quaestionibus, l. divo Marco. Ninth, it is proved thus: because privileges of parents pass to children, even if they assume the cause from time, as in C. qui potiores in pignore habeant, l. assiduis, §. exceptis; and noted in l. etiam, in principio, D. solutione matrimonii. Therefore the grandson succeeds to the paternal privilege and to the right of preference, because it is not a privilege written in the person, but in the cause, namely, primogeniture; therefore the virtue flowing passes to the grandson. Tenth, it is proved: because all privileges which are not only begun but also executed pass to posterity, as noted in C. ad Velleianam, l. etc., through Cynus. But the right of primogeniture was executed in many things while the king was alive, such as sitting at the right hand of the father, and in many other things, 7. q. 1, c. quam periculosum. And therefore it is a matter not entire, but somewhat executed. Clearly therefore it makes passage to posterity. Eleventh, it is proved: if there is only one son, no one doubts that the virtue of primogeniture passes to the grandson; otherwise the kingdom remains without an heir of blood, since the grandson is not the firstborn. Or we would say that the virtue of custom fails, which is false. He succeeds therefore as firstborn, therefore he excludes the second-born. Twelfth, thus: that which the grandson does not have by himself, he must have through another, in whose place he succeeds, as in D. quae res pignori obligari possunt, l. Aristo. Thirteenth, thus: the cause of the first is always represented in the second cause, in which it flows, as in D. de procuratoribus, l. licet, §. ea obligatio. But the firstborn is the first cause, which transmits its force, power, and dignity to his son, just as the root to the shoot; therefore, just as the son is of the nature of the father, so he must be of the legal judgment; because legal judgment, i.e., that which the law judges, imitates nature, as in D. de adoptionibus, l. nam adoptio. Fourteenth, it is proved: because those things which proceed by seminal reason endure in their being as long as the seed or its fruit is found to be present, as the law says regarding subrogation in place of deceased heads, as in D. de usufructu legato. But this succession proceeds by seminal reason; therefore it passes to the grandson. Fifteenth, it is proved: because when more things are required for preference, one of many is not sufficient to obtain preference, as in C. qui potiores in pignore habeant, l. qui balneum. But for the second-born to succeed, more things are required, namely, that at the time of the king's death he be prior in age, and also more effective in reason; but it is not so that he is more effective in reason; therefore he does not exclude the grandson. Sixteenth, it is proved thus: the succession edict has place from renunciation just as from death, as in D. de inofficioso testamento, l. si is, qui.

† Suppose, therefore, that the firstborn renounces the kingdom, or that the younger brother becomes such after having begotten a son; shall we exclude the grandson and grant the kingdom to the uncle? Certainly not at all: for the way is open to the grandson, as in C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. Si quis filium.

† Furthermore, suppose the firstborn is insane with perpetual madness; would we therefore deprive his son and give [the inheritance] to the uncle? Certainly not at all. The text is in c. Grandi, de supplemento negligentiae praelati, lib. 6. Seventeenth, because if we were to say otherwise, an absurdity would follow.

† Suppose, for instance, that both the firstborn and the second-born have children: yet the second-born married first and had children first. It would then follow that, if both sons died during the lifetime of the king, the son of the second-born would be preferred to the son of the first-born, if the primogeniture of the parent were not taken into account; which is absurd. Therefore, it follows that the prerogative of primogeniture is transferred to the descendants. And if this is so, the conclusion follows that the grandson is preferred.

† And note that according to the law of nations, kings hold the supreme pivot, as is also the case among infidels; and therefore no appeal lies from them. It also appears that that species of dominion which is called universal resides with kings, whereas particular dominion pertains to individuals in their own right, and to the king only by accident, i.e., by an accidental cause, for example, on account of a delict; and therefore it is established that the king cannot impose a tax, or diminish the funds or patrimony of individuals, except for cause, according to Petrus and Cynus, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. neminem; nor can he revoke concessions made by them without cause. Nevertheless, for cause arising from public necessities, they can impose new conditions on fiefs; because this is a preeminent right of the prince, as is proven in de omni agro, from l. qui fundos, in Auth. de referendo, in princ., in 10th col., de natura feudorum, c. 1. And if the lord does not treat the vassal as a vassal, the vassal is not bound to treat the lord as a lord, as stated in 10th col., per quos fiat investitura, c. final., in the gloss, and in forma fidelitatis, c. 1, §. dominus quoque. And if the Pope does not treat the bishop as a bishop, the bishop is not bound to treat the Pope as the Pope. And by withdrawing obedience from him in that which he commanded as if he were not a bishop, he is not said to be a schismatic, as is openly proven, 95th dist., c. esto subiectus. Or say, as noted there. It does not matter whether he is emancipated or not; because this name of firstborn is a natural name, de capite, dist., l. tutelas. The office of governing is a public office, de re militari; but the office does not pass to the heir, l. tutela, de tutelis. Moreover, if he were an infant, he would govern others, although he cannot govern himself, contrary to l. ultima, de legatis tutoribus. The same applies if he were a prodigal, or a slave to lusts, contrary to l. final., C. de sententia paschali, 7th q. 1, c. factus est Cornelius, in fine, v.g. Moreover, in a king, counsel and understanding are required, 23rd q. 4, c. duo ista. Let discipline watch over the office of the name, which can be absent from the son of a king, and especially from the daughter, de cura furiosi, l. cum bonis, l. final., C. de testamento militis. Moreover, it is expressly stated in the royal dignities in the title, quis dicatur dux, c. 1, col. 10. Moreover, it is confirmed by canon law, as appears in the decrees, 8th q. 1, c. Moyses; 7th q. 1, c. denique. Moreover, it is expressly stated here in the gloss, ordinatio, that election makes the king, as if to say not by birth. Moreover, it seems absurd that the world should be ruled by blind fortune; since it is a grave fault, by reason left aside, to commit oneself to fortune. Moreover, Aristotle says, 3rd Politics, that those who were made kings from the beginning because they were very good, behold, now at the end, because they are very good, not because they are sons. Moreover, we have an example in the book of the Romans, de iure iurando, c. ad apostolicae, and in apostolicus, 23rd dist., c. in nomine domini. Moreover, all nations use the contrary, that the firstborn becomes king; therefore, the conclusion holds by the law of nations, per l. 1, §. finali, supra eodem. Moreover, the firstborn is called king, etc., during the lifetime of the father, and has his seat to the right of the father, 7th q. 1, c. quam periculosum; 23rd q. 4, c. quaesitum; and 23rd q. 5, c. non frustra; and q. 5, c. dicat. Moreover, it is expressly stated in c. licet, de voto et iureiurando, c. 5, and is confirmed by new law by c. grandi, de suppletione negligentiae praelatorum, lib. 6. Moreover, it is confirmed by divine law, i.e., to the Hebrews, 2; Psalm: those who do not follow divine testimonies have lost the weight of human testimony, 23rd q. 3, q. 4, c. ipsas pietas. Moreover, plurality of principalities is not good, therefore, etc., as appears in 12th Metaphysics. Moreover, the king ought to be more noble, according to nature; and no one is more noble than the son of the king, 23rd q. 4, c. Nabucodonosor. Even an infant could be elected king, de iure iurando. What B. So. says: kingdom in production is by the force of election; kingdom in procession is by the force of transmission; kingdom outside the church is the same as the king's. The act cannot be censured when God is the author, 23rd q. 4, cap. quaesitum. By punishing and acknowledging, this alone is done well, so that the lives of men may be preserved, 23rd q. 5, c. prodest seueritas. Vengeance feeds the mind with another's evil, 23rd q. 5, c. de occidendis. One takes the rule of governing one's neighbor from oneself, 23rd q. 5, si non licet. He adorns the doctrine of the Lord, who does those things which are suitable to his condition, 23rd q. 5, c. si apud carnales. A severed limb does not hold the spirit of life, 23rd q. 3, c. quam amen. God is not to be tempted, 23rd q. 8, c. si nulla. The Emperor is within the church, 23rd q., c. conuenior. Nature accustomed to guard, 23rd q. 6, c. iam vero. We tolerate those whom we cannot correct or punish, idem. My dove is one, de consecratione, dist. ultima, c. aliud est. The avaricious man does not seek a co-possessor, nor does he inflamed with the desire to dominate seek a partner, 23rd q. 7, c. quod autem nobis obijcitur. On the contrary, it seems that an immature birth deprives of privilege, de excusatione tutoris, l. sed et milites. Moreover, in a favorable act, the inclusion of both is more just than the exclusion of each, noted in l. aretusa. Moreover, he is prior whom no one precedes, l. qui duos, de rebus dubiis, in constitutionibus. Moreover, an equal is not excluded by an equal, nor by another, therefore by no one, de acquirenda possessione, l. 1, §. veteres. Moreover, it is not possible for two to reign simultaneously, since they are held in the place of one, l. cui fundus, §. fide metropoli. Moreover, royal dominion is indivisible, therefore it can be held by several in solidum, l. final., ff. uti possidetis; l. final., de rerum divisione. Moreover, an office can be held by several in solidum, l. 1, de officio consulis; l. 1, §. si plures, de exercitu; l. decreto, de administratione tutoris. Moreover, both are in possession of the primogeniture, therefore each makes his own way by authority, as noted in l. edicto. Unless one yields to the other, which he can, 7th q. 1, c. quam periculosum; nor is this case doubtful and uncertain to man; because it is clear and certain to the law, de majoribus, l. cum inter veteres. And thus I hold, notwithstanding l. cum duo, de in diem adiectum; because there it is about not vitiating the uncertain by the uncertain; here it is not so, l. 1, de libertate praetoria, in constitutionibus, §. per Cynum.

† Here begins the doubt whether the firstborn can defer [his right] to the third-born. It seems that he can, because the right of primogeniture can be donated. D. c. quam periculosum. Also, it appears from this: because if the one first to be admitted consents to another being invested, the investiture holds, in 10. col. quibus modis feudum amittatur. c. 1. §. praeterea. Also, it was so in the case of King Robert, whose action, on account of his wisdom, is our instruction, and the decretal pronounces in his favor in c. pastoralis. de re iudicata. in Clem. On the contrary, it seems: because dignity is not in commerce, nor can honor be ceded. §. Iul. si quis omni causa testamentaria. Because he who has something for life cannot grant it to another after his death. de periculo et commodo rei venditae. l. necessario. §. fin. de legatis 2. l. peto. §. praedium. Also, in conditions, the adversary’s extinguishing principle suffices, l. antepen. de institutionibus et substitutionibus. Also, a successive edict is not without a change of degree. Also, the right being resolved, in which something successive is founded, that which depends on it is resolved. de pignoribus. l. lex vectigalis. locato conducto. l. si quis domum. and in 10. col. qui succedunt in testamento. C. de legatis. l. uxor patrui. Also, a personal cause limits the caused thing personally, 10. col. de controversia investiturae. §. rursus. Also, nothing can be done by the first to the prejudice of the firstborn. de legibus. 1. l. filius. §. diuus. and in auth. res, quae. cum si. l. si fundus. §. 1. Also, this is a gift of law and nature, which cannot be taken away from the second-born. de adoptionibus. l. si arrogator. §. sed an impuberi. If, however, it were valid, it would be valid perpetually. C. de adoptionibus. l. si tibi filius. It makes for de his, qui in prioribus criminibus laesi sunt, successionis. l. 1. Also, the condition of a permanent act requires the perseverance of the fact. de arbitris. l. inter Castellianum. Also, every act proceeding from an influencing power deserts when the power ceases. in c. ultimo. de procuratoribus. in Clem.

† The following doubt arises: if one of the co-kings dies leaving a son, whether that son will be co-king with his uncle. And it seems that he will not, because he ought not to concur with the firstborn. To the contrary: because this is not a concurrence, but a division. Moreover, because the father transmits to his son, not to the brother. On the nature of succession, c. 1; and on two brothers invested by the captain, c. 1, C. de donis, l. si auia. For here the course was according to Leg. 3, l. pater, § 15, and this if he died with the kingdom firmly established for him. But if he was only in hope, as because the old king was still living, the uncle is preferred to the nephew, because he is closer to the king. For where true proximity is considered, and not fictitious, the uncle is preferred to the nephew. ff. de legatis tertio, l. 3, § sciendum; de bonis liberti, l. libertus qui, in fine. And this is not the son of the firstborn, but of a co-born. And from equality by nature one departs through inequality. c. duobus, de rescriptis, lib. 6.

† Another doubt follows, whether the right of primogeniture, not to speak of equal primogeniture, is transmitted, so that the son of the firstborn excludes the uncle. And it was determined and observed in the Kingdom of France and England that it is so; the contrary was the case with King Robert. Chapter *Pastoralis*. Which opinion is more just is a matter of dispute. The words are of Cicero. In favor of the uncle it is argued: because he ought not to be in a worse position than the nephew. C. *de bonis matri.* l. *Si viua matre*. Also, because the right of age, as it disposes, is not transmitted for the future. *de temp. in inte.* re. l. *Ea quae*. Also, because while the father is alive, all sons are called kings and lords of the fief. *qui mo. feu. amit.* c. 1. Also, because upon the death of the first, the derivative right is cut off at the root. C. *de nup.* l. *Si liber*. Also, when one comes through another, he cannot come if that intermediary is extinguished in the meantime. ff. *ad l. aqui.* l. *Proinde*. l. *Receptum*. Common principles. In favor of the nephew it is argued: because succession is his own right in innate dignity, which is transmitted by right of blood; because the son is something of his father, hence the father is in the son. Also, the efficient cause ceasing, the effect produced does not cease in the matter. l. *Patre furioso*. Also, the qualities of innate dignities are transmissible. l. 1. *de epis. et cle.* per Ia. Alex. and Cy. Also, this succession is the very same thing as innate dignity, which is inseparable. *de pac.* l. *Ius agnationis*. Also, the substitution of the nephew in place of the parent is natural. *de libe. et post.* l. *Gallus*. *de iniu. te.* l. *Posthu.* 9

† I hold, for the sake of argument, in favor of the grandson, unless the wording of the custom required that he be the firstborn of the king: for his father is not truly king, since the crown was not due to him. L. bene a Zenone. It is established in the Digest on testaments, L. Titius. And thus, what is not provided for by custom is decided by reason. De feudis, compilatio.

And if the grandson is a minor, the guardian will govern the kingdom in his name. C. de tu. et cu. illustrium personarum, l. 1. This guardian will receive oaths of fidelity in the name of the guardianship, and will confer caduc feuds, as in 10. col. per quos fiat inue., c. 1. col. 10. de aqua quot., l. j. §. si quod vi, aut clam, I. prohibere, §. plane. For this is customary, therefore also C. de pig. act., l. vel universorum, de do., l. filius, 23. q. 6. Indeed, there nature preserves the customary practice. The first part of the law ends; I come to the second part. In the Name of Christ, Amen. These verbal obscurities tire the intellect: the aforementioned Master Baldus declares his conclusions in this manner: namely, that the first conclusion is this. That the authority and counsel for undertaking war against infidel kings resides primarily with the Apostolic See, however, with cause. 23. q. 3, §. his continentur, and §. huic etiam, and §. breuiter, in fi. dist., and c. vnusquisque. And that in justifying war, given the supposed cause, the conscience of the judge, concurring with the truth, suffices, even if proof is lacking. The second conclusion is declared thus: that the subjects of the realm, widowed of the royal house, and the royal lineage, can elect a new king for themselves; that the kingdom passes to the firstborn, or to twins born together in a certain order of birth. And that when one of them, reigning with his son, dies, the grandson will be co-king with his uncle; but if these are not yet reigning, and one dies, the uncle alone will be king. And that this is consistent with the fact that the son of the firstborn, predeceased, excludes the second-born uncle of the king. It follows the third principal conclusion, that royal jurisdiction in universal matters is always in act. I declare that there are two extremes: namely, personal and real, i.e., subtle and territorial, by which the royal sanction always sanctions, and authority always commands. It is always in act, because universal jurisdiction has a continuous cause, but it does not fall discretively upon Peter or John, except by accident, for example, due to a delict or contract; otherwise, the prince does not have power over the things of individuals, as is fully noted in consti. omnem. And therefore, without cause, he cannot impose a tax that has exhausted the resources of the citizens, as noted by Cy. after Pet. C. de sac. san. ec., l. neminem. And dignity, because it is universal and incorruptible, is always present through its form. In Auth. quo oportet episcopos, §. et forma is called act. Arist. de anima, in prin. Corollary: because discretionary jurisdiction is not prescribed, except like a discontinuous servitude, because it requires a human act. l. foramen. But universal jurisdiction is prescribed in 30 years, like duchies, counties, and feuds. In c. si quis per 30, col. 10, and de feudo dato in vicem, l. commissoriae, c. quidem, where this is discussed, l. vires, and l. mortis. The fourth conclusion is declared thus: that a contract is an act, and its potency is to produce an obligation in its times; and that an action in general is nothing other than a reason concluding to the attainment of the proposed end; or a vigor produced by the obligation when it arises, but when it is brought forward, it is an instrument of pursuing. And that civil obligation is not a natural quality, but is a secondary species: and not in the contract, but from the contract. The fifth conclusion is not declared otherwise. The sixth conclusion is not declared otherwise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. At what time is a person presumed to have been born, how this should be pleaded, and whether the child is to be judged as born of a marriage or of illicit intercourse, etc.
2. What is meant by doubtful proof.
3. The argument from commonly occurring events is valid.
4. Whether, with regard to kinship, conception or animation is to be considered.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The Imperial Advocate has spoken so profoundly and copiously that one might close the mouths of others; nevertheless, because the points you touch upon are useful and diverse, and have been discussed by Jacobus Bellus and others, and by the gloss of Bernard in the chapter *Adferte* on presumption, it must be considered,

† That sometimes a conception presumed at a certain time presupposes a lawful beginning and what is possible according to nature. And if that were not presumed, maleficium or fornicatory intercourse would be presumed, and then that is presumed which gives a lawful beginning to the conception. D. de adulteriis, l. Miles, § Defuncto, there where it says “since it is possible,” etc., where it is said that although the mother is proven to be an adulteress, nevertheless if the child could have been born from the marriage, we ought not to judge the child to be illegitimate. Sometimes, due to the diversity of menstrual cycles, a diversity of times of birth could occur, and the child could be justly born at any of those times. And then the question of two uncertain fathers arises, to which of them the child should be attributed. And they define this by natural presumptions, such as by similarity; and by temporal ones, such that the time which is more suitable to nature and to the region is believed to be the correct one. For in some regions gestation is completed sooner, in others later: as in l. 7, Mense, per Cynus. And in the case of two mothers who gave birth in the same bed, on the same night, one a male and the other a female, and each claims the male as her own. For the matter is decided by presumptions, D. Afferte. Sometimes the question is not of fathers or mothers, but only of time, namely, at what time one was born, whether earlier or later. And this occurs in two ways: in one way, with respect to some disposition referring to the earlier moment; for example, if someone says, “I institute the firstborn,” and two are born simultaneously. And this is the subject matter of the Lex Aretusa, D. de statu hominum. In the second way, with respect to some agnation or cognation, where there is no doubt about the offspring, because this, as I said, is not our case, but there is doubt about the cognation between certain offspring with regard to being born, but uncertain with regard to being recognized, because it may be that one is a cognate, and it may be that one is not. And this is our case. To understand this case, let us proceed through the paths of the laws, i.e., through the rules of law. The rule is that proof of genus is required of him who is sent from the genus. D. de probationibus, l. 1; C. eodem, l. Matrem tuam. Another rule is that the fuller and more certain proof of two adversaries prevails. And therefore he wins who better grounds his intention. C. de edicto divi Adriani, l. Si. From this rule two conclusions, or decisions, seem to be inferred. The first is that if two claim to have been full brothers of Martin, deceased, and one proves fully and the other semi-fully, the one proving semi-fully does not make a part of the one proving fully, but rather the one proving fully wins in toto; because the certain draws the uncertain to itself, not vice versa. To this effect is what Cynus notes, C. de rebus creditis, l. In bonae fidei. The second seems to be proper to our case. For the second full sister fully proved cognation and consanguinity, whereas the uterine brother did not prove clearly or conclusively the necessity. If therefore in the former case the one proving dubiously does not make a part, much less in this second case does he exclude the one proving clearly from the whole.

But here it must be considered what is meant by doubtful proof. And I say that it is that which holds the middle ground between certain proof of a fact and no proof of a fact, as noted by the doctors in C. de procuratoribus, l. 1. And this, so to speak, medium fides sometimes, with the aid of the law, concludes sufficiently according to the disposition of the law, and then it is given effect; otherwise, a son would never exclude an uncle, or the uncle would be certain. But the son is known only through presumptions, as in de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Lucius, which is certainly false, as in Auth. de hereditatibus ab intestato, § 1. Moreover, it concludes nothing on account of the certainty of the fact, and then it operates for nothing. Extra de probationibus, c. In presentia; probationes liquidae esse debent. C. de competentiis, l. Si. And sometimes they can be drawn probably to either side, because both are possible; then, in this doubt, those who are in possession are more favored than those who bring the action. D. de liberis causis, l. Liberi, § Si; D. de probationibus, l. Circa; Inst. de interdictis, § Commodum; C. de probationibus, l. Non nudis epistolis, and l. Neque natales. An example is that of two wills made on the same day with the institution of different heirs, as noted in l. Edicto, cum si. And many other examples can easily be given, in which possession or quasi-possession decides doubtful matters.

Furthermore, it must be considered that although the age of those born begins from the hour of birth, nevertheless the age of those being born begins from the day of conception and extends until the day of birth. Hence, our question, so to speak, is one of age: whether, while this child was in the womb, the age was nine months, and thus he was conceived during the life of his brother, or whether it was not nine completed months, but perhaps eight and a half months of the ninth, or not so precisely. And it is a question of a point that is known only to God and to the mother conceiving in that first instant. What, therefore, shall we say? I answer that we must adhere to what seems more credible. Thus, it is said notably in Iure consensus, D. de probationibus, l. Cum de aetate. And this concludes the first point.

I come to the second point, and I say that it is more credible that which commonly occurs. For, in doubtful cases, the presumption is drawn from what commonly happens, as noted in the gloss beginning "probabilitatis" in the law *Neque natales*, Codex, *De probationibus*. Nor are we here concerned with the certainty of nature, to which all things are certain, Digest, *De iure*, law *Sed et si restituatur*, at the end, and this is assumed by Rasponius, *Metaphysics*. Rather, we are dealing with legal art and presumption, which, as I have said, is that the law adapts itself to what is more frequent, than does the judge, its minister, Digest, *De legibus*, law *Nam ad ea*. Nor is it to be supposed that one swallow makes a spring, or that one woman is a solitary sparrow in her homeland. For the more frequent things are more probable, Digest, *De fundo instrato*, law *Cum delationis*, section *Asinam*. And it is most likely that what is more probable is also more believable, Digest, *De infaustis*, law *Athleta*, word *Generaliter*. And in this matter, recourse must be had to the common opinion of women, because they know their own peculiarities better, Digest, *De venditionibus inspicendis*, law 1, in the beginning, and the argument, Digest, *De fluminibus*, law 1, section 1. And this is true, unless some signs, which would indicate conception according to the judgment of physicians, showed otherwise. For commonly, women do not carry for more than nine months. And if she said that she had carried in her womb for longer, and did not give birth before nine months were completed, and no contrary presumption resulted, the crime would not fall upon her, unless I had other certainty about the beginning of conception, according to the conclusions of medical canon.

The third question follows, whether, with regard to cognation, conception or animation is to be considered. And I say that conception is to be considered; otherwise it would follow that if the father died during intercourse with his wife, from which intercourse the woman remained pregnant, that the posthumous child would not be acknowledged by the father, nor would he succeed him. Which is contrary to all truth. For indeed, that which is in the womb is considered as born, although not formally, but casually. D. de stat. hom. l. qui in utero; D. si pars haer. pet. l. antiqui; D. de acqu. haer. l. cum quidam. §. quod dicitur. Where it must be considered that, speaking naturally, at the beginning of conception there is neither the body of a man nor the soul, but afterwards the body is formed, and then it is animated; nevertheless, a man is not called such while he is in the womb. D. de coll. bon. l. si; D. de ass. leg. l. ult. However, what nature lacks, the law supplies by regarding him who is in the womb as a man, if he comes to the light. C. de posth. haer. inst. l. si; C. de fid. leg. l. cum inter veteres. From the hour of effective insemination in the womb, at which time the mother conceived. D. de suis et leg. haer. l. Titius and l. item praetor; D. unde cog. l. 1. §. si quis proximior; D. de haer. quae ab intest. ven. §. cum autem. Therefore, the issue is to be articulated regarding conception, not regarding animation. So it seems to me, always saving your judgment, and that of any ingenious man. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a notary may add something to an instrument.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. After the instrument has been restored to the parties, the notary may add nothing or change anything, unless by order of the judge, and the truth has been established for him by witnesses, and a petition concerning the conception of an error has been presented, and the party has been cited, as is fully set forth in the Digest, *de statu hominis*, in the beginning, through the doctors, especially through Cynus. Nevertheless, I have seen an instrument returned, and that one, although perhaps not examined as it ought to be, nevertheless suffices to recover its force of 350 florins, and two hundred can be recovered by the force of another instrument, as in the Digest, *de actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Lucio*; *de probationibus*, law *quinquaginta*; and *de dote prædata*, law *si*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ. The point is this: Cecharellus of Monte Martata married his daughter, the noblewoman Alena, to the nobleman Gausta of Radicofano, and in the name of her dowry promised 500 florins. Thereafter, the said Cecharellus made a will, in which he instituted his full brother Peter as heir, without making any mention of the said Alena, his daughter. Then, after the death of the said testator, another daughter, named Piera, was born to the said Alena, who married Stephen of Urbe Veteri. Then the said Alena died, with the said Piera, her daughter and the testator’s granddaughter, surviving her. Piera intends to bring an action against the will of the said Cecharellus on the ground of the omission of Alena, her mother and the testator’s daughter; or on the ground of the omission of her own person, although she was born more than a year after the death of the testator. The question now arises whether such a will can be overturned for the said reason.

Another point is this: the said Gausta granted a lease (affictum) of certain plots of land, which formerly belonged to Cecharellus, to the aforementioned Peter for a certain quantity of grain per year; and concerning this lease they drew up a public instrument, in which mention is made of another instrument, in which it was stated that the said plots of land had been pledged to the said Gausta in respect of the aforementioned dowry promise; but the instrument mentioned does not appear. The question now arises whether, upon the expiration of the term of the lease of the said plots of land, by virtue of the instrument initiating the lease of the said lands, the said Piera, daughter and heir of the said Gausta, can claim the said lands as universal heir of the said Gausta, or not.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a will in which a son is passed over is void under civil law.
2. For how long the right to declare it void endures.
3. Whether a void will, in which a son is passed over, is drawn into a fideicommissum by a codicillary clause.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be stated for clarity that a testament in which a father omits a son or daughter, which is indeed void by operation of law, when he made no mention of them, is so for two reasons. First: because he did not care for the natural affection towards his son, like a madman. Second: because he did not observe the formalities in such a testament, as in D. de lib. et post. l. si filius, qui in potestate; and l. Gallus §. in omnibus; and l. inter cetera. D. de iniur. test. l. posthum. Inst. de exh. li. in principio. C. de inoff. test. l. omnimodo. §. 1. In Auth. ut cum de ap. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum. And therefore the said testament, as a testament, was void by operation of law. The glossa, however, says that it is void by operation of law, if it is said to be void, as in C. de inoff. test. l. scimus. in principio. de iniusto testamento. l. filio praeterito. and C. de contrah. l. posth. The Doctors say that rather it is entirely void by civil law. But if it is not said to be void, it is validated by praetorian equity, so that possession may be granted according to the tablets, which, unless claimed by an instituted heir who is an outsider within one hundred useful days, it is impossible that it be validated. See D. de iniur. testa. l. posth. and what is noted in the same title, l. cum in secundo. D. de leg. praestan. l. si duo. However, the possession according to the tablets could be claimed by the instituted heir after the lapse of one useful year granted to the omitted son in power to claim against the tablets: because such is the order of the aforementioned praetor, that instituted heirs do not wait forever, but for a time set by the praetor, as in D. ad car. l. si impubes. §. 1. D. de secun. tab. l. aequissimum. §. expectandi, on account of which the goods were not lost or recognized as possession according to the tablets by Peter; the testament could not be validated: because it was not confirmed. D. de stip. serv. l. si servus communis meus. and castrensis peculii. in fine principii. But suppose that, by civil law, it were validated by the equity of the jurists, according to which the simple ancient doctors and the glossa said, then it would have to be seen whether, from the fact that the omitted daughter suffered her uncle to possess for the whole time of her life, she is understood to have approved by silence. And it seems so, especially since this was for a long time, and particularly on account of the connection of persons. D. l. filio praeterito, C. de pet. haer. l. si filius. D. de prob. l. procula. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. si servus communis. And the granddaughter, who was conceived after the death of her grandfather, does not have the right to break the will in her own person. D. de iniur. te. l. si quis hereditatis. in principio. de suis, et leg. l. Item praetor. and what is noted in C. de inoff. te. l. si quis filium. in principio. Nor from the person of the mother: because she tacitly approved not only by the passage of time, but also by other indications joined together with the passage of time, as I said, although Bartolus says, and wrongly, that she seems to approve by the mere passage of one useful year.

† For it would follow that the right to bring an action would not be subject to any annual limitation under civil law, which is false. For if the complaint lasts for five years, as it is odious, therefore at least for five years the right to bring an action persists. Moreover, the new law imposes a limit, therefore it is perpetual. I readily admit that by the lapse of a year one appears tacitly to repudiate the inheritance under civil law, and not to confirm the will. C. de iure delib. l. suum heredem. For tacit renunciation of one remedy does not extinguish the other. de bonis liberis l. si filius. Otherwise it would follow that an instituted heir, who did not petition according to the tablets within the time limit, could not subsequently enter upon the inheritance under civil law: which no one understanding of civil law says. C. de iure delib. l. cum antiquo. and l. licet.

† I return to the point at issue, and I say that the said testament is null according to the direct law. But whether it is drawn into a fideicommissum by virtue of the codicillary clause, the glossa says that it is not, in the authenticum *Ex causa*. To this effect is what I said concerning insanity, in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Titia*. For he made no mention of the daughter, as if he were of unsound mind; but even if he had made some mention of the daughter, he would not have added it under the title of institution. Then he would have fulfilled paternal affection, although he erred in law. And then the force of the codicillary clause would have place. And in this opinion was Oldradus. Others say indiscriminately, as do Decius and Cynus, that the clause is valid and is drawn into a fideicommissum, and this opinion has prevailed among the moderns, and they are among the summits of the law. On the second question I say that the thing ought to be restored to the lessor and to his heirs, as in the Code, *De locato*, law *Si quis conductionis*, and law *Conductores*, and in the Code, *Unde vi*, law *Non ab re*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How it is proved that someone is a manifest usurer.
2. The term "only" — what it signifies.
3. How manifest status is proved by reputation, and how a witness is bound to testify.
4. Unless someone is proved to be a usurer, he cannot be proved to be manifest.
5. Whether singular witnesses prove.
6. Reputation is not proved by a single witness testifying to reputation.
7. When a statute or constitution states that reputation suffices, what kind of reputation is meant.
8. Who are called singular witnesses.
9. How it is proved by singular witnesses that someone is a heretic.
10. Whether a confession made before a priest proves someone to be a usurer, and whether it can be made by constitution.
11. Whether, by the constitution of a bishop, it can be established that a crime is proved by a single witness.
12. What is known by the multitude cannot be denied to be notorious.
body: In the name of the almighty God, of the Blessed Mary, his mother, Virgin, and glorious. Amen. In the case of Ludovicus Mascus and others, it must be considered,

Whether it is proven according to the common law that John was a manifest usurer, such that his testament is invalid; and that this cannot be known unless the testimonies of the witnesses are seen and examined. I shall proceed through each witness in order: and I permit, for the sake of clarity, that the one alleging a manifest usurer raises two objections: the fact and the quality, as in the chapter *Ab eo*, *De electione*, Book 6. From these two joined together results one thing, namely, that he is intestable, as in the chapter *Quanquam*, *De usuris*, Book 6. Nor is it sufficient to prove that someone is a usurer, unless the quality necessary for this is proposed and proven, as in the Digest, *De adulteriis*, law *Denuntiasse*; *De vi bonorum raptorum*, law *Praetor*, section *Docere*; *De itinere actuque privato*, law 3, section *Itaque*. Because the effect arises from the quality itself, not from the simple fact, as in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Divus*, according to Bartolus and the noted glosses in the chapter *Si forte*, *De electione*, Book 6.

Secondly, I premise that the word "however" is exclusive, as is noted in C. de probat. l. rationes and l. obesse C. de praediis minorum. Hence, if the article to be proven contains a qualified fact, and the witness says that he however knows that the fact occurred, but says nothing about the quality, it appears that he is saying that he knows nothing about the quality, because the word "however" in a witness has a negative sense both in meaning and in proof.

Third, I premise that when notoriety is proved by reputation, if the witness first said that he did not know whether it was notorious, but afterwards affirms the reputation without correcting his statement or explaining it, he is understood to be wavering. It is otherwise if he says, “I correct” or “I interpret.” As noted in c. ult. de iureiurando, lib. 6.

Fourth, I premise that unless it is proven that someone is a usurer, he cannot be proven to be manifestly so. D. de probat. l. si arbiter. Unless it were very notorious, as in the case of Albrico, who was aware, and of Bonibello: the fame of them is authentic, and by reason of their place and name they are notorious. D. de iur. cal. c. cum causam. According to Innocentius, since no one would dare to testify or hold a contrary opinion.
† Fifth, I premise that singular witnesses do not prove a certain and determined fact, as is noted in C. de testibus, l. testibus, and in the Speculum de inquisitione, § nunc videndum.

Sixthly, I premise that fame is not proved by one witness as to fame, nor is there an indication, and perhaps half-proof; because half-proof of half-proof is not found in law, nor half-indication, as is noted in C. de fideicommissis hereditatibus, l. si.

Seventh and finally, I premise that when a statute or constitution states that reputation suffices, it is not understood to refer to a perfunctory or chance-born reputation, but to one deriving its origin from certain causes and conjectures, which ought to move the populace to believe in such a manner, as noted by Bartolus in the question *de minoribus*, § *tormenta*, at the end. And it was an ancient saying, as reported by Johannes Andreae and Innocentius in the chapter *Cum oporteat*, where it is also stated that when reputation is highly prejudicial, it must be established that it arose among prudent, discreet, and unsuspected men; or that among them prevails the credulity of the discreet, which constitutes an acceptance and a foretelling of the truth. Having therefore premised these matters, let us consider the statements of each individual witness.

It must be known, however, that every witness is singular, because he is contained in one spirit and one sense, as stated in the law *rerum mixtura* under the heading *de usucapione*. But not every witness is called singular; rather, that witness is called singular who testifies about that which he alone knows and no one else knows, or, if another knows it, does not testify about the same thing.

† Likewise, the same person is said to be doubtful in the same genus of heresy, if one says that he is a heretic, and another says that he is likewise a heretic: but in the matter of knowledge, one says that he heard him denying the Incarnation, another the Resurrection. Jacobus de Belvisi says that heresy is proved in the genus, because they agree in the end of the matter. Others, however, say the contrary, because these do not prove the genus, except insofar as the genus is represented in the species. But this species is not proved by anyone, because it is singular. On this point, see *de testibus*, l. *ob carmen*, § *fin.* The same thing is not proved in the species, unless by witnesses who comprehend knowledge of the matter in the same sense, in the same place, at the same time, without any discrepancy, as in *Codex de testibus*, l. *testium*. Let us therefore examine the testimonies. The first witness, Fr. Francis, deposes concerning a certain market conducted in fraud of usury. "Fictitious commercial transactions," says the law, "we condemn, lest we leave room for frauds." He deposes nothing concerning manifest fact or fame. And because he said that he nevertheless knew, it follows that beyond what he deposes, he says that he does not know. The second witness, John Marini, deposes concerning a certain other act tending to the crime of usury, and that it was public voice and fame, and common opinion, that the said John trafficked and practiced usury by means of the *cambio sicco* [dry exchange]. Here it must be observed that he does not say that it was public voice and fame that he was a public or manifest usurer, but that he was a usurer; hence, by this fame, it is proved at least co-adjuvatively that he was a usurer. But because he says that he nevertheless knew, and does not speak of manifest fact, it seems to follow that by this fame, which can also be concerning hidden things, and even concerning untrue things, manifest fact is not proved. Thus, those who say that manifest fact is proved by other indications and fame must be understood as meaning when the fame is that he is manifest, not when he is simply a usurer; because fame concerning a simple [usurer] does not prove a mixed [usurer], of which the fame does not speak, nor does the witness speak. For it is possible for there to be fame when someone secretly and colorably lends alone to another at usury; and yet no one would say this is manifest, which cannot be known except by the subtlety of the judge and a scrupulous inquiry. See *de lege*, l. *si servus vetitus*, *Codex de dolo*; l. *dolum*, *Institutiones de actionibus*, § *curare*. Thus, although there is fame that someone is a prostitute, it is not proved thereby that she is a public prostitute, unless she openly makes her profit; see l. *palam*, *de ritu nuptiarum*. The third witness, Lord Pucius, a priest, proves the confession. Here it must be observed,

† Although the constitution states that a confession made before a priest renders one a manifest usurer, it does not state that the priest alone suffices to prove this confession. Rather, this confession must be proved according to divine and human law by two witnesses. C. de test. l. quam; Alberi. de succ. ab int. 11; c. si. de testibus; c. in nomine Domini; and what is noted, fa. haer. l. si.

† Nor would the bishop’s constitution be valid if it provided that a crime, or a manifest crime, could be proven by a single witness, because it is not reasonable. Nor is it to be tolerated, especially in serious cases: as in l. maritus, D. 3, q. 3; c. erit autem lex, C. de officio praefecti praetorii; l. normam, a contrario sensu. And because a lower law cannot abrogate a higher law, especially a divine or natural law. The fourth witness, s. d. Nico., does not prove anything unless some subscription induces a doubt in conscience: because his statement is ambiguous and too general. D. de probat., c. in praesentia. The fifth witness, s. d. Io. Angelini, proves manifest fame, but not manifest sin: because the adverb “manifestly” in his speech qualifies the verb “heard,” not the verb “to exercise,” as appears from the construction of the sentence: and because he had previously used the words “I only know,” he does not prove manifest sin, but manifest fame, i.e., common report of the sin. Ugolinus Ioan. says that the fame was that he was a manifest usurer: because he says, “I heard from all who had dealings with him.” Here it must be observed from whom this fame originated: because it came from usurers, who hoped for profit from the fame, i.e., repayment of usury; in such a case, they introduced it as their own fame, which is of no value, since it originates from suspicious persons. D. de adulteriis, l. miles, §. pe., and there by Bartolus. Simbaldus Gerii proves usury, but does not prove it to be manifest, because he does not testify about manifestness. D. de furtis, l. fur est, and l. si quis in servitute, per Bartolus. Matiutius, s. Marini, does not testify about manifestness. Nor does Gilicus Nardi, if I am not mistaken, nor do the records speak to it. Now Ser Marini refers to a writing not written by this person, but by another, and it is a private writing, by which a crime is not proven, because its credibility can be called into doubt. And a private writing does not make anyone manifest, as the text clearly states. D. de legibus, l. in tacitis. Many others speak of these usuries, calumnies, shiftings, and frauds, but they do not prove the qualities of manifestness. Nevertheless, it must be considered whether so many things seen with the eyes, so many things handled by the hands, and so much knowledge of the usurious faction, make it manifest in his case: so that, given so many acts and so many frauds, manifestness results ipso facto, as if it were publicly known, just as in the case of a prostitute whom many have individually and separately defiled. 12

† Quod. n. it cannot be denied that it is not notorious, that there is a multitude, as C. de acq. l. ea quidem. per Cy. et ar. C. qui test. fac. present. l. hac consultissima. §. si. Witnesses. n. prove acts, and the frequency of acts, and a certain duration of time: from which custom is induced, and from custom manifest evidence flows. C. que sit longa consue. l. 2. per Pet. et Cy. In this certainly my conscience pricks me, and in these matters the discretion of the judge has much place. says In. de acq. c. cum oporteat certainly the thing known by so many people is as if it were common, it seems necessary to be,

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Force is twofold, namely absolute and conditional.
2. The case of a ship having suffered force to which resistance is impossible appears to be specifically excepted from the promise.
3. The act of an official excuses the subject, and the official himself is excused on account of the king's command.
4. The clause "notwithstanding": how it is to be placed.
5. Whether the seller is bound for force inflicted, and what is the case regarding fortuitous event; and number 6.
6. The word "another": what it signifies.
7. Whether a fortuitous event excuses from interest, or whether fault brings about interest.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The following reasons are advanced on behalf of Lord Dinaldo.

The first reason is that force is twofold, namely absolute and conditional. Absolute force occurs when someone is seized by robbers, or drowned in deep water, or detained by a powerful person against whom resistance is impossible, as in D. locata conducto, l. si fundus, in fine; D. de baptismo, c. maiores. Thus, when a ship is committed to the winds, its course is not determined by your will, but by the impulse of the wind, as in D. de publicaniis, l. Caesar. In such a case, the person impeded is considered to have observed the law with regard to the avoidance of damage or penalty; and thus the text there interprets the law of the agreement.

The second reason is that the case of a ship suffering force majeure, against which resistance is impossible, appears to have been expressly and specifically excepted from the promise; and in case of doubt, it is better to adhere to the words of the contract, especially since natural reason supports this, as stated in D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, § pactorum; D. de usuris, l. si stipulatus; and X. de privilegiis, c. porro. The third reason is that, although the seller has assumed upon himself all adverse, i.e., fortuitous and unfortunate, events except two, nevertheless this royal decree should not be termed an adverse or fatal event, but is rather a certain edict of the Prince, who is the living law of his subjects and can impose law upon them, especially for the public utility of the kingdom, which lies in the supply of provisions or foodstuffs, and in any other matter of public utility, as stated in D. de decretis ab ordinariis factis, l. si; C. de commercio et mercatoribus, l. mercatores; C. de eunuchis, l. 2. Therefore, if this is not a fortuitous event, although it constitutes an impediment for them, the risk does not appear to have been assumed, as stated in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fistulas, § frumenta; and D. de locato, l. opus, quod in advectione.

The fourth reason is: because the act of the official excuses the subject. The official himself is also excused on account of the king’s mandate, as in D. de pi. act. l. si, §. ult.; D. de lege commissoria, l. mulier fundos; D. de regu. iur. l. non videtur, §. quid iussu; X. de appel. c. cum parati and c. nouit; and D. de aqua plu. arcen. l. quod Principis, and as noted in the proemium of the title Hoc ius regis erit praedia, and c. Quinto. Fifthly, because if anyone were to bind himself expressly against an edict of the Prince, the obligation would not hold, as noted in D. de pac. l. pacisci and l. iurisgentium, §. praetor ait, and §. et generaliter, even with an oath, as appears there, and l. quemadmodum, D. de agri. et censi., and D. de leg. 1, l. si quis inquilinos, §. si. For such an oath contains the stigma of transgression, not the bond of religion, as in C. de nup. auth. quod eis and C. quae res venire non possunt, l. pen. and l. si.

To the contrary, against the lord Arnald, that he is bound to the penalty, these reasons are made. And first: because the exception of violence is understood to apply to that which is inflicted by a stranger, not by oneself or one’s own, as in D. loc. l. qui insulam, §. Colonus, where the text is found, and thus the Summa with Bartolus there, although the law si vendita insula, D. de peri. et commo. rei vendi., seems to go to the contrary. But this does not avail, because there the matter was not one of hostility, as it was here. If, therefore, violence was inflicted here by his own men, it harms him who chose such unfaithful ministers, as in D. nau. ca. l. si, §. seruorum, and D. furti aduersus naul. l. in fin., and D. de publi. l. 3.

Secondly, because the violence inflicted upon the seller was not reasonable, but injurious, since the Florentine, to whose prejudice the precept was directed, was not of the king’s land, as in X. de postu. prae. c. 1. Therefore, it harms the seller, not the buyer, as in D. loca. l. si merces, §. culpae; D. solu. matri. l. in his.

Thirdly, because he who binds himself to a risk is not released by a supervening risk, D. de peri. et commo. rei vendi. l. si in venditione. But this man bound himself to the risk of the impediment to transport; therefore, he is liable for the risk, not because it is a risk, but because of the agreement, as noted in l. quaesitum, C. commo. l. 1.

Fourthly, because after the occurrence of the risk, the lord Arnald ought to have approached the king and insisted on the removal of the impeding risk, and exerted every effort to have the said precept removed, as in D. de pigno. ac. l. si, §. si, in the text and gloss. Princeps. n. praesumitur iustitiae plenus; l. 2, §. merito; ne quid in loco pub. l. ex facto, in prin.; de vulga. substitu. And therefore, it ought to have been probable that he did not wish his precept to prejudice justice, already established by the preceding contract, as in the said l. Caesar, and C. de rescin. vend. l. ratas, and de preci. impe. offe. l. quo.

† By which law it is clear that it is not sufficient for the Prince merely to oppose the clause “notwithstanding the contract,” unless he expressly states “notwithstanding.” L. quo, ut notum est, D. quod quisque iure; L. 3, § si is, pro quo, D. pro quo; and C. si contra ius, vel uti publicum; L. si, and especially when neither, or one of the contracting parties, is subject to his jurisdiction, and consequently neither to his law nor edict. D. de bonis auctoritatis iudicis possessoribus, L. cum unus, § is, qui; regnum non est suis limitibus coarctatum, and to those limits the king’s power adheres both extensively and restrictively. C. de re iudicata, C. pastoralis, in the title. And although one ought not to express what is irrelevant, D. de negotiis gestis, L. nam et servus, nevertheless, that which may plausibly be of assistance should be attempted, as in D. quibus causis maior, L. sed si per praetorem, § haec clausula. And this is required by good faith; otherwise, one could easily conclude agreements with the king’s officials. Moreover, the simple ears of the king are deceived, as is said in the book Aestiva. Fifthly, because at least he ought to have notified the buyer, as in D. de locato, L. Item quaeritur, § exercitu; and to perform acts which not only imply good faith but also manifest it openly, as in D. de poenis, L. bonafides. Nor should a way be opened for frauds or affected dolus, as in D. si quis cautio, L. 2, § nam si ipse; for dolus is presumed from the omission of remedies. D. de manumis, L. idemque, § si ignorantes; to this effect, C. de temporibus appellationum, L. si, § illud, in the word “summa ope”; and Extra, de electione, C. eis. Coming to the solution of this question, I say that if any fault, even the most severe, can be found in the seller, there is no doubt that he is bound to the penalty on account of the pact regarding risk, made without any specification of perilous cases, as noted in the said § quaesitum. And much more so if he had arranged something out of precipitous avarice, as in D. de nautico fenerato, L. cum proponas. And the same applies if, when he could have obtained permission from the king before the act, he had not done so, by argument from D. de locato, L. in locationis; D. de pactis, L. non impossibile. But if the navigation was precisely impeded by the king’s edict, because the king rules by law, as in the epistle Inter claras, and from his mouth comes the sword, as in C. ex ore, de privilegiis, and his word is said to be armed force, then this case is doubtful to me on account of the words of the pact in the second case, excepting the peril, where it says “armed force,” etc. For what difference does it make whether the impediment is established with one or with a thousand, if one is as effective as a thousand? For the terror of the king’s arms makes the force armed, as in L. 3, § qui armata, D. de vi et vi armata.

† It must be considered that the owner is liable for violence inflicted by his own persons, because his own persons are at fault; otherwise, if they are not at fault, as is the case here, since the king's command excuses them. And this is what the text considers in the aforementioned law *Qui insulam*, § *Colo*, where it says, "not by chance, but by fault." However, I say one thing,

† But if the seller could have foreseen this event, he would then not be excused: as in D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. Si vina, quam in doliiis, § Plane. For example, he was a friend of the king, and thus knew his intention, or he observed an urgent scarcity, and knew that in such cases the king was accustomed to act; yet he did not warn the buyer, who was ignorant of the conditions of the king or the kingdom, as stated there. Certainly, if the words of the agreements are carefully considered, it must be noted that the exception applies only to an armed predicative, not to an impediment to the delivery of wheat: since the contrary is provided for regarding this matter not only in Sicily, but everywhere on that voyage. And this is what those words mean: "or in another case," i.e., even if delayed by an impediment.

† For the term “another,” when it signifies a similarity of quality despite a diversity of substance, as noted in C. de servis fugitivis, l. Si fugitivus. But that the parties to the contract should have considered a future law, when this is not expressed in the agreement, is not probable: as in ff. de evictionibus, l. Lucius; and de legibus 2, l. Qui solidum, § 1. And it is deemed impossible to act against that which depends solely on the Prince: de legibus 1, l. Apud Iulianum, § Finis; de verbis obligandi, l. Continuus, § Cum quis. But to this it is answered, because he imputes it to himself if he bound himself, since it was possible from the beginning. Hence the disposition is not vitiated: de legibus 1, l. Si mihi et tibi, § Si quis servos. Just as sailing is sometimes impossible, when sailing is said to be placed in fortune, as in that condition, “if the ship comes from Asia.” Which condition is casual, not potestative, because it depends on the snares of fortune. And if anyone wishes not to be able to plead the excuse of a storm at sea, the agreement is valid, and the penalty is incurred, as in the cited § Quaesitum. Nor is the act of the king stronger than the act of nature, but weaker: because the prince is supplicable, whereas truly the waves of the sea and the winds are implacable: unless it is said that the case is different with the Prince, because one cannot bind oneself to act against the command of the king, because one would bind oneself to commit a sin, which cannot be effected by any agreement: as in ff. de pactis, l. Si unus, § Illud. And those who sin against heavenly counsels incur infamy and damages: as in C. de officio rectoris provinciae, l. Ne quis iudicum. And he who sins against the king is immediately certain of the penalty, but he who commits himself to the sea is not immediately certain of the danger, but places himself in doubt, because navigation is uncertain: eo. tit. l. Civitas Phodiorum. Therefore, on account of equity, he seems to be excused from the penalty by the occurrence of an unforeseen event: ff. ad legem Rhodiam de iactu, l. Si vehenda, § Idem iuris. Which has a natural understanding and reason: ff. de transactionibus, l. Cum aequo; de testamento militis, l. Militis; eodem, § Miles. Certainly someone will say that this event should not be called unforeseen, but rather it could easily have been foreseen, and an obscure agreement is interpreted against the seller: ff. de pactis, l. Veteribus. And he who speaks with loose words falls into immediate danger: C. de dotis promissa, l. Finis, in fine. And general and indefinite speech comprehends all things: ff. de pactis, l. Empto, § Lucius; ff. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. Si servitus. And much more so universal terms: C. de manumissionibus, l. A procuratore; C. sine censu vel reliquis, l. Omnes. Because the same reason and condition apply to all fortuitous events: ff. de acquisitione emptionis, l. Si ea res. And those words are explained as meaning: in every case of contrary fortune: ff. ad trebellianam, l. Epistolam, in principio; and extra de aetate et qualitate, c. Tuam. Just as a favorable event is called “dexter” [right-handed], when the ship goes to the second port, as noted in ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Pretia rerum, § Si dexter. Therefore “prosper” is said, and “sinister” is put for unfortunate: ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. Non solum, § Finis. It would be certain that if this lord Arnald had delayed the voyage, and could have done so, he would be effectively bound to the penalty: as in ff. si quis cautio, l. 2, § Quod diximus. Because fault causes this: ff. de locato, l. Peculium, § Navem. The same if he could have held by ways secure from all impediment. Therefore, this matter should be referred to the discretion of a good man according to the circumstances of how it is proven: de verbis obligandi, l. Continuus, § Cum ita; de annuis legibus, l. Mevia, § Finis. And this as regards the penalty.

I say, as for the interest, which arises from the agreement due to the loss, it may be doubted whether they are bound, such that only the value of the grain at the designated place is to be considered in each case, or whether it was a generic obligation, and he is bound: because the casualty does not release him: as in the law *Incendium*, and the law *Vinum*, and the law *Si* of the title *De tritico*. But if it is a specific thing, then otherwise, unless delay or fault preceded the casualty. Digest 10, law *In nave* of Saufeli. And thus it matters whether the grain was bought in genus, as so many bushels, or under a demonstrated body. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An absolute surety does not fall again under the obligation.
2. In case of doubt, collusion is not presumed, nor simulation, and no. 3.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A surety, who has been judicially released by the benefit of a sentence, does not fall back into the obligation under the new law mentioned against the principal debtor. For the words of the reform are directed against the person of the principal debtor, and they are contrary to the common law, and therefore must be restricted. For the words state that such chamberlains do not say anything about sureties. D. de pactis, l. si. Unless the first sentence had been rendered after conclusion of the case, because then it would benefit no one, neither the principal debtor nor the surety. C. de sententiis adversus fiscum latis, l. 1. § 10.

† In doubt, however, collusion is not presumed. L. fin. C. ad I. Iul. repe. I say the same of the buyer as of the surety: because a law enacted against the seller after the purchase has been contracted does not harm the buyer, unless simulation is proven.
† which is not presumed in case of doubt. D. de probat. l. si superatus. arg. D. de evict. l. Lucius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the executors sell any property on account of debts incurred before the birth of the posthumous child, the posthumous child, once born, may claim it.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having seen the will of Angelo, son of the late Davino Jacobo of Clanciano, from which it appears by the hand of Bartholomew Ser Mierii, it is alleged in the case that the executors sold that house before the birth of the posthumous child, whom the posthumous child wishes to claim.

† The question is: what is the law? I answer that the sale did not hold, because that sale could not be made unless it was established that there were debts of the testator, since it ought not to be made to satisfy debts. But it could not be established that there were debts, nor could proof be made, before the posthumous child was born, nor even after the posthumous child was born, and without being duly cited regarding the liquidation of the debts, because a testament requires proof of the debt. Such proof was not made: nor could it be made except in court. L. Haec autem, Qui ex causa in possessionem eatur, De verbis obligatis; L. Qui Romae, § Augerius. And therefore the said posthumous child can claim the said house from the possessors, notwithstanding the said sale. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether death is proved by reputation, and how, and whether one witness proves the truth and another the reputation of the death.
casus: CASE. The point is as follows: A certain A. by name made a testament, in which he instituted B., his son, as his universal heir. However, during his lifetime, and after the death of the said B., the said A. wished that an oratory be made from his house, in which he dwelt, and for which he wished his goods to be given. This B., the son and heir, after the consumption and sale of his father’s goods, went to the parts of Hungary, and there he served for a time on the pay of the lord king. Finally, returning from there, he began to fall ill on the journey, and in that illness on the journey, it is said, he died. To prove whose death, three witnesses are introduced, two of whom say that they heard it said by C. that the said B. was dead. D. attended his burial. s. of the said B. Many other witnesses also testify to public voice and fame. Now the question is: whether such witnesses suffice to prove the death of the said B., and if they do not fully prove it, whether they at least induce a presumption which transfers the burden of proof to those claiming that the said B. is alive. Which doubt is greatly caused by the distance of the road and the length of time, because what happened here was over ten years ago.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. An ancient death is proved by mere reputation, but not a recent death: as noted in C. soluto matrimonio, l. si quidem, and l. 2, § si dubitetur, ff. quemadmodum testamentum, unless the reputation is accompanied by indications which lead the mind of a man to a reasonable conjecture. I say a discerning man. It is possible in such a place for a person to have died, or in such an act, which could not be proved by sight. An example regarding place is that it is said he died in a very remote or wooded place; because he entered the forest and was not afterwards seen to exit, or the sea. Regarding an act, for example in war. It is relevant what is noted in C. de repudiis, auth. hodie, and ff. de secundis tabulis, l. qui ex liberis, in principio. I believe that in our case the presumption is sufficiently proved, yet it is not fully proved, because no one proves by a congruous sense of the body, nor does he testify conclusively to prove the truth. C. de causis, l. nec nos, and it is relevant. C. de naufragio, l. de submersis, and l. quotiens, lib. 11, and what is noted by Innocentius de iuramento calumniae, c. cum causam, and ff. de adulteriis, l. miles, § socer, and ff. de hereditate instituenda, l. Paccumeius Androtenus. However, if the said citizen had testified, testifying to his presence, then one witness to the truth with two others to the reputation would suffice; because then the reputation would confirm the faith of the man. ff. de triticario, l. 3, § idem divus, with similar authorities. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether legitimation is rendered void if there were multiple impediments, and only one was expressly stated.
2. Whether one who is not capable of receiving restitution, yet is asked to receive it, may do so in order to restore it to a capable person.
casus: CASE. The case is as follows: Bartholomew had a natural son named Dominic from a certain woman named Jacoba. He had this Dominic legitimated by having authority from the Lord Emperor, stating that this Dominic was born from him, Bartholomew, being bound [in marriage], and the said Jacoba being free [from marriage]. Appended to this privilege of legitimation was the clause, "notwithstanding § si in Auth. qui modo naturales efficiuntur sui, or any other law, edict, or constitution acting to the contrary." Finally, the said Bartholomew made a testament, in which, among other things, he said thus: "Furthermore, I leave to John, son of the said Bectia, formerly my sister, my nephew, 50 pounds of Pisan denarii. And I order him to be content with these, and that he cannot ask for anything else in my goods and inheritance, since I have acquired all the goods I have by the industry of my person, and the said Bectia has had from paternal and maternal goods more than the portions falling to her and due to her according to the form of the present constitution. In all my other goods, however, I institute as my heir Dominic, my son legitimated by the most excellent man, Lord Peter, citizen of Pisa, son of Lord Albizius, Count of the Sacred Lateran Palace. And if the said Dominic should die at any time without children, I substitute the work of the major church of Saint Mary of this city. And finally, at the end of the said testament, it is contained thus: 'And I say and will that this my testament be valid by the law of testaments, valid by the law of codicils, and of the present constitution, and by every other law, way, and mode by which it can better be valid; for so it pleases me and I will, and such is my last will.'" Finally, the above-named Bartholomew, the testator, dies, having made the above-named testament as stated, leaving the above-named Dominic, his legitimated son, instituted as heir as stated, and the above-named John, son of the above-named Bectia, formerly sister of the said testator, his next closest relative after the said Dominic. Now the above-named John opposes and says that the above-named legitimation does not hold, because in truth the above-named Dominic was born from the said Bartholomew being bound [in marriage] and the above-named Jacoba being bound [in marriage], whereas in the privilege of legitimation it was said she was free; consequently, he says the inheritance of the above-named Bartholomew pertains to him. On the other side, the contrary is said. Now, assuming as constant without prejudice that the said Jacoba was bound [in marriage], whereas in the privilege it is said she was free. Because the above-named legitimation is valid in law: and also assuming without prejudice that the said legitimation was invalid, it is asked whether the above-named John can and ought to have, ask for, and obtain the inheritance and goods of the above-named Bartholomew deceased, or not; since the said Dominic, the instituted heir, possesses the said inheritance and goods. And on the other side, the said John asks for it and them. It is asked, according to law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† As to the first point, I say that the legitimation is invalid, because whenever it is necessary to remove several impediments, if one is expressed and the other is concealed or suppressed, the act is vitiated: as in D. de haereditatibus instituendis, l. Si non lex eliescentia; it is required that mention be made of the defect, if one awaits the care of the dispensing authority: c. 2, de filiis presbyterorum, lib. 6; and l. 2, C. si servus aut libertus ad decurionatus aspiraverit, lib. 10; and l. Barbarius, according to the reading of the moderns, which holds that Barbarius was not, as the praetor, by the fact that the people had freed him, made free. Moreover, it is easier to remove one inconvenience than several: as in l. 1, C. de dote promissa. Furthermore, whether we say that legitimation is assimilated to dispensation, it is certain that dispensation does not extend to suppressed defects: as in D. de peculio, l.
