Cum dominus, in principio, through Jacobus de Aretio; or whether we say that it is a restitutio in integrum, it is certain that restitutio in integrum does not extend to those matters which have not been implored: C. si saepius in integrum restitutio postulatur; or whether we say that legitimation is a benefit of the Prince, it is certain that benefits of Princes do not extend to that which has not been considered: D. de vulgari substitutione, l. Ex fratre. One laboring under double defects must make mention of both, according to the noted doctrine of D. de verbis obligatorum, l. Stipulationum quaedam; and D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Si scriptus. And it makes the whole general rule that obreption vitiates; the laws are well known.

† Regarding the second point, it appears that one who is not capable of taking [an inheritance] when charged with restitution cannot take it in order to restore it to a capable person. D. 36.6.1 (Cogi) § Qui solidum. And the reason is that he acts as a minister, from whom no benefit is retained. D. 24.1.1 (Mulier, also beginning Sulpicius). How could a spurious son be an executor of a will, since he is not prohibited by any law? He could also be appointed guardian to a legitimate son, even though he cannot take the goods for himself. D. 26.1.1 (Impuberi filio centurio).

To the contrary, it is said: for the instituted heir who is charged with restitution is charged as an heir, as D. 36.1.1 (Mulier) § Fin. Therefore, it is necessary that he be an heir; otherwise, he cannot restore the hereditary property. But those who come in intestacy should restore, for whenever the institution of an heir is invalid due to the testator’s error regarding the quality of filiation, those coming in intestacy appear to be charged, and they must restore upon the fulfillment of the condition, and not before. The case is: C. 6.42.1 (Eam quam). Here two things must be investigated. First, because the substitution made to a spurious son could not stand. C. 6.24.1 (Cum proponas). For if a spurious son is instituted, a vulgar substitution can be made. The text is noted in the same title, D. 28.5.1 (Non poterit). And this is true immediately upon the death of the testator, and the matter is not one of intestacy as long as it is possible to accept the inheritance under the will, D. 28.5.1 (Quod diu) and C. 6.53.1 (Antequam) and D. 29.2.1 (Equissimum) § 1. And this opinion should be defended by the note of Cynus in D. 4.1.1 (Precibus).

Another consideration: if this spurious son had children, and thus the substitute would be excluded. What would be the law then? And the question arises whether the children are understood to be substituted. This article is determined, and the substitution would be abolished; however, here it cannot be certain as long as he lives. The way is not open to the intestate successors. It is true that regarding what I said about the children, there are opinions. For some say that children are called descendants, because as regards children, indications of will are sufficient to include them and exclude strangers. To this effect, D. 35.2.1 (Titiae Seio) § Seia. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the founder of a certain church has provided that upon his death his sons shall succeed, whether, if he leaves alien heirs and not sons, they do not succeed in the right of patronage.
2. Whether the concession made to the sons is denied to alien heirs.
3. If one refounds a hospital and constructs a new hospital, and by reason of the land is the first founder the patron, or rather is the one who refounded and constructed something in the passage or at the fountain.
casus:
CASE. The point is this: A certain person in the city of Arezzo, with the consent and authority of the bishop, constructed and endowed a certain hospital with a chapel from goods granted to him by God. And he ordained and disposed that the election of the hospitaler of the said hospital should be made in this manner, namely, that the election of the hospitaler or rector, which was to be made then as it was first made, should be made by Andrew alone. And if it should happen that the hospitaler elected by him should die before the death of the said Andrew, then the election of the successor should be made by the said Andrew and a certain prior of a fraternity of certain clerics of the city of Arezzo, and his council. And the said Andrew, while living, would have two votes in the said election, and the aforementioned prior with his council in the past election had two votes; but the sons of the said Andrew would have only one vote. And in the aforementioned form, several elections were celebrated. Afterwards, the sons of the said Andrew died, leaving John, son of Bartholomew, brother of the paternal uncle of the said sons of Andrew, surviving. This John, as the nearest relative, accepted the inheritance of Margaret, one of the sons of the said Andrew who had most recently died, and was heir to his brothers. Now it is asked whether the said John, universal heir of the said Margaret, male and legitimate son of the said Andrew, and universal heir, also succeeds in the right of patronage of the aforementioned, which the said Margaret, son of the said Andrew, had.

Furthermore, when the case of the destruction of the said hospital and chapel occurred, because they were too close to the retaining walls of the city, a certain Bartholomew, then hospitaler of the said place, founded a certain other hospital in another place, larger and more spacious than the first, on the land and ground of the aforementioned Margaret, also with the consent of the bishop. And he first laid the foundation with the goods of the portion of the hospital. He later increased and completed it with the goods left to the newly founded hospital; which goods and legacies of the new hospital have increased to such an extent, both in number and amount, as were, or are, the goods of the old hospital, or more and greater. However, he named the said hospital by the same name by which the old one was named. Now it is asked whether, by reason of the ground upon which the said new hospital was refounded and constructed, the right of patronage in the said new hospital belongs to the aforementioned Margaret, lord of the ground, and his heirs; and what right belongs to him in total, considering the prior right of the destroyed old hospital and the right of the new hospital by reason of the ground. And what right of patronage the aforementioned prior of the fraternity of clerics and his council would have in the said hospital.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the first point, it is asked whether, when a hospital is founded and its founder has provided that, upon his death, his sons should succeed in one voice of presentation, and some other person in two voices, the heirs of the sons, upon the sons’ death, acquire any right in the said patronage or not. It must be known, however, that our question does not proceed in respect of patronage simpliciter, but only concerning the voice. For patronage has many rights beyond the voice, and although the right of patronage were restricted in the voice, it would not be understood to be restricted in other respects, as is stated and noted in a similar case in the chapter *Hi qui*, *De aetate et qualitate*, in the gloss beginning *Stallum cor solummodo*. Therefore, it remains to consider the voice, which is twofold, both ordered to a single end. The first voice is that of choosing the person to be presented. The second voice, or writing, is that of presenting the person to be instituted. Both of these must be determined here, and it appears that an alien heir is not entitled to that which was reserved to the sons by the founder, and this for several reasons. The first reason is the form of the thing assumed from the origin of the foundation. And the argument runs thus: the builder gives the form to the right of patronage; because the right of patronage proceeds from him, as in the Authenticum *De ecclesiasticis*, title, § *Si quis*, column 9. I do not, however, exclude other processes, such as from donation, transmission, and endowment; nevertheless, I say that the founder, with respect to himself and his sons and successors, can give the form to the thing then his. Question 16, last; chapter *Pie mentis*; and chapter *Quicunque*; and throughout.

† The question therefore stands on this point: whether the concession made to the sons appears to be denied to other extraneous heirs to whom the right of voice and election would otherwise pass. And it seems that, since special mention was made of the sons, it does not pass to extraneous heirs, even that which would otherwise pass to them; because this term, "sons," is a restrictive term. C. ad trebel. l. iubemus. And because that laymen have the right of presentation is a benefit which the church grants to them. But in such benefits words ought to be restricted, because the nature of ecclesiastical things is sufficiently exorbitant from secular discretion, and accedes more to privilege than to common law; therefore it ought not to be extended. c. privilegium personale, per Dy. And because what is permitted to one is prohibited to another. de iud. l. cum prætor. and in Auth. de non ali. §. emphy. And because the founder could provide for one quality of heirs, without providing for another. ff. de pac. l. auus. Thus we say concerning a sepulchre, that a family sepulchre differs from an hereditary one by a pecuniary constitution: as ff. de religio. l. si familiaria filii. Therefore they do not transmit this right: because it is personal by form, although not by nature. Moreover, the right of patronage consists in the act of making, as regards voices; therefore it can be granted to one of the heirs. ff. de assignandis lib. l. 1. For the right of patronage can be remitted to the church; therefore it can also be restricted by a pact appended in the foundation, and even afterwards. as C. de bonis lib. l. fi. And thus I believe it ought to be said on this point.

† On the second point, I say that if one hospital builds another, the first is the patron of the second; nevertheless, if someone was the patron of the first, his rights do not perish, if the first has been transferred in fact and in name to the second. D. 8.4.11 (Filiae) § 1. Does the patron of the first therefore present in the second? This is similar to the case of one who has a toll right on a bridge, and that bridge is destroyed and another is built: whether he will levy the toll on the new one. I say that if it is destroyed by force or by accident, not maliciously, those who were constituted to bear the burden of the bridge are bound to whatever they were obligated to bear, for they would undoubtedly be bound even now. D. 39.3.1 (Eum debere columnam). If, therefore, it is destroyed by the force of another or by nature, and it seems that this question is determined such that the first founder ceases to be patron, as if the hospital had perished by chance. D. 8.3.1 (Hoc iure) § Si aqua. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the subject matter. The law *hac edictali*, concerning the three laws imposing a penalty on those who remarry.
2. Whether that which returns to the children of the first marriage by virtue of the law *hac edictali* is to be imputed to their legitime.
3. Whether the entire amount exceeding the permitted limit is to be considered as not written and applied to the children, or whether only that portion is to be considered as not written which reduces the husband and them to equality.
4. Whether, regarding the excess left to the spouse, the testator may institute the children of the second marriage as heirs by vulgar substitution, or by simple fideicommissum, or after death.
body: In the Name of Christ.

† Because the aforementioned points touch upon the matter, it must be premised, in accordance with *l. hac edictali*, that there are three bodies of law to be considered, which impose a penalty on those who marry a second time regarding the alienation of their own property to the spouse to the prejudice of the children of the prior marriage.

The first is the law of Emperor Leo, which provides that one who enters into a second marriage cannot leave or give more by way of a lucrative cause, or where the final effect is gain, even if the title is originally onerous; nor can they give or leave to the children of the first marriage a dowry greater than that given or left to the others. If more has been given or donated, it passes to the persons of the children, to be divided among them, as stated in *C. de secundis tabulis*, *l. hac edictali*, up to § *his illud*. Here, two points are noted: the penalty imposed on the spouse, and the provision of the Emperor. For the penalty is with respect to the spouse, from whom the faculty to alienate their own property to the spouse is removed. The provision of the law, however, is with respect to the children. The penalty was just, for certain reins of temperance were imposed on those marrying a second time, especially women, who abandon not only the property of their children but also their lives to new husbands, as in *C. de administratione tutorum*, *l. lex, quam tutores*. Hence, it was just to restrain such persons regarding immoderate affection, considering the person making the disposition and the person receiving it; otherwise, it would be easy for the hope of succession of the children to be removed by step-parental blandishments, as in *ff. de inofficioso testamento*, *l. non est*.

The provision was also just against the impiety of a parent who offends the children in two ways: first, by entering into a second marriage, for thereby they abandon the children, as in *ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, *l. sed si hoc*, § *si*, and in *Auth. de nuptiis*, § *si autem tutelam*. Second, by an immoderate legacy or donation, which offenses regard only the children of the prior marriage, and therefore the provision refers only to them, as in *l. hac edictali*. However, since it was just that all children, both of the first and subsequent marriages, should be equal in the parent’s goods, as in *C. communia utriusque iuris*, *l. si*, and *C. de collationibus*, *l. illud superuenit*, Justinian provided that what was taken from the spouse should be applied to the children of the common marriage. For all are children and ought to be called by equal right of nature, as in *ff. de actionibus et obligationibus*, *l. obligationum*, § *lege*, and therefore they are rightly to be executed. See *C. de libris praetoris*, *l. maximum vitium*. Otherwise, it could happen, due to the inequity of the law, that if there were one child from the first marriage and three from the second, these three would have one share each, and that one would have a *dodrans*. Suppose the case where the spouse had left a *bessem* to the spouse, and a legitime to each of the children, i.e., one share for each, since there are four for this justice of weight and measure to be removed among the children. To this end, the law *quiam praeterea* was issued, *C. de secundis nuptiis*. The reason supports this, for that excess is as if not written, therefore it remains with all heirs without any burden, as in *C. de caducis tollendis*, § *in primo*. And that it is not as if not written is declared in *Auth. de nuptiis*, § *optime*. And this was according to the law of Justinian, namely that law *quiam praeterea*.

Subsequently, it pleased Justinian to revert to the constitution of Leo, because penalties should benefit those in whose favor they were established, and should be applied to these, not to others, as in *ff. de litigiosis rebus*, *l. si*. Also, because an absurdity could follow in some case, for it happened that if it was taken from the stepfather and applied to his son, then through the interposed person it returned to the spouse, i.e., to the stepfather himself, the usufruct through the person of the son, which was inconvenient, as in *l. hac edictali*, § *omnes*. And therefore, by the latest law, Justinian provided that what was taken from the spouse should pertain to the children offended by the transition alone. This is the third and last law, in which we reside, as in the said § *optime*. And it is confirmed by reason: for to the prejudice of the common children, one can alienate to the husband, i.e., their father, from their legitime; hence, as to the prejudice of the children, the mother has judgment, and without complaint; therefore, to the children of the first marriage, who alone are called to the revocatory complaint, all that beyond is applied, because no one makes a part for them, since no other is admitted to a part. This is the truth, and the reason of the truth. Nor can the children of the second marriage insult the first, since it was permitted to the mother and the law in regard to strangers, as in *C. de inofficioso testamento*, *l. cum quaeritur*, in *Auth. de restitutione*, and that which bears, § *quamobrem*. But two doubts occur,

† First, whether that which returns to them by virtue of this edictal law is to be imputed to the children of the first marriage in respect of their legitime. The gloss in §. optime states that it is not. Iac. de Ra. holds the contrary. I adhere to the gloss, because it is not by natural law, but by penal law, that it is applied to them, and thus by a different law, as appears from ff. de bonis possessoribus, l. sed cum patrono, and ff. de calumniis, l. si. Nor could the testator provide that this benefit should be imputed to them in respect of their legitime, as appears from de inofficiosis testamentis, l. si arrogator, §. sed an impuberi. The second doubt is whether the whole,

† that which exceeds the said mode, shall be deemed unwritten, and shall be applied to the aforementioned children, or rather, that part shall be deemed unwritten which reduces the husband and them to equality: for example, 10 are left to the spouse, 5 to the son. Will the son have five of those 10, and thus would have double what the husband has? Or two and a half? The text in l. hac edictali, lib. ibi, and it adds, and the same is stated textually in §. optime. There, Pet. and Cy. hold the contrary, and this is the mind of the gloss in l. hac edictali, s. quod coniunx expresse potest virum testari, for example, out of 15, only seven and a half remain with him. And thus here, that which is beyond equality, is reduced to equality, arg. de usur. l. placuit, as is in the example nihil, i. quando nihil, etc., which the gloss and all authorities place in l. hac edictali. For this opinion, ff. de leg. prestan. l. Salinus Aristo, strongly supports it. Thus it shall be done, because the son of the first marriage, and also of the second, must first have their legitime, and that which remains after it is divided equally between the wife and the son of the first marriage. So holds Ia. de Bel. in §. optime, and this is the truth.

† Certainly, other doubts arise, namely whether, in that which is left over to the spouse, the testator may make a vulgar substitution of the children of the second marriage, or a simple fideicommissary substitution, or a substitution after death: this is what our question seeks. And indeed, it is held that the substitution is not valid, because the law gives [the portion] to another, namely to the son or grandson of the first marriage; for the testator cannot substitute in the right of a third party, as stated in the Digest, *de vulgari substitutione*, law *ex facto*, in the beginning. On the contrary, it seems that a capable person may be directly substituted for any incapable person, as in the Code, *de hereditatibus instituendis*, law 2. But that more may be left to the children of the second marriage than to those of the first, and that they are capable, is expressly stated in the Authenticum, *de nuptiis*, section *et quam*; and therefore the substitution seems valid. In the Digest, *ad Trebellianam*, law *cogito*, section *hi qui solidum*, it is stated that a pure and simple, and conditional [substitution] in the event of the condition, is valid for this reason: that it may increase the dowry; because even to a mere executor, with whom there was not even the making of a will, this power may be given, as in the Digest, *de dote praelegata*, law *Theopompus*; *de legatis* 2, law 1; *ad Trebellianam*, law *ex facto*, section *ex facto*. However, this power is understood to be at the discretion of a good man, as in the said law *I* and law *si filiae*, *de legatis* 3. The conclusion is that, in favor of the children of the second marriage, the testator may ordain more than he ordains in favor of the first, if it pleases the testator; but not in favor of the spouse. But if the spouse had repudiated from the beginning, she would have caused the law to cease by this edictal rule, because that which is repudiated is not said to be left, as in the Digest, *si certum petatur*, law *penultima*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Sons and daughters, without regard to any difference of sex, succeed equally per stirpes; however, daughters who have received a dowry must collate the dowry.
2. Sons and daughters in the father's power transmit the father's inheritance to all.
3. An inheritance may be accepted within thirty years.
casus: CASE. In the Name of the Lord, Amen. The point of doubt, upon which counsel is requested to be given, is as follows. The noble man Stephen Ghechi of Alviano died without having made a will, that is, intestate, with his children surviving and succeeding him. These children all took part in the inheritance of the said Stephen, their father, by taking and possessing the goods of the said Stephen. Afterwards, all the said children died, having made wills or intestate, with their heirs surviving, namely the said Francis, the said James, and the said Philippa, with their heirs surviving. Now there is a dispute between the heirs of the said Francis on one part, and the heirs of the said James on the other. The heirs of the said James allege that the said James’s mother, and heir daughter of the said Stephen, succeeded to one-third part of the said Stephen, her former father, together with the said Philippa and together with the said Francis. The heirs of Francis allege that a female daughter does not succeed equally with a male under the common law when the father dies intestate, but says and alleges that female daughters ought to be dowered according to the capacity of the estate and the paternal inheritance. Anthony says that a female daughter succeeds equally with a male under the common law. It is presupposed that in the said Castle of Alviano there are no statutes nor customs disposing on this matter, but this doubt consists solely in the disposition of the common law. Now it is asked, what is the law: whether the inheritance of the said Stephen devolved upon his children, male and female, per stirpes [or pro rata], or not. And how the heirs of the said children [shall take] the said inheritance of the said Stephen, their father, concerning whose inheritance it is treated, upon which it is asked, what is the law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Sons and daughters succeed equally, without regard to any difference of sex. C. de lib. praete. l. maximum vitium; and in Authen. de hęre. ab intest. §. ex his. However, daughters who have received a dowry must collate the dowry. C. de colla. Auth. ex testamento.
† and sons and daughters who were under the power of the father transmit the inheritance to all

† And the inheritance may be accepted up to 30 years. C. de iure delib. l. licet. de mili. testa. l. ex militari. §. si. de iure fis. l. Luc. and fully noted in l. apud hostes. cum si. and this is the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In a fideicommissary substitution, whether a condition of substitution collectively existing in the person of the last survivor gives rise to the substitution in his share.
2. Whether a son who is an heir and has not made an inventory deducts the legitime, and
3. The Trebellianic portion, and transmits it.
casus: CASE. In the Name of the Lord Amen. The point is as follows: a certain Cola Cocii of Thomas John made his last will, in which he instituted Ang., his legitimate and natural son, as universal heir, and made a substitution for him, that if the said Ang. died in pupillary age, or later at any time without sons, that Mathucius and Barnabeus, the testator’s own brothers, would succeed him. After the death of the said Cola, the said Ang. was his heir; because Ang. died intestate and without any son, surviving a certain niece, daughter of the said Ang.’s own sister, who sister was dowered and married by the aforementioned Cola, father of the said Ang. and sister. The said Cola and his sister being survived by their own uncles, brothers of both parents of the late Cola. Now it is asked about two things: whether the said Ang. was free in any respect, and in what, and in what part of the inheritance of the said late Cola, assuming without prejudice that the said Ang. died over 13 years of age. And who, or whom, succeeded him, whether the said niece, or the said uncles, both of them, and in what part. Also it is asked: because the said Ang. died with the said substitutes surviving, and in what part, and what is the law regarding the aforementioned, having seen the will of the said Cola, and having seen the statutes of the commune then and now in force, which are transmitted to you, lord consultant, namely, copies thereof. And having seen the narration of the said facts. Afterwards the said Cola in the said will further provided for his house and progeny, that if all the said together, and brothers, and aforementioned substitutes died without sons, that those of his house and progeny would succeed them, as contained in the will. The said son, as stated, died, and also the said Barnabeus without sons, and the said Mathucius died with sons. It is now asked whether the said substitute was in the place and at least in the person of the said Barnabeus. And although the other party wishes to say that because all died without sons, that the said Mathucius died with sons, that there was no place for substitution. It seems that it is not so, since the said Barnabeus, dying last, died without any son, by l. heredes mei. §. eum ita. ad Tre. Rather it will be said that because the said Mathucius died with sons, and made his male sons heirs, and for whom he made a substitution, that if all died without male sons after the said Mathucius. It is asked if the part which came to the said Mathucius by virtue of the substitution of the said Cola, considering the aforementioned, pertains to the said substitutes by the said Mathucius of those of the progeny, and of the house, whether it comes by right to be restored to the other substitutes: and thus that which came to Mathucius by virtue of the substitution of Cola. And because the said Mathucius substituted those of the progeny to his sons dying without male sons surviving the said substitutes, it ought to come to those substitutes by Mathucius, if he had made an inventory. It is asked in a similar manner, what is the law, having seen also the will of the said Cola in the first part of the first point, where it is said, in what part those coming intestate succeeded the said Ang., son of the said Cola, and heirs of the said Cola, who died without sons. I say that, assuming without prejudice that the said Ang. died over 13 years of age, and thus those coming intestate would succeed at least in the Trebellianic portion, because those coming intestate would succeed. Lord Baldus of Perugia in a certain counsel of his advised that if the heir does not make an inventory, that those coming intestate cannot deduct the Trebellianic portion. And thus that all goods are due to the said substitutes of the said Ang. Nevertheless, let the consultant deign to advise, what is the law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In a fideicommissary substitution, a condition of substitution existing collectively in the person of the last survivor gives rise to substitution in the share of that person. D. ad Trebellianum, l. Haeredes mei, §. Cum ita; and l. Lucius, §. Gayo; and noted in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Pater filiae, §. Duobus; and C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. Penultima. And the reason is that, in a fideicommissary substitution, the testator intended to burden both; hence, although one is exempted on account of children received by him, this does not benefit the other, who is not found to be exempt. Argument from D. de duobus reis, l. Licet: when two free persons liberate one who has children, they do not liberate the other, who did not receive children; because, since the children are placed in the condition and in the final cause of the extinction of the fideicommissum, they extinguish it only to the extent that they are relevant. We therefore divide the will according to the reason of the will, and from the nature of the relationship; also from the nature of a plural obligation to be resolved into its singularities, as noted in D. si quis cautio, l. Si servus, §. Si plurium. And these things are true: the sons, who remain from the first deceased, exclude the substitutes by the presumed will of the deceased, which is presumed from the order of charity. Argument from D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. 1: if from the ordered providence of the testator; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Publicianus, §. Finis; D. de legatis secundum, l. Cum ita, §. In fideicommissum; D. ad Trebellianum, l. Haeredes mei, §. Finis. And therefore, the substitution made by Cola concerning others of the issue expired in the person of all, by reason of the children of one, who are to be preferred according to ordered charity, according to the aforementioned doctrine, which was that of Nicolaus de Mathea, Digestum, in consilium; and Bartolus. However, from the new testament of Mathuicius, those of the issue come. That testament refers to all the goods of the testator, insofar as he can make a will. We do not care about that matter, whether a preceding fideicommissum is included in a subsequent fideicommissum, D. ad Trebellianum, l. Marcellus, §. Quidam; because here we are in the testament of the burdened party, not in the testament of Cola, the first substitutor. For a fideicommissary may make a will concerning the fideicommissum left to him, just as concerning his other goods, D. de legatis secundum, l. Cum filius, §. Lucio; D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Paterno.

† Here I return to the testament of Cola, and to the first point, concerning how much could freely be transmitted by Angelo, and I say that as regards the legitima, if he made an inventory, because it is in the place of a light burden, and as regards the Trebelliana, if he made an inventory, according to the opinion approved by Cynus in the Authentica "Sed cum testator," Codex, On the Falcidian Law, which Bartolus follows in his consilia. For he who did not make an inventory is presumed to have schemed and subtracted, if anyone administered the goods. Authentica "De haereditate et Falcidia," § "Sancimus." And therefore he is unworthy of the benefit. Digest, On the Falcidian Law, Law "Haereditatis," § final; Digest, On the Trebellian Law, Law "Paulus." And although no express statute is found in the Trebellian Law, the express reason of the statute is found. Bartolus, however, says that the Trebelliana is deducted indiscriminately in Law "Marcellus," § "Quod autem," On the Trebellian Law, and he makes a distinction whether the Trebelliana is prohibited by the privilege of the Falcidia by the will of the deceased, and then the same applies to the Trebelliana, or from another cause, and then otherwise, according to Bartolus. I say that the delict excludes the Trebelliana, and here, if no inventory is made, a delict is presumed, hence I hold the opinion of certain glossators, who hold this, and also Cynus in the additions he made there. I also say that we are in the ius commune as regards Angelo succeeding intestate, because the statutes of the city do not touch our case. But if he were a minor, a woman, or a soldier, in whom a delict would not be presumed, then the Trebelliana would not cease even if no inventory were made. Others say indiscriminately that, although no inventory is made, the Trebelliana does not cease, and this is the more common opinion, which Jacobus de Belvis held, and Rodolphus disputed in his libelli, and it is more observed by custom, and things should not be changed, etc. But as to the subtlety of the law, it is more true that which I said. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws. And to the faith of this I have subscribed and sealed with the seal of my name.

Furthermore, beyond the above said, if anyone wishes to defend the custom, he can prove this by such reasoning: the universal fideicommissary can compel the heir to make an inventory, because for caution with specification of things, as in Codex, "Ut in possessionem legatorum," Law "Cum Archimedoram." If therefore he did not do this, let him impute it to himself, for the fault of the heir and the fault of the universal fideicommissary are compensated, indeed the fault is greater of him who obtains the status of a petitioner. Digest, On Verbal Obligations, Law "Si servus," § "Sequitur." And note in Law "Si mora," On the Dissolution of Marriage. But if, when required to make an inventory, he refused to make it, then it is presumed that he subtracted and concealed. This matter is among the opinions of the doctors, and therefore some hold one thing, some another, and whoever holds what he holds cannot be convicted of falsehood. Baldus.

CASE. Point. Picham Ciccheus of Perugia gave a certain donkey of his to a certain Vannuccio Acocseti for carriage, for the purpose of buying salt at the castle of Crenqueti of the land of Grosseto. It happened that, since the said beast did not know how to reach the determined place with the saltworks, the said Vannuccio left it in the care of a certain host, and it remained for two days before he returned to the place where he had left the beast; finally, returning, he found it dead. Now it is asked, whose is the risk, that of the lessor or that of the lessee.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the lessee of a horse is liable for the death of the horse.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In this contract celebrated for the benefit of both parties, dolus, lata culpa, and levis culpa apply, but not levissima culpa; that is, malice, stupidity, and negligent custody are included, but not the utmost diligence or excessive curiosity. D. 17, 2, Si ut certo, § Nunc videndum. Whether this hirer fatigued the animal with too great a burden or too long a journey: for then he is liable. Likewise, he is liable if he did not entrust it to a good custodian, because he is liable for levis culpa. Likewise, he is liable if he did not exercise the diligence he usually exercises in his own affairs. D. 17, 2, In rebus; and the aforementioned § Nunc videndum. If the donkey had been his own, he would not have stood for two days watching to see what had happened to his donkey; but he did not care about another’s donkey, and thus he is liable, unless it had died of natural causes. I, Baldus.

Note this following opinion, given on behalf of the nurse of Guiglioti. Consilium 405, summarized.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the testament of Mitra, or Rota, formerly of Massi of the village of Popegii in the district of Sellano, in which he instituted Vannucia, Divitia, Catharina, and Vendricia, his daughters, as his universal heirs, and provided that if any of them should die without children, one should succeed to the other; and if all should die without children, he substituted to them Petrus, Dominicus, and Bella, his brothers and sister. And assuming that Vannucia died first, survived by one legitimate and natural daughter, and afterwards the other three died without children. The question is whether the said substitutes are called. I answer that they are not called, for the daughter of Vannucia is called, according to the will of the testatrix. As is fully noted by Bartolus, D. 36, 1, Cum acutissimi; D. 4, 4, De impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, Generaliter; D. 28, 5, De hereditatibus instituendis, Lucius; D. 35, 1, De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, Cum avus. Therefore, the testatrix appears to have reserved the right of legitimate inheritance to her said granddaughter, and thus excludes the collateral substitutes and those more remote. D. 28, 6, De vulgari substitutione, Vel singulis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a tutor appointed by the testator for a minor as his substitute can be a tutor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having viewed the testament of Ugutionis Franci, lord of Nimaldi, and having examined that clause in which he appointed as guardians of his sons and heirs John and Nimaldus with full right, and since the said John has died and Nimaldus has reached the age of majority, and there remains also another son named Farolfus, who is not of the age of majority, I say that both the guardianship and the upbringing of the daughters of the said testator, since they are wards, belong to the said Nimaldus; but the said Nimaldus is a suitable person for the management of the said wards, because, unless something else is proven before the judge, the testament of the father must be upheld.

And because, although Nimaldus is a substitute, nevertheless the close proximity of blood removes all ambiguity of suspicion. D. 26, 2, 1 (where a ward ought to be educated); D. 26, 16, 1 (on the confirmation of tutors); C. 5, 57, 1 (in confirming); D. 38, 10, 1 (of humanity); D. 38, 10, 1, § 1 (not only). And thus I conclude that the guardianship and upbringing of the said wards pertains to Nimaldus, and that he ought to rule and govern them, especially on account of those words “by full right,” which words confirm this sense, namely, that the governance of the patrimony and of the persons pertains to him whom the testator deemed suitable for all these things. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Statutes enacted by a superior and not confirmed do not bind in the lands of the church.
2. Cities and peoples who govern themselves may enact statutes without the authority of a superior.
3. Whether confirmation at one’s pleasure terminates upon death.
4. Whether a woman who is prohibited from making donations by statute is also prohibited from making donations to her children.
5. Whether those who are outside the church may enact statutes, and whether they possess jurisdiction.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be presupposed that in the territories of the Church, statutes which have not been confirmed by a superior do not bind, nor are they to be observed, just as it is not contained in the constitutions of the Roman Church; indeed, they ought to be of common law, and all peoples understand the law when the confirmation of a superior intervenes. And this is Riza Ma.

† Nevertheless, the common opinion is that cities and peoples who govern themselves may also live according to their own customs and statutes, even without the authority of a superior; for they possess this jurisdiction to enact statutes by virtue of written law. Hence, a prohibition is uselessly sought against that which is granted by the common law, as stated in l. 1, C. de thesauro. On this point, we have sufficiently treated in d. l. omnes populi, and in ff. quod quisque iure, l. 1, in principio; and in c. 1, de constitutionibus, lib. 6; and in c. 1, de iureiurando, in the same book. Unless such statutes were expressly reproved by a superior, or unless bad customs contrary to law had given rise to a cause, as in ff. de sepulchro violato, l. 3, §. diuus; or unless the right of a superior is touched, as in extra, de iureiurando, c. venientes; C. de decurionibus, l. vacuatis. For if universities can make statutes, if the municipal magistrate and the leading men of the people approve the cause, as in l. 2, in fine, de constitutionibus peculiaribus; then, a fortiori, the entire people can do so. But it is not necessary to dispute this here, because the situation is different in the lands immediately subject to the Roman Church; for all their status and statutes depend on a superior; and unless their statutes are confirmed by the provincial governor, they are not valid, since they are contrary to the common law.

It must therefore be considered whether the confirmation and approval of the said statutes is terminated, so that it has no force after that time, or not. And that it is terminated appears thus: the said confirmation was granted until the good pleasure of the Lord Pope’s legate, etc. But the aforementioned lords have died, and their good pleasure is extinguished; therefore, the confirmation is terminated. And although jurists and canonists formerly disputed this matter, today it is settled by c. Si gratiose, de rescriptis, lib. 6, where this is fully examined; and by Arch., 16 q. 2, c. Frater, at the end of the great gloss; and de verbis oblig., l. Centesimis, according to Bartolus. For the Pope who then reigned is meant, and thus the words must be understood as referring to the person, not to the See. And thus, with the death of the person, the confirmation is terminated, as l. 4, ff. locati conducti; and this is the truth.

† Therefore, this donation is to be considered under the ius commune, such that if it does not exceed five hundred gold coins, it is valid without insinuation; but if it exceeds that amount, insinuation is required, otherwise it is invalid to the extent of the excess. C. de donat. l. scimus. Moreover, even if this statute is presumed to be valid and in force, nevertheless this donation, since it was made to the children out of piety, is valid by reason, because a mother is not understood to be prohibited from making donations to her children. C. de imp. lucra. describ. l. 1, lib. 10; C. de fideicomm. l. voluntas. For the statute was enacted on account of the weakness of women, but this [donation] arises not from weakness, but from piety, as in C. de captiv. et postlim. revert. l. liber captus. Furthermore, it must be considered that, with the presence and consent of the nearest relatives, a woman may make a donation according to the form of the statute; but here the nearest relatives consented, and the same children who were the donees also consented. For here consent is not required by way of authority to be given, for then she could not act in her own property and in her own contract in the place of both the authority and the contracting party, but she can properly act in the place of the consenting party. And thus there is no objection from l. 1, in fine, ff. de auctor. tutor. And the reason is that these are the nearest relatives, and thus no others have the right to consent, nor a reasonable cause, except these. Hence this donation is valid, either because the nearest relatives consent, or because she has no others whose consent ought to be required, since the others are more remote, concerning whom the statute does not speak. Otherwise an absurdity would follow, namely that a woman could make no donation to her own children, which would be most unjust, as in Inst. de lege Falcidia. And although the said confirmation of the privilege obtains in a similar manner, nevertheless it confirms a statute made against the ius commune, as in C. de contrah. stipul. l. dudum, and C. de donat. l. si a matre. But it is certain that those rebellious against the Church fall back into the crime of lèse-majesty, and by that very fact lose all privileges, and all benefits, and all jurisdiction, as in c. ad apostolicam, §. nos itaque, de re iudic. lib. 6.

† Therefore, the statutes of schismatics, since they are outside the Church, ought not to be upheld by the Church, as in the Authentica *De priuilegio dotis*, "haereticorum mulieribus non praestandis," in the *Liber Iuris Canonici* (the "tubro" and "nigro"). Among schismatics there is no jurisdiction *habitu* (by right), although they may exercise it *actu* (in fact), *de facto*, and by tyranny. Hence, statutes which are sustained by jurisdiction *habitu* do not exist among them, as stated in Distinction 8, chapter *Quo iure*, and in the Codex, Title *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, law *Decernimus*, because outside the Church no jurisdiction can be lawfully possessed by rebels, Codex, Title *De Iudaeis*, law *Si*, and the note by the doctors, Extra, Title *De voto*, chapter *Quod super dubium*. Nevertheless, it might be argued that what the daughter-in-law donated to her father-in-law was valid; or it is answered that the marriage had been dissolved. Moreover, because she donated for the sake of her children, not so that it might be acquired by the father-in-law, and this false premise is dispelled, Codex, Title *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, in the law *Si constante*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution made by means of a word, whenever it occurs, is always a fideicommissum, even if it vanishes because the inheritance cannot be accepted by the instituted heir, or whether it is rather a compendious substitution.
body: In the Name of Christ. The facts are as follows: Nicolutius Andreae Bilacque of Saint Severin made his will, in which he instituted as universal heir his son Nicolaus, and any posthumous child to be born; and he made such a substitution, namely: And if all his sons, both those born and those to be born, should die at any time without legitimate children, he substituted his wife, Lady Casnelina. Finally, the said son Nicolaus died while his father Nicolutius was still living; then, after some years, the said father Nicolutius died. The same testator died while the said Cathesna, his wife and mother of the aforementioned Nicolaus, was still living.

It is asked whether the said testament was broken by the death of the said Nicholas, or whether there is room for substitution, so that the said Cathelina succeeds by substitution, excluding those who would otherwise succeed intestate? And it seems that the said testament is in the case of caducity. C. de cad. to. §. pro secunvnde there is nothing about which substitution can be questioned. ff. de capti. l. gt si filius. ff. vul. sub. l. lex Cornelia. Moreover, the said substitution is considered at all times fideicommissary, as noted. C. de impu. et al. subl. s. precib. Hence it vanishes if the heir instituted has not petitioned for the inheritance: as C. de fideic. l. eam, quam. To the contrary is the truth itself. The said substitution was compendious: and therefore, upon the death of the son while the testator was alive, it contains vulgarly; because it cannot be valid in any other way: as noted by Cy. in l. precib. and Bar. in l. Centurio. And this whether the said substitution is made to one already born, or to a posthumous child, or to both, as is proven. ff. de ven. inspi. l. pe. ff. de le. 1. l. ab haeredita. C. de insti. et substi. l. fi. non ob. glo. l. precibus. Because that gloss speaks of the case where the son did not die after the inheritance had been accepted, and thus the substitution can be valid by the law of fideicommissum. Here, however, he died while the testator was alive. Furthermore, l. quod si filius does not apply, because there it speaks of a purely pupillary substitution; here, however, we speak of a compendious one. And therefore I say that this mother succeeds directly by vulgar substitution, excluding the case of intestacy. And this is true if the testament appears by instrument, or by seven witnesses summoned. Let the witnesses therefore be examined, and upon proof being made, sentence ought to be rendered entirely in favor of the said Catharina, the mother substituted, and these witnesses ought to be examined for the eternal memory of the matter. And this is supported by what is expressly noted. C. de edi. diui adri.l. edicto. in glo. ordina. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The right of patronage of the church passes to all universal heirs.
2. Whether the rights which were in a destroyed hospital pass to the one who caused it to be restored or rebuilt, and whether the right of patronage is acquired by him.
3. Whether another patron can be added by reason of an increase in goods.
casus:
CONSULTATION.

The first point is this: A certain Margaritus, who was in possession of the right of patronage of a certain hospital and chapel built together, died intestate. Serloannes, the nearest relative of the said Margaritus, accepted his universal inheritance. Now it is asked whether the said right of patronage passes to the said Serloannes, the aforementioned heir, along with the universality of the inheritance.

The second point is this: A certain hospital, which has two different patrons, one with two voices and the other with one, is destroyed by necessary accident, not maliciously; and another is built in another place, and of another material, and in another form; yet it is considered under the same name as before; and it is begun and founded from the goods of the destroyed hospital; it is completed and built from the goods left to the newly founded hospital; which goods left to the new hospital have multiplied to such an extent that they are more numerous and greater than the goods of the destroyed hospital, which were transferred to the new hospital. Now it is asked whether the rights of the patrons, which were in the destroyed hospital, pass and are in the newly constructed hospital, as stated above, or have they perished entirely?

Furthermore, since the new hospital was founded and constructed, and is situated on the proper land of the aforementioned Margaritus, with the license of the diocesan, it is asked whether the said Margaritus, lord of the land, and his universal heir, are entitled to the right of patronage by reason of the land.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the first point, it must be said that the right of patronage of a church passes not only to the sole blood heirs, but also to any other universal heirs: because it passes with the universality, as is read and noted in c. ad audientiam, de iure patronatus, according to Innocentius. For he who succeeds in the other goods, succeeds universally in the right of patronage, as is noted in 16. q. 7, c. piae mentis, etc., to the sons. And this right, adhering to the universality and passing with the universality, as is noted in ff. de acquisitione rerum dominii, l. quaedam; de re iudicata, c. cum Bertolus; de contrahenda emptione, l. in modicis; ff. ad Trebellianum, l. quia per indebitum. And this is the decision on the first point: because such is its nature.

† On the second point, it must be said, according to Innocentius, that either the first person was patron by reason of the fund on which the church or hospital was built; and then, if the location is changed, the right of patronage is extinguished, for which the following authorities support: D. de aqua pluviali arc. l. hoc iure § si aqua; and D. de servitutibus amittendis l. si locus, where the servitude returns only if the location returns to its former state, which it cannot do when the place and form are destroyed: D. de solutionibus l. quae res § aream. Or, someone was patron by reason of a donation; and then he remains patron in the subsequent location just as in the preceding one. And the reason is: because the dowry follows the substituted location, according to Innocentius. To this effect: D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus l. filiae § a Titia; D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem l. si donante § si sponsus. Therefore, if the first hospital passed into the second together with its dowry, the patrons of the first have two voices, and one has one voice. And this is true if this transfer was made by the authority of the diocesan bishop, so that the hospital is solemnly constructed, as stated in Extravagantes de religiosis domibus c. de xenodochiis, and noted by Hostiensis in Summa de ecclesiis aedificandis, and noted in c. per literas de praebitis in clerico. I therefore say in our case that the voices of the aforementioned remain valid.

† On the third point, I say that it is not novel that several, and very many, are patrons, one or more from the beginning, and afterwards another is added to them by a cause generating the right of patronage, such as is the fund, in which there is a second foundation in the order of the foundation: as is the case here. And although otherwise this fund precedes as the beginning of the thing, and the final cause of the whole in the origin of the right to acquire, here it follows: but it is not a right, because on account of the new fund this one is co-patron of the others, because the fund and the dowry are equated. It is established by what is noted by Hostiensis in the Summa, On the Right of Patronage, §. ex quibus, and §. qualiter, and there the laws are cited which it is expedient to cite. And by the Archdeacon in c. 1, On the Right of Patronage, Book 6, with the si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether he who received, held, and bargained for certain goods, knowing afterwards that they had been stolen, is bound to answer for reception and is to be punished. And nos. 5 and 10.
2. Whether a cleric accused of a crime before a secular judge may vary his plea before an ecclesiastical judge, and no. 3.
3. When a partner is said to commit theft of common property.
4. Good will and intention exclude all guilt.
5. When the presumption is in favor of the respondent, it is presumed in favor of his defense.
6. Whether one who confesses the article of receiving stolen goods is deemed to confess fraud and knowledge of the stolen nature of the goods.
7. Good reputation is tarnished by a single offense.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case and question of Antonio de Oldegradis entrusted to me by my lord, Doctor Paul, bishop of Emona, vicar of the most reverend father and lord in Christ, the lord bishop of Csanád. The acts from which the right to condemn or to acquit arises must be divided into three parts. For first, it must be divided as to what is objected against the accused, as in the Digest, On Adultery, law *denuntiasse*, section *quid tamen*. Second, as to what the accused is convicted of, as in the Code, On Those Who Are Received, law *observare*. Third, as to what is brought forward for the excuse and purification of the accused, as in the Digest, On Public Judgments, law *qui reus*.

† It is therefore objected against him that he knowingly received, retained, and contracted certain stolen goods from the vault of the dwelling of Nico. Mengosi, located in the contrada of Saint Bartholomew in Venice, situated in the said contrada, which goods are said to belong to the common partnership of Ser Nicolai Quarterio and the said Nico. Mengosi; and that the said An. received the said goods from the said Nico. Mengosi, who had broken the wall of the said vault and had extracted the aforementioned goods therefrom, and afterwards had carried them to the said Nico., so that he might hold and preserve the said goods at the request of the said Nico. Mengosi, as the aforementioned breaker-and-enterer. It is certain, however, that this inquisition concludes from its own tenor that reception, contracting, and fraud are imputed to Antonio: for where there is fraud, there is a malicious act, and an atrocious malicious act, as in D. de re iudicata, l. ad ea; and noted in D. de compensatione, l. si ambo and l. si quid a fideiussore; and D. de deposito, l. 1, § si apud; and l. 1; and l. non solum, § si; D. de alieno iudicio; D. de acquisitione et obligatione, l. ex maleficiis. The contracting of another’s property is also prohibited by natural law against the will of the owner, as in Inst. de obligationibus ex maleficio, § 1; and D. de furtis, l. 1, § fin. And it is established that receivers are punished in the same manner as thieves, as in D. de receptatoribus, l. 1. And whether you say that the receiver is a thief by contracting, or whether you call him a receiver in his own name, it makes no difference, for the crime must be punished which is derived from the written law, as in D. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. famosi; and therefore the said inquisition contains all that pertains to the substance of the form of the inquisition and of this kind of malicious act. And thus I have finished with the first point, namely, that which is imputed to the defendant. But because it is not immediately the case that whoever is accused or inquired into is therefore presumed guilty, unless it is proven, as is read and noted in l. 3, C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis.

Therefore, I come to the second point to be examined, namely, whether this Antonio, the accused, is convicted of the crime charged, or not. It is certain that by the proceedings in the secular court, this cleric is not considered convicted, as stated in Extra, De iudiciis, chapter At si clerici. Hence, it is lawful for him to vary his statement, since the confession does not bind him, as noted by Guillaume de Coulanges in the law Qui tamen, De arbitris. Although Innocentius says that the bishop should compel him based on what he said, the better view is that found in the Authenticum, De sancta ecclesia, section Si vero crimen, as noted by Bartolus in the law Divus, Digestum, De captivis et postliminio. Or one may say that Innocentius means this only if it appears to the bishop, having regard to the judicial proceedings; otherwise, the opposite holds. Digestum, De quaestionibus, law Milites, section Oportet. This is especially so in our case, because this Antonio confessed before the secular judge under torture illegitimately inflicted: I say this with respect to the whole matter, not with respect to those who inflicted the torture, who were ignorant that he was a cleric. Digestum, De locato, law Si quis ignorans. Nevertheless, in any case, the law annuls an unjust confession, as in Digestum, De quaestionibus, law Maritus. Therefore, what was confessed before the secular judge should not be taken into account here, so that we may consider it as a foundation or argument for establishing the bishop’s claim. Thus, according to Innocentius, regard should be had to what was confessed before the bishop, whose procedure is solemn, as stated in Extra, De accusationibus, chapter Qualiter et quoniam, and in Extra, De simonia, chapter Licet Helias. And much more so if he confessed the same thing before both judges, because truth appears from the persistence of the confession. And thus I presuppose here, because it is true, and especially considering the court of the Venetians, which shines with the sanctity and clarity of its judgments.

Let us therefore discuss whether the confession made before the bishop constitutes valid proof of witchcraft, or at least an indication thereof, such that the truth ought to be extracted by torture, as is done in atrocious and especially clandestine cases of witchcraft, in which proof is more difficult. See Digestum, De quaestionibus, l. De minore, § Tormenta; and l. Edictum divi. I argue for both sides. First, that the witchcraft is fully proven: for it is certain that witchcraft is fully proven by a confession made voluntarily in court, even if no prior indication exists, as in Codex, De episcopis et clericis, l. Si quis in hoc genus, where it states “conjoined, or confessed.” For this alternative wording “or” shows that one suffices, as in Digestum, De custodia rei, l. Confessus; and Codex, De custodia rei, l. 2; and Extra, De appellationibus, c. Romana, lib. 6, where this is fully noted; and in c. 1, De accusationibus, eod. lib.; and 2 q. 1, c. Nos in quemquam. The first confession at least suffices for torture, as noted by Innocentius, De confessionibus, c. Cum super. This will be clear in l. Capite, 5, De adulteriis; Digestum, De aedilicio edicto, l. Quaero, § Fin.; and as noted in Digestum, De infamia, l. Ictus; and Extra, De accusationibus, c. Cum dilectus. Moreover, in cases of witchcraft, which are prohibited by natural law, we always presume the worse part, i.e., that fraud is present, and not absent. See Codex, De iniuriis, l. Si non convicii. To the contrary, it appears that nothing has been proven or confessed against this Antonio that conclusively induces or causes it to be presumed that the alleged crime is tainted with truth.

† And for the sake of clarity, I premise that although a partner ought not to commit theft of common property against his partner: as in D. de furtis, l. si socius; and D. pro socio, l. merito; and although things purchased by one of the partners in the common name immediately become common property: as noted in l. 1, on the word "universae," D. de usucapione, l. pro dote; nevertheless, this is true if the partner acted with the intent to conceal: but until the anger of the partner ceases, and so that he may not suffer violence from him. The text is to the letter, with its gloss, D. de furtis, l. qui vas, §. qui ex voluntate. This is also supported by reason and natural justice, because one ought not to wait for the other partner to inflict violence upon him and to despoil him of the common property; and therefore he may bring the common things to safety, just as he could if he wished to preserve them from any other thief. And this is not theft, but precaution: D. de aedilicio edicto, l. quis sit fugitivus, §. si autem. And this is especially permissible in the forum of conscience: as noted by Innocentius, Extr. de immunitatibus ecclesiarum, in c. quia plerique. Nor does the fact of breaking the roof or the door aggravate the act, for this is permissible for the sake of saving one’s own things to him who has detention of the house, as fully noted by Innocentius, Extr. de immunitatibus ecclesiarum, c. 1. Moreover, the act itself is not to be considered, but the cause of acting: D. de furtis, l. verum. But the cause here was not to make a profit, but to avoid suffering damage through the injustice of the partner. Moreover, the law is express that he who describes and marks things, in order to return them to the owner, does not commit theft; because he does not have the intent to intercept anything, unless he later, having changed his purpose, conceals the things: D. de furtis, l. falsus, §. qui alienum, ver. plerique. And although it indicates [the rule] when he does not know the owner, the same applies if he begins to know, as in the following verse. And therefore Nicolaus Mengosi truly did not commit theft; and especially because of the administration committed above, by contract of partnership, which could not be taken from him against his will: C. de pignori, l. 3; and D. de furtis, l. cum creditor rem. Whose innocence also renders Antonio innocent; because in real delicts, if the principal did not offend, the accessory did not offend either: as noted, D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. si quis id quod, §. si; and D. de furtis, l. si is qui, §. si tu Titium. Moreover, any occasion excuses from theft: D. de abigeis, l. 1, in fine. And this truth is credible; because although he may have committed an act, he believes that he can act justly: C. ad legem Flaviam de plagio, l. si plagii; and l. praeses; Inst. de vi bonorum raptorum, §. sed nedum; D. de furtis, l. Inter omnes, §. recte. Nevertheless, assuming that Nicolaus Mengosi had offended, which I do not commend, who, although not with evil intent, yet by example: D. de poenis, l. si quis aliquid, §. qui abortionis; nevertheless, he is not a thief.

† Moreover, Antonius has in no way committed a fault, nor has any evidence, however slight, been proven against Antonius that includes fraud or gives rise to a presumption thereof. The law states that if a thief deposits the spoils he stole from me with Seius, who is unaware of the depositor’s malice, Seius is bound to and must return those spoils to the thief, unless I convict him in court. D. 16, 3, *bona fides*. Likewise, the law states regarding the borrower. D. 13, 6, *ita ut furtum*. And in the case of the ship, *ca. sta.*, as in D. 47, 12, *adversus nautas*, l. 1, § *quod si recepit*, joined with l. *itaque fullo*, in the beginning, D. 47, 2. For what opportunity for sin did this Antonius give to Nicolaus Mengosus to steal or to pilfer? Certainly none; rather, he gave him sounder, safer, good, and friendly counsel, because in a doubtful matter it is safer to abstain, D. 23, 2, *adoptivus*, § 1. Again, these goods were entrusted to Antonius for safekeeping, but it does not appear that he knew that these items had been brought there illicitly or by some breaking and entering, nor was it established for him what, or of what kind, or whose, or of what value they were; and even if he had learned this afterwards after an interval of time, it matters nothing, because he is already bound by contract to restore them to the depositor; and this obligation excuses him from wrongdoing. Likewise, the beginning of possession and detention must be considered, which was without defect. D. 41, 2, *clam possidere*, in the beginning; and C. 7, 31, l. 1, § *tantum modo*. Likewise, we judge from the words and deeds of persons. C. 9, 22, l. 1. And a good reputation greatly benefits a person in excluding presumptions of crimes, and especially of heinous ones. D. 37, 11, *non omnes*, § *a Barbaris*; for a good reputation is a kind of law that shows a person’s quality, as in D. 48, 18, *de minore*, § *tormenta*. From all these things, having seen and weighed the acts, I conclude that the said Antonius should be absolved by sentence. Notwithstanding, if it is said that this Antonius foresaw Nicolaus’s intent: as in D. 44, 3, *apud Celsum*, in the beginning, and l. *Fulcinius*, § *animus enim*, *quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur*; for it is fitting to observe with what mind something is said. D. 46, 3, l. *pe*. And because an act does not speak from a word, for often one thinks to do more than one does, and says more than one effects, as is noted. C. 4, 38, l. *in ementis*. Likewise, ignorance of another’s fact is justified, as in l. *si pro suo*, unless it were notorious: as noted in l. 1, D. 4, 8; and C. 5, 59, l. *si tutor*. Likewise, he who ignores the subtleties of the law is excused from fraud. C. 4, 10, l. *senatus*. And I say further, that even if he had fully known the fact, nevertheless, by receiving the things so as to satisfy both parties, he does not commit theft, nor does he commit malicious fraud. And because it was an act for the preservation and saving of the things for both partners, there is no hope of crime here: as is noted. C. 4, 29, l. *si testitio*. Where the intent was not evil, which is accustomed to give the name to human action, just as if one manages the affairs of the whole partnership by the mandate of one partner.

† Moreover, good will excludes all guilt: and intention gives life to the act, just as the soul does to the body. Since this matter has not yet been fully discussed through responses to the contrary, I shall briefly summarize, directing my attention to the proceedings. For Article 11 of the aforementioned prediction states: and the statute is confessed only in a qualified manner, namely, that he dissuaded.

† It is therefore asked whether, in that he dissuaded, he has answered the question. And it seems that he has not, because no one is believed for himself. I say the contrary, because when the presumption is in favor of the respondent, it is presumed in favor of his answer. But here the presumption is in his favor: because no one is presumed to give bad counsel, but either good or none, as in D. de probat. l. quo. §. quidolo. and l. fin. C. ad l. iul. repetundarum.

† Moreover, Article 12 states the seizure of goods; this article is confessed. It is asked whether the fraud or the knowledge of the breaking and entering is confessed. I answer: no, because fraud from knowledge is not contained in the article; therefore, it is not by this confession, because such are the subjects as the predicates demonstrate. D. de interrog. actio, l. si defensor, § 1. This is also clearly shown by the following article, which provides that he was informed of the breaking and entering on the following day, and not before, which precedes the fact of the deposition of Antonio’s knowledge, as appears from all the chapters distinguishing times up to this day, as Article 13 says that Antonio seems to have been innocent. And note this third article: Antonio confesses to subsequent knowledge of the breaking and entering; therefore, the breaking and entering came to his notice. And stop here, and consider. After this, the said Antonio went to the house of Philip and extracted certain things, as Article 27 says, for the purpose of selling and converting the price to his own benefit, which article Antonio confesses. However, he says that he did this for a cause, namely, with license, and because he was a creditor. Here it must be observed, and more severely, that if this is against Antonio, namely, after he knew the thing was alien, as it is said, and stolen, he ought not to have removed it from place to place, since in this way theft is committed. Moreover, in contingent matters, after knowledge, past ignorance does not help. C. de incest. nu. l. si quis ancillis; Extr. de consti. c. nam concupiscentiam. Moreover, he did this with the intent of profiting from another’s thing. How then can there be intent in this case, if not in others, and no transmutation is pardonable. Furthermore, it is not presumed that he had license. Moreover, he ought to have known that such license could not be given over an alien thing in whole or for the greater part, and which remained alien, as D. de fur. l. interdum, § qui furem; D. de condi. ob causam, l. pe. melius de contrah. em. l. si in emp., § item si emptor. Nor can he now say, I wanted to preserve the society, since, as it appears, rather he wanted to sell for himself. D. de neg. ges. l. si pupilli, § 2, there, he studies his own advantage. Therefore, this alone suffices for the condemnation of Antonio. Moreover, the claim is founded, because a depositary commits theft by selling, as D. de furtis, l. in faciendo, in prin. Nor is the offense palliated by the fact that he deposited it with another; rather, it is doubled or increased, because more are enrolled from it, as D. de infa. l. athletas, § pompo.

† Nor does good reputation avail Antonius; for by a single crime it is tarnished, whatever good works a man may have done in the world. C. ubi senatores, vel clarissimi. I. 1. and in c. deficiat peccator. For good reputation, as a bare conjecture, has place in uncertain, not in certain matters. ff. de verb. oblig. l. continuus. §. cum ita. just as we say of rumor. ff. de haer. inst. l. si.

But having considered all these points, I do not depart from what I said, namely that Antonius should be absolved. For he is not acting in bad faith who executes good faith according to law and by the force of the contract; but this Antonius received the deposit before having knowledge of the alleged plunder, with that simplicity and good presumption which a good merchant ought to have in a faithful merchant, which is presumed in a merchant long trusted through experience, as in D. 17.2.1 (l. argenti). From this deposit he was bound to custody, and by the duty of custody he was bound to keep the things with himself or with another trustworthy person, notwithstanding supervening knowledge, not only of another’s property, but of the theft itself, as in D. 16.3.1 § si praesto (l. 1 § si praesto). It supports what we say: D. 47.2.1 (l. ancillae) with its material, and D. 47.2.2 (l. in civile) with its authorities. And it is impossible that anyone should simultaneously exercise good faith due to the contract by right reason and commit theft; rather, once good faith is established, all bad faith is excluded, and vice versa. C. 9.13.1 (l. 1) and D. 47.2.1 (l. ancillam) pro suo, which is very apt. Also D. 11.3.1 (l. doli verbum) in D. de servo corrupto. And thus it remains that Antonius should be absolved. For because of the just beginning of the thing as regards the said Antonius, it must be concluded justly in his favor, as expressly noted in D. 3.5.1 (l. item) in the principal part, in the glossa necessarium est. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute providing that the paternal uncle shall come with the mother is also extended to grandmothers.
2. Whether the term "paternal uncle" includes the great-uncle.
casus: CASE. In the name of the Lord, amen. The facts are as follows: A certain daughter named Joanna, daughter of Andreutius Bentinenghus Pisanellus, having been endowed by the said Andreutius, her father, in his last will, died, leaving surviving her Cola Pisanellus, her uncle Magnus, and Piso and Lello, sons of Ianuarius Pisanellus, another uncle of Magnus, and her maternal grandmother and paternal grandmother. Now the question arises, having examined the statute of the commune of Perugia, to whom or to whom the inheritance of the said daughter of Andreutius pertains.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Considering that the statute provides for concurrence, namely that the paternal uncle comes to the inheritance together with the mother in this manner, namely that the paternal uncle succeeds in the remaining goods and rights in the legitime, I say that such a statute is also extended to grandmothers, as is noted in C. ad Tertul. Authen. defuncto. Indeed, some have wrongly stated that he who takes what pertains to the mother excludes the grandmother entirely; but the truth is that the grandmother succeeds in the place of the mother and is considered to have the same right, as is fully noted there.

But there is a doubt whether the term "patruus" includes the "patruus magnus" (great-uncle); for this addition, "magnus," makes a difference between the term used simply and the term used with qualification, as in L. Iurisconsultus, De gradibus; just as when I say "frater" (brother), I understand it to mean a full brother, not a paternal cousin or a maternal cousin, as in the aforementioned Authentica Defuncto. On this point, I say that if there exists such a person who, by the presumed will of the deceased, reasonably excludes the great-uncle—for example, if the nearest uncle has died, and the great-uncle succeeded in his place, as is the case here considered—then the final ratio of this statute, which is favorable, is verified even in the case of the great-uncle, as in L. 1, De venditionibus insipientibus. I also hold that the great-uncle should benefit from the statute. For this statute is not odious, since it reserves the legitime to the mother; and the same should be understood regarding the grandmother. Hence, this statute is not one of simple exclusion, but of a certain concurrence. And I would say the same if the testator said, "Furthermore, I bequeath to my uncles 10." For if he had immediate uncles, they would come; but if they do not exist, the great-uncles would come. For these indefinite or collective names are understood according to the order of justice, affection, or nature. It is true that in this matter much can be alleged, and especially the notable opinion of Cynus in L. 1, Quae sit longa consuetudo, which I do not pursue. I would not say this if the statute were openly inequitable, for example, if it stated that if an uncle exists, the daughter does not succeed; for then, in order to restrict the odium, I would understand it to refer to the first uncle, not to the great-uncle, by argument from De liberis et posthumis, L. Cum quidam. Although even in this case, a certain great doctor has advised in favor of the great-uncle. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a condemnation arising from a delict, paid by one of the brothers standing in community, ought to be imputed solely to the share of the condemned brother.
2. Whether the fruits derived from the dowry ought to be shared among the brothers.
3. Whether expenses incurred for the common utility may be recovered by one of the brothers standing in community.
4. Whether expenses incurred for studies are common, or whether they ought to be imputed to the individual share.
5. Whether expenses incurred for maintenance and for marrying off daughters ought to be shared.
body: John Penetenga, the sons and heirs of Bentonolius, held their paternal inheritance in common and lived together at one table, sharing bread and wine, and they conducted almost all their profits and business affairs jointly. Finally, the aforementioned Benetenga died, leaving behind his sons Frantutio and Angelo, who likewise retained their property together with the aforementioned John and conducted their business jointly. While they were thus situated, the aforementioned John and also a certain son of his committed certain crimes, and the resulting condemnations were paid from their common funds. Now, at the time of division, the sons of Benetenga claim that the said condemnations should be charged to the share of the said John and not to their own. The question is: what is the law?

† Regarding the aforesaid matters, I state that the aforementioned bans, or condemnations from the common fund, ought to be imputed solely to the share of the said John; nor are the sons of the said Benetenga bound to contribute in any way. The text is in *l. inter fratres*, § *si*, D. *pro socio*, and note the gloss in *l. fratres parentum*; otherwise, it is found in *l. cum duobus*, D. *pro socio*. Furthermore, while they remained in this state, the aforementioned John took a certain wife, who had had another husband; and for the dowries which the first husband had possessed, she acquired certain possessions and goods.

It is asked whether the fruits of the said possessions ought to be shared in the house where the said wife was maintained, or whether they ought to belong to the said John or to his wife. Regarding the aforesaid, I say that the dowries which were given to the first husband appear to have been recovered in the name of dowry even in the second marriage, tacitly, even if nothing was said to that effect; especially when no children survive from the first marriage: as in *l. dotem, quae* and *l. Ligias*, D. *solut. matr.*; *l. pen.* § *uxor*, D. *de pact. dot.*; and it supports what is noted by Cynus in *Auth. quamvis*, C. *de rei uxoriae actione* and *de pact. dot.*; *l. cum maritus* § *Titius*. And consequently, the fruits ought to be common, and not separate: since the burdens of the marriage were undertaken jointly: as in *l. si his* § *si tibi*, D. *de iure dotium*; and *l. si filia* § *damnis*, D. *fam. ercisc.*. Moreover, in a certain house, or houses, which were part of the said dowries, and also in certain possessions of the aforesaid, rebuilding was carried out, and many expenses were incurred from common funds.

† Now it is asked whether the aforementioned sons of the said Benetenga ought to recover their share of the money spent for the benefit of the said houses at the time of the division.
