Regarding the above, I say that the aforementioned sons of Benetenga may recover their share of the expenses incurred for the permanent benefit of the houses or the aforementioned things; the text is in l. 2, throughout, § fin., and the following law, and l. utilium, ff. de impensis in re dotali factis. Moreover, while the aforementioned situation remained, the said John and certain of his sons went to school and spent certain sums of money from the common funds of the aforementioned parties for the purpose of acquiring learning.

† It is asked whether, at the time of the division, the said sons of the said Benetenga can recover the aforementioned expenses incurred in the studies of the said [sons], and what is to be imputed to the share of John? Regarding the above, it seems to be said that they ought to be imputed to the share of John, and the sons of the said Benetenga are not bound to contribute anything: because the said expenses were not made from the common inheritance and goods; thus noted the gloss in l. cum duobus, §. Papi., otherwise beginning lex si fratres parentum, ff. pro socio, in the gloss which begins, sic ergo econtra in damnis, et expensis, etc. Moreover, while they remained thus in common, the said John had more sons and daughters to educate and maintain than the said sons of Benetenga; and the said John also married certain daughters, whose maintenance and dowries were made from the common [funds].

† Now it is asked whether the sons of the said Benetenga can impute the said expenses and dowries to the said John, so that they are not bound to contribute. Regarding the above, I say that they can recover a portion of the said dowries and maintenance: because it is the father's duty to maintain his daughters and to provide dowries for them: as in l. si quis a liberis, § si vel parens, ff. de liberis agnoscendis, and l. fin., C. de pactis dotalibus; and consequently, the sons are not bound to contribute, as noted in l. alimenta, C. de negotiis gestis, and in the aforementioned l. si fratres parentum. And thus it seems to me, Bonacursus, doctor of laws. And see in the following consilium on the same matter.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a payment made on account of a delict is common property, or whether it ought to be deducted before the division of shares.
2. The fruits of the dowry: to whom they belong, and whether they are subject to contribution.
3. Whether useful expenses are subject to contribution.
4. Whether expenses incurred for education are subject to contribution.
5. Whether an uncle living with his nephews must collate the acquisitions made by him.
6. Whether a widow who has returned to her father’s house is entitled to the fruits of her dowry in addition to her maintenance.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
† On the first point, it must be said that what has been paid on account of a wrongful act should not be deducted from the common fund, but only from the share of the wrongdoer. D. 17.2.14.

† On the second point, since it is put to me that the dowry appears to have been constituted in money, I say that other things are presumed to be paraphernal. C. de pac. conuen. l. si. And therefore the fruits of those things belong to the wife, namely those which are extant. Likewise, those converted into the purchase of lands, or other extant benefits, consumed for the sake of marital affection ought not to be restored, de donatione inter virum, et vxorem. l. si seruus communis.

† On the third point concerning useful expenses, I say that in voluntary matters, it is permitted for both parties to contribute; [this is supported by] the rule on negotiorum gestio, in the law *Ex duobus*.

† On the fourth point, I say that the expenses of study pertain to the father alone. D. 10.2.12 § si idem scribit. On the last point, I say that fruits consumed in common maintenance are not recovered when shared among partners; but if not as among partners, then the law *Nesennius* applies, D. 3.5.1 and C. 3.28.1 and l. *alimenta*.

† It is also to be known that an uncle has no partnership with his nephews while the nephews are minors. On the administration of tutors, *l. si Titium, et Meuium*, § *altero*. It is also to be known that the uncle is bound to render an account to the nephews themselves of what he has done and received. And if the uncle acquired something in the meantime by himself, it is his own, as in the Codex, On the Arbitration of Tutors, *l. si defunctus*; but if he had acquired it in partnership and during the time of the partnership, it ought to be shared. *l. si socius*, *si certum petatur*. The time during which there could have been a partnership is after twenty years.

† Concerning a widow who has returned to her father’s house, she must either contribute the fruits of the dowry or restore the maintenance she received, since she was not a partner and possessed her own patrimony, according to the matter discussed in the law *Nesennium*. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given the statute in question, which person is to be preferred in a sale to two persons.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The facts are as follows: A certain Lady Joanna of Callio executed an instrument in the form of a sale to a certain illegitimate stepson of hers regarding certain things, with the constitution of a precarium. At the time of said instrument, an agreement was made to rescind said contract if said Lady, being ill, recovered from her illness. Although nothing concerning this is contained in said instrument of sale, in truth it was so acted between said parties at that time; and it is proved by the notary and witnesses that it was so. After said Lady Joanna was recovered, two days after said sale was made, both parties, being in agreement, had said contract of sale, or protocol, cancelled. And said stepson confessed with these express words in said cancellation, namely: “Cancelled and annulled was said contract by me, the notary written below, by the license and will of said Lady and of said such stepson, the buyer, because said parties confessed that said contract and instrument of sale was and is simulated, and does not hold.” And these words were appended in the cancellation, and furthermore the word “etc.” was appended. And said protocol is found cancelled in the manner of a cross, according as is handed down and required by the law *Inductum*, Codex, *De solutionibus et liberationibus*. And at the time of said cancellation, said stepson was under twenty-five years of age.

Then said Lady Joanna made an instrument of sale of said things to a certain Lady Jacoba of said place, with the constitution of a precarium; and she remained in possession. Then she made another instrument to said stepson with the constitution of a precarium, and similarly she remained in possession. And between said stepson and said Lady Jacoba, the buyer, there is contention regarding the priority of right and possession of said things.

And for the part of said stepson it is said that he has the stronger rights, because he bought first. And it is said that the aforementioned cancellation does not stand in the way, because he was under 25 years, as is said above; and the form of the statutes was not observed, which require certain solemnities to be observed in contracts of minors. A copy of which statute is described below. Alleged for this part is the law *Quo*, Codex, *De rei venditione*.

And for the part of Lady Jacoba it is said that said first instrument does not assist said stepson by reason of said cancellation, and the solemnity of said statute was not observed, because said cancellation and confession appears to have been made by force of the agreement made at the time of the first sale contract, in which permission to rescind was granted, as is said above. And although it is not said in said cancellation “rescinded,” nevertheless, since the word “etc.” is opposed, and the confession of simulation, it follows from the nature of this word “etc.” that it comprehends rescission and all things required by the nature of the contract, as in law 1 and 2, § *Si quis iurauerit*, with the gloss and doctors there, and especially by the said Bartolus, Digest, *De iureiurando*. Hence, just as the sale holds, so all agreements inserted at the time of said sale, namely rescission, hold and are to be observed, as is the text in the law *Bene a Zenone*, Codex, *De quadrienaria praescriptione*. And thus said Lady Jacoba, who first received the instrument, is stronger because of the constitution of the precarium, by which possession was transferred to her, as in the law *Quod meo*, Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*. And where two have a cause at the same time, he is stronger to whom possession was first delivered, *De publiciana*, law *Secundum autem*, § *Si duobus*. Hence, between said stepson and Lady Jacoba, regarding the possessory action, he holds who was first, because possession was first delivered to him, whose title of said Lady Jacoba precedes. *Extra*, *De probationibus*, chapter *Licet causam*; Digest, *Uti possidetis*, law *Si duo*. And this part, in consulting, was held by Master Angelo of Perugia, doctor of laws.

Now two questions are asked: First, whether said Lady Jacoba ought to prevail in the possessory action; and whether said first cancelled sale prejudices her, and the minority of age of said stepson making the cancellation. Second, what must be extended regarding the nature of the contract of said notary who cancelled said contract and appended said word “etc.,” and what words are to be appended which said notary ought to append by law.

Copy of the aforementioned statute.

On contracts to be made by pubescent minors.

Rubric.

We therefore establish and ordain that all and singular contracts, however made and to be made by pubescent minors, that is, males over 14 years and females over 12 years, be ratified and firm by the authority of the present statute, provided that they are made, and have been made, in the presence of two of their blood relatives of the closest degree, namely from the father’s side, or two from the mother’s side, with an oath given by the aforementioned pubescent minors, and with the authority of a judge; otherwise, if any of the aforementioned is lacking, said contracts are to be understood as extorted by fraud and fear, and are null by the law itself. We also establish that if in the aforementioned cases any of the closest blood relatives of a minor were falsely and knowingly added to the contract of the minor, who in truth were not blood relatives or closer, and then the one contracting with the minor knew that the contract is null by the law itself as to the prejudice of the minor; and let that one contracting be punished, if it was a contract of a thing worth more than 10 pounds, and from 1 pound up to 25 pounds, in 100 pounds to be applied commonly and to be exacted in fact. But if he was ignorant, and the minor knowingly and fraudulently added them, then the contract shall nevertheless have firmness.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The formality required in contracting is required in dissolving.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

†That solemnity which is required in contracting is required in rescinding the contract: as in C. de praediis minorum, l. si ad resoluendum; and see also l. 1, C. si aduersus transa. But there is a great difference between the rescission of a contract and its observance. For if, at the time of the contract, it was agreed to rescind, this rescission is not a rescission, but is the execution of the first contract, which was truly celebrated, although otherwise simulated in writing: as in ff. de manumi., l. 3, § si ab ignoto; and l. 1, in fi., de rebus eorum. Nevertheless, it must be proved by witnesses that it was agreed at the time of the said simulated sale; which being proved, the said Lady Jacoba has a stronger right: C. de rei ven., l. quo. And therefore the opinion of Lord Angelus in this case is the very truth. And so I say and advise, I, Baldo de Perugia, doctor of both laws. And to the faith of this I have subscribed and affixed my seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In depositum, just as in mutuum, there may be a numeratio, and a stipulation that is conforming in two limbs and non-conforming in the other two.
2. When someone makes an agreement with another concerning a thing that did not belong to the party making the agreement, no right is sought for him; it fails.
3. Where the creditor and the debtor who made the deposit appear, along with a third party whose money was not deposited, which of them shall be preferred.
4. Money paid to someone is presumed to be whose. And no. 5.
5. What this clause, that someone may [act] in all places, etc., imports.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for clarity that, just as in a loan for consumption (mutuum), so too in a deposit there can be a counting (numeratio) and a stipulation that are conforming in two respects: namely, when one counts in his own name and stipulates in his own name; or when one counts in another’s name and stipulates in another’s name. And they are non-conforming in the other two respects, in which the counting tends to acquire for one person, and the stipulation for another, for example, when I count in my own name and stipulate in another’s name, or vice versa, as in l. si absentis and in § si nummos. I say this to this extent, because here a counting intervenes, whereas there, when it speaks of the imposition, ff. depositi, l. publica, § si, and the stipulation there, when it says “and thus we promise,” as in Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, § si scriptum, and C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. 1. And both the counting and the stipulation, or promise, were conforming, because they were in the names of the same persons. And I do not here call into doubt the validity of the contract, because I presuppose that it is valid.

† For although Bartolus says that when someone contracts with another concerning a thing which did not belong to the contracting party, no right is sought for him, nevertheless, according to him, this fails in two cases, namely in loan for use and in donation, as he notes in l. certi condictio, §. quoniam, D. si certum petatur, and D. de pignoris actione, l. solutum, §. per liberam. I say the same regarding deposit: because by its nature it is contracted with the thing, even if ownership is transferred, as when a quantity is deposited for counting, by which deposit one may make use. D. de deposito, l. die sponsaliorum. And I say this more strongly in deposit than in loan for use: because deposit is a good faith contract, to which it does not befit to dispute over legal subtleties, nor to allege rules of civil law to enrich oneself at another’s loss; and because by writing even a stipulation is presumed to have been made solemnly, as it ought to have been done, in order to be valid in law. D. de legibus, l. huiusmodi, in principio; C. de fideicommissis, l. finalis. Therefore, presupposing the validity of the contract and the subsistence of the obligation, let us examine its derivation and the transfer of the obligation. However, I premise that, even if through an interposed stipulation with the same names there does not appear to be a right as to the essence of a stipulation usefully made, of which the money was the subject: as C. si certum petatur, l. quamvis; nevertheless, on account of the creditor having the pledged goods, it seems useful and necessary to know this.

† Suppose my debtor, whose goods were pledged to me, deposited his money in another’s name, or by having a contract spoken in another’s person, or by a minor, or if something else happened to him humanely, which signifies death, whether natural or unnatural, such as by sword. ff. depositi. l. publia. in prin. The creditor appears and sues for this money hypothecarily: because although ownership is transferred with the cause of the pledge. ff. de pig. l. si superatus. yet in doubt ownership is not presumed to be transferred, unless use is transferred: or unless it is agreed that it is to be returned not as a certain body, but as a quantity, as noted. ff. si cer. pet. l. cum quid. and l. certi condictio. §. fin. or unless interest intervenes: as ff. de priuileg. credito. l. si neuter. §. in bonis. Also appears he in whose name the deposit was made: and sues for it. It is asked, who should be preferred: the text says, that he should be preferred who has the more just claim. ff. deposi. l. bona fides. §. j. but the creditor has the more just claim, who exists prior in time, as ff. de eui. l. si cum venditor. in prin. hence this pledge can and should be extinguished, lest injury be done to the creditor by a harsher adversary, or another of the forum, or of impossible genus, as noted. C. deposi. l. fi. huc accedat suspitio. ff. de l. commissoria. l. mulier fundos. ff. ad Treb. l. haeres cum debuerat. in fi. huc accedat suspitio competitoris, for even if it were restored to him, it would still need to be sequestered. ff. qui satisd. cog. l. si fideiussor. §. fi. and this if the money has not been consumed, but if it has been consumed in good faith, the hypothecary action competent to it seems to cease, as noted. ff. si cer. pet. l. nam et si fur. ff. de pign. l. si fundum. §. in vendicatione. But a useful action would be given against the name. i.e. against the debtor of the debtor. Whether this is true, I will say immediately.

It remains, therefore, to consider whose money is presumed to have been involved. Indeed, if someone counts money in his own name, it is presumed that the money belongs to him, as stated in C. si certum petatur, l. non unde originem; and in D. de privatis creditoribus, l. si neutri, §. fin. This presumption holds even more strongly in the case of deposit, which must be returned even to a mere detainer and to a robber. Hence, it suffices for him that he was in possession. D. de deposito, l. 1, §. si praedo; and l. bona fides.

However, if someone counts money in another’s name: if he is a father or a husband, it is presumed to be his own money. C. de pignoribus, l. fin.; D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. uxor marito. If he is an institor (manager) or a procurator, it is presumed to be the principal’s money, by argument from D. de institoria, l. fin.; and D. de obligationibus ex verbis, si ita stipulatus, §. Griso; D. si certum petatur, l. lecta. If he is a mother, the same rule applies as for a father. d. l. Publia, in principio.

If, however, he counts money in the names of several persons in different ways, and under the conditions of another, as is the case in our present question, it is probable that the money was primarily and principally named in the instrument for one person, and that the others were added at his will. Argument from D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. si communis servus ita, versio: sed cum ad nomina; and what is noted there by Jacobus de Arena; and that a prudent counsel of a brother to a brother, after death, as to a legitimate heir, would have provided for him. D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. fin.

Certainly, the mixture of outsiders here seems to oppose such a conjecture; but I answer that it does not at all oppose the argument on his side. And that it is presumed in favor of the heir seems to be proven by what is read and noted in D. de pactis, l. si tibi, §. si pacto. But against this is the aforementioned law Publia. And because these were not the words of Lord William, but the words of the deponent, and because from the order given it appears that nothing was done in view of a future inheritance, nevertheless, as I said, it is also credible that this was done for the benefit and with the money of Lord William. Nor is it surprising if he loved his comrades and associates in labor and danger as brothers. D. de donationibus, l. si pater.

† I therefore return to the question asked, whether the Lord Bartholomew has a right in this money. And I say that he does: if it has not been consumed, for consumption is not presumed in a deposit; he therefore has this money bound, since it is presumed originally and principally to have belonged to the Lord William, as I said. If, however, this money has been consumed, then we are not dealing with a hypothecary right over the thing owed, but with a hypothecary right over the name of the debtor, or an action in personam. C. quae res pignori obligatae possunt, l. Nomen; D. de pigneratitia actione, l. Si convenerit, in principio. It must therefore be considered whose name this is today: if it is an hereditary name, the heir is also bound, and if not, as D. de pignoribus, l. Paulus; or if it is entirely that of strangers, similarly not bound, as D. de pigneratitia actione, l. Rem alienam. And it is certain that these named persons have useful actions in their own name, not as heirs, but outside the right and name of the inheritance; therefore, in effect, it is their name. Hence, the Lord Bartholomew would have no right in this name for two-thirds, but only in the third part which falls to the brother of the Lord William. Either that brother is not the heir of the Lord William, and the result is the same, because he is bound by no obligation; or he is the heir, and then he is bound as heir. Although this name is not bound, nevertheless, because he is suspect and does not possess immovables, if the forum permits, this money should be seized, just as other movable goods of the heir. It is certain that the statute of Florence does not bind him to the necessity of accepting the inheritance; nevertheless, he should not be permitted to depart with another’s money. D. de iudiciis, l. Si legationis, and l. De eo; just as not to a vagabond and wanderer through the world, who has no home where he flees. C. ubi de crimine agi oporteat, l. 1 and 2, cum si. For a vagabond is similar to mercenaries, who perhaps will never be in their own forum; I say this not as regards the quality of the person, but as regards the justice of the forum.

† Moreover, see the obligation of Lord Guli. there, where he says, in all places and courts. For this pact also binds his heir to the Florentine forum, in which he himself or his procurator is found. D. 2.1.14 (Haeres absens); D. 16.3.1 (Lucius Titius). Although some say that if no place is expressly stated, this pact operates for nothing. Cynus says that it is a case in which the pact is valid in the said law Lucius. For by this pact no rule of law is restricted, nor any natural equity, and the intention appears, especially with an oath. It is supported by D. 26.1.1 (Tutores) and by Bartolus on D. 12.1.3 § Si quis ita. Therefore, it being established that Nicolaus Filinbach is the heir, justice undoubtedly favors Lord Bartholomew. The law also aids the pious party. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a mandate that is void due to a defect of formality, or otherwise invalid, can be ratified by ratification.
2. Whether sureties who intervened in a void mandate are bound, even if it is subsequently ratified.
3. Whether a void suretyship is ratified by ratification.
4. Whether ratification has any effect after the expiration of a term fixed by law: and whether the expiration of the term implies a renunciation.
1. If a procurator must be appointed by women with the advice of two relatives and with the authority of the magistrate, and if the magistrate’s authority is lacking, whether the judgment rendered in proceedings with him is valid, or whether it is rendered void.
casus:
CASE

The case is as follows: A certain person was appointed procurator without observing the form of the statute, so that his mandate was null by operation of law, according to the express disposition of the aforementioned statute. This alleged procurator caused a certain sequestration to be made and submitted a petition within eight days for the confirmation of the said sequestration, in accordance with the form of another chapter providing that, once the sequestration has been made, a petition must be submitted for its confirmation within eight days; otherwise, the sequestration is null by operation of law, as if it had never been made. Finally, the said alleged procurator substituted another person, and with this substitute many matters were litigated in law for the release of the said sequestration. Sureties were given for the return of the sequestered property when necessary, or for the payment of its estimated value, and the sequestration was released. After these many proceedings, it was objected that the mandate of the said alleged procurator and of those substituted by him was and had been null; and consequently, all things done by them or with them were and had been null, and that the said sequestration did not hold, nor does it hold, and that the sureties given for the restitution of the said sequestration were not, nor are, effectively bound. After this, seeing this, the opposing party appointed another procurator, whose appointment was made lawfully and with the due solemnities intervening, and who ratified all acts and deeds performed by the said alleged procurator and by those substituted by him. This ratification occurred not after the expiration of the eight days, but much later.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The first doubt arises because the first mandate was defective in formality, and that which is lacking due to formality cannot be ratified: as is noted by the doctors in C. de bonis, quae libe., l. cum non solum, §. necessita, and by Innocentius in c. dudum, de reb. ecc. non alie., and in c. prudentiam, de testamento, deleg. Furthermore, because the mandate was null by operation of law, it does not appear to be validated by ratification, as in extra de rescrip., c. nonnulli, and c. ex parte decani. But the truth is to the contrary: for it is not the mandate of the principal that is ratified by the principal ratifying, but rather the management of the procurator that is ratified; just as it could be ratified where there was no mandate at all, so much more strongly can it be ratified where the mandate was invalid, as in ff. de iud., l. licet; ff. de exce. rei iudi., l. si iur., §. hoc iure; and in c. rati, through the gloss and Dynus. And this is demonstrated by the following reason: for here there is no defect in the ratifying party, since he ratifies formally, but the defect lies in the mandate; hence the acts performed in judicial proceedings and in contracts are validated. This is shown to us by all the laws that speak of the caution de rato: ff. de procurato., l. Pompo., §. rati; and l. non solum, §. si status; and l. qui absente; and l. mutus, §. is, qui curatorem. For if it could not be effectively held as ratified, one ought not to be required to give caution de rato: ff. de procurato., l. non cogendum, §. fin. And these statements are true even if a decree were required on the part of the actor, as is evident in the case of a false tutor or one lacking a confirmatory decree, whose acts in court and out of court can be ratified: ff. de administra. tuto., l. vulgo, quod falso tu., l. 1. Moreover, these statements are true even if a decree is required on the part of the ratifying party: it is certain that if a city appoints a syndic, in such an appointment a decree of the magistrate is required, as is noted in ff. quod cuiusque vniuer. nomine., l. nulli. Suppose that the decree did not intervene, yet later the city ratifies with the decree; certainly all acts are validated, just as in the cases of individual persons: ff. quod cuiusque vniuer., l. item eorum, §. sed interdum; and l. actor, rem rat. hab. The gloss in c. rati responds to the contrary arguments by stating that they are special cases and cannot be in suspense; for those things that cannot be in suspense cannot be ratified, because they are not in potency toward their effect: as in l. receptum, communia praediorum.

The second doubt is, assuming that the ratification is valid, whether the sureties are bound. And it seems that they are not, because they intervened by mistake, not intending to intervene for a false procurator. And a suretyship given by mistake is void: no right has been acquired for the surety, therefore it cannot be taken away from him without his own act: as in D. de pactis, l. fin.; and noted in the cited c. rati., vers. et hoc facit; D. qui potiora in pignore habent, l. qui balneum, § Titia; D. quomodo servitus amittitur, l. si partem, § 1; C. locata, l. si cum heres; rem ratam habere, l. si videntur; and in Speculum, de obligationibus et solutionibus, § 1, vers. item pone, in contrarium est casus; D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. Iul. Nor is it said that the condition of the surety is made worse than he had intended in his mind: D. de fideiussoribus, l. si quis pro eo, § si nummos. For the right of ratifying is established for the principal by the disposition of the law, which right cannot be taken away from him: D. de constitutione pecuniae, l. unde falsam. Which ratification, since it represents [the act as if done by the principal], makes him retroactively a legitimate procurator, so that the suretyship is said to be erroneous.

The third doubt arises, because satisfaction ought not to have been given, and satisfaction given without due cause is not effective unless it was given with certain knowledge, or through an intolerable error of the common law, as in D. si quis caut. l. sed et si quis, §. fin., and D. de fideiuss. l. Graece, §. tutore. Indeed, the glossa there seems to say that it does not harm the fideiussor who acted in bad faith. To the contrary, it appears from the above, for the nature of a sequestration is that it is not revoked if made at the instance of the true creditor, unless a fideiussor is provided. D. qui satisdare cog. l. fideiussor, §. fin. And if it be said that this is true when the sequestration was valid, but here it was not valid, I answer that it is argued that it was valid, because ratification legitimizes all that has been done, as in D. de damno infecto, l. inter quos, §. alieno. Hence the principal debtor is bound, and the fideiussor accedes to him. And these things are true if there were nothing else in the case, and thus I advised in Genoa. But furthermore, then, as much as from me

† Now another question arises, which was not then considered, namely, because the statute states that, after the sequestration has been made, a petition for its confirmation must be given within eight days; otherwise, the sequestration is null by operation of law, as if it had never been made. Now, within the eight days, the petition was given by a less-than-legitimate procurator. The question is whether the principal can ratify after the eight days. And the answer is yes. For in judicial proceedings, one proceeds through dilatory periods; nevertheless, after all of them, and even after sentence, ratification has place. D. de negotiorum gestione, l. Servus autem, § 1. Moreover, according to Decius, the lapse of a term, even one given by law, is an obstacle to the principal only when it induces a tacit renunciation; otherwise, it is not, as he notes in D. de rerum venditione, l. Bonorum, and in c. Rati, per Decius, and this is the ordinary gloss in l. Si ego, D. de negotiorum gestione. But here the principal never renounced; on the contrary, he always accepted and wished it; therefore, etc. And this is clear from the examples in bonorum possessio, in which time does not run unless against one who knows; and one who knows is deemed to renounce. The same applies to the time for appealing, because one who does not appeal is deemed to consent. D. de appellationibus recipiendis, l. 1, post principium; 2 q. 6, c. Anteriorum, quasi circa medium. But Bartolus rejects this distinction and says that tacit repudiation is not necessary, but that the mere lapse of a term given by law prevents ratification. And he argues against Decius in a fanciful manner. First, by l. Si is cui, D. de rerum venditione, which is irrelevant, because there transmission is prevented due to ignorance, not due to the lapse of time. Also, he offers another reason which is worth not a straw; for it is not doubtful that one who effectively renounces cannot later ratify; otherwise, if the renunciation is ineffective. L. Si ita, § Si sub conditione, D. de legatis. Hence I wonder that he does not bring forward better reasons against Decius. These are the reasons: First, regarding the prescription of an action, it is certain that the creditor does not consent to the prescription of time, as noted in D. de dolo, l. 1, § 1. And yet, if the gestor did not wish to interrupt the prescription by performing the acts required for that purpose, he cannot have it ratified after the time has elapsed. D. de rerum venditione, l. Finis. Second, in bonorum possessio, the days run against one ignorant of the right. For one who errs, even in law, does not renounce. D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. Obediamus. And yet, after one hundred days, it is not considered ratified, as in D. quis ordo in bonorum possessionibus servandus sit, l. Finis. The same applies to appeal, for time runs against one ignorant of the right, and yet after the time, the intermediate act cannot be ratified. But in similar cases excluding the right of ratification by the course of time, consider whether the term is fixed for the principal, and then he cannot ratify after the term; or for the agent, who in fact observed the term, and then ratification is not prevented by the lapse of judicial terms. To know which this is, observe three cases: sometimes the term is fixed by law without the intervention of a judge; sometimes by a judge, yet with the intervention of a judge; sometimes by a judge, and not by law. In the first case, the term is deemed fixed for the principal himself, to perform that act by himself or by a legitimate person. The law, namely, which disposes all things with effect, is not understood to fix the term for a false procurator, but for the principal, as in l. Bonorum, cum si. In the second and third cases, the judge is often mistaken, and it depends on the fact to whom he speaks and to whom he directs his words, whether to the agent or to his principal. Therefore, a term assigned to the principal affects him more than a term assigned to the gestor. It must therefore be seen whether this statute assigns the term to the one who caused the sequestration to be made in another’s name; and then it seems that the proceedings of that sequestration can be ratified. Or whether it is understood to be assigned to the one for whom, i.e., for whose benefit, the sequestration is made; and then the contrary holds, because neither he himself offered the petition, nor a legitimate person. Let us suppose that the procurator, or the principal himself, caused the sequestration to be made, but a false procurator gave the petition within eight days for the confirmation of the sequestration, which the principal ratified after the time had elapsed. I do not believe such ratification to be valid; for those words, “a petition must be given,” are understood to mean by a legitimate person. C. qui dari tutores possunt, l. In universis. Within eight days, i.e., continuous days from the day of the sequestration, for its confirmation. The act and the law require confirmation. D. de legibus, l. Tali scriptura. So that within eight days it is null by operation of law, by the definitive sentence of the law, as if it had never been made, but it can never be ratified; for that which is non-existent cannot be ratified. And therefore, according to what is newly proposed, a new response must be given. For I do not change my opinion, but the theme has changed for me. It supports what I noted in the rule Non confirmatur, namely, that one who supervenes to confirm then confirms when he has no obstacle; but here he has the obstacle of the eight-day period. But he would not have this obstacle if the sequestration were certainly valid and the sureties were bound.

† However, since the statute of the gate was transmitted to me when I was first consulted, and I cannot pass it over in silence without a clear conscience, I will set forth the words of the statute. It states: “women may act, demand, and seek, etc., by themselves and their procurators, provided that the aforementioned actions are done with the advice of two relatives and with the authority of the magistrate.” The question arises: if the authority of the magistrate did not intervene, is the procurator a procurator and a true procurator, namely, subject to judgment, unless an exception is raised? D. de procuratoribus, l. Filius, §. Veterani; and l. Qui procuratorem, §. Ult.; and l. Pomponius, §. Rati. C. eod., l. Ita demum. And certainly it seems that he is, as stated above, a procurator, because the words say that in the opinion of the procurators they cannot act unless they are constituted with the authority of the magistrate. The word “procurans” speaks thus to procurators; nevertheless, it does not grant him the exercise of the procuratorship, which is to be understood if they are excepted, not by the law itself, because the law does not say that they cannot be constituted; but it says that they do not act. For it is one thing to speak of essence, another of mere exercise, as noted in C. de regulis iuris, c. Ratum, lib. 6; and D. ad Macedonianam, l. 1; and D. ad Velleianam, l. 1. Therefore, at least it is valid for the benefit of the woman herself, in whose favor the statute was made, from which it was not conceived. C. de procuratoribus, l. Non eo minus; C. in quibus causis in integrum restitui non est necessarium, l. Si tutor; D. de pactis, l. Contra iuris civilis regulas; D. de novis, l. Cui bonis; de transactionibus, l. Cum hi, §. Eam. And therefore it seems to be treated here in vain regarding ratification, since it is valid from the very beginning; because the substance of consent does not fail. D. de procuratoribus, l. 1; nor the substance of the essential form, but only the form of exercise. To the contrary, because the form which gives being to the thing truly fails; and because the incapable and the null are equivalent. D. quod cuiusque universitatis, not., l. 1, §. Pen.; de transactionibus, l. Cum hi, §. Si praetor. Whether this is so, I do not examine, because I was not asked. What therefore I have said above, I have written assuming the title of the question to be true; I leave the rest to others. By the excellent doctor, Lord Dominic, it was presented to me differently formed, to be considered differently at least in secret, by l. Ult., C. de pacis conventionibus, and by other reasons.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A pronouncement concerning age must be made solemnly, and especially after a time limit has been set for both parties to prove their case.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A pronouncement concerning age, where a great prejudice is at stake, as is the case here, must be made solemnly, and especially after a term has been granted to each side for proof. D. de minoribus, l. de aetate; D. de probationibus, l. cum de aetate; C. de restitutione in integrum minorum, l. si minorem te; D. de interrogationibus et actionibus, l. de aetate. This was not done here, and therefore this sentence was invalid. To this point, it is most helpful that we note C. de iuramento calumniae, l. 2, § quod observari; D. de interrogationibus et actionibus, l. de aetate, in principio. And it is noted that when minority of age is raised in the manner of obtaining some benefit, or as an excuse, or as an exception, the one who excuses himself must prove it. D. de iureiurando, l. nam et postea, § si minor; C. si minor se maiorem dixerit, l. penultima, cum si. Since, therefore, the mother here did not prove that she was a minor with respect to the jurisdiction of the forum, judgment must be rendered against her, namely, that by the lapse of a year she is excluded from the succession. The law is harsh, yet it must be observed. But if the mother had proved that she was of age, or if it were evident from her appearance, then judgment should have been rendered in favor of the mother. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having seen the testament of Cecolo Cola, and having seen the concession made by the reverend father in Christ, Lord Faglard, Bishop of Spoleto, to the monastery of Saint Clare of Spello for the heir and goods of the said Cecolo. It is asked whether, according to law, the said concession is valid, as appears from the form of the testament: the testator instituted three heirs, namely Cecolo, Iverus, and Lord Peter, and disposed that the heirs could not sell immovable property, and that they should distribute the fruits to the poor of Spello, as they shall see fit for the soul of the testator. And if any of the said Cecolo, Iverus, and Lord Peter should die, that the other two, in place of the predeceased, should elect another within a month, who shall have authority in the aforementioned matters, just as the heirs themselves. It is also proposed as a matter of interest that, after the death of the testator, and subsequently after the death of the said Cecolo, the aforementioned Lord Peter elected Vannes Philippus in place of the predeceased Cecolo. And finally, after the death of the aforementioned Vannes, because the aforementioned Lord Peter did not elect anyone in place of the said Vannes within a month, the aforementioned Lord Bishop, saying that the right of distribution had devolved to him, made the aforementioned concession to the said monastery regarding the inheritance of the said Cecolo, the testator. And in that concession it is expressed that the institution made by the said testator concerning the aforementioned Cecolo was vacated, because the notary summoned for the said testament could not inscribe in the testament the said institution concerning his son, as more fully appears from the tenor of the said concession.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a father who is a notary may inscribe something to his son.
2. Due to negligence, the right of election devolves to the bishop.
3. The right of election does not run against one impeded by a legal impediment.
body: It must be premised,
† Piter, being a notary, may write down laws or an institution for his emancipated son; but not for a son who is under his power. ff. de falsis, l. si puberem, § 1, where this is discussed.

Secondly, I premise that, due to the negligence of Lord Peter in not having elected anyone to the place of Vannis, the right to elect another to the said place of Vannis devolves to the diocesan bishop, according to the chapter *Nos quidem* in the title *De testamento*.

Thirdly, I premise that the right to distribute the fruits of the hereditary estate among the poor belongs to Lord Peter and to another person to be elected by the diocesan bishop in place of the predeceased Vannis; because this right of execution cannot be said to devolve to the diocesan bishop due to the negligence of the executors. For negligence in distributing the fruits of the inheritance among the poor cannot be imputed to Lord Peter, since he alone does not have the power to distribute them, but only together with his colleagues, that is, together with the person elected in place of the predeceased Vannis. Therefore, before another is elected in place of Vannis, it is clear that Lord Peter is impeded, and prescription does not run when there is an impediment of law, nor is he considered negligent. See *de concess. praeb.*, c. *Quia diversitatem*; *de iure dot.*, l. *Ubi adhuc*; C. *de ann. exc.*, l. *Si nec ob.*; *de test.*, c. *Fin.*, lib. 6. Where, upon the death of one executor, the surviving colleague has the office and power of execution. For that statement is true when, upon the death of an executor, the right of execution did not transfer from the person of the deceased to another. But here it transferred to another, namely, to the person to be elected by the diocesan bishop in place of the predeceased Vannis.

Fourthly, it must also be premised that the right of execution imposed on the executors pertains to the fruits of the hereditary goods, not to the goods of the inheritance itself; for the ownership of the goods belongs to Lord Peter and Cecolus; and upon the death of Cecolus, it belongs for one-half to the heirs of Cecolus; because those heirs could not be deprived of their half by the diocesan bishop, since no one can be deprived of his ownership without cause, as stated in l. *Id quod nostrum*, *de reg. iur.* Since, therefore, the right of execution devolves to the diocesan bishop due to the negligence of the executors, and no execution regarding the ownership was imposed on the heirs by the testator, there is therefore no negligence in execution regarding the ownership; for negligence does not attach to that which was not imposed, because deprivation presupposes possession. And by this it is concluded that, from the right which the diocesan bishop claimed had devolved to him, the diocesan bishop could not grant the dominion of that inheritance to the aforementioned monk. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia. Peter, etc.

And I say the same, and I advise, I, Flonorius Deeru, doctor of laws, as above advised by the eminent V.I.D. Lord Peter: and that this is true is proved not only from the precept of the testator supported by a cause, in which case it must be observed, ff. de legat. 1, l. filius, §. diui, as was the case here, because the testator forbade the alienation of immovables, so that the fruits might be divided among the poor. But also by another reason, because, assuming but not conceding, that the power of distribution had devolved to the diocesan, nevertheless neither he nor the first executors could distribute before the time to the prejudice of future poor, as ff. de legat. 2, l. cum pater, §. cum filia, and C. de fideiuss. l. praemotus, and in both places by Bartolus, who thus advised many times. Now, to the point, I say that the testator, by providing that the fruits be distributed among the poor every year, has set this time, which is not instantaneous but extended to the end. Hence, it could not rightly be done in one year or moment; and thus, because the ownership does not pass in the legacy, and because the fruits cannot be distributed to the prejudice of future poor, I say that the concession does not hold, and also by the reason assigned by the learned Peter, because no negligence can be imputed; for where no exception or petition is granted, there is no delay, C. si certum petatur, l. lecta. And if there had been any delay, which is denied, it would not have been perpetual, except in the right of choosing. And to the truth of this I have subscribed, and sealed with the seal of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A dowry asset may be sold to the prejudice of the seller, who binds himself regarding eviction.
2. Those measures which tend to strengthen the proceedings may be taken while the case is pending.
3. Whether the fruits of the dowry diminish the principal.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A dowry asset may be sold to the prejudice of the seller, and with the obligation of the seller in case of eviction. On usucapion, l. cum vir praedium. On fideicommissa, l. cum lex. According to Dy. On laws, C. l. non dubium. According to Cy. And therefore, for the eviction of goods then obligated, and by express promise of eviction. On eviction, C. l. si fundum sciens. Furthermore, they are hypothecated for the defense of the matter in court, so that the possessor may relinquish possession or defend it. On eviction, ff. l. si plus, vel minus. §. mota quae sunt. Where it is expressly stated. And it is not necessary in this case to await the judgment, as appears there. And therefore, he who brings a hypothecary action should strengthen his proceeding by effecting excussion and having a pronouncement made thereon. For

† Those [measures] which tend to the fortification of the process, such as excussio, may be undertaken while the case is pending. D. de pignoribus et hypothecis, l. si rem, §. si; S. Ma. l. si mulier; fructus rei hypothecatae computet in dotem, D. de solutionibus, l. Titia; S. Ma. l. insulam, per Bar., si habet ultra, quam sint alimenta dotis; C. de re iudicata, l. exactio.
† I say that alimony is due for as long as the widow lives; but upon her death, the fruits indiscriminately diminish the principal. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the grandfather is the legitimate guardian when the mother has died or been excluded.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Datalis Abrami married his daughter to Abram Allemichi; and the said girl remained a widow; and the said girl is twenty years of age or thereabouts; and there remained from the said Abram and the said girl two young female children; to whom the paternal consanguineous relatives caused appointed guardians to be given; and among these was the paternal grandmother, who caused two guardians to be appointed for them; now the mother of the said wards is entering into a second marriage; wherefore the said maternal grandfather wishes to assume the said guardianship as the legitimate guardian,

† It is asked whether it is possible? I answer that it is possible, because the mother being perpetually excluded, the grandfather will undoubtedly succeed according to some colleagues, according to others together with the grandmother, as noted in Auth. matri, et auiae. And thus the testamentary guardianship ends, and the legitimate guardianship begins. On the appointment of guardians and curators by them. L. si impuberi. And thus there is no objection from what is noted in D. de excus. tu. L. non solum. §. libenter. And I say the same if the said mother says that she wishes to enter into a second marriage: because by this she is rendered perpetually ineligible for guardianship, and therefore the grandfather succeeds. Although there are opinions on this point, and so I hold. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one bound to a certain sum or a certain thing is released from the part paid by payment of that part.
2. "Less" is said in many ways.
casus: CASE. Peter bought from John a certain possession for the price of one thousand florins. Of this price, the said Peter paid to the said John five hundred, and retained the remainder with the consent of the said John, until certain promises made by the aforementioned John in guarantee of the said purchase were observed, by this agreement made between them, that the said Peter promised to the said John to deposit the said remainder, i.e., five hundred florins, on the said Monte of Florence, which is called by the name of the Moon, for which five hundred florins there were recorded in the books of the said Monte one thousand five hundred florins. And the said Peter promised to the said John to give interest on the aforementioned money, which the said Commune gives to its other creditors, until the said John has observed the aforementioned promises of guarantee for the aforementioned purchase. And John, after some time had elapsed, during which time he always received from the said Peter the interest that the said Commune gave to its other creditors for the said sum of 1,500 florins, observed the said pact of guarantee for the said purchase. And the aforementioned Peter caused the aforementioned quantity of 1,500 florins to be entered to the account of the said John. These 1,500 florins, on the day on which they were entered to the account of the said John, were worth, due to the bad statute of the aforementioned Commune, three hundred florins. These 1,500 florins the aforementioned John accepted, taking fruits and interest for a long time, after they had been entered to his account, and before the lawsuit set forth below arose. And after another period of time had elapsed after the aforementioned entry of 1,500 florins to the account of the said John, the said Commune of Florence made a reform containing that all its creditors recorded in the books of the said Monte should be reimbursed, and that lots should be drawn by chance, and that such drawing should entitle one to recover from the said Commune one-fourth part of his credit in this manner, namely, that whoever is drawn should recover the said part of the money which it is truly established is owed to him, in which the aforementioned person was found recorded in the books of the said Monte, so that if it happens that 100 florins are expended, they should recover one-fourth part thereof. Hence John was drawn for his said fourth part, and the officials of the said Commune appointed for these matters wish to give to the said John one-fourth part of 300 florins, since the aforementioned 1,500 florins were worth this much on the day on which they were entered to the account of the aforementioned John. But John says that he ought to have one-fourth part of five hundred florins, since this is the true sum of his money. It is asked whether the aforementioned Peter is in any way obligated to the said John, or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† These words, that whoever is thus extracted must restore the fourth part of the coins which were truly established as due to him, in which said such person is found described, have in themselves a clear meaning, as C. man. l. per diuersis. in prin. there: "thus, however," etc., as l. ab Anastasio. there: "indeed, by the contract itself, he performed in fact." And C. qui po. in pig. ha. l. assiduis. There: "in fact, they were given to the husband's party." But let us suppose that three hundred were established for my actor; but for me, placed in the position of my actor, five hundred were established, or vice versa: what do we examine? I answer: my contract establishes the formal price, as ff. ad l. fal. l. si hęres. And it supports what is noted in C. de rei ven. l. mater. But here it must be seen whether these coins were established for this John as five hundred or three hundred? And to see this, one must consider whether said Peter was released from said five hundred florins by said assignment of 1500 florins made by the monte. If therefore he was released, then nevertheless it was established for said John as five hundred florins, ff. ad l. Falc. l. quęrebatur. But if said Peter was not released except in three hundred, with the inducer remaining obligated, it follows that these coins were not established for John except as three hundred. Another: he has two hundred in credit against Peter; and therefore it must be seen what is the law.

It must be known, however, that “less” is said in many ways: for sometimes less is paid in quantity, sometimes less in substance, sometimes less in quality, sometimes less in time, sometimes less in place, sometimes less in cause. If, for example, I owe ten and I pay five, release occurs only as to five; because I pay less in quantity. For a particular payment releases only partially. D. Si certum petatur, l. Quidam aestimaverunt; C. De transactionibus, l. Siquidem; C. De exemptionibus, l. Si ex maiore; D. De solutionibus, l. Qui stipulatus est, §. Qui decem. But if I owe a certain body, for example a certain estate, and I give it by delivery, similarly release occurs as to that part, if the obligation is divisible, for example to give or restore the thing; otherwise, if the right is considered indivisible and the thing is to be handed over. D. De verbis obligatis, l. Stipulationes non dividuntur. And this is true when payment is made for the same thing; but if something else is paid for something else, for example an estate of lesser value for a greater quantity, the debtor is released in full, Inst. Qui modis tollantur obligationes, in principio; not so with quantities, for example if I pay one gold coin for six pounds of denarii, when it is worth only four, unless perhaps that gold coin was paid as a species, not as a quantity. D. De legatis secundis, in principio, §. Si; C. Si vero plus qualitate, i.e., goodness, and I pay less, i.e., worse, then a distinction must be made, as in the aforementioned D. De donationibus, l. Eleganter; §. Non solum, D. Communia, l. 3, §. Si redditur. I do not follow the other members, because they are not relevant to the purpose. Against Peter, therefore, it is argued, because he promised to deposit five hundred florins and deposited only three hundred. But in his favor it is argued, because he promised to deposit at the end, so that 1,500 [units] would be described, which final description was fulfilled, and the thing attained its end. And whether we say that this description of 1,500 was purchased by Peter deliberately, this benefits him. D. Ad legem Falcidiam, d. l. Si haeres; or by chance and fortune, because this description began to be worth less, this loss pertains to the seller; because it concerns the thing. D. De evictionibus, l. Lucius; and D. De periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. Necessario. Moreover, these civil possessions are reduced to the likeness of a corporeal immovable thing; as C. De sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. Iubemus; and in Auth. De non alienando, §. Si; and this revenue, paid for five hundred and accepted by John, must release Peter from the whole; as D. De manumis, l. Inter causas, §. Abesse; D. De re iudicata, l. A divo Pio, §. Nam si creditor; D. De pignoratitia actione, l. Solum, §. Solutam; and D. De solutionibus, l. Satisfactio. Viturius says: “Something else for something else is paid,” just as if I had promised you ten in honey, and you accepted for these ten honey worth only one. For you would be released from the whole, as is clear in the aforementioned laws and similar ones. So here that description was accepted for the said five hundred florins to be deposited. Nor was there any thought from the beginning of a larger sum, nor of a more abundant one. And if it is so, that this description was accepted for the said five hundred florins, it is as if a less valuable militia were estimated at a higher price; as C. De pignoribus, l. Si; and D. De legatis tertio, l. His verbis, §. Alumno. And thus Peter would be released in full, and John would be owed a quarter of five hundred, because that is what this scriptio cost John. D. De hereditate vendenda, l. Si nomen.

CASE. The fact, among others, which are found in the testament of Francis, Master Peter of Cierqueto, is found thus: “Moreover, he left and judged Lady Enida, his widow, as lady and stewardess, and usufructuary of all his goods and chattels, and the habitation of a certain house situated in the said castle, while chaste, etc.”

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The wife, left as mistress, housekeeper, and usufructuary, to whom also the use of a certain house is left, what she ought to have.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The lady, by virtue of the said legacy, must have maintenance, as noted in l. 1, C. si secundo nupserit, and l. 3, per Bar., de leg. 2. However, her dowries, since they consist in money, she cannot recover within a year from the day of the testator’s death, as stated in C. de rei uxoriae actione, § exactio. Furthermore, she must have status and habitation together with the heir, if she can conveniently reside with him; otherwise, she is also to be maintained outside, as noted by the doctors in l. diuortio, so. mat. To the extent that the assets permit, after deducting the legitimate portion of the son, as in l. vxori, de usufructu legato, and in Auth. nouissima, C. de inofficioso testamento. I, Francis, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The mother succeeds to the usufruct, but not to the ownership, of the goods of her son who died in pupillary age, to whom a substitution had been made. And add the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Conclusively, the truth is that Dame Vanarella, having provided security for the use and enjoyment according to the discretion of a good man, must have the full usufruct upon the death of the minor. However, she does not succeed to the ownership, because the pupillary substitution excludes her. This is proved first by the law *uxori* in the title *De usu et usufructu legato*, and notably by Bartolus in the law *Titia*, section *si*, in the title *De legatis secundum*. This is proved secondly in the law *Papinianus*, section *sed nec impuberis*, in the title *De inofficioso testamento*, and in the chapter *Si pater*, in the title *De testibus*, Book 6.

The objection is not valid if it is said that the pupillary substitution was not confirmed by acceptance of the paternal inheritance; because, if it was made to his own heir without acceptance, it is confirmed by the existence of his own heir, according to the common opinion of the doctors in the title *De militari substitutione*, the law *Si filius qui patri*, and the law *Apud Iulianum*, section 1. And this opinion has gained strength by custom in these parts, and should not be changed, etc., although if anyone wished to dispute, much would have to be said; especially that, if the infant died, the mother would be excluded even by the vulgar substitution, even if included in a compendious form, according to the Digest, title *De ventre in suspectum addendo*, law *Qui neutri*; the Code, title *De institutionibus et substitutionibus*, law *Si*; and the Digest, title *De vulgari substitutione*, law *Lucius*.

And therefore the truth is that the mother ought to have nothing of the ownership; but she ought to have the usufruct, from which the inheritance passes to strangers; because it appears from the words that the substitution was pupillary, compendious, and direct in the pupillary age, as noted by the gloss and all the commentators in the law *Precibus*. And to say the contrary is not to speak reasonably. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Upon the death of the said minor, the said mother ought to have full usufruct, according to the law *uxori* in the title *De usufructu legatorum*. When the inheritance comes to strangers, those stranger heirs are bound to perform the legacy from their own person. And therefore, their person, and not that of the son, is to be considered. Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Si fundum*, section *Si pater*. Moreover, the custom written in the common court is written in personam, not in rem, that is, in respect of existing children. Since therefore there are no existing children, we are in the common law. Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, law *Si vero*, section *De viro*. Moreover, that which is granted to sons as a privilege is not extended by custom to strangers. Code, *De testamentis*, law *Hac consultissima*; Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, section *Ex imperfecto*; Digest, *De legatis secundo*, law *Paulus*, section *Finis*; Digest, *De legatis secundo*, law *Cum patronus*; Code, *De impositione lucris descriptionis*, law 1, book 10. From which I conclude that the said lady, until etc., ought to have full usufruct. Digest, *De usufructu legatorum*, law 9, origin. And thus holds Bartolus in law 4, *De legatis secundo*. And he senses these same reasons, although not so clearly. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a guarantor of one of the partners, who has paid on his behalf, may recover from the other by virtue of the preservation and indemnity promised to him.
2. Whether a guarantee is a contract.
3. If there are two partnerships, the beginning of the time of each must be examined.
4. By what acts a partnership is formed.
casus: CASE. Since it often happens that money-lenders and practitioners of the exchange trade of the City of Perugia make promises and oblige themselves to give, pay, and restore moneys which are deposited with them and in their books, and also those which come to them by reason, or trade, or occasion of the art of exchange, and also they often make promises for the debts of others for the honor of the said art and of the money-lenders, that such money-lenders making such promises shall pay and satisfy without any delay, or exception, or opposition, and within the terms established. We say, we establish, we ordain, that whoever, as a money-lender, has made or shall make to anyone any promise, of which promise there appears a writing in the hand of the money-lender himself, or in the hand of any disciple standing at the bench with the money-lender, or by order of the money-lender, or in his presence without contradiction. And by virtue of such writing something is demanded before the said auditors from the money-lender who made or ordered to be made the written promise, as is said, the said auditors, having seen the said writings summarily, without the offering of a libel, without contest, and without the noise and form of judicial process, shall order and command the money-lender who wrote or ordered to be written such writing or acknowledgment, if the money-lender is present, to him personally, or to his place of residence, to be commanded and ordered by one of the messengers of the said art, that within ten days next coming from then he give and pay, and ought to have given and paid, to his creditor whatever appears in the said writing or acknowledgment that such money-lender ought to give or pay. And if within the said term he does not pay and satisfy with effect, let the said creditors, after the said ten days have elapsed, have such money-lender, at the petition of his creditor, pledged, burdened, seized, and put in prison and held: and he shall not be released without the license of his creditor, until he has satisfied him of the quantity, debt, and expenses. And if the writing appeared in the book of the table, in which all the partners write, or in which facts pertaining commonly to all partners are written, any one of their partners, of whom the said book was, or to whom the things written in the said book pertained, may be sued for the whole; and conversely, all may be proceeded against for the whole by the said auditors in the manner and order aforesaid. But if the writing were found in any other book, only the writer, or he who caused it to be written, shall be bound to the satisfaction of the contents of the said writing or acknowledgment, and because also it is. By the form of this ordinance, any one of the partners is bound for the whole to the deposer in the tables of the said partners; and also in those things which, by reason, or trade, or occasion of the art of exchange, come to any one of the said partners. But Peter, who was a partner of Bernard, is not sued by the heirs of Andreutius on account of the deposit made with the said Bernard by the said Andreutius, nor even on account of those things which, by reason and occasion, come to any one of the said partners; but the said Peter is sued as a partner of Bernard, by reason and occasion of the suretyship made by Andreutius for the said Bernard, and by reason and occasion of the preservation made by the said Lord Bernard for the said Andreutius.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. If a surety

† One of the partners having paid for the other, seeks from the latter, by virtue of the stipulation of indemnity promised to him by the person for whom he stood as surety, to be indemnified. The question is whether he can do so. And it is argued first that he cannot, because this claim is founded on the stipulation of indemnity: but from a stipulation one cannot sue anyone other than the promisor, for a stipulation could not have been contracted with another who was absent and unaware. D. de verb. oblig. l. 1 and l. inter stipulantem in princ. Moreover, if the promisor had expressly promised that the partner would keep the surety indemnified, the promise would not have been valid: because no one can promise that another will give or do something. d. l. inter stipulantem and l. stipulatio ista in princ. and Inst. de inutil. stip. § si quando and C. de const. pec. auth. si quando. Moreover, the surety, by paying, did not manage the business of another for whom he did not intervene, although he may have labored for him: because that was by the nature of the obligation, which is consumed by one payment, not by the office of management, since it was paid by virtue of the promise and out of necessity, as is noted. D. de neg. gest. l. facto. Furthermore, this surety cannot be sued for the act of him for whom he did not stand as surety: therefore he ought not to be able to act against him for whom he did not intervene: because the rule is the same for contraries. D. de act. empt. l. Iul. § si procurator where therefore by the contrary. Moreover, the law says that if one surety stands surety for the father, and another for Martinus Conreis, that these are not sureties, because they did not both intervene for both: but each for each, as D. de fideiuss. l. si a Titio. Moreover, suretyship is of strict law. And therefore it is not extended to another person. D. de fideiuss. l. fideiussores magistratuum and D. ad mun. l. 2 and D. de mag. conv. l. 1. 2. responso. Unless therefore the creditors have assigned their rights to the surety, the surety does not seem to be able to act by his own right. D. de sol. l. modestin. and l. Stichum § si mandato D. man. l. Pap. but that is true, that he cannot bring the action of the creditors: but his own, from his own contract, if he has one. To the contrary it seems, that the surety is bound and acts, when they are partners: because one represents the other, and they are seen as mutual institors. D. de exerc. l. 1 in fi. and therefore the surety employed by both, since both are participants in the risk, arg. D. de arbit. l. si duo and it seems expressed. D. de institoria l. cuiusque. Also this is confirmed for the surety by the municipal law, which wants that whoever contracts with one of them be bound in solidum, but

† A suretyship is a contract in the broad sense, as the authorities teach in l. 1, D. si certum petatur. But it seems that the third opinion should be embraced. That is, that the surety cannot bring an action unless against either of the two debtors, insofar as the partnership creates a shared risk. D. de pactis, l. si unus, vers. idem in duobus. Unless he pays due to the fault of one only: for then he would have recourse against that one alone, since the effect of the risk does not pertain to the blameless party, arg. D. de tutoribus et curatoribus distr. bon., l. 1, § nunc tractemus; and C. de transactionibus, l. 1; and C. de duobus reis, l. 1. For he by whose act the surety has fallen into the obligation seems to be the only one who should be sued. Solution: If indeed at the time of the suretyship the partnership had been contracted, and the rule is that the partnership for which one had given surety would have one bound by stipulation, and the other bound by an obligation arising from negotiorum gestio or by a useful institoria action. D. de negotiorum gestione, l. 3, in fine, together with the following law. But if the partnership in which the debts were contracted had not then been formed, then this surety cannot bring an action in any way: for neither by stipulation, nor by a useful institoria action, because there was no institor, nor by negotiorum gestio, because the business did not pertain to him who was not a partner. Moreover, it matters greatly whether one gives surety for the person sinking in the partnership, or in the exercise of the trade: and then the suretyship does not touch, except him for whom; or whether for the social commerce and social profit, and then it touches both: hence, with respect to the suretyship, the force of the claim must be founded. arg. D. de fideiussoribus, l. si Titius, § pro socio; l. socium qui, § fin.; D. de minoribus, l. 3, § si quid; D. de institoribus, l. cuiuscunque, § non tamen omne; D. de procuratoribus, l. si procurator meus, § fin.; and what is noted there by the gloss and by Guillaume de Cuyk; and what is noted there is to be weighed.

† And understand that if there are two partnerships, the beginning of the time of each partnership must be ascertained. D. pro socio, l. si id quod, § si filius. And note D. de negotiorum gestis, l. Pomponius, in negotiis.

It must also be known that a new partnership is not created by new acts subsequent to and explanatory of the old ones; otherwise, if they are entirely new. C. loca. l. si cum hermes. Therefore, the quality of the acts must be weighed. ff. de neg. ge. l. at qui natura. §. si eum. and l. eum actum. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus.

casus: CASE. The point is as follows. And having seen the acts and proceedings in the case being litigated between Ludouicus Guidarelli on one part, and the heir of Bartholomaeus Bontagni on the other part, and especially on the points inscribed. It is asked, what are the duties of the lords consuls in the aforementioned case. And on the part of the said Ludouicus it is said, and alleged, that notwithstanding the petition produced, and other acts made before the judge instituted on the nullity, nevertheless the lords consuls ought to execute the sentence given by them against do. Magdalenam, heir of the said Bartholomaeus, and to adjudge and give to the said Ludouicus what remains unpaid, because it can appear from the acts through the lords consulting, that no cause of nullity exists in the said sentence, or in its process, per no. per Inno. in c. cum mater. de officio, et po. iu. deleg. Secondly, because in the said cause of nullity it ought not, nor can it, proceed further before the judge before whom the nullity was claimed: for the judge of nullity, by the will of the parties, set a term of three days for paying the tenth, and for contesting the litigation in the aforementioned cause, and nothing was ever paid in the name of the tenth. Hence, from the form of the statutes of the commune of Perugia, especially by virtue of the statute under the heading de decimo soluem. in casi. ciuilibus, it appears that before the judge where the said cause of nullity is pending, it ought not be heard further, nor can he cognize it of his own right: and the sentence which would be rendered there on the part of the non-paying party would not be valid. Hence, having seen the said statute, it is similarly asked, what is the law. Thirdly, that a year and more, by four months or so, has elapsed since the nullity was claimed, and thus it is chosen on the part of the said Ludouicus that the cause of nullity is deserted. Fourthly, the reformation issued by the priors, and the cause in the year of our Lord 1333, in the month of April, is alleged, and also the reformation recently issued. Since in the first reformation the jurisdiction and cognition of the judge of appeals and nullities, etc., is removed, as they are shown to us in form, to all of which are inserted, and also other acts and proceedings between the aforementioned, it is asked, what are the duties of the said lords consuls.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Before the judge pronounces on the nullities, the matter of nullities is pending before that same judge, and therefore in the meantime the lords consuls cannot execute [the sentence]: because a prejudicial question is pending before a superior judge. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an uncompleted delict in cases of assassination is to be punished.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† He who wished another to be assassinated, and made a deposit, yet the act did not proceed further, nevertheless, according to Johannes de Monarchia and Johannes Andreae, is punished by a temporal penalty, as if the crime were consummated. Thus we note in c. Humanitatis, de Homicidio, lib. 6, because it is an atrocious crime: but this is true with regard to temporal penalties, which are expressed in that chapter: not with regard to the penalty of municipal statutes, which require the consummated act. C. ad l. Cornelia, de Sicariis; l. Is qui cum telo, de Poenis; l. Aut facta, §. Eventus. And therefore I say that the penalty will be arbitrary, and it will be the ultimate punishment, and mutilation of a member. ff. de Extraordinariis Criminibus, l. 1. and fully in l. Si quis non dicam rapere. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the emphyteutic right fails in the person of one, when it accrues to another.
2. Whether an ecclesiastical emphyteusis passes to heirs.
3. When an emphyteusis goes per stirpes, and when per capita according to hereditary shares.
4. Whether division is prejudicial in an emphyteusis.
5. If in a division someone renounces the emphyteusis, whether the renunciation is prejudicial to himself.
6. A church cannot confer upon another a right not yet vested in itself: unless with consent, even if that right is merely in expectancy.
7. Although a prelate may enfeoff and grant in emphyteusis, nevertheless he cannot, by acting prematurely before the proper time, prejudice his successor.
casus:
CASE. The point of the question is as follows. Lord Bartolus, Abbot of the monastery of San. Christophani de Duran., by himself and his successors, with the consent of Lord Benedict, a monk of the said monastery, present there, gave, consented, and renewed, for a canon not paid, to Lord Guidon, clerk, or tutor of Francis and Dynus, sons of the late Ser Nando, stipulating and receiving for the said Lords Francis and Bartolus, and for their sons and grandsons up to their third generation completed, so that the share of the deceased shall devolve upon and accrue to the survivors, certain pieces of land contained in the instrument, over the course of time. After the death of the said tutor, the said Francis, Dynus, and Bartolus made a division of the said things: and the said Dynus and Francis, as to the share falling to them, were renewed by the said monastery: And the said Bartolus, as to his share, was similarly renewed by the aforementioned monastery; nor does it appear in the instruments of the second renewal that Bartolus, Dynus, and Francis consented. Each of the aforementioned held and possessed their part of these things in severalty for 10 days and more. It is asserted that the said Bartolus was renewed a second time by the said monastery for the said share together with the said Jacoba, his wife, the said Dynus and Francis being ignorant thereof. In the year past, the said Bartolus died, the said Francis surviving, and leaving Nardus, his son; after the death of the said Bartolus, the said Nardus, his son, was last renewed by the aforementioned monastery for the said share, which, upon his dying without sons, was to devolve to the said Lady Jacoba, his mother, and to Angelus Saluecti, cousin of the said Lady Jacoba. After the death of the said Nardus, son of the said Bartolus, the said Francis, by virtue of the first renewal made to his tutor, entered into possession of the said share, before the said Lady Jacoba and Angelus apprehended possession of the same thing; then the said Lady Jacoba and Angelus likewise entered into the said possession without the will of the said Francis; a sequestration of the fruits of the said share was made, and a term was given to the parties to state their right.

Alternatively, on behalf of Lady Jacoba and Angelus, that the said Lady Jacoba and Angelus are in a stronger right.
