First, because of the division made; Second, because of the last renewal made to the said Nardus, and the said Lady Jacoba and Angelus. And because they say that they possess the said share on behalf of the said Francis, it is said that the said Francis is stronger in dominion and in possession in the said share of Bartolus, by virtue of the instrument made to the said tutor, and the pacts therein to which they were unwilling, by which the portion of the failing party accrues to the survivor. Nor does the division and remission of right contained in the instrument of division made between the said Francis, Dynus, and Bartolus, oppose this, because an emphyteutic thing cannot be divided. And Dynus and Francis, by remitting the right competent to them in the share of the said Bartolus, could not by dividing abdicate such right from themselves. Nor do the renewals made afterwards by Bartolus and the said Nardus, his son, oppose this, because they could not be made to the prejudice of the said Francis and his mother, the said Francis being ignorant and not consenting. From which it follows, and it seems, that the right to the said share devolved upon the aforementioned Francis; and he is stronger in possession, and Dynus excluded, against the said Lady Jacoba and Angelus aforementioned. Who, Angelus and Lady Jacoba, seem to have incurred the penalty from the aforementioned molestation. And consequently, the fruits are to be restored to the said Francis. Which being inserted, it is asked, who is prior in the said thing, and to whom the fruits are to be adjudged.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† To make the matter evident, it must be premised that emphyteusis sometimes takes its root and beginning in the person of one individual; but afterwards, on account of the multitude of successors, it comes to several persons. And in this case, without any agreement, it reverts from one who fails to another who supervenes from the same stock. And there is a manifold reason for this. The first reason is that he alone is found to represent the stock and to retain its image; hence, through whatever hands it may have passed, it returns to him who represents its beginning and its stock, as in c. j. §. cum vero Conradus, qui feudum dare possunt, col. 10; and cf. C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi, §. 1, in ratione sui. The second reason is that this emphyteusis runs by way of acquisition mortis causa, and has its nature; and therefore the right of accretion applies, not only conventional but also legal, as in D. de fideicommissis, l. Thais ancilla, §. Stichus servus. The third reason is that it does not matter whether it always remains with one, or whether several revert to one. l. sicut, §. si, quod cuiusque universitatis. Therefore, whether it goes from one to one, or reverts to one, the law is the same. The fourth reason is that every number of those who are substituted in the place of one is considered as one and a single person. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cui fundus, in fine. The fifth reason is that this is by virtue of consolidation due to the emphyteutic nature, as in Inst. de locat. et conduct., §. adeo; and cf. C. de re in praesenti, §. videamus. When the person who formed part fails, the whole consolidates into one through concurrence. l. 1, in fine, de usufructu accrescendi; and what is noted in l. 2, si pars haeredum, per haereditatis petitionem. And therefore the lapsed portion consolidates with another portion by reason of the person into whom alone, as into a new shoot, all the remnants of the ancient root stand. And just as in a tree there are many shoots upon the stock: for if you cut off all, leaving one upon the stock, the whole sap of the stock flows there; therefore, in the case at hand, the natural example should be followed. This one is indeed bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, Gen. 2. Therefore, it pertains to him by the law of the law, by the law of signification, and by the law of nature; and it does not revert to the church; and this by tacit ordination and with every right of accretion circumscribed. D. de legatis secundis, l. Titium Seio, §. cum inter patrem. The sixth reason is that, when the person is extinguished, whether by sword, impediment, or successive order, the person or degree which is not found to be extinguished remains, as in Auth. de non alienando, §. emphyteusis; and D. de in ius vocando, l. posthumorum; de legatis secundis, l. cum ita, §. si. And thus the edict concerning succession has place. We see this by example in the Kingdom of Apulia, which is emphyteutic; which by its nature goes to the posterity of the royal blood according to their degrees, and does not revert to the church. Seventh, this is proved expressly in ro. col., an filius vel agnatus, c. 1. Eighth, this is proved by the Auth. doc., because the word "until" the third or until the fourth generation always renewed from generation to generation by repeating and renewing. D. qui modis ususfructus amittatur, l. si cum in annos; D. de verborum obligationibus, l. stipulatio ista, §. si quis ista. Hence, if one is diminished in head or removed by death, another is called to the whole. The same if he renounces. D. de inofficioso testamento, l. si is qui, in the word "nolit, aut non possit." Of this, however, I will say below. Regarding this repetitive reason and the main point, see fully Bartolus, de verborum obligationibus, l. si mihi et Titio. Ninth, it is proved because it seems tacitly agreed that provision is made for the genus as long as they exist in the designated degree. de legatis secundis, l. peto, §. fratre; or in perpetuity, if in perpetuity. D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si; C. de contrahenda et communi stipulatione, l. secundum responsum domini Ulpiani. Tenth, this is proved: it is certain that the patronage of the church passes to the heirs, especially of blood, who are to be preferred, de iure patronatus, c. 1, per Innocentius. Also, it is certain that the right of patronage, although as to substance it is not divided, yet as to the voice it is divided; hence it is said that such a one has half the voice: when there are two, each has half the voice. c. 1, de iure patronatus, lib. 6. And yet if one of the heirs dies without an heir, the survivor will have the whole and entire voice, and nothing of liberty reverts to the church. 16 q. 7, c. considerandum; D. de assignmentibus, lib. 1, vtrum. Therefore, a similar rule should be said with regard to emphyteusis and fief. And this is the very truth.

† Whenever an emphyteusis takes its origin in the person of several individuals—for example, in the persons of Titius and Seius—one must then consider the derivation. For, from Titius, derivation occurs to his descendants with the right of accretion among themselves, that is, with the right of devolution; for here I broadly understand the right of accretion as the right of augmenting and reverting. This is supported by what is noted in the Authenticum on Marriage, in the beginning, column 4, and in the Authenticum on Incestuous Marriages, in the beginning, column 3. And similarly, from Seius, derivation occurs to his descendants, as stated in the Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations, in the law “Pater Severinam,” § 1; and in the Digest, On Vulgar Substitution, in the law “Cohaeredi,” § “Qui discretas.” However, there is no place for the right of accretion from the heirs of Titius to the heirs of Seius, because they are distinct in their respective stems, as stated in column 10 of the title “De duobus fratribus” in the Decretals, On New Benefices, chapter 1. And this is true, unless the pact of reverting from one to the other has been added; for then it reverts by the force of the form of the contract, as in the Code, On Donations, in the laws “Quae sub modo” and “Quotiens”; in the Digest, On Deposit, in the law “Publia,” in the beginning; and as noted in the Digest, On Donations, in law 1, in the great gloss. The reason of the law supports this. In the Digest, On Deposit, in law 1, § “Si convenerit,” it is stated that, in this case, it exceeds its simple nature. The cited § and the Code, On the Right of Emphyteusis, chapter “Quaedam,” require two qualities: namely, that the person be of the descendants, and that he be an heir. And this passes to posterity, if they are heirs; otherwise, if they have repudiated the inheritance of their progenitors, from whom it came. This is supported by what is noted in the Digest, On the Petition of Inheritance, in the laws “Et non tamen” and “Liberti, libertaeque,” according to Cynus; and in the Code, On Free Persons, in the law “Qui se patris,” according to Nicolaus de Tudeschis. The chapter “Quaedam” requires only one quality, namely, that the person be of the descendants; and here, repudiation by the heir does not harm. This is supported by the Digest, On the Trebellian Trust, in the law “Quia perinde”; and in the Digest, On the Work of Freedmen and on Defamation, § “Si liberi,” and there according to Bartolus; in the Digest, On Acquiring an Inheritance, in the law “Pro haerede,” § “Si sepulchrum”; in the Digest, On Violation of a Sepulcher, in the law “Quaesi”; in the Digest, On Urban Servitudes, in the law “Si domus”; in the Digest, On Free Goods, in the law “Si filius.” And this is what must be premised.

Thirdly, it must be premised that sometimes the mention of an heir is a distributive addition, and then the emphyteusis proceeds according to the hereditary shares. Sometimes it is disjunctive, or demonstrative, and then it operates according to the virile shares, which is not the case in the cited chapter 1 in the Clementines.

Fourthly, it must be premised that in emphyteusis, a division ad oculum [i.e., a physical division] is not prejudicial; just as that division which occurs by operation of law among heirs is not. For this physical division proceeds from the other, intellectual division, as its execution, and by equity it does not alter the nature of the thing. This is supported by the Digest, On the Action of Sale, Law Julius, Section Idem Celsus.

† Fifth, it must be premised that, when it is asked whether a renunciation made in a division is prejudicial, it matters whether the renunciation was made in the hands of the owner: and it is prejudicial to him, according to the edict of the aediles, in the law *Quaeritur*, § *Si venditor*. Whether it was made in the hands of a co-heir: and then it is not prejudicial except as regards the co-heir, and insofar as it concerns his interest. D. *De pactis*, l. *Nemo*; and, the facts being thus, D. *De verbis obligatorum*, l. *Qui Romae*, § *Si*. And because this renunciation made upon division is not absolute, but is accessory to the division, and is causative with respect to the co-heir, because the renunciation was made for his benefit. C. *Ad Velleianum*, l. *Iubemus*. And therefore, upon his death, without an heir of the blood, it does not revert to the church, but pertains to the survivor. It supports what we have said, D. *De pactis*, l. *Idem in duobus*, in the beginning; and D. *De manumissionibus*, l. 1, in the reasoning of itself.

Sixthly, and lastly, it must be premised that the church cannot confer upon another a right not clearly established in its own favor, unless with the consent of the right-holder, even if that right is merely in prospect. D. de aqua pluviali arc. l. diem, at the end, where the text is noted, and col. 10, tit. 2, c. 1, where it is expressly stated, unless the right subsequently accrued to the church, which would confirm the preceding act done by the chapter and the prelate, but not by the prelate alone. D. de rei vend. l. si a Titio.

† Although it is noted that sometimes only the prelate may enfeoff and grant in emphyteusis, nevertheless, by acting beforehand before the time, he cannot prejudice his successor, as is argued from Leg. 1, l. a filiis, §. diuus, Leg. 2, l. vnum ex familia in principio. However, the Chapter is always one and the same, and has no successor, because it does not die, as is noted in ff. si quis ius dicendum non obtemperauerit, l. 1, §. fin., and it is established in c. vltimum, de procuratoribus, in the Clementines. From the foregoing it appears that the prior, with respect to the ancient concession, is preferred to the most recent one. ff. de pignoribus, l. si superatus; l. si partem, §. 1, quemadmodum servus amittitur; ff. de publicaniis, l. si autem, §. si duobus; Cod. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. si ante; and it is established in Cod. communia de legibus, l. fin., §. si autem ob avaritiae; and Auth. res, quae. That which is subject to acquisition by reason of death seems to be subject to the last will. Cod. familiae herciscundae, l. filiae cuius. And therefore the rule of the said Auth. has application, which is noted. Weigh well, which I say: because you will not find them so perfectly stated elsewhere. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the mother is bound to request a guardian for her son, and whether she can purge delay, and within what time she must make the request.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows: Benevenuto died intestate, leaving his wife Berta, who was pregnant and then aged thirty years and more, who, after the death of the said Benevenuto, bore a male child after six months and more, who was named John. And after the death of the said Benevenuto, the said John died in pupillary age, namely at the age of fourteen months, without having accepted the inheritance of his said father, either by himself or by another in his name; and without guardianship of the said John having been requested or assumed by his said mother Berta, or by any other person, nor a guardian having been requested to be appointed for him, leaving his said mother surviving him, and leaving surviving him Antonio, son of the said Berta and uncle of the said John, and leaving surviving him Francisco, paternal uncle of the said John and full brother of Benevenuto, father of the said John, and Baldutia, cousin sister of the said John and daughter of the late Paulucius, full brother of the said Benevenuto; who Francisco and Baldutia had held property in common between them during the lifetime of the said Benevenuto, and after the death of Benevenuto, the said John remained and dwelt with them in common until the time of his death.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This case very rarely occurs in fact, and the question does not appear to proceed under the new law. For, since a woman today has a year to make a claim, as stated in C. de legatis tutoribus, l. sciant, and Inst. ad Tertullianum, §. si et quandocunque, and within that year she may purge the delay, which was not the case under the old law, ff. ad Tertullianum, l. 2, §. confestim, and this opinion is maintained by general custom. It is impossible to find this year in one who is in the womb, as in Auth. de restitutione, and that which she bears, §. si. Certainly, if while pregnant she does not seek a curator for the womb, in this respect nothing has been changed by the new law. And therefore the mother is deprived of the succession of the child born before puberty, ff. ad Tertullianum, l. 2, §. quod si cum praegnans. And although it may never seem so, nevertheless, in favor of minors, it is so established, lest the goods which ought to come to them be dissipated beforehand, or taken away in custody, before they are born. And therefore, in our case, the mother being excluded, the uterine sister of the said John comes: because she is nearer than others, as in Auth. post fratres. And sometimes the very truth makes it so that the mother does not have a full year to make a claim: for example, if her son at the time of the father’s death has 13 years and one month, and dies, let us say on the penultimate day of pupillary age, certainly the mother will not be excused; rather, the mother will be deprived, as in the aforementioned §. confestim, since this penalty was established for the sake of the pupilli, and the mother committed the delay, and did not purge it, nor can she purge it, she is excluded from the succession. And the same applies to others who hope for the first place in legitimate succession.

CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact, briefly stated, upon which counsel is now required, is as follows. A certain man named Ciolus Ioan. de Gualdo was condemned to death by the podestà of the land of Gualdo aforesaid; because it is said that at the place and time set forth in the inquisition formed against him, he had conversation, dealings, and conspiracy with Ludouico Anlocti de Micolotis of Perugia, and his emissaries, a traitorous rebel and enemy of the commune of Perugia, with the intent and purpose of subverting the good state of the land of Gualdo; and that he had done and committed other things, as contained in the said condemnation. After this, before the condemnation was passed against him, he made his last will and testament, in which, among other things which he made and disposed, he left by way of legacy to a certain woman called Ciola, daughter of the late Gioli Citroli formerly of Assisi, and Mina de Gualdo, for her salary, because the said Ciolus asserted in the said testament that she had served him for 8 years past by right, and had stood by his family, one piece of land situated in his holding, as set forth in the said testament, bounded: and also a piece of land under cultivation, likewise declared in the said testament. After this, the said Ciolus, as stated, was condemned to death for the causes declared in the said condemnation; and execution was carried out on his person according to the tenor of the said condemnation. After this, a lawsuit was brought by the said Ciola against the heirs and possessors of the goods of the said Ciolus. The said Ciola came to this agreement with the heirs and possessors of the goods of the late said Ciolus, namely, that the said cause and lawsuit, the said heirs on one part and the said Ciola on the other, by order of the judge, the podestà of the said land of Gualdo, and they compromised, in law and fact, and truth, and equity, according to the form of the statute of the land of Gualdo prevailing in the said land of Gualdo, into two good men: reserving and excepting the cases placed by the said statute under the rubric "de causis compromittendis" [on causes to be compromised], who did not wish to come to the said compromise. Now two doubts arise. The first is on the principal matter, namely, that the heirs and successors of the said Ciolus, to whom restitution was made of the goods of the said Ciolus, say that the said Ciolus, on account of the crime which was said to have been committed by him, was condemned to death; and could not make a will; and that his said testament is not valid in law. Another doubt is also, namely, that they say the said cause and lawsuit pending between the said Ciola and the agent on one part, and the said heirs and possessors of the goods of the late said Ciolus, on the occasion of the legacy made to the said Ciola in the testament of the late Ciolus, do not fall within the aforementioned compromise, notwithstanding the said reservation and exception made in the said compromise regarding the cases reserved and excepted in the said statute. And for the part of the said Ciola, servant of the late Ciolus, it is answered thus, namely, to the first doubt, that the testament of the said Ciolus was and is valid in law. First, because according to the form of the statute of the land of Gualdo placed under the rubric "de poena turbantis bonum statum comunis Gualdi" [on the penalty of one disturbing the good state of the commune of Gualdo], the penalty shall be pecuniary according to the form of the said statute: and in default of payment it was capital, and therefore it is said that the condemnation was null; and that the aforementioned testament is valid and holds in law. And furthermore, that the said legacy was not a simple legacy, considering the words appended in the said testament, namely, where it is said that the said legacy was made to the said Ciola, because the said testator asserted that the said Ciola had served him for the time of 8 years, and had stood by him as his servant for the said time, by which the said legacy ought to be conferred rather as a fact for compensation and satisfaction of the said service and servitude, than by right of donation or simple legacy. And furthermore, that in the case where the said testament would not be valid as a testament, at least that it is valid and ought to be valid as to the said legacies, as codicils, or by right of codicils. To the second doubt it is also answered thus, that the compromise was not made simply between the said parties regarding the said legacy, but regarding the cause and question which was between the said parties regarding the said things left to the said Ciola for her service and servitude, and the fruits thereof, and also on the occasion of the salary of the servitude and service of the said Ciola, and that the compromise, notwithstanding the said exception, is valid and holds, that the arbitrators, in whom the compromise was made, are and ought to know and terminate the said cause and lawsuit, considering the form of the said compromise. And that the said cause was and is pronounceable according to the form of the said Statute. Now, having seen the condemnation of the said Ciolus, having seen his testament, and the statute on the penalty of one disturbing the good state of the commune of Gualdo, on causes to be compromised, and the aforementioned compromise made between the aforementioned parties according to the pronouncement of the judge of the said commune, who pronounced the said cause to be compromiseable, it is asked, what is the law regarding the two said doubts: to which your prudence deigns to respond in law, and your counsel to respond on each of the said doubts clearly and openly, as is your custom: so that every doubt which could arise from the aforementioned doubts is totally removed. And your counsel to respond on the aforementioned matters with the laws by which your aforementioned prudence is moved to counsel and respond to the said doubts, and others which could be objected to the contrary.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute defining a penalty is seen to have departed from all common law.
2. What a capital sentence entails and what execution it brings with it.
3. Whether a person condemned to death may make a will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be considered that when a statute defines a penalty, it has departed from all common law, as in l. qui cum uno, §. qui post., de re militari, because even magistrates swear to observe statutes, as in Extra, de iureiurando, c. venientes. Secondly, it must be known that

† A capital sentence, as regards infamy and certain other effects, draws after it execution, unless the sentence is void by operation of law itself, as in D. de poenis, l. qui ultimo; or unless an appeal has been lodged, as in l. 1, in fine, ad turpil. and l. furti, § 1, de infa. For then the appeal rescinds the pronouncement: and the person is deemed not to have been made infamous, nor to have been rendered liable, who has suffered injury and corporal execution; or unless within the time for appealing a notoriously unjust execution has been carried out. It is supported by what is noted in D. de accusat., l. ex iudicio.

† However, this third case does not apply according to some: because he was immediately made a slave of the penalty by the sentence; therefore he could not make a will. Others say that he who does not lose his property does not become a slave of the penalty; for if he became a slave of the penalty, he would leave no property in the city. D. 28, 5, l. lex Cornelia. There are many other opinions on the matter. I say that since this sentence was passed contrary to the form of the statute, and in fact such most unjust sentence did not induce penal servitude. And since the right of appeal was at least notorious, execution could not be carried out within 10 days. This case is similar to that in which a decurion was condemned to the beasts. This unfortunate man was illicitly condemned to death, and through the gross negligence of the judge, without observing the statutes in condemning, nor the common law in executing. Hence, just as he could have donated his property, so too he could make a will regarding it. This is a new case. And on this point I judge that it should be decided thus. And so the said will is valid: due to the defect in the pronouncement, which was issued contrary to the form of the statute. I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. During the pendency of a dilatory exception and the term, execution cannot be carried out.
casus: CASE. Punctus. John is condemned to 1800 pounds and to a heavier penalty in the fourth degree: and it is added in the sentence that if he does not pay within 40 days, and then comes into the fortress of the commune of Perugia, his head shall be cut off by the executioners. Now the directors, who are the executors of sentences passed for the commune, carried out execution of the said quantity within the said 40 days. It is asked whether they could justly do this: or whether it is within the power of the said John to pay the said quantity, or not, and whether he remains under the ban of having his head cut off.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It appears to me that, while the alternative and disjunctive delay is pending, the judge’s office remains inactive. C. de dila. siue pars. Moreover, because it is the election of the condemned, not of the fisc, in this case it has the effect that it does not. C. de ser. fug. l. quicunque. Furthermore, before the term granted to those sentenced, which is these 40 days, execution cannot be carried out against the principal; therefore, neither can it be carried out against the father, just as it cannot be carried out against the surety, as C. de us. rei iud. l. si. in fi. Also, if an heir is ordered to pay a penalty within 40 days, and if he does not pay, to pay a thousand, he cannot be sued in the meantime; but the day must be awaited. l. i. de pen. leg. Moreover, the matter is in suspense regarding the genus of the final penalty. de cond. inde. si non sortem. §. si. Also, the benefit of election ought not to be taken away, as Inst. de act. §. plus. de eo quod cer. lo. l. non utique. Wherefore I say that the directors cannot in the meantime carry out execution of the said quantity, because we are uncertain in the meantime of the final outcome and the subsistence of the condemnation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a promisor who undertakes to see to it that another person shall deliver or give something is released from his obligation upon a change in the status of the person for whom the promise was made, or whether he remains bound to pay the penalty or interest.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Whether one who promises to do and to see to it that another will do, deliver, or give, is released if the status of the person for whom he promised changes; or whether he is bound to the penalty or to damages, is discussed. C. de exce. l. defensiones. ff. qui sat. cog. l. si decesserit. ff. de fideiuss. l. ubicunque. C. de fideius. l. 1. And briefly, the truth stands thus: either the person to whom the power and authority over the matter principally belongs changed his status after the delay of the promisor; and then the promisor is bound to damages, or to the penalty, if a penalty was promised. As in the said l. si decesserit. Or the status was changed without preceding delay; and then it matters whether it was such a debt or act that can be fulfilled notwithstanding the change of status, and even then the promisor is not released; but he is bound to fulfill it, as in the said l. 1. C. de fideius. Or it is such a debt or act that cannot be fulfilled on account of the change of status; and then the promisor is released, as in the said l. si decesserit. And note, as in l. si vero. in prin. However, in that case, if he received anything on account of that promise, he must restore it; since the contract could not be fulfilled on his part. ff. de condi. ob cau. l. si hęres. Now it must be seen whether this act of sale and obligation can be performed by another. And it is held that it can; because those things which are in giving can be carried out by any giver. l. fi. de condi. instit. nihil. It does not matter from whom it is given, provided it is given. C. de ca. tol. §. ne autem. Also, he who promised to give a certain promisor and solver is released by giving another equally good, if the first who was to promise does not wish or cannot bind himself. arg. ff. de consti. pe. l. promissor Stichi. §. fi. and ff. de arb. l. labeo. in fi. And it seems expressed. ff. de exce. do. l. fideiussor euictionis. To the contrary it seems, because it is in the interest of the buyer to have had it from the owner rather than from the fiscus; especially when confiscation arises from partiality of lands; because eviction depends on fortune, to which the stipulator is not bound to subject himself. ad Treb. l. qui ita. §. etiam. Therefore, I think the price ought to be returned, because: in this way both parties are provided for. arg. ff. de solu. l. cum Stichus. But damages or penalty are not due; because delay did not precede. And so I say and advise. I, Baldus.

In the name of Christ, Amen. Lord Nicolaus and Franciscus were instituted if no male child should be born; and from the universal institution, or the vulgar substitution made in the event that a son should not be born or should not be heir, they are not repelled by reason of a suspect statutory guardianship (tutela legitima), or on the grounds that a guardian (tutor) was not petitioned for.

† But there is a doubt, because they were substituted to daughters already born under the condition "if she should die without children," and, having considered the terms of what was left for a dowry in that legacy or bequest, a vulgar substitution is included under this expectation, "if she could not be endowed," because they died before marriageable years, de vulg. sub. l. qui habebat. And in an express vulgar substitution, as I have said, the law sciant cuncti does not apply. Wherefore I say that the substitutes, and the same institutes, Lord Nicolaus and Franciscus, would have the better rights if they had petitioned for a guardian, C. de insti. et subst. l. fi. per doc. Nor is the testament null, since meanwhile the daughters were substituted in maintenance and other amounts; for an institution or substitution made under the designation of an amount includes also the maintenance left to the person to whom the substitution was made, ad Treb. l. ita cogi. Nevertheless, the legitime is owed to the mother as if from the goods of the daughters, except insofar as the substitution appears to be pupillary. But certainly the substitutes are excluded under this head of pupillary substitution, because they did not petition for a guardian; therefore, the mother has a right in the legitime of her daughters. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The collation of an abbot existing in quasi-possession of the right of conferring holds good, notwithstanding that another claims to be the patron.
2. Whether an excommunicated person can confer a benefice.
3. Whether one who has been absolved after a presentation made by patrons can freely confer.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Inasmuch as the Abbot of San Vito was, and is, in quasi-possession of the right of conferring, the collation made by him held good: notwithstanding that another claims to be the patron; de elec. c. querelam; de iu. pat. c. consultationibus; de caupos. c. cum olim, I speak of where indeed that canonical impediment does not stand in the way of the ordinary collator. For if he were excommunicated, or suspended from office, or from benefice, or even from office alone, he could not confer if his excommunication were public,

† because he would have been publicly denounced as excommunicated; de consuet. c. cum dilect.; de re iud. c. ad probandum; de sen. excom. c. si quem, and c. latores; de cle. excon. If, however, it were secret, the acts done by him would be valid, as above by the cited laws; to this effect the notable gloss in ff. de testa. l. cum l. and there by the gloss and Bald.; and in the Auth. de tab. §. pe. in the singular ordinary gloss, which says that what a secretly deposed notary does is valid, and it is not found elsewhere. And the aforesaid applies while the suspension lasts; but once it ceases he can freely confer, nor does the six-month period run in the meantime, as in c. quia diuersitatem, de conces. pręb., and the note in c. fi. de elec.

† and, the Abbot conferring after absolution within the six-month period, a presentation previously made by the patrons would not stand in the way, even if they were truly patrons, by the aforesaid laws, since it is customary for the said benefice to be conferred by the Abbot of the said Monastery of San Vito. I, Franciscus, etc. And I, Petrus, say the same, etc. THE CASE. In the name of the Lord, Amen. The fact is set forth thus: a certain person having property, and a broad substance of movables and immovables, entered the religion of the Friars Preachers, and there made profession. The prior of the said order and the convent, in the person of the said professus, claims the goods that belonged to the professing person at the time of profession, which are now possessed by those who would succeed the professing person upon intestacy if he had died naturally without making profession. The question now is whether the said goods are owed to the said order, or to those coming upon intestacy. Having considered the words of the Blessed Dominic uttered with the last breath of his life, the founder of the said order, enacting thus: “These, most beloved brothers, are what I leave to you to be possessed as sons: have charity; preserve humility; possess voluntary poverty. But with all the strictness I can, I forbid anyone to bring possessions into this order, imprecating the curse of God upon anyone who does the contrary.” Having also seen the constitution of the Friars Preachers, in which, among other things, it is contained that possessions and revenues are in no way to be received. Having also seen a certain apostolic privilege granted to the same order in the form written below, namely: “Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the Master and Friars of the Order of Preachers, greeting and apostolic blessing. Whereas formerly on your part it had been set forth to Pope Clement of happy memory, our predecessor, that certain prelates, clerics, and laymen situated in various parts of the world, asserting that you were dead and unable to possess property, were striving on such occasion to exclude you from any successions whatsoever; and it was nevertheless humbly petitioned from the same predecessor that, lest it should happen that you incur any harm on account of such people, he should apply a suitable remedy in this regard; the same predecessor by apostolic authority declared that you could succeed in the temporal goods to which you would have succeeded had you remained in the world, and could take possession of the goods themselves, and sell them, and convert their price to your utility as it should seem most expedient to you. We therefore, inclined in this part to your supplications and following in the footsteps of the same predecessor, declare by the tenor of the present letters that you can succeed to his goods and take possession of them, as shall be just, and moreover convert their price to the aforesaid utility.”

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The Preaching Brothers are called mendicants.
2. Who are called mendicants.
1. Whether the mendicant brothers, and those of Saint Dominic, can hold anything in their own or common property. The same opinion is held by Lauro de Arezzo in the law *Deo nobis*, under the title *De episcopis et clericis*.
2. Whether the goods of one entering the monastery of the Preachers should belong to the monastery, or rather to the intestate heirs.
3. In those dedicated to God, a fourfold status is found.
4. Under the name of possessions are included movables, actions, and the names of debtors.
5. Add also that it was consulted below by Niccolò de' Cassoli, in consultation 476.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the aforementioned point, and having read the words which the blessed Dominic, at the end of his life, entrusted to his brothers, and also having examined the constitution of the Friars Preachers disposing that possessions are not to be accepted, and having examined the privilege of Pope Nicholas, it must be considered to whom the said inheritance is due. Having considered the common law. Having considered the words of the blessed Dominic. Having considered the constitution of the said Friars Preachers. Having considered furthermore the apostolic privilege.

It must be premised that, according to the common law, the Friars Preachers are mendicants: and they serve Christ the poor in the strictest poverty. On the concession of prelates, c. *Nimis*; on elections, c. *Quorundam*; on regulars, c. *Constitutionem*; on the status of regulars, c. 1; on the excesses of prelates, c. 1, Book 6; on penalties, c. *Cupientes*; on sentence of excommunication, c. 1, in the *Clementinae*; and in the *Extravagantes*, c. *Quia quorundam*; on regulars, c. *Ut professores*, in the *Clementinae*.

† And those are called mendicants whose profession, rule, or constitutions forbid them to have revenues or possessions for adequate sustenance, but who are accustomed to provide for themselves through public begging, which is an uncertain mendicancy. On the matter of dowry, c. 1, bk. 6, in the word *confirmatos*; and according to the gloss on excesses of prelates, c. 1, bk. 6, in the second gloss: they do not indeed have anything certain from which to take their livelihood, and they beg, suffering a defect, to which they are sometimes succored. And thus is the uncertain support of the mendicant, as stated in the aforementioned c. 1 on the matter of dowry. But those are not properly called mendicants who can have property of their own, even if they do not have it and in fact beg. For if they are actually begging, they are not so in status; since we consider a thing according to its status, not merely according to its act. Hence it is that even a church which was established as parochial from its beginning does not cease to be parochial, although it does not actually exercise the care of any souls. On elections, c. *Licet canonici*, Innocentius III; on new works, c. 1. Likewise, it is not considered a cure of souls, although it actually exercises care, since the care was not given to it by a superior, as noted on prebends, c. *De multa*. But they are considered mendicants by virtue of their constitutions, even if the constitutions are not approved by the Pope. For although a constitution could be revoked, as noted by John Andrea with sound reasons, and the Abbess in the aforementioned c. 1, which is noted by the gloss on rescripts, c. *Si*, bk. 6; although otherwise in the aforementioned election, c. *Ut professores*.

† Since, therefore, according to the common law, mendicants are constituted in the strictest poverty, it is clear that this Order cannot have property in common: for, since they are not permitted to appropriate anything to themselves, and they are to serve Christ the poor in the strictest poverty, such alienation must be understood both in the particular and in the common. That it applies to the particular is evident, because this accords with the profession by which one renounces property, as is shown in c. Cum ad monasterium, in fine, de statu monachorum; and in the decretal Exiit, under the word “proinde.” That it applies to the common is evident in the decretal Exiit, in c. Proinde, and in the extraneous constitution c. Quia quorundam, Ad conditorem.

† Therefore, what will be the case regarding such goods according to common law? It is not established that, as is provided for minors, they are incapable of succession. In which case, nothing comes to the order; rather, those who succeed intestate inherit, as noted by Bartolus in his *Minorica*, leaving it in doubt as to other mendicants. Guillaume, in the *Speculum*, under *De statu monachorum*, word 3, argues that the goods do not pass to the order, as it is incapable, citing *Obiectum*, Law *Mulier*, *De legatis* 1; Law *Apud Iulianum*, in the end, *De hereditatibus instituendis*; Law 1, *De actione empti*; Law *Transactio*, § *Si tibi*; and that they come to the sons or grandsons, *Institutiones*, *De qualitate hereditatum*, § *Sui*; *Pro herede*, Law 2, § *Si*; or, if they do not exist, to those succeeding intestate, such as collaterals, since the entrant is considered dead. But there he holds that they come to the order: which, if it cannot hold them, can nevertheless sell them for its necessities, *Digestum*, *De iure dotium*, Law *Cum in fundo*. For even a slave cannot have property, yet he holds what is left to him, *De legatis* 2, Law *Debitor*, § *Si*; and that the order can demand said goods, although individuals cannot retain them, yet they wish to live, *De officio ordinarii*, Chapter *Intereram*, 86, *Distinction*; Chapter *Pascae*. For co-slaves can demand whereof they may live, Law *His*, *De his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt*; Law *Servos*, *De alienis legatis*; and Law *Si in metallum*, *De his quae pro non scripto habentur*. And the poor, *Clementina*, per Law *Caetera*, § *Si duobus*, *De legatis* 1; Law *Si servi*, and *Digestum*, *De legatis* 3, Law *Fideicommissum*, § *Si servo*. Innocentius, *De probationibus*, Chapter *In praesentia*, puts forth an opinion saying that, according to some, the goods are held as derelict, and thus are granted to the occupant, Law 1, *Pro derelicto*; and they are in the case of caducity, Law *Unica*, *De caducis tollendis*. Others say that they come to those succeeding intestate, from which the professed is feigned dead, as in the said Law *Deo nobis*. Others say that they come to the diocesan of the place, 16, q. 1, Chapter *Qui vere*, *De episcopis et clericis*; Chapter *Nulli*. Others say that the order takes them, not to retain for itself, but to sell; it helps *De relictis dotis*, Chapter 1, Book 6, in the gloss. For since they must live by alms, these [goods] yield in place of alms. It helps *De donationibus*, Chapter *Cum dilecti*. But as John and Hostiensis say there, let them observe by what right they do this. Generally, a pact succeeds in place of a thing, *Digestum*, *De usufructu*, Law *Quia qui precio*. From which it appears that nothing is sought for the order, since among religious some are non-mendicant, and these lack property in common, as proved above; therefore, nothing is sought for the order: because it cannot have it in common, nor in particular, as Chapter *Cum ad monasterium*. And because, having to beg and seek sustenance from another, now they would not beg, nor seek sustenance from another, but would have it from themselves, and receive it certainly, not uncertainly, which suits a beggar, as in the said Chapter 1, *De relictis dotis*. It helps *Clementina*, *Exivi*, in the end, that in the times there they could pass their life without their begging. And because if it were sought for the order, it would be against the substance of their rule and would be altered, and such a state is permitted, which also should not be, as in the said Chapter *Cum ad monasterium*. Therefore, let them live in poverty, as thus instituted; for indeed the state is more perfect, and by the addition of poverty in common, because thereby the solicitude of temporal things, love, and pride are removed, according to that, "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all." Therefore, they are incapable of such successions, as Law *Apud Iulianum*, in the end; and neither do they take those goods to sell, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, Law *Neque*. It is established that incapacity is in the order and persons. Therefore, let original acquisition be impeded, let charity itself be impeded; and because they are incapable of seeking: therefore also of selling: because incapacity as to acquiring equally applies, since it retains, whether to have perpetually, or to sell similarly, *De Iudaeis*, Chapter *Si*. The foregoing are assisted by the words of Blessed Dominic emitted in the last spirit of life, when he said, "How strictly I forbid that anyone introduce possessions into this order, invoking the curse of God upon him who does the contrary." Therefore, this constitution is prohibitive with the addition of a spiritual penalty. Similar *De locis*, Chapter 1; *De eo quod furatus est*, the order received, Chapter 1; *De simonia*, Chapter *Sicut tuis sagittariis*, Chapter 1; *De electione*, Chapter *Licet devitanda*. But the aforementioned words, "let no one introduce," can equally apply to tacit transfer, which is otherwise induced by confession; as *Authenticum*, *Ingressi*; and as is declared expressly by words, *De donationibus*, Chapter 1, *Cum taciti*. And tacit and express have the same reason, as in a similar case by the doctors in *Authenticum*, *Consequenter*. This is proved by the words of the constitution disposing that possessions are not to be received. Therefore, the constitution itself seems to prohibit not only reception, which is caused by another instigating, but also that which is by one's own motion; although these otherwise differ among themselves, *De praedictis*, Chapter 1, *De praebendis*, supra *Motu*, Book 6, *Eodem titulo*, Law *Romanus*; *Clementina*, *De executione*, Chapter *Cum ecclesiasticae*. And thus, as to possessions, the words of the constitution are related, and if such a professed had movables at the time of profession, yet because acquisition by reason of profession is indivisible and proceeds universally, movables cannot be separated from immovables. It is established that such acquisition is *in ius universum*; therefore, it did not receive separation, Law 3, *De bonis possessionibus*. It helps *In ratione sui*, *Digestum*, *De administratione tutorum*, Law *Cum quaeritur*, *De negotiis gestis*, Law *Eum actum*. Nor does an apostolic privilege cooperate with acquisition as to the order: because the privilege disposes of things coming to one already professed; because it disposes that they take what they could take while existing in the secular world. But this belonged to the one professing before the profession itself. And it differs whether something comes to a professed or not professed: because in the first case, advents are sought for the order, *De privilegiis*, Chapter *Cum olim*. But in the case where it is sought, it is in the power of the holder to profit, as in *Authenticum*, *Si qua mulier*, joined with *Clementina*, *Exivi*. Furthermore, the privilege disposes over new acquisition, there they strove to exclude from successions. But not over the retention of what is already acquired. These differ among themselves, as is clear *De Iudaeis*, Chapter *Iudaei*; and *De relictis dotis*, Chapter 1, Book 6. Furthermore, the privilege disposes of acquisition to be made by the person, not the place. These differ among themselves, *De officio*, Law *Quam abbas*, *Eodem titulo*, Law *Is cui*, Book 6; and *De legatis* 2, Law *Quod principis*; and Law *Si Augustae*. Again, the privilege is considered subreptitious: because the urgent constitutions were tacitly omitted, *De constitutionibus*, Chapter 1, Book 6, since the second mission must be expressed, because it contradicts the constitutions, *De constitutionibus*, Chapter *Utili porrecta*. Furthermore, the privilege disposes of acquisition by way of succession, which agrees with succession by will or intestate, as in *Clementina*, *Exivi*, and in *Authenticum*, *De successionibus ab intestato*. But the acquisition of the goods of the professed by reason of profession is induced not by reason of succession, and the monastery does not take the goods of the professed as heir, but by legal disposition, as noted by Innocentius, *De probationibus*, Chapter *In praesentia*. Therefore, a privilege expressing a certain case, or mode of acquiring, does not go beyond another case, or mode of acquiring, *De privilegiis*, Chapter *Sanctum*; *De rescriptis*, Chapter *Successio*, Book 6.

† It must be observed that in things dedicated to God, a fourfold status is found. Some have property in common, but not in particular: as those professed in non-mendicant orders, who do not have property in particular, as in c. Cum ad monasterium, but in common, as appears there. Some have property in common with respect to certain things, and with respect to others not, as in the Carthusian order, which, although it is not permitted to have villages and castles in common, nevertheless has other goods in common, such as fields and other possessions, de statu monachorum, c. Recolentes. So also with the Preachers, who have certain things in common which do not repugn against their rule and statutes, as in the Extravagant, c. Quia quorundam. This appears from the form of the said privilege, where they receive inheritances devolving upon their professed members, although Blessed Dominic and his constitution dispose regarding the non-reception of his possessions. Therefore, these are not simply mendicants in common; and although they cannot receive what is prohibited by the constitution in order to retain it, they may do so in order to convert it into that which they can retain in common, as is the case expressly stated in de statu monachorum, c. Recolentes, in the end, where the Cistercian order, which can hold certain things in common and others not, can receive, when transferred to itself by another order, those things which the constitution prohibits, in order to convert them into that which the constitution permits. For this, it is responded to c. 1, de reliquiis et donationibus, because the Preachers are not simply mendicants, since they can hold some property in common; nor does it matter that Blessed Dominic disposed, and his constitution, because these seem to be understood regarding the reception of possessions which are acquired by the act of a man without translation of person; but acquisition by reason of profession is induced by the disposition of law with translation of person. And it matters between this whether something accrues from a man or from law, as in l. Licet obvenire haereditatem, and ff. de legatis, l. Legitimationis, there "nemo dat," and de probationibus, c. In praesentia. Nor does it matter what is said about subjection, because according to our norm, since a privilege is granted to another than the one making the constitution. But where the one making the constitution impetrates a privilege, by which derogation is made to himself and his constitution, and not to another, then the expression of the constitution in the privilege is not required. de praescriptionibus, c. Veniens, where this is expressly stated. By rightly understanding this, it is responded to that which is said a second command should issue, because this is true when a privilege issues against public law, but here against private law. But that nothing should be sought for the order, seems to be sustained by the previously alleged. For Blessed Dominic, constituting regarding the non-reception of possessions, constituted the same regarding the changing of poverty; but it would not be a changing of poverty to receive an inheritance to be sold and the price received. Such a constitution equally applies to reception caused by a man or by the ministry of law. Since, namely, the prohibition is induced so that they may keep poverty, they would no longer keep it if they received an inheritance by right or by the benefit of a man. To c. Recolentes, § Caeterum, it is responded that there the order, because it was transferring itself to the Cistercian order, by that translation did not lose dominion over those things which it previously held, therefore as lord it could abandon them. ff. pro derelicto, per totum. And also to exchange them, de exceptionibus, c. Cum venerabilis. That exchange therefore is not made by the Cistercian order to which the translation is made, but by the order which transfers itself. But in the present case, such an exchange cannot be made by the professed member, as lacking discretion, de electione, c. Si religiosus, c. Quia quorundam, unless by the Order of Preachers, as proved above. And thus § Caeterum supports the proposition. And even if in that inheritance there are movables, immovables, rights, and actions, nevertheless none of these rights are sought for the order, because whatever is sought repugns against poverty, which the constitution considered, nor does such a division seem to be possible in those who are transferred by way of universality, which is this case, as in d. l. Cum quaeritur, and l. Eum actum, de acquisitione haereditatis, l. 1, and l. 2, and de legatis 2, l. Grege.

And because under the name of possessions, movables also seem to be included, l. si, C. de pace, since possession falls upon them just as it does upon immovables, l. 1, de acquisitione possessionis. The transfer of rights and actions also seems to be prohibited; for it is not fitting for poverty to hold names of debts; indeed, an inheritance is estimated to be so much the greater, the more there is in the names of debts, ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. 1, § non solum; and l. si debitor; and l. si haeres; and l. pe; and l. in quantitate. And because the prohibition concerning the hindering of possessions seems to include rights, in which, even if no possession falls, there is nevertheless a quasi-possession, ff. de usucapione, l. sequitur, § si viam; de rebus dubiis, l. servus, § in corporibus; de causa possessionis, l. cum etiam; and they are compared to immovables, de praescriptione longi temporis, l. si; and de sacrosancta ecclesia, l. iubemus; de peculio, l. quam Tuberonis, § in peculio; de re iudicata, l. amodo, l. si; in quibus causis res non est necessaria, in Auth. de non alienando, § quia vero; Dy. in l. potest, ff. de auctoritate tutorum; de verborum significatione, l. moventium. From which it seems to be concluded that the said goods are not sought for the aforementioned Order; that regarding immovable goods, it seems sufficiently juridical, considering the words of Blessed Dominic and the aforementioned constitutions, and this seems to accord with the purity of conscience. But as regards movable goods, this is quite doubtful on account of the Extravagant *Quia quorundam*, in which, among other things, it is contained thus: "The Friars Preachers and Minorites serve Christ the poor in strictest poverty; and yet it is established that the said Preachers hold in common, as to ownership, certain things, which does not repugn against the statute of their rule. And therefore we leave this under doubt as to movable goods only; although it has been proven by most valid reasons, and authentic and most excellent counsels of doctors, that even those movable goods, considered according to the mind of the rule of Blessed Dominic, are not transferred to the Order of Preachers."

Conclusively, therefore, we say that immovable goods do not belong to the Order; because the words of Blessed Dominic impede the principle of acquisition. But as to movables, concerning which the prohibition does not speak, it does not seem so secure to advise, unless they were annual revenues; for example, those which are received from the Monte di Firenze; because they are compared to immovables, whence such things would not belong to the Friars Preachers. And thus we say and advise, we Baldus and Petrus de Perusio, Doctors of Law, to whose faith we have caused to be subscribed, and we have appended our customary seals. Always saving the sounder counsel.

CASE. The point of the question, upon which counsel is requested, is as follows: A certain Cola Cuchi of Nursia, having a pregnant wife, coming to death, made a testament; and after many legacies, he thus disposed: "In all my other movable and immovable goods, present and future, rights and actions, and names of debts, I institute and make as my heir or heirs the posthumous child or children, one or more, to be born from the womb of the said Catherine, his wife, if they come to light. And if they do not come to light, I institute as my heirs Benedict and Jacobus Marchi; except that in a certain piece of land situated in the instrumentum of Nursia among his other boundaries, and in another piece of land situated in another of his said instrumentum in his other boundaries, in which he substituted the said Colucia upon the happening of the aforementioned condition, namely, in the said two pieces of land. And if they come to light, and die without legitimate children, he substitutes to her or them the aforementioned Jacobus and Benedictus Marchi in equal portions upon the happening of the aforementioned condition."

Then the said testator, after the testament, made codicils, in which, after certain preambles, he thus disposed: "Furthermore, adding to the said testament, the said testator willed that the substitution made to his posthumous child or children, one or more, to be born from the womb of the said Catherine, his wife, contain in itself an express pupillary substitution. Furthermore, that the said Catherine, mother of the said posthumous child or children, shall not have, or be able to have, the legitime by natural right, or the Trebellianic quarter, from the said inheritance." Then the said testator died, the said wife remaining pregnant; then the said wife gave birth to a son; and he lived for a certain time. After this, the said pupillus died. Now, from the above-mentioned theme arises the question: For the mother of the said pupillus says that she is admitted to the legitime and the Trebellianic quarter, notwithstanding the said codicils. On the other side, Benedictus and Jacobus, the aforementioned substitutes, say that the said mother is to be totally excluded both from the legitime and from the Trebellianic quarter by virtue of the said codicils. It is asked now, what is the law, having seen the said testament and codicils, which are transmitted to you.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution of this kind, if they were born, etc., contains an implied pupillary substitution against the mother.
1. The Trebellianic action may be prohibited by the testator.
2. Whether a pupillary substitution in codicils excludes the mother, and below in the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. First, it must be considered, assuming that no codicils were made, whether the said substitution excludes the mother. And regarding this, two points must be examined. For

† First, it must be considered whether the first limb of the substitution, which is “if they are not born,” contains an implied pupillary substitution against the mother; and it seems that it does, as in D. de ventre in possessionem missa, l. Qui ventri, where it appears that an express pupillary substitution, if the pupillus is born and dies in pupillary age, contains an implied vulgar substitution, but if he were not born, it excludes the mother. Therefore, the same applies if he is extracted from the womb. That law is irrelevant: for the implied vulgar substitution does not exclude the mother there by virtue of the substitution, but because that woman who bears no one is not a mother, since she has not given birth; for how can she succeed to a son whom she does not have? And therefore those who allege that law, that an implied vulgar substitution is admitted against the mother, do not understand themselves: for there it speaks of a son not born. And where there is no son, there is no mother. One must therefore, for the true understanding, resort to the understanding of the last law, C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, where the text determines that the substitute is called in only two cases. The first is when the posthumous child is not born. The second is when he is born, and the mother dies before the death of the posthumous child. But where the mother survives, the implied substitution is not understood to have been made to the prejudice of the mother: because the burdensome inheritance of the son ought not to be taken away from the mother, as the text there expressly says. Note that Ulpian and Papinian said it is a question of intent. And I do not believe their opinion to be entirely abolished, except in a case of doubt: but when the intent is certain, even an implied substitution is admitted against the mother, as we note in l. Precibus. How much more so if the testator expressed it? Someone will say: not in a will; because according to c. Substitutionis, s. Nato posthumo, according to the common opinion, it is a fideicommissary substitution, and codicils do not avail: for one cannot directly substitute in them, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Si seyum. Therefore the mother ought to have her legitime and the Trebellianic portion: or at least her legitime.
† holding that the Trebellian substitution may be prohibited by the testator, as is the common opinion.

† of the learned: it seems to me that the codicils do not contain a new substitution, but rather a declaration of the substitution in the will; because the testator declares that his intention is that said substitution be pupillary. And the words permit this, because they were common words. Hence, I say that the mother is excluded by the force of the will as declared by the codicils. D. 28, 5, l. heredes palam, §. sed si notam. Nevertheless, these words are contrary to this, adding “and so forth,” for one thing is to add, another to declare. And he says, “I add,” therefore he had not previously sensed nor considered this. But I answer: he adds by declaring; for an obscure interpretation is in a manner to add. Let us therefore adhere to the opinion of Ulpian and Papinian, who say that it is a matter of will. And because the will appears, let us say that the mother is repelled by two wills joined together, namely, the will as declared and the codicil declaring: from which it follows that, having been made briefly in the will implicitly and declared afterwards by the codicils explicitly, the mother is excluded, not by the mere force of the codicils. Argument: D. 28, 5, l. a se toto, cum si. Codicils alone would not suffice, but just as the will could be declared by witnesses alone, so also by codicils. I, Baldus of Perugia.
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Most Reverend Father. I had already given my opinion on this point against the mother, following the will of the testator. For although in the codicils the pupillary substitution turns into an oblique one, and does not exclude the mother from her legitime portion, as stated in the Digest, ad Trebellianum, l. Scaevola, nevertheless the codicils are rather declaratory of the will than operative in themselves: as is clear there, where it is said that the substitution made contradicts, etc. For it may be contained, if the testator so wishes. Therefore, the codicils do not dispose, but declare what has been disposed. Which can also be done before two witnesses. Digest, de testibus, l. haeredes palam, sed si et notam. Wherefore I excuse myself to you: because I cannot, with a clear conscience, write in favor of your client. Farewell, my lord. And I was with Master Peter, who, having seen the opinion, did not wish to involve himself, although he says he is in doubt: because the force of the will favors the oblique and not the direct substitution. And it is also true, unless the mind of the testator were certain, as it is certain. I remit both the messenger and the fee, since I do not give an opinion on your behalf. Due to many impediments, I could not dispatch the messenger sooner, who arrived in this city on Saturday evening. Baldus, yours, from Perugia, on the 21st day of September. Doctor of both laws. CASE. A certain Paulitius was appointed, or decreed, tutor to a certain ward by a judge, and the said tutor administered the guardianship of the said ward, and finally, during the guardianship, in order that he might more conveniently have care of the person of the said ward, he retained the said ward in his own house: he had all the goods of the said ward removed from the house of the said ward, in order that he might be able to let the house of the said ward: and in order that he might better safeguard the goods of the said ward: which goods the said tutor deposited in his own house, in which the said tutor dwelt: finally, at the time of the Nativity, namely when the shepherds of the church entered the city, a great fear and tumult of the people arose, and through the said tumult the house of the said tutor, together with his goods, and also with the goods of the said ward, were burned, along with many houses of many citizens. Now it is asked, whether the said tutor is liable for those goods burned and stolen.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A guardian is not liable for an unforeseen accident, as stated in the Digest under the heading *de casu fortuito* and the following sections.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If no fault can be imputed to this guardian, because he placed [the ward or the ward’s property] in a place that was believed to be safe, and the house did not burn down due to his special enmity, the loss is not at the guardian’s risk, because it is a fortuitous event. His adversary, however, must prove fault or enmity. C. de periculo tutorum. l. si res; l. si mores. §. si culpae. locati. de pignora. ac. l. quae fortuit. ff. pro socio. l. cum duobus. §. damna. et l. contractus. de re. iu. And if he does not prove it, the guardian’s heir ought to be absolved. And so I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, advise. V. l. D. And I have subscribed to my faith, and [affixed] the seal of my name.
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This was a fortuitous event, and therefore the tutor is not liable for such an event, nor is his successor. D. de negotiorum gestione, l. sed an ultro, §. his autem; C. eodem, l. tutori; C. de periculo et commodo tutoris, l. si res; D. de communi dividundo, l. si ut certo, §. quod vero senectute; D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. damna; D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. si vendita insula; D. de actionibus emptoris, l. si ea res. I, Baldus. On the restitution of dowries according to the old statute. We establish and ordain: that whenever any other dowry is to be restored because the marriage was dissolved by the death of the wife, namely, the wife predeceasing the husband, notwithstanding any common children descending from them, or the children of those children, the husband, or his heirs, or any other person who might be sued for the restitution of the dowry, shall be bound to restore only two-thirds of the dowry; the remaining third part of the dowry shall remain with the husband, or his heirs, or another person who might be sued or bound to restore the dowry, notwithstanding any pact contained in the dowry instrument regarding the restitution of the dowry without diminution, which would speak to the contrary. And this shall have effect and be observed in past, present, and future cases, notwithstanding any statute on rendering justice, or any other ordinance speaking to the contrary. On the form of the dowry instrument, day, month, witnesses, etc. Anthony Pasci Cuitii confessed and acknowledged, not in expectation of a future payment, but in actual payment having had and received from Angelo of Benevento, given to him as a dowry, and in the name of a dowry on account of the marriage celebrated between the said Anthony on one part, and Lady Nicolina, daughter of the said Angelo, on the other, 78 livres. Renouncing and c. which dowry he, by himself and his heirs, permitted, agreed with the said Angelo, stipulating, etc., to hold, preserve, and keep safe well and diligently, and to render and restore it in this manner: namely, if the said marriage should happen to be dissolved on the part of the said Anthony by death, divorce, or other just cause, or if perhaps the said Anthony should fall into poverty, or misuse his goods, or die without children, or with children, to render and restore the said dowry, not diminished, to the said Angelo stipulating and receiving for the said Lady Nicolina. But if the said marriage should be dissolved on the part of the said Nicolina without children, or with children born from the said marriage, or if the said children, one or more, should die without children before the age of 25, then he promised to render and restore the said dowry to the said Angelo stipulating and receiving for himself and his heirs, for whom and c. Form of the new statute on the restitution of dowries. Therefore we establish and ordain that if the marriage should be dissolved by the death of the woman with children, or with other descendants from the said marriage, that the entire dowry shall remain with the said children, or descendants, or their successors. But if the marriage should be dissolved by the death of the woman without children, or other descendants from the said marriage, the husband shall acquire one-third part of the said dowry. And if the dowry had been given, he to whom the dowry is to be restored shall be bound to make a quittance to the husband, or his heirs, or another who, if it had been given, would be bound to restore it, to give and pay one-third part of the promised dowry, adding that the husband, or his heirs, shall not be compelled to restore to the woman, or her heirs, the fruits of paraphernal goods, or those which are not dowry goods; but the husband, or his heirs, shall acquire the fruits received; adding further that no renunciation may be made to this statute by the parties, notwithstanding any form of dowry instrument, or any pact.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a husband shall not acquire the dowry when children are living, whether he will acquire it when children are living.
2. Whether an argument from the contrary sense applies to statutes.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The first statute provides that, notwithstanding the children, the husband shall acquire one-third part upon the predecease of his wife, and shall restore two parts, unless there is any agreement speaking to the contrary. Now it is asked whether, when children are present, anything is to be restored, the custom mentioned in the law *dos a patre* being set aside. And it seems that the entire dowry is to be restored, as noted in the law *Beblius*, *De pactis dotalibus*. For the case of children is a case unforeseen by the statute; therefore, the custom ceasing, we are in the common law, and thus it ought to be restored, as in the final law, *C. de bonis utriusque iudicis*, and in the text of the aforementioned law *dos a patre*. The contrary seems to follow from an argument taken from the contrary sense of the statute itself, *ff. de pactis dotalibus*, law *inter socerum*, § *cum intra*. And thus it remains with the father for the children. It supports this what is noted by Dy. in the chapter *quod ob gratiam*, *De restitutione iuris*, book 6. And in the law *quod favore*, *De legibus*, by Cy.

† I hold that from this statute an argument *a contrario sensu* may be drawn, as if from the contrariety of the final cause, whereby two-thirds ought to be restored when there are no children. A contrary final cause produces a contrary effect. The objection from *Sed obiectio*, *Sic ostenditur*, *Maior*, *Lex*, *Si cum dotem* does not hold, because there the unforeseen case was not contrary in the final reason for the restitution of the dowry to the case expressly stated in the contract; here, however, it ought not to be called unforeseen, because the conception of the mind understands both contraries simultaneously. But it is doubted whether one can renounce this argument *a contrario sensu* by virtue of an agreement, just as one can renounce the custom of the law *Dos a patre*. And it seems that one can. D. *De pactis*, l. *Pacisci*. To the contrary it seems, for the statute prohibits renouncing its own provision, but this contrary sense is a tacit provision of the same statute; therefore, one cannot renounce it, because this contrary sense appears to be the text of the statute itself. D. *De testamento*, l. *Qui testamento*, §. *Mulier*. And if this is true, even under the old statute the dowry remains for the children with the father, notwithstanding a stipulation made to the contrary by the father of the woman. For if one could renounce it, the father would gain nothing; and thus the children, who ought to be the cause of gain, would be the cause of loss, which is most absurd. But this seems false, because this argument *a contrario sensu* ought not to be drawn against the *ius commune*; for the *ius commune* is expressed, but the argument *a contrario sensu* is tacit; and therefore it is removed by the express provision. Likewise, the custom mentioned in l. *Dos a patre* is derogated by agreement, as noted there. From this it seems to be concluded that the said dowry ought to be restored in its entirety according to the form of the stipulation, as in l. *Rem in praesenti*, §. *Videamus*. For contracts receive their law from agreement, as in D. *De deposito*, l. 1, §. *Si convenerint*.

And therefore it seems that recourse should be had to the second statute; nevertheless, that statute does not seem to apply, because the case of the restitution of the dowry arose before the new statute was enacted. And thus one must adhere to the old statute and the common law, and not to the new statute, as stated in C. de legibus, l. leges, et constitutiones, cum si. And although the father is bound to provide a dowry for his daughter, nevertheless, according to the common law, he may stipulate that, in the case of restitution of the dowry, the whole amount be returned to him alone, as stated in ff. sol. matr. l. si cum dotem, and C. com. utriusque iud. l. si. Hence, according to the strictness of the law, the dowry in question ought, in the case of restitution, to be returned to the father; nevertheless, because the intent of the old statute was certainly to the contrary, one might perhaps argue the contrary on grounds of equity, pursuant to l. inter, § cum inter, de pactis dotalibus. Nevertheless, the first opinion is more correct, namely, that the common law be observed.

There is no doubt regarding the third part of the dowry, which remains with the husband, because the case of children who existed (whose death is the cause for triggering the stipulation for the restitution of the dowry) is similar to the case of children who did not exist at the time of death. And in that case as well, there is a greater cause or reason for gaining; therefore, etc., as stated in ff. de legatis, l. non potest, l. illud, and ff. ad legem Aquiliam, and C. de interdictis, l. 1, cum si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the edictal law. C. on second marriages, and whether a husband may leave to his second wife more than to the daughter of his first marriage.
2. A restrictive interpretation in the pursuit of gain has no place in statutes.
casus: CASE. In the name of the Lord, amen. In the year of our Lord 1369, indiction 7, in the pontificate of Pope Urban V, on the 21st day of the month of March, acted in the Castle of the Plebs, in the church of Saint Gervasius, present being Bernardo son of Benevenuto, Christophoro Cechi of Vannis Casellae, and An. Ioannis Amadeus of the said Castle, witnesses called and requested for this purpose. Since Nico., formerly Vanuti, son of Monaldi of the said Castle, has come of age, several years have now elapsed, and he is now absent from the said Castle, and there is no one who takes care of the goods of the said Nico., or governs, manages, and holds them in hand; and it is equitable and proper that a curator be appointed for the aforementioned goods, lest those goods be dissipated or alienated. Therefore, the wise man Do. Nico. of Volterra, judge and assessor of the commune of the Castle of the Plebs, for the noble man Bartholo. Nicolutii of Perugia, holder of the power of the said Castle, having learned through the assertion of the lady Antonia, mother of the said adult Nico., and of several of his blood relatives present there, that Titius Munitii of the village of Catissani, within the district of the said Castle, is useful and suitable for the confirmation and governance of the said goods, and for receiving the aforementioned care, and especially because the said Titius was, during the absence of the said Nico., administrator of the said goods, and had repeatedly administered the said goods well, faithfully, and legally, he gave, constituted, and decreed the said Titius, present there and accepting, as curator of the goods of the said absent adult Nicolaus, and in defense, at the instance and petition of the said lady Antonia, mother of the said Nico. He said to the said Titius: "Be curator of the said goods." And moreover, he swore on the holy Gospels of God, touching the written text corporally, to perform and conduct the said care well and legally, in good faith and without fraud, and to diligently seek out, investigate, defend, keep, and save the said goods, and to do all and each thing which he should see and know to be useful to the said goods, and to omit what is useless; provided always that he may use them in accordance with the truth, and to make and render an inventory of the said goods according to the order of the law, and to assign it; and to render and assign an account for such curatorship, as well as for the administration and care of the said goods, according to the order. For such curatorship, and at his prayers and command, Benevenuto, son of the lord Staphani of the said Castle, acted as surety for all and each of the aforementioned matters, and even in every case and event, promising the said Benevenuto to me, the notary subscribed below, stipulating for the said Nico. and the said goods, that he would cause and ensure that the said curator would attend to and observe all the aforementioned promises; which, if not observed, he promised to observe from his own property, under the obligation of all his present and future goods. The said Benevenuto renounced the benefit of suretyship and every other aid of the laws and law competent to him and to be competent to him. All these and each of these things having been thus performed, the said lord judge, sitting on the tribunal in the said place, which place the said judge chose for himself as suitable and juridical for this act, interposed his authority and that of the commune of the Castle of the Plebs, and decreed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
