† It is certain in the common law that a husband cannot leave to his second wife more than to the daughter of his first marriage; and that whatever is left beyond what is due to the said daughter of the first marriage, if she is the only one, is applied [to her]; and if there were several from the first marriage, it is distributed among them, as is stated in C. de secun. nup. l. hac edictali, and in Auth. de nup. §. optime, co. 4. But because the statute provides that daughters, granddaughters, and others are bound to observe the will of the father and grandfather, and their testament, and cannot demand more when males exist; and in the said statute follows, adding, that the said women are always bound in every other case to observe the last will of the aforementioned, provided that they are not burdened in their legitime; it is doubted whether the said statute derogates from the said law hac edictali. One point was omitted: for in that statute, before that clause, the following words are added: provided that the females are not defrauded of the right due to them by law, in the presence of male descendants. And afterwards follows the clause adding, etc. And it seems that the said daughter of the first marriage has the benefit of the law hac edictali. And this for several reasons. First, because a statute is distinguished by common law, and is reduced to common law, if the words of the statute allow; because they are not expressed against common law, as C. de nox. l. si serui, extra de consue. c. cum dilectus. But here they are not expressed against common law; because in the statute no mention is made of second marriages; therefore, in the case of second marriages, common law will be observed. C. ad tertu. auth. defuncto, in fi. Second, because a statute should be understood as applying to one who can make a will, C. de sac. san. ec. l. 1. But he who has passed to second vows does not have testamentary capacity in this regard; indeed, he is prohibited from making a will in this manner, as d. l. hac edictali, §. si vero, there: as if not written, etc. Third, because the statute provided that, when males do not exist, daughters are not defrauded of their right; but the right of the law hac edictali is their right; therefore, that right is reserved to them. And thus it seems that the said daughter of the first marriage has a right against the stepmother. On the contrary, however, three reasons are taken from the words of the statute. The first reason is from the word adding, which is an extensive and augmentative word, as extra de elec. c. statuimus, li. 6. And therefore it does not remain within the limits of strict speech; but it must operate something beyond. l. si quando, ff. de leg. 1, ad mun. ff. de vsu, l. stipulatus. The second reason is from the word always in every, which words are universal affirmatives, as all embrace cases. so. ma. l. 1, in the word always, and everywhere, §. manda, l. a procuratore, de ver. sig. l. cum quaerebatur. The third reason from those words, provided that they are not burdened in their legitime. I believe that the words of the statute should be understood in such a way that they have some meaning in understanding, as ff. de leg. 2, l. cum pater, §. cum imperfecta. Then I argue thus: legitime is said to be that which is owed by natural law. For the portion that accrues from l. hac edictali is not owed by natural law; for it is computed in the legitime, because it is received as if owed, as elegantly noted by the gloss in d. §. optime, de nup. l. statutum. Therefore, it wants daughters to be content with their legitime in every case; therefore, it allows the father to freely dispose of the other goods. C. de inoffi. testa. l. cum quaeritur. And so I hold, because what is prohibited to the father regarding the legitime, it seems to be allowed regarding the rest. And the words of the statute say, in every other case. Hence, the statute does not distinguish, nor do we distinguish; because
† A restrictive interpretation has no place in statutes when seeking to gain an advantage. Add the following opinion.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How adultery is to be proved.
2. How a legacy is to be proved.
3. Rosellus, lover of truth.
4. Whether a legatee loses the legacy if he alleges adultery against the testator.
5. Whether a husband loses the gain of the dowry if he brings his adulterous wife back into his home.
6. Whether one alleging the contrary is to be heard.
body: On the aforementioned points, it has been excellently alleged by the most excellent doctor, Lord Baldus. Likewise by the most distinguished man, Lord Marcus. But as the glossa says in C. de rescindenda venditione, l. ratas: if it is posited that it is not expedient, it follows that it ought not to be done. This is often the case; but so that this may not happen, it is excellently distinguished in the point previously set forth by me, by inquiring into several matters.

And regarding the first question, whether adultery has been proven, Lord Marcus argues very subtly and well in his counsel; but I shall dispose of the matter briefly, without a multitude of citations. And I say that adultery has not been legitimately proven, either truly or presumptively. It is only proven that Ser Laurentius, son of Paul Vencan, [confronted] his wife, namely Lady Lena, and that the wife of Ser Paul said that she was not there, and that he, upon entering, quarreled with Agabito; and that Agabito was with his shoes untied; and that the wife of Ser Laurentius left the house in shame, and that Ser Laurentius wished to kill her, and certain other similar things. Certainly, from the foregoing, it is not proven that the said Lady Lena committed adultery with the said Agabito, which the statute and the common law require in order for the husband to forfeit the dowry. For an obscure statement is always interpreted against the party producing the witness. Extra, De probat., c. In praesentia; No., De testib., c. Cum clamor. Moreover, a statement that does not conclude of necessity does not assist the party producing it. C., Unde legi., l. Non ob hoc; De probat., l. Neque natales; and d. c. In praesentia. But the statements of these witnesses are obscure and do not necessarily conclude adultery, as I shall prove; therefore, they are obscure and do not necessarily conclude adultery, as is apparent to the senses, because it was possible that all the aforementioned things, and more, might have occurred, and yet she had not committed adultery. These points are clear: that the presumption was obscure and did not necessarily conclude, and such a presumption as would suffice for condemnation. Lord Marcus labored very subtly, and said whatever could be said; but, with all due reverence to that most valiant man, they do not conclude necessarily, nor even presumptively, for, as I said above, when the matter could be otherwise, even presumptively, from the fact that he found Agabito with the said Lena in the house, concerning whom, as the witnesses say, he otherwise had a bad presumption. And because the door was fastened, and Lady Clara denied that she was there, and he found Agabito with his shoes untied and disheveled, such that he could justly suspect that he had come for the purpose of adultery, it appears so, but he was prevented by him from consummating it; from this alone he would have been moved against him. Moreover, he could justly suspect this from the fact, and make a quarrel, from all of which such suspicions could arise. And because he found her in an indecent manner, as if she had been adulterated, it is fitting that, through the aforementioned things, the witnesses do not presumptively, nor necessarily, conclude that adultery was committed; which is apparent, because it could have been for another reason, as I said above; they do not even presumptively prove that adultery was committed, which the statute expressly requires, especially with the will of the lady, when there is a presumption of law to the contrary, because no one is presumed to be forgetful of eternal salvation. C., Ad l. Iul. repetund., l. Si. Nor is it true, upon correct examination, that the fame of adultery has been legitimately proven. For although the witnesses seem to say this, none of those interrogated knows what fame is, or how many people make fame. And no one can prove that which he ignores what it is, since his testimony must be perceived by the senses, as C., De testib., l. Testium; and Extra, eod., c. Cum causam, and there by Innocentius. Furthermore, all, except the last, when interrogated, say that they know it because it is said by the public; they do not say that they heard it said publicly; and thus they do not prove it, because they do not state by which bodily sense they perceived it, according to the note by Bartolus, ff., De quaestionibus, l. De more, § Si, in the question how fame will be proven. And thus I conclude that adultery has not been proven, either truly or presumptively, such that the said Ser Laurentius should be relieved. In support of this, it is that Ser Laurentius brought her back into the house. Moreover, because at the time of his death, or of Lady Lena, he asserted that he was bound to restore the dowry, as his witnesses prove, and thus it should be believed that he did not believe that he had lost the dowry for that cause, and consequently that adultery had been committed. For no one says what he does not hold in mind, as ff., De solutionibus, l. Labeo.

† Regarding the second point, whether it is a legacy, it is proven, first premising that legacies can be left by a nod, as in D. de legatis 3, l. nutum. Also, an adulterer questioned. As in C. qui testare facere possunt, l. hac consultissima, and §. at cum humana, no. de testibus, I. iubemus. Also, it suffices to say thus, and it appears to respond to the questions asked. As in D. de verbis obligatorum, l. 1, §. si quis interroget, de interrogatione et actione, l. si defensor, §. qui interrogatur, cum si. Now, only the first witness creates doubt, who differs in words from the others.

† But I, who am a lover of truth, say that the legacy is proven: and I understand the statement of the first witness, who recited the effect of the testator’s mental intent, not the words, so that it may be reconciled with the others; which ought to be done, as in Extra, De testibus, c. Cum tu. For even one Evangelist says that Christ said, “Put your sword into its sheath,” and another says that he said, “Put it in its place”; yet they are not discordant, because the Holy Spirit has no discord, but they are understood as to sense and the same effect, since the sheath is its place. Likewise, what one omitted, the other supplied. And thus there is no objection if one says thus, and the other that he said it twice; and especially on account of the length of time. And thus it is not surprising regarding the very words if they are not remembered, since oblivion is induced by a decade, as noted in C. De acquisitione possessionis, l. Licet; ff. De usucapione, l. Furtum, § 1. That he was of sound mind is presumed, especially since he responded to questions, and especially because the heir was present there and said nothing; he would have complained if he had seen that she was not of sound mind; since no one is presumed to throw away his own rights, as in ff. De probationibus, l. Cum de indebito, § 1. And I would hold this part in judging. I by no means believe that it had the force of a deliberatory pact; since from this a donation is presumed, which is prohibited between husband and wife. Hence it is rather presumed that it was by way of a legacy, as in ff. Pro socio, l. Merito, cum si. But perhaps in this case it would not be affirmed by death, as in ff. De donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Papinianus. On the third point,

Whether Brother Laurentius loses the legacy on account of the exception of adultery, I say that he does, because he defamed her of a most heinous crime after her death; and thus he loses the legacy, even if he had acted justly, as in D. de his qui ut indigni, l. 1. But I observe that there is a great difference when the legatee acts during the lifetime of the testator; for then he loses the legacy as if by a change of the testator’s will, as noted in C. de fideiussoribus, l. Fideiussor; in that case, the property remains with the heir. Thus is understood l. 3, §. Si, D. de adimendis legatis; and D. de his qui ut indigni, l. Si inimicitiae, at the end, unless he had acted with some color of justice for his own interest; for then it would be applied to the fisc, as in the said l. Si inimicitiae, at the end, and there by Bartolus, and more fully in the same title, l. Si. But since it is after death, he does not lose the legacy ipso iure, but it is taken from him as from an unworthy person by sentence, and applied to the fisc, as in l. Papinianus, §. Meminisse, D. de inofficioso testamento. And thus, since he does not lose the legacy ipso iure, Joanna, the heiress, cannot alter the right of the fisc to repel Brother Laurentius. This is the case, and the gloss in D. familiae herciscundae, l. His consequenter, §. Sed an famulus. It supports what is noted by Bartolus in the said l. Si, D. de his qui ut indigni, near the end, and what is there noted by Raymond de Peñafort.

† On the fourth point, whether, because she is taken back, she loses the dowry’s profit, etc.: I hold that adultery has not been proven, nor is it necessary to examine this; but even assuming it were proven, I believe Lord Baldus speaks truly when he says that, in this manner, the husband cannot oppose her by means of the laws he has alleged. Nor does it matter that statutes do not admit of a restrictive interpretation, so that no one may suffer undue harm, according to the doctrine of Bartolus in *l. omnes populi* and in the Code, *de legibus*, *l. non dubium*. For, even assuming his doctrine is true, this is not restricted so that someone suffers undue harm, but rather so that someone does not gain undue profit. For, since the laws intend that the husband profits from the dowry on account of the wife’s adultery if he takes her back, kept her, and did not accuse her morals, he would gain unduly if the statute were understood without distinction. Nor does it matter that he profits by operation of law according to the form of the statute, because it is conditional, namely, where he takes her back, so that the statute is drawn to the common law, as I said above. On the sixth point, the answer has been given above: for, since it must be taken away from him as from an unworthy person, it must be applied to the fisc, as stated in § *meminisse*, *de his qui ut indigni*, and *l. Claudius cum sequentibus*. From the foregoing, the answer to the last point is clear: for the dowry instrument merits execution for three hundred livres; in other respects, the exception of a legacy and of liberation and satisfaction may be raised according to the form of the statute; although, as I said above, the said three hundred livres left to the said Ser Laurence may subsequently be taken away from him by the fisc.

† However, that which Lord Baldus says, namely that he who alleges the contrary is heard, provided that they are proposed conditionally according to the opinion of Dynus in the chapter *Nullus pluribus*, is not true in law: when I oppose, both exceptions must be proved, as is required to be proved, as in our case, as is fully declared by Bartolus in the Digest, *De exceptionibus*, law *Nemo*; and Baldus himself reproves Dynus and holds the opinion of Laurentius de Arezzo, and in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Cum de indebito*, § 1. And perhaps Ser Laurentius does not allege the contrary. And thus it seems to me that it should be said in law, to Rosello de Rosellis of Arezzo, doctor of laws: therefore I have subscribed, and signed with my usual seal. On the same facts as the preceding opinion.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Adultery cannot be committed except during the lifetime of the adulteress.
2. If a legatee, after the death of the testator, commits causes of ingratitude by which he is deprived of his right by operation of law, the fiscus does not acquire the legacy; rather, the heir retains the legacy as caducary due to the fault of the legatee.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. If I said that you had weighed the matter, you would not have advised the contrary, you lover of truth.

† For adultery cannot be committed except during the life of the adulteress. And if a husband, under the false impression that she has committed adultery, conceives capital enmity against his innocent wife, there is no doubt that he is a tacit capital enemy, whom the wife would not have left her estate to, had she known him to be an enemy, and who will pursue this enmity even after death; and since this enmity was conceived during the lifetime of both parties, a legacy made on account of it is not considered a valid legacy: nor can the legatee claim it, because a legacy is left on account of merit, whereas an enemy does not merit it. And if he harbors capital enmity in his heart, as stated in l. 3, in fine, and l. ex parte, de adimendis et querendis legatis, and de legatis 2, l. Lucius, §. Lucius, de manumissionibus testamento, l. testamento Centurio, Inimicitia: enmity which arises between living persons and is revealed after death is similar to a posthumous child who breaks the will. And I say this with respect to legacies and fideicommissa; otherwise with respect to the institution of an heir or intestate succession: because one cannot be disinherited by tacit will, but the fiscus (public treasury) takes the inheritance, as stated in the text and gloss of the aforementioned l. ex parte, which speaks in the context of inheritance. And l. nam et consequenter, §. 1, quod interficiens testatorem succedit in hereditate, states that although the fiscus may take it away, the situation is different with regard to a legacy, which remains with the heir, and the killer does not succeed to it. ff. soluto matrimonio, l. ab hostibus, §. si vir uxori. And observe this: because you said that in the case of capital enmity which existed at the time of the testator’s death, there is no doubt, even according to your view, and that it existed at the time of the wife’s death. This is not a matter of belief, but of capital enmity lying in the husband’s heart due to his own temerity, whereby, according to your view, the wife was innocent. Therefore, you contradict yourself, Master Consultant, brother, and my dear friend. For this reason, I stated in my opinion that it was affirmed at the time of death, with continuity. These words you did not weigh, as it appears to me.

† Now, beyond the first opinion, I say further that if the legatee, after the death of the testator, commits causes of ingratitude by which he is deprived ipso iure, the fiscus does not come in; but the heir retains the legacy as caducum due to the delict of the legatee. And this is the text in the law which I cited for the case in l. 1. de his qui ut indigni, in the word "carere." Hence, what Bartolus says there is not true in that case when the legatee offends the mind of the legator, who, if he had known, would not have made the legacy, arg. ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si. Hence, consider whether it is feigned retroactively during the life of the deceased, for example, that he would not have left it, and the legacy is not due; but if, after the legacy has been acquired, indignity supervenes, then the fiscus comes in. Believe the glossator in this, C. de his qui ut indigni, l. sororem. For he who commits adultery with a widow is presumed to have schemed during the life of the deceased, and loses the legacy. This is said by the gloss there, citing l. 3. in fine, de adimendis legatis, because the gloss is understood according to the law which it cites. And the same is noted most expressly by the gloss and all the doctors before Bartolus, Petrus de Ancharano, and Cynus, Petrus de Dyaco, Butrius, and all others. Therefore, no one can say that this man, who persecuted his wife with capital hatred during her life, at her death, and after, and attempted to defame her memory, is not deprived of the legacy, l. inimicitiae, ff. de his qui ut indigni. And therefore, this man cannot act regarding the alleged legacy, whether it exists or not, since the mind or intention of the legator is lacking, and especially in our case.

Then this man says that the statement of Master Dyaco is not true; therefore neither is mine, since I follow Dyaco in our case. And he cites the statement of Bartolus. I merely recited the statement of Dyaco; I did not defend it. And in our case, I adhere to and hold that what he says is true as the Gospel, for three reasons. First, because when the excepting party alleges a crime, he can never simultaneously with the exception of the crime, for example adultery or similar, allege a contrary exception; because the allegation of a crime is a kind of impeachment; and therefore it cannot be denied, as in de iniuriis, l. praetor edixit. Second, he can swear de calumnia, that he believes what he alleges to be true, for he cannot be excused from perjury; the text is in c. vult, de iureiurando, lib. 6. But he proposes disjunctively that it is true, or unless he proposes a second contrary exception, receding from the first, as in l. si quidem and l. arator, ff. de conditione indebiti. And if this is so, in the case known from execution, having previously placed the legacy, he would be seen to have receded from it and renounced it, ff. de minoribus, l. si filius. Third, because a benefit, for example of a dowry to be gained or similar, cannot be obtained by one who denies that which is the cause of that benefit, de fideiussoribus, l. si dubitetur, §. 1. And all contradiction is perplexing to the matter, and no one can believe that both parts of the contradiction are true; whoever says the contrary should strive in his own mind to find the truth, because he has not yet found it.

Note also that when the delict excludes the will of the legator, the legacy is presumptively not confiscated there, but the legatee loses his right by means of an exception; on this, note Jacobus de Belvisio in §. si quis autem non implens, there, "uideas." And thus I say and advise, I, Baldo de Ubaldis, Doctor of Both Laws. And to the faith of this I have subscribed, and with the seal of my name.

I also said in the first opinion that this legacy was not proven due to the discrepancy of the witnesses, I mean real discrepancy, because the statement of one does not conclude what the statement of the other concludes. And this friend of truth did not consider in law that the words of witnesses do not conclude to one end. And although Master Rosellus is truly an excellent man, nevertheless when his opinion is not conformable to the laws, it should not be held, and the power of the castle should follow justice.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The buyer, who is compelled to submit to arbitration in accordance with the form of the statute, has a right of recourse for eviction. The notice required to be given to the buyer may be waived by the father.
2. The word "unless," when placed after a negation, affirms.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It is certain that a buyer who is compelled to submit to arbitration in accordance with the form of the statute has a right of recourse for eviction on two grounds. The first is that he did so out of necessity, as is proven by the reason given in the text of the Digest, *De evictionibus*, law 10, § *Si compromisero*. The second is that the arbitrator succeeds to the place of the judge, as stated in the Code, *De iudicibus*, law 1; and he performs the function of an arbitrator when he renders a condemnation. And even if it were assumed that he was both an arbitrator and an arbiter, the law would be the same, because he possesses jurisdiction by virtue of the statute of the place. Furthermore, it is certain that if the right to give notice has been waived by agreement, an action for eviction may be brought without any notice having been given, as stated in the Digest, *De evictionibus*, law *Habemus*. It is also established that when the form of one instrument is impressed upon another instrument by the nature of the reference to it, both instruments are deemed to contain the same clauses and the same waivers. See law *Hæc sententia*; and law *In summa*; and the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Instituti*; and the Digest, *De hereditate instituenda*, law *Asse toto*; and the Extravagantes, *De verborum significatione*, chapter *Abbate*. Therefore, it must be considered that although the instrument executed by the Palatine does not expressly state that he waived the necessity of giving notice by agreement, it sufficiently contains such a waiver, inasmuch as he does not wish to be bound by the *gritta* in the same manner and form in all respects as Gracanellus, who is mentioned above regarding the *Gritta*; thus, the entire formal and literal series of Gracanellus’s instrument was repeated in the Palatine’s instrument. Nor does it matter if it is said that that clause was added in negative terms; for he stated that he is not bound to the aforementioned preservation, unless and insofar as, and as, and in the manner and form in which the Palatine, as heir to one-half of the said Gracanellus’s share of the said house, apart from the said cellar.

For the phrase “unless” placed after a negation sets forth common law principles, as stated in § Qui in iure and in l. Ac in c. Pactum, according to Dy. Moreover, even if a denunciation were required, when the person having entered into possession does not know the name of the successor against whom he must denounce eviction, it suffices to denounce at the house, as held in ff. De evictionibus, l. Si dictum, § Pe. Furthermore, an error in a proper name, when the person is identified by a descriptive term, does not invalidate the citation or the judgment; this is the general rule, and Bartolus expressly notes this in ff. De legibus, l. Si quis in fundi vocabulo. But here the person is clearly identified, because there was only one daughter of the Palatine; hence the citation could not be understood as referring to anyone other than her alone, as stated in ff. De liberis et posthumis, l. Nominatim. To this effect also ff. De rebus dubiis, l. Qui habebat; ff. De hereditate instituenda, l. Quotiens; ff. De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Demonstratio. And thus the objection based on ff. De iudicibus, l. Eum, quem temere, does not apply, because there the citation was ambiguous and obscure, since Titius was cited and there were several Titii; whereas here the citation was certain by the addition of the heir’s name, and there were not several heirs, nor several persons under guardianship, but only one girl, who was properly cited, as appears from the foregoing. And this is the truth.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. The following case is proposed. The Magnificent and distinguished knight, Lord Bartholomew de Casalibus, General Lord and Imperial Vicar of the city of Cortona, died, leaving behind Lord Francis, his son from his first marriage, and also Lord Raynerius and Ugutio, his sons from his second marriage. He had made a testament in which he instituted the aforementioned Lord Francis, Lord Raynerius, and Ugutio, his legitimate and natural sons, as his general and universal heirs in equal shares. Then, during the communion [undivided co-ownership] among the said brothers, the same Lord Francis was constituted General Lord and Imperial Vicar of the said city. It is also proposed that no division having been made among the said brothers, but while they lived together familiarly in communion, and with the said Lords Raynerius and Ugutio being under the age of 25, the aforementioned Lord Francis created John Guelfi of Florence as factor and manager of the greater affairs, and for many years, up to the time of the death of the said Lord Francis, he placed in the hands of this John the administration. After the death of Lord Francis, there survived Nicholas, John, and Francis of Siena, his sons and universal heirs instituted by him, and also the aforementioned Lords Raynerius and Ugutio, his brothers. Therefore, during the aforementioned communion, the aforementioned Nicholas John was elected and made General Lord and Imperial Vicar of the said city of Cortona. During whose time the aforementioned John administered the aforementioned goods for many years. During the aforementioned communion, the said Lord Raynerius also died, having made a testament in which he instituted as his heirs the said Beatrice, his mother and former wife of the aforementioned Lord Bartholomew. Finally, the aforementioned Nicholas John died. After his death, the aforementioned Ugutio, Francis of Siena, and Alionigio, son and heir of the aforementioned Nicholas John, were elected and made General Lords of the said city of Cortona. To Francis of Siena and Alouisio, as pupils, a certain tutor, Antonius Guidonis of Cortona, was appointed. During the aforementioned communion, no division having been made among the aforementioned brothers or their heirs, it is also true that during the aforementioned communion, the said Lord Francis made certain deposits in florins and purchases in his own name, from which fruits and annuities came into the hands of the said John, the factor and manager of the greater affairs. It is also true that the said Lord Bartholomew died in the lordship and vicariate of the said city of Cortona, and in all his goods and rights, he instituted as his universal heirs Lord Francis, Lord Raynerius, and Ugutio in equal shares. That he wished his sons to be equal in the aforementioned lordship appears in the testament itself, where he says: "Item, he left his wife, Lady Beatrice, as Lady Mayor and Stewardess in the house of the testator, etc." Because in the hands of the said Lady Beatrice, his wife and mother of the said Lords Raynerius and Ugutio, he disposed and wished that the custody and governance for the heirs of all the fortifications of the said city of Cortona and of any other goods of the testator should reside; from which custody the said Francis later deprived her and brought it back into his own hands. It is also presupposed that the aforementioned Lords Francis, Raynerius, and Ugutio were heirs of the aforementioned Lord Bartholomew, their father, and accepted his inheritance, and acted as heirs of their father by virtue of the aforementioned testament. Now, the aforementioned Lady Beatrice, as testamentary heir of the aforementioned Lord Raynerius, and also the aforementioned Ugutio, with their own hands, and also the aforementioned Antonius, tutor, in the tutorial name of the aforementioned Francis of Siena and Alouisio, wish to sue the aforementioned John Guelfi, so that, intervening in the said names and manners, he render an account of the administration of the said revenues and incomes, with the restitution of the remainder; namely, to the same Lady Beatrice, heir of the aforementioned [Raynerius], for one-third part, to the same Ugutio for another third part, and also to the same Antonius, the aforementioned tutor, for the aforementioned reasons, for Francis of Siena and Alouisio for the other third part; since he is found to have rendered no account of the aforementioned to them. It is therefore asked whether the said John, constituted as above as major factor and manager of affairs, is bound to render an account with the full restitution of the remainder to the same Lady Beatrice, heir of the aforementioned [Raynerius], for one-third part, and to the aforementioned Ugutio for another third part, or not; concerning all the incomes of the common goods of the aforementioned Lords Francis, Raynerius, and Ugutio, and the heirs of the said Lord Bartholomew, and specially all the incomes of the said city of Cortona, and all the fruits or annuities of all and each of the deposits in florins and purchases made by the said Lord Francis in his name, considering the aforementioned, and also considering that brothers during communion among them are bound to share the fruits and revenues of adventitious goods and of any other goods acquired by any of them; and because those acquired goods and lordships appear to be profectitious [derived from paternal substance] from the paternal substance and from the common goods of themselves, and from the work of the fortifications and the lordship of their father, namely of the said Lord Bartholomew. Finally, inasmuch as Lord John is bound to render the aforementioned account, and renders no account, because perhaps he deceitfully does not show the account books, since the said John, at the time when he became major factor, had nothing of his own in the world, and has become very rich in possessions, money, merchandise, and debtors, and movables, perhaps from the aforementioned revenues, presuming that he was accustomed during the time of the said administration to exercise certain mercantile activities with those revenues and to derive profit therefrom; and especially since at the time of the death of the same Lord Francis, the entire treasury remained and was in the hands of the said John, whether the aforementioned Lady Beatrice, Ugutio, and Antonius, tutor, can vindicate those possessions, money, merchandise, debtors, and movables then existing with the said John, obtained by him, as goods rescinded, as above, pertaining by right from the aforementioned causes; or what they ought to demand from the said John, who does not render the aforementioned account. How, however, the rendering of the account of the said administration, or of the said possession, or something else is to be demanded from the said John in the case where the aforementioned have right, you shall found, we ask, before arbitrators in juridical form.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, and by what action, a negotiorum gestor (manager of another’s affairs) is bound to render an account of his administration.
2. A negotiorum gestor is not presumed to have enriched himself from the principal’s assets, unless this is proven.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This is a subtle matter.

† Lord Francis proposed that he and his brothers had appointed a manager for their common affairs. This manager, following the mandate of Lord Francis alone, conducted the business of Lord Rayner and Ugutio, who had given no mandate. The question is whether the said manager is bound to render an account of the administration to the said Lord Rayner, or his heir, and also to the said Ugutio, by means of the action for management of affairs (negotiorum gestio) or another action, or not. And it seems that he is not bound: as in D. 17.1.13 (Si tibi mandaveris), § Si curator. And to the contrary it seems that he is bound: as in C. 4.6.1 (Si mandatum solius). This question is debated in the gloss to D. 3.5.3, § Apud Marcellum. John, however, distinguished: either the manager knew that the affairs were common affairs; and then the action for management of affairs arises reciprocally; or he was ignorant, and then the action for mandate belongs solely to the mandator, and to the others in no way; because he did not have the intention of obligating himself to others, or of others to himself. But Azo said indistinctly that the action for management of affairs lies, because the truth is inspected rather than the proposal of the manager: D. 3.5.1 (Quae utiliter), § Si. But in the aforementioned law Si mandatum solius, a sub-distinction is made in the case of the ignorant manager: either the affair was truly theirs who did not mandate, or by ratification. In the first case, the opinion of Azo is true. In the second case, the opinion of John is true. And this is the truth, and so hold Odofredus and other doctors commonly. From this solution we conclude that the said manager is bound to render an account to all of the revenues of the common things; but of the revenues of the proper things of Lord Francis, he is not bound to render an account to Lady Beatrice, nor to Ugutio, nor even of the mercantile transactions made in the name of Lord Francis, nor of the revenues of his own name in his behalf; but of all these he is bound to render an account to the heirs of Lord Francis, namely Francis of Siena and Louis. And the reason for the confirmation of the above is: because trading is not an affair truly of anyone, but by ratification, which has no place when it was not managed in consideration of him: D. 26.7.1 (Titium), § Altero. Moreover, the fruits of lordship are not shared with brothers, just as neither are the fruits of any dignity, or otherwise of an office: D. 38.2.1, § Nec castrense; D. 38.10.1 (Si filia), § Idem scribit, in the second response. From these things it appears by whom action should be brought, and concerning which things; and how the libel should be formed. Thus it will be formed on behalf of Lady Beatrice and Ugutio, that a general account of the administration of all the goods of the late said Lord Francis be demanded, namely to the said Lady Beatrice as heir of Lord Rayner, continging to the said Lord Rayner while he lived, and for the other third part to the said Ugutio, with the return of the remainder; that which is noted in D. 43.1.1, § 1. Francis and Louis, however, will form the libel concerning all that was administered, namely concerning the revenues of the common goods for the other third part which falls to them, and for the other things which pertain to them alone, between the two of them jointly and severally, and in the libel they will conclude.

† It must be known: that the said manager is not presumed to have enriched himself from the goods of the owners, unless it is proven, as in C. arbitrium tutelae, l. si defunctus. Although in the case of public administrators the glossa says the contrary in l. facultas, C. de iure fisci, lib. 10. For these owners have a double patrimony, namely fiscal and private, as in l. bene a Zenone, with similar authorities. Furthermore, to remove all doubt, it should be stated in the libellus of the lady Beatrice and Ugutio, that the said manager knew the goods to be common. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A minor cannot, even with the father’s authority, nor by obligation, nor by cession of rights, nor by any other act, principally and directly prejudice himself; but what is the case with an adult, and with an oath, and number 1.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In

† It is not doubtful that a ward is not bound, because even with the father’s authorization he cannot be bound, nor can he alienate, nor cede rights, nor do anything else by which he would principally and directly prejudice himself, as stated in D. de pactis, l. contra iuris civilis regulas; in the beginning of D. de verbis oblig., l. si; §. fin. of Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. pupillus; at the end. Nor is an oath valid, nor does it harm the ward, as in l. qui iurasse, D. de iureiurando. Nor does the perfunctory testimony of the father harm him, nor the pronouncement of the judge, if the contrary is proven. D. de minoribus, l. minor 25; an. ex aspectu, D. de in integrum restitutione minorum, l. de tutela; D. de probationibus, l. etiam matris.

But let us assume that he was an adult, yet still under 25 years of age; whether he could cede his rights with an oath: I say that he could not, because two consanguineous relatives did not consent; and this by the aforementioned statute, which orders everything to be annulled. D. 34.1.1, *Si quis inquilinos*, § *Si*; and note Bartolus, D. 46.1.1, *Si quis pro eo*; and D. 4.4.1, *Etiam*, 1, response. The objection based on that particle of the statute does not hold. Moreover, the objection that it is for the debtor does not hold, because it does not speak of alienation; but the cession of rights is an alienation of actions; hence those words do not obstruct. Furthermore, there it says, "as if he were not a son under paternal power"; hence it openly disposed the same for a son under paternal power as for one who is not in power: this is the truth. The objection based on the pronouncement regarding age does not hold, because against a minor in defense, and *ex abrupto*, it is not valid. And because it created only a presumption, which transfers the burden of proof, and does not operate anything else: as is fully read and noted, D. 4.4.1, *De aetate*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If, after the promise to buy and to sell, the price is paid in full or in part, the sale is immediately consummated.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Lord Nicolaus, as appears from what he writes due to excessive haste, was unable to deliberate fully. For I know that he is an excellent man and one who reveres justice, and that he would have advised otherwise had he weighed the proceedings and the truth of the matter.

And so that the truth may be clearly understood, it must be known that if, after the promise to sell and to buy, there follows the payment of the price in whole or in part, the sale is immediately perfected by consent; and this is indicated by the very term “price,” as shown in l. si, C. de praediis curialibus, lib. 10. And although there was an agreement to sell, who doubts that the sale can immediately follow thereafter? For subsequent acts perfect prior ones, when regard is to be had to what follows. D. si certum petatur, l. lecta, and l. pacta novissima. Moreover, concerning this sale, preceded by a pact to sell, a written instrument was drawn up containing an express sale, which instrument the parties formally and entirely approved, and this is clearly demonstrated by many witnesses on the sixth article, not by only one witness. Furthermore, a private writing has some legal effect; indeed, in a certain sense, this contract was solemnized in writing. C. de fide instrumentorum, l. contractus. And therefore the aforementioned absolving sentence was not merely unjust, but horrible, and was rendered badly, very badly, and most unjustly. I do not write this out of excessive haste, but I write as I am accustomed to write, seeing and thinking well, so as not to offend anyone unjustly. And an appeal may be taken from it, and the appellant ought to prevail entirely.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Concerning paternal power, no compromise may be made, nor is an award valid that orders the emancipation of a son and commands that something be given to him as a reward for the emancipation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Patria potestas cannot be the subject of a compromise; nor is valid an award ordering the emancipation of a son and directing that a gift be made to him as a reward for emancipation; and such an award was null and inequitable. D. de arbitris, l. non dissimili, § liberali; D. de adoptionibus, l. non potest filius. Moreover, no mention was made in the compromise of the emancipation to be effected, nor of the gift; hence these matters are not included in the generality of the words. D. de pactis, l. contra iuris civilis, § si; D. de donationibus, l. filius; and D. de pignoribus, l. obligatione generali; C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. possessionum. For this must be obtained from the father out of grace, not imposed by a contrived scheme. C. de sententiis passim, l. finalis, ad finem. For the father may be induced, upon receiving a reward from the son, to grant emancipation; D. de verbis obligatorum, l. ob turpem. But it is not the case that the father must give a reward to the son, whether he wills it or not. And from this principal defect arises a defect in all its consequences.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An inheritance not taken up from a testator pertains to the intestate successors who take it up, but not to the bishop, on account of the right of taking up the inheritance belonging to the daughter.
2. If the Church is instituted or substituted: whether, if it does not accept, the bishop is the heir; whether the institution is lapsed.
3. If the poor are instituted or substituted: whether the bishop can take up the inheritance and sell it, so that a chapel may be built.
4. The bishop is the father and guardian of the poor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If the inheritance is not accepted by virtue of a will, then such inheritance pertains to the intestate successors, that is, to those who accept it, as in C. de fideiussoribus, l. eam, quam. On account of the right of acceptance, the inheritance of the said pupil does not belong to the bishop, but to the uterine brother and sister of the said pupil.

† And for the understanding of this, it must be known that sometimes a specific church is instituted or substituted; and then, if such church does not accept, the bishop does not thereby become heir in the name of the church, but the institution and substitution become void, without prejudice to what will be said below.

† Sometimes the poor are instituted or substituted in general: then the bishop may enter upon the inheritance on behalf of the poor, just as a father enters upon the inheritance on behalf of his infant child, as in C. de epis. et cle. l. si quis ad declinandam.

For the bishop is the father and guardian of the poor; and the poor are equated with infants, because just as an infant does not understand what he sees, so too do the poor in general, since they constitute a certain mystical body lacking understanding. Therefore, the bishop, whether he is equated with a father or a guardian, may then intervene, as provided in C. de iure delib. l. Si infanti; C. de episc. et cler. l. Orphanotrophos. What, then, is the situation in our case, in which the church of the Friars Minor is a church substituted for the construction of a chapel? I answer that the substitution is void; nevertheless, the chapel must be constructed, because a pious use ought not to be abandoned but fulfilled with the care of the bishop. And if it cannot be built in the place of the Friars Minor, it must be built elsewhere, as stated in l. Lege, de usufructu legato; l. De relictis domibus; c. Quia contingit, in the Decretals; and l. Legata, de administratione rerum ad civitatem pertinentium; as well as extra de testamentis, c. Nos quidem.

But it must be observed that the vicar was too hasty in selling the goods, for he could not do this, especially before declaring where the chapel was to be constructed; because the words of the will state that the said goods cannot be held unless at the time the chapel is being made. Furthermore, because the legitimate heir was not in default, he ought to be compelled here to sell and to do what the testator commanded, especially on account of the codicillary clause, which binds those who come intestate. The bishop, although he is the legitimate executor, could not sell so abruptly. See C. de distractione pignorum, l. Creditor; and in Auth. de ecclesiasticis, tit. § Si quis aedificationem; and ff. de alimentis et cibariis legatis, l. Alio haerede, where this is concluded in the ordinary gloss. It is therefore concluded that the chapel must absolutely be constructed, that the legitimate heirs succeed, and that the vicar could not sell by any right.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one can be bound in his own name, and principally, and in the name of others as a surety.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. As to the point,

Whether one could bind oneself principally in one’s own name and as a surety in the name of others is not in doubt, but rather it is so. Argument: Digest, On the Usufruct of Those Things; On Tutors and Curators; On Those from Whom [Tutors/Curators] are Demanded, l. Romanus Apostolus; and fully noted: Digest, On the Velleian Law, l. vir vxori, §. fin. As for the principal point, I say that, since execution has been made for a thousand florins, one thousand pounds cannot be further exacted from the first promise for the same offense. As in Digest, On Praetorian Stipulations, l. Valerianus, and there fully on the matter. For when the principal debtors are released from the last promise, which contains more, an exception is prepared for them and for their sureties in the first promise, which contains less. Digest, On Verbal Obligations, l. qui vsufru. And this applies when the principals are the same persons liable for the debt. But if any principal were in the first obligation who was not repeated in the second, then by the second stipulation it would not be mentioned or novated as to him, nor as to his sureties, nor as if the first obligation. And I speak of living persons in this case; an action could be brought against him and his sureties from the first stipulation. And this supports the point: Codex, On Leases, l. cum in plures, §. l. dicta; and Digest, On Constituted Peculium, l. qui autem, §. pen.; and Digest, On Compromises, l. 3. personam, §. qui pecuniam. And if anyone examines this matter, he will find that one thing is a change, another is the addition of a new security without repetition of the principal obligation. The first releases by operation of law, if this is the issue; the second by means of an exception; the third in no way.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a daughter, with the consent of her father, in the absence of her husband, and without his consent, may make a donation causa mortis.
2. Whether a statute speaking of alienation applies to delivery.
3. Whether a donation causa mortis is an obligatory contract.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether a daughter, with the father consenting and the husband absent, and without the husband’s consent, may make a donation causa mortis. It is certain that she cannot bind herself, nor her heir; and therefore she cannot promise to make a donation, because from such a promise she would be bound with effect, as is fully read and noted by Bartolus, and also by Decius, in l. 1, ff. de donis causa mortis. But by delivery she does not seem to be prohibited: because he who delivers does not bind himself. de aedificio edito, l. ad res donatas; and noted by Bartolus in l. 3, de legatis primo.

† And thus the statute has no place in a donation causa mortis beginning with delivery. I say the same if a daughter, with the father's consent, promises a donation causa mortis: because it is one thing to promise, another to permit; for he who promises is not bound by the donation, but extrinsically, and if it were inter vivos, an action on the donation arises. If he later hinders it, see ff. de donationibus, l. qui saxum; ff. de donationibus, l. si cum mihi; cf. ff. de donationibus, l. Aquilius regulus.

It must be considered whether a donation causa mortis is properly an obligatory contract. If a stipulation or pact intervenes, it is a contract, as noted in the great gloss on l. 1, ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, and in the Authentica sacramenta puberum. But if only a promise intervenes, it is not an obligatory contract. That which is noted in l. 2, de donationibus praeelegatis, de legatis 2, l. legata, supports this. What then, if both intervene, namely a promise and a permission? I answer that after the permission it does not have effect so that an action may be brought therefrom; nevertheless, if the donee possesses, he has an exception and a right of retention; because certain things are valid for retaining which are not valid for bringing an action. But this is so on account of the reason for which I write: because the instrument contains permission to take possession by one’s own authority; and the useful is not vitiated by the useless, but it is valid insofar as it can be valid. And this is true if the donation is made without defect and fraud; otherwise it would not be valid, as in ff. de auctoritate tutoris, l. 1, in fine, joined with l. pupillus, § per interpositam, in the same title, holding the opinion of the gloss. For the legitime of the children must always be preserved, if this daughter had children. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A loan for consumption is threefold.
2. A dowry is threefold.
1. A dowry, which does not appear to have been paid by confession or by instrument, can never acquire the privilege of priority.
2. A dowry released by acceptance is recovered as if it had been given.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.
It should be known that there are three types of mutuum: namely, natural, civil (to which nature cooperates), and civil simpliciter, as noted in l. 2, ff. si certum petatur.

† Moreover, dowry is threefold: namely, natural, when the counting is truly performed without stipulation; also civil, to which nature cooperates, when the counting is truly performed with stipulation, or when the counting follows a preceding written acknowledgment of confession; and civil simpliciter, when only the acknowledgment of the dowry intervenes, and the time for raising the exception of non-numerated money has elapsed.

† Moreover, it must be known that if it appears from a confession or an instrument that the dowry was not actually paid, such dowry can never acquire the privilege of any priority; hence, in this case, a second dowry truly paid is preferred to the first dowry which was merely confessed and not paid, as noted in *l. Assiduus*, *Qui potior in pignore habeatur*. Therefore, the distinction should be made as follows: either both were truly paid, and the first dowry is preferred; or both were merely confessed, and the time limits have lapsed, or the exception of *non numerata pecunia* has been waived, and the same rule applies: because, all other things being equal, the earlier dowry is preferred, as in § *Exceptis*. Or, if it clearly appears that the first was not paid, but the second was paid, or even confessed and thus deemed paid by legal fiction, then the second is preferred. In our case, however, according to the facts alleged, there was no payment of the first dowry, but a confession appears to have been made in hope of future payment; and this is evident from the stipulation immediately appended, which seems to be inherent, as in *l. Lecta*, *Si certum petatur*. Here it must be noted that if the first dowry had remained merely at the stage of confession, the action would have belonged jointly to the father and the daughter, and both would have had to bring an action for the dowry; thus, the confession benefited not only the daughter but also the father, as in *l. 2*, *De solutione matrimonii*. This confession is inherent in the *acceptilatio*; because the words there sound to this effect, when it is said: "I have accepted, I have received, what I took."

† and therefore the dowry accepted by acceptilatio is recovered, just as if it had been given, as in l. 2, ff. sol. mat. I do not say, however, that acceptilatio and confession are in all respects the same. ff. de sol. l. si ex pluribus. But when it appears from a contrary document that no money was actually paid, one must adhere to the truth, as in ff. si cert. pet. l. qui pecuniam, and note in c. 1, de confess., lib. 6. For the father could have confessed the contrary immediately, especially under the common law, as I said. This reasoning regarding the community of dowries is not acceptable according to l. quotiens, sol. mat., and l. ex morte, in fin., de pact. convent. But other reasons are acceptable. Moreover, the acts of the parties should not operate beyond their true intention, as in l. non omnis, si cert. pet. But it was never the true intention of the husband to be effectively bound to restitution without having received the dowry from the father of the woman. ff. de iure dot. l. si extraneus. But against the foregoing it is argued that, because of the confession, a right seems to have been acquired solely by the daughter, which right could not even be immediately taken away from her by the father. See the arguments we make in the case of loan: for if I pay in the name of one person, and then immediately make a stipulation, the payment prevails, as in ff. si cert. pet. l. certi condictio, §. si nummos. But there a true payment took place, whereas here it did not. Furthermore, it does not seem to be an obstacle that, although no payment took place here, a promise did take place, which is considered equivalent to payment: for it seems sufficient that the woman is deemed to have received payment if the husband is content with the promise, as in the aforementioned l. si extraneus, and ff. mand. l. inter causas, §. obesse. I answer that here it appears that the act was done in expectation of a future payment to be made by the father himself in the name of the daughter, as in ff. de ritu nup. l. qui libros. For if it is said that the confession was made in expectation of a future promise, I concede this; but the end of a promise is performance, as in l. 2, §. credi, si cert. pet. Therefore, considering the ultimate end, it was a species of payment. It is not an obstacle that the noted Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus in the aforementioned l. penult., §. penult., sol. mat. say that what they state is true where there is no question of the priority of dowries: however, where a privilege of priority is at issue, their statement should not be extended to this case; but one must follow the gloss in the aforementioned §. except., from which it is concluded that the second dowry is preferred here, not as the only one, since it does not appear that any payment was made, either in fact or by legal fiction, regarding the first. Moreover, it does not appear here that the father received the confession from the husband in the name of the daughter, nor that any right was acquired by the daughter through the instrument that I saw. Furthermore, it is not proven by the fact that he made mention of another document.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A tacit substitution is not admitted against the mother.
2. Legacies left for the soul do not require acceptance of the inheritance.
3. Whether a substitution made to a child in pupillary status, who has since died, excludes the mother, given that the said substitution was made to religious brothers, and considering that the testator ordered a church to be built at the expense of the inheritance, thus for divine worship and in favor of the soul.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Having examined the testament of John Gilii, and having considered the substitution he made in favor of the male descendants of the instituted heirs, namely the spiritual brothers known as the Apostles, which was a pupillary substitution; having considered that the posthumous son died in pupillary age after the death of his father; and having considered that the said spiritual brothers repudiated the inheritance devolved to them by virtue of the pupillary substitution, it is doubted what should be done with the goods of the said testator, in light of the substitution made in favor of the spiritual brothers of the Order of the Brothers of the Body of Christ, who are called the Apostles, who were substituted in the place of the said Apostles in two cases, namely if the Apostles should alienate, and if the testator should die without sons. For the understanding of this, it must be known that although a direct substitution made for one case contains a similar case, nevertheless, where the mother is in the middle, as is the case here, because the mother of the posthumous son is alive, the rule is different, because a tacit substitution is not admitted against the mother. C. de impub. et aliis substitutio, l. fin. From this it follows that the said pupil died intestate, and that the mother succeeds to him intestate; nevertheless, the pious judgment of the deceased ought to be brought to effect by pontifical authority, as ff. de annuis legatis, l. Quintus Mutius, § ad auctoritate, especially on account of the codicillary clause, which may be appended to a pupillary substitution, since a father may make a codicillary disposition in favor of his son. ff. de legatis primo, l. quod fideicommissum.
And because legacies for the soul do not require the acceptance of the inheritance, and by the sole authority of the law they have effect according to the common opinion.

† Now therefore let us see how that which the testator commanded is to be put into execution. The words of the will state that the Apostles are to be built at the expense of the inheritance in a certain farmhouse situated in a certain estate, to be made into a church and a penitential place, and adapted for dwelling for the sake of prayer and the divine office: and that the said brothers and chapter etc. must stay and reside there. It does not specify what or how much he bequeaths to that church, because he had left all his patrimony to those spiritual persons; and therefore it would seem to be said that, saving the legitimate portion due to the mother, which is one-third part, only so much should be spent from the testator’s goods as would suffice for the construction and endowment of the said church and spiritual place. So that at least three, who make up a chapter, may sufficiently live there and celebrate the divine ministries. D. de legatis secundo, l. quidam in testamento, where the case appears. It is also certain that those who reside there must be maintained there. D. de annuis legatis, l. Quintus Mutius, at least from the fruits of that estate where the church is to be constructed. D. de usufructu legato, l. Sempronio, §. fin. And it supports this, Extr. de praebendis, cap. Cum secundum Apostolum. It can also be said that, except for the said legitimate portion, everything ought to be assigned to divine worship and given to the church. And the reason is that it was left to those spiritual brothers in contemplation of the church and divine worship; hence all the goods seem to have been left to the church and divine worship, and honor given to God. D. de legatis tertio, l. fideicomissa, §. plerunque. Hence also, if the Apostles are removed from the scene by renunciation, a pious and universal bequest for the sake of God remains. And thus it is probable that the testator intended: hence we must follow this, as in the said l. quidam, §. si modo, which can be said fairly and plausibly in favor of the soul, for which interpretation ought to be made as broadly as possible. It supports this in Auth. de ecclesiasticis titulis, §. si quis aedificatione, col. 9. For this purpose, the brothers of the Body of Christ are to be chosen and appointed. For the case of repudiation is similar to alienation, as in D. de bonis libertorum, lege liberto octoginta, and D. de rebus creditis, l. magis puto, §. fundum autem. I conclude therefore that the bishop is bound by duty to appoint and confirm the said brothers of the Body of Christ, and to assign to them the goods of the said testator, saving the legitimate portion due to the mother; but no legitimate portion is due to the collateral heirs, because the donation and intention of the said testator ought not to be defrauded.

CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. The point and case is as follows: Lord Arnaldus de Ferner of Barcelona sold to Matthew Antonii of Florence, a merchant residing in the city of Pisa, a certain quantity of Sicilian grain, which he promised to deliver to him within a certain time. And among other agreements of that second sale, in the document of that market, such a clause was added. From which arises the doubt:

"Furthermore, the said Master Arnaldus is bound and must in every way conduct, or have conducted, onto the said ship, without making or changing any voyage, the said ship loaded with the said grain, in the manner as in this writing. And for him no action may be brought, or have brought, in any way, and for any reason, except if by a fortuitous case of God or of the sea the ship should perish, or if the said ship were taken by an enemy fleet able to force it, may God in His mercy save and guard it. In these two cases only the said Master Arnaldus is not bound to this market. But in every other adverse case, or fortune of whatever condition it may be, or if a disaster were made as one might wish, or in another case, whatever it might be or could be, he is bound and must observe, or keep, and put into execution the whole of the said market."

And then in the document of the merchant, if there were a breach, a penalty was appended, and an oath interposed by both parties to keep the promises; finally it happens that the said Arnaldus, the seller, went with the said ship to the island of Sicily, and loaded it with grain: And while thus loaded it stood in the port of that island, a certain messenger of the Lord Duke, the eldest infant, having two sealed letters, one, it is said, of the general bailiff of that kingdom, by which he commanded all and each patron and sailor of whatever condition, as to the mandate of that messenger of the bailiff, that all their ships with grain must be conducted and go to load at the port of Barcelona, by command of the King, since there was great scarcity in those parts, under penalty of fine and person. The other was a letter of the consuls or councilors of Barcelona, by which they notified all persons and sailors that the will by command of the King and the bailiff was in their commands and letters, notwithstanding whatever pacts, promises, and obligations contracted and entered into with whatever communities and persons, although in the letters of the bailiff they are not contained. Likewise they entreat and request all patrons and sailors that they come to unload their ships in Barcelona, so that they do not incur the threatened penalty, and to this they exhort. And copies of those letters are sent to you together with this present point. That messenger with these letters boarded the ship, which was then secure in that port, the patron then being on land, and having made the command to the sailors, who were then at sea. Finally the patron returned and expelled that messenger from the ship: and thence after certain days he set sail with the ship. And while he was on the voyage and navigation, and that messenger was in another ship existing in the convoy with the aforementioned one, at night time that messenger descending into the ship of the inundated went to the said seller then present: and alone he boarded it, and made the command to that patron present and the sailors of that ship by virtue of those letters under penalty of fine and person, that they must go to unload in the port of Barcelona. Then the sailors, recalling the patron to such command, although this is not established, pretending to recall, and placing another in his place, led the ship to Barcelona: and there they unloaded, not delivering the grain to the above-mentioned buyer. Now that buyer, on account of the non-observance of the contract and pact, demands the penalty against the seller and his sureties, assuming as constant that the facts were as the seller alleges and is written above. It is asked, what is the law.

Finally another doubt occurs in the course of the cause, although the force of the question does not rest on this, on account of other things which were brought forward and proved in the cause for the liquidation of the fact. The doubt therefore occurs, because on all the clauses of that market, and those contained in the document of that market made by the scrivener, the plaintiff made his interrogations and positions. The defendant responds to them in this way: he believes, unless a case of just impediment occurs, as it occurred, and nothing the defendant proceeds on the case of just impediment; finally the plaintiff produces the document of that market: in which the case that occurred is not described; which document was subscribed by the seller and the sureties: and thus they confess. Now it is asked, whether this confession, thus qualified and conditioned, constitutes proof against the confessor, so that it stands against him and not for him, or not: it is asked, what is the law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is lawful for one who holds no public office to resist by force.
2. Whether a superior's command excuses from punishment.
3. What the mere utterance of words imports.
4. Whether a case that cannot be removed by human ingenuity is said to be fortuitous.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. That Lord Arnaldus has incurred the penalty, notwithstanding the force alleged by him, appears from several reasons.

† And first, because he ought to have resisted him with force, since the latter was in no way exercising any office in this case, as is stated in C. de iure fisci, l. prohibitum, lib. 10; and C. de metallis, l. devotum, lib. 12; and D. loc. cond., l. item quaeritur, l. exercitu, and the notes thereon.

For the King’s command did not touch the case of a ship laden with Sicilian wheat: since Sicily is free from it, nor placed under his jurisdiction. D. de auctoritate iudicis positi, l. cum unus, § is qui; and in l. cunctos populos, with its subject matter. Nor ought one to fear the Prince’s indignation, who does not say that he violates his mandate: and if he fears, it is a vain fear, which does not excuse. D. quod metus causa, l. nec timor. And it is expressly stated in X. de appellationibus, c. cum parati. Secondly, because it is not probable that Lord Arnald was unwillingly compelled by his men, over whom he commanded on the ship, as C. de servis exponendis, l. moueor. Thirdly, because, excepting two cases, Lord Arnald assumed every other fortuitous case; therefore, apart from the two cases, no other case excuses him from the penalty, as fully noted in D. l. sed et si quis, § quaesitum; and l. 1, C. communi. The first case excepted was if the ship should perish by a chance of the sea. The second case was if danger should occur by irresistible force; for in that case he wished to be bound to the wheat, because by such force the thing promised, that is, the wheat, was taken from him; hence, because he would then have nothing to give, as D. locati, l. in nave saufelli, he excepts this case. However, our case is not conformable to this, neither in terms nor in the decisive reason: because here there is no intervening right of confirmation, nor loss of wheat, but rather gain: because the ship arrived safely with the wheat at the place where wheat was very dear: and the letters of the King and of the Barcelonians testify to this, namely, to the extreme dearth; therefore, it must be considered that Lord Arnald did this through precipitous avarice. C. de nautico faenore, l. cum proponas; so that he might go to a nearer place, where the danger of the sea is more quickly incurred, and where he would sell the wheat at a higher price, as C. de nauicula, l. cum procuratores, lib. 11. And in the true and pure conscience of the judge, this ought to weigh heavily. Fourthly, because when an exception is made by the number of exceptions, and not by their qualities, as is the case here, because it says in two cases

† With a taxative word, namely "only," no extension can ever be made to a third or fourth case on account of some similarity, as is read and noted in C. de annua exceptione, l. ut perfectis; C. de praediis minorum, l. ob aes. For an exception does not limit the disposition except in the case of the exception itself, l. ff. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. si vendita, with similar authorities. The direct office of an exception is to except directly, and tacitly it confirms the rule in the rest of the wording, as in l. 1, de regulis iuris, with the common material. Fifth, this is proven, for even if the said lord Arnaldus had truly been prevented from sailing, it must be considered that he was bound to deliver a quantity of wheat in general; hence the difficulty did not release him, ff. de verborum obligatione, l. continuus, §. illud. For in this case the risk is that of the seller, as Bartolus elegantly notes, ff. de locato, l. si uno, §. item cum quidem. Nor was anything said here in the contract by way of taxative specification, e.g., that it was grown in Sicily, but simply, de verb. oblig., l. inter stipulantes, §. sacramentum. If therefore he did not cross the sea, he ought to have delivered at the term, or at least could, without contestation of the lawsuit, offer in the persons themselves or in a warehouse good wheat, as stated in the contract; or, by undertaking the voyage again, fulfill his promise, ff. de constituta pecunia, l. sed et alia, and l. item illa. Therefore, the final compromise ought to be observed, ff. de arbitris, l. Celsus, §. idem ait; de eo quod certo loco, l. quod si Ephesi; ff. de locato, l. pen., §. navem. For he is not released from the principal obligation, therefore neither from the penal one; for even in l. Caesar, de publicanis, one must sail again and depart from the port, so that the intent of the contracting parties and the utility of the agreement may be preserved; otherwise one incurs the penalty. Moreover, it is no objection, ff. ad legem Rhodiam de iactura, l. pen., §. idem iuris, there "publicly detained" etc., because there the ship perished by the act of public persons together with the goods contained therein; here not, as noted there. Moreover, there the thing was that of the charterer of the ship, and that specific species perished; here it is a genus, and nothing perished here. Moreover, the persons were not public here; for the axes of the empire are not extended beyond the territory, l. secunda, de officio proconsulis et legatorum, and C. de decuriis, l. divinarum, lib. 10. Moreover, what right does the fisc have in another's calamity or prosperity? Certainly none, as l. prima, C. de naufragio, lib. 11; C. de furtis, auth. navigia. Moreover, it was not the intention of the King to do injury to the buyer, de vulgari substitutione, l. ex facto, in principio; no objection, de evictionibus, l. Lucius, because there the specific will and power of the prince appear; here not. Sixth, this is proven here by a notable law, which my beloved lord Ludovicus de Plumbis alleges. And I, after Bartolus, ff. de locato, l. qui insulam, §. colonus. For since it is certain that the fault was either in this lord Arnaldus or in his agents, because the definite command of the King did not touch them, I say that if they used force against them, he is liable for the fault of his agents, no objection, ff. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. si vendita. For there there was no agreement on an adverse event, here there was. Someone will say, nor does an agreement on an adverse event bring about a fortuitous event, as ff. de locato, l. opus. I answer, there no specification of an adverse event was made, here it was, and thus it is no objection. Seventh, and finally, it must be considered that events have causes, and are judged fortuitous or culpable according to the originating causes leading to the event, ff. communi dividundo, l. si ut cer0, §. sed interdum, as noted there.

And if indeed the counsel of a free man cannot remove the case, this is called a case with this adjective, fortuitous. On pledge, action. L. fortuitis. D. On action. Sale. L. si ea res. But if by the skill of man the facts can be avoided, as Ptolemy says, the wise man will rule the stars. Then it is otherwise; but in our case, by the skill of man and by the skill of the law, the case should not have been feared: because he who is a good man does not despise discipline, he preserves his legality. Deposit. L. bona fides. Indeed, the better he is, the more pleasing he is to the King: for he cultivates justice, otherwise he is a tyrant, as in Auth. de man. princi. §. si quis autem, cui tale. And there no. From these, therefore, which my mind conceives, and because it was applauded, as it seems to me, in the instrument of precept, I think the aforementioned lord Arnald was as culpable as if he had bound himself to the case: and therefore he is not excused from the penalty: which I say always saving the conscience of the judge, who may know better: but I am in the aforementioned sentence. CASE. The point on which counsel is requested is as follows. In the volume of statutes of the land of Terreti there are two statutes. The first is that no person dare or presume to incite men to uproar, or brawl, or fight by crying to arms to arms, or by doing other things, especially at the time of any brawl or fight to the injury of anyone: whoever contravenes this shall be punished in twenty-five pounds each time. Another statute is that if anyone strikes another with arms, wood, stick, and club, and similar things or any of them, or with iron in the face, face, or head with effusion of blood, he is condemned in twenty-five pounds. Now the case has occurred that a certain Paul armed himself with a wooden staff, made an assault against a certain John, and struck him with the said staff on the head with effusion of blood: on account of which a great uproar was made in the land of Terreti. Now assuming that these things are clearly proven, it is asked whether the aforementioned Paul, the offender, can be punished by the force of the said statutes both for the blow given and also for the uproar made in the land of Terreti, please advise, and affix your seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that anyone is to be punished for making a disturbance, and another statute providing that anyone is to be punished for assault, if someone committed an assault accompanied by a disturbance, is he to be punished for both? And no. 2.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The crime arising from the assault, the striking, and the other acts committed and perpetrated after the striking, as appears from the inquisition, is distinct from the crime of incitement to public disturbance, which is a crime in itself; hence one may be punished both for the wounding and for the incitement, because one is not merged with the other, as stated in D. de priv. del. l. nunquam placatur and C. de accus. l. qui de crimine. Consider, indeed, that this person committed a twofold offense, for by inciting public disturbance he offended the public, and principally the private individual; and therefore, since he intended to commit both crimes, he ought to be punished for both. The objection based on D. de capt. et postlim. revert. l. si quis ingenuam § in civilibus does not hold, because there the disturbance occurred only incidentally and as if through a very remote cause; here, however, it occurred immediately and through many other acts closely connected and tending toward incitement and public disturbance. Moreover, it is not said that such disturbance, if attached to wounds or to a delict, is not a separate delict. This is supported by C. de sepulcr. viol. l. qui sepulchra, where it states "a twofold offense," and by C. de accusat. l. senatus esse censuit, according to Bartolus. For here there are two titles of crime, two forms of action, and two persons principally offended, namely the public through the disturbance, and the private person through the affliction of his body.

† Suppose that someone made a disturbance, and in the course of the disturbance killed a man; he is not to be punished for both, certainly not in this way, lest you leave the homicide unpunished: certainly not. Moreover, here there are many acts committed after the initial blow; and therefore they are not merged into one another. I, Baldus.
