consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a dowry can be claimed back by the wife's heir, from whom the husband confessed to having received it, even though he had not in fact received it.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked what is the law, namely whether the aforementioned Angelo can recover the said dowry as heir of the late Lady Ludovica, his former sister: and it seems that he can, because Francesco Orlandi confessed to having received from the aforementioned Angelo, in the name of the dowry of the said Lady Ludovica, sister of the said Angelo and wife of the said Francesco, 1,075 pounds of denarii, by the hand of a public notary; from which confession the right of the said Lady Ludovica was acquired; hence the heir of the said Lady can sue as heir. Notwithstanding the objection that subsequently the said Angelo promised to give to the said Francesco, on account of the said dowry, notwithstanding the said confession, 1,075 pounds of denarii, as appears by the hand of a public notary; for if the right to demand was already acquired by the woman, it could not be novated, nor impeded by a contrary contract, as in D. de pactis, l. si; and D. sol. mat., l. quo; and C. de rem in praesenti, §. accidit; D. de transact., l. 3, in principio; D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. ante omnia. Even if he who later contracted to the contrary should become the heir of the woman, see D. de pactis, l. si tibi, §. si pactus. And see D. de exceptionibus, l. Modestinus. To the contrary is the truth itself, for it matters greatly whether one confesses to having received from the woman; and then a subsequent act to the contrary by his own procurator does not prejudice the woman, D. de manum., l. si hominem. Or whether he confesses to having received from the procurator, who procurator immediately, and before turning to other acts, confesses the contrary; and then the last statement must be believed, D. de acquirenda possessione, l. si quis ante. Indeed, it is certainly always to be believed that what is said last is true, and whatever is permitted by way of confession appears to be done in hope of future provision, D. sol. mat., l. pen., §. si vir, according to Bartolus. Moreover, the heir suing as heir is bound to prove that his own claim is true; nor can he, as heir, sue against himself, as noted by the gloss and Dino, D. de re iudicata, l. Is qui haeres, §. si te. Therefore I say that whether carnal intercourse took place or not, it is irrelevant; for he who sues for the recovery of what was not truly paid acts in bad faith, and ought to be repelled. Nor is it a matter for dispute here how much Angelo can demand, or how much he cannot, because he can recover nothing, except up to the said amount; but this may be doubted, whether Francesco, or his heir, can demand from the said Angelo that half of the dowry remain with the said Francesco on account of carnal intercourse. For the dowry is said to be promised, although not yet paid. Response: When it is asked whether those who succumb by way of exception are admitted to sue, I answer that if the exception was fully cognized, then he is not admitted to sue, D. de compensatione, l. quod in diem, §. si in rationem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A substitution by which the transfer of an already vested inheritance is made through another is fideicommissary.
2. The opinion that an inheritance transferred to another by fideicommissum is transferred under the same condition fails, etc.
3. Where delay and penalty are to be incurred and triggered by interpellation, it is required that the person interpellated knows, or ought to know, that he is bound.
body: In the Name of Christ.

† On the first point, it seems to be said that a substitution, by which the transfer of an already acquired inheritance is made through another, is a fideicommissary substitution. D. de legatis 3, l. uxor, § haeres, where the text, the gloss, and Dynus so presuppose: and this is true. The law *ciuilibus* supports this, as does the law *cum si*.

† On the second point, I say that when an inheritance is transferred to another by fideicommissum, it appears to be transferred under the same condition, as in D. de administratione legatorum, l. legatum; and D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. sub conditione. This fails, however, if by such repetition the disposition would be vitiated, as in D. de legatis 2, l. si quis a filio, in principio. It also fails if the condition is attached to the prior person, as if a legacy is left to a woman upon bearing a child, and ownership is transferred by restitution of that legacy to another; it is impossible that this condition be transferred, as in l. legatum and C. de caducis tollendis, § ne autem. In the present case, this Pierus was burdened with a penalty, having arrived after two months, once he had reached the age of majority. For if this time has passed, and therefore Brusius is deprived of the benefit of the inheritance, it is impossible to repeat the time that has already elapsed, and it is attached to the person; and therefore Brusius is understood to have been purely requested, without repetition of that time, as in the aforementioned l. sub conditione. For a delay, the expiration of which opens the way to the substitute, is not understood to be repeated in the substitution. It follows that the substitute is to be constituted in default, and consequently in deprivation, if any could threaten the said Brusius, by interpellation, and not by the lapse of a day as if appointed, as in C. de fideiussoribus, l. quaestionem, in fine. And by this, also, a response is given to the third doubt.

† On the fourth doubt, I say that where delay and penalty are to be incurred and provoked by interpellation, it is required that the person interpellated knows, or ought to know, that he is bound; as stated in D. si certum petatur, l. quod te. However, this is not the case as long as the matter remains unliquidated, or until liquidation by sentence, as in Auth. de haereditatibus et falcidia, §. si quis autem implens. This supports what is stated in D. de pignoribus et hypothecis, l. si convenit; and see the argument in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. cum falsum; and C. de bonis possidendis, l. quandiu; and fully noted in Inst. de actionibus, §. item mixta est actio contra eos. It is certain that the last disposition was codicillary and valid by the law of fideicommissum, because the testator stated that he did not wish it to be codicillary to the testament which he did not wish to be valid, except in the exchange. Therefore, let it be valid as it can be valid, given the institution of the heir by virtue of the testament which he first ordered. This supports what is noted by Bartolus in l. 1, D. de iure codicillorum; and D. ad Trebellianam, l. secundum. And thus it appears that the Trebellian institution is necessary.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether knowledge of the will and codicils is presumed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Knowledge of the will and codicils is presumed here: because it is presumed that one knows what one speaks; nor is he to be believed if he says that he knew one part of the same writing, but was ignorant of another part pertaining to him, as in D. de transactionibus, l. non est ferendus. This is clear from the notes of Bartolus in D. de verbis oblig., l. qui Romae, § duo fratres, in the third question. But although Brutius is presumed to have known the series of the will and codicils, which are mentioned in the said private writing, nevertheless it is not presumed that he knew that the said Pierus had not observed those conditions, the non-observance of which the testator declared would deprive the said Pierus of the inheritance; for this depends on the act of another, not on the act of Brutius himself; and in the act of another, ignorance is presumed. D. pro socio, l. si; D. de probationibus, l. numerus. Therefore, it is not presumed that he knew that the case of substitution had occurred. However, that he knew the words of the will and codicils appears from their formal recollection; because he made mention of their proper form, whence it is presumed that he knew it integrally and had examined the whole, as in the aforementioned l. non est ferendus. And all this was to be read to him, insofar as it pertained to him; but of those parts which were not to be read to anyone, knowledge is not presumed from the recollection of other parts; because it is not probable that those things were read to him which ought not to be read, as in c. contingit, de fide instrumentorum. It supports this what is noted in D. de liberis et legatis, l. cum heres; D. de transactionibus, l. qui tutorem, § fin.; and D. de his, ff. quemadmodum testamentum aperitur, l. 1; D. si certum petatur, l. eius, qui in provincia; and in the rule praesumitur; and D. de regulis iuris, l. qui cum alio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The fourth [point] concerns which things are to be left to the bishop.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Of all legacies to churches or pious places, a fourth part is due to the diocesan bishop as of right, Extra, de testibus, c. fin. Hence, of a legacy to another bishop, a fourth part is due: which is to be understood, except in reserved cases, for example if it is left for the fabric of such a church, and similar cases; then a fourth part is not due, as in c. fin. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A substitution made by these words: "the dowry of the deceased, or owed to her, shall remain for the other daughters who survive." What kind of substitution is this, and whether the daughter could then institute her mother as heir. And no. 4.
2. A legacy of a dowry, when she shall be of marriageable age, if it should fail, to whom it shall be acquired, or accrue, and what if the girl herself, dying, is the universal heir. And no. 3.
3. If anyone asks to be seen, what is said in law to constitute raising a brawl, or a dispute.
4. Whether one ignorant incurs a penalty: or if it is done against an ignorant condition, whether the condition is said to be defective.
5. If the testator left a quantity of one hundred pounds in coins to his daughter, or to be created at her election, whether the guardians, without a judicial decree, can assign to her possessions worth more than the said quantity.
6. Whether the testator can permit alienation by a minor, without a decree.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Beginning with the first point, it must be premised for clarity that a substitution made in common terms is sometimes in a specific thing or quantity, and sometimes in the inheritance. In the first case, common terms are used for oblique substitutions. D. ad Trebellianum, l. cogi, §. et generaliter, according to Dynus and the note in l. illa institutio, de haeredibus instituendis, according to Bartolus. In the second case, the matter applies. l. precibus and l. Centurio. Now, therefore, let us consider the substitution made among the daughters. The words of the will state: "the dowry of the deceased, or that which is due to her, shall remain to the other surviving daughters." The father bequeathed a dowry to his daughter and substituted in that same dowry: what kind of substitution is this? I answer that this substitution is a particular fideicommissary substitution, not a universal fideicommissary one; and much less is it a direct universal one. The law states that a father may substitute for his daughter in the dowry by means of a fideicommissum. D. de legatis 2, l. si, §. filiae, and the text there says that the word "perueniat," which is a common term, in this case implies a particular fideicommissum.

But suppose that the legacy of the dowry has lapsed, because the girl to whom the dowry was bequeathed when she would be of marriageable age died before reaching marriageable age. I answer that it remains with the heir, together with its burden. Codex, On the Abolition of the Falcidian Law, § pro secundo.

But suppose that the same pupilla, upon her death, is the universal heir. I answer that, although the legacy is extinguished by confusion, the fideicommissum does not accrue to others, nor is it altered. And therefore, only the dowry is contained within the fideicommissum, namely, the quantity of the dowry specifically designated by name; for no account is taken of increase or decrease, since the substitution was fixed by the testator in the dowry, as stated in the aforementioned §. et generaliter, where it says, "if he was asked concerning the thing or the quantity." Therefore, the words of the testament speak of the dowry of the deceased. Although, therefore, the legacy of the dowry, or the institution made specifically in the dowry, is extinguished by confusion due to the case of a male child not being born, as per ff. de legatis 1, l. legatum, §. haeredi, and l. ab omnibus, §. si a Titio, nevertheless, the formal particular substitution is not changed. And therefore, it is true that the sisters were not substituted to that infant in a pupillary substitution, but only in the one thousand pounds left for the dowry. In this quantity of one thousand pounds, the substitution of the surviving sisters takes place upon the death of Joanna, because no one is substituted to himself in a pupillary substitution; Veronica succeeded to her intestate for one-third part, and Leonarda, if she accepted the inheritance of Joanna, for another third part. That she accepted it is evident from the testament of Leonarda, who disposed of the succession of Joanna; for in a testament, an inheritance offered to the testator can be accepted. C. de iure deliberandi, l. si auia. It is true that, because Veronica passed to a second marriage, she loses ownership, and only the usufruct of those things which came to Joanna, her daughter, from her father's estate through the existence of her heir or through intermingling, remains to her. C. de secundis nuptiis, auth. ex testamento. It is also true that the said Antonia must have, before all else, five hundred pounds of those one thousand specified for the dowry of Joanna. Hence, on the first point, it is to be adjudicated by the arbitrators that, of the third part of the inheritance of Peter which belonged to the said Joanna, the said Antonia shall first have five hundred pounds, and the entire remainder shall belong to the said Antonia by right of ownership; as for the usufruct, one-half shall belong to Veronica, provided she gives security for using and enjoying according to the discretion of a good man and for restoring the property upon the termination of the usufruct; and the other half of the usufruct shall belong to Antonia freely. And this concludes the first point.

† On the second point, it must be said that Dr. Leonarda could have instituted her mother as universal heir; nor do the second marriages prejudice this, as stated in the aforementioned authority *Ex testamento*, in the first response, and in the inheritance of the said Domina Leonarda there are five hundred pounds out of the one thousand pounds left to Joanna; because the day had arrived before the said Domina Leonarda died, and she transmitted it by act. C. de cad. to. §. *In nouissimo*. Furthermore, there was her own hereditary portion of the paternal inheritance, that is, one-third of the inheritance of Peter, but with the burden of restoring the one thousand pounds left to Domina Leonarda as dowry, concerning which it must be seen whether Dr. Antonia ought to have those one thousand pounds and the other bequests made in the testament of Domina Leonarda; and certainly I say that Dr. Antonia ought to have those one thousand pounds from the paternal testament, and the legacy made by her sister from the testament of the sister, as in l. *Creditorem*, de leg. 2. And so it is to be judged by the arbitrators. But this is true provided the conditions of the sister’s testament are observed; otherwise she would lose the legacies made to her by her sister, as is provided in the testament. As C. de his, qui per not. l. 1. ad Trebel. l. *Lucius*. §. *Tres haeredes*. The words of the testament of Domina Leonarda are thus stated: if, and insofar as no lawsuit, question, dispute, or annoyance is raised, etc.

† But if the lady Antonia seeks to be heard, what right she herself has, and what right she has in the goods of Joanna, and that her right be assigned to each of them, whether by this she is said to be raising a dispute or a question. And it must be said that by her own right she ought to pay a thousand [units of currency] of her own motion; and if she does not wish to do so, she is at fault; nor from this does the said Antonia incur the penalty which the law demands. D. de verb. oblig. l. venditores. However, concerning the goods possessed by the mother, or concerning the administration of Joanna's goods, because it appears that a certain release was left to the mother, if she were to claim such things, she would incur the penalty.

† But here it is doubted whether one who acts in ignorance incurs the penalty, or if one acts contrary to a condition out of ignorance, the condition is said to be defective; and it must be said that this is not so, because a stipulative condition requires knowledge. D. de cond. et demonstr. l. 2. Therefore, the sister must fulfill the will of her sister, and she will rejoice in her judgment: and I speak of wealthy inheritances. Therefore, I advise that wills be observed as they sound; nor should the wills of testators be transgressed and altered. C. de codic. l. fin. And this is the second point.

† On the third point, the words of Peter’s testament must be considered, which are as follows: “and let the said quantity of six hundred pounds be had in cash or in wax candles, namely at the election of the said lady.” The question is whether the guardians, without a judicial decree, could have assigned to her, for the said quantity, possessions worth more than the said quantity.

And it is certain that the testator may permit this alienation to be carried out even without a decree, as stated in l. 2, C. quando decreto opus non est. And thus the formality is dispensed with; nevertheless, it must be done at a fair price, as stated in l. non dubium, §. fin., de legatis 3. And if the price was not adequate, it must be reduced to an adequate one, even if the deception was less than half of the just price; because the guardians could not be more lenient in any respect without a judicial decree than the testator intended, l. qui fundum, §. si tutor, de usucapione pro emptore. And therefore, to the extent that the property is of greater value, the fruits must also be restored to that extent; because good faith does not appear to have intervened due to the inadequacy of the price, argumentum C. mandati, l. per diversas; ff. de minoribus, l. et si sine; and argumentum ff. de iure dotium, l. sive generalis. And thus it ought to be pronounced by the said arbitrators on the third point. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a commune may take away or diminish something from the purchasers of tolls, or enact anything to their prejudice. And no. 5.
2. One thing is the object, another is the price of the object.
3. When the leased thing is destroyed, to what is the lessee bound.
4. Rights have their own deaths.
5. If a toll is taken away from purchasers who bought it from the commune, or if anything is enacted by the commune to their prejudice, whether the commune is bound for damages, and what concerning profit.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Given the tenor of the ordinance issued concerning the raising of one-third of the tax on ground grain for the current year, which began on the 15th day of the month of June last past, for the inhabitants of the territory of Perugia and those paying taxes, and regarding the exemption and exception from the said one-third part, and that if they have paid anything of the said one-third part, they shall be reimbursed in other payments. And the purchasers for the said one-third part for the said year are to be understood and are exempt, and for the said one-third part of the said tax they cannot be compelled to pay to the commune. And that the said purchasers cannot demand the said one-third part, etc. It is proposed by the said purchasers, and it is said that since the commune has taken away from them the said part of the tax, which is fixed by the ordinances of the tax, therefore the commune is bound to remit to them the amount which the said purchasers for the said one-third part received from the inhabitants of the territory and those considered as inhabitants of the territory; if they received a thousand, the commune is bound to remit a thousand to them; if a hundred, a hundred. On the other hand, it is said that the commune, which must make a remission of one-third of the price owed to the commune, so that just as one-third of the tax has been raised, so one-third of the agreed price should be abolished; but not that the commune is bound to restore to the said purchasers the profits which they would have made therefrom. The question is, what is the law: whether regard should be had to the quantity of the benefit, or to the quality of the price.

And it seems that, since this ordinance considers quality, it should be understood as having provided equally with respect to quantity, not with respect to frequency, as in C. de pactis conventis, Authent. aequalitas. Moreover, this ordinance must be understood without prejudice to the buyer. D. ne quid in loco publico, l. 2, § si quis a principe; C. de emancipatis liberis, l. nec auus; D. de usufructu legato, l. fundi tres. Furthermore, just as the common law cannot entirely remove the benefits from the buyer, so too it cannot diminish them, according to the note in l. quod semel, de decretis ab ordinario factis, together with its subject matter. The primary nature of a relative relation is to refer its antecedent specifically, not generically, if there is someone in that statement, as in “the woman condemned, who saved.” For it would not be so regarding its proper meaning, nor does it signify that if Berta condemned, Berta saved, as noted in D. de hereditate instituenda, where the text and the notable gloss are found. If the adjective indicates a relative, therefore it refers to the third part which the buyers are to receive, not to the third part which they are to pay. That this is a relative term, and consequently representative of the thing previously stated, is clear from all the laws in which this term is found: D. de pactis, l. quod dictum; de excusatione tutoris, l. dixit; de actionibus et obligationibus, l. cum infinitis similibus. Furthermore, by the nature of equal proportion, restoration must correspond to the loss; and this ordinance speaks restitutively, just as the law says in C. de submissione, cap. loco, de mortuis, and de renovatione semis, as in D. de usufructu, l. item si fundi, § seminarios; and D. de usufructu, l. vetus. Moreover, it is by the nature of the contract that interest arises in a place where industry is considered: l. 3, in fine, de eo quod certo loco; or the contract is celebrated in good faith, de actionibus, emptio, l. 1, in principio; C. de senatusconsulto quod pro eo, l. 1, § pe. Furthermore, this ordinance speaks of a toll: but a toll is one thing, and the price of the toll is another.

† just as one thing is the thing itself, another is the price of the thing. D. de rerum permutatione, l. 1; D. de contrahenda empt., l. 1. Another thing is the expenditure on the thing. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Quibus diebus, § 1. Hence, to draw an analogy to this case from l. Pretium ad conventum seems impossible, because the words do not signify this. And these are the six reasons which favor the buyers against the common opinion. Now let us consider those arguments which support the common opinion, where it must be observed that the jurisdiction to impose the toll is that of the Commune of Perugia, and the toll itself is owed, as regards the direct obligation, to the Commune of Perugia; whereas the exercise [of collection] belongs to the contractors or buyers, as in l. 1, D. de locatione publica fructuum; and D. de procuratoribus, l. Qui stipendia; D. de furtis, l. Si apes, § fin. And since this toll has been abolished in the person of the Commune, the very substance of the leased thing has been destroyed, as in D. de legatis 3, l. 11, § Si rem, at the rubric “Hic enim.” For just as the toll arises from law, so it is caused to cease by contrary law. C. de edicto Divi Adriani, l. Edicto, in principio. For that twentieth part introduced by Adrian was a certain toll, namely 12 denarii per pound, which is abrogated by Justinian, so that it is no longer in existence in the nature of things, nor can it be alleged. C. de novo codice conficiendo, l. 1, § Sed si quae; and there, the glossators note.

† From this I argue as follows: just as the lessor is not bound, except to remit the rent pro rata temporis, when the substance of the leased thing is destroyed, if the substance consists in a corporeal thing, so it is when the substance consists in a right.

For laws also have their own deaths, and this is proven. D. loc. cond. l. si quis domum § 1, where the right perished, but not the thing; and l. habitatores; and l. si fundus; and fully noted in the same title, l. si uno § item cum quidam, and there an example is given of a thing destroyed, and when houses are burned down. And these are most true according to the common law. Someone will say, these are true, unless this happens by the act of the lessor: because on account of his own act he is liable for all damages. But here it must be observed and distinguished between a necessary act, or one that ought to have been done by law, and an act de facto, or voluntary, because an act out of necessity is not culpable. And in this contract, that which is not fault does not come into play, as D. comm. div. l. si ut certo § nunc videndum; and D. loc. cond. And this distinction is true: but here, on account of pressing necessity and the poverty of the subjects of the county, the third part of the tax was remitted no less justly than piously, as noted C. de annona et trib. l. indictiones, lib. 11, in the last gloss. Secondly, this is manifest from the words of the law, which says that the buyers are absolved for the said third part. For their absolution is not from the tax, because they do not owe the common tax, but the price of the tax: for this quota inserts itself into the obligation, and the obligation into the price. For this reform is a certain distraint made for a certain part of the quota, and therefore the commune is not bound to them henceforth, as if it had been distrained in its entirety. C. quando lic. ab empt. disce. l. 1; D. de pactis l. ab emptione. And as I said, this could be done for a cause, as expressly stated and noted D. de publ. l. content. § agri, although the gloss there gives an example when the cause arises from the fault of the redeemer. D. pro socio l. si convenerit. This first law is general as to the whole county, although it runs against the redeemers. l. Antiochenisium. Thirdly, this is clear: because this ordinance disposes only of liberation, not of obligation or damage to the commune: for it is absurd to say that the commune of Perugia succeeds to the obligation of the subjects of the county, and is regarded as a single peasant, so that what the peasant’s purse does not pay, the commune’s purse pays, receiving so much the less: and the acts of agents do not operate beyond their intention: and especially when the lord disposes concerning his subject or his debtor. The text is noted D. de pecul. leg. l. si peculium § sicut. Fourthly, this is clear, because the reform refers backwards, as appears from the word “incepta” etc. For it wishes that it be understood from now as if from the beginning: as if it said, let this sale remain without beginning as to the third part. Argue therefore from the defect of the beginning, and you will find that the commune is not bound to the benefits in question: just as when a thing is redhibited, the benefits of the intermediate time are returned to the seller. D. de aedil. edict. l. cum autem § cum redhibetur, provided that the buyer is not in damage. eod. tit. l. ediles § fin. with the following law. For this retroactivity seems similar to redhibition and restitution in integrum. eod. tit. l. redhibere in princ. For the virtue and power of the law of fiction draws the end of time to its beginning. D. ad leg. Aquil. l. huic scripturae; and l. ita vulneratus. Fifthly, this is clear from a similar case of an heir burdened, whose portion is diminished. For by the quota part by which it is diminished, he performs legacies for the whole less, not for so much. D. de iur. codicill. l. licet cum ea, which law weighs heavily the mind of the speaker. And thus it must also be weighed in the case at hand as to the commune, D. de leg. 2 l. cum filius in princ.; D. de cond. et demonstr. l. Plautius § item scinditur. And it is confirmed, because the nature of the thing must be considered no less than the bark of the words. D. de usur. l. si stipulatur. But the nature of resolution in correlatives is to resolve on both sides, not to increase, as D. de accept. l. fin. For in dissolving obligations there should not be limping, as noted in l. 1 D. de rescind. vendit. Sixthly, because this contract is resolved by repentance: for in this case the commune repented of having sold: and it draws its repentance backwards: and the act of the commune by way of law is regarded as also the act of the buyers under the universality of the citizens. And therefore the commune does not remain bound by the said contract. Moreover, these buyers ask for that, the contrary of which they would not have claimed if they had expected damages: therefore they are not heard. Also, since there is one fruit of the whole year, as D. sol. matr. l. divortio § quod in se mentem, the preceding things seem still to depend on the future on account of the uncertain event of the fruits, as C. de usur. l. si ea lege. Finally, if we were to say otherwise, this absurdity would follow: suppose that the commune, by reason of the third part, ought to have in three months 10 in the name of price, but the buyers would claim 20 from the peasants, certainly if they deducted 20, they would have this tax for another trimester free of charge, so that for another trimester nothing would come to the purse of the commune. And certainly the sale would be converted into the species of a donation, which is impossible. And thus the law argues from the little to the much: and it shows by such an argument the arising absurdity, which must be entirely avoided, as D. de leg. 3 l. Offidius in the verse pater interrogavit. From which reasons it seems evident to conclude and say for the commune, that for the time from the day the law was enacted, the commune has clear justice, namely, of remitting the price pro rata temporis, so that insofar as the cause ceases, the effect ceases. l. domum D. de contrah. empt. But for the time before the law was enacted up to the day of the contract, the buyers have their own rights from their contract, which for the past time could not be undone against their will. l. in bello § factae. But they, by using this law, consented to the law: and for the time before the law was enacted, they collected according to the tenor of the law itself, the contract being resolved retroactively, as has been fully proven above. I judge for the commune, that the rent be exonerated. And this is the plain way, and without the thorns of calculation: for if we were to come to calculation, as they ask, the prior lords and chamberlains ought to appoint viewers, that is, good men, or a good man, who neither deceives nor is deceived, as l. fin. C. de pondera auri; and l. 2 C. de usur. et fruc. leg. And by the same reform it is established that truth and justice be ministered to both parties, and both public and private good, both of the buyers and of the subjects of the county, shall be satisfied. Which must undoubtedly be done over their damages: because the reform says it does not hinder. l. fina. C. de contrah. empt. For there it is over the substance, here over the coherences and accidentals. D. de contrah. empt. l. officio. And such are the aforesaid matters, as if your commune had let its urban properties for one rent, and finally one had been taken by the prohibition of some official, or for another necessity impending upon the republic, argument C. loca. l. eden. secundo responso; and the verse autem et quod, and what is noted there.

† Assuming as true that it may be removed on the ground of damages, I say that they must be entirely kept indemnified for the time of the whole year. As for the profits, which they claim they would have made after the law was enacted, it must be considered that this can hardly be known: because then dangerous times were at hand; and one must look at what was probable, and for how much more it could have been sold; and if it is not probable that it could then have been sold for more, they must remain silent and content. For where future considerations are discussed, it is more just to estimate hope penitentially than to defer it casually. D. ad Trebellianum, l. 1, § si haeres, where is the notable text; D. de conditione furtiva, l. si servus. I, however, believe that after the law was enacted, the contract was dissolved on both sides: but for the time before the law, the contract is firm. C. de fidei instrumentis, l. contractus. And I presuppose natural law, because public utility and unavoidable necessity prejudice the private: I do not speak of public utility as regards the common purse, but as regards the state of the city, as was the case here. And thus it does not obstruct [the rule] de pollicita. D. qui et a quibus, l. totum; l. si privatus, with its material. And what is noted in l. ambitiosa, by Bartolus in the second column, under the rubric “item ex virtute alicuius.”

Furthermore, the commune sold the benefits of its law, from which the toll was imposed, and the law can be changed if it has not passed into contract: but when it has passed into contract, otherwise, unless from a great and necessary cause, as is the case here. D. de legatis 2, l. qui solidum, § 1, with similar cases.

Furthermore, because, as I said, by a general law prejudice can be inflicted on individuals, when the law is in itself generally just and necessary, as is the case here.

Furthermore, that which from many subjects hangs in the balance of mortality, in doubt is rather considered damaging than profitable; and from this cause the minor is understood to be harmed. D. de minoribus, l. verum, § locupleti. Or, as a medium between contrary possibilities naturally induced, it is introduced. C. de transactionibus, l. si de fideicommissa. Or recourse is had to moderators. D. de actionibus emptoris, l. si iactum rectis. And in this I rest, insofar as I say: reformation. I, Baldus of Perugia.

CASE. The point of the question is this, namely: Angelutius and Christophorus, brothers and sons of Nicolutius, made and granted to each other peace and concord, and remission of all and every injury and offense made and committed by one party to the other, and conversely. And they promised to each other that the said parties would hold the said peace and concord perpetually firm and valid, and not act or come against it, under a penalty of fifty pounds, of which penalty the half, which the party who violated it would give and pay to the observing party; and the other half to the treasurer of Lord Galeotto. After these things, the said Christophorus offended the said Angelutius in the street, made him fall to the ground, from which fall blood came from the face of the said Angelutius, and for the said offense the said Christophorus was condemned to twenty-five pounds. The said Angelutius, however, sued the said Christophorus, and within the term given to the parties for proving, the said Christophorus made one position of the following tenor, namely:

Furthermore, the said Angelutius and Christophorus, now for several years, solemnly agreed among themselves, and by common accord, that the said instrument of peace and the promises contained therein should be of no effect, efficacy, or value; and they wished and declared them to be void and null, and wished to have them as void and null. And of the said agreement and accord made together, they requested Ser Sanctus, son of Ser Francisci, notary of the borough, to draw up a public instrument thereof. Who Ser Sanctus, through his negligence and being prevented by death, omitted to draw up any public instrument thereof, or to write any. Which position was proved, as you can see, by two witnesses: and not obstructing the said proof, the said Christophorus was condemned to give to the treasurer of Lord Galeotto twenty-five pounds, and as much to the said Angelutius.

Now, however, the said Christophorus sues the said Angelutius; and demands from him a similar penalty, because he says that the said Angelutius struck the said Christophorus with an empty hand on the chest of the said Christophorus, and fully proves the aforesaid by three witnesses, although one of those witnesses, before he gave his testimony, being questioned by the said Angelutius whether he ever saw that he struck the said Angelutius, as is said in his petition, answered that he did not, in the presence of several witnesses: and this was fully proved. It is opposed by the said Angelutius that the said Christophorus cannot sue him by virtue of the said instrument of peace, which he in the aforesaid position said that the brothers agreed should be null, as was especially proved.

It is asked whether the said witness, who gave different testimonies, one to the party and another to the judge, is false; and then whether the said Angelutius can be condemned for breaking the peace in the said penalty, and by virtue of the said instrument of peace, which he first said by another [instrument] had been annulled.

These matters are doubtful, because the said Lippus and Vannutius say that they are not bound to the said Bartolus to any defense, unless given and made only of them. Secondly, they say that the said ordinance, that one may not measure spelt and barley, proceeded from fact and not from law: and that their promise succeeds in the place of a stipulation, having license. Which looks to law and not fact, and thus the said ordinance does not bind them, since it proceeded from fact. Thirdly, they say that the said ordinance is not valid: because it takes away the right of the said Lippus and Vannutius; which it cannot do without their act and consent.

On the part of the said Bartolus, it is responded that the said Lippus and Vannutius promised to the said Bartolus, among other things, that they would do and see to it that the said Bartolus could collect and receive the said fruits, revenues, and proceeds of those measures without any impediment, which words bind the said Lippus and Vannutius both to law and to fact. And especially because of the word “freely,” which is in the said promise. And because of the word “without any impediment,” and it is not true that the said promise refers to law only.

Secondly, the said Bartolus says that the said priors could make the said ordinance by the authority and discretion granted to them. And that they can take away another’s right for a cause, as is in our case. Because a cause has supervened, that the commune of Perugia needs money in abundance for the causes occurring, for the event of the Pope, for the defense of the city and county of Perugia and the recommended lands. And thus the said ordinance was valid by reason of the cause, and the other ordinances following from it.

Thirdly, the said Bartolus says that it is not true that the said Lippus and Vannutius prove any damage from the said ordinance, hence they receive profit, because, since before where they received three denarii for each measure, now by virtue of the said ordinance they receive three denarii. And also the said Bartolus says that the said Lippus and Vannutius approved the said ordinance by receiving three denarii for each measure by virtue of the said ordinance.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one is said to accept an ordinance made concerning a tax from the collection of that tax itself.
2. Public necessity takes precedence over private interest.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because the aforementioned Lippus and Vamnurius accepted the said ordinance and acknowledged the said judgment by collecting the toll, which includes under itself all the tolls of the boroughs, suburbs, and the entire city, and they collected it with a profit of three denarii where only two were due, it seems that one must say that by acknowledging or accepting the benefit of the law, they cannot refuse the burden of the law. D. de legatis 2, l. ex duobus; and l. tertia, § si centum. Nor can they avail themselves of the contract made with Bartolus: for they voluntarily departed from him by the very fact that they collected the toll universally, which includes the toll of the cess. Arg. D. de pactis, l. ab emp.; D. de fideiussoribus, l. si est opus. Just as if one who had assigned an action for a certain price were to sue the debtor and also wish to claim the price promised for the assignment. For one ought not to have both the thing sold and the price. And if it be said that the statute is invalid, I answer that the consensus of the parties confirmed it.

† Moreover, public necessity derogates from the rights of individuals. C. de rei vend. l. item si verbe. §. 1. de euic. l. Lucius. de excu. tut. l. sed reprobari. with similar authorities. I, Bal. de Per. V. l. D., advise that the path of the said ordinance should be followed. And to my faith I subscribed, and [affixed] the seal of my name. Seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the mother is excluded from the succession of her children because agnates exist up to the second degree, is the grandmother also understood to be excluded by virtue of the statute?
casus: CASE. In the name of God, amen. The facts are proposed thus: My [client] Stephen of Venice, of Sarthiano, died without having made a will, surviving him were Joanna, Peter, and Antonio, his sons and heirs, and his wife and mother of the aforementioned, and Gherius, maternal grandfather of the aforementioned Joanna, Peter, and Antonio. After this, the said Lady Maria, mother of the aforementioned, passed on to a second marriage. Then the aforementioned Gherius, grandfather of the aforementioned, assumed the guardianship of his said nephews, and involved himself in the guardianship estate in the name of the guardianship. After this, the aforementioned Peter died at the age of 7 years, surviving him were Joanna and Antonio, the brothers mentioned above, and the said Lady Maria, their mother, and Gherius, their grandfather, named above. After this, the said Gherius, guardian, married the said Lady Joanna from the goods of the inheritance of his said father. Then the said Antonio died at the age of 10 years, surviving were Lady Joanna, his married sister, and the said Lady Maria, his mother, and the said Gherius, grandfather and guardian, and possessor of the goods of the said inheritance. Then Gherius, the aforementioned grandfather, took possession of the inheritance of the aforementioned deceased, and possesses all the goods. Now a question arises between the said Gherius, the aforementioned grandfather, on one side, and Lady Joanna on the other side, and the said Lady Maria, mother of the aforementioned, on the other: and each of them wants the inheritance of the said deceased. It is asked, what the law [is]. Whether they ought to belong to the said Gherius, the maternal grandfather, or to the said Lady Joanna, the carnal sister of the aforementioned, or indeed to the said Lady Maria, their mother. Having seen these statutes, it is said on behalf of the aforementioned Gherius that they did not take possession of the inheritance of the aforementioned within the time established by law, as they ought to have done by law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. According to the common law, the brothers would succeed to the entire ownership of the goods formerly belonging to their father, which came to their brothers, namely Peter, Anthony, and the said Maria; because she entered into second marriage, she succeeds only to the usufruct of one-half of the said goods derived from the husband’s estate to the common children, as stated in the Codex, *De secundis nuptiis*, in the constitution *Ex testamento*, in the section *Sed eorum*. However, Gherius would succeed in no way, because the mother of the children precedes the grandfather, as stated in the Codex, *Ad Senatusconsultum Tertullianum*, in the constitution *Defuncto*, there: “saving the prerogative of degree.” But according to the form of the Sardinian statute, the said mother succeeds in no way to her children, but the nearest relatives up to the second degree succeed according to the form of the statute, as appears in the title *Quod mater non succedat*, in the section *Sed succedant*, etc.

It must therefore be considered that, the mother being excluded by the statute, whether the grandfather or the sister succeeds, since both are in the second degree. And it is true that the sister does not succeed, because she is dowried, as in another statute, "that a dowried woman, etc." and thus only the grandfather succeeds. On the contrary, it is argued that the maternal grandfather in no way succeeds, but only the sister, for the statute which excludes the mother seems also to exclude the grandfather and every more remote relative; because it seems to have been made in favor of agnates, as noted by the doctors, C. de adulteriis, l. publica. And although the grandfather is in the second degree and is contained under those words of the statute, "up to the second degree," nevertheless the intent and reason of the statute seem to be different, which prevails, ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, §. et si maxime. Nor does it obstruct this that the noted doctors in the aforementioned auth. defuncto, s. quod frater, vel soror, state that a brother or sister does not exclude a grandfather; for that is true according to the common law. But by the form of the statute, from which the mother is excluded, the maternal grandfather is all the more excluded, as noted by Cynus in l. 1, in 5, q. C. quae sit longa consuetudo, and so held the aforementioned Rizzardi de Malo. Likewise, it does not obstruct the sister that she is dowried, because not by her father. Likewise, it does not obstruct her the person who might exclude her, nor does the statute speak in our case. But it seems that the sister and the maternal grandfather succeed equally; for the mother being excluded, they thus succeed according to the common law; nor does the statute expressly provide the contrary; hence, since I find the common law not corrected, I will adhere to it, nor can an unwritten reason of the statute correct a written law, as noted, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, auth. quas actiones. Likewise, the statute must be drawn to the common law, as noted, C. de noxalibus, l. 2. Finally, although in this question there are various opinions, nevertheless, considering the said and alleged arguments on both sides, I think that the sister alone succeeds, the maternal grandfather being excluded, according to the intent of the statute; for the reason of the law or statute is the law or statute itself, as noted, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum tale, §. pen., and l. quoniam ius, de in ius vocando, cum similibus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a libel that concludes presumptively is sufficient.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the petition presented by Ballutius, son of the late Saluti of Fulgineo, against Lillus Tilli of the same place, before the noble and learned man, Master James of Spoleto, Vicar, etc., whereby the said Ballutius, through the said Master James, seeks to compel and constrain the said Lillus by the remedies of the law, etc., as is declared in the said petition, namely that he requests that the latter be condemned according to a statute of the commune of Fulgineo placed under the rubric: “That the podestà shall cause public instruments to be made of unwritten contracts,” etc. I say briefly that, in law, it must be said that the said petition proceeds both under the common law and according to the form of the said statute.

† I prove this as follows: it is certain that, according to the common law, even in a civil case, a libel proceeds without a conclusion. This is proven by *l. omnes*, § *Luc.*, and the gloss thereon beginning “in libello tuo,” and *c.* ff. *de his, quae in fraudem creditorum fiunt*; and there by the learned Francesco Tingrino of Pisa, who alleges to this effect *l. Paulus*, § *querere*, ff. *de bonis libertorum*. This is also held by Guillaume de Cuggione in *l. edita*, near the end, C. *de edendo*, where he says: “I say the same if the fact is not narrated, as when I sue you on the action on the contract of sale.” Certainly, I say that this libel proceeds; nor is it necessary to narrate it, etc. He alleges the gloss in the body of *Auth. de exhibendis rebus*, § *Sancimus*, where the gloss expressly holds this, on which point the doctors speak fully in *l. minorum*, C. *in quibus causis in integrum restitui non est necessarium*. For it suffices that the libel presumptively concludes, as noted by the gloss in the aforementioned § *Luc.* But if a libel proceeds without a conclusion, much more ought it to proceed even with an inept conclusion, by argument from *l. 1*, § 1, C. *de rei uxoriae actione*. Moreover, if a libel cannot stand according to its proper meaning, it is drawn to an improper one, as in ff. *de iureiurando*, in *l. sed et si possessori*, § *sed si rerum*; and C. *de his, qui ex publicis rationibus*, *l. 1*, in the gloss at the end, where it explains “commodauerit” as “mutuauerit.” And this improper meaning occurs, as noted by the gloss in *l. et puto*, § 1, ff. *familiae herciscundae*. For the words of a libel are to be understood broadly, as noted by Innocentius in *c. licet causam*, extra *de probationibus*, in the gloss at the end; and ff. *de iudiciis*, *l. solemus*, with the following. To this effect it is pertinent that which is noted in 1 q. 4, *c. quia praesulatus*, in the gloss, where it is said that it suffices to complain of the possessor, even though restitution is not demanded, as in extra *de causa possessionis et proprietatis*, *c. cum ecclesia*. Moreover, when the Church is the plaintiff, even if the libel is inept, it proceeds, according to what is noted by Innocentius in *c. examinata*, extra *de iudiciis*. But in the case proposed, it is of this kind; therefore, etc.

Furthermore, I say that the said petition proceeds according to the form of the said statute. For, since it is possible to proceed to contestation in the said petition without a libel, as is shown by the form of the aforementioned statute, it appears that this excludes all meticulousness and the form of drafting a libel; but it suffices that what is intended is demanded, as is fully noted in *c. saepe contingit*, § *verum*, extra *de verbis significandis*, in the Clementines, and there by the Lord Paulus de Liazza. But in the said petition, what is intended is sufficiently clearly demanded; therefore, etc.

The objection from *l. nimis propere*, C. *de excusationibus rei iudicatae*, does not hold. For the said law speaks of a judge who cannot execute before he condemns. No mention is made there of a libel, although the said Bartolus wishes to hold that it concerns a libel by the said law, whereas he holds the contrary in *l. 2*, § *penes*, ff. *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*.

I therefore conclude briefly that the said petition proceeds both according to law and according to the form of the said statute, and that the said Lillus can be condemned by the said judge to contestation in the said petition, even though it is not expressly demanded by the plaintiff; for it suffices that it be presumptively demanded, as proven by the laws alleged above.

And thus, as written above, I say and advise, I, Francesco, son of the Lord Bernardino of Spoleto, always reserving the sounder opinion. In testimony of which thing, I have written with my own hand and affixed my accustomed seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the action brought by Tibellus, in which it was sought that someone be compelled only, but not condemned, proceeds according to law.
2. What effect the giving of an earnest money (arrha) produces, and whether it is proved by two witnesses.
3. Who is called a prosoneta.
4. Whether a prosoneta is a competent witness in a contract.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Three doubts are raised concerning the libel: first, whether it is incompetent or not; second, whether the contract has been proved or not, considering the form of the deposition of the witnesses; third, whether James Vangoli can be repelled as a prosoneta.

† On the first point, Master Bartolus says in l. j. C. de executione rei iudicatae that the libel does not proceed, “I ask that such a person be compelled,” unless it is asked that he be condemned; because he cannot be compelled unless he is condemned; he cannot be condemned unless it is asked that he be condemned, as in l. si. de fideicommissis. I say, however, that if, after narrating what needs to be narrated, I conclude thus: “whom I ask to be given or done to me,” even though I do not say, “whom I ask to be condemned as defendant,” the petition proceeds; and the ordinary gloss so formats the libel, and says that all other words are superfluous, in Auth. de exhibendis reis, §. sancimus. And so it was here, if the petition is properly examined.

† On the second point, I say that two witnesses prove by bodily sense the agreement and the giving of the earnest money; hence the contract is perfected by consent, as noted in C. de contrahenda emptione, l. in ementis. Moreover, because the earnest money was given as part of the price, the thing was not entire, as noted in ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. quod saepe; nor could one of the subsequent parties dissolve the contract from the consent, as in l. ab emptore de pactis. On the third point

I say that a *prosoneta* is understood in two ways: in one way, he who receives a price; in another way, he who acts gratuitously, yet through whom the agreement and the forum are established. But where the forum is established by the principals themselves without an intermediary, he who brought the parties together or summoned witnesses is not called a *prosoneta*, because he provides no service to the contract, nor does he thereby merit a *prosonetionum*. And thus stands the common understanding. And this is proved in the Authentica *De testibus*, § *Quoniam vero*; and in Chapter 1, *De testibus*, Book 6; and as we note in the law *Eleganter*, in the beginning, *De dolo*.

† Hence, Jacobus was not properly a Prosoneta, because he did not provide an internal and substantial service, but only an external one in bringing the parties together in one place; hence I do not believe that one should properly be called a Prosoneta to whom the term Ptosoneticum does not correspond, but he is a certain friend, as in l. sciendum, ff. de usu. Nor do I believe that the reason for prohibition applies to him, because the contract was not his by arrangement or for his benefit, but of the principal parties. Hence nothing repels him, neither utility nor affection, which are the two reasons assigned in the said §. quoniam, in the gloss. For one is not affected by that which was done by another and not by oneself, and no law provides that this person should be repelled; therefore, and so forth, l. 1, ff. de testi., with similar authorities. He therefore proves at least the convention, although whether he proves the Artha is doubtful, because he says that he gave it, and in this he was an intervener and minister. It supports what is noted in l. differre, §. 1, de iu. fis., and what is noted in cap. Romana, de testib., lib. 6, in the gloss si igitur. And thus, concerning another’s act, he is believed as concerning his own act, whereas a witness is not believed, because these are separable. But according to the accurate gloss in the said §. quoniam, one should believe the whole, if he does not hope for advantage, because he is not gathered together according to the gloss. The canonists say that a Prosoneta, even if willing, will not be heard unless by the will of both parties, as noted in 1. quaestio. 1, cap. si quis episcopus, and de testib., cap. dilectorum, per Ber. Whatever may be said about the Prosoneta, I say that in the act of convention this person was not a Prosoneta, because the parties agreed by themselves immediately. And from the acts of both parties it can sufficiently be weighed by the judge, who must investigate all things, that this was the truth of the matter, our pacts shall be observed, as in extra de pact., cap. 1, with similar authorities, the praetor says, I will observe pacts. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the bishop may visit the brothers and the convent of Saint Mary of the Servants by ordinary right, since they had a general minister, who ought to visit them, by virtue of a privilege.
body: Por

† L. quod de rerum, § si quis, in fine, D. de legatis praestandis; and there Jacobus de Aretino makes an argument for the question of the Humiliated Brethren of Milan, to the effect that they ought not to be visited by the bishop, since they have been granted a privilege that they shall have a general minister who is to visit them. For what is appointed for some is deemed to be taken away from others. And D. de administratione tutorum, L. iste. On the contrary, it is argued from D. de administratione tutorum, L. quotiens, § final, verse quae res; and what is noted there by the aforementioned Jacobus, who thus says: Here it is argued that when someone founds a church so that it is under an abbot, it will nevertheless be under the bishop. To the same effect it seems, because jurisdiction granted to one is not seen to be taken away from another, as L. 1, C. de officio praefecti urbis. To the same effect it is argued, because although the collegiate clergy are under their prior, they are nevertheless also subject to the power, as L. final, C. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum. I scarcely do not hold the aforementioned opinion; for one thing is in a concession by privilege, for a privilege is to be strictly observed, as C. ad Silenum, L. de criminibus, Book 12; and by its nature it follows the rules of law. And it is supported by D. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, L. ex facto, in principio; and what is noted in D. de legatis, L. beneficium domi, by his doctor Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In criminal cases, proof clearer than light is required for condemnation; for torture, presumptions or certain and probable indications are required.
2. Torture has no place unless in an atrocious crime, and where the truth cannot otherwise be obtained.
3. Whether a witness examined before one judge proves anything if he says the contrary before another.
4. One single witness is not sufficient for a judgment of torture.
5. Whether a proceeding conducted by one who is considered a notary is valid.
6. An instrument lacking the date and the consuls makes no proof.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, consulted whether the said Dominic should be condemned or absolved, having examined the entire inquisition and the whole said procedure, and having reviewed the inquisition drawn up by the vicar of the castle of Camera, and the procedure conducted thereon, and especially the testimonies of the witnesses, and above all that of Jacobus Pucioli Chiali, a witness examined in both procedures, I declare that the said Dominic ought to be absolved and not condemned, nor ought he even to be tortured, all circumstances being considered. And I declare that it has not been proven, either fully or to the extent sufficient for torture, and therefore he deserves to be absolved.

† And this is proven thus: in criminal cases, for condemnation, proofs clearer than light are required. C. de proba. l. sciant cuncti. For torture, certain, probable, and verisimilar presumptions or indications are required. C. de quaestionibus. l. milites. §. oportet.

† Nor is torture applied to defendants in all crimes, but only in atrocious ones; nor in every case, but only when the truth cannot be ascertained otherwise. D. de quaestionibus, l. edictum and l. diuus. But here there has been no clear proof of the crime; hence a condemnatory judgment cannot be rendered; nor has there been clear proof of indicia; hence an interlocutory order for torture cannot be issued, nor can a confession be extorted by torture. For here four witnesses were examined: Iacobutius Cialli, Andreutius, Angelutius, and Pet.

† Faith is not to be given to Iacobutio: because, concerning the same fact, he was examined in the form of a trial before another tribunal and stated that he knew nothing. Hence, when he subsequently testifies to the contrary before another tribunal, he is not believed: as in D. de falsis, l. eos enim. And in Raesen. For since he is perjured, his statement is not to be believed: as is read and noted in D. de his who are not infamous, l. Lucius. And in Extr. de testibus, c. testimonium vacillosus. Which is a species of falsity in testimony and inconsistency. And D. de testibus, l. qui falsa, vel varia. And if it is said that the first deposition was made before an incompetent judge, since the Camera does not have cognizance, jurisdiction, nor power of inquiry in the contrary case without a special commission, as in c. 2, Extr. de officio vicarii, lib. 6, it is responded that this applies to a commission made by a person; but where the commission is by statutes or by law, the words are to be interpreted most broadly, arg. D. de officio praefecti urbis, l. 1, §. cum verbum. And thus the judge was elected here by counsel. For if this is against the custom of the place, the people themselves conferred this jurisdiction. According to the note in Auth. de mandato principis, §. non habere, at the end, the great gloss. Moreover, since from this crime no penalty of death or other affliction is imposed, but extra ordinem, as l. 1, D. de extraordinariis criminibus, the vicar could be construed for this purpose. C. de his who exercise the office of another judge, l. insurgerent. And note in l. 1, §. 1, D. de officio eius cui mandatum est ius dicere. And D. de officio proconsulis, l. nec quicquam, §. vbi decretum, at the end, the great gloss. Moreover, even assuming that he was not a competent judge, nevertheless, in whatever judicial order he was received as a witness, he is not excused from perjury, nor from the defect of falsity or the crime of stellionatus, according to the note in l. si quis legatus, D. de falsis. And D. de sepulchro violato, l. praeterea. P. Cy. One loses faith because he has removed faith from himself, according to us, C. de transactionibus, l. transigere. In 2. q. per Cyn. For one loses the office of witness who, in the office of testifying, offends by breaking faith. C. de susceptis et archis, l. si aliquid. D. de his who are not infamous, l. 2, §. miles. This question. The statement of the witness does not even suffice for torture: because the witness is not suitable, nor faithful, as he ought to be, to proceed from his statement to torture. And D. de quaestionibus, l. maritus. Moreover, perhaps this crime is not so atrocious that one should come to torture by right from presumptions or indications; but this does not please, for rather the contrary: for it is atrocious against one who attacks chastity, as l. 1, de extraordinariis criminibus, in the gloss which says that the crime is enormous, namely not on this ground, but on the first, namely because such faith should not be given to the aforementioned witness as would make room for torture on account of the defect of the witness, as in the said l. maritus. Angelus does not prove violent entry: for in his reasoning he makes no mention of force, nor does he prove chastity, although he says that he heard certain words which could have been uttered. This is proved, and for another reason, and it does not prove this to be so, as l. non nudis, l. neque tales. Moreover, because in this hearing there is a single witness.

† By means of a single individual witness, one does not proceed to torture on the basis of an indication, as noted by Innocentius in the Extravagantes, *De simonia*, chapter *Sicut facit*; this accords with the note in the Code, *De familiae erciscundae*, *De hereditatibus*, law *Si probatio famae*: because bare [evidence] is not sufficient for torture; otherwise, if reputation were joined with other probable presumptions: as in chapter *Tormenta*, *De confessionibus*. Nor does it say that the witness is to be rejected, who is not merely solitary, but also bad; thus, the law *Capite quinto* does not oppose. I therefore advise that the said Dominic, the facts being thus, should be absolved. And to the faith [of this document] I have subscribed, and with the sign of my name I have signed.

† On the first point, a distinction must be made: whether the proceedings brought against the notary were publicly known, in which case his instruments are invalid; or whether they were not publicly known, but he was commonly regarded as a notary and publicly drew up instruments, in which case his instruments are valid on account of a probable and common error, as noted by the gloss in the corpus of the Digest, title *De testibus*, § *Peccant*, and supported by the law *Barbarius* and similar authorities. And thus I previously advised on this point in this very same litigation.

† On the third point, I say that an instrument lacking the date and the consuls makes no proof, as in Auth. ut praeponatur nomen imperatoris in principio; and note in l. generaliter in principio de tabulis. From this, the fourth question is resolved, because if the original is not valid, neither is the copy, especially when the party was not cited in the exemplification, as in Auth. si quis in aliquo. The solution to the fifth point also appears, for since a solemn instrument is not presumed false, C. de testamento l. iubemus §. si, it provides no cause for demanding [a challenge]: as C. de falsis l. ex initio. Having premised these things, it remains to resolve the second point, and I say on it that, the writing of the said testament being valid, the testator’s inheritance must be divided into two parts: and one part belongs to the aforementioned B., heir of the son intestate, because he ought to have the legitime and the trebellianic portion; the other part ought to be held by those instituted, as in c. Raymundi and c. Raymundi. And upon B.’s death, this right belongs to the chapter and the chapel instituted by her, if the lady B. accepted the inheritance of the son’s inheritance. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who obtains a vacant prebend by reason of death in a church where there is no fixed number of canons ought to obtain it.
2. Prebends that do not have certainty in themselves, but are sometimes greater and sometimes lesser according to the discretion of the superior, cannot be obtained.
3. Whether one who obtains a prebend includes in himself a canonry.
body: In the name of Almighty God, in the case of the prior of the church of Saint Michael and of Fran. Iacobelli, since a pleading ought not to be verbose, I shall use few words.

† Innocentius says that if I obtain a prebend vacant by the death of such a person in a church in which there is no certain number of canons, I ought not to obtain it: since it appears to be a subreptitious grace, because such a prebend is not said to be vacant by death, but to cease. On prebends, c. Dilecto, § 1, according to Innocentius; and the same is held there by Hostiensis and Johannes Andreae. And although their reason and authority ought to suffice for everyone, I nevertheless confirm it with another reason: when something is obtained or granted which does not have the form of existence in the nature of things, nor is it expected to have it, the disposition is as if not written, because it has no subject upon which to be founded, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. Non moriturum, where it is said that if I promise that I will give you an immortal man, the promise is not valid, because such a man is not found in the nature of things. But if I promise a slave, and he dies after default, the obligation is perpetuated by reason of the default. And for the purpose at hand, that law, if introduced, is well suited. For where there is a distinct number of canons and prebends, the prebend never dies, although it is vacant; but where there is no distinct number, the prebend is never perpetual, but just as a man dies and is born, like a peculium, as in l. Peculium nascitur. Therefore, this prebend, which arises and dies, is similar to a man; and when it is obtained as vacant, it is obtained as if immortal; hence, if such a thing is not found in that church, the obtaining is not valid. And thus I introduce the law Non moriturum, joined with the aforementioned law Peculium.

2. Response: Therefore, it is vainly obtained that which cannot be given. D. de verbis oblig., l. Si stipuler. 2. Response: But a vacant prebend in such a church cannot be given, because this is not found; therefore, the grace does not bind, if it can. For whose execution is impossible, his disposition does not bind; the testator condemns the heir to give wheat of such weight that it is not found, which is useless. D. de vino legato, l. Quoddam, § fin. Thus, therefore, in this church a vacant prebend is not found; therefore, the letters for this purpose are not valid. D. de herede instituendo, l. Item quod Sabinus, ver. Aliter, atque ubi dicitur. And where it is said that one instituted in a vacant portion is in no way an heir, if no portion is vacant, the portion or prebend of the deceased is not a portion, nor a prebend. D. de herede instituendo, l. Quo loco, § fin. And there it is also proven that in matters depending on will, the opinion of the speaker is rather inspected than the true status of the person or church; but it is the opinion of the prince, whose words resonate. For in the mouth and in the mind it is presumed to be one and the same, as in D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. Ex his apparet, and Extr. de decimis, c. Ad audientiam, de sepulchris, l. Labeo. For if he had wished otherwise, he would have written otherwise. C. de caducis tollendis, l. Si autem indeficienter.

Furthermore, if there is doubt whether an error occurred in the cause of fact, therefore the rescript does not bind, as in D. de tutoribus et curatoribus, da. ab his, l. Tutor si petitus, and D. de contrahenda, l. Filium, § Si quis, and D. de Carbo, l. 3, § Impuberi, cum si. Moreover, those things which require a person qualified in a certain manner cannot belong to others, as in D. de capite diminuto, l. Tutelas, D. de rebus dubiis, l. Si cognatis, as in c. Statutum de prebendis, lib. 6. But a canonical prebend requires that the prebendary be a canon and be qualified, just as a canonical portion, because it is qualified, requires such quality to be present in the person. Arg. D. de milite testamento, l. Titius, D. de opere liberti, l. Opere in rerum. 2. Response: That text is well suited in its own reason. C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. Non plures, C. de propositionibus sacri cubiculi, l. 1. For that which custom has ascribed to canons ought not to belong to others, as in C. de primicerio, l. Praeclaram, lib. 12.

Furthermore, to be a canon is prior in time and law than to be a prebendary. For it is absurd to seek stipend before serving in the military. And thus, he who is repelled from guardianship is repelled from the legacy annexed to the guardianship. D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. Nescennius Appolinaris, with the following law, and l. Amicissimos. Thus, he who is repelled from the canonry, especially by his own fault, because he obtained the canonry by subreption, is unworthy of the prebend: namely, rewards and favors are not proposed to those who obtain by subreption; but those who obtain by subreption are not worthy that favor be shown to them. D. de in ius vocando, l. Sed si hac, § Patronum, D. de fideiussoribus, l. Cum no, D. de herede instituendo, § Subuentum. Although in Jacob it was contravened, as noted, D. de herede instituendo, l. Quotiens, and de testamentis, l. Heredes palam. But that was not subreption, which conformed itself to divine law; just as neither was the theft of the Hebrews, as noted by Azo in Summa Institutionum, de obligationibus ex delicto.

I conclude that subreption in the canonry is subreption in the principal, de constitutionibus, c. Cum M. Ferra. And therefore, the accessory is vitiated when the principal is vitiated, as in D. de adiecto legato, l. Alumne, § Seia, D. de peculio, l. Tunc inutile.

It remains to be considered,

† That prebends which do not have certainty in themselves, but are sometimes greater and sometimes lesser at the discretion of the prior, and thus, because they do not have a certain quantity or nature, cannot be obtained as if they were certain, as in D. de annuis legatis, l. Seio, § medico: there, “uncertain,” and as we say, that a legacy does not bind, l. Diuus, in principio, de legatis; and there, note, or at least regarding this custom: because it touches the right of the prior and the statute of the church, mention should have been made by the petitioner; because it is not probable that the prince or legate would wish to change the form established from ancient times. C. de exact. trib., l. missi opinatores, lib. 10; nor to prejudice the right of another. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. ex facto, with similar cases.

It is not an obstacle that the noted authorities, for this, de conceptione prebendarum, cap. Ex parte Astensis, and by the gloss of Ioannes Andreas in cap. ultimo, de concessionibus prebendarum, lib. 6, because it matters greatly whether mention is made of the number by way of amplification; and then it does not restrict the grace, as in D. de usufructu, l. Proculus; or by way of limitation, and then it restricts the grace. We say the same in legacies and donations. For words spoken by way of qualification restrain and restrict; otherwise, if by way of designation. D. de legatis 1, l. Quidam testamento; and another law, l. Lucius, de legatis 2, l. Lucius; l. 1, per Dy., de donationibus, l. Donationes in concubinam, § speciei, de usufructu; donationes in principio, de transactionibus, l. Cum hi, § si pluribus, de alimentis et cibariis legatis, l. Quaero.

And I say that where the clause “non obstantibus” is not added, the grace seems to be restricted. And an omitted case is held as omitted. D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Si cum dote, and l. Si vero, § de viro, de liberis et posthumis, l. Commodissime. But where the clause “non obstantibus” is added, certainly to the number of canons, etc., because such a clause is added to amplify and confirm the grace, it should not restrict, nor should it operate against the intention of the writer. l. Si quando, in principio, de legatis 1. And this is also clear from the argument from the contrary, for just as that which is done to strengthen an act does not confirm the act against nullity, de legatione prestanda, l. Legata inutiliter, nor induces a new disposition, as in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. Ex facto etiam agitatam, so, by the contrary, that which is done to amplify does not diminish. D. de legatis 3, l. Ea tamen adiectio; and to this effect, D. de supellectili legato, l. Legata supellectilis, in principio. Although the case of vacation through ignorance of fact is enumerated, it does not restrict the general grace. And it supports what is noted, composed in c. Capitulum Sanctae Crucis, where he holds that which I held above.

† It is doubted, however, whether one who obtains a prebend thereby includes in himself the canonry. For whenever one of connected things is granted, the other tacitly follows: for that which is similar is drawn to it, without which it cannot exist. D. de peculio, l. nam quod liquide. Likewise, C. de fideiussoribus, l. quamvis; D. de usufructu, l. Item si fundus, §. fin.; and l. sed et si quid, §. proprietatis. To this it is responded that when both are expressed in the letters, one is not tacitly contained under the other, as in D. de vulgari et extraordinaria substitutione, l. cum ex filio, §. filio, and what is noted there. And this question is pertinent to our case. Finally, the motive of contemplation must be considered. D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. tutor petitus, §. 1; Extr. de testamentis, c. requisisti; C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum aliquis; D. de vulgari et extraordinaria substitutione, l. sed si plures, §. in atrogato; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. filio; D. de solutione matrimonii, l. si vero, §. item quicquid. And I speak of final and immediate contemplation, not of impulsive and remote contemplation. D. pro socio, l. socium, §. fin.; D. de iure dotium, l. profectitia. For because he thought him to be made a canon, he conferred the prebend. If, therefore, error induced him to confer the prebend, it is not valid, as in C. de hereditate instituenda, l. cum proponas, vers. nam si credens. For this quality imports a final reason, which must always be taken into account, as in D. ad Senatum consultum Trebellianum, l. a filio, §. alumno; and D. de hereditate instituenda, l. pacta meus; C. de hereditate instituenda, l. si pater; and l. nec apud Peregrinos, which are well-reasoned in their own right. And thus I say that when the final reason ceases, the provision ceases. Moreover, "vacant" and "not vacant" differ no less when they are juxtaposed than do diverse species of vacancy when they are distinct. But if one expresses one species of vacancy, and it does not become vacant by that species, but by another, he obtains nothing, as in c. Susceptum, de rescriptis, lib. 6, unless fraud were committed, as in l. filiae meae, de solutione matrimonii; and C. de repudiis, l. dubium. Therefore, much more strongly, by expressing vacancy, he does not obtain the desired effect through non-vacancy. Furthermore, the order of words designates the order of understanding. D. de consecratione, dist. 2, c. In Christo pater; D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. quidam recte; D. de usufructu, l. quotiens; D. ad Senatum consultum Trebellianum, l. heredes mei, §. fin. Hence, that which is first in speech is presumed to be principal in intention. D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. si communis servus ita. But since in the letters the canonry is named before the prebend, it follows that the prebend is mentioned accessorially to the canonry: therefore, if the principal is vitiated, the accessory is vitiated.
