C. si penes apud quem mors intercesserit, l. 3; for it does not have a reason for subsisting by itself. C. de usu, l. eos, in principio; and note D. de pignoribus, l. si tibi, §. pignore, with similar authorities. And these suffice. Nor can it be said that he is received to the prebend. For it may happen in fact that he will become a canon; certainly it would be absurd to order first the thing, then the person. D. de testamento, l. si quaeramus; C. de hereditate acquirenda, l. ut debitum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the priorate of a fraternity is a dignity or an honor.
2. Argument from a similar case regarding executors: whether the act of those elected is valid, and when an act performed by several or by one is valid.
body: Most Reverend Father,

† That the dignity, or honor, of the fatherhood is sufficiently able to be proven by those things which Innocent notes in the gloss on the chapter Dilectus, extra, de excessibus praeparatorum, in the first gloss after the principal text, where it is held that a college of laymen, which is established for the sake of religion or piety, is lawful, and that it can appoint for itself a rector, or prior, as in the principal gloss there; and this rector will have ordinary power, as the same author notes in the gloss on the chapter Cum ab ecclesiarum, extra, de officio ordinarii, in the first gloss after the principal text. And thus, by consequence, he is said to have dignity, or honor, since he has jurisdiction, or administration, just as we say in a similar case concerning an ecclesiastical prelate, by those things which the same Innocent notes in the gloss on the chapter Sedes, de rescriptis, where some say, for a secular prerogative is called dignity, 23 q. 5, c. Administratores; note of the Archdeacon, de consuetudine, c. 1, in the first gloss, book 6. And this is true in the broad sense, according to which the prior is recognized to have a certain preeminence over the others of his college, de verbis significandis, l. Quamvis. And thus there would be room for the successor of the said prior to bring an action for contempt, as in the gloss on the chapter Quod sicut, extra, de electione, as appears at the end thereof. But, with respect to sounder counsel, I would not believe that in the present case we should consider contempt: since there is no similarity between those who elect and those who execute, as is evident in itself. For the former, insofar as they are members of the college, have the right of election by the common law, extra, de electione, c. 1; whereas the latter have the duty to execute the will of the testator, de testamento, c. Tua, and c. Ioannes. And concerning this execution, they can do nothing except what pleased the testator, ut eodem titulo, c. Religiosus, § Sane, at the end, book 6.

† And thus the argument from similarity regarding executors appointed to elect would not proceed: for an argument from similarity is destroyed where a dissimilarity can be noted. 1. q. 1. c. Cum ergo. and 27. q. 1. c. Nuptiarum. And this same opinion is held by Fe. de Se. in his Consilium 64 regarding executors appointed to guardians. But we must rather consider, concerning executions, whether they are granted with a clause, or simply. I. Without a clause, or *in solidum*: if with a clause, either with that clause, “if not all,” or “if both,” and then the form must be observed. c. Prudentem, in principio, extra de officio delegati. Or with that clause, “so that all,” or “two,” or “one,” etc., and then the form must be observed. c. Cum plures, eodem titulo, lib. 6. If simply, i.e., without a clause, even then it is not valid that it be done by one without the others, or by the others without one. extra de officio delegati, ca. Communi. and e. Cum tamen. and c. Penult. in glossa 2. and de procuratoribus, c. Duo, in principio, lib. 6. Unless in the cases expressed in c. Religiosus, §. Sane, eodem titulo, lib. 6, if *in solidum*, and then the form of the aforementioned c. Si duo, in principio, must be observed. If, however, they are all present, and one wishes to execute in one manner, and another in another, then the form of c. Ult., extra de ordine iudiciorum, must be observed, as noted by Ber. in the aforementioned law, cap. Causam, de officio delegati, in glossa 3. Or something else will be done, as Spe. says in Speculum de instrumentis edicti, §. Nunc vero aliqua. There, but what will it be, unless the testator had otherwise provided for himself? Because then that will be observed in the aforementioned chapter, c. Religiosus, §. Sane, in fine, lib. 6.

CASE. In the name of God, amen. The case is such, namely, that John, son of the late Francis Cioni of Magalotti, of the parish of San Fiorenzo, in the year of our Lord 1472, in the month of October, made his nuncupative testament without writing: in which he disposed of many things, and made many legacies, and among other things he instituted, made, left, and wished to have as his universal heir Philip Ducii of Magalotti of Florence, and the sons and descendants of said Philip, one or more legitimate or natural males, begotten through the male line, as is contained more fully here and elsewhere in the public instrument of said testament, written by the hand of a public notary. Afterwards, said John, in 1462 [note: text says 1362, likely error for 1462 given context], in the month of February, made his codicils, publicly written by the hand of a public notary, in which he disposed of and bequeathed many things, and among other things, which are contained and written in said codicils, and are found to be, and etc., together with said testament, as above, it is said that the same John instituted, made, left, and wished to have as his universal heir in all his movable and immovable goods, rights, actions, and persons, Philip Ducii of Magalotti of Florence, and the sons and descendants of said Philip, one or more legitimate and natural males, begotten through the male line, as, how, and in what manner as is contained in said testament, as is read and noted. Now today, said John, knowing that said Philip was dead and deceased, and that there existed from said Philip a single son of said instituted heir, correcting, declaring, and adding to the same, and cancelling it, and disposing of his last will in that certain way, he cancelled the person of the females of said Philip Ducii, leaving to himself Joanna; but in all other his movable and immovable goods, rights, actions, and names whatsoever, the same John instituted, made, and wished to have as his universal heir a certain Philip, son of the late other Philip Ducii of Magalotti of Florence, and the sons of said Philip, son of the late other Philip, and descendants, legitimate and natural males, one or more, begotten in legitimate marriage, wishing that said institution made in said testament regarding the sons and descendants of said Philip Ducii remain in its force. Then also afterwards, in the year of our Lord 1477 [note: text says 1377, likely error for 1477], in the month of July, said John made his last codicils, publicly written by the hand of a public notary, in which he disposed of many things, and made many legacies, and among other things, which are contained and written in the last codicils, are found, contained, and written, and is found to be, thus and such a chapter, and in such a series, manner, and form, namely: Item, he wished, disposed, and ordained, and left and commanded, said John, that said Philip, son of the late other Philip, heir of said John and instituted by him, be bound and ought to stand by and be content with the testament and codicils all made by said John, as is said above: and also with the legacies and bequests and dispositions made therein: and with all and each thing contained therein: and not to do or come against them, or any of them, in any way, by himself or otherwise, directly or indirectly, against said testament and codicils, of which mention is made, nor against the legacies and bequests made by the same John therein, and all and each thing contained therein, from now for four years and two months next future, to begin today; but after the lapse of said four years, because then he will be of legitimate age, solemnly to approve and confirm by present instrument, made by the hand of a public notary, and to execute in all things according to the disposition of said John, and within the times ordained by him; so that within said term said instrument comes to the knowledge of said Lady Lisa, or of her daughters, or of one of them; nor also is said Philip bound to freely, and without any question, trouble, or contradiction, or payment, permit, stand, remain, and inhabit in the house, or Palace of said Philip, situated in the Palace of San Fiorenzo, in which, and in that part in which now resides and inhabits said John, his wife Lady Lisa with her family, at least from now for one year next future, beginning at the death of said John: and with the condition, and saving the honor of observing and doing, said Philip, and the same John wished to be his heir, and not otherwise. And inasmuch as said Philip, son of the late other Philip, did not observe, or effectively do and fulfill the aforesaid, the same John deprived said Philip of said inheritance, and in said case, and not otherwise: the same John wished that said inheritance devolve, and in said case instituted, made, left, and wished to have as heir, Dominic Teri, Bartholomew Taldi, and Besse Guidonis of Magalotti, and their sons and descendants, males and natural, in stirpes, not in capita, and them, and their sons and descendants, legitimate and natural males, substituted one for another with the condition, saving the honor of observing and doing all the aforesaid, which said Philip is bound and ought to observe and do. And he bequeathed and left in said testament and codicils, of which mention is made above, and in the aforesaid made and described, to be paid in the modes, forms, times, and at the terms contained and described therein, willing and commanding said John that said Philip in said case could make no deduction or retention of said inheritance, or goods of said John, and after the death of all of them, Dominic, Bartholomew, Besse, if there remain no sons or descendants, legitimate and natural males, of the same in said case, and not otherwise, he made and wished to have as universal heir the Society of the Blessed Virgin Mary of the Order of Saint Michael of Florence, with the condition and honor of observing, fulfilling, and doing all the aforesaid, and also in said testament and codicils, of which mention is made above, and preserved, contained, and legacies and bequests made and described therein, to be paid in the modes, forms, and times, and at the terms contained and described therein, and at the end of said codicils he appended the following clause, namely: And he asserted his last will to be, which he ordered and wished to have value by the right of codicils, or of any other last will, and by any other right, mode, and form, by which and by which it may more effectively have value and hold. And then afterwards said John, testator and codicillator aforesaid, died and passed away, surviving and succeeding him said Philip, sole son and descendant, legitimate and natural male, of said late other Philip Ducii of Magalotti: who Philip, after the death of said John, entered upon and apprehended the inheritance of said John with the benefit of law and inventory: but first he began the inventory, but did not complete it, and within the time and term aforesaid of four years and two months he did not ratify said testament and codicils by public instrument, as was disposed above in said codicils, disposed and ordained, made; and also he did not fully do and observe those things which, and as, were disposed in said testament and codicils by the same John. Now it is asked, having seen said testament and codicils, institutions, and substitutions, and conditions, and burdens, and other things contained therein appended, what is the law in and upon the aforesaid, above written and narrated: and especially in and upon said last codicils made by said John, as is said above, by the condition, or said chapter of said last codicils, and whether said Philip, heir aforesaid, is deprived, or can be deprived, or ought to be, or is deprived, or is understood to be deprived, of said inheritance of said late John, or not: and whether said inheritance of said John, or any part thereof, can devolve, or revert, or be applied, or pertain, or belong, or ought to, to said Dominic, or Bartholomew Taldi, and Besse Guidonis, substituted in said last codicils, by virtue of said last codicils, or said chapter of said last codicils above narrated, or whether it can remain, or ought to, to said Philip, heir aforesaid, and pertain and belong to said Philip, or not: and if so, how, and by what right, and mode, and whether in whole, or in part, for which, or for what quota part.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How manyfold the impossible condition is.
2. An inheritance is not given by codicils: and therefore the condition is rejected.
3. Whether direct words are drawn to a fideicommissum.
4. An express vulgar substitution made in codicils is not drawn to a fideicommissum.
5. Whether a reciprocal substitution is drawn to a fideicommissary one.
6. Whether the Trebellian rule can be prohibited in codicils.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† To make the matter clear, it must be premised that some conditions are impossible, some void, some superfluous, and some proper, which it is necessary to fulfill. An impossible condition is said so in two ways: in one way, it is impossible even in itself, which occurs in four modes, namely, by nature, by law, by fact, and according to good morals. D. de cond. et demonstr. l. filius. In another way, it is said to be impossible to impose, although in itself it is necessary. C. de his, qui poenae nomine. l. 1. To reconcile this, see G. and Petrus. A void condition is one when the testator considered its existence in vain, as in D. de cond. et demonstr. l. quidam in suo. §. si. A superfluous condition is one that is expressed in vain, because it was inherent by necessity. D. de legat. 1. l. haec. A proper condition is one that is prescribed for form, without which the thing cannot even be done. D. de cond. et demonstr. l. qui heredi. §. si. and l. meus. Secondly, it must be premised that a testator who leaves a fideicommissum in codicils made before the acceptance of the inheritance contemplates the necessity of the acceptance of the inheritance from the will; for it would be absurd and impossible for rights to be transferred by the heir to another before the heir himself is made. If, therefore, the testator does not wish the heir to be made, he does not wish restitution to be made through him, as in D. ad trebell. l. sed et si alio. §. si. Thirdly, it must be premised that words spoken in codicils made to a will are sometimes spoken under the form of an obstructive condition of acceptance of the inheritance, sometimes under the form of a presupposed condition of acceptance of the inheritance, and sometimes under an oblique or derogatory form. Therefore, sometimes the words are direct according to the nature of the words, obstructing acceptance, and such words never obstruct, because the testator considered such a condition in vain, as noted in the aforementioned l. quidam in suo. §. final. For in the case of a failing condition, the testator, who did not even wish the heir to be made, is not understood to have burdened him by the fideicommissum. C. de fideicommissis. l. ab eo. If I do not transfer to the fideicommissum on account of the contradiction that exists between the will and possibility,

† The second point remains, that in codicils an inheritance is neither directly given nor taken away; hence not only is the condition vitiated, but also the thing conditioned, as being consequent to the condition. D. de iure codicillorum, l. quod poenitentiam; and Inst. de codicillis, § neque.

† Sometimes the words of codicils are under the matter and form of a suppletive acceptance of inheritance; and then direct words are drawn to a fideicommissum, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. An cum quis, §. Si eam; and thus it is understood, that in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Verbis civilibus, and in Inst. de codicillis, §. Penes. And the reason is, because such direct and fideicommissary [substitution] has a symbol concerning the required acceptance of inheritance; and therefore the transition is easy from the more plain, i.e., direct, to the less comprehensive, i.e., fideicommissary substitution: whereas pupillary substitution, which requires acceptance of inheritance at least made by common words in codicils, is contrary, as in l. Si eum.

But an express vulgar substitution made in codicils is not extended to a fideicommissary one, because they are entirely contrary, according to Guillaume de Cuyk, who thus notes in his treatise on substitutions, §. Now let us see, on fideicommissary substitutions, in the gloss “But it is asked, what on the contrary, whether a direct substitution, until someone.” This statement of Guillaume is contrary to l. Seium and contrary to the gloss placed there by G., and contrary to the summary case of Dynus, who thus summarizes that law: “A direct, vulgar, pupillary, or reciprocal substitution made in codicils is extended to a fideicommissum.” Therefore, the aforementioned opinion of Guillaume is false. Solution: Rather, it is the very truth, if one understands the case in the terms of l. Seium, where the father instituted his son, a pupillus and in his power, as heir, and in his will; finally, in codicils, he substituted three persons for him, whom he substituted to receive from one another. It is said there that, if the pupillus dies, the brother of the pupillus, who succeeds the pupillus intestate, is bound to restore the inheritance to the substitutes, if they are alive; but if any of the substitutes predeceased, the entire fideicommissum arising from the oblique pupillary substitution is owed to the survivors, namely by the brother of the pupillus. For that reciprocal substitution, “if you shall not be heir,” is explained as meaning “if you shall not be fideicommissary”; the others who survive are fideicommissaries and take from the hand of the heir of the pupillus. For the same result would follow by the right of accretion, the reciprocal substitution ceasing.

† Thus, reciprocal substitution is drawn to that which comes into the fideicommissum, since it can also be made in a fideicommissum, as stated in the delegation. 2. L. ut haeredibus. But that law does not say that if someone is substituted in the ordinary way, it is understood that he is substituted by fideicommissum: for this is false according to civil and natural reason; for he who substitutes in the ordinary way loves the instituted heir more than the substitute in order and in the fruit of the order, and if it were drawn to the fideicommissum, the opposite would follow. This reason is clear in the aforementioned L. verbis civilibus. Therefore, an oblique interpretation against the testator's will is impossible, but this seems expressly contrary. §. Sey. But here consider that a disposition made by one who disposes by way of privation, especially in codicils, requires the acceptance of the inheritance: for every disposition of last will must be confirmed by acceptance, as in L. si servus communis meus, de castrensi peculio, in the end; principium, de stipulationibus servorum; and ff. de haeredibus instituendis, L. sed et si in conditione, §. final; ff. de legatis 3, L. si iure. And therefore it has a similarity with fideicommissary substitution. Moreover, those words, "I wish him to be heir," are drawable to a fideicommissum, because the fideicommissary is in a certain sense an heir. ff. de militum testamento, L. quaerebatur; ff. quod cum eo, L. si filius, §. 1. The enumeration of law and the general nature of words allow substitution to be interpreted obliquely. From these I infer two conclusions. The first is that if those words of the superior testament, cum condit. et c., imply a condition strictly and properly, so that in the event of the failure of the condition an ordinary substitution has been made, as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. pro secundo, the inheritance remains with Philip without the burden of restitution under the Trebellian law. The second conclusion is this: if it is not a proper condition, but a certain tenor, as noted in ff. pro socio, L. si societur, in the beginning, such inheritance must be restored under the Trebellian law, according to some, with the deduction of the Trebellian fourth; but according to others, with no fourth deducted, because it was prohibited, and because it is a penalty for not observing the judgment of the deceased. On this point, see auth. sed cum testator, through the doctors; L. Marcellus, §. quod autem, ad Trebellianum, through Bartolus. Therefore, only this remains to be considered: whether the condition required by the testator to be fulfilled for the power to enter upon the inheritance is a proper condition or not; on which point I do not stand firm, because the words of these codicils are ambiguous, applying to many intentions, and sounding in many cases and in various ways, and especially because of the clause more than codicillary placed at the end.

The third point concerning the form of the deprecatory clause is clear, because it is possible that, although the Trebellian share may be prohibited in codicils, this is not clear: nor does *l. cautum* [so hold]; on the contrary, even in a will. The glosses are contrary: and if the Trebellian fourth could be taken away in codicils, *l. quae* distinguishes between direct heirs and those by fideicommissum, it would have been imposed by words, and not by things: since the name of heir would remain empty, *inst. de fideicommissis hereditatibus* § *sed quia*. Hence also, according to those who say that the Trebellian share can be prohibited, I nevertheless say that in codicils it cannot be prohibited so as to be entirely exempted, and the institution of the heir in the will by codicils would be rendered void, with no effect remaining for the heir instituted in the will. For this is contrary to the intent of the said law, *quod per manus*. And for this is the ordinary gloss, also *l. 2* C. *de codicillis* in the gloss which begins, *cum preces*: for everything which is subalternated to another, and subjected to another’s power, is inferior to it, and under it not more powerful, because not dominant. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the goods of one entering the monastery of Saint Dominic ought to belong to the monastery or to the intestate heirs.
2. Whether immovable and movable things are included in a general lease.
3. See what is consulted above by Balduinus and Petrus, consilium 438.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case, on which legal advice is requested, is as follows. Iitius of Viterbo, under 25 years of age, having movable and immovable property, entered the Order of Preachers and made profession to the convent that would otherwise have succeeded him intestate, that it should hold the goods he had in the secular world against the will of the prior and the order and the entire convent. However, the prior of the convent and the aforementioned place, or its syndic, the canon, could have the aforementioned goods, pertaining to him at the time of his entry, restored to him by all. It is asked whether these goods can in any way be retained or even, by any right, be claimed from the said convent: and whether the convent itself can be held liable by any right?

† And first it seems that the said prior, or syndicus, ought to be admitted in petitioning for the restitution of the said goods to himself: because by the entry into the said order, all the goods of the said professed person were acquired for the convent, as in the Authentica *De monachis*, § *Illud*. And although they are mendicants, nevertheless they can acquire for themselves; which is proven by the fact that it is special for the Minorites that they cannot have property nor acquire for themselves, as in the Clementina *Exiit* *De Paradiso*. Therefore, the contrary will be the common law, and in the Preachers and others they acquire indiscriminately, and can have property, as in l. 1, in fine, ff. *Ad municipalia*; l. *Ius singulare*, ff. *De legibus*; and *Cum si*. Moreover, it is not prohibited to Preachers by any law or case to have movables, even by the rule of Blessed Dominic, or even by their constitution: therefore, although they can acquire and have movables indiscriminately; for all things are permitted which are not found to be prohibited. l. *Memoriae*, § *Sed quod*, ex qui. *Causa maioris*. They will therefore, without doubt, be able to claim and demand all movables which belonged to him upon entering, indiscriminately. Furthermore, by the precept of Blessed Dominic, it seems prohibited to induce possession into the convent; therefore, they are prohibited from inducing movables. For when something is specifically prohibited, its consequence is understood, namely that other things are permitted. ff. *De iure*, l. *Cum praetor*; and movables are distinguished from immovables by law. l. *A Diuo Pio*, § 1, ff. *De re iudicata*; and l. *Monetium*, ff. *De verborum significatione*; ff. *Uti possidetis*, l. 1, § *Pe*. They can therefore have and demand movables without doubt. Furthermore, and even if it seemed that the acquisition of immovables was prohibited, and the acquisition of movables permitted, they can acquire immovables, not to hold them, but to sell them, and convert the price thence derived into their utility and necessary uses. ff. *De legatis 1*, l. *Caetera*, § *Si duo*; and l. *Si seruo*, § *Si cui*, *Cum si*. They can therefore without doubt also claim, demand, and sell immovables, and convert them into necessary and useful acts and uses of the convent for food, books, and similar things. Furthermore, although it were true that they could not acquire immovables in any way or case, nevertheless, since they have the Roman Church as their lady, and thus their head, since they do not have to petition, the order acquires, and since it could not retain for itself, it acquires for the Roman Church, as they ought to give an account of their preeminence, just as a common slave, who if he cannot acquire for one of the masters, acquires for the other in solidum. ff. *De stipulationibus servorum*, l. *Si servus communis*. And because the Roman Church is their head and is in the order as a head, just as a father is in a son, and a master in a slave, as in ff. *De operis liberti*, l. *Pamphilo*; and ff. *De stipulationibus servorum*, l. 1, § 2, and § *Parvi*, with similar cases. And from these the brothers will be supported, argument from C. *De episcopis et clericis*, l. *Raptorem palam*; l. *Servos*, *De aliis legatis*; and l. *In metallis*, ff. *De his quae pro non scriptis habentur*, with similar cases. Moreover, for this makes the constitution of the Clementina and of the supreme pontiffs Nicholas, where they seem to admit the acquisition of land by them through succession, and largely of possessions and all things indiscriminately, just as they could acquire while existing in the secular world, and take from possession; and that they sell and convert into their necessity and utility. And it is certain that if they were in the secular world, they could acquire; therefore, existing in the rule, they can acquire: which constitution agrees sufficiently with the above said. The tenor of whose constitution is as follows: Clement, bishop, to the master and brothers of the order of Preachers, and with the pretext of the divine name, to whose cult, under the observance of our sacred religion, we gladly assent to your vows, and we favorably hear your petitions, and having duly deposited these. For indeed, it was proposed on your part before us, that certain prelates, clerics, and laymen situated in various parts of the world, asserting that you are dead and cannot validly possess property, attempt to exclude you from any successions on this occasion. Wherefore, on your part, it was humbly requested by us that, lest any harm be done to you through the presumption of such persons, we should provide a proper remedy for this with paternal diligence. We therefore, more benignly assenting to your supplications, by apostolic authority declare that you may lawfully succeed in temporal goods in which you would succeed while existing in the secular world, apprehend the possession of those goods, and freely sell those goods, and convert their price into your utility, as it seems best to you. Having inspected the privilege, and its series and sentence, it will be seen indubitably that they can claim and demand the said movables and immovables for the aforementioned effects; and especially because if this proceeds from the benefit of the Prince, it ought to be interpreted most liberally, as in C. *De bonis vacantibus*, lib. 10; ff. *De constitutionibus Principum*, l. 1; it makes extra *De donationibus*, cap. *Cum dilecti*. Furthermore, when they can take, so that they may sell and convert into their utility, it seems expressly to sound and hold the gloss of the order, extra *De relictis*, c. 1, on the word *domini*. For although they beg, nevertheless it is expedient for them to live from alms and others, in which all kinds of goods can consist. Proven extra *De donationibus*, c. *Cum dilecti*. This also determines Speculum, *De statu monachorum*, § 1, versi. 3; and the same, *Eodem*, § *Vero*, l. 3, where he holds expressly that relatives do not succeed in their goods by such entry, but the monastery itself, because no one is nearer to himself than he who is coupled to him in dominion. *De pecuniis*, cap. 2; and as John Andrea touches upon more widely there, concordant with the first place said, that such mendicants can acquire such goods, not to hold them, but to sell them, as is placed in the Novella *De probationibus*, cap. *In praesentia*. And this we see continuously observed by custom, which is the best interpreter of laws. As in ff. *De legibus*, l. *Minime*; l. *Barbarius*, ff. *De officio praetoris*, with similar cases.

Against this makes: because what Blessed Dominic, the founder of this religion, left for his brothers to observe, he seems to have given them in command by these words, namely: "Most dear brothers, I leave these to you as to sons to possess: Have charity; keep humility; possess voluntary poverty, I forbid you with as much strictness as I can: for whoever induces possession into this order, let the maledictions of the Almighty be against him." From this verse *inducat*, every act of acquisition seems to be prohibited; I say of possession, as both the act of acquiring by oneself, and also from another offering, etc. Moreover, this seems to be shown and proven by the pre-constitutions of the Preachers, by which it seems to be disposed of possessions, not if sought, etc. But regarding money to be acquired, it does not seem to be disposed of by the aforementioned words, nor even by the sentence, which is inferred from this, especially so that they may have wherewith to live. It remains therefore that they can have and seek money, but it seems to be noted by what law they receive, whether offered, or another offered, they can. But if by hereditary right, which is not of itself, but together with possession, and otherwise is found in the patrimony of the professed, it seems they cannot receive it by reason of the form of this act of taking; because they must take as heirs and universal successors of the professed, in whom they are successors, movables, nor can they be divided before acquisition; because the right of acquiring by reason of entry into dominion of goods is indivisible. Another reason seems to be, that if they can take the goods of the professed by reason of entry, and also goods which afterwards happen to them, they receive by virtue of privilege, statute, rule, not mendicancy; because in no respect is it distinguished from monks in the acquisition of dominion of things, and even in having goods, whence this monk, by acquiring, although by entry, contradicts the constitution of the rule and the form, which is that he be in poverty and mendicancy, nor can they even by virtue of the aforementioned privilege; because the privilege grants them those things which are deferred to them after profession: but not the retention of those which they had before: whence this case is not included in the privilege, but rather seems omitted, and consequently excluded. ff. *Solutis matrimonii*, l. *Si cum dote*, in principle. Another reason, for the aforementioned privilege grants the brothers to take what would be acquired to them existing in the secular world: but this, which they claim by virtue of entry, would not be acquired to the brothers in the secular world; because if they were in the secular world, there would be no convent, and thus it is a conventual acquisition, by this reason it is inferred that the privilege does not concern those things which are deferred principally and directly to the order itself, but those which happen singularly to the brothers, which are those which they would have existing in the secular world. But against the interpretations of the aforementioned constitution, the constitution of the Clementina makes, which does not admit such interpretation, and reserving to itself alone the interpretation, of which constitution the tenor is as follows: Clement, bishop, etc., to the master and brothers of the order of Preachers, etc., of your sacred religion, which you serve to the Lord in humility of spirit, deserves to be praised, that we do not grant you those things by which the matter of the subject grievance is procured for the tranquility of your state, with a willing mind. Indeed, the complaint transmitted to you shows that certain bishops, and archbishops, and prelates of other churches, derogating from your liberties, attempt to interpret indulgences or privileges granted to you by the Roman Church, and to draw them to their own understanding, although the words of such indulgences and privileges do not seem to express them with such understanding, and they compel you to conserve those privileges according to their interpretation, to your no small prejudice and grievance: because, however, you have implored the remedy of the apostolic see on this, we strictly forbid by the authority of these presents that the aforementioned archbishops and prelates presume to interpret the aforementioned privileges, indulgences, or whatever they contain, whether they do not need interpretation, or are doubtful or obscure, from now on: willing that, since it is for him to interpret who has made it, interpretation on such doubtful and obscure matters be left to the judgment of the said see, etc. Given at Viterbo, etc.

Moreover, another reason seems that the said prior and syndicus cannot claim nor demand: because Titius was under 25 years of age at the time of profession. Whence he could not tacitly nor expressly alienate without a tutor and a decree, as in l. *Lex quae*, C. *De administratione tutorum*; and *De bonis minorum*, *Sine decreto non alienentur*, per totum, *Cum si*. But here no decree, no solemnity intervened: therefore, the deduction otherwise did not hold, and thus the right was transferred to the convent of movables and immovables, therefore the prior, or convent, or syndicus cannot act; because without action he would experience against the laws. ff. *De negotiis gestis*, l. *Si pupilli*, § *Videamus*; l. *Quotiens*, § *Finalis*; l. *Si temporali*, ff. *De administratione tutorum*, with similar cases. And from these, and others to be supplied in law by the lord consultant, it is asked, what is the law.

Regarding the above, it is to be considered that such a contract is one of good faith, as in the Institution *De actionibus*, § *In bonae fidei*; and C. *Locatio*, l. *Adversus*. And in such a contract, it is permitted to the lessor to speak more clearly. l. *Apertius*. And if, as is proposed, then the said Bartholomew had and possessed all and each thing stably, he could oppose in exception all which were not of his intention in the lease. Since therefore the lease appears obscure or ambiguous, that he said that he leased all and each stable thing which he Bartholomew now has, holds, and possesses in his name and that of his wife, except the weight, etc., an interpretation is to be made against the lessor, namely against Bartholomew; and this is what is said in l. *Veteribus*, *De pactis*, there, "and to him who leases," etc. In the case, however, proposed, it can sufficiently be said that all stable things come into the lease, since it is proposed that then he Bartholomew had and possessed all the said stable things, and leased them thus generally, except the weight, etc. Therefore, the exception cannot comprehend other cases than those named and applied, says l. *Si servus eius*, *De acquirenda hereditate*; and l. *Si duo*, *De administratione tutorum*. Moreover, these three words, namely *habet*, *tenet*, and *possidet*, import almost the same effect. To have is with respect to dominion, and not with respect to possession alone. l. *Stipulatio ista*, *Habere, licere*, *De verborum obligatione*; and l. *Is apud*, and l. *Habere*, *De verborum significatione*. If from this there arises obscurity or ambiguity, whether in contemplation of dominion or possession, then the aforementioned l. *Veteribus* has place, so that interpretation be made against the lessor. Which interpretation is, that it be understood to have by right of sole possession, one could hold the same regarding the word *significatione*, to hold and possess. Thus simply pronounced, it refers to naked detention, as in l. *Stipulatio ista*, § *Hi quoque*, and § *Habere*, where it is openly said that natural question, or to possess naturally, and to hold, and this in effect import the same. Since therefore it is proposed that Bartholomew at the time of the said lease had, held, and possessed, it sufficiently appears that all those stable things came into the said lease, except the weight of grain, etc. And consequently, the lord Bartholomew, by the acts, was bound by condition to the lord Francis of Clu, as by the law *Ex conducto*, ff. *De locatione*; and l. 2, C. *Eodem*. But why in the beginning he said it was against the chapter of good faith, because in it come all promised and received things, and in certain things not said and not expressed, all good and equitable things are observed, as in the Institution *De obligationibus ex consensu*, § *Finalis*; and l. *Circa*, C. *Locatio*. By which I conclude, as I premised, that the said Bartholomew was thus bound and held to the said. And also in the said lease comes every possession, whether stable, of which mention is made above, for the two weights excepted, namely the weight of Conta, etc. Nicolinus de Casulis, yours always. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An appeal from a sentence passed by the authority, or its judge, to whom the case is devolved.
2. Whether the prior citizens have any jurisdiction. And below, in the following opinion.
3. If it is established before the judge that the appeal has been abandoned, or was not duly interposed, he must execute his sentence.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the point of fact narrated above, the acts and proceedings carried out before the Lord of Fons and the judge, and the sentence of the said Lord Defender and the appealed judge, the facts presented to the said Lords Priors and accepted, and the facts opposed and produced on behalf of the said Lelli before the said Lords Priors, and all acts produced and carried out before the said Lords Priors, and having seen the statutes thereof, as they were transmitted to me: and presupposing that the appeals intended for the time being were made to the aforementioned Lords Priors, and that more than a year had passed, and that there was neither then nor is there now a Captain in your city, but only a Podestà in that city of yours; and that the sentence passed against the said Lelli, from which the said Lelli appealed, and the said Lord Defender and Judge, did not emanate from the said Lord Podestà, who is now and was at the time of the said appeal and sentence passed by the said Lord Defender, nor from any of his office, but from his predecessor, etc.

† I state briefly that, in law, it must be said that the aforementioned Lords Priors were not, nor are, competent judges in the said case. The reason which moves me is this: It is certain that, according to the form of the statute of your commune, placed under the rubric "On appeals to be interposed in civil cases," as at the end: "But if the definitive sentence from which appeal was made has been annulled by the said Judge of Appeals, or declared null for being imprecise, etc., when the sentence pronounced by the Potestate or his judges is annulled by the Judge of Appeals, appeal must be made to the Capitano; and vice versa, if the sentence was pronounced by the Capitano and annulled by the Judge of Appeals, appeal must be made to the Potestate." But in the case at hand, the sentence pronounced against the said Lello, and finally annulled by the said Lord Defender, was pronounced by the Judge of the Potestate; and thus appeal ought to have been made to the Capitano of your city, if at that time the office of the said Lord Capitano had been in force in your said city. But since at that time the said Capitano was not present in your said city, appeal ought to have been made to the people, or to the council, or to the order of decurions: these decurions are called councilors. This is noted by the gloss in *l. nulli*, D. *quod cuiusque universitatis*; in the gloss on the verse "omnimodo"; and in D. *de decurionibus*, Book 10, in the gloss on the rubric. And not to the Lords Priors; because when the rectors are not in the city, the jurisdiction of the said rector remains with the order of decurions, that is, with the councilors of the said city, and not with the Priors. This is proven by *l. ubi absunt*, D. *de tutoribus et curatoribus datis ab his*; and there by Lord Bartolus; and by the same author in *l. 1, § si quis in appellatione*, D. *de appellationibus*. Similarly, see Extravagantes, *de maioribus et obediencia*, cap. *Iste*; and cap. *Cum olim*, Extravagantes, *de haereticis*; and cap. *Ad abolendam*, in which it is said that, upon the death of the bishop, the vacant jurisdiction remains with the chapter. For decurions, or consuls of the city, have that power which the whole people has. This is proven by *l. plane*, and the notes thereon, D. *quod cuiusque universitatis*; and *l. nominationum*, C. *de decurionibus*, Book 10.

But the former [priors] are not so: for they have limited jurisdiction, as is evident from the statute of your commune, placed under the rubric "On the Election of Officials and the Authority of the Lords Priors and the People," etc. Nor can they be called the greater powers or the Captains of the said city of Todi. And thus an appeal could not be made to them: for an appeal must be made to a superior, not to an inferior or an equal, as is proved by L. 1, § Si quis, in the title De appellationibus of the Digest, and in the body of the Authenticae, De appellationibus, and infra, Quae tempora debeat appellari, § Illo. And this appeal ought to have been made, namely, to the people or the decurions of the said city of Todi, if the said city of Todi is a free people and acknowledges no superior. But if it acknowledged a superior authority, then, the office of the said Captain being vacant, the appeal ought to have been made to the superior of the said city of Todi, namely, to the Pope or the Emperor, if there are no other intermediate superiors. This is proved by L. Imperatores, in the Digest, De appellationibus, and by those things noted by Doctor Bartolus in the aforementioned § Si quis, in the title De appellationibus, and L. 1, § Solenniter, in the Digest, Quando appellatio sit, by the same said Bartolus, with his followers. Concluding, therefore, I say, in the name of Christ invoked, that the aforementioned priors were not, nor are, competent judges in the aforementioned appeal, by the law and authorities cited above. I, Francis. To the same effect. In the name of Christ, amen.

If it is established that the appeal has been abandoned or was not duly interposed, the judge must execute his sentence, as noted in C. de appellationibus, l. eos in principio, and l. contra; and in Extra de appellationibus, caput 1 in Clementinis; and according to Bartolus in l. 1, in fine, nihil novi, apud penult., where it has been so extensively consulted that it is not expedient to say anything further, except that it was wisely consulted by the most excellent doctor, Lord Bartolus de Saliceto, and by my most dear colleague, Lord Francis of Spoleto. The prior of the city has no other contentious jurisdiction except that which the municipal law, because their office is deficient, grants to them, as noted in ff. de pace, l. item magistrorum.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A release must be effective, not void or ineffectual.
2. A release is not considered a mere fact.
3. Whether to order payment and to order release are the same thing.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In this dispute, which originates with the servant, by virtue of which agreement this Iosfredus, a true debtor formerly, now wishes to recover what has been paid from the lord John, it is said first that it must be stated that Iosfredus has a just and clear

† because he ordered the debtor to be released, if he meanwhile demands payment, he is bound to restore what has been collected. And thus the act of release is converted into the truth of restitution, as in D. de exceptionibus doli, l. pure, in principio. For it is not understood as an empty and futile release, but as one effective at the time when the obligation subsists; because he ordered something to be done, he must do it in such a way that it takes effect according to law. D. de legatis 1, l. huiuscemodi, in principio, and § si ita cui legatum, and in both places, numero.

† And release is not said to be a mere fact. D. de cond. ob causam, l. si mulier; C. de transac., l. siue apud acta; because he who remits is deemed to give. D. de calum., l. 2; D. de re iur., l. si quis obligatione.

† Hence, it is as if one were to order payment and order release. And thus the petition of Losfredus appears to be properly formulated. And since there is no question regarding the pronouncement, it remains to be seen that the said Losfredus should be the one who carries off the palm of victory. To the contrary, it could be argued that the said pact was naked, and thus no action could lie therefrom: because it did not have a cause pertaining to the matter. D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, §. sed cum nulla. But I do not insist on this point: because it was pronounced according to the pact, even if perhaps it was judged erroneously. Nevertheless, authority of the sentence must be obeyed. D. de iudiciis, l. si praetor, §. in omnibus; D. de pignoribus, l. si fundus, §. si plures; D. de re vendita, l. si ex diverso. And therefore I come to the second reason: for the words stated that it should be regarded as if the said Losfredus had obtained [the judgment]; thus, therefore, it should be regarded as such. But if he had obtained [the judgment] by sentence and paid the true debt, he would not recover it. D. de condictione indebiti, l. Iulius; Inst. de exceptionibus, §. item si in iudicio; l. procurator, ad proximum, §. 1, in fine; D. rem ratam habere. Therefore, with what face and with what conscience he recovers, I do not concern myself: for he cannot recover from Nicolaus, because he made no convention with him; nor from Lord John, because Lord John received his own. D. de condictione indebiti, l. repetitio. Which certainly would also be due to him naturally by an absolving sentence: for in this case the pact does not extinguish the natural obligation, because it operates no more by the form of the convention than does a sentence. Moreover, this Losfredus brought about his own act so that he could not be released, because he paid, and the substance was extinguished. Objections. D. de legatis 3, l. 1, §. si rem. And if he says that he was compelled to pay. I answer: the act of the judge harms him as if he had previously consented; therefore Lord John could have obtained the release of this pact through another, etc., and if he could not have done so himself. D. de liberatione legati, l. si is qui duos. Also, a debt, although exacted in civil law, cannot be recovered. D. quod metus causa, l. fin., §. fin.; to the same effect, D. de iureiurando, l. sed et si postor, §. si non admiserit. To the same effect is what is noted in D. si certum petatur, l. pactum, in the gloss on the words "hinc autem." To the same effect, C. de transactionibus, l. si pro fundo. And the whole of that which is not done to raise an exception does not give rise to an action, as noted in D. de pactis, l. si intra. And it is supported by D. de iureiurando, l. si quis cum debitore, in the gloss 3, or better, Baldus. And therefore I say that the said John has justice: and especially because the said pact was captious, since nothing could accrue to Lord John therefrom, who also had justice without the pact, as clearly appears from the following: therefore I say that Losfredus has no right, and that Lord John should be absolved from his latest recovery, presupposing that Losfredus was his true debtor, or a common debtor of both him and Nicolaus, as the theme indicates, or rather, and principally, was the debtor of Nicolaus. The objections to the contrary do not stand: first, the reason does not stand, which says that it obtains if he had not suffered execution; for rather he would have been compelled to pay the said Nicolaus: because the temerarious pact of the said Nicolaus and John would not have harmed Nicolaus, nor the sentence pronounced expressly stating the cause of the said temerarious pact. Also, they could not have made a pact concerning the right of a third party. D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. ante omnia. Also, nor concerning another’s fact, as Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. si quis alium. Also, if he was compelled to pay, this was just and equitable. And because the question seems to have been principally with Nicolaus alone, it is supported by D. de pactis, l. si unus, in principio; D. de iureiurando, l. duobus; D. de negotiis gestis, l. ex duobus, cum simili. Also, l. auunculo does not stand, because there natural equity favors the one recovering, otherwise the defendant would be enriched there at another’s loss: here it is quite the contrary: because Losfredus is the one who wishes to be enriched. And therefore he must be repelled from an immoderate and inordinate intention, as far as is possible without breaking the pact of obtaining the palm, which must be observed when it concerns some virtue of body or mind. D. verum obiectum, l. in excusatione, §. fin., in the gloss. But here, as I said, it is not broken, because we are in the third case, of which the pact does not speak, nor does equity. Also I say: the dog barks, and if he does not bark, I wish to lose the case; it is also foolishness and ineptitude, and the diligence of the laws would be small and wretched, which would draw that pact to terms not its own.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a staircase existing above the door of someone is to be called common.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On this point, the truth of the facts must be examined, which can be seen with ocular evidence. L. Si cum in emptione, §. Ad officium, D. De finium regundorum. For this one says that, although he has now found his office on the said staircase, it is therefore manifest that the staircase was common to those dwelling on both sides. D. De communi diviso, L. Arbor, §. De vestibulo. In which case, if one can conveniently ascend by the staircase, the building constructed with the knowledge and acquiescence of the co-owner ought nevertheless not to be demolished. D. De communi diviso, L. Sabinus, 2. Responsio. But if the staircase belonged to the other as his own, then the building ought to be demolished. And therefore the arbiter, having inspected the quality of the place and seen the truth with his own eyes, had ruled according to the aforementioned opinion. And consider that if he has nothing else in his intention except to annoy his co-owner, he ought not to be heard. Arg. D. De rei venditione, L. In feudo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The Church of the Friars Minor cannot be instituted as an heir, nor can it be substituted universally.
2. A mother may, on behalf of her son, deduct the legitime from the assets subject to substitution.
3. Whether the adverb "freely" is included in the burden of the restitution of a fideicommissum after death.
casus:
CASE. The facts are proposed as follows. Vannutius Levi made a testament, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows: “I also leave to Lady Luchella, his wife, all the cloths of wool and of linen for the use of clothing of the said Luchella, however. I also freely bequeath and leave to the said Luchella, his wife, his houses situated in Assisi at the Gate of St. Francis, in the borough of St. Peter, alongside the road on two sides, and the property of Lippus Martius and the heirs of Blasius Vannis. I also leave, by right of institution and legacy, to Francisca Maria and Clarella, my daughters, for each of them four hundred pounds of denarii, a quantity which the said testator ordered and willed that each of them should have when they lived, and he substituted them to one another if they should die without legitimate sons or daughters; and in the case that all the said daughters should die without legitimate sons or daughters, in the said case he substituted to them, thus dying, the said Luchella, his wife and their mother. After the death, however, of the said Luchella, he willed and commanded that the said quantity of money left to his said daughters should freely devolve to the Church of St. Francis of Assisi. In all his other movable and immovable goods, etc., he instituted and made the said Lady Luchella, his wife, his universal heir. After the death, however, of the said Lady Luchella, the said testator willed and expressly commanded that all the goods of his said inheritance should freely devolve to the Church of St. Francis of Assisi, etc.”

Now it is asked: assuming as constant, although the law is otherwise, that the aforementioned Church could be admitted to take the aforementioned inheritance after the death of the aforementioned daughters of the testator and the aforementioned Luchella, and that the prelegacies made to the said Lady Luchella come into the restitution to be made to the aforementioned Church.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Assuming, without prejudice to the truth, that the legacy, etc., made to the Church of the Friars Minor is valid, at least with respect to a certain usurpation, since I hold as a matter of law that the Church of the Friars Minor could not be instituted as an heir, nor could it be substituted universally,

I come to the question, and I say that the mother could deduct the third, i.e., the legitime, on behalf of her children, which she appears to have acknowledged by taking possession of the hereditary assets; and therefore she transmitted this legitime to the agnates and to her own heirs. C. de Amet. inoff. testam. l. si quis filium. And thus the Church will have two parts; and it has the third part of all the goods, both those left to the daughters and those to the wife; because the legitime of the daughters is deducted from the whole of this estate. As for all the legacies made to the woman at the beginning of the will,

† Whether the adverb “freely” is included in the burden of restitution of the fideicommissum after the wife’s death is sufficiently doubtful, due to the universal words and the testator’s intent encompassing everything: as in C. de fideicom. l. cum virum. But that it does not apply is supported by the fact that the adverb “freely” would have no effect, which it ought not to have; and because a special, indeed singular, provision derogates from the general rule. Cap. factum haereti. l. quot. de le. tertio. l. haeres meus. §. duae statuae. de alimen. leg. l. alimenta. §. basilicae. and l. Stichus. And by way of disputation, this part is more defensible.

On descendants intestate without children. Rub. TEM We establish and ordain that if anyone, male or female, from the land of Saint Severinus or its district should die intestate, without legitimate children, all goods and rights thus devolving intestate shall come and revert to the nearest blood relatives descending from the paternal line, or from the line of the paternal grandfather, of the person dying intestate; since it is sufficiently consonant with reason that such goods return to their original state, from which they are known to have originated. And the foregoing shall apply in present, past, and future cases. Otherwise, it is a case without decision; therefore, I have annulled it, and I marvel that these first correctors did not seek decisions, or did not occupy the membranes.

In the Name of Christ. Having premised the aforementioned statute, the following case is proposed. Otherwise, it is a case without decision; therefore, I have set it aside. In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows: Petrutius Panlelii of Gualdo gave and granted to Panlelio, his son. CASE. The facts are such: Titius, having Jacoba, his mother, and Margaret, his wife, and Joanna, the infant daughter of said Titius by his wife; this Titius killed Margaret, his wife. Now, the said Lady Jacoba, mother of said Titius and of the slain Margaret, wishes to be admitted to the guardianship of said Joanna. The uncle of the said Lady Margaret, who was killed, says that he ought to be admitted and that the said grandmother ought to be excluded. Now the question is: what is the law?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a guardian may be appointed for a person outlawed both in property and in person.
2. Who is to be preferred in guardianship, the grandmother or the maternal uncle: and with whom the guardianship ought to remain.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

First of all, it must be known whether, when a person is banned, there is room for any guardianship in respect of his estate and person. And following the gloss in § relegatis, under the heading “locus tutelae”: because the son is released from paternal power, and there is an irregular guardianship, as Bartolus states in l. si quis sub conditione, de testamento, in the verse quis, where he says that when the father is banned to death, the mother assumes the guardianship of the underage son. And the same was held by Master Federicus of Siena. But Jacobus de Arezzo and the same Bartolus in his disputation hold that he does not lose paternal power, and therefore there is room for a curator, and not a tutor: which he fully reported in l. 1, C. de haeredibus institutis. Whatever the case may be, since the guardianship or curatorship ought to be administered by one who loves the ward with full affection, and of whom no sinister suspicion can be entertained (ff. de suspectis tutoribus, l. si tutor aliquis), when such cases arise from which the grandmother’s mind may reasonably be thought to oppose the ward’s interests, or at least to act with negligence, the judge ought not to decree the grandmother’s administration.

† It must be observed that, although guardianship is conferred upon the mother and grandmother by the law *Sicut* in the Code on legal guardianship, nevertheless the decree of administration is never legitimate or anomalous, but always appointive. Therefore, if the judge judges in his mind that the legitimate or anomalous guardian would not be suitable, he should not appoint himself, but appoint another. See the Code, *When a woman can perform the office of guardian*; the law *Second*; § *Is illud*. For how can this grandmother love this granddaughter, who is the enemy of her father? And if she administers, the murderer himself will effectively administer; indeed, he will dissipate and tear apart like a dog. Moreover, because the grandmother and the father are considered one person, see the last law in the Digest on substitution for infants and others. And this would be a sorrowful administration. See the Code, *On those suffering from insanity*, law 3; which testator, Digest, *He who is the closest friend of the ward’s capital enemy is repelled from guardianship*, law 1, § *Cum patronus*, on the office of the urban prefect; and the Code, *On inofficious wills*, law *Liberi*, § *Fin*. But this grandmother is of this kind; therefore, either she should not be removed, or at least so that she may not act maliciously, the aforementioned uncle should be joined to her, and the girl should be educated with the uncle. But it is better that it be decreed to the uncle alone, because they do not get along well together due to enmities. And thus I hold, because she will be educated more securely with the uncle, and with fuller affection, without stain, and with greater peace and consolation for the girl, and the way will not be open to proving that the grandmother should be repelled and guardianship conferred upon the uncle. I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws. That word, *or care*, I, Baldus, added after other opinions. And the same I advise, I, Peter of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, as advised by the said Baldus, to whose faith I subscribed and affixed my seal. And the same, as above written and advised, I say and advise, I, Julian Bini of Perugia, Doctor of Laws: in testimony of which I subscribed the aforementioned and sealed with my usual seal, saving the sounder opinion. And the same, as above advised by the aforementioned and excellent doctors of laws, I say and advise, I, Crispolitus, doctor of laws of Perugia. In testimony of which I subscribed the aforementioned and sealed with my usual seal, always saving the sounder opinion. And thus I say and advise, I, Sanctes Collae, as advised by the above-mentioned excellent doctors; for the principal reason that, in the case of a ward, the uncle excludes the grandmother not only on account of enmity, but on account of suspicion regarding the succession. And there is a text in the case proposed in the last law of the Code, *Where the ward should be educated*, and it is proven in the Digest, same title, law 1 and law penultimate. And the aforementioned of me, the least of doctors of laws, always saving the better judgment of one who sees more clearly. The same, as advised, I say and advise, I, Ludovicus Petrus of Perugia, doctor of laws. In faith of which I subscribed and sealed with my usual seal. And that which is above said and advised by the aforementioned most excellent doctors, I say and advise, I, Antonius de Scallolis of Perugia, doctor of laws, although the least, always saving the more abundant and sounder opinion. In testimony of which matter I subscribed and sealed with my own seal.

SUCH AGREEMENT. In the Name of God, Amen. The facts are as follows: A certain Ser Petrus Ceni of Gualdo made his last will, and among other legacies left, etc., he instituted his son Ambrosius as his heir with this condition, that if the said Ambrosius, the heir, should die without legitimate and natural children, he substituted his brother Jacobus Ceni with this condition, that the said Jacobus, the substitute, is bound to spend from the goods of the said testator for the new Church of Saint Mary of Mercatali of Gualdo, for the soul of the said testator, 100 gold florins. Moreover, the said Ambrosius, son and heir of the said testator, being over 14 and under 25 years of age, with the consent and will of his nearest blood relatives, and with the authority of the judge, sold all his goods to the said Jacobus Ceni. Later, wishing to attain the clerical habit, he made his will, in which he left and made the aforementioned Jacobus his universal heir, etc. Now it is asked: if the said Jacobus, while the said Ambrosius was alive in the clerical habit under the Order of Saint Francis, and the aforementioned goods having been sold, and the will made, is he bound by law, against his will, to spend the said 100 florins for the said new Church?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A brother who has entered a religious order is considered as naturally dead.
2. Whether the acts performed by one who enters a religious order before he entered are valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A minor friar is considered, according to Bartolus, as naturally dead; because natural death can effect no more in the dispossession of goods than can religious profession, as he himself notes in his treatise on the sentences of the Minorites. And he posits this in the Authentica Si qua mulier.

† And it is true in this respect, that he can no longer revoke the testament which he made. But generally, as regards other effects, it is not true, if we speak of what he did before entering religion, or of what he committed afterwards. For it is certain that if he first contracted and promised me ten, or committed theft, he is not thereby released because he enters religion, as is noted in Auth. de monachis, in the beginning; and Extra, de obligationibus et solutionibus, ad ratiocinia, c. 1. Likewise, if afterwards he commits theft against me, he is similarly bound, punished, and imprisoned, as we see every day. It is provided in de donationibus et conditionibus, c. fin., § litibus, in the end; C. de accusationibus, l. hos accusare, § omnibus; ff. de negotiis gestis, l. eum actum. Therefore, since it is given that he lives naturally, civil and natural obligations, by which he is bound as one person, manifest that if he lives to the contrary, the condition has not yet occurred; for it is in his interest to be considered living, so that he may not be liable for eviction if any of the sold things were evicted by hypothecary or otherwise, ff. de evictionibus, l. si cum venditor, in the beginning. Since therefore the father loved his son more than the church, with the son certainly living, whose interest it is to be considered living, the condition of the said 100 florins did not occur; and thus it is probable that the father intended, namely, that while the son lived, he should not suffer trouble directly or indirectly on account of that legacy; as ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, § fin. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a university may enact statutes concerning burdens, forced labor, tolls, and the like, is distinguished.
2. Whether public duties, both real and personal, pass to heirs.
3. Whether a grant of immunity made in recognition of merits may be revoked.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the immunity granted to Master Nicolaus Petri of Carnetis of Gualdo by the general council of the territory of Gualdo, and the confirmation made by the rector of the duchy in the following form, namely, that the aforementioned Master Nicolaus, as well as his present and future goods, shall be freely exempt from all real, personal, and mixed burdens, corvées, and menial services; and from all tolls, guidages, subsidies, impositions, and superimpositions, whatever name they may bear; and in the aforementioned commune, by the said commune and its officials upon its inhabitants, and among the inhabitants of the said territory, or upon the commune itself and its inhabitants by any lords and superiors of the said commune, several doubts arise. First, whether the said immunity is valid. Second, if it is valid, whether it endures after the death of the said Master Nicolaus. Third, whether it can be revoked, even if it would otherwise endure.

† Regarding the first point, it seems to be said that it was not valid, because such decrees are ambitious and contrary to the public utility; and also by them others are more heavily burdened, as in the law and notes, C. de anno et tribu., l. in fraudem; and C. de decur., l. vacuatis; and C. de decre. decur., l. 1, book 10; and C. de censi et peraequatoribus, l. 1, book 11. Nor does the confirmation of the president obstruct, since it is similarly ambitious, and out of favor; for the decrees in this case do not seem to be valid. ff. quod vi, aut clam, l. 3, § plane. On the contrary, this question is resolved with a distinction. For either it is asked whether it is valid to the prejudice of those granting, and it is valid; or to the prejudice of the superior in indictments, because they are made by superiors, and it is not valid. Thus says Andr. de Baruli in the said l. in fraudem. Nor is it called ambitious when merits precede, and it is not done at the request. de praeben., c. si motu proprio, lib. 6; and arg. in l. 3, ff. quod quisque iur. And this is true if those who granted it had authority; otherwise, otherwise. ff. de pac., l. item magistri. For since this immunity is a kind of gratuitous release, it cannot be done without the mandate of the people, unless the university itself, when assembled, grants it, which is the mistress of its goods and rights, as noted in the said l. item magistri. But the general council has the force of the whole university by common law. de reg. iur., l. aliud, § refertur.

† Regarding the second point, it must be said that, as far as personal offices are concerned, in which the person is burdened on account of himself, they do not pass to the heir, because mention is made of the heir; although, as far as real offices are concerned, which descend from the patrimony alone, without any act of the heir, they pass: because what is granted under the name of real, and by a conjunction, which every conjunction is placed extensively, of law 3. l. ea tamen adiectio. ff. de aqua quo. l. 1. §. permittitur ff. de cens. l. forma. §. quamquam. C. de excu. mu. l. maximarum. de serui. l. pater. de pac. l. iurisg. §. pactorum.

And therefore the said concession, which was made in recognition of merit, cannot be revoked except on account of ingratitude; hence, if the sons of this privileged person were ungrateful, it appears that the privilege may be taken away from them on account of their own ingratitude, I do not say that of the deceased, just as a fief and a benefice are taken away from a son on account of his own felony, as in c. 1, quae fuerint privata causa beneficii amittendi, col. 10, ad hoc, de sacrosancta ecclesia; l. privilegia, in Auth. constitutio, quae de dignitatibus; §. illud, ff. de decurionibus; l. Aquilae regula; l. si pater, ff. de decretis ab ordine factis; l. quod semel. For privileges granted in recognition of merit are to be regarded in the place of these and of stipends awarded for merit, from which a deserving person ought not to be defrauded, as in ff. de iustitia et iure, l. 1, in principio; and ff. de commodato, l. in commodato, §. sicut. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws. And to the truth I have subscribed, and [affixed] the seal of my name. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a substitution has been made, such that the testator instituted and substituted [an heir] in the event that the son should die at any time, whether it contains a direct vulgar substitution and not a fideicommissary one; and thus, whether the substitute in the fourth share acquires the whole by right of accretion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be considered that the words of the substitution state thus: "if the son should die at any time, I institute and substitute Munaldus Cioli and Guadagninus as heirs to me in a fourth part of the inheritance." The word "institute," because the son died during the mother's lifetime, signifies a direct vulgar substitution, and not a fideicommissary one. For this reason, a remarkable result occurs: the entire share accrues to these substitutes in the fourth part by the right of accrual, as is proved here, and not by Cynus in l. precibus and de hereditatibus instituendis l. si te solum. And thus, by law, the daughter of the said testatrix must have her legitime in the entire third part, because at the time of the mother's death she alone was alive, since her brother had predeceased her. The substitutes, however, must inherit two parts, considering and applying to them the virtue of the vulgar substitution with the inseparable right of accrual. Someone might ask: why does it not accrue to the daughter in the same way as to the substitutes? I answer: because the daughter has her legitime by virtue of the disposition of the legacy, and by another law than the law of the testament, namely, by the mere benefit of the law. ff. de bonis possidendis l. si cum patruos. And thus these substitutes, on account of the word "institute," succeed beyond what the testatrix believed. And therefore notaries, often erring through ignorance and not knowing the force of words, bring greater damage to others. For if the word "institute" were not present here, this substitution would be fideicommissary, and the substitutes ought not to have [the inheritance] to the exclusion of the codicillary heir, because the institution would be caducous, unless [they had] the fourth part. Others, however, say that it would be vulgar, etc. Nevertheless, whether it is true that "institute" is used, because it contains the vulgar substitution in a compendious manner, and they decide, whence in another case where the daughter would not be excluded from the inheritance by such understanding, and the substitution would be total, that is, in the whole, not quantitative, l. in re or l. pars, because then the part would not be drawn to the whole, since the substitution would be fideicommissary; otherwise, where she would be excluded. But in our case, on account of the word "institute," the truth seems, as I said, that the daughter succeeds in the third, and the substitutes succeed in the two parts. It is supported by ff. ad Trebellianam l. recusare §. Titius, and l. cogi §. generaliter, because the word "institute" is merely direct, and expressly direct, and directis sinum. Legacies and bequests, however, must be paid by these substitutes, for
† L. cum pater, § ab instituto, de legatis, 2. Cum si, quia the legitima is owed to the said daughter without burden. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a prescribed debt releases the creditor.
casus: Point. The matter on which counsel is sought is as follows: A certain man made a will and instituted his son as heir, and in the said will, among other things, he wished, ordered, and commanded that satisfaction be made to all and each of those who ought to receive something from the said testator or his father; because if there is anyone who ought to receive from the said testator or his father, but [the claim] is prescribed, whether the heir is bound to pay the said true debt, although prescribed, having regard to the words added in the said will. Secondly, whether if the said heir or fideicommissaries paid without raising the said exception of prescription, they could freely pay, so that they are not bound to restore from their own property, nor can any fault be imputed to them, or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A debtor is said to be so in two ways, namely, in conscience and according to natural truth, and artificially, or judicially: in the first way, prescription does not release the debtor, because prescriptions were introduced for the public good only. In the second way, it releases the debtor from the necessity of performance. I say, therefore, that either the testator uses civil words, for example, that I owe; or natural words, for example, that I received on loan, or that I promised. In the first case, it matters whether the testator considered the prescribed debt, for example, because he made mention of it, and the will must be followed. Hence, in this case, if the father died after such a long time that the son had acquired prescription, the executors could pay; otherwise, they could not. On solutions, l. si is, cui. §. Flavius. In the second case, without doubt, they could satisfy the obligation, arg. in l. fin. de iureiurando. I, Baldus. This is the ordinance of the commune of Perugia, placed in the volume and reformed. Moreover, they established and ordained that from the sentence of any judge one may appeal only once, and not more often: and that the appeal must be made to the judge of appeals appointed by the commune of Perugia, and not to another. And that if it should happen that the office of said judge is vacant, or the judge himself is absent, that then, and in that case, if the sentence was passed in the court of the podestà, one may appeal to the court of the captain and to the captain himself and his assessor; and if it was passed in the palace of the captain, one may appeal to the court of the podestà and to the podestà himself and his assessor; and those assessors shall be the judges of said appeals according to the form of the Statute of the commune of Perugia. And secondly, the appellant shall be ordered to carry out the execution due in the appeal case, and the aforementioned sentence shall be carried out. And all and each of the aforementioned things, the podestà, the captain, and the judge of justice, and any judge and official of the commune of Perugia, shall be bound to observe under the penalty, and to the penalty, of five hundred pounds of denarii, to be taken from them in fact during their term of office. Moreover, it is placed in the Statutes of the commune of Perugia in l. 1. lib. under Rubric 18i. de appellationibus. And the judge of appeals shall admit the appeal if he knows it to be admissible, and it is lawful for each person to appeal twice: and if he fails in the first appeal in the case of appeal, and wishes to appeal a second time, such appellant shall be bound, both for himself and also for the adversary for whom the first sentence was passed, to pay a tenth; and otherwise the appellant shall not be heard, which second appeal from the sentence, which would be passed by the major syndic and the judge of justice confirming the first, if it is for the sentence passed in the court of the podestà, may be appealed to the lord captain and his assessor. Who assessor shall be as judge and decider of said case of second appeal. And if it is upon the sentence, which would be passed in the court of the captain, one may appeal to the lord podestà and his assessor; and that assessor shall be judge, cognizor, and decider of said case. And if said assessors are, and are understood to be, judges of said appeals, as stated.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute providing for the judge of appeal, when an appeal is taken from a confirmatory sentence, is deemed to provide for the same judge when an appeal is taken from an infirmatory sentence.
