2. Whether a statute enacted in one matter is considered to be a statute in another, if the constitution is penal.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute providing for the judge of appeal, when an appeal is taken from a confirmatory sentence, and when it is taken from an infirmatory sentence, does not appoint a judge of appeal: and this appears from a weighing of the words of the Statute. Hence this seems to be an omitted case, in which recourse must be had to the subsidiary judge, that is, to the Lords Priors of the Arts, as in *l. ubi obsunt*. For they are the judges of justice when other rectors are lacking, just as formerly jurisdiction was with the college of pontiffs, as in *l. secunda*, D. de origine iuris. And it is not new that jurisdiction is contentious, if it is with colleges, as in *cap. primo*, de maioritate et obedientia, Book 6; and see the note in *cap. 1*, de haereticis, by Innocent. And therefore, if in the city of Perugia the general judge of appeals were vacant, and also the office of the Potestas were vacant, then from the sentence of the Capitano appeal would undoubtedly be made to the Lords Priors. For there must always be in the Republic one who gives the law. D. de origine iuris, *l. secunda*, § *post originem*.

Our question therefore stands thus: whether this is an omitted and unforeseen case; and it seems that it is, from the nature of the words; because, however much you search the text of the statute, you will not find this case specified; and therefore recourse must be had to the Prince on account of the new case. C. de legibus, *l. cum de novo*, and *l. si Imperialis*. But the Prince now is the college of the Priors of the Arts. D. de pactis, *l. iuris gentium*. And I prove this by such reasoning: A provision for one case excludes the contrary case, as in *l. inter*, § *cum inter patrem*, D. de pactis. But here the statute provides for a judge in the confirmatory case; therefore in the contrary case, namely the infirmatory, it is not understood to provide the same: but either it did not consider it, so that it is a case omitted in words and mind; or it meant the contrary by an argument from the opposite.

Secondly, it is proved, that to whom the words of the law do not apply, the mind of the law is not understood to be adapted; because one must not depart from the words. D. de exercitoribus, *l. prima*, § *si is, qui navem*. But here the words do not agree, nor the signification, that is, the plain exposition of the words. D. de legatis tertio, *l. ille, aut ille*, § *cum in verbis*; D. de suppleto legato, *l. idem respondeo*.

Thirdly, it is proved, because the force of the words of the law is to effect something, as in *l. prima*, D. ad municipalia. But if appeal were permitted to the Potestas simply, then those words "confirmatory" would effect nothing: which ought not to be, as in *l. si quando*, D. de legatis primo.

Fourthly, it is proved, because that which is placed for the sake of a difference always usually constrains both the disposition of a man and the legal disposition. D. de legatis tertio, *l. hoc legatum*. But those words "confirmatory" seem to signify a primary difference. For if they are not placed for the sake of a difference, they occupy parchment in vain.

Fifthly, let it be posited that the Pope commits all confirmatory causes; does he seem to commit infirmatory causes? Certainly not, because this cannot be conceived from the words, as in Extra, de privilegiis, *cap. porro*. And if you attend carefully, this statute is contrary to the common law. For by the common law no one appeals to one who is not superior; but the Potestas is not a superior judge of justice in such a way that from the Potestas, as from a lesser, appeal is made to the judge of justice. Since therefore this statute is contrary to the common law, it ought not to be extended, as in D. de solutione matrimonii, *l. si vero*, § *de viro*.

Sixthly, it is proved, because the limits of a commission, of delegated jurisdiction, are to be carefully observed, and are not to be extended, so much so that in appeals prorogation has no place even with the consent of the parties. D. de iudicibus, *l. secundam*, § *etiam quoque*; de mutatione petitionis, *c. 1*, per Innoc. For the authority of the superior, not the consent of the parties, makes judges of appeal; but here is the mode: in things, there are certain limits, beyond which and short of which right cannot consist. As noted in D. de verbis obligatis, *l. si ita quis*, § *ea*.

Seventhly, it is proved by the ordinary gloss, which says that *c. prudentiam*, de mutatione petitionis, has place when the judge is given at the postulation of a party; otherwise if by law, or on his own motion, as noted in Extra, de regulis iuris, *c. quod ob gratiam*, in the ordinary gloss. It helps *l. 3*, in principio, D. quod quisque iuris.

Eighthly, it is proved, because this statute in the confirmatory sentence is conceived by reformation; therefore this statute, as conceived, cannot henceforth be extended. C. de edicto divi Adriani tollendo, *l. sin*.

Ninthly, it is proved, that jurisdiction given in a certain case seems to be denied in others. D. de iudicibus, *l. cum praetor*; C. de pacis conventione, *l. si*. For there is much difference between the genus and the species of committed jurisdiction. D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, *l. solet*, and *l. praetor*; and D. quis et a quo appellatur, *l. 1*.

Tenthly, and lastly, it is proved from the nature of statutes, which are of strict law and of the most rudimentary sense, in which words ought to be understood materially and in a gross manner according to the bark of the words. Hence that which the people does not speak, it is not believed that they feel. Laws are most vulgar and most certain.

To the contrary, it seems by several reasons: first, because equal favor ought to be given in the cause of appeal to each party; the text is in the said *cap. 2*, de mutatione petitionis. Nor does that response avail, that there it is so because at the postulation of a party; for the same if on his own motion, as noted in the Novella.

Secondly, on account of the equality to be preserved in judgments both concerning the judge and concerning the order of the judgment and the whole process. C. de proximo sacro scripto, *l. in sacris*; C. de fructibus et litis expensis, *l. fin*.

Thirdly, because of contraries the discipline is the same. *l. fina*, D. de legatis 3.

Fourthly, posit that the confirmatory sentence is given for the defendant; it is certain that, according to the statute, it is permitted for the plaintiff to appeal to the Potestas. To say the contrary, that it is not permitted for the defendant, is contrary to the rule of law, which says, that what is not permitted to the defendant is not permitted to the plaintiff. Since therefore the defendant appeals, the Potestas is his judge, just as it is the judge of the appealing plaintiff.

Fifthly, because the continuity of the cause ought not to be separated as regards judges. C. de iudicibus, *l. nulli*; C. de appellationibus, *l. ampliorem*. Posit that the sentence is partly confirmatory, partly infirmatory, and both appeal simultaneously, so that one does not interpose an appeal against the other; one therefore will go to the Potestas, the other to the Priors, with the judgment split: which is absurd.

Sixthly, because whenever a general determination follows, a special promise does not restrict the subsequent genus. D. ad legem Aquiliam, *l. si servus servum*, § *inquit text*. Since therefore the last clause, which says "and thus the said judges etc.", ought to effect something and establish a certain rule which comprehends all cases on which provision of the law is necessary: rightly this end of the statute concludes all. The words "as has been said" do not obstruct. For I say that what has been said above is so by this reason and mind considered. For often under the silence of words the mind of the legislator is apparent, and does not hide. C. de furtis, *l. si quis servum*, with similar cases.

Seventhly, because although when appeal is made to the Capitano, those words "confirmatory" are placed, even if I do not believe this true, let them be placed conditionally, "if it has been given," it says, "in the court of the Potestas"; but when appeal is made to the Potestas, it does not repeat the said speech, but "in the confirmatory first", nor ought the ignorance of the dictator of the statute or the writer to be understood as repeated. C. de testamentis, *l. ambiguitatem*. For that which lacks reason is to be extirpated, as in C. de liberis praeteritis, *l. maximum vitium*. But to this it might be responded, that one construction is that those words were emitted; because disjunctively, namely "if it has been etc.", they are common to all the following by force of construction.

Eighthly, because the statute ought to be reduced to the understanding of equity, even vulgar equity, which is commonly apparent. D. de deposito, *l. bona fides*, and note. C. de transactionibus, *l. si maior*. But the equity of the law ought to be, as the equity of the judge and of the good man, which ought to be a column in the middle: not a corner, nor a partial favorer. C. de iudicibus, *l. rem non novam*.

Ninthly, because the same law is established as regards the judge and the forum, when appeal is taken from infirmation and confirmation.

† Moreover, a statute enacted in one case is deemed enacted in another, even if the constitution is penal, as is evident from two chapters joined together in the extrajudicial collection on election: cap. Cupientes, cap. Generali, and cap. Si postquam, §. Cum autem, in Book 6; and Si vero, and there note. Tenthly, and finally, that since by the common law of Perugia no other judges are appointed than three judges, alternating in their cases according to the latest reform, perhaps by the said reform the former judges would not be judges: and the case would be terminated without a judge: which is absurd, and therefore our case cannot be attributed, unless to the power to whom, whether I will or not, the stream of this appeal is directed. And although the question is difficult to decide, with arguments imaginable for and against, yet because in the case of appeal the judge is appointed to the case, not to the person, the appeal should be introduced to the power, and to other proceedings, as reason dictates: so however that neither party may appeal, unless once only, and conversely the other once, parity being observed, as in C. Ne lic. In una, eademque causa. And it is the text of the reform in the word, and the second appellant: if therefore the syndic rendered a confirmatory sentence of the first, he cannot now appeal: because since the sentences are contrary, it is equitable that it be reviewed, which of them is more just. And as I said, the question is doubtful, because the words of the statute and reform enumerate cases and judges, yet because these constitutions are favorable, not odious, nor penal, and the mind of the legislator ought to have been prospective of the law, as cap. Si is, cui causa. De offic. Delega. Book 6. The more equitable and just opinion is that which I described above, according to which appeal may be made to the power, and in similar cases may be: and thus I hold, and I have written at length, so that others may have the opportunity of alleging in all similar cases: and also of impugning me, if I err in opinion: I believe, however, that the intention of the statute is to provide equally for both parties as to judge and judgment, and speediness in an indifferent nature. And to this effect is the gloss. Ord. In c. Cupien. §. Denique. De elect. Lib. 6. In glo. Seruent quod no. Ff. De iuris. Omn. Iudi. L. Si per errorem. In glo. Fina. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws: to the faith of which I have subscribed, and signed with my name and seal, saving the judgment of any one determining better.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the term "sons" includes grandsons, and thus the sons of sons.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. On this point I have much doubt due to the various opinions of the doctors, which it would be tedious to cite at length. Nevertheless, I shall not cite any, except one argument for one side, and another for the other.

† And it appears that by the term "sons" the sons of sons are not included. The text is in the Institutes, Qui dantur tutelae, in the section on testamentary possession, §. fin., and there the gloss says that this is due to common usage of speech: because commonly people call sons one thing and grandsons another; and especially the laity, who do not know the letter of grammar, for which reason "son" is said to come from the Greek *philos*, meaning love in Latin, as noted in the Digest, De testamento tutorum, l. Si quis filiabus. And to the contrary it holds, because the meaning of "son" includes the grandson. Digest, De verbis significandis, l. Liberatorum. And it seems expressly stated in substitution. Digest, De hereditate instituenda, l. Lucius. And natural reason supports this. L. Sanguinis proprii dilectio, and civil reason, because if he had been asked about the grandson, he would have ordered the same. Digest, De pactis, l. Tale pactum; Codex, De conditionibus insertis, l. Praeterea. Solution: According to Andreas de Pisa, etc., the grandson is not included; rather, he is said to be passed over, if mention is made of the son and not of the grandson. Digest, De liberis et posthumis, l. Titius and l. Gallus, §. Instituens. But according to me, if mention is made of the son, it matters whether the mention is made in disinheritance, and the grandson is not included; argument from Digest, De contrahenda tutela, l. 3, §. Si emancipatus; or in institution and substitution, and then it matters: Either mention is made of a son who is entirely an outsider, and the grandson is not included; because service must be rendered to the voice of the speaker. Argument from the said §. Ultimi. Or mention is made of the son of a brother, or another relative by blood, and then he is included, as in the said l. Lucius, and Codex, De conditionibus insertis, l. Prima. Or mention is made in guardianship, and then, because guardianship contains a burden on a third party, that is, the guardian, and not a favor, a strict interpretation is made. In the ordering of the testator's goods, a broader interpretation is made, mixed with favor for the testator's children and the substitute, than in imposing honors. Digest, De administratione tutorum, l. Impuberi filio centurio. And thus speaks the said law Lucius, when it equates sons and children. And this is sufficiently equitable and consonant with natural reason, when the testator provides not only for those born, but also for those to be born: because he directed his meaning without a certain and determined affection: not on account of merits, which do not apply to those not yet born; but on account of the honor of his family and agnatic line: and we are in a matter that is indifferent and favorable, otherwise in a matter containing a burden, as noted in the Authenticum, De restitutione fideicommissi, §. Manifestum. In substitutions, Bartolus holds this, and well, although, as I said, many say the contrary. Concurring: Jacobus Butrigarius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The father is preferred to the brothers.
casus: CASE. In the name of the Lord, Amen. The point is as follows. A certain lady Catelina married Cechus, and gave him in dowry forty gold florins; from which marriage were born two sons, namely Matthew and Cia; after this Cechus died; and Catelina again married John; and gave him the aforementioned dowry; from which marriage was born one son named Dominic. Afterwards this Catelina died, with the said Dominic her son and John her husband surviving her; after some days this Dominic died in infancy, with the said John his father surviving him. From this lady Catelina survived only lady Cia and her brother Matthew, although there is doubt rather about death than about life: because he has been absent for three years and more; and nothing has been heard of his death, nor of his life, nor any news? Wherefore the blood relatives of this lady Cia on the father's side married her to a certain Matthaeolus; and gave her in dowry all her rights, especially concerning the dowries of her mother, the said lady Catelina; Wherefore Matthaeolus demanded this dowry from this John, husband of the late lady Catelina; and this John contends to give to this Matthaeolus for lady Cia and her brother, namely Matthew. Now I ask, what is the law: furthermore, it is asked here, considering that this John has retained this dowry in his possession for three years and more, whether he can demand the fruits of the dowry of the said Matthew and lady Cia.
body: In the Name of Christ.

† John has retention of one-third part of the said dowry, and of the other goods of the lady Catelina, in the person of Dominic, his son, who died in infancy. For the father is preferred to brothers united on one side only. Another third part may be claimed by Mattheolus in the person of Cies. The other third part of Mattheus, however, on account of the uncertainty of life or death, cannot be claimed, unless a curator of the goods be appointed, as in C. de capt. l. nec nos. and l. ab hostibus. ex quibus cau. maio. and this if Mattheus had accepted the inheritance of his mother. But if he did not accept it, then the curator appointed for the goods could not accept it, nor bring an hereditary action; hence it is necessary then that it be ascertained whether he lives or is dead. One-half part of the dowry, and of the other goods, remains to John, the other half, however, must be restored to Mattheolus in the person of Cies. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, and to the faith of my writing and signature of my name and seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Proof must be certain and conclude with necessity; hence, proof that someone took grain, without the quantity being proven, is said to be uncertain.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Because the examination and re-examination of the documents has wearied me greatly, I shall say only a few words.

And I presuppose for clarity that proof must then conclude with necessity, or in such a way that it is sufficient with the aid of the law; hence proof must be certain, as noted in D. 16.3.1 § si quis argentum (de deposito); D. 46.3.117 (de praetoria stipulatione); X. 2.19.1 (In praesentia, de probationibus); D. 2.4.10 § pen. (ne quis eum qui in ius vocatus est); and C. 6.30.1 (Non hoc, unde leges). Regarding these points, I find that Francis proved the debt. I also find that he proved the sequestration. I also find that he proved a certain quantity of grain in the street. And although the wheat in the ears could not be seen well, nevertheless, because the eye can hardly be deceived, it is certain, since proofs are not to be treated harshly, but are to be understood with natural discretion, according to the note by Innocentius in X. 1.33.1 (Causa, de rescriptis). On the contrary, I find that Paulotus proved how the people went to the fields and by force took away all the grain that had been mentioned. But I do not find proved a certain quantity of grain to have been in the fields at that time, since the case was so violent; hence how much quantity was taken away is uncertain, and consequently the proof does not exclude Paulotus’s excuse, because it is uncertain. For the word “wheat,” whether in the field or in the ears, is uncertain: D. 45.1.1 § sacramentum (de verbis obligatis); D. 18.1.1 § verisimile (de contrahenda emptione). And therefore, in the point of law, Francis has the right, considering the acts; but in the point of conscience, it is left to the proof of his conscience: and I advise him not to act against conscience. For if truly that quantity had been taken away from the said Paulotus, it is certain that the sequestrator would not be liable for the accident, as in D. 16.3.1 (Si sine causa); D. 16.3.11 (Quod Nerua); D. 19.2.1 § nunc videndum (de commodato), with similar authorities. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It is proposed that Angelus Benedictoli of the Hospital of the Castle of Funtigano made a will, in which he disposed as follows among other things: namely, in all his goods he instituted Francis, his legitimate and natural son, as universal heir; and if the said Francis should die at any time and in any age without legitimate children lawfully descending from him, he substituted to himself Sanctutius, Benedictus, and Nellolus, or their heir, in one part of the land; the other goods he also wished for the restitution of the dowry of Lady Florentia, wife of the said testator; and he also substituted to himself in those same goods, together with the said Florentia his wife, Cechus Pauloti, and the heirs of the said Cechus. The testator died, the said son surviving; finally, the said son died in pupillary age. It is asked to whom the inheritance of the said testator ought to belong.

See the summary with the following. In the Name of Christ, Amen. This substitution made by the said Angelo to the said Francis is a pupillary substitution, because it was made to a pupil, and by words which include the time of pupillary age, as is held in l. precibus, de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus; by virtue of which pupillary substitution, the inheritance of the said testator ought to belong to the aforementioned Cechus and Lady Paulutia. ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papinianus; and de testamento, c. 1, lib. 6. And thus I advise, I, Peter of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, to whose faith I have subscribed and affixed my seal.

TO THE SAME. In the Name of Christ, Amen. In few testaments have I found these words: “in whatever age he shall have died”; but more distinctly, it has been customary to insert words distinguishing ages, saying, “if he shall have died in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time.” And sometimes more vaguely, “whenever he shall have died.” In our case, however, so that those words “in whatever age” may have effect, as if the ages had been named, I believe the substitution to be considered direct upon the death of the son in pupillary age, as in C. de fideiussoribus, l. si frater, from the contrary sense of the first response; and what is noted in Inst. de pupillari substitutione, §. quaestio; the same in l. precibus, with similar authorities.
If you wish to summarize, do so yourself. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because brothers conducting business separately, but each buying for himself, his children, and his heirs, are not partners, since they do not contribute their profits to a common fund, it must be judged, from what is proposed in the first point, that the mother, Fucius, and Io. or their children were not partners, nor did they contract any general partnership, nor should the goods bought by them in their own names be shared: it is true, however, that if it were proven that they were bought from common revenues or funds, those should be shared: or at least restitution should be made, insofar as one had converted the other’s share into the purchase of properties, as in D. de admin. tutor. l. Titium. §. altero.

† Concerning dowries, however, it must be said as follows: if dowries have been converted into common utility, that estate must be restored to the person to whom the dowry belonged, if a purchase was made in her name; if it was made in the common name, the share of the valuation must be restored, as stated in the Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law *Uxor marito*.

† Regarding capture, damages, and penalties for offenses, it must be said that one person is not bound to communicate or share anything with another. And this is certain in the case of offenses. D. 17.2. l. cum duobus. §. si. In cases of fatal damages, the same applies unless they had encountered a robber in common affairs. D. 17.2. l. cum duobus. §. quidam sagariam.
† Indicia, and legacies ought to be paid from the share of the testator: because even a full partnership does not extend to last wills, as in l. cum duobus. §. Idem respondit.

† If fruits are to be divided, if the fruits have been acquired through the labor of persons, they are divided according to the number of persons; but if they have been acquired from common things, they are divided in proportion to the share in the thing from which they were collected. D. de rei vindic. l. solum. §. meum. C. pro socio. l. 1. I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In a fideicommissary substitution, general words do not include the own property of the person burdened.
2. That is to say, what is the import of an institution of this kind: I institute Cola, and the descendants issuing from him.
3. A mother may bring an action for the supplement of her legitime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† There is no doubt that, when a fideicommissary substitution is made in general terms, the property of the person burdened does not pass to the substitute. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, § cum filiae.

† And therefore it must be considered what were the separate property of Matthew: because the substitution made by Cola Angelus, his father, does not extend to those assets. And therefore it must be investigated what it means to say, “I institute Cola Angelus and his descendants.” And Bartolus clarifies the matter, stating that Cola Angelus himself and his descendants come after him, that is, if Cola is not the heir. For among these there exists an ordered affection, whereby the primary love excludes the subsequent one. D. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus, § ibi; and there fully by Bartolus. Others say that the father and son come together. D. de usufr. accresc. l. si quis Titio and l. si mulieri; and C. de impub. et aliis subst. l. fi. But according to Jacobus de Arena, either the latter was already born, and thus the affection and love fell upon him; and then they come together, otherwise not. It can be said that this conjunction “and” is placed rather subjunctionally than principally copulatively. That is, that Cola Angelus, the testator’s grandson, should have it during his lifetime, and afterwards his descendants; because this is an ordered and due affection, as D. de haer. inst. l. Lucius; and this interpretation is friendly to nature. D. de leg. 2, l. cum ita legatur, § in fideicommiss. But arguing from the force of the conjunction properly taken, a division would be made between Cola Angelus the father and Matthew the son; but according to Bartolus, Cola Angelus would exclude Marcus both during his lifetime and at death, since he had acquired it for himself. But to me it seems from the word “descendants,” and because Matthew, the son of Cola Angelus, is not alleged to have been in existence at the time of the testament of Lord Matthew; nor could it then be hoped with certain expectation, that the testator disposed successively. That is, so that succession should descend from one to another, like the right of blood.

† On another point, I say that the mother can bring an action for the supplement of the legitime, in the Authentica de trien. et semis. § 1, in the gloss. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, and for the faith of this I subscribe and sign with the sign of my name, always reserving the sounder opinion, which question is sufficiently doubtful and subtle. To declare the same, explaining the opinion, In the Name of Christ, Amen. The declaration of the above-written opinion is this: Cola Angelus was heir in solidum during his lifetime of the said Lord Matthew; but after the death of the said Cola Angelus, the said inheritance ought to be restored to Matthew. For two cannot directly succeed according to the common opinion of the doctors in the law *hereditas ex die*, de hereditatibus instituendis, although William of Conchis says that one can be heir in solidum during his lifetime, and afterwards, after the first has died, another: as if the first hereditary right were found to be extinguished by death in the first, and begins anew in the second, as he notes in the Codex, de hereditatibus instituendis, law *extraneum*. But this is not true, as in the Digest, de vulgari substitutione, law *verbis civilibus*, de trebellianica. Therefore, counting also the fruits therein, Cola Angelus could be considered. Likewise, concerning his other own goods, which were not part of the inheritance of the said Lord Matthew, Lucia, mother of the said Lady Rita, must have her legitime from all the goods of the said Lady Rita, however acquired; because all have become one patrimony, as most prudently says the said John Ranaldus, as in the Digest, de vulgari substitutione, law *plures*, § *filio*, and law 1, § *sciendum*, de separatione. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A license granted to the testator is deemed granted to his heir and successor; hence, the heir cannot disturb one entering into possession by authority of the testator.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Since the license granted by the testator is deemed granted to his heir and successor, as stated in D. qui in rem vindicant potest pig. vel hypo. sol. l. sicut, §. si debitori, and D. de pignoribus et hypothecis l. solutum, §. si creditori; so conversely, if I sell a thing possessed by me at that time, or which I subsequently begin to possess, and I grant the buyer license to take possession, my heir must suffer what I would have suffered: and thus he must allow entry and possession. D. de legatis 2, l. Titia, §. 1, unless the heir alleges another cause than that of the deceased, as in l. an vitium, §. ex facto, de diversis et temporibus praescriptionum. Therefore, if after this reasonable entry the entry is disturbed by one who knows that he is disturbing it, an action for disturbing violence may be brought; because injury is done to him, by argument from D. de actione empti l. qui pendentem, because injury is done to the one disturbed: provided that the disturber knew of the fact through notification made to him, for one who is ignorant is not said to commit violence. D. de actionibus et obligationibus l. ex maleficio, §. longe minus. Therefore, in the case proposed, if the facts narrated are true, the accused ought to be condemned, unless some just cause excuses him, as noted in l. 1, si quis testamento lib. esse ius, fue. per Bartolus; and it is supported by D. de abigeo l. 1, in fine, and D. ne vis fiat ei l. si quis missum, cum sequentibus. And having seen the acts and proceedings in the case, it does not appear to me that anything has been proven by which the said license is infringed, as in C. de pignoribus l. 3, and D. de pignoribus actione l. qui ratiocinatio. And after the right of the entrant has been notified, the disturber appears to be in bad faith. And it is supported by what is noted in D. quod metus causa l. extat, in the gloss beginning, in casibus.

CASE. IN the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen. A certain house is situated in the city of Forlì near its boundaries, which is held in emphyteusis, and belongs to the right of the church of Saint Julian of Forlì, and is customarily granted in emphyteusis by the rectors of the aforementioned church, which was granted in emphyteusis to Lady Pelegrina by a certain Don Simon, who held and governed the said church during his life by virtue and force of the rights set forth below, which are transmitted to you. The instrument of the said concession made to the said Lady Pelegrina is also sent to you. It is asked, whether, having seen the aforementioned documents and others pertaining to the law concerning the aforementioned matters, the said Don Simon could lawfully have made the said concession in emphyteusis to the said Lady Pelegrina: and by this means whether the said Lady Pelegrina acquired some right in the said house.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If an ecclesiastical emphyteusis is customarily granted to the rector of the said church, whether the said grant is valid.
body: In the name of Christ, and of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and of the Blessed Martyrs Blaise, Pontiff, Gratiosus, and Gregory, the glorious soldier, and of the entire heavenly court, amen. I return to the aforementioned matters, I, Gaspar, the above-named consultant, having examined the said instrument of concession in emphyteusis made to the said lady Pelegrina by the said Don Simon, lessee of the fruits and revenues of the said church of St. Julian, from Antonio Nicolai de Sala, rector of the said church of St. Julian, and having examined the instrument of the said lease, or its copy, which are presumed to be true, and assuming the said Antonio to be the true and legitimate rector,

I argue that, at first glance, it appears that the said Lord Simon could not have made the said concession in emphyteusis: because such a lessee, indeed even a perpetual one, cannot alienate without the consent of the owner. D. loc. c. potuit; and L. fi. C. de iure emphyteuticario. Whether the name of alienation includes a perpetual emphyteutic contract, as in the decision of Nulli, D. de rebus ecclesiasticis non alienandis. Therefore, such a contract is not valid. And thus, at first glance, it seems that the Speculum holds this view, tit. de loc. §. nunc vero aliqua, ver. centesimo vigesimo quinto, quaeritur.

On the contrary, this donor Simon leased the church. §. l. domos, possessiones, bona, et iura ipsius ecclesiae, et ad ipsam quomodolibet pertinentia; therefore, all goods and rights of the said church, and whatever pertains to it in any way; therefore, goods and rights. D. de privilegiis, c. quia circa, with its subject matter. Therefore, the right to grant in emphyteusis, because it is part of the right of the church. For this is numbered among the contracts of good faith. Inst. de actionibus, §. et not. D. de exceptionibus, c. cum venerabilis, in the third gloss. Therefore, all things come which can come. D. de donationibus, L. eleganter; §. non solum, D. de legatis tertio, L. praediis, D. de causa possessionis; c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, and what is noted there.

Furthermore, it is permitted to this lessee by the nature of the contract to enjoy and use the leased thing. D. loc. L. ex conducto, and L. si in lege, §. colonus. Therefore, also to make this contract of emphyteusis, since it was customary to be done with ecclesiastical things, just as he could lease a forest to be cut down at the proper time; if it occurs to be cut down during the time of the lease, by the argument of what is noted in D. de electionibus, c. generali, lib. 6, in the last gloss.

Furthermore, the lessor ought to have foreseen that this could happen. D. loc. L. si quis domum, §. pe. contra. Therefore, when interpretation is made, if he did not foresee it for himself. D. de pactis, L. veter.

From these, it is concluded that the said Lady Pellegrina could have received the said houses in perpetual emphyteusis through the said Lord Simon; and thus I think and advise that this part is true in law, provided that those houses were accustomed to be given in such perpetual emphyteusis.

The objection raised to the contrary does not hold, because they must be understood regarding a thing which is not accustomed to be granted in such a manner, nor does it fall under the name of alienation. D. de fructibus, §. 2. And therefore, the other things usually observed in alienation are not necessary in this case, as the Speculum says in tit. de loc. §. sequitur, ver. caeterum si emphyteoticaria, and there Johannes Andreas says that these are observed. And by this also a response is given to L. fi. C. de iure emphyteuticario.

Thus I think and advise it to be in law, saving the counsel of a wiser one. I, Gaspar de Caldari, doctor of decrees and knight, wrote the above with my own hand, and ordered my usual seal to be affixed.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case granted to me by the Magnificent Lord Pius of the Ordelaffi family, having examined the formal legal opinions issued on both sides and the subtle arguments presented, I consider, on one hand, the common rules of law which state that no one can convey to another more right than he himself possesses, as in the Digest, *De acquirenda re*, law *Traditio*; another rule states that when the right of the grantor is resolved, the right of the grantee is also resolved, as in the Digest, *De legatis 2*, law *Peto*, section *Praedium*; Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Vectigali*. Another rule states that one who holds a usufruct or a temporary benefit cannot grant it to another beyond his own term, as in the Digest, *De periculo et commodo rei venditae*, law *Necessario*, section *Si*; Digest, *De locato conducto*, law *Si quis domum*, section *Et hic*. It may be added to this what is noted by Innocentius regarding prebends, in the chapter *Si ne praepositi*, *Vices suas*.

On the other hand, I also consider the rule that when the thing is resolved, the right of the grantor does not resolve the right of the grantee, when, with the will of him who could grant in perpetuity, a perpetual grant was made, as noted in column 10, *De controversia investiturae*, section *Rursus*, by Jacobus de Belvis. But here it is certain that the rector of the church of St. Anthony could grant the things in emphyteusis according to the usual custom; therefore, the one holding the cause from him can do the same: because one holding the cause is said to hold the will of the actor, as in the Digest, *De pignoris actione*, law *Solutio*, section *Unde si domum*. Moreover, Lord Simon leased not only the things, but the right of leasing, which consists in law; therefore, for the same reasons, as is now said here, he can grant it to another for an intermediate period according to their nature and ancient custom, as in the Digest, *De aqua quotidiana et aestiva*, law *Permittitur*. Nor is this transfer prohibited: because custom induces it, as in chapter 1, *Episcopum vel abbatem*, chapter 1, and as noted in law *Si ut certo*, section *Si duobus vehiculum*, in the major gloss, Digest, *De communibus*, first part.

I approve the first part, namely that they cannot grant to another beyond their own term, according to the laws cited above, and according to law *Epistola*, section *Si*, *De pactis*, and as noted in the Code, *Si pignus pignori datum sit*, law 1, in the final gloss; and in the Digest, *De legatis 1*, law *Si domus*, section *Si*; and in the Digest, *De contrahenda emptio*, law *Qui tabernas*; and in the Code, *De communibus divisionibus*, law *Si*, section *Si autem avaritiae*. Moreover, this person leased the things and rights with respect to the fruits: but the price, which is demanded for the useful owner, is not called the fruit of the thing, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Quibus*, section 1. Moreover, he who enjoys the price is considered to enjoy the thing, as in the Digest, *De usufructu*, law *Quia qui precio*. Therefore, the first lessee would enjoy it, because he leased for a time in perpetuity, which is absurd according to the laws; therefore, he can enjoy all things temporarily, not in perpetuity. And thus I hold, especially considering the pact of non-alienation, Code, *De rebus alienis non alienandis*, law *Si*; Digest, *De legatis 2*, law *Codicillis*, section 2, by Decius.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a toll should be paid for goods that are carried to the army for the purpose of trade.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Those who voluntarily carry goods to the army for the purpose of trade and their own benefit must pay the toll; for they carry them by their own will and for their own advantage. D. de publicanis et vectigalibus, l. licita, § mercatores. But if anyone carries goods unwillingly, by order of the prince and for the public good, the prince has the power to determine what he deems just; for when the toll is imposed, it is not understood to apply to this case, since fortuitous events are unusual. Arg. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fistulas, § frumenta. And out of favor for the army, freedom should be granted to those carrying goods. Ibid., l. § fiscus, and § res exercitui paratas. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a person arrested for one debt may be detained for another.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A doubt always arises from the discordance of laws, unless it is removed by some distinction,

† I therefore say that sometimes someone is arrested for a fiscal debt only, and then reformation has place: because the arrest is made for a public or private debt, or it is tacitly included without any other specification, and then the statute speaks, which wishes its arrest to extend its force to both: because therefore he seems to be arrested for both offenses simultaneously, although one debt is paid, he can be detained for the other, until that annexed or connected debt is satisfied: because the reason for connected things is one and indivisible. And this was said by the law in the case of one arrested for the criminal penalty of theft: for he is not released until the theft is restored, as in Auth. ut iud. sine quoquo suf. §. oportet enim. col. 2. and in Auth. ut lic. ma. et auiae. §. illud valet. near the end, col. 8. Moreover, reformation speaks when someone is arrested for what he has to do with the community, or in the community: but this is a certain fine, which is imposed in the statute if anyone does not observe the judgment, which statute simultaneously and connexedly provided for the fisc and the creditor. D. si quis iud. non ob. l. 1. §. fi. Moreover, here he is not attacked at the instance of another: but of the creditor himself, and from the same law both arise. Therefore I say, unless he pays, he should not be released. Thus I say, and I advise, I, Bal. de Perusio. The case, on which you, most excellent Lords, ask for my counsel, is as follows: The statute of the city of Genoa, placed under the heading that contracts of minors and women are valid, as is provided below, provides among other things that all contracts, obligations, or settlements which any woman over the age of 25 years has made to any person, are valid and binding with the consent of her husband, and with an oath taken with the advice of two of her better relatives, who must swear that they believe the said contract, obligation, or settlement is not made to the detriment of the said woman, but for her utility. Moreover, that all women having their husbands, who have in their affairs and businesses by themselves and their proxy, may act, demand, require, acquit, enter into inheritance in court and out of court, and bind themselves and their property, as if it had been done in the presence and with the consent of their husbands, provided that the aforementioned things are done with the advice of two relatives on the part of the husband, and with the authority of the magistrate. It happens that three women, two of whom had husbands absent from the city of Genoa, and another had a husband present, having certain reprisals against a certain university, constituted Arzon, present, as proxy of one of the said women, with additional and general powers, and all etc., and mandates, voluntarily accepting: in whose proxy’s creation intervened the consent of the said Arzon, the present husband, and the advice of two relatives of the aforementioned absent husbands, and swearing that they believe the said contract is not made to the detriment of the said women etc. However, the authority of the magistrate was lacking in the creation of the said proxy, which was required by the form of the aforementioned statute in women having their husbands absent. Moreover, Arzon, the husband, and the proxy thus constituted, as above, made, by mandate of the magistrate, seize and sequester certain possessions on the occasion of the reprisals granted to the aforementioned women, which were goods of the aforementioned university in the hands of a third person. By this sequestration thus, as above, made by the said Arzon, proxy, the said Arzon appeared before the magistrate, and offered a libel, in which he asked that the said goods be adjudged, and delivered, and given to him unsold up to the amount due, namely. c. Upon the offering of the said libel, the proxy of the said university appeared, opposing and defending, and doing many acts with the said Arzon as proxy of the said women, causing the said Arzon to be cited as proxy to many acts without any prestation or opposition against the person of the said Arzon, proxy. Indeed, what is more, he caused the said Arzon to be cited as proxy of the said women to see provided and to receive a bail or surety on the said sequestration, which the said proxy of the said university requested, and wished to be released according to the form of the statute of the city of Genoa, by virtue of which statute the said sequestration had been made. Who, the proxy of the said university, in the release of the said sequestration, promised in court to the said Arzon, in the said proxy name, and the notary receiving in the name and on behalf of the said Arzon, in the said name, and of all and each of those whose interest it is, was, or may be, to demand the said seized goods, or their estimation, to the higher magistrate. And of this he gave sureties: nor did the said proxy of the said university cause the said Arzon, and proxy of the said women, to be cited to see exceptions, and to respond to certain interrogations or positions deposited by the said proxy of the said university in the acts. And in the citation it is said that Arzon, as proxy of the said women, will come to respond to the said positions: these things thus acted and agitated, no opposition being made against the person of the said Arzon, the said Arzon, wishing to leave Genoa, substituted another proxy, called Caena. This Caena, appearing in court, wishing to prosecute the said judgment begun by the said Arzon, was opposed by the proxy of the said university, that he, Caena, the substituted proxy, was not proxy, nor was the said Arzon, because in the creation of the proxy of the said Arzon, the authority of the magistrate did not intervene, which was absolutely necessary by the form of the aforementioned statute: and who, the proxy of the aforementioned university, appearing in court, asked that by the said magistrate it be pronounced that the process made with the said Arzon, proxy, and Caena, substituted, be and have been null, as made and agitated with persons less legitimate. This being thus asked, these women, wishing to validate the said process, ratified, approved, and confirmed all acts, deeds, done, procured in the name of the said women both by the said Arzon in their name, and by the said Caena, substituted by the said Arzon, with certain knowledge, and expressly, and especially such and such acts done by their said proxies of the said university, making special mention of the said acts: and without revoking the said Arzon, their proxy, and the substitute by him, they made anew another proxy, called Philosopher: in which ratification, and approval, and constitution of the new proxy, above Philosopher, intervened all solemnities required by the form of the aforementioned statute of Genoa, namely, consent, and advice, and oath of the relatives of the husbands of the said women absent from the city of Genoa, and also intervened the authority of the magistrate, so that the said ratification of the deeds and acts was made solemnly, and in form. Now, this theme being thus presupposed, three doubts, or points, on which counsel is asked, briefly arise. The first is, whether, because the proxy of the said university approved the person of the said Arzon, litigating with him, doing many acts with him as with the proxy of the said women, and whom he asserted as proxy in the acts of the said women without any opposition or protestation made by him against the person of the said Arzon, it suffices for this, that by the said approval the said Arzon is said to be a legitimate proxy, and the acts and deeds done by him are valid to the prejudice of the proxy of the said university thus approving his person. The second doubt is, whether the ratification and approval afterwards made by the said women solemnly with the advice and consent of the said relatives, and with the authority of the magistrate, and of all acts and deeds in court by the said Arzon, proxy, and Caena, his substitute, makes valid the said process, and the said acts and deeds done by the said Arzon validate and corroborate, although in the creation of the proxy of the said Arzon the said authority of the magistrate did not intervene. The third doubt is, whether the promise made by the said proxy of the said university in court before the magistrate in the release of the said sequestration, which was made to the notary receiving in the name and on behalf of the said Arzon, in the said name, and of all and each of those whose interest it is, may be, remains valid, and is valid, provided that the said Arzon was not the legitimate proxy of the said women, or did not have sufficient mandate.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person is deemed to have ratified a procurator with whom he has litigated as if with a procurator.
2. If an exception is raised against a judge, and I subsequently litigate before him, whether I am deemed to have ratified him.
3. Whether acts performed by a procurator in the name of the principal can be ratified by the principal, if the former was not a procurator.
4. Whether a caution furnished by a procurator of a corporation in the execution of a sequestration, or in a relaxation, when he was not bound to do so, is valid and binds the sureties.
5. Whether a judicial stipulation is confirmed by ratification.
6. Add the following opinion.
body: Regarding the first point

† It seems doubtful to say that, on account of the approval of the person of Arzoni, which the procurator of the said university made by litigating with him, the person of the said Arzoni appears to have been legitimated, and that the acts and proceedings with the said Arzoni are valid; for this is the opinion of Innocentius on the text in c. Quoniam contra falsam, in the gloss on the word “in fine,” and in the same chapter in the gloss on the word “facit.” To the same effect is what Innocentius notes in c. Statuimus, Extra, de electione, in the gloss on the word “in abbatia.” And the same is held by Johannes Andreae in c. 1, Extra, de electione, lib. 6, in the gloss on the word “absentia.” The same seems to be held by Laurentius de Butrio, Lumen iuris civilis, in l. Pomp., § rati, ff. de procuratoribus, where he says that if one has admitted a procurator in judgment and has litigated with him without demanding security from him, it is as if one had litigated with him contentiously. The same seems to be held by Bartolus in three places. First, in l. Licet, C. de procuratoribus, where he says that if I opposed the person of the procurator and protested that by any act I did not intend to approve the person of the said procurator, but after such protestation I voluntarily litigated with him, I appear to approve the person of the said procurator. Second, in l. Inter quos, § qui in alieno, ff. de damno infecto, where he says that if I do not wish to approve the person of the procurator, I must protest in every act that I do not intend to approve his person. The same is noted by the said Bartolus, and more clearly, in l. Pomp., § rati, ff. de procuratoribus. The same is held by the Speculum in tit. de procuratoribus, § ratione autem formae, in the verse “Sed nunquid pars procuratorem semel approbans per haec.” I allege the text at the end of l. Si proponas, § haereditatis, ff. de inofficioso testamento, where if anyone claims or performs any act with someone as an heir, he appears to approve him as an heir. To this effect is what Cynus notes in l. Mercalem, ff. de conditionibus ob causam, where Cynus says that in such responses and rejoinders which anyone makes in court, judgment is given against the confessor, and it is held against him as full proof. Moreover, this is demonstrated by another reason,

† For I see that if an objection is raised against the person of the judge, and afterwards he voluntarily litigated before the said judge, he appears to have renounced the aforementioned exception of suspicion, as in c. Exceptio, Extra de exceptionibus, and there noted; and in c. Inter meum, Extra de re iudicata, and there noted by Innocentius and Bartolus, who places it in l. Quidam consulebant, ff. de re iudicata; and this is supported by l. Si susceperit, ff. de iudicibus, and what is noted in l. Non videtur, ff. eodem titulo. Therefore, the same will apply in our case, arguing from the person of the judge to the person of the procurator. And this is the first point. On the second

And the second doubt being posed, without prejudice to the point that the said approval would not ratify the acts performed, it seems to be said that, at least by virtue of the ratification and approval made solemnly by the said women with the authority of the absent husbands’ relatives and with the authority of the magistrates according to the form of the aforementioned statute, the acts and proceedings in court by the said Arzonus and his substitute are valid and binding. For this is expressly held by Cynus in *l. si tutor*, in fine, Cod., *qui causae in integrum restitutione non est necessaria*, where Cynus expressly holds that ratification and approval made by the principal of acts and proceedings done in court before judgment by one who was not a procurator, for example, concerning the contestation of the lawsuit and other acts, makes the aforementioned acts and proceedings valid and binding, however invalid they might otherwise be due to a defect of mandate. And for this, *l. licet*, D., *de iudicibus*, is alleged, where there is a text on this point. And this is true of acts performed before judgment, because before judgment the prejudice or benefit to the ratifying party is not yet established. Therefore, ratification operates well. Otherwise, if judgment had been rendered: for a distinction is made, either it was rendered for the principal or against the principal. Also, either he was a minor or a major: but this distinction does not apply in our case, because the ratification was made before judgment. Also, this is proven by reason, for I see that if someone, who had no mandate at all, were to act in court as my procurator, and I, knowing this, ratify and approve, such ratification makes the acts performed by him in my name valid, as is the gloss in *c. per tuas*, Extr., *de arbitris*. Raymond puts it in *l. non utiliter*, D., *de eo qui pro tutore*, and in *l. multum*, Cod., *si quis alteri vel sibi*. And Jacobus de Belvisus seems to hold this in *l. licet*, in fine, Cod., *de procuratoribus*. And Bartolus in *l. recte*, § *si procurator*, D., *de praecipiis signatis*: the ratification of the principal makes valid the acts of the procurator who from the beginning had no mandate at all, nor the foundation of a mandate, nor the will of the principal, even if less solemnly. Therefore, in our case, by virtue of the ratification, the aforementioned acts will be valid. To this also, the authority of the magistrate, which intervenes in the ratification, should greatly contribute, which supplies both the defect of the common law and makes the acts valid according to the common law, as well as the defect of the said statute. And it is a notable text, which Dynerus said he could not find elsewhere in the body of the law, in *l. 1*, in § *idem Pomp.*, in the verse, D., *quod falsum*. Also, thirdly, it is sufficiently proven to the same effect that that authority of the magistrate, which ought to intervene in the said procuratory instrument, was a solemnity that ought to intervene in the contract outside of court, i.e., in the constitution of the said procuratory instrument. Now, if the said solemnity did not intervene, I admit that it renders the said procuratory instrument null, and that he is not the procurator of the said ladies, and it is as if he had no mandate. But if he had no mandate, such ratification would make the acts valid, as is the round text in *l. licet*, D., *de iudicibus*. Therefore, it will be the same in our case. Nor does the gloss object to this, which is in *l. cum non solum*, § *necessitatem*, in the gloss on the word there, in the verse, Cod., *de bonis quae liberis*, where the gloss says that if a *filiusfamilias* intervenes in court without the consent of the father, and the father later ratifies, such ratification does not benefit, nor make the acts done by the son valid. For to this it is answered in two ways, because there it is so to that extent, because that solemnity of the father’s consent was not required in court from the beginning of the instituted lawsuit, because the *filiusfamilias* is not a whole person to stand in court without the consent of the father, and thus the lawsuit was begun with a less legitimate person. And thus the said lawsuit was null from its beginning due to the defect of a less legitimate person, who could not be in court; to that extent, the ratification of the father operates nothing. But in our case, such solemnity of the authority of the magistrate was not required in court, nor at the beginning of the lawsuit, but only in the contract, i.e., in the making of the said procuratory instrument, and that procurator Arzonus, who intervened in court, had a legitimate person in himself to stand in court, if he had a legitimate mandate. Therefore, ratification in our case ought to operate, and not in the case of the said gloss. Secondly, it can also be answered otherwise, because when a *filiusfamilias* is in court without the consent of the father, the son acts in his own name, not in the name of the father, and therefore if the father later ratifies, he does nothing; because the father cannot ratify what was not done in his own name, as in *l. si pupilli*, § *sed si ego*, D., *de negotiis gestis*. But in our case, the said women ratified what was done in their own name; because the said Arzonus intervened in court and acted in the name of the said women, and consequently the ratification would be valid as of acts done in the name of the ratifying party. And this reason is given by the gloss and Cynus in the said *l. cum non solum*, § *necessitatem*, Cod., *de bonis quae liberis*. By this, it makes good that which is noted there by Jacobus de Belvisus in the said § *necessitatem*, where Jacobus de Belvisus distinguishes in this case: either the litigation is with a legitimate person, but consent is required so that prejudice may be drawn to another, as in a procurator who litigates in another’s name; and then it suffices that it be ratified whenever, so that the acts may be legitimately drawn to the judgment of another, as in *l. 3*, D., *rem rati habere*. Sometimes litigation is with a less legitimate person, and consent is required in court for the perfection of the person, but outside of court for the perfection of the mandate. Therefore, the said ratification, whenever made by the said women, makes valid the acts performed by the said Arzonus, their procurator. And this concludes the second step, or doubt. On the third and last doubt

† Assuming, without prejudice, that the acts performed with the said Artono, procurator, were invalid by virtue of the approval and ratification of the said women, it seems that one should hold that the promise made in court by the procurator of the said university to the public stipulator and recipient, acting in the name and on behalf of all and each of those who have or may have an interest, to present the said goods, and the subsequent suretyship that followed, whereby such promise and suretyship were acquired and would be acquired by the said women, whose reprisals' execution...

† The said suretyship and promise were made, because through the judge, or in the name of those stipulating, the said stipulation and suretyship were acquired for the said women, as is stated in l. 2, 3, and 4, in the beginning, ff. rem pupilli salvam fieri; and in Auth. libellum, C. de litis contestatione; and in Auth. de executione et his qui eam, § 1; and in Auth. de haereditate ab intestato, § ex his; and as noted in Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, § si quis alii, in the gloss on the word “igitur alii,” etc. This is also well-founded, because even if it were assumed that the said Arzonus did not have a mandate through the ratification made by the said women of the acts and transactions performed by him, the aforementioned stipulation would still be acquired for them, as is the text in l. si ego hac mente, ff. de negotiorum gestione; and as noted by Bartolus in l. stipulatio ista, § alteri, ff. de verbis obligatorum. Nor does it matter if it is said that this suretyship or caution was made or provided upon a sequestration being carried out at the instance of a person less legitimate; and thus, since the principal is invalid, the accessory is also invalid, as l. cum principalis, ff. de regulis iuris; and l. non dubium, C. de legibus. But if the said sequestration was invalid because of the less legitimate person, therefore the promise and caution provided by virtue of the said sequestration are invalid. To this, it is responded in two ways: first, that through the said procurator of the said university, the said sequestration was approved, as appears from the records, because the said procurator of the said university, appearing in court, stated that, having knowledge of the sequestration made for the procurator of the said women, and desiring that the said sequestration be released, he offered to the judge to provide suitable sureties for presenting the said goods according to the form of the statute of the city of Genoa, placed under the heading “de interdicto” and following; and he summoned the said procurator of the said ladies to come and accept the said sureties for the release of the said sequestration. Now, by these words, it is said and alleged that they approved the said sequestration: similarly, it is said of one who is condemned and asks for a delay in payment, that he seems to approve the sentence, as l. ad solutionem, C. de re iudicata; and that act which I once approved, I cannot thereafter disapprove, as l. Pomp. and l. eum actum, ff. de negotiorum gestione; and l. venditioni, C. de usucapione pro emptore. Likewise, it is responded to the same effect: a caution is always interposed upon that which could be claimed by some right, and it always remains valid; indeed, even if it were interposed upon a right that could not be claimed by any law, if it were interposed knowingly, it would be valid and binding, as l. sed et si quis, § final, ff. si quis cautionem; and in l. si, C. ad legem Falcidiam; and l. damnum, § cum pariete, ff. de damno infecto; and in l. quaerat, ff. familiae herciscundae; and as noted by Bartolus fully in l. si patronus, ff. de donationibus; and Bartolus places this in the said l. sed et si quis, § final, ff. si quis cautionem. Now, to the point: either the procurator of the said university was bound to give the said caution, and then the caution is valid and the sequestration held; or he was not bound by any right, and this the procurator of the said university knew, because he said he was not bound; therefore, by providing this caution, knowing that he was not bound, the said caution is valid and binding, as the said l. sed et si quis, § final; and as noted by Bartolus in the said l. si patronus. And in this third doubt, it is concluded that the said promise and caution provided by the procurator of the said university in the release of the said interdict are valid and binding, and that the said sureties are obligated. I, Dominic Imperialis, doctor of laws, have alleged as above written, and I have subscribed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person, by litigating with someone as if he were a procurator, appears to approve of him.
2. Whether acts performed by a non-procurator as if he were a procurator can be ratified by the principal.
3. Whether a judicial stipulation is validated by ratification.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It has been fully and excellently alleged by the excellent Doctor, Lord Dominic, that it would not be expedient to speak further, except for the sake of preserving the good custom of those who give counsel. Therefore, having retained the aforementioned copious allegations,

It must be noted that, although where a magistrate’s decree is required, the act does not hold by operation of law if the decree is lacking, because the formal and substantial solemnity is missing, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si praetor; and l. qui neque, de rebus eorum; and l. 1, de rebus curialibus, lib. 10; and although such decree is sometimes also required even in a power of attorney for an individual person, as in c. ult., de iudicibus, lib. 6; there is no doubt regarding a universitas, according to the gloss, as noted in l. nulli, quod cuiusque universitatis nomine. Nevertheless, it must be considered whether, if the adversary knowingly litigated with him as with a duly appointed procurator, the proceedings are valid; because this nullity favors the constituent, for whose benefit the statute was made, but does not favor his adversary. For that which cannot be valid from the beginning by the consent of both parties cannot be made valid by the consent of one, according to the doctrine of the gloss in l. a divo, de ritu nuptiarum. But if it is not established that the solemnity was lacking, which is presumed to have intervened, if what is true is presumed, since in judgment each party puts forward what is true, according to the note in C. de procuratoribus, l. licet; in c. 1, de electionibus, lib. 6; C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam, according to Cynus; and l. cum precum; and the note in l. rura, de omni agro deserto, with Innocentius, who does not admit this, but that what is not apparent to have been done is presumed to have been done, although these proceedings are those which are the cause of the foundation, in cap. innotuit, de eo qui furtive ordinem suscepit. And this mandate is null by operation of law, otherwise if by means of an exception, as in C. de exceptionibus, l. fin.; and in § ratificatio, cum si. It supports what is noted in l. actor, rem ratam haberi; and in l. 1, C. de fide instrumentorum; and iure hastae fiscalis, lib. 10. I therefore conclude that an act done with a less than legitimate procurator, whose mandate is null by operation of law, is not valid, as in D. de iureiurando, l. ius, joined with § pupillus, and the note there; and in the same title, l. tutor, § prodigus. And this is to the first point.

† But as to the second point, I say that a solemn ratification makes that which was done valid, according to the law *Si tuor*, Codex, in the title *In quibus causis in integrum restitutio non est necessaria*, prudently alleged by the saying of the most excellent doctor, and from the argument in the Digest, title *De procuratoribus*, law *Non est minus*; and in the Digest, title *De transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, section *Eam*. Likewise, those things which I ratified without a decree, as is clear from the Digest, title *De negotiis gestis*, law *Si autem*, section 1, joined with the gloss on the said law *Nulli*; and in the Digest, title *De administratione tutorum*, law *Vulgo*; and in the Digest, title *De conditione indebiti*, law *Neque*; in the Digest, title *De exceptione rei iudicatae*, law *Si mater*, section *Hoc iure*; and what is noted in the Codex, title *Qui admissi sunt ad bonorum possessionem*, law 1, *Si maior factus*, because ratification is drawn back to the beginning, therefore also the decree, which is its accessory. But ratifications of those who are not owners are not drawn back to the beginning, as is noted in section *Necessarium* and in the Codex, title *De iure fisci*, law *Instar*, book 10; and in the Codex, title *Qui pro sua iurisdictione*, law 1, in the gloss. Likewise, where the consent of the ratifying party is not valid, it is similarly not drawn back to the beginning, as is noted in the Codex, title *De pedali iudicio*, law 1; and in the Digest, title *De auctoritate tutorum*, law *Obligari*. I therefore say that by the said ratification, the procedure is deemed to have been carried out properly, and this as regards the second point. As to the third

I say that by the said ratification the judicial stipulations appear to be confirmed: certainly this is a subtle doubt, which one must weigh. D. qui satisdare cogantur, Iul. de procuratoribus in causis, §. fin.; D. de iudiciis solutis, l. si ante. For here ratification intervenes on the part of the plaintiff, and thus it becomes valid. Moreover, emerging securities are to be received even in contentious jurisdiction, and in any stage of the litigation, as D. de in ius vocando, l. eum, pro quo. However, if the defendant were absolved from observing the judgment, that security would revert to having no cause, and thus amicably, even if it had been interposed by one with knowledge, as noted in C. de sponsionibus, l. si, in the last question. Nor do I deny that in the meantime it binds by certain knowledge. D. de fideiussoribus, l. Graece, §. a tutore; and l. sed si quis, §. fin. In securities which have a principal foundation, cause is not required, but certain knowledge suffices; however, where the judgment does not bind, these judicial stipulations do not bind, as D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. 2, §. si quid ex his. Pertinent to the foregoing is what is noted in D. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit, l. spontaneus. Furthermore, the proceedings did not legitimize the person, unless followed by the ratification of the principal, as in the said §. alieno, and l. 3, §. fin., rem ratam habere. For this concerns those who act without the will and authority of the principal. Pertinent is what is noted by Innocentius, de rescriptis, c. ex parte decani.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What executors having power under these words and so forth can do. And whether. 2.
2. If executors choose a certain cleric not in consideration of the Church, whether the Bishop ought then to have the fourth part.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. That

† The words “among churches, ecclesiastical persons, and the poor,” because of the words that follow, “as it shall seem best to them,” do not compel executors to give one-third to churches, one-third to ecclesiastical persons, and another third to the poor; rather, they may distribute equally or unequally according to good conscience. This is noted by Bartolus expressly in the Digest, *de annuis legatis*, and thus it is true.

But suppose they choose churches for the work of the church; whether they can do so, when by this the Bishop is defrauded of his canonical portion, as stated in the extrajudicial decretal *Extra de testam.*, c. *fina.* I answer: yes, provided it is done in good faith and not under a pretense. And this is conveyed by the adverb "as," regarding the meaning of which adverb, as noted in *C. de eden.*, l. *edita*; *de dolo, et contumacia*, c. *prout*.

But whether, if they choose some cleric not in consideration of the church, but in consideration of some special service, the Bishop ought to have the fourth part: and what concerning the poor of no certain place, so that those who are chosen are truly poor. I answer that by law the bishop ought not to have the fourth part of these, as noted by Bartolus in chapter 2, *De sepultura*, and by Johannes Andreae in chapter 1, *De testamento*, book 6, in the gloss *igitur quia*, and noted in chapter *Dudum*, section *Verum*, *De sepultura*, in the Clementines. Of other digressions nothing need be said. I, Baldus of Perugia. END.
